## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library, complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all extant monuments of Catholic tradition through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the most extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following the individual volumes or authors of some importance; arranged with chapters suitably placed within the text, and also with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; amplified with works both doubtful and apocryphal which nevertheless possess some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: one, namely, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other, of Holy Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on individual texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in what places of their works. A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if the following are considered: the clearness of its type, the quality of its paper, the completeness of its text, the perfection of its correction, both the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the course of the whole work, the modest price, and above all this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library, from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**Second Series, in which are issued the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.—The twelve hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the thirteen hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for one thousand eight hundred francs.—The wholly Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.**

## Twelfth Century

### The Complete Works of Hugh of Saint-Victor

Regular Canon of Saint-Victor in Paris, distinguished alike for piety and learning.

Arranged in three volumes; carefully corrected and emended from manuscripts of his works preserved in the Victorine library; together with his Life, previously nowhere published, through the diligence and industry of the Regular Canons of the royal abbey of Saint-Victor at Paris (Rouen, 1648, folio). A new edition, with spurious and alien works relegated to an appendix, provided with a superior arrangement, enlarged and illustrated with very extensive prefaces and various minor works, under the editorship of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Clergy Library, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

## Prologue to Raynerus the Convert: On Beasts and Other Things

[Col. 0013]

Hugh sends greetings to his Raynerus.

Dearest brother, wishing to satisfy the requests of your desire, I have resolved to paint the dove “whose feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of whose back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]), and through the painting to edify minds, so that what the mind of simple people could scarcely grasp with the eye of understanding, it may at least discern with the bodily eye; and what hearing could scarcely conceive, sight may apprehend. Nor have I wished merely to paint the dove by forming it, but also to describe it in writing, and through writing to display the painting, so that whoever is not pleased by the simplicity of the painting may at least be pleased by the moral sense of the writing.

Therefore for you, to whom the dove’s wings have been given; who, fleeing, have gone afar off, so that you might remain and rest in solitude; who seek not delay in the raven’s voice, repeating “Tomorrow, tomorrow,” but contrition in the dove’s groaning—for you, I say, I shall paint not only the dove now, but also the hawk. Behold: on the same perch sit the hawk and the dove. For I came to conversion from the clergy, you from military service, so that we might sit in the regular life as though upon a perch; and you, who had been accustomed to seize domestic birds, might now draw wild birds—that is, secular persons—to conversion by the hand of good works.

Let the dove therefore groan, and let the hawk also groan and utter a voice of grief. For the dove’s voice is a groan, the hawk’s voice a plaint. At the beginning of this work I have set the dove first for this reason: the grace of the Holy Spirit is always prepared for one who repents, and forgiveness is attained only through grace. After the dove comes the hawk, by which persons of noble rank are signified. For when a noble person is converted, he is set before the poor as an example of good action. Concerning certain birds and animals which Holy Scripture mentions as examples for conduct, I shall attempt, as soon as I can, to give a brief account.

## A Second Prologue

By this prologue the author, whoever he may be, intimates that he painted the animals themselves and the little stones; but because in printing we cannot preserve the colours, and because most animals are known in themselves, we shall refrain from reproducing their pictures.

[Col. 0015]

Since I must write for the unlettered, let not the diligent reader wonder if, for the edification of the unlettered, I speak simply about subtle matters. Nor should he attribute it to frivolity that I paint a hawk or a dove, since blessed Job and the prophet David have left such birds to us for instruction. For what writing intimates to the more learned, painting conveys to the simple. Thus, just as the wise person delights in the subtlety of writing, so the mind of the simple is held by the simplicity of painting. I labour more, moreover, to please the simple than to speak to the more learned and, as it were, pour liquids into a vessel already full. For one who instructs the wise with words is like one who pours liquids into a full vessel.

# Book I

[Col. 0015]

## Chapter I. On the Three Doves Mentioned by Scripture

[Col. 0015A]

“If you sleep among the lots, the dove’s feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

Brother, in reading Holy Scripture I have found three doves, from which, if they are carefully considered, the minds of simple persons can be instructed unto perfection: namely, Noah’s dove, David’s dove, and Jesus Christ’s dove. Noah is interpreted “rest”; David, “strong of hand”; Jesus, “Saviour.” But to the sinner it is said: “Have you sinned? Rest” (Ecclus. 21). If, therefore, you wish to be Noah, rest from sins. That you may be David, do mighty deeds. If you desire to be saved, ask salvation from the Saviour. “Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace” (Ps. 33 [Vulgate]). Turn to Noah’s ark. [Col. 0015B] Fight the Lord’s battles with David. Seek peace with Jesus in Jerusalem. Turn to repose of mind, resist temptations, and patiently await the benefit of salvation.

Of Noah’s dove it is said: “The dove returned at evening, bearing in its mouth a branch of green olive” (Gen. 8). The dove returns to Noah’s ark when the mind is recalled from outward things to repose of mind. It returns at evening when, as the light of worldly prosperity fails, it flees the pomp of vain glory, fearing lest it incur the darkness of mind—that is, the depth of everlasting damnation. It carries an olive branch because it seeks mercy. It bears the olive in its mouth when, by prayers, it asks that it may be forgiven for what it has sinned.

Of David’s dove it is said: “And the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.” [Col. 0015C] Gold is found in the hinder parts of the back because forgiveness is promised in the future to the person who does good works. Likewise, we read of the Saviour that, at the dove’s descent upon him, this voice was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). The dove is the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is seen to have descended upon Jesus in the Jordan, because grace is prepared for every humble person cleansed from sins. Mercy, therefore, is granted to the penitent; forgiveness is promised to the worker; grace is given to the one who loves.

## Chapter II. On Comparing the Dove to the Church

[Col. 0016A]

“If you sleep among the lots, the dove’s feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

The silvered dove is the Church, taught by the doctrine of divine speech. By analogy it is said to possess a beak of preaching divided by reason, with which it gathers grains of barley and wheat—that is, the sayings of the Old and New Testaments. It has a right and a left eye: the moral and mystical senses. With the left it looks upon itself; with the right it contemplates God. It has two wings, the active and contemplative life. Sitting, it is covered by these two wings; flying, it is raised by them to heavenly things. We fly when we transcend in mind. We sit when we are sober among the brethren. On these wings, indeed, are feathers. The feathers are teachers, attached to the wings of upright action and divine contemplation.

[Col. 0016B] We call *cleros* “lots” in Latin. The two lots are the two Testaments. Those sleep between these lots who agree with and rest in the authorities of the Old and New Testaments. “And the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.” They say that the dove’s back is that part of the body in which the roots of its wings are naturally joined to one another. There the heart is situated, which, being close to the back, will in the future be covered by the gold of everlasting blessedness. As gold is more precious than silver, so the blessedness of the age to come is more precious than present happiness. Therefore the hinder parts of the dove’s back will be in the pallor of gold, because the righteous will shine with surpassing brightness in eternal blessedness.

## Chapter III. On Comparing the Dove to the Faithful Soul

[Col. 0016C]

“If you sleep among the lots, the dove’s feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

The dove is every faithful and simple soul, silvered in its feathers, made illustrious in virtues by the reputation of good opinion. It gathers as food as many grains of seed as it adopts examples of righteous people for good action. It has two eyes, [Col. 0017A] right and left: memory and understanding. With the one it foresees future things; with the other it bewails things past. Our fathers closed these eyes in Egypt, because they did not understand the works of God, nor were they mindful of the abundance of his mercy.

It has two wings: love of neighbour and love of God. One is extended through compassion toward the neighbour; the other is raised through contemplation toward God. From these wings proceed feathers, that is, the virtues of the soul. These feathers shine with silvery brightness when, through the reputation of good opinion, they offer hearers a sweet ringing like silver. We call *cleros* “lots” in Latin.

[Col. 0017B]

There are four lots: fear, hope, love, and desire. They are called lots because they assign a place in the paternal inheritance. Fear and desire are the outer lots; hope and love the middle ones. Fear unsettles the soul; desire torments the mind; and unless something intervenes between them, the soul departs from repose. Therefore we must place hope and love between desire and fear. Hope refreshes fear, and love moderates desire. The person who sleeps peacefully between hope and love, as between the middle lots, is vigilant and disturbed between the outer lots, namely fear and desire. If, therefore, you are a dove, or a feather of a dove, when you fear and desire, you are awake between the outer lots. When you hope and love, you sleep peacefully between the middle ones.

“And the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.” Burdens are customarily carried upon the back; and by these burdens the labours of works may be signified. [Col. 0017C] By the hinder parts of the back, however, is indicated expectation of reward. For after enduring present labours, we believe that rewards for merits will follow the righteous in the future. “For God will repay the saints the reward of their labours, and will lead them in a marvellous way.” And we believe that this is in the pallor of gold, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115 [Vulgate]). Thus silver is in the feathers, because utterance is in the tongues; but gold is in the hinder parts—that is, reward after labours.

## Chapter IV. On Comparing the Dove to a Prelate

“If you sleep among the lots, the dove’s feathers are silvered, and the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

The silvered dove, lacking the gall of malice, is every prelate who is still living and who sleeps between the middle lots. *Clerus* is Greek; in Latin, “lot.” [Col. 0017D] Hence *cleronomia* properly means an inheritance conveyed by testament. It consequently came about that the sons of Levi had no lot—that is, no share of inheritance—among the children of Israel, but lived from tithes.

There are two inheritances: the earthly inheritance of the Old Testament and the eternal inheritance of the New. The person who, in contempt of earthly things and hope of heavenly ones, brings his life to its end between these sleeps, while neither craving present things too ardently nor failing patiently to await future things. “And the hinder parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.” For “the eyes of the righteous shall see the king in his beauty.” Then you will have gold in the hinder parts, when the glory of divine majesty appears in the future.

[Col. 0018A] The crowns of kings are fashioned from the purest gold, whereas coins are made of silver, and images of kings are stamped upon them. A coin signifies imitation of the form; a crown, the sign of victory. The coin of divine speech teaches imitation of Christ’s life, but the crown teaches victory. Battles come after the labours of the present age. Therefore, there is gold there, as it were, in the hinder parts; here, silver in the feathers of preaching. For when the dove has come to those gifts, it will no longer need the utterance of preaching, but will live without end, in the purity of perfection, in that which it receives as recompense.

## Chapter V. On Comparing the Red-Footed Dove to the Church

The dove of which there is discussion here is said to have red feet. This dove is the Church, which had feet by which it traversed the space of the entire world. [Col. 0018B] The feet are the martyrs, who traverse the earth by as many steps as they show the way of righteousness to their followers through examples of good works. They touch the earth when they rebuke earthly acts and desires with fitting reproaches. But while the earth is trodden, the feet are wounded by the harshness of the earth—that is, by the cruelty of earthly people. Thus the feet of the Church became red because the martyrs shed their blood for Christ’s name. The redness of the feet, therefore, is the blood of martyrs.

## Chapter VI. On the Dove’s Silvered Feathers, Compared to Preachers

The dove said to have red feet is shown by prophetic words to have had silvered feathers. David says: “The dove’s feathers are silvered” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]). [Col. 0018C] The silvered feathers of the dove are the Church’s preachers. Silver is divine speech; the ringing of silver is the sweetness of the word; it has heat and brightness. Silver retains its brightness when any teacher preaches purity in words and has purity in himself, when he loves what he teaches and shows outwardly in deeds what he loves inwardly.

“These are the chaste utterances of the Lord, silver tested by fire.” The Lord’s utterances are chaste because they are corrupted by no pretence and impregnated by no seed of greed. Silver tested by fire is made firm in every disturbance. The silvery brightness in the feathers, therefore, is the gentle charm of speech in the tongues of teachers.

## Chapter VII. On the Sapphire Colour of the Dove’s Wings, Compared to Contemplatives

[Col. 0018D]

I have not found the colour of the wings written down, but it may be determined from the likeness of a material dove: if you look at a painted dove, you will not deny that it has the colour of a material dove. The surface of the wings is suffused with sapphire colour because the mind of the contemplative imitates the appearance of heaven. But the sapphire colour is marked out with white lines, so that snowy white is mixed with sapphire. The snowy colour mixed with sapphire signifies purity of flesh and love of contemplation.

## Chapter VIII. On the Dove’s Colours, Compared to Moral Qualities

“The hinder parts of the silvered dove’s back” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

The prophet mentions this and then morally shows the end of the present life in every human being. By gold he signifies purity of mind; [Col. 0019A] by the pallor of gold, mortification of the flesh. For pallor is the natural colour of a patient mind and mortified flesh. The hinder parts of the silvered dove’s back, therefore, will be in the pallor of gold when purity of mind and mortification of flesh obtain the end of every dying person.

The golden colour is also joined to the sapphire colour on the hinder parts of the dove’s back because the glory of future blessedness will follow the contemplative mind. Thus the golden colour on the hinder parts signifies the gift of eternal recompense.

## Chapter IX. On the Saffron-Coloured Eyes and Watchfulness of the Dove, Compared to the Church’s Watchfulness

“Your eyes are doves’ eyes” (Song 1 [Vulgate]).

The dove very frequently sits over waters so that, when it sees the shadow of an approaching hawk, it may flee aside. [Col. 0019B] The Church arms itself with the Scriptures so that it may avoid the snares of the devil who lies in wait. This dove, therefore, has saffron-coloured eyes because the Church, by mature consideration, indicates and foresees future events. Thus saffron colour in the eyes signifies the discernment of mature reflection: when someone maturely considers what to do or think, he adorns the spiritual eyes as it were with saffron. For saffron has the colour of ripe fruit. The saffron eye, therefore, is maturity of understanding.

## Chapter X. On the Dove’s Remaining, Changeable Colour Compared to a Troubled Sea, and the Sea Compared to Flesh

The colour of the rest of the body resembles the colour of a troubled sea. The sea, raging in the motion of its waves, boils up. [Col. 0019C] The flesh, raging as sensations boil up in motion, behaves similarly. The sea moves and raises the sands in its disturbances; the flesh assails the levity of the soul with its pleasures. The sea, passing beyond its boundaries, meets fresh waters; the flesh, given to wantonness, dulls the sweet streams of tears. The sea obstructs the courses of sailors by the diverse whirling storms of tempests; the stormy flesh plunges into the deep the conduct of those who live rightly.

While the sea is agitated by so many storms, land is mingled with waves through the collision of the waters; and thus, from the collision of sea and land, the sea receives a mixed colour. Similarly, when the flesh suggests and the mind does not consent, a colour is produced in the body as though from black and white; this colour, made from diverse colours, is called intermediate. The sea-colour in the dove’s breast, therefore, signifies tribulation in the human [Col. 0019D] mind.

## Chapter XI. On the Dove’s Diverse Properties

In different places I have found diverse properties of the dove; by inserting them into this work, brother, I have taken care to set them down for you. The dove’s first property is that it gives forth a groan in place of song; the second, that it lacks gall; the third, that it persists in kisses; the fourth, that it flies in flocks; the fifth, that it does not live by plunder; the sixth, that it gathers the better grains; the seventh, that it does not feed on a corpse; the eighth, that it nests in the holes of a rock; the ninth, that it perches above flowing waters so that, on seeing the shadow of a hawk, it may more swiftly avoid its approach; the tenth, that it nourishes two young.

The dove uses groaning in place of song because it groans in lamentation over what it willingly did. [Col. 0020A] It lacks gall, that is, the bitterness of anger. It persists in kisses because it delights in an abundance of peace. It flies in flocks because it loves community. It does not live by plunder because it does not disparage its neighbour. It gathers the better grains, that is, the better sayings. It does not feed on corpses, that is, carnal desires. It nests in the holes of the rock because it places hope in Christ’s passion. It perches above flowing waters so that, on seeing the hawk’s shadow, it may more swiftly avoid its approach, because it studies the Scriptures in order to turn aside the fraud of the devil when he comes upon it. It nourishes two young, that is, love of God and love of neighbour. Therefore, whoever has these natures should take for himself the wings of contemplation, by which he may fly to heaven.

## Chapter XII. On the North and South Winds
Rise, north wind, and come, south wind (Song 4), etc. The north wind [Col. 0020B] is the coldest wind. “From the north,” says Jeremiah, “every evil shall be opened out” (Jer. 1). There is Satan’s seat; thence comes the beginning of ruin. The north wind is a grave temptation. Its blast is the prompting of temptation; its cold is the numbness of negligence. The north wind therefore comes when a grave temptation assails anyone’s mind. But the north wind rises when temptation departs from the soul. “They shall come from the north and from the sea,” he says (Isa. 49). The north wind is temptation; the sea, the world. Therefore Christ gathers his own from the north and from the sea when he separates from the tumult of temptations not only the righteous but sinners also. “I will set my seat in the north,” he says, “and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14). He whom the feather of pride raises on high desires to set his seat in the north. He longs to be like the Most High when, by a spirit of arrogance, he makes himself equal to him to whom [Col. 0020C] he ought to be subject; indeed, to say more, he not only compares himself with his master but even considers himself better than him. The devil fell when he wished to exalt himself. A human being is humbled when he longs to exalt himself.

The south wind is the warmest wind. “God shall come from the south,” he says (Hab. 3). There is the seat of the Most High; there is the ardour of love; thence comes the purity of truth. The south wind proceeds from a clear region, because God rests in serenity of character: there he feeds, there he lies down, there is rest for the mind, there is the refreshment of contemplation. The south wind signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit; its breath, the kindness of the Holy Spirit; its warmth, love. Thus the south wind comes whenever the grace of the Holy Spirit kindles anyone’s mind. It rises [Col. 0020D] whenever grace departs from the mind. “God shall come from the south,” he says. From the north comes the devil; from the south, God. The one inhabits the darkness of ignorance; the other loves the serenity of charity. The cold of the north wind constricts the pores of the flesh; the warmth of the south wind opens those that are shut. For what the cold of avarice holds back by constriction, generous charity supplies with hands opened in almsgiving. The old feather, indeed, sinks one into hell; the new raises the mind to heavenly desires. For sins weigh down, whereas virtues raise up.

## CHAPTER XIII. How the hawk moults by spreading its wings toward the south wind

“Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south?” (Job 39). Hence blessed Gregory:

> “It is the habit of wild hawks, when the south wind blows, to spread their wings, so that the warmth of the wind may heat their limbs for shedding the old feathers. But when the wind is lacking, they spread their wings against the sun’s rays and, struck by them, make for themselves a warm breeze; thus, when their pores are opened, either the old feathers fall out or new ones grow.” [Col. 0021A]

What, then, is it for the hawk to grow feathers in the south wind, except that each of the saints, warmed by the breath of the Holy Spirit, casts off the practice of the old way of life and takes on the form of the new human being? Saint Paul the Apostle urges this, saying: “Putting off the old human being with his deeds, and putting on the new” (Col. 3). And again: “Although our outer human being is being corrupted, yet our inner human being is renewed from day to day” (2 Cor. 2).

> “To cast away the old feather [Col. 0021B] is to abandon ingrained pursuits of deceitful action. To take up the new feather is to retain a gentle and simple disposition for living well. For the feather of the old way of life weighs one down, while the plumage of new transformation raises one up and makes one lighter for flight in proportion as it is newer. And fittingly it says, ‘spreading its wings toward the south.’ For to spread our wings toward the south is, at the coming of the Holy Spirit, to open our thoughts by confession, so that we no longer delight in covering ourselves by self-defence, but make them public by accusation. Thus the hawk grows feathers when it spreads its wings toward the south, because each person then clothes himself in the feathers of virtues when, through confession, he lays his thoughts bare before the Holy Spirit. Whoever does not uncover the old things by confession does not at all bring forth the works of the new life. [Col. 0021C] Whoever does not know how to mourn what weighs him down cannot bring forth what raises him up. For compunction itself opens the pores of the heart and pours forth the feathers of virtues; and when the mind diligently rebukes itself for its sluggish oldness, it is made young by some renewal. Therefore let it be said with blessed Job: ‘Does the hawk grow feathers by your wisdom, spreading its wings toward the south?’ That is: Have you bestowed understanding upon any elect person, so that, when the Holy Spirit blows, he may spread the wings of his thoughts, cast off the burdens of his former life, and take up the feathers of virtues for the use of a new flight? Thus he may understand that he does not possess in himself, of himself, the vigilance of understanding—he who is altogether unable to bestow it upon others from himself.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On the two kinds of hawk

[Col. 0021D]

There are two kinds of hawks: the domestic and the wild; yet they are the same. At different times, however, one and the same hawk may be wild and domestic. The wild hawk is accustomed to seize domestic birds, and the domestic hawk wild ones. The wild hawk immediately devours those which it seizes; the domestic hawk keeps its captives to be left for its master. Then its master opens the bellies of the captured birds and takes their hearts to give the hawk as food. He throws out the entrails of the belly with the dung, for if these remain within, they produce the putrefaction of flesh with its stench.

In the moral sense, the wild hawk both seizes and devours captured birds, because every perverse person does not cease to scatter the deeds and thoughts of the simple. [Col. 0022A] The domestic hawk, however, is the spiritual father, who seizes wild birds as often as he draws secular people to conversion by preaching. He kills those he has captured when he compels worldly people to die to the world through mortification of the flesh. But his master, almighty God, opens their bellies when he rebukes and dissolves the softness of the fleshly through the Scriptures. He draws out their hearts when he makes the thoughts of worldly people manifest through confession. He casts out the entrails of the belly with the dung when he makes the memory of sin odious to the sinner. Thus captured birds come to the Lord’s table when sinners, chewed by the teeth of teachers, convert themselves into the body of the Church.

## CHAPTER XV. On the treatment of domestic hawks

[Col. 0022B]

For domestic hawks, if they are to grow feathers better, protected and warm places are required. Protected places are cloisters, in which a wild hawk is kept enclosed so that it may become domestic. There it loses its old feathers and acquires new ones, because any cloistered person who is stripped of former vices is not adorned with human virtues; nor is he taken from there until, after the old feathers have been cast out, the new ones are made firm. But when he is strong in flight, he comes to the hand. Likewise, if anyone converted leaves the cloister, he must come to the hand of good action; and, released from it, he must fly, so that with the whole striving of his mind he may raise himself toward the heavenly things to be desired.

## CHAPTER XVI. On carrying a hawk on the left hand

[Col. 0022C]

A hawk is customarily carried on the left hand so that, released toward the right hand to seize something, it may fly. “His left hand,” he says, “is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2). The left hand is temporal goods; the right hand, eternal goods. Therefore he sits on the left who presides over temporal goods. But he flies to the right who desires eternal things with the whole affection of his mind. There the hawk catches the dove: that is, anyone changed for the better receives the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the perch on which a hawk stands or sits

The hawk’s perch signifies for us the uprightness of the regular life. It is suspended far above the ground because such a life is separated from earthly desires. Upon this perch [Col. 0022D] he sits bound who firmly observes the ordinances of the regular life. It is said to be attached to two walls, by which it is supported on both sides. The two walls that support the perch are the active and contemplative lives, which uphold the uprightness of those who live devoutly.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the hawks’ fetters or shackles

A hawk is accustomed to have what are, as it were, shackles upon its feet, lest, whenever it wishes, it be able to fly off at any opportunity that arises. He binds the hawk’s feet as with shackles who restrains the affections of the mind by fear of judgment and sorrow at punishment. “They humbled,” says the Psalmist, “his feet in fetters” (Ps. 104). He humbles Joseph’s feet in fetters who, recalling present and eternal punishment, binds the soul’s affections lest they advance toward their desires.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the leash or strap, and the hawk’s tether

[Col. 0023A]

The strap by which the hawk is tied to the perch is the mortification of the flesh, by which every convert is kept in the regular life. For the strap, made from the hide of a dead animal, signifies the mortification of the flesh. This strap is not broken, but loosened when the hawk is urged to catch something. Similarly, if any brother goes out on some temporal business, his profession is not broken; but when he returns, he binds himself more firmly with the same strap as before.

## CHAPTER XX. On the turtledove and the sparrow

After the dove’s groaning and the hawk’s complaint, dearest one, you ask that I delay no longer but swiftly write to you of the turtledove’s lament and the sparrow’s cry. [Col. 0023B] Nor shall I merely write: I shall also portray how the turtledove loves the wilderness’s solitude and how the solitary sparrow does not cease to cry upon the roof, so that under the turtledove’s example you may preserve the purity of chastity, and under the sparrow’s example may love the vigilance of cautious watchfulness—so that you may both live chastely and walk cautiously.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the palm tree, and how the righteous person is compared to it

“I shall multiply my days like the palm tree” (Job 29). The palm tree multiplies its days because it grows slowly before rising to its height. Likewise, the righteous person advances slowly before reaching that toward which he strives. For it is the righteous person’s desire to attain the heavenly kingdom. But the world obstructs this desire, so that he can attain what he seeks only slowly. The palm tree multiplies its days, [Col. 0023C] yet neither winter’s cold nor summer’s excessive heat prevents it from always remaining green. Likewise, the righteous person lives and is prevented by nothing from persevering in the purpose of good action. Winter’s cold is the numbness or negligence of a mind grown cold. Summer’s excessive heat is the heat of lust, the flame of anger, or the blaze of covetousness. Therefore, just as the palm tree neither withers in winter’s cold nor is scorched by excessive summer heat, so the righteous person is not destroyed by any temptation of prosperity or adversity.

In another sense, the palm tree multiplies days because the righteous person recalls ancient days and meditates in his mind upon eternal years. He makes known to himself the small number of his own days, while on the other hand he hopes for the length of days to come. Therefore whoever gathers these things within himself grows upward, like the palm tree multiplying its days, by conquering the world.

## CHAPTER XXII. How the Church and the faithful soul are compared to it

“Your stature is like a palm tree” (Song 7). The stature of the Church, or of any faithful soul, is compared to a palm tree. In the stature of any human being, smallness or greatness of the limbs is indicated by the body’s outlines. The righteous person has the stature of a palm tree if he is small in his own estimation but great before God, humble in himself yet exalted before God. This palm tree is Christ, to whom the righteous person is compared. For when he suffers the tribulations which Christ suffered, the righteous person is made like the stature of the palm tree. Hence the Apostle: “Those who share in tribulations shall share also in glory” (2 Cor. 5). Therefore whoever is a member of the body ought to feel what belongs to the head. [Col. 0024A]

Now the palm tree has grown tall. Now its summit has penetrated heaven. Now with the head are the head’s tresses, namely the lofty palm fronds—that is, the chosen souls. Yet the trunk, surrounded with rough bark, that is, the Church surrounded by the harshness of tribulations, is fixed in the earth; and the branches, that is, the saints, rejoice in eternal blessedness: “For the righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Ps. 91). The righteous person is planted, flourishes, and bears fruit, planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God. The house of our God is the house of conversion. Now a court stands before the inner house. Before the house of conversion, indeed, is the court of renunciation. For the person who renounces the world plants in the courts of the Lord’s house the palm of victory by which he conquers the world. Thus he is planted in the house of conversion, flourishes through [Col. 0024B] the reputation of good opinion, and bears fruit through good action.

But where does he put down a root? How does he grow? How is he strengthened? He takes root through faith, grows through hope, and is strengthened through charity. Yet it is remarkable what is said of the righteous: “They who are planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of the house of our God” (ibid.). It is remarkable that they are planted in the house and flourish in the court. Perhaps they are planted inwardly through faith; outwardly they flourish through the example of good work; and thus the fragrance of the flower goes forth through the reputation of good opinion. Or otherwise: they are planted in the house and flourish in the court because the righteous are planted in the present Church and shall flourish with an unfading flower in eternal life. There they shall receive fruit together with the flower: that is, with purity of flesh and soul, [Col. 0024C] the reward of future recompense.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the turtledove’s nest—that is, the faithful soul’s nest—in the palm tree, that is, the tree of the cross, through faith in the Passion; and how the palm is carried in the victor’s hand

“I shall climb the palm tree and grasp its fruits” (Song 7). Near the ground, the palm tree is slender and rough; toward heaven it is thicker and beautiful. Therefore the ascent is difficult, but the fruit sweet. The labour of the climber is diminished while he perceives the fragrance of the fruit on the tree; the sweetness of its taste removes the difficulty of ascent. The palm tree is Christ; its fruit is salvation. David says: “Say to my soul: I am your salvation” (Ps. 34); and, “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33). Hope of salvation is in the wood of the cross. Therefore climb the palm tree: that is, contemplate the victory of the cross. For by the ladder [Col. 0024D] of the cross you shall ascend to the victor’s throne. Take up your cross also and follow him. Whoever afflicts his flesh takes up his cross.

The palm adorns the victor’s hand, and the righteous person carries the palm of victory in his hand by doing good. There are said to be three things from which the righteous person ought to win victory: the world, the flesh, and the devil. The righteous conquers the world when he scorns its pleasures; he overcomes the flesh when he tames it by abstinence; he masters and subjects the devil when he expels him from his own bounds. Therefore he carries the palm in his hand who triumphs over these three by good action.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the turtledove’s voice as compared to the soul, and on our land and a foreign land

“The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2). [Col. 0025A] The turtledove’s voice is the grief of an injured mind. The turtledove’s voice signifies the groaning of every penitent soul. The land spoken of here is the mind, entangled in the occupations of earthly frailty. There is, however, our land and a foreign land. The foreign land is a mind subjected to the devil’s dominion. Hence: “Strangers have risen against me, and the mighty have sought my soul” (Ps. 53). The foreign land is Babylon; our land is Jerusalem. Babylon means “confusion”; Jerusalem is interpreted “vision of peace.” Strangers devour our land when demons ravage the mind by their assaults. We are held captive in Babylon; we are free in Jerusalem. “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136).

Our land is said to be ours when nothing proprietary is found in our mind. [Col. 0025B] We call our land ours when we possess our mind together with our master and brothers, so that a soul devoted to God may serve the brothers through charity, its neighbour through compassion, itself through moderation, and thus become common property. Therefore the turtledove’s voice is heard in our land when the inner ear is humbly inclined to repentance.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the turtledove as compared to the Church and the faithful soul, on its nest, and on Christ as the husband of such a turtledove

The turtledove loves the wilderness’s secluded place, yet sometimes descends to poor people’s little gardens and to the fields of cultivators, in order to gather the grains of seed by which it may live. The turtledove is the Church or any faithful soul; the wilderness’s seclusion is the solitude of the cloister; the grains of seed are the sayings [Col. 0025C] of teachers. The gardens or fields are the books of teachers. From these the soul is refreshed; in them is the life of the spirit. “For thus one lives, and in such things is the life of my spirit.”

The turtledove finds for itself a nest in places most secure and pleasant, where it may lay up its young. It places its nest among the branches of a dense tree and lays eggs, from which young birds may be produced in due time. By the tree we understand the cross; by the nest, salvation; by the eggs, hope; by the young, twofold charity, namely love of God and of neighbour. Let us therefore seek the turtledove’s nest; let us seek the egg in the nest, the nest in the tree—that is, hope of salvation in the wood of the cross.

I think it is also well known to many that the turtledove’s nature is such that, if it has once lost its mate, it always goes without a mate. Christ is the bridegroom of the Church [Col. 0025D] or of any faithful soul. Ascending the tree of the cross, Christ drew the nest together on every side. “I shall climb,” he says, “the palm tree” (Song 7), that is, the cross; and: “When I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). Christ died; the Church, or any faithful soul, waits for him until he returns, meanwhile keeping the law of chaste companionship. It often returns to the tree, frequents the nest, sees the shedding of blood—the judgment, that is, of death—and, as it contemplates these things, groans. Likewise, every faithful soul often recalls the mystery of the cross, contemplates the price of the blood, and, while considering it attentively, summons its mind to lamentation with multiplied groans.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Lebanon and the cedar in a mystical sense; and on sparrows nesting in the cedar’s branches

[Col. 0026A]

Lebanon and the cedar are sometimes used in a favourable sense, as Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen as the cedars” (Song 5). Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, at the boundary of Judaea toward the north. Its trees surpass the timber of other forests in height, beauty, and strength. By Mount Lebanon, we may properly understand the eminence of virtues. It is the boundary of Judaea toward the north, lest the devil enter the minds of those who truly confess through temptation. Its trees surpass other trees in height, beauty, and strength when faithful souls surpass others [Col. 0026B] in the loftiness of desire, the beauty of chastity, and the strength of perseverance. By the cedar we understand Christ. This is the lofty cedar of Lebanon, made like hyssop: though exalted, he became humble.

Of these things the Prophet says: “The trees of the field shall be satisfied, and the cedars of Lebanon which he planted; there the sparrows shall nest” (Ps. 103). The sparrows are preachers; the young are those begotten by the word of preaching; the nest is the place of a tranquil mind. Thus those nest in this cedar who, living peacefully, do not despair of eternal blessedness. The cedars of Lebanon which the Lord planted are the rich of this world. The sparrows are the rulers of monasteries; the young, disciples; the nest, the place of workshops. Sparrows nest in these cedars because rulers of souls establish monasteries on the estates of the rich. There the sparrows do not cease to cry, in order to seek food for themselves [Col. 0026C] from God. They seek food from God for themselves when they desire to be satisfied, as with food, by the words of divine utterance. They cry out day and night because with all the striving of their minds they pray to God for their benefactors. In the nest of a tranquil mind they nourish the feathers of contemplation, with which they endeavour to fly as swiftly as possible to the aforesaid cedar. They flutter about the trees of Lebanon because they desire to know the life or character of the lofty who are living.

Solomon is recorded to have made a litter from these trees of Lebanon (Song 3), because the Church is built from lofty and tireless men. There are cedars which the Lord did not plant. He did not plant them in self-will; he did not spread them abroad through covetousness. “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted” (Matt. 15). These cedars [Col. 0026D] of Lebanon are proud rich people. In them herons and hawks—that is, plunderers—nest (Ps. 103). They make nests because plunderers build strongholds upon the possessions of the rich. Their young are the accomplices or servants of plunderers. These birds hide in the cedars in order to plunder, because plunderers derive the power to harm from perverse rulers. But “the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 28): that is, the rich of the world—some by repentance, others by judgment. By repentance, because “he shall break them in pieces like a calf of Lebanon.” “He shall break [them] in pieces like a calf of Lebanon” (Ps. 28), bringing them to imitation of Christ’s life, so that they may become a calf fit for sacrifice, mortify the flesh, and carry the cross with Christ. By judgment he shall break others, because he shall reserve them to be burned in eternal fire.

The aforesaid cedar, cut down, profits greatly, [Col. 0027A] because Christ redeemed the world by his own death. “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12). Thus the cedar is cut down when Christ dies. Christ’s death, indeed, benefited many. For descending to hell, he led captivity captive; rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he gave hope of resurrection to those who die. What benefit would there be in living miserably, being shaken by tribulations, and finally dying, unless the hope of resurrection followed? And what benefit would there be in having risen unless there were firm faith that a human being remains immortal, without punishment, and without end?

Likewise, when the cedar which the Lord planted is cut down, it profits greatly, because it is transferred to the building of eternal blessedness. But if the cedar which the Lord did not plant is cut down, it will be of no small benefit, because that which bore no fruit in Lebanon—that is, in the world—when cut down supports the weight of the building in the spiritual temple. I say this if you cut down the cedar’s pride by repentance. But if you cut it down by judgment, you reserve it to be burned for ever in the fires of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Who is to be understood mystically by the sparrow

“In the Lord I trust: how do you say to my soul, ‘Migrate to the mountain like a sparrow’?” (Ps. 10). By the name of the sparrow is signified the instability of mind in any human being. For the sparrow is an inconstant and unstable bird, and therefore signifies the mind’s mobility. [Col. 0027C] By the mountain, moreover, we understand the height of pride. Like a sparrow, therefore, that person migrates to the mountain who raises his mind from the valley of humility into pride.

It may also be said otherwise: by the sparrow we understand any unbeliever, while the aforesaid mountain is the loftiness of intellectual perception. If anyone strikes upon this mountain, he wrecks his ship. Thus, like a sparrow, that person migrates to this mountain who abandons the humility of Christ’s Incarnation and denies that Christ is God and man. Answering heretics who oppose the faith, the Prophet therefore says that he will not depart from the faith, because he trusts in the Lord. For he does not trust in his own strength, nor does he glory in the abundance of his riches.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the house found by the sparrow and the character of the tamed sparrow

[Col. 0027D]

“The sparrow has found herself a house” (Ps. 83). “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). The sparrow, which knew how to fly from branch to branch, now flies from the woods to the house. So many who had clung to the various occupations of the world now lift their minds toward the house not made by hands which is in heaven. The sparrow, once clothed in light feathers—that is, worldly cares—now advances winged with virtues and commandments. It ascends and makes a nest. God provides that the nest may be made: for the Father’s Word clothed himself in the hay of flesh. Thus the nest is raised on high, because human nature is placed above angelic creation. It nests in the holes of the rock because it places hope in Christ’s Passion. “For the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10). This is the lofty [Col. 0028A] cedar of Lebanon, made like hyssop; there the sparrows shall nest.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the sparrow’s watchfulness—that is, of the newly converted monk

“I have kept watch and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Ps. 150). The sparrow finds a place to remain in the house of faith; and he who was formerly unstable does not cease to watch lest he be seized by the hawk. Thus every faithful person acts, lest he be held captive after being seized by the devil. He watches over himself through vigilance; he watches over his neighbour through teaching. The sparrow dwells upon the roof so that he may be far removed from earthly things. He remains in the house and sits upon the roof who holds fast the firmness of faith and teaches those subject to him from the summit of virtues. See how the sparrow, once accustomed to migrate to the mountain of unbelief, now keeps watch for the truth of faith [Col. 0028B] and cries aloud from on high. He is called solitary because he is far removed from earthly desires.

## CHAPTER XXX. How the sparrow resembles the soul in avoiding snares

“Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of hunters. The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered” (Ps. 123). The soul bears the likeness of the sparrow when, in what it does, it employs an example of shrewdness. For when the soul frequently examines itself, it sometimes happens that, through the practice of continual self-examination, the mind becomes shrewder, so that it avoids the snare placed in its path.

There are three snares of hunters. The first snare is the deceitful prompting of demons; the second, the subtle deception of heretics; the third, the sweetness of the fleshly life. These snares are set in the footpath, the road, and the open field. The footpath is the narrower life; the road, the broad life; the field, the spacious life. Religious persons walk by the narrow and difficult way; married persons by the broad and straight one; pleasure-seekers by the spacious and wandering one. The snare holds the sparrow captive when the devil possesses the mind, when the sweetness of the present life pleases it, or when a heretic cherishes one deceived by flatteries. But the snare is broken and the sparrow delivered if, having cast aside fleshly desires, the soul turns to God. This, however, is not achieved by our own power but by grace: “For our help is in the name of the Lord” (Ps. 123).

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the mystical explanation of the price of two and five sparrows according to the Gospel

According to the sequence of the Gospel, two sparrows are sold for an *as*; [Col. 0028D] and five for a *dipondium* (Matt. 10; Luke 12). Sparrows are wandering and inconstant people. A *dipondium* consists of two *asses*, though each is of small weight. Therefore sparrows are sold for an *as* and a *dipondium* when sinners are subjected to the devil, to be tormented in eternal fire, for transient and temporal things. Yet not one of them shall be forgotten before the Lord, because the Redeemer’s mercy is always prepared for sinners. “But you,” he says, “are worth more than many sparrows” (Matt. 10). This he said of the disciples. The righteous are of greater value: when in this present world they offer themselves and what is theirs for the Lord, in future blessedness they shall possess eternal things in exchange for things transient and changeable.

Some interpret the two sparrows jointly as soul and body. The five [Col. 0029A] sparrows they refer to the five bodily senses. Again: “Are not two sparrows sold for an *as*? And not one of them shall fall to the ground without your Father” (ibid.). Hence Jerome [Note: [Col. 0029D] St Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 10, book 1, vol. 26 of the *Patrologia*]:

> “If other small and worthless things,” he says, “do not fall without God as their agent, you, who are eternal, ought not to fear that you live without providence.”

“Therefore do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the two sparrows to be sacrificed under the Law for cleansing from leprosy

The Law of Moses commanded that, if anyone had been cleansed from leprosy, he should offer two living sparrows. Of these, the priest was to sacrifice one in an earthen vessel over living waters, while the other he was to dip in the blood of the sacrificed sparrow [Col. 0029B] and permit it to fly freely into the field (Lev. 14). The two sparrows are body and soul. The earthen vessel is the frailty of mortal flesh; the living waters are the streams of divine Scripture, which provide us with spiritual drink and washing. We offer two sparrows when we consecrate body and soul to God.

The fact that one sparrow was sacrificed, with its head bent back toward its little feathers, so that its blood was poured out but its head was nevertheless not torn from its neck, signifies that our flesh is to be so afflicted through abstinence that it is not entirely extinguished from life. The fact that the other sparrow is allowed to fly freely into the field morally signifies that, when fleshly desires have been subdued, our soul is to be lifted to heavenly things on the wings of contemplation.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the nature of the pelican

[Col. 0029C]

“I have become like a pelican of the wilderness” (Ps. 101). The pelican is an Egyptian bird dwelling in the wilderness of the river Nile. This bird is said to kill its young with its beak, to groan over them for three days, and after three days to strike itself with its beak and sprinkle its young with its own blood; thus it washes those whom it had previously killed in life-giving fashion by sprinkling them with blood.

Mystically, the pelican signifies Christ; Egypt, the world. The pelican dwells in solitude because Christ alone deigned to be born of a Virgin without union with a man. The pelican’s solitude is Christ’s life free from sin. This bird kills its young with its beak because by the word of preaching it converts unbelievers. It does not cease to groan over its young because Christ mercifully wept when he raised [Col. 0029D] Lazarus. Thus after three days he gives life to his young by washing them in blood, because Christ washes them by redeeming them with his own blood. For the pelican’s death is Christ’s Passion.

Morally, however, by the pelican we may understand not merely any righteous person, but one far removed from fleshly pleasure. By Egypt we understand our life enveloped in the darkness of ignorance, for Egypt is interpreted “darkness.” Therefore we make solitude in Egypt when we are far removed from the cares and pleasures of the world. So also the righteous person makes solitude in the city when, as far as human nature permits, he keeps himself free from sin. The pelican kills its young with its beak because the righteous person judges and condemns with his own mouth the thoughts and deeds which he has wickedly performed, saying: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the ungodliness of my sin” (Ps. 23). [Col. 0030A] He laments over them for three days because he teaches that whatever they have done wickedly in thought, speech, and deed should be erased by tears. Thus he gives life to his young sprinkled with blood when he lessens and destroys the works of flesh and blood, and preserves spiritual deeds by living well.

The nature of this bird is also said to be such that it is always afflicted by hunger and quickly digests whatever it swallows, because its stomach has no chamber in which it can retain food. Thus such food does not fatten the body, but only sustains and strengthens it. The eremitic life is made like this pelican: it is fed with little and does not seek the filling of the belly; it does not live in order to eat, but eats in order to live.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the night-raven, that is, the owl

[Col. 0030B] “I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling-place” (Ps. 101). The *nycticorax* is a bird that loves the darkness of night. It dwells among ruins, because it makes its habitation in the ruins of walls that have no roof. It shuns the light; flying by night, it seeks food.

Mystically, the *nycticorax* signifies Christ, who loves the darkness of night because he does not will the death of the sinner but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18). For God so loved the world that, for the redemption of the world, he gave his Son over to death (John 3). The Apostle testifies that sinners are called darkness, saying: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). The *nycticorax* dwells in the ruins of walls because [Col. 0030C] Christ willed to be born from the Jewish people. “I was not sent,” he says, “except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15). But Christ is crushed by the ruins because he is killed by the Jews. He shuns the light because he abhors and hates vainglory. For when he healed the leper, to give us an example of humility, he said to the leper: “See that you tell no one” (Matt. 8). Of this light it is said: “Their light shall be taken away from the wicked” (Job 38), that is, the joys of this present life. Yet he himself is the inaccessible light which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). Therefore light shuns light: that is, truth shuns the vanity of worldly glory. Flying at night, it seeks food because through preaching Christ converts sinners to the body of the Church.

Morally, however, the *nycticorax* indicates to us not merely any righteous person, but one who, while living among people, hides himself from human sight as far as he can. He shuns the light because he pays no heed to the glory of human praise; of this light it is said: “Shall not the wicked person’s light be extinguished, and shall not the flame of his fire shine?” (Job 18). [Col. 0030D] By light he means the prosperity of this present life. But the wicked person’s light is extinguished because the prosperity of future life ends together with it. “Nor shall the flame of his fire shine.” By fire he means the ardour of temporal desires. The flame is outward splendour or power, which proceeds from his inward burning. But it shall not shine, because on the day of departure every outward splendour and power shall perish. He watches in the night when, attending to sinners’ darkness, he avoids their errors. He dwells in the ruins of walls when he considers the world’s decline and awaits its end. He seeks food at night because, reflecting upon the life of sinners, he nourishes his mind and life from the examples of the righteous.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the raven
The raven is understood in various ways in the sacred page: by the raven are sometimes meant a preacher (for the raven, croaking, is a teacher who preaches), sometimes a sinner, and sometimes the devil. Isidore says in the book of *Etymologies* that the raven first seeks the eye in corpses. The raven, then, is the devil, who first seeks the eye in corpses because, in carnal persons, he extinguishes the understanding of discernment; and thus he draws out the brain through the eye, because, once the understanding of discernment has been extinguished, he overthrows the mind’s perception. Again, by the raven is understood any sinner, who is, as it were, clothed in the blackening feathers of sins. Now some sinners despair of God’s mercy. There are others who pray in order to be aided by the prayers of religious persons; of these it is said: “Ravens fed Elijah” (3 Kings 17). By the ravens, therefore, sinners are intended who support religious persons from their own substance. For Elijah signifies those whom the place and habit of religious life conceal. There are others, however, who despair, crave earthly things, look outward when they ought to be within; of them Scripture says: “The raven did not return to the ark” (Gen. 8), because perhaps it perished, caught by the waters of the flood, or perhaps, having found corpses, remained there.

[Col. 0031C] Likewise, the sinner who feeds upon carnal desires is held fast by outward cares, like the raven that did not return to the ark. But the raven is taken in a good sense when by it is meant any learned preacher. Hence it is said through blessed Job: “Who prepares food for the raven, when its young cry to God, crying out because they have no food?” (Job 38).

> “The raven,” as blessed Gregory says, [Note: [Col. 0031] St Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXX, on Job 38:41, chapter 10, §§33–35, vol. LXXVI of the *Patrologia*.] “is every learned preacher, who cries aloud while bearing the memory of his own sins, as a certain blackness of colour. Certain disciples are born to him in faith, but perhaps they do not yet know how to consider their own weakness; perhaps they turn their remembrance away from past sins and thus fail to display the blackness of humility which ought to be assumed against the glory of this world. These open their mouths as though to take food when they seek to be taught concerning lofty hidden matters. But the teacher gives them the nourishment of lofty preaching all the less insofar as he recognizes that they are less worthy to mourn their past sins. For he waits and admonishes them first to become blackened from the brightness of this present life through the laments of repentance, and only then to receive the fitting nourishment of most subtle preaching. The raven looks at the gaping mouths of its young, but first seeks that their bodies be clothed with the blackness of feathers. So too the discerning teacher does not administer inward mysteries to the minds of those whom he sees have not yet cast themselves off from this [Col. 0032A] world. And the less they empty themselves of temporal glory, the more they fast from spiritual refreshment.

> “But if, in confession of their former life, they put forth the groans of their lament as though they were blackening feathers, immediately the teacher, in contemplation, thinks of bringing down food from on high for their nourishment; like a raven he flies, and brings food back to their gaping mouths, when, from the understanding which he himself has received, he supplies by speech the food of life to hungry disciples. He refreshes them with things above all the more ardently as he knows more truly that they are becoming blackened from the world’s brightness by the lament of repentance. Moreover, when the young clothe themselves in the black colour of feathers, they promise flight from themselves as well; for the more disciples think lowly of themselves and afflict themselves in self-contempt, the more they promise hope of their future growth into higher things. Hence the teacher hastens more eagerly to feed those whom he now foresees, from certain indications, able to benefit others also.

> “When this discernment in teaching is cautiously maintained by the preacher, then a more abundant supply of preaching is granted him by God. For because he knows, through charity, how to suffer with afflicted disciples, while through discernment he understands the fitting time for instruction, he receives greater gifts of understanding, not only for himself but also for those upon whom he bestows the efforts of his labour. Hence it is aptly said: ‘Who prepares food for the raven, when its young cry to God, crying out because they have no food?’ For when the young cry in order to be satisfied, food is prepared for the raven, because when good hearers hunger for the word of God, greater gifts of understanding are bestowed on teachers for their refreshment.” [Col. 0032C]

Its young—that is, the preachers begotten from it—do not presume upon themselves, but upon the strength of their Redeemer. Hence it is rightly said: “When its young cry to God”; for they know that they can do nothing by their own strength. And although with devout voices they hunger for the gain of souls, they nevertheless desire this to be accomplished by him who works all things inwardly. For by true faith they grasp that neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase. But in the words, “crying out because they have no food,” this crying signifies nothing other than the desires of devout minds for saving food through preaching or the reception of the sacraments. For the desire for one’s own salvation, and for knowing and understanding, is innate in everyone. Therefore, when good preachers perceive this, they long to receive all their young—that is, the peoples subject to them—into the bosom of the Church; and, inflamed with great ardour, they send forth their desire now to gather these, now those. For this very agitation of thought is a kind of crying. Some read *wandering* (*vagantes*) and refer it to the ravens, that is, the preachers, who pass through various places with changing movements, while, for the increase of souls, they run with hungry minds in countless ways and into diverse regions.

[Col. 0033A] This passage can also be explained otherwise, so that by the raven are meant prelates of the Church, black with the soot of sins, who do not merely prepare their own food for themselves, but prepare it so that they may live more delicately than others. Their young are their disciples, who cry to God and murmur because their masters take more delicate food for themselves; they wander out from their cloisters and thus seek for themselves an abundance of provisions. There are also other ravens, greater in power and higher in rank, who, whenever they gather peoples in churches, preach fasting, while they themselves eat meat on fasting days and thus scandalize and offend the simple. Hence the people, wandering in mind, doubt whether the prelates who teach fasts believe that these benefit the people; or the good cry out and groan, hungering for the food of good example, while those corrupted by their evil examples desire like indulgence. And this is enough for the present concerning the raven, until someone says weightier things about it.

## Chapter XXXVI. On the moral nature of the domestic cock

“Who gave understanding to the cock?” The question is asked from whom understanding is bestowed upon the cock. But this question is quickly resolved if blessed Gregory, speaking in the *Moralia*, is heard.

> “For the cock receives understanding,” as blessed Gregory says, [Note: [Col. 0033D] St Gregory, *ibid.*, verse 36, chapter 3, §§11–14, *ibid.*] “first to discern the hours of the night, and only then to utter the voice of awakening. Thus every holy preacher first considers in his hearers the quality of their life and only then forms the fitting voice of preaching for their instruction. For to discern the hours [Col. 0033C] of the night is to judge the deserts of sinners; to discern the hours of the night is to rebuke the darkness of actions with the fitting voice of correction. Therefore understanding is bestowed from above upon the cock, because the power of discernment is divinely supplied to the teacher of truth, so that he may know to whom, what, when, and how he should apply instruction.

> “For one and the same exhortation is not suitable for all, because not all are bound by an equal condition of character. Things that benefit some often harm others. Thus herbs which nourish some animals kill others; a gentle whistle calms horses but excites puppies; a medicine that lessens one disease adds strength to another; and bread which strengthens the life of the strong kills little children. Therefore the speech of teachers ought to be fashioned according to the condition of their hearers, so that it may give each person what is his own and yet never depart from the art of common edification. For what are the attentive minds of hearers but, as it were, the tensions of strings on a lyre? The musician strikes them differently so that, when touched, they may produce no discordant harmony. The strings give forth harmonious modulation precisely because they are struck with one plectrum but not with one and the same stroke. Therefore every most prudent teacher, in order to build all up in the one virtue of charity, ought to touch the hearts of hearers from one doctrine, but not with one and the same exhortation.

> “We have something further to consider concerning this cock’s understanding: namely, that in the deeper hours of night it commonly gives stronger and more prolonged songs; but when morning time is already drawing near, it produces altogether lighter and shorter calls. In this understanding of the cock, the discernment of preachers, when considered, shows what is intimated to us. When they preach to minds still wicked, they announce the terrors of eternal judgment in lofty and mighty voices, since they cry, as it were, amid the darkness of deep night. But when they know that the light of truth is near the hearts of their hearers, they turn the greatness of their cry into the gentleness of sweetness, and utter not so much the dreadful things concerning punishments as the gentle things concerning rewards. Then they also sing with small notes, because, as the morning [Col. 0034B] of divine light approaches, they preach very subtle things concerning heavenly mysteries, so that their followers may hear things more subtle and refined concerning heaven the more certainly they now approach the light of truth. And those whom the cock’s long cry had awakened while asleep may, when awake, be delighted by the shorter and more modulated song which follows, so that each corrected person may gladly learn subtle and sweet things concerning the kingdom, having first feared the adverse things concerning judgment.

> “This is well expressed through Moses when, for setting the army in motion, the trumpets are commanded to sound in short blasts. For it is written: ‘Make for yourself two hammered silver trumpets’ (Num. 10). And a little later: ‘When the short blast sounds, the camps shall move’ (*ibid.*). For the army is led by two trumpets because the people are summoned to the battle-line of faith by the two commandments of charity. They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may be clear with the brightness of light and may not confuse the minds of hearers by any obscurity of their own. They are hammered because it is necessary that those who preach the life to come should grow through the blows of present tribulations. It is rightly said, ‘When the short blast sounds, the camps shall move,’ because indeed the more subtly and briefly the discourse of preaching is given, the more ardently the hearts of hearers are stirred against the contests of temptations.” [Col. 0034C]

There is yet another thing carefully to observe in the cock: when it is preparing to utter its song, it first shakes its wings and, striking itself, renders itself more wakeful. We plainly see this if we watch attentively the life [Col. 0034D] of holy preachers. For when they admonish through words of preaching, they first exercise themselves in holy actions, lest, sluggish in work within themselves, they awaken others by their voice. Rather, they first shake themselves by sublime deeds, and then make others attentive to acting well. The cock striking itself with its wings is the teacher setting forth an example of good life. They first strike themselves with the wings of their thoughts, because, when by careful investigation they detect what lies uselessly dormant within them, they correct it through exact examination. They first strive to punish their own faults with tears, and then denounce what must be punished in others. Therefore they first sound with their wings before uttering songs, because before they bring forth words of exhortation, they proclaim in deeds all that they are about to say. And indeed, while they are watchful within themselves, they then call others who sleep to vigils.

But whence has the teacher so great an understanding: both to watch perfectly over himself and, by certain effects of his cry, call those asleep to vigils; first carefully to examine the darkness of sins and afterward discerningly show the light of preaching; to suit each person according to measure and time, and at once show all who follow him? Whence is he rendered effective for such great and subtle matters, unless he is taught inwardly by him from whom he was created? Therefore, since the praise of such great understanding belongs not to the preacher’s power but to the Creator’s, it is rightly said by that same Creator: “Who gave understanding to the cock?” [Col. 0035B] As though he said: “No one but I, who have wonderfully instructed the minds of teachers, which I created from nothing, to understand hidden things.”

It may also be said of the cock that there are certain prelates of the Church to whom understanding is given by God, but who do nothing in accordance with the understanding given them by God. They do not awaken themselves with their wings, nor do they admonish others to rise to good works. They love themselves and so devote themselves to idleness and pleasure. Like the cock, they do not announce the hours of the night, because they do not accuse the faults of offenders. They give no attention to the rigor of confession and repentance, but employ the understanding given them by God in acquiring transitory things. They are unwilling to seek the gain of souls, yet with their whole mind seek things that belong to the pleasure of the flesh.

[Col. 0035C] There are also others, excessively simple and unlearned, who, like a cock, sit upon the perch of governance—that is, occupy a place in the chair of prelacy—yet do not know the office of divine law. They sit and are silent and feed themselves, but do not lead the flock entrusted to them to the pastures of eternal greenness. Thus both he to whom understanding is given but who does not preach God’s word to the people, and he who is silent because he does not know what to say, should beware lest, like a cock, he fall from the perch. Eli often rebuked his sons; but because he did not apply the hand of correction, he fell from his seat with his neck broken; before he died, he saw the death of his sons and learned that the ark of the Lord had been captured by the Philistines (1 Kings 4).

## Chapter XXXVII. On the ostrich and its feathers, by which hypocrites are denoted; and on the hawk and heron, by which the elect are signified

[Col. 0035D]

“The feather of the ostrich is like the feather of the heron and the hawk” (Job 39). Who does not know how greatly the heron and hawk surpass other birds by the speed of their flight? But the ostrich has a resemblance to their feathers, not the swiftness of their flight. For it cannot be lifted from the ground; it raises its wings as though for flight merely in appearance, yet never suspends itself from the earth by flying. Such indeed are all hypocrites: while they imitate the life of the good, they have an imitation of holy conduct [or “vision,” *visionis*], but do not have the truth of holy action. They have the wings of flight in appearance, but creep upon the ground in action; for they spread wings under the figure of holiness, but, weighed down by the burden of worldly cares, are in no way raised from the earth.

In reproving the appearance of the Pharisees, the Lord censures, as it were, the feather of the ostrich, which displays one thing outwardly in deed and another in colour, saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. 23). As though he said: The appearance of a feather seems to raise you, but the weight of your life presses you down into the depths. Of this weight the Prophet says: “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Ps. 4). The Lord promises through the Prophet to turn this ostrich’s hypocrisy to his own glory, saying: “The beast of the field, the dragons, and the ostriches shall glorify me” (Isa. 43). For what is expressed by the name of dragons except openly malicious minds, which always creep along the ground in lowly thoughts? And what is denoted by the term ostrich except those who pretend to be good, who retain the life of holiness as the feather of flight in appearance but do not exercise it in works? Thus the ostrich in the desert is pretence in one converted. Therefore the Lord declares that he is glorified by dragon or ostrich, because he often turns both those openly evil and those falsely good to his service from the depths of their thought.

[Col. 0036B] We have yet something to weigh more attentively, in considering this ostrich, concerning the hawk and the heron. The bodies of the hawk and heron are small, but supported by denser feathers; and therefore they fly swiftly across, because they contain little that weighs them down and much that lifts them up. By contrast, the ostrich is clothed in sparse feathers and burdened by an enormous body, so that, even if it desires to fly, the very scarcity of its feathers cannot suspend so great a mass in the air. Thus the persons of the elect are aptly signified in the heron and hawk: while they are in this life, they cannot be without even the slightest contagion of fault; yet, because they have little in them that presses down, they possess much strength of good action which lifts them upward. Conversely, even if the hypocrite performs a few things that lift him, he commits many things that weigh him down. The hypocrite does not indeed do no good at all, but he commits many perverse acts by which he weighs down even those good acts themselves. Therefore the ostrich’s few feathers do not raise its body, because the multitude of evil actions weighs down the hypocrite’s small good.

[Col. 0036D] This same feather of the ostrich has a likeness of colour to the feathers of the heron and hawk, but not a likeness of strength. Their feathers are joined together and therefore stronger; by the force of their union they can press the air in flight. By contrast, the ostrich’s feathers are loose and therefore cannot take flight, because they are passed through by the very air which they could not press down. What then do we see in these things, except that the solid virtues of the elect fly forth so as to press down the winds of human favour? Yet the action of hypocrites, however upright it may appear, does not suffice for flight, because the breeze of human praise passes through the feather of unstable virtue.

But behold: when we see one and the same outward habit in good and bad alike, when we see the very appearance of their profession in elect and reprobate alike, how is our understanding enabled to discern the elect from the reprobate, the true from the false?
