Yet we recognize this more quickly if we impress upon our memory the uncorrupted words of our Teacher, who said: “By their fruits you shall know them.” For we must not weigh what they show in appearance, but what they preserve in action. Hence, after introducing the appearance of this ostrich, he immediately adds its deeds, saying: “Which leaves its eggs upon the earth” (Job 39).

[Col. 0037A] For what is expressed by eggs except offspring still tender, which must be brooded over for a long time so that it may be brought to the state of a living bird? Eggs are senseless in themselves, but when warmed become living birds. So too it is certain that little hearers and children remain cold and insensible unless they are warmed by the careful exhortation of their teacher. Therefore, lest they be left in their insensibility and grow numb, they must be brooded over by the continual voice of teachers until they can live through understanding and fly through contemplation.

But because hypocrites, though always acting perversely, nevertheless do not cease to speak rightly, they beget children in faith or conduct by speaking well; yet they cannot nourish them by living well. Thus it is rightly said here of the ostrich: “Which leaves its eggs upon the earth.” For the hypocrite neglects the care of his children because, from inward love, he subjects himself to outward matters; and the more he is exalted in these, the less he is troubled by the failure of his offspring. To have left eggs on the earth, therefore, is not to suspend the children born through conversion above earthly actions by setting between them the nest of exhortation. To have left eggs on the earth is to offer children no example of heavenly life. Since hypocrites do not burn with the inner affections of charity, they do not grieve at the numbness of their offspring—that is, at the coldness of their eggs; and the more willingly they involve themselves in earthly actions, the more negligently they permit those whom they beget to act earthily.

But because heavenly care does not abandon the children left by hypocrites—for it warms some even from among such persons, foreknown by inward election, through the regard of bestowed grace—it is rightly added: “Perhaps you will warm them in the dust” (*ibid.*). As though he said: “I, who warm them in the dust,” because the Lord kindles with the fire of his love the souls of little ones abandoned by the care of their preachers and set in the midst of sinners. Hence we see many living amid peoples and yet not adopting the life of a numb people. Hence we see many not fleeing the crowds of the wicked and yet burning with heavenly ardour. Hence also we see many, if one may say so, becoming warm amid coldness. For whence do some, placed among the dullness of earthly people, burn with desires of heavenly hope? Whence are they inflamed amid cold hearts, unless because almighty God knows how to warm abandoned eggs even in the dust and, having driven away the insensibility of their former coldness, to animate them with the perception of vital spirit, so that they do not lie numb in the depths but, transformed into living birds, raise themselves to heavenly things by contemplation—that is, by flight? [Col. 0038A]

It should be noted, moreover, that in these words not only is the perverse action of hypocrites reproved, but the pride of good teachers also, should it perhaps creep in, is restrained. For when the Lord says of himself that he himself warms the eggs left in the dust, he plainly indicates that he himself works inwardly through the words of the teacher, he who even without the words of any human being warms what he wills amid the coldness of dust. As though he openly said to teachers: “That you may know that I am the one who works through you when you speak, behold, whenever I will, I speak even without you to human hearts.”

Thus, having humbled the thought of teachers, the discourse turns to portray the hypocrite, and still more fully shows under the deed of the ostrich the foolishness in which he grows numb. For it follows: “It forgets that a foot may trample them or that a beast of the field may crush them” (*ibid.*). What is understood by the foot except the course of action? What is signified by the field except this world, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “The field is the world” (Matt. 13)? What is expressed by the beast except the ancient enemy, who, lying in wait amid the plunder of this world, is daily sated by human death? Of it the Lord, promising through the prophet, says: “No evil beast shall pass through it” (Isa. 35).

[Col. 0038B] Therefore, in abandoning its eggs, the ostrich forgets that a foot may trample them, because hypocrites abandon the children whom they beget in conversion and take no care at all lest, deprived either of the attentive concern of exhortation or the guard of discipline, they be perverted by examples of wicked deeds. For if they loved the eggs which they produce, they would greatly fear that someone might tread them down by displaying perverse deeds in action. It also forgets that the beast of the field may crush them, because if the devil raging in this world seizes children brought forth in good conversion, the hypocrite takes no care whatever.

True teachers, therefore, have within them the affections of fear for their disciples by the power of charity; hypocrites fear the less for those entrusted to them insofar as they do not detect in themselves what they ought to fear. And because they live with hardened hearts, they do not acknowledge even the children whom they beget with any piety of due love. Hence it is further added under the image of the ostrich: “It is hardened toward its children as though they were not its own.” The person into whom the grace of charity is not poured looks upon his neighbour as a stranger, even if he himself has begotten that neighbour for God. Such indeed are all hypocrites: because their minds always seek external things, they become insensible within; and in all they do, because they always seek their own interests, they are not softened toward affection for their neighbour by any compassion of charity.

[Col. 0038D] Because they know not the inward affections of charity, the more their mind dissolves outward through worldly desire, the more it hardens inward through its lack of affection; it grows numb inwardly with insensible torpor because outwardly it is softened by condemnable love. It cannot consider itself because it makes no effort to think upon itself. But a mind cannot think upon itself when it is not wholly present with itself. Nor can it be wholly present with itself, because, through as many desires as draw it away, it is scattered from itself into as many forms; dispersed among low things, it lies fallen, though, if it wished to gather itself, it would rise to the heights.

The mind of the just, by contrast, because through the custody of discipline the flow of appetite toward all visible things is restrained, is gathered together and inwardly made whole within itself. It fully sees what it ought to be toward God or neighbour, because it leaves nothing of itself abandoned outwardly. And the more tightly it is restrained from outward things, the more it is enlarged and inflamed in inward things. The more it burns, the more brightly it shines in detecting vices. Hence holy men, when they gather themselves within themselves, perceive even the hidden faults of others with wonderful and penetrating keenness.

It follows: “When the time comes, it lifts its wings on high” [Col. 0039B] (Job 39). What are understood by this ostrich’s wings except the hypocrite’s thoughts, now pressed down and, as it were, folded together? When the time comes, it lifts them on high because, having found an opportunity, it reveals them in pride. To lift its wings on high is to disclose thoughts through unbridled pride. But now, because it pretends to be holy and, as it were, constrains within itself what it thinks, it folds its wings against its body by humility. Let the hypocrite, then, go and now seek his own praise, later oppress the lives of his neighbours, and at some time exercise himself in mockery of his Creator, so that, the loftier the things he continually devises, the more deeply he may plunge himself into more atrocious punishments.

Hence it is also added: “It forgets that a foot may trample them and that a beast of the field may crush them” (*ibid.*). Then the foot treads on the eggs and the beast of the field crushes them when they are abandoned on the earth, because human hearts, while always thinking earthly things, always desire to do what is low; they lay themselves open to be crushed by the beast of the field—that is, the devil—so that, having long been cast down by lowly thought, they may at last be broken by the commission of greater crimes.

It follows: “It is hardened toward its children as though they were not its own” (*ibid.*). It looks upon as not its own those whom it finds living otherwise than it taught them; and, growing fierce in cruelty, it applies terrors, exercises itself in their torments, and, inflamed with the fires of envy, labours that those in whom it did not labour so that they might live should perish. Hypocrites, then, who are understood through the ostrich, are said to be of such a disposition that they care for no one else, but glory in what they do and ascribe to themselves alone, above others, the good that they do.

## Chapter XXXVIII. On the vulture and its nature applied to Christ

“The bird has not known the path, nor have the vulture’s eyes [Vulgate: *eye*] seen it” (Job 28). Who is signified here by the name of bird except him who, in ascending, raised into the heavens the fleshly body which he assumed? He is fittingly also expressed by the designation of vulture. For when the vulture flies, if it sees a corpse lying down, it swoops down to feed upon the corpse and is often caught unto death in this way, while it descends from the heights to a dead animal. Thus the mediator between God and human beings, our Redeemer, is rightly signified by the designation of vulture: remaining in the height of his divinity, he saw, as though in sublime flight, the corpse of our mortality lying below, and lowered himself from heavenly things to the depths.

[Col. 0040A] For he deigned to become human for our sake; and while he sought a dead animal, he found among us death, though he was immortal in himself. But the eye of this vulture was the very purpose of our resurrection, because, dead for three days, he freed us from eternal death. That faithless people of Judaea saw him mortal, but did not at all consider how by his death he would destroy our death: they indeed saw the vulture, but did not see the vulture’s eye. Since they would not consider the paths of his humility, by which he would lift us to the heights, they did not know the bird’s path. For they did not take pains to weigh how his humility would raise them to heaven and the purpose of his death restore them to life. Therefore, “the bird has not known the path, nor has the eye of the vulture seen it,” because although it saw him whom it held by death, it would not see how great a glory for our life would follow from his death.

Accordingly it also burned with the cruelty of persecution, refused to receive the words of life, and repelled the preachers of the kingdom of heaven by forbidding, raging, and striking. These preachers—the apostles, of course—having been repelled, abandoned Judaea to which they had been sent and were dispersed among the gathering of the Gentiles. Yet the vulture is also said to be of such a nature that any sinner may be understood through the vulture. For the vulture follows an army in order to be filled with the corpses of the dead, because the sinner follows wicked people, who belong to the devil’s army, in order to imitate their wicked customs. It feeds upon corpses of the dead because it delights in carnal desires that produce death.

[Col. 0040C] The vulture also willingly walks on its feet. Hence it is called by some *gradipes*, “the walking-footed,” because the sinner loves earthly things and craves what is earthly. At times the vulture also flies high, because the sinner at times raises his mind to heavenly things; but with what intention he does this another does not know. For who sees the vulture’s eyes—that is, the intention of its thought? The Almighty has reserved this to himself, for he alone knows human thoughts. Note also that the vulture, as Isidore says, is named from its slow flight. For when it begins to fly, it departs slowly from the earth, because the sinner scarcely, or never, abandons earthly desires.

## Chapter XXXIX. On cranes following one that flies ahead of them in a letter-shaped formation, and so forth

[Col. 0040D]

As cranes travel, they follow one in a letter-shaped formation. They seek lofty places, so that they may more easily see the lands for which they are heading. The one that drives the flock reproves the rest with a piercing cry; but when it grows hoarse, another succeeds it. At night they divide the watches and take turns in the order of guard duty, holding small stones in the toes of the other foot raised from the ground, by which they ward off sleep. Their cry indicates what must be guarded against. Their colour reveals their age: for in old age they become black. When cranes fly from place to place, they preserve an order of advance in flying. They signify those who study to live in an ordered manner. For cranes flying in a letter-shaped formation signify those who live in an ordered fashion.

[Col. 0041A] When they proceed in ordered flight, they trace letters in their flight. They signify those who form within themselves the precepts of Scripture by living well. One of them goes ahead of the others and does not cease crying, because the prelate who holds the first place of governance ought to go before his followers in character and life, but in such a way that he always cries out and shows his followers, by preaching, the path of good action. If the one that goes ahead of the others becomes hoarse, another then succeeds, because if a prelate does not preach God’s word to those subject to him, or does not know how to preach it, once he has become hoarse another must succeed him.

But if night comes, the one that goes ahead descends to the earth with the others and seeks a place of rest; then all together arrange watches for their protection, so that the rest may take the repose of sleep more safely. By the watchers we may understand any discerning brothers who jointly provide temporal necessities for the brethren and take special care for each individual. To the extent of their ability, they keep watch for the service of the brethren, prudently repelling from them the assaults of demons and the approaches of secular persons.

The cranes, moreover, chosen to keep watch for the others, hold a little stone in the foot raised from the ground, fearing that if one of them should fall asleep, the stone, slipping from its foot, will fall. If it falls, the crane wakes and cries out. The stone is Christ; the foot is the mind’s affection. For as someone walks with feet, so the mind, endowed, as it were, with its affections as feet, advances. Therefore, whoever watches over himself or the brethren should carry the little stone in his foot—that is, Christ in his mind. But he should especially beware lest, if he falls asleep in sin, the little stone fall from his foot—that is, lest Christ depart from his mind. If it falls, let him cry out through confession to awaken those who sleep—that is, let him invite the brethren, both for his own transgressions and for theirs, to the watchfulness of vigilance.

[Col. 0041C] Their colour reveals their age, for in old age they become black. Here this colour suits an old person in old age when he groans, mourning for his sins. For when an old person remembers the evil he has done, he changes colour in old age. He changes the love of former pleasure into the pain of contrition. Behold how the way of religious persons can be taught through the nature of birds.

## Chapter XL. On the nature of the kite, applied to the vicious
The kite is weak in strength and flight, as though a soft bird; hence also its name. Yet it is extremely rapacious [Col. 0041D] and is always lying in wait for domestic birds. For, as is read in Isidore’s book of *Etymologies*, the kite is named from its gentle flight. The kite, then, is weak in strength and signifies those whom the softness of pleasure tempts. The kite feeds on carcasses, because the voluptuous delight in carnal desires. For the kite, which snatches flesh, is idle and seeks pleasures. It constantly circles around kitchens and butcher-shops, so that, if any raw flesh is thrown outside from them, it may seize it swiftly. By this the kite indicates to us those whom concern for the belly makes anxious. Those who are such seek luxurious things, frequent butcher-shops, and hanker after kitchens. The kite is timid toward great things but bold toward small ones: it does not dare to seize wild birds [Col. 0042A], but is accustomed to lie in wait for domestic ones. It lies in wait for chicks in order to snatch them, and kills more swiftly those whom it finds unguarded. Thus soft and pleasure-loving persons seize tender chicks, because they adapt the simpler and more prudent to their own habits and drag them toward perverse uses. Flying slowly over them, they deceive the unwary, while they seduce them by flattering with bland speech. See how birds devoid of reason teach skilled people, endowed with reason, to guard themselves by examples of perverse conduct.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Nature of the Swallow, Morally Applied to the Penitent Soul

“The turtle-dove and the swallow and the stork knew the time of their coming; but Israel did not know the judgment of the Lord” (Jer. VIII). We have spoken above concerning the turtle-dove. It remains now for us to discuss the swallow, and afterwards [Col. 0042B] the stork. Hence Isidore says:

> “The swallow is so called because it does not take food while sitting, but catches and eats its fare while hovering in the air. It is a chattering bird, flying through winding curves and twisting circuits; it is most diligent in building nests and rearing its young. It also possesses a certain foreknowledge, so that it abandons structures about to fall and does not seek lofty roofs. Nor is it attacked by other birds, nor is it ever prey. It flies across seas and remains there during the winter.”

It observes the times of its arrival; it knows also when to come and when to return. This devout bird knows how, by the sign of its arrival, to announce the beginning of spring. By the swallow, as authority testifies, is understood at one time pride of mind, at another contrition of an afflicted [Col. 0042C] heart. That pride is denoted by the swallow is said concerning Tobit: “When Tobit,” it says, “had thrown himself down beside the wall and fallen asleep, it happened that warm droppings from a swallow’s nest fell upon his eyes as he slept, and he became blind” (Tob. II). Therefore Bede, on Tobit:

> “The swallow, because of its light flight, signifies the pride and fickleness of the heart. Its filth immediately blinds; for it does not allow one to see what one has been.”

But that contrition of heart ought to be understood through the swallow is shown by the prophet, saying: “Like a swallow’s chick I shall cry out” (Isa. XXXVIII). Therefore, by the swallow we understand any discerning teacher; by the crying chick of the swallow, a disciple; and by its cry, contrition of mind. The swallow’s chick cries when it seeks from [Col. 0042D] its master a word of preaching. The swallow’s chick cries when, through confession, it reveals to its master the disposition of its contrite heart. If you know the swallow’s cry, unless I am mistaken, it signifies the lament of the penitent soul. For the swallow’s cry is the sorrow of one repenting.

The swallow does not take food while sitting, but eats fare while hovering in the air, because one who does not love earthly things, removed from earthly things, seeks heavenly things. It is called a chattering bird because it often delights in plaintive prayers. It flies through winding circuits in order that one subject to obedience may bend the mind toward the various commands of obedience. Most diligent in building nests and rearing its young, it builds its nest on high because it fixes firm hope in faith in Christ’s Passion; it is diligent [Col. 0043A] in rearing its young—that is, in teaching subject brethren. It also has a certain foreknowledge, so that it abandons things about to fall and does not seek lofty roofs. Those who truly repent likewise have a certain foreknowledge, because they flee the downfall of the present age and seek things that shall remain without end. The swallow is not attacked by other birds and is never prey; for birds of prey never seize a swallow, because those contrite in heart never become prey to demons. The swallow flies across seas because one who truly repents desires to leave behind the bitterness and tumult of this world. And it remains there in winter. For when winter presses on and cold approaches, then the righteous person passes to the warmth of charity and patiently waits there until the cold of temptation departs from the mind.

The devout bird knows how, by the sign of its arrival, [Col. 0043B] to announce the beginning of spring. The swallow returns after winter’s cold in order to announce spring’s beginning. In the same way, after the cold of excessive temptation the righteous person returns to the moderation of a balanced mind, so that, having escaped the cold of temptation, he may advance moderately, by the ascents of good work, toward summer—that is, the warmth of love. Such, then, is the nature of the swallow, that is, of the penitent soul, which always seeks spring’s beginning because in all things it keeps the measure of discernment and moderation. See how a simple bird instructs those whom divine providence makes discerning from the beginning.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Nature of the Stork

Storks are called from the sound with which they clatter—a sound plainly belonging to the mouth rather than the voice, because they make it by shaking their beaks. These heralds of spring, companions in society, enemies of serpents, fly across seas and proceed to Asia in a gathered flock. Crows go before them as guides, and they themselves follow like an army. Their devotion toward their young is extraordinary. [Col. 0043C] They cherish their nests so earnestly that by constant brooding they shed their feathers. And for as much time as they spend in rearing their offspring, they in turn are fed by their own young for the same length of time.

Storks make the sound of the mouth instead of a voice by shaking their beaks. They represent those who, with weeping and gnashing of teeth, utter with their mouth what they have done wrongly. They are heralds of spring because they show others the moderation of a converted mind. They are companions in society because they gladly live among brethren. It is also said of the stork that [Col. 0043D] it is hostile to serpents. Serpents are perverse thoughts, or perverse brethren; the stork strikes them with its beak when the righteous person restrains evil thoughts or reproves perverse brethren with a piercing rebuke. Flying across seas, they proceed to Asia in a gathered flock. Asia is interpreted “elevated.” Therefore those fly across seas and proceed to Asia who, despising the tumults of the world, strive toward higher things.

Their devotion toward their young is extraordinary, so that by constant brooding they shed their feathers over them. Storks shed their feathers over their chicks through continual brooding because prelates, while nourishing those subject to them, pluck from themselves the feathers of superfluity and frivolity. And for as much time as they spend in rearing their offspring, they in turn are fed by their young for the same length of time. So long as their chicks need them, storks [Col. 0044A] ought to nourish them; because so long as disciples need instruction, prelates ought to feed them with the word of teaching. Likewise, subjects ought to support prelates by their labours, providing them with the necessities they need. Thus the turtle-dove, the stork, and the swallow rebuke those who do not believe that Christ came in the flesh and who do not dread the coming judgment of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Nature of the Blackbird, Morally

Isidore on the blackbird:

> “The blackbird was formerly called *modula*, because it sings melodiously.”

Others say that the blackbird is so called because it flies alone, as though *mera volans*, “flying alone.” Although it is black in other places, in Achaea it is white. The blackbird is a small black bird. It indicates those whom the blackness of sin stains. The blackbird [Col. 0044B] moves the mind toward an affection of delight by the sweetness of its own voice. Figuratively, it represents those whom carnal pleasure tempts through suggestion. Concerning it, indeed, blessed Gregory writes in the book of the *Dialogues* how it came flying to blessed Benedict, and how so great a man, after the bird’s departure, was tempted by the ardour of lust. For he says:

> “One day, while the blessed Benedict was alone, temptation came. A little black bird, commonly called a blackbird, began to fly about his face and to press itself importunately upon his countenance, so that the holy man could have caught it in his hand had he wished to hold it. But when he made the sign of the cross, the bird departed; and when that same bird had departed, such a temptation of the flesh followed as the man of God had never before experienced.
>
> [Col. 0044C]
>
> “For he had once seen a certain woman, whom the malign spirit brought before the eyes of his mind; and it so inflamed the soul of God’s servant, in the image of that woman, with the fire of desire that the flame of love could scarcely be contained in his breast. Indeed, overcome by pleasure, he was almost resolved to abandon the wilderness. But suddenly visited by heavenly grace, he returned to himself. Seeing dense thickets of nettles and brambles growing nearby, he stripped off the garment he was wearing, cast himself naked into those barbs of thorns and burning nettles, and rolled there for a long while. He emerged with his whole body wounded by them, and through the wounds of his skin drew the wound of his mind out of his body, because he turned pleasure into pain.”

The flying blackbird, then, is suggestion tempting by pleasure. Those [Col. 0044D] who desire to cast off the blackbird’s pleasure must pass to the corrective discipline of blessed Benedict, and thus draw the mind’s delight out through affliction of the flesh. In the regions of Achaea, as Isidore testifies, there are white blackbirds. The white blackbird is a pure will. Achaea, however, is interpreted “the labouring sister.” There are two sisters, Rachel and Leah: namely, the active and the contemplative life. Leah is interpreted “laborious.” The active life teaches one to give alms, instruct the unlearned and simple, maintain the purity of chastity, and work with one’s own hands. This is the labour of the active life; this is the labouring sister; this is Achaea, namely, the active life. Thus in Achaea, as it were white blackbirds are those who live purely in the active life.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Nature of the Owl, Morally

[Col. 0045A]

Isidore on the owl:

> “The owl has a name formed from the sound of its cry. It is a funereal bird, indeed laden with feathers, but always held down by heavy sluggishness; it frequents tombs day and night and always dwells in caves.”

Hence Rabanus says: “The owl signifies those given over to the darkness of sins and fleeing the light of righteousness.” Therefore it is counted among the unclean animals in Leviticus (Lev. XI). Accordingly, by the owl we may understand any sinner. The owl is said to be named from the sound of its voice, because “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart.” For what it thinks in the mind, it utters with the voice (Matt. XI). It is said to be a foul bird because the place where it lives is defiled by its dung; for the sinner disgraces those with whom he lives by the example of his perverse [Col. 0045B] conduct. It is a bird laden with feathers—that is, with superfluity of flesh and levity of mind—but held down by a certain heavy sluggishness. It is held by inertia and grave sloth because sinners are inert and slothful in doing good. It remains in tombs day and night, for it delights in sin, which is the stench of human flesh. It also dwells in caves, and does not come out through confession, but hates the light of truth.

When seen by other birds, it is exposed by their loud cries and harassed by great attacks. For if a sinner comes to the light of recognition, where his sins are made known, he gives great occasion for derision to those who do good; and when he is caught in sin, he hears words of rebuke from others. They pluck out his feathers and tear him with their beaks, because those who do good rebuke the sinner’s carnal [Col. 0045C] acts and condemn the excess of his frivolity. Therefore the owl is called unhappy, because unhappy is the person who does the things described above.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Nature of the Jackdaw, Morally

Rabanus on the jackdaw:

> “The jackdaw is named from its chattering, not, as some wish, because jackdaws fly in flocks, although it is evident that they are named from their voice. It is a most talkative and noisy kind, which can signify either the talkativeness of philosophers or the harmful verbosity of heretics.”

Still something else may be said about the nature of the jackdaw. For the jackdaw signifies chatterers and gluttons. Those who devote themselves to gluttony willingly recount idle reports after eating, and either slander others or lend their ears to slander. The jackdaw lives in woods and, chattering, flies from one tree to another; so the talkative person never ceases to tell others, even shameful things that he knows, about those among whom he lives. When the jackdaw sees someone passing by, it chatters; and when it finds persons in hiding, it acts likewise. So the talkative person slanders not only secular people but also those whom a religious place conceals. The jackdaw is sometimes caught and shut in a cage, in order that it may be taught to speak articulated words. Likewise, when a secular person comes to conversion, he learns the language of religion, so that the tongue of a bird may speak the words of a human being: one who had been accustomed to speak disorderly may thereafter become accustomed to speak orderly.

Yet it sometimes happens that the jackdaw [Col. 0046A] held shut up escapes, and one who had formerly chattered cries out more loudly after leaving. In the same way, when a talkative person adopts religious life, he scarcely abandons his tongue; but if he should leave the habit and go outside, he turns the good of religion toward evil by slandering it, as though chattering. Therefore the nature of the bird should warn us whom to receive into the fellowship of religion. A prudent teacher, when he must receive someone, should at least first test him through some period of living together.

I learned from a certain prudent and religious man that there are some kinds of people who can scarcely be kept in proper order in religious life. If you ask who they are, so that they may be avoided, they are painters, physicians, entertainers, and certain others accustomed to travel through various regions [Col. 0046B]. Such persons can scarcely be stable. The painter’s art is very attractive. For when a painter has painted a church, chapter-house, refectory, or some workshops, he goes to another monastery, if permission is granted him, at someone’s request, in order to paint. He paints the works of Christ on a wall; but would that he held them in mind, so that he might know how to paint them in colours—that is, by example and conduct.

The medical art, however, needs many things and scarcely ever lacks private possessions. Whoever practises it must necessarily abound in aromatics and kinds of medicines. When someone living near the church is oppressed by illness, the physician is asked to come to the sick person. But if the abbot does not allow him to go, he incurs the anger and indignation both of the sick person and of the physician. A physician [Col. 0046C] sometimes sees what he ought not fittingly to see. He touches what it is not fitting for a religious person to touch. He speaks of uncertain things from experiments, but experiment is deceptive, and therefore he is often deceived. Yet it is not suitable for a religious person to speak anything other than what is true. He promises gain to his church if he goes to the sick person, but keeps silent about scandal and harm to his own soul.

Perhaps, brother, you know what blessed Gregory says concerning the monk physician named Justus—just in name, but would that he had been just in deed—who had hidden three gold pieces in a medicine. Although Justus had served him in his illness, Gregory nevertheless did not spare him in correction:

> “Before his death, he forbade the brethren to speak with him; after his death, however, he ordered him to be buried on a dung-heap. And thus after death he was absolved: ‘May your money be with you unto destruction’” (Acts VIII).

Entertainers also, frivolous before conversion, when they come to conversion often make use of frivolity and depart lightly. Those accustomed to travel through various regions, if they are burdened by weariness of the cloister, leave their cloisters more quickly because they know the variety of lands.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Nature of the Goose, Morally

The goose attests the night watches by the constancy of its honking. No animal, however, senses the smell of a human being as does the goose. Hence, by its honking the ascent of the Gauls to the Capitol was discovered. Therefore Rabanus says: “This bird can signify prudent persons, keeping good watch over their own protection.” There are two kinds of geese: domestic and wild. Wild geese fly [Col. 0047A] high and in order, and signify those who, removed from earthly things, keep the order of good living. Domestic geese, however, live together in villages, cry out often, tear themselves with their beaks, and signify those who, although they love gatherings, nevertheless occupy themselves with talkativeness and slander.

Wild geese are all ash-coloured; I have seen none of them pied or snow-white. Among domestic geese, however, there is found not only ash-grey colouring but also pied or white. Among wild geese is found ash-grey colouring—that is, among those removed from the world, the humble garb of penitence. But those who live in villages or cities wear clothing of more beautiful colour. More than other animals, the goose senses the smell of an approaching person, because the discerning person recognizes others, even though far distant, by good or bad repute. Therefore, [Col. 0047B] when the goose senses the smell of an approaching person, it does not cease to cry out at night, because when the watchful brother sees the negligences of ignorance in others, he ought to cry out. Long ago the goose’s cry benefited the Romans on the Capitol, and in the chapter-house the cry of a prudent brother benefits daily when he sees negligence. The goose’s cry drove the Gallic enemy from the Capitol. But the cry of a provident brother drives the ancient enemy from the chapter-house. The goose’s cry kept the city of Rome free from the assault of enemies; the cry of a prudent brother guards the life of those living in common, lest it be disturbed by wicked people. Divine providence, I think, would not set the natures of birds before us unless it wished them to benefit us in some respect.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Nature of the Heron

[Col. 0047C]

The heron is called, as it were, *ardua*, “lofty,” because of its high flights. For it fears rain and flies above the clouds so that it cannot feel rainstorms. When it takes flight, moreover, it signifies a storm. Many call it the *tantalus*. Hence Rabanus says:

> “This bird can signify the souls of the elect, who, fearing the disturbance of this world lest perhaps, at the devil’s prompting, they be enveloped by the storms of persecutions, lift their minds, raising their purpose above all temporal things, to the serenity of the heavenly homeland, where the face of God is continually beheld.”

Although the heron seeks food in waters, it nevertheless places its nest in woods and high trees, because the righteous person, who nourishes himself upon falling and transitory things, nevertheless sets his hope in divine and lofty things; and although his flesh is sustained by transient things, his soul delights in eternal things. The heron tries to defend its chicks in the nest with its beak, lest they be seized by other birds. In the same way, the righteous person strikes with vigorous rebuke those whom he knows to be perverse and intent on deceiving his subjects. Some of them are white in colour, others ash-grey; yet both colours are understood positively, if purity is signified by white and penitence by ash-grey. Those who do penance and those who live purely belong to the same kind. Thus both the heron’s colour and its manner of life offer an example of salvation to religious men.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Bird Caladrius

[Col. 0048A]

The *Physiologus* says of the caladrius that it is wholly white, and that the inner part of its thigh removes dimness from the eyes. The nature of the caladrius, then, is said to be such that, if it is brought several times to a sick person, it makes those standing by certain whether the sick person is to die or live. For if it looks at the person’s face and does not turn away its eyes, but attentively considers the sick person’s face, it is a sign that he will live. But if it turns its eyes away from the sick person’s face, it is a sign of death.

By the caladrius we understand Christ, who came into the world in order to save humankind. He is said to be snow-white in colour because he was free from every sin. The inner part of whose thigh wipes the darkness of dimness from the eyes. By the thigh is understood propagation [Col. 0048B] of the race. The inner part of the thigh, therefore, is the incarnation of the Saviour. For the incarnation of the Saviour was inward and hidden, and it was hidden even from the devil. Christ came into the world to save humankind. He turned his face from the Jews; he looked upon the Gentiles; he bore our iniquities; and he who committed no sin bore our sins on the wood of the cross.

Moreover, this aforesaid caladrius visits our infirmities daily, considers the mind through confession, and heals those to whom it grants the grace of repentance; but it turns its face from those whose heart it knows to be unrepentant. It rejects these, but makes sound those upon whom it fixes its face.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Phoenix

The phoenix is called a bird of Arabia either because it has a purple-red [Col. 0048C] colour, or because it is singular and unique in the whole world. For Arabs call a singular thing *phoenix*. Living for five hundred years and more, when it sees that it has grown old, it gathers little branches of aromatic plants and builds itself a pyre; then, turning toward the sun’s ray, it kindles a voluntary fire for itself by the beating of its wings, and thus rises again from its ashes. Hence Rabanus says:

> “The phoenix can signify the resurrection of the righteous, who, having gathered the spices of virtues, restore to themselves after death the renewal of their former vigour.”

The phoenix is a bird of Arabia. Arabia is interpreted “a plain.” The plain is this world; Arabia is secular life; Arabs are secular persons. Arabs call the phoenix singular. Singular is any righteous person altogether removed from secular concerns. [Col. 0048D] The phoenix is believed to live for five hundred years, as Scripture testifies. Now the number one hundred in years morally signifies the limit of perfection. The number of five hundred years can be assigned to the five senses of the body. When sight fails, the first hundred years pass; when hearing fails, the second passes. When the three remaining senses—that is, touch, taste, and smell—fail, then five hundred years have morally passed.

But when the phoenix approaches death, it prepares various kinds of aromatic plants. The spices are good works; the various kinds are the various virtues of the soul. It builds a heap of spices and places itself amid the kinds of aromatic plants. The righteous person does this [Col. 0049A] as often as he brings to mind the multitude of his good works. At the sun’s ray it kindles voluntary fire with its wings, because the righteous person inflames his mind, roused by the wings of contemplation, with the ardour of the Holy Spirit. Thus the phoenix is burned, but from its ashes a phoenix is born again. Therefore, when the phoenix dies and another phoenix is born again from its ashes, this example is given so that the truth of the future resurrection may be believed by each person; and the phoenix’s resurrection is the hope and image, or specimen, of the future resurrection. Faith in the future resurrection, then, is no greater miracle than the phoenix’s resurrection accomplished from ashes. See how the nature of birds supplies the simple with an argument for the resurrection, and how the work of nature confirms what Scripture proclaims.

## CHAPTER L. On the Nature of the Partridge

[Col. 0049B]

“The partridge cries out and gathers and broods over eggs that it did not lay, making riches for itself without judgment: ‘For in the midst of its days it will leave them, and at its end it will be foolish’” (Jer. XVII). Hence Isidore says:

> “The partridge has its name from its voice. It is a deceitful bird, so fraudulent that it steals another’s eggs and broods over them.”

But deceit has no fruit. For when the chicks hear the voice of their own mother, by a certain natural instinct they leave the bird that brooded over them and return to the one that gave them birth. Hence Rabanus says:

> “Through the leaders of heretics the devil gathered peoples whom he had not begotten, and joined to himself a multitude of deceived persons, whom he afterwards abandoned; and by the judgment of all he is proved most foolish [Col. 0049C].”

We may therefore understand the devil by the partridge, and hope by the egg. The partridge whose eggs the devil steals is undoubtedly understood as the Church. Thus Scripture indicates to us in the partridge the devil, who steals, broods over, and nourishes another partridge’s eggs—that is, those possessing hope of salvation. He steals them when he takes their hope of salvation away; he broods over them and nourishes them with idleness and pleasure; he broods over them with earthly desires and nourishes them with carnal enticements. But when the chicks hear the voice of their own mother, they recognize her by a certain natural instinct. Likewise, when someone has been subject to the devil and hears the voice of ecclesiastical preaching, leaving the devil he flies back to the Church as to his own mother, so that henceforth he may live in peace beneath the wings of divine protection.

[Col. 0049D] See how the partridge loses, in the chicks, the eggs that it steals and gathers; for it is no wonder if the devil loses, by the judgment of truth, those whom he had gathered wickedly. Therefore, at his end the devil will be foolish, because on the day of judgment he will lack eternal blessedness, and then the partridge with the lost—that is, the devil with his subjects—will hear: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV). Those who fall while serving the devil in this life tend toward this end.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Quail, or the *Qualea* Bird

Quails are plainly named from the sound of their voice; the Greeks call them **ὄρτυγες** (*ortyges*), because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They have [Col. 0050A] seasons for coming. For, when summer has been driven away, they fly across the seas. The *ortygometra* is the bird that leads the flock; when it approaches land, the hawk sees and seizes it. Therefore all take care to make the leader wary of the alien kind, through whom they may first avoid dangers. This bird alone, like the human being, suffers from the falling sickness.

Quails have seasons for coming. For, when summer has been driven away, they fly across the seas. The quail flying over the sea is the soul trampling upon all things that pass away. Summer’s heat is the ardour of charity. Winter’s cold is the temptation of a mind grown cold. Therefore the righteous person crosses from love of neighbour, over the sea of this world, to love of God, so that he may always remain in the warm region—he who always burns within himself with the warmth of love—in order to avoid winter’s cold, namely the storms and winds of unforeseen temptation. [Col. 0050B]

The *ortygometra* is called the bird that leads the flock. When it approaches land, the hawk sees and seizes it. Land is earthly desires; seas are the perils of the world; the hawk lying in wait is the devil tempting through suggestion. Thus, when it approaches land, the hawk sees and seizes it, because the devil draws after himself those who seek earthly things. Therefore the prelate who goes before the flock should carefully consider with what intention he seeks earthly things: whether he turns them to his own use or seeks them for the brethren’s need, lest the hawk—that is, the devil—seize one who, setting spiritual things aside, does not cease to hanker after earthly ones. Therefore all take care to make the leader wary of the alien kind, through whom they may first avoid dangers.

There are two kinds of human beings: the good and the evil. Those of the alien kind are perverse [Col. 0050C] people. Therefore the righteous set the perverse before themselves, while they carefully observe their falls and outcomes. When they consider these attentively, they avoid, by reflection, the first perils of sinning. This bird, like the human being, suffers from the falling sickness, because the spiritual person, like the carnal person, is said sometimes to sin; yet he does not die every time he sins, because the grace of repentance is not denied him. Hence it is written: “The righteous falls seven times a day” (Prov. XXIV), and yet does not cease to be righteous. For as often as the righteous person sins, so often does he add the resolve to rise again.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Nature of the Hoopoe

The hoopoe is called by the Greeks **ἔποψ** (*epops*), from **ἐποψάομαι** (*epopsaomai*), meaning “I procure provisions,” because it notices and collects human excrement and feeds on foul-smelling dung. It is a most filthy bird, helmeted with projecting crests [Col. 0050D], always dwelling among tombs and human dung. Hence Rabanus says: “This bird signifies wicked sinners, namely those who constantly delight in the filth of sins.” The hoopoe is also said to love mourning, because the sorrow of the world works death of the spirit. Therefore one who loves God ought always to rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things (I Thess. V), because joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Gal. V).

The *Physiologus* also says of the hoopoe that, when it has grown old and cannot fly, its children come to it, pluck the very old feathers from its body, and do not cease to brood over it; and until new feathers grow again, they support it with food, until, as Scripture says, [Col. 0051A] having recovered its former strength, it can fly again. Thus, by their own example, hoopoes rebuke perverse people who expel their fathers from their own homes when they have grown old and refuse to support them when they fail, although those fathers reared them when they were still little. Let the rational creature, therefore, consider what it owes to father or mother, since the irrational creature repays its parents in their need, when they have grown old, with what has been described above.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Olor, or Swan

The olor is a bird which the Greeks call **κύκνον** (*kyknon*), “swan.” It is called *olor* because **ὅλος** (*holos*) means “whole,” since it is wholly white in its feathers. For no one remembers having seen a black swan. The swan is named from singing because it pours forth the sweetness of song in modulated tones. It is said to sing sweetly because it has a long, curved neck, and its voice, forced out through a long and winding passage, must produce varied modulations. It is reported that in the Hyperborean regions, when cithara-players sing beforehand, many olors fly up and sing together very fittingly.

The swan has snow-white plumage but black flesh. Morally, the olor snow-white in its feathers signifies the effect of pretence, by which black flesh is covered, because sin of the flesh is veiled by pretence. When the swan swims in a river, it carries its head and neck upright, because the proud person, though drawn toward destruction along with transitory things, nevertheless takes temporary glory even in possessing things that pass away. It is reported that in the Hyperborean regions, when cithara-players sing beforehand, [Col. 0051C] many olors fly up and sing together very fittingly, because those who greedily cling to pleasures with all their desires, as though flying up, accord with pleasure-lovers.

It is also said that, when the swan dies at the end, it sings very sweetly. Likewise, when the proud person leaves this life, he still delights in the sweetness of the present world and, in dying, brings to memory the things he has done badly. But when the swan is stripped of its snow-white feathers, it is placed on a spit and roasted at the fire. Likewise, when the rich and proud person dies and is stripped of worldly glory, descending into the flames of hell he will be tormented by punishments; and one accustomed to consume food excessively, descending into the abyss, becomes food for fire.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the Fleet of Solomon and Jehoshaphat

[Col. 0051D] Solomon’s fleet went by sea once every three years to Tarshish, bringing back gold, silver, elephants’ teeth, monkeys, and peacocks (*pavos* or *pavones*) (I Kings X). Tarshish is interpreted “exploration of joy.” There is a joy of the present age and a joy of the future. The joy of the present life is enclosed by an end; the joy of the future is bounded by no end at all. Sorrow and sadness follow the joy of the present life; neither sorrow nor sadness follows the joy of the future. The joy of the present age is to be exalted in honours, to enjoy transitory things for a time, to abound in a multitude of relatives, and to delight in their presence. But when someone is deprived of honours, stripped of possessions, or loses a friend through death, sorrow follows. Thus this joy is always mingled with sorrows.

[Col. 0052A] Once in every three years Solomon’s fleet is sent by sea to Tarshish. Solomon’s fleet is the power of confession. By this fleet we are carried across the sea of this world, lest we be submerged. The fleet is therefore sent to Tarshish, from which it is said to bring gold and silver, elephants’ tusks, apes, and peacocks. Gold and silver are said to be in Tarshish—that is, men distinguished for wisdom and endowed with eloquence—who, while they explore and seek out the joy of the present age, come to know themselves. And when, by Solomon’s fleet, they come from Tarshish to Jerusalem and bring pure gold, they are made purer in the peace of the Church through confession. From this most pure gold King Solomon made golden shields. The golden shields are those who live purely and defend others from the assaults of the devil. From the aforesaid [Col. 0052B] silver, too, are made silver trumpets—that is, the teachers of the Church. It also brought apes and peacocks: that is, mockers and sensual persons, so that those who had been mockers and sensual persons in Tarshish may become humble in the peace of conversion. Solomon’s fleet also brought elephants’ tusks—that is, the slanders of the proud. For while by slanderous words they detract from the good works of the simple, they gnaw, as it were, at their bones with their teeth. Note that elephants’ teeth become the material of ivory, and from ivory is made Solomon’s throne. Those, indeed, who had been accustomed to live by plunder, once made subject to Solomon, afterwards prepare themselves, through the virtue of justice and charity, to be his throne. Once in every three years Solomon’s fleet was accustomed to go to Tarshish. Morally understood, the first year is thought, the second speech, and the third action. [Col. 0052C] Therefore, when confession is made concerning these three together, it is as though Solomon’s servants go once in three years to Tarshish.

But King Jehoshaphat of Judah also, as the history relates, made fleets upon the sea to sail to Ophir for gold; and they could not go, because they were wrecked at Ezion-geber (III Kings XXII). Jehoshaphat means “judging”; Ezion-geber means “the tongue of a man,” that is, confession. Jehoshaphat is understood, or said, to be king of Judah when judgment rules over confession. For when the sinner judges himself in confession, then King Jehoshaphat reigns in Judaea. Ophir, however, means “grassy.” Grass-covered ground is said to be land which no one tills, where an abundance of grass grows so as to move [Col. 0052D] one’s inclination toward pleasure. In this Ophir—that is, in this luxuriant place—the pleasure-loving sit, the idle lie down. They sit through persistence; they lie down through dissipation. This grassy place is this barren and unfruitful world. Jehoshaphat’s fleet therefore strives to go to Ophir for gold, so that, while the world’s downfall is considered, purity of mind may be gained. But while this is being done, Jehoshaphat’s fleet is said to have been wrecked at Ezion-geber. Geber, as Jerome says, means “young man” or “strong man.” It is therefore no wonder if the surge of youth wrecks the fleet of confession.

## Chapter LV. On the nature of the peacock

Since we have already spoken of certain matters mentioned above, it remains for us to say something about the peacock, which we intend to discuss. “The peacock, as Isidore says, received its name from the sound of its voice.” For when it suddenly begins to cry out, it strikes sudden terror into its hearers. Thus the peacock is named from terror (*pavor*), because terror is caused to hearers by its cry. While the peacock dwells in Tarshish, it signifies sensual persons. But when it has been brought by the fleet to Jerusalem, it represents learned preachers. Its flesh is tough and resistant to decay; it is scarcely cooked by a cook’s fire, or digested in the stomach by the heat of the liver. Such are the minds of strong teachers: neither does the flame of greed burn them up nor the heat of lust inflame them. The peacock has a terrible cry, a simple gait, a serpent-like head, a sapphire-blue breast; it also has somewhat reddish feathers on its wings, a long tail, [Col. 0053B] and, so to speak, one full of eyes. The peacock, I say, has a terrible cry when the preacher threatens sinners with the inextinguishable fire of Gehenna. It walks simply whenever it does not exceed humility in its deeds. It has a serpent-like head when the head of the mind is held under the guard of shrewd circumspection. The sapphire colour on its breast signifies heavenly desire in the human mind. The reddish, ruddy colour in its feathers signifies the love of contemplation. The length of its tail indicates the duration of the life to come. Its having what seem to be eyes in its tail signifies that every teacher foresees the peril threatening each person at the end. There is green in its tail, so that the end may correspond with the beginning. Thus the variety of colours signifies the diversity of virtues.

[Col. 0053C] Note also that, when the peacock is praised, it raises its tail, just as any prelate, through vainglory, lifts up his mind at the praises of flatterers. It arranges its feathers in order, because whatever the teacher does, he believes that he has done it properly. Yet when the tail is raised, its hinder parts are uncovered; thus what is praised in the work is ridiculed in the self-exaltation. The peacock must therefore keep its tail lowered, so that the praiseworthy thing which the teacher does may be done with humility.

## Chapter LVI. On the nature of the eagle

The eagle is so called from the sharpness of its eyes. Its sight or gaze is said to be so great that, when it is borne motionless of wing over the seas, plainly visible to human eyes, it sees little fish swimming from so great a height and, descending like a whirlwind, draws its seized prey with its wings to the shore. It is also said not to turn aside its gaze from the rays of the sun; hence it suspends its young by the claw and exposes them to the sun’s rays, preserving as worthy of their kind those that it sees hold their gaze steady, but casting aside as degenerate those whose eyes it sees turn away.

Therefore blessed Gregory says: “By the name of eagle, Sacred Scripture sometimes signifies evil spirits, snatchers of souls; sometimes the powers of this present age; sometimes the most subtle understandings of the saints; or the incarnate Lord, swiftly flying over the depths and soon returning to the heights.” By the name of eagles are expressed the spirits who lie in wait, as Jeremiah testifies when he says: “Our persecutors were swifter than the eagles of heaven” (Jer. [Col. 0054A] IV). For our persecutors are swifter than eagles of heaven when wicked men do such great things against us that they seem, by their inventions of malice, even to outstrip the powers of the air.

By the name of eagle earthly power is figured. Thus it is said through the prophet Ezekiel: “A great eagle with great wings, with a long extension of limbs, full of feathers and variegation, came to Lebanon; and it took the pith of the cedar and plucked away the topmost part of its branches” (Ezek. XVII). Whom, indeed, does this eagle signify but Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon? On account of the immensity of his army he is described as having great wings; on account of the long duration of his times, a long extension of limbs; on account of his many riches, as full of feathers; and on account of the innumerable array of earthly glory, as full of variegation. He [Col. 0054B] came to Lebanon and took the pith of the cedar and plucked away the topmost part of its branches, because, attacking the eminence of Judaea, he took away the nobility of its kingdom as though the pith of a cedar; and, when he carried away into captivity the tenderest offspring of the kings from the summit of their kingdom, he plucked away, as it were, the topmost part of its branches.

“By the name of eagle is expressed the subtle understanding of the saints. Thus, when the same prophet described himself as having seen the four Evangelists under the figure of living creatures (Ezek. I), he signified by an eagle the fourth living creature among them, namely John, who in flight abandoned the earth because, by subtle understanding, he penetrated inwardly into the mysteries of the Word through vision.” Likewise, those who abandon these earthly things in mind, like an eagle with John, seek heavenly things through contemplation.

Again, blessed [Col. 0054C] Gregory says of the eagle: “Like an eagle flying to its food. For it is the eagle’s habit to gaze upon the rays of the sun with an undazzled eye; but when the need for food presses it, it lowers the same gaze of its eyes, which it had fixed upon the sun’s rays, to look upon a corpse. Though it flies to the heights, it nevertheless seeks the earth in order to take flesh. Such, too, were the ancient fathers, who, insofar as the infirmity of human nature allowed, contemplated with minds raised up the light of the Creator. But foreknowing that he would be incarnate at the end of the world, they turned aside, as it were, from the sun’s rays. And they come, as it were, from the heights to the depths when they acknowledge God above all things and man beneath all things. Since they discern that he will suffer and die for the human race—by which death, that is, they knew that they themselves would be nourished and renewed unto life—they seek food in the corpse, after contemplating the sun’s rays, according to the eagle’s manner.”

Otherwise: “Like an eagle flying to its food. The eagle, indeed, is suspended in a very high flight and by swift striving is set free into the ether; but by the appetite of its belly it seeks the earth and suddenly pours itself down from the heights. Thus the human race fell in its first parent from the heights to the depths. The dignity of its condition had suspended it, as it were, in the freedom of the air through the loftiness of reason; but because it touched food contrary to the command, it came to the earth through the desire of the belly, and, as it were, after flight feeds upon flesh, having lost those free breaths of contemplation and delighting below in bodily pleasures.”

[Col. 0055A] Again, concerning the eagle: “My youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII). It is commonly said of the eagle, when it is weighed down by old age, that its beak becomes hooked and bent so that it cannot take food and languishes from emaciation; but it comes to a rock, sharpens its beak, takes food, and becomes young again. The rock is Christ; the eagle is any righteous person who sharpens its beak upon the rock when, through good action, he makes himself conformed to Christ.

## Chapter LVII. On the bird *ibis* or *ibis*

There is a bird called the ibis. Under the law it is unclean beyond all birds, because it feeds upon dead bodies and carrion. It remains day and night on the shores of sea, rivers, or pools, [Col. 0055B] seeking dead little fish or any corpse which the water has already cast out, putrid or soaked. For it fears to enter the water because it cannot swim, nor does it try to learn, because it delights in dead bodies. Therefore it cannot enter the depth of the water, where clean little fish dwell, so as to take food for itself there; but it always wanders around outside, fleeing the purer and deeper waters, from which it might live cleanly.

You therefore, Christian, who have been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, enter into intelligible and spiritual waters—that is, into the depth of Christ’s commandments: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, long-suffering, goodness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity (Gal. V). For if [Col. 0055C] you refuse to enter into the higher waters and to take and receive from them spiritual food for yourself, but, wandering about outside, should wish to fatten yourself upon dead and most foul corpses—of which the Apostle says, “Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are uncleanness, adulteries, fornication, shamelessness, debauchery, drunkenness, revelry, avarice, covetousness” (ibid.)—you will come into the company of the unclean. These are carnal and death-bringing foods, by which unhappy souls are nourished for punishment.

Learn therefore to swim upon “this sea, great and broad in its reaches; there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. CIII). Nor will you overcome them otherwise than by the sign of the cross. Thus the saints, like ships passing through, come to the kingdoms of heaven [Col. 0056A] as to a most tranquil harbour. But those who do not know how to swim spiritually will be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, and the dead will perish with the dead, as it is said in the Gospel: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. VIII). Accordingly the *Physiologus* fittingly says of the ibis that it drives serpents violently away. And you, when you pray, stretch out your hands to heaven, because the power of the cross always defends those who pray and say: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. IV). For even the sun itself does not shine unless it extends its rays; birds cannot fly unless they spread their wings; ships, unless they raise their sails, are not moved when the wind blows. Finally, while Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; when he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed (Exod. XVII).

## Chapter LVIII. On the coot

There is a bird called the coot, very intelligent and most prudent among all birds. It does not feed on corpses, nor does it fly and wander restlessly from one place to another; rather, it remains and stays in one place until the end, and there it has its food and rests. Thus every faithful person is preserved and lives according to God’s will. He does not fly about, wandering here and there through various places, as heretics do. Nor does he delight in worldly desires and bodily pleasures; rather, like that bird which does not feed on flesh, he always holds himself and rests in one and the same place—that is, in the Catholic and Apostolic Church—and remains there [Col. 0056C] until the end, as the Gospel says: “But whoever perseveres until the end, this one shall be saved” (Matt. X). There he keeps himself, and there the Lord “makes those who are of one mind dwell in a house”; and there he has the daily bread of immortality, and as his precious drink the blood of Christ, refreshing himself with holy feasts and with the most sweet words of the Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. “For man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. IV). The coot is a pool-bird, having its nest in the middle of the water or upon rocks surrounded by water; it always delights in the depth of the sea, and when it foresees a storm, it flees and plays in its nest.

# Second Book, Principally Concerning the Natures of Animals

[Col. 0055]

## Prologue

[Col. 0055D]

The term “beasts” properly applies to panthers, foxes, tigers, wolves, apes, bears, and the rest that are savage either with mouth or claws, serpents excepted. Beasts are so called from laying waste and from the force with which they rage. They are called wild animals because they exercise natural freedom and are borne along by their own desire. For their wills are free: they wander [Col. 0056D] here and there and are carried wherever their inclination leads them.

## Chapter I. On the lion

*Leo* is a Greek word adapted into Latin, for in Greek it is called λέων (*leōn*). It is king of the beasts and prince of all four-footed animals. Its kind is said to be threefold. Of these, those that are short and have curled manes are timid; [Col. 0057A] those that are long and have plain hair are fiercer. Their spirit is indicated by their brow and tail. Their strength is in their breast, their firmness in their head. When enclosed by hunters, they look at the ground, lest the sight of hunting-spears terrify them. They fear the noise of wheels, but fire still more. And though they fear no encounter, they are said to be very much afraid of a white cock.

Natural philosophers, moreover, say that the lion has five natural properties or natures. The first is that it loves to travel along mountain summits. But if it happens to be sought by hunters, it detects their scent and covers its tracks with its tail, so that hunters cannot track it by its footprints. So too our Saviour, the spiritual Lion from the tribe of Judah (Apoc. V), the root of Jesse and son of David, sent by the heavenly Father, concealed [Col. 0057B] the traces of his divinity by assuming flesh from the Virgin Mary, so that even the devil, the enemy of humankind, ignorant of the mystery of his Incarnation, attempted to tempt him as though he were a mere man. For when our Lord Jesus Christ had long fasted in the wilderness and, in respect of the flesh, hungered for our sins, the tempter approached him and said: “If thou art the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread” (Matt. IV). But when he willed to suffer for us, having been delivered by a disciple into the hands of the Jews, the devil thought that he would conquer by death him whom he had been unable to overcome while living. Yet when Christ rose from the dead by his own power, he not only returned from the lower world, but also led captivity captive, displaying his divinity.

The lion’s second nature is that, when it sleeps, it appears to have its eyes open. This is aptly said of Christ in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, and my heart watches” (Cant. V). For the flesh slept in dying on the cross, but the divinity watched, protecting all things; whence the Psalm: “Behold, he that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. CXX).

Its third nature is that, when the lioness gives birth, she gives birth to her cubs dead and guards them for three days, until their father comes and breathes upon their faces so that they are brought to life. Thus the almighty Father raised our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, from the dead on the third day, as Jacob says: “He shall sleep as a lion, and like a lion’s cub he shall be raised up” (Gen. XLIX).

The lion’s fourth nature is that, unless it has been injured, it is not easily angered. Its mercy is evident in that it spares those who have fallen. Hence the verse:

> The noble anger of the lion knows how to spare the fallen.  
> Do thou likewise, whoever rulest in the world.

It permits captive people whom it encounters to return, and kills only under extreme hunger. Rational human beings ought to look to its example: they grow angry without having been injured and oppress the innocent, though Christian law commands them to let such persons go free.

## Chapter II. On the animal *antula*, or *anto*, or antelope

There is a very fierce animal called *antula*, such that no hunter can approach it. For it has long horns like a saw, with which it can cut down the greatest oaks; it cuts down every dense and superfluous growth of the trees without stopping anywhere. But when it thirsts, it goes to the great river Euphrates and drinks. There are there green, soft willow twigs. The animal begins to play among those twigs, and in playing entangles its horns; and, its horns being entangled, it cries out with a great roar because it cannot escape while surrounded by the slender twigs. Then any hunter hunting in concealment, hearing its cry, runs up and, finding it bound, kills it.

Take heed, therefore, servant of God, against drunkenness; do not become bound by the pleasure of lust, lest you be slain by the devil. “Wine and women cause wise men to fall away” (Ecclus. XIX). But the truly wise and prudent man will turn away from wine and woman. There are also two fire-bearing stones, male and female. Therefore you who profess wisdom, understand that many have perished through wine, as through a man, and through women, that is, pleasures; and be watchful, that you may escape safely.

Therefore this animal described above signifies persons possessing the horns of good works, or knowledge of the two Testaments. So long as they apply themselves to these, they cut away not only minor but even great vices. But if they turn back from these things and attend to the enticements and pleasures of this life, serving gluttony and seduction, they lose not only the power of good works but also the rewards which they ought to possess.

## Chapter III. On the onocentaur

The *Physiologus* declares that the onocentaur consists of two natures, saying: its upper part is like a centaur—that is, a human being—[Col. 0058C] but its lower part like an *onos*, that is, an ass. Foolish and double-tongued people are likened to it. Hence Paul says: “Having the promises of godliness, but denying them by their deeds” (II Cor. VII); and the Psalmist: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII).

## Chapter IV. On the hedgehog, or urchin

The *Physiologus* says of the hedgehog that it has the form of a suckling pig and is wholly covered with spines. At vintage time it enters a vineyard; where it finds a vine laden with fruit, it climbs upon it and shakes the clusters to the ground. It then descends and rolls itself upon the gathered clusters, so that they lodge in its spines, and thus carries food to its young. It is useful medicinally; when cooked and eaten, it is beneficial.

But you, servant of God, guard your vineyard and all its spiritual fruits, lest the anxiety of this age and pleasure in temporal goods seize you, and lest the spiny devil fasten all its spiritual fruits upon his spines, make them food for beasts, and leave your soul bare, empty, and void, like a vine-shoot or vine stripped of its grapes. For afterwards you will cry out in vain: “I have not kept my vineyard” (Cant. II). It is also the nature of this hedgehog that, whenever it senses a human being, it protects itself against all that person’s snares by fencing itself with its spines, gathering itself into a ball, and creaking like a cart. But you, foreseeing the enemy of your salvation, fortify yourself against him with the virtues given to you and with the sacraments of the Church; and, that you may live to God, feign yourself dead to the works of the world, the flesh, and the devil.

## Chapter V. On the fox and its nature

The fox is called *vulpes*, as though *volupes* [“swift-footed”]. For it is quick with its feet and never runs in a straight path, but by winding turns. It is a deceitful and ingenious animal. When it is hungry and finds nothing to eat, it rolls itself in red earth so as to appear bloody, throws itself upon the ground, and holds its breath so that it does not breathe. Birds, seeing it motionless and seemingly bloody, with its tongue thrust from its mouth, think it dead and descend to perch upon it. Then it seizes and devours them.

The devil bears this figure. [Col. 0059B] For to all who live according to the flesh he feigns himself dead, until he has them within his throat and punishes them. But to spiritual persons living in the faith which works through love, he is truly dead and reduced to nothing. Those, however, who wish to perform his works die, as the Apostle says: “Knowing this: that if you live according to the flesh, you shall die; but if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you shall live” (Rom. VIII). And David says: “They shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall be portions for foxes” (Ps. LXII). And the Lord says of Herod: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke XIII); and in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards” (Cant. II).

## Chapter VI. On the *monoceros*, or unicorn

There is an animal called the *monoceros*. In Greek, μονόκερως (*monokerōs*) means “one-horned”; in Latin it is called *unicornis*, because it has one horn in the middle of its head. The *Physiologus* says that this unicorn has the nature of being a small animal, like a kid, with one very sharp horn on its head. No hunter can either overcome, outstrip, or capture it by force; but they capture it only by this contrivance and deceit. They bring a beautiful virgin maiden to the place where it dwells and leave her there alone. When it sees her, she opens her bosom; at this sight, laying aside all ferocity, it places its head in her lap. Thus, while sleeping, it is caught by those lying in wait and brought to the king’s palace.

So too the Lord Jesus Christ, the spiritual unicorn, descending into [Col. 0059D] the womb of the Virgin, was taken by the Jews in the flesh received from her and condemned to death on the cross. Of him David says: “And the beloved one, like the son of unicorns” (Ps. XXVIII); and elsewhere: “My horn shall be exalted like that of a unicorn” (Ps. CXI); and Zechariah: “He hath raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant” (Luke I). Since this animal has one horn in its head, it signifies what the Saviour said: “I and the Father are one” (John X). For the head of Christ is God (II Cor. XI). Since it is said to be most fierce, this signifies that neither principalities, nor powers, nor thrones, nor dominations can understand God as he is. Since it is said to be small, this refers to his Incarnation and humility, as he himself says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI).

[Col. 0060A] Yet he is so fierce that the most subtle devil could not understand or investigate the mystery of his Incarnation; but by the Father’s will alone he descended into the Virgin’s womb, “and the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). The unicorn is like a kid because, according to the Apostle, the Saviour was made “in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might condemn sin concerning sin” (Rom. VIII).

## Chapter VII. On the *hydrus* and the hydra

There is an animal in the river Nile called the *hydrus*, a water-serpent—that is, one living in water. For the Greeks call water ὕδωρ (*hydōr*). Hence the *hydrus* is a water-serpent; from its bite people swell, a disease which they call *boa* [the printed reading *fiboam* is uncertain], because it is cured by cow dung. According to the poets, the hydra is a dragon with many [Col. 0060B] heads, such as was in the Lernaean marsh in Arcadia, which Hercules wished to kill; when one head was cut off, three heads arose. But this is fabulous. For it is established that the many-headed thing called hydra was a place vomiting forth waters that devastated a neighbouring city; when one channel was closed, many burst forth. Seeing this, Hercules burned the places themselves with fire and closed the channels.

But this aforementioned *hydrus* is an enemy of the crocodile and has this nature and habit: when it comes and sees the crocodile sleeping on the shore, it goes and rolls itself in mud so that it may more easily slip into the crocodile’s jaws. The crocodile suddenly swallows it alive; but the *hydrus*, tearing open all its entrails, comes out not only alive but unharmed. Thus death and hell bear the figure of the crocodile, [Col. 0060C] whose enemy is our Lord Jesus Christ. For, assuming human flesh, he descended into hell and, breaking open all its entrails, brought forth those whom it unjustly held in death. For, rising from the dead, he put death itself to death and taunts it through the prophet, saying: “O death, I shall be thy death; I shall be thy bite, O hell” (Hos. XV), because at that time the bodies of many saints also arose with Christ (Matt. XVII, 27).

## Chapter VIII. On the nature of the crocodile

The crocodile is named from its saffron colour. It is born in the river Nile, a four-footed animal living on land and in water, commonly twenty cubits in length and armed with enormous teeth and claws. Its skin is said to be of such hardness that, although struck upon the back by blows of stones, it is not harmed at all. It rests in water by night and on land by day. If it ever finds a human being, it eats him, if it can overcome him, and afterwards always weeps for him. Alone among all animals, it moves the upper part of its mouth but keeps the lower part unmoved. Its dung becomes a cosmetic; old and wrinkled women anoint their faces with it and become beautiful until running sweat washes their faces.
