It is the figure of hypocrites, or of the lustful and avaricious. For though they are inflated by the wind of pride, stained by the corruption of lust, and darkened by the disease of avarice, nevertheless they display themselves before all people, advancing rigidly and as though most holy in the sanctifications of the law. It rests in water by night and on land by day, because although hypocrites [Col. 0061A] live lustfully, they delight in being called holy and just. Conscious in heart of their own wickedness, they lament, though by practice and habit they are continually drawn back to deeds already committed. It moves the upper part of its mouth because such persons show others, in word, the examples from the lives of the holy Fathers and the teaching of their words, yet display in themselves not even the least of what they say. From its dung a cosmetic is made because wicked people are often praised by the ignorant for evil perpetrated and exalted by this world’s favour. But when the strict Judge advances his wrath to strike their evil deeds, then all that splendour of praise vanishes like smoke.

## Chapter IX. On the nature of the beaver

There is an animal called the beaver, or *fiber*, an animal of very keen intelligence and great gentleness, whose testicles are medicinally useful for various ailments and the treatment of diverse diseases. The *Physiologus*, describing its nature, relates that when it has been tracked and pursued, and greatly fears being taken by hunters, it looks back at them, bites off its own testicles, and throws them before them as it flees. The hunter comes, gathers them, and pursues it no farther, but turns back. But if it happens that another hunter finds it, when it sees that it cannot escape, it rises up and shows the hunter that its genitals have been torn out. Seeing this, the hunter leaves it.

So too one who wishes to live chastely according to God’s command cuts off from himself all vices and casts every indecent act in the devil’s face. Then, seeing him without the testicles of vices, the devil departs from [Col. 0061C] him in confusion. Thus, without doubt, all who wish to live chastely must cut off from themselves every vice of heart and body, throw them in the devil’s face, and live in Christ. Let the servant of God therefore have nothing in common with the devil, so that he may safely say with the Lord: “The prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (John XIV). Hence the Apostle says: “Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute is due; tax to whom tax; honour to whom honour” (Rom. XIII). First of all, let us render to the devil what is his, renouncing him and all his works; then, having been converted to God from the whole heart, let us render him honour as to our Father. With his help let us shake off from ourselves the tax and tribute of the devil, that we may gain [Col. 0061D] spiritual fruits and charity in good works, in almsgiving, in visiting the sick, in comforting the poor, in the praises of God, and in continual prayers. Beavers are so called from castration (*castrando*); they are also *fibers*, and are called Pontic dogs.

## Chapter X. On the hyena, concerning which verses are commonly circulated

For this reason he calls the night by the name “hyena”:

> It snatches the summoned one and tears him with a savage wound.

The hyena is an animal said to dwell in the tombs of the dead and devour their bodies. Its nature is that it is sometimes male and sometimes female, and for this reason it is an unclean animal. Julius Solinus also relates that it goes around houses at night and utters certain words, so that those within the house suppose it to be a human being because it speaks like a human; when they go out, they are suddenly devoured by it.

The children of Israel are likened to this beast: at first they served the living God, but afterwards, given over to riches and luxury, they worshipped idols. For this reason the prophet compared the Synagogue to an unclean animal, saying: “My inheritance has become to me like a hyena’s den” [the Vulgate reads: “like a lion in the forest”] (Jer. XII). Therefore, whoever among us serve luxury and avarice are compared to this beast, since they are neither male nor female—that is, neither fully faithful nor faithless—but undoubtedly are those of whom the Apostle James says: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (Jas. I), and of whom the Lord says: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI).

This beast has in its eyes a stone called *hyaenium*, which, if someone holds it beneath his tongue, is believed to enable him to foretell the future. Yet Julius Solinus relates of this stone that it is found in the stomachs of hyena cubs and that, if anyone’s tongue is touched by it, he is said to prophesy.

## Chapter XI. On the wild ass

There is an animal called the wild ass (*onager*), that is, an untamed or unbroken ass roaming in the wilderness. For ὄνος (*onos*) means “ass,” male or female; and ἄγριος (*agrios*), “wild,” “untamed,” or “fierce.” Individual males rule over herds of females. When males are born, the males become jealous and bite off their testicles; mothers, guarding against this, hide them in secret places.

The *Physiologus* says of the wild ass that on the eleventh day of the month Phamenoth, that is, March, it brays twelve times at night, [Col. 0062C] and likewise in the day. From this it is known that the equinox has come, and they ascertain the number of hours of day or night by the single braying of the wild ass in each hour. The devil bears its figure: when he knows that night and day are becoming equal—that is, when he sees that the people who walked in darkness are converted to the Lord and made equal to the faith of the righteous, as night is equalized with day—immediately he brays by night and day in every hour, seeking his food. For the wild ass does not bray except when it seeks food for itself, as Job says: “Will the wild ass bray when he has grass?” (Job VI). Likewise the Apostle says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (I Pet. V). Africa has these animals in great size.

## Chapter XII. On apes

[Col. 0062D]

Monkeys are so called in Latin because in them a likeness of human reason is perceived. They are keen observers of the elements: at the new moon they rejoice, and at mid-moon they are sad. There are five kinds of them, of which the cercopitheci have tails. For a cercopithecus is a tailed monkey, which some call *dura*. Sphinxes are shaggy and tame enough to forget their wildness. Cynocephali likewise resemble monkeys, having a long tail and a face very like that of a dog; whence they are so named. Satyrs have a very pleasing face and are restless in their gesticulating movements. Gallitriches differ from the rest in almost their whole appearance: for they have a pointed face, a long beard, and a broad tail. The nature of the monkey is such that, when she bears twin young, she loves one [Col. 0063A] and hates the other. If it should happen that she is pursued by hunters, she clasps before her the one she loves, while she carries on her neck the other whom she hates. But when, walking on two feet, she falls, she unwillingly throws away the one she loves and unwillingly preserves the one she hates.

The devil has this as his figure: he has a head but no tail; and although he is altogether ugly, his hind parts are especially foul and horrible. For the devil had a beginning with the angels in heaven; but because he was a hypocrite and inwardly deceitful, he lost his tail, since in the end he will wholly perish, as the Apostle says: “Whom the Lord Jesus will slay with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. II [printed: XXV]). According to others, *simia* or *simius* is a Greek name. For σίμος (*simos*) means “snub-nosed,” because this beast, with its compressed nostrils, [Col. 0063B] is ugly and foul with wrinkles—although goats too may have a flattened nose. Of it the ancient poet Ennius says:

> “The monkey, that most ugly beast, how like us!”

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Nature of the Goat

There is an animal called the goat (*caper*), because it seeks out rough places. Some derive the name from the cracking of its legs and maintain that wild goats were called *capteae*. The Greeks called these *dorcades*, because they see sharply. Of them the *Physiologus* says that they love high mountains and graze in mountain valleys. For it is a very watchful animal, seeing everything from a great distance extremely well, so that, if it sees men walking in any region, it immediately distinguishes whether they are hunters or not.

Thus too our Lord [Col. 0063C] Jesus Christ loves the high mountains—that is, the prophets, patriarchs, apostles, and all the saints. And, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “Behold, my kinsman comes like a roe, leaping upon the mountains” (Cant. II). This is our Lord Jesus Christ, who feeds in the Church through the works of mercy performed by believers, as he says in his Gospel: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. XXV), together with the other praiseworthy things there enumerated.

The mountain valleys, moreover, signify the Church in its various places, as in the Song of Songs: “Return, my kinsman, and be like a roe or a fawn of deer upon the mountains of the valleys” (Cant. II). Therefore the roe, possessing the keenest vision and looking from afar upon the snares of hunters, signifies [Col. 0063D] our Lord Jesus Christ; for, as Scripture says, “The Lord is a God of knowledge” (1 Sam. II), and elsewhere: “The Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly; but he knows the lofty from afar” (Ps. CXXXVII).

As the most prudent one, he watches over, sees, and governs the creature he created for the honor of his name. Before we fall into the devil’s snare, he protects us by inward foreknowledge; and, lest we be oppressed by the darts of thoughts, he urges and counsels us to seek the heights of the mountains and examine the meanings of the divine utterances, so that there, as in a mirror, we may consider what in ourselves pleases, and what displeases, our Creator. For just as the roe foresees the hunter, so our Lord Jesus Christ, long beforehand foreseeing Judas the traitor, said: “One of [Col. 0064A] you will betray me” (Matt. XXVI); and more plainly: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke XXII).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Nature of Deer

Deer are called ἀπὸ τῶν κεράτων, “from their horns,” and they are said to live for nine hundred years. When they feel themselves failing through illness or old age, they draw serpents from their caves with the breath of their nostrils; having overcome the destructive power of their venom, they are restored by feeding upon them. They shake out arrows lodged in them by eating dittany. They are delighted by the sound of pipes. With their ears raised they hear keenly; when lowered, not at all. Whenever they swim across immense rivers or seas, they place their heads upon the rumps of those going before, succeeding one another, and feel no burden of weight. Their collected tears and bones found in their heart are suitable as a drink for those suffering [Col. 0064B] from palpitations of the heart.

The deer also signifies our Lord Jesus Christ, who, drawing out by the breath of divine wisdom the devil—the enemy of the human race—lurking as it were in a cave among every nation, crushed his head beneath the foot of power; and by the food of the venomous death which he voluntarily underwent renewed our nature, weighed down by the old age of sins. For the Psalmist says to him: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help will come to me” (Ps. CXX). By “mountains” he means the apostles and prophets; by “deer,” faithful people lifting their eyes to the mountains—that is, their prayers to the apostles—from whom help will come to us.

Again, there are two kinds of deer. One, when it finds a serpent hidden in a cave, breathes into it so that it may come out; then, striking the emerging serpent’s neck [Col. 0064C] from one side and the other, it kills and devours it. Afterwards, because of its swelling, it runs to the purest waters and vomits up the poison; but because of this swelling it sheds its hair and casts off its horns. The deer is a figure of penitents, who, repenting, are inwardly constrained by consciousness of their sins. They go to the springs, to the teaching of the Scriptures, and are cast out, because by penitence they separate themselves from the body and blood of Christ until they are received again through a priest’s reconciliation.

Another kind of deer, when it finds a serpent, kills it; and after its victory seeks a mountain where it may find food. So too every saint, when he perceives the devil pouring into himself or others the poisons of evil persuasion, should strive, through the Lord’s power, to kill him and cast him away, and should come to Christ the mountain, where he may seek and find food for the soul.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Ibex

There is an animal called the ibex, having two horns of such strength that, if it is cast down from a high mountain to the depths below, its whole body is supported unharmed by these horns. It signifies learned persons, who are accustomed to temper whatever adversity befalls them by the harmony of the two Testaments, as by a healing blend; and, supported as it were by two horns, they uphold the good deeds they perform through the attestation of the Old Testament and Gospel reading.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Stellio and the Salamander

[Col. 0065A]

There is a reptile which some think to be the salamander and others the *stellio*. It resembles a small lizard of variegated color, concerning which Solomon says: “The *stellio* supports itself with its hands and dwells in the houses of kings” (Prov. XXX). The *Physiologus* says of it that, if by chance it falls from anywhere into a fireplace, furnace, or any conflagration whatever, the fire is immediately extinguished.

Thus the righteous are admirable to all people, as Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were in the furnace of burning fire; and the fire did not touch them at all. But that the righteous can come forth untouched and undefiled from the furnace of fire is more plainly declared by the Apostle Paul when he says: “We suffer tribulation, but are not distressed. We are cast down, but do not perish” (2 Cor. IV). Again: “They stopped the mouths of lions” (Heb. XI). Thus every person who believes in God with his whole faith and perseveres in good works passes through the fire of Gehenna, and its flame does not touch him, concerning which it is written in the prophet Isaiah: “If you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you” (Isa. XLIII).

Again, concerning the same creature: the salamander is so named because it has power against conflagrations, and among all venomous things its force is the greatest. For other creatures strike individuals; this one kills many at once. If it climbs into a tree, it infects all its fruit with poison and kills those who eat fruit from it. If it falls into a well, the force of its venom kills those drinking from it. Resisting conflagrations, it alone of animals extinguishes fires. For it lives amid flames without pain or consumption, [Col. 0065C] and is not only unburned but even puts out the blaze.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Dogs and Their Natures

There are many kinds of dogs. Some track the wild beasts of the forests for capture; others pursue birds; others guard flocks of sheep together with their shepherds against the attacks of wolves; others, as watchmen, guard their masters’ household property vigilantly, lest it be stolen by night. They are also said unable to live without humans. Therefore they are reported to love their masters so greatly that the dogs of a certain king, captured by enemies and held in custody, formed a troop and brought him back from exile through the midst of enemy ranks. And when a man had been killed, while his friends did not know upon whom this crime might be charged, a dog revealed in the midst of the people the murderer and author of that death.

A dog’s tongue, when it licks a wound, heals it. It is said to subsist on very little food. Finally, a puppy tied to the body is commonly a remedy for the entrails of the wounded. Its nature is to return to its vomit and eat it again. When it crosses a river holding meat or some such thing in its mouth, upon seeing its reflection it opens its mouth; and, hoping to obtain another real piece of meat, it loses the very one it holds.

In certain respects preachers bear its figure: by continually admonishing and carrying out what is right, they drive away the devil’s snares, lest he seize and carry off God’s treasure—that is, Christian souls. A dog’s tongue, when it licks [Col. 0066A] a wound, heals it, because the wounds of sins are cleansed in confession made to a priest. A puppy applied to a person likewise heals the entrails, because the hidden things of the heart are often cleansed through the deed or speech of a teacher. A dog is said to live on exceedingly little food because one who presides over others and keeps watch over the pursuit of wisdom ought utterly to avoid gluttony. For Sodom perished through surfeit of bread. Indeed, by no entrance does the enemy take possession of a Christian more swiftly than by greedy appetite.

A dog’s return to its vomit signifies that some, after a confession has been performed, heedlessly return to committing the same crimes. Its leaving meat in the river for the sake of a desired reflection signifies people abandoning even what is their own by right through ambition for an unknown thing. Thus, while they cannot attain what they desire, they uselessly refuse to lose what they have abandoned.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Weasel and the Asp

The Law commands that the weasel not be eaten, because it is an unclean animal (Lev. XI). A weasel (*mustela*) is so called as though it were a “long mouse,” for τέλος (*telos*) means “long” in Greek. Cunning by nature, when it has borne young in the house where it lives, it transfers them from place to place and settles them after changing its dwelling. It also pursues serpents and mice.

There are two kinds of weasel. One is wild and differs in size; the Greeks call these *ictidae*. The other wanders about houses. Some say that they conceive through the ear and give birth through the mouth. Others say, on the contrary, that they receive seed through the mouth and give birth through the ear. [Col. 0066C] They are said to be skilled in medicine, so that, if their young have perhaps been killed, they can restore them alive if they can find them.

Thus some believers freely receive the seed of the divine word, but, becoming disobedient, neglect and disregard what they have heard. Such people are compared not only to the weasel but also to the deaf asp that stops its ears so as not to hear the enchanter’s voice. The *Physiologus* says that the asp has this nature: if someone comes to the cave where it lives and charms it with every incantation in order that it may come out from its hiding places, then, so as not to hear the enchanter’s voice, it puts its head to the ground, presses one ear into the earth, and stops the other with its tail.

Such are the rich people of this [Col. 0066D] world: some press one ear down into their earthly desires, while others, always adding new sins to their former sins, harden their hearts; and so they do not hear the voice of the enchanter, that is, the preacher of God’s word.

Isidore: “Those who say that the weasel conceives through its mouth and gives birth through its ear are mistaken.”

## CHAPTER XIX. On Fire-Bearing Stones

There are fire-bearing stones on a certain mountain in the East, which the Greeks call *chiroboli*, that is, “handfuls.” They are said to be male and female. When separated from one another, no fire is kindled in them. But when by some chance they approach one another, so great a fire is immediately kindled in them that everything around them burns.

Therefore you, people of God who lead the monastic life, separate yourselves far from women; for if you approach them, a harmful fire will immediately be kindled within you, and every good thing that Christ the Lord has bestowed upon you will be consumed. For they are angels of Satan, who continually assail holy men as well as chaste women. You must remember the struggles which holy men underwent, such as Samson and Joseph. Both were indeed tempted by women; one conquered, the other was conquered. Eve too and Susanna were tempted: one was defeated, the other conquered. Therefore do not be secure or trust in your habitual chastity; rather, fortify your hearts with divine commands, so that the deceptive love of women may not frighten you. Their sin has raged from the beginning—that is, from Adam until now—among the children of disobedience [Col. 0067B]; nor let the works of demons set you aflame.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Nature of Wolves

The wolf is called in Greek λύκος (*lykos*), and λύκη (*lykē*) means “morning light,” which is fitting for beasts of prey; thus it is named from rapacity. Hence we call prostitutes *lupae*, “she-wolves,” because they lay waste the possessions of their lovers. Others say wolves are called as though they were *leopedes*, because, as the lion has strength in its feet, so do they. Hence whatever they press beneath their foot does not live. It is a rapacious beast, desirous of blood.

Concerning it country people say that a person loses the power of speech if a wolf sees him first. Hence, when someone suddenly falls silent, it is said, “The wolf is in the story.” Certainly, if it senses that it has been seen first, it lays aside the boldness of its ferocity. Wolves mate no more than twelve days in the whole year. The wolf has strength in its forelegs or shoulders, or in its mouth, but least of all in its loins. The *Physiologus* describes these as deadly animals. It can never bend its neck backward. Sometimes it is said to live on prey, sometimes on earth, and at times on wind.

The she-wolf, moreover, bears its young in no month except May, when there is thunder. Its cunning is so great that it does not seize prey near the place of its young, but far away. If it needs to seek prey by night, it proceeds everywhere to the sheepfold like a gentle dog; and, lest the dogs happen to smell the odor of its breath and awaken the shepherds, it goes against the wind. If a branch or something similar makes a sound by breaking under its foot, it punishes that very foot with a harsh bite. Its eyes shine at night [Col. 0067D] like lamps.

Its nature is such that a person loses the power to cry out if it sees the person before it is seen by him. But, as Julius Solinus relates, who says much concerning the natures of beasts, it carries an amatory tuft or hair at the tip of its tail, which it tears out with its own teeth if it fears it may be caught.

The devil bears its figure, for he continually envies the human race and goes about the churches of the faithful in order to slaughter and destroy their souls. Its being born at the first thunder in the month of May signifies that the devil fell from heaven at the first stirring of pride. Its strength in the front members but not the rear signifies that this same devil was once an angel of light in heaven, but is now an apostate cast down; he is powerful at the first onset, but, if you resist him, he will flee from you. Its eyes shine at night because certain works of the devil seem beautiful and beneficial to blind and foolish people.

When it rears its young, it takes prey only far away, because the devil cherishes them with temporal goods, of whom he is certain that they will suffer eternal punishments in the prisons of Gehenna. But he especially pursues those who are far removed from him by good works, as is read of righteous Job, from whom he took all his possessions and also struck his sons and daughters, so that his heart might depart from the Lord (Job I). Its never turning its head backward without its whole body signifies that the devil is never bent toward the correction of repentance.

But what is a person to do when the wolf has taken away his power to cry out? Whoever lacks the power of calling aloud loses the help of one who stands far off. What then should be done? Let the person cast off his garment; trampling the earth with his feet, let him take two little stones in his hands and strike them together. What follows? The wolf, losing the boldness of its strength, will flee; while the person, safe through his own ingenuity, will be free as at the beginning.

This must be understood spiritually and applied allegorically to the preceding sense. For what can we understand by the wolf except the devil, by the person except the human race, by the garment except sin, and by the stones except the apostles or other saints, or our Lord Jesus Christ himself? For all other saints are called living, adamantine stones by the prophets. Our Lord himself is also called in the Law “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” (1 Pet. II), of whom the prophet says: “I saw a man standing upon an adamantine mountain.”

Before we were redeemed, we were under the enemy’s power and had lost the voice of crying out, because, our sins demanding it, we were not heard by God, nor did we invoke any saint to help us. But after the merciful God bestowed grace on us in his Son, we laid aside in baptism the old man with his deeds and put on the new, who, according to the Apostle, is created according to God in righteousness (Eph. IV). Then we took stones and struck them against one another, because we strike the saints of God, who already reign in heaven, with the speech [Col. 0068D] of our own mouths, that they too may appeal to the Judge’s ears and obtain pardon for our sins, lest Cerberus, rejoicing in our destruction, swallow us up unawares.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Nature of the Viper

The *Physiologus* says of the viper that, when it mates, the male puts his mouth into the female’s mouth; she swallows the seed, bites off the male’s head, and the male immediately dies. Understand, then, what illicit intercourse does. When the young have grown in the womb, they pierce the viper by biting and so emerge, their mother dead. This example is directed against the Pharisees who committed such a deed: “Brood of vipers, who will show you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. III).

For the Pharisees are compared to vipers, serving obscene deeds and desires. For they killed their father Christ and persecuted their mother the Church. The *Physiologus* also says: “There are three harmful kinds of vipers, and three of their natures.”

The first, when it has grown old, has an impediment of the eyes so that it cannot see. But see what it does: it fasts for fifty days and nights until its skin becomes loose; then it goes and seeks a cut and rough rock, passes through it, and so casts off that skin and becomes young. “Narrow is the gate and constricted the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII).

The second viper’s nature is that, when it goes to drink, or to mate with an eel, it first vomits its venom into its cave or pit. Let us imitate its prudence, so that, when we come to drink water—that is, to hear divine words in the Church of God—we may not bring with us dusty and stained desires for worldly things; but, with consciences cleansed through humility and true confession, may enter the Lord’s temple praying and singing psalms in our hearts to the Lord.

The third viper’s nature is this: when it sees a naked person, it fears and flees from him; but if it sees him clothed, it leaps upon him. So let us understand spiritually that, as long as our father was naked in paradise, the devil, the ancient serpent, did not prevail against him. But after he was clothed in a tunic—that is, with the mortality of the body—the serpent leapt upon him.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Sawfish, a Sea Monster

[Col. 0069C]

There is a monster in the sea called the sawfish, having enormous fins. When it sees a sailing ship, it raises its wings and strives to race against the ship for thirty or forty stadia. But when it becomes exhausted, it lowers its wings and at last, drawing them back to itself, stops in weariness; the waves then customarily carry it back into the depths of the sea, to its proper place.

The sea signifies this world. Ships are therefore an example of the righteous, who pass through the storms and tempests of this world without any danger or shipwreck of faith, and conquer its deadly waves—that is, the adverse powers of this age. But the sawfish, which wishes to sail against ships, bears the figure of those who begin with good works but do not remain in them; conquered by greed, drunkenness, luxury, and diverse kinds of vices, they are submerged by the sea’s tossing waves down to hell.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Nature of the Panther

There is an animal called the panther, variegated in color, exceedingly beautiful and very gentle. The *Physiologus* says that it is hostile only to dragons. Therefore, when it has eaten and satisfied itself from every kind of prey, it returns to its cave, lies down, and sleeps for three days. Rising from sleep, it immediately sends forth a roar from on high and, along with the roar, an odor of surpassing sweetness, so that its scent surpasses every spice and perfume. When all beasts, whether far away [Col. 0070A] or near, hear its voice, they gather together and follow its exceeding sweetness. But when the dragon alone hears its voice, terrified by fear, it hides beneath underground caves. There, unable to endure the force of its fragrance, contracted within itself, it becomes stunned and numb, remaining motionless and lifeless as though dead. All the other animals follow it wherever it goes.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, the true panther, drew to himself through his incarnation the entire human race that had been captured by the devil and made liable to death; he rescued it and, “leading captivity captive, gave gifts to men” (Eph. IV). For *panther* is interpreted as “every beast,” as though it caught every animal by its odor. So God, as we have said, seeing the entire human race captured by demons, enslaved to idols, and altogether made the devil’s prey, descended from heaven with the abundant fragrance of his incarnation and rescued us; and we follow the Lord and the Lamb wherever he goes.

Thus the prophecy is fulfilled: “I became,” he says, “a panther [moth] to Ephraim, and like a lion [rottenness] to the house of Judah” (Hos. VII). By this it was signified already then that Ephraim served idols, and that the calling of the Gentiles and of the Jewish people ought to be fulfilled through Christ’s coming.

Because the panther is a variegated animal, it signifies Christ, who is incomprehensible wisdom—wholly simple, good, merciful, firm, stable, and shining with diverse wisdom. And because the panther is a beautiful animal, so is Christ, as David says in the Spirit: “Fair in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV). Again, [Col. 0070C] because it is a gentle animal, as Isaiah says of Christ: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter Zion, because your king comes to you, gentle and saving” (Matt. XXI; Zech. IX; Isa. LXII).

And again, just as the panther, when satisfied, immediately rests and sleeps, so our Lord Jesus Christ, after he had been sated with Jewish mockery, scourges, blows, insults, indignities, thorns, spitting, and finally had been hung on the cross, nailed fast, given gall and vinegar to drink, and pierced by a lance—sated, I say, by these violences of the Jews—Christ slept and rested in the tomb. Descending into hell, he bound there the great dragon, the greatest enemy of the human race, namely the ancient serpent.

That this animal rises on the third day after its satisfaction and sleep, sends out a great roar, and breathes a sweet fragrance from its mouth signifies that our Lord Jesus Christ, rising from the dead on the third day, fulfilled David’s prophecy concerning him: “The Lord awoke as one sleeping, like a mighty man overcome with wine” (Ps. LXXVII). Immediately he cried out so that his voice was heard throughout the whole earth and his words to the ends of the world, saying: “Now rejoice, take courage, and do not fear: I have conquered the world” (John XVI). And again: “Father, those whom you gave me I have kept” (John XVII). “I go to my Father and your Father, my God and your God. I will come again to you and will not leave you orphans” (John XIV). Again, at the end of the Gospel he said: “Behold, I am with you all [Col. 0071A] days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII).

And what can be sweeter or more delightful than the fragrance of our Lord Jesus Christ? It is so sweet that all who are near through faith and works, as well as those still far away, burdened by weakness, hear his voice. Filled and refreshed by the most sweet fragrance of his commandments, we seek him and always follow him, crying with the Prophet: “How sweet are your words to my palate, O Lord—more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. CXVIII). And with the sage in the Song of Songs: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Cant. I). And a little later: “The king has brought me into his chamber; we shall exult and rejoice with him” (ibid.).

Therefore, as soon as it is granted us, we ought—as souls renewed in Christ like young women and coming through baptism to newness of life—to run after the ointments of Christ’s commandments and pass from earthly things to heavenly, so that the king may bring us into his palace, Jerusalem, the city of the Lord of hosts and mountain of all the saints. There let us exult and say: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts” (Ps. XLVII).

The panther is a beast marked all over with small circles, its tawny circles resembling eyes, distinguished by a black or white variety. It bears young only once, and the reason for this is clear. When the young, formed in their mother’s womb, have attained mature strength for birth, they tear the burdened mother with their claws as though she were obstructing their delivery; and she pours out—or rather lets go of—her offspring under the compulsion of pain. Thus, after the mother’s passages and chambers have been damaged, generative seed later introduced does not adhere when received, but rebounds uselessly outside.

Hence Pliny says that animals with sharp claws cannot give birth frequently, for they are injured inwardly by the young moving within them. But Isidore says: “The panther is so called either because it is the friend of all animals except the dragon, which it greatly hates; or because it delights in fellowship with those of its own kind, since whatever it receives it returns in the same likeness.” In Greek πᾶν (*pan*) means “all” in Latin, and θήρα (*thēra*), “wild beast.”

Again, Isidore on spices: “Spices,” he says, “are all fragrant substances which India or Arabia sends, or any other region whatsoever.” The name *aromata*, moreover, seems to have been derived either because, placed upon altars, they appear suitable for divine invocations, or because they are shown to enter and mingle with the air. For what is odor except air drawn in through the nostrils after it has been imbued by a fragrant thing?

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Dragon, the Greatest of Living Creatures

The dragon is the greatest of all serpents, indeed of all creatures upon the earth. The Greeks call it δράκων (*drakōn*), while the Latins call it *draco*. It is often said to be drawn from caves into the air, and the air shines when it is stirred by it. It has a crest, a small mouth, and open breathing passages through which it draws breath and puts forth its tongue. Its power lies not in its teeth but in its tail: it harms by its lash rather than by bite or jaws. It is harmless with respect to venom; but it has no need of venom to kill, because if it binds anyone, it kills him. Even the elephant, despite the unrestrained size of its body, is killed by it. For, lying hidden near the paths by which elephants customarily travel, it binds their legs in the knots of its tail and kills them by suffocation. They are found in Ethiopia and India, where the sun’s very heat produces continual warmth like summer.

The devil is compared to this dragon, for he is a most huge serpent. He is often driven from his cave into the air, and the air shines through him, because from the beginning the devil, exalting himself, transforms himself into an angel of light and deceives fools with the hope of false glory and human joy. He is said to have a crest because he is himself the king of pride. He has venom not in his teeth but in his tongue, because, his powers [or: rights] having been lost, he deceives by lying those whom he draws to himself. He lies hidden near the paths on which elephants walk because the devil always pursues great men. He binds their legs in the knots of his tail and, if he can, ensnares them, because he entangles their road to heaven in knots of sins and kills them by suffocation: whoever dies entangled in the bond of crimes is without doubt condemned to hell.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Nature of Elephants

There is an animal named the elephant. The *Physiologus* says that it has great intelligence and is said to have very little fleshly desire. When it wishes to produce offspring, it goes with its female to the East, as far as a place near paradise. There is there an herb called mandrake, whose fruit the female tastes first; then she leads the male so that, persuaded, he may eat. After both have eaten, they mate with one another, and the female immediately conceives.

When the time to give birth comes, she goes to a great lake, enters it up to her breasts, and there gives birth upon the water. She does this because of the dragon, which lies in wait for her young and for the parents themselves. The male does not leave the female but guards her as she gives birth over the pool of water, to ward off the enemy dragon, as I have said.

These two elephants, male and female, signify Adam and Eve, who were in God’s paradise before transgression, clothed with glory and knowing no evil—neither the desire of lust nor sexual intercourse. But when the woman tasted of the forbidden tree, she gave to her husband, who ate and was deceived. Then they were cast down from paradise into this world, as into a lake of many waters. David indicates that water sometimes signifies the present world because of its various disturbances and pleasures, when he says: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. LXVIII). And elsewhere: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he looked upon me and drew me out of the lake of misery and the mire of filth” (Ps. XXXIX).

When, therefore, they had departed into this lake of misery, Adam knew his wife Eve and begot Cain in the mire of filth. Accordingly our pious and merciful Lord Jesus Christ, descending from the bosom of the Father, took our flesh [Col. 0073A] and drew us out of the lake of misery and the mire of filth; setting our feet upon a rock, he put a new song in our mouth (ibid.), saying: “Thus shall you pray: Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. VI), and so forth. He himself taught us this hymn—he who set our feet upon the rock. “And the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X). “May the Lord of peace sanctify you wholly, so that your spirit and soul and body may be preserved complete and without blame for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. V).

I shall say what the bones and skin of elephants do. Wherever they are burned—in any place or house—their odor immediately drives out every serpent or any venomous animal whatsoever. Thus, finally, do God’s commandments and devout works. For if they are kindled in a person’s heart, they drive out every venomous work of the devil from every part.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Again, on the Nature of Elephants
Again there is an animal which in Greek is called *elephas* [ἐλέφας], from the greatness of its body. Among the Indians it is called *barrus* from its cry; hence its cry is called a *barritus*. Its teeth are ivory; its snout is called a *promuscis*, because with it it gathers food and brings it to its mouth. It is like a nail and is fortified with an ivory barrier. The ancient Romans are thought to have called these “Lucanian oxen”: oxen, because they had seen no animal larger; Lucanian, because Pyrrhus first deployed them against the Romans in battle in Lucania. For this kind of animal is suited to warfare: Persians and Indians, placing wooden towers upon them, fight with missiles as though from a wall. They are remarkably strong in intelligence and memory; they travel in herds, salute people as best they can by a gesture, fear a mouse, and mate facing away from one another.

When they give birth, they do not leave their young in water or woods because of dragons, which are most hostile to them and kill them when they have entwined them. When the time for giving birth comes, the female enters a pond or other water up to her breasts and gives birth there because of the dragon that lies in wait for her. If she gives birth outside the water, or even outside the forest, the dragon immediately snatches and devours her young. The male guards her while she gives birth. They carry their young for two years; they give birth no more than once, and not to several, but only to one. They live for three hundred years. Elephants were formerly born only in Africa and India; now India alone produces them. They never lie down when sleeping; but when they yield to sleep or are wearied by labour, they lean against great trees and, supported by them, sleep. Their hunters or ambushers, carefully observing this, mark the place and the trees, and almost cut through the trees against which they suppose the elephants will lean in accordance with their habit. The trees fall, and the elephants with them are thrown to the ground; and thus they are captured.

When the time comes for their procreation, when they must join together to produce offspring, the female finds mandrake for herself and eats it first; afterwards she gives her male the fruit of the mandrake. Thus she entices the male to eat, and they mate; and immediately the female conceives. These two elephants, male and female, signify Adam and Eve, who were in Paradise, knowing and experiencing no evil, no desire of concupiscence, nor the embrace of intercourse. But when the woman tasted of the forbidden tree, seduced her husband, and he ate, they went out of Paradise as exiles and wretches into this world, as into a pool of many waters, a valley of tears, and a place of misery.

If the bones and hide of an elephant are burned anywhere, their smell drives serpents from the place; and, if any harmful poisons are present, venomous creeping things do not approach it. So too the commandments of God purify the person, and that person’s heart, who keeps and observes them within; and no suggestion of the enemy prevails there to find an entrance.

Isidore: “Mandrake is so called because it has *mala*, that is, sweet-smelling fruits the size of hazelnuts.” Hence the Latins also call it the “apple of the earth” (*malum terrae*). Poets call it *anthropomorphon*, because it has a root imitating the shape of a human being. Its bark, mixed with wine, is given to drink to persons whose body must be cut for treatment, so that, put to sleep, they may not feel pain. There are two kinds of it: the female, with leaves like lettuce and bearing fruits resembling plums; and the male, with leaves like beet.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Nature of the Pelican

The pelican is an Egyptian bird, dwelling in the river Nile. Two kinds of pelican are reported: one lives in the water, and its food is poisonous animals—namely lizards, serpents, crocodiles, and onocrotali, that is, birds with a long neck and beak which, when drinking, imitate an ass’s braying and farting.

The *Physiologus* relates of the pelican that it loves its children excessively. For when it has produced chicks and they begin to grow, they strike their parents in the face. The parents, angered by this, strike them back and kill them. But on the third day after their death, the mother, out of compassion, wounds herself with her beak in the rib, side, or breast, pours her blood over her chicks, and thus raises them from death to life.

This bird signifies the Lord speaking through the prophet Isaiah: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” [Isa. 1]. Almighty God, the Father of all creation, made us when we did not exist, that we might serve him. Yet we struck him in the face, because, abandoning and despising both him and the commandments of life, we rejected him. Nevertheless, for our sake he gave up his Son; and when the side of the Son was pierced on the cross by the soldier’s lance, blood and water immediately came forth for our salvation and redemption. For water is the grace of baptism, and his blood is the cup of the New and eternal Testament, which, holding it in his holy hands, he blessed while giving thanks to God the Father, and gave us to drink for the remission of our sins.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Lizard, Stellion, and Lacerta

The lizard is a kind of creeping animal, so called because it has, as it were, muscles and arms. There are several kinds of lizards, such as the *botrax*, salamander, *saura*, and stellion. The stellion receives its name from its colour, for its back is marked with shining spots like stars.

There is a winged animal called the *lacerta*, bright in both eyes like the sun. The *Physiologus* says of it that, when it has grown old, its sight becomes so obstructed that it cannot see even the light of the sun. But its nature provides this remedy: it seeks out a wall facing east and goes out through a narrow opening with its eyes open, and is thus renewed.

And you, O man, who are clothed in the old garment: when the eyes of your heart grow dim, seek a place facing east—that is, turn yourself toward Christ our Lord, the Sun of righteousness, whose name is called the East [Zech. 3]—so that he may rise in your heart through the Holy Spirit and show you the light of his mercy, he who enlightens every person coming into this world [John 1].

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Nature of the Ant

[Col. 0075B] Solomon says thus concerning the ant: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her: though weaker in strength, she stores up much grain during the summer” [Prov. 6].

The *Physiologus* says that the ant possesses three virtues. Its first virtue is this: when ants leave their hole, they walk in order and seek grains of every kind of seed. When they find them, they seize each grain with their mouths and carry it into their hole. Other ants, however, having no grains in their mouths but coming empty-handed to meet those carrying food in their mouths, do not say to them, “Give us some of your provisions.” Rather, they go on, following their tracks, and take grain as the others did, and carry it to their own hole.

These things are said concerning irrational animals and weak creeping things: they act so prudently that none of them remains foolish, but all are found—or become—clever and wise. How much more ought those five rational virgins, who became foolish through their negligence, to have imitated the five wise ones, and likewise to have taken oil into their vessels from the source from which those others took it, rather than, through idleness and their foolish hope, asking the wise ones, “Give us some of your oil” [Matt. 25]. O what foolish folly! For if they could not understand for themselves that they should seek it from the same place from which the others sought it, they ought at least to have imitated the ants’ diligence. But while they hoped for oil from others’ vessels, the bridegroom arrived, and the foolish women remained outside with their lamps extinguished.

The ant stores grains in its hole so that, moistened by dampness, they may not germinate, and so that it may not perish of hunger in winter. And you, O man of God, divide the Scripture of the Old Testament into two parts: according to history and according to spiritual understanding. Divide truth from figure; separate bodily things from spiritual, and spiritual things from bodily. Pass beyond the letter that kills to the spirit that gives life, lest, when the letter germinates on the day of winter—that is, on the day of judgment—you perish from hunger. For the Apostle says: “The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal” [Rom. 7]. “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” [2 Cor. 3]. And elsewhere: “These things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” [1 Cor. 10].

For the Jews, following the letter and despising spiritual understanding, became despisers of the prophets and killers of their own Lord; and therefore they still perish from hunger, because, occupied with empty chaff, they lost the wheat. You therefore, O man of God, peel the branches and remove their bark, so that your sheep may produce offspring that are pure and spiritual, not carnal and vicious. All these things are intelligible to spiritual believers, but unintelligible to unbelievers.

At harvest time, among the crops, the ant knows by smell whether an ear contains barley or wheat. If it is barley, it passes to another ear and smells it; when it has detected which ear is wheat, it climbs up into the ear, takes out a grain, sets it down, and carries it to its chamber. Barley, however, is food for brute animals; hence it signifies heretics, who, feeding human souls with perverse food, kill them. Flee therefore, O Christian—flee Sabellius, Donatus, and Photinus, from whom serpent offspring came forth as from a dragon’s womb. The teachings of these men are false and therefore hostile to truth.

**Etymology.** The ant is so called as though “carrying crumbs of spelt” (*ferens micas farris*). Its diligence is great. It provides for the future and prepares in summer what it will eat in winter. At harvest it chooses wheat, but does not touch barley. When rain falls upon its grain, it throws the whole store out. It is also said that in Ethiopia there are ants as large as dogs, which dig golden sands from the ground with their feet and guard them so that no one may take them away; and they pursue those who take them to their death.

But those who wish to snatch gold from them take mares with their foals and afflict the mares with hunger for three days. Then they tie the foals at the bank of the water which runs between them and the ants, and drive the mares across that water with panniers placed upon their backs. When the mares see green grass beyond the river, they graze in the fields on the far side. The ants, seeing the chests and panniers upon their backs, carry golden sand into them, wishing to store it there. At evening, after the mares have eaten their fill and are laden with gold, they hear their foals neighing from hunger; and so they return to them with much gold.

There is also another animal called the ant-lion, which is either the lion of ants or at once ant and lion. It is a small animal, so hostile to ants that it hides itself in dust and kills ants carrying grain. It is therefore called lion and ant because, as the lion is stronger than other animals, so this creature is stronger than other ants.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Nature of the Asp

According to Isidore, the asp is so called because it injects and spreads poison with its bite. For *as*, as he holds—or rather *ios* [ἰός] in Greek—means poison. It has diverse genera and species and unequal effects in causing harm. Some prefer to say it is so named from defending, for *aspizō* [ἀσπίζω] means “I defend,” since *aspis* [ἀσπίς] also means a shield.

It is said that when the asp begins to suffer an enchanter, who summons it out of its cave by certain spells, it does not wish to come out. It presses one ear to the ground and stops and covers the other with its tail; thus, not hearing those magical sounds, it does not come out to the enchanter.

The dipsas is a kind of asp, called in Latin *scythale*, because one whom it has bitten dies of thirst. The hypnale also is a kind of asp, so called because it kills by sleep; Cleopatra applied this one to herself and was thus released by a death like sleep. The haemorrhois too is called an asp because a person bitten by it sweats blood, so that, with the veins dissolved, all that constitutes life pours out through the blood. For blood is called *haima* [αἷμα] in Greek. The praester is an asp which runs with open, steaming mouth; the poet mentions it thus:

> “The greedy praester, stretching wide its smoking jaws.”  
> —Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book IX, verse 713.

The person it strikes is swollen and killed by monstrous distension, for putrefaction follows the swelling. The seps, a corrupting serpent, is likewise of the race of asps. If it bites a person, it immediately consumes that person, so that the whole body melts in the serpent’s mouth.

In the nature of asps there is something to imitate and something to avoid. We should imitate them by closing the inward ears against the Sirens—that is, against the enticements of pleasures and deceitful flatteries—so that, according to the Lord’s word, we may be wise as serpents. We should avoid them lest the ancient serpent strike us, like the dipsas, with the thirst of avarice; overwhelm us, like the hypnale, with the sleep of sloth; stain us, like the haemorrhois, with the bloodiness of anger; or puff us up, like the praester, with the gaping of ambition or the poison of another sin.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Charadrius, or Charadrus, a Sea-Bird

It is given this distinct heading because Theodore Gaza calls it *charadrius*; Suidas, *charadrus*, saying that it is a large, voracious sea-bird. Those who look at it are freed from jaundice, perhaps the same bird which Pliny calls the *icterus* bird, so named from its effect. But let us hear the author.

There is a bird called the charadrius. It is written in Deuteronomy that it must not be eaten [Deut. 14]. The *Physiologus* says that it is entirely white, having no black part in itself, and that its internal dung cures dimness of the eyes. Whoever is held by illness is commonly recognized through this bird as one who will live or die. For if the sickness is fatal, the charadrius immediately turns its face away from that person, and there is no doubt that the person will die. But if the person is to recover and be healed, the charadrius gazes intently at him; approaching, it lays its mouth upon the person’s mouth, and by its breath draws all the person’s illness into itself. Then, flying in the air toward the sun, it burns and disperses the illness; the sick person is healed and becomes sound.

So too Christ testified concerning himself: “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” [John 14], because “he committed no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” [1 Pet. 2]. But coming to the infirmity of the Jewish people, he turned himself away from it and turned his face toward the nations; taking away our iniquities and bearing our sins, he was lifted up on the cross. Ascending on high, he led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings. “He came into his own, and his own did not receive him; but to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” [John 1].

If anyone now wonders why unclean animals are referred to as signs of a good thing, such as the cleansing of conscience and instruction—serpent, dragon, lion, eagle, and the like—let that person know that they sometimes signify Christ’s strength and kingship, but at other times the rapacity of the devil, and thus can be applied in various ways.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Nature of the Sirens

Isaiah says of Babylon: “Sirens shall dwell in its shrines of pleasure” [Isa. 13]. Sirens are creatures deadly to those who yield to them. As the *Physiologus* describes them, from above down to the navel they have the form of a woman, while their lower part down to the feet has the shape of a fish. They sing a wondrously sweet melody, so that by the sweetness of their voice they entice sailors from afar, draw them to themselves, delight their ears with the excessive sweetness of their song, and, lulling them and their senses, turn them to sleep. Then, when they see them sunk in the deepest sleep, they attack them and tear their flesh; thus by sweet-sounding voices they deceive and kill ignorant and foolish people.

So too those who delight in the pleasures of this age, its pomp and theatrical entertainments, dissipated by tragedies and comedies, become the adversary’s prey as if lulled by heavy sleep. They imagine that there were three Sirens, partly maidens and partly fishes, having scales and a fish’s tail. One sang with her voice, another with pipes, the third with a lyre; by the allurements of their songs they caused unsuspecting people sailing through those places to be endangered by shipwreck. But in truth they were prostitutes who reduced travellers to poverty; therefore they were said to inflict shipwrecks upon them. They are said to have had scales and to have lived amid waves because the waves created Venus.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Again, on the Onocentaur

The same prophet says: “The onocentaur and the hairy one shall cry one to another” [Isa. 34]. As we have also said above, the *Physiologus* declares that the onocentaur consists of two natures: its upper part is like a centaur—that is, a horse-man—while the limbs of its lower part are those of an onager, that is, a wild ass. It resembles foolish and double-tongued people: human in appearance but misshapen in character. The Apostle says: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” [2 Tim. 3]. Hence in the Psalm: “Man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared to foolish beasts and became like them” [Ps. 48].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Power of the Diamond

The *Physiologus* says that there is a stone called the diamond (*adamas*), found on a certain mountain in the East. Yet it must be sought at night, not by day, because it shines at night and reveals where it is; by day it does not shine because the sun dulls its light. Neither iron, nor fire, nor any other stone can prevail against the hardness of this stone. The prophet says of it: “I have made your face like a diamond and like flint” [Ezek. 3]. Since a creature cannot prevail against the Creator, the diamond is Christ.

From that diamond all the saints are called diamond stones by the prophet, just as Christians are called and named from Christ’s name. Therefore the eastern mountain, in which the *Physiologus* says the diamond is found, is Christ: as he is known in the Father, so the Father is in the Son. For he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” [John 4]; and again: “Whoever sees me sees the Father” [ibid.].

That the stone is not found by day signifies that Christ concealed his descent from the heavenly virtues, dominions, and powers, who stand as God’s luminaries; yet they never knew the mystery of his descent and incarnation which he was to accomplish on earth. Finally, after all his wonders had passed—those which he performed for the redemption of humankind—when he had ascended into heaven, bringing there a complete and perfect human being, even the hosts of the heavenly city, seeing him, said: “Who is this King of glory?” [Ps. 23]. “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” [Isa. 63]. As if to say: Who is this who ascends from blood, and whose garment’s redness comes from flesh?

And that stone is found in the night, because he descended into the darkness of this heaven and enlightened all this race which sat in darkness and in the region of the shadow of death. Thus David the prophet, in the person of the whole human race: “For you light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” [Ps. 17]. Therefore the Lord came and, taking to himself the lamp extinguished by the devil—that is, soul and body—enlightened it with the splendour of his grace, giving it life and restoring it. More plainly, the Apostle speaks of the sacrament of so wonderful a mystery: “Indeed, manifestly great is the mystery of godliness: which was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, believed in the world, and taken up in glory” [1 Tim. 3].

What the *Physiologus* says of this stone, that iron cannot prevail against it, means that death will not rule over him: for he destroyed and trampled down death, as the Apostle testifies, saying: “Death has been conquered in victory. Where, O death, is your contention [victory]? Where, O death, is your sting [goad]?” [1 Cor. 15]. Nor can fire harm him—that is, the devil, who with his fiery darts sets ablaze the whole earth and its cities, that is, the lustful, drunken, and angry, of whom Isaiah says: “Your land is desolate; your cities are set ablaze with fire” [Isa. 1]. For the Lord Jesus Christ will slay him with the spirit of his mouth [2 Thess. 2]. Nor did another stone harm him—that is, no person whatsoever, nor any creature, prevailed against him. “For all things were made through him, because without him nothing was made” [John 1].

The diamond is small and unattractive, having an iron-coloured hue and crystalline brilliance. It is found in the shape of a hazelnut kernel and yields to no material—not to iron, not to fire—nor does it ever grow warm. Hence, in Greek interpretation, its name derives from its unconquerable power. Yet although invincible by iron and contemptuous of fire, it is softened by fresh, warm goat’s blood and is then broken by many blows of iron. Engravers use its fragments for marking and piercing gems. It is hostile to the magnet stone, so much so that, when it is placed near it, it does not allow iron to be drawn toward the magnet (*magnetem*; variant *magneti*). But if the diamond is removed, the magnet then seizes, grasps, and carries off the iron. It is also said, like amber, to drive away poisons, banish groundless fears, and resist magical arts. There are six kinds of it; since they contribute little to our present purpose, I pass them over.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Shell, or Pearl-Bearing Shell

Among pearl-bearing shells—that is, shells which produce pearls, called in Latin *uniones* and commonly *perlae*—there is a certain kind called by some *marmaetholion* and by the Latins the Sabaean shell, because it is hollow and round. It is divided into two parts, so that it opens itself when it wishes and closes itself when it wishes. This shell rises from the bottom of the sea and nourishes its flesh within itself with morning dew. When it rises from its place above the sea, it opens its mouth and receives within itself the dew of heaven; the sun’s rays shine around it, and thus within it is formed a pearl, precious and very bright, having indeed been conceived from heavenly dew and made radiant by the sun’s ray.

This stone called *conchus* signifies holy Mary, of whom the prophet Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” [Isa. 2]; and again: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” [Isa. 7]. The rod is said to be the holy Virgin Mary; the flower born from holy Mary is our Lord Jesus Christ. For as the shell, in which the stone *conchus* is born, rises from the sea, so holy Mary rose from her father’s house to the temple of God and there received heavenly dew. These are the words spoken to her by the angel Gabriel: “The Spirit of the Lord shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore the holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God” [Luke 1]. Behold, these words are that heavenly dew.

Likewise, long before, the patriarch Isaac, blessing his son and signifying that Christ would be born from his seed, said to him: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth” [Gen. 27], signifying the chaste and untouched Virgin Mary. The morning dew which it receives describes the time of morning prayer. The shell’s opening of its mouth signifies the occasion when Mary said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” [Luke 1]. At once she received the Holy Spirit within herself, and the power of the Most High, like the sun of righteousness, made her bright. What was born from her is life and light: “The true light came, which enlightens every person coming into this world” [John 1]. Of this Paul also says: “Who, being the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” [Heb. 1], etc.; and elsewhere: “In whom it pleased all the fullness of divinity to dwell” [Col. 1].

Of this pearl it is read in the Gospel that “the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. Having found one precious pearl, he sold all his substance and possessed this pearl” [Matt. 13]. This merchant is certainly the choir of the apostles. For all the apostles are called one merchant because of the unity of faith. “For there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, neither Scythian nor barbarian, neither male nor female; for we are all one in Christ Jesus” [Col. 3].

Thus the same good and wise merchant—that is, the holy choir of apostles—seeks good pearls, namely the Law and the Prophets; or every believing soul seeks God. The just man also seeks good pearls, namely apostles, prophets, and patriarchs, through whom he may arrive at that true and precious pearl. These are the holy stones that roll upon the earth. When that good merchant finds the precious and good pearl, namely our Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, he purchases it by selling all his possessions: that is, by disdaining and rejecting not only the substance of this life but also wife, children, every carnal kinship, and moreover his own body and soul, as Truth says: “Whoever loses his soul for my sake shall find it” [Matt. 10].

Seeing all this, the choir of apostles accepts neither gold nor silver, as blessed Peter said to the lame man asking alms: “Silver and gold I do not have; but what I have I give you: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Nazarene, arise and walk” [Acts 3]. And Paul says: “Whatever things were gains to me, these I have considered losses for Christ, because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ” [Phil. 3]. Therefore, whoever has confidently despised all possessions, wife, children, and all kinship, and even body and soul, in order to acquire the one pearl—if that person has placed the surest trust in it and believes that the one pearl can be acquired—will possess resources of wealth far greater and better, more excellent honour, and moreover a crown of glory. All these things are possessed by that merchant, the choir of apostles, through the one precious stone, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true pearl, our way, truth, and life [John 14].

Finally, hear him himself saying in the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you authority over unclean spirits, to tread upon all serpents and scorpions and over all diabolical power, and to heal every sickness and infirmity” [Luke 10]. And again: “Go and preach, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near; heal the sick, cleanse lepers, give light to the blind, raise the dead, cast out demons” [Matt. 10].

See now how beyond valuation this pearl is to the holy martyrs, who performed wonders not only while they were in this life, but even after their departure from it. For now we see how unclean spirits in possessed bodies are tortured and tormented by their power and authority, beaten with invisible whips until they are cast out and driven away from people. The demons themselves cry out—as we hear them—shouting and begging the martyrs to cease tormenting them. In their many and varied forms, some crying out, others roaring, others hissing like serpents, they are driven from the possessed bodies of people by the virtues of apostles and holy people, given to them by the Lord according to their merits.

They received from that precious stone the honour surpassing and exceeding every earthly honour, for whose sake they abandoned all their goods so that they might possess that heavenly treasure. They say to the Saviour: “Behold, we have left wives and children and all possessions for your sake. What will you do for us in your kingdom?” [Matt. 19]. And he says to them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: when the Son of Man sits upon the seat of his majesty to judge the world, you too shall sit upon twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” [ibid.]. Hence the Apostle Paul says with full confidence: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? And this world shall be judged by us” [1 Cor. 6].

The choir of apostles was rewarded with such glory and honour that, while still placed in this world, Paul, that lawful athlete of Christ, foresaw in heaven the crown of his righteousness. Rejoicing, he says: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will give to me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love the appearing of his kingdom” [2 Tim. 4]. Such a crown does the choir of good apostles deserve from Christ; such a recompense will the apostles receive for perishable things.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Aspidochelone, an Aquatic Monster Having the Form Partly of an Asp and Partly of a Tortoise

For *chelone* [χελώνη] is a tortoise, a sea-monster; it will also be mentioned in the following work.

There is a monster in the sea called in Greek *aspidochelone* [ἀσπιδοχελώνη], and in Latin the asp-tortoise. It is a great sea-creature, having upon its skin something like a mound of sand or gravel and often living near the seashore. In the middle of the sea it raises its back above the waves, so that sailors see it as nothing other than an island—especially when they see that the entire place is covered with sand like every seashore. Thinking it an island, they bring their ship alongside it; disembarking, they drive stakes there and tie up their ship. Then, in order to cook food for themselves after their labour, they make hearths and fires upon the sand as though upon land.

But when it feels the heat of the fire, it suddenly plunges into the water and draws the ship with it into the sea’s depths. Thus suffer all unbelievers and all who are ignorant of the devil’s wiles: placing their hope in him and binding themselves to his works, they are submerged with him in the hell of burning fire. This is his cunning.

The second nature of this monster is as follows. When it is hungry, it opens its mouth and exhales from it a certain sweet-smelling scent. As soon as the smaller fish perceive it, they gather inside its mouth. But when its mouth has been filled with diverse small fish, it suddenly closes its mouth and swallows them. Thus suffer all who are of little faith. Enticed by pleasures and seductions, like certain diabolical fragrances, they are suddenly swallowed by him like tiny fishes. The larger fish keep themselves from it and do not approach it. Likewise, those who always have Christ in their mind are great before him; if they are perfect, they recognize the devil’s manifold wiles, guard themselves from him, and resist more strongly; but he flees from them. Those who are doubtful and of little faith, however, are deceived when they follow the devil’s pleasures and luxuries, as Scripture says: “They delight in ointment and diverse perfumes” [Prov. 27]; and so the soul is broken by ruin.

The whale is so called from the immensity of its body. These kinds of monsters have enormous bodies, equal to mountains, so that ships are brought alongside them as if alongside an island. Such was the creature that received Jonah, whose belly was so vast that it was thought to be hell, as Jonah the prophet himself says: “From the belly of hell I cried, and you heard my voice” [Jonah 2].

## BOOK THREE

Since in this book very many of the same matters as those discussed above are repeated, I have not wished to repeat them, but to indicate where they have been discussed. (G)

[Col. 0083]

[Col. 0083B] For the derivation of *bestia* (“beast”) and what beasts are, see Book II, in the prologue.

On the lion and its natures, Book II, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER I. On the Tiger

The tiger is named from its swift flight; for the Persians and Medes call an arrow by that name. It is a beast marked by varied spots, marvellous in strength and speed. The River Tigris is named after it, because that river is the swiftest of all rivers. Hyrcania produces these beasts in particular.

When the tiger finds the empty den of its stolen offspring, it immediately follows the tracks of the thief. Although he rides a swift horse, seeing nevertheless that the beast’s speed may overtake him and that no means of escape can assist him, he softens the tiger by this trick: when he sees that she is near, he throws down a sphere of glass, that is, a round mirror. She is deceived by her own reflection and takes it for her offspring; she checks her rush, wishing to gather up her young. Again, when she discovers the empty image, she throws herself forward with all her strength to seize the horseman and presses hard upon the swiftly fleeing man with the goad of anger. Again he delays her as she approaches by throwing down a sphere. Yet the mother’s diligence and memory of the trick do not fail: she turns the empty image about and crouches down as though to suckle her young. Thus, deceived by devotion to her offspring, she loses both her vengeance and her child.

## CHAPTER II. On the Pard and the Leopard
The pard is a species of wild beast, variegated and exceedingly swift, and headlong in its thirst for blood. For it rushes by a leap to [Col. 0083D] kill. The leopard is born from the adulterous union of a lioness and a pard, and constitutes a third kind; as Pliny also says in his *Natural History*, the lion mates with the female pard, or the pard with the lioness, and from either coupling degenerate offspring are produced—such as the mule and the hinny, born from different species.

[Col. 0084B] On the panther see Book II, chapter 23. On the antelope or antula, Book II, chapter 2. On the unicorn see Book II, chapter 6.

## CHAPTER III. On the lynx.

It is called lynx because it is counted among the wolf kind: a beast marked on its back with spots like a pard, but resembling a wolf. They say that its urine turns into the hardness of a precious stone, called *lygurius* or *lycurius*, as Pliny and Solinus call it. The lynxes themselves are shown to be aware of this: they cover their discharged liquid with sand as thoroughly as they can, through a certain envy of nature, lest such an excretion pass into human use. Pliny says that lynxes do not have more than one young in a litter.

## CHAPTER IV. On the griffin.

[Col. 0084C] The griffin—or, as Isidore writes, the griffins—is a winged quadruped animal, born in the Hyperborean mountains, resembling a lion in every part of its body, but an eagle in its wings and face, and violently hostile to horses. For it tears living people to pieces and carries them whole to its nest.

On the elephant see Book II, chapter 26. On the beaver see Book II, chapter 9. On the ibis see Book II, chapter 15. On the hyena see Book II, chapter 10.

## CHAPTER V. On the bonasus.

In Asia there is born an animal called the bonasus. It has the head of a bull; the rest of its body is upright; it has a horse’s mane; and its horns are bent back upon themselves in many curves, so that anyone who strikes against them is not [Col. 0084D] wounded. But whatever protection its forehead denies this monster, its belly supplies. For when it takes to flight, it discharges a flood of dung from its swift belly for the length of three *iugera*; its burning quality scorches whatever it touches. Thus, by a harmful discharge, it drives off its pursuers.

[Col. 0085A] On monkeys see Book II, chapter 12. On stags see Book II, chapter 14. On the he-goat see Book II, chapter 13. On the monoceros or unicorn see Book II, chapter 6.

## CHAPTER VI. On the bear.

The bear is said to be so called because it forms its young with its mouth, as though *orsus* (“formed”). For they say that bears produce shapeless offspring, and that a kind of lump of flesh is born which the mother, by licking, shapes into limbs; but this immaturity produces deformed young. Finally, it gives birth on the thirtieth day; whence it comes about that, because gestation is hastened, shapeless offspring are produced. A bear’s head is weak; its greatest strength is in its forelegs and loins, which is why it sometimes stands upright. Nor do bears neglect the art of healing. Indeed, when badly injured in a fight and wounded, [Col. 0085B] they are accustomed to treat themselves by applying to their sores an herb named *floinus*, so that they are healed by its touch alone. A sick bear eats ants. Numidian bears surpass the rest only in fierceness and in deeper shaggy coats; for their reproductive capacity is the same wherever they are born. They do not mate in the same way as other quadrupeds, but, fitted to mutual embraces, they couple as in human unions. Winter arouses their desire for intercourse. The males respectfully keep apart from pregnant females, and, though they occupy the same dens, they are divided by separate sleeping-hollows. Their time of delivery is unusually quick, since on the thirtieth day the womb is released; whence it comes about that hastened pregnancy produces shapeless offspring. They bear very small pieces of flesh, white in colour, [Col. 0085C] without eyes. By licking them they gradually give them shape, and sometimes warm them at their breasts, so that, heated by continual brooding, they may draw animal breath. Meanwhile they take no food.

Indeed, during the first fourteen days the mothers fall into such sleep that they cannot be awakened even by wounds. Thus, when they emerge shortly afterwards from the cavernous mountains in which they hide into the open day, they suffer such an unfamiliarity with the light that you might think them blinded. They lie in wait for hives of bees, especially desiring honeycombs, and pursue nothing more eagerly than honey. When they have tasted mandrake apples, they die; but, lest the evil grow into destruction, they seek out ants and devour them to recover their health. Whenever they fight bulls, they know which parts chiefly weaken them, and attack only the horns and nostrils: [Col. 0085D] the horns, so that their weapons may fail them; the nostrils, so that pain may be inflicted in the most tender spot.

## CHAPTER VII. On the leucrocota.

In India there is born a beast which surpasses all wild animals in speed and is called the leucrocota. It is of an ass’s size, with the haunches of a stag, the breast and legs of a lion, the head of a horse, cloven hoofs, a mouth opening as far as its nostrils, and, in place of teeth, one continuous bone. Such is its form; in voice, however, it imitates the sounds of speaking human beings.

On the crocodile see Book II, chapter 8.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the manticore.

In India there is born an animal called the manticore, having three rows of teeth meeting in alternating succession, [Col. 0086A] a human face, blue-grey eyes, a blood-red colour, a lion’s body, and a tail armed with a stinging spike like a scorpion’s. Its voice is so hissing that it imitates the notes of pipes.
