It craves human flesh most greedily; its feet are so powerful and its leaps so great that neither the widest stretches nor the broadest obstacles can delay it.

## CHAPTER IX. On the tharand.

Ethiopia sends a beast called the tharand: of the size of bulls, with cloven hoofs, the colour of a bear, branching horns, a stag’s head, and deep shaggy hair. They affirm that this tharand changes its appearance through fear and, when it hides itself, becomes like whatever object it has approached—whether that object be white like a stone, green like a shrub, or of any other appearance.

On the fox see Book II, chapter 5.

## CHAPTER X. On the animal called the eale.

[Col. 0086B]

There is a beast called the eale, as large as a horse, with an elephant’s tail, black in colour, the jaws of a boar, and horns of extraordinary length. Its horns are adapted to its command, as though responsive to movement; for they are not stiff, but move as the need of fighting requires. It bends one back and fights with the other, so that, if the point of one is struck by some blow, the other’s edge may take its place.

On the wolf see Book II, chapter 20.

## CHAPTER XI. On the dog and its nature.

The Latin name *canis* seems to have a Greek etymology. For in Greek a dog is called *kynos* [κύων], in Latin *canis*, although some think it is named from the melodiousness of its barking, because it sounds forth in song, whence it is also said to “sing” (*canere*). Nothing, however, is more sagacious than dogs. They have more perception [Col. 0086C] than other animals; for they alone recognize their own names and love their masters. There are many kinds of dogs. Some track wild creatures in the forests for capture. Others guard houses and protect their masters’ property, lest it perhaps be carried away by thieves at night. They even willingly expose themselves to death for their masters; they run after prey with their master; they guard even their master’s dead body and do not abandon it. Finally, it is their nature that they cannot exist apart from human beings.

It is recorded that dogs loved their masters so greatly that, when a king of the Garamantes had been captured by enemies and committed to custody, two hundred dogs, advancing in formation through the midst of the enemy lines, brought him back from exile, [Col. 0086D] fighting against those who resisted. When Jason of Lycia was killed, his dog rejected food and died of hunger. The dog of King Lysimachus threw itself into the flames of its master’s burning pyre and was consumed by the fire along with him. When, in the consulship of Appius Junius and Publius Silius, a master condemned to death was led away, his dog, which could not be driven off, accompanied him to prison. Soon afterward, when the man had been executed, the dog followed him with howling. When, out of pity, the Roman people gave it food, it carried the meal to the dead man’s mouth; finally, when the corpse had been thrown unburied into the Tiber, it swam alongside, trying to support it.

But when a dog finds the track of a hare or stag, comes to a fork in the path, and to a meeting of roads divided into many directions, it goes around the beginning of each separate track and silently reasons with itself, as though uttering a syllogistic argument by the acuteness [Col. 0087A] with which it gathers scent: “Either it turned in this direction, or in that; or it betook itself to this winding path. But it entered neither this nor that; therefore it remains that it went in this direction.” Thus, having rejected falsehood, it arrives at truth.

Often too, by the manifest force of a voice laid against someone, dogs have furnished evidence to convict the accused, so that their mute testimony has often been believed. At Antioch, they relate, a man was killed in a remote quarter of the city at twilight. He had a dog with him. A certain soldier, impelled by desire for plunder, had been the agent of the murder and, still concealed in the dim beginning of day, had withdrawn elsewhere. The body lay unburied; a large crowd of onlookers stood around; and the dog, with mournful cries, [Col. 0087B] bewailed its master’s misfortune. By chance the man who had inflicted the death, such being the cunning of human disposition, eagerly desiring to avoid danger and to make his presence attest his innocence, approached that circle of people standing around and drew near the funeral as though in grief. Then the dog, setting aside for a while the cry of sorrow, took up the weapons of vengeance: it seized and held him and, murmuring as though it were reciting some lamentable song, moved all to tears and supplied proof and demonstration, because it did not release the one man whom it alone had held among many. At last the man was disturbed; and he could not repel so manifest an indication of the deed by alleging hatred, enmity, any injury, or envy, because of the accusation brought by nature itself. Therefore, what was consonant with reason occurred: [Col. 0087C] he suffered punishment, because he could offer no defence.

A dog’s tongue, when it licks a wound, heals it. Its licking is said to be highly medicinal. Indeed, a puppy’s tongue is often the salvation of wounded entrails. Its nature is to return to its vomit and eat it again. And when it has swum across a river holding flesh or something of that kind in its mouth, upon seeing its shadow it opens its mouth; and, hurrying to take another piece of flesh, it loses the very one it holds.

In certain respects preachers have its figure: by always admonishing and practising what is right, they drive away the devil’s snares, lest he take away God’s treasure, the souls of Christians. A dog’s tongue, while licking a wound, heals [Col. 0087D] it, because the wounds of sins, when laid bare in confession, are cleansed by the correction of priests. A dog’s tongue also heals a person’s inward parts, because the secrets of that person’s heart are cleansed by the work and speech of a teacher. The dog is said to be very medicinal because one who is set over others ought to devote himself to the pursuits of wisdom and to avoid excess of food in every way. For Sodom perished through fullness of bread. Finally, in no way does the enemy take possession of a person so quickly as through a voracious appetite. The fact that a dog returns to its vomit shows certain people who, after making confession, carelessly return to the sins they have committed. The fact that it leaves flesh in a river for a desired shadow signifies foolish people who, because of the ambition for an unknown thing, often abandon what is within their own power. Thus it happens that, while they cannot obtain what they desire, they vainly refuse to lose what they have left behind.

[Col. 0088A] Lycisci are said to be dogs born from wolves and dogs when they happen to mate with one another. The Indians customarily tie female dogs in forests so that they may mate with tigers; from these, dogs of the same litter are said to be born exceedingly fierce, so strong that they bring down lions in an embrace.

## CHAPTER XII. On the names, species, and properties of animals in general.

Adam was the first to assign names to all living creatures, giving each one a name, according to the character of the nature it served, from its present constitution. The nations, however, gave each kind of animal names from their own languages. Adam did not impose those names in Latin, Greek, or any barbarian language of the nations, [Col. 0088B] but in that language which before the Flood was one for all and is called Hebrew.

In Latin, living creatures are called *animalia* because they are animated by life and moved by breath. Quadrupeds are so called because they walk on four feet. Although they resemble livestock, they are not under human care, such as stags, fallow deer, wild asses, and so forth. Yet they are not wild beasts, such as lions, nor beasts of burden, such that they can be useful to human purposes. We call that a *pecus* (“beast, livestock”) which lacks human speech and form. More properly, however, the name of livestock is usually applied to animals fit for food, such as sheep and pigs, or provided for human use, such as horses and oxen. There is a difference between *pecora* and *pecudes*. [Col. 0088C] For the ancients called *pecora* all animals in general, but *pecudes* only those animals which are eaten, as it were, “grazing animals.” Generally, every animal is called *pecus* from grazing (*pascere*).

Beasts of burden (*iumenta*) derived their name from the fact that they help our labour or burden by carrying or ploughing. For the ox draws carts and turns the hardest clods with the ploughshare. The horse and ass carry loads and lighten the labour of people in walking. Hence they are called *iumenta* because they help people; for they are animals of great strength. They are likewise called herds (*armenta*), either because they are fitted for arms—that is, war—or because we use them in warfare, or because they have large shoulders (*armi*). Others understand *armenta* to mean only oxen, from ploughing (*arare*), as though *aramenta*, or because they are armed with horns. There is, moreover, a distinction [Col. 0088D] between herds (*armenta*) and flocks (*greges*). Herds belong only to the larger animals, such as horses and oxen; flocks also include goats, sheep, and the other smaller animals which live in groups.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the sheep.

The sheep is gentle livestock, with a woolly body: an unarmed animal of placid disposition. It is called from offering (*oblatio*), because among the ancients not bulls but sheep were at first slain in sacrifice. Of these, some are called *bidentes*, those which have two teeth higher than the other eight; these were especially offered in sacrifice by the pagans—or else the term means sheep that were two years old. At the approach of winter, the sheep, because it is insatiable in feeding, crops grass without satisfaction, since it senses the coming harshness of winter, [Col. 0089A] so that it may fill itself beforehand with the fodder of grass before every blade of grass fails under the scorching frost.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the wether.

A wether (*vervex*) is said to be named either from strength (*vires*), because it is stronger than other sheep, or because it is a male (*vir*), though emasculated. For the uncastrated male is called a ram (*aries*), and the castrated one a wether; or because they have worms in their heads, and, like rams aroused by the itching, shake one another. Hence *aries* is called ἀπὸ τοῦ ἄρεος, “from the mother”—the name by which males among sheep are called among us—or because this livestock was the first to be sacrificed on altars by pagans, so that it was called *aries* because it was placed upon altars (*arae*). Hence the saying, “A ram is slain at the altar”; but this explanation is less pleasing, and the quantity of the first syllable does not support it.

## CHAPTER XV. On the lamb.

[Col. 0089B]

A lamb (*agnus*) is called, as it were, *hag(n)es*, ἄγνης, “chaste.” The Latins, however, think it is so called because, more than other animals, it recognizes its mother. Even if it wanders in a great flock, it immediately recognizes its parent’s voice by its bleating, hastens to its mother, and seeks the familiar sources of maternal milk. The mother, moreover, recognizes her own child alone among many thousands of lambs; though the bleating of many is one and their appearance the same, she nevertheless recognizes her own offspring, distinguishes it from the rest, and, by the impulse of silent affection, recognizes her child alone.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the he-goat and kid.

The he-goat is a lustful animal, wanton and always ardent for mating. Because of its lust, its eyes look sideways, whence it derived its name; for, according to Suetonius, *hirquii* are the corners of the eyes. Its nature is so hot that its blood alone dissolves the adamant stone, which neither fire nor iron can overcome. According to some, kids (*haedi*) are named from eating: for when small they are very fat and pleasant in flavour, whence they are called *haedus* and *haedulus*. But because *haedus* is spelled thus, it seems to others to be called so because, if *h* is changed to *f*, it becomes *foedus* (“foul”).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the wild boar.

The wild boar (*aper*), that is, the wild pig or swine, is named from its fierceness, with a letter removed, as though *asper* (“rough”), according to Varro. Hence among the Greeks *agrios* [ἄγριος], “of the fields,” means wild and fierce; for everything wild and untamed we loosely call rustic or savage. Others think [Col. 0089D] it is called from the Greek word ἀφρός, “foam,” because it emits foam from its mouth.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the young ox and the bull.

A young ox (*iuvencus*) is so called because it begins to help human use in tilling the soil, or because it was always everywhere sacrificed among the pagans, and never the bull; for in sacrificial victims age was also taken into account.

*Tauros* [ταῦρος], “bull,” is a Greek name, as is *bous* (“ox”). Indian bulls are tawny in colour, swift as birds, with hair growing in the opposite direction and a great gaping mouth. They also turn their horns about, and, with every flexibility of the head they wish, reject every missile by the hardness of their back. They are so immensely savage that, when captured, they cast away their lives rather than be tamed.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the ox, the urus, and similar creatures.

[Col. 0090A]

The Greeks say βούς (*bous*), masculine and feminine alike, with genitive βοός (*boos*); the Latins call this the *trio*, because it wears down the earth, as though *terio*. Oxen have an exceptional affection for their companions. One seeks another with whom it has been accustomed to draw the plough by the neck, and testifies to its loving attachment to its companion by frequent lowing if it happens to be absent. Oxen know how to remain at their stalls when rain is impending; and, when by natural perception they have discerned a change in the weather, they look outward toward clear skies and stretch their necks beyond the stalls, all in one direction, to show that they wish to go out. Uri are wild oxen with enormous horns, so large that, because of their remarkable capacity, they are made into drinking-vessels among royal tables.

[Col. 0090B] In India there are also one-horned oxen, solid-hoofed rather than cloven-hoofed, and extremely fierce. Buffaloes derive their name from this, that they resemble oxen; they are so untamed through fierceness that they do not accept the yoke.

The cow (*vacca*) is called as though *boacca*. It belongs to the class of names formed from masculine forms, as lioness from lion, dragoness from dragon, and so forth. Calf (*vitulus*) and heifer (*vitula*) are named from greenness (*viriditas*), that is, youthful age, just as is *virgo* (“maiden”). We call a *vitula* small and not yet having calved; for one that has calved is a *iuvenca*, that is, a young cow.

## CHAPTER XX. On the nature of the camel.

The Greek κάμα (*kama*), “labour,” gave the camel its name, because it is a laborious beast of burden; or it comes from χαμαί (*chamai*), the Greek adverb meaning “on the ground.” [Col. 0090C] For when they are loaded, they lie down, in order to become lower and humbler, and thus it would be written *chamelus*. Or it is because its back is curved, from *chamiro*, “bent.” Although other regions also send them, Arabia produces the most camels, and Bactria the strongest. Yet they differ in this: Arabian camels have two humps on their backs, Bactrian ones a single hump. Their feet never wear away, for their soles are fleshy and furnished with certain yielding pads. Hence their feet are suited to walking, with no support hindering their exertion in placing the foot. They are kept for a double service. Some are suited to carrying burdens; others are swifter and readier for travel. The former accept extraordinarily great weights; the latter do not wish to go beyond their customary distances. [Col. 0090D] They are so inflamed by the desire of reproduction that they become savage when they seek intercourse. They hate the horse kind. They also endure thirst for three days; but when an opportunity to drink is given, they fill themselves as much as both satisfies their former thirst and serves them for a long time to come. They seek muddy waters and avoid clear ones. Finally, if no muddier water is available, they themselves stir up mud by continual trampling, so that it may be clouded. They live for a hundred years. If they are carried into foreign places, they contract illnesses because of the unfamiliar change of air. Females are prepared for war, and a practice was devised by which their desire for intercourse is removed by a kind of castration; for they are thought to become stronger if kept from mating.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the dromedary.

[Col. 0091A]

The dromedary is a kind of camel, indeed of smaller stature but greater speed, whence it has its name. For δρόμος (*dromos*) in Greek means “running” and “swiftness”; it commonly covers a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal, like the sheep, ox, and camel, chews the cud. Rumination is so called from the prominent part of the throat called the *rumen*, through which food once swallowed is brought back by many animals.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the ass and the little ass.

The ass (*asinus*) and little ass (*asellus*) are named from sitting upon (*assidere*), as though “sat upon by man” (*assessus ab homine*). But this name, which was more fitting for horses, was assumed by this animal because, before people rode horses, they began to ride it. [Col. 0091B] For it is a slow animal and in no respect resistant to commands; as soon as a person wished, it submitted itself. Arcadian asses are so called because they were first brought from Arcadia; they are large and tall. The smaller ass is called the *asellus*, and it is more useful because it both endures labour and almost does not resist the neglect of soft rearing.

On the wild ass see Book II, chapter 11.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the horse and its nature.

Horses (*equi*) are said to be so called by removal of the first letter, namely *a* from *aequus, aequa, aequum* (“equal”), because when they were yoked in pairs or fours, they were joined as equals in height, strength, and speed. The nag (*caballus*) is named from hollowing (*cavare*), because, as it walks, its hoofprint [Col. 0091C] hollows the ground, which other animals do not do. Hence it is called *sonipes* (“sounding-footed”) because it makes a sound with its feet.

Horses have great spirit and intelligence. They leap about in fields, smell out war, and are stirred by the trumpet’s sound to battle. They are incited to running by the voice. They grieve when conquered and exult when victorious. Some horses perceive enemies in battle, so that they attack opponents with bites. Others even recognize their own masters and, if their masters change, forget their gentleness. Some admit no one but their master upon their back.

We may give the example of Alexander the Great, whose horse was called Bucephalus, either because of the fierceness of its appearance or because of its conspicuous nobility, since it had a bull’s head, or because on its forehead there projected something like the threatening horns of a bull. When on another occasion it was gently mounted by its own groom, wearing the royal cloth, it never deigned to carry anyone except its master. Many were its proofs in battles, in which it brought Alexander safe through its own aid from the cruellest contests. The horse of Gaius Caesar admitted no one but Caesar upon its back. When a king of the Scythians was killed in single combat and his victor wished to strip him, he was torn by kicks and bites from that king’s horse. When King Nicomedes was killed, his horse ended its life by starvation. When Antiochus had defeated the Galatians in battle, he mounted in triumph the horse of the commander, named Centeretrios, who had fallen in the battle; but the horse so despised the bit that, intentionally made savage and frenzied, it brought both itself and its rider down in a fall.

[Col. 0092A] In this kind of animal, the males have a longer lifespan. We indeed read of a horse that lived to seventy years. We have also observed recorded a horse named Opuntes [possibly “Opinices”] which remained capable of ordinary mating until forty years of age. Mares’ lust is extinguished when their manes are shorn. At their delivery there is produced a love-charm, which the newborn foals bear on their foreheads: tawny in colour, of the size of a dried fig, called *hippomanes*. If it is immediately snatched away, the mother gives no milk at all to the foal. The sounder and more promising a horse is, the more deeply it plunges its nostrils while drinking. They have shed tears over masters who were killed or dying. For they say that the horse alone sheds tears on account of a human being and experiences the effect of grief. Hence the nature of horses and humans is mingled in feeling. From the sadness or cheerfulness of horses, they are also accustomed to infer the future outcome of a coming battle.

[Col. 0092B] In well-bred horses, as the ancients say, four things are looked for: build, beauty, quality, and colour. Build: that the body be strong and solid, the height suitable for strength, the side long and tucked up, the haunches very large and rounded, the leg knotted and lean, the hoof firm with a hollow horn. Beauty: that the head be small and lean, with skin closely adhering to the bones; the ears short and pointed; the eyes large; the nostrils open; the neck erect; the mane and tail thick; the hooves sound; and the feet fixed and round. Quality: that it be bold in spirit, lively on its feet, with quivering limbs (which is an indication of strength), easily roused from complete rest, and not difficult to restrain once its speed has been excited.

[Col. 0092C] A horse’s movement is understood from its ears; its strength, from trembling limbs. Among colours these are especially sought: bay, golden, rose-coloured, myrtle-coloured, deer-coloured, yellowish, blue-grey, spotted, grey, shining white, white, dappled, black; next in rank is variegated colouring distinguished by black and bay, whereas every remaining variegated colour—ash-grey, for example—is the poorest. The ancients called *badius*, or, as the common people say, *baius* and *baiadus*, as though *vadius*, because horses of that colour go more strongly among other animals. It is also the *spadix*, called “phoenix-coloured,” and is named *spadix* from the colour of the palm, which Syrians call *spadix*. *Glaucus* means having eyes as though painted and suffused with a certain brightness. *Gilvus* is a midway, whitish colour. *Guttatus* is white with intervening black [Col. 0092D] spots. *Candidus* (“shining white”) and *albus* (“white”) differ from one another: *albus* has a certain pallor, but *candidus* is snowy and suffused with a more intense whiteness. *Canus* (“grey”) is named for a colour made from white and black. *Scutulatus* is so called from the white circles it has among purple ones; *varius*, from its streaks of unequal colours. Those which have only white feet are called *pedici*; those with a white forehead, *candidi*. *Cervinus* is what the common people call grey. *Onosinus* is so called because its colour is the same as that of an ass; it is also ash-grey.

There are horses born of a rustic stock, which we call wild horses; accordingly, they cannot rise to the dignity of city life. *Maurus* is black, [Col. 0093A] for the Greeks call black *mauron*. A *mannus* is a smaller horse. The ancients called *verhedi* those which drew carriages (*raedae*), or travelled public roads along which carriages were customarily driven.

There are three kinds of horses. One is noble, suited to battle and burdens. Another is common and herd-bred, suited to drawing loads, not to riding. The third arises from the mixing of different kinds; it is also called *bigenum* (“double-born”), because it is born from different parents, as the mule. The mule has a term coined from Greek, namely because, harnessed to the yoke of millers, it drives slow millstones in a circle while grinding. The Jews assert that Anah, Esau’s great-grandson, was the first to make herds of mares be mounted by asses in the wilderness, so that new animals, contrary to nature, might be born from beasts of burden. [Col. 0093B] They also say that wild asses were admitted for this purpose to she-asses, and that he discovered this kind of mating so that very swift asses might be born from them. Human ingenuity, indeed, compelled unlike animals to mate and thus, by adulterous mixture, discovered another breed—as Jacob too contrived differences in the colours of sheep contrary to nature. For his sheep produced offspring such as the rams mounting them beheld in the reflection of water upon the rods. It is further said that this is done with herds of mares: noble horses are presented to the sight of females conceiving, so that they may conceive and produce offspring like them. For those who keep pigeons also place painted and very beautiful doves in the places where the females live, so that, when their sight has seized those images, they may produce marked offspring. Hence some instruct pregnant women [Col. 0093C] not to gaze upon the most ugly faces of animals, such as dog-headed creatures and apes, lest, encountering them with their eyes, they bear similar offspring. For they say this is women’s nature: whatever they look upon, or conceive in the mind during the extreme heat of pleasure as they conceive, offspring of that kind they produce. For in sexual intercourse the soul transmits external forms, and, filled with their images, draws their appearances into its own character.

Among living creatures those born from different parents are called *bigena*: the mule from a mare and an ass; the hinny (*burdo*) from a horse and a she-ass; hybrids (*ibridae*) from wild boars and pigs; the *tityrus* from a sheep and a he-goat; and the *musino* from a she-goat and a ram, which is the leader of the flock.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the cat, or *musio*.

[Col. 0093D] The *musio* or *muscio* is called by most people *muriceps* (“mouse-catcher”) or *murilegus* (“mouse-hunter”), because it is hostile to mice. The common people call it *catus* (“cat”) from catching. Others say that it catches things with its eyes—that is, sees them. For it sees so sharply that it overcomes the darkness of night by the brilliance of its light. For *catus* means sharp and clever.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the mouse and shrew, etc.

The mouse is a small animal; its Greek name is μῦς (*mys*), while whatever is derived from it is Latin. Others say that mice (*mures*) are so called because they are born from the moisture of the earth: for *humus* is earth, and hence *mus*. Their livers grow at the full moon, as do certain marine creatures which increase as the full moon approaches and again diminish when the moon wanes. Some draw a distinction between the shrew (*sorex*) and mouse (*mus*): the shrew is the smaller animal which [Col. 0094A] cats stalk; the mouse is the larger animal, incorrectly thought to be the dormouse (*glis*).

On the weasel see Book II, chapter 18.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the mole.

The mole is a little black creature condemned to perpetual blindness. For it lives in darkness without eyes, always digs the earth and raises the soil, and beneath the crops eats roots. In Greek it is called ἀσπάλαξ (*aspalax*).

On the ant see Book II, chapter 29. On the hedgehog or urchin see Book II, chapter 4.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On birds in general.

Birds have one general name, but their kinds are different. For as they differ in species, so too they differ in the diversity of their natures. Some are simple, such as doves; others cunning, such as the partridge; some submit themselves to the hand, [Col. 0094B] such as hawks; others fear it, such as *garamentes* [reading uncertain]; some delight in human society, such as the swallow; others love a secluded life in deserts, such as the vulture; some utter the sweetest songs, such as the swan and blackbird; others imitate human words and voices, such as the parrot and magpie. And, as they are innumerable in kind, so too in habits. For no one can discover how many kinds of winged creatures there are. No one could have penetrated all the deserts of India, Ethiopia, or Scythia and thereby known their kinds or distinctions.

Birds (*aves*) are so called because they do not have straight paths but wander through every trackless place (*avia*); they are called *alites* because by wings they strive upward and rise to heights by the oarage of their wings. *Volucres* is from flying (*volare*). For “to fly” and “to walk” (*ambulare*) derive from the same source: the *vola* is the middle part of the foot or hand, and in birds the *vola* is the middle part of the wings, by whose motion the feathers are stirred; hence *volucres*. The young of all birds are called chicks (*pulli*). The young of quadruped animals too are called *pulli*, and a little human being is a *pullus* or *pusio*. Thus newly born young are called *pulli* because they are dark-coloured (*polluti*); hence a black garment is called *pulla*. Some have feathers fixed in order, providing the function of flight; these are called wings (*alae*) because birds, enclosing their chicks with them, nourish and warm them. A feather (*penna*) is named from hanging (*pendere*), whence also “to hang.” Winged creatures move by the aid of feathers when they commit themselves to the air. Down (*pluma*) is, as it were, *piluma*: for as hairs are on the bodies of quadrupeds, so feathers are on birds. Many names of birds are evidently composed from the sound of their voice: crane, raven, swan, owl, kite, screech-owl, cuckoo, jackdaw, and the rest. The variety of their voices taught people how to name them.

On the eagle see Book I, chapter 56. On the vulture, Book I, chapter 38. On cranes, Book I, chapter 39.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the parrot.

India alone produces the parrot, green in colour, with a crimson collar, a large tongue broader than that of other birds; therefore it articulates words, so that, if you did not see it, you would think a human being were speaking. By nature it gives a greeting, saying *ave* (“hail”) or χαῖρε (*chaire*, “rejoice” or “greetings”). It learns other names by instruction. Hence Martial:

> Through me it learned to say: “Caesar, hail.”

[Col. 0095A] Its beak is so hard that, when it falls from a height onto a rock, it catches itself by the force of its beak and uses it as a kind of foundation of regular strength. It strives to say what human beings say; and while it is still a chick, still under its second year of age, it both learns more quickly what is taught and retains it more firmly.

On the caladrius see Book I, chapter 48. On storks see Book I, chapter 42. On the *holor* or swan see Book I, chapter 53. On the ibis or *ibi*, Book I, chapter 57. On the *assida* or ostrich, Book I, chapter 37. On the coot, Book I, chapter 58.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the halcyon.

[Col. 0095B] The halcyon is a sea-bird which usually brings forth its young on the shore, laying its eggs in the sand about the middle of winter. For it has that season appointed for brooding its offspring, when the sea most violently rises against the shores and the stronger surf is dashed upon them. Then, by a sudden calm, in favour of—or in accordance with—the nature of this bird, the breeze subsides; once the eggs have been laid, the sea lowers itself, every storm falls, the blasts of the winds grow gentle, and the sea stands calm despite the winds until the halcyon has brooded its eggs. There are seven days in which it hatches its chicks and at once completes the bringing forth of its offspring; it adds another seven days in which it nourishes its chicks, until they begin to grow. Nor should you wonder that the period of feeding is so brief, since the hatching of the young also occupies so few days. They say that so great a favour has been granted and divinely bestowed upon this bird that sailors observe these fourteen days as a period of assured calm; they call them the halcyon days, during which no disturbance of storm is to be feared.

On the phoenix see Book I, chapter 49.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Cinnamulgus

The cinnamulgus is likewise a bird of Arabia, so called because it weaves its nests in lofty groves from cinnamon fruit. Since people cannot climb there because of the height and fragility of the branches, they attack these nests with lead-weighted missiles, thus knock down the cinnamon, and sell it at higher prices, because merchants value this cinnamon more highly than other kinds.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Hercynian Birds

[Col. 0095D] Hercynian birds are named from the Hercynian Forest of Germany, where they are born. Their feathers shine so brightly in darkness that, although night is covered by dense shadows, feathers cast down to guide one’s journey gleam through the dark, and the course of the road is made visible by the indication of their shining plumage.

The hoopoe has been discussed under “Hoopoe,” Book I, chapter 52; the pelican, Book II, chapter 27; the owl, or *nycticorax*, Book I, chapter 34; the sirens, Book II, chapter 32; the partridge, Book I, chapter 50.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Magpie and the Woodpecker

Magpies are, as it were, *poeticae* (“poetic birds”), because they articulate words with a discrimination of sound like a human being. Hanging among the branches of trees, resounding with importunate chatter, although they cannot articulate languages in speech, they nevertheless imitate the sound of the human voice. Accordingly, someone fittingly says (Martial):

> Chattering magpie, with a distinct voice I greet you, master.  
> If you do not see me, you will deny that I am a bird.

[Col. 0096A] The woodpecker (*picus*) took its name from Picus, son of Saturn, because he himself used that bird in augury. For they relate that this bird possesses something divine, as is shown by the fact that in whatever tree it has nested, a nail or anything else driven into it cannot remain fast for long, but immediately falls out when the bird has settled there.

On the hawk see Book I, chapter 13.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Nightingale

The nightingale takes its name from the fact that by its song it is accustomed to signify the dawning rise of day—thus, as it were, *lucinia* (“light-announcer”); for it is an ever-watchful sentinel. When it broods its eggs in a certain hollow and lap of its body, it lightens the sleepless labour of the long night by the sweetness of its song. And, as it seems to me, this is its chief concern: that it may quicken and cherish its offspring no less with sweeter melodies than with the warmth of its body.

Such a life, it seems, is led by a widowed woman who is poor but chaste: drawing the distaff with her fingers in order to earn food for her little children, she softens the sorrow of poverty by nocturnal song; and though she cannot imitate the sweetness of the nightingale, she nevertheless diligently imitates it in the duty of maternal affection.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Bat

The bat, a lowly animal, takes its name from evening (*vesper*). [Col. 0096C] It is a flying creature and at the same time a quadruped, and it uses teeth, which is not usually found in other birds. It gives birth like quadrupeds, not to eggs but to living young; it flies, however, not by any winged flight, but supported by the oarage of its membrane, by which it is borne and animated in the air as though by the flight of wings.

This mean animal has another feature: they cling to one another and hang from a high place like a cluster of grapes. But if each of the lowest ones lets go, all come loose. This occurs through a certain gift of charity, which is difficult to find among human beings, yet is found to some extent even among creatures of this kind.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Crow and the Raven Again

The crow, a long-lived bird, is called by the Greek name *korōnē* (κορώνη) among the Latins. Augurs say that by its signs it reveals human concerns, warns of ambushes on the road, and foretells the future. It is a great impiety to believe that God entrusts his counsels to crows. Among its many auguries, they also ascribe to it the foretelling of rain by its cries; hence:

> Then the shameless crow calls for rain with her voice.  
> —Virgil, *Georgics* I.388

[Col. 0096D] Let people learn to love their children from the usefulness and affection of ravens, which, even while flying, diligently follow their young in attendance; anxiously fearing that they may perhaps fail, they provide them with food and do not abandon the duties of nourishment for a very long time.

But women of our time quickly wean even those children whom they love; if they are wealthier, they disdain to nurse them, while if they are poorer, [Col. 0097A] they cast out and expose their little ones, and deny them when they are found. Rich mothers too, lest their estate be divided among more children, kill their own offspring in the womb; with parricidal juices they extinguish the pledges of their womb within the very generative belly. Life is taken away before it is bestowed.

Who taught this but human beings: to disown their children? Who made brothers unequal within nature’s fraternal fellowship? The children of one rich man fall to different lots. One enjoys the registration of the whole paternal estate; another laments his narrow and impoverished share of a wealthy paternal inheritance. Does nature divide the deserts of children? From equal resources it gives all alike what enables them to possess the means both of being born and of living. Nature herself, O parents, teaches you not to distinguish by inheritance those whom she has made equal by the title of kinship. For those to whom you have given in common the fact that they are born, you ought not begrudge their jointly receiving and possessing the same share.

On the dove see Book I, chapters 1, 2, and 3; on the turtle-dove, Book I, chapters 20, 23, 24, and 25; on the swallow, Book II, chapter 41; on the quail, or *qualea*, Book I, chapter 51; on the peacock, Book I, chapter 55; on the hoopoe, Book I, chapter 52; on the cock, Book I, chapter 36.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Duck

The duck (*anas*) received its apt name from its continual swimming. Certain birds of this genus are called German ducks because they nourish their young more than the rest. Pontic ducks live on poison and therefore are not fit for human food. It is also thought that the duck gave its name to the goose (*anser*), because it too, although it lives on land, swims continually; but we have spoken elsewhere of the goose.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Eggs and What Is Born from Them

All kinds of birds are born twice. First eggs are produced and laid; then they are formed and quickened by the warmth of the mother’s body. Eggs (*ova*) are so called because they are moist (*uvida*). Likewise grapes (*uvae*), because they are inwardly full of moisture. For *humid* is what has moisture externally, whereas *uvid* has it within. Some think that *ova* has a Greek origin, for the Greeks say ὤ, and in the singular ὠὸν (*ōon*), with the letter *v* removed.

[Col. 0097D] Some eggs are conceived from empty wind, but they are not reproductive unless conceived through male intercourse and penetrated by seminal breath. Their power, they say, is so great that wood drenched with them does not burn, nor indeed is even cloth shrunk by fire scorched; mixed with lime, they are also said to cement fragments of glass together.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Bees

Bees (*apes*) are so called either because they bind themselves by their feet, or because they are born without feet; for later they receive both feet and wings. Industrious in their allotted task of producing honey, they inhabit their appointed seats, construct dwellings with inexpressible skill, make honeycomb from varied flowers, and fill their camps with countless offspring and woven wax. They have an army and kings; they wage battles, flee smoke, and are provoked by disturbance.

[Col. 0098A] Many have found by experience that they are born from the carcasses of oxen. For, to produce them, the flesh of slaughtered calves is beaten, so that worms may be produced from the decaying blood, which afterwards become bees. More properly, however, bees are said to arise from oxen, as hornets from horses, drones from mules, and wasps from asses.

The Greeks call them *castro* [*castoras*], those larger bees produced in the outermost parts of the honeycombs; some think that these are called kings because they lead camps. Bees alone, among every kind of living creature, have offspring held in common by all. All inhabit one dwelling, are enclosed within the threshold of a house of one homeland; their labour, food, work, function, produce, and flight are common to all. What more need be said? Since their generation is common to all, the integrity of a virginal body and childbirth are likewise common to all. For they neither mingle with one another in any intercourse, nor are they loosened by lust, nor are they shaken by the pains of childbirth; but suddenly they send forth a vast swarm of children, gathering leaves and grasses with their mouths and thereby generating offspring for themselves.

They themselves make and appoint their king. They themselves create their peoples. Although they are placed under a king, they are nevertheless free. For they retain both the prerogative of judgment and an affection of faithful devotion, because they love their king as one set up by themselves and honour him with the whole swarm. The king is not chosen by lot, because in a lot there is chance, not judgment, and often by the irrational accident of the lot an inferior is preferred to better persons. But among bees the king is fashioned with the bright distinctions of nature: by size and appearance of body, and, what is chief in a king, [Col. 0098C] by gentleness of character. For although he has a sting, he does not use it for revenge. For theirs are laws of nature written not in letters but impressed upon their manners: that those who possess greater power should be more restrained in punishment.

Bees that have not obeyed the laws of the king also punish themselves by the penalty of repentance, so that they die from the wound of their own sting. The peoples of Persia are said to observe this among themselves, executing upon themselves the sentence of their own death according to the value or gravity of the offence committed. Thus no people observe their king with such reverent devotion as bees do—not the Persians, who have very severe laws for their subjects, nor Indians, nor Jews, nor Sauromatians—so that none dare leave their homes or go forth to any feeding-ground unless the king has first departed and claimed for himself the leadership of flight.

[Col. 0098D] Their departure is into fragrant fields, where gardens breathe upon flowers, where a running stream passes through scented grasses, where the riverbanks are delightful. There is the sport of lively youth; there the exercise of the open field; there the release from cares; there the work itself is sweet among flowers and fragrant herbs, and the first foundations of their camps are laid. For what else is a honeycomb but a kind of camp? Finally, the drone is excluded from these bee-stalls. What camps can possess as much artistry and grace in their square arrangement as the lattice-work of honeycombs, in which tiny round cells support one another by their mutual joining?

What architect taught them to construct those hexagonal cells with their distinct equality of sides, [Col. 0099A] to suspend tender waxes between the partitions of their homes, to pack away honey, and to extend storehouses, interwoven with flowers, with a kind of nectar? You might see all competing in their task: some keeping watch in seeking food, others maintaining anxious guard over the camp, others exploring coming rains and observing the gatherings of storm-clouds, others shaping wax from flowers, others gathering the inward dew from flowers. Yet none plots against another’s labour or seeks life by plunder—though would that they did not have to fear the plots of plunderers.

They nevertheless have their poisons and, if provoked, pour venom amid their honey; in the heat of revenge they lay down their lives in the wound. Therefore, in the middle of the ramparts of their camp, that fresh liquid is poured in; gradually, through the passage of time, it is condensed into honey. At first liquid, it begins, by the combining of wax and the scent of flowers, to breathe forth the sweetness of honey.

Rightly does Scripture commend the bee, like the ant, as a good worker, saying: “Go to the ant, O sluggard, and consider her ways, and learn wisdom” (Prov. VI). It is as though it said: See how diligently and providently she has worked, and imitate her work. For bees undertake an honourable labour, whose toil kings and ordinary people alike take up for their well-being. For sanctification is desirable and dear to all. You hear what the prophet says. Thus he sends you to follow the example of that little bee and imitate its work. See how laborious it is, and how pleasing. “The bee is small among flying things, and its fruit has the beginning of sweetness” (Eccl. XI). [Col. 0099C] Therefore its fruit is desired and sought by everyone; it is not distinguished according to differences of persons, but by its undiscriminating grace it becomes sweet with equal pleasantness to kings and ordinary people alike.

Nor serves it pleasure only, but health as well. It sweetens the throat and heals wounds. It also applies medicine inwardly to ulcers. Thus although the bee is weak in bodily strength, it is powerful in the vigour of wisdom and the love of virtue. Indeed, bees defend their king with the greatest protection and think it noble to perish for him. While the king is safe, all have one mind; when he is lost, they break faith. While he is safe, they do not know how to change their judgment or bend their intention elsewhere. When he is lost, they abandon the task of maintaining allegiance and plunder their own honey, because he who held the chief place in this office has been killed.

Thus, whereas other birds produce young only once each year, bees bring forth new swarms twice or three times, and therefore surpass other animals in their wondrous fecundity.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On a Certain Tree in India

There is a hanging tree in India. The fruit of this tree is wholly sweet and very pleasant. Doves delight in the fruit of this tree and dwell in it, feeding on its fruit. But a dragon is the enemy of the doves; it fears the tree and its shade, where the doves remain, and cannot approach either the tree or its shade. For if the tree’s shade falls westward, it flees eastward, and conversely. But if it happens that a dove is found outside the tree or its shade, [Col. 0100A] the dragon kills it.

Understand this tree as God the Father, and its shade as his Son, as Gabriel says to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I). Understand the heavenly fruit as the wisdom of the Lord, namely the Holy Spirit. Take heed, therefore, O human being, lest, after you have received the Holy Spirit—that is, the spiritual and intelligent dove abiding upon you—you become outside eternity, alien from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, lest the dragon, that is, the devil, kill you. For if you possess the Holy Spirit, the dragon cannot approach you. Take heed, therefore, O human being, and remain in the catholic faith. Beware, as far as you can, lest you be found outside the house and that dragon, the ancient serpent, seize you outside and devour you like Judas, who, as soon as he went outside the house [Col. 0100B] and away from the brother apostles, was immediately devoured by the demon and perished.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Kinds of Serpents

*Anguis* is the general name for all serpents that can be coiled and twisted; hence *anguis*, because it is angular and never straight. *Coluber* is so called because it inhabits shadows, or because it is drawn or glides along slippery courses in winding coils. For “slippery” is said of whatever slips when held, such as an eel or a serpent. A serpent (*serpens*) received its name because it crawls by hidden approaches, not by open steps, but creeps by the slightest efforts of its scales. Creatures that move upon four or more feet, such as lizards and stellions, are not serpents but reptiles, because they crawl upon belly and breast. Their poisons are as numerous as their kinds, their forms of destruction as numerous as their species, and their pains as numerous as their colours.

On the dragon see Book II, chapter 24.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Basilisk and the Sibilus

The basilisk, Greek βασίλισκος, is translated in Latin as *regulus*, “little king,” because it is king of serpents: those that see it flee, since it kills them by its smell. Indeed, if it looks upon a human being, it kills him. No bird flying past escapes unharmed from its sight; though far away, it is burned by the basilisk’s mouth and devoured. Yet it is overcome by weasels, which people introduce into the caves in which it lies hidden. At the sight of one, it flees; the weasel pursues and kills it. For that parent of all things established nothing without a remedy.

It is half a foot long and marked with white spots. Little kings, like scorpions, seek dry places; when they come to waters and there bite someone, they make them hydrophobic and mad. The *sibilus* is the same as the *regulus*. It kills by hissing before it bites or burns.

On the viper see Book II, chapter 21; on the asp, Book II, chapter 30.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Cerastes

The cerastes is so called because it displays on its head horns like those of rams; for κέραστα, that is, *cerata* (“horned things”), is the Greek term for horns. It has four little horns, by the display of which it lures animals as if by bait and kills them. It covers its entire body with sand and gives no sign of itself except in the part by which it catches the birds or animals it has invited. It is more sinuous than other serpents, [Col. 0101A] so that it seems to have no spine.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Scitalis, from Pliny and Solinus

The serpent *scitalis* is so called because it shines with such a varied brilliance of back that it delays those who look at it for the beauty of its markings. Since it is slower in crawling, it catches by the wonder of itself those whom it cannot overtake. It is of such great heat that even in winter it casts off the hot slough of its body. Lucan says of it:

> And the scitalis alone, even now when frost is scattered abroad,  
> is about to shed its slough.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Amphisbaena

[Col. 0101B] The amphisbaena is so called because it has two heads, one in its proper place and the other in its tail; it moves from either head with the circuit of its body coiled. Alone among serpents, it exposes itself to cold and is the first of all to come forth. Of it Lucan likewise says:

> And the heavy amphisbaena, inclining toward its twin head.

Its eyes shine like lamps.

On the *hydrus* and hydra see Book II, chapter 7.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the Boa Serpent Again

The boa, a serpent of Italy of immense size, pursues herds of cattle and buffaloes, entwines itself around udders wet with abundant milk, and kills by sucking. It consequently received the name *boa* from its ravaging of cattle (*boves*).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Javelin-Serpent

[Col. 0101C] The *iaculus* is a flying serpent, of which Lucan says:

> … and the flying javelin-serpents.

They leap down from the trees where they lay ambushes; when some animal comes in their way, they hurl themselves upon it and kill it. Hence they are called *iaculi*, “javelins.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Siren Serpents

In Arabia there are also serpents called sirens, with wings, which run faster than horses and are also said to fly. Their venom is so potent that death follows the bite before pain does.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Seps Serpent

The seps is a small serpent which consumes with its poison not only the body but even the bones. The poet mentions it thus:

> The seps, melting the bones together with the body.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Dipsas Serpent

[Col. 0101D] The dipsas is said to be so small that when it is trodden upon it cannot be seen. Its venom kills before it is felt, so that the face, overtaken by death, causes no grief to the person dying. Of it the poet says:

> The standard-bearing youth Aulus [or *almum*, “nourishing”], of Tyrrhenian blood,  
> was bitten by a dipsas, twisted backward at the head, when trodden upon.  
> There was scarcely pain or sensation of the tooth, etc.

## CHAPTER L. On the Lizard Again, and the Batracha

The lizard is a kind of reptile, so called because it has arms. There are many kinds of lizards, such as the batracha, salamander, saura, and stellion. The batracha is so called because [Col. 0102A] it has the appearance of a frog; for the Greeks call a frog *batrachon* (βάτραχον).

On the salamander see Book II, chapter 16.

## CHAPTER LI. On the Saura

The saura is a species of lizard whose eyes become blind when it grows old. It enters a hole in a wall, looks toward the east, fixes its gaze upon the rising sun, and receives sight.

## CHAPTER LII. On the Stellion Again, and Other Serpents

The stellion takes its name from its shining colour, for its back is marked with bright spots in the manner of stars. Ovid says of it:

> It has a name suited to its colour,  
> starred upon its body with varied spots.

It is so opposed to scorpions that, as is reported, the sight of it strikes them with fear and brings them numbness. There are other kinds of serpents also, such as *admordicae*, *elephantiae*, *chamedracontes*, and many others. All are deadly to human beings, so that the number of deaths is as great as the number of names.

All serpents are by nature cold and do not strike unless they grow warm. For when cold, they touch no one. Hence their poisons harm more by day than by night; for they are numbed by the night’s chill, and rightly so, since they are chilled by nocturnal dew. Within themselves they draw in the vapour of the numbness of their cold pestilence and nature. Thus in winter they twist themselves into knots, and in summer they uncoil. Hence anyone struck by the poison of a serpent is first numbed; then, when the venom itself has grown hot and flared up within him, it immediately kills the person.

[Col. 0102C] Poison (*venenum*) is so called because it travels through the veins (*venae*). For when its pestilence has been introduced through the veins, it runs through the body after destroying its vital activity and extinguishes the soul. Therefore poison cannot harm unless it has touched a person’s blood. Hence Lucan:

> The pestilence of serpents is harmful when mixed with blood.

Every poison is cold; therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees cold poison.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the Various Nature of Serpents

Among the natural goods which we see are shared by us and irrational animals, the serpent excels in a certain liveliness of perception. Hence it is read in Genesis: “Now the serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Gen. III). The serpent has three natures.

The first is this: when it has grown old, its eyes grow dim; and if it wishes to become new, it abstains from food and fasts for many days until its skin loosens. Then it seeks a narrow crevice in a rock, enters it, rubs and constricts itself, and casts off its old skin. So we too, through great bodily hardship and abstinence for Christ, should put off the old human being and his garment, seek Christ the spiritual rock, and the narrow fissure—that is, the gate.

Its second nature is that, when it comes to a river to drink water, it does not carry poison with it but leaves it in a hole. So we too, when we come to the gathered water to draw living and everlasting water—that is, the divine word in the Church—must cast away from ourselves poison, that is, earthly [Col. 0103A] and evil desires.

Its third nature is that if it sees a naked person it fears him, but if it sees him clothed, it leaps upon him. So let us understand spiritually that the first Adam, while he was naked in Paradise, was not overcome by the serpent. But after he was clothed with a tunic—that is, with the mortality of the body, or with the consent through which our death and his own followed—the serpent then leapt upon him. If therefore, O human being, you have within yourself the mortal garment, that is, the old human being, and have become old in evil days, the serpent will leap upon you. But if you strip yourself of the garment of the rulers and powers of this age and of darkness, then the serpent—that is, the devil—will not be able to leap upon you.

The serpent also dispels acquired blindness by feeding on fennel. Thus, when it feels its eyes becoming covered over, it seeks known remedies and is not disappointed of their effect. If a serpent tastes the saliva of a fasting person, it dies. Pliny says: “It is believed that if the head of a serpent escapes with two fingers [of its body], it nonetheless lives. Hence it exposes its whole body to those striking at it, in defence of its head.”

All serpents have dull sight and rarely look straight ahead. For they have their eyes not in the forehead but at the temples, so that they hear more readily than they see. No animal moves its tongue with such rapidity; it seems to have a triple tongue, though it has only one. The tortoise, too, after feeding on the entrails of a serpent, when it perceives poison creeping upon it, employs oregano as the medicine of its preservation.

[Col. 0103C] The bodies of all serpents are moist, so that wherever they go they mark their route with moisture. The tracks of serpents are such that, although they seem to lack feet, they nevertheless crawl by the efforts of their ribs and scales, which they have arranged in like fashion from the top of the throat to the lowest belly. They rely upon their scales as upon claws, and upon their ribs as upon legs. Hence if they are struck in any part of the body from the belly to the head, they are rendered weak and cannot move, because wherever that blow falls, it dislocates the spine through which the feet formed by the ribs and the motions of the body were driven.

Serpents are said to live a long time, so that when they have cast off their old covering, they are reported to put away old age and return to youth. The coverings of serpents are called *exuviae*, because when they grow old they strip them off. They are also called *exuviae* and *induviae*, because they are taken off and put on.

Pythagoras says that a serpent is produced from the marrow of a dead human being which is in the spine. Ovid also mentions this in the books of the *Metamorphoses*, saying:

> There are those who believe that, when the spine has decayed in a closed tomb,  
> human marrow is changed into a serpent.

If this is believed, it fittingly follows that, just as human death came through a serpent, so the life of a serpent follows from human death.

## CHAPTER LIV. On Worms

A worm is an animal generally produced, without any intercourse, from flesh, wood, or any earthly matter whatever, although at times they are also born from eggs, as is the scorpion. Worms belong to earth, water, air, flesh, foliage, wood, or clothing.

[Col. 0104A] The spider is a worm of the air, so named from its nourishment from the air. With its tiny body it draws out long threads; ever intent upon its web, it never ceases from labour, continually suffering loss in its work.

The many-footed worm is an earth-worm, named from its multitude of feet; when threatened by a blow, it contracts itself and coils into a ball.

The leech is a water-worm, so called because it sucks blood; it lies in wait for those drinking. When it slips into the throat or fastens anywhere, it draws blood; when soaked with excessive blood, it vomits out what it has swallowed, in order to suck afresh.

[Col. 0104B] The scorpion is an earth-worm and is classed more among worms than among serpents. It is an animal armed with a sting; from this it is called *nepes* in Greek, because it fixes its tail and spreads poison through an armed wound. A peculiarity of the scorpion is that it does not strike the palm of the hand.

The silkworm (*bombyx*) is a worm of foliage, from whose weaving silk cloth is made. It is called by this name because it empties itself while producing threads, so that air alone remains within it.

The caterpillar (*eruca*) is a worm of foliage, wrapped in vegetables or vine-leaves, and named from gnawing. Plautus mentions it: “The caterpillar, a wicked and harmful beast, wrapped in a vine-leaf, having imitated [something uncertain; *imitatus*], wraps itself in it; it does not fly in like the locust, so as, running here and there, to leave things half-eaten, but remains among crops destined to perish and consumes everything by slow movement and sluggish bites.”

[Col. 0104C] Wood-borers are called *teredones*, some saying that they are worms because they eat by rubbing, or because they bore; τέρετρον (*teretron*) is Greek, and in Latin means “auger” or “drill.” Among the Greeks δήξ (*dēx*) means “a biter,” and δῆξις (*dēxis*) “a bite.” In Latin we call these *termites*, for this is what wood-worms are called among us, which trees generate from themselves in an unfavourable season.

The clothes-moth (*tinea*) is so called because it persists and remains upon a thing until it has gnawed it away. Hence one is called *pertinax* (“persistent”), because one repeatedly presses upon the same thing.

Worms of flesh are *hipscratos*, the intestinal worm (*lumbricus*), lice (*pediculi*), fleas (*pulices*), nits (*lendes*), *tarmus*, the dog-tick (*ricynus*), *usia*, and the bedbug (*cimex*).

The *hipscratos* is called a worm of the head.

The *lumbricus* is a worm of the intestines, named as though from *lubricus* (“slippery”), because it glides, or because it is in the loins (*lumbi*).

Lice are worms of the skin, called from feet (*pedes*); hence those in whose bodies lice teem are called *pediculosi*.

Fleas are so named because they are nourished from dust.

The *tarmus* is a worm of bacon.

The *ricynus* is a worm of the dog, so called because it clings in dogs’ ears. For κύων (*kyōn*) is Greek for “dog.”

[Col. 0105A] The *ustula* is a worm of the pig, so called because it burns: where it has bitten, it burns so severely that blisters immediately form there.

The bedbug is a foul-smelling worm, born in walls and beds, named because it resembles the herb *cima*, whose stink it has. Strictly speaking, however, the worm is born in decaying flesh; the moth in clothing; the caterpillar in vegetables; the wood-borer in wood; and the *tarmus* in bacon.

A worm does not crawl like a serpent by open steps or by the efforts of scales, because it does not have the rigidity of spine possessed by a snake. Rather, by extending in succession the contracted parts of its little body and contracting the extended parts, it performs its movements and thus, when set in motion, glides along.

## CHAPTER LV. On the Different Natures of Fish

Fish (*pisces*), and likewise livestock (*pecus*), are named, that is, from feeding (*pascere*). [Col. 0105B] Swimming creatures are called reptiles because they have the appearance and nature of creeping: although they plunge into the deep, they creep in swimming. Hence David says: “This sea is great and broad of hands; there are creeping things without number” (Ps. CIII).

Amphibians are certain kinds of fish so called because, living on land and in water, they have the capacity of walking on land and the function of swimming in water. For Greek ἀμφι (*amphi*) is rendered in Latin “both,” that is, creatures which live on lands and in waters, such as seals, crocodiles, and hippopotami—that is, river-horses.

On the asp-turtle see Book II, chapter 36.

Whales are beasts of immense size, so called from emitting and pouring forth waters. For more than other sea beasts they vomit up waves. For βάλλειν (*ballein*) in Greek means “to emit” and “to hurl.” The male whale is the *musculus*; this creature is said to conceive through intercourse with it. There is also a sea monster called the sawfish (*serra*), on which see Book II, chapter 22.

Dolphins have their established name or designation because they follow the sounds of human beings, or because they gather in herds for harmony. Nothing in the sea is swifter than they are, for they often leap over ships in flight. When they sport amid the waves and carry themselves onward by a headlong leap through the movements of the waters, they seem to indicate storms. These are properly called *simones*. There is also a kind of dolphin in the River Nile with a serrated back; by cutting open the tender bellies of crocodiles, they kill them.

[Col. 0105D] Sea-pigs, commonly called *suilli*, are so called because, while seeking food, they dig the ground beneath the water in the manner of swine. They have the function of the mouth around the throat, and unless they plunge their snout into the sand, they gather no food.

The swordfish (*gladius*) is so called because it has a pointed snout, with which it pierces ships and sinks them.

The sawfish (*serra*) is named because it has a serrated crest and, swimming beneath ships, cuts them apart.

The scorpion-fish is so called because it injures when lifted in the hand. Some report that, if ten crabs are tied together with a bundle of basil, all the scorpion-fish in that area gather at that place.

The crocodile, named from its saffron colour, is born in the River Nile. It is a four-footed animal living on land and in water, generally twenty cubits long, armed with terrible teeth and claws, and with skin so hard that if its back is struck by the blow of strong stones, it suffers no harm. At night it rests in water and by day on land. It broods its eggs on land; the male and female take turns sitting upon them. The sawfish kills it by cutting open its belly.

[Col. 0106A] A fish is called the wolf (*lupus*) because of its greed and ingenuity in catching prey. Thus, when surrounded by a net, it is said to plough up sand with its tail and thus, hidden, pass through the net.

The red mullet (*mullus*) is so called because it is soft and tender. They say that eating it restrains sexual desire and dulls the sharpness of the eyes. People who eat it frequently smell of fish. A mullet killed in wine produces an aversion to wine in those who drink from it or eat the fish itself.

[Col. 0106B] The mullet (*mugilis*) has its name because it is very agile. As soon as it perceives the fishermen’s nets arranged for it, it immediately turns back and leaps over the net, so that you would think the fish was flying.

There are, therefore, countless kinds of fish and countless uses of them. Some produce eggs, such as the larger variegated fish called trout (*tructae*), and entrust them to the waters to be brooded. Water itself generates and creates, and still performs the office of that command of the perpetual law, like a kindly mother of living creatures.

Others bring forth living young from their own bodies, as the huge whales, dolphins, seals, and other such creatures. When they swallow their offspring, if they perceive that any snares or terror are at any time being directed against their young, they are said, in order to protect them or to calm the fear of their tender age [Col. 0106C] by maternal affection, to open their outer mouths, suspend their offspring from their teeth, receive them into the inner body, and hide them in the womb that bore them. What human affection could imitate this devotion of the fishes? Their mouths are sufficient for our satiety; for them it is not enough to open their entrails, receive their young, call them back unharmed, revive their offspring again with their warmth, nourish them with their breath, and admit two into one body, until they bring them to safety or defend their young from dangers by the interposition of their own body. Who, seeing these things, would not yield to such great devotion in fishes? Who would not marvel and be astonished that nature preserves in fishes what it does not preserve in human beings? Very many women, seized by suspicion of a stepmother’s hatred, have killed their own children; others, as we read, in famine [Col. 0106D] have eaten their own offspring, and a mother has become a tomb for her human pledges. But for the young of fishes, the parent’s womb is like a wall: by a sort of rampart of maternal entrails it keeps its pledges unharmed. Therefore the different kinds of fish have different uses. Some lay eggs; others produce living and fully formed young. Those that lay eggs do not weave nests like birds, do not clothe their offspring by prolonged labor, and do not rear them with trouble to themselves. The egg falls; the water, like a kindly nurse, receives it into a certain lap of its own nature and quickly brings forth the creature by warming it. For the egg, animated by the parent’s continual touch, falls, and a fish emerges.

Then how pure and inviolate is their succession: none mingles with another, but each with its own kind. For they do not know [Col. 0107A] the adulterous contamination of alien fishes, as do those animals which mate—horses and asses—which, though of different kinds, human beings with great care cause to breed with one another; or again when horses and she-asses are mixed together: these are truly adulteries against nature. For surely the offense committed in the pollution of nature is greater than that committed in the injury of a person. And you, O man, procure these things, interpreter of beastly adultery! You consider that animal more valuable than the rest which is adulterous, rather than that which has been produced according to nature’s law. You yourself confuse alien kinds and mix different animals; you commonly compel unwilling creatures to forbidden intercourse, and call this ingenuity, because you cannot do the same with human beings—so that a mixture of different kinds may produce offspring. Yet you take from a human being that with which he was born, [Col. 0107B] strip manhood from a man, and, cutting off a part of the body, destroy sex: you make a eunuch, so that human audacity may accomplish what nature denied. Consider from this how good a mother water is. You, O man, have taught fathers’ repudiation of their children, separations, hatreds, and injuries; learn what the reciprocity of a parent ought to be. Fish cannot live without water; they cannot be separated from the fellowship of their parent, nor distinguished from the service of their other nourisher [altricis]; and by a certain law of nature they die immediately when separated.

What shall I say of the density of their teeth? They do not have teeth only on one side, as sheep and oxen do; rather, both parts are armed with teeth. Since they live in water, if they chewed their food for too long and did not swallow it quickly, their [Col. 0107C] food might be swept from their teeth and dissolved by the wash of waters. Therefore they have close-set and sharp teeth, so that they may cut and consume food swiftly and swallow it without delay or hesitation. Accordingly, they do not chew the cud; only the scarus, however, is reported to ruminate, by those who have either had occasion, experience, or zeal to ascertain such matters.

Indeed, fish themselves have not escaped the violence of the more powerful; for everywhere the weaker are subject to the greed of the stronger. The weaker anyone is, the more swiftly he lies exposed to the prey of predators. Many feed on plants and tiny worms. But there are some that devour one another, feeding upon their own flesh. Among them the smaller is food for the larger, and then the larger itself is attacked by one stronger; and the predator becomes the food of another predator [Col. 0107D]. Thus it comes about that, when one fish has devoured another, it is devoured by another, and both come together into one belly: each, swallowed with its own devourer, becomes together in one entrail a partnership of prey and revenge. Envy itself perhaps willingly agrees to this, as it does among us. For this did not begin from nature, but from greed; or rather, fish have been given for human use as a sign, so that in them we may see the vices of our own conduct and guard against them by their examples, lest any sinner attack one weaker than himself and thereby offer against himself an example of injury to someone stronger. Thus whoever harms another prepares for himself a snare into which he himself may fall. You too are a fish: you who attack another’s entrails, sink the weak, and pursue the fallen into the depths. Beware lest, while pursuing him, you yourself fall into the hands of one stronger [Col. 0108A], and he whom you pursue—who fled from your snares before awaiting your misery, and feared you while you pursued him—lead you into another’s ambushes.

A certain fish is called *scarus* because it alone is said to chew its food again, since other fishes do not ruminate. It is also said to be ingenious. When enclosed in wicker fish-traps, it does not burst out by the front opening or force its head through the hostile withes; rather, with repeated blows now of its teeth, now of its tail, it loosens the barriers and thus withdraws backward. If another *scarus* happens to see its struggle, it takes hold of the escaping fish’s tail with its teeth and assists its efforts to break out.

The little fish *echineis*, about half a foot long, has its name because by clinging to a ship it holds and delays it [Col. 0108B], from the word ἔχω (*echō*), “I have,” or ἔχομαι (*echomai*), “I cling,” and the noun ναῦς (*naus*), “ship.” For though winds rush and storms rage, the ship nevertheless seems to stand in the sea as though rooted there; and it does this not by holding it back, but as though clinging to the earth. The Latins call it *remora*, “a delay,” because it compels ships to stand still.

Its resemblance to a snake gave the eel (*anguilla*) its name. Its origin is from mud and heavenly dew. Wherever and whenever it is caught, it is so slippery that the more firmly it is pressed with a bare hand, the more quickly it slips away. They report that the eastern river Ganges produces eels thirty feet long. Eels killed in wine give those who drink that wine an aversion to wine.

The Greeks call the moray eel μύραινα (*myraina*) because [Col. 0108C] it coils itself into circles. It is said to be exclusively female and to conceive by a serpent. For this reason fishermen summon and catch it, as if by the serpent’s hiss. It is difficult to kill by a blow from a stick, but immediately killed by a blow from a rod. It certainly has its life in its tail: they say that when its head is struck it is scarcely killed, but when its tail is struck it is immediately deprived of life.

The polypus—that is, the many-footed creature, for it has very many feet—is ingenious: it goes after a hook and, embracing it with its arms rather than biting it, does not let it go until it has gnawed away the bait around it.

The torpedo is so called because it makes the body numb. If anyone touches it while it is alive—even from a distance, whether with a spear or a rod—it makes numb [Col. 0108D] anyone, however powerful his arms may be, and binds the feet of the most robust man for running. So great is its force that even the emanation from its body affects the limbs.

The crab, an animal that walks sideways, devises these tricks for the sake of food. It too delights in the oyster and seeks the feast of its flesh, but in desiring food it foresees danger. This hunt is difficult and dangerous. It is difficult because the inner food is enclosed by the oyster’s stronger shell. Nature, the interpreter of the royal command, has fortified the softness of its flesh, as with certain walls; it nourishes and warms it in the hollow recess at the center of its shells and spreads it, as it were, into a kind of valley. Therefore all the crab’s attempts are futile, because it cannot by any force [Col. 0109A] open the closed oyster. And it is dangerous if the oyster shuts upon its claw. Therefore the crab resorts to stratagems and devises snares by a new trick. Since every kind of living creature, however different, is soothed by some pleasure, it watches for the time when the oyster, in a place remote from every wind, opens that dwelling to the sun’s rays and unbars the enclosure of its shells so as to receive, through the free air, a certain pleasure in its inner parts. Then the crab secretly throws in a pebble—that is, a small stone—which prevents the oyster from closing; and thus, thrusting its claws into the open shell, it feeds upon the oyster’s inner flesh. So also vicious people, after the fashion of the crab, creep by deceptive contrivance into the use of another’s property, and support the weakness of their own virtue by a kind of cunning. They weave deceit against a brother and feed upon another’s [Col. 0109B] misfortunes. But be content with what is your own, and do not let another’s losses feed you. A good food is the simplicity of innocence, which possesses its own goods, knows no plotting against those of another, and does not burn with the offspring of greed. To it every unjust profit is a loss to virtue and fuel for desire. It is therefore blessed if it knows its own goods, since the virtue of poverty is to be preferred to all treasures. Is not a little thing with the fear and love of God better than a great treasure without that fear and love? For hospitality with vegetables and grace is better than a preparation of fattened calves with discord. Let us therefore use ingenuity to seek grace and preserve salvation, not to entrap another’s innocence. It is nevertheless permissible for us to use examples drawn from the sea [Col. 0109C] for the advancement of our salvation, not for another’s peril.

The sea-urchin is a small, cheap, and contemptible marine creature. It is commonly a sign of an approaching storm or a herald of calm to sailors. When it senses a storm of winds, it seizes a heavy pebble and carries it as ballast, drawing it like an anchor lest it be tossed by the waves. Thus it balances itself not by its own strength but is made stable and guided by another’s weight. Sailors take this indication as a sign of coming disturbance and take precautions for themselves, lest an unexpected tempest find them unprepared. What mathematician, astrologer, or Chaldean can thus comprehend the courses of the stars, the movements of heaven, and the signs? By what ingenuity does it gather these things? By what teacher does it learn them? Who interpreted for it so great an omen? Human beings often see a disturbance in the air and are often deceived, because it is commonly dispersed without a storm. The sea-urchin is not deceived. Its own signs never pass the sea-urchin by. Whence has so small a creature such foreknowledge, that it announces what is to come?
