Accordingly, it has nothing greater than possessing so great a prudence. Believe that through the favor of God, Lord of all things, it has received this gift of foreknowledge. For if God so clothes the grass, so feeds the birds, if he prepares food for ravens—for their young cry to the Lord—and if he has given women wisdom in weaving; if he has not left the spider without a share in wisdom, though it so subtly and skillfully hangs its loose nets in doorways; if he [Col. 0110A] has given strength to the horse and loosed fear from its neck, so that, coming from the plains, it meets kings with a neigh, scents battle from afar, and is aroused by the sound of the trumpet; if he has filled these irrational creatures and other insentient things, such as grass and lilies, with the wisdom of his ordering, why do we doubt that he has also bestowed on the sea-urchin the grace of foreknowledge? He has left nothing unexamined, nothing neglected. He who feeds all sees all; he who made all things in wisdom fills all things with wisdom, as it is written (Ps. CIII [104]). Therefore, if he did not pass over the sea-urchin in the gift of his visitation, if he considers it and informs it by signs of future things, does he not consider you? Indeed he does, as his divine wisdom testifies, saying: “If he watches the birds, if he feeds them, are you not worth more than they?” “If God so clothes the grass which is today [Col. 0110B] and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith?” (Matt. VI.)

Shellfish and snails (*conchae* and *cochleae*) are so called because they are hollowed when the moon wanes. For in all enclosed sea creatures and shells, their bodies swell with the moon’s increase and are emptied with its waning. When the moon is increasing, it increases moisture; when it is waning, moistures diminish. This is what the natural philosophers say. *Concha* is the original name; from it, by derivation, comes *cochlea*, as though “little shell” (*conchula*). There are many kinds of shellfish, including pearl-bearing ones, called *cocaeloae*, in whose flesh the precious little stone called a pearl (*unio*) is formed. Those who have written on the natures of animals report that at night [Col. 0110C] they seek the shore and conceive pearls from heavenly dew; hence *cocaeloae* are named as though “conceiving from heaven.”

The murex is a sea-snail, so called from its pointedness and roughness. It is also named *conchylium*, because, when cut around with iron, it emits tears of purple color, from which purple dye is made. Hence it is called *ostrum*, because this dye is extracted from the moisture of the shell.

They wish crabs to be called so because they are shells with legs, creatures hostile to oysters; for they live on their flesh. As I have already said, it is an animal of unusual ingenuity. Unable to open the oyster’s strong shell, it watches for the moment when the oyster opens the fastenings of its shells [Col. 0110D], then secretly inserts a small stone, and, preventing closure, gnaws the oyster’s flesh. There are two kinds of crabs, freshwater and marine. The oyster (*ostrea*) is named from the shell by which its softness is protected; for the Greeks call a shell ὄστρακον (*ostrakon*).

Mussels (*musculi*) are snails, and oysters conceive from their milk. They are called *musculi* as though *masculi*, “males.” The tortoise (*testudo*) is called a fish because it is covered by a shell like a vaulted roof. There are four kinds of tortoises: land tortoises; sea tortoises; mud tortoises—that is, those living in mud and marsh; and a fourth kind, river tortoises, which live in fresh water. Some report, though this is incredible, that ships carrying a tortoise’s right foot proceed more slowly. Frogs are so named from their chattering, because they resound about their native marshes and make vocal sounds with importunate cries [Col. 0111A]. Some of them are called aquatic, some marsh frogs, some *rubetae*, because they live among brambles and thorns and are larger than the rest. Others are called *calamitae*, because they live among reeds and bushes; they are the smallest of all, very green, mute, and voiceless. *Agredulae* are little frogs that remain on dry land or in fields, and are so called from this. Some deny that dogs bark if a live frog has been given to them in a morsel.

Pliny says that there are one hundred and forty-four names of all animals living in water, belonging to the kinds of sea-monsters, snakes common to land and water, crabs, shellfish, *pelorides*, soles, lizards, squids, and similar creatures.

## CHAPTER LVI. On Trees

[Col. 0111B] Some think that the name for trees (*arbores*) is derived from strength (*robur*), just as that for herbs (*herbae*) is believed to derive from clinging (*haerere*), because they adhere to the earth by their roots. The two are almost alike for this reason: one is produced from the other. For when you cast seed into the earth, first an herb arises; then, when nourished, it grows into a tree, and within a short time what you had seen as an herb you behold as a young tree. An *arbustum* is a young and tender tree in which grafting may be done, or a tree to which a vine is wedded and clings; hence it is called an *arbustum*, as it were, “a tree’s stake.” Others take *arbustum* to mean a place in which trees stand, like willow-groves (*saliceta*) and green thickets (*vireta*), where there are willows, young shoots, and green growth. A shrub (*frutex*) is rightly called smaller than a tree because with its foliage it covers the ground [Col. 0111C]. *Nemus* is a Greek word, from νέμω (*nemō*), “I pasture,” because flocks pasture in it; and it is planted for pleasure. Others wish it to be called, as though it were Latin, from *nemo* (“no one”) or from *numina* (“divinities”), because pagans sacrificed there to their idols. A grove (*lucus*) is a thick stand of trees that takes light away from the ground, by antiphrasis because it does not shine; or it comes from *lux*, “light,” because torches or candles shone there amid the darkness of woods. A wood (*saltus*) is a tall density of trees, so called because it leaps (*exsilit*) upward and rises on high, or because wild animals and cattle sometimes leap there. Grafting (*insitio*) is when, after a trunk has been split, a shoot of a fruitful tree is inserted into a barren one. Plants (*plantae*) are slips taken from trees. Nursery plants (*plantaria*) are those grown from seeds with roots and transplanted from their native soil. A root (*radix*) is so called because [Col. 0111D], fixed in the earth by certain rays, it sinks into the depths. For natural philosophers say that the depth of the roots and the height of certain trees are equal. The trunk (*truncus*) is the stock and upright body of the tree, standing upon the root. The ancients called bark *corux*. Bark (*cortex*) is so called because it covers wood as hide (*corium*) does. The inner bark (*liber*) is the inner part of the bark, so named because it is freed—that is, removed—from the bark; it is something between the wood and the outer bark. Branches (*rami*) flow out from the trunk, just as shoots (*surculi*) come from branches or root. Shoots are named from the cutting of the saw. A thicket (*virgultum*) is what sprouts from the root; a branch (*ramus*) is what comes from the very strength of the tree; a twig (*virga*) is what comes from branches. Properly, however, a *virgultum* is that which grows at the tree’s root and is cut off by farmers as nearly useless; hence it is called *virgultum*, because it is taken away from the twig [Col. 0112A]. A twig (*virga*) is named from force (*vis*) or strength (*virtus*), because it has much force in itself; or from greenness (*viriditas*); or because it is a sign of peace, in that it restrains force. Hence magicians use the rod called a caduceus to reconcile serpents with one another, and for this reason they depict them bound upon it. Philosophers, kings, messengers, masters, and envoys also use it. The upper parts of trees are called *flagella*, because they endure frequent blasts of wind. The tops of plants are called *cimae* and *cimata*, as though “hair” (*comae*). Leaves are called φύλλα (*phylla*) in Greek; hence the word has come to us by derivation. Flowers (*flores*) are named because they quickly flow down (*defluunt*) from trees, as though *fluentes*, since they quickly dissolve. They have a twofold charm: color and fragrance. By the south wind flowers are dispersed; by the west wind they are produced. We call a pregnant shoot a bud (*germen*), from begetting (*generare*); hence also germination. [Col. 0112B] Fruit (*fructus*) takes its name from *frumen*, that is, the projecting part of the throat by which we eat; hence also grain-crops (*fruges*). Properly, fruits are those of fields and trees which we use; in animals, however, “fruit” is applied improperly and metaphorically. Apples or fruits (*poma*) are named from *opimus*, that is, from abundance of plenty. They are called ripe (*matura*) because they are fit to eat, and likewise unripe (*immatura*), because before they become ripe they are hard to eat. *Poma* are whatever fruits do not enclose their principal fruit in a kernel. According to Varro, firewood (*ligna*) is so called because it is gathered (*leguntur*) to build a fire; according to some, because when kindled it is transformed into light. Hence also a lamp is called *lychnus*, and the *elychnium*, which burns in it, supplies light. A firebrand (*torris*) is burned wood [Col. 0112C], which the common people call a *titio*; a *foce* is wood half-burned and extinguished. *Quisquiliae* are stalks mixed with dry shoots and leaves; they are the refuse of the earth.

The palm is so called because it is the emblem assigned to a victor’s hand, or because its branches are spread out like the palm of a human hand. It is a tree, the sign of victory, clothed with tall and graceful foliage and long-lasting leaves, preserving its leaves without any succession. The Greeks call it *phoenix*, because it lasts a long time, in likeness to that Arabian bird which is said to live for many years. Its fruits are called dates (*dactyli*) from their likeness to fingers.

[Col. 0112D] The laurel (*laurus*) was called *laudus*, from the word “I praise” (*laudo*), for victors’ heads were crowned with it amid praises. Among the ancients it was called *laudus*; later, with the letter *d* removed and *r* substituted, it was called *laurus*, as with *auriculae*, which were originally called *audiculae*, and *medidies*, which is now called *meridies*. The Greeks call this tree *daphne*, because it never loses its greenness, and for this reason victors were formerly crowned with it. This tree alone is also commonly believed never to be struck by lightning. The apple tree (*malus*) is said to be named from Greek because its fruit is the roundest of all fruits; hence true apples are those that are especially round. Some say that apples are called *mala* because the Greeks call them *mela*; others say that they are named from sweetness, because its fruit has the taste of honey or because they are preserved in honey. The pomegranate (*malum punicum*) is so called because its kind was brought from the Punic region [Col. 0113A]. It is likewise called the seeded apple (*malum granatum*), because within the roundness of its rind it contains a multitude of seeds. The fig (*ficus*) is called in Latin from fecundity. For it is more fertile than other trees, producing fruit three and four times in each year; while one crop ripens, another arises. Hence dried figs (*caricae*) are also named from abundance. The Egyptian fig is said to be more fertile: when its wood is thrown into water, it immediately sinks; and when it has lain in mud for a while, it then rises to the surface, by a reversal of nature, since, once soaked, it should have sunk through the weight of moisture. Figs frequently eaten by old people are said to smooth out their wrinkles. They also say that the fiercest bulls, tied to a fig tree, become tame. [Col. 0113B] The mulberry (*morus*) is named from Greek; the Latins call it *rubus*, because its fruit or shoots are red. It is a wild mulberry bearing fruit, by which shepherds’ hunger and want are sustained in the wilderness. Its leaves, laid upon a serpent, are said to kill it. The names *sycomorus* and *morus* are Greek. The sycamore is called the “foolish fig,” because σῦκον (*sykon*) is Greek for “fig” and μωρός (*moros*) for “foolish.” It is also called *marisca* by the Latins and *celsa*, “tall,” from its height, because it is not short like the others. The walnut (*nux*) is so called because its shade or the dripping of its leaves harms neighboring trees. The Latins also call it *juglans*, as though “Jove’s acorn.” For this tree was consecrated to Jupiter. Its fruit has such power that, when thrown among suspected foods of herbs or mushrooms, it draws out, carries away, and extinguishes [Col. 0113C] whatever poison there is in them. “Nuts” generally means all fruits covered in a harder skin, such as pine nuts, hazelnuts, acorns, chestnuts, and almonds. Hence kernels (*nuclei*) are so called because they are covered by a hard skin. By contrast, all soft fruits are called apples (*mala*), but with the addition of the lands in which they were first produced, such as peaches (*persica*), pomegranates (*punica*), Matian apples (*matiana*), and so forth. Almond (*amygdala*)—ἀμύγδαλον (*amygdalon*)—is a Greek name; in Latin it is called the long nut. Before all trees, it clothes itself with flowers and is earlier than succeeding trees in producing fruit. The Latins call the chestnut by a Greek name; for the Greeks call it κάστανον (*kastanon*). Some think it is named from castration, because its paired fruits are hidden in the husk like testicles and, when they are cast out, are as though castrated. Once cut down, this tree customarily sends up shoots like a forest [Col. 0113D]. The holm oak (*hex*) is a tree bearing acorns, named from “chosen” (*electus*), because people first chose the fruit of this tree for their food. Hence the poet:

> All mortals belched acorns from their throats.

For before the use of grain, ancient people lived on acorns. The beech (*phagus*) and the oak (*aesculus*) are thought to be called acorn-bearing trees because people once lived and took food from their fruits. For *aesculus* is named from food (*esca*). *Phagus*, however, drew its name from Greek: φαγεῖν (*phagein*) means “to eat” in Greek. *Xylicon*, which the Latins corruptly call *siliqua*, received such a name from the Greeks because its fruit is sweet. For ξύλον (*xylon*) in Greek [Col. 0114A] means “wood,” and γλυκύς (*glykys*) “sweet.” The juice pressed from this tree’s fruit is called *acatia* by the Greeks. The pistachio tree (*pistacia*) is so called because the rind of its fruit has the scent of spikenard (*nardus pistici*). The pine is a pitch-producing tree, called from the sharpness of its leaves; for the ancients called “sharp” *pinnum*. They call one pine *pitin*, another *peucen*; we call the latter *picea*, because it sweats out pitch. On the islands of Germany this tree’s tears produce amber. A drop flowing down hardens into a solid through cold or heat and becomes a gem, taking its name from its quality: *succinum*, because it is the tree’s juice (*succus*). The pine is believed to benefit everything stored beneath it, just as the walnut harms everything. The fir (*abies*) is so called because it goes far beyond other trees and rises high above them. Its nature lacks earthly moisture and is therefore considered serviceable and light [Col. 0114B]. Some call it Gallic, because of its whiteness. It is without knots. The cedar is also called κέδρος (*kedros*) in Greek. Its leaves resemble the cypress; its wood has a pleasant scent and endures for a long time, never being destroyed by moths. Therefore ceilings in temples are made from this wood for their durability. The resin of this wood is called *cedria*; it is so useful in preservation that things coated with it suffer neither moths nor decay with time. Cypress is called κυπρίασσος (*kypriassos*) in Greek, from the name of a boy, because its head rises to a point from its rounded form; hence its tall roundness is also called *eonos* [uncertain reading]. From this its fruit is called a cone (*conus*), because its rounded shape resembles a cone; hence cypresses are called cone-bearing. [Col. 0114C] Such wood has a virtue almost equal to cedar, is also fit for temple beams, and, by its impenetrable solidity, never yields to a burden, but remains with the firmness it had at the beginning. The ancients used to set cypress branches near a pyre, so that, while corpses were burned, they might overpower the smell of the bodies with its pleasant fragrance.

The juniper is thought to be called ἄρκευθος (*arkeuthos*) in Greek; by some it is called in Latin *junipyrus*, as though “helping fire.” *Pyr* either comes from its ending in a narrow point from a broad base, like fire, or because it retains fire enclosed within it for a long time, so that if embers are covered with its ashes, they last for a whole year. For πῦρ (*pyr*) is Greek for “fire.”

[Col. 0114D] The plane tree (*platanus*) is so called from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and broad; for the Greeks call “broad” πλάτος (*platos*). Scripture expressed this tree’s name and shape when it says: “I have spread out like a plane tree in the streets [I have been exalted beside water].” It has very tender and soft leaves.

The oak (*quercus* or *querna*) is so called because the gods of the nations were accustomed to give answers through it to those seeking them. It is a very ancient tree, as we read of the oak of Mamre, beneath which Abraham dwelt, which is said to have endured through many centuries until the reign of Emperor Constantine. The fruit of its leaves is called a gall; that of its branches, an acorn or little acorn.

The ash (*fraxinus*) is said to be so called because it grows chiefly among rough [Col. 0115A], mountainous, and broken places. Of it Ovid says:

> …and the ash, useful for spears.

The alder (*alnus*) is so called because it is nourished by a river (*amnis*): it grows near water and does not readily live away from waters. It is tender and soft because it is nourished in a wet place. The elm (*ulmus*) takes its name because it thrives better in marshy and damp places; in mountainous and rough places it is less luxuriant.

The poplar (*populus*) is so called because a multitude (*populus*) of leaves and shoots arises from it. It differs, however, from *poly* and from *populus* meaning “a people” in the quantity of the first syllable. There are two kinds: one white, the other black. The white poplar is so called because its leaves are white on one side and green on the other. Thus it has two colors, as though signs of day and night, which periods are determined by the rising and setting of the sun. Poplars also produce resin and amber about the river Eridanus or, as others relate, in the regions of Syria. The willow (*salix*) is so called because it leaps quickly—that is, grows swiftly—a pliant tree suited to binding vines. Its seed is said to have this property: if anyone drinks it in a cup, he will be without children; it also makes women infertile. Poplar, willow, and linden are of soft wood and suited to carving. A wicker shoot (*vimen*) is so called because it has much force of vigor or greenness. For its nature is such that even if, when dry, it is washed, it becomes green; then, when cut and fixed in the ground, it itself sinks its roots into the earth. [Col. 0115C] Boxwood (*buxus*) is a Greek name, partly corrupted by the Latins. The Greeks call the evergreen tree *byxos*; its light wood is suited to the letter-forms of the alphabet. Hence also Scripture says: “Write on boxwood” (Isa. XXX).

## CHAPTER LVII. On the Discovery and Generation of Pearls, Also Discussed in Book II, Chapter 35

Craftsmen who seek pearls find them by means of the agate or achates stone. They tie an agate stone to the diver’s cord and lower it into the sea. When the agate stone comes to a pearl, the divers, following the cord, immediately find the pearl. I shall now explain how a pearl is born. There is a stone or fish called *conchus*, which comes to the seashore in the early morning before dawn, opens its mouth, and swallows the heavenly dew, the ray of the sun, and the stars which are above; and thus the pearl is born from the higher stars [Col. 0115D]. Thus the agate is John the Baptist. For this John showed us the intelligible pearl, our Lord Jesus Christ, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John I). The sea signifies the present age; the divers signify the company of the saints who are above, whereas those below are sinners.

On fire-bearing stones, see Book II, Chapter 19.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the Twelve Precious Stones

Jasper is placed first in the foundation of the house of the Lord. It has this nature: it is green in color. Whoever wears it fears no apparitions. It signifies those who hold the faith of God and [Col. 0116A] never wither away from it, but are always green in it; nor do they fear the deceits of the devil, who, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour: “Resist him, steadfast in the faith” (I Pet. V).

Second is placed sapphire, which is sky-colored—indeed, it has the color the heaven has when it is clear. It signifies those who, while still placed upon earth, give their attention to heavenly things and despise all earthly things as though they were not on earth. Such persons can say with the Apostle: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III).

Third is chalcedony [*catchedonius*]. While it is in a house, it does not shine; outdoors in the open it shines. It resists those wishing to engrave it. Warmed by a ray of the sun or by the rubbing of fingers, it draws chaff to itself [Col. 0116B]. By this stone are represented those who conceal their good works and perform in secret their fasting, almsgiving, and prayers, not wishing to be seen by people, as God commanded: “But when you fast” (Matt. VI), etc.; again: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand does” (ibid.); and again: “When you pray, go into your chamber” (ibid.). But when their master—that is, a bishop or abbot—commands them to go forth, then their goodness appears and they shine, whether they wish to or not. And if anyone wishes to flatter them and, as it were, engrave or portray them, they do not accept such people’s praise and vain glory; rather, they firmly resist and do not yield to them, as Solomon warns when he says: “My son, if sinners have praised you”—“do not consent to them” (Prov. I). [Col. 0116C] Such persons, breathed upon by the rays of the true sun—that is, Christ—or, as it were, drawn together and warmed by the fingers—that is, the gifts—of the Holy Spirit, draw chaff, that is, sinners, to themselves by the word of their preaching and the example of their goodness, and join them to themselves.

Fourth is the emerald. Its nature is as follows. It is of such great greenness that it surpasses in its green color all herbs, all leaves of trees, and all gems. It is born in Scythia, a land uninhabitable because of cold. There dwell only griffins, which are partly terrestrial beasts and partly birds. They have four feet and resemble lions in body, head, and feet, and eagles in wings. That land is exceedingly filled with such gems, and these griffins [Col. 0116D] guard them, so that no nation can take them except the Arimaspi, a people having only one eye in the forehead. They fight the griffins for these gems, for the griffins that guard them wish to take them away when the Arimaspi seize them; and it is through these Arimaspi that we have them. This gem signifies those who, strengthened by faith and greener than others, overcome unbelievers by that faith; these, like griffins, are always cold to charity and goodness because they do not possess it, and they harm those who do. The griffins guarding the gems signify devils, who begrudge to people the precious pearl of faith. They wish to have it and to take it from them, not because it benefits themselves, but because they do not wish those whom it benefits to possess it. They are rightly called griffins, as it were terrestrial beasts and birds, because [Col. 0117A] they are like terrestrial beasts, cast down into hell for their deserts, and like birds flying through pride. Against them fight the one-eyed—that is, those who do not walk by two ways, do not have a double heart or a double will, do not serve two masters, but always have one good intention toward the Lord, firmly hold the faith of God against all, and defend the grace of faith, which the griffins—that is, the devils—wish to take from them. Yet by God’s help they overcome them.

The fifth is sardonyx. It has three colours: dark brown and almost black at the bottom, white in the middle, and red above. This stone is compared to people who endure scourges and the punishments of suffering in their bodies for love of Christ, while inwardly they are white in spirit and pure without pretence; yet they despise themselves and regard themselves as sinners, and say with the Prophet: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21).

The sixth is sard, which is of one colour, like blood. It signifies the martyrs who poured out their blood for Christ’s love. David: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115).

The seventh is chrysolite, which gleams like gold and sends forth burning sparks. By it are signified those who understand divine Scripture and show to others, by deed and word, what they understand; they cast out from themselves, as it were, sparks of good work and speech, by which others are enlightened and kindled. They do not hide God in the earth, nor place the lamp under a bushel [Col. 0117C], but set it openly, that it may give light to all who are in God’s house (Matt. 5), doing as the Lord commanded: “Let your light shine before men” (ibid.).

The eighth is beryl, which shines like water struck by the sun and is said to warm the hand of the person holding it. It signifies persons enlightened by heavenly grace and shrewd in secular learning, who warm those with whom they associate by the fire of divine love and the example of good conduct, as beryl warms its holder’s hand. It also has two colours, green and pale, through which is indicated the life of those who are green through contemplation of heavenly things and pale through the activity of earthly administration.

The ninth is topaz. This stone is found rarely and is therefore the dearer and more precious the rarer it is. It has two principal colours: one utterly pure, like gold; the other like the sky when it is clear. It surpasses the brightness of all gems, and nothing is more beautiful to behold. If anyone attempts to polish it, it grows dim; if it is left by itself, it is brighter. Kings love it above all gems and all riches. It signifies those who have been tested and cleansed of the desire and filth of this age, like pure gold, and who direct their attention to the brightness of heavenly life. Those who possess this virtue and love the aforesaid life are brighter, purer, and more beloved of God than other people. Even the kings of this world reverence and honour this contemplative life. For the Lord [Col. 0118A] praised it with his own mouth, saying to Martha: “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken from her” (Luke 10). Those of this kind whom men wish to adorn with worldly rank are, as it were, made more worthless and of less merit by that adornment. It is read of blessed Martin that he performed many miracles before he became bishop; but, once adorned with the episcopate, lest he be lifted up, he performed fewer signs: he laid aside not his merits but his adornment.

Alternatively, it may be called the stone *topatius*, which contains within itself the colours of all stones, yet possesses one colour of its own; for Greek πᾶν (*pan*) means “all” in Latin. It signifies saints filled with every virtue, each having his own particular virtue.

The tenth is chrysopassus, purple in colour and speckled with drops of gold. It signifies those who [Col. 0118B] always lead their life amid tribulation and the labours of suffering, and finally end it by martyrdom, as the martyrs did. It is so called because *chrysos*, χρυστός, signifies “gold,” and the verb πάστω signifies “I scatter.” There is another stone, chrysoprase, blended of golden and green colour, because πρᾶσον (*prason*) signifies a leek, which is green.

Hyacinth is the eleventh. It changes its colour with the appearance of the sky: if the sky is bright, it shines; if dark, it becomes dark. By this stone are shown those who so adapt themselves that among the wise they are wise, perfect, and strong; then they descend to the foolish, imperfect, and weak, making themselves equal to them, so that, according to the capacity of their hearers [Col. 0118C], they speak wisely to the wise and humbly to the less wise and weak. Thus did Paul, who adapted himself to the qualities of those to whom he spoke. To the wise and perfect he spoke wisdom: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2). To the less perfect he said: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons, but as to carnal persons; I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). To the weak he said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11). Thus he accommodated himself to all, so as to become all things to all, as he says: “I became all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9). Alternatively, hyacinth, resembling water struck by the sun’s ray, denotes those filled with wisdom and suffused by the ray of the true sun.

Amethyst is the twelfth stone. It is red [Col. 0118D] like a rose, sending forth certain little flames from itself. It signifies those who, amid the torments of suffering which they endure for God, possess flames of charity: praying for those who kill them, and grieving more for the sins of their killers than for the penalty they themselves endure. It is suitably placed last, because it signifies those who pray for their enemies; for the virtue of virtues is to pray for one’s persecutors, and we find few who do this. Alternatively, amethyst is sprinkled with three colours: purple, violet, and rose. By purple are marked the saints who wear a heavenly habit on earth; by violet, their humility together with the fragrance of good action; by rose, charity, which flourishes so greatly in them that they come even to suffering.

[Col. 0119A] Its name is interpreted as “least intoxicated,” because α is a privative particle, and μεθυσθείς (*methystheis*) means “intoxicated,” while μέθυ (*methy*) means “intoxication.” Those who live in charity toward God and neighbour are least intoxicated by the wine of this world’s pleasures.

## CHAPTER LIX. On nature in general, and on the nature of man, the prince of natural things, created last and narrated here last.

Nature is so called because it causes something to be born. For it has power to generate and make. Some said that it was God, by whom all things were created and exist. *Genus* (“kind”) is named from generating; some derive its name from earth, from which all things are generated, for γῆ (*gē*), that is, *ge* in Greek, means “earth.” Life is called so because of vigour, or because it possesses the power of being born and growing; hence trees too are said to have life, because they generate and grow.

Man is called *homo* because he was made from *humus*, earth, as Genesis says: “God created man from the mud of the earth” (Gen. 2). By an improper usage, the whole human being is spoken of from both substances—that is, from the union of body and soul; properly speaking, however, *homo* is called so from *humus*. The Greeks called man *anthrōpos*, as it were “turned upward,” having branches downward and a root—that is, the mouth—upward, because he looks upward, raised from earth to contemplate his maker. This is what the poet Ovid indicates when he says:

> While all other animals look downward at the earth,  
> he gave man an uplifted face,  
> and commanded him to look upon heaven  
> and raise his upright countenance to the stars.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, bk. 2)

[Col. 0119C] He stands upright and looks toward heaven, that he may seek God, and should not attend to the earth like cattle, which nature made prone and obedient to the belly (Sallust, preface to *Catiline*).

The soul takes its name from winds, because it is wind. Hence wind in Greek is called ἄνεμος (*anemos*). It seems that, by drawing air through the mouth, we live; but this is plainly false, because the soul is generated much earlier than air can be drawn through the mouth, since it already lives in the mother’s womb. Therefore the soul is not air, as some supposed because they could not conceive its bodily nature.

The Evangelist calls spirit the same thing as soul, saying: “I have power to lay down my soul, and power to take it again” (John 10). Concerning this soul of the Lord, at the time of the Passion the Evangelist quoted above says: “He bowed his head and gave up the spirit” (John 19); and another says: “He sent forth the spirit” (Matt. 27 [printed “XVII”]). What is it to give up or send forth the spirit except to lay down the soul? But the soul is called so because it lives; it is called spirit, or a spiritual nature, because it breathes in the body. Likewise, *animus* is the same as soul; but the soul pertains to life, the *animus* to deliberation. Hence philosophers say that life remains even without *animus*, and the soul endures without mind. Thus they call people *amentes*, “out of their minds”; for they call mind that by which one knows, and soul that by which one wills. Mind is so called because it stands out in the soul, or because it remembers.

[Col. 0120A] Hence the forgetful are also called *amentes*. Accordingly, not the soul, but that which excels in the soul is called mind, as its head or eye. Hence man himself, according to the mind, is called the image of God. All these things are joined to the soul in such a way that they are one thing. The soul receives different names according to the effects of its functions. For while it gives life to the body, it is soul; while it wills, *animus*; while it knows, mind; while it recollects, memory; while it judges rightly, reason; while it breathes, spirit; while it senses something, sense. For *animus* is called *sensus* in respect of the things it perceives; hence *sententia* (“judgement”) also receives its name.

The body is called so because, once corrupted, it perishes. For it is dissoluble and mortal, and is someday to be dissolved. Flesh is called either from lacking (*carendo*) or falling (*cadendo*), because it lacks life—for properly speaking it belongs to the dead—or because it falls into death, whence also *cadaver* (“corpse”). Semen is the male seed, from which the bodies both of animals and of human beings are conceived; hence parents too are called creators. Flesh, considered as body, is composed of four elements: earth is properly in flesh, air in breathing, moisture in blood, fire in vital heat. For the elements each have their own share in us, which is restored to each when the composite is dissolved.

There are five bodily senses: taste, smell, hearing, sight, and touch. Of these, two—that is, two of their organs—open and close: sight and taste; two are always open: hearing and smell; [Col. 0120C] and the fifth, touch, does both and neither. They are called senses because through them the soul, with the power of perception, most subtly moves the entire body. Hence they are also called “presences,” because they belong to things present, just as things before the eyes are present to the eyes. Sight is what philosophers call the vitreous humour. Some maintain that seeing comes about either through external ethereal light or through an inner bright spirit, issuing through fine veins from the brain, passing through the membranes, and entering the air; then, by a mingling of similar matter, it produces sight. Sight is called so because it is livelier, more excellent, and swifter than the other senses, and has greater power, as memory does among the other functions of the mind. For it is nearer to the brain, from which all things flow. Thus we say that we “see” matters belonging to other senses, as when we say, “See how it sounds; see how it tastes,” and so forth.

Hearing is so called because it hears or drinks in voices—that is, receives sounds produced by air struck. Smell is as though touched by the scent of air, for the air touching the nostrils is perceived. So too *olfactus*, because it arises from odours. Taste is named from the throat or from tasting. Touch is so called because it handles and touches, spreading the vigour of sensation through all the limbs. For by touch we test whatever we cannot judge by the other senses. There are two kinds of touch: either something comes from outside to strike, or it arises within the body itself. Each sense is given its own organs. What is to be seen is apprehended by the eyes; what is to be heard, by the ears; soft and hard things are assessed and judged by touch [Col. 0121A]; flavour by taste; odour by the nostrils.

## CHAPTER LX. On the limbs and parts of man.

The first part of the body is the head. It received this name because all senses and nerves take their beginning from it; it in some way bears the role of the soul itself, which directs the body.

The crown is the highest part of the head, where the hairs turn back—that is, hang downward—as we descend from the summit of a mountain.

The skull is so named from “bald bones,” by loss, and the word is grammatically neuter.

The occiput is the rear part of the head, as it were opposite the head, or because it is at the back of the head.

Hair is, as it were, the “hairs of the head,” made to provide beauty [Col. 0121B], fortify the brain against cold, and protect it from the sun. Hairs are called from the skin from which they grow, just as *pilum* (“pestle”) is named from *pila*, where pigment is pounded.

A man’s cut hair is called *caesaries*, from cutting; hence it belongs only to men. For it is fitting for a man to be shorn.

*Comae* are properly cut hair, and the word is Greek; for the Greeks call locks κόμας (*komas*) from cutting, whence also κείρειν (*keirein*), “to shear.” Thus they are also called curls, which the Greeks likewise call *mallon*.

*Tresses* (*crines*) properly belong to women. They are called *crines* because they are separated by headbands; hence also the partings, by which they are divided and bound again, are called *discrimina*.

The temples are the regions lying beneath the skull on the right and left. They are so named because they move, and by that very movement, as it were, change the times (*tempora*).

The face is so named from its likeness or representation (*effigies*), for there is the whole form of a human being and recognition of each individual person. Countenance (*vultus*) is named because through it the will of the mind is displayed; according to the will, it changes into various expressions. Thus they differ: *facies* is understood simply as an individual’s natural appearance, whereas *vultus* denotes the qualities of the mind.

The forehead takes its name from the openings of the eyes, or from being carried before the rest. It too is a certain image of the mind and expresses its movements by its appearance, whether joyful or sad.

[Col. 0121D] The eyes are called either because coverings of eyelashes conceal them lest they be harmed by the blow of any injury that falls upon them, or because they contain hidden light—that is, secret or inwardly placed light. Of all the senses, they are nearest to the soul. Every indication of the mind is in the eyes; thus disturbance or cheerfulness of spirit appears in them. Eyes and lights are the same thing. They are called lights because light flows from them, or because from their beginning they hold enclosed light, or return to sight light received from without and set before it.

The pupil is the centre of the eye, in which the power of sight resides. Because little images are seen there, it is called *pupilla*, for small children are called *pupilli*. Many call it *pupilla* because it is pure and unstained, like girls. Physicians say that persons who will die within three days lack the pupils which we see in [Col. 0122A] the eyes; when these are not seen, despair of life is certain. The circle by which the white portions of the eye are separated from the pupil by distinct blackness is called the crown, because its roundness adorns the circumference of the pupil. Some call the very corners of the eyes “valves,” from their resemblance to folding doors.

The eyelids are the folds of the eyes, named from fluttering, because they are always moving and meet one another so as to refresh sight by continual motion. They are fortified with a rampart of hairs, so that anything which falls may be repelled even when the eyes are open, and, when they close in sleep, the eyes may rest hidden as though wrapped up. At the edge of the eyelids, at the points where the two meet when closed, hairs grow in an ordered row, providing protection to the eyes so that they may not easily receive sudden injuries and thereby be harmed; they keep away the contact of dust or any thicker matter, and by closing themselves exclude even disturbed air, thus making sight fine and clear.

Some think tears are so called from a laceration of the mind; others believe they are called *lacrymae* because the Greeks call them δάκρυα (*dakrya*). Eyelashes are the coverings by which the eyes are covered, and are called *cilia* because they conceal the eyes which they cover with safe guardianship. Eyebrows are so called because they are placed above the eyelashes. They are covered with hairs in order to provide the eyes with a stronger defence than the eyelids and to repel sweat flowing down from the head. The space between the brows, however, is the hairless middle between the eyebrows and eyelids.

The cheeks are the lower parts beneath the eyes, where the beard [Col. 0122C] begins; for in Greek *genos* means “beard,” and hence cheeks are so called because beards begin to grow from them.

The cheekbones are the projecting parts beneath the eyes, placed there for their protection. They are called *malae* either because they project below the eyes in a rounded form like apples, which the Greeks call *mela*, or because they are above the jaws.

The jaws (*maxillae*) are so called by diminutive formation from the cheekbones, as *paxillus* from *palus*, and *taxillus* from *talus*.

The mandibles are parts of the jaws, from which their name too is made.

The ancients called the beard so because it belongs to men, not women. The ears received their name from drawing in voices. Hence Virgil:

> “And with these ears I drank in her voice.”
> (*Aeneid*, book 4, line 359)

Or they are called so because the Greeks call the voice itself ἀνδήν (*audēn*), from hearing. By a change of letter, *aures* (“ears”) are called as it were *audes*. For a voice reflected through the windings of the ears makes the sound by which they receive the sense of hearing.

The pinna is the uppermost part of the ear, named from its point. The ancients called something pointed *pinnon*. Hence also *bipennis* and *pinna*.

The nostrils are so called because through them odour or breath never ceases to flow; or because they warn us through smell, so that we may be knowing and aware. Conversely, the ignorant and untrained are called *ignari*, “not knowing.” The ancients said “to have smelled” for “to have known.” Terence: “And not [Col. 0123A] to have learned anything for a full six months before he began anything at all.” The straight part of the nose, because it extends evenly in length and roundness, is called the column; its tip is the little pear, from the form of the pear fruit; the parts on the right and left are the little wings, from their resemblance to wings; the middle is the dividing boundary.

The mouth is so called because through it, as through a doorway, we bring food in and cast spittle out; or because food enters through it and speech comes out from it.

The lips are called from licking. Some maintain that the upper one is called *labium*, while the lower, because it is thicker, is *labrum*. Others call men’s lips *labra* and women’s *labia*, but the terms are confused.

Varro thinks the tongue is named from licking food; others, because it binds articulated sounds into words. For just as a plectrum strikes strings, so the tongue strikes against the teeth and brings about the emission of vocal sound.

The Greeks call teeth ὀδόντες (*odontes*), and Latin seems to derive its name from this. The front teeth are called incisors or cutters because they are the first to cut everything received. The following are called canines: two are in the right jaw and two in the left, and they are called canines because they resemble dogs’ teeth. People, because the front teeth can cut, hand food on to these so that they may break it up. The common people call them little columns because of their breadth, length, and roundness. The last are the molars, which work over, grind, and chew what has been cut by the former teeth and broken up; hence they are called molars. [Col. 0123C] The number of teeth is differentiated by sex: men have more and women fewer.

The gums are named from generating teeth. They were also made for the beauty of the teeth, lest bare teeth seem an object of horror rather than an ornament.

Our palate, like the sky, is placed above; hence *palatum* derives by derivation from *polus* (“pole,” “heaven”). Likewise the Greeks call the palate οὐρανίσκον (*ouraniskon*), because in its hollow shape it resembles the sky. The throat is named from pouring forth voices, as though *foces*, or *fauces* because we speak through it.

The windpipes are called so either because through them air—that is, breath—is carried from the lungs, or because they contain the vital breath in narrow and constricted passages. Hence they emit the sounds of the voice, which would sound in only one manner unless the tongue’s movement produced the distinctions of speech. In the Gallic language the tonsils are called *toles*; the common people call them, by a diminutive, tonsils, which are apt to swell in the throat.

The chin is so called because the mandibles arise from it; or because things are moved there; or because, when we mention something in speech, we move it.

The gullet takes its name from the throat. Its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils and has a route by which voice is conveyed to the tongue, so that it may strike words together; hence we say “to chatter.”

The oesophagus is next to the gullet, and through it food and drink are swallowed. Hence beasts that bring food back and chew it again are called ruminants.

[Col. 0124A] The sublingual [membrane] is the covering of the gullet, like a little tongue; it opens and covers the opening of the tongue.

The neck is named because it is stiff and round like a column, bearing and supporting the head, as it were a capitol; its front part is called the throat, its rear the nape.

The nape is so named because through it the brain is directed toward the spinal marrow, as it were the brain’s way. The ancients used *cervices* only in the plural; Hortensius was the first to say *cervix* in the singular. In the singular, *cervix* now denotes the member itself; in the plural, *cervices* often denotes stubbornness. Cicero in the *Verrines*: “You accuse the praetor of breaking necks.”

The shoulders are called, as it were, *armi*, to distinguish man from dumb beasts: men are said to have *humeri*, while they have *armi*; properly speaking, *armi* belong to quadrupeds.

The *hala* is the upper, rear, and more concealed part of the shoulder.

The arms are named from strength; for Greek βαρύ (*bary*) means “heavy” and “strong.” In the arms are the rounded masses of the muscles, and there is a conspicuous strength of musculature. In them are *tori*, that is, muscles, called *tori* because the entrails seem twisted there.

The elbow is named because we lean upon it when taking food.

According to some, the ulna is the extension of each entire arm; according to others, it is the elbow—which is more correct—because in Greek ὠλένος (*ōlenos*) means “elbow.”

[Col. 0124C] The armpits are so called because the movement of the arms begins from them in the manner of wings. Some call them *ascillae* or *axillae*, because the arms are *cillentur*—that is, moved—from them. Hence *oscilla* are so called because mouths are *cillentur*, that is, moved; for *cillere* means “to move.” Some call these places “goats,” because in most persons they give off a goat-like smell.

The hand is called so because it is the service (*munus*) of the whole body. It supplies food to the mouth, performs and administers everything, and through it we receive and give. By improper usage, *manus* also means an art or craftsman; hence we speak of the price of handiwork and of armed forces.

The right hand is called from giving: it is given as a pledge of peace and is offered as a witness of faith and safety. This is what Cicero means when he says: “By order of the senate I gave the public pledge—that is, my right hand.” Hence the Apostle says: “They gave to me and Barnabas the right hands of fellowship” (Gal. 2).

The left hand is called because it is smooth, that is, without the roughness and callus which labour produces on the right hand.

The *sinistra* is called as it were “without the right hand,” or because it allows a thing to be done and does not do it. For *sinistra* is named from allowing (*sinendo*).

The palm is the hand with fingers spread, just as the fist is the hand with fingers contracted. The fist is named from pricking (*pungendo*) or from fighting (*pugna*), or conversely the palm from spreading (*pandendo*).

The fingers are so named either because they are ten in number or because they are fittingly joined together; for they contain both a perfect number [Col. 0125A] and a fitting order. Hence the first is called the thumb because it prevails over the others in strength and power. The second is the index finger, the greeting finger, or the pointing finger, because we commonly greet, show, or indicate with it. The third is the indecent finger, because reproach is often expressed through it and the anus is cleaned with it; this is the middle finger. The fourth is the ring finger, because a ring is worn on it. It is also the medicinal finger, because physicians apply eye-salves with it, or because the pulses of sick people are felt with it. The fifth is the little-finger, because we scratch and clean the ear with it.

We call nails from Greek, for they call them ὄνυχες (*onyches*). Others wish the word to be derived from anointing (*unguendo*), because the nail is smooth and shining as though anointed. Nails belong to animals with distinct fingers, such as humans, apes, [Col. 0125B] birds, lions, dogs, and so on. Hooves belong to animals without distinct fingers, such as horses, mules, asses, oxen, deer, and similar animals, some of which have cloven hooves.

The trunk is the middle part of the body from the neck to the groin. Nigidius says: “The head is carried by the neck; the trunk is supported by the hips, knees, and legs.”

The thorax, as the Greeks call the front part of the trunk from the neck to the stomach, is what we call the chest (*arca*), because there is there a secret (*arcanum*) from which the other parts are excluded. Hence *arca* and *ara* are so named, as a secret thing. Its projecting parts are called breasts; between them the bony part is called the breastbone, and on the right and left are the ribs.

The chest (*pectus*) is so called because it is combed (*pexum*) between the projecting parts of the breasts; hence *pectus* is also so called because it produces combed hair.

The breasts are called because they are round, like little apples by diminutive formation. The nipples, however, are the heads of the breasts, which nursing infants grasp. They are called *papillae* because infants, while sucking milk, as it were touch them repeatedly. Thus *mamma* is the whole prominence of the breast, while *papilla* is the small part from which milk is drawn.

The udders are named either because they are fruitful (*ubera*) with milk, or because they are moist (*uvida*), filled with the moisture of milk like grapes. Milk draws the force of its name from its colour, because it is a white liquid; for Greek λευκός (*leukos*) means “white.” Its nature is transformed from blood. For after childbirth, whatever blood has not yet [Col. 0125D] been consumed for the nourishment of the womb flows by a natural passage to the breasts and, through their power, becomes white, taking on the character of milk.

The skin is the body’s outermost layer. It is called so because, being laid over the body, it suffers the first cutting; for Greek *cutis* means “cutting” in Latin. It is also called *pellis*, because by covering it drives away external injuries to the body and bears the first heat of wind and sun.

Skin when removed and treated is called hide (*corium*), and is thicker skin. *Corium* is so called by derivation because flesh is held or covered by it, but this properly belongs to brute animals.

The body’s pores are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are properly called breathing-holes, because through them the life-giving breath is supplied from outside.

[Col. 0126A] *Arvina* is fat adhering to the skin.

Pulp is flesh without fat, called so because it quivers; indeed it often springs back. Many also call it *viscum*, because it is sticky.

Members are parts of the body.

Joints are the means by which members are joined, named from fastening tightly (*arctando*). Or they are called joints because, bound together by sinews, they are tightened—that is, constricted. Their diminutives are *articuli*: we call the larger members, such as arms, *artus*, and the smaller ones, such as fingers, *articuli*.

Sinews are named by Greek derivation, for the Greeks call them νεῦρα (*neura*). Others think they are called *nervi* in Latin because the junctions of the limbs cling together by them. It is most certain that sinews furnish the chief substance of strength; for the denser they are, the more readily they increase firmness.

[Col. 0126B] The *compagiae* are the ends of bones, so called because, joined together by sinews, they adhere as if with some kind of glue.

Bones are the body’s supports; in them all posture and strength rests. Bones are called from being burnt (*usto*), because the ancients burned them; or, as others think, from the mouth (*ore*), because there they are exposed, whereas everywhere else they lie concealed under skin and entrails.

Marrow is so called because it is in the middle of bones, or because bones are moistened by it; for it fattens and strengthens them.

The vertebral processes are the upper parts of the bones, gathered together in thicker knots, so called because at them the limbs turn in bending.

Cartilages are soft bones without marrow, of which kind are the ear, the division of the nostrils, the ends of the ribs, and the coverings of bones that move. They are called cartilages because they lack pain when bent with slight rubbing.

Some think the ribs are called so because the internal organs are guarded by them and all the softness of the belly is safely enclosed.

The side is so called because, when we lie down, it lies hidden. It is the left and right portion of the body extending on either side between front and back. The right side has the more dexterous motion; the left is stronger and more suitable for carrying burdens. [Col. 0126D] It carries the shield, sword, quiver, and other burdens, so that the right hand may be free for action.

The back extends downward from the nape to the loins. It is called *dorsum* because it is the harder surface of the body, like the hard back of a bear, strong both for carrying and enduring.

The rear parts are so called because we lie on them supine upon the ground, which only man can do; dumb animals lie only upon their belly or side. Hence the term is improperly used of animals. The shoulder-blade is called from climbing. The space between the shoulder-blades is called the interscapular space.

The shoulder-blades are the projecting members on the right and left of the back, so called because in wrestling we press and throw them about, which the Greeks call πάλιν (*palin*).

[Col. 0127A] The spine is the jointing of the back, called so because it has small rays like sharp thorns. Its joints are called *spondylia* on account of the portion of brain that is said to travel through them in a long course to the other parts of the body. The sacred spine is the lowest part of the continuous spine, which the Greeks call ἱερὸν νῶτον (*hieron nōton*), “sacred back,” because it is the first thing formed when the child is conceived; hence among the Gentiles it was the first part offered to their gods in a sacrifice, and it is therefore called the sacred spine.

Varro says that the kidneys are named because streams of obscene moisture flow from them, ἀπὸ τοῦ ῥεῖν, from the verb *rhein*, “to flow.” For veins and marrow sweat a thin liquid into the kidneys; this liquid, again dissolved from the kidneys by sexual heat, flows down.

The loins are named from the wantonness of lust, because in men the cause of bodily pleasure is in them, as it is in women in the navel. Hence at the beginning of his speech Job was told: “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 38), so that there might be readiness to resist in the very places where lust customarily finds an occasion to rule.

The navel is the middle place of the body, called so because it is the boss of the flanks; hence the central projecting part of a shield, from which it hangs, is called a boss.

The flanks are called by a Greek term because we wrap ourselves around there; for Greek εἰλέω (*eileō*) means “to turn” and “to wrap around.”

The buttocks are so called because they are near the *colum*, which is long; they are the swellings of the buttocks.

[Col. 0127C] The buttocks are so called because we lean on them when sitting. Hence flesh is massed together in them, lest the weight of the pressing body cause the bones pain.

The genital parts of the body, as their name itself teaches, received their designation from generating offspring, because offspring is procreated and generated by them. They are also called the shameful parts because of modesty, or from puberty; hence they are covered by clothing. They are also called indecent because they do not have the same beauty of appearance as members placed openly and in view. The male organ is also called *veretum*, either because it belongs only to a man (*vir*), or because *virus* issues from it; for *virus* properly means the fluid flowing from the male nature; or it derives from sweeping (*verrendo*), or finally from truth (*vere*).

[Col. 0127D] The testicles are called by a diminutive from witnesses (*testes*), whose number begins with two. They supply seed to the penis, which they receive from the spinal marrow, kidneys, and loins for the purpose of procreation.

The scrotum is the skin in which the testicles are.

The posterior parts are so called because they are behind and turned away from the face, so that, when we evacuate the bowels, we may not defile our sight.

The passage is so called because through it excrement passes—that is, is discharged.

The thighs are called so because at that part the male sex differs from the female. They extend from the groins to the knees.

The *feminae*, by derivation from thighs, are the parts by which we cling to the backs of horses when riding; [Col. 0128A] hence in old times combatants were said to have lost horses “under their thighs.”

The hips are like joined axles, for the thighs move in them; their hollow sockets are called vertebrae.

The hocks are the folds at the back of the legs, borrowed from quadrupeds; they bend backward, as the knees in the front legs bend forward. They are so called because they are broken or bent below (*suffringuntur*), not above like knees.

The knees are the junctures of thighs and legs, and are called *genua* because in the womb they are set opposite the cheeks of the eyes. There they cohere and are related: knees are kin to the eyes, the indicators of tears and pity, for knees are named from cheeks (*genae*). Indeed, they say that a person is born and formed folded up at the knees, so that [Col. 0128B] the knees are raised, by which the eyes are formed hollow, round, and hidden; for in the mother’s womb the knees press upon them. Ennius: “And, brought to the cheek, he presses the knees.” Hence, when people prostrate themselves at the knees, they immediately weep. Nature wished them to recall and remember the maternal womb, where they sat, as it were, in darkness before coming into the light.

The legs are so called because with them we run and take steps, and they extend from the knees to the heels.

The shins are called as it were trumpets, since they resemble them in length and form. They are the bones, or front parts, of the leg; the calves are at the back.

The ankle is called from *tolus*, for *tolus* is a projecting roundness, and thus the dome of a round temple is called *tolus*. [Col. 0128C] The ankle is beneath the leg, and beneath the ankle is the heel.

Feet derive their name from a Greek etymology; for the Greeks call them *podas* [πόδας]. Some think they are so called from seeking the ground, because, fixed to the soil by alternating motions, they move forward.

The soles of the feet are named from flatness, because they are not rounded as in four-footed animals—lest a two-footed human being be unable to stand—but were formed flat and rather long, so as to make the body stable. The soles are the front parts of the feet and consist of many bones.

The heel (*calx*, *calcs*, or *calcis*) is the first part of the sole. It received its name from treading (*calcare*), because we tread the ground; hence also *calcaneus*, “heel.”

[Col. 0128D] The sole is the lower part of the foot, so called because by it we imprint our steps upon the earth. But “sole” is also said of anything that supports something else, as though “solid”; hence the earth too is called a sole because it supports all things: the air is the support of birds, and the sole of the foot supports the whole weight of the body.

By *viscera* we mean not only the intestines, but everything beneath the skin, between the skin, flesh, and bones. Likewise, the vital viscera are the regions surrounding the heart, so that *viscus* is, as it were, the force of the heart, because life—that is, the soul—is contained there. Likewise, the viscera are the heads of the sinews, joined together from blood and nerves.

Likewise, the muscles (*lacerti*) are named from their resemblance to crawling lizards (*lacertae*), because in each limb there are places from which they take their names, as the heart, which is in the middle of the body, is called after the name of similar animals living upon the earth. Thus muscles (*musculi*) are so called from their resemblance to mice (*mures*), just as *lacerti* derive from *lacerta*, “lizard.” Hence also the *tori*, because there the viscera seem twisted.

[Col. 0129A] The heart (*cor*) takes its name by Greek derivation, since the Greeks call it *kardian* [καρδίαν]; just as our word *cura*, “care,” is said to come from *cor*, “heart,” and *uro*, “I burn,” for in the heart resides every care and concern of life and knowledge. It is near the lung so that, when anger is inflamed, it may be tempered by the lung’s moisture. It has two arteries, of which the left has more blood and the right more breath; hence we observe the pulse in the right arm.

The precordia are regions near the heart through which sensation is perceived. They are called *praecordia* because there is the source of the heart and thought, or because they surround the heart; for they are membranes about the heart, in which is the seat of the affections.

[Col. 0129B] The pulse is so called because it beats; by its indication we understand either illness or health. Its movement is twofold: simple or composite. A simple pulse consists of one beat. A composite pulse consists of several irregular and unequal movements. When these movements have fixed intervals, they call it a dactylic pulse, so long as it remains free from defect.

Veins are so called because they are the paths of swimming blood, streams distributed throughout the whole body, by which all the limbs are irrigated.

Blood derives its name from a Greek etymology, because it is enlivened, sustained, and lives; for *saos* [σάος] means “sound” or “safe.” Blood is so called while it is in the body; when poured out, it is *cruor*, “gore.” It is called *cruor* either because, when shed, it runs, or because it falls while running. Others interpret *cruor* as ichor, corrupted blood that is discharged. Others call blood so because it is sweet. Blood is not sound except in the young. For physicians say that blood diminishes with age, whence old people tremble. Properly speaking, blood is the possession and seat of the soul; therefore women customarily tear their cheeks in mourning, so as to make an offering with their hands. Hence purple garments and purple flowers are also presented to the dead.

[Col. 0129C] The lung takes its name from Greek, for they call the lung *pleumon* [πλεύμων], because it is the heart’s fan, in which is *pneuma*, that is, breath or spirit; through which it is stirred and moved; hence the lungs too are so named. For in Greek *pneuma* [πνεῦμα] means “breath” or “spirit”: it emits and receives air by blowing and moving it. By this the lungs are moved and throb; they open to take in breath and contract to expel it. They are like an instrument of the body.

[Col. 0129D] The liver (*jecur*) takes its name from having a place near the heart. From there it draws in blood, which flies upward to the brain and is then diffused to the eyes, the other senses, and the limbs. By its heat it turns into blood the juice drawn to it from food, which it supplies to each limb for nourishment and sustenance. According to those who discuss natural philosophy, pleasure and desire, anger and love, reside in the liver.

[Col. 0130A] The fibres are the extremities of the liver, like the outermost parts of leaves on vines, or like protruding veins resembling tongues. They are said to be called *fibrae* because, among the pagans, diviners carried them in sacrifices to Phoebus’ altars, so that, after they had been offered and burned, they might receive answers.

The spleen is so called from “supplement,” being on the opposite side of the liver so that it should not be empty. Some think it was made for the sake of laughter: for we laugh with the spleen, grow angry with gall, think wisely with the heart, and love with the liver. When these four are in proper balance, the animal is whole.

Gall is so called because it is a small bag carrying the fluid called bile.

The Greek word *stomachos* [στόμαχος] means “mouth,” because it receives food like the doorway of the belly and sends it on to the intestines.

[Col. 0130B] The intestines are so called because they are enclosed in the interior part of the body. For this reason they are arranged in long interconnected coils, in the manner of circles, so that they may digest food received gradually and not be obstructed when further food is added.

The omentum is the membrane that contains the greater part of the intestines; the Greeks call it *epitolin*.

The diaphragm is the intestine or partition that separates the belly and the other intestines from the lung or the heart.

The caecum is the intestine that has no opening or outlet; the Greeks call it *tisonenteron*.

The jejunum is the thin intestine; hence it too is called “empty” (*jejunum*).

[Col. 0130C] The belly, the abdomen, and the womb differ from one another. The belly is that which digests food received; it is visible externally and extends from the breast to the groin. It is called *venter*, “belly,” because it supplies nourishment for life throughout the whole body.

The abdomen (*alvus*) receives food and is customarily cleansed through excrement; for the filth of dung flows from it. Sallust: “Pretending to cleanse his bowels.” It is called *alvus* because it is washed (*abluatur*).

Only women have a womb, in which they conceive, resembling a little stalk; nevertheless, authors often use the word for the belly of either sex, not poets only but others as well. The womb is called *uterus* because it is double and divides from each side into two parts, which spread and curve in opposite directions, twisting about in the manner of a ram’s horn; or because it is internally filled with a foetus. Hence also a skin or vessel (*uter*), because it contains something within, such as limbs and viscera.

[Col. 0130D] The *aqualiculus* properly belongs to a pig; from this comes its transferred use for the belly.

The matrix is so called because the foetus and embryo are generated in it. It cherishes the seed it receives, gives body to what it has cherished, and distinguishes what has received a body into limbs.

The vulva is named as though from *valva*, “a door,” that is, the doorway of the belly; or because it receives seed, or because the foetus proceeds from it.

The bladder is so called because it is, as it were, a vessel of water. It is filled with urine collected from the kidneys and is distended by fluid. Its use is not found in birds.

[Col. 0131A] Urine is named from Greek *oureō* [οὐρέω], “I urinate” or “piss,” and Greek *ouros* [οὖρος], by whose indication both health and disease are shown. In Latin this fluid is called *lotium*, because clothes washed with it are made clean.

Seed is that which, when cast either into the earth or into the womb, is received for the generation of fruits or offspring. It is a fluid produced from the digestion of food and body, diffused through the veins and marrow; then exuded, it grows in the kidneys like bilge-water. Expelled through intercourse and received into a woman’s womb, it is formed into a body by a certain heat of the viscera and by irrigation with menstrual blood.

Menstruation is women’s superfluous blood. The menses are so called from the cycle of the moon’s light, by which this discharge customarily occurs. For the moon is called *mene* [μήνη] in Greek; these are also called “the female matters.” For woman alone is a menstruating animal. By contact with this blood crops do not germinate, wine turns sour, plants die, trees lose their fruit, rust corrupts iron, and bronze objects blacken. If dogs eat it, they are driven into madness. The bitumen adhesive which is dissolved neither by iron nor by fire, when polluted by this blood, separates of its own accord. After many menstrual days, moreover, seed is not fertile because there is no longer menstrual blood by which it may be moistened and irrigated.

[Col. 0131B] Thin seed does not adhere in the female organs, for it slips away and lacks the power of adhesion. Likewise thick seed lacks generative power because, owing to its excessive density, it cannot mingle with female blood. Hence they say males and females become sterile either because of excessive thickness of blood or seed, or because of their excessive thinness. They say, however, that the human heart is formed first, because in it are both human life and wisdom. Then, on the fortieth day, the whole body is completed—a conclusion, they report, drawn from abortions. Others say that foetuses begin from the head; hence in the offspring of birds we see that the eyes are first formed in eggs. A foetus is so called because it is still kept warm in the womb. They likewise say that children are born resembling their fathers if the father’s seed is stronger, their mothers if the mother’s is stronger; by this same principle facial likenesses are produced. Those who reproduce the form of both parents are conceived when paternal and maternal blood or seed is mixed equally.

[Col. 0131C] They also say that children become like their grandfathers and great-grandfathers because, just as many seeds lie hidden in the earth, so within human beings are concealed seeds that will reproduce their parents’ forms. Girls are born from paternal seed, boys from maternal seed, because every offspring consists of double seed; and whichever part is greater envelops and takes possession of the likeness of its sex.

In our body some things were made solely for utility, such as the viscera; some for both utility and beauty, such as the senses in the face and the hands and feet on the body—limbs whose usefulness is great and whose appearance most becoming. Some exist solely for beauty, such as male nipples and the navel in both sexes. Some serve distinction: in men, the genitals, a long beard, and a broad chest; in women, smooth cheeks and a narrow chest, while, for conceiving and carrying foetuses, the loins and flanks are expanded. Since what pertains to the human being and to the parts of soul and body has been discussed in part, let us now add the stages of life.

[Col. 0132A]

## Chapter LXI. On the Ages of Human Beings and Their Names, Even unto Death and the Dead

There are six stages of life: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, mature adulthood, and old age. The first stage is infancy, from a child’s birth into the light, extending to seven years. The second stage is childhood, that is, purity, not yet fit for generation, extending to the fourteenth year. The third is adolescence, fit for generation, extending to twenty-eight years. The fourth, youth, the strongest of all ages, ends in the fiftieth year. The fifth age is that of the elder, that is, mature adulthood: a decline from youth toward old age, not yet old age but no longer youth, because it is the age of the *senior*, whom the Greeks call *presbytēn*; for an old man among the Greeks is not a *presbyter* but a *gerōn* [γέρων], whose genitive is *gerontos*. From the fiftieth year begins old age, which is bounded by no fixed number of years; after the preceding five ages, however much life remains is assigned to old age. Senility is the final part of old age, so called because it is the boundary of the seventh age. Within these six periods philosophers have described human life, in which it is bounded, runs its course, and reaches life’s end. Let us therefore proceed briefly through the aforesaid stages of life, showing their etymologies in the human being.

[Col. 0132B] An infant is a person of the first age. He is called *infans* because he cannot yet speak (*fari*), that is, talk: since his teeth are not yet properly arranged, his articulation of speech is less complete.

A boy (*puer*) is so called from purity because he is pure and does not yet have the down and bloom of the cheeks. Those who possess it are called *ephebi*, from *hēbē* [ἥβη], “puberty.” Boys are not yet men by reason of birth, but lightly built adolescents. “Boy” is used in three ways: first, of birth, as in Isaiah: “A boy has been born to us” (Isa. IX); likewise, of age, as of an eight-year-old or a ten-year-old, whence the verse:

> “Already he bore the childish yoke upon his tender neck.”

[Col. 0132C] Second, it is used for service and purity of faith, whence in the Virgin’s song: “He has received Israel his servant-boy” (Luke I). Third, it is used for immaturity and ignorance: “A boy of a hundred years shall die” (Isa. V). A little girl (*puella*) is, as it were, a little young creature (*pulla*); hence we call wards (*pupilli*) so, not by condition but by childish age.

Wards are so called as though without a little girl of the eye (*pupilla*) and eyes, that is, bereft of parents. But those are properly called wards whose parents died before they received a name from them; the others are called orphans.

Orphans are the same as wards: that term is Greek, this Latin. For where the Psalm often reads, “You will be a helper to the ward” (Ps. IX), the Greek has “to the orphan.”

[Col. 0133A] Those of pubertal age (*puberes*) are so called from the *pubes*, the down covering the shameful parts of the body; at that time these places first put forth down. Some reckon puberty by years, holding that one is pubescent upon completing fourteen years, even though puberty may come very late. But it is most certain that one is pubescent who shows puberty in bodily appearance and is now able to generate.

*Puerperae* are those who give birth while still in the years of childhood, whence Horace:

> “Already she is praised as a mother who has borne offspring.”

Or they are called *puerperae* because girls give birth, or because they bear boys.

[Col. 0133B] An adolescent is so called because he has grown (*adultus*) fit for generation, or because he is still growing (*adolescit*), that is, increasing and developing.

Young men (*juvenes*) are so called because they begin to be able to help (*juvare*), as young bulls (*juvenci*) are called so when they have left calfhood. The young man stands in the very increase of age and is ready to render assistance. For to help is the work of one who contributes something. As the thirtieth year is the year of perfect age in human beings, so the third is the strongest in cattle and beasts of burden.

A man (*vir*) is so called because there is greater strength (*vis*) in him than in women; hence he also receives the name of virtue (*virtus*), or because he acts by force upon a woman.

[Col. 0133C] A woman (*mulier*) is called from softness (*mollities*), as though *mollier*, with the letter *l* removed or altered. The two sexes are distinguished by the strength and weakness of their bodies. Yet the man has greater strength and the woman less, so that she might endure and obey the man—namely, lest women resisting should compel lustful men to seek something else or rush toward another sex. Thus *mulier* is said with reference to the female sex, not to the corruption of virginity; this usage comes from the language of Holy Scripture. For Eve, made from her husband’s side and not yet touched by a man, was called woman, Scripture saying: “And he formed her into a woman” (Gen. II). And the Lord said to his mother: “Woman, behold your son” (John XIX).

A virgin (*virgo*) is named from the fresh or green age (*viridis*), as are a twig (*virga*) and a heifer (*vitula*); alternatively, from incorruption, as though *virago*, because she does not know female passion.

[Col. 0133D] A *virago* is so called because she acts like a man—that is, performs manly deeds—and possesses masculine vigor. The ancients called strong women by this name. A virgin, however, is not properly called a *virago* unless she performs a man’s office. But a woman who performs manly works is rightly called a *virago*, as are the Amazons. She who is now called *femina*, “woman,” was anciently called *vira*, just as from *servus* comes *serva*, and from *famulus*, *famula*, so from *vir*, *vira*. Hence some think the name *virago* derived. But *femina* is named from the regions of the thighs (*femora*), where sex is distinguished from the male.
