Others think, by Greek etymology, that *femina* is named from fiery force because she desires the man intensely; for they say women are more lustful than men, both among human women and among animals. Hence excessive love was called “feminine” among the ancients.

[Col. 0134A] A *senior* is still greener, that is, younger, than an old man. Ovid, in Book VI:

> “Between the young man and the old man, an elder.”

Terence:

> “By what right are we younger?”

Here *adolescentior* does not mean “more adolescent,” but “less so,” just as a *senior* is less old than a *senex*, where the comparative degree signifies less than the positive.  
> **Note:** [Col. 0133D] Valla denies this.

Therefore a *senior* is not sufficiently old, just as a *junior* is below a *juvenis*, and *pauperior* below *pauper*. Some think old men (*senes*) are so called from the diminution of sensation, because through age they become foolish. For physicians say that foolish people have colder blood and prudent people warmer blood; hence old people, in whom it is already cold, and children, in whom it is not yet warm, are less wise. In this respect the age of infants and that of old people agree. For old people rave through excessive age, while children, through playfulness and infancy, do not know what they are doing.

[Col. 0134B] *Senex*, “old man,” is masculine only, just as *anus*, “old woman,” is feminine. For *anus* is said only of a woman. An old woman is so called from many years, as though *annosa*, “full of years.” If it were a common noun, why would Terence not say *senem mulierem*, “an old woman”? Hence also *vetula*, “little old woman,” as though from *vetusta*, “old.” As *senectus*, “old age,” comes from *senex*, so *anilitas*, “old-womanhood,” comes from *anus*.

Grey hair (*canities*) is named from whiteness (*candor*), as though *candities*. Hence the phrase, “blooming youth, milky grey hair,” as though it said “white.” Old age brings us both many benefits and many evils: benefits, because it frees us from most imperious masters, sets bounds to pleasures, breaks the onrushes of lust, increases wisdom, and gives more mature counsels; evils, because senility is most wretched through weakness and hatred. For diseases and sad old age come on. There are two things by which bodily strength is diminished: old age and disease.

[Col. 0134C] Death (*mors*) is so called because it is bitter, or from Mars, the maker of deaths, or from the bite (*morsus*) of the first man, who, biting the fruit of the forbidden tree, incurred death. There are three kinds of death: bitter, untimely, and natural. Bitter death belongs to infants, untimely death to the young, and mature—that is, natural—death to the old.

It is uncertain from what part of speech *mortuus*, “dead,” is declined. For, as Caesar says: “Just as a dead man cannot do anything after his death, so a human being cannot know its origin”—that is, the origin of the word *mortuus*. From *morior*, “I die,” the past participle ought to end in *-tus* with one *u*, not two *uu*; for where the letter *u* is doubled, there is a noun, not a participle, as *fatuus* and *arduus*. It was therefore fitting that, just as what the word signifies cannot act, so the word itself cannot be declined in speech.

[Col. 0134D] Every dead body is either a funeral object (*funus*) or a corpse (*cadaver*). It is a *funus* if it is buried; *funus* is so called from the lighted ropes that they carried before the bier, made of papyrus wrapped round with wax. It is a *cadaver* if it lies unburied; for *cadaver* is named from falling (*cadere*), because it can no longer stand. While it is being carried to burial, we say that funeral rites (*exsequiae*) are performed for it; when it has been burned, that its remains are extant; when it has been laid away, that it is now buried.

[Col. 0135A] It is called a body (*corpus*) by customary usage, because while it lived it was a body, as in the line:

> “... then the bodies deprived of light.”  
> (Virgil, *Georgics*, Book IV, verse 355.)

The deceased (*defunctus*) is so called because he has completed life’s duty. For we say that persons are *defuncti officio*, “finished with an office,” because they have completed their required duties; hence also *honoribus functus*, “having discharged public offices.” Therefore one is *defunctus* because he has been relieved from the duty of life, or because he has completed his day. One who is buried (*sepultus*) is so called because he is without pulse or palpitation, that is, without movement. To bury (*sepelire*) is to lay bodies away, that is, to hide them. For to inter (*humare*) is what we call covering over, that is, casting earth upon and covering with earth.

# Book Four. On the Properties and Epithets of Things, Arranged in Alphabetical Order (G)

[Col. 0135]

## Chapter I. On Those Whose First Letter Is A

[Col. 0135B]

One weaned from the breast is separated by bitterness, returned to his father, and uses stronger food.

The fir tree is tall and lofty, with a most beautiful crown.

The wild or woodland hawk seizes domestic birds and immediately devours those it catches. As it grows feathers, it seeks suitable places from which it cannot be drawn out. Having cast off its feathers, it catches wild birds, pursues the dove, and keeps its prey for its master. A tame hawk is carried on the left hand, so that it may fly to the right; it is confined by fetters and fastened with a strap. When that strap is not broken but loosened, it is allowed to fly. At the sight of meat it returns to its master.

A grape berry turns black, retains the scent of wine, and gives off a stench.

[Col. 0135C] The active life preaches, is solicitous, will have a fruitful end, applies itself to works, undergoes martyrdom, and is perilous.

A needle is slender, rigid, smooth, sharp at one end and pierced at the other, suited to the work of sewing.

The diamond is uncuttable and unconquerable; it attracts iron; it is not held by gold or another metal, but by steel; and it is crushed only by the blood of a he-goat.

All fat belongs to the Lord by perpetual right. Fat is the inner richness of the heart or belly, liver (*jecur* or *hepar*), kidneys, or lesser kidneys.

Air is thin, mobile, full of birds, and easily corrupted; it is the breath of living creatures, darkened by clouds, illuminated by the sun, condensed in winter, stirred by wind, and made clear in summer. When cloudy, it signifies coming rain.

[Col. 0135D] The letters *E* include *es* (“you are”), *aethiops* (“Ethiopian”), and *aestas* (“summer”).

A field is cleared of harmful things, manured, ploughed in many ways, levelled with a rake, sown, and has its seed covered. It is surrounded with ditches, enclosed, allowed to lie fallow, and fitted with signs to drive birds away.

A farmer rises in the morning, dresses in humble clothing, yokes oxen together, urges them with a goad, observes the proper seasons for ploughing and sowing, is not driven away by weather, makes a straight furrow, returns home as evening comes on, and patiently awaits the seed he has cast.

A lamb is innocent, pious, and simple. Among many females it knows its mother, recognizing her by her bleating alone. It is very like its mother and fit for sacrifice; when to be sacrificed, it does not cry out. Its mother supplies milk for nourishment, wool for clothing, and flesh for food. It is silent when shorn, splits the hoof, and chews the cud.

[Col. 0136B] A wing is double, fixed upon the back, and lifts up the bird.

The alb is a priestly garment covering the body; it is tight at the sleeves, broad below, and made of linen.

A channel contains water, is deep, and is enlarged by inundation.

The almond is sweet food for the sick and is covered by a hard, rough shell.

A maidservant is humble, obedient, modest, timid, faithful, diligent, unadorned, and has no authority.

An anchor is strong, hooked, and iron; it is cast in harbour, has a rope, holds a ship against storms, and is scarcely pulled up.

[Col. 0136C] An angel is pure in nature, faithful in guarding, gracious in reconciling, obedient in carrying out commands, contemplative in favouring, and active in announcing.

A ring has neither beginning nor end; it is round, adorned with a stone, encircles and tightens the finger, and ornaments it. A tighter ring does not fit; a looser one falls off. It is suited to betrothals and to the consecration of virgins, and is affixed to royal seals.

A year varies by the succession of four seasons, is distinguished by twelve months, turns back upon itself, and consumes within itself the things born in it.

Wild geese fly high and in disorder; all are ash-coloured. By their continual honking at night they attest their watchfulness; they live together and cry out repeatedly. Domestic geese tear themselves with their beaks; when they sense a human being, they cry out. They are variegated and snow-white in colour and are harmful to seeds that have been sown.

[Col. 0136D] A bee is born without intercourse and arises from a decaying ox. It is industrious, feeds on flowers, and flies in swarms; it works for others, not itself; it casts out those killed and dead; it is quickly injured and hostile to cold; rough outside, it has sweetness within and loves cleanliness. When it stings, it loses its sting; having lost it, it never produces fruit.

Water is common to all, washes filth away, flows downwards, does not leave its channel, returns to the sea, follows every flood, and is naturally cold. Mixed with wine it benefits the sick; boiled with barley it is healthier; mixed with earth it makes mud. It is the drink of the poor, clear enough for a mirror, quenches thirst, leaves no track of a ship, and extinguishes fire.

[Col. 0137A] The eagle is named from the sharpness of its eyes, because it gazes upon the sun’s ray with eye and vision unblinking; it casts off its young if, though its own, they do not gaze upon the sun in this way. Flying high in the air, it sees little fish in the sea, which it snatches in a swift descent and devours. It flies higher than other birds. In old age, when its beak grows excessively, it strikes it against a rock and becomes young again. It nests in high places, smells carrion across seas, lives by plunder, and places amethyst in its nest, which drives away poison.

The north wind freezes waters; hence *aquilo*, as though “binding waters.” It is cold, harms flowers and plants, and blows from the north.

[Col. 0137B] The spider has seven feet, wastes away with poison, disembowels itself, weaves webs from its own entrails, ensnares flies, sucks flies dry, and thus withers and dies. Swollen, it raises itself into the air on its web without wings or any other support.

A plough is made of wood and iron, cleaves the earth, is held by the farmer, improves the soil, and is left in the field.

The more deeply a tree fixes its root, the more firmly it clings; it gives shade, is green in summer, flowers and bears fruit, withers in winter, and, when superfluous growth is cut away, bears more and richer fruit.

The Ark was made of shittim wood, covered with gold inside and out. Its breadth was a cubit and a half. On each side it had two golden rings, with gilded poles of shittim wood in the rings. Within it were the tablets, Aaron’s rod, Deuteronomy, and a vessel containing manna.

[Col. 0137C] A bow has an immovable and inflexible middle and two movable ends. It is held in the left hand; if kept drawn long, it becomes slack and is quickly damaged. In it hardness is tempered by softness. Its string is drawn, and it sends forth an arrow.

Water channels are made of hollowed stone and carry water to a garden.

A ram has two horns on its forehead. While vigorous it is lustful, leads the flock, protects the flock with its horns, rules the flock, and makes it fruitful.

Silver is white, clean, has a sweet ring, and possesses an attractive nature.

[Col. 0137D] An earnest payment is part of the price, confirmation of a contract, and assurance of possessing the thing.

The wild ass, that is, the onager, is fierce in tooth, inhabits dreadful places, and tears pursuing dogs apart. The domestic ass is pierced by the wild one, attacks no one with its teeth, is foolish, stronger in its hindquarters and weaker in its forequarters, bears a cross on its back, is beautiful in youth and ugly in old age, brays horribly, is lustful, sluggish, fond of thistles, gentle, pricked by the goad, delighted by the lyre, and was the first animal ridden by man.

The asp harms by poison and lives in caverns. Against enchanters it blocks one ear with its tail and the other with earth. If it strikes someone, that person immediately falls asleep, and it kills in this way.

[Col. 0138A] An athlete cuts his hair round, anoints his head with oil, does not burden himself with clothing, guards himself on every side, wears red, holds his weapons firmly, does not yield to hardships, and, in hope of victory, does not cease to make his opponent rest. He perseveres in combat, does not overstep the boundaries, and keeps his eye always upon victory.

A bird-catcher has various nets, snares, and birdlime. He seeks places more frequented by birds, conceals his snares and himself, imitates birds’ calls, sometimes deceives one bird by means of another, and adds to himself all the birds caught except one.

Dawn drives away darkness, glows red, brings on the day, and is darker when the sun rises. It lies between night and day; when it reddens, it signifies coming rain.

Gold is the most precious of all metals; it is solid, delights the eye, and the redder it is, the better. It is purified in a furnace, is brilliant, and suited to kings.

[Col. 0138B] The south wind is warm, melts frost, nourishes the flower, and blows from the south.

Autumn gathers what has been produced in the year, strips trees and fields bare, abounds in fruits, and produces late and useless flowers.

## Chapter II. On Those Whose First Letter Is B

A staff is long, smooth, rigid, inflexible, suitable for support and fit for defence.

A bath washes and dries the body, kindles natural heat, softens flesh, nourishes, and restores loosened limbs.

[Col. 0138C] Balsam is fragrant and wards off decay. Its trunk resembles a vine; it preserves youth. Its drop is adulterated when mixed with Cyprian oil or honey, but is proven free of honey if someone curdles it with milk. With oil added it makes chrism. Pure balsam cannot endure the blazing sun. It is supported and cultivated like a vine. The tree is distinguished by an everlasting crown, rises two cubits, and is cut with sharp stones and bone knives because iron’s touch is harmful to it.

A military belt is golden; it girded or bound the loins and breast, and encircles and belts the whole body.

A beard signifies strength, denotes sex, and adheres to the head.

[Col. 0138D] The basilisk is king of serpents. By its gaze alone it kills a human being; by its breath it kills birds in flight. It is so full of poison that it is wholly translucent. If a human being sees it first, it does not harm that human being; and the basilisk rules in an empty desert.

The Blessed Virgin was poor, humble, obedient, quiet, modest, simple, wise, announced by an angel, sanctified in the womb, and the first to offer a vow of virginity to God her bridegroom. She was greeted by an angel, proclaimed full of grace, the Mother of the Lord, lady of angels, star of the sea, earth that brought forth the Saviour, earth from which the true Adam was formed, earth from which truth arose, earth from which the true bread was brought forth, earth that gave its fruit, earth whose fruit is exalted, earth blessed by the Lord, earth of which it is said: “The seed fell into good ground, a land flowing with milk and honey” (Luke VIII); the Ark of the Testament—or rather, of the Covenant; the star that arose from Jacob; the vessel containing manna; Solomon’s throne; the house of salvation; the closed gate; the fleece drenched with dew; the bridegroom’s chamber; Solomon’s Temple; Aaron’s rod; the high priest’s tunic; the woman clothed with the sun; the house hewn with seven pillars; the enclosed garden; the sealed fountain; the dining room of the Trinity; Noah’s Ark; beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, and dawn rising.

[Col. 0139A] Beryl shines like water struck by sunlight and warms the hand of its holder.

An ox has two horns, chews the cud, and splits the hoof; it ploughs the earth, is pressed beneath the yoke, eats chaff, is sacrificed, is driven by a goad, and is strong.

The owl calls like a bird; it is ill-omened, laden with feathers, held back by heavy sluggishness, frequents tombs by day and night, loves darkness, is hated by other birds, and always remains in caverns.

[Col. 0139B] A trumpet is narrow at the bottom and broad at the top; it encourages the bold, terrifies the timid, gathers the scattered, and sounds dreadfully.

Butter is sweet, white, rich, quickly melts, is made from coagulated milk, and removes hoarseness.

The box tree is hard, a low-growing tree, clings to rocks, is barren, stays green in winter, and does not shed its foliage.

## Chapter III. On Those Whose First Letter Is C

A corpse is rotten, foul-smelling, and food for worms.

An onion causes tears, is covered with different skins, and soon rots.

[Col. 0139C] The caladrius or charadrius is a bird which, when placed before a sick person, if it looks at him, drinks up the whole illness and the sick person recovers; if it will not look at him, this is a sign of death.

A reed is hollow, fragile, light, and suited to the work of writing.

Shoes cover and protect the feet; looser ones do not fit, tighter ones hurt, and they are tied around the foot.

Chalcedony, or carchedonius, has the colour of a pale lamp. It shines in daylight but is dark in a house; it resists the skill of engravers; when heated by the sun’s ray or by rubbing with fingers, it draws chaff to itself.

A pebble is a hard, rolling, flat, round stone, found in rivers and not softened by water.

[Col. 0139D] Heat dissolves, opens, compels, warms, causes blackening, and, when excessive, burns and dries out.

A camel is huge in body, burden-bearing, humped, and misshapen; it kneels down to be loaded.

A bell awakens sleepers and marks the hours. It is broad at the bottom and narrow at the top; if silver is mixed into it, it sounds more sweetly.

A field is a spacious, uncultivated place, very rich in flowers and pastures.

A candle has wax and wick, gives light, consumes itself, and is straight, flat, long, narrow above, broad below, and pierced and hollow beneath.

[Col. 0140A] The lampstand in the Temple was of the purest gold, ductile; its shaft was iron, clothed with five golden reeds. At the heads of the reeds were cups in the form of nuts; lilies proceeded from the bases of the cups; above were little spheres; six branches with the shaft, of iron, clothed with seventy golden reeds. It had upper parts, a stem below on which it stood, seven lamps, seven vessels for pouring, and seven snuffers.

A dog is hostile to a robber, is born blind, recognizes no one but those among whom it lives, has a healing tongue, remarkable keenness, commendable fidelity, drives off wolves and thieves, is powerful in scent, has very sharp teeth, licks blood, is ravenously hungry, returns to its vomit, and gnaws bones.

[Col. 0140B] Song rouses the sluggish, incites the devout, and preserves concord.

Hair is smooth and slender, adorns the head, and is firmly rooted.

A goat chews the cud, splits the hoof, is foul-smelling, raises its two feet upward while feeding, its hair is made into haircloth, it is shaggy, sacrificed, and grazes on high places.

A roe deer is clean, sharp-sighted, splits the hoof and chews the cud, is very swift of foot, and grazes on high places.

The head is the highest and most principal limb; it contains the five senses, is adorned with hair, and is set upon the neck.

Coal comes back to life from dead matter; it changes from blackness into redness, produces cinders, and, when it disintegrates, becomes ashen.

The carbuncle is a very brilliant little stone; it puts the darkness of the night to flight [Col. 0140C]; it is found in the land of Havilah.

A prison is dark, foul-smelling, dreadful, deep, punitive, solitary.

Flesh is frail; it urges and lusts against the spirit, produces depraved impulses, and is weak.

Cassia is a plant, also called a tube (*fistula*), which grows in waters; it is hollow and grows to an immense height.

A castle is situated in a secure place, fortified with ditches, surrounded by walls, encircled with bulwarks; in it are defenders, weapons, provisions, and watchmen.

A chain is heavy, iron, hard; it binds tightly and does not allow movement; in it one ring encloses another.

A chair is the seat of teachers; it has four feet by which [Col. 0140D] it is supported.

The cedar grows in Lebanon; it is tall, barren, fragrant. Wood smeared with its resin does not rot or decay with age. As high as it raises itself into the air, so deep does it root itself in the earth; it clings firmly, is imperishable, and its scent drives serpents away or kills them.

Wax is dry, hidden in the honeycomb, pure, fragile; it softens at fire, and, being tenacious and soft, receives the form of a seal. It reduces swelling, is fragrant and pale.

The brain is in the head, inviolable short of death [the printed *immolabile* perhaps reads *inviolabile*]; it is the seat of memory, the power of understanding, and reason.

A pillow is square, short, sewn with fine linen, filled with very light feathers, and placed beneath the head.

Stags, departing from their native land at the season of love, [Col. 0141A] proceed in an orderly fashion; one bears another, with its antlers laid upon its back. They pass unharmed through thickets; they draw serpents out of their dens, eat the serpent when it has been drawn out, and, after drinking from a spring, recover their sight. They shed their superfluous antlers and grow young again; they play, chew the cud, and split the hoof.

Chrism is consecrated from balsam and oil; with it priests and kings are anointed.

Christ was valued at a paltry price; he prayed with a bloody sweat, was betrayed by a disciple, most shamefully seized, bound, struck with slaps, scourged, accused by false witnesses, declared guilty of death, and his beard was plucked out, as the gloss on Isaiah says: “Before Pilate he is accused by many; by Herod he is despised; he is clothed in a white garment; a robber is chosen in his place; he is unjustly condemned; he is clothed in a scarlet [Col. 0141B] cloak; crowned with thorns; his head is struck with a reed; he is stripped of his own garments; he carries his cross for himself; he is crucified, blasphemed, given vinegar to drink; crying out and weeping, he gave up the spirit; his side is pierced with a spear; he is laid in the tomb.”

Christ is also the Temple of Solomon; the cluster brought from the promised land into the wilderness; the pillar of fire and cloud; David, whom Saul—that is, the Jewish people—wished to pierce through, but the spear was planted in the wall and he escaped unharmed; the scapegoat and the spotless goat; the pair of sparrows, one of which is sacrificed and the other flies away; the mercy-seat; the spotless lamb; the high priest who entered once into the Holy of Holies; the red heifer; the serpent raised upon a pole [Col. 0141C]; mighty Samson; the true Solomon; David, mighty in hand or desirable in appearance; Isaac carrying the wood; the true Joshua; Joseph, handsome in face and comely in appearance; Elisha the great one, fitting himself to the boy.

Chrysolite is a little stone with a golden gleam; it seems to emit fiery sparks.

Chrysoprase, or chrysopassus, is a green little stone of a golden nature, growing in India; there is also a purple kind with golden drops.

A scar is the trace of a wound; it readily renews the wound, cauterizes the flesh, and retains pain.

The stork is the herald of spring, an enemy of serpents, a friend of society; it flies across seas and goes to Asia in a gathered flock. Quails go before them as guides. They have extraordinary devotion toward their young: they so warm their chicks in [Col. 0141D] their nests that from constant brooding they lose their feathers; and for as long as they feed their offspring, for just so long are they fed by their offspring.

Haircloth is made from goats’ hair; it breeds worms and is foul-smelling and prickly.

Cinnamon has bark like a reed; it grows in the middle of Ethiopia, on a short shrub two cubits high, gray or somewhat black in colour. The thicker kind is held cheap; the more slender is dearer. It has a round and slender stem: when it is broken, a visible breath flies forth like mist or dust.

Ash is made from wood by fire; it is fine and heavy, washes cloths, and is best made from twigs—that is, from vine prunings.

[Col. 0142A] A cistern is deep, cold, a receptacle for rain, a storehouse of water.

A cithara is made from the skin of a dead animal stretched over wood; its ordered strings produce sound from within. If they are stretched too tightly, they break; if too loosely, they grow hoarse; they are regulated with a plectrum.

A key is an implement for insertion; it turns a large lock, opens a door, and makes a noise.

A cloister is a voluntary prison for clerics, a place of quiet. It makes one secure from outward matters, joyful in inward matters, certain of eternal matters; though it restrains the body, it cheers the mind.

An oven is round, solid, white, low, open, dark.

Scarlet twice dyed had the colour of fire.

[Col. 0142B] Heaven conceals what is in it; it is the dwelling of God, the place of angels and blessed souls: quiet, peaceful, high, light, soft, pleasant, level.

The neck adheres to the head; it is long, joins the head to the body, draws food into the body, and through it the voice is formed; it is smooth, white, and rounded.

The dove is simple, persists in kisses, lacks gall, has red feet, and has keener vision than other birds. It harms none with beak or claws; it is humble, feeds its young from its beak with what it has itself been fed, does not eat carrion, eats pure grain, cherishes other birds’ young as its own, sits over streams so that it may see the hawk coming, nests among rocks, defends itself with its wings, flies in flocks, is fertile, gives a moan instead of song, and rears twin young.

[Col. 0142C] A column has a capital, shaft, and base; it supports a building. It is strong, straight, slender, long, rigid, twisted, smooth.

The consecration of a church is performed thus: relics are carried away, and twenty-one crosses are at once made on the walls; bodies are removed; the bishop knocks at the door and goes around the church, sprinkling it three times with holy water. Within, it too is sprinkled with water, wine, salt, and ash. Twelve candles are placed and lit upon the walls beside the crosses, or beside images of the apostles. The alphabet is written on the pavement in the form of a cross; incense is burned upon the altar; the altar is anointed with chrism, covered, adorned; Mass is celebrated; the church’s banner is placed above it.

[Col. 0142D] A basket is outwardly humble, woven from rushes and palm leaves; it is a dung-befouled vessel.

The heart is on the left and inviolable short of death; it is the seat of heat in the middle of the body; it is the seat of the soul and the dwelling-place of the Trinity alone.

A horn is of flesh, firmly attached, projecting beyond the flesh; it is hard, yet softer than bone and harder than flesh, rigid and shining.

A crown has neither beginning nor end, surrounds the whole head, is woven with flowers, adorns the head, restrains the hair. A broader one falls off; a tighter one does not fit; when shifted, it is unsuitable.

A strap is long, thin, made from a dead animal; it surrounds the whole body, binds the limbs, has nails, binds and restrains garments, and has an opening [Col. 0143A] like a gate; pierced by a needle, it is tightened or loosened with a buckle.

The curtains were of five colours; there were ten of them; one covered another; they had loops and were ornamental (Exod. XXVII, XXXVI).

The raven is black and feeds on corpses. It first seeks the eye in a corpse, and thus draws out the brain through the eye. It lives by plunder, calls in a hoarse voice, is noisy, does not feed its offspring until they become black, and heaps its nest together from many things into one.

The quail is named *qualea* from the sound of its call; it desires seasons of pleasantness. Driven away in summer, it crosses seas. Alone among birds, like man, it suffers from the falling sickness.

A crater is turned on a lathe, round, deep.

[Col. 0143B] *Cremium* [an uncertain term] is dry; it contracts and is burned by fire, so that the fire may draw out the blood.

A sieve separates the clean from the unclean, retains coarse things, and expels fine things.

The Cross: the pole of the bronze serpent, Isaac’s wood, Jacob’s ladder, Moses’ rod, the wood of Marah, the sign of Tau upon the lintel of the house, the wood of the widow of Zarephath, Zacchaeus’s sycamore, Rahab’s scarlet thread, David’s key, the pole on which the cluster was carried. It had four parts and was composed of four woods: olive, cedar, palm, and cypress. It drives away phantoms and removes venial sins. Ships run over the seas in the form of a cross; birds fly in the air, people swim, and churches and cowls are made in the form of a cross.

A knife is held by its handle, cuts with iron, and is kept in a sheath [Col. 0143C].

The more heavily a cart is loaded, the more it creaks. It rolls on four wheels, leaves tracks, turns with difficulty, has a pole, runs easily when greased, has steps on either side, and its wheels have spokes.

The swan, while swimming, raises its neck; it is strong in its wings and has black flesh. It is named from singing; it has a long neck and white feathers. When death is at hand, it thrusts its feather into its own brain and sings most sweetly. It is said that very many swans fly to the Hyperborean regions and sing very fittingly in accompaniment to cithara-players who sing before them.

The cypress is fragrant, suitable for healing bodies, and does not lose the beauty of its foliage through any assault.

## Chapter IV. Of those whose first letter is D

[Col. 0143D]

The doe lives in mountains; it is a clean animal, sharp-sighted, swift in running, chews the cud, and splits the hoof.

The ten commandments of the Decalogue; the ten virgins in the Gospel; the ten lepers cleansed; the ten tribes of Israel, apart from the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin; the ten horns of the beast; the ten cities; the ten curtains over the tabernacle; ten fingers on the hands and as many on the feet.

A denarius is of silver, round, contains four quadrants, whole, undiminished, of equal weight, and bears an image and inscription.

Teeth are white, hard, well rooted, orderly, grind food, and are strong.

[Col. 0144A] A desert is barren, rugged, uncultivated, solitary, pathless to human beings, and a dwelling-place for wild beasts and full of serpents.

Day restores colour to things, permits work, is clear and bright when the sun shines; it opposes thieves, robbers, and evildoers; it contains twelve hours, is warm, puts night and darkness to flight, and is divided into morning, noon, and evening.

A finger is distinguished by its joints, long, straight, rounded, has a nail, and is slender and flexible.

A disciple ought to be humble, holy, obedient, attentive, patient, ready, diligent, holding and honouring his teacher in place of a parent in disposition, not bodily relation.

Riches are lost with pain, acquired with labour, [Col. 0144B] possessed with fear; they pass away quickly, produce pride, prick the mind with anxiety, obstruct the way to the Lord, and are denounced by the devil. They are thorns that choke good seed and do not allow it to take root, yet are good for those who use them well. They consist in metals, gems, provisions, utensils, treasures, and possessions.

Teaching ought to concern faith and morals; it should be catholic—that is, universal—public, sound, discerning, true, mature.

A cask is round, hooped, woven, deep, open.

The Lord God is ready to forgive, slow to vengeance, inclined to reward, appeasable, [Col. 0144C] kind, patient, and free from suspicion or unbelief.

A house is built thus: first the earth is dug out, then the foundation is laid; first the walls are raised, afterward various ceilings are inserted, and the roof is laid on. The wall is square; rooms are separated off; it contains many doors and windows and has various entrances and exits. It affords rest to its inhabitants, protects from rain and winds, makes one household, tames wanderers, and provides knowledge and prudence to those resting and meditating within it.

The two Testaments; the two tablets of the Law; the two walls in the tabernacle; the two choirs in the church; the two bearers of the cluster; the two fishes in the Gospel; the two men going up to the Temple; the two columns in the porch of the Temple; [Col. 0144D] the two cherubim over the mercy-seat; the two lampstands and two olive trees; the two lights in the firmament of heaven; Jacob’s two wives; Lazarus’s two sisters; the two altars of the tabernacle; in a human being, two eyes, two nostrils, two ears, two feet, two legs, two knees, two shins, two sides, two arms, and almost all other things in pairs.

The twelve patriarchs; the twelve apostles; the twelve years after the Ascension during which they preached in Judaea; the twelve stones in the breastpiece; the twelve springs at Elim; the twelve seats of the judges; the twelve tribes of Israel; the twelve loaves of presentation; the twelve dishes; the twelve handfuls; the twelve divisions of the Red Sea; the twelve spies; the twelve stones brought across from the Jordan; the twelve watches around the tabernacles; the twelve gates of the city; the twelve [Col. 0145A] little lions upon Solomon’s steps; the twelve fruits of the Spirit enumerated in the Epistle to the Galatians; the twelve fruits of the tree of life in the Apocalypse; the twelve stones there likewise; the twelve stars likewise seen in the woman’s crown.

## Chapter V. Of those whose first letter is E

Drunkenness arises from frequent drinking; it provokes vomiting, makes a person more daring, causes the steps to stagger, hinders the tongue and makes it as if stammering, alters one’s gait, makes one insensible, exposes secrets, provokes weeping, takes away the function of the limbs, brings forgetfulness, makes one forget oneself, and removes discernment.

Ivory is white and cold; first dull, it becomes bright when polished with files [Col. 0145B], smooth; the older it is, the more reddish and beautiful it becomes.

Elephants are huge in body, suited for battle, travel in herds, and are caught by deceit.

A sword is sharp, shining, flat on both sides, kept in a sheath, and inscribed.

A horse, untamed, is scarcely tamed and scarcely restrained; it is strong, swift, proud, not frightened by the sound of weapons, bridled, often recognizes its rider, bolder when armed, furnished with a saddle, bound with straps, lustful, urged by spurs, and has a hard hoof upon which it is shod.

A hermit is solitary, uncultivated, pale, thin, ragged, hairy, rough-looking, and bearded.

A hedgehog, or *hericius*, is spiny and quickly angered; when touched it gathers itself into a heap in which it extends itself; it has the form of a pig; it rolls itself in apples and grapes, so as to load itself and later feed itself.

Bronze is solid, resonant, imperishable.

Summer is warm and clear, has days longer than nights, abounds in flowers and fruits, dries moisture, flashes with thunder and lightning, and distinguishes fruitful from fruitless trees.

An Ethiopian is curly-haired, has white teeth and black flesh, and begets one like himself.

The four Gospels; the four living creatures in Ezekiel; the four feet of a table; the light and pleasant yoke; the bronze laver at the entrance of the tabernacle; the pillar of fire and cloud; the star of the Magi; the four chariots in Zechariah; Elijah’s chariot; the four rivers from Paradise; [Col. 0145D] the manna in the ark; the book sealed with seven seals.

## Chapter VI. Of those whose first letter is F

The smith passes night as though it were day; he sits beside the anvil, considers the work of iron, the vapour of fire burns his clothes, and he wears away his flesh in the heat of the furnace. The voice of the hammer resounds in his ear, and his eye fixes upon the likeness of the vessel. He will give his heart to completing the works, and by his wakefulness he will adorn their imperfection (Ecclus. XXXVIII). He has a workshop or furnace, an anvil, tongs, hammer, grinding stone for sharpening, fire, bellows, and sprinkler.

The face has form, and as the countenance declares a person’s will, so it makes recognition and discernment possible.

Lees settle at the bottom; they are bitter, a muddy [Col. 0146A] substance, produced from wine, and retain its odour.

A sickle is sharp, curved, and cuts more closely.

Hunger constricts the vital passages, weakens work, produces squalor, reckons cheap things precious, makes the skin swollen and hairy, and excites sluggishness and appetite.

Flour is fine and clean, acquired with labour, bound together by water, leavened, and takes on sourness.

A bundle is made from many things gathered together; unless it is well tied, it falls apart.

A spark is light, is reduced to nothing, and remains after fire.

A honeycomb is cellular, light, sweet, and contains or yields wax.

[Col. 0146B] A torch is hollow, dry, fragile, consumes itself, gives off the greatest light, and burns with a crackling sound.

Fever brings heat, causes trembling, spoils the palate, ends in sweat, and leaves symptoms behind.

A window turns on hinges, is open, receives light and the sun’s rays.

A wild beast inhabits forests, is untamed and cruel.

A little leaven is put into a mass of kneaded flour.

Iron is heavy, is quenched in water, follows the magnet, makes a harsh sound; weapons are made from it. It softens in fire, is stretched by frequent hammering, is placed in a horse’s mouth, governs the horse, readily turns it about, [Col. 0146C] leads it, and is extended by two straps with certain attachments.

The fig tree has broad leaves; their juice produces itching. It afterward bears *grossi* (unripe figs), which readily fall and are not edible; its fruit is sweet.

The potter sits at his work, turns the wheel with his feet, is always anxious over his work, and all his labour is innumerable. With his arm he shapes the clay, and before his feet he forms its strength. He will give his heart to completing the coating, and by his wakefulness will clean the furnace.

A son awaits an inheritance, is obedient, resembles his father; if ungrateful, he is expelled from the inheritance.

[Col. 0146D] Thread is slender, twisted, long; it sews a garment and follows the bristle.

Dung, when scattered, fertilizes the earth; it gives off a stench and arises from an animal.

A pipe is hollow and perforated, sounds thinly, is blown through the mouth, and deceives a bird.

A flame is made from many sparks, rises upward, glows or shines, and is reddish.

A flower delights the sight, affects by its scent, is the hope of fruit, quickly withers, is exposed to the air, arises in spring, adorns the field, is sweet, is harmed by cold, burned by excessive heat, or struck down by untimely hail.

A river is swift, rises from an abundance of waters and rains, is deep, and does not leave its accustomed channel.

[Col. 0147A] Linen breeches were tight, voluntarily assumed, and cover the genitals.

Hay is green in summer, soft, readily feels injury when struck, immediately dries when cut, is cast into the oven, and is food for beasts of burden.

A leaf is thin, broad, light, gives shade, adorns a tree, gathers the tree’s fruit, grows pale in autumn, is cast down by wind, is green, is stirred by wind, and rustles.

A bellows is made from wood and leather, has an opening on the inner side, draws in breath, and emits air to stir up fire.

A spring gushes from the earth, is cold, divides into streams, is pure, murmurs sweetly, relieves thirst, is warm in winter, clear, lightly disturbed, and sends its springs [Col. 0147B] upward.

Tongs have two arms; they divide; while they divide, they are drawn tight; they are joined by a rivet and connected in the middle.

A furnace is small and hot, purifies gold, turns wood to ash, and annihilates dross.

Cold constricts pores, contracts the limbs, and does not permit fruitfulness.

The forehead is tender and quickly reddens; it is the place of modesty and does not conceal a stain.

Fruit delights by scent, refreshes by taste, displays the nature of the tree, is coloured by the sun’s heat, falls when ripe, and is shot straight forth.

The *frusus* is a kind of bramble which grows of itself, shoots up thickly, is thorny, impenetrable, dark, [Col. 0147C] dense, full, intertwined and clinging to itself, bristly, uncultivated, barren.

A drone does not work, stings, and devours the labours of others.

Lightning strikes and flashes from the edge of the sky, arises suddenly, is bright and shining, and proceeds from heat.

Smoke is born from fire, rises straight upward, and provokes tears.

A sling is swung by motion, made of leather, turned about the head, holds a stone, hangs from two straps, and strikes hard.

A foundation is laid deep, is firm, made from unhewn stones, cast into the lowest earth, covered with earth, broad, and supports a building.

A thief comes at night, plunders, suddenly attacks, and [Col. 0147D] kills the unwary; he catches birds, undermines a house, hides when observed, is merciless, seeks secret entrances, and fears every sound.

A curved little clasp has two hooks and is almost of iron.

A spindle is wrapped with thread, pointed at both ends and broad in the middle, and is turned with the right hand.

## Chapter VII. Of those whose first letter is G

The scent of galbanum drives serpents away; it is the sap of a certain ferula-like tree growing in Syria.

A hen warms her chicks beneath her wings, protects them from the kite, falls ill from grief for her chicks, grows hoarse and loses her feathers, and feeds from warmth.

[Col. 0148A] A cock is accustomed to utter stronger and more prolonged calls in the deeper hours of night, and in the morning forms shorter cries. Before crowing, it beats itself with its wings; it announces the day, awakens the sluggish, and bends itself to every wind.

A gem is precious and bright, powerful in virtue, smooth, altogether beautiful.

A cheek is beautiful, white, smooth, and suffused with blush because of modesty.

A hump is an excess of nature; it makes one smaller and produces deformity.

A giant is huge in body, remarkable in limbs, pre-eminent in strength, but lacks piety and good intelligence.

Ice is hardened from water by cold, melts in the sun, and is fragile, slippery, clear, shining.

[Col. 0148B] An acorn comes from the oak and is food for pigs.

A ball is round, rolling, wound around with many threads.

Hail is hardened in the air, cold; in falling it is bruised and dissolved, and it harms flowers and tender plants.

Grain is sown, dies, then sprouts into grass, then into an ear, and afterward into wheat; it is gathered, threshed, separated from chaff by wind, dried, and ground by a millstone.

Cranes proceed in a letter-shaped formation; they seek the heights, so that they may more easily see the lands for which they are bound. One goes ahead and regulates the flock with its voice; when that voice becomes hoarse, another takes its place. They divide the watches of the night; and, in the order of their watches, they always rest upon one foot, in which they hold a stone [Col. 0148C].

A whirlpool is deep, dark, dreadful, engulfing, and otherwise motionless.

A drop is heavy, quickly dries, is small, and provides refreshment.

The throat is the vehicle of the voice and a channel for food.

## Chapter VIII. Of those whose first letter is H

An inheritance is cultivated by the Lord, feeds the Lord, and is firmly possessed.

A hook is curved, covered with bait, slender, and suspended from a line.

Sand (*harena* [*arena*]) is innumerable, fine, bitter, barren, heavy, moist, absorbent.

A reed (*harundo* [*arundo*]) is hollow, fragile, yields to every wind [Col. 0148D], is rustling, grows in a marsh, wounds the hand that handles it, is green outwardly, and withers inwardly.

A spear is long, rounded, straight, flat, smooth, slender, rigid, penetrating, and armed with iron.

Ivy creeps, is always green, grows like a rose, is barren, does not shed its foliage, has an attractive nature, drives away foul smells, and crowns victors.

Hermit: see *Eremita*.

The herodius is a most rapacious bird, the largest of flying creatures; it conquers the eagle and nests on the highest rocks.

Winter freezes waters, is cold, has nights longer than days, and is wet.

A fawn remains in high places, is swift, sharp-sighted, and feeds on the highest rocks.

[Col. 0149A] A he-goat is foul-smelling, lustful, shaggy, unclean, fit for sacrifice, chews the cud, splits the hoof, and is distinguished by horns.

The swallow is chattering, lives in houses, flies in winding circuits, is most skilful in building nests and rearing its young, abandons and does not seek lofty places likely to fall, attacks no other birds and is not attacked by them, crosses seas and remains there in winter, and by its arrival announces the beginning of spring.

Man is frail, prone to sin, incapable of rising again, weak in maintaining constancy.

*Honus*: see *onus*.

*Hortus*: see *ortus*.

A guest dwells in another’s place, is deferential, passes quickly, and does not trust well in another’s house.

[Col. 0149B] The Eucharistic host is white in colour, small in size, round, wheaten, unmixed, unleavened, inscribed.

*Hostium*: see *ostium*, because it is derived from *os* (“mouth”).

The shoulder bears burdens; it is double, inflexible, strong, broad.

Moisture joined with heat nourishes; it rises from the earth into the trunk and from the trunk into the branches.

The hyacinth changes with the air: in clear weather it is transparent, in cloudy weather dark.

A hypocrite conceals his own evils, is pale, proclaims his own good deeds, goes about uncouthly, does everything in order to be seen, and is proud and impatient.

Hyssop is a lowly herb; it clears the chest, clings to a rock, and its root calms swelling of the lung.

## Chapter IX. Of those whose first letter is I and J

[Col. 0149C]

Fasting disciplines the body, restrains vices, wards off lusts, raises the mind, and enriches the soul.

Fire glows; things placed in it are drawn toward its heat. It gives off brightness and smoke, produces smoke, supplies heat, consumes wood, has an attractive nature, dries, cooks foods, and follows its own material.

An image has outlines, makes a shadow, resembles the thing of which it is an image, and is useless.

An anvil is a very hard iron block, solid and firm, upon which works are fashioned, useful for nothing else.

An island is beaten by waves and breaks the waves, but is gradually [Col. 0149D] diminished.

An envious person is pale, wasted by thinness, quickly bursts into anger, changes expression through envy, fierce in the eyes, restless in mind.

The rainbow has two colours, glows red; it is fiery on the outside and watery within, and signifies rain.

Isopus: see Hyssop.

A yoke joins two, is heavy, presses down toward the earth, rests upon the neck, is fastened to the head, is curved, disciplines the untamed, and rubs bare flesh.

A beast of burden rolls and rests in its own dung, feeds on cheap things, bears loads, and does not distinguish its riders.

A rush grows in water, flexible, sharp at the top, [Col. 0150A] slender, green outwardly, smooth, long, straight, soft, decayed inwardly, and without a node.

The juniper is a low-growing shrub; as is said, fire is preserved in its ashes for a year; its shade and smoke are most healthful.

Youth is slippery, inconstant, unreflective, hot, immoderate.

## Chapter X. Of those whose first letter is L

Milk is white, nourishes little children, when curdled dries, and is sweet, rich, pleasant; when boiling, it rises.

A tear is brief, clear, quickly dries, strong, bitter, and salty.

A small cask is woven from several boards, bound with iron hoops, has a vent, and preserves wine [Col. 0150B].

A plate is thin and extended by frequent hammering; it was golden upon the priest’s forehead and bore the divine name, the Tetragrammaton, in the shape of a crescent moon.

A lamp is fragile, somewhat dark, narrow below, broad above, contains oil, and supplies light.

Wool is curly, white, soft, pleasant, light; first it is shorn, then washed, dyed, and spun.

A stone is hard, rolling, trips the foot, is not softened by water, and is hollowed by a constant drop.

A brick is formed from mud, hardened by fire, square, red, fragile, raw; if, when newly made, it is washed more, it is dirtied more; it covers a house.

A bed is private, soft, adorned, raised, clandestine.

[Col. 0150C] The lion is king of beasts; its mouth stinks. As if born dead, on the third day it is awakened by its father’s roar. It erases its tracks with its tail when pressed by a pursuer; all beasts fear its roar. When it makes a circle with its tail, no wild animal dares cross it. It is proud, strongest, and always clings to its prey.

The hare is swift, makes its bed among rocks, weak, has hind legs longer, is long-eared, does not chew the cud, and sleeps with eyes open.

The Law is the base beneath the column; the base beneath the bronze laver; the five barley loaves; death in the pot; Elijah’s staff; the priest and Levite passing by the wounded man; the water of Marah; the flute-players around the dead girl; the woman with the flow of blood; [Col. 0150D] the six stone jars; the other ear of the servant of the high priest, cut off.

*Libanus* is a tree in Arabia, with broad bark and leaf, resembling frankincense, exuding sap like that of an almond tree. It is gathered twice yearly, in autumn and spring. When its bark is cut in the heat of summer, white frankincense comes out; when the bark is cut in spring, contracted and thickened foam comes out red—not comparable with the former, but nevertheless more fragrant.

A book is made from the skin of a dead animal, written with ink through a quill, has many leaves, is punctured, pressed in a press, bound, preserves ancient deeds and secrets; unless it is frequently opened, it becomes mouldy. It is adorned with emblems, closed with seals, easily defiled, contracts in fire, and is washed away by water.

[Col. 0151A] A balance has two equal pans and a tongue above, where it is suspended; fairness follows the heavier weight, settles disputes, and by weight inclines to whichever side it leans.

Shittim wood is low-growing, imperishable, incombustible, like white thorns; the more it is in fire, the more it is hardened.

A lily readily sprouts, grows from uncultivated ground, rises in valleys, is fragrant and white. When closed it contains its scent; when opened it pours it out. It has six leaves, grows among thorns, and has twigs and a stalk in the middle; it is pricked by thorns and yet retains its whiteness, stands straight on its stalk, heals burned limbs, and when uprooted does not immediately wither as other flowers do.

[Col. 0151B] A file is toothed, sharpens iron, and while sharpening is drawn and drawn back; it consumes itself with rust.

A threshold is the entrance of a house and both its beginning and its end.

The tongue is small, slippery, swift, situated in moisture, forms words, exalts great things, is a cold member, and declares the will.

Flax is first sown, quickly harmed, slender and sparse, covered because of birds, gently gathered into bundles, put into water, dried in the sun, whitened by many beatings, and sheds its varied colour; it is rubbed, separated from tow, spun, knotted, unwound, washed again, and warped into cloth.

A locust washes away dirt and makes itself dirty, adds colour to water; when born it is called *bruchus*, when formed *achelabus*, and when complete, *locusta*. One devours another; in winter it hides, in summer it leaps, and its hind legs are longer.

[Col. 0151C] A breastplate is woven from diverse rings, covers and protects the body, is iron and heavy, and becomes rusty through lying unused.

A lamp gives a modest light; it is made from a potter’s clay vessel, which, when large, appears broken.

The morning star rises in the morning, announces the glowing day, and drives away darkness.

The moon receives its light from the sun; it shines by night when the other lights have departed, is lower and nearer the earth than the others, and, when the sun has departed, alone gives light to the night. It has a spot: the brighter it appears, the larger the spot. It is round, sometimes crescent-shaped, increases and decreases through its phases, quickly completes its course, is very great, and yet appears small.

[Col. 0151D] A wolf is foul-smelling, swift, cruel; it observes the absence of dogs and shepherds, lies in wait for sheepfolds, howls horribly. If it is seen before it sees, it does no harm; if it sees first, it takes away the voice.

The laver was bronze, at the entrance of the tabernacle; it had a rim all around above, held water for washing the priests, and had a base beneath, long and straight in line and smooth.

Lust removes without cost, corrupts the soul, brings the disease of paralysis upon the body and blindness upon the eyes, defiles the body, despoils reputation, takes away money, is an enemy to one’s neighbour, stinks before God, pleases the devil, is hateful to angels. Its fire descends into hell; its smoke, demanding vengeance, rises to heaven [Col. 0152A].

## Chapter XI. Of those whose first letter is M

A teacher ought to be learned, gentle, diligent, and attentive.

A hammer is hard, strong, heavy, and raised for striking.

A pomegranate is reddish on the outside in its rind, pale within, contains various red grains that quench thirst, and has a hard rind.

A nipple is situated on the breast, paired, soft, white, round, containing milk, pleasant; in a virgin it is firm, in a woman it is loosened; in it blood is changed into milk.

A sheaf is made from many things gathered by hand; it is collected with labour [Col. 0152B], but possessed with joy.

Manna was a small seed as though beaten with a pestle, white like coriander seed; to those eating it, it tasted like whatever they wished; it melted in the sun, hardened in fire, was ground in a little mortar, had the taste of oily bread, and, if gathered beyond measure, swarmed with worms.

The hand is distinguished by fingers, flexible, suited to work, white.

The sea is full of monsters, salty and bitter, generates winds, dangerous, deep, broad; every human being lives in it. There the larger fish devours the smaller; it receives all running rivers, holds living bodies, casts out dead ones, flows and ebbs, and never rests.

[Col. 0152C] A mother is anxious in giving birth, solicitous in rearing, diligent in guarding, fervent in love.

Honey is sweet, pleasant, tenacious.

The table was made of shittim wood and overlaid with gold, having four feet and two crowns; above, it had a bronze rim, and was round all around. Twelve white loaves are to be placed upon it on the Sabbath; twelve dishes over the loaves; twelve handfuls of incense over the dishes; it has rings in its feet and poles in the rings.

A blackbird is a small black bird, flying alone, not in flocks like a starling; in the regions of Achaia they are white.

The soldier rejoices in hardships and endures them; he is brave and thus armed: he has iron greaves, a breastplate over his thigh-pieces, an iron cap as an adornment over the breastplate, and [Col. 0152D] a helmet; over the helmet a certain emblem like a cone; a sharp sword and a spear. He rides on horseback and does not yield to blows.

The kite is feeble in strength and flight, exceedingly rapacious, and feeds on carrion. It constantly flies about kitchens and slaughterhouses; cowardly before large creatures, bold toward the smallest. It lies in wait for domestic birds, does not dare attack wild ones, preys upon chicks, and very quickly kills those it finds off guard.

A millstone turns swiftly; it is rough, double, round, supported by iron, heavy; it grinds grain, is worn away by use, and produces flour.

A mountain is firm, high, barren; it receives the sun’s rays before the valley does, is broader below and narrower at the summit, and is stirred by greater impacts.

[Col. 0153A] Death has mercy on no one; it feels compassion for none, makes all equal, comes unexpectedly, spares no one, separates body and soul, and is the end of labors and the final line of all things.

The world is passing, vain, anxious, false, and deceptive.

The cat is cunning, lies in wait for mice, is caught in a snare, sees by night, has gleaming eyes, does not quickly drown, and is strong in its claws; it leaps down from a height and is not harmed.

A wall is made of cut stones; it fortifies towns, keeps enemies away, and confines those shut within.

A mouse dwells in holes, fears the cat, and is caught by a small bait.

New wine is sweet wine; it swells the belly, causes looseness, and is hot. Without a vent it bursts new skins; it hisses. While it is clearing, it expels everything that must be purged, and produces drunkenness.

Myrrh is a tree in Arabia, five cubits high, resembling a white thorn. Its drop is green and bitter; the drop that flows of itself is more precious than that drawn out by a wound in the bark. It wards off worms and decay in wounds; it is fragrant and of a drying nature; it calms swellings and tumors.

## CHAPTER XII. On those whose first letter is N

Nard is a herb with a pressed, small leaf. Its tops spread out into ears; spice-dealers lay aside its spikes and leaves for preparing nard. It is a hot and fragrant herb.

[Col. 0153C] A nostril is straight, hollow, breathes, and perceives smell.

The nose is straight, flat, and white. The appearance of the face consists chiefly in it; it emits breath through the nostrils.

A swimmer’s body in the water keeps its head above the water and moves its feet, throwing the waves backward.

A ship is narrow at the beginning and end, broad and laden in the middle; it is carried on the waters. When pierced, it sinks; it has a mast, is driven by a sail, governed by a rudder, and held by an anchor. Without this protection it is moved by the wind; it is shattered on rocks, emptied by bailers, pressed and broken by waves, and battered on every side by the billows.

A sailor sits at the end of the ship, carefully watches the stern, controls the helm, considers and fears the route, dreads the storm, and continually inspects the ship lest it be damaged anywhere. He does not overload it beyond what is right; he wears cheap clothing and seeks his wage in port.

[Col. 0153D] Mist arises from moisture and spreads widely; it is cold. Rising, it heralds rain; it is dissolved by the sun’s heat; descending, it indicates fair weather; remaining motionless, darkness.

The night-raven dwells in houses and walls, flies at night, and avoids the day.

A nest is made for birds in a secluded place; it is warm inside, rough outside, and piled together from many things.

Snow is hardened from water, white and cold; it quickly melts, falls in small particles, comes down from above, is resolved into water by heat, covers the earth, and cherishes the crop.

[Col. 0154A] A razor shaves smoothly; it is sharp, cuts away superfluities, and is securely kept in a case.

Nine orders of angels; nine lepers healed and not returned.

Night is dark, quiet, and cold. In the night rotten wood and a certain little worm shine. It is solitary, sluggish for work, troublesome, full of dangers and phantoms; it takes color away from things and is illuminated by stars.

Clouds are light; they nourish rain and are dark and swift.

A nurse suckles an infant, protects it, treats it tenderly, carries it diligently, kisses it, chews its food beforehand, bears its illnesses, and restrains it from crying by promises and threats. She teaches it to walk and speak, and goes before it wherever [Col. 0154B] it goes; she directs a kiss to it; sometimes she allows it to fall, so that, hurt, it may beware of falling again. She soothes it when angry, wipes its eyes when it weeps, calls it back when it has taken offense, and lifts it into her lap.

A nut has a bitter outer husk, a hard shell, provides fodder, has a sweet kernel, and supplies or affords a pleasant light.

## CHAPTER XIII. On those whose first letter is O

There are eight beatitudes; eight ages of man and of the world; an eight-cubit vestibule of Ezekiel’s gate (Ezek. 40).

An eye is clear, flat, extended, and most delicate; it gives light to the body and is quickly injured. It has a pupil; the pupil is covered by an eyelid; it is darkened by a spot or excessive brightness; [Col. 0154C] it is double.

Smell delights, permeates the air, and remains for some time after the fragrant object has been removed.

Oil is rich and pleasant; it nourishes, is of an invisible nature, floats above, permeates, and refreshes the weary.

The olive tree is a sign of peace, yields oil, and is beautiful.

A clay pot is hardened by fire, fragile, and useless when broken.

A burden is borne; it is carried easily if it is gathered together; it inclines toward the ground and is heavy when bound upon the shoulders.

Onycha is a sea-fish whose crushed bones yield a most pleasant fragrance.

Barley is rough, food for beasts of burden, lowly, full of awns, sweet; mixed with water it benefits the sick, [Col. 0154D] and has tough chaff.

An organ has pipes; the pipes stand arranged like a tower, sound harmoniously, are easily damaged, and are set in motion by bellows.

A garden is dug around and enclosed around, adorned by the variety of trees, delightful with flowers, pleasant with green growth, gentle and calm when the breeze blows, outstanding for the charm of its shade, delightful with the murmur of a fountain, full of varied fruits, unharmed by dew, and praiseworthy for the song of birds.

A bone is strong, hidden, white, supports flesh, hard, solid, and hollow.

A kiss joins two bodies, delights, confirms, is a sign of peace, a pledge of love, and an earnest of betrothal.

[Col. 0155A] A door turns on hinges, affords entrance, is secured by a bar, protected by a bolt, has two thresholds, upper and lower, and hangs on pivots.

A sheep provides milk and meat for food, wool for clothing, and is sacrificed. It is a simple animal, clothed in its own fleece and clothing others; it is fruitful, and its dung is useful. It eats and feeds on dry things, is satisfied with little, chews the cud and divides the hoof; it is timid and quiet, has a skin suited to many uses, and is of a sociable nature.

An egg is translucent, fragile, white, the hope of offspring; it is born from an animal, and from it an animal is born.

## CHAPTER XIV. On those whose first letter is P

[Col. 0155B] A palm tree is exceedingly slender near the ground, broad above, with wrinkled bark; outwardly it has sweetness, roughness at the root, great height, long-lasting leaves, and pleasant fruits. It spreads out like the palm of a hand, bears fruit at a hundred years, and is the crown of victors, because it does not yield to weight but resists it.

A shoot bears fruit on the vine; outside the vine it withers. When luxuriant it is pruned; the pruning is given to the fire.

An eyelid covers and protects the eye. A person whose eyelids are cut off does not sleep and is made ugly.

Chaff is dry, light, barren, and tough; it is thrown out by the winnowing fan, separated from grain, and burned in fire; it makes a most fierce and powerful fire.

A stake is long, pointed, and rigid; [Col. 0155C] a hole is dug beforehand for it so that it may enter more easily. It is fit for a hedge, is sharpened, hardened by fire, and set in order.

Linen cloth is spread out, moistened, put into hot lye, heated, rubbed clean, beaten, twisted, and dried.

A marsh is watery, muddy land, impassable, slippery, full of pools, soft, deep, and fit for frogs to inhabit.

A vine leaf is broad and makes shade; it protects the grape against excessive heat. If it grows luxuriantly, it is cut back, so that the grape may receive the warming of heat.

Bread is made thus: first flour is ground, kneaded, sifted, sprinkled with water, leavened, rolled out, formed into bread, and baked.

Cloth is woven from many threads. Its wool is carded, [Col. 0155D] spun, shorn, warped, pressed, pricked, trodden by the fuller, washed, dyed, stretched by skill, cut into a garment, and sewn.

The panther means “every beast.” It has a spotted skin and is very beautiful, gentle, and hostile only to dragons. Having eaten its fill of dragons, it withdraws into a cave and sleeps for three days. On the third day it rises, emits an odor of marvelous sweetness, and gives out a roar; at its roar animals everywhere stop their steps and follow it in order as it goes before them. The dragon alone, hearing its voice, hides in its cave and, stupefied as though defeated, becomes mute.

[Col. 0156A] A paralytic loses the function of the limbs, trembles, grows cold, and becomes numb.

A leopard is cruel and spotted.

A sparrow is small, lustful, fickle, unstable; it stays on the roof and nests in a cleft of the rock.

A shepherd recognizes his sheep, strengthens the weak, leads them to pasture and brings them back, keeps wolves away with voice and staff, heals the sick and diseased, binds up the injured, brings back the wandering, carries the feeble, shears the strong and fat, seeks the lost, carries pregnant ewes, lifts lambs into his bosom, and is known by them.

A father begets, calls back, nourishes, loves, enriches, gives an inheritance, raises up, corrects, and sustains.

A pavement is beautiful, painted in diverse ways, and, lying beneath the feet, is trodden underfoot.

[Col. 0156B] The peacock suddenly strikes fear into hearers by the sound of its cry; hence it is named from fear (*pavor*). Its flesh is tough and resistant to decay, scarcely cooked and indigestible. Its gait is simple, its head serpentine, its breast sapphire-colored; on its wings are somewhat reddish feathers. It has a long tail marked with eyes. When praised, it raises its tail; it raises the feathers in order like a wheel, but lowers its tail when it sees its feet, because when it raises the tail its hind parts are exposed. It takes great pride in its tail; its head is weak, crested, and unlike the rest of its body. It very often devours its young unless the mother hides the eggs.

A comb is toothed with close-set and wider-spaced teeth; it arranges and orders hair, cleans the head, and is made of bone, [Col. 0156C] flat, shining, and broad.

The pelican is an Egyptian bird. It kills its young with its beak and mourns them for three days; after three days it tears itself with its beak and heals them with its own blood. It is a bird of excessive thinness.

Skin protects from an animal’s force and is adapted to diverse uses.

A pouch hangs from the neck by two straps, preserves what is put in it, belongs to travelers, is made of leather, and is carried at the side.

The partridge takes its name from its call, for it is a deceitful bird. It steals the eggs of others and broods them as its own. Chicks thus brooded, when they hear the voice of their own mother, recognize her again by natural instinct and follow her. It flies near the ground, goes about in flocks, [Col. 0156D] its flesh is wholesome, it is drawn into a net by the sound of a little bell, and seeks grain.

A traveler considers where he is going, measures the length of the road beforehand, carries with him necessities for sustenance, burdens himself as little as possible, provides himself with sturdy footwear, has a pouch, carries a staff, does not dress in costly garments, joins himself to good company, is not hindered from completing the right journey by any troublesome weight, is not drawn back by transient things, commends himself to the faithful amid dangers, is not without fear and apprehension, bears hardship through love of his homeland, does not show his own possessions to many, does not proclaim himself rich, always speaks and thinks of the journey’s end, and sighs for it.

Parchment is taken from a dead animal; it is stretched, [Col. 0157A] scraped, thinned, whitened by much soaking, carefully cleaned. It is thin, white, and smooth; water makes it soft, and it is suitable for the task of writing. It is pleasant, contracts and is prepared by fire, is made smooth with pumice, whiter with chalk, and marked with lines, so that at last writing may be done upon it.

The foot seeks the ground, is the lowest part of the body, is protected by a shoe, and carries the person.

A bolt fastens a door; it is movable, drawn forward and back.

A ball is spherical, rolling, light, and filled inside with rags, refuse, or hay.

Pepper is a small grain, very strong in taste, black, wrinkled, and hot.

A fisherman has a boat with his equipment, wears cheap [Col. 0157B] clothing, sails silently, casts nets into the water, frightens fish by casting nets, sets nets of different kinds, washes and repairs his nets, does not set them in muddy water, carefully watches where he has cast them, and knows which baits suit each fish.

A fish has fins and scales, is guided by its tail and fins, is nourished in water, dies outside water, is generated without intercourse, foresees the wind and, when it comes, lets itself down to the bottom; it leaps toward warmth, always rises upward, and is caught by a hook hidden in bait.

A wound quickly makes flesh rot, stinks, and is scarcely healed.

The plane tree is tall and spreading, grows near waters, has soft leaves resembling those of the vine, and possesses a most foul sap.

A feather is light, covers the body, is soft, takes root in flesh, [Col. 0157C] and is pleasantly or lightly drawn out.

Lead is a heavy metal; it increases in water, is burned in place of gold, and is very soft for cutting.

Rain comes from above, is fine, softens the earth, dispels cold, waters the earth, produces mud, moderates the weather, increases waters, and calms the wind.

An apple is spherical, beautiful to see, sharp yet pleasant to taste, fragrant; when ripe it becomes pale, and when it touches the ground it rots.

A bridge is placed over water and carries those crossing a river; it is sometimes destroyed by floodwater and supported by piers.

Unless it runs, a pig walks slowly; it runs readily, is prolific, bristly, grunts horribly, roots up mud with its snout, does not chew the cud, delights in mud, feeds on unclean things, [Col. 0157D] is fed on acorns; when one is struck, the rest gather and grunt together.

A preacher ought to be holy, learned, discerning, mature, eloquent, of honorable conduct, steadfast, of unblemished reputation, humble, approachable, and sent.

Frost is born from moisture, is dark, and spreads widely.

A boy is innocent, pure, clean, simple, truthful, generous, placable, and temperate. When hurt he does not rage; when offended he runs to his mother. On seeing a woman he does not lust after her.

The lung is soft, draws in breath, does not suffer injury, and moderates the heart’s heat.

Dust is earth like the smallest atom, lowly, barren, [Col. 0158A] mobile, light, dry, whirled by the wind, and harmful to the eyes.

The pupil is small, black, and has sight; vision is directed through it. It is quickly injured and darkened by a whitish film.

Purple is blood-colored and a royal adornment.

## CHAPTER XV. On those whose first letter is Q

A square has six sides; however it is thrown, it falls back and rests upon a side.

There are four Gospels and Evangelists; the chariots of Amminadab; four thousand fed in the wilderness; four rings on the ark; four feet on the table; four living creatures of Ezekiel; four cardinal virtues; four coverings of the tabernacle; four rivers of Paradise; four parts of the cross; four sides of the city in the Apocalypse; four watches of the night; four parts of the Lord’s garments in John; four parts [Col. 0158B] of the measure in Matthew; the sheet shown to Peter was suspended by four cords [Vulgate: “beginnings”] (Acts 20).

The oak is a tree seeking heights, strong, supplying food to pigs, and very durable.

The five books of Moses; five robes given by Joseph to Benjamin; five loaves in the Gospel; five thousand men; five portions given by Joseph before his other brothers; five Samaritan men; five columns before the Holy of Holies; five foolish and five prudent virgins; five stones which David took from the torrent; five sheddings of the Lord’s blood; five wounds in Christ’s body; five senses in the human body.

## CHAPTER XVI. On those whose first letter is R

[Col. 0158C] A cluster of grapes is spherical, full within, contains berries, is at first bitter and hard, and sweetens as it ripens.

A ray of sunlight is bright, fine, hot, and straight.

A root is fixed in the earth, rough and hidden; it supports the tree, spreads itself widely, and sends moisture to the branches.

A frog is talkative, disturbs the spring, hops about, dwells in a marsh, and from the grass upon which it hops plunges itself into the pool.

The breastpiece, or *logion*, was upon the breast of the ancient priest; twelve stones hung upon it, on which were the twelve names of the sons of Israel. On it [Col. 0158D] were written “truth and judgment”; it was attached to the ephod by certain golden chains.

An oar is broad, parts the water, drives the ship, and directs it.

A net is woven with various meshes, washed, and enfolds a fish or bird; it is folded up, visible in clear water, and hidden in troubled water.

The buckthorn is first soft and then thorny; it is low-growing, always green, and glue is made from its bark.

A stream is born from a spring, separated from the spring, and takes flavor and color from the spring.

Dew descends invisibly, cools, makes fruitful, is pleasant and clear, and is dried by a little heat.

A rose is ruddy, fragrant, beautiful, born from thorns, [Col. 0159A] quickly withers; when withered it becomes white and shrinks; it is cold in its leaves and hot in its seed.

A wheel has spokes around the center—that is, the axle—is rolling; in rising it falls; when dry it creaks, and likewise when new; overloaded, it creaks and breaks.

## CHAPTER XVII. On those whose first letter is S

A priest ought to be honorable in life and strong in wisdom.

A sack is rough, hard, heavy, conceals grain, and is quadrangular.

The goat-hair cloths were over the horns of the altar, touched the ground, and were rough.

A dragnet has many meshes, is broad, catches good and bad, large and small fish, and is drawn through the middle [Col. 0159B] of the water.

An arrow has a wooden shaft, flies swiftly, is feathered, is kept in a quiver, has a notch, moves straight ahead, is armed with sharp iron, straight, rigid, flat, slender, shot from a bow, whistles, and strikes suddenly.

Salt is fine; it seasons foods, dries meat, wards off decay, kills worms, crackles in fire, relieves swelling, is made in great quantity from water boiled down by fire or sun, and makes the earth barren.

Willows grow near water, sprout easily, are unfruitful, blossom but bear no fruit, and grow tall.

The Holy of Holies had the mercy-seat, the ark of the covenant, a veil at the entrance, a golden censer, and four columns; it was open only once a year to the high priest alone [Col. 0159C].

The sanctuary had an altar, incense, a larger veil at the entrance, five columns, a table, and a candlestick; it was open to all priests.

Blood is warm, purple, scarlet-colored, thick, flows gently, and is the seat of the soul.

A leech lives in a marsh, is long, and sucks blood; but first it wounds the skin, and when full, vomits up what it had sucked.

Sapphire resembles a clear sky; struck by a ray, it emits a gleam.

Sard is not of one color: black at the bottom, white in the middle, red at the top; it has the appearance of red earth and is blood-colored.

[Col. 0159D] Vine branches are worthless when cast out from the vine, fit for no use except fire.

A broom cleans a house, is made of many twigs, and soils itself.

A shield is broad, triangular, light, and movable; it protects and defends, is carried in the left hand, and held by a strap.

Seed is entrusted to good ground, scattered, hidden, cast into the following year, multiplied by frost, choked by excessive flooding, and rises with much increase. On the path it is trampled and carried off by birds; in stony places it withers; among thorns it is choked; in good, well-cultivated earth it multiplies. First the blade comes up, second the ear, third the grain; then flour is made from it.

[Col. 0160A] Old age is fastidious, cold, complaining, sluggish, weak, bent, and barren.

A hedge is woven from stakes and twigs, made beside a road, guards fruit, breaks when dried, is carried off by passers-by, and, after the fruit is gathered, is carried away and removed; it keeps off wild creatures and beasts and is fortified with thorns.

Seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer; seven virtues; seven beatitudes; seven capital vices; seven fat and seven lean cattle; seven fine ears of grain and as many blighted ones; seven columns of the Church; seven small bowls opposite the arms of the lampstand; seven lamps in the land of promise; seven snuffers; seven pouring vessels; [Col. 0160B] seven penitential psalms; seven sacraments of the Church; seven churches in Asia; seven loaves in the Gospel and seven baskets; seven works of mercy; seven kings in the land of promise; seven circuits in the dwelling-place.

A tomb is beautiful outside, but foul inside.

A bar is fastened to a door, has various turnings, is wound around wood, compounded with iron, and is easily disturbed.

Speech ought to come first to the file and then to the tongue: it should be premeditated, discerning, mature, distinct, infrequent, reliable, lively, constant, authoritative, humble, patient, and careful.

[Col. 0160C] A serpent moves upon its breast, eats earth, harms secretly, is venomous in its tail, exposes its whole body to protect its head, dwells in deserts, creeps lightly, flees a naked person, is scarcely extinguished, and dies from the spittle of a fasting person.

A servant ought to be obedient, faithful, wise, cheerful, and ready.

A bristle is sharp, rigid, introduces thread, is slender, and clings firmly.

There are six cherubim in Isaiah, jars in the Gospel, cities of refuge, works of six days, and six gifts Joseph offered his brothers.

A seal has an image and inscription, confirms a document stamped with wax, and keeps secrets.

[Col. 0160D] A wood is planted with trees, shady, dark, thick, inhabited by wild animals, uncultivated, solitary, muddy, unfruitful, and damp.

An emerald is of intense greenness beyond all grasses and leaves; it makes the surrounding heap green. It is found more precious in Cilicia than elsewhere.

Dreams quickly pass, are vain, and fashion vanity.

Sleep takes away the use of the limbs, creeps on gradually, brings in phantoms, weighs down the body, and afterward restores it for labor.
