A mirror is clear, fragile, flat, and polished; it represents an image, is set in wood, and, when broken, represents as many images as it has pieces.

[Col. 0161A] An ear of grain is protected by awns, supported by a stalk, filled with kernels, and has its grains arranged in it.

A thorn clings firmly; it is low, rough, prickly, dense, springs up of itself, makes a sharp fire, crackles in fire, and is hard.

A sponge is light, empty, porous, soft, and receptive of moisture.

Spittle descends from the brain; it is salty and white.

A star is fixed on high, is large though it seems small, round, illuminates the night, guides sailors, does not swerve from its course, is carried along with the firmament, is fiery, seems to change its place, sends forth rays from itself, and adorns the firmament.

A dung-heap is foul and a receptacle of filth.

[Col. 0161B] A gutter is hollow, receives rain, lets out what it has received, and is placed at the edge of a roof.

Stubble clings to the ground; it is light, barren, remains after crops are gathered, dry, fit for burning, hard, rough, fragile, crackling, and hollow.

Storax, or styrax, is a tree of Arabia; it distils an aromatic tear. The tear that flows down is clean and white; its resin has a pleasant, moist scent and emits a liquid almost of no use.

The ostrich is a bird huge in body, scanty in feathers or featherless; it has wings like those of a hawk and a heron, cannot fly, yet sometimes raises its wings. It leaves its eggs and forgets that a foot may crush them and a beast of the field break them; it is hardened against its young as though [Col. 0161C] they were not its own.

Study sharpens the mind, drives away idleness, engenders love of learning, preserves learning, turns the mind away from vain and useless things, produces hatred of sin, and seeks rest and peace.

Tow is the refuse of flax; it is soft, light, and quickly catches fire.

A stylus is long, flat, slender, sharp, straight, and broad at the other end.

Sulphur is white, foul-smelling, and sticky.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On those whose first letter is T

The tabernacle of the Lord had four sides. On each of two sides there were twenty boards; [Col. 0161D] on the western side, ten. Each board rested upon two silver bases; on each board it had golden rings, and in the rings gilded bars. It was divided into the Holy Place and the Holy of Holies. In the Holy Place was the altar of incense; its horn was covered with red-dyed skins. In the open court was the altar of burnt offerings.

The mole, very black, eats earth, digs earth, and in digging piles earth up over itself; the more it digs, the more it increases the mound of earth above itself. It has a smooth skin, dwells under the ground, and could not live above ground.

A bull has two horns, is strong, is held by the horn, goes before the herd, is wild, draws the yoke, makes the herd fruitful, and is lustful.

[Col. 0162A] Cloth is warped, cut, woven, whitened by frequent beatings and washings; it is fine, white, and soft.

A church is clean, enclosed in vaulted chambers, hung and adorned with cloths, strewn with flowers; candles are lit and bells rung within it.

Darkness is dark and drives away light; lest it itself should exist, it is driven away by light.

The terebinth is a small tree in Macedonia but fruitful and large in Damascus, with black, shining, solid wood like boxwood. It has flowers in clusters like those of the olive, but red; it has dense leaves and little pods emitting creatures like gnats. Its resin, called *terebinthina*, commonly *tereminthina*, is very pure. The spots of this tree are fruitful [reading uncertain]; its fruit is of two kinds: one kind red and the size of a lentil, the other pale, no larger than a bean, with a pleasant odor.

[Col. 0162B] A pot is fragile, made from clay, and hardened by fire.

A bridal chamber ought to be secluded, adorned, closed, and quiet.

A treasure is gathered from precious things, stored away, guarded, increased, and reserved for a time of need.

The throne was of ivory, great, clad within and without in exceedingly bright and pure gold. Its ascent was by six steps, the ascent being of marble; six little lions stood on the six steps, on either side. The rounded rear of the throne rested over a calf looking forward; two arms on either side held it, and two lions stood beside each arm. No such work existed in all kingdoms.

[Col. 0162C] Frankincense sends forth a little column of smoke; it is gathered in spring and autumn and smells more strongly when burned. The frankincense-producing region is called Saba, which means “mystery,” and is inaccessible on every side because of cliffs. It flows from trees like a tear and restrains motions of the flesh.

A censer has two properly fitting parts: the lower part is solid and the upper perforated. It has a ring above; five chains extend it, four of which are immovable. It is raised and lowered by the lower part, holds fire, and incense is shaken and stirred in the upper part so that it may breathe out greater smoke; [Col. 0162D] it is round and pierced with carved work.

Incense was compounded from vinegar or myrrh, from onycha or *albeola*, from sweet-smelling galbanum, and from the purest, brightest frankincense; all these were reduced into one mixture.

Thunder is terrible, arises from heat, sends lightning ahead, and emits the thunderbolt.

A winepress rises and descends by turning, separates wine from the grape, presses grapes, and rises step by step.

A torrent is rapid, passes swiftly, breaks all obstacles, is sudden, and arises from an excess of rains.

Three fruits of good ground in the Gospel.

[Col. 0163A] The Lord raised three dead persons; the earth held the Lord for three days; three places occur in the Lord’s parable; the title of Christ on the cross was written in three languages; there were three temptations of the Lord. Three places will contain two persons, rightly unequal: namely, a field, a mill, and a bed. Three persons are in the Trinity; three theological and principal virtues; three measures of flour; three sons of Noah; three bands of Chaldeans against Job; three principal vices; three Magi and their three gifts; three days of the Lord’s burial; three men—Noah, Daniel, Job; three orders of those saved in the field, bed, and mill; three baskets of the baker in Genesis; three grains of bad ground in the Gospel.

A trumpet is made by many hammerings, narrow at the bottom and broad at the top; it sounds through the breath of the mouth, is hollow, [Col. 0163B] gives forth a very great sound, awakens, gathers, and terrifies.

Aaron’s tunic was hyacinth-blue and reaching to the ankles; little bells and pomegranates hung below, and it covered the whole body.

A tower is surrounded by a ditch, high, fortified, strong, and firm.

The turtledove is a bird of pleasant and wooded places; it makes its nest in the branches of a dense tree. If it loses its mate once, it remains without one always; it wanders alone, does not feed on carrion, and feeds its young by night.

A drum is struck with the hand and made from the skin of a dead animal, whose hide is stretched over hollow wood.

## CHAPTER XIX. On those whose first letter is U and V

A cow is frisky, draws the yoke, treads grain, provides milk, is fruitful, has horns, is sacrificed, chews the cud, [Col. 0163C] and divides the hoof.

A valley is low, quiet, secluded, moist, and shaded.

The sacred veil was made with embroidered work, interwoven in four colors, hung from columns and bars. A ship’s sail gathers wind, is broad, drives the mast, and is hung from the mast with a crosswise piece of wood; in calm weather it is reefed, in a storm spread out, and by some piece of wood is turned in its course.

A vein contains blood; when struck or cut, it emits the same; it is hidden.

Poison infects, corrupts, and kills.

The belly receives food, is soft, and is swollen.

Wind is swift, invisible, gentle, whistling, strong; a great wind is moderated by a little rain.

[Col. 0163D] Spring is temperate, produces flowers, makes plants sprout, and brings forth the songs of birds.

A worm is born from earth without intercourse, moves gently, draws itself along by its mouth, is fragile and soft, and looks about with raised head so that it may move more softly.

A bladder is round, light, empty, swollen, and expanded by air.

The garments of the priest are these: drawers of twisted fine linen, a very close linen shirt, a turban on the head, a hyacinth-blue tunic, and a golden belt. They also had a golden ephod, a shoulder-piece made like a scapular, a square breastpiece upon the breast, and, as I have said, a turban upon the head with a golden plate.

[Col. 0164A] A bond binds and constricts; it is heavy or burdensome.

A vineyard buds, is trenched, propagated, pruned, dug, staked, bound to stakes, and hedged. It bears buds, leaves, and flowers. Shoots are pulled out so that the moisture of the stock may not pass to them; vine leaves are removed because of excessive shade, so that the garden may have the heat of the sun; there should be a shelter in it, so that it may be guarded. In winter no wood is cheaper; in summer none more useful.

Wine is clear, white, somewhat sweet; it intoxicates, produces blood, gladdens the heart, sharpens the mind, sometimes turns sour, and unmixed wine kills little children.

[Col. 0164B] The violet is purple, low-growing, fragrant, cold, and soft.

A rod is straight, slender, long, smooth, flexible, has a flower at its top, and chastises and instructs.

Glass is clear, smooth, solid, and fragile.

A band encircles, adorns, and binds tight.

The sacred heifer was red, unblemished, and had not drawn a yoke.

A calf is a priestly victim, has horns, and is frisky and simple.

Shade moderates heat, is welcome to those weary in heat, preserves the outlines of the body, and through it one comes to the body—for it is produced by the body’s interposition before a luminous object—and is insubstantial.

Eleven disciples were in Galilee. Eleven goat-hair cloths were in [Col. 0164C] the tabernacle.

Good ointment is made from choice myrrh, cinnamon, calamus, cassia bark, and olive oil. These, reduced to powder, were prepared with olive oil in the prescribed measure.

A nail is the horny part of the fingers, hard, shining, thin, and flat.

Birds are light and unstable; they nest and sing in the air, fly with two wings; when one is struck, the others flee; they are timid.

Pleasure dissipates virtues, softens the body, destroys natural goods, and seeks idleness.

Let the voice of a modest person be simple, restrained, quiet, humble, modest, guarded, and cautious.

[Col. 0164D] A bear produces disgust, knows no study, has no companionship, is huge in body, covered with a very hard skin, cruel, very strong in its forelimbs, and exceedingly fond of honey. It climbs trees; it is born an unformed lump of flesh and is shaped by its mother’s licking tongue.

A wineskin is made from the hide of a dead animal. It holds and preserves wine; when it has grown old, it is useless.

A fox is cunning, biting, foul-smelling, dwells in holes, deceitful, and [reading uncertain: *inesibilis*].

A vulture is said to scent corpses across seas; if it sees a corpse lying there, it descends to eat it. It follows an army so as to gorge itself on corpses, and readily walks on its feet.

[Col. 0165]

## Four Books on the Soul and Its Formation for the Knowledge of Itself and of God, and for True Piety

The first and third of these, because of the supreme fervour of pious devotion shining forth in them, have been ascribed under the titles *Meditations* and *On the Interior House* to the devout doctor Blessed Bernard of Clairvaux. The works of Blessed Augustine, however, have wrongly laid claim to the second, both because of its subtlety of argument and because of the dignity of its style; for it cites Boethius, apart from Augustine’s practice and against the chronology. (G)*

## Book I

(It is found among the Works of St Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIV, col. 485.)

## Book II

(See *Patrologia*, vol. XL, Works of St Augustine VI, col. 779.)

## Book III

(It is found among the Works of St Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIV, col. 507, down to the words of chapter 49: “Than earthly occupation.”)

### Chapter L. A contemplation upon the words, “The Word was made flesh,” not found in the other works, and apparently a new treatise.

[Col. 0165A]

“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1). Truly, the Word was made flesh; and we truly receive the flesh of the Word as the Lord’s food. Therefore he must be understood to remain in us naturally: he who, having been born human, assumed for himself our nature of flesh, now inseparably united to himself, and mingled with us, under the sacrament of flesh to be communicated, the nature of his own flesh.

For thus we are all one, because the Father in Christ and Christ in us make us one in them. Therefore, we who receive the body have become Christ’s body; and, by his mercy, we are what we receive. We are Christ’s body, and we are Christ himself, [Col. 0165B] because, although we are many, all his members are one body (Rom. 12; Col. 2). Therefore, we who are Christ’s members and are Christ must be united not only to the Head through love, but also mutually with the members.

For whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not preserve the bond of peace receives the mystery not for his own benefit, but as testimony against himself. Our mystery has been set upon the Lord’s table. Therefore be what you see, and receive what you are. In the bread is received that which hung upon the cross; and in the cup is received that which was poured out from Christ’s side.

[Col. 0166A]

For the invisible Priest, by the hidden power of his word, changes the visible creatures of bread and wine into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “This is my body”; and, repeating the consecration: “This is my blood.” Therefore, when you ascend to the venerable altar to be satisfied with food, behold with faith the sacred body and blood of the Lord your God; touch it with the mind; marvel at it with honour; venerate it with devotion; receive it with the hand of the heart; and take it inwardly with the draught of the soul.

For to believe in him is to receive the living bread. We believe and affirm that Christ’s body is such to each person as the person who approaches to offer is, and such as the person who approaches to receive is. For one and the same body is always holy on account of the Lord’s name which is invoked, and it becomes such for each person as is the heart with which that person approaches to receive it.

[Col. 0166B]

If an evil person offers to God and a good person receives, it is such for each as each has been. We believe and confess that the body which God assumed from the Virgin, and in which he rose again, is always in heaven, and is wherever he wills and in whatever form he wills. He who sits above at the right hand of the Father is held in human hands at the time of sacrifice.

We receive in the sacrament Christ’s body as it is in itself after the resurrection. When it is received, it is not consumed; but, when the office for which it is sacrificed and eaten has been completed, it is transferred into that which is in heaven. Christ [Col. 0167A] was offered once in himself, and is sacrificed daily in the sacrament (Heb. 9).

Therefore, when the priest has invoked the Holy Spirit, offered that venerable victim, and then touched the common God, where, tell me, shall we place that in our estimation? Consider what sort of hands ought to minister such great things; what sort of tongue ought to pour forth such words; and what soul, purer and holier than others, ought to receive such a Spirit.

For then angels are present with the priest, and the tribunal and place of the altar are filled with heavenly powers in honour of him who is sacrificed. At the very hour of the offering, the heavens are opened at the priest’s voice; in that mystery of Jesus Christ the choirs of angels are present; the lowest things are joined to the highest; [Col. 0167B] earth is united with heaven; and one thing is made from visible and invisible things.

But while we do these things, it is necessary that we sacrifice ourselves in contrition of heart; and we who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion ought to imitate what we perform. For then the victim will truly be for us before God, when it has made us ourselves a victim. In Christ the victim was offered once by eternal power for salvation; but we offer daily, because we sin daily. We offer, however, in remembrance of his death; and the victim is one, because Christ was offered once.

This sacrifice is an image of that one: always the same, the same in substance, though different in form. While the victim is broken and the blood is poured from the cup into the mouths of the faithful, it signifies the sacrifice of the Lord’s [Col. 0167C] body on his cross and the outpouring of his blood from his side.

Yet, although Christ is daily sacrificed in the sacrament, it is not said that he is killed again; rather, his true sacrifice, represented anew, accomplishes now in the sacrament what it then accomplished on the cross. Here and there the substance of Christ’s body and blood is the same, although under another form; and the grace of our salvation is likewise the same.

For the true flesh of Christ is that which we receive in the sacrament, covered by the form of bread; and the true blood of Christ is that which we drink beneath the form and taste of wine. The food of mortality appears outwardly, because what appears outwardly from us is mortal. Nothing outwardly is changed, because nothing outwardly in us is renewed. But inwardly we receive in ourselves the same thing [Col. 0167D] that we believe concerning him: for we receive life from life, by which we are re-formed unto life.

For just as true flesh is created from the Virgin by the Spirit without intercourse, so by that same Spirit Christ’s very body is mystically consecrated from the substance of bread and wine. And just as that which is offered everywhere is one body and not many bodies, so one sacrifice is sacrificed in diverse places by diverse persons, and everywhere it is the same. It is divided into portions and received by many, yet it is always whole. Just as it is indivisible when divided, so it is incorrupt when received.

Christ is eaten in portions in the sacrament and remains whole: whole in heaven, whole in your heart, whole in what is broken, whole in what is unbroken. In the small portion there is as much as is known to be [Col. 0168A] in the whole. Individuals have no less than all together have. One person, two persons, or many receive the whole without diminution, because grace is not in the form or quantity of the sacrament, but in Christ’s power.

However the signs in the sacrament may vary, Christ is always the same in himself. He made this more clearly manifest when, at supper, being present, he distributed his body and blood to his disciples. He gave them himself in the sacrament as though another, and yet the same. And although he was eaten and drunk in the sacrament as received by each person, he nevertheless remained one and whole in himself.

Divine grace is so free that it is bound by no human merits or offices, but pours itself forth when it wills, how it wills, and wherever it wills.

Therefore, within the Catholic Church, nothing greater is performed in the sacrament [Col. 0168B] of Christ’s body by a good priest, and nothing less by an evil priest, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. Yet all the sacraments, though they harm those who administer them unworthily, benefit those who receive through them worthily.

For communion with evil persons does not stain anyone by participation in the sacraments, but by consent to their deeds. Just as Judas, to whom the Lord handed the morsel, made room for the devil within himself not by receiving an evil thing but by receiving a good thing badly, so everyone who receives unworthily makes room for the devil within himself.

Therefore those who have not yet worthily repented of grave sins, or who are still inclined to sin, or who hate any human being, should not receive Christ’s body, lest they die. But incestuous and lustful persons [Col. 0168C] receive it more dangerously, because nothing is so opposed to the lover of purity as filth.

But one who has ceased to sin, although still wounded by sin, should nevertheless not cease to communicate, provided that he has no intention henceforth of sinning. As we are tempted and fall daily, Christ is daily sacrificed for us in the sacrament.

Therefore, when we receive Christ’s body with the mouth, let us consider in our hearts his friendship and benefits: how he suffered and died for us, and by his death delivered us from eternal death. By participation in his body he incorporated us into himself, so that he may pass in us to the Father, and we too may pass in him, made one with him: that through himself we may have the taste of him on the way, fullness in the homeland, here provision for the journey, and there reward.

[Col. 0168D]

It is asked why Christ’s body and blood are consecrated in bread and wine rather than in other bodily kinds. The answer is that, just as bread is made from many grains and wine from many grapes, so the Church is gathered from different persons. It was also fitting that, in the same forms by which flesh in every human being is naturally nourished and produced, they should be consecrated potentially in the Lord’s human nature.

If bread is naturally transformed into the flesh and wine into the blood of any person, much more, if God wills, will they be transformed potentially into his own flesh and blood. Therefore, since bread is changed into flesh and wine into blood by the Lord’s word, let the rational creature no longer despair of being transformed into Christ’s body, [Col. 0169A] into which even the brute creature is transformed, if it ceases to be what it had wrongly been of itself, so that in Christ it may rightly become what it was not.

For just as food and drink are our temporal life, for as long as God pleases, so much more will that heavenly bread be eternal life for those for whom he wills it. For he who has life and is life ought more to be believed to confer eternal life than one who does not have it.

It is not surprising that the Creator can confer everlasting life upon a creature, when a creature can preserve and keep another creature eternally. For just as the tree of life was placed in paradise, by which a human being would live eternally in the body had he not sinned, so Christ placed himself in the Church as the tree of life, that eternal life might be in those who believe in him.

Therefore [Col. 0169B] faith is so greatly required in the sacrament, because the world perished through false faith when Adam presumed to believe the devil making false suggestions more than God making true promises. But when, as is fitting, more faith is given in the sacrament to God than to the enemy, that treacherous faith is healed by this true faith.

And because we live by food and drink in such a way that we cannot lack either, Christ willed that both should be present in his sacrament, lest it be imperfect if either were absent. Therefore neither body without blood nor blood without body is rightly communicated. Bread and wine are properly food not for beasts but for human beings. Therefore Christ employed the ministry of both, so that it might be believed to be the distinctive and proper refreshment of human beings; and afterward he willed water to be mixed with it through the apostles, in order to signify that fellowship in the dignity [Col. 0169C] of so great a mystery belongs not only to the righteous but also to sinners, if they are willing to repent.

Because we are regenerated through water and redeemed through blood, blood and water came forth from Christ’s side. Therefore, when wine and water are sacrificed for Christ on behalf of the people, and both become one blood, this signifies the unity of Head and members. Therefore, just as you see that what has been made is one, so be one yourselves by loving one another. For whoever receives the mystery of unity but does not preserve the bond of peace receives the mystery not for his own benefit but as testimony against himself. But whoever hates one person will lose wholly whatever he has offered to God in good works.

All sacraments are fulfilled by faith. Therefore, whoever approaches them with faith and devotion, even though through carelessness or ignorance he inserts some erroneous words, is not for that reason believed to make the sacrifice any less, since the disposition of the supplicant overcomes the defect of the prayer. It is not to be considered what a person does, but with what intention and will that person does it.

The Church’s sacraments chiefly consist in four kinds: [Col. 0170A] water, oil, bread, and wine. Although water is necessary for everyone, it is not precious because of its cheapness and abundance. Oil, bread, and wine, on the other hand, so escape the measure of price through their low cost that they seem to claim for themselves no usefulness except in spiritual grace.

Water extinguishes, cleanses, and whitens beyond other liquids. Therefore in baptism it extinguishes the incitements of the flesh, washes away the stain of sins, both original and actual, restores the brightness of innocence, and, thus reforming the image of the heavenly Father, regenerates children of adoption. Whence comes such power, that it touches the body and cleanses the heart, except from the working word? Not because it is spoken, but because it is believed; for all sacraments are fulfilled by faith.

Baptism is such as is the person in whose word it is given, not such as [Col. 0170B] is the person through whose ministry it is administered. Oil, moreover, gives light, anoints, and nourishes: it illumines the soul by faith, anoints it by devotion, and nourishes it by love. Bread and wine incorporated into a human being are temporal life.

Accordingly, in this sacrament Christ willed to be united, as Head, to the members, through whom we are regenerated to God the Father. Through participation in Christ’s body and blood we are incorporated into the Son of God unto life. Through the anointing of oil we are strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit.

The faithful God will never drive from participation in his kingdom those whom he deigns to unite to himself so intimately in this world’s exile. Rather, he will repay them with the great recompense of honour in the manifest vision of his majesty, since he has been received and ordered by them so worthily in the hidden and foreign figures of the sacraments. There [Col. 0170C] cannot be made different what has been made one here.

Whatever deformity or change may happen merely in appearance in Christ’s sacrament ought not to tear from us faith in its truth. For he who, being true God, endured many unworthy things in his body would endure nothing unworthy in his body until the end of the age, although he is truly present there. Since all things except sin are clean to him, he does not appear more unclean in the belly of a mouse or dog than in the belly of an impenitent sinner.

If it is said to be burned by fires, this is impossible, since he is God of all the elements. If it appears to be corrupted by the gnawing of mice or the change of age, this does not concern the substance of the sacrament—namely Christ, who cannot be corrupted, [Col. 0170D] because he is incorruptible. Such things and similar occurrences come only to correct or punish some persons’ negligence, or to test and exercise faith, so that the faithful may be exercised and the reprobate hardened. Therefore it must be guarded with the devotion with which it is received.

## Book IV

Which concerns the raising of the soul or mind to God, devout prayer and discourse addressed to God, and certain instructions and admonitions for salvation.

[Col. 0171]

### Chapter I. That it is necessary for us to invoke God, and what it is to invoke him.

[Col. 0171A]

Because we are set amid snares, we easily grow cold toward heavenly desire. Therefore we need continual admonition, so that, awakened when we drift away, we may return to God, our true and supreme good.

For this reason, not through the rashness of presumption but through great love for my God, I have devoted effort to this little work for his praise, so that from the elegant sayings of the holy Fathers I might always have with me a brief, handy word concerning my God, and, whenever I grow lukewarm, might be kindled into his love by the fire of its reading.

Now be present with me, my God, whom I seek, whom I love, whom I praise and adore with heart, mouth, and such strength as I possess. My mind, devoted to you, [Col. 0171B] inflamed by love, sighing for you, yearning for you, desiring to see you alone, finding nothing sweet except to speak of you, hear of you, write of you, confer concerning you, and frequently turn over your glory beneath the heart, so that the sweet remembrance of you may be some rest for me amid these storms.

Therefore I invoke you, most desired one; I cry to you with a great cry in my whole heart. And when I invoke you, I surely call you into myself, because I would not exist at all unless you were in me, and unless I were in you. You are in me because you remain in my memory from the time when I came to know you; and there I find you when I remember you and delight in you and in speaking of you—from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

### Chapter II. How God, remaining unmoved in himself, causes all things to move, and either acts or acts together with all things.

[Col. 0171C]

You fill heaven and earth, bearing all things without burden and filling all things without enclosure. Ever active, ever at rest; gathering, yet needing nothing; seeking, though nothing is lacking to you. You love but do not grow hot; you are jealous and secure. You repent, yet do not grieve. You are angry, yet tranquil. You alter works, yet do not alter your counsel. You receive what you find, yet have never lost it. Never needy, yet rejoicing in gains. Never greedy, yet demanding interest. It is always given out to you, so that you may owe; and who has anything that is not yours? You repay debts while owing no one; you forgive debts while losing nothing.

You who are everywhere and wholly everywhere, who can be perceived but cannot be seen; who are absent nowhere and yet are far from the thoughts of the wicked. Nor are you far from where you are absent, [Col. 0171D] because where you are not by grace, you are present by judgment. You who are present everywhere and can scarcely be found; whom we follow while you stand still, yet cannot apprehend. You who hold all things, fill all things, embrace all things, surpass all things, sustain all things.

[Col. 0172A]

You who teach the hearts of the faithful without the sound of words; who are not extended by places, changed by times, or subject to arrivals and departures; who dwell in inaccessible light, which no human being has seen or can see. Remaining at rest in yourself, you move everywhere throughout the whole.

For you cannot be split or divided, because you are truly one. Nor are you poured out into parts; rather, wholly you hold the whole, wholly you illumine and possess the whole. Though books filled the whole world, your ineffable knowledge could not be narrated. Because you are unspeakable, you cannot in any way be written or enclosed.

You are the fountain of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness. For you are great without quantity, and therefore immeasurable; good without quality, and therefore truly and supremely good; and no one is good except you alone. Your will is deed; for you, to will is to be able; and all that you created from nothing you made by will alone.

[Col. 0172B]

You possess every creature of yours without any need, govern without labour, and rule without weariness. Nothing can disturb the order of your sovereignty, whether in the highest things or the lowest. You are had in all places without being in a place; you contain all things without bodily form; and you are present everywhere without position or motion.

You are not the author of evil, which you cannot do. Nor has anything that you made ever caused you regret: by your goodness we were made, by your justice we pay penalties, and by your mercy we are delivered. Your omnipotence governs, rules, and fills what it created.

We do not say that you fill all things so that they contain you, but rather so that they themselves are contained by you. Nor do you fill all things part by part. Nor should it be thought in any way that each thing receives you according to the magnitude of its portion—the greater thing more, the lesser less—when rather you yourself are in all things, or all things are in you.

[Col. 0172C]

Your omnipotence encloses all things, and no one will be able to find an avenue of escape from your power. For whoever does not have you propitious will by no means escape you when angry.

### Chapter III. Again, on the devout invocation of God, the tranquillity and joy of the mind through it, and the misery of the soul that does not seek God.

Therefore I invoke you, most merciful one, into my soul, which you prepare to receive you through the desire which you inspire in it. Enter into it, I pray, and fit it to yourself, that you may possess what you made and remade, and that I may have you as a seal upon my heart.

I beseech you, most gracious one, do not forsake one invoking you; for before I invoked you, you called and sought me, so that I, your servant, might seek you, find you by seeking, and love you when found. I have sought and found you, Lord, and I desire to love you. Increase my desire and grant what [Col. 0173A] I ask; for if you gave me all that you have made, it would not suffice for your servant unless you gave me yourself.

Therefore give yourself to me, my God, mine; restore yourself to me. Behold, I love; and if this is too little, let me love more strongly. I am held fast by love of you; I burn with desire for you; I delight in your sweet remembrance.

Behold, while my mind sighs for you and meditates upon your ineffable mercy, the burden of flesh weighs less heavily; the tumult of thoughts ceases; and the weight of mortality and miseries does not dull me as it ordinarily does. All contrary things are silent, and all things are tranquil. The heart burns, the spirit rejoices, memory is vigorous, understanding shines, and the whole spirit, kindled by desire for your vision, sees itself caught up into love of invisible things.

May my spirit take wings like an eagle; may it fly and not fail; may it fly and attain unto the beauty of your house [Col. 0173B] and the throne of your glory, so that there it may be fed, at the table of refreshment of the citizens above, upon your hidden things, in the place of pasture beside most abundant streams.

Be our exultation, you who are our hope, salvation, and redemption. Be our joy, you who will be our reward. May my soul always seek you, and grant that it may not fail in seeking. Woe to the wretched soul which neither seeks nor loves Christ; for it remains dry and miserable. Whoever does not love God loses the very life he lives. Whoever cares to live apart from you, Lord, is nothing and is for nothing. Whoever refuses to live for you is dead. Whoever has no taste for you has lost sound judgment.

Most merciful one, I commit, surrender, and entrust myself to you, through whom I am, live, and understand. In you I trust, hope, and place all my hope; through you I shall rise again, [Col. 0173C] live, and rest. I desire, love, and adore you; with you I shall remain, reign, and be blessed.

The soul that neither seeks nor loves you loves the world, serves sins, and is subject to vices. It is never at rest, never secure. May my mind always serve you, most gracious one; may my pilgrimage sigh for you; may my heart burn in love for you. May my soul rest in you, my God. May it contemplate you in the ecstasy of the mind. May it sing your praises in jubilation, and may this be my consolation in this exile.

May my mind flee beneath the shadow of your wings from the heat of this age’s thoughts. May my heart rest in you—my heart, a great sea swelling with waves. God, richest in every good, most bountiful giver of the banquet of heavenly fullness, give food to the weary, gather the scattered, free the captive, restore what is torn apart.

Behold, he stands at the door and knocks (Rev. 3). I beseech you through the bowels of your mercy, by which the Dayspring from on high visited us: command that the wretched man knocking be opened to, [Col. 0173D] so that with free steps he may enter to you, rest in you, and be refreshed by you with heavenly bread. For you are bread and the fountain of life. You are the light of eternal brightness. You are all things from which the upright live, they who love you.

God, light of the hearts that see you, life of the souls that love you, and strength of the thoughts that seek you so that they may cleave to your holy love: come, I pray, into my heart, and intoxicate it from the abundance of your delight, that it may forget these temporal things. I am ashamed and weary of suffering such things as this world performs. What I see is sad to me. What I hear concerning transitory things is grievous. Help me, Lord my God, and give gladness in my heart.

[Col. 0174A]

### Chapter IV. He prays that he may receive God according to the measure of his mind; that the house of his soul may be enlarged by the expulsion of evil desires and the reception of good ones; and he recalls how great is the happiness of the soul received into heaven.

Come to me, that I may see you; but the house of my soul is narrow. Enlarge it, so that you may come into it; it is ruined: restore it. It has things that offend your eyes—I confess and know it—but who will cleanse it? Or to whom else besides you shall I cry: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18)?

Make me, sweet Christ, good Jesus—make me, I pray—through love and desire for you lay aside the burden of carnal desires and earthly lusts. Let my soul rule my flesh; reason my soul; your grace my reason; [Col. 0174B] and subject me inwardly and outwardly to your will.

Grant me that my heart, my tongue, and all my bones may praise you. Enlarge my mind and raise the gaze of my heart, so that, even by the swift thought of my spirit, I may touch you, eternal wisdom abiding above all things. Release me, I pray, from the bonds by which I am held fast, so that, leaving all these things, I may hasten to you, cleave to you alone, and attend to you alone.

Blessed is the soul which, released from its earthly prison, freely seeks heaven; which sees you, sweetest Lord, face to face; which is troubled by no fear of death, but rejoices securely in the incorruption of perpetual glory. It is tranquil and secure; it fears neither enemy nor death. It already possesses you, the gracious Lord whom it long sought and always loved; joined with hymn-singing choirs, it sings forever the honey-sweet songs of the perpetual feast to the praise of your glory, Christ the King.

[Col. 0174C]

For it is intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you give it drink from the torrent of your delight. Blessed is the society of the citizens above, and glorious the solemn festival of all those returning to you from the sorrowful labour of our pilgrimage.

Your citizens continually behold the loveliness of every beauty, the splendour of every radiance, and the dignity of every excellence. Nothing at all that disturbs the mind is brought to the ears there in you. What songs, what instruments, what chants, what melodies are sung there without end! For there continually sound the honey-sweet instruments of hymns, the most sweet melody of angels, and wondrous songs of songs, which the heavenly citizens sing forever to your praise [Col. 0174D] and glory.

Bitterness and every harshness of gall have no place in your realm. For there is no evil one there, nor evil. There is no adversary or assailant, nor any enticement of sin. There is no want, no disgrace, no quarrel, no reproach, no accusation, no fear, no disturbance, no punishment, no uncertainty, no violence, no discord; but highest peace, perfect love, jubilation and eternal praise of God, secure rest without end, and joy always in the Holy Spirit.

Blessed shall I be if I hear the most delightful songs of your citizens, honey-sweet hymns rendering praises to the supreme Trinity with due honour; but exceedingly blessed if I myself deserve to sing to the Lord a song from the sweet [Col. 0175A] songs of Zion (Ps. 136).

O life that gives life, eternal and eternally blessed life, where joy is without sorrow, rest without labour, dignity without trembling, riches without loss, health without weakness, abundance without diminution, life without death, perpetuity without corruption, and blessedness without calamity. There every good is perfected in love; there are form and vision face to face; there is full knowledge in all things and through all things. There the supreme goodness of God is seen, and the illuminating light is glorified by the saints. There the present majesty of God is beheld, and the mind of those who contemplate it is satisfied without failure by this food of life.

They see and desire to see; they are satisfied without anxiety and without weariness. There the true sun of righteousness refreshes all by the wondrous sight of his beauty, and so illumines all the citizens of the heavenly [Col. 0175B] homeland that they themselves shine: the light illumined by God, illuminating light beyond all brilliance of our sun and all brightness of the stars. Cleaving to immortal deity, they are thereby made immortal and incorruptible, according to the promise of the Lord and Saviour: “Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory; that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John 17).

O kingdom of heaven, most happy kingdom, lacking death and free from end! No times succeed one another there through eternity, where continuous day without night knows no time. There the victorious soldier is heaped with ineffable gifts.

> A noble head, enfolded by a perpetual crown.

### Chapter V. He prays with longing to enjoy heavenly goods and be delivered from earthly evils, and recounts them.

[Col. 0175C]

Would that, with the burden of sins remitted, your divine mercy might command me, the least of Christ’s servants, to lay down this burden of flesh, so that I might pass into the eternal joys of your city to find rest; might join the most holy choirs above; might stand with the most blessed spirits before the glory of the Creator; might behold the present face of God; might be touched by no fear of death; might rejoice secure in the incorruption of perpetual immortality; and, joined to him who knows all things, might lose every blindness of ignorance.

Then I might count all earthly things of little worth and not deem myself worthy any longer either to behold or remember this valley of tears: where life is laborious, corruptible, [Col. 0175D] full of every bitterness; life, mistress of evils and servant of hell, which bodily humours swell, pains weaken, fevers dry up, air makes diseased, foods inflate, fasts emaciate, jokes dissolve, sorrows consume, anxiety constricts, security dulls, riches make proud, poverty casts down, youth exalts, old age bends, weakness breaks, grief depresses, the devil lies in wait for, the world flatters, the flesh delights, the soul is blinded, and the whole human being is troubled.

After all these great evils furious death follows, and puts such an end to vain joys that, once they have ceased to be, they are not even thought to have been. Yet what praises or thanksgivings can we render to you, our God, who do not cease to console us, even amid these great miseries of our mortality, by the wondrous visitation [Col. 0176A] of your grace?

Behold, I am wretched and full of many sorrows. I fear for my life; I consider my sins; I dread your judgment; I think upon the hour of death; I shudder at the punishments of Tartarus; I do not know with what strictness my works will be weighed by you; I utterly do not know with what end I shall close them. While I turn over these things and many others in my heart, you come, intending to comfort me, with your accustomed mercy.

Amid these complaints, excessive weeping, and deep sighs of heart, you take up my sad and anxious mind to the lofty ridges of mountains, even to the beds of spices, and set me in a place of pasture beside rivulets of sweet waters. There you prepare before me a table of abundant provision, which refreshes the weary spirit and gladdens the heart exhausted by sorrow. Refreshed at last [Col. 0176B] by such delights, forgetful of many miseries, I rest in you in true peace, above the height of the earth, amid an abundance of many delights.

### Chapter VI. He professes his love for God, that God may make it grow, and adds the causes of love.

I love you, my God; I love you, and I desire to love you more and more. Grant me, O fairest of the children of men, that I may desire you, that I may love you as much as I wish, as much as I ought. You are immeasurable; you ought to be loved without measure, especially by us, whom you have so loved, so saved, for whom you have done things so great and such as these. O Love, ever burning and never extinguished; sweet Christ, good Jesus, highest charity, my God: kindle me wholly with your fire, with love of you, affection for you, longing for you, your charity, your gladness and exultation, your mercy [Col. 0176C] and sweetness, your will and desire—which is holy and good, chaste and pure—that, wholly filled with the sweetness of your love and wholly made fervent by the flame of your charity, I may love you, my sweetest and most beautiful Lord, with all my heart, with all my soul, with all my strength, and with my whole intention (Luke 10), with great contrition of heart and a fountain of tears, with great reverence and trembling; having you in my heart, on my lips, and before my eyes always and everywhere, so that no place in me may lie open to adulterous loves.

O most beautiful bridegroom of my soul, I beg you, through that most sacred outpouring of your precious blood by which we were redeemed: grant me contrition of heart and a fountain of tears, especially when I offer prayers and supplications to you; [Col. 0176D] when I sing the psalmody of your praise; when I recall or proclaim the mystery of our redemption, the manifest token of your mercy; when, though unworthy, I stand at the holy altars, desiring to offer with every reverence and devotion worthy of it that wondrous and heavenly sacrifice which you, my Lord, immaculate priest, instituted and commanded to be offered in remembrance of your charity—namely, of your death and passion for our salvation and for the daily restoration of our frailty.

May my mind, amid so great mysteries, be strengthened by the sweetness of your presence. May it feel that you are present to it, and may it rejoice before you: fire ever shining, love ever burning, sweet Christ, good Jesus, eternal and unfailing light. Bread [Col. 0177A] of life, who restore us and do not fail in yourself: you are eaten daily and yet always remain whole. Shine upon me; kindle, enlighten, and sanctify me. Empty your vessel of wickedness; fill it with grace, and preserve it full, so that for the salvation of my soul I may eat the food of your flesh; that, by eating you, I may live from you, go by you, arrive at you, and rest in you.

O sweetness of love and love of sweetness, may my belly consume you, and may my inward parts be filled with the nectar of your love, so that my mind may utter a good word. Living charity, my God, sweet honey, snow-white milk: you are the food of the mature. Make me grow in you, so that you may be eaten by me with a healthy palate. You are my life by which I live, the hope to which I cling, the glory that I long to attain. Hold my heart, govern my mind, direct my understanding, [Col. 0177B] raise my love, lift up my spirit, and draw the mouth of my spirit thirsting for you toward the streams above.

Let, I pray, the tumult of the flesh be silent; let the phantasms of earth and water, air and sky be still. Let dreams and imaginary revelations, every tongue, every sign, and whatever comes to pass in passing away, be silent. Let even the soul be silent to itself, and pass beyond itself, not thinking of itself but of you, my God, because you are truly my whole hope and confidence. For in you, God and our sweetest, kindest, and most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, are the portion, blood, and flesh of each one of us.

## Chapter VII. He recalls the grounds and arguments of his hope and confidence, that they may become firmer.

Where, then, my portion reigns, I believe that I reign; where my blood holds dominion, I trust that I hold dominion; [Col. 0177C] where my flesh is glorified, I know that I am glorious. Although I am a sinner, I do not despair of this communion of grace. Even if sins prevent me, my substance lays claim upon me; and though my own offences exclude me, communion of nature does not repel me. For the Lord is not so harsh that he does not love his own flesh, his own members, and his own inward parts.

Indeed, I might have despaired because of my excessive sins and vices, faults and countless negligences, which I have committed and daily commit without ceasing, in heart, speech, deed, and every way in which human frailty can sin, unless your Word, O God, had become flesh and dwelt among us. But now I do not dare despair, because he, made subject to you even unto death—indeed, death on a cross—[Col. 0177D] took the bond recording our sins, and, fastening it to the cross, crucified sin and death (Col. 2). In him I breathe securely, for he sits at your right hand and intercedes for us. Trusting in him, I desire to come to you—in him in whom we have already risen and come to life, have already ascended into heaven, and have sat down in the heavenly places.

To you be praise, to you glory, to you honour, and thanksgiving, most merciful Lord, who so loved and saved us, so justified and exalted us. Most merciful Lord, how sweet is remembrance of you! The more I meditate on you, the sweeter and more lovable you become to me. Therefore it gives me great delight, in the place of my pilgrimage, according to my measure and for as long as I remain among these frail [Col. 0178A] members, to contemplate your blessings with the pure gaze of the mind and the sweetest affection of devout love. For I have been wounded by the dart of your charity; I burn fiercely with longing for you; I desire to reach you and to see you.

Therefore I shall stand upon my watch, and with wakeful eyes I shall sing psalms in spirit and with understanding; with all my strength I shall praise you, my maker (1 Cor. 14). I shall pierce the heavens; in mind and desire I shall be with you, so that though in this present misery I am held only by the body, yet in thought, longing, and every desire I may always be with you. Thus may my heart be where you are, my desirable, incomparable, and supremely lovable treasure.

But behold, my most merciful God and compassionate Lord: when I desire to contemplate the glory of your immeasurable goodness and mercy, my heart is insufficient. For your beauty, loveliness, power, glory, magnificence, majesty, and charity surpass every capacity [Col. 0178B] of the human mind. As the splendour of your glory is beyond estimation, so the kindness of your charity is beyond speech: by it you adopt as sons and join to yourself those whom you created from nothing.

O my soul, if we had to endure torments daily, if we had to bear hell itself for a long time, in order that we might see Christ in his glory and be joined to his saints, would it not be worthy to suffer everything sorrowful, so that we might be made participants in so great a good and glory? Therefore let demons continually prepare their temptations; let fasts weaken the body; let garments press upon it; let labours weigh it down; let vigils dry it up; let cares rouse it; let this person cry out against me and that one, or another, disturb me; let cold bend me; let conscience [Col. 0178C] murmur; let heat burn; let my head ache, my breast burn, my stomach swell, my face grow pale; let me become wholly infirm; let my life fail in pain and my years in groanings (Ps. 30). Let rottenness enter into my bones and bubble up beneath me, that I may rest in the day of tribulation and go up to our people that are girded (Hab. 3).

## Chapter VIII. On the excellence of heavenly glory, its contemplation, and the manner of obtaining it.

What then shall be the glory of each one of us, how great the joy of the saints, when every face shines like the sun; when, with ranks distinguished, the Lord begins to review his people in the kingdom of his Father and restores to each person the promised rewards [Col. 0178D] according to merits and works—heavenly things for earthly, eternal things for temporal, great things for small? Truly, there will be a fullness of happiness when the Lord brings the saints into the vision of the Father’s glory and makes them sit in heaven, so that God may be all in all.

O happy delight and delightful happiness: to see the saints, to be with the saints, and to be holy; to see God and to possess God for ever and beyond. Let us think on this with diligent mind. Let us desire this with our whole desire, so that we may be able quickly to come to them. If you ask how this may be done, or by what merits or helps, listen. The matter is placed in the power of the doer, because the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (Matt. 11). O human being, the kingdom of heaven asks no price but yourself. It is worth as much as [Col. 0179A] you are. Give yourself, and you shall have it. Why are you troubled about the price? Christ gave himself in order to acquire you as a kingdom for God the Father. So give yourself, that you may be his kingdom; and let not sin reign in your mortal body, but the spirit unto the gaining of life (Rom. 6).

O my soul, let us return to the heavenly city, in which we are enrolled and decreed citizens. Therefore, as fellow citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, and as heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ (Rom. 8), let us consider, insofar as it is possible to consider it, the illustrious happiness of our city. Let us therefore say with the Prophet: “O how glorious are the things spoken of you, city of God! The dwelling of all those who rejoice is in you. For you are founded as the joy of the whole earth” (Ps. 86).

In you there is no old age, nor the misery of old age. There is no dwarf, [Col. 0179B] nor lame person, nor hunchback, nor deformed person, since all come together into a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ (Eph. 4). What life is happier than this, where there is no fear of poverty and no weakness of sickness? No one is injured; no one is angry; no one envies; no covetousness burns; no desire for food exists; no ambition for honour or power presses upon anyone. There is no fear of the devil there, no snares of demons, no terror of hell; no death, either of body or soul, but a pleasant life through the gift of immortality.

There will nowhere then be discord, but everything harmonious and consonant, because all the saints will possess one concord. Peace and joy contain all things; all things are tranquil and at rest. There is unceasing radiance—not that which now exists, but [Col. 0179C] brighter by as much as it is happier. For that city, as we read, will not need the light of the sun; rather, the Lord Almighty will illuminate it, and its lamp is the Lamb (Rev. 21). There the saints will shine like stars for everlasting eternities, and like the brightness of the firmament, those who instruct many (Dan. 12).

Accordingly there is no night there, no darkness, no gathering of clouds, nor any harshness of cold or heat; rather, such a tempering of things as eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2), except for those found worthy to enjoy these things, whose names are written in the book of life. Yet above all these things, to be joined to the choirs of angels and archangels and of all the heavenly powers; to behold the patriarchs and [Col. 0179D] prophets, to see the apostles and all the saints, even to see our parents—these are glorious things. But far more glorious is to behold the present face of God, to see the unbounded light. Surpassing glory will be ours when we see God in himself, see and possess within ourselves him whose vision is an end without end.

## Chapter IX. Why the soul is endowed with the likeness of God; how great a hope and confidence it may derive from this; and the merits of the soul’s love for God.

The soul, illustrious through the noble image of God, has in itself a likeness from God, by which it is continually admonished either to remain with him or to return if it has been moved by its own affections—or rather defects. And it possesses not only a ground on which it may breathe again in hope of pardon through hope in mercy, [Col. 0180A] but also one on which it may dare to aspire to marriage with the Word, enter into a covenant of fellowship with God, and bear the sweet yoke of love with the king of angels.

Love accomplishes all these things if the soul presents itself as like God in will, as it is like him in nature, loving as it has been loved. Of all the soul’s motions, perceptions, and affections, love alone is that in which the creature can—if not repay its maker equally—at least render a reciprocal return in kind. When love comes, it draws all other affections into itself and captures them. Love is sufficient in itself, pleasing in itself, and for its own sake. It is merit, reward, cause, fruit, and use. Through love we are joined to God.

Love causes one to will and to refuse the same things; love first brings character into harmony, then [Col. 0180B] makes one consider all present things as though they were absent, and in the third place enables one to behold things above and within with the pure gaze of the heart. Through love, first honourable things are rightly done in the world; afterwards even the honourable things of the world are despised; finally, the inner things of God are beheld.

God the Father is charity. God the Son is charity. The Holy Spirit is the love of Father and Son; this is charity, and this charity requires in us something like itself—namely charity—so that by a kind of affinity of shared blood we may be associated and joined with it. Love, ignorant of rank, knows no reverence. One who loves approaches God confidently of himself, speaks to him familiarly, fearing nothing and hesitating over nothing. Whoever does not love God loses the very life he lives. But whoever loves always has his eyes upon [Col. 0180C] God, whom he loves, whom he desires, in whom he meditates, delights, feeds, and is made fat.

Such a devout person sings in this way, reads in this way, and in all works is so provident and watchful as though God were present before his eyes—as indeed he truly is. Thus he prays as though he had been assumed and presented before the face of Majesty upon the lofty throne, where thousands upon thousands minister to him and ten times a hundred thousand stand before him (Dan. 7).

Love, when it visits a soul, awakens it sleeping, moves and softens it, wounds its heart, illumines dark things, opens things shut, inflames cold things, tames the mind when harsh, irascible, and impatient, drives away vices, restrains carnal affections, corrects manners, [Col. 0180D] reforms and renews the spirit, and checks the impulses of slippery youth and frivolous actions. Love does all these things when present; but when it departs, the soul begins to lie languid, as though you had removed the fire from a boiling pot.

Love is a great thing, by which the soul confidently approaches God of itself, clings steadfastly to God, and speaks with God familiarly, consulting him about every matter. A soul that loves can think of nothing else and speak of nothing else; it despises everything besides and is weary of all things. Whatever it meditates, whatever it says, tastes and smells of love: love of God has thus claimed it for itself.

Whoever wishes to have knowledge of God, let him love. In vain does one approach reading, meditation, or prayer who does not love. God’s love begets the soul’s love and makes it direct itself toward him; God loves in order to be loved. When he loves, he wants nothing but to be loved, knowing that those who love him are blessed by love itself. When [Col. 0181A] the loving soul renounces all its own affections and leans wholly upon love alone, so as to answer love by returning love, and when it has poured itself wholly into love, what is that beside the outflow of a perennial fountain? Love and lover, God and soul, Creator and creature, do not flow with equal abundance; nevertheless, if the soul loves God with its whole self, nothing is lacking where all is present.

Let the soul that loves not fear; let the soul that does not love be afraid. The loving soul is borne on prayers, drawn by desires; it disregards merits, opens its eyes to Majesty, and closes them to pleasure—setting itself upon salvation and acting confidently in it. By love the soul withdraws and passes beyond bodily senses, so that it does not feel itself because it feels God. This happens when the mind, enticed by the ineffable [Col. 0181B] sweetness of God, in some manner steals itself from itself—or rather is snatched and slips away from itself—in order to enjoy God in delight.

Nothing would be so delightful, if only it were not so brief. Love gives familiarity with God; familiarity gives boldness; boldness gives taste; taste gives hunger. The soul touched by God’s love can think of nothing else and desire nothing else; it often sighs, saying: “As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, God” (Ps. 41). God comes to human beings through love; he comes into human beings; he became human. Through love, God who is invisible became like his servants. Through love he was wounded because of our offences.

## Chapter X. On safe and firm rest in the wounds, inward parts, and death of Christ, which protect against every evil and snare.

[Col. 0181C] For the weak and sinful there is safe and firm rest in the wounds of the Saviour. There I dwell securely; through the wounds his inward parts lie open to me. Whatever I lack in myself, I claim for myself from the inward parts of my Lord, because they overflow with mercy and there is no lack of openings through which it may flow out. Through the openings of the body the secret of the heart lies open to me; the great sacrament of mercy lies open; the inward parts of the mercy of our God lie open, in which the Dayspring from on high has visited us (Luke 1).

The wounds of Christ Jesus are full of mercy, full of loving kindness, full of sweetness and charity. They dug through his hands and feet, and pierced his side with a lance (Pss. 21, 33). Through these clefts I am permitted to taste that my Lord is sweet, truly sweet and gentle, and abundant in mercy to all who call upon [Col. 0181D] him in truth, to all who seek him, and especially to those who love him. Abundant redemption has been given to us in the wounds of our Saviour (Ps. 129): a great abundance of sweetness, fullness of grace, and perfection of virtues.

When some shameful thought assails me, I flee back to Christ’s wounds. When my flesh oppresses me, I rise again through remembrance of my Lord’s wounds. When the devil prepares snares for me, I flee to my Lord’s inward parts, and he departs from me. If the heat of lust stirs my members, it is extinguished by remembrance of the wounds of the Son of God. In all adversities I have found no remedy so effective as Christ’s wounds. In them I sleep secure and rest unafraid.

Christ died for us. There is nothing tending toward death [Col. 0182A] which is not undone for us by Christ’s death. My whole hope is in my Lord’s death. His death is my merit, my refuge, my salvation, life, and resurrection. My merit is the compassion of the Lord. I am not without merit as long as he has not forgotten mercies. And if the Lord’s mercies are many, I am abundant in merits. The more powerful he is to save, the more secure I am.

I have sinned a great sin, and I know myself guilty of many offences. Yet I do not despair, because where offences abounded, grace abounded still more (Rom. 5). Whoever despairs of pardon for sins denies that God is merciful. Whoever distrusts his mercy commits a great wrong against God. So far as lies in that person, such a one denies that God possesses charity, truth, and power, in which my entire hope consists: in the charity of adoption, the truth of promise, and the power of fulfilment.

Let my foolish thought murmur as much as it wishes, saying: “For who are you, or how great is the glory for which, and by what merits, do you hope to obtain it?” And I answer confidently: “I know in whom I have believed, because in his exceeding charity he adopted me as a son, because he is true in promise, powerful in accomplishment, and is permitted to do what he wills.” I cannot be frightened by the multitude of sins when my Lord’s death comes to mind, because my sins cannot conquer him. The nails and lance cry out to me that I am truly reconciled to Christ, if I love him. The lance opened Christ’s side more deeply for me; I entered, and there I rest secure. Let one who fears, love, because perfect [Col. 0182C] charity casts out fear (1 John 4).

There is no medicine so powerful and effective against the heat of lust as the death of my Redeemer. He stretched out his arms upon the cross and spread out his hands upon the cross, ready to embrace sinners. Between the arms of my Saviour I desire both to live and to die. There I shall sing securely: “I will exalt you, Lord, because you have taken me up and have not made my enemies rejoice over me” (Ps. 39). Our Saviour inclined his head in death in order to give kisses to his beloved. As often as we are pierced with compunction in his love, so often do we kiss the Lord.

## Chapter XI. The soul is stirred to love Christ and, through love, to conform itself to him.

O my soul, marked with God’s image, redeemed [Col. 0182D] by Christ’s blood, betrothed by faith, endowed by the Spirit, adorned with virtues, appointed among the angels: love him by whom you are so greatly loved. Attend to him who attends to you. Seek him who seeks you. Love your love, by whom you are loved, whose love has gone before you, who is the cause of your love. He is merit, reward, fruit, use, and end.

Be diligent with the diligent, at leisure with him who is at leisure, pure with the pure, and holy with the holy. As you prepare yourself for God, such must God appear to you. He who is sweet, gentle, and abundant in mercy (Ps. 85) seeks those who are gentle, sweet, humble, and merciful. Love him who drew you out of the pit of misery and the mire of mud (Ps. 39). Choose as your friend, before all [Col. 0183A] your friends, him who, when everything else has been taken away, will alone keep faith with you.

On the day of your burial, when all your friends withdraw from you, he will not abandon you, but will protect you from the roaring beings prepared for prey; he will lead you through an unknown land and bring you to the streets of the heavenly Zion. There he will place you with the angels before the face of Majesty, where you will hear angelic melody. For there is the song of joy, the voice of exultation and salvation, thanksgiving, the voice of praise, and everlasting alleluia. There is a fullness of happiness, surpassing glory, overflowing joy, and every good.

O my soul, sigh ardently and long intensely, that you may reach that heavenly city of which such glorious things are spoken, in which is “the dwelling of all who rejoice” (Ps. 86). By love you can ascend; for one who loves, nothing is difficult, nothing impossible. A soul that loves frequently ascends and familiarly traverses the streets [Col. 0183B] of the heavenly Jerusalem: visiting the patriarchs and prophets, greeting the apostles, admiring the hosts of martyrs and confessors, and contemplating the choirs of virgins.

Heaven and earth, and all things in them, never cease telling me to love my God. But what do I love when I love my God? Not bodily beauty; not the splendour of time; not the brightness of light dear to these eyes; not sweet melodies of tuneful songs; not the fragrance of flowers, ointments, and spices; not manna and honey; not limbs pleasing to the embraces of the flesh. These are not what I love when I love my God. Yet I love a certain light, a certain voice, [Col. 0183C] a certain fragrance, a certain food, and a certain embrace of the inner person: where there shines for my soul what place cannot contain; where there sounds what time does not carry away; where there smells what no breeze disperses; where there tastes what eating does not diminish; where there clings what satiety does not tear apart. This is what I love when I love my God.

I love a certain light, voice, fragrance, food, and embrace. And what is this? I questioned the earth and said, “I am not [God].” And whatever is in it confessed the same. I questioned the sea, the depths, and the creeping things with living souls; and they replied, “We are not your God; seek above us.” I questioned the sky, the sun, moon, and stars. “Neither are we the God whom you seek,” they said. And I said to all these things surrounding the doors of my flesh: “Tell me something about [Col. 0183D] my God, whom you are not; tell me something of him.” And they cried out in a great voice: “He made us” (Ps. 99). Then I directed myself to myself and found you in my memory, my God, because you deigned to dwell there from the time I learned you; and there I find you when I remember you and delight in you.

## Chapter XII. On the restoration of our life through Christ’s death, and on the praise and breadth of charity.

It was an old thing that a human being should die; it became a new thing that God should die, in order that by the newness of his death he might dissolve the oldness of our death, and through the mockery of the cross destroy the corruption of our flesh. Against the oldness of our death he brought [Col. 0184A] the newness of our life; against old sin he brought the new commandment—namely, charity.

Extinguish covetousness if you wish to embrace charity. For as covetousness is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6), so charity is the root of good things. Charity is the fulfillment of the law (Rom. 13); the end of the commandment is charity (1 Tim. 1). Charity securely possesses the whole greatness of the divine utterances, by which we love God and neighbour. On these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets (Matt. 22). If you lack leisure to search all the holy pages, unfold every wrapping of words, and penetrate every secret of Scripture, hold fast to charity, on which all things hang. Thus you will hold what you have learned there, and also what you have not yet learned. For whoever keeps charity in conduct holds both [Col. 0184B] what is open and what is hidden in the divine words.

Charity is not present if it is not patient and kind. Charity is not present if it is jealous, behaves improperly, is puffed up, or seeks its own interests. Charity is not present if it is provoked, thinks evil, rejoices in wrongdoing, or does not rejoice in truth. Charity bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails (1 Cor. 13). By this you can test whether you have charity.

Without charity the rich person is poor, and in it the poor person is rich. Charity is strong in harsh sufferings, joyful in good works, most secure amid temptations, and most expansive in hospitality. Among true brothers it is most joyful; among false ones, most patient. This is the sum of apostolic teaching: that we should owe no one anything except to love one another [Col. 0184C] (Rom. 13).

Let charity so embrace all friends that it extends even to enemies. Let it give itself to friends who desire it and offer itself to enemies who do not desire it. Let it keep the former and gain the latter. Let it delight the former, lest friends become enemies; let it invite the latter, that enemies may become friends. The Lord commands charity to be extended even to enemies, saying: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5). Tell us, Lord, what reward you will give if we love our enemies. “That you may be,” he says, “sons of your Father who is in heaven” (ibid.). If what is commanded seems bitter to the hearer, let what is promised be sweet to the obedient.

Those who love their enemies and do good [Col. 0184D] to those who hate them shall be children of God. If children, then heirs—indeed heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ (Rom. 8). Hear therefore, Christians; hear, children of God and co-heirs of Christ: in order to possess your Father’s inheritance, bestow charity not only upon friends but also upon enemies. Let charity be denied to no one, since it is held in common by all good people. All of you possess it together; and, that you may possess it more abundantly, bestow it upon both good and evil.

The charity of God is God, because the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5). The more charity is multiplied, the more generously it is bestowed by God. While charity is returned, its giver becomes rich. Charity calls enemies to concord. Charity delights to pardon an injury inflicted upon it.

[Col. 0185A] Who can unfold the praise of charity in words fitting to it? It is neither alone in heaven nor left bereft upon earth. On earth it has the companionship of friends; in heaven it possesses fellowship with angels. It labours in the world; it rests in God.

## Chapter XIII. On guarding the inner person through the cardinal virtues; on fear, the messenger of death, and its answers; on the devil’s assault and the torment of hell; likewise, counsel of the virtues for escaping the evils of hell.

To indicate the need for guarding the inner person, the Lord Jesus offers this comparison: “Know this: if the householder knew at what hour the thief was coming, he would surely keep watch and would not allow his house to be broken into” (Luke 12). This householder may be understood as the mind, [Col. 0185B] whose household consists of thoughts and their movements, perceptions too, and actions, both outward and inward. This household will be excessively wanton and unruly unless it is restrained and ordered by the vigour of its master. For if he grows even a little sluggish in his vigilance, who can say how, through thoughts, eyes, tongue, ears, and the other organs, they may become insolent?

The house is the conscience, in which this householder dwells and gathers the treasures of virtues; to prevent the house from being broken into on account of these treasures, he keeps the greatest watch. The thief, however, is not one but many, because particular vices lie in ambush for particular virtues. Yet the chief thief is understood to be the devil. Against him and his satellites, the same householder—if he is not negligent—must fortify his house with a strong guard, [Col. 0185C] establishing prudence at the first entrance, to discern what ought to be admitted, avoided, or excluded. Beside it let fortitude be stationed, so that it may repel the enemies whose coming prudence has announced. Let justice sit in the middle, that it may render to each what is due.

And because the hour at which the thief will come is unknown, he must be feared at every hour; and, lest the sleep of sin creep in, we must keep watch constantly. Once these things have been arranged, prudence ought to bring in certain messengers who may recount matters profitable for exercise. Accordingly, the messenger of death, requesting entrance, is admitted. Asked to say who he is, whence he comes, and what he has seen, he answers that he will say nothing unless complete silence is kept. This having been obtained, he begins as follows:

[Col. 0185D] “I am the fear of death, and I announce to you that death is coming.”

Prudence speaks for all and asks:

**Prudence.** Where is death?

**Remembrance of Death.** I know that it is not slow to come and is near. But I do not know the day and hour of its arrival.

**Prudence.** And who comes with it?

**Remembrance.** A thousand demons, carrying with them great books, iron hooks, and fiery chains.

**Prudence.** What do they intend with all these things?

**Remembrance.** In the books are written all human sins; and they say that those whose sins are written there belong to their jurisdiction. They carry hooks so that, after proving that persons belong to their jurisdiction, they may violently drag out their souls and, bound in chains, draw them into hell.

[Col. 0186A] **Prudence.** What is hell like? Or what did you see in it?

**Remembrance.** Hell is broad without measure, deep without bottom, full of incomparable burning, full of intolerable stench, full of innumerable pain. There are misery, darkness, no order, eternal horror; there is no hope of good, no despair of evil. Everyone in it hates himself and everyone else. There I saw every kind of torment, the least of which is greater than all the torments that can be inflicted in this world. There are weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matt. 22); there one passes from the cold of snows to the excessive heat of fires, and both are intolerable. There all are burned and gnawed by worms, yet are not consumed. “Their worm [Col. 0186B] does not die, and their fire is not quenched” (Isa. 66). There is no voice there except “Woe, woe”; they have woe and sound woe. Demonic tormentors both torment and are tormented together, and they shall never have either end or remedy. Such is hell, and a thousand times worse; these things I saw in hell, and things a thousand times worse.

**Prudence.** God, what shall we do? Now, brothers, hear my counsel and give your own. Be faithful and prudent, and keep watch in prayer, providing what is good not only before God but also before human beings (1 Cor. 8).

**Temperance.** “Let us come before his presence” (Ps. 94), etc. “Be sober and keep watch” (1 Pet. 5), etc.

**Fortitude.** “Resist him, strong in faith” (ibid.). “Be strengthened in the Lord; put on [Col. 0186C] the armour of God: the breastplate of justice, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation. Take also the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6).

**Justice.** “Let us live soberly, justly, and devoutly” (Titus 2): soberly toward ourselves, justly toward our neighbour, devoutly toward God. And let us not do to others what we do not wish done to ourselves, for this is just.
