## Chapter XIV. On the second messenger, namely love and desire for eternal life, and the joys and inhabitants of heaven which he announces.

**Prudence speaks.**

Another messenger comes, beautiful and cheerful, who appears to bring good things.

**Justice.** Let him be admitted. Perhaps he will make us glad, for the former one frightened us.

[Col. 0186D] **Prudence.** I shall admit him. Enter, and state who you are, whence you come, and what you have seen.

**Messenger.** I am love of eternal life and desire for the heavenly homeland. If you wish to hear me, keep silence and stillness; for I cannot be heard amid cries and tumults.

**Justice.** If we were silent while fear and remembrance of death spoke, it is right that we should be much more silent while you speak.

**DESIRE FOR ETERNAL LIFE.** Be silent, therefore. I saw such things as no human being can fittingly describe. Yet I shall say something, as far as I can. I saw God, but through a mirror and in an enigma. I contemplated that ineffable majesty of the indivisible Trinity, without beginning or end. But because he dwells in inaccessible light, [Col. 0187A] my eyes were dazzled by that very light and my sight was blunted. For that brightness, that beauty, surpasses every sense and every act of vision. Yet for a little while I beheld the Lord Jesus Christ sitting at the right hand of the Father, reigning in eternal life; although surpassingly beautiful above every creature, so that angels desire to look upon him (I Pet. I), he nevertheless bore in his body the wounds of the Passion by which he redeemed us, attending upon the Father on our behalf. I saw beside him his glorious Mother, seated upon a wonderful throne with every honour and reverence, exalted above all the ranks of blessed angels and human beings, interceding for us with her Son and showing mercy to whomever she wills. But, unable long to endure this wondrous brightness [Col. 0187B] of Mother and Son, I turned my gaze to those orders of blessed spirits who stand before God, whose everlasting blessedness, derived from the vision and love of God, is neither diminished nor ended, but always increases and endures. Yet no human being could suffice even to conceive, much less to recount, their ranks and dignities, or the praises which they render to their Creator.

Then I beheld the prophets and patriarchs rejoicing with wonderful joy, who possess that homeland which long ago they had greeted from afar, and who behold fulfilled the things which they had foreseen in the Spirit. I saw the apostles sitting on thrones, ready to judge all tribes and tongues; and I marvelled greatly that those who had been poor and infirm had been made so glorious and so exalted by the Lord Jesus. [Col. 0187C] I saw, but could not fully discern, the innumerable host of blessed martyrs crowned with glory and honour, who regarded the sufferings of this present time which they had endured as very slight in comparison with that glory which had been revealed in them. Long delighted by their happiness and glory, I looked back upon the glorious multitude of confessors, among whom apostolic men and teachers—who fortified the holy Church by their teachings—shine like stars for everlasting ages. There are monks there who, in exchange for narrow cloisters and cells, possess immense palaces brighter than the sun; in exchange for rough tunics, they are clothed in garments whiter than snow and softer than every delight. From their eyes God has wiped away every tear. They behold the King in his beauty. [Col. 0187D] Finally, I looked upon the choir of virgins, whose glory, adornment, and melody are sweet. For they sang a song which no one else could utter (Apoc. XIV), and which no human eloquence can worthily recount. But the fragrance in their region was so sweet that it surpasses every kind of aromatic perfume.

## CHAPTER XV. On the common activity of the citizens of heaven, and their first exultation.

**PRUDENCE SPEAKS AGAIN.**

What you say pleases us. You speak wondrously of each order of the blessed; we ask you to tell us what their activity is in common.

**DESIRE FOR ETERNAL LIFE.** I shall say what I can. The common activity of all together is sevenfold: they live, know, love, rejoice, praise, are swift, and are secure.

[Col. 0188A] **PRUDENCE.** Although I understand this to some extent, nevertheless say a few words about each point for the sake of the hearers.

**DESIRE.** So be it. They live a life without end, without distress, without diminution, without any adversity. Their life is the vision and knowledge of the blessed Trinity, as the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they may know thee, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom thou hast sent” (John XVII). They know the counsels and judgments of God, which are a great abyss (Ps. XXXV). They know the causes, natures, and origins of all things. They love God beyond comparison, because they know from what and to what God has raised them. Each loves every other as himself. They rejoice in God ineffably. They rejoice in so great a blessedness of their own. And because each person loves every other as himself, each has [Col. 0188B] as much joy in the good of every individual as in his own good, because the good which he does not possess in himself he possesses in another.

It is therefore evident that each person has as many joys as companions, and each joy is as great to each as the proper joy of every one of them. Since, however, each loves God more than himself and all the others together, he rejoices more in God’s happiness than in his own and that of all the others together. If, therefore, the heart of each can scarcely contain its own joy, how can it contain so many and such great joys? Therefore it is said: “Enter into the joy of thy Lord” (Matt. XXV); not, “May the joy of thy Lord enter into thee,” because it could not be contained. Hence they praise God without end and without weariness, as it is written: “Blessed are they who dwell in thy house, O Lord; they shall praise thee for ever and ever” (Ps. LXXXIII). They are swift, because wherever [Col. 0188C] the spirit wishes to be, there the body also is. All are secure. They are secure concerning such life, such great wisdom, such great love, such great joy, such praise, such swiftness: that these will suffer no end, no diminution, no loss. Behold, I have told you a few things which I saw in heaven. For I was unable either to speak as I saw or to see them as they are.

**PRUDENCE.** We understand that you truly were in heaven, truly saw true things, and truly related them.

**FORTITUDE.** Who, therefore, shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, and so forth. I am certain that neither death nor life nor any of the other things can separate us from the love of Christ (Rom. VIII).

**JUSTICE.** Let that former messenger be cast out, for it is [Col. 0188D] not right that he should remain in the same house with this one. For perfect love casts out fear (I John IV).

**FORTITUDE.** Depart, Fear. You shall no longer be within our borders.

**FEAR.** What evil have I done? Come now, come now—I said what I said for good.

**TEMPERANCE.** Brothers, I say that one ought not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly (Rom. XII). But you, Fear, depart, and bear with equanimity the judgment which Justice has pronounced. Perhaps you will be admitted if Desire for Eternal Life should at some time cease speaking.

**AUTHOR.** Thus each person ought to shake off his sluggishness and pass from fear to desire for the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the blessed conditions of the soul and the banqueting provisions of eternal life; and a description of the virtues by which they are attained.

[Col. 0189A]

For in that heavenly homeland there is life without death, youth without old age, health without sickness, rest without labour, joy without sorrow, peace without discord, delight without weariness, light without darkness, beauty without ugliness, agility without heaviness, strength without weakness, freedom without servitude, pleasure without anxiety, long life without an end of life, wisdom without foolishness, friendship without enmity, concord without discord, honour without disgrace, security without fear.

Charity is the movement of a rational soul to love itself for God’s sake, a friend in God, and an enemy for God’s sake. Humility is contempt for the world and [Col. 0189B] self-abasement. Obedience is vicarious service. Discipline is the necessary duty of holiness, reproving vices and correcting sins. Again, discipline is the ordered correction of conduct and the regular observance of the elders and predecessors; from it clemency is born. Clemency is the kindness of a superior toward inferiors. From it, in turn, justification is produced. Justification is the completion of a perfected thing. Chastity is purity of body together with integrity of mind. Perseverance is the outcome of a matter through the completion of faith. Charity is the root of virtues; humility, the guardian of good things; obedience, the promoter of commandments; discipline, the corrector of vices; chastity, the adornment of monks; perseverance, the crown of all good things.

## CHAPTER XVII. Description of certain vices that suffocate religion, such as gluttony, drunkenness, idleness, and the evil thoughts that creep into idle persons; and that no sin remains unpunished.

[Col. 0189C]

Against these virtues opposing vices wage continual war: gluttony, drunkenness, and idleness, from which comes evil thought. For varied foods produce gluttony, and frequent drinking produces drunkenness. Drunkenness, moreover, brings forth disturbance of mind, frenzy of heart, and the flame of lust. Drunkenness so estranges the mind that it does not know where it is, and it often consents to the evil that drunkenness introduces. Hence that saying which occurs in the prophet: “Fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. IV). Fornication makes even a wise man foolish, as it did Solomon. Drunkenness, as in the case of Lot himself, [Col. 0189D] enslaves the senses, stripping them of reason. Hence in Proverbs: “Do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments” (Ps. XXXI).

To many it seems worthy of praise to drink [Col. 0190A] much and not become drunk. Let such persons hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness!” (Isa. V). Concerning idleness, Gregory says: “Into an idle mind malignant spirits introduce evil thoughts, so that, if it rests from work, it may not rest from delight in evil works.” Therefore do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. For the ancient enemy, as soon as he finds an idle mind, comes to speak to it under certain pretexts, and recalls to its memory certain past deeds. He makes some words formerly heard resound improperly, and, if any things were shamefully done long ago, he sets their image before the eyes of the heart. Thus he whom he cannot defile through present things, he assaults through evils that have passed; [Col. 0190B] and he often restores the deceived mind to delight. Hence he long afflicted it by assault, so that it truly says with the Psalmist: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my folly” (Ps. XXXVII).

Thus a scar returns to decay when the wound of sin, already healed through repentance, shakes the soul into delight in itself. Often, through the snares of the crafty enemy, we see before the eyes of the heart things which we have never done. And when delight has insensibly crept in here, although the soul now weeps over what it has done, the unhappy soul is nevertheless troubled that it did not do certain things which it weeps over. These are the darknesses of our heart which we knowingly and willingly endure in this life. What help against these evils should be sought except “a helper in due seasons, in tribulation”? The devil [Col. 0190C] harms not by compelling but by persuading. There is nothing in which the devil rejoices more than when a human being says that he made him sin.

Gregory: “When pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also becomes dominant in action.” Augustine: “No one can do anything unless the command of thought has preceded it, because deeds proceed from thought.” But it cannot happen that one who has good thoughts should have evil deeds. We must firmly believe that no sin is left without punishment. Either each person here destroys his own sin through repentance, or the Lord mercifully purges it by his chastisement, or after death it shall be cleansed by purgatorial fire. But if a person’s sin has not been destroyed by these means, after this life he shall descend into eternal fire. For the sinner who does not deserve to be chastised in [Col. 0190D] this world shall be tortured in hell. Certainly no one can sin as greatly as God’s power can forgive; we shall pray that he forgive us all our debts. Amen.

[Col. 0191]

# TWENTY-FOUR BOOKS OF ALLEGORICAL EXCERPTS, with the scholia of Master Thomas Garzoni of Bagnacavallo, theologian of the monastery of St Victor at Paris (G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0191] Receive, dearest brother, the gift of *Excerpts* which you requested. In it you will find many things collected from many books, arranged in an ordered sequence, joined, continued, and connected with one another as the logic of their meanings requires, and sufficiently useful for the purpose of your love. For, ranging through the fertile fields of the sacred books and gathering from them whatever is best, we omit few or no things necessary for your simplicity as you enter upon the reading of Holy Scripture.

By what we write, however, we do not wish to teach grammarians or instruct the wise, but to satisfy your request and desire, and to assist your study toward improvement. We also wish you to know that we claim no glory for ourselves from the things we write to you, but rather for God and the holy teachers, from whose books we have taken them—although we set down many things which we have conceived in our own understanding and dictated in our own words.

We observe the following method of writing. We divide the whole sequence of this little work into two parts. In the first part, our subject is the origin of the arts, the situation of lands, and the course of histories running down from the beginning to our own time. In the second part, our subject is the meanings of allegories and tropologies, arranged according to the sequence of the underlying historical narrative.

We divide the first part into ten books. In the first book we briefly discuss the origin of the arts and their division. In the second we set forth the subject matter of secular and divine Scripture, and show how secular learning serves divine Scripture, with certain additions. In the third we describe the situation of lands. In the fourth we give a summary of sacred history from the beginning to the birth of Christ. In the fifth, the rise, course, and fall of the kingdoms of the world, from the time when they first began to exist down to the birth of Christ. In the sixth we treat the Roman emperors from Octavian [Octavius] to Trajan. In the seventh, from Trajan to Constantine the Great. In the eighth, from Constantine the Great to Zeno. In the ninth, from Zeno to Charlemagne. In the tenth we treat the origin and kings of the Franks down to Charles, and afterwards from Charles down to our own time.

We divide the second part of this work into fourteen books. The first book treats the mysteries of events from the beginning to Abraham. The second, the mysteries of events from Abraham to Moses. The third, the mysteries of events from Moses to Joshua. The fourth, the mysteries of events from Joshua to Elkanah, the father of Samuel. The fifth, the mysteries of events from Elkanah to David, at the place where it is written: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and has given it to thy neighbour, who is better than thou” (I Kings XV). The sixth, the mysteries of events from David to Solomon. The seventh, the mysteries of events from Solomon to the Babylonian captivity. The eighth, the mysteries of events contained in Ezra. The ninth, the mysteries of events contained in the books of Esther, Tobit, and Judith. The tenth contains various discourses, each composed on its own subject matter. What remains, which we set forth afterwards, we take from the New Testament and delimit in four books. Thus we complete the whole work in twenty-four books. We cultivate brevity in the individual chapters, lest we burden the imperfect beginning of your undertaking with excessively lengthy words. We arrange the books and chapters of the first part as follows.

# FIRST PART: CONTAINING THE ORIGIN AND DIVISION OF THE ARTS, THE SITUATION OF LANDS, AND A SUMMARY OF HISTORIES

[Col. 0193]

# BOOK I. Treating of the origin and division of the arts, and containing 25 chapters.

## CHAPTER I. On the creation of the rational creature.

[Col. 0193A]

God, supremely good and unchangeably good, knowing that his blessedness could be shared and could in no way be diminished, made the rational creature in order to make it a participant in his blessedness. He made it in his image and likeness according to love: in his image according to the knowledge of truth; in his likeness according to the love of truth; in his image according to understanding; in his likeness according to affection. Thus God the Creator made the rational creature in his image and likeness, so that, through being made in God’s image, it might know God, and, through being made in God’s likeness, it might love God; and, by knowing and loving [Col. 0193B] God, might possess him, and by possessing him might be blessed.

For just as in one element, namely fire, there are two things different from one another and wholly separate from each other, namely brightness and heat—and brightness is not heat, nor heat brightness, because brightness shines and is seen, whereas heat burns and is felt; nor does brightness burn or come to be felt otherwise than by sight, nor does heat shine or become visible—so in the spiritual creature the image of God and the likeness of God are different from one another and in a certain manner separate. For according to that original good by which it was made in the [Col. 0194A] image of God, the spiritual creature itself shines forth toward knowledge; and according to that good by which it was made in the likeness of God, it grows warm toward love. The Creator commanded one part of it, namely the angelic nature, to remain in its simple purity; but another part, namely human nature, to exist in bodies of clay.

> **Note:** [Col. 0193B] How the rational creature—that is, the human being—is said to have been formed in the image and likeness of God is notably set forth by various authorities. First, from Aureolus’s *Compendium of Truth*, a threefold designation of image is drawn.
>
> First: one image is one of most perfect equality; in this sense the Son of God alone is the image of the Father. Another is an image of imitation; in this sense the human being was made in the image of God, namely so that he may acknowledge God himself and, by imitating him in virtues, endeavour to love him. Another, however, is an image of representation; in this sense the world is called a mirror and image of God’s goodness.
>
> The second distinction, for clarification, is this: one thing is an image not “unto an image,” as is the Son of God. Another is an image “unto an image,” as is a human being or angel. Another is not an image but is “unto an image,” as is the world: it is not an image because it is not capable of God through love and knowledge, but is only a trace of the Creator.
>
> The third distinction explains this further: one image is naturally begotten, as the king’s sons are in relation to the king; such is Christ in relation to God the Father. [Col. 0193D] Another image is created, such as the human soul and an angel. Another is an image made in an almost artificial manner, such as the image on the king’s coin or denarius, or a statue [Col. 0194B] representing the king himself.
>
> Moreover, it should be known that in Holy Scripture the name “image of God” is understood in two ways, namely according to substance and according to likeness. According to substance, the image of God, as Eucherius says in the first book [Col. 0194C] of his *Commentaries on Genesis*, is nothing other than the mind naturally bestowed by God upon every human soul, by whose privilege other animals lack it. But the image of God according to likeness is the conformity with God of a righteous and holy soul, acquired through divine grace and the practice of holy actions. On this point St Ambrose, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Colossians, on the Apostle’s words, “Putting on the new man, who is renewed according to the image of him who created him” (Col. III), speaks thus: “This image must be understood as consisting in the conduct of a good life.”
>
> Further, from Nicholas of Lyra on the words of Genesis, “Let us make man in our image and likeness,” it should be noted that the image of God consists in the soul with respect to its natural properties, namely memory, understanding, and will. Likeness, however, consists in gratuitous gifts; [Col. 0194D] therefore likeness is a kind of perfection of the image, because grace perfects nature.

## CHAPTER II. On the three primordial goods and the two external goods given to humankind.

God gave human beings three primordial goods in creation. The first good was that God made them in his image; the second, that he made them in his likeness; the third good was immortality of body, if the human being had remained in obedience to the Creator. These three goods were divinely given to humankind in its creation [Col. 0194B] and naturally and originally implanted. There were also two other human goods, as though outside the human being: one beneath him, the other above him. Beneath him was the world; above him, God. The world is a visible and transitory good; God, an invisible and eternal good. In the one the human being was created; in the other he was to be made blessed. Under God the human being stood by condition; above the world by dignity; destined to depart from the lower good and to attain the higher good. Therefore the three primordial goods of humankind, given to it in its creation [Col. 0195A] and substantially implanted, are the image of God, the likeness of God, and immortality of body, if it had wished to persevere in obedience to the Creator.

> **Note:** [Col. 0195D] Scotus and his followers hold a very different view concerning bodily immortality. They maintain that the human being would have been subject to death, even had original innocence remained, because of the condition of mortal nature. Yet they call this not a penal death but a most gentle dissolution of the spirit, like a breath issuing from the mouth.

## CHAPTER III. On the three principal evils.

There are three principal evils which corrupt the three preceding goods: ignorance, concupiscence, and weakness. Ignorance of good, concupiscence for evil, and weakness of the human body. By the first evil the first good was corrupted; by the second, the second; by the third, the third. For through ignorance the divine image in us was corrupted; through concupiscence, the divine likeness; through weakness, bodily immortality. Thus the human being’s way became darkness and slippery ground, with the angel of the Lord pursuing him (Ps. XXXIV): darkness through ignorance; [Col. 0195B] slippery ground through concupiscence; and the angel of the Lord—that is, bodily weakness, inflicted upon the body as punishment—pursuing him by mortality until he returns to the earth from which he was taken.

According to some, however, what we here call concupiscence is specifically called vice, so that the three evils are said to be ignorance, vice, and weakness, through which the three preceding goods were corrupted.

> **Note:** [Col. 0195D] The evil of ignorance fittingly opposes the understanding; concupiscence opposes the sanctity and purity of life; bodily weakness opposes immortality. Thus the whole human being recognizes himself as wounded by Adam’s sin: he who before could have remained wholly sound, had he not sinned, became wholly infirm by sinning.

## CHAPTER IV. On the three remedies against the three evils mentioned.

There are three principal remedies against the three aforesaid evils, so that through three remedies the three evils may be driven back and the three goods restored. They are wisdom, virtue, and necessity. Wisdom against ignorance, virtue against vice, necessity against weakness. [Col. 0195C] Wisdom is the comprehension of things as they are. Virtue is a disposition of the mind, in the manner of nature, consonant with reason. A disposition is a quality arising through the application of a subject and difficult to change, just as a state is a quality arising through the application of a subject and easy to change. By “subject” we mean the mind, which is applied to receive that quality. Necessity is that without which we cannot live, though we would live more happily without it. Therefore these three remedies—wisdom, virtue, and necessity—stand against the three aforementioned evils: ignorance, vice, and weakness.

> **Note:** [Col. 0195D] Wisdom heals the wounds inflicted, by assisting the understanding; virtue, by restraining concupiscence; necessity, by supporting weakness. For the most merciful Lord offered remedies for our infirmities [Col. 0196D] suited both to his compassion and to our weakness.

## CHAPTER V. On the three sciences.

For the sake of these three remedies every art and every discipline was invented. For finding [Col. 0195D] wisdom, theoretical science was invented; for finding [Col. 0196A] virtue, practical science; for finding necessity, mechanical science. Theoretical science, expelling ignorance, illuminates wisdom. Practical science, excluding vice, strengthens virtue. Mechanical science, guarding against want, alleviates the deficiencies of the present life.

Theoretical science chooses to investigate truth in everything that is and is not. Practical science orders the proper manner of life and the form of discipline according to the instruction of the virtues. Mechanical science, administering perishable things, strives to provide what is necessary for the human body. For the end and intention of all human actions or studies regulated by reason ought to look to this: either that the integrity of our nature be restored, or that the necessity arising from the deficiencies to which the present life is subject be alleviated. The integrity of our nature is restored by wisdom, to which theoretical science belongs, and by virtue, to which practical science belongs; and necessity is alleviated by the administration of temporal things, to which mechanical science belongs.

Last of all, logic was invented for the sake of eloquence, so that wise persons investigating and combining the aforementioned principal disciplines might know how to treat and discuss them more correctly, more truthfully, and more elegantly: more correctly through grammar, more truthfully through dialectic, and more elegantly through rhetoric. For logic, through the correctness of speech, administers truth and beauty of expression. *Theorica* means contemplative; *practica*, active; *mechanica*, adulterine; *logica*, concerned with discourse.

> **Note:** [Col. 0196D] In order that wisdom might be found—assisting understanding, excluding ignorance, and offering the truth of things—God taught us theoretical learning; in order that virtue might be found—expelling or restraining concupiscence—he showed practical learning; in order that necessity might be found—supporting and helping weakness—he showed mechanical learning, which guards against want and moderates the miseries or deficiencies of this life. In all these things the charity of the Most High God shines forth toward us.

## CHAPTER VI. On philosophy and its parts.

[Col. 0196C] Therefore there are four sciences into which all philosophy is divided: theoretical, practical, mechanical, and logical. Philosophy is the love of wisdom, which is a living mind needing nothing, and the sole primordial reason of things. “Philosophy is the love of wisdom” pertains more to the etymology of the name. The addition “a living mind needing nothing” signifies that divine wisdom lacks nothing, but beholds all things—past, present, and future—once and together. It is a living mind because whatever has once existed in the divine reason is never erased by any forgetfulness. It is the primordial reason of things because all things have been formed in its likeness. Again, philosophy is the discipline that probably investigates the reasons of all human and divine things.

> **Note:** [Col. 0196D] “Philosophy,” says Ammonius in his commentary on Porphyry, “is a good than which no greater or more desirable good has been given, or can be given, to human beings by the gods.” And Themistius, in the first book of the *Physics*, chapter 4: “Philosophy is the perfection of the soul, as medicine is of the body.” Plato defines philosophy in another way as a meditation on death. Philosophy, according to Albert, *On Animals*, book I, “is nothing other than victory over and abstinence from [Col. 0197D] things subject to concupiscence.” The nature of philosophy is to seek the greatest investigations, as Averroes says, *Metaphysics* II, text and commentary 15.

## CHAPTER VII. On theoretical science and its parts.

[Col. 0197A]

Theoretical science is divided into theology, physics, and mathematics. In another division, theoretical science is divided into the intellectual, physiology, and the intelligible. In another, it is divided into the divine, natural, and doctrinal. Theology, the intellectual, and the divine are the same; physics, physiology, and the natural are the same; mathematics, the intelligible, and the doctrinal are the same.

Theology treats invisible essences of invisible things. Physics treats invisible causes of visible things. Mathematics treats visible forms of visible things. Theology is present when we discuss, in some respect, the ineffable nature of God or spiritual creatures in their most profound quality. Physics is that which discovers causes of things from their effects, and effects from [Col. 0197B] their causes:

> Whence trembling comes to the earth; by what force the deep seas swell;  
> The powers of herbs and stones, and the rages of wild beasts;  
> Every kind of swimming creature, and likewise of birds and creeping things.

Mathematics is that which considers abstract quantity. Abstract quantity, however, is nothing other than a visible form impressed upon the mind according to linear dimension. Every form of visible things consists in quantity. One kind of quantity is discrete, called multitude, as a flock or a people; another is continuous, called magnitude, as a tree or a stone. Again, one kind of multitude is discrete in itself, as two, three, four; another is related to something else, as the ratio of one and a half, or of one and one-third. One kind of magnitude is immovable, as the sphere of the earth; another movable, as the sphere of the firmament. Discrete multitude in itself is the subject matter [Col. 0197C] of arithmetic. Discrete multitude in relation to something else is the subject matter of music. Immovable magnitude is the subject matter of geometry. Movable magnitude is the subject matter of astronomy.

> **Note:** [Col. 0197D] Theology has no higher mystery than the divinity and knowledge of the Father and the Son, and likewise of the Holy Spirit, as is found in Steuchus, *On Perennial Philosophy*, book I. Hence it is aptly said to treat invisible essences of invisible things.

## CHAPTER VIII. On mathematics and its parts.

Thus there are four branches of mathematics: arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy. Arithmetic treats number; music, the proportion of sounds; geometry, the space of places; astronomy, the movement of stars. The element of arithmetic is unity; the element of music is unison; the element of geometry is the point; the element of astronomy is the instant. [Col. 0198A] Arithmetic is the science of numbers. Music is the harmony produced by bringing several dissimilar sounds into one. Geometry is the discipline of immovable magnitude and the contemplative description of forms, by which the boundaries of each thing are customarily made clear. Astronomy is the discipline of movable magnitude, investigating the spaces, movements, and returns of heavenly bodies at fixed times.

> **Note:** [Col. 0197D] Since natural bodies have surfaces, solids have lengths, and points exist in a body, mathematics agrees with physics; yet it differs in its manner of consideration and in other respects which Aristotle sets forth in *Physics* II, chapter 2. For mathematics selects a definite part of the universal body to examine and concerns itself with lines, angles, numbers, or some other such thing. Its four branches are mentioned by Hugh; they are speculative disciplines, according to Aristotle, *Metaphysics* VI, chapter 1, and necessary for knowledge of natural things and other things, as Plato says in the *Epinomis*.

## CHAPTER IX. On arithmetic.

Writers of secular literature wished arithmetic to be first among the mathematical disciplines because it needs no other discipline in order to exist. But music, geometry, and astronomy, which follow it, need its assistance in order to exist and subsist. Arithmetic is therefore first, because number is found in [Col. 0198B] proportion, space, and movement, but not conversely. In number, proportion or space or movement is always seen to be present. Hence arithmetic is proved to be both one of the four and the instrument of the other three.

> **Note:** [Col. 0198C] “All things that exist,” says Boethius, “consist in numbers,” since God made all things in number, weight, [Col. 0198D] and measure (Wis. X). It is therefore not surprising that the Pythagoreans sometimes said that all things were made from numbers, as Aristotle says, *Metaphysics* I, chapter 5. Macrobius also says that the soul is joined to bodies by a determinate ratio of numbers, book I of the *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*. Proclus, however, in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, reports that the Pythagoreans established four orders of numbers: one musical, as in music and songs; another natural, as in the composition of things; another rational; and another divine.

## CHAPTER X. On music and its parts.

Of musics, one is mundane, another human, another instrumental. Of mundane music, one kind is in the elements, another in the planets, another in the times. Of that which is in the elements, one kind consists in weight, another in number, another in measure. Of that which is in the planets, one kind consists in position, another in movement, another in nature. Of that which is in the times, one kind is in years, as in the changes of spring, summer, autumn, and winter; another in months, as in the waxing and waning [Col. 0198C] of the moon; another in days, as in the alternation of light and night.

Human music is one thing in the body, another in the soul, another in the union of the two. In the body, one kind is in vegetative powers, another in humours, another in operations. The first belongs to all things that are born, the second to sentient beings, the third to rational beings. Music in the soul is one thing in powers, such as anger and reason; another in virtues, such as justice and fortitude. Music in the union of soul and body is that natural friendship by which the soul is held fast to the body, though not bound by bodily bonds. Instrumental music is one thing in percussion, as in drums and strings; another in wind, as in pipes and organs; another in voice, as in songs and melodies.

> **Note:** [Col. 0198D] The ancients placed music among the disciplines because nature seeks the ability to live commendably not only in business rightly conducted but also in leisure, as Aristotle says, *Politics* VIII, chapter 3. To many, moreover, music appeared to be a shaper and inventor of character, as Aristotle says, *Politics* VIII, chapter 5, and Plato, *Laws*, Dialogue 6. Macrobius held that even the minds of barbarians can be bent by musical sounds toward virtue or dissolved into the softness of pleasure, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II, chapter 3.

## CHAPTER XI. On geometry and its parts.

[Col. 0199A]

Geometry has three branches: planimetry, altimetry, and cosmimetry. Planimetry measures length and breadth, extending forward and backward, to the right and to the left. Altimetry measures height and depth, extending upward and downward. Cosmimetry measures spherical, that is, round, things.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] It was written on the doors of Plato’s school: “Let no one ignorant of geometry enter.” In the seventh book of the *Republic*, Plato likewise writes that geometry raises the mind to truth, prepares thought for philosophy, and is of the greatest importance in acquiring the disciplines, whether one has studied geometry or not.]

## CHAPTER XII. On Astronomy and Astrology

Among the mathematical sciences astronomy is not only last in order, but also higher in place and more exalted in dignity; for, while the other three are in some manner occupied with lower things, this alone has undertaken to investigate and treat the arrangement of heavenly and supernal things. Astronomy is divided into two branches: spherical astronomy [Col. 0199B] and gnomonics. Spherical astronomy considers the spaces and positions of heavenly bodies. Gnomonics observes the movement of the clock.

The difference between astronomy and astrology appears to be this: astronomy discusses the law of the stars and the revolution of heaven, investigating regions, circles, risings and settings of the stars, and why each thing is so called. Astrology, however, considers the stars in relation to the observation of birth, death, or any other events whatsoever. It is partly natural and partly superstitious. It is natural in bodily constitutions, from which come sickness, health, barrenness, fertility, storm, and fair weather, things varying according to the higher tempering influence. It is superstitious in contingent events; this rests upon constellations, and this branch is handled by mathematicians—that is, vain interpreters [Col. 0199C].

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Knowledge arising from the observation of the stars and from reasoning is called astrology; consequently, the subject of this science is the heavenly bodies. It has two parts, theoretical and practical. The theoretical, also called speculative, is occupied with contemplation: it observes the natures, motions, spheres, circles, and other accidents of the stars; Ptolemy treats this fully in the *Almagest*. The practical part considers the same matters, but not absolutely: rather, insofar as they concern lower things—that is, insofar as they exert their powers upon, or influence, lower things. This is transmitted by Ptolemy in the work called the *Quadripartite*.]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Practical Philosophy and Its Parts

Practical philosophy is divided into solitary, private, and public. In another way, practical philosophy is divided into ethics, economics, and politics. In another way, it is divided into moral, administrative, and civic philosophy. Solitary, ethical, and moral philosophy are the same; private, economic, and administrative philosophy are the same; public, political, and civic philosophy are the same. The first forms morals; the second orders the household; the third governs cities. The first pertains to individuals, the second to heads of households, the third to rulers of cities.

Ethics is that discipline which, taking care of itself, [Col. 0200A] raises, adorns, and increases itself by every virtue, admitting nothing into life over which it may not rejoice and doing nothing to be regretted. Economics is that which, ordering the care of household duty by a moderate arrangement, distributes it. Public philosophy is that which, undertaking care for the commonwealth, remedies the welfare of all by the resourcefulness of its prudence, the balance of its justice, the steadfastness of its courage, and the endurance of its temperance.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] The same author supplies fine divisions of practical philosophy concerning these matters; Gregory of Toulouse gives a summary account of them in [Col. 0200D] *Syntax*, books XXI–XXII.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On Mechanics and Its Parts

Mechanics has seven branches: cloth-making, armature or construction, navigation, agriculture, hunting, medicine, and theatrical art. The making of all things seems to converge upon it. For all things which are found pleasing, useful, convenient, or necessary to human needs belong to it, and whatever can be shown to be included under [Col. 0200B] its aforesaid seven branches.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] A mechanic is a craftsman of things accomplished jointly by ingenuity and hand. Hence not every worn and commonplace craft is properly to be called mechanical, but only those which, as Aristotle says at the beginning of the *Mechanical Problems*, bring ingenuity to bear on difficulties arising contrary to nature and serve practical usefulness.]

## CHAPTER XV. On Cloth-Making

Cloth-making is the first branch of mechanics. It includes every operation of spinning, twisting, sewing—everything done with the instrument, distaff, spindle, needle, comb, curling-iron, reel, balance, or awl; in materials of flax, wool, hemp, and cork; and every use of flocks, felt, cloaks, pack-saddles, water-vessels, and baskets.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] In the *Politicus*, Plato divides the art of cloth-making into two parts: the separating and the combining. The separating part is drawing out or extending lengthwise and breadthwise, as with the twisted spindle or wheel; the combining part performs the work of weaving by the interlacing of warp and weft.]

## CHAPTER XVI. On Construction

Construction has two branches: architecture and smithing. Architecture is divided into masonry, belonging to stonecutters and masons, and carpentry, [Col. 0200C] belonging to carpenters and timber-workers. Smithing is divided into hammer-work and extrusion-work. Construction includes every craft of carpenters, timber-workers, masons, stonecutters, and smiths: everything done with the tool, axe, adze, mattock, trowel, plumb-line, hammer, chisel, square, and anvil; in materials of wood, stone, sand, gypsum, and bronze.

[Note: [Col. 0200D] The kinds of smithing are various, since this name is general for all who work in some hard material—stone, wood, iron, gold, or silver. Craftsmen are accordingly named with the addition of the material in which they work. If you wish, see Gregory of Toulouse in his *Syntax* on all these matters.]

## CHAPTER XVII. On Navigation

Navigation is the third branch of mechanics. It includes every activity of selling and buying. It approaches shores previously unknown, establishes peace and intercourse with foreign [Col. 0201A] nations, and makes private goods common.

[Note: [Col. 0201C] Navigation requires knowledge of the seas and of the variety, routes, and positions—according to the nautical chart—of the places which one has resolved to sail to. It also requires foreknowledge of storms, the dangers posed by winds, [Col. 0201D] the various courses and aspects of the sun and moon, and the risings and settings of certain stars.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Agriculture

Agriculture has four kinds of land: arable land (*arvum*), that is, land which is ploughed and assigned to sowing; planted land (*consitum*), assigned to groves, such as orchards, vineyards, and olive-groves; pasture land (*pascuum*), assigned to grazing, such as meadows, valleys, and waste-lands; and flowering land (*floridum*), devoted to flowers, such as gardens, rose-gardens, and apiaries.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] In the *Epinomis*, Plato does not regard agriculture as a human art, but holds that from the beginning human beings undertook it without art, through God’s beneficence. Xenophon, however, in the *Oeconomicus*, calls it the art of arts and the nurse of all. According to Ennius, its principles are the same as those of the world—namely water, earth, air, and sun—as Varro also says, book I, chapter 4.]

## CHAPTER XIX. On Hunting

Hunting has three kinds: the hunting of beasts, bird-catching, and fishing. The hunting of beasts is carried out in many ways: by nets, snares, nooses, precipices, bow, javelins, spear-point, a line of feathers, scent, dogs, and hawks. Bird-catching [Col. 0201B] is carried out by nooses, snares, nets, bow, birdlime, and hook. Fishing is carried out by seines, nets, fish-traps, hooks, wicker fish-traps, and javelins. Hunting includes every occupation of bakers, butchers, cooks, and innkeepers.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] Julius Pollux, writing to the emperor Commodus in book V of the *Onomasticon*, urges him at the beginning to be zealous for hunting, because this pursuit is heroic, contributes to the sound condition of body and soul, and is an example of military boldness. Hunting is therefore greatly celebrated among the Persians, as Xenophon writes in book I of the *Cyropaedia*; and Athenaeus, in book I of the *Deipnosophists*, says: among Homer’s people young men engage in hunting, in order to avoid the dangers of war and by every pursuit to become stronger and healthier.]

## CHAPTER XX. On Medicine

Medicine includes circumstances and treatments. There are six circumstances: the air surrounding us; food and drink; sleep and waking; motion and rest; evacuation and repletion; and affections of the soul. Treatments are carried out inwardly and outwardly. Inwardly, as are the things introduced through the mouth, through the anus, or to provoke sneezing, vomiting, and purgation. Outwardly, as plasters, incision, and cautery.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Medicine is so called from the mean; and the mean lies between excess and deficiency. Hence in Hippocrates it is called “the addition of what is lacking and the removal of what exceeds.” In short, it brings excessive extremes [Col. 0202D] to a balanced state, or preserves that mean. Thus medicine has two aims: to cure and to preserve health, as Galen testifies in *On Sects*, and Aristotle in *On Youth and Old Age*.]

## CHAPTER XXI. On Theatrical Art

[Col. 0201C] Theatrical art includes games. Some games were performed in theatres, others in *gabula* [uncertain term], others in gymnasia, others in arenas, others in amphitheatres, others at banquets, and others in temples. In theatres, deeds were recited. In *gabula*, they led dances. In gymnasia, they wrestled. In arenas, boxers were trained. In amphitheatres, they competed in races on foot, on horseback, and in chariots. At banquets, they played musical instruments. In temples, they sang praises of the gods.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Various kinds of games may be found both in the workshop of Textor and in that of Julius Barbarana. You may also draw much from the book of our *Platea* in the vernacular tongue.]

## CHAPTER XXII. On Logic and Its Parts

Logic is divided into grammar and the art of [Col. 0202A] reasoning. Grammar is divided into letter, syllable, word, and sentence. Reasoning is divided into probable, necessary, and sophistical reasoning. Probable reasoning is divided into dialectic and rhetoric. Necessary reasoning pertains to philosophers; sophistical reasoning, to sophists. Grammar is the knowledge of speaking correctly. Dialectic is keen disputation, distinguishing truth from falsehood. Rhetoric is a discipline suited to persuasion in every case.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Logic is nothing other than the art of reasoning. Its matter is the general question, not the particular one. Its end is to prove and to reason—that is, to examine something through disputation. Its instruments and means are definition, division, and argumentation.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. How the Arts Are to Be Read

In studying the arts, the following order must be observed. First of all, eloquence must be acquired, and therefore logic must be sought; then the eye of the mind must be purified through ethics, and thus one must pass on to rhetoric. Egypt is the mother of the arts: from Egypt they came into [Col. 0202B] Greece, and from Greece into Italy. Physics alone treats things; all the others treat concepts of things. But logic treats things according to their predicamental constitution; mathematics according to their dimensional extension. Therefore logic sometimes uses pure understanding, whereas mathematics is never without imagination.

It should be known, however, that physics is sometimes taken broadly as equivalent to theoretical philosophy; ethics likewise as equivalent to practical philosophy. In that case philosophy is divided into only three sciences: physics, ethics, and logic. It should also be known that mechanics is contained under philosophy with respect to its theory, not with respect to its execution. For example, the theory of agriculture belongs to the philosopher; its execution belongs to the farmer.

[Note: [Col. 0202D] Marsilio Ficino finely joins eloquence with ethics, which has the task of purifying the eye of the mind. For why, he says in his *Georgias* of Plato, is eloquence without wisdom a sharp sword in the hand of a madman?]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Inventors of the Arts

[Col. 0202C]

Among the Greeks, Linus was the first theologian; among the Latins, Varro; and in our own times, John Scotus, in *On the Ten Categories in God*. Thales of Miletus, one of the seven sages, invented natural physics. Pythagoras invented arithmetic; Boethius translated it. Sacred history records Jabal as the inventor of music; the Greeks and others name different persons. The Greeks invented geometry; Abraham, astrology. Neharot, after whom it is also named, invented astronomy. Socrates taught ethics. Minerva is said to have given the Athenians the use of cloth-making. Ninus was the first of all to wage wars. The Pelasgians invented the use of ships. Ceres is said to have discovered grain. Aptius likewise discovered the refinements of cookery. Apollo is thought to have invented medicine. The Lydians invented games: having once left Lydia, they settled in Etruria and there instituted games among the other kinds of their religious rites. Hence the Romans, having summoned instructors, held games at Rome.

Abraham invented the letters of the Syrians; Phoenix, those of the Greeks; Isis, those of the Egyptians; Moses, those of the Hebrews; Carmentis, those of the Latins. A certain Alcmon is said to have invented fables. Parmenides is said to have devised dialectic upon a certain rock; Demosthenes, to have invented rhetoric.

[Note: [Col. 0203B] On the inventors of the arts, one should consult partly Polydore Vergil and partly Alexander Sardi of Ferrara. Yet, if you wish, you may think to sample more in our *Platea*.]

## CHAPTER XXV. On Magic and Its Parts

[Col. 0203B] Magic is not contained under philosophy, but lies outside it. By a false profession it lies concerning truth, and, truly harmful, leads human beings away from divine religion, commends the worship of demons, and drives its followers toward every crime. It contains five kinds of evil arts: mantic art, mathematics, sorcery, lot-casting, [Col. 0204A] and illusions.

*Mantic* is interpreted as divination. It has five kinds: necromancy, geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy. The first is carried out among the dead; the second in earth; the third in water; the fourth in air; the fifth in fire. Mathematics is vanity in many respects. It has three branches: haruspicy (*aruspicina*), augury, and horoscopy. Haruspicy is said to derive from the inspection of *haræ* (*aræ*, “altars”); it occurs when events are sought in the entrails of animals—animals placed in *haræ*, that is, pens or lairs. Augury is named from birds. It sometimes pertains to the ears and is called augury from the cries of birds; sometimes it pertains to the eyes and is called auspice from the observation of birds. Horoscopy rests upon constellations. Sorceries are performed by incantations; [Col. 0204B] lot-castings by lots; illusions by phantasmal deceptions.

Zoroaster, king of the Bactrians, invented magic, and after a long time Democritus enlarged it. The Persians are said to have invented hydromancy; the Phrygians, auguries; Mercury, illusions; and a certain Etruscan boy named Tages, haruspicy.

[Note: [Col. 0203B] Nothing more copious or more complete can be read on magic than all that is stored up and concealed in our palace [Col. 0204B]. For if either ancient or recent authors have produced anything commendable on this subject, all of it will be made manifest in that volume. Let the reader keep these things in mind and, when it occurs to you, put them to the test.]

# BOOK TWO

Which treats of the subject matter of secular and divine Scripture; and that secular learning serves divine learning; with certain additions; containing ten chapters.

[Col. 0203]

## CHAPTER I. On the Subject Matter of Secular and Divine Scripture

[Col. 0203C]

Certainly, secular writing has as its subject matter the work of creation. Divine Scripture has as its subject matter the work of restoration. For there are two works of God: the work of creation and the work of restoration. The work of creation is that by which things that did not exist were made to exist; the work of restoration is that by which things that had perished were made better. The work of creation is the creation of the world with all its elements. The work of restoration is the incarnation of the Word with all its sacraments. The work of creation was accomplished in six days. The work of restoration can be accomplished only in six ages. Yet the six correspond to the six, so that the Redeemer may be known to be the same as the Creator.

## CHAPTER II. Why the Three Visible Things of the World Demonstrate the Three Invisible Things of God

[Col. 0203D]

Nor should it be passed over that, through the work of creation, three invisible things of God are demonstrated. “For the invisible things of him, understood through the things that are made, are clearly seen from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1). God has three invisible things: power, wisdom, and goodness. From these three all things come; in these three all things subsist; by these three [Col. 0204C] all things are governed. Power creates, wisdom governs, goodness preserves. Yet, just as these three are ineffably one in God, so in operation they cannot be separated. Power creates wisely through goodness. Wisdom governs kindly through power. Goodness preserves powerfully through wisdom.

The immensity of creatures manifests power; their beauty, wisdom; their usefulness, goodness. The immensity of creatures consists in multitude and magnitude. Multitude exists among similar things, diverse things, and mixed things. Magnitude consists in bulk and extension. Bulk consists in mass and weight. Extension consists in length and breadth, depth and height. The beauty of creatures consists in position and motion, form and quality. Position consists in composition and order. Order consists in place, time, and property. [Col. 0204D] Motion is fourfold: local, natural, animal, and rational. Local motion is forward and backward, right and left, upward and downward, and around. Natural motion is growth and diminution. Animal motion is in senses and appetites. Rational motion is in actions and deliberations. Form is a visible appearance discerned by the eye, such as colors and bodily shapes. [Col. 0205A] Quality is an inward property perceived by the other senses: melody in sound by the hearing of the ears; sweetness in flavor by the taste of the throat; fragrance in smell by the nostrils’ sense of smell; lightness in a body by the touch of the hands. The usefulness of creatures consists in what is pleasing, fitting, advantageous, and necessary. What is pleasing delights; what is fitting is suitable; what is advantageous is profitable; what is necessary is that without which something cannot exist.

## CHAPTER III. On the Threefold Mode of Treating Divine Scripture

Divine Scripture treats its subject matter in three ways: according to history, according to allegory, and according to tropology. History is the narration of events, contained in the primary signification of the letter. Allegory is when, through something said to have occurred, another occurrence—past, present, or future—is signified. Tropology is when, through what we read as having occurred, we recognize what we ought to do. In this respect divine Scripture is far superior to secular learning: in it not only words but also things are significant.

Therefore, just as knowledge of words is necessary for the meaning that concerns words and things, so knowledge of things is necessary for the meaning that concerns things and mystical deeds, whether accomplished or to be accomplished. Knowledge of words consists in two things: pronunciation and signification. Grammar pertains only to pronunciation; dialectic only to signification. Rhetoric pertains at once to pronunciation and knowledge. Knowledge [Col. 0205C] of things lies in form and nature. Form lies in outward arrangement; nature in inward quality. Every arrangement is either in number, which pertains to arithmetic; or in proportion, which pertains to music; or in position, which pertains to geometry; or in motion, which pertains to astronomy. Physics concerns inward quality.

## CHAPTER IV. That Secular Learning Serves Divine Scripture

All the arts, therefore, serve divine wisdom, and lower knowledge, rightly ordered, leads to higher knowledge. Under the meaning that concerns words and things is contained history, and three sciences serve it: dialectic, rhetoric, and grammar. Under the meaning that concerns things and mystical deeds is contained allegory. Under that which concerns things and mystical deeds [Col. 0205D] to be done is contained tropology. Arithmetic, music, geometry, astronomy, and physics serve these latter two.

## CHAPTER V. On the Signification of Words and Things

Words have no more than two or three significations. Things, however, can have as many significations as they have properties. These primary things, which signify secondary things, are considered as distinguished by six circumstances: thing, person, number, place, time, and action.

Here “thing” is understood as any material or inanimate substance constituted among heavenly or earthly things, such as stones and wood. A thing signifies in two ways: by nature and by form. By nature, as snow, because it is cold, [Col. 0206A] signifies the extinguishing of lust. By form, because it is white, it signifies the purity of a good work. A person signifies: Isaac signifies God the Father; Jacob, the people of the Gentiles.

Numbers signify in nine ways in divine discourse. According to the order of their position: unity, because it is first among numbers, signifies the origin of all things; two, because it is second and first departs from unity, signifies sin, by which there was a departure from the first good. According to the quality of their arrangement: the same number two, because it admits division and can be divided into two, signifies corruptible and transitory things. But three, because—with unity intervening in the middle—it does not admit division into two equal parts, signifies incorruptible things. According to the manner of extension: seven, beyond six, [Col. 0206B] signifies rest after work. According to the form of their arrangement: ten, because it extends in length, signifies the rectitude of faith; a hundred, because it expands in breadth, the breadth of charity; a thousand, because it is raised in height, the height of hope. According to calculation: ten signifies perfection, because in it the progression of counting comes to an end. According to multiplication: twelve signifies universality, because it is completed by the mutual multiplication of three and four, since four is the form of bodily things and three of spiritual things. According to the aggregation of parts: six is the form of perfection, because its three, two, and one, added together, complete the whole and neither exceed it nor fall short. According to [Col. 0206C] multitude: two, because of its two units, signifies love of God and neighbor; three, because of its three units, the Trinity. According to intensification: as in Leviticus, “I will add your punishments sevenfold for your sins” (Lev. 26). Here nothing other than a multitude of punishment, expressed by the number seven, is signified.

Places signify: Jericho signifies worldly falling-away; a stable, the Church; Jerusalem, eternal life. Time signifies, as when we read that the feast of the Dedication was held at Jerusalem, and it was winter. Winter in this place signifies the cold unbelief of the Jews. Action signifies, as when Jesus came to Bethany and raised Lazarus. Bethany is called “the house of obedience,” and Christ comes to the obedient person in order to raise Lazarus—that is, [Col. 0206D] the soul dead in sins.

## CHAPTER VI. Why Scripture First Sets Forth the Work of Creation

As was said above, secular writing has as its subject matter the work of creation; Sacred Scripture, however, has as its subject matter the work of restoration. The first was done so that it might be subject to a person standing upright; the second was done so that it might raise a person who had fallen. Sacred Scripture, therefore, in order to approach more suitably the treatment of its own subject matter, first recalls the work of creation.

For just as the human spirit was made for God, and the body for the spirit, so the world was made for the body: that the world might serve the body, the body the spirit, and the spirit the Creator. Sacred discourse could not explain [Col. 0207A] the restoration of humanity without its fall; its fall without its creation; or its creation without the creation of the whole world. It therefore wished first to recount the work of creation.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Creation of the World and the Works of the Six Days

Scripture recounts the creation of the world thus: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). By “heaven” it calls the three elements—fire, air, and water—which, mingled together in one confusion, or confused in one mingling, were fluctuating about the fourth, earth. Earth, at the center and balanced in a single position by its own weight among the other three, settled downward.

Sacred Scripture then calls the three elements which were mingled together “waters” and “darkness”: waters when it says, “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” (ibid.); darkness [Col. 0207B] when it says, “Darkness was upon the face of the deep” (ibid.). They are called heaven because of their suspension, waters because of their mobility and fluctuation, and darkness because of their confusion. The deep is the hollow of the earth, destined to become the receptacle of the lower waters.

Thus, in the beginning heaven and earth were created—that is, the four simple elements, the material of all things to be made. Scripture then adds: “And God said, ‘Let there be light’; and there was light” (ibid.). That first light is believed to have been made in the place where the sun now rises daily; and it is believed to have traveled the same path by which the sun is believed to have traveled, thus accomplishing evening and morning. This was the work of the first day.

On the second day the firmament was made in the midst: that is, in the midst of that confusion of the three elements which at first is known to have been called heaven, then water, [Col. 0207C] then darkness; and here, in the work of the second day, it is named by the term “waters.” The firmament was made in the midst of the waters so as to enclose part of them within itself and have them beneath it, while excluding another part from itself and having them above it. For in the mass of the universe, that which is innermost is lowest, and that which is outermost is highest. For example, earth among bodily things is innermost of all and itself lowest of all. The waters above the firmament are outermost and themselves highest of all. Among intermediate things, whatever is more inward is lower, and whatever is more outward is higher.

The firmament is shown to be movable by the stars fixed in it, but it is unknown of what material it was made. On the third day, by the divine command, the mass of waters which occupied the space between heaven and earth turned downward and descended into the deep; thus the air remained pure and clear in the middle. God then commanded the earth to bring forth herbs and trees according to their kinds, and it brought them forth. On the fourth day he made the lights, which are shown to be fixed in the firmament, except for the seven planets, whose names are: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. On the fifth day he made fish and birds from water; but he left the fish in the water and appointed birds to dwell in the air. On the sixth day he made beasts upon the earth.

Therefore, once the world had been created, arranged, and adorned, and once what was necessary, useful, and pleasing [Col. 0208A] for the human body had been prepared, God made humanity, the possessor of all things and lord of the universe. Though later in time, humanity is found earlier in cause and higher in dignity. God made the human body from the mud of red earth, breathed into its face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul.

The Lord God had planted from the beginning a paradise of delight (Gen. 2). Paradise is a place in the regions of the East, which, because of the great moderation of its air, is never touched by cold or heat; rather, perpetual springtime, vernal pleasantness, and serenity endure. In it was the tree of life: so long as a human being ate from it, he would never become sick or grow old, but, once obedience had been fulfilled, would be transferred to the fellowship of angels—then without death, just as now [Col. 0208B] through death. There was also in it the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, by which a human being was to experience good if he did not eat from it, evil if he ate.

In this place God put the human being whom he had made, forbidding that person only the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Then, after all living creatures had been brought to Adam and he had given names to all of them, God made Eve, whom he gave as a companion to the man from whom she had been made. “And God saw all the things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). “And he rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished” (Gen. 2).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Four Works of God

But what does it mean that God is here said to have rested from all work, when Christ says in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5)? It should therefore be known that God’s operation is distinguished in four ways. The first work of God is the work of creation; the second, the work of ordering; the third, the work of propagation; the fourth, the work of governance. God performed the first before every day, the second in six days, and from this he rested on the seventh day. He performs the third from the beginning until the end of the age, and will not cease to perform the fourth for eternity.

In this way Sacred Scripture proceeds through the work of creation toward its subject matter, namely the work of restoration. It treats that subject matter in three ways, as was stated above: according to history, allegory, and tropology. But before we enter upon the historical narrative, [Col. 0208D] we must say something about the situation of the lands. For we propose first to sketch the outline not only of sacred but also of secular history, and thereafter, insofar as we are able, to explain the mysteries of allegory and tropology.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Two Testaments

All divine Scripture is contained in two Testaments, namely the Old and the New. Each Testament is distinguished into three orders. The Old Testament contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. The New contains the Gospels, the Apostles, and the Fathers.

The first order of the Old Testament—that is, the Law, which the Hebrews call *Torath* (“Torah”)—contains the Pentateuch, that is, the five books of Moses, in this order: first, *Bresith* [*Bereshit*], that is, Genesis; second, *Hessesmot* [*Shemot*], [Col. 0209A] that is, Exodus; third, *Vagethra* [*Vayyiqra*], which is Leviticus; fourth, *Vagedaber* [*Bemidbar*], which is Numbers; fifth, *Adabarim* [*Devarim*], which is Deuteronomy.

The second order is that of the Prophets. It contains eight volumes: first, *Josue Hennum* [probably *Jehoshua bin Nun*], that is, Joshua son of Nun, who is also called Joshua, Jesus Nave, and Jesus; second, *Soptim* [*Shoftim*], which is the book of Judges; third, Samuel, which is First and Second Kings; fourth, *Malachim* [*Melakhim*], which is Third and Fourth Kings; fifth, Isaiah; sixth, Jeremiah; seventh, Ezekiel; eighth, *Thareastra* [*Trei Asar*], which is the book of the twelve prophets.

The third order is that of the Hagiographa. It contains nine books: first, Job; second, the Psalter; third, *Maslot*, which in Greek means *Parabolai* (“Parables”) and in Latin *Proverbia* (“Proverbs”); fourth, *Celeth* [*Qoheleth*], which is [Col. 0209B] Ecclesiastes; fifth, *Sira sirim* [*Shir ha-Shirim*], that is, the Song of Songs; sixth, Daniel; seventh, *Dabreniamin* [probably *Divrei ha-Yamim*], which is Chronicles; eighth, Ezra; ninth, Esther. These are twenty-four in all.

There are, moreover, other books, such as the Wisdom of Solomon, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the book of Maccabees, which are indeed read but are not written in the Canon. To these twenty-two books of the Old Testament are added eight of the New. In the first order of the New Testament are the four Gospels, written by Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. In the second are likewise four: the Acts of the Apostles; the fourteen Epistles of Paul in one volume; the Catholic Epistles; and the Apocalypse. In the third order the first place belongs to the decrees which we call canons; [Col. 0209C] then come the writings of the holy Fathers—Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and others—which are innumerable.

Yet these writings of the Fathers are not counted in the text of the divine Scriptures, just as, in the Old Testament, as we have said, there are certain books which are not written in the Canon but are nevertheless read, such as the Wisdom of Solomon and the others named. [Col. 0210A] The text of the divine Scriptures, therefore, as though one whole body, is principally contained in thirty books: twenty-two, as stated above, in the Old Testament, and eight in the New.

## CHAPTER X. Why It Is Called a Testament
Sacred Scripture is called a testament, human custom having furnished the occasion for the term. For in ancient times those who lacked children adopted children; and when they appointed them heirs, they summoned witnesses and drew up a written instrument—yet not one so binding that it could not be altered while the testator lived. Likewise God, having one Son by nature, wished to adopt many by grace; and first he chose Abraham, commanding him to depart from his kindred and promising him [Col. 0210B] the land of Palestine (Gen. 12). Afterwards, when he had brought the children of Israel out of Egypt, he promised it again; and, lest they should doubt, he made a testament as assurance of the promised inheritance—namely, the Law, which was given through Moses. But because God could not die, and a testament had to be confirmed by the death of its testator, a mystical lamb was slain for it; with its blood the book and the whole people were sprinkled, in confirmation of the promised inheritance. In the same way the Lord Jesus Christ, calling not one man but all nations to an eternal inheritance, made a testament, namely the Gospel. For its confirmation, that ancient lamb was not slain, but he himself—because he was human and could die—underwent death. And just as God, when giving the Old Testament, called witnesses—[Col. 0210C] namely Aaron, his sister Miriam, and Hur—so Christ, because he promised greater things, called more witnesses: namely, the apostles and martyrs. The first Testament is called Old because it was given earlier, or because it was instituted concerning things that grow old. It is called the New because it speaks of things unchangeable and ever new.

## BOOK THREE. On the Situation of Lands. With Annotations by Master Thomas Garzoni, Theologian. It contains eight chapters.

[Col. 0209]

## CHAPTER I. On the Three Parts of the World.

[Col. 0209D]

There are three parts of the world: Asia, Europe, and Africa. Asia occupies that half of the earth which lies toward the east. The other two occupy that which lies toward the west, and they are divided from one another by the great sea.

> [Note: [Col. 0209D] Modern writers add to these three parts of the world three others: namely America of the West Indies, unknown to the ancients; Greenland, lying farthest north, recently discovered but still not well known; and a sixth, most southerly part, discovered but unknown and unnamed. [Col. 0210A]]

## CHAPTER II. On Asia and Its Parts.

Asia has many provinces and regions, whose names and locations I shall briefly set forth, beginning with Paradise. Paradise is a place in the eastern regions [Col. 0210D], planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree. It has the tree of life. There is neither cold nor heat there, but a perpetual temperateness of the air. It has a spring which divides into four rivers. “Paradise” in Greek, and in Hebrew “Eden,” together mean in our language “the garden of delights.”

India is a region of Asia between the Ocean and the river Indus, and it derives its name from the Indus. It has many peoples and towns; the island of Taprobane, full of gems and elephants; and Chrysa and Argyria, rich in gold and silver [Col. 0211A]. It reaps twice a year; it produces dark-complexioned people and enormous elephants, the rhinoceros beast, the parrot bird, ebony wood, cinnamon, pepper, and aromatic reed. It sends ivory, beryls, chrysoprases, diamonds, *lignetes* [uncertain gem-name], carbuncles, pearls, and large pearls, for which the ambition of noblewomen burns. It also has golden mountains, which are exceedingly difficult to approach because of dragons, tigers, griffins, and races of gigantic men.

Between the rivers Indus and Tigris are Arachosia, Parthia, Assyria, Media, and Persia. Arachosia took its name from its own city. The Parthians, having come out of Scythia, occupied Parthia and called it Parthia after their own name. Assyria was named from Asshur, son of Shem, who first inhabited it after the Flood. [Col. 0211B] In it the use of purple was discovered. From there came fragrances for the hair and ointments for the body. Media and Persia were named after the kings Medus and Perseus. In Media is found a tree which no other region possesses. The Persians worship fire and are said to have invented pyromancy.

Between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates are Mesopotamia, Chaldea, and Arabia. By Greek etymology Mesopotamia is so called because it is surrounded by two rivers, the Tigris and Euphrates. Arabia is called “sacred,” because it contains the frankincense-bearing region. This was called Saba after Saba, son of Cush. In it are found the frankincense tree, myrrh, cinnamon, the phoenix bird, and the sardonyx gem.

Between the Euphrates and the Mediterranean Sea are Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine, which contains Judaea, Samaria, and Galilee. Syria, [Col. 0211C] it is said, was named after a certain Syrus, from his own name. There is found in it the Syrian stone, which is said to float when whole but sink when crushed. Phoenicia received its name from Phoenix, who reigned there. Tyre is in it. Palestine is named from Philisthiim, its chief city; Judaea from Judah. This is Canaan, called after Canaan son of Ham. In the middle of Judaea is Jerusalem, the navel of the whole earth, rich in diverse resources, fertile in crops, splendid in waters, and abundant in balsam. Samaria takes its name from the town called Samaria. Galilee is so called because it produces fair-complexioned people; it is a land sufficiently fertile in crops.

On Asia’s northern side, Scythia stretches from the Eastern Ocean westward; it is enclosed on all sides by mountains, and at its eastern extremity are the Seres. [Col. 0211D] In it are found the finest emerald and the purest crystal. Below Scythia, from the Caspian Sea to the Euxine Sea or the Hellespont and the river Tanais [Col. 0212A], are Amazonia, Albania, Hyrcania, Bactria, Iberia, Armenia, Cappadocia, Colchis, Asia Minor, and Cilicia. Amazonia is so called because women rule there; lest they be hindered in archery, they remove the right breast of their girls. Albania is named from the whiteness of its people. The dogs of this land are of such enormous size and ferocity that they overpower bulls and kill lions. Hyrcania is named from the Hyrcanian forest, abundant in wild animals, herds, panthers, and leopards. The river Bactrus gave Bactria its name. It has camels whose feet never wear down. Armenia derives its name from a certain Armenus. Upon its mountains the ark came to rest after the Flood. A city properly gave Cappadocia its name; the land is above all others a breeder of horses. Asia Minor has the provinces of Bithynia, Phrygia, Galatia, Lydia, Caria, Pamphylia [Col. 0212B], Isauria, and Lycia. Cilicia, named after a certain Cilix, has Tarsus as its chief city.

On Asia’s southern side the Red Sea extends from the Eastern Ocean westward as far as the borders of Arabia and Palestine. Between the Red Sea and the Southern Ocean, eastward above it, is Upper Ethiopia, which is enclosed crosswise on the west by the Ethiopian mountains. Below Ethiopia are Upper Egypt, the deserts of Egypt, Lower Egypt, and Libya. Egypt is a region unaccustomed to rain; it has the crocodile beast, and the ibis and pelican birds.

> [Note: [Col. 0211D] Asia is divided into two principal parts. One, facing northward, corresponds to Europe; the other, facing southward, corresponds to Africa. The first is again divided into three further parts. One extends from the river Tanais and Lake Maeotis to the river Rha and the Hyrcanian Sea; the second, from the Euxine Sea to the farthest part of the Hyrcanian strait. The third extends from the river Rha and the eastern extremities of the Hyrcanian Sea to the furthest bounds of Asia, which lie northward of the established line. The other principal part of Asia is subdivided into three further parts. The first is from Lycia and the Red Sea to the Persian Gulf. [Col. 0212D] The second is from the Persian Gulf to the river Indus. The third is from the river Indus to Asia’s furthest boundary, beyond the line of Mount Taurus toward the south. The aforesaid author explains in his treatise *On the World* how many provinces are contained in all these divisions.]

## CHAPTER III. On Africa and Its Parts.
