The regions of Africa stretch from east to west as follows: Ethiopians, Nadaberes, Garamantes, [Col. 0212C] Cyrenaican Libya, Tripolitania, Futhensis, Zeugitana, Gaetulia, Numidia, Tingitania, and Mauretania. The Syrtes, extending obliquely from the Mediterranean Sea to the Atlantic Ocean, divide Zeugitana, Numidia, and Mauretania from the deserts of Africa, beyond which are the Ethiopians. The Nadaberes are named from the place Nadaber. The Garamantes likewise are named from the town Garama. Cyrenaican Libya is called after the city Cyrene. Tripolitania is named from its three cities. Futhensis is thought to be named after Futla. Moreover, Carthage is in Zeugitana. Gaetulia, it is reported, has no fishermen. Numidia derives its name from inhabitants wandering through pasturelands; for in their language *Numidae* means “people of uncertain dwellings.” Tingitania is named from its chief city Tingis. Mauretania is named from *mauro*, meaning “black” [Col. 0212D].

> [Note: [Col. 0212D] Africa is divided by Mount Atlas, which runs alike from west to east in an uninterrupted chain as far as Egypt, into two principal parts. The first, facing northward and situated opposite Europe, extends to the Mediterranean Sea. The other extends to the farthest Southern Ocean, but narrows both from west and east, so that at its southern extremity it forms, as it were, an angle, where the promontory popularly called the Cape of Good Hope is situated. [Col. 0213D] The provinces contained in each part may be seen in the same author.]

## CHAPTER IV. On Europe and Its Parts.

These are the regions and peoples of Europe, extending westward from the river Tanais [Col. 0213A] along the shore of the Ocean: Lower Scythians, Dacians, Goths, Alans, Gepids, Rugians, Bulgars, Huns or Hungarians, Noricans, Slavs, Germany, Alemannia, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Spain. Germany is so called because of the fertility with which it produces peoples. It also produces Hercynian birds, whose feathers shine at night, bison beasts, and crystal stone. Alemannia, with its fertile soil, is suited to the use of animals. Gaul is named from the whiteness of its people. The ridges of the Alps protect it on the east, and the Ocean encloses it on the west. To the south it has the steep slopes of the Pyrenees; to the north, the waters of the Rhine and Germany. Aquitaine takes its name from the winding waters of the Loire. Spain was first called Iberia after the river Iberus, then Spain after King Hispanus; it is a land [Col. 0213B] exceedingly rich in every kind of crop and full of stores of gems and metals.

Between the Danube and the Mediterranean Sea, beneath the Euxine Sea and the Hellespont, are Moesia, Istria, and Macedonia; and beneath Macedonia, from north to south, Arcadia, Hellas, Thessaly, and Achaea. Moesia is so called from the ripening of harvests. Istria is named from the Hister, that is, the Danube. Thyras, son of Japheth, is said to have given Thrace its name. Macedonia is named from Macedon, the homeland of Alexander the Great. Arcadia was formerly called Sicyon; it has asbestos stone, which once kindled is never extinguished, and it also has white blackbirds. Hellas is called after King Hellen. In it was Athens, the city that nursed philosophers. Thessaly is called after King Thessalus. There the practice of taming horses was discovered. Achaea is called after [Col. 0213C] King Achaeus. Its chief city is Corinth.

After passing across the Dalmatian Gulf, between the Alps and the Mediterranean Sea, are Campania, Apulia, Tuscany, Calabria, Liguria, Italy—also called Latium—and Umbria. Italy, moreover, was named after King Italus; it is a land most beautiful in every respect, most pleasing in the fertility and abundance of its soil. It produces gems, *sertites* [uncertain stone-name], lynx-stone, coral, the boa serpent, the lynx beast, and Diomedean birds. Between the Cottian Alps and the Apennines are Lombardy and Valeria. Between the Tyrrhenian Gulf and the Pyrenees is the province—

> [Note: [Col. 0213D] Europe may conveniently be divided by the Adriatic Sea, the Alps, Mount Adula, and the river Rhine into two principal parts. That which extends from these boundaries toward the Fortunate Islands is called the western part. The other, which from these boundaries faces the river Tanais, Lake Maeotis, the Euxine Sea, and the Aegean Sea, is called the eastern part. You may learn from the aforesaid author how these parts are in turn divided into others; in dividing the earth, he declares that he followed Strabo, Ptolemy’s maps, and the world-map of Jacopo Gastaldi of Piedmont. [Col. 0214D]]

## CHAPTER V. On Mountains Famous throughout the World.

Above the Indian Ocean, in the southern part, is Calidargamera; to the north, Samara. In Scythia are Imaus, Caucasus, Parapamisus, Taurus, Oscabares, [Col. 0213D] Parcan, Memarmoli, Ariobarzanes, Acroceraunus, and Caucasus. In Armenia is Parcoatras; in Cilicia [Col. 0214A], Taurus; in Boreas, the Riphaean Mountains; in Phoenicia, Lebanon; in Arabia, Nysaeus; in the Arabian desert, Mount Phasga, Mount Scorpion, Mount Sinai, Mount Hor, and Mount Abarim. In Idumaea is Mount Seir; in Judaea, Mount Hermon, Carmel, and Gilboa. In Thessaly, Olympus, Pindus, and Ossa. In Phocis, Parnassus. In Macedonia, Athos. In Sicily, Etna. In Italy, the Apennines and the Alps. Between Gaul and Italy, Licabantos. Between Aquitaine and Spain, the Pyrenees. In Spain, Solurius and Calpe. In Africa, Atlas.

> [Note: [Col. 0214D] The mountains of Armenia, where Noah’s ark rested, are inferred from sacred Genesis to be exceedingly high.]

## CHAPTER VI. On Rivers Famous throughout the World.

The Ganges is a famous river in India. The Indus lies west of it. In Parthia, the Tigris. The Bactrus in Bactria. Likewise the Tigris between Assyria and Mesopotamia. The Euphrates between Mesopotamia and Syria. The Nile in [Col. 0214B] Egypt; the Jordan in Judaea. The Cydnus in Cilicia. The Araxes in Armenia. The Timaus in Lower Scythia. The Pactolus, Hermus, and Maeander in Asia Minor. The Hebrus in Thrace, and the Eurotas in Thessaly. The Inachus in Achaea. The Po and Tiber in Italy. The Danube and Rhine in Germany. The Rhône, Saône, Meuse, Seine, and Loire in Gaul. The Iberus in Spain. The Minho in Galicia. The Tagus and Bagrada at Carthage.

> [Note: [Col. 0214D] You will find the rivers of the whole world more fully—though summarily—enumerated in the book on hydrography by Johann Thomas Freigius.]

## CHAPTER VII. On the Islands of the World.

In the Eastern Ocean, from south to north, are Taprobane, Thule, Argyria, and Chrysa. In the Northern Ocean, from east to west, are the island of the Phanesians, Albania, Hyperborea, Apolitana, Gangania, Glossaria, Northmannia, the Orkneys, Thule, Scotland, Britain, [Col. 0214C] and Ireland. In the Western Ocean are the Fortunate Islands, the Hesperides, and the Gorgades. In the Southern Ocean are Gauleum, the Island of the Fish-Eaters, Adamus, Coneus, and Malicus. In the sea which divides Europe and Africa from west to east are Gades, the Balearics, the Stoechades, Sardinia, Corsica, Sicily, and Cephalonia. In the Great Sea are the Cyclades, Rhodes, Tenedos, Carpathos, Cythera, then Cyprus, Sidon, and Crete. In the Syrian Sea is Patmos.

> [Note: [Col. 0214D] The Diomedean Island, now belonging to the Canons Regular of the Lateran, is celebrated by Pliny, book 10, chapter 44, because of the birds of Diomedes, famous among the poets. But anyone who seeks a complete knowledge of all islands should not hesitate to read the volume commonly called *The Book of Islands*, as well as Peter Apian’s *Catalogue of the Islands of the World*.]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Famous Cities and Towns.

Babylon is in Chaldea; Nineveh in Assyria; Nysa in India; Media in Media; Persepolis and Susa in Persia; Ctesiphon in Parthia; and in Mesopotamia, Carrae, Edessa, and Calamiae. This is Seleucia, Philadelphia. In Scythia are Hortogoria, Samarkand, Aripti, Alexandria, Scythopolis, [Col. 0214D] and the village of Saphir. In Syria are Antioch, Damascus, and Seleucia. In Phoenicia, Tyre and Sidon. In Cilicia [Col. 0215A], Tarsus. In Asia Minor, Nicomedia, Nicaea, Chalcedon, Sardis, Ilium, Ephesus, Pergamum, and Thyatira. In Samaria, Bethany, Samaria, and Caesarea. In Galilee, Nazareth, Chorazin, Bethsaida, Tiberias, Cana, Capernaum, and Nain. In Judaea, Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Jericho, and Hebron. In Thrace, Constantinople, Panisus, and Nicopolis. In Macedonia, Philippi. In Egypt, Thebes, Tahpanhes, Memphis, Heliopolis, Pelusium, and Alexandria. In Cyrenaican Libya, Cyrene, Parthenium, Berenice, Apollonia, Ptolemais, and Adramyttium. In Italy, Rome, Alba, Capua, Benevento, Sipontum, Naples, Tivoli, Ostia, Luna, Genoa, and Ancona. In Lombardy, Milan, Ticinum or Pavia, Brescia, Verona, Vicenza, Padua, Bologna, Ravenna, Mantua, and Cremona. In Valeria [Col. 0215B], Aquileia. In Calabria, Tarentum. These are the cities beyond the Alps: Cologne, Mainz, Salzburg, [Col. 0216A] Regensburg [Ratisbona], Würzburg, Strasbourg, Basel, Trier, Sens, Paris, Lyon, Rouen, Rheims, Arles, Vienne, Parentasia, Embrun, Bourges, Tours, Bordeaux, Toulouse, and Narbonne. In Spain are Pamplona, Huesca, Barcelona, Tarragona, Tortosa, Carthage, Hippo, Megala, Caesarea, Leptis, Byzantium, and Clupea. The twelve Alexandrias: Alexandria Bucephala, Alexandria of the Mountains, Alexandria by Porus, Alexandria in Scythia, Alexandria by Babylon, Alexandria in Egypt, Alexandria among the Massagetae, Alexandria by the Orgalas, Alexandria by the Granicus, Alexandria in the Troad, Alexandria beside the Tigris, and Alexandria by the Xanthus. Having thus briefly dealt with the situation of lands, let us proceed to what follows [Col. 0216B].

> [Note: [Col. 0215B] Many cities famous today are passed over, such as Venice, Pisa, Siena, Florence, Ferrara, Perugia, and very many others, because he wished partly to enumerate older ones, and partly to include only some, not all, even of the ancient cities in his catalogue. More recently Gerama Frigius used the same method in his *Catalogue of Cities*. [Col. 0216B]]

## BOOK FOUR. It Treats of History from Adam to Christ; It Contains Thirteen Chapters.

[Col. 0215]

## CHAPTER I. The Course Which the Following Narrative Will Follow.

[Col. 0215C]

It should certainly be known that this whole sequence and extension of time is to be divided into two states, old and new; into three periods, of natural law, written law, and grace; and into six ages. The first is from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian Captivity; the fifth from the Babylonian Captivity to Christ’s coming; and the sixth from Christ’s coming to the end of the world. Again, the five preceding ages from Adam to Christ are divided by four successions. The first succession, that of the patriarchs, was from Adam to Moses; the second, that of the judges, from Moses to David; the third, that of the kings, from David to the Babylonian Captivity; and the fourth, that of the priests, from the Babylonian Captivity to Christ. Therefore I shall extend my account from Adam to Christ through the eminent men of these four successions; then, from Christ’s coming to our own times, I shall continue the narrative first through the Roman emperors and then through the kings of the Franks.

## CHAPTER II. These Are the Patriarchs.

Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Salah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, Nahor, Terah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Levi, Kohath, Amram.

## CHAPTER III. The Judges Who Were.

Moses, Joshua, Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, [Col. 0216C] Abimelech, Tola, Jair, Jephthah, Ibzan, Elon, Abdon [Labdon], Samson, Eli, Samuel.

## CHAPTER IV. The Kings Who Were.

Saul, David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Azariah, Athaliah, Joash, Amaziah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, Josiah, Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah.

## CHAPTER V. High Priests.

Jesus, Joachim, Eliasib, Judas, John, Simon the Just, Eleazar, Manasseh, Onias, Simon, Onias, Jesus also called Jason, Onias also called Menelaus, Alcimus, Judas, Jonathan, Simon, John, Aristobulus, Alexander, Alexandra, Hyrcanus.

## CHAPTER VI. History from Adam to Moses.

The first parents, therefore, having transgressed the command of obedience, were cast out of Paradise and thrown into the misery [Col. 0216D] of this world. Adam knew his wife and begot Cain, whose descendants were called “men.” He begot Abel, whose descendants were called “sons of God.” Seth, moreover, begot Enos; Enos begot Cainan; Cainan begot Mahalaleel; Mahalaleel begot Jared; Jared begot Enoch, who was translated; Enoch begot Methuselah; Methuselah begot Lamech; and Lamech begot Noah.

In those days there were giants on the earth, and all flesh had corrupted its way. For the sons of God—that is, those who were of Seth’s stock—seeing the daughters of men, who were of Cain’s race, that they were beautiful, mingled the holy with the profane and took them as wives. Therefore God, angered, said [Col. 0217A] that he would destroy mankind and every living creature which he had made for humankind’s sake, by the waters of the Flood. But Noah found favour before the Lord; and, by God’s command, he made an ark for himself, in which he, his wife, his three sons, and his sons’ wives might be saved. Of the clean animals he brought in seven each; of the unclean, two by pairs. Thus every living creature was destroyed by the waters of the Flood, except those that were in the ark.

When the Flood was over, Noah came out of the ark with all his sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. From them the entire human race was dispersed over the earth after the Flood. But before their descendants were divided from one another, they began the tower of Babylon, where their speech was confounded. After they were divided, the sons of Shem possessed the southern part of Asia from the rising of the sun [Col. 0217B] to the Phoenicians. Ham’s descendants occupied the southern land from Sidon to the Strait of Gades. The sons of Japheth occupied the northern part of Asia from Mount Taurus, and all Europe to the British Ocean, leaving their names to places and peoples. Some of these names remain still: from Elam, the Elamites; from Asshur, the Assyrians. Others have been changed: from the river Indus, Indians; from King Aegyptus, Egyptians.

Shem begot Arphaxad; Arphaxad begot Salah; Salah begot Eber, from whom the Hebrews are called. In his family, after the confusion of languages, remained that primordial language common to all, which is called Hebrew. Eber begot Peleg, in whose time the tower called Babel was built. Peleg begot Reu, or Ragau, under whom gods were first worshipped. Ragau [Col. 0217C] begot Serug; Serug begot Nahor; Nahor begot Terah; and Terah begot Abram, in whose time Zoroaster discovered magic.

God brought this Abram out of Chaldea, when the worship of idols was already fervent everywhere, and led him into the land of Canaan (Gen. 12), and promised that he would give it to his offspring. When a famine arose, Abram journeyed into Egypt and returned from there enriched. Finally, he received a divine command to circumcise himself and his offspring. Abraham begot Isaac, who took Rebecca as wife and by her begot Jacob and Esau. After Jacob had obtained his brother’s birthright for a dish of lentils and had supplanted him in their father’s blessing, he went to his uncle Laban; in return for his [Col. 0217D] service, he took Laban’s daughters as wives and fathered the twelve patriarchs by them and by their handmaids. Having become very wealthy, he returned to his homeland and buried his father with Esau his brother. Then Joseph was sold into Egypt by his brothers; there, by God’s wondrous providence, he was exalted, and his father followed him there with his entire household.

## CHAPTER VII. History from Moses to Joshua.

After Jacob’s death, and after Joseph’s death, the children of Israel multiplied greatly in Egypt. Another king arose who did not know Joseph, and he began to oppress the children of Israel in the building of the cities Pithom and Rameses. But God saw their labor and heard their cry; he sent Moses and Aaron and brought them out of the land of Egypt, after Egypt had been scourged with ten plagues.

[Col. 0218A]

> First, a reddening wave; second, pestilence and frogs.  
> Then grievous gnats; after these, a more harmful fly.  
> The fifth struck down cattle; the sixth produced blisters.  
> Next came hail; then the locust with its dreadful tooth.  
> The ninth covers the sun; the last kills the firstborn offspring.

But because Scripture, from Moses onward, relates the sum of events not according to the generations of patriarchs but according to the succession of rulers, we shall set down Moses’ own generation from Jacob, and then shall briefly comprehend the deeds done under him and the two who followed him. Jacob, therefore, begot Levi; Levi begot Kohath; Kohath begot Amram; and Amram begot Moses. Under his leadership God performed many mighty deeds in the Red Sea and the wilderness. For he scourged Egypt with the ten plagues mentioned above and divided the Red Sea before the children of Israel. In the wilderness [Col. 0218B] he made bitter waters sweet, rained manna from heaven, with which he fed the children of Israel for forty years, brought water from the rock, defeated the people of Amalek, gave the Law on Mount Horeb, and commanded that the tabernacle of the covenant and the ark of testimony be made, and that Aaron and his son be consecrated to him for the priesthood and clerical office.

When these things had occurred, after the children of Israel had departed from the mountain under Moses’ leadership with the pillar preceding them, God again filled them with quail meat. Dathan and Abiram, contending against Moses, he condemned when the earth swallowed them. He caused Aaron’s rod, contrary to nature, to put forth leaves, blossom, and bear fruit. He punished the murmuring children of Israel by the conflagration of heavenly fire; he sent fiery serpents among them, and healed them from their bite by their looking upon the bronze serpent. When, moreover, at the return of the twelve scouts, they murmured, [Col. 0218C] he kept them in the wilderness for forty years. During those years all those murmurers and unbelievers died, while their children grew up and afterwards possessed the land of promise. The Lord destroyed Og king of Bashan and Sihon king of the Amorites, as the children of Israel fought, and he overthrew Balak and his people. Aaron died in the wilderness and was buried on Mount Hor. When the forty years were completed, Moses too died, by the Lord’s command, on Mount Abarim; Joshua son of Nun succeeded him.

## CHAPTER VIII. History from Joshua to King Saul.

Joshua brought the people of God into the land of promise, killed the Canaanite peoples and thirty-one kings [Col. 0218D] in that land, and distributed the land among the victorious people. Othniel succeeded Joshua. He delivered Israel from the hand of Cushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and the land rested forty years. After him came Ehud, of the tribe of Benjamin, who used either hand as his right hand. He delivered Israel from the hand of Eglon king of Moab. For when he was bringing the tribute of the people of Israel to King Eglon, whom that people then served, he sent away his companions as they were returning, went back to Eglon, killed him in secret, gathered his people, conquered Moab, and delivered Israel.

After his death Deborah [Delbora], with Barak, went to battle against Sisera, commander of Jabin of Hazor. The Lord terrified Sisera before Barak; he leapt from his chariot and fled to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite [Col. 0219A]. After covering him with a cloak, she took a nail and drove it into his temples, and he died. After Deborah arose Gideon, who delivered Israel from the hand of Midian and struck Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna.

Then, after Gideon’s death, Abimelech son of Jerubbaal, whom his concubine of Shechem bore him, killed all his seventy brothers, except the youngest, Jotham, who escaped. The men of Shechem made Abimelech their ruler. After this God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; Abimelech himself killed many of them, and at last he perished with his brains dashed out by a fragment of millstone which a woman threw upon his head. After him arose Tola; after Tola, Jair; and after Jair, Jephthah. Finally Jephthah delivered Israel from the hand of [Col. 0219B] the children of Ammon. As he went to war, he vowed to God that, should he gain victory, he would sacrifice whatever first met him on his return. His only daughter met him as he returned; he sacrificed her and fulfilled the vow that he had made.

After Jephthah, Ibzan was judge; after him Elon [Achialon]; after him Abdon [Labdon]; and after him Samson. He killed a lion, took a wife from Timnah, burned the Philistines’ crops by fastening lighted torches to foxes’ tails, and slew a thousand men with an ass’s jawbone. He carried the gates of Gaza up onto a mountain. At last he revealed to the woman Delilah that such great strength was in his hair; after she had shaved his hair, she handed him over to the Philistines, who gouged out his eyes and made him grind. When his hair [Col. 0219C] had grown again, and he was performing before the Philistines as they held their feasts, he shook the pillars of the house and killed those who were in it, while he himself also died.

Eli succeeded Samson. Under him the prophet Samuel became famous, the ark of the covenant was captured, and Hophni and Phinehas, the priest’s sons, were killed. Finally, when Eli heard that the ark of the Lord had been captured, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died. The Lord struck the Philistines in the more hidden part of their buttocks, and mice were born in their fields; compelled by this plague, they returned the ark of God. Samuel succeeded Eli.

## CHAPTER IX. History from Saul to Hezekiah.

When Samuel had grown old, the children of Israel asked for a king. This displeased the Lord; nevertheless he gave them a king, [Col. 0219D] Saul son of Kish, who, though he had a good beginning and defended Israel, came to a bad end because he disobeyed the Lord in the war which he waged against Amalek. Therefore, being rejected, he was tormented by an evil spirit. David was anointed king in his stead. Afterwards David was brought into Saul’s house; and whenever the evil spirit of the Lord seized Saul, David played the lyre, and Saul was relieved.

But after David struck down the Philistine, Saul removed him from his presence and made him commander over a thousand men. Jonathan, Saul’s son, loved David as his own soul. And when Saul suspected David in regard to the kingdom, he laid many snares for him in order to kill him; but the Lord did not deliver him into his hands. At last David fled to Achish, king of Gath. When Saul had died, [Col. 0220A] David went up to Hebron and reigned over the tribe of Judah. Then, after the death of Abner, he reigned over all Israel. Gad, Nathan, and Asaph prophesied. Now the time during which David reigned was forty years.

After David, his son Solomon reigned. He built the temple of the Lord. He too had a good beginning, but his end was not good, because he worshipped foreign gods. Therefore the Lord, angered, tore the kingdom from the hand of his son Rehoboam and gave it to his servant Jeroboam. For when the people asked that the yoke of his father be lightened, he answered them harshly. And the ten tribes appointed Jeroboam son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam, moreover, defiled the people through the worship of idols.

The kingdom of Israel continued for three hundred and forty years and through nineteen kings, [Col. 0220B] whose names are these: Jeroboam, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri, Ahab, Ahaziah, Joram, Jehu, Jehoahaz, Joash, Jeroboam, Zechariah, Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, Pekah, Hoshea. In the days of Hoshea king of Israel and in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians deported the ten tribes and settled them in the cities of the Medes; and he brought Cushites into Samaria. These are the Samaritans, with whom the Jews did not associate.

Therefore, after Solomon, Rehoboam reigned in Judaea, and after Rehoboam, Abijah. He walked in the sins of his father. After Abijah Asa reigned; Asa’s heart was upright with God, and he had war with Baasha king of Israel. When Baasha had died, Jehoshaphat reigned. He did what was right before the Lord and went to war with Ahaz against the king of Syria. [Col. 0220C] In these days Elijah prophesied.

After Jehoshaphat Joram reigned and walked in the ways of the kings of Israel. In those days Edom revolted so as no longer to be subject to Judah; then Libnah also revolted. Joram slept with his fathers, and Azariah, son of Athaliah, reigned in his stead. Azariah went down to visit Joram king of Israel, whom the Syrians had wounded, and Jehu killed them both. Now Athaliah was the daughter of Omri king of Israel; when she saw that her son was dead, she killed all the royal offspring. But the sister of Azariah took Joash, son of Azariah, and kept him safe for six years, during which Athaliah reigned over the land. In the seventh year, however, the priest Jehoiada summoned the centurions and showed them the king’s son; they appointed him king and killed Athaliah. [Col. 0220D]

In those days the king of Syria wished to fight against Jerusalem; Joash gave him those things which his fathers had offered to the treasuries of the Lord, and he withdrew. At last the servants of Joash killed him, and his son Amaziah reigned in his stead. Amaziah challenged King Joash to battle, and Amaziah fled. Joras, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem and took from there the gold and golden vessels found in the house of the Lord. Then a conspiracy was formed against Amaziah; he was killed at Lachish, and his son Uzziah reigned in his stead.

Moreover, when a great solemn feast was at hand, Uzziah clothed himself in priestly garments and entered the temple to offer incense; immediately he was struck with leprosy. Thereafter he lived privately outside the city, while his son Jotham administered the affairs of the kingdom. The Olympiad is instituted by the Greeks. [Col. 0221A]

After Uzziah’s death, his son Jotham reigned in his stead. Jotham built the gate of the house of the Lord which was called the Beautiful Gate. Romulus is born. After Jotham had died, his son Ahaz reigned in his stead. In those days Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah went up to make war against Jerusalem. Ahaz hired Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians, who killed Rezin and delivered Ahaz. Rome is founded. Ahaz died, and his son Hezekiah reigned in his stead.

## CHAPTER X. History from Hezekiah to the return from Babylon

In the days of Hezekiah, Sennacherib attempted to carry Judah away, but the Lord did not permit him; rather, he struck down one hundred and eighty [Col. 0221B] thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians. Afterwards Sennacherib himself was killed by his sons in the temple of his god.

After Hezekiah, his son Manasseh reigned. He did evil according to the rite of the Gentiles and worshipped all the host of heaven; he caused his son to pass through fire and did evil beyond all the kings who had been before him in Jerusalem. And the Lord spoke through the hands of his servants the prophets, saying: “Because Manasseh has committed these abominations, I will destroy Jerusalem and deliver it into the hands of its enemies.”

When Manasseh died, his son Amon reigned in his stead. He walked in the way of his father, and his servants killed him. Josiah then reigned in his stead. Josiah walked in the way of David his father and did not turn from it either to the right or to the left. He caused the temple to be cleansed [Col. 0221C] and the Passover to be celebrated, such as had not been celebrated from the days of the Judges until that time. He also destroyed the altar which Jeroboam had made at Bethel and burned upon it the bones of the priests who had offered incense on it.

Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn from his wrath which he had spoken against Judah. Finally, Josiah met Necho king of Egypt in battle and was killed in the plain of Megiddo. Joahaz reigned for three months; when these were completed, the said Necho took him, led him into Egypt, and set in his stead Eliakim son of Josiah, whom he called Jehoiakim. He also condemned Judah to pay one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.

In the eleventh year of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem and demanded from him the tribute which he had been accustomed to pay the king of Egypt. [Col. 0221D] He did not hesitate to pay it for three years, but in the third year, hearing that the Egyptians were going to fight Babylon, he delayed payment. Therefore Nebuchadnezzar killed him as a rebel, carried about three thousand men captive from Judah, and appointed in his place as king Jehoiakim, who is called Jeconiah.

Not many days later Nebuchadnezzar besieged this Jeconiah. When he came out to meet him with his mother and some of the people, he captured him and carried him to Babylon, appointing in his place his uncle Zedekiah. But this Zedekiah also soon began to rebel against Nebuchadnezzar. Nebuchadnezzar then returned a second time, carried him captive to Babylon, overthrew the city wall, burned the temple, carried away the [Col. 0222A] holy vessels, and placed them in the temple of his own god.

Nebuchadnezzar lived twenty-five years after the destruction of the temple. When he died, Evil-merodach reigned; after him Labosordach; after him Egesar; and after him Belshazzar. In Belshazzar’s reign the seventy years were completed during which Jeremiah had prophesied that the captivity of the Jews was to be ended.

Accordingly, in those days Cyrus captured Babylon and released the Jewish captivity, as is written in the book of Ezra the Prophet:

> In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, that the word of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom in writing, saying: “The God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the world, and he himself has commanded me to build for him a house in Jerusalem. [Col. 0222B] Whoever among you belongs to all his people—may the Lord his God be with him—and let him go up.”

## CHAPTER XI. History from Cyrus to Judas Maccabaeus

Cyrus, therefore, after releasing the captivity of the Hebrews, permitted nearly fifty thousand persons to return to Judaea. He also ordered Jozadak, a priest of Aaron’s line, who had been carried away with the fathers, to return, so that the rite of the ancient solemn observance might be restored through the knowledge of an experienced priest. His faithful son Jeshua ruled the people after him. Thus, after the return from Babylon, the chief administration of affairs was conducted through the high priests.

Those who came from Babylon immediately laid the foundation of the temple; and when the temple had been founded, they offered sacrifice. The priests stood [Col. 0222C] in their attire, and the Levites praised the God of Israel; and there was great rejoicing among the people.

After Cyrus king of Persia had died, the Samaritans brought an accusation against the Jews before his son, who is called Cambyses, Ahasuerus, and Artaxerxes. The work was therefore interrupted until it was completed under Darius, in the second year of his reign. In the second year of this Darius, while Zerubbabel was governor, the building of the temple was completed, in the forty-sixth year after it began to be built. Hence the Jews are reported to have said to the Lord in the Gospel discourse: “This temple was built in forty-six years,” etc.

Darius was succeeded by his son Xerxes. In the seventh year of his reign Ezra, the scribe of the law of God, went up from Babylon. He brought sacred monies from Egypt to the temple of the Lord: [Col. 0222D] six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels worth one hundred talents, and golden vessels worth twenty talents. He also celebrated the feast of Tabernacles.

Nehemiah, cupbearer of this same king, also returned from the fortress of Susa in the king’s twentieth year and rebuilt the walls of the city. The aforesaid Ezra, inspired by the divine Spirit, restored the library of the Old Testament after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans. He corrected all the books of the Law and Prophets which had been corrupted by the nations, and arranged the whole Old Testament in twenty-two books, so that there might be as many books in the Law as there are letters.

Nehemiah also sent the descendants of those priests who, at the time of the deportation, had preserved the sacred fire in a dry well. [Col. 0223A] But they did not find fire, only thick water. Nehemiah ordered this water to be sprinkled over the wood and the burnt offerings; and fire was kindled from that water, and all marvelled.

The tabernacle of the covenant, the ark, and the altar of incense, which Jeremiah the prophet hid on Mount Abarim, remain on that same mountain to the present day.

Jeshua was succeeded by Joiakim; Joiakim by Eliashib; Eliashib by Judas; Judas by John; and John by Jaddua. Finally, in Jaddua’s time Alexander the Great undertook to conquer the king of the Persians and ordered Jaddua henceforth to observe toward himself the loyalty which he had promised and maintained until then toward Darius king of the Persians. Jaddua replied that he had sworn fidelity to Darius and could by no means do what Alexander requested while Darius was alive. [Col. 0223B]

Alexander, angered, threatened to destroy the city of Jerusalem. Jaddua therefore became afraid, summoned the clergy and people, and informed them of the matter. Sacrifice was offered and prayers were poured out to the Lord. When these had been completed, the high priest dismissed everyone, while he himself remained alone. Immediately, overcome by sleep, he saw a vision, and it was said to him:

> “Do not fear Alexander; but put on the sacred garment, let the priests put on their vestments, and when he comes go out and receive him with honour. For Alexander will do you no harm.”

Meanwhile Alexander the Great was hastening toward Jerusalem with great forces. When he drew near the city, the high priest went out with all the people and clergy. The Macedonians thought that Alexander would immediately kill them and destroy the city. But when he saw the high [Col. 0223C] priest, he greeted him, and all Alexander’s soldiers were greatly astonished.

Since they hesitated to ask the king about this, one who was more intimate with him than the others asked him, saying: “Why, O king, did you greet this man before all others?” The king answered: “When I was still in my own land, I saw this man in a dream telling me that I could obtain the kingdom of the Persians; therefore I greeted him before all others.”

The high priest, accompanied by the splendour of the clergy and the multitude of the people, led the king to the temple, and sacrifice was offered for him. Finally, as he departed, Alexander promised that henceforth he would love, honour, and exalt that place.

Jaddua was succeeded by Onias; Onias by Simon the Just; Simon the Just by Eleazar. Eleazar sent seventy [Col. 0223D] translators to Ptolemy Philadelphus, who reigned in Egypt second after Alexander. Eleazar was succeeded by Manasseh; Manasseh by Onias; Onias by Simon; and Simon by Onias, whose brother was Jesus. Jesus, also called Jason, desiring to seize the priesthood, began not merely secretly to violate the ordinances of the Jewish Law, but openly to overthrow them before all, as though he could not obtain the priesthood which he coveted except by wickedness.

For he dared, beneath the very citadel of the temple, to construct a gymnasium and to place the finest of the young men in brothels; and he enrolled those who were in Jerusalem as Antiochenes. But divine vengeance overtook this impious Jason’s heinous and unheard-of crime—a crime not of a priest. For one does not act wickedly against the divine laws with impunity. Therefore, after three years, Jason himself, who had violated the laws [Col. 0224A] of God and imprisoned his own brother, was expelled by order of King Antiochus into the region of Ammonitis; and a certain Menelaus of the tribe of Benjamin obtained the priesthood.

Through the machinations of this Menelaus, the pious high priest Onias was murdered by a certain deputy of the king, Andronicus. Not long afterwards Menelaus died, his brother Lysimachus succeeding to the priesthood. But because Lysimachus did not cease even then from evil, he was finally cast down from a tower fifty cubits high and miserably breathed out his unhappy soul. Lysimachus too, after much temple gold had already been carried away, perished when a popular crowd stoned him near the treasury.

After these things Antiochus, king of Syria, went up to Jerusalem, entered the sanctuary arrogantly, took away the golden altar, the lampstand, the table of the presence, the veil, and the other ornaments [Col. 0224B] of the temple, and departed. Finally, he commanded all the peoples of his kingdom to be one people; he forbade burnt offerings to be made in the temple of the Lord and required the Jews to defile themselves with unclean foods.

## CHAPTER XII. History from Judas Maccabaeus to Christ

In those days Judas Maccabaeus had withdrawn into the wilderness, where he and his companions lived among wild beasts, so that he might not share in the defilement. Yet although those with him were few, they nevertheless wore down the commanders of King Antiochus in war, so that they recovered the temple at Jerusalem and, by their fortunate persistence, restored the laws which were being abolished.

When Antiochus had died, Demetrius reigned. The utterly wicked Alcimus came to him and began [Col. 0224C] to inflame the king against Judas. For he said to the king:

> “Judas and those with him foster wars and do not permit the kingdom to be at peace. Therefore, deprived of the glory of my ancestors—that is, the high priesthood—I have come to you, first indeed to preserve loyalty to the king’s interests, and secondly to provide for my fellow citizens.”

Then the king sent Nicanor to Jerusalem, to seize Judas and appoint Alcimus high priest. But Alcimus, possessing the spirit of a wild beast, when he came to Jerusalem ordered the walls of the inner holy house to be destroyed. Yet the wretch could not long evade punishment for these crimes. Suddenly his mouth was paralysed and he could not speak. Then, disabled by paralysis, he died miserably.

Thus, when the priests of Aaron’s line had failed, and Judas Maccabaeus, who was fighting for the laws of his country, had now died by the chance of war, his brother Jonathan obtained leadership of the Jews and the priesthood together. Now the deeds of Judas and his brothers are very numerous and are contained in the books of the Maccabees; I have not wished to insert them into the present brief account. [Col. 0224D]

Jonathan was succeeded by his brother Simon. After Simon, the priesthood came to his son John, who, fighting against the Hyrcani, received the name Hyrcanus. John Hyrcanus was succeeded by Aristobulus. Aristobulus became both king and priest, and Aristobulus was succeeded as both king and priest by Alexander.

When Alexander died, he left two surviving sons, Aristobulus and Hyrcanus. But until the boys should come of age, he wished his wife Alexandra to govern with royal moderation, at the same time appointing her judge as to which of them should especially be entrusted with the high priesthood. She put Hyrcanus in his father’s place in the priesthood because of the prerogative of his greater age, entrusting no public office to his brother Aristobulus. [Col. 0225A]

After Alexandra’s death, Aristobulus seized the kingdom, and at last Hyrcanus relinquished the priesthood to him. Afterwards Hyrcanus himself, stirred up by Antipater, father of Herod, first went to the king of Arabia in repentance for what he had done, and finally brought his complaint to Pompey, commander of the Romans, who had come into Syria to wage war against King Tigranes. On this occasion Pompey, Roman consul, captured the city of Jerusalem, defiled the temple, and sent the high priest Aristobulus in chains with his children to Rome. He left Hyrcanus the high priesthood and appointed the aforementioned Antipater administrator of the whole kingdom. [Col. 0225B]

Thus thereafter the Jewish people became tributary to Roman power; and so, as has been said, the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus, fighting one another, were the first to give the Romans an opportunity to invade Judaea.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Herod and his lineage

In the time of the aforesaid high priest Hyrcanus, certain bandits came out from Jerusalem and plundered around Ascalon. Among the other captives there, a certain young man named Antipater, son of a certain Herod, an Idumaean by descent who had been priest of Apollo’s temple at Ascalon, was taken captive and brought to Jerusalem. This Antipater, serving for some years in Hyrcanus’s household, [Col. 0225C] became distinguished for ability and integrity and won the favour of his master Hyrcanus, so much so that Hyrcanus entrusted to him the management of his whole house.

Antipater, however, was not unmindful of his former favour toward Hyrcanus, but proved kindly disposed toward him. He carried out his entrusted office with such moderation [Col. 0226A] that he pleased both Jews and Romans. He had a son named Herod, who after his father’s death received a crown from the Romans, both because of his own merit and because of the favour due to his father’s loyal service.

Having crept, contrary to the law and religious right of the Jewish people, into an undeserved dignity, Herod began to appoint to the priesthood the most unworthy and obscure persons whom either his will or chance presented to him. He also kept the high priest’s garment locked up under his own seal and never allowed the high priests of his time either its use or control. In order to unite his offspring with the royal line of the Jews, he put away his wife Deside, whom he had married while a private person, and took to himself Mariamne, daughter of King Aristobulus and granddaughter of Hyrcanus, high priest of the Jews.

But this desired union with the woman, as will later be shown, brought down rather than raised his power and afflicted him with domestic griefs. For, in pursuing nobility, he fell into turmoil, as though his own household did not suit him. [Col. 0226B]

But now that the legitimate anointing of the Jewish people had ceased, the Lord Jesus Christ, the expectation of the nations according to the prophetic utterance, was imminent: the true king and priest, taking flesh from the line of kings and high priests, he came into the world bringing the saving faith, in which he would join and unite to himself the Gentile and Jewish peoples by sanctifying them. In the ordered course of events, he was born in the thirty-first year of the aforesaid King Herod, which is, according to the Hebrews, the four thousand nine hundred and fifty-first year from the creation of the world. Moreover, as blessed Maximus testifies in his sermon on Easter, and as Greek calculators reckon, it is the five thousand four hundred and seventh year.

# BOOK FIVE

It treats of the kingdoms of the world from the time when they arose after the Flood until they came under Roman power, containing 21 chapters, with annotations by Master Thomas Garzoni, theologian.

[Col. 0225]

## CHAPTER I. On the kingdoms of the world

[Col. 0225D]

I shall now recount how the kingdoms of the world proceeded from the beginning until the coming of Christ. After the Flood, four pre-eminent kingdoms first arose among humankind: that of the Scythians in the north, where Tanus reigned; that of the Assyrians in the east, where Belus reigned; that of the Egyptians in the south, where Mineus reigned; and that of the Sicyonians in the west, where Aegialeus reigned. But Scripture makes rare mention of the kingdom of the Scythians and the kingdom of the Sicyonians, because the Scythian kingdom was far distant and the Sicyonian kingdom quickly declined.

## CHAPTER II. On the kingdom of the Scythians

[Col. 0226D]

The Scythian people, therefore, an exceedingly ancient people situated in the north, had beginnings no less illustrious than their dominion; nor did they shine more through the courage of men than through that of women. The Scythians, accustomed to wander through uncultivated wildernesses, do not cultivate the soil, but carry their wives and children with them in wagons, protecting themselves from rain and winter’s harshness with hides. They drive their herds and flocks with them. They live on milk and honey; they are a people hardened by labour and war, with enormous bodily strength. [Col. 0227A] The kingdom of the Scythians is thought to have arisen under Ragan.

> **Note:** [Col. 0227D] In order to understand of what nations the kingdom of the Scythians consisted, the peoples of Scythia should briefly be noted. John Hunter, in his *Rudiments of Cosmography*, declares them to have been: the Moschi, Arimaspi, Agathyrsi, Basilides, Roxolani, Hamaxobites, Basternae, Taurians, Getae, Nomads, Georgians, Axiaci, Thyssagetae, and Geloni.

## CHAPTER III. On the kingdom of the Assyrians

The kingdom of the Assyrians arose under Belus, its first king, and continued from the twenty-fifth year of Serug, Abraham’s great-grandfather, until the seventh year of Uzziah king of Judah. Others begin the Assyrian kingdom with Ninus, son of Belus, because under him it was first extended among foreign nations.

After Ninus’s death, his wife Semiramis feared to entrust the kingdom to her son Ninus because he was under age, while she herself did not dare to administer the kingdom. She therefore had her son remain in his chamber; and, because she resembled him, she put on male clothing, pretended to be of the male sex, and passed herself off as a boy rather than a woman, and as Ninus’s son rather than his wife. [Col. 0227B] Thus she held and greatly enlarged the kingdom, and performed very many deeds with manly courage. When her son had come of age, she delivered the kingdom to him; but at last, inflamed with desire for him, she compelled him to shameful intercourse. Afterwards, overcome by grief, he killed her.

The Assyrian kingdom continued for one thousand three hundred and two years and through thirty-seven kings, down to Sardanapalus, after whom it was transferred to the Medes. The kings of the Assyrians were these: Belus, Ninus, Semiramis, Zameis, also called Ninias; Arius; Aralius; Xerxes, also called Baleus; Armamitres; Belochus; Balens; Altadas; Mamintus; Machaleus; Sparreus; Mamillas; Sparretus; Ascatades; Amintes; Belochus; Bellopares; Lamprides; Sosares; Lampares; Pamas; Sosarinus; Mitraeus; Tautories; Theutheus; Tineus; [Col. 0227C] Pergilius; Eupales; Laosthenes; Piorithiades; Offrateus; Offratenes; Acrazepes; Thonos; Conolores, who in Greek is called Sardanapalus.

Moreover, these are the kings thought to have reigned in Assyria after Sardanapalus, as sacred history relates: Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sennacherib. But the aforesaid Sardanapalus was a man more corrupt than a woman. For he always lived among companies of women. When, one day, Arbastus, prefect of the Medes, also called Arbaces, had obtained admission to him, he found him among crowds of prostitutes spinning purple wool with a distaff and dividing wool-work among maidens. Having seen this, Arbaces returned to his companions, told them what he had seen, declared that he could not possibly obey one who preferred to be a woman rather than a man; and a conspiracy of the Medes against the Assyrians was immediately formed [Col. 0227D] and war declared upon Sardanapalus.

Since Sardanapalus could not resist so many rebels, he withdrew into the royal palace. There, after a pyre had been kindled, he burned himself and his riches in the fire. Thus the kingdom of the Assyrians was transferred to the Medes.

> **Note:** [Col. 0228D] The kingdom of the Chaldeans, or Assyrians, called the Babylonian kingdom, took its beginning from the building of the Tower of Babel, as Berosus the Chaldean says, in the one hundred and thirty-first year after the universal inundation of waters. All its kings and the changes of its kingdom are finely described by Joannes Lucidus in his *Chronicles*, book IV, at the beginning; it is fitting to consult him.

## CHAPTER IV. On the kingdom of the Medes

The kingdom of the Medes arose under Arbaces, its first king, [Col. 0228A] and continued from the seventh year of King Uzziah until the nineteenth year of the Babylonian captivity: two hundred and fifty-eight years and eight kings, whose names are these: Arbaces, Sosarinus, Medus, Cardiceas, Diocles, Phaartes [Phraortes], Arsaces, Astyages.

Finally Cyrus, grandson of Astyages, when he had grown up, declared war upon Astyages. In the ensuing battle he routed his army and captured Astyages, but took nothing from him except his kingdom. Thus this Cyrus transferred the dignity of the Medes to the Persians.

## CHAPTER V. On the kingdom of the Persians

The kingdom of the Persians, arising under Cyrus as its first king, continued for two hundred and eighteen years and through fourteen kings, whose names are these: [Col. 0228B] Cyrus, Cambyses, the Magian brothers, Darius, Xerxes, Artabanus, Artaxerxes also called Longimanus, Xerxes II, Sogdianus, Darius Nothus, Artaxerxes also called Mnemon, Artaxerxes also called Ochus, Arses son of Ochus, Darius Arsynius.

Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, raised among the Persians, after obtaining the monarchy subjected Syria and all Scythia to himself. Having accomplished these things, he besieged Babylon, then stronger than all other cities. Its circuit extended for four hundred and eighty-six stadia. It stood on a plain and, like a camp, was laid out square, its walls corresponding in length. The walls were fifty cubits wide and four times as high. On the outer face of the walls were one hundred bronze gates. The Euphrates ran through the middle of the city, and outside it a broad ditch flowed all around like a river. The citadel which rose within was that tower which the giant Nimrod began to build after the Flood.

Croesus, king of the Lydians, had come there to assist the Babylonians. When Belshazzar had completed the seventeenth year of his reign, reckoning vain the prophecy of Jeremiah that the Jewish captivity would be ended in the seventieth year, he had the sacred vessels of the Lord’s temple brought to his table [Col. 0228C] and drank from them against law and right. But he immediately paid the penalty for this crime: before daylight he was killed, and King Croesus fled with many other kings who had assembled there. Thus Cyrus entered the city.

Afterwards Cyrus defeated Croesus, king of the Lydians, and acquired his kingdom. Then he made war upon the Scythians, where Queen Tomyris [Tamaris], having arranged an ambush, killed him. For when the queen learned that Cyrus was present, she sent her son with an army to pursue him. But Cyrus entered Scythia, prepared wine and a feast, and, feigning fear, immediately abandoned the feast. Those who came upon the camp, finding it filled with Cyrus’s abundant preparations, threw themselves down as if invited to a banquet. [Col. 0229A] Cyrus then returned and slaughtered them all together.

Queen Tomyris pretended that she had lost hope because of the disaster inflicted, called the enemy—proud in victory—to herself, and so, in a valley where she had set an ambush, destroyed two hundred thousand Persians by a sudden attack. When this was done, she ordered Cyrus’s head cut off and placed in a wineskin full of human blood, saying: “Satisfy yourself with the blood for which you thirsted.”

His son Cambyses, also called Artaxerxes and Ahasuerus, reigned in his stead. Cambyses subjected Egypt, stopped the work on the temple, and is called by the Jews the second Nebuchadnezzar. The events contained in the history of Judith are thought to have occurred under him. When he died, two Magi reigned. After they were killed, Darius, son of Antipater, was made king. He took the daughter of King Cyrus in marriage and established his kingdom by royal nuptials, so that the monarchy appeared not so much to have been transferred to an outsider as to have returned to Cyrus’s family. [Col. 0229B]

Xerxes succeeded him. He is said to have had in his army seven hundred thousand armed men, with three hundred thousand auxiliaries, when he set out to conquer Greece; also one thousand two hundred beaked warships and three thousand transport ships. But such a host lacked a leader: Xerxes always appeared last in battle and first in flight. Accordingly, before experiencing war, relying upon vast resources, he levelled mountains into plains, burdened seas with bridges, and made immense gulfs of water passable. But when he came to the narrows of Thermopylae, where the entrance into Greece lies open, he was shamefully defeated. Afterwards, when he had been overcome both by land and sea, he even began to be held in contempt by his own people. Therefore, as royal majesty daily failed in him, his prefect Artabanus killed him.

Artabanus was succeeded by Artaxerxes, also called Longimanus. He is the Ahasuerus under whom occurred the events contained in the history of Esther. Artaxerxes Longimanus was succeeded by Xerxes II; Xerxes II by Sogdianus; and Sogdianus by Darius Nothus. Then Egypt revolted from the Persians and began to have its own kings. [Col. 0229C] Darius Nothus was succeeded by Artaxerxes, also called Mnemon; and after him by Artaxerxes, also called Ochus.

Afterwards Ochus drove Necho, king of Egypt, into Ethiopia, recovered Egypt, and from that time until Alexander the Great the Persians reigned in Egypt: namely Ochus, Arses son of Ochus, Darius son of Arses, and Alexander the Great. But before I proceed to the Persian war and the deeds of Alexander, I shall first briefly set forth the origin of the Macedonian kingdom, in which Alexander himself first reigned.

> **Note:** [Col. 0229D] After Sardanapalus, the monarchy of the Medes and Persians began, divided between the Medes and Babylonians. It was afterwards reunited under the first Cyrus and Darius. How it began and how the division followed may be found clearly and fully in Joannes Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book IV, chapter 2. [Col. 0230D]

## CHAPTER VI. On the kingdom of the Macedonians

The kingdom of the Macedonians arose under Cranaus as its first king, from the thirteenth year of Uzziah king of Judah until [Col. 0230A] the ninth year of Onias the high priest, also called Menelaus. It continued for six hundred and thirty-six years and through thirty-nine kings. Before Alexander the kings were: Craneus, Crenus, Tyriminas, Perdiccas, Argus, Philip, Europus, Alcetas, Amyntas, Alexander the Great.

Accordingly, Alexander the Great, when he was twenty years old, began to conquer the Persian kingdom. He had in his army thirty thousand infantry and four thousand five hundred cavalry. No one younger than sixty led the ranks of these forces, so that, if you saw the leading positions of the camp, you would think you saw a senate rather than commanders of troops. None of them thought of flight in battle, but of victory; no one placed hope in his feet, but in his arms.

King Darius, however, trusting in his strength, judged it more glorious not to keep the enemy from the borders of Persia but to receive him within the bosom of his kingdom. He allowed Alexander without hindrance to cross the river Euphrates and Mount Cilicia, that wall, and finally drew up his battle line against him on the plains of Adrastus. [Col. 0230B] Darius had six hundred thousand soldiers in that engagement. But that immense army quickly turned its back, overcome no less by Alexander’s skill than by Macedonian courage.

There was great slaughter of the Persians in that battle. Of Alexander’s army only nine infantrymen and one hundred and twenty horsemen fell. After this victory, the greater part of Asia immediately defected to Alexander. Finally, he waged many wars with Darius’s generals, whom by this time he overcame not so much by arms as by the terror of his name. For Alexander’s soldiers already considered Persian gold and all the wealth of the East as their own spoil, and remembered not war and dangers but riches.

After this Darius advanced into battle with four hundred thousand infantry and one hundred thousand cavalry. Alexander met him, and battle was joined with immense spirit. In that battle both kings were wounded; nevertheless the issue remained uncertain until Darius fled. Thereupon a great slaughter of the Persians followed: sixty thousand and one infantrymen and ten thousand cavalry were killed, and forty thousand were captured. Of the Macedonians one hundred and thirty infantrymen and one hundred and forty horsemen fell. [Col. 0230C]

Much gold and other wealth was found in the Persian camp. Among the captives taken in the camp were Darius’s mother, his wife, his own sister, and Darius’s two daughters. Though Darius offered even half his kingdom for their ransom, he did not obtain it. Yet Alexander ordered that they be treated in his household as queens and commanded that the daughters expect a marriage not unworthy of their father’s rank.

Afterwards Darius, to win the favour of the victorious Alexander, was bound in golden chains by his relatives. Bound, he ended his life together with the Persian kingdom. Alexander buried his body with royal honours. Thus the kingdom of the Persians passed into the power of the Macedonians after it had stood for two hundred and thirty-one years.

[Col. 0231A] Meanwhile Alexander captured Tyre, a most flourishing city; founded Alexandria upon the river Tanais; and marched against India, so that he might set the boundaries of his empire at the furthest edge of Ocean. There, riding a very powerful horse, he fought in single combat with Porus, the king of that people; but when his horse was killed beneath him and he was thrown down, he escaped death through the rush of his attendants. Having then subdued all the peoples of the East as far as the river Indus and the Ocean, he resolved to return. But, having outlived King Darius by only five years and returned to Babylon, he ended his life by poison in that same city, through the treachery of his own men, in the very flower of his age and victories: namely, in the thirty-second year of his life and the twelfth of his reign.

After his death his successors divided among themselves the whole world [Col. 0231B] that had been subdued by Macedonian arms; but later, as they contended amid the changing fortunes of war, power was concentrated in the hands of a few. The first division was as follows: Ptolemy received Egypt, Africa, and Arabia; Laius of Miletus, Syria; Philotas, Cilicia; Philo, Illyria; Acropatus, Greater Media; Sother, Lesser Media; Schynus, the Susian people; Antigonus son of Philip, Greater Phrygia; Nearchus, Lycia and Pamphylia; Cassander, Caria; Menander, Lydia; Leonatus, Lesser Phrygia; Lysimachus, Thrace and Pontus; Eumenes, Cappadocia and Paphlagonia; Seleucus, the supreme command of the camp; Cassander son of Antipater, the king’s guards and attendants; Traxiles, the Seres between the Hydaspes and the Indus; Phiton son of Agenor, the colonies founded [Col. 0231C] among the Indians; Oxiarches, the Paropamisadae at the edge of the Caucasus; Subitores, the Arachosians and Gedrosians; Statanor, the Drangians and Areans; Amyntas, the Athrians; Sicheusita, the Sogdians; Canor, the Parthians; Philip, the Hyrcanians; Frataphanes, the Armenians; Tlepolemus, the Persians; Peucestes, the Babylonians; Arthous, the Pelasgians; and Archesilaus, Mesopotamia.

After this, as was said above, power was concentrated in the hands of a few. Philip, who was also called Arrhidaeus, eventually obtained Macedonia; Seleucus, Syria; Antigonus, Asia Minor; and Ptolemy, son of Lagus, Egypt. These, therefore, are the kings who ruled in Macedonia after Alexander the Great: Philip, also called Arrhidaeus; Cassander; Antigonus; Alexander, son of Cassander; Demetrius; [Col. 0231D] Pyrrhus; Lysimachus; Ptolemy Ceraunus; Meleager; Antipater; Sosthenes; Antigonus; Philip; and Perseus. After this the kingdom of Macedonia came to an end. For, after Perseus had been killed, the Romans ordered the Macedonians, Illyrians, and Galatians to be free.

> [Note: [Col. 0231D] On the proper monarchy of Alexander of Macedon, and on the kings succeeding him in Asia and Syria, you may excerpt several noteworthy matters from John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book IV, chapter [Col. 0232D] 3.]

## Chapter VII. On the kingdoms of Syria

Moreover, these are the kings of Syria who ruled there after Alexander the Great: Seleucus, Nicanor, Antiochus Soter, Antiochus Theos, Seleucus Callinicus, and Seleucus Ceraunus. This Antiochus exempted the priests, scribes, and singers of the Temple of the Lord [Col. 0232A] from tribute, royal taxation, and the many other burdens.

After him his son Seleucus Philopator ruled. This is the Seleucus who sent Heliodorus to Jerusalem to plunder the treasury that was in the Temple of the Lord. But Heliodorus, struck by divine judgment, returned to the king without having accomplished his business. Finally Seleucus left as his successor his brother Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes—that is, “illustrious,” “noble,” or “renowned.” This is the Antiochus called the root of sin at the beginning of the first book of Maccabees, who committed so many abominations in Jerusalem.

Upon his death his son Antiochus Eupator reigned for two years. After him Demetrius, son of Seleucus, left the city of Rome and came into Syria, that is, into his father’s kingdom. When the army that had been with Antiochus Epiphanes learned [Col. 0232B] of his arrival, it killed Antiochus Eupator, that Antiochus’s son, who had already begun to reign. Thus Demetrius, son of Seleucus, also called Soter, obtained the kingdom. But Alexander, son of Antiochus Eupator, arrived, assembled an army, overcame Demetrius, and recovered the kingdom. Later Demetrius, son of Demetrius, drove out Alexander and recovered power for himself. Then Tryphon killed Antiochus, the young son of that same Alexander, whom he had undertaken to rear; but when Tryphon was finally overthrown, the kingdom remained in the line of Seleucus.

Moreover, Antiochus Cyprius succeeded Demetrius; Antiochus Cyzicenus succeeded that Antiochus; and Philip succeeded Antiochus Cyzicenus. In the thirteenth year [Col. 0232C] after the death of Alexander the Great, Seleucus began to reign in Syria, and in Asia in the fortieth year. The kingdom continued through seventeen kings and for two hundred and twenty years, down to the aforesaid Philip. After this Syria came under Roman rule. For Antiochus, fleeing to the Parthians, surrendered himself to Pompey, after Philip had been captured by Gabinius.

## Chapter VIII. On the kingdom of Asia

In Asia Minor, Antigonus ruled for nineteen years after Alexander the Great. After him Demetrius Poliorcetes ruled for seventeen years. Then Demetrius surrendered himself to Seleucus, king of Syria, and Seleucus ruled in Asia and Syria. Having thus dealt briefly with these matters, let us proceed to what follows. But [Col. 0232D] before speaking of Ptolemy, son of Lagus, who ruled in Egypt after Alexander the Great, I shall briefly set forth the origin of the Egyptian kingdom, which I mentioned above, and its course down to these times.

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] What our Hugh discusses here may be noted in John Lucidus, in the book and chapter mentioned above.]

## Chapter IX. On the kingdom of Egypt

Some report that gods or certain heroes first ruled in Egypt, as follows: Festus first, for 680 years; Sol second, for 77; Sosinosiros third, for 320; Orontoliarchus fourth, for 18; and Typhon fifth, for [Col. 0233A] 45. After these came the kingdoms of the Mirthei, as follows: Procaanubes for 83 years; Apion for 67.

But the true account maintains that, from the birth of Abraham, the sixteenth dynasty—called by the Egyptians the supreme power—of the Thebans began among the Egyptians and lasted for 190 years. For fifteen dynasties in the Egyptian kingdom had already passed, and the sixteenth, as we have said, in which the Thebans ruled, arose. Thus, in the sixteenth dynasty the Thebans ruled for 190 years. In the seventeenth dynasty, the Shepherds, eight [kings]. In the eighteenth dynasty of the Diapolitans: Amasis first. He was at the time of the famine, beginning to reign in its sixth year; Chebron second; Menophis; Mephres; Miffar; Mutosis; Theutemosis; [Col. 0233B] Amenophis; Ortus; Achencheres; Achoris; Ebencres—he was drowned; Acherres; Cherres; Armeus, also called Danaus; Ramesses, also called Egyptus; and Menophis.

In the nineteenth dynasty: Zetus, Rampses, Amenophis, Ammenephus, Thuores, also called Polybus. Menelaus and Helen lodged with this man after the destruction of Troy. In the twentieth dynasty: the Diapolitans. In the twenty-first dynasty: Sinendis, Psusennes, Nefercheres, Amenophis, Osochor, Psinaces, Psusennes.

In the twenty-second dynasty: Sesonchosis, Osorton, Tacelosis. In the twenty-third dynasty: Petubas, Orsochon, Psannios. In the twenty-fourth dynasty: Bochoris. In the twenty-fifth dynasty: Sabachon, Aethios, Sobicus, Tharacus the Ethiopian. In the twenty-sixth [Col. 0233C] dynasty: Merres the Ethiopian, Stephinatis, Neheompos, Nechao Psammeticus, Nechao the Second, also called Necepsos, Psammites, also called Psammeticus, Vafres, Amasis. In the twenty-seventh dynasty of the Persians, for 111 years: Cambyses, the Magian brothers, Darius, Xerxes son of Darius, Artabanus, Artaxerxes, Xerxes the Second, Sogdianus, Darius Nothus.

After this Egypt revolted from the Persians and began to have its own kings, as follows. In the twenty-eighth dynasty: Amarcheus the Saite. In the twenty-ninth dynasty: Nephrites, Achoris, Psammites, Nephrites, Nectanebus. After this Artaxerxes, also called Ochus, drove Nectabo, king of Egypt, into Ethiopia and took possession of Egypt. From the seventeenth year of Ochus down to the seventh of Alexander, the Persians held the Egyptian dynasty; [Col. 0233D] and now Egypt came under Greek rule.

Moreover, at the time when the aforesaid Ochus ruled in Persia and Egypt, Brennus, who ruled among the Senonian people, came into Italy with three hundred thousand Gauls. He occupied it as far as Senogallia, situated above the Adriatic Sea, [Col. 0234A] and there they separated from one another. About one hundred thousand of them went to Delphi and perished by Greek swords. Another hundred thousand remained in Italy; founding Ticinum, Mediolanum, Bergamum, and Brixia, they gave their name to Cisalpine Gaul. Hence the term Transalpine Gaul, which lies beyond the Alps from Italy’s point of view, and Cisalpine Gaul, which lies on this side of the Alps. Let this brief account of Brennus and the Gauls suffice.

Arses, his son, succeeded Ochus; Darius, son of Arses, succeeded Arses; and Alexander the Great succeeded Darius, as stated above. In the seventh year of Alexander’s empire Egypt came under Greek rule. Finally, after Alexander the Great, Ptolemy son of Lagus ruled in Alexandria of Egypt.

## Chapter X. On the kingdom of the Egyptians after Alexander the Great

[Col. 0234B]

It should be known that all the kings of Egypt were initially called Pharaohs by the common title; but from Alexander the Great to Cleopatra they were called Ptolemies or Lagids, after Ptolemy Lagid, son of Lagus. Thus the kingdom of Alexandria continued down to Octavian [Octavius] Augustus through twelve kings, whose names are these: Ptolemy Lagid. He took Jerusalem by deceit and led the Jews into captivity. Ptolemy Philadelphus. He caused the Old Testament to be translated from Hebrew into Greek and released the Jewish captivity. Ptolemy Euergetes; Ptolemy Philopator; Ptolemy Epiphanes; Ptolemy [Col. 0234C] Philometor; Ptolemy Euergetes; Ptolemy Physcon, also called Soter; Ptolemy Alexander; Ptolemy who was driven out by his mother; Ptolemy Dionysius; Cleopatra. After this Egypt came under Roman rule. Its kingdom always followed effeminacy and was at last brought low in a woman; I shall explain its end below.

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] The kingdom of the Egyptians began at the same time as that of the Chaldeans, namely in the 131st year after Noah’s Flood, as we have learned from Berosus. Egypt received its final name from King Egyptus, as Manetho, an Egyptian priest, says in the *Supplement of Times*. For it was formerly called Oceana and Nilea, according to Diodorus Siculus in book I; later it was called Aeria, as Eusebius says in *On Times*. [Col. 0234D] It was also called Osyriana by the Egyptians from the name and surname of Osiris, and Mizraim by the Hebrews, according to Moses. Finally, as stated, it was called Egypt after Egyptus, brother of Danaus, who was called Ramesses. These details are from John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book V, chapter 1, where you may find several other matters worthy of notice for the present purpose.]

## Chapter XI. On the kingdom of the Sicyonians

The kingdom of the Sicyonians, arising under Aegialeus as its first king, ran from the twenty-fourth year of Nahor, Abraham’s grandfather, to the seventeenth year of Eli, priest and judge of Israel: 961 years and thirty-one kings. Their names are these: Aegialeus, Europs, Felchim, Apis, [Col. 0234D] Telon, Aegiorus, Thurimachus, Leucippus, Mesaspus, Eratus, Plemeus, Orthopolis, Marathias, Maratus, Echireus, Chorax, Epopeus, Laomedon, Sichon, Polybus, Inachus, Phestus, Adrastus, Polyphides Pelasgus, Zeuxippus. After these, the priests of Carni governed for twenty-eight years. Their names are Archelaus, Antomidus, Mecludutus, [Col. 0235A] Heuneus, Theonaus, Amphicius, and Caridus. After this the kingdom of the Sicyonians ended.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] According to Eusebius, *On Times*, the kingdom of the Sicyonians in Greece began seventy-three years before the birth of Abraham, namely in the thirty-second year of Belus, and endured for 961 years. You may derive the remainder of its course from John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book VI, chapter 4.]

## Chapter XII. On the kingdom of the Argives

The kingdom of the Argives, arising under Inachus as its first king, continued down to Acrisius, its last ruler, for 544 years: from the first year of the patriarch Jacob to the twelfth year of Deborah and Barak, judges of Israel. The kings of the Argives, therefore, were Inachus, Phoroneus, Apis, Argus, Criasus, Phorbas, Triopas, Crotopus, Sthelenus, Danaus, Lynches, Abas, Proetus, and Acrisius. After this the sovereignty was transferred to Mycenae. Perseus, having killed Acrisius unintentionally, departed from Argos. The kings of Mycenae were Perseus, Sthelenus, Eurystheus son of Sthelenus, Atreus and Thyestes, Agamemnon, [Col. 0235B] Aegisthus, Orestes, Tisamenus, Pentilus, and Comethes.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] Soon after Esau and Jacob were born, in the second year of Baleus Xerxes, the eighth king of the Assyrians, the kingdom of the Argives began, as Eusebius calculates. A brief reckoning of its kings and their times may be seen in John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book VI, chapter 5.]

## Chapter XIII. On the kingdom of the Athenians

The kingdom of the Athenians, arising under Cecrops as its first king, ran from the twenty-second year of Moses—that is, the forty-fifth year before Israel’s departure from Egypt—to the twenty-ninth year of Manasseh king of Judah, for 953 years. The kings were Cecrops, Cranaus, Amphictyon, Erichthonius, Pandion, whose daughters were Procne and Philomela; Erechtheus; Cecrops son of Erechtheus; Pandion son of Cecrops; Aegeus son of Pandion; Theseus son of Aegeus; Menestheus; Demophoon son of Theseus; Oxintes; Aphicitas; Thimotes; Melanthus; Codrus son of Melanthus. Up to this point there were kings; afterward rulers were [Col. 0235C] appointed, each of whom held authority until the end of his life: Medrus son of Codrus, Acastus, Archippus, Theusippus, Phorbas, Mezades, Diognetus, Pheredus, Ariphron, Thespieus, Agamestor, Aeschylus, Almeon, Carops, Aesimedes, Elidicus, Hippomenes, Leocrates, Absander, Eurixias. Afterward nine annual magistrates were appointed at Athens from the nobles of the city.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] As Berosus says in book V, the kingdom of the Athenians began in the fourth year of Sparetus, the seventeenth king of the Assyrians, which was the first year of Jasius king of Etruria and the thirtieth of Ori king of Egypt. John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book VI, chapter 6, derives from Eusebius the number of years for which their kings ruled.]

## Chapter XIV. On the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians

The kingdom of the Lacedaemonians, arising under Eurystheus as its first king, ran from the seventh year of Samuel, judge of Israel, to the forty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah: 325 years [Col. 0235D] and nine kings. Their names are: [Col. 0236A] Eurystheus, Agis, Echestratus, Labores, Doristeus Agesilaus, Archilaus, Thelectus, Alcamenes.

> [Note: [Col. 0236D] According to Eusebius, the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians began in the fourth year of Dercis, the thirty-first king of the Assyrians. Some, however, say it began two years earlier, which, Lucidus says, better accords with our reckoning. For this was the seventy-eighth year of the twentieth Egyptian dynasty, the sixth year of Aeneas Silvius, king of the Latins, and likewise the twelfth year of Saul, king of the Hebrews. In the same author you have, from Eusebius, the kings of the Lacedaemonians.]

## Chapter XV. On the kingdom of the Corinthians

The kingdom of the Corinthians, arising under Alethes as its first king, ran from the eighth year of Samuel, judge of Israel, to the first year of Jotham son of Uzziah: 320 years. The kings were Alethes, Trion, Agilaus, Primiras, Bacis, Agelas, Eudemus, Aristomedes, Agemon, Alexander Thelestes, and Pritanis.

> [Note: [Col. 0236D] According to Eusebius, the kingdom of the Corinthians began at the same time as the kingdom of the Lacedaemonians. Their kings numbered twelve. John Lucidus, book VI, chapter 10.]

## Chapter XVI. On the kingdom of the Lydians

The kingdom of the Lydians, arising under Ardisus as its first king, ran from the forty-eighth year of Uzziah king of Judah to the forty-third year of the Exile: 330 years and [Col. 0236B] nine kings. Their names are Ardisus, Alyattes, Meles, Candaules, Gyges, Ardis, Sadyattes, Alyattes, Croesus. After this the kingdom of the Lydians was overthrown by the Persians. For Croesus, king of the Lydians, while the Mede and the Persian were besieging Babylon, brought aid to the Chaldeans against them. Therefore, after Babylon had been overthrown, he was attacked and defeated in war by Cyrus king of the Persians. Thus the kingdom of the Lydians passed under Persian rule.

> [Note: [Col. 0236D] According to Eusebius, the kingdom of the Lydians began immediately after the end of the Corinthian kingdom, that is, two years before the first Olympiad. John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book VI, chapter 13.]

## Chapter XVII. On the kingdom of the Parthians

After the Parthians revolted from King Seleucus, they began to have kings of their own. Their names are Arsaces, Arsaces, Priapacius, Phrahates, Mithridates, Phrahates, Artabanus, Mithridates, [Col. 0236C] Orodes. In their time Crassus, having obtained the Roman consulship, was proceeding through Mesopotamia toward Parthia. Contrary to the treaty made by Lucullus and Pompey, Roman consuls, he crossed the river Euphrates and reached Carrhae, where the Parthians surrounded him; he lost his army and was himself slain.

Pacorus succeeded Orodes; Mithridates the Great succeeded Pacorus; and Pharnaces, his son, succeeded Mithridates the Great. This is the Pharnaces who brought assistance to Pompey in the Pharsalian War and whom Julius Caesar defeated in Pontus after Pompey’s death.

## Chapter XVIII. On the kingdom of Numidia

The kings of Numidia are Gala, Masinissa, Mycipsa, [Col. 0236D] Adherbal, Hiempsal, Jugurtha.

## Chapter XIX. On the kings of Babylon

[Col. 0237A]

The kings of Babylon are Merodach, Baladan, Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuchadnezzar, Evil-merodach, Egesar, Labosordach, Balthasar. These are the Chaldean kings who, though distinguished by their deeds, are nevertheless not reckoned among the illustrious kings.

## Chapter XX. On the kingdom of the Latins

The kingdom of the Latins, arising, as they say, under Janus as its first king, ran from the seventy-sixth year of Othniel, judge of Israel, to the eighth year of King Darius—which was the eightieth after the Babylonian Exile, the tenth after the return, and the fourth after the rebuilding of the Temple—for eight hundred [Col. 0237B] twenty-nine years; and it had six Latin kings, fourteen Alban kings, and seven Roman kings down to Tarquinius Superbus.

The Latin kings were Janus, Saturn, Picus, Faunus, Latinus, Aeneas. The Alban kings were Ascanius; Silvius Posthumus, son of Aeneas; Silvius; Aeneas; Silvius Latinus; Silvius Epithus; Silvius Capis; Salvius Capetus; Silvius Tiberinus; Silvius Agrippa; Silvius Aremulus; Silvius Aventinus; Silvius Procas; Silvius Amulius. The Roman kings were Romulus, Numa Pompilius, Tullus Hostilius, Ancus Martius, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius Tarquinius, and Tarquinius Superbus.

After this, when Brutus had expelled the kings from the city, consuls governed the republic until Julius Caesar—that is, until the twentieth year of Hyrcanus, king and priest of the Jews—for 462 years [Col. 0237C], as follows. Brutus was first consul in the first year after the expulsion of the kings; then ten men were appointed in year 40; Camillus was consul in year 136; Quintius dictator in year 148; Papirius consul in year 186; Manlius and Regulus in year 243; Publius Cornelius Scipio in year 292; Fabius Maximus dictator in year 298; Lucius Aemilius Paulus and Terentius Varro in year 299; Levinus and Marcellus in year 304; Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator in year 305; Scipio Africanus the Elder in year 311; Scipio Africanus the Younger in year 364; Scipio Nasica in year 391; Posthumus and Metellus in year 393; Marius and Gnaeus Mallius in year 401; Sulla in year 422; Marcus Tullius Cicero in year 469; Pompey and Crassus in year 457; Caesar ruled alone [Col. 0237D] in year 462.

We have extracted these items concerning the times of the consuls, noting from the expulsion of the kings down to Julius Caesar the successive years and periods in which they governed the republic after the kings. We have especially marked those whose times saw great deeds performed either by themselves or by others: for example, in the time of the consul Papirius, the events written about Alexander the Great; in the time of the Scipios, the Punic Wars; in the time of Marius, the Jugurthine War; and in the time of Cicero, the Catilinarian affair. Julius Caesar was therefore the first monarch of the Romans; I shall set forth his deeds briefly.

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] You have all these matters more fully in John Lucidus, *Chronicles*, book III, chapter 3; but Robortellus [Col. 0238D] and Paulus Manutius have supplied them in certain extensive tables.]
