## Chapter XXI. On Julius Caesar, first Roman emperor, and Pompey the Great

[Col. 0238A]

Julius Caesar subdued the fiercely warlike people of the Gauls in many battles. Then, crossing to Britain by ship, he extended Roman power beyond the boundary of land, namely the Ocean Sea; he completed all this within ten years. After this, he requested that the Roman Senate decree him a second consulship. Marcellus, three times consul, opposed him, with Pompey supporting the opposition. The Senate then decreed that he should not come into the City unless he had dismissed his army.

Caesar took this bitterly and, gathering forces from every side, advanced upon Rome as an enemy. Having crossed the river Rubicon, he took Ariminum and moved to Ravenna. But Pompey and the entire Roman [Col. 0238B] Senate, alarmed by Caesar’s growing strength, went to Greece as though driven from Italy, choosing Dyrrachium as the base for conducting the war. Caesar, after already fighting many engagements against Pompey’s commanders, finally entered Rome. Breaking open the doors of the public treasury, he took money and distributed it to his soldiers.

Meanwhile many kings of the East came with auxiliaries to Pompey at Dyrrachium. Hearing of this, Caesar drew up his army and came through Epirus into Thessaly. Pompey arranged eighty-eight cohorts in triple line; his army contained forty thousand infantry, with six hundred cavalry on the left wing and five hundred on the right. Among them were many kings, senators, [Col. 0238C] and very many Roman knights. Against him Caesar likewise arranged eighty cohorts in a triple formation. Caesar’s army had fewer than thirty thousand infantry and one thousand cavalry. Yet, as the battle was fought on both sides, Pompey’s entire army finally fled. Twelve thousand of Pompey’s men and thirty-four centurions were slain in that battle.

Pompey fled, found a merchant vessel, hurried to Asia, and from there crossed through Tyre to Egypt. There, as soon as he reached the shore, he was killed by order of the young Ptolemy, to win the favor of Caesar the victor. After Pompey’s death Caesar traveled through Syria and came to Alexandria. At the request of the Alexandrians, he granted the aforesaid young Ptolemy the kingdom of Alexandria. Yet Ptolemy immediately rebelled against Caesar and began a war. In that war, it is reported, [Col. 0238D] twenty thousand men were slain, and twelve thousand surrendered in seventy ships. Ptolemy, frightened by this, boarded a small boat to flee; but when many others leapt into the same boat after him, it sank, and he was killed. When his body was cast upon the shore, he was recognized by the evidence of his golden breastplate. Caesar sent it ahead to Alexandria and compelled the Alexandrians, in despair, to surrender. When these affairs had been accomplished, he again gave the Egyptian kingdom to Cleopatra.

Finally, traveling through Syria, he defeated Pharnaces in Pontus. Returning to Rome for the second time, he was called [Col. 0239A] dictator and consul; then, crossing into Africa, he defeated all the commanders and nephews of Pompey the Great. He fought near the city of Munda against Pompey’s commanders Labienus and Accius Varus and prevailed. He also killed Pompey’s daughter Pompeia, Faustus, Sulla, Afranius, and Petreius. Cato, however, killed himself at Utica. Returning thence to Rome, Caesar seized for himself alone the supreme power and authority in affairs, which the Greeks call *monarchia*, “sole rule.” But while there he mercifully restored the constitution of the republic, contrary to the custom of wicked men, Brutus and Cassius instigated a conspiracy, and he died in the senate-house, stabbed with twenty-four wounds [Col. 0240A] three years and six months after he had begun to rule. They say that 260 persons were involved in this conspiracy. The Roman people, stirred by grief, wished to burn the Capitol together with the authors of the murder. Later he became so memorable among them that all emperors after him were called Caesars.

Thus I have briefly set forth the rise, course, and fall of the kingdoms of the world which existed from the time when the human race was scattered over the earth after the Flood down to the time of Hyrcanus the high priest.

> [Note: [Col. 0239A] The most exact writer Plutarch has most diligently set out, in their vices, what may be said concerning Caesar and Pompey both in praise and in reproach. [Col. 0239B] Very much may be noted about Caesar in Suetonius, and about both men in Appian and the other writers of Roman history. [Col. 0240B]]

# Book Six

It treats of the Roman emperors, from Christ’s birth—that is, from Octavian—down to Trajan; it contains thirteen chapters.

[Col. 0239]

## Chapter I. On the concordance of what precedes and follows

[Col. 0239B]

Henceforth I shall endeavor to explain in similar order the succession and names of kingdoms and kings as they have run from the Incarnation of the Word down to our own times. [Col. 0239C] For we have divided the line of reckoning by which we measure the course of the present age into two parts: extending its upper portion from the beginning of the world to the Incarnation of the Word, and its lower and later portion downward from the Incarnation of the Word to ourselves.

After the period of the consuls, monarchs acquired imperial power in the Roman republic, Julius Caesar being the first to seize the empire. The Roman practice of obedience to one ruler was restored in the 722nd year from the founding of the City and the 580th after the expulsion of the kings; after Augustus, the ruler was called emperor in place of king, or by a more sacred name.

## Chapter II. On Octavian, the second monarch, and Christ’s birth

[Col. 0239D]

The second monarch of the Romans, after Julius Caesar had been killed, was Octavian [Octavius]. He occupied Illyricum and Pannonia, conquered the Sicambri and the Artures, peoples of Spain, and civilized them by laws and customs. The Noricans, Dalmatians, Moesians, Bosporans, Thracians, Dacians, and Sarmatians were conquered by the valor of his commanders.

But before Augustus himself had obtained the monarchy of the kingdom, he possessed Italy, Gaul, and Spain, while Antony possessed Asia and Pontus. Antony, who was Augustus’s brother-in-law, repudiated Augustus’s sister, took Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, as his consort, and declared war against Augustus. But when battle came, Antony, unable to withstand the emperor, killed himself with his own hand; Cleopatra, having brought serpents to herself, was lulled into death [Col. 0240B] by them. Augustus then took possession of the exceedingly wealthy city of Alexandria and entered Rome in triumph.

When these things had been accomplished, the Parthians, frightened by the glory of his illustrious name, voluntarily restored to him the Roman standards that they had seized when Crassus was killed; having given hostages, [Col. 0240C] they were granted a treaty with him. The Indians, Garamantes, and Ethiopians also sent ambassadors to him with gifts. Herod king of Judaea likewise came to him, having laid aside his diadem and put away the insignia of royalty because he had been among Antony’s friends. He came, I say, in humble dress but with a royal mind. When before the emperor he had most eloquently explained the loyalty which he had preserved toward Antony, Caesar, admiring the man’s loyalty and goodness, said: “Hail, and now possess your kingdom all the more; for we do not envy virtue, but delight in it.” Saying this, he placed a crown upon his head and enlarged his kingdom, giving him Gadara and Hypona, Samaria and Joppa, and also the Tower of Straton. Herod adorned the Tower of Straton [Col. 0240D] with splendid courtly buildings and ordered it to be called Caesarea.

Therefore, when all regions throughout the whole world had been pacified: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled. This first enrollment was made by Quirinius, governor of Syria. And Joseph went up from Nazareth of Galilee to Bethlehem of Judaea, because he was of the family of David, to be enrolled with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant” (Luke 2).

Accordingly, in the forty-second year of the reign of Octavian Augustus, the thirty-first of Herod’s reign, and the 193rd Olympiad, when a most secure peace prevailed throughout the world, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was born at Bethlehem of Judaea according to the faithful promises. At his birth angels sang in exultation: “Glory to God in the highest [Col. 0241A] and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2). The Magi also came from the East to worship him, offering him gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matthew 2). But Herod, terrified by evil suspicion, killed all the boys, hoping to kill Christ among those of the same age.

Moreover, ill-fated Herod was driven by evil suspicion to many crimes. So that he might not appear low-born, he married Mariamne, daughter of Aristobulus. Then he married nine women, but Mariamne excelled among all of them in the exceptional grace of her beauty. Herod therefore loved her and was unwilling that she should be offended. Yet a charge of adultery was contrived against Mariamne: that she had sent Antony her portrait, so as to arouse in him the unrestrained desire of a man captivated by her beauty. When [Col. 0241B] Herod heard this, he ordered her killed. But repentance for the deed followed not long afterward. Mariamne seemed to him to be heard and seen, and at times he seemed to stand with her and converse with her.

Others added further goads, warning him that he must beware of plots by his sons and maintaining that hands avenging their mother’s death were being armed against him. At last Alexander and Aristobulus—for these were their names—were brought to the city of Sebaste and strangled by their father’s command. Herod also had his son Antipater killed. Finally, brought low by a disease beneath the skin, he took to his bed and at last ended his life in a most dreadful death.

Herod was succeeded by his son Archelaus, inferior indeed in majesty but not in vices. At the same time Virgil, Sallust, Terence, [Col. 0241C] Horace, Livy, and Hortensius flourished at Rome. Augustus Caesar was sparing in entering friendships, but most steadfast in retaining them. He was gentle, gracious, civil, and agreeable in disposition; beautiful in all his body, but especially in his eyes. He enlarged Rome with many buildings, glorying in the saying: “I found a city of brick; I leave one of marble.” He died of illness at Nola and left his stepson Tiberius as his successor.

## Chapter III. On Claudius Tiberius Caesar
Claudius Tiberius, raised to the imperial throne, reigned for about twenty-two years. At first he was of such moderation that he said it was the part of a good shepherd to shear the flock, not to flay it. Under him, King Archelaus, accused of arrogance, was banished to Vienne, a city of Gaul [Col. 0241D]; and, in order to diminish the power of the Jewish kingdom, the brothers of Archelaus—Lysanias, Philip, and Herod—were established as tetrarchs. In the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, Pilate was appointed governor of Judaea. And in the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate governed Judaea and the aforesaid sons of Herod administered the territories entrusted to them, the word of the Lord came upon John, son of Zachariah, in the wilderness. And he came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism for the remission of sins (Luke III).

In the same year our Lord Jesus Christ began his evangelical teaching and chose the twelve apostles. Afterwards he chose seventy-two disciples. But Herod the tetrarch took away from his brother Philip his wife Herodias. When John the Baptist rebuked him, he bound him, cast him into prison, and finally had him beheaded at the fortress called Machaerus. Moreover, in the same year in which Saint John was beheaded, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered and rose again on the third day.

It was an ancient custom among the Romans that the governors of provinces should report by letter to the senate if anything unusual occurred in the provinces which they governed. Pilate therefore wrote a letter to Tiberius concerning the things perpetrated against our Lord Jesus Christ, informing him that he was truly the Saviour of the world. Then Tiberius, with the support of great favour, laid the letter before the senate, requesting that Christ be regarded as God. But the senate rejected Christ, indignant that the letter had not first been brought before it according to custom [Col. 0242B]. From that day the previously most praiseworthy moderation of Caesar began to be changed into punishment of the dissenting senate.

Meanwhile, at Jerusalem the apostles ordained Matthias (Acts I), and afterwards seven deacons, whose names are these: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas of Antioch (Acts VI). From this arose the heresy of the Nicolaitans. At the same time Philip, going down into Samaria, preached the word of God there, and many believed. Simon Magus also, who had driven that same city mad by magical arts, was baptized. When Peter and John came there, and Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given to believers through the laying on of their hands, he offered them money, asking that this power might be granted to him [Col. 0242C]; but, severely refuted by Peter’s words, he departed.

About these days the Apostle Paul was chosen, Stephen was stoned at Jerusalem, and James the son of Alphaeus was appointed patriarch. The apostles also, when Judaea had now rejected the word of God, visited individual provinces. Peter went to Cappadocia and Antioch; John to Asia; Paul to Greece; Andrew to Achaia; Matthew to Ethiopia; Philip to Scythia; Simon and Judas to Persia; Bartholomew to Lesser India; Thomas to Greater India. Moreover, the disciples who were converted to the faith were not called Christians. But the Church, gathered and flourishing greatly at Antioch, was the first to call believers in Christ “Christians.”

Furthermore, when Caesar was already punishing his own people and foreigners alike, and military discipline had been relaxed in the city of Rome, Armenia was ravaged by the Parthians, Moesia by the Dacians, Pannonia by the Sarmatians, and Gaul by neighbouring peoples. At last he was killed through the plots of Gaius Caligula.

## CHAPTER IV. On Gaius Caligula

Gaius Caligula, having been made emperor, gave the kingdom of Judaea to Agrippa Herod, son of Aristobulus, son of Herod the Great and Mariamne. Gaius accordingly gave him the tetrarchies of Philip, Lysanias, and Herod the tetrarchs; and he condemned the incestuous Herod, together with Herodias, to perpetual exile in Spain. He also caused the daughter of Herodias, who had danced at the beheading of Saint John, to be swallowed alive by the earth.

Nor did the governor Pilate remain unpunished [Col. 0243A], but, while exiled at Vienne, killed himself by his own hand. At this time Matthew wrote the Gospel. Meanwhile Caesar, setting out in search of an enemy for his idle forces, traversed Germany and Gaul and received into submission Bellinus, son of the king of the Britons. Thus he returned to Rome.

In those days also, after a sedition had broken out among the Jews at Alexandria and they had been crushed by slaughter, they sent to Caesar a certain most eloquent Philo, in order to lay their complaints before him. But Caesar despised his embassy. At last he ordered the temple at Jerusalem to be profaned, and himself to be worshipped as God. Finally, rendered hateful to all by the obscenity of his conduct, he was killed by the Praetorian soldiers.

## CHAPTER V. On Claudius, Caligula’s Uncle

[Col. 0243B]

Claudius Tiberius, Caligula’s uncle, was therefore made emperor. Having crossed into Britain, he received part of that island into submission and added the Orkney Islands to the Roman Empire. On returning to Rome, he gave his son the name Britannicus.

In these days the aforesaid King Herod stretched forth his hands to afflict certain members of the Church. He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword; and he seized Peter and put him in prison, intending to bring him before the people after Passover (Acts XII). But divine providence did not permit this. Finally, while Herod was celebrating spectacles in honour of Caesar, and the people, because of the splendour of his gilded garments, cried out, “A god and not a man,” he was lifted up in pride, struck by an angel [Col. 0243C], and, having contracted an illness, died. His son Agrippa succeeded him.

Thus Herod the Great was the first foreigner to reign among the Jews. After him came his son Archelaus; after him Herod the tetrarch, brother of Archelaus; after him also Agrippa Herod, son of Aristobulus; and finally Agrippa, son of Agrippa Herod. He endured until the final destruction of the Temple, always a friend to the Romans and entirely secure from that Jewish rebellion.

At this time also Peter went to Rome, and Mark wrote the Gospel. But Claudius Caesar excluded his son Britannicus from the succession and left Nero, husband of his daughter Octoviana, as his successor.

## CHAPTER VI. On Nero

Nero, having obtained the Roman Empire, proved very troublesome during five years [Col. 0243D]; and in the second year of his reign he placed Festus over Judaea. After his case had been heard before him, Paul was sent bound to Rome, where he was kept for two years in free custody. Afterwards, when released, he went to Spain; but on returning thence to Rome he was again arrested and bound.

At the same time Albinus succeeded Festus as procurator of Judaea, and Florus succeeded Albinus. In the presence of Berenice [Beronice], sister of King Agrippa, Florus flogged honourable Jewish men at Jerusalem on a solemn day and fastened them to crosses. Unable to endure this, the Jews began to rebel against the Romans. Vespasian, commander of the army, was sent by Caesar with his son Titus to subdue them.

About these days Simon Magus began to lead the Roman people so far astray that images of him were sent beforehand and worshipped as God [Col. 0244A]. But when Peter raised, in the name of Jesus Christ, a young relative of Caesar whom Simon had been unable to revive by magical arts, Simon, confounded, declared himself offended by the Galileans. He threatened to leave the city and promised the day on which he would be borne up into the heavenly seats. As he flew, he fell at Peter’s prayer and died broken to pieces.

But Caesar Nero, angered at this, ordered Peter to be seized. When Peter, overcome by the tears of the faithful, had promised that he would leave the city, he saw Christ the Lord coming to meet him. Worshipping him, he said: “Lord, where are you going?” The Lord replied, “I am coming to Rome to be crucified again.” Peter therefore understood this saying to concern his own suffering [Col. 0244B], and, having returned and been arrested, he was crucified. The Apostle Paul also was beheaded.

Moreover, in Nero’s time the Gospel was written by Luke, and James the patriarch was struck in the head and killed at Jerusalem with a fuller’s club. Nero Caesar, enemy of justice, was the first to instigate persecution against Christians. He also killed his own mother, sister, wife, and nearly all his relatives. He killed the poet Lucan and his own teacher Seneca. But while he was committing these and many other evils, Galba was made emperor in Spain. Nero, abandoned by all, fled from the City and killed himself.

At the same time there flourished at Rome the poets Lucan and Ovid; the satirists Juvenal and Persius; Seneca the tragedian; the philosopher Musonius; and Plutarch [Col. 0244C].

## CHAPTER VII. On Caesar Galba

After Nero’s death Galba came to Rome and ruled for six months and the same number of days. He adopted the young man Piso as his son, but Otho killed them both in the middle of the forum and seized the empire.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Otho

Otho therefore ruled for three months. Vitellius, born when Lucius Vitellius was consul for the third time, fought against him. But Otho, seeing himself and his men defeated in battle, killed himself.

## CHAPTER IX. On Vitellius

Vitellius, having gained the empire, ruled for eight months. Meanwhile Vespasian was waging war against the province of the Jewish people. As rumours of the civil wars—the death of Galba and Otho, and the rule of Vitellius, who had settled, as it were, like dregs after the others—grew stronger in the army [Col. 0244D], men of long military experience and commanders made Vespasian emperor against his will, judging him mature in counsel and strong in battle.

Then Vespasian left Judaea with his son Titus and hastened to enter Alexandria. For he knew that the greatest strength of the commonwealth was there. After arranging matters there favourably for himself, he returned to Antioch. From there, having sent the commander Mucianus ahead to Italy, he himself directed his route through Cappadocia and Phrygia.

Vitellius, alarmed by the unfavourable news, entrusted the whole danger to Caecinna, commander of his army. Caecinna, leaving Rome, learned that a strong force was approaching and summoned the centurions, urging them to desist from war because the glory of the opposing emperor outweighed all else. But while Caecinna was delaying, the commander of the opposing party, named Antonius, met him and defeated him in battle [Col. 0245A].

When Vitellius learned this, he first planned to lay down the empire; but afterwards, encouraged by certain persons, he killed Sabinus, Vespasian’s brother, who suspected no evil. Two days later Antonius arrived. He was met by the enemy; and after three engagements around the city, the Vitellians were routed and slaughtered. When the Vitellians failed, Vitellius shut himself in a little chamber. He was dragged shamefully from it to the forum, killed, and finally dragged into the Tiber; he was denied a common burial.

## CHAPTER X. On Vespasian and the Destruction of Jerusalem

[Col. 0245B]

Vespasian, raised to the imperial throne in the seventy-first year of the Lord’s Incarnation, reigned for nine years, eleven months, and twenty days. Meanwhile, because the ordinances of the law among the Jews had been corrupted and their religion violated, divine Providence deserted them. Not only were they pressed by the Romans, but they themselves also suffered internal seditions among one another.

There were two leaders of the whole rebellion. One was a certain John, a frivolous man, a plague of the people, clever in deceit, an artificer of deception, who considered fraud a virtue and regarded entrapping his closest associates as refinement. The other was Simon, no less cruel, although inferior in wealth.

Titus, executor of his father’s triumph, returned from Alexandria with a powerful force to besiege Jerusalem. He besieged it on the solemn day of Passover [Col. 0245C], when a great multitude of Jews had gathered there, by God’s just judgment: so that those who had killed our Saviour on the day of Passover, shut up as though in a single prison, might receive the destruction of the deadly punishment which they deserved.

The leaders of the factions consequently urged the people, in their united zeal, to defend their homeland. John fought in the fortress called Antonia. Simon undertook the defence of the city in the vicinity of John’s tomb. Thus desperation gave courage to the Jews, while desire for glory added valour to the Romans. Titus advised his soldiers to fight with deliberation, saying that courage alone was true courage when providence accompanied it.

Many people were killed. As the battering rams shook it, the wall gradually fell; and, when the first part of the walls had been breached, the Jews withdrew to the second wall. When the Jews fled, the Romans entered and demolished the outer wall. The city was full of terror: everywhere grief, everywhere fear, the cries of women, the wailing of old men, the groans of the dying, and the despair of the living.

Then Caesar ordered a battering ram to be brought against the second wall. At length the second wall was broken by the force of Caesar’s attack. One wall remained: this was the third. Titus now ordered his soldiers to restrain themselves, and urged the Jews not to involve themselves in the burning of the city [Col. 0245D]. Since it was already in Roman arms, he said he would grant pardon if only they would take thought either for themselves or for their country.

After three days had passed, because the Jews offered nothing peaceful, Titus attacked the fortifications. Meanwhile a terrible famine had overtaken those who were shut in [Col. 0246A]. They now ate uncooked food in secret—miserable fare, food worthy of tears. Parents snatched food from their children’s very mouths, and children from those of their parents. But why need one set forth even the full weight of this famine? For there was committed there a deed such as no report has ever received either among Greeks or among barbarians.

There remained in the city a certain wretched woman who killed, roasted, and ate her own infant. While it was roasting, the smell of the burning reached the leaders of the rebellion. Driven by hunger, they followed it and entered the woman’s lodging. Thus what had been done was discovered. Immediately the horror of so great a crime filled the whole city, and every person shuddered at the food of that parricidal banquet set before his eyes. Many also, terrified by the horror, fled to the enemy.

When he learned this [Col. 0246B], Caesar cursed the contagion of the unhappy land and, lifting his hands to heaven, protested in these words:

> We have indeed come to war, fellow soldiers, but we are fighting against men more cruel than beasts. Wild animals love their offspring, whom they nourish even in famine. It surpasses every horror that a mother should devour the limbs she has borne. From this contagion I absolve myself before you, whatever power you are in heaven. For you know that I have frequently offered peace. O unhappy city, in which there is such a workshop and such a service! Let its own ruins cover it, and let them conceal this contagion of the world, lest the sun see it, lest the sphere of the stars behold it, or the breaths of the winds be polluted. We thought the feast of Thyestes a fable; we see the crime; we behold a reality more terrible than tragedies. Let us therefore finish the war more swiftly [Col. 0246C] and depart from this accursed and destructive land.

Having said this, he ordered the battering rams to be brought against the wall.

When two full years had passed after the city was besieged, Titus the victor broke through its walls by engines and other instruments of war, though not without the blood of his own men. Once the wall had been broken, the sound of the trumpet rang out more terribly than usual. Hearing the crash of the wall and the trumpet blast, Titus ordered his army to run to arms. The enemies had already rushed in; they had already thrown everything into confusion. Wounds followed wounds, and the sword was blunted by the hardness of the iron. One might see the land flooded with blood as with a river: everywhere slaughter, everywhere grief, everywhere danger, everywhere shouting, everywhere despair. But when night came, each army rested.

At daybreak Caesar ordered the silver-covered doors of the Temple to be set on fire [Col. 0246D]. Titus wished to preserve the Temple; but, when the leaders said that the roots of rebellion must be uprooted completely, one of the Romans set fire to the gate of the Temple called the Beautiful Gate. The molten hardness of the gold stripped bare the wood, and then the fury of the fire, entering the inner recesses of the Temple, rushed onward.

The flame was already consuming the chambers of the Temple. Titus ran up, wishing to inspect what sort of building it was. Moved by its splendour, he acknowledged it to have surpassed the works of his own temples, and believed that so noble a structure could be no dwelling except that of the highest God. He marvelled at the size of the stones, the brightness of the metal, the beauty of the workmanship, and the grace of its loveliness.

Meanwhile, one of the priests surrendered himself and certain vessels: two lamps [Col. 0247A], tables, bowls, golden cups, and the hangings of the Temple. Phinehas also, keeper of the treasury, was seized and showed much priestly purple, scarlet, cinnamon, incense, spices, vessels, and the sacred vestment of the high priest.

Finally John surrendered himself to Titus, and Simon, captured by Terentius Rufus, was presented to Titus. The city was burned, and the wall cast down to the very ground. Vespasian and Titus, bringing back a magnificent triumph over the Jews, entered Rome and immediately proclaimed peace throughout the whole Roman realm.

Thus the Roman commonwealth obtained Vespasian, as though by a certain fate, lest it should fall utterly. But in the seventieth year of his life, mingling serious matters with the jokes in which he delighted [Col. 0247B], he died. For, when weakened by a flux of the belly, he had risen, he said: “An emperor ought to depart this world standing.” Thus he expired, and his son Titus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XI. On Titus, Son of Vespasian

Titus, chosen emperor, reigned for two years. He was remarkable in every kind of virtue and adorned with the flowers of imperial character. He was so eloquent that he pleaded cases in Latin verse and composed tragedies in Greek. But when two years of his assumed sovereignty had elapsed, he died of a fever among the Sabines, amid the immense grief of his people.

## CHAPTER XII. On Domitian

[Col. 0248A]

Domitian, Titus’s younger brother, reigned for fifteen years and six months. He conquered the Chatti and the Germans and constructed many buildings at Rome. He built the temple called the Pantheon, which is now consecrated in honour of all the saints. But Domitian, having become cruel, killed many illustrious men and sent many into exile. Among them he banished the Apostle John to the island of Patmos.

In Domitian’s time Pope Clement sent men to Gaul to preach: Photinus to Lyons, Paul to Narbonne, Gratian to Tours, and Julian to Le Mans. But while Domitian cruelly slew the people in the city of the Flavians and the army outside it slew enemies, he was killed by the senate, and his body was denied burial [Col. 0248B].

## CHAPTER XIII. On Nerva

Nerva, raised to the imperial throne, recalled by his first edict all exiles whom Domitian had condemned to banishment. Thus blessed John returned to Ephesus. Meanwhile many heresies of Cerinthus, Ebion, and others who deny that Christ came in the flesh sprang up throughout Asia. The apostle calls them antichrists. Therefore, against their perversity, the aforesaid apostle, at the request of many, wrote his Gospel.

Finally Nerva Caesar served the commonwealth greatly by adopting Trajan, an energetic man, as his son.

# BOOK SEVEN

Treating of the emperors from Trajan to Constantine the Great; it contains twenty-three chapters.

[Col. 0247]

## CHAPTER I. On Caesar Trajan

[Col. 0247C]

Trajan, a Spaniard by origin, received the insignia of empire at the city of Agrippina. Soon he conquered Germany and many peoples beyond the Danube; reduced the nations beyond the Tigris and Euphrates to provinces; and, after Alexander the Great, advanced as far as the borders of India. At home he possessed uprightness, and in war courage.

In his time the Apostle John died. In his time also, when persecution flared up, Pope Clement was thrown into the sea, Simon son of Cleophas was crucified, Ignatius was given to the beasts, and Pope Alexander was crowned with martyrdom. But Pliny the Younger, orator and historian, wrote to the emperor that, apart from their confession of Christ and their honourable assemblies, Christians did nothing contrary to Roman laws [Col. 0247D]. Soon, by God’s prompting, Caesar moderated the edict.

Finally, Trajan Caesar died of a flux of the belly at Seleucia, a city of Isauria.

## CHAPTER II. On Aelius Hadrian

Aelius Hadrian, having obtained the empire, reigned for twenty-one years. He was a musician, geometer, painter [Col. 0248C], worker in bronze, and witty—that is, exceptionally sharp in serious or playful provocation and reply, and in abuse. Instructed by Quadratus and Aristides, he wrote a letter to Minucius, proconsul of Asia, declaring that no one might condemn a Christian without accusation and proof of a crime.

Finally, he utterly subdued the Jews, who were ravaging the province of Palestine, formerly their own; rebuilt Jerusalem; and called it Aelia after his own name. By his works it came about that the holy places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, once lying outside the city, are now enclosed by the city’s northern wall. He ordered that no Jew should enter it, while the city was permitted only to Christians. At the same time Aquila the orator and Aquila the translator flourished.

## CHAPTER III. On Antoninus Pius

[Col. 0248D]

Antoninus Pius, adopted by Hadrian as his son, obtained the empire. Justin the philosopher made him kindly disposed towards Christians. Antoninus was so peaceful that he was deservedly called Pius. He was without boasting or display. The Indians, Bactrians, and Hyrcanians sent envoys to him [Col. 0249A], having learned of the justice of so great an emperor. He died in the twenty-second year of his reign. At the same time there flourished Galen, the distinguished physician; Justin Martyr; and Justin the philosopher.

## CHAPTER IV. On Marcus Aurelius and Aurelius Commodus

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, having obtained the empire, reigned for nineteen years and eleven months. He admitted his relative Aurelius Commodus to a share in the empire. Both triumphed over the Parthians. At this time the fourth persecution dripped down upon Christians.

But a great plague followed the persecution and devastated many provinces, especially Italy. There was nowhere any rest from warfare; wars raged throughout the East, Illyricum, Italy, and Gaul. But Aurelius Commodus, while riding with his brother in a carriage, was suffocated by the disease which the Greeks call *apoplexia* [Col. 0249B], “apoplexy.”

Marcus Antoninus moderated the harsher laws by new provisions. In these days the Marcomanni, Quadi, Vandals, Sarmatians, and nearly all the peoples of Germany surrounded the Roman army within the territory of the Quadi. The Roman army, hemmed in by thirst and danger from the enemy, poured itself out in prayers; and at the invocation of Christ’s name it obtained so abundant a rain that it was most generously refreshed. But the barbarians, terrified by thunderbolt strikes, turned to flight.

At the same time Hegesippus the historian and Theodotion the translator flourished. Moreover, the emperor died while stationed in Pannonia [Col. 0249C], and his son Lucius Aurelius Commodus succeeded him.

## CHAPTER V. On Lucius Aurelius Commodus

Aurelius Commodus reigned for thirteen years. Given over to luxury, he killed a great many senators. The punishment of the city followed the emperor’s crimes: the Capitol was struck by lightning, which burned the Roman library. In these days a question concerning Easter arose; as was decreed by a council celebrated at Caesarea of Palestine, it was to be observed on the Lord’s Day. Commodus, harmful to all, finally died strangled in the house of a Vestal.

## CHAPTER VI. On Aelius Pertinax

Aelius Pertinax, made emperor by the senate, reigned for six months; scarcely had these elapsed when he was killed in the palace by the crime of Julian [Col. 0249D], the jurist.

## CHAPTER VII. On Julian

Julian reigned for seven months. He was killed in civil war near the Milvian Bridge. In these times Africanus the historian flourished.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Caesar Severus

Severus, having been made emperor, cruel by nature and harassed by many battles, governed the commonwealth very bravely indeed, but with great labour. He killed Pescennius, who had aspired to tyranny in Egypt and Asia. He restrained the Jews and Samaritans, conquered the Parthians and Arabs, killed Claudius Albinus, who had made himself Caesar in Gaul, and recovered the island of Britain by great battles.

But he instigated the fifth persecution against Christians. He died at York [Col. 0250A] and left his sons Bassianus and Geta. Symmachus the translator flourished in these times.

## CHAPTER IX. On Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus

Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus, son of Severus, having obtained the empire, reigned for seven years. He was more unrestrained in lust than his father and even took his stepmother as wife. In these times Symmachus the heretic preached that Christ had been born from the seed of Joseph and that the law was to be observed in the Jewish manner.

Finally, Caesar Aurelius Antoninus Bassianus marched against the Parthians and was killed at Edessa. Macer Macrinus, prefect of the palace, succeeded him, though in no way by the will of the senate.

## CHAPTER X. On Macer Macrinus

[Col. 0250B]

Macer Macrinus therefore seized the empire after Antoninus, but after a year had passed he was killed.

## CHAPTER XI. On Marcus Aurelius Antoninus

Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Gabalus, having acquired the empire, left behind no memory of himself except obscenity. When a military uprising had arisen at Rome, he was killed with his mother.

## CHAPTER XII. On Alexander Mammaea

Alexander Mammaea, having obtained the empire by the will of the senate and the soldiers, launched an expedition against the Persians and, victorious, crushed their king Xerxes. His mother Mammaea, a Christian, took care to hear Origen. In these times also Tiburtius and Valerian were martyred at Rome with the virgin Caecilia. Alexander was killed at Mainz by Maximus, his son [Col. 0250C].

## CHAPTER XIII. On Maximus Julius

Maximus Julius, also called Maximinus, having obtained the empire, instigated persecution against priests and clerics on account of Mammaea and Alexander’s Christian household. But in the third year of his reign he was killed at Aquileia by the tyrant Pupienus. Pupienus also, while he usurped the empire with his brother Balbinus, was killed with him in the palace.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Gordian

Gordian, raised to the Roman throne, after fighting successfully against the Parthians, was killed by the treachery of his own men beyond the Euphrates. At this time flourished Africanus, a man most renowned among ecclesiastical writers [Col. 0250D], and Porphyry the philosopher.

## CHAPTER XV. On Philip, Also Called Marcus Julius, and His Son

Philip, also called Marcus Julius, having been made emperor, reigned for seven years from the two hundred and thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Incarnation. He made his son Philip his colleague in empire and was the first of the Roman emperors to be a Christian. But both emperors were ensnared and killed by the treachery of Decius.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Decius

After seizing the Roman Empire, Decius, alone after Nero, issued deadly edicts for the persecution of Christians. Indeed, we cannot set forth how great multitudes were consumed while this persecution raged [Col. 0251A]. At this time Novatus founded a heresy, saying that repentance was not to be accepted from brethren who had lapsed during persecution. Decius, before two full years had elapsed, was killed among the barbarians with his son.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Gallus Hostilianus, His Son Volusianus, and the Tyrant Aemilianus

Gallus Hostilianus, having obtained the empire with his son Volusianus, though flourishing at first, began to persecute holy men who prayed for the peace of his kingdom. But when persecution arose, vengeance also arose for the violated Christian name. For there was scarcely any Roman province, city, or household which was not emptied by plague.

While Gallus and Volusianus, distinguished by this calamity alone, were preparing civil war against Aemilianus, who was striving for revolution [Col. 0251B], they were killed. Aemilianus also was destroyed in the third month of his usurped tyranny. About these days Origen died.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Valerian and Gallienus

Valerian was made emperor by the army in Raetia. He took a certain man named Gallienus as partner in empire. At first Valerian so venerated God’s holy ones that his household was thought to be a church of God. But later, corrupted by a certain magician, he began to detest the faith of Christians. Eighth after Nero, he ordered Christians to be compelled by tortures to idolatry.

But he did not enjoy impunity for this persecution. For after he ordered Christians to be killed, the barbarian nations suddenly, with loosened reins [Col. 0251C], entered Roman territory. Greece and Macedonia, Pontus and Asia, were devastated by the invasion of the Goths. The Germans advanced as far as Ravenna. The Alemanni entered Gaul. The Quadi and Sarmatians ravaged Pannonia. The Parthians took Mesopotamia. Posthumus seized tyranny in Gaul and held it for ten years, but afterwards was killed in an uprising of his own soldiers.

At last Valerian was captured by Sapor, king of the Persians, and, as long as he lived, endured this punishment of disgraceful service: stooping to the ground, he raised the king as he mounted his horse, not with his hand but with his back. Gallienus, terrified by so clear a judgment of God, having obtained sole control, began to act more gently and granted peace to the Churches. Immediately the wrath of God was turned into mercy: Aemilianus [Col. 0251D], the tyrant, was killed while attempting revolution near Mainz; Marius, who had seized the empire in Gaul after Posthumus’s death, was killed; and Victorinus, made Caesar by the Gauls, was overthrown. In the East also the Persians were defeated by Odenatus, Syria was defended, and Mesopotamia too was recovered. Finally the emperor Gallienus died, Claudius succeeding him.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Claudius and Quintilius

Claudius, a vigorous man of upright character, having been made emperor, checked with great slaughter the Goths, who for fifteen years had been ravaging Illyricum and Macedonia. Therefore a golden shield and an equestrian statue were erected to him in the senate-house.

In these days a certain heretic Paul, holding unworthy opinions concerning Christ, preached that he had been a man of common nature and had taken his beginning from the earth [Col. 0252A]. But after the death of the emperor Claudius, his brother Quintilius was chosen by the army and raised to the throne; yet on the seventh day of his reign he was killed and died.

## CHAPTER XX. On Aurelius, or Aurelian, and the Emperors Tacitus and Florian

Aurelius, a man exceedingly experienced in military enterprise, having obtained the empire, routed the Gothic people in fierce battles, established Roman dominion within its ancient boundaries, and claimed all Syria, now recovered, for himself. In these days a famous council assembled at Antioch, at which the aforesaid Paul was convicted and condemned.

But when he refused to leave the Church’s house [Col. 0252B], Aurelian was appealed to, and he ordered him to be expelled by public force. For Aurelian had not yet been corrupted by the wicked counsels through which, as time went on, he changed his good purpose. But when Aurelian, most impious, was shedding the blood of the pious, he was destroyed by divine action between Constantinople and Heraclea.

After his death Tacitus ruled for six months. When he was killed in Pontus, Florian obtained the Roman Empire. He too was killed at Tarsus in the third month of his reign.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Probus

Probus, finally obtaining the empire, freed Gaul, long occupied by barbarians, after many wars and the eventual destruction of its enemies. He fought two civil wars: one in the East, in which he crushed the tyrant Saturnus; and another in which he killed Proculus and Bonosus at the colony of Agrippina [Col. 0252C].

At this time a certain Mani, a Persian by birth, keen in intellect but barbarous in life and character, called himself the Paraclete. From him the heresy of the Manichaeans spread. He asserted that there were two principles, one of good and the other of evil. Emperor Probus was killed in a military uprising at Sirmium.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Carus of Narbonne and Numerian

Carus of Narbonne, having obtained the empire and made his two sons partners in the realm, set out for war against the Parthians and died in camp when struck by lightning. Numerian, who had gone out with his father, was killed by the treachery of his father-in-law Aper while returning from there.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Emperors Diocletian and Maximian

[Col. 0252C]

Diocletian, therefore, having been elected emperor by the army after Numerian had been killed, in the year 276 of the Lord’s Incarnation, ruled for almost twenty years. Once made emperor, he killed with his own hand Aper, Numerian’s murderer, and killed Carinus, Numerian’s brother, in Dalmatia. In these days Amandus and Elianus, having gathered a band of peasants in Gaul, stirred up destructive disturbances. Therefore Diocletian chose Maximian Herculius as Caesar and sent him into Gaul; he easily restrained the peasant band by military strength. But on the very journey the Theban Legion willingly died for Christ at the Gallic place of Autun, under Ganno, subordinate to the aforesaid Maximian.

[Col. 0253A] In the nineteenth year of Diocletian’s reign, while the Church of God was spreading and increasing throughout the whole world in prosperous growth, suddenly the storm of persecution broke out. This persecution burned so fiercely that it even crossed the rim of Ocean, and the rage once begun did not cease to seethe until the seventh year of Constantine the Great. Moreover, at this time eighteen thousand martyrs suffered within Rome. But while these things were taking place, severe crashes of rebellions resounded through all the territories of the Roman Empire: Carausius rebelled in Britain and Achilleus in Egypt; the Quinquegentiani also ravaged Africa, and Narseus, king of the Persians, pressed the East with war. Moved by this danger, Diocletian made Maximian Herculius, formerly Caesar, Augustus; and chose Constantius [Col. 0253B] and Galerius Maximian as Caesars.

Carausius, moreover, was killed through the treachery of his associate Allectus. Allectus was overthrown by the prefect Asclepiodotus. The Alamanni too, who likewise rebelled, were defeated by Constantius Caesar; and the Quinquegentiani were subdued by Maximian Augustus. Diocletian killed Achilleus at Alexandria. Galerius Maximian, having engaged Narseus in battle, was defeated for the third time and fled; but, returning again against the enemy, he overcame him with great force.

Finally Diocletian compelled Maximian, against his will, to lay down the imperial office together with him, [Col. 0254A] so that, with younger men appointed in their places, they themselves might grow old in private dress. Thus on one and the same day Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan laid aside the purple. Then Galerius Maximian and Constantius, as Augusti, were the first to divide the Roman Empire into two administrations, namely those of East and West: Galerius Maximian held Illyricum, Asia, and the East; Constantius possessed Gaul and Spain.

Maximian, however, raised a most grievous persecution against the Christians. Constantius acted more mildly and held worshippers of Christ in honor. Therefore the destruction of the aforesaid tyrants promptly followed through God’s grace. For Herculius Maximian, wishing again to seize the imperial power which he had cast off, was killed at Marseilles by Constantine, who was not yet emperor. [Col. 0254B] Galerius Augustus sent Severus Caesar with an army to Italy. There, although he had occupied Rome, he was abandoned and betrayed through the treachery of his soldiers, and killed at Ravenna. Diocletian also, as has already been said, having laid aside royal rank, died at Salona. Finally Constantius, a most vigorous emperor, died at York in the fifteenth year of his reign; he appointed Licinius Caesar of the Spains, and his son Constantine Caesar of the Gauls.

## BOOK EIGHTH

Treating of the emperors from Constantine the Great to Zeno; it contains fourteen chapters.

[Col. 0253]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning Constantine, I mean, the Great.

[Col. 0253C]

Constantine the Great, son of Constantius, a most moderate and distinguished ruler, was made emperor in Britain by God’s direction and ruled for thirty-two years. In the eastern regions Maximian Galerius still reigned as Augustus; at Rome Maxentius, son of Maximian Herculius, had been made emperor by the Praetorian soldiers. He afterwards wallowed in such a cesspool of vices that no dreadful crime was foreign to his life or deeds.

Accordingly, when Constantine was spending the seventh year of his reign, he prepared war against Maxentius, Licinius, his colleague, joining him in the conspiracy. And while he was considering much concerning the necessity of the impending war, he saw in a dream in heaven the sign of the holy cross, τὸ ταῦ—that is, Tau—and angels [Col. 0253D] standing by him and saying: “In this sign you shall conquer.” When he awoke, he painted upon the military standard the sign which he had seen. Having pitched camp not far from the Milvian Bridge, Maxentius, driven by frenzy, came out of the City across a bridge made of boats and met him in battle. When both sides were fighting fiercely and Maxentius’ army was being overthrown by the power of the holy cross, Maxentius attempted to return by flight to the City. He mounted the bridge, made as we have said of boats, [Col. 0254C] but immediately the boats sank; and he himself, falling from his horse, was drowned in the depth of the river-bed.

Then Constantine entered Rome in triumph, and thus the rule of the entire West came to Constantine and Licinius. Yet Maximian, an impious and fierce-minded man, still ruled in the eastern regions. Licinius, departing from Rome, prepared to attack him. When Maximian’s army had already fallen by Licinius’ sword, the remaining part submitted to Licinius, and Maximian fled shamefully. But after he had raised another army and wished a second time to fight the enemy, he was seized by pain in his inner organs; at last, having lost his sight through illness, he ended his life.

Meanwhile Constantine was covered with a severe and loathsome leprosy. Since he could not be cured by physicians, [Col. 0254D] the priests of the Capitol told him that a pool should be made for him in the Capitol and filled with the blood of innocents, and that, bathed in it while it was warm, he could be healed. But when the innocents had been assembled, the pious ruler saw the mothers’ tears and heard their wailing. He immediately recoiled in horror from the deed, and, moved by compassion, ordered their children restored to their mothers. When the day had passed, the apostles Peter and Paul appeared to him in a dream and told him to summon Pope Sylvester from Mount Soracte, because [Col. 0255A] he would show him the pool in which he should wash and be healed. Thus the pope was summoned; he expounded Christ’s faith to Constantine and baptized him when he believed. Emerging from the font, Constantine was healed alike of leprosy of body and soul.

Constantine the Great, having become a Christian, publicly commanded by edict throughout the Roman Empire that temples of idols should be closed and churches built. Indeed, it is incredible to recount how swiftly, through his zeal, the holy Church grew widely throughout the world. Licinius, however, pricked by envy, planned dissension, making this his complaint: that Christians did not keep vigil in solemn prayers on his behalf as they did for Constantine. But when he understood that his schemes profited little, he openly declared war on the emperor. Battle having been joined, [Col. 0255B] Licinius was defeated near Chrysopolis in Bithynia, captured, and beheaded at Thessalonica. Thus Constantine, by God’s direction, alone secured the stability of the Roman Empire.

After this Constantine built the coastal city of Byzantium and called it Constantinople after his own name. He granted the city of Rome, together with his palace called the Lateran, to the apostles Peter and Paul and to holy Pope Sylvester, and established Constantinople as the imperial seat. Nevertheless, emperors’ successors continued to be called Roman emperors until the time when the Roman Empire was transferred to the kings of the Franks. Thereafter those who ruled at Constantinople were called rather emperors of the Greeks. From that point the sequence of times is reckoned by the kings [Col. 0255C] of the Franks.

Constantine further decreed that all matters pertaining to ecclesiastical order should receive their settlement by the judgment of the bishop of Rome. Helena also, his mother, a woman of singular magnificence, instructed by divine visions, went to Jerusalem, sought the wood of the Lord’s cross, and found it miraculously through the restoration to life of a certain dead man. Constantine also, by a law promulgated for this purpose, prohibited the punishment of the cross, which had been in Roman use, and ordered its image inscribed on solidi.

At the same time there was at Antioch a certain heretical presbyter named Arius. He preached that the Son, in divine matters, was a creature, and that the Holy Spirit was created by him. He also added that there was a time when the Son himself did not exist. Hearing this, Constantine caused a synod to be assembled at Nicaea, a city of Bithynia, in the year 316 of the Lord’s Incarnation; three hundred and nineteen bishops met there. [Col. 0255D] At this synod it was determined that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and Arius was condemned and separated from the Church.

At the same time, among other anchorites or hermits, Panutius, a man of God in Egypt, flourished. Saint Evurtius also, subdeacon of the Roman Church, who had by chance then come into Gaul to seek his brothers, was designated for the third time in the church of Orléans, before the clergy and all the people, by a dove sent down from heaven, as the man to be chosen bishop; and he was consecrated pontiff of that Church.

The often-mentioned Constantine [Col. 0256A] died in the sixty-fifth year of his age. So long as he lived, he adorned his clothing with gems and his head continually with a diadem. He also always fostered the liberal arts, but especially literary studies; he himself read, wrote, and reflected. His three sons succeeded him: Constantine at Rome, Constantius at Constantinople, and Constans at Antioch.

These are those who, after Constantine the Great, ruled when the Empire was divided between Rome and Constantinople. At Rome: Constantine; Julian the Apostate. At Rome and Constantinople: Jovian. At Rome and Constantinople: Valentinian, Gratian, Theodosius. At Rome and Constantinople: Honorius, Valentinian, Maximian, Avitus, Majorian, Athemius, Olybrius, Glycerius, Nepos, Augustulus, Odoacer, Theoderic, [Col. 0256B] Athalaric, Theodahad, and Witigis, Totila. At Constantinople: Constantine; Julian the Apostate. At Constantinople and Rome: Valens, Valentinian, Theodosius. At Constantinople and Rome: Arcadius, Theodosius, Marcian, Leo the First, Leo the Second, Zeno, Anastasius, Justin, Justinian.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the brothers Constantius, Constantine, and Constans.

Constantius, therefore, after his father’s death, obtained the Roman Empire and ruled for twenty-four years. As soon as he became emperor, he was corrupted away from the Catholic faith by his intimates. Supported by his patronage, the Arian bishops devastated the Church’s prosperity through domestic disturbance and condemned to exile many Catholic men who manfully resisted them for the justice of the faith. Finally Constantine Augustus of Constantinople died in the suburb of Nicomedia. His brother Constans, too, having given himself over to intolerable vices, was killed by the treachery of the tyrant Magnentius.

After Constans’ death, Constantius Augustus summoned a certain Julian, nephew of Constantine the Great, and appointed him Caesar of the Gauls. Julian, made Caesar, defeated the Gauls with remarkable success. Since he was popular with the soldiers, they hailed him Augustus. Rejecting the authority of Constantius Augustus, he seized Italy and Illyricum. Hearing this, Constantius abandoned his expedition in the Parthian war and came against him, but died on the journey, in the forty-fifth year of his life. After his death Julian [Col. 0256D] came to Constantinople and became emperor.

Moreover, at this time the heresy of the Anthropomorphites arose. Its originator was a certain Andes, who said that the Godhead has form and that God is distinguished by bodily parts—contrary to Catholic teaching.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Julian the Apostate.

Julian the Apostate, having become emperor, reopened the temples of the pagans and became a more cunning persecutor of Christians than all other persecutors. He said, moreover, that the military belt, provincial administration, and the office of administering justice ought not to be entrusted to Christians, since their own law had forbidden them to use the sword. Therefore he subsequently commanded soldiers by a public edict either to sacrifice to idols or to leave military service. [Col. 0257A] Yet certain Catholics preferred to abandon military office, through zeal for God, rather than their faith.

At the same time Valentinian, who afterwards became emperor, did not conceal the zeal that was innate to him. For one day, as the Augustus was entering a temple and an attendant was sprinkling those entering with water, Valentinian saw a single drop upon his cloak. He struck the attendant with his fist, saying that by this sprinkling he had been polluted rather than cleansed. When Julian saw this, he ordered Valentinian taken into custody and finally sent into the wilderness. But when a year and a few days had passed, Valentinian received the Empire as the reward of his confession.

Julian, moreover, profanely washing away baptism with the blood of sacrifices, did everything by which demons are customarily appeased. He also persecuted Athanasius, but by God’s direction could not capture him. In these days the martyrs of Christ John and Paul suffered at Rome. Also, at Sebaste, a city of Palestine, a crowd of pagans with sacrilegious hands broke open the tomb of Saint John the Baptist, burned the relics of that martyr, and scattered the ashes, mixed with dust, over the fields. Yet some pilgrims from Jerusalem were present; they secretly removed a few bones from the fire and carried them back with them.

Finally, as Julian was about to set out for the Parthian war, he began with still more unbridled rage to persecute the worshippers of Christ. But when he had moved his camp from Ctesiphon and was already drawing up his army for battle, he was wounded in the abdomen by an unknown person and was punished. As he died, he began to blaspheme Christ God, [Col. 0257C] saying, “You have conquered, Galilean; you have conquered.” And with these words the criminal expired.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning Jovian.

Jovian, having obtained the Empire, ruled for eight months. When, after Julian’s death, he was forcibly drawn to the imperial office by the soldiers, he said that he did not wish to rule pagan men, since he himself was a Christian. When the voice of all proclaimed that they too were Christians, he accepted the Empire. He made a treaty with Sapor, king of the Persians, and ceded to him the town of Nisibis and part of Upper Mesopotamia. Immediately the king of the Persians caused a market for goods for sale to be prepared for him in the desert. Thus Jovian led the Roman army unharmed from the midst of the enemy.

[Col. 0257D] But as he was returning to Illyricum through Galatia, he entered a newly built chamber, where he was overcome and suffocated by the heat of charcoal and the fumes of walls recently coated with lime. He ended his life in the eighth month of his reign. Thus an untimely death ruined beginnings so pious and so joyful.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning Valentinian the Great.

Valentinian the Great, whom we mentioned above, was made emperor at the city of Nicaea by the will of the soldiers and ruled for eleven years. He admitted his brother Valens to partnership in the Empire, retaining the western regions for himself and granting his brother the eastern regions to govern. But Valens was led by his wife’s persuasion into the Arian heresy, though he had previously been Catholic in faith. He was baptized a second time [Col. 0258A] by Eudoxius, an Arian bishop who appeared to hold the see of Constantinople. By that very baptism Eudoxius bound wretched Valens by oath to remain in impiety and to banish those holding contrary beliefs. But Valens long concealed his malicious persecution and, while his brother lived, did not add power to his will, being restrained by Valentinian’s authority.

In these days Auxentius, defender of the Arian doctrine, who had long held the episcopal see of Milan, at length died. Ambrose, still a catechumen and a man of consular rank, was chosen as his successor through the voice of a child in the public assembly.

Meanwhile Valentinian, a worshipper of Christ, subdued the Saxon nation, terrible in strength, and so crushed the Alans that he compelled them to seek the Maeotian marshes. But pursuing them again there [Col. 0258B] and being hindered by the terrain and difficulty of the places, he summoned to his aid the Trojans who inhabited Sicambria. He remitted their tribute for ten years if they would assist him. Encouraged by this promise, and being familiar with the terrain, they easily drove the Alans from the marsh. Admiring their valor, the Augustus called them Franks, from their ferocity. I shall explain their origin and succession more fully below.

At the same time Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, flourished. Finally Valentinian Augustus died at the town of Brigetio in the eleventh year of his reign. When he was deprived of life, the soldiers of Italy raised his very young son Valentinian to the Empire, while his brother Gratian and their uncle Valens survived.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Valens.

[Col. 0258C]

Valens, therefore, an emperor hateful to God, after his brother’s death ruled with his nephews Gratian and the younger Valentinian for fourteen years. Justina, mother of this Valentinian, an Arian, revealed after Valentinian her husband’s death the malignant sect that she had concealed while he lived, and began to harm the orthodox. Finally she tried to send Saint Ambrose into exile. But when he refused to leave the church at the queen’s command, Justina began to inflame the people against him. Yet the people showed such reverence and persevering love toward Ambrose that they preferred to lose their lives rather than their bishop.

[Col. 0258D] Therefore, judging herself wronged, she began to complain to her son. Then the young man, inflamed by his mother’s complaint, sent an army to besiege the church, so that no Catholic might enter it. But almighty God turned the soldiers’ hearts to the church’s defense: they did not permit those within to leave, but did not prevent others from entering. Ambrose, with the orthodox enclosed within the church, devoted himself to God in fasting and continual vigils. On this occasion vigils, hymns, and antiphons first began to be celebrated in the church of Milan; the custom of this observance thereafter spread through all the provinces.

But while these things were happening in Italy, Valens, an emperor hateful to God, commanded by a cruel edict in the eastern regions [Col. 0259A] that monks should serve as soldiers, and ordered those unwilling to do so killed. While this persecution raged, many companies of holy monks are reported to have been slain for Christ. After he had deprived almost all the churches of the East of their shepherds, he came to Caesarea in Cappadocia. There he tried, both personally and through his prefect, to bend Basil the Great, bishop of that city, toward Arian unbelief, using promises and threats. When he could not turn him from the uprightness of the faith, he decided to send him into exile. As he wished to ratify with his own hand the decree which he had commanded to be written concerning Basil’s exile, the pen broke in his hands three times. Then, his mind filled with terror, he tore the sheet with both hands.

But in the thirteenth year of Valens’ reign, four nations of Scythia—[Col. 0259B] namely the Goths, Hypogoths, Gepids, and Vandals—using one language and differing only in name, crossed the Danube in a divided host. For the nation of the Huns had expelled them from their ancient settlements. Two leaders ruled these nations, Fridigern and Athalicus. Since they disagreed with each other and raged in war, Athalicus sought refuge with Valens. Valens gave the said Athalicus assistance against Fridigern. Thus Athalicus, relying on the aid of Valens Augustus, overcame Fridigern.

In gratitude for this benefit, the simple Goths asked that bishops be sent to them, from whom they might learn the rule of faith. Then Valens, employing malicious perversity, sent them teachers of Arian doctrine, from whom they received the first rudiments of faith. There was also a certain bishop among them, Vulfila, whose episcopal words they preserved as though immutable laws. He invented Gothic letters, translated both Testaments into their own language, and corrupted them in accordance with the Arian sect.

The Goths themselves, after a short interval, compelled by hunger through the greed of the general Maximus, revolted from Valens and spread through Thrace. Valens marched out from Antioch and prepared a most fully equipped war against them. At the first shock of battle the disordered squadrons of cavalry abandoned the unprotected infantry. Soon the legions of infantry, encircled on every side by the enemy’s cavalry and overwhelmed by clouds of arrows, perished. The emperor himself, wounded, hid in the cottage of a certain small farm; discovered by the pursuing [Col. 0259D] enemy, he was burned up when they set fire to the cottage, in the fifteenth year of his reign.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Gratian and Valentinian.

Gratian, son of Valentinian, after Valens’ death ruled with his younger brother Valentinian for six years. He was a Catholic and modest man, very learned, restrained in food, and a conqueror of lust. But because he neglected his army and preferred to the Roman soldiers a few Alans whom he had bound to himself with gold, a certain Firmus in the regions of Africa, having stirred the nations of the Moors to support him, assumed the purple and began to ravage Africa and Mauretania. He also treacherously captured Caesaraugusta, a most renowned city of Spain, and gave it to barbarians as plunder.

[Col. 0260A] Hearing this, Gratian Augustus, and seeing the afflicted and desolate state of the commonwealth, summoned from Spain Theodosius, a man mature in character and age and energetic in military service. For this man had recently been sent to Spain by Valentinian the Great and had subdued the scattered nations of the Moors throughout Africa and Mauretania in many battles. Gratian accordingly made this man, renowned for his personal valor, emperor against Firmus.

Theodosius, as soon as he became emperor, subdued the barbarian nations in the East and freed Thrace from every tumult of war. Gratian too defeated the Huns and Goths in great battles and entered Constantinople in victory. Meanwhile in Britain a certain Maximus, a vigorous man and worthy of empire—had he not aspired against the commonwealth—seized tyranny. His prefect Andragathius killed Gratian by treachery and ambush. But Valentinian, learning of his brother’s death, fled into Illyricum, saying that he suffered this evil because of his mother, who was an Arian.

Theodosius, leaving his son Arcadius as emperor at Constantinople, hastened to avenge Gratian. On arriving in Italy, Valentinian met him. Theodosius received him with paternal kindness; then he crossed the Alps, captured Maximus, and killed him. Andragathius, learning of Maximus’ death, threw himself headlong into the waves.

Thus the younger Valentinian was established in the kingdom. After Maximus had been killed and his son defeated—the son whom Maximus had left as emperor to the Gauls—Valentinian himself withdrew into Gaul. There, while he governed the tranquil commonwealth in peace, he was, as they say, strangled at Vienne through the treachery of his count Arbogast.

After Valentinian Augustus died, Arbogast immediately dared to make the tyrant Eugenius emperor. He chose a man on whom he might place the imperial belt, while himself increasing the imperial power. Immediately that man, barbarous in spirit, excessive in courage, boldness, and power, joined with his son and gathered innumerable forces, supported in some places by Roman garrisons, elsewhere by barbarian auxiliaries, by authority in one place and by kinship in another.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Theodosius the Great.

Theodosius the Great, after the death of the emperor Gratian, ruled for fifteen years. As [Col. 0260D] has been said, after the younger Valentinian had been killed, Eugenius and Arbogast deployed their armed battle lines on the plains. They had also cunningly occupied the high slopes of the Alps and the impassable passes with ambushes set in advance; although inferior in number and strength, they were nevertheless victorious by their position in war alone.

But Theodosius, stationed on the high Alps, without sleep or food, knowing that he was deserted by his own men but not knowing that he was enclosed by strangers, prayed to the Lord Christ—alone, to the only One who can do all things—his body prostrate on the ground, his mind fixed in heaven. Then, after passing a sleepless night in continual prayer and leaving pools of tears as witnesses, which he had added to his prayers for heavenly aid, he confidently seized his weapons. Knowing himself to be [Col. 0261A] not alone, though alone, he gave the sign of the cross for battle and committed himself to war, destined to conquer even if no one followed him.

The first path to safety was Count Arbitio of the enemy party. Having caught the unaware emperor in surrounding ambushes, Arbitio turned in reverence toward the present Augustus and not only freed him from danger but also supplied him with assistance. When they reached positions close enough for battle to be joined, a great whirlwind of winds rushed into the faces of the enemy. The missiles of our men were borne through the sharp air and carried across empty space beyond the measure of a human throw; they were not allowed to fall anywhere before striking. The missiles which the enemy themselves had hurled forcefully were caught by the violence of the wind, turned upside down and driven backward, and unhappily pierced their own men.

Thus fear for their human consciences took thought for itself. For immediately, when a small band of their own men had been routed, the hostile army threw itself down before the victorious Theodosius; Eugenius was captured and killed, while Arbogast struck himself with his own hand. Thus civil war was extinguished by the blood of these two.

Finally the most faithful emperor, rising against the error of the pagans, took care to overthrow it utterly. He therefore promulgated a law commanding the temples of idols to be razed to the ground. For until his time fire was kindled on the altars of idols, and libations and sacrifices were offered. But Theodosius, a Catholic emperor, commanded all these things to be eradicated from the roots: he uprooted, suppressed, and condemned them.

Theodosius the emperor, with the commonwealth now peacefully settled, fell ill at Milan. As the illness worsened, [Col. 0261C] he found the rest of a natural death in the sixteenth year of his reign and the fortieth year of his life. At the same time Jerome the presbyter flourished, an interpreter of the divine law after the Seventy.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the rulers Arcadius and Honorius.

After the death of his father Theodosius, the emperor Arcadius obtained the Empire and ruled with his brother Honorius for thirteen years. Arcadius ruled in the eastern regions and Honorius in the western. The care of both their palaces, however, remained entrusted to two most powerful men, Rufinus and Stilicho.

The soldiers who had gone out against the tyrant Eugenius while Theodosius was still alive returned to Constantinople with the aforesaid Rufinus as leader. When the emperor met them at the gates according to custom, [Col. 0261D] the soldiers immediately killed the aforesaid Rufinus, for he was suspected by the emperor of being able to seize tyranny.

The prefect Count Stilicho, calling the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Burgundians to arms, began to assail Gaul in war, hoping under this emergency to transfer the Roman Empire to his son Eleutherius. When this was made known to the emperor Honorius, he ordered Stilicho killed. His son Eleutherius was also killed in those days.

After these events, the king of the Goths besieged Rome, having first issued an order that anyone who fled to holy places should remain free and unharmed. Not long afterwards Alaric, also called Athalaric, died. His kinsman Athanulf succeeded him and likewise broke into Rome. In that invasion he carried off as captive Placidia, daughter of Theodosius and sister of Arcadius and Honorius, [Col. 0262A] and married her. This afterwards greatly benefited the commonwealth, for Athanulf ultimately served the Augustus Honorius quite faithfully.

The emperor Arcadius, after ruling thirteen years with his father Theodosius and fourteen with his brother Honorius, died, leaving behind his eight-year-old son Theodosius. Under him arose the heresy of the Priscillianists, whose adherents endeavor to maintain that human beings are bound to the fateful stars. The Pelagian heresy also arose; those contaminated by it endeavor to destroy the prayers which the Church makes for the faithful.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the emperors Honorius and Theodosius the Younger.

[Col. 0262B]

After Arcadius’ death, the emperor Honorius ruled with his nephew Theodosius for sixteen years. Honorius, as has already been said, governed the western regions, whereas the eastern provinces were subject to Theodosius, Arcadius’ son.

Athanulf, king of the Goths, whom we mentioned above, was killed through the treachery of his own people at Barcelona, a city of Spain. Segeric succeeded him. He established an excellent peace with the emperor Honorius and honorably restored to him his sister Placidia, whom he had kept with him. Honorius gave her in marriage to Count Constantine and made him emperor at Ravenna.

In these days the body of Stephen the protomartyr was revealed to the venerable presbyter Lucian. Augustine, bishop of the church of Hippo and an outstanding teacher, also flourished at the same time.

But Honorius, after the ten years during which he had ruled with his brother Arcadius and the other fifteen during which he had ruled with his nephew Theodosius, departed from human affairs. After his death, a certain John, a tyrant, seized the western Empire. But Ardabur, a patrician sent by Theodosius, killed him within Ravenna. Theodosius then took the boy Valentinian, son of the aforesaid Placidia and Constantine, crowned him, and sent him with his mother Placidia to Italy, appointing him emperor and Placidia Augusta.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the rulers Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian.

[Col. 0262D]

Theodosius the Younger ruled with Valentinian for twenty-one years. At the same time the nation of the Saxons reached Britain in three long ships and occupied almost the entire island from its eastern side to its western. Then too, since the Pelagian heresy had stained the faith of the English, the Gallic bishops sent Germanus of Auxerre and Lupus of Troyes, distinguished bishops, to eradicate that heresy.

At that time also Eudoxia, Theodosius’ daughter and Valentinian’s wife, the empress, brought the chains with which Saint Peter had once been bound by Herod.

In these days, in the city of Constantinople, a certain bishop named Nestorius, endowed with secular eloquence, taught against the Catholic faith: that holy Mary was not the Mother of God, and that a mere human being was born from her, but that God was afterwards mingled with the man. Therefore the third holy synod was convened at Ephesus by order of Pope Celestine. Two hundred fathers assembled, and there Nestorius was condemned and anathematized; it was confirmed that blessed Mary should be called *Theotokos*, Θεοτόκος, that is, “Mother of God.”

At the same time Saint Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, flourished; he instituted the three Rogation Days. But Theodosius Augustus died at Constantinople in the forty-second year of his reign.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning the emperors Marcian and Valentinian.

[Col. 0263B]

Marcian, having been raised to the Empire, ruled with Valentinian for six years. While the Parthians and Vandals were harassing the Roman realm, he established peace with them. In the times of these emperors—Marcian and Valentinian, that is—the fourth holy universal synod was celebrated at Chalcedon, comprising six hundred and thirty venerable bishops and gathered through the diligence of holy Pope Leo. There the heretic Eutyches, together with Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, was deposed and condemned.

Meanwhile the emperor Valentinian, at the instigation of the eunuch Heraclius, killed Agerius, a patrician. But not long afterward Valentinian himself was killed by Agerius’ retainers through the treachery of Count Maximinus of the palace. At once Maximinus seized his Empire and compelled Valentinian’s wife to enter into marriage with him. [Col. 0263C] Yet he did not enjoy this licentiousness for long. For after a second month he was torn limb from limb by the king’s servants and thrown into the Tiber. After his death the Romans made Avitus Caesar. Marcian, however, died in the sixth year and likewise the sixth month of his reign.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning Leo the Great.

Leo the Great, having obtained the empire after the death of Marcian, reigned sixteen years. In his first year Avitus, emperor of the West, having been despised and abandoned by his army in Gaul, returned to Italy and, after a few days, laid aside the honor of his rank and was ordained bishop of Piacenza. In the same year [Col. 0263D] Majorian was appointed Caesar of Italy at Ravenna by the Roman soldiers. He went to [Col. 0264A] Spain and proposed to cross from there against his own people to Carthage; but, wholly disappointed in his hope, he returned to Italy, where, scarcely having completed the third year of his rule, he died. Then Emperor Leo sent Arthemius as Caesar into Italy. When he reached Rome, he dispatched his son-in-law Ricimer against the Alans; through him he put a great multitude of Alans to flight and slew their king Beorgicus, overcome in the first onset of battle. But not long afterward Arthemius himself, murdered through Ricimer’s treachery, left the kingdom to Olybrius. Olybrius, however, did not live to complete the eighth month of his rule. When he died, Glycerius presumed to seize the empire for himself.
