But scarcely a year having elapsed, a certain man named Nepos drove him from the kingdom, caused him to be ordained bishop [Col. 0264B], and seized the kingdom for himself.

Seeing such changes and vicissitudes among Roman rulers, Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, occupied the city of the Arverni. Against him Nepos Caesar ordered Orestes, master of his army, to advance from Italy. But when Orestes came with an army to Ravenna, he made his own son Augustulus emperor. Hearing this, Nepos, stripped of his guard, fled to the Dalmatians, where he died in private life. While Augustulus was residing at Ravenna, Odoacer, king of the Totilingi, having with him Heruli and auxiliary troops of various nations, occupied Italy. He killed Orestes, drove his son Augustulus from the kingdom, and condemned him to exile in the Campanian fortress of Lucullanum. Thus the western kingdom of the Roman people—which Octavius [Octavian] Augustus, the first of the Augusti, had held in the seven hundred and [Col. 0264C] ninth year from the founding of the city—lost the privilege of its dignity in this Augustulus and at last, having fallen into the hands of kings of foreign nations, collapsed. Finally, the aforementioned Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, occupied Illyricum and a great part of Italy. Leo, emperor of the East, made his son-in-law Zeno master of the whole East; he appointed Basiliscus, brother of the Augusta Verina, commander of Thrace; and he crowned his own son Leo as Augustus.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Leo the Second, Basiliscus, and Zeno

Leo the Second, after his father’s death, reigned one year. When he died, Basiliscus, brother of Verina, was acclaimed Augustus by the palace soldiers; but Zeno eventually [Col. 0264D] became emperor.

# BOOK NINE

Treating of the emperors from Zeno to Charlemagne; containing twenty-three chapters.

[Col. 0263]

## CHAPTER I. On Zeno

[Col. 0263D]

Zeno therefore, having received the diadem, reigned two years with Basiliscus and fifteen alone. Moreover, [Col. 0264D] this Zeno composed the *Henoticon* against the ecclesiastical faith. He also caused Theodoric, king of the Visigoths, to come to him, entrusted to him the charge of his palace [Col. 0265A], and, not many days later, once again distinguished him with the honor of the patriciate and dispatched him to Italy. When he arrived there, he defeated Odoacer, king of the Heruli, in various engagements and finally killed him after driving him from the kingdom. Then he presumed and usurped the kingdom of Italy for himself.

In order to establish it permanently for himself, he married his daughters to neighboring kings: he gave one to Alaric, king of the Goths; another to Sigismund, king of the Burgundians; his niece to Hermenfrid, king of the Thuringians; and his sister to Thrasamund, king of the Vandals; he also united the daughter of Clovis, king of the Franks, to himself in marriage. Finally, he established his seat at Ravenna, a man of the Arian sect, bearing in his heart a bestial cruelty against Catholics. At the same [Col. 0265B] time, the crypt of Saint Michael the Archangel was discovered on Mount Gargano. After Emperor Zeno’s death, a certain Anastasius, chosen by the Augusta, became known to all both as emperor and as husband of the Augusta.

## CHAPTER II. On Anastasius

Anastasius therefore, assuming the purple, reigned twenty years. Corrupted by Acacius, bishop of Constantinople, he favored heretics and persecuted Catholics. The venerable Pope Hormisdas sent to rebuke him for his error. But the faithless Anastasius gave this answer through his envoy: “We wish to command, not to be commanded.” But while he persisted in his perfidy, he perished by a stroke of lightning. At the same time Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, flourished.

## CHAPTER III. On Justin the Elder

[Col. 0265C]

Justin therefore, a most Christian emperor, succeeding the faithless Anastasius in the kingdom, reigned twenty-three years in the five hundred and eleventh year of the Lord’s Incarnation. To him the venerable Pope Hormisdas sent from the imperial city Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua; the priests John and Claudinus; the deacons Felix and Dioscorus; and also his notary Peter, so that he might restore to their own churches the bishops whom Anastasius had caused to go into exile for the Catholic faith. The most merciful emperor received them all with great joy and honorably sent them back.

After Hormisdas [Col. 0265D], John ascended the apostolic chair. He too came to the same ruler. When he arrived at Constantinople and the man of God was honorably received there by the emperor and by almost all the people of that city, he immediately granted sight, before their eyes, to a blind man who asked for it at the gate called the Golden Gate. Having at last secured the things for which he had gone, he returned to Ravenna. There the oft-named tyrant Theodoric, through jealousy and envy because he had heard that John had been honorably received and treated by the Augustus, detained him with his companions and killed him by the affliction of imprisonment; he also killed the patrician Symmachus.

The same tyrant condemned to exile Boethius, a consular man of the highest wisdom, who had ennobled dialectic, arithmetic, and music in his own language and had composed other treatises [Col. 0266A] with the greatest elegance; and he caused him to be beheaded in the territory of Milan. Yet Theodoric did not long enjoy impunity for this monstrous cruelty. Not long afterward he breathed out a soul polluted with sins in a horrible and unexpected death. A certain solitary living on the island of Lipari even saw, with bodily eyes, that soul plunged into Vulcan’s cauldron, where the sea boils like a kettle from fire.

Theodoric the king was succeeded by his grandson Athalaric, and Athalaric by Theodald. While the Lombards were still dwelling in Pannonia, Alboin son of Aldoin ruled over them; not long afterward he brought the Lombard people themselves into Italy. Meanwhile Justin, the most Christian Augustus, fought successfully against the Parthians and finally established a most firm treaty with their king. When he too was approaching death, he designated as his successor his nephew Justinian, son of his sister.

## CHAPTER IV. On Justinian the Great

Justinian the Great, having obtained the empire, reigned thirty-eight years and eleven days. He triumphed over many peoples. For in the seventh year of his reign the Vandal wars took place, and Belisarius recovered Africa. With God’s favor he proceeded there with great speed, defeated the unbelieving Vandals, and at last restored all Africa, formerly torn away, to the body of the ancient commonwealth. For Gelimer, king of the Vandals, unable to endure Belisarius’s power, fled to the Moors. But Belisarius swiftly pursued and captured him there, brought him with him bound in a silver chain [Col. 0266C], and celebrated a triumph over him at Constantinople.

Not long afterward Emperor Justinian sent that same Belisarius to Italy. On arriving, Belisarius seized Sicily at his first approach, besieged Naples, captured it, and plundered it. When Theodald, king of Italy, heard this, he sent Vitigis, commander of his army, against him. But after Vitigis entered Campania and was made king by the army, he abandoned the expedition and returned. Then, rejecting Theodald and repudiating his first wife, he married Matasuntha [Mathesuntha], niece of King Theodoric. But while he delighted in his new marriage, Belisarius entered Rome and was received with rejoicing. He immediately occupied the neighboring places, Rome, [Col. 0266D] and the garrisons of the towns. When these things had been accomplished without delay, King Vitigis attacked Rome and surrounded it with a siege for a whole year. But Belisarius finally consumed his engines with fire, drove him thence in flight as far as Rimini, and, after not many days had passed, received him at Ravenna, where he was shut in, upon surrender; he transported him with his wife and the wealth of the palace to Constantinople. Thus Justinian, the orthodox Augustus, in a brief interval of time nobly triumphed over two powerful nations through the hand of the illustrious commander Belisarius.

After Belisarius’s departure, the Goths dwelling beyond the Po and in Liguria rebelled against the Romans and made Totila, also called Baiola, their king. Fighting the Romans often, he repeatedly broke and overcame their forces. At the same [Col. 0267A] time in Italy there shone, both by grace and by name, Benedict, a man of the Lord. When the aforesaid Totila came to him in order to discover whether he possessed the spirit of prophecy, the man of God foretold what would happen to him, saying: “You do many evils and have done many; now at last cease from wickedness. You shall indeed enter Rome, you shall cross the sea, you shall reign nine years, and in the tenth you shall die.”

Thus, not long afterward, when he had crossed the sea, laid waste Sicily, returned from there, surrounded and captured Rome, he ordered his men to sound their trumpets throughout almost the whole night, so that the Romans might hide themselves from the Goths by whatever means they could. Rome was therefore captured by the aforesaid King Totila in the twenty-first year of Emperor Justinian. [Col. 0267B] Hearing this, Justinian appointed the wise man Narses patrician of the Romans and sent him to Italy. Upon arriving, he defeated King Totila, and Totila died in accordance with the prophecy of Father Benedict.

At the same time a great mortality occurred at Byzantium. For this reason, in that same year the feast of the Purification of Saint Mary, Mother of God, began to be celebrated on the second day of February, and that mortality ceased. This feast is customarily called in Greek the Lord’s *Hypante* (ὑπαντή), “Meeting,” because on that very day, when the Lord was brought into the Temple, Simeon and Anna came to meet him; for Greek ὑπαντάω (*hypantaō*) means “I go to meet,” as a mark of honor.

After this, in the thirtieth year of his reign, Emperor Justinian, led astray by Anthimus [Col. 0267C] the bishop, began to depart from the Catholic faith. And when he turned the ear of his heart away from the divine commandments, by the just judgment of God he fell into madness. Therefore, summoning the most Christian Justin, he made him *curopalates* and entrusted to him the care of the entire empire. Having done this, he died in the thirty-eighth year and seventh month of his reign. In these times Priscian the grammarian flourished in the imperial city, and at Rome a certain subdeacon named Arator, who sang [expounded] the Acts of the Apostles in hexameter verse.

## CHAPTER V. On Justin the Younger

Justin the Younger, a Thracian by birth, having been made emperor from the office of *curopalates*, reigned twelve years, ten months, and twenty days in the five hundred and seventy-second year of the Lord’s Incarnation. [Col. 0267D] In his time Narses, patrician of the Romans, mentioned above, had made all Italy peaceful by repelling incursions of various enemies; but for his great benefits he suffered great envy from the Romans. They sent word to Justin in the imperial city that it was better for the Romans to serve the Goths than the Greeks, where Narses, a eunuch, ruled and exercised dominion according to his own pleasure. Moved by these words, the emperor appointed his prefect Longinus in Narses’s place.

The Augusta Sophia also sent this insult to Narses: that he should return to Constantinople with his girls and distribute the bundles of wool in the women’s gynaeceum. Narses is said to have replied that he would weave for her a web which, while she lived, she would never unravel. Then, withdrawing to Naples, he sent word to the Lombards that they should leave the poor fields of Pannonia which they inhabited and flock to take possession of the fertile soil of Italy. [Col. 0268A] Hearing this, Alboin king of the Lombards entered Italy with a great multitude of Lombards in the five hundred and seventy-eighth year from the Lord’s Incarnation. He then entered Milan and, within a short space of time, subjected to himself almost all Italy except Rome and Ravenna.

Accordingly, in the eighth year of his reign Emperor Justin began to suffer in his feet. Therefore he took Tiberius, commander of the excubitors, adopted him as a son, and declared him his successor.

## CHAPTER VI. On Emperor Tiberius L [the Fiftieth]

[Col. 0268B]

Tiberius therefore, the fiftieth emperor of the Romans, having assumed the empire in the five hundred and eighty-second year of the divine Incarnation, reigned three years, ten months, and nine days. He was a Catholic and devout man. Accordingly, he restored many churches in Constantinople. He also entered the land of the Persians and most powerfully defeated them; returning from there, he brought back so vast a mass of booty, together with many elephants, that it might have been thought sufficient for human greed.

Moreover, when this same Augustus Tiberius foresaw that the end of his life was near, he chose for the empire a certain man, a Cappadocian by birth, vigorous and most wise, named Maurice. He gave him his daughter Constantia, adorned with royal ornaments, saying: “Let my empire be granted to you together with this girl. Use it happily, therefore, and keep constantly in mind that equity and justice are the foremost insignia of an excellent emperor.” [Col. 0268C] After saying this, he breathed out his spirit. When Tiberius died, Maurice, clothed in purple and crowned with the diadem, proceeded to the circus; amid acclamations of praise and distributions of customary gifts, he became the first man of Greek descent to possess the Roman empire.

## CHAPTER VII. On Maurice, the First Greek Emperor among the Romans

Maurice, a Cappadocian by birth, having obtained the Roman empire, defeated the Huns with great skill. At this same time Saint Gregory [Col. 0268D] established the sevenfold litany because of the plague called the groin-plague, and the people were swiftly delivered. It was called a sevenfold litany because all the people were divided into seven groups. In the first choir was all the clergy; in the second, all abbots with their monks; in the third, all abbesses with their communities; in the fourth, all children; in the fifth, all laypeople; in the sixth, all widows; and in the seventh, all married women.

The same Saint Gregory sent Augustine, Mellitus, and John, with many others, into Britain, in order to convert the English people to the faith of Christ. Through the labor of these men he won that people for God. Moreover, while Emperor Maurice was a God-fearing man, he preferred in this world to pay the penalty for his sins by bodily punishment [Col. 0269A] rather than to be tormented by the pains of hell; and because he continually prayed to the Lord for this, he deserved to be heard.

One night, as he rested in his bed, he saw in a dream before him the bronze image of the Savior that stood before the palace gate. From it a voice was sent forth to him, saying: “Give me Maurice.” Some officers of the court brought him forward. Then the image of the Savior said to him: “Where do you wish that I should repay you the evils you have deserved: here or in the world to come?” And he said: “O Lord, lover of humankind, here rather than there.” Then the divine voice ordered that he, his wife Constantia, and all their kindred should be handed over to the soldier Phocas.

Upon waking, he sent for his son-in-law Philippicus. When Philippicus stood by him, [Col. 0269B] Maurice said: “Do you know any soldier in our ranks named Phocas?” He answered: “I know one.” The emperor asked: “What kind of man is he?” He replied: “Young, swollen with pride, and rash.” Then Emperor Maurice, recounting his dream to Philippicus, greatly glorified God for such a revelation.

After this, while Emperor Maurice was in enemy territory and compelled his soldiers to refrain from violence and plunder, yet did not distribute their customary pay to them, they began to urge Phocas to accept imperial rule over them. Phocas, so often mentioned, complying with them, took the imperial purple. When Maurice heard this, broken in spirit and beset by adverse circumstances, he yielded and fled into a certain forest adjoining the sea. There, by order of Caesar Phocas, he was killed with his wife and five sons. [Col. 0269C]

## CHAPTER VIII. On Phocas

Phocas therefore, invading the Roman empire through his own rashness, reigned eight years. When he became emperor, he crowned his wife Leontia Augusta. In the second year of his reign the venerable Pope Gregory departed from this life. Sabinus was ordained in his place to the apostolic office; Sabinus was succeeded by Boniface III, and Boniface III by Boniface IV.

At the latter’s request, the aforesaid Augustus decreed [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Decreed,” that is, declared, against the insolence of the bishops of Constantinople; for this did not belong to the secular power, and all Roman pontiffs from Peter to Boniface exercised the primacy without interruption. See, among others, Melchior Cano on this matter.] that the see of the Roman and apostolic Church was the head of all churches. For previously the Church of Constantinople styled itself the first of all churches. The same Pope Boniface also obtained from the aforesaid ruler [Col. 0269D] the grant to Christ’s Church of the temple at Rome which in ancient times was called the Pantheon.

Because Phocas raged cruelly against his own household, he was killed by order of Heraclius, patrician of Africa, who after his death claimed the commonwealth for himself.

## CHAPTER IX. On Heraclius

Heraclius, having obtained the Roman empire in the six hundred and fifteenth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, reigned thirty years. He found the commonwealth greatly disordered and worn down. For the Avars had grievously devastated Europe. In his days also Chosroes, king of the Persians, [Col. 0270A] captured Damascus, laid Jerusalem waste, burned the venerable places in it, took a multitude of people captive together with Zacharias, patriarch of that city, and carried with him into Persia the precious wood of Christ’s cross.

Heraclius defeated Chosroes’s commanders Sarabbagas and Sabasas, Sain and Razates, and captured many fortifications. Finally Chosroes was captured by him and sent into prison, where he also died. These things having been accomplished, Heraclius returned to Byzantium with the holy wood of the Lord’s cross. Then, having bestowed generous rewards on his soldiers and rested a little, he brought the wood of the holy cross back to Jerusalem, giving God very great thanks for such victories.

But at the same time Cyrus, bishop of Alexandria, [Col. 0270B] and Sergius, patriarch of Constantinople, were preaching the heresy of the Monothelites. Corrupted by them, Emperor Heraclius departed from the Catholic faith. Therefore, by divine judgment, the Hagarenes, also called Saracens, under the leadership of Hummar, began to tear apart his empire. At this same time the Saracens, also called Turks, led by Mahomet the false prophet, left their settlements and began to devastate Heraclius’s empire. This Mahomet, leader and false prophet of the Saracens and Arabs, was of the race of Ishmael, son of Abraham.

Finally Emperor Heraclius died in the thirty-first year of his reign. After his death, his son Heraclius Constantine reigned four months. When these were scarcely completed, he was killed by poison administered by [Col. 0270C] his stepmother Martina. Thus, when he died, his brother Heraclonas reigned in his place with their mother Martina.

## CHAPTER X. On Heraclonas

Heraclonas, son of Heraclius, reigned with his mother Martina six months. During this reign Machinas, admiral of the Arabs, sent by Hummar, captured Caesarea of Palestine and killed seven thousand people in it. In the same year the senate expelled Heraclonas with his mother Martina; having cut out Martina’s tongue and cut off Heraclonas’s nose, it raised to the empire Constans, son of Heraclius Constantine and grandson of Heraclius.

## CHAPTER XI. On Constans, Son of Heraclius Constantine

Constans, son of Heraclius Constantine and grandson of Emperor Heraclius, obtained the Roman empire at Byzantium in the six hundred and forty-fourth year of the divine Incarnation and reigned twenty-six years. [Col. 0270D] He too fell into the heresy of the Monothelites, as had his grandfather Emperor Heraclius, through the poison of perfidy suggested to him by Paul, bishop of Constantinople, who succeeded Pyrrhus in the episcopate. He condemned many of the orthodox to beatings and exile because they would in no way assent to his heresy.

Since he was hateful to almost everyone at Byzantium, he sailed to Italy, wishing both to rescue it from Lombard power and to remain there for some time. Departing from the imperial city, he came to Athens and, crossing the sea from there, invaded the territory of Benevento. But Grimoald, duke of that province, severely crushed his army. Seeing, therefore, that he achieved nothing against the Lombards, the Augustus went to Rome. At the sixth mile from the city Pope Julian reverently met him and led him, amid a great crowd of people, to the shrine of Saint Peter. [Col. 0271A] When he arrived, he offered Saint Peter an excellent pallium woven with gold.

After he had remained in the city for twelve days, moved by great greed, he carried off to the Tiber diverse kinds of ornaments of bronze and marble with which the city was adorned, so as to transport them to Constantinople. Among these, he stripped the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and of All Martyrs—which was formerly called the Pantheon—of its bronze roof tiles. [Col. 0271B] Having done this, he resolved to return. Departing from Rome, he sailed to Sicily. There, while one day he was bathing more privately in a bath, he was killed by his own men.

After his death the soldiers chose a certain Armenian, Mezentium, and made him emperor. But not many days later Constantine, son of the deceased Augustus Constans, arrived there with many ships, assumed the imperial purple, and condemned Mezentium and the murderers of his father to a most wretched death.

## CHAPTER XII. On Constantine, Son of Constans

Constantine, son of Constans, after his father’s death, obtained his empire in the six hundred and eightieth year of Christ’s Incarnation and reigned sixteen years. He was [Col. 0271C] a man Catholic in faith and restrained in character. Employing wise counsel, he made a most firm peace with the Arabs dwelling in Damascus and with the Bulgars. He also restored churches that had been destroyed since the time of his great-grandfather Heraclius. Moreover, he rose against the Monothelites, striving to overthrow their opinions, who believed and preached that there was only one nature in our Lord Jesus Christ.

When Constantine, the orthodox Augustus, died in the imperial city, his son Justinian received by hereditary right the governance of the empire.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Justinian

Justinian, succeeding his father in the kingdom, reigned ten years in the six hundred and ninety-sixth year of the divine Incarnation. [Col. 0271D] Being about sixteen years old, he acted with youthful rashness and broke the peace which his father had established with Abimelech, leader of the Arabs, disturbing peace with the Bulgars and the arrangements that his father had made in good order. He also renewed the army of the Marcianites, by which he defended his empire from Arab attack. After they had been restrained, the Arab rule possessed peace and quiet until the present day. From that time the barbarians more freely ravaged Romania.

Afterward Justinian marched against the Slavs and overthrew many of them. But while returning from there, hemmed in by the Bulgars in a narrow defile, he scarcely managed to return, with slaughter and wounding among his own people. He also supported Stephen the Persian, his *sacellarius*, a cruel and utterly wicked man, who grievously oppressed many leaders of the commonwealth. In the emperor’s absence, this man presumptuously had his mother, the Augusta Anastasia, whipped like a child. [Col. 0272A] This made him especially hateful to all the leaders and members of his household.

Therefore the patrician Leontius rose against him, with Patriarch Gallinicus conspiring with him; opening the prisons and releasing many confined persons—who had been kept in chains for six or eight years, many of them soldiers—he went out into the forum. Immediately he exiled Justinian to Cherson, having cut off his nose; then, fortified by the arms of the aforesaid men, he seized the Augustal dignity.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Emperor Leontius

Leontius, having assumed the empire in the seven hundredth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, [Col. 0272B] reigned three years. In the third year of his reign the Arabs were defeating Africa. Against them he sent the patrician John with a numerous fleet. When he reached Carthage, he put the Arabs to flight and wintered there. At length he returned to the emperor, intending to ask him for a larger fleet. But the army remaining in Africa, during the absence of the patrician John, chose a certain Apsimar, whom it also named Tiberius, and made him emperor. Apsimar, taking the fleet that was with him, sailed to the city and without delay entered it through the wall of Blachernae, seized Leontius, and sent him into exile.

## CHAPTER XV. On Apsimar, or Tiberius

Apsimar, also called Tiberius, reigned about seven years. [Col. 0272C] He exiled Philippicus, son of Nicephorus, who asserted that in a dream he had seen his head overshadowed by an eagle, because such a dream seemed to signify that he himself would become king.

While Apsimar was ruling, Justinian, living at Cherson, began openly to proclaim to the people that he would again recover his empire. For this reason the inhabitants of the place, stirred by zeal for the Augustus, were preparing, because of this claim, either to kill him as one plotting against the king or to seize and send him to the emperor. But when Justinian learned this, he fled and presented himself to the khagan of the Turks. The khagan received him honorably and gave him his own sister as wife. [Col. 0272D] From there he sailed to Terebellus, king of Bulgaria, who likewise gave him aid and restored him to his empire.

## CHAPTER XVI. Again on Justinian Restored, and His Cruelty

Justinian then reigned a second time for six years. As soon as he recovered the empire, he killed all who had formerly expelled him; and he ordered Apsimar, led into the circus and worn down by many humiliations, to be beheaded. He also sent Patriarch Gallinicus to Rome after tearing out his eyes, and installed Abbot Pyrrhus in his place. Finally, he killed an innumerable multitude of citizens.

He resolved to destroy Cherson, where he had lived in exile. Gathering all the vessels he could obtain—dromons, that is, triremes, skiffs, [Col. 0273A] *chimaerae*, and boats as far as the *chelandria*—he sent them there, ordering that all its inhabitants, from the least to the greatest, be killed. When they arrived, the patrician Maurice and the *spatharius* Elias, following the emperor’s command, killed everyone except infants. They sent Tuduinus, leader of the city, together with forty other leading men, to the emperor; and they fastened seven other chief men of the same city to wooden spits and roasted them over a fire.

Then Justinian sent another fleet in October, ordering that all the children who had been spared be put to death. But almost the entire fleet was sunk in the sea, and seventy-three thousand persons perished there. Learning this, Justinian, still raging with great cruelty, sent another fleet again, ordering the whole city to be ploughed up and dashed to the ground. [Col. 0273B] Hearing this, the people of that province took Philippicus, who was in exile there, and made him emperor. Then Philippicus came to Constantinople and killed Emperor Justinian and his son Tiberius together.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Philippicus Bardanes

Philippicus, also called Bardanes, made emperor at Cherson in the seven hundred and twenty-second year of the divine Incarnation, reigned one year and a half. Being a heretic, he exiled Cyrus, bishop of Constantinople, and placed in the same see a pseudo-bishop of his own opinion, a monk named John. Philippicus himself [Col. 0273C] sent letters of corrupt doctrine to Pope Constantine at Rome. The holy man, with the counsel of the Roman people, rejected them and ordered that Philippicus’s name should not be entered in documents, that no coinage bearing his stamp should be accepted, and that his name should not be recited at the solemnities of the Mass.

After Philippicus had reigned one year and half a year, Anastasius rose against him, deprived him of his eyes, deposed him from imperial dignity, and claimed his empire for himself. In Italy, however, after the death of Aripert, his son Liutprand ruled.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Anastasius Artemius

Anastasius, also called Artemius, reigned three years and six months. Being a Catholic man, he sent letters to Pope Constantine through Scholasticus, patrician and exarch of Italy, [Col. 0273D] declaring himself a defender of the Catholic faith and a proclaimer of the holy Sixth Council. After this he sent a fleet to Alexandria against the Saracens. The entire army, adopting another plan, returned midway from its journey to Constantinople; seeking Theodosius, an orthodox man, it elected him emperor and compelled him to ascend the imperial throne. Theodosius defeated Anastasius in a severe battle near the city of Nicaea and afterward ordered him to become a priest.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Theodosius

Theodosius, after Anastasius’s death, reigned one year. When it was over, a certain most powerful man named Leo rose against him. He deposed him from the imperial [Col. 0274A] throne but allowed him to depart unharmed. Theodosius himself, afterward made a cleric, passed the remainder of his life in peace.

## CHAPTER XX. On Leo

Leo, having obtained the Roman empire in the seven hundred and twenty-seventh year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, reigned twenty-four years. In his days the people of the Saracens besieged Constantinople hostilely for almost three years. But as the citizens earnestly entreated God with many prayers, that powerless nation at last took flight and subsequently, while sailing on the open sea, was overwhelmed and perished in a sudden storm.

In the eighth year of his reign Emperor Leo ordered all holy images to be destroyed. He abhorred them with the greatest hatred, as well as all miracle-working relics of the saints. After this, King Liutprand of Italy, hearing that the Saracens had ravaged Sardinia and defiled the place where the bones of Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, rested—bones which had long before been transferred and honorably buried there because of the ravages of barbarians—sent there and, paying a price, received them and transferred them to Pavia. There he placed them in the monastery called the Golden Cell. [Col. 0274B]

Afterward a great earthquake occurred at Constantinople; many churches collapsed, and many people perished. In the same year Emperor Leo died, in both soul and body; and his son Constantine became successor alike to his empire and his impiety. The year from the creation of the world was, according to the Romans, six thousand two hundred and forty; but according to [Col. 0274C] the reckoning of the Egyptians and Alexandrians, six thousand two hundred and thirty-two.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Constantine the Impious

Constantine, persecutor of the laws handed down by the fathers, having assumed the empire, reigned thirty-four years, two months, and twenty-six days. Throughout his life he constantly devoted himself to magical sorceries, bloody sacrifices, and sensual excess. Under him many clerics, monks, and devout laypeople suffered danger because of the true faith. He also had in all things as his ally, through love of earthly rule, Anastasius, falsely so called patriarch of Constantinople. Therefore divine wrath came upon the citizens of that city, warning the impious emperor [Col. 0274D] to restrain himself from the madness by which he burned. But he remained uncorrected, like Pharaoh of old.

For a pestilential death came, beginning from Sicily and Calabria, to the imperial city, and devastated it so that even many entire houses in it were shut up because there was no one to inhabit them. The corpses of the dead were carried on wagons for burial. At the same time stars appeared falling from heaven, so that all who saw this thought the end of the age was at hand. Meanwhile the utterly wicked Emperor Constantine, marching against the Bulgars, contracted a terrible illness and died from it, no less full of the blood of martyrs than Diocletian. His son Leo IV succeeded him.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Leo

[Col. 0275A]

Leo, having obtained the empire in the seven hundred and eightieth year of Christ’s Nativity, reigned five years. He was succeeded by his son Constantine, a most Christian man.

### Chapter XXIII. Concerning the Emperor Constantine and His Mother Irene

Constantine, therefore, together with his mother Irene, obtained the Roman Empire in the year of the divine Incarnation 786, and reigned for ten years. Having made peace with the Arabs, he triumphed over the Slavs through the patrician Stauracius. At this time, moreover, Irene sent her sacellarius to Charles, king of the Franks, in order that he might give his daughter in marriage to her son, the Emperor Constantine; but she afterwards annulled this arrangement. For in the tenth year of the reign of Constantine and Irene [Col. 0275B], the devil stirred up the poison of discord between Irene herself and her son the emperor; she confined him under guard and reigned for five years.

When these years were completed, her son, relying on Armenian assistance, recovered the Empire once more. As soon as he had regained it, he immediately sent into exile the patrician Stauracius and Aetius the protospatharius, his mother’s friends, together with all her eunuch household servants. Irene herself, however, he placed, with abundant provision, in the palace of Eleutherius, which she had built and in which she had hidden much money. Afterwards he led his army against the Bulgars; but, defeated by them, he returned to the city having lost many men. On this account certain princes, angered against him, were preparing to make Nicephorus, son of his great-grandfather Constantine, emperor. When Constantine learned this [Col. 0275C], he immediately deprived that same Nicephorus and his brother Christopher of their tongues. He also blinded Alexius, patrician of the Armenians [Col. 0276A]. He further compelled his wife, named Maria, to become a nun, and crowned his chamberlain Theodora as Augusta.

Meanwhile Irene truly began, by gifts and possessions, to win over the generals and princes of the realm to her counsels, so that Augustus was seized a second time by his own household. For his mother’s counsellors deprived him of his eyes so cruelly that death immediately followed the torture. Thus Irene reigned a second time, for nearly five years. During this period the Roman Empire was transferred to the kings of the Franks, Charles the Great, son of Pippin, being made its first emperor. At Constantinople, however, the kingdom of the Greeks remained, and after Irene Nicephorus seized the Empire.

After Constantine the Great, the imperial seat was indeed at Constantinople [Col. 0276B], because that most pious and most Christian emperor, leaving for ever to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and to those holding his place, the privilege of the Roman see, had established the imperial seat for himself in that same city. Nevertheless, they continued to be called Roman emperors in dignity until the time when the Roman Empire was transferred to the kings of the Franks. Thereafter those who ruled at Constantinople, retaining only the name of empire, were called rather emperors of the Greeks. From this point the sequence of times is reckoned by the kings of the Franks. But before we describe the empire of Charles the Great, it is pleasant to sketch briefly something concerning the origin and kingdom of the Franks, lest we seem to pass over in complete silence the beginnings and achievements of so great a people [Col. 0276C].

## Book Ten

Treating of the people and kings of the Franks, from the origin of the Franks down to Charles the Great, and afterwards from Charles the Great down to the successors of Charles the Simple; containing ten chapters.

### Chapter I. Concerning the Origin of the Franks

[Col. 0275C]

The Franks were Trojans by origin. After the destruction of Troy, they departed thence under a certain leader Priam and settled near Thrace along the banks of the Danube. There they built a city [Col. 0275D] and called it Sicambria. They remained there until the time of the Emperor Valentinian, who expelled them because they refused to pay tribute to the Romans, as other peoples customarily did. Departing from there under the leaders Marcomir, Sunno, and Gennebaud, they came and settled around the bank of the Rhine on the border of Germany and Alemannia. Although Valentinian subsequently attacked them in many battles, he could not conquer them; he called them by a name of his own, Franks, as though *furnicos*, that is, fierce men. From that time the strength of the Franks grew so greatly that at last they subjugated all Germany and Gaul as far as, and beyond, the ridges of the Pyrenees.

Others maintain that the Franks were named after a certain Francio. For they say [Col. 0276C] that, after the ruin of Troy, a great multitude fled thence and then divided itself into two peoples: one part made a certain Francio its king, while the other followed one named Turcus [Teucrus]; and that from him the two peoples, taking their names, have been called Franks and Turks [Teucrians] down to the present day [Col. 0276D].

### Chapter II. Concerning the People of the Franks and Their Kings

After Marcomir’s death, the Frankish people made Pharamund their king. Clodio succeeded Pharamund; he captured Cambrai and, expelling the Romans from it, extended the boundary of his dominion as far as the river Somme. After Clodio, Meroveus reigned; after him the Merovingians were named, who are now called Franks. Childeric reigned after Meroveus, and Clovis after Childeric. Now Clovis married Clotild, a most Christian and very beautiful maiden [Col. 0277A], daughter of Childeric, formerly duke of Burgundy.

### Chapter III. Concerning King Clovis

Meanwhile the kingdom of the Franks began to expand, and the aforesaid King Clovis, son of Childeric, wished to be baptized by Saint Remigius, archbishop of Rheims, on the following occasion. One day, as he fought against the Alemanni and his army was being severely cut down, he raised his eyes to heaven and said: “O Lord Jesus Christ, whom my wife Clotild worships and adores, I devoutly beseech your aid; and if you grant me victory in this battle, I promise you that henceforth I shall believe in you and shall be baptized in your name.” When he had said this, the Alemanni were put to flight, and King Clovis returned triumphantly to his own land.

Then, having summoned the holy bishop Remigius [Col. 0277B], he faithfully fulfilled what he had vowed to God, and was baptized with his people in the fifteenth year of his reign. Clovis, moreover, desiring to enlarge his kingdom, invaded the kingdom of Aquitaine, which King Alaric held. When he had crossed the channel of the Loire, he turned aside at Tours to the basilica of Saint Martin. As he entered it, there resounded in the choir the voice of those chanting: “You have girded me, O Lord, with strength” (Psalm XVII), and so forth. On hearing this voice, he became more joyful and, giving thanks to God, continued his intended journey.

When he wished to cross the river called Vienne and could not find a ford because the swollen river had overflowed, a hind suddenly crossed by that same river and showed him the ford. Then he met Alaric ten miles from the city of Poitiers [Col. 0277C], where the two met and fought one another. But at length Alaric was there pierced and killed, and his army was scattered in every direction. Having achieved this victory, Clovis spent the winter at Bordeaux. When winter’s severity had passed and spring arrived, he made for Toulouse, the capital of the Gothic kingdom, and captured it. Taking Alaric’s treasures from there, he hastened to Angoulême. At his arrival, the city wall, by divine prompting, fell down of its own accord and offered the approaching king an open way.

From there he came to the city of Tours. While he rested his weary army there, he received letters from the Emperor Anastasius, by which Anastasius designated him consul and Augustus of the Roman commonwealth. Receiving this gratefully, he immediately put on the consular robe, and from that day deserved to be called both consul and Augustus [Col. 0277D]. Returning thence to Paris, he built there a royal church in thanksgiving for such great honours and benefits bestowed upon him by God, and ordered it to be consecrated to the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

Thereafter, through the enterprise of his son Theoderic, he joined to his kingdom the people of Limoges, the Rutenians, the Cadurci, the Arverni, and likewise the remaining peoples or provinces of Aquitaine, from the river Rhône to the channel of the Loire, and again from the Pyrenees to the whole Ocean—that is, all Alaric’s kingdom. Alaric’s son Amalaric also yielded to him unwillingly and migrated from Aquitaine into Spain. Thus, when the Arian Goths had been expelled from Aquitaine, the Catholic Franks immediately filled it with the religion and faith of a better rule.

Having accomplished these things, with God’s favour [Col. 0278A], and having extended the kingdom of the Franks far and wide, King Clovis died in the thirtieth year of his reign and the forty-fifth year of his life, leaving four sons as heirs to his kingdom. Succeeding their father, they divided the Frankish kingdom among themselves. Theoderic received Metz as the seat of his kingdom; Clodomir, Orléans; Clotaire, Soissons; and Childebert, Paris.

### Chapter IV. Concerning the Sons of Clovis

The three sons of Clovis—Clodomir, Childebert, and Clotaire—therefore made an alliance with one another and, desiring to enlarge the borders of their realm, entered the kingdom of Burgundy and attacked Sigismund and his brother Godomar in battle. At the first onset of war Sigismund was immediately captured by Clodomir [Col. 0278B], taken to Orléans, killed there, and thrown into a well. Not long afterwards, however, he was taken up from there and honourably buried in the monastery which he had built at the place called Agaune for Saint Maurice and his companions.

Then, after not many days had passed, the above-named brothers returned to Burgundy and again attacked Godomar, Sigismund’s brother. But Clodomir was killed in that expedition. His three sons, Guntram, Gerbald, and Clodoald, succeeded him. Childebert and Clotaire, however, besieged and killed Godomar at Autun and reduced all Burgundy to their power. Theoderic, the elder son of the aforementioned Clovis, entered the territory of the Thuringians with his brother Clotaire and his son Theodebert; having put Hermenfrid to flight [Col. 0278C], he reduced Hermenfrid’s kingdom to his own power.

On returning from there, Clotaire took with him Radegund, daughter of King Berthar and niece of Hermenfrid, and joined her to himself in lawful marriage. But after a short time she left the marital bed, took the religious habit within the city of Poitiers, and, persevering in it, honourably completed the course of her life. The son of the aforesaid Theoderic, named Theodebert, being a vigorous warrior, entered Italy while his father was still alive and made it tributary to himself from the Alps as far as the borders of the maritime regions. As he returned from there, he left the commander of his army, named Buccelinus, to overrun Sicily and the remaining places in Italy which he had not visited.

Again, the aforesaid brothers [Col. 0278D], Childebert and Clotaire, departing from Gaul, entered Spain. Having grievously devastated it, they carried away with them a great quantity of gold, together with the robe of Saint Vincent the martyr. Theodebert and Theobald succeeded Theoderic. At length the monarchy returned to Clotaire. After he had reigned at Soissons for sixty years, he died, leaving four sons as his successors: Chilperic at Soissons, Charibert at Paris, Guntram at Orléans, and Sigebert at Metz.

### Chapter V. Concerning the Sons of Clotaire and Certain Other Kings

Sigebert married Brunhild [Brunechild], daughter of Leovigild, king of Spain. His brother Chilperic, however, being licentious and vain [Col. 0279A], had many wives. Among them he had Fredegund, indeed sufficiently beautiful, but rich in most evil arts; she held the aforesaid Chilperic bound to her pleasures. She was accustomed to commit adultery with Landric, count of the palace. Chilperic eventually learned of this. But when she sensed the danger threatening her, she used feminine cunning, prepared to conceal one crime by a greater crime, and laid snares for her husband as he returned from hunting. For when Chilperic had dismounted from his horse and was being received by his own attendants, he was pierced with two daggers and killed. His son Clotaire nevertheless succeeded him.

Before these events, the aforesaid King Sigebert, son of Clotaire king of the Franks, had been killed. His son Childebert undertook to govern his kingdom together with his mother Brunhild. Not long afterward [Col. 0279B], Guntram, Chilperic’s full brother, died, leaving his kingdom to his nephew, the aforesaid Childebert. Childebert himself, after reigning twenty-three years in Austrasia and four in Burgundy, died, leaving two sons as his heirs. One of them, named Theobert, governed the kingdom of the Austrasians, while Theoderic governed Guntram’s kingdom.

But when Theobert and Theoderic had died by varying fortunes, Clotaire obtained the Frankish kingdom. At the judgment of the Franks, Clotaire ordered Queen Brunhild to be tied to an unbroken horse and torn apart for her various wicked deeds. Dagobert succeeded Clotaire. When Dagobert saw death pressing upon him, he granted the kingdom of Austrasia to his son Sigebert and the kingdom of Neustria to Clovis.

Austrasia lies between the Rhine and the Meuse; Neustria, as it were “new Austrasia,” lies between the Meuse and the Loire, and is now called Franconia and Francia [Col. 0279C]. After this, Clovis died, leaving his two sons as successors: Clotaire in Neustria and Childeric in Austrasia. Clotaire lost both kingdom and life after three years of rule. On his death his brother Theoderic succeeded him. But after a short time the Franks expelled him from the kingdom and forced Ebroin, overseer of the royal court, into the monastery of Lupionio, since they could no longer endure his wickedness. They then chose Theoderic’s brother Childeric and made him their king. But Childeric was killed not long afterward, and Theoderic was recalled to the kingdom.

When Ebroin heard this, he laid aside the monastic garment he wore, left the monastery, gathered forces about himself from every side, and again became mayor of the royal household [Col. 0279D]. Raging against the men who had governed the royal court during the reign of King Childeric, and especially against Leodegar, bishop of Autun, he seized him and, after many kinds of torture, ordered him beheaded.

After Ebroin’s death, Pippin, son of Ansegisel, began to exercise power under the kings in Austrasia. By his wife Plectrude he had two sons, Drogo and Grimoald. But by a concubine he begot Charles Tudites. Theoderic was succeeded by his son Clovis; Clovis by Childebert; and Childebert by his son Dagobert. At this period the kings of the Franks [Col. 0280A] began to decline from their customary strength and to administer affairs of the kingdom through the mayors of the royal household—that is, through the seneschal, constable, and chamberlain.

After this Pippin died, and his son Charles Tudites succeeded him. He was called Tudites from the large smiths’ hammers by which a mass is customarily struck and beaten thin. Having become mayor of the royal household under the younger Dagobert, he fought quite vigorously against the Saracens. For in the preceding period the Saracens, crossing the sea from Africa into Spain, had subjugated it; then, in Dagobert’s time, advancing with wives and children, they invaded Aquitaine, a province of Gaul, and, devastating everything, reached the borders of Septimania and the Viennese province. But Charles Tudites defeated them so thoroughly in two great battles—one [Col. 0280B] in Aquitaine and the other near Narbonne—that he compelled them to return to Spain. In that war he killed three hundred thousand Saracens.

This is Charles Tudites, who, because of the continual wars, gave ecclesiastical property to laymen. He also fought against the Saxons and Bavarians [Bavarians], whom he overcame with great difficulty. He fought also against Eudo, duke of the Aquitanians, and expelled Ragnfred, count of the royal palace, from the palace; but he granted him only one city, namely Angers.

Dagobert, king of the Franks, was succeeded by his son Theoderic. Charles Tudites also died, and his sons Charles the Great and Pippin took over his authority. When the aforesaid Dagobert died, his son Theoderic reigned in his place [Col. 0280C]; Theoderic was succeeded by Childeric, who is also called Hilderic. Since he was an ineffectual and indolent man, Pippin, mayor of the royal household, endeavoured through envoys to ask Zachary, bishop of Rome, whether he ought to be king of Francia who, given over to idleness, was content with the royal name alone. The pope replied that he ought to be called king who governed the commonwealth well. Encouraged by this answer, the Franks thrust Hilderic into a monastery, clothed him in a monk’s tunic, and made Pippin their king.

When Pippin died in the fifteenth year of his reign, his sons Charles and Carloman obtained the kingdom. Charles received the royal crown in the city of Noyon, and his brother Carloman at Soissons. But Carloman died after the completion of the second year from his elevation to the kingdom [Col. 0280D]. His wife and sons fled, without any compulsion, to Desiderius, king of the Lombards. Thus Charles alone obtained the monarchy of the entire kingdom of the Franks.

### Chapter VI. Concerning the Reign of Charles the Great

In the first year of his reign Charles entered Aquitaine and attacked Duke Hunold, who, after the death of Waifar, was preparing to keep that province for himself; Charles compelled him to seek Gascony. Charles then ordered Lupus, duke of the Gascons, to surrender the fugitive, threatening to make war upon him unless he promptly did so. Lupus, adopting the wiser course, not only surrendered Hunold but also committed himself, along with the province over which he presided, to Charles’s power.

When, as has been said, the Frankish kingdom had wholly come to Charles, Peter, an envoy of the Roman Church sent by Pope Adrian, came to the same glorious King Charles [Col. 0281A], seeking aid against Desiderius, king of the Lombards, who, following the example of his father Aistulf, harassed the Roman Church. Charles obeyed and prepared war against Desiderius with great forces. He entered Italy by Mount Cenis, strongly besieged Ticinum, now Pavia, a city of Italy, captured King Desiderius there, and sent him into exile. Furthermore, he drove Desiderius’s son Adalgisus from his paternal kingdom; after subduing Italy, he made his own son Pippin king.

When matters in Italy had been settled, he undertook the Saxon war. The Saxons were so thoroughly conquered and subdued by his strength that he took ten thousand of them, with their wives and little children, and distributed them in many separate settlements throughout Gaul and Germany [Col. 0281B]. The war was at last concluded on the condition that they would abandon the worship of demons, receive the sacraments of the Christian faith, and, united with the Franks, become one people with them.

While this war was being carried on, having stationed garrisons in appropriate places, Charles entered Spain. He crossed the pass of the Pyrenean mountains and, after receiving into surrender all the towns and fortresses which he visited, returned. But while returning he experienced Basque treachery on the very ridge of the Pyrenees. For as the army proceeded in a long column, extended as the nature and narrowness of the place required, the Basques, having placed ambushes in a hollow of the mountain, attacked the rear of the column and threw it down into the valley beneath.

Engaging them in battle, they killed all whom they found. In that battle Eggihard, overseer of the royal table, Anselm, count of the palace, and Roland, prefect of the Breton march, were killed with many others [Col. 0281C]. Roland was carried to and buried at the castle of Blaye. In those same days, the great king of the Franks Charles, returning from Spain, found that his wife Hildegard had given birth to twins [Col. 0281D].

After this, Charles subdued the people of Narbonne and returned to Francia. Not much later he went through Italy to Capua, a city of Campania; returning thence, he declared war on the Beneventans. But Arigisus, duke of the province, unable to endure the king’s forcefulness, sent his sons Romuald and Grimoald as hostages to secure his fidelity. Charles the Great afterwards returned again to Gaul.

Then the Bavarian war arose and was quickly concluded. War was also waged against the Suebi, and the Danes were allied with the Suebi. Charles subdued all of these in a single expedition. He also attacked the Huns and Avars in war. This war was successfully concluded within the eighth year from its beginning [Col. 0282A]. Moreover, he subjected all Frisia and Brittany to his dominion.

### Chapter VII. How Charles the Great Was Made Emperor

At Rome, Leo succeeded Pope Adrian. The relatives of the aforesaid Pope Adrian stirred up the Roman people against Pope Leo, seized him, and blinded him; yet they were unable completely to extinguish his sight. He fled to Charles, king of the Franks, who avenged him and restored him to his see. Leo crowned him emperor in the church of Saint Peter, clothing him with the imperial vestments. Then all the Roman people acclaimed him: “To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor: life and victory” [Col. 0282B].

### Chapter VIII. Concerning the Empire of Charles the Great

Charles the Great, therefore, having been made emperor of the Romans from king of the Franks, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 784, ruled for about forty-seven years. Having taken up and arranged the commonwealth, as stated above, he began many works appropriate to imperial dignity. Among these the chief seem to have been the basilica of Saint Mary at Aachen and a bridge over the Rhine at Mainz, five hundred paces in length. Above all, wherever he found sacred buildings fallen into ruin throughout his whole realm, he took care through envoys to command the bishops, to whose responsibility their restoration belonged, that what had been ordered should be carried out [Col. 0282C].

Above all, he defended the Roman Church and adorned it with his resources. He always cultivated the Christian religion with the highest devotion, and diligently attended church morning and evening, at the night offices, and at the time of sacrifice. He was also endowed with the greatest generosity toward the poor, aiding not only those in his own realm but also those in lands beyond the sea; he strove to send large sums of money to Syria, Egypt, Africa, Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage. Histories and deeds were read to him. He also delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those entitled *On the City of God* [Col. 0282D].

He had three sons: Charles, Pippin, and Louis. At last, when the magnificent Emperor Charles saw the end of his life drawing near, he left the imperial crown to his son Louis. He died in the seventy-second year of his life, the forty-seventh of his reign, and the year 814 of Christ’s Incarnation, in the fourth indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February [28 January]. He was buried in the church of Blessed Mary at Aachen. At that same time Saint Giles, the eminent confessor, a Greek by nation, flourished. By God’s prompting he came to Gaul and led an eremitic life in the province called Septimania.

### Chapter IX. Concerning Louis the Pious and Certain Other Kings

[Col. 0283A]

Louis the Pious, son of the Emperor Charles the Great, obtained the Roman Empire after his father’s death in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 814 and reigned for almost twenty-seven years. He was a man of most merciful disposition. Yet, though he administered the commonwealth in accordance with the gentleness of his character, he met an end full of adversities, being cruelly attacked both by his children and by the great men of the kingdom. He was also a most fervent executor of the Lord’s commands and a most vigorous defender of the holy law. In his time gem-laden belts and secular ornaments began to be laid aside by bishops and clerics.

That most serene emperor had three sons by his first wife Hermengard: Lothair, Pippin, and Louis; and by his second wife, Judith, Charles, king of the Franks [Col. 0283B]. Lothair, the emperor’s firstborn, having been appointed by his most kindly father king over Italy, came to Rome and on holy Easter Day received the crown and the title of Augustus in the church of Saint Peter from Pope Paschal. But this Lothair later seized his father Louis and ordered him guarded at the monastery of Saint-Médard. He also banished Louis’s wife Judith and committed Charles, whom Louis had begotten by her, to the fortress of Prüm.

Not long afterward, however, the princes of Francia released Emperor Louis from custody [Col. 0283C] and reconciled his son Lothair to his father. Afterwards the most merciful emperor divided his empire among his four sons: he assigned Italy to Lothair, Germany and Saxony to Louis, Aquitaine to Pippin, and Francia and Burgundy to Charles. But Lothair did not bear this division of the empire patiently and attempted to subject the entire empire to himself. When his father learned of this, he immediately set out against him; but, seized by illness on the journey, he ended his final day.

After his death, his four sons fought one another fiercely at the field of Fontenoy. In that war nearly all the soldiers of Francia, Italy, Aquitaine, Alemannia, Saxony, and Burgundy killed one another with mutual wounds [Col. 0283D]. Charles the Bald nevertheless gained the victory. In these times Theodulf, abbot of Fleury and bishop of Orléans, also flourished. When he had been accused before Emperor Louis of many crimes, he was banished to Angers. While he was held in custody there, it happened that the aforesaid emperor came on the very day of Palm Sunday. As the procession passed beside the house in which Theodulf was confined, silence having been made, he sang through the window in the emperor’s presence the beautiful verses he had composed, which are still sung throughout Gaul at that solemnity. Their opening is: “Glory, praise, and honour be to you, Christ the King, Redeemer” [Col. 0284A]. Moved by these words, the emperor immediately ordered him released from his bonds and restored him to his former favour. Rabanus likewise flourished at the same time.

Not many days after his father’s death, Lothair was seized by illness, became a monk, and left the dignity of the Italian Empire to his son Louis. Charles alone held Francia, Burgundy, and Aquitaine. Louis in Italy was succeeded by Lothair, and Lothair by Hugh. These also are those who ruled in Germany after Louis: Louis, Charles, Arnulf, Louis, Conrad, Henry, Otto, Otto, Otto, Henry, Conrad, Henry, Henry, Luiter. Charles the Bald was succeeded by Louis the Stammerer [Gallus], and he by Carloman, Carloman by Louis, and Louis by Charles the Simple [Col. 0284B].

### Chapter X. Concerning the People of the Northmen and the Successors of Charles the Simple

During this period, while Charles the Simple was reigning, the Northmen, Danes by origin, under a certain leader named Rollo, departed from Lower Scythia and travelled by sea across the Ocean. Having often before harassed both Germany and Gaul in piratical fashion by raids along these shores of the Ocean, they finally disembarked and overran the part of Gaul facing Brittany. Having occupied the city of Rouen, they called it Normandy after their own name, as it is called to this day. For “Northmen,” in their barbarian language, means, as it were, “men of the north,” because they first came from that quarter of the world [Col. 0284C].

Charles, king of the Franks, made a treaty with them, gave his daughter to Rollo in marriage, and granted him the land now called Normandy. Rollo, when baptized, took the name Robert. From that time the people of the Northmen, believing in Christ, became subject to the faith. Once the Northmen had established themselves in the part of Francia which they had overrun, they sought to stretch out their hands farther still. William the Bastard, duke of Normandy, subjugated England to himself. Others went farther and occupied Apulia, Calabria, and Sicily.

Charles the Simple was succeeded by Robert, who was outside the royal line and reigned two years; Robert was succeeded by Ralph, likewise outside the royal line, who reigned thirteen years [Col. 0284D]. Afterwards the kingdom was restored: Louis, son of Charles, reigned; he was succeeded by Lothair, Lothair by Louis, and Louis by his brother Charles, who reigned for half a year. After this the kingdom was transferred to Hugh. Hugh was succeeded by Robert. This Robert was a good man and Catholic in faith, who always endeavoured to honour and exalt the holy Church and churchmen. He also founded a church for the eminent confessor of Christ whom he loved greatly and venerated with the highest honour, at Avianum in the suburb of the city of Orléans. After him came Henry, Philip, Louis the Fat, Louis the Younger, and Philip.

[Col. 0285] *(Part II of the Excerpts appears above in the Appendix to the exegetical works; Part III, consisting of one hundred sermons, appears in the Appendix to the mystical works.)*

[Col. 0285]

## On the Union of Body and Spirit

[Col. 0285A] “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John 3). If there were nothing intermediate between spirit and body, neither could spirit be joined to body nor body to spirit. But there is a great distance between body and spirit; these two are far apart. Therefore there is something by which body rises, so that it approaches spirit, and again something by which spirit descends, so that it approaches body. That by which body rises is higher than body; likewise, that by which spirit descends is lower than spirit.

Nor are all bodies themselves of the same quality; rather, some have been made higher, some lower, some highest, and almost transcending bodily nature. Likewise among spirits, some are higher, some lower, some lowest, and almost fallen beneath spiritual nature, so that in this manner the lowest may be joined with the highest. Moses went up the mountain, and God came down upon the mountain. Unless Moses had gone up and God come down, they could not have met as one. Great mysteries are present in all these things. Body rises and spirit descends. Spirit rises and God descends. That by which body rises is above body; that by which spirit descends is below spirit. Again, that by which spirit rises is above spirit; and that by which God descends is below God.

Body rises by sense; spirit descends by sensuality. Likewise spirit rises by contemplation; God descends by revelation. Theophany is in revelation; understanding is in contemplation; imagination is in sensuality; and in sense [Col. 0285C] are the instrument of sensuality and the source of imagination. See Jacob’s ladder: it stood on earth and its summit touched heaven. Earth is body; heaven is God. Minds ascend by contemplation from the lowest things to the highest: from body to spirit, by means of sense and sensuality; from spirit to God, by means of contemplation and revelation. But the Lord leans upon the ladder, so that the highest may bend down to the lowest.

Therefore let us also ascend by reflection as far as we can; for even if we cannot do everything, perhaps we can do something. If we are not angels flying, yet we are human beings walking. Angels do not need a ladder, because they fly by divine contemplation; but human beings, who creep—or, at most, walk—by human reason do. I do not think angels sought the ladder for their own sake, but in order to teach human beings what they themselves ought to do. The ascent is from the lowest to the highest. Set down first, therefore, the things which are lowest, so that beginning from them you may ascend in order to higher things.

There are, then, in this body of the world four elements distinguished by their proper qualities: earth, water, fire, and air [Col. 0286A]. Of these the first, earth alone, is immovable in itself, because it cannot move unless it is externally impelled. The remaining three are movable because they move of themselves without external impetus. Yet there is this difference: water can be held so that it does not move; air and fire cannot. Again, air cannot be kept at rest, but it can be held in place. Fire, however, can be held neither at rest, so as not to move, nor in place, so as not to rise. Whatever things can be held externally either in place or at rest can also be moved externally: either so that they may move, if they are immobile, or so that they may move more, if they move less. Fire alone [Col. 0286B], just as it cannot be held, cannot be moved externally either, having every movement within itself and from itself.

In these four [elements], then, whatever is more subject to sense is called body in a fuller sense; whereas whatever is farther removed from sense departs further from the nature of bodies and approaches the nature of spirits. Hence air itself, because in its subtlety it cannot be seen, is called *spiritus* (“spirit”), although it is a body; for, in that respect in which it exceeds bodily sense, it comes so near to spiritual nature that it even assumes its name in its designation. But fire, which is much subtler and more mobile than air, and which does not, like air, move earthly bodies from without by blowing upon them, but gives them life inwardly by animating them, is more properly called spirit. [Col. 0286C] Yet this spirit—that is, fire—is one thing in bodies which it merely animates but does not endow with sensation, and another in bodies which it both animates and endows with sensation. For it animates some things without endowing them with sensation, such as trees, plants, and everything that sprouts from the earth; but it both animates and endows others with sensation, such as all brute animals. Among these there are some which have sensation only and lack imagination, and others which have both sensation and imagination. Since, therefore, to be endowed with sensation is greater than merely to be animated, it is certainly evident that this power is subtler where it confers sensation than where it bestows vegetation alone. Where it is subtler, moreover, it is in a manner more spirit, because, insofar as it more closely approaches incorporeal [Col. 0286D] nature, it assumes both that nature’s name and its property. Yet it does not assume it properly, since even in being called spirit it is demonstrably not raised beyond the property of bodily nature.

The weakest [Col. 0287A] body, and preeminently body, is that which cannot move at all by itself. Next after this, and less bodily, is that which can indeed move by itself but can nevertheless be restrained externally in a fixed state. Then follows that which, while still belonging to bodily nature, already receives the name spirit: it can move by itself and, though it may be held externally in place, cannot be held at rest; it is not seen and is always in motion. The highest body, and that nearest spiritual nature, is what always has motion in itself and can never be restrained from without. Insofar as it confers sensation, it imitates rational life; insofar as it confers imagination, it forms living wisdom. Nothing in body can be higher, or nearer spiritual nature, [Col. 0287B] than that in which, after sensation and above sensation, the power of imagining is conceived. This is so lofty that whatever is above it is nothing other than reason.

That same fiery power which, when formed from without, is called sensation, is called imagination when that form has been conveyed inward to the inmost part. For the form of a sensible thing, apprehended externally through the rays of sight, is drawn back by the working of nature as far as the eyes; and, being received by them, it is called vision. Then, passing through the seven coats of the eye and its three humours, it is at last purified, brought inward as far as the brain, and becomes imagination. Thereafter the same imagination, passing from the anterior part of the head to the middle, touches the very substance of the rational soul and [Col. 0287C] arouses discernment, having by then become so purified and subtle that it is immediately joined to spirit. Yet it truly retains the nature and property of body, so that what is written may be plain: “What is born of flesh is flesh” (John 3). For just as body is not born from spirit, so spirit is not generated from body. Although body is raised up as far as spirit and spirit lowered as far as body, nevertheless neither is spirit transformed into body nor body into spirit. Rather, “what is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (ibid.). Yet what is highest in body is near to spirit, and in it the power of imagining is grounded; above it [Col. 0287D] is reason. That imagination is outside the substance of the rational soul is shown by the fact that brute animals, which have no reason at all, are proved to possess the power of imagining.

Imagination, therefore, is a likeness of sensation: at the summit of bodily spirit and at the lowest point of the rational [nature], it gives form to the bodily and touches the rational. For sensation—whether through sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch—is formed by outward contact with a body; and, drawing inward the form conceived from that bodily contact through channels arranged for each sense to issue forth and return inward, it gathers it into the phantastic cell and impresses it upon that purer part of bodily spirit, thereby producing imagination. [Col. 0288A] In brute animals this imagination does not pass beyond the phantastic cell; in rational beings, however, it advances as far as the rational [faculty], where it touches the incorporeal substance of the soul and arouses discernment. Therefore imagination is nothing other than a likeness of body, conceived outwardly through the bodily senses from contact with bodies, then led inward through those same senses to the purer part of bodily spirit and impressed upon it. In rational beings it becomes purer where it is refined so as to touch the rational and incorporeal substance of the soul; yet even there it remains outside that substance, because it is a likeness of body and is grounded in body.

The rational substance is bodily light; imagination, [Col. 0288B] insofar as it is an image of body, is shadow. Therefore, after imagination has ascended as far as reason, like a shadow coming into light and falling upon light, insofar as it comes to that light it is made manifest and circumscribed; insofar as it falls upon it, it clouds, overshadows, enfolds, and covers it. If reason itself receives imagination solely in contemplation, as if it were a garment, imagination remains outside it and around it, so that it can easily be taken off and laid aside. But if reason also adheres to it with delight, imagination itself becomes like skin to it, so that it cannot be stripped off without pain, since it has clung to it with love.

This is why souls stripped of their bodies can still be held by bodily passions: namely, because they have not yet been cleansed from the corruption [Col. 0288C] of bodily affections. Spirit itself has, indeed, a certain mutability in its own nature, according to which it approaches the body by giving it life. In this mutability that spiritual and incorporeal substance lays aside somewhat of its purity and, as it were, meets the body by assuming a certain grosser property. If this adaptation occurs according to nature alone, it involves change but not corruption. But if it is vicious, it corrupts the purer nature precisely by compelling it to pass into association with the bounds of an inferior nature. The more deeply this vice cleaves to the soul while it remains in the body, the more difficult it is for it to leave the soul when it departs from the body; and the passion is not removed even when the cause of the passion is removed. For the soul itself, insofar as it is affected by delight in [Col. 0288D] the body and thereby, as it were, draws on a certain corporeality, is deformed by the phantasms of bodily imaginations; and, when these are deeply impressed upon it, it does not cast them off even after being released from the body. But those who have endeavoured in this life to cleanse themselves from such dregs, when they depart hence carry nothing bodily with them and remain free from bodily passion.

Thus there is a kind of progression from the lowest and outermost bodies upward as far as incorporeal spirit, through sensation and imagination; these two belong to bodily spirit. Then, in incorporeal spirit, nearest after body is the imaginative affection by which the soul is affected through its union with body; above this is reason acting upon imagination. Then comes pure reason above imagination, and in reason is the soul’s highest ascent above body. [Col. 0289A] But when one ascends from the soul to God, first comes intelligence: this is reason formed from within, because the divine presence, meeting and joining itself to reason, forms it from above into wisdom or intelligence, just as imagination, forming reason from below, produces knowledge.

## How God’s Word Is One—Namely, the Incarnate Word—Yet Living, Effective, and Penetrating; How All Things Are Naked and Open to God; and Concerning Christ’s Priesthood

“God spoke once” (Ps. 61), because He begot one Word, through whom He made all things. This Word is His utterance. Therefore God’s utterance is one, because God’s Word is one. And it is truly one because it is the one utterance of the One: it does not contain multiple judgments, but [Col. 0289B] is brought to completion in one simple word. Why then is it said in the Psalm, “That thou mayest be justified in thy words” (Ps. 50), and elsewhere, “Give me life, that I may keep thy words” (Ps. 118)? If God’s utterance is truly believed to be one, how are His utterances spoken of in the plural?

It must be understood that God speaks one way through human mouths and another way through Himself. For nearly all the Scripture of both the Old and New Testaments testifies that God speaks in human beings through human beings. Thus God speaks through human beings, and He speaks through Himself: many utterances through human beings, one through Himself. But whatever He uttered through human mouths, that one [Word] was present in them all; and all are one in that one Word, since without it they cannot be uttered in any place or time. Let us therefore consider [Col. 0289C] the great mystery: the Word of God, clothed in human flesh, appeared visibly once, and now every day that same Word, embodied in human speech, comes to us. Although He is made known to human beings one way through flesh and another through human speech, nevertheless in one manner the voice of the Word here ought to be understood as the flesh of God there. Even evil and unbelieving people could not only see Christ’s humanity but also kill it; and still today they hear God’s utterance outwardly and despise it. Just as those people would not have dared kill the man if they could have known God, so these likewise would by no means reject the divine words they hear if they could taste their power by an inward savour.

God’s utterance, then, is living because life is in it. In what is heard outwardly [Col. 0289D] it awakens; in what is inwardly present it gives life to the heart. It enters through the ears and is inspired into the heart. What is outward passes away; what is inward admits no change. What unfolds outwardly in the course of words, immutable truth declares inwardly. Therefore, He says, “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Luke 21). They will surely not pass away where they are not transient; for just as the one Word is not divided among many [utterances], so many [utterances] are not altered in the one Word.

Having briefly explained these matters concerning God’s utterance, let us now examine the Apostle’s words: “The word of God,” he says, “is living and effective and more penetrating than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4). It is living because it does not change; effective [Col. 0290A] because it does not fail; penetrating because it is not deceived. It does not change in what it promises; it does not fail in what it accomplishes; it is not deceived in judgment. Its promise does not die through forgetfulness or change through alteration of purpose. Its operation is not overcome by difficulty. Its judgment is not deceived by ambiguity. It promises truly, acts powerfully, and discerns subtly. God’s utterance is living, that you may believe; effective, that you may hope; more penetrating, that you may fear. It is living in commands and prohibitions, effective in promises and threats, and more penetrating in judgments and condemnations. But since the truth of its promises and the omnipotence of its works are to be believed rather than investigated, let us consider the subtlety of its judgments.

“The word of God,” he says, “is more penetrating than any two-edged sword.” A two-edged sword cuts on both [Col. 0290B] sides; when it is thrust in, penetrating from either side, it opens a path for itself. Yet it cuts only flesh. God’s sword, however, cuts both ways, because it can destroy both soul and body in the hell of fire (Matt. 10). Or it cuts both ways in judgments, because it judges both, cuts, and distinguishes. It follows: “Reaching unto the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4). In every human being there are three things: flesh, spirit, and mind. Delight belongs to flesh; thought to spirit; discernment to mind. Delight is the serpent, thought is Eve, discernment is Adam. In delight is the desire of excess. In knowledge is provision for necessity. In discernment is the judgment of truth. Delight, under the pretext of necessity, hurls provision into excess. [Col. 0290C] Through compassion for what is lower, provision bends reason away from the judgment of truth.
