The first division is between the serpent and Eve—that is, between carnality, or soul, or animality, and spirit; between delight and thought; between excess and necessity. The second division is between Eve and Adam: between thought and intention, or between prudence of the flesh and the judgment of truth.

The utterance of God likewise divides, as it were, between soul and spirit when sacred discourse shows us what conflict there is between carnal and spiritual desires. It follows: “And of joints and marrow” (ibid.), that is, the utterance of God reaches even to the division of joints and marrow. [Col. 0290D] What we should understand by “joints” and “marrow” is explained in what follows: “Of thoughts and intentions” (ibid.). The joints are thoughts; the marrow, intentions. First outwardly are works, like skin; then delight, like flesh; then thoughts, like bones; then intention, like marrow. As skin covers flesh, so works cover delight; as bones support flesh, so thoughts nourish desires; and as marrow lies within bones, so intentions lie hidden within thoughts. Thoughts are also called joints because in some manner they join desires to one another, as the joints of limbs bind their members together. For a joint is a connecting bond placed between things and joining their extremities. Likewise thoughts, because they are born from desires and in some sense [Col. 0291A] generate desires, binding both to one another by nourishing the former and bringing forth the latter. They connect succeeding things, as it were, with those preceding, because they themselves proceed from the former and the latter from them.

That desires generate thoughts can be unknown to no one who knows himself, since we turn over in thought more frequently the matter by whose love we are more strongly affected. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. 6). This is as though He said: Where your desire is, there is your heart also—that is, where your affection is, there is your thought also. Conversely, that thoughts generate desires the Psalmist shows when he says: “In my meditation fire shall blaze” (Ps. 38). For when the thought of something frequently settles in the mind, love for it [Col. 0291B] burns more keenly in the heart.

Accordingly, we rightly understand intentions by marrow, which is more hidden and concealed in the body; intentions are, as it were, the marrow of our thoughts, because the intention of thought lies hidden in the thought of the heart. When we examine it subtly, we penetrate, as it were, to the interior of the bones.

It is clear, therefore, that joints are rightly called thoughts and marrow intentions. It remains to inquire how God’s utterance reaches to their division. The first division is between soul and spirit—that is, between carnal and spiritual pleasures. The second division is between joints—that is, between carnal and spiritual thoughts. First, then, pleasures are distinguished, and whether the mind is affected by a good or an evil desire. [Col. 0291C] This discernment comes first because each person can more easily judge his own desires. Then follows discernment of thoughts, which is more hidden and more difficult to grasp. For good thoughts sometimes arise from wicked desires, and, conversely, wicked thoughts arise from good desires. Therefore it is not easy to discern or examine the quality of thoughts, since they must be judged not only from the preceding desires from which they arise, but also from the subsequent things which they themselves generate.

But, so that it may be seen more plainly how good thoughts arise from wicked desires and wicked thoughts from good desires, let this be shown by an example. No one is unaware that the desire for plunder is evil. [Col. 0291D] Yet sometimes from the desire to plunder there arises the desire to kill, and often from the desire to kill there arises horror of homicide. Thus, when from an evil desire there emerges a thought generating a good affection, a good shoot, as it were, bears sweet fruit from an evil root. Likewise, sometimes an evil thought arises from a good desire: when, for example, abhorring pollution of the flesh, we begin to think about the foulness of carnal desire, and from that very thought we are inflamed toward unlawful delight. It is as though water had begun to flow from a pure spring, but, gradually failing, was making its way into the cesspool of foulness. At other times thoughts both proceed from good desires and generate good desires, or, arising from evil desires, likewise bring forth evil ones. Since in this ambiguity [Col. 0292A] truth can be discerned with greater difficulty, the division of joints—that is, of good and evil thoughts—is rightly placed after the division of soul and spirit, that is, of carnal and spiritual wills, as the more intricate and difficult division. Finally, because discernment of intentions is known to be more secret than all these, the division of marrow is rightly added last.

God’s utterance penetrates all these things in judging them, because He who inwardly distinguishes our secrets by subtly understanding them through His wisdom outwardly enables us, through His teaching, profitably to understand the same things. Therefore, because God’s utterance is living, let us believe that it promises truth; because it is effective, let us hope that it will fulfill what it promises; because it is penetrating and cannot be deceived, let us repent of having offended it and henceforth fear to offend [Col. 0292B] it. For He understands our wills, sees our thoughts, and comprehends our intentions. It follows:

“No creature is invisible before Him” (Heb. 4). God’s eye takes in things far off because He is present everywhere; things most inward because He is in all things; subtle things because it is penetrating; and the greatest things because all things are in Him. He continues: “All things are naked in His sight” (ibid.), because all things are in Him; “and open” (ibid.), because He is in all things. Or the creature is called naked; naked also are human action, thought, and intention. One kind of eye is outward and not inward, like the eye of flesh; another is inward with respect to one thing and outward with respect to another, like the eye of the heart; and [Col. 0292C] there is an eye which is inward only and not outward, namely, the eye of God. The bodily eye sees only the outermost things of bodies; the eye of the mind sees the outermost things of hearts. God’s eye sees what is inmost. The eye of the heart is inward in relation to the bodily eye but outward in relation to God’s eye. And just as the bodily eye does not take in what the eye of the heart takes in, so the eye of the heart does not take in what God’s eye takes in; but God’s eye takes in what the eye of the heart takes in.

Thus the bodily eye takes in only the outermost things of bodies. The eye of the heart takes in both outer and inner things of bodies, but only the outer things of hearts. God’s eye takes in at once the outer and inner things not only of bodies but also of hearts. Therefore no creature is invisible before Him. All things are naked and open before Him. Even things visible are often covered from our eyes; things invisible are shut away. An action is visible; an intention is invisible. Yet human actions, although visible by their nature, are covered from our eyes in many ways so that they cannot be seen. Intention, however, cannot be seen even if the action itself is visible. Therefore all things are naked to God’s eyes, because He sees all human actions wherever they occur: for “there are no darknesses, nor a shadow of death, where those who work evil may hide themselves”; neither covering conceals, nor veil protects, nor wall shuts us out, nor darkness hides us from His eyes. Therefore all things are naked because He sees everything done; all are open because He sees with what intention it is done. It follows:

“To whom is our word/account” (ibid.), that is, to God or to His utterance; one must supply either “is,” “will be,” or “ought to be” [Col. 0293A] our word/account. God’s utterance first comes to us; afterward our utterance comes to God. God’s utterance comes to us in two ways: inwardly and outwardly. Inwardly through inspiration, outwardly through preaching. Inspiration likewise occurs in two ways: through nature and through grace. Through nature, when He inspires created beings with knowledge of the good; through grace, when He suggests love of the good to those restored. Our utterance also comes to Him in two ways: either by consulting reason or by rendering an account. If we are unwilling now voluntarily to consult reason in acting, then we shall necessarily render an account of our actions. Thus in the Apocalypse books are said to be opened, and then another book is opened, which is the book of life; afterward the dead are judged from the things written in the books (Rev. 20).

The books are [Col. 0293B] human hearts. The book of life is wisdom. God’s books are opened when the secrets of hearts are made manifest. The book of life will be opened when everything that ought to be done is clearly revealed to each person by inward light. The dead are judged from what is in the books, not from what is in the book, because sinners shall be judged from their own works. Our books are written in relation to God’s book, because our hearts are made in the likeness of God’s wisdom, as is said: “The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is marked upon us” (Ps. 4). Our books must still be written according to the pattern of the book of life, as the Apostle says: “Be imitators of Christ, as most dear children” (Eph. 5). And if they have not been written, at least they must be corrected. Let us therefore compare our books with this book, so that, if they contain anything different, [Col. 0293C] they may be corrected, lest at that final comparison, if they are found to contain anything different, they be cast away.

Thus “to whom” may be understood as “to whose utterance is our utterance.” Or otherwise: “To whom is our word/account?” Let us speak to Christ concerning ourselves, so that He may speak to the Father on our behalf, because He is high priest, to present to God the vows of the people, and great. He is great according to divinity because He is the Son of God; great according to humanity because He penetrates the heavens. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of His grace—that is, Himself, in whom grace reigns. Grace reigns in Him in two ways: because no wickedness is in Him to hinder the affection of grace from willing, and no misery is in us to hinder it from being able. Let us therefore approach with confidence, [Col. 0293D] since it is both His office to pray for us, because He has been appointed high priest, and His merit to obtain what He asks, because He is righteous. Finally, He will readily have compassion, because for our sake He too was surrounded by infirmities.

He was appointed because He was appointed by God. For He did not appoint Himself; rather, God glorified Him, who said: “Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee” (Ps. 2; Matt. 2, 17; Mark 9). When this was spoken over Christ at baptism, [Col. 0294A] He was then, as it were, chosen for the high priesthood. When it was spoken on the mountain, He was then, as it were, ordained high priest and clothed in the garment of glory. Afterwards, in the third voice which came to Him from heaven, saying, “I have glorified, and I will glorify again” (John 17), He was approved and confirmed in His dignity, just as Aaron, after his ordination, was approved and confirmed by God because he had certain rivals who disparaged his priesthood. On the mountain He received the garment of glory at His ordination; in the resurrection He put it on in order to offer prayers to God for us.

For every high priest, taken from among human beings, is appointed for human beings in matters pertaining to God, that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins (Heb. 5). The appointment of those who are set over others ought to be twofold: first, they ought [Col. 0294B] inwardly through grace to be raised to excellence in virtue; then outwardly, through obedience, they ought to be called to excellence in dignity. Some are raised inwardly but not outwardly, like good subjects. Others are raised outwardly but not inwardly, like evil prelates. Others are raised both outwardly and inwardly, like good prelates. Others are raised neither outwardly nor inwardly, like evil subjects. It follows:

“He is appointed for human beings in matters pertaining to God” (ibid.). It is said in the Gospel: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Luke 20). Just as Caesar has his officers over the people to exact what belongs to Caesar, so God has His officers over His people to require what belongs to God. And just as Caesar’s officers perform an embassy on behalf of the people [Col. 0294C] in order to intercede, and an embassy from Caesar to the people in order to command, so God’s officers—that is, prelates in the Church—perform an embassy on behalf of the people to God, in order to entreat Him, and an embassy from God to the people, in order to command them.

For the office of a prelate, insofar as he is an envoy of the people to God, is one thing; and insofar as he is God’s envoy to the people, another. In the office in which he is the people’s envoy to God, he ought to offer devotion, so that by offerings, spiritual sacrifice, and prayers he may render God propitious. In the office in which he is God’s envoy to the people, it belongs to him to teach the ignorant and correct sinners. Of the office in which he is the people’s envoy to God it was said, “that he may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.” Of the office in which he is God’s envoy to the people it was said, [Col. 0294D] “that he may know how to have compassion on those who are ignorant and go astray, since he himself also is surrounded by infirmity” (Heb. 5).

There are some who know themselves to be in infirmity but do not think themselves surrounded by infirmity: namely, those who consider themselves strong in certain of their actions. But those who perceive themselves to be weak in all things are, so far as their own estimation is concerned, surrounded on every side by infirmity.

[Col. 0295]

## APOLOGY CONCERNING THE INCARNATE WORD, APPARENTLY BY JOHN OF CORNWALL, CONTAINING OBJECTIONS AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT CHRIST IS NOT SOMETHING INSOFAR AS HE IS HUMAN. (G)

[Col. 0295A] Faith is certainty concerning invisible things pertaining to religion, placed above opinion and below knowledge. From this definition of faith it is clear that one may not doubt or hold opinions concerning articles of faith. For where there is opinion, there is no certainty; and where there is no certainty, there is no faith. In natural opinions, poetic judgments, allegorical interpretations, or tropological meanings, it is permissible to advance diverse views. Concerning faith, it is not permissible not merely to establish something else, but even to doubt the truth itself to the slightest degree; rather, one must profess it firmly. Hence in the Athanasian Creed: “This is the catholic faith, which unless each person believes faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.”

But if it is not permissible to hold differing opinions about any article of faith, this is especially so concerning that article which is more principal than the rest, [Col. 0295B] upon which the others rest as upon a foundation, and which is expressed in these words: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1), that is, a human being composed of flesh and soul. Hence Augustine says: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that He who was eternally born of the Father is He who was essentially conceived and born of the Virgin, of one nature with His mother.” Behold, Augustine forbids doubt and commands us to hold most firmly that in Christ there are two natures: the divine, according to which He says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10); and the human, according to which He says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14).

### QUESTION I

I ask, therefore, of those who say that Christ is not something insofar as He is human: what is signified by [Col. 0295C] “me” when it is said, “The Father is greater than me”? Is it that which is Christ, or that which is not Christ? If it is said that something not Christ is signified by “me” in such a passage, it follows that Christ says that He is something which He Himself is not—something inconsistent with truth. Again, if something which is Christ is signified there by “me,” it is either an uncreated or a created substance. But no uncreated substance is less than the Father. If, however, it is a created substance, it is either rational or irrational. But it cannot be an irrational substance. Therefore it is a rational substance. Thus it is either angelic or human; but it is not angelic; therefore it is human. Accordingly, what is signified there must be a created, rational, human substance—that is, a human being composed of soul and flesh.

Hence Augustine says that, when it is said, “The Word [Col. 0296A] was made flesh,” a part is put for the whole, namely, flesh for human being. Therefore a human being is necessarily some whole of which flesh is a part, and that whole is Christ. Hence the same author says: “God received into the eternal person of divinity the temporal substance of flesh.” What does “received into a person” mean except that He united it personally to Himself—that what was assumed might be one person with the Assumer? Hence in the book *On the Christian Conflict*: “Immutable truth, receiving a soul through spirit and a body through soul, liberated the whole assumed human being.” In the same work: “Let us not listen to those who say that the man born of the Virgin was assumed by eternal wisdom in the same way as other human beings become wise through it. For it is one thing merely to become wise through the wisdom of God, and another to receive the very person [Col. 0296B] of the wisdom of God.” You hear that this man received the person of God’s wisdom. Accordingly, through grace the human being passed into God, not by changeability of nature but by God’s gracious condescension, being wonderfully assumed into unity of person. Therefore that wise man who bears the person of Wisdom is wise in one way, and other people in another.

Hence Augustine, commenting on the Epistle to the Galatians: “By putting on Christ through faith, all become sons—not by nature, as the only Son, who is the Wisdom of God. Nor [do they become sons] through the power and singularity of being assumed so as naturally to possess and exercise the person of Wisdom, as the Mediator Himself is one with the Wisdom which assumes Him.”

### QUESTION II

I ask further how Augustine can say that the assumed man has been assumed so as naturally to possess the person of the Father’s Wisdom, when elsewhere he says that the man was assumed in [Col. 0296C] unity of person by grace, not by nature.

**Solution.** “Natural” is used in two senses: both for what belongs to a thing’s substance and for what is original—that is, given from the origin of its creation. Therefore, because the assumed human being was, from the moment he existed, a divine person—though not by nature but by grace—it is in some sense natural for him to be the person of God; but this naturalness does not exclude grace. Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “In the assumption of human nature, grace itself was in some fashion made natural to that man. For from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son, and this unique Son: so that, just as rational soul and flesh are one person, so God and human being are one person.”

“Son” is said in three ways: by adoption, as we are through faith; by assumption, as the Mediator—that is, the assumed human being; and by nature, as the Word, which is the same [Col. 0297A] substance as the Father but not the same person, and the same person as the Mediator but not the same substance. Hence Augustine says in the book *On the Trinity*: “Although the Son is God and human being, God is one substance and human being another substance.”

### Question III

It is asked whether the human substance in Christ is to be adored.

**Resolution.** The power of dignity is not lost when humility is adored, as Hilary says. Augustine likewise says: “The earth, assumed by the Word of God, is adored, because no one eats his flesh unless he first adores it”—yet not on its own account, but on account of him to whom it is united.

Authority says that the Creator is created, the predestining One predestined, the unmade made; this must be understood according to the human nature. “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20).

If Christ is not some created substance, he does not have God, since God belongs only to creatures; but he himself necessarily says that he has God. Therefore he is something that has God or a Creator.

Elsewhere it is said that the union of man and God is so great that he is wholly God and wholly man. What is signified by “man” when it is said, “he is wholly man”? What does the following statement mean: “not in the substances of man”? For if it is understood thus—“God is man,” that is, he has a man—then one may say, “the soul is flesh,” that is, it has flesh.

Augustine says on John that the Word of God is one thing and man another. What is signified here by “man”? For if, as some suppose, soul and flesh are understood here by “man,” and not something composed [Col. 0297C] of the two, he ought to have said, “The Word of God is one thing; man is several things,” since by “man” several things, not one, are signified.

Augustine says elsewhere, on the Epistle to the Colossians: “The man, assumed in the most excellent manner, bears the person of Wisdom.” If, therefore, that which is assumed is not a person, as some maintain, neither does it bear the person of Wisdom. How then do they dare deny that the assumed man is a person, when authority says so plainly: “He who descended,” that is, God, “and he who ascended” (Ephesians 4), that is, man? For the expositor says that deity and humanity are the same person.

Hence Pope Leo: “Humility becomes more wonderful to us in God than power; and the emptying of the divine majesty is grasped by us with greater difficulty than the supreme advancement of the servant’s form.” And afterwards: “Although the Creator is one thing and the creature another, nevertheless the property of each nature converges in one person. Humanity and deity alike accomplished all things belonging to God and to man.”

It is read that Christ, just as he is *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιος, “of the same substance”] with the Father, is likewise *homoousios* [ὀμοούσιος] with his mother. But if Christ is not that which is man, but only that which is the Father, nothing that is consubstantial with the mother is substantial to the Son, and conversely; therefore he is not consubstantial with her, since he has nothing substantial in common with her.

But perhaps they will say: Christ is called *homoousios* [ὀμοούσιος] with his mother because he is of the same nature as his mother. And I ask what they understand by human nature when it is said that Christ is of the same nature as his mother. Let them say: body and soul. [Col. 0298A] But Christ’s soul is one thing and the Virgin’s soul another. Hence, if human nature is the same thing as soul and body, then, if they are not of the same soul and flesh, neither are they of the same nature. Or, if they are of the same nature, though they are not of the same flesh and soul, one thing is understood by “nature,” another by “soul and flesh.”

It should be noted, however, that “human nature” is taken in three ways: namely, for the substantial form called humanity; for the thing existing under such a property, namely, that composite of body and soul, which is sometimes signified by the name “humanity”; and sometimes human nature means body and soul.

Therefore it is true that Christ assumed body and soul, that composite, and that form—namely, humanity. [Col. 0298B] Nor can it be denied that this form was assumed, since not only body and soul were assumed, but all properties also were assumed.

### Question IV

Therefore I ask those who say that in Christ there is nothing that is man: what is the subject of humanity, this form? For neither deity nor flesh nor soul can be its subject. What then? If nothing composed of Christ’s body and soul exists which is Christ, in which humanity may exist, as it were, in a subject, then necessarily Christ is some whole consisting of soul and body; or else he does not possess this form, humanity.

We confess, therefore, a union of two substances in Christ—not a change, convertibility, admixture, or confusion.

### Question V

[Col. 0298C] Hilary says in the ninth book *On the Trinity* that it was acquired for man that he might be God. I ask, therefore, who is this man for whom it is acquired that he may be God? Is it for soul or flesh? Certainly not, but for the man consisting of both.

The same author, in the eighth book *On the Trinity*: “He plainly does not know his own life who does not know Jesus himself to be true God and likewise true man.” For if he is not that which is man, he is not man; and if he is not man, he is not true man. How great, then, is the rashness of denying that Christ is some man, while nevertheless proclaiming him to be true man!

Augustine says on “Lord, you have been our refuge” (Psalm 89): “Christ began to be what he was not, while the property of the substances was preserved.” [Col. 0298D] What was creatable remained creatable; and what was uncreatable, uncreatable; what was mortal, mortal; and what was immortal, immortal. Yet both are one immortal person, and truly immortal.

Hence Isidore says in *On the Supreme Good*: “The humanity assumed by Christ is the third person in the Trinity.” This agrees with what Augustine says in the second book *On the Trinity*: “The form of the assumed man is the person of the Son.” What could be clearer? How then do you dare say that nothing which is assumed is the person of the Son? Return to your heart and heed the truth. Consider who it is that speaks. Recall that you incur danger to your soul if you deny so manifest a truth.

Remember also that the man who denied that Christ is something was himself a man, and therefore could [Col. 0299A] be deceived. And would that he had been deceived alone, and had not deceived others!

If you do not yet believe the authorities cited, hear what Augustine says in the same book: “The Trinity wrought that human form from the Virgin Mary, but it is the person of the Son alone.” The same, in book thirteen *On the Trinity*: “Human nature was joined to God the Word, so that with him it became one person.”

Note that in places of this kind “humanity,” “the form of a servant,” or “human nature” does not signify body and soul, or that property properly and according to ordinary speech called humanity; rather, it denotes the thing existing under such a property. Therefore one must firmly maintain that by the name “humanity” that which is man is sometimes signified. Do not therefore wonder that humanity is called a person, when in such a passage the assumed man is signified by the name “humanity.”

Hilary says thus in the eighth book *On the Trinity*: “It is proper to God to have become other than he remained, and yet not to cease being what he remained.” Hilary says that God is other than he was, while remaining what he was. And since it cannot belong to any creature to remain at once what it is and become something else, he says that it is proper to God to be other than he was and to remain what he was.

Say, then, how you presume to say that Christ is not something which he was not from eternity. Behold, we have several authorities that Christ became something that he was not. I ask you to show at least one authority which says that God is not something in so far as he is man, or that he did not become something when he became man.

[Col. 0299C] Now the objections of certain persons against us must be set forth.

“If God is essentially man, or man is God, then, if God had assumed a human being of the female sex, woman would be God and God would be woman. But God could have assumed a human being of that sex; therefore God could have been woman.”

**Resolution.** Augustine says: “He who was essentially born of the Father is essentially the one who was conceived and born of the Virgin.” Therefore I confess that God always could, can, and will be able to assume a human being of either sex.

Would that you saw yourself where I see you, you who raise these objections. Since, therefore, both sexes had to be redeemed, it was fitting that the more honorable sex should be assumed, and that it should be assumed from a woman, so that both sexes might thus be shown to belong to redemption. Hence Augustine, *On the Creed*: “That dispensation showed that both sexes are honored and are subject to care—not only the sex which he assumed, but also that through which he assumed it, by taking the role of man and being born from a woman.” [Col. 0299D]

### Question VI

I ask those who say that nothing is composed of Christ’s soul and flesh: how was sex assumed? For no sex exists in flesh or soul, but only in the whole constituted from the two parts.

It was fitting that the divine quaternity be completed. For God made the first human without the joining of sexes. He brought forth woman from man. From marital intercourse, however, he formed both. There remained a fourth possibility: that, as it were, woman should return the favor to man; this [Col. 0300A] was fulfilled when a virgin gave birth contrary to reason and above nature.

**Objection.** “If God could assume a woman, therefore a woman could be God.”

**Resolution.** It does not follow. Just as this does not follow: “God can make a stone from a man; therefore a man can become a stone.” For God can do impossibilities, yet impossibilities are not thereby possible.

Again they object: “If that substance which was united to the Word began to be God, and conversely God began to be that substance, then some substance is God which was not always God; some substance is God which is not the divine substance; and God is something that he was not always.”

They add: “If the assumed man is a person, then he is either the third person in the Trinity or another person; but not another; therefore he is the third person in the Trinity, and thus God.”

**Resolution.** [Col. 0300B] In this very point they prove themselves not to be Catholics, since they regard as absurd what is established by so many authorities. Does not Isidore say that the humanity assumed by Christ is the third person in the Trinity? And does not Hilary assert that it is proper to God to have been other than he remained, without ceasing to be what he remained? And Augustine says: “The Creator of times was found in time, himself also made.” And elsewhere: “Man is new, but God is not new.”

This is the absurdity that we adore. This is the abuse through which we have been redeemed.

I know where your eyes are held captive, you who regard it as absurd that God should be something he was not always, because you do not grasp the manner in which something is said to be other on account of the ineffable union. For in this, that God poured himself into man according to fullness [Col. 0300C] and brought all that was his to him, and assumed into himself all that belonged to man, it is truly said—and is true—that God is man and man is God.

Man is God not by nature but by grace: not by the grace of adoption, but by the grace of union or assumption. God is man by condescension. Therefore, when we proclaim God man or man God, we do not signify that one nature is changeable into the other, but the mutual and complete participation of both natures.

It should be noted that some do not regard this as a valid argument: “That substance united to God is God; therefore some substance that has not always existed is God.” This is evident in the following parallel: “A candle shines; therefore some substance which is not fire shines,” since fire shines of itself, whereas the candle shines from [Col. 0300D] fire.

There is another parallel: “This man was made in the image of God; therefore [it would follow that] some substance which is neither animal nor angel...” The inference does not follow. Thus the Word is God in himself, just as fire shines; but man is God from the Word, just as a candle shines from fire, and man is an image from the soul.

Nevertheless, it must in no way be denied that the substance united to the Word of God is the Son of God. But, as has already been said, man is God by grace, while the Word is God by nature.

### Question VII

If you do not yet believe, hear still the words of Truth on Luke, where it is written: “He will be great” (Luke 1). It is read that the power which the Son of God has naturally, man was to receive in time, so that God and man might be one person.

I ask what is signified by “man”; and when it is said that man [Col. 0301A] was to receive, and so forth, whether divine or human substance is meant. But nothing was given in time to the divine nature; therefore it was given to the human. Thus human substance has the power which the Son of God has by nature; therefore man has omnipotence, and thus is omnipotent, and thus God—as he himself professes, saying: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28).

To whom was all power given? Hear the expositor on the same passage: “This is not said of the divinity coeternal with the Father, but of the assumed humanity.” Whatever you may say about Christ, I believe Christ himself speaking of himself better than I believe you. Do you not contradict Christ when you deny what he affirms? See, therefore, that your interpretation is contrary to Christ and to the orthodox Fathers.

You say that the assumed man does not possess omnipotence; he himself says: “All power [Col. 0301B] has been given to me.” Hence the Apostle: “In him dwells all the fullness of divinity bodily” (Colossians 2). Judge for yourself. What is this: “In whom dwells all the fullness of divinity”? Is it the Word of God? Why then does he add “bodily”?

Hilary says in book eight: “True faith is neither ignorant that God is man, nor ignorant that flesh is the Word.” Recall what is signified by the name “flesh.” Hear Augustine: “The Word became flesh,” that is, man; a part is put for the whole. This agrees with John: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5).

In matters of this kind, which cannot belong to God, they are accustomed to explain: “The person received this according to the human nature.” Do you understand what you say? If the person is not something according to humanity, as you assert, how did the person receive anything according to it?

Again, it is said to you: if human nature did not receive this, then neither did the person receive it according to that nature—just as, if your body is not white, neither are you white according to the body; or, if your soul is not rational, neither are you rational according to it.

It must indeed be granted that the person received, according to humanity, the power which he has naturally; and the man himself received it, and thus the person itself in him. Other authorities make clear that this is the proper understanding.

Hence Hilary says: “It must not be ignored that flesh is the Word, and that all power in heaven and on earth was given to humanity.” Let them assign, if they can, what that is to which all power of judgment was given, which is called Son of the Most High, and which is related to the mother by a temporal relation.

For he is not called the mother’s son by eternal sonship. How is he the son of his mother if he has nothing of being from his mother? Is someone to be said to derive his origin from a sheep because his garment comes from it? If, therefore, Christ is not something from the Virgin, but his garment comes from her, how is he the Son of the Virgin?

Therefore, just as the Word is light in himself and the assumed man is light from the Word, so the Word is person in himself, whereas man has “personhood,” if I may so speak, from the Word.

But someone will say: “Would not the assumed man be a person if he were not united to the Word?”

**Resolution.** He would indeed be a person and would have his own personhood from his rationality. But now, since the whole splendor [Col. 0302A] of divinity has poured itself into the lamp of humanity, the lesser light yields to the greater: that is, the assumed man draws his personhood from the Word, and is called, and is, one person with him through the same personhood which the Word possessed from eternity.

Every rational creature is called a person because of what it has most excellent. Therefore, because the splendor of divinity is incomparably more excellent than the lamp of humanity, man is rightly a person from it.

Hence it is written: “Nature does not consume nature, but person consumes person, because ‘person’ is a term of law.” Consider this carefully, reader, and you will understand why man is said to be assumed into person, not into nature; and why the Word is said to have assumed nature, not person.

For the assumed man was taken into the divine person because he became a participant in the divine light, so that through him he might be distinguished from all others, as the Word is. He was not taken into nature, although the divine person is divine nature, because that would be to be changed and converted into it.

But the Word assumed human nature, not person—although that which was assumed is a person—because he does not draw personality or personhood from that which is assumed, having a far more worthy personhood from the nature of divinity.

Just as a lamp at night is called the light of the Church, but by day, when the greater splendor of the sun arrives, the lamp is no longer called the light of the Church, but rather the light of the sun; so a man would indeed be a person from his rationality if he were not assumed. But now, as has been said, he is a person from that which is more worthy in him, namely, the divine light. [Col. 0302B]

Whoever does not see this should ask the Lord for understanding. I find no exact likeness of this matter among creatures. For nothing which remains what it is can become something else; that is proper to God alone, as Hilary says.

Yet how the splendor of the Word pours itself into man so as to illuminate him, although it does not depart from the Word, may be shown by some sort of comparison. For the brightness or heat of fire comes to a candle or coal and does not depart from the fire, but is at once in the fire and in the candle. Yet in the fire it is by nature, in the candle accidentally. Nevertheless, the union between God and man is greater.

Hence the Word grants to man that he may be with him not one substance, but one person. Therefore God is one thing and man another, but not one God and another man: rather, one and the same is God and man, as many authorities plainly show.

Thus body and soul are one man and one person, though body is one thing and soul another. Christ, therefore, has a double substance, namely divine and human, but only one person, because both substances are one person. [Col. 0302D]

Since Christ, therefore, has human substance, must it be granted that he is a creature, since every man is a creature?

**Resolution.** It should not simply be granted that Christ is a creature unless “according to man” is added. But do we not simply grant that Christ is man? Why then is it not likewise granted that he is a creature?

**Resolution.** Without qualification, the usage of the holy Church does not customarily grant simply that Christ is a creature, [Col. 0303A] lest this be understood according to both natures, and lest it appear to assent to Arian perfidy, which said that Christ is only a creature. Catholic faith, however, says that he is both Creator according to divine nature and creature according to human substance.

Hold firmly, therefore, that the assuming Word is naturally God, while the assumed substance is naturally a creature; and that, by reason of the ineffable union and the sacrament of wondrous assumption, the Word is man and man is God, while each substance remains unconfused and unchanged.

Hence Hilary says in the fifth book *On the Trinity*: “It belongs to the power of the mighty nature that, while it remained what it was, it could nevertheless become what it was not.”

I warn you to give the assent of faith to what is read in Holy Scripture. Let it not seem strange to you if you do not yet understand everything fully. Recall that faith has no merit when human reason supplies demonstration.

Some are more troubled by ignorance of natural things than by ignorance of things to be believed: for example, what an image in a mirror is, or how it exists; how the same spring is now this water, now that; how different utterances are the same word.

Friend, if you do not understand these light and almost childish matters, with what face do you presume to attempt the ineffable sacrament of the Incarnation?

Do not therefore reason thus about Christ: “If Christ is some simple or uncreated substance, then he is not some composite or created substance,” since he is both, though not in the same respect. Why do you not reason thus? “In the days of his flesh he was mortal; therefore then he was not immortal.” Or: “Then he was passible; therefore then he was not impassible.” [Col. 0303C]

Someone will say to me: “I see that you are an Arian, because you say that Christ is a creature.”

Let us therefore examine more carefully whether this is true. Arius said that Christ was a mere creature, not begotten consubstantially from the Father but only a creature; and therefore less than and later than the Father. He did indeed affirm that Christ was God, but not by nature—only by adoption.

Now I ask whether Jerome thought the same as Arius when he says: “We boldly proclaim Christ to be a creature.” And Hilary, who says: [Col. 0303D] “What is that which was not?” Or the Apostle, who says: “Who is faithful to him who made him” (Hebrews 3). And elsewhere: “Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1). And Augustine, who declares the divine substance immutable and the creature mutable, according to which Christ endured all that Scripture recounts concerning him.

Although, therefore, heretic and Catholic have the same words on their lips, it does not follow that the same meaning is in the heart of each. Thus it does not follow that, if certain things share the same name, they therefore share also the reality named: God and an idol share the name “god,” but not the same deity.

Therefore what is written—“Whoever says that Christ is a creature, let him be anathema”—must be understood as referring to a mere creature, as Arius understood or said. By the same reasoning must be understood what Ambrose says: that Christ is not subjected to futility and therefore is not to be numbered among creatures, because every creature is subjected to futility.

Does it follow that because Christ is man, and every man is a liar, Christ is a liar? Many things are said generally of man, yet not of Christ the man, because he is not mere man but God and man.

Augustine says: “He through whom every creature was made is not a creature.” Behold, he denies that Christ is a creature; this seems contrary to what has been said.

**Resolution.** “He through whom every creature was made is not a creature”—that is, that in Christ through which every creature was made is not a creature, but the creative essence. For he is treating of the person according to divine nature.

Again Hilary says: “The Son of Man is not one thing and the Son of God another”; and we say and believe that the Son of Man is one thing and the Son of God another. What then? Are we contrary to Hilary?

**Resolution.** More frequently these grammatical endings signify substance. Yet sometimes, though rarely, the neuter signifies person. The sense is: the Son of Man is not one person and the Son of God another person, but one and the same.

Hence Augustine, speaking of the three persons, says: “And these three are one.” Elsewhere he says that the Mediator himself is one with the Wisdom that assumes him. By these words the difference of substances is not confused, but personal union is proclaimed.

Hilary, however, does not say: “The Word is not one thing and man another”; rather, this neuter “another” is not other than Christ. And Augustine says: “That man was not made other than the Son of God,” that is, he was not made something that is not the Son of God. For whatever belongs to the person of the divine essence is not other than that person itself, though it is other than divine nature.

Hence Jerome: “God the Word is not the assumed flesh.” By these words the difference is shown not of nature from person, but of nature from nature. But if by “flesh” a part, not the whole, is understood, it is clear that the Word is not flesh. Yet by “flesh” the whole man is signified. Nevertheless, as Ambrose says, one thing is that which is assumed, another that which assumed.

Otherwise, if Christ is not something according to that in which he is man, he himself is not something according to which he is *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιος] with his mother; or he is *homoousios* [ὁμοούσιος] with Father and mother in the same respect. [Col. 0304A]

Hilary elsewhere explains himself, saying: “Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in death. And though each set of deeds belongs to its own nature, remember that Jesus Christ is nevertheless one, he who is both.”

He would not have said “both” of one nature, nor “one” of two persons. “Both” excludes singularity of natures; “one” excludes plurality of persons.

Some say that, just as the Son of God is not one person and the son of man another, so the Son of God is not one thing and the son of man another. But if this is so, then just as person is undifferentiated, so nature is undifferentiated. [Col. 0304B]

Some say that when the Word became flesh, a certain composite whole came to be from Creator and creature—namely, deity, flesh, and soul. That composite is a creature because it did not always exist; and deity is a part of that composite. Therefore the Creator is a part of some creature.

But what could be more absurd—indeed, more false? Again, every whole is greater than any of its parts. Therefore, if deity is a part of something, something must be greater than deity itself. Or, if deity is greater than every thing, it is greater than that of which it is a part, and thus either it deprives its own whole of the law and right of totality, or its whole circumscribes it.

Again, if deity is an integral part, wherever it is, its whole is also; but it is everywhere, therefore its whole is everywhere. Again, no integral part is predicated of its whole. Therefore, if Christ were a certain [Col. 0305B] whole of which God or deity were a part, Christ could in no way be God, since no whole is its part.

Therefore Holy Scripture much more rightly says that there is a personal union between God and man, or between the assumed man and the assuming Word, than an integral constitution or composition. [Col. 0305A]

It must be known that there are several kinds of composition. A house is composed of its parts in one way; bread of water and flour in another; a statue of matter and form in another; a species of genus and difference in another; man of flesh and soul in another.

Things united are also sometimes called composite, as when it is read that a hypostasis is composite from two natures. This must be understood thus: two natures are united in one person without change or confusion.

Therefore, just as fire is infused into coal, yet is not joined to it as a part so that some whole may be completed from fire and coal which is neither fire nor coal, so the Word is united to man; yet no whole is thereby produced which is neither man nor Word. [Col. 0305C]

### Question VIII

I ask you who deny that anything assumed is the Son of God: what do you say is the seed of Abraham? Is it that seed whose coming the Apostle proclaims in speaking of the state of the law, saying that the law was ordained through the hand of a Mediator until the seed should come to whom the promise was made? (Galatians 3.)

Will you call “the seed of Abraham” something that is not from Abraham? God the Father begot nothing except what he himself is, that is, God from God. What then did Abraham, a man, beget except that which is [Col. 0305D] man—the offspring of his own nature? This is the seed which was to come when the promise was made to Abraham. What, then, is this seed if that which is assumed is not man? Did not man beget man?

### Question IX

I ask whether Christ is something which, through the Virgin, is from Abraham—that is, man from man, creature from creature. “Christ Jesus is the mediator of God and men” (1 Timothy 2). A middle term exists only between extremes.

I ask, therefore, what this middle term is and what the extremes are. You have one of the extremes where it is written, “Mediator of God”; the other where it says, “and of men.” I ask what the middle term is. Hear the Apostle: “The man Christ Jesus” (ibid.). He does not say “the Word,” because he is not mediator in so far as he is God, but is one of the extremes.

If, therefore, that which is [Col. 0306A] assumed is not Christ, neither is it mediator. What then? Say what those three are, two of which are extremes and the third mediator. For God and human beings, reconciled, are the two extremes. But what will the mediator be?

Hear at least what the Apostle says on this matter: “The man Christ Jesus,” whom a communion of natures joins to us, but whom the union of one and the same person joins to God—not an integral composition, a composition unworthy of God.

But that God is not a part of this person Augustine says in these words: “Christ is a person of double substance; nevertheless God is not a part of this person.”

The word “whole” sometimes has the collective force of integral parts, as when it is said, “The whole man was created by God,” namely, every part of man—soul and flesh, form and the joining of the parts—exists by God’s creation.

Sometimes the same word excludes every composition, as when it is said, “The whole God is everywhere essentially.” By these words it is denied that he has parts. For if, through diversity of parts, he occupied a diversity of places, he would not be wholly everywhere. The sense here is: God is everywhere wholly, that is, nowhere is anything of his essence absent.

Sometimes “whole” signifies the association of things not united totally, as when we call the union of soul and body a whole, or call burning coal a whole. Baptism also is said to consist of two things, namely the elements and the word of life; and the sacrament of the Eucharist, of the visible species and the body and blood of Christ.

Thus we call Christ, as it were, a whole with respect to deity and humanity, because these two natures are joined in one person, just as the element and word in baptism, and the visible species and Christ’s flesh in the sacrament of the altar, are joined to each other. [Col. 0306C]

Yet they differ very greatly, because the union by which God and man are united is incomprehensible. In none of the aforementioned unions is one said of the other: for fire is not coal, nor coal fire; visible species is not Christ’s flesh, nor flesh soul, and conversely.

But in the person of Christ an ineffable reciprocal predication is found. For God is man and man is God; and he is wholly God and wholly man. What is the whole? Christ. For just as the union of soul and body is called man, so the personal union of human and divine nature is called Christ, likewise, as it were, a certain whole with respect to the two natures united in Christ.

Yet reciprocal predication is not the same in man, because two rational substances capable of personhood are not united in him. Therefore in Christ or in his sacraments there is no ordinary composition of partial integral constitution. [Col. 0306D]

Some say that nothing is composed of Christ’s soul and flesh, just as nothing is composed from the two natures. Consequently they add that nothing which is man is God or the third person in the Trinity.

We believe and confess both: that something is composed of Christ’s flesh and soul, and that this is God and the third person in the Trinity by grace, not by nature. This must first be demonstrated by authoritative testimonies and then by arguments.

But this must first be understood: neither canonical Scripture nor the holy Fathers say that no composite substance exists from the two aforesaid things. How, therefore, do you dare proclaim what cannot be proved by any authority?

Say yourself, if you can, which saint has used these words: “Christ is nothing in so far as he is man”; or “nothing consists of Christ’s soul and flesh”; or “nothing that is man is God”; or “nothing that is man is the third person in the Trinity”?

Yet he confesses with us that God is man and man is God.

### Question X [Cols. 0307B–0308A]

I ask, then, what is the thing denoted by the name “man”? Is it not a thing consisting of soul and flesh? How can they deny the thing denoted by the name, and attribute the name itself to God without its thing? For man is not a pure body and a naked soul, but an ensouled body, or a soul having flesh.

Since, therefore, Christ’s soul wholly animates his body and makes it live, just as my soul does my body—indeed, far more excellently—how is it that from the conjunction of my body and my soul there exists a true man, while from that most holy soul and body there does not exist a true man? If, then, as some say, nothing exists from those two, there was in Christ no conjunction of soul and body like that in other human beings.

Against them Hilary says in Book IX: “Although Christ was born according to the law of human beings, he was nevertheless not conceived, having in himself, even in his origin, the constitution of the human condition.” Let us therefore consider what the constitution of man is in us, and let us believe with Hilary that this was in Christ.

The same author, in the same place: “We do not doubt that Christ is God the Word; nor, again, are we ignorant that the Son of Man consists of soul and body.” Let us therefore confidently believe what Hilary thus affirms. Augustine agrees with him when, expounding “And the Word was made flesh,” he asserts that a part is put for the whole. What part for what whole? Flesh for man. Therefore man must be a certain whole of which flesh is a part.

This same point has already been stated above. Yet it is not superfluous to repeat other things already said as testimony to the truth. Jerome agrees with these: “We say that the very Son of God, at the end of the ages, assumed a perfect man of our nature.” If, then, there is nothing from Christ’s soul and flesh, what is the perfect man which he says was assumed?

Does not Athanasius say in the Creed concerning Christ: “Perfect God, perfect man, subsisting from a rational soul and human flesh”? If, after so many testimonies of truth, you still doubt, hear Jerome saying: “We anathematize Apollinaris and those like him, who say that the assumed man was unlike those for whose sake he was assumed.”

Tell me, I ask, what does your soul do in your body, as regards natural things, that Christ’s soul does not do in his body? Someone says: “From the soul and body of this man there consists a certain person who is not the Son of God.” Is there not, then, from Christ’s soul and flesh a certain person who is not the Son of God?

**Reply.** It must be granted that that which is composite is a person; nevertheless, it does not derive its personal distinction from the assumed nature, but from the Word of God to whom it is united. Hence we say that the assumed man is in the person of the Word; but the Word did not assume the person of a man. For the higher is not said to be in the person of the lower; rather, the lower is said to be in the person of the higher. Recall what has been said above concerning person.

### Question XI [Cols. 0308A–B]

If Christ is not something consisting of body and soul, I ask what in him was capable of the things said of him in the Gospel. For we read that he fasted, ate, sat, stood, slept, kept watch, rested, was weary from the journey, wept, groaned, sighed, and walked upon the sea. Was, then, the thing capable of such acts a substance or not a substance; created or uncreated; animate or inanimate?

Let no one say that these names were bare names in Christ. For, as Hilary says in Book VI, properties follow names. Is it not madness, then, to take away from the profession of names the truth of their properties?

What, then, was capable of death: that which assumed, or that which was assumed? That man died. Will you explain this in the customary way: “That man—that is, the one having a man—died”? Here this course is not allowed. Far be it that the Word which assumed man should have died, for the fountain of life did not dry up!

When, therefore, it is read, “The Lord of glory was crucified,” and “life dies upon the wood,” only that which was assumed must be understood to have been subject to death. But the soul cannot die. Therefore either the body, or something constituted from soul and body, died. Yet a body that is not capable of reason never lived human life; how, then, could it die by that kind of death by which human beings die?

### Question XII [Cols. 0308C–0309B]

I ask what in Christ was subject to sensation. For neither the soul nor the flesh was sensitive, since what is not an animal is not capable of sensation. If, therefore, in Christ there was no composite from soul and flesh, Christ was neither truly sensitive nor mortal, and thus not truly dead.

Again: was he not capable of receiving instruction, or visible? If these belong to him, how was he not that which is man? Or, if the species “man” is not predicated of him, how can its proper attribute belong to him? Will anyone say that Christ could weep but could not laugh? If, then, things are said of Christ which can belong only to a substance constituted from soul and flesh, who dares deny that he himself is a substance constituted from body and soul?

It has not been heard since the beginning of the world that any soul did not, together with a body, constitute a person or a man. In this the soul differs from an angel. Since, therefore, Christ’s soul is a spirit and not an angel, its natural condition requires that it constitute some substance together with the body.

The Lord says, speaking to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). I ask, then, of what thing was that destruction? For it is written concerning the flesh: “Thou wilt not give thy Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15 [16]). Therefore that separation was necessarily a separation of soul and flesh. For the divinity was separated from neither. But how did death follow their divorce if they had not been united to constitute something living?

John says: “But he spoke concerning the temple of his body” (John 2). This should not be understood as though the flesh had been dissolved in itself, since, as has already been said, it did not see corruption. In what, then, was that dissolution? Or what was subject to dissolution? You will find nothing unless you say that there was some composite from body and soul.

Therefore they were united in living which were separated in dying: a living, breathing animal; a temple that could die and be raised from death; a living, breathing animal, the temple of which he had said, “I will raise it up in three days.”

They grant with us that Christ is man; for they do not dare, with a change of understanding, to alter the words too. We indeed understand it thus—and all Catholics have understood it thus: “Christ is man,” that is, a created substance consisting of body and soul. They explain it thus: “Christ is man,” that is, “having a man.”

### Question XIII [Cols. 0309B–C]

I ask, then, whether Christ and Enoch are men. If Christ is not man in the same sense in which any one of us is, how is he our brother? Peter was a man; he did not have a man. Christ was a man—that is, according to their explanation, he had a man. May one, then, infer in the plural: “Therefore Christ and Peter were men”?

Again, was he not passible and mortal like one of us? If, then, “passible” can belong to us and to him in the same sense, why not “man”? Why do we rather grant that accidents are common to us and him, but not being man? Does he agree with us in accidental matters and not in substantial ones?

Augustine says that the assumption of man is like a garment which does not change that which is clothed. Many glory in this statement. Yet Augustine does not say that the assumed man is the garment of the assuming Word, but “as a garment.” He explains wherein the similarity lies when he says that it does not change that which is clothed. By these words he intends to show nothing other than that, in the assumption of man, the Word of God was not changed or converted into something else. For God became man, as Scripture says, not by conversion of divinity into flesh but by assumption. Therefore he who was found in form as another man did not lack the truth of human nature.

Does any garment become so united to a man that the name “garment” passes over to the wearer, so that the man is called a garment or of the same nature as the garment? Just as God is man and of the same nature as man?

### Question XIV [Cols. 0309D–0311B]

I ask what that state or “garb” is which is predicated of the Word when, according to these men, it is said, “God is man.” For, as they say, having soul and flesh is predicated of him. Let them answer whether it is an accident, a substance, or something which is neither. For it cannot be said to be nothing, since by it Christ is like other human beings.

Peter is that which man is; he does not have a man. Christ is not that which man is. In what, then, are they alike? How, then, are they brothers? Perhaps they will say: “They are alike in this, that each has flesh and soul.” But when Peter is said to be man, a substance consisting of flesh and soul is predicated of him. When Christ is said to be man, having flesh and soul is predicated of him, not a substance consisting of flesh and soul. According to their opinion, therefore, they are not alike in this but very unlike. If there is any likeness there, it is understood solely according to the equivocal application of a name.

But this likeness is slight or nonexistent, since Christ is not the same thing as man; nor is even the clothed thing something that is man; nor does he participate in flesh and soul in the manner of other people.

The Apostle says in the Epistle to the Hebrews that Christ likewise shared with us in flesh and blood—that is, in soul—when he said: “Since the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same” (Hebrews 2), that is, he was a man consisting of soul and flesh, as the commentator says.

And elsewhere, on the First Epistle to Timothy, where it reads, “To the King of the ages” (1 Timothy 1), the commentator says that the assumed man was not always King of the ages, but in time began to be King of the ages. Let every believer consider these things and judge whether Scripture plainly says that Christ is that which man is, so that he has with us a true brotherhood and not a fictitious humanity.

The same Apostle says: “He nowhere takes hold of angels, but he takes hold of the seed of Abraham” (Hebrews 2), that is, he united it in the unity of person. “Whence it behooved him to be made like his brethren in all things” (ibid.). But if he is not that which man is, he is like us in nothing substantial. How, then, was he made like his brethren in all things? At least acknowledge that the Apostle thinks otherwise than you do concerning Christ; or answer, if you can.

If Christ is made like his brethren in all things, then he is like them in substantial things, in genus and species, and in other substantial and all natural things. Consider whether the apostolic sentence, whether you wish it or not, convicts you who say, “This species, man, does not belong to Christ.”

Again, what is more natural to man than to consist of flesh and soul, since this is the being of an animal according to the wisdom of this age? Nor is one capable of human nature to whom such a composition does not belong. If, therefore, that without which no one can be man does not belong to Christ, how is he made like his brethren in all things?

If a rupture befell a man like you, would he still be called like you? If, then, Christ does not consist of body and soul, how is he made like his brethren in all things?

Therefore either confess Christ to be a complete man, a participant in our nature in all things, consisting of soul and flesh; or deny that he is made like us in all things except sin. In him there is nothing lowered but something exalted, since he alone was able to enter into his creature without any diminution of his own substance.

For everything belonging to God belongs to him by nature and to man by grace; and everything belonging to man by nature belongs also to God by condescension. Hence God is most truly predicated as man and man as God: God because of his humanity, and man as God because of his divinity. The person of both is the same, as Augustine says: Christ is that which God is, and is that which man is.

This we too believe and confess, because it is the common faith of all the saints. “In that,” he says, “in which he is the Word, he is equal to the Father; in that in which he is man, the Father is greater.”

If Christ is not that which man is, how does the Apostle number him among human beings, saying: “The first man Adam was made into a living soul; the second man, [the last Adam], into a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15); and: “The first man is from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly” (ibid.)?

Hence, if Christ were not that which man is, he would not be called the second man or the last in relation to the first. Just as no one says of a non-garment: “This garment is first; this clothed person is the last garment.” If, therefore, the first man was a true man, how is the second man not that which man is, but one having a man? Remove every order between them, and the former will not be called first nor the latter last.

For if he had only the matter of the first man and were not some substance consisting of flesh and soul, how would he be from the same matter as the first man? Can a man clothed in purple and this purple be said to be of the same matter? Was that which was animal in Christ without a soul? Or was it animal yet not sensitive? If it could not feel, was it not animal? For that which was devoid of every sense was not animal. See, then: if Christ could feel, something animal and sensitive existed, and thus a substance consisting of soul and flesh existed.

### Question XV [Cols. 0311B–D]

I ask, then, whether the animal which Christ was was rational or irrational. But it could not be irrational, since it did not live by a brute soul. Therefore that which was first animal in Christ, but is now spiritual, was rational and mortal. This is proved by the following enumeration: “The first man, from earth, earthly; the second, from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15). If, therefore, the second man were not that which man is, he would by no means be numbered with the first under the same name. For who counts in this way: “The first man Adam; the second man Gabriel”?

They are accustomed to answer these and similar arguments by saying: “Christ was said to be of human nature because he was clothed with flesh and soul.” Is the nature of a garment said to be that of the wearer? “Such as is the heavenly, such also are the heavenly” (ibid.), as the Apostle says. The relation made by the Apostle through “such” and “as” requires identity of uniform nature. And elsewhere he says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear the image of the heavenly” (ibid.).

Who is this heavenly one? Is he not the man united to the Word of God, who was called heavenly because, above the law of human generation, he was conceived of the Holy Spirit? Augustine says in the homily *On the Creed*: “This was the nature of the man who was made from the Virgin: the nature which belonged to the Virgin from whom Christ was formed and born, just as according to divinity he is of the same nature as the Father.”

### Question XVI [Cols. 0311D–0312A]

I ask what is of the same nature as his mother, if some man does not consist of Christ’s soul and flesh. Again, if flesh and soul are united in Christ differently than in other human beings, how is he like his mother? He is one with her in humanity, just as he is one with the Father in divinity. Hilary says in Book II *On the Trinity* that Christ wished himself to be bodily.

### Question XVII [Cols. 0312A–B]

I ask what that bodily thing was or is which Hilary confesses Christ to have been, if he is not a man consisting of soul and flesh. Would you rather that Christ have the members of a human body than that he truly be a man?

A ram, a living victim, was offered in place of Isaac; but for Christ—impassible according to divinity—what was offered? Was it flesh alone, or rather the partnership of soul and flesh—that is, man?

It has not been heard that what is not a man should be called a true man; the Paschal ram or lamb prefigured Christ. Was the figure something, while Christ according to humanity was nothing? Was the figure something, while the truth itself was nothing? For that ram or lamb was a figure not of divinity but of humanity. Yet humanity is nothing—rather, according to the novel doctrine, there are several things.

If, therefore, the assumed man was not one thing but several things, Christ offered not one thing but two. The Church confesses two natures united in Christ.

### Question XVIII [Cols. 0312B–C]

I ask what we ought to understand by the two natures. By the two natures we must understand either two substances, or properties of essences, or one substance and one property.

That one nature is the divine *ousia* [essence], no one doubts; it is not composite, so that one thing in it possesses and another is possessed. For nothing exists in God that is not God. What conjunction of parts or form with substance could exist in him by whom every form and every structure has been created?

What, then, is understood by the other nature: substance or property? Perhaps you will say in the customary way: not one thing but several are understood by the other nature, namely soul and body.

### Question XIX [Cols. 0312C–0316A]

I ask: if God were now to create soul and flesh not united to constitute anything, would they be called one nature or one substance? Why say more? More properly Christ would be called of three substances than of two; nor would there be anything bodily, contrary to Hilary. Nor would the substance of humanity be contained in soul and flesh, contrary to Jerome.

Nor should Augustine and Hilary be heard when they say: “The Word is one thing, the man another, but not another person.” For to be is one thing; to have is another.

This is the Word of life, of whom John says: “What we have heard and seen, and our hands have handled” (1 John 1). He was not only heard, for the voice of the Father also was heard (Matthew 3); but he was also seen and handled by hands. Will you deny that he was visible and tangible, whom John confesses that he handled? For it is one thing to touch the thing of a garment and another to touch the garment itself. Yet John says that he exercised the effects of these senses upon the Word himself.

If you can, take these things away from Christ and assign them to a garment: “Why do you call me good? No one is good except the one God” (Mark 10). The purpose of him who denied the title was that he who saw him as a true man and called him a good teacher should also believe him to be God, to whom the name of goodness belongs uniquely and incomparably.

“I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8). In “the beginning” understand him to be true God; in “who also speak to you,” recognize true man.

The prophet says: “After this a man was seen upon earth and conversed among human beings” [the Vulgate omits *homo*, “man”] (Baruch 3). “Who will know him?” How, then, do you dare deny that he is true man, or that which man is, when the Holy Spirit through the prophet declares that a true man was seen upon earth and conversed among other human beings?

“I humbled my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Psalm 34 [35]). Whose voice is this? That of the assumed man, who prays not to another, but to one personally united to himself, as the commentator says.

It is established, therefore, that person is not united to person, nor is one having a man united to himself. Who, then, prays? Who is personally united to the one praying? The assumed man spoke to the Word united to himself.

“This is the man who shall live and shall not see death, and shall deliver his soul from the hand of hell” (Psalm 88 [89]).

That great centurion says: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15). What, I ask, did he point out? What did he proclaim to be the Son of God? Was it not that assumed man? For, as Hilary says, he confessed that creature to be the Son of God.

Augustine says that “that man was assumed into the unity of person, so that he who assumed and that which he assumed might be one person.” What could be clearer?

Yet they say this must be explained thus: both are Christ and one person, because one person and one Christ subsists in each. Likewise, the assumed one is one person with the assuming one, because the assumed is united to the one assuming into unity of person—that is, so that unity of person remained. In saying this they deny that it was granted to the assumed man to be God, which Hilary says.

But, as they say, this means that the assumed man was taken into the assuming person, while the person was not divided but remained one in the incarnation as before. They confess that Christ is in both; therefore there must be two things in both. Let them specify in which of them Christ exists personally, or let them condemn Augustine, who distinguishes what assumed and what was assumed as different.

If Christ bestowed upon the assumed one only this, that one person exists in it, while it itself is not a person, what did that united thing receive beyond any other creature? For in what creature is not that person essentially present? Did he not assume soul and body and the parts of the human body, such as hands and feet? Would one say that he personally assumed each of these because, in assuming them, he did not cease to be one person?

Did not the Holy Spirit, appearing in a dove or in tongues of fire, remain the one and same person that he was before? Yet it is impious to say that the Holy Spirit personally assumed those things.

Again: what is it for man to be united into the same person except to become one and the same person? Or do you think it the same thing to be assumed into a person and to be united into a person? Did Christ assume the members of the human body, or did he assume each individually into unity of person?

My hand is not personally united to my spirit, nor is it said to have a soul, although the soul is in it, because, like the other parts, it is animated. Note that man is either a body having a rational soul, or a rational soul having a body.

If the Virgin had borne that man not united to the Word, would he not have been a person?

**Reply.** He would indeed have been a person, but a human one, deriving his personality from his rationality; whereas now, by the sacrament of union, he has become a divine person.

If the assuming person were not that which it assumed, but the assumed were merely the clothing and garment of the one assuming, why would the Son be said to be less than the Father because of the garment alone?

Again, he appeared to Moses and the other saints in many forms, yet he was not thereby made less than the angels. Therefore there must be a difference between this incarnation and those appearances. This incarnation was not garment-like, but rather personal; those appearances were merely garment-like, not personal.

Hence one nowhere reads that the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit or that the Holy Spirit is less than the Father, because the creature in which the Holy Spirit appeared was not assumed as the Son of Man was assumed, in whom the person of the Word might be manifested: not so that he might have the Word of God as other wise men do, but so that he himself might be the Word. It is one thing for the Word to be in a man; another for the Word to be man.

By these words Augustine plainly expresses what we believe concerning the incarnation of the Word. For he says that the Son of Man was assumed. Whether you wish it or not, you must grant that what the Word assumed is the Son of Man. Tell me, I ask, what is this which was assumed and which is the Son of Man? See, at least, now taught by so many proofs, that something which is man consists of Christ’s soul and flesh.

Therefore, if that which was assumed is the Son of Man, it must also be the Son of God, or the Son of God is not the son of the Virgin. But far be it that the Word and that which was assumed should not be the son of the Virgin, since authority says of both that he is the son of the Virgin.

Again, observe that Augustine says that the Son of Man was assumed, not merely so that he might have the Word, but so that he might himself be the Word. For he says: “It is one thing for the Word to be in a man, another for the Word to be man.”

Christ says: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20). If, then, Christ is nothing except what he was from eternity, explain how he has God. For nothing has God except something created.

Elsewhere Christ himself says: “No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down of myself” (John 10). The Word did not separate the soul from himself. Since God became man, he did not lay aside the soul, nor, according to some, did he cease to be man; nor could the soul be absent from him. Therefore it was necessarily separated from the flesh.

But what separation was there in the flesh unless a vital union had joined the soul to the body? Therefore the assumed man himself laid down his soul, when the sensitive animation departed from the flesh. Thus the partnership by which man came to be from soul and flesh was dissolved, while the union of the Word with each remained.

The flesh was stripped of the soul, or the soul of the flesh; and these two were joined to one another at the hour of resurrection. Hence Scripture says that Christ was made man anew. Nothing else is understood by this than the renewed conjunction of flesh and soul. So also blessed Job says: “I shall wait until I am made again [until it comes into my hand]” (Job 14).
