Augustine says: “If anyone says and believes that the man Jesus Christ was not assumed by the Son of God, let him be anathema.” Bede agrees: “May the memory perish from the earth of those who deny that Christ is true God and true man.”

Therefore the same substance was both made and predestined: predestined from eternity and made in time. Thus man bears all that belongs to God, and God has and bears all that belongs to man except sin.

Hence true religion professes of Christ both the acts of each substance and the truth of each substance. Thus he is called unmade according to divinity and made according to humanity, as the Apostle says, speaking of Christ: “Who was predestined Son of God in power” (Romans 1).

For what is predestination? A preparation in time for grace to be bestowed, or a pre-election of those to be saved. What, then, in Christ was predestined that was capable of living blessedly? For what always existed cannot be subject to predestination.

Perhaps they will grant that the soul of the man was predestined. But why will they call it the soul of a man when it never constituted any man together with flesh? Again, the Apostle does not say, “The Son of God whose soul was predestined,” but “who was predestined.” The relative pronoun requires that the Son of God himself be understood as predestined.

Here they answer that the Son of God was predestined, though not according to that which assumed, but according to that which was assumed. These words are sound; would that they had a sound understanding of them!

Answer, I ask: if Christ is nothing which is said to be assumed, how is he himself predestined according to that which is assumed? Or, if that which is assumed is not predestined, how is Christ predestined according to that which is assumed? But if you say that what is assumed is predestined, you must grant with us that what is assumed is the Son of God.

The expression *secundum* (“according to”) sometimes indicates a cause: as when someone is called rational according to rationality, because that quality is formally the efficient cause why he is rational. Sometimes it signifies that from which something comes to pass, as though materially: as when one says, “A man is rational according to the soul,” or “visible according to the body.” Neither would be said if the soul were not rational or the body visible.

Sometimes *secundum* indicates the tenor or quality of a thing from an author, as when one says, “This Gospel is according to Luke or Mark.” Somewhat akin to this is the way someone is said to judge or speak according to conscience. Sometimes *secundum* signifies, as it were, that in which something is found: as when one says, “This expression is of this property according to this word, or of that property according to that one.”

### Question XX [Cols. 0316A–C]

I ask, then, what is signified by *secundum* when it is said that Christ was predestined according to humanity. They reply that it expresses unity of person. Therefore I ask how unity of person is expressed by this word *secundum*, when it is said, “Christ is predestined according to that which is assumed,” if that which is assumed is not one person with him.

Augustine, speaking of the assumed and the assuming, says: “Both are not two, but one Christ, who, according to that in which he is man, was indeed predestined, that he might be Son—not an adoptive but a natural Son; not by nature but by grace; not by adoption but by union. Thus in our head the fountain of grace appears. For by the same grace every believer becomes a Christian as that man by grace became Christ.”

The same author elsewhere says: “He who made that man such that he never had and never would have an evil will, himself made a good will from an evil will in his members.” In the book *On the Trinity* the same author says: “He made us believe in Christ, who made for us the Christ in whom we believe. He makes in human beings the beginning of faith who made the man Jesus the author and finisher of faith.”

Who, then, carefully considering what has been set forth, can doubt that from Christ’s soul and flesh there subsists a man capable of predestination and of the other things mentioned above? I admonish you, reader, to gather what has been said into one view of reason, and you will see that it was granted to man to be a person of divine substance, and that, remaining God what he was, he was made man what he was not.

[Col. 0315]

## Three Conferences, or Disputations, on the Incarnate Word [Cols. 0315, 0315D–0317C]

### Conference I. On the Three Silences, in the Second of Which the Incarnation of the Word Is Treated

[Col. 0315D]

“While all things held the middle [quiet] silence” (Wisdom 18).

There are three silences. The first silence is ignorance of sickness. The second silence is despair of healing. The third silence is the attainment of health. The first silence was before the Law; the second, between Law and grace; the third will be after this life.

The first silence existed when man did not recognize his disease; therefore he was silent and did not seek a remedy. But after the Law entered and showed the sick their wounds, the silence was immediately broken, and the sick at once began to seek health. Yet because they wished to be healed through the works of the Law, where health is not found, they could not find what they sought.

At last, therefore, when man considered through the Law that no one could be justified, he was, as it were, wearied by long cries and already despairing; he again ceased to speak, and the second silence followed.

Then the almighty Word of God the Father, coming into flesh, broke the silence: he spoke peace, gave grace, offered mercy, and promised pardon. The sick began to run to the physician and, as though with great cries, to demand a remedy through the pure faith of the heart and true confession of the mouth.

This, then, is what takes place in the present life: that man may receive health through the grace of God. But when he has received full health and has been brought to the blessedness of future immortality, he will have nothing further to ask; then that third blessed silence, which will never end, shall follow.

Between the first and middle silence many words sounded; between the middle and last silence one Word sounds. The many words were the manifold commandments of the Law, which was given through Moses. The one Word is the one grace of God, which came through Jesus Christ—or rather, Jesus Christ himself.

Moses, God’s servant, uttered many words and many discourses. God the Father sent one Word and one discourse. But Moses’ discourses were not almighty, because they could not accomplish what they said; and therefore at length they fell silent, at some point failing in the promise.

Then came the almighty Discourse, who not only spoke, but did whatever he said—indeed, whatever he willed. This discourse, this Word, still speaks so long as he works his promises in his faithful. But when he has fulfilled what was promised, he will then, as it were, cease speaking.

Once the promises have been fulfilled, because nothing will be lacking that might further be asked, there will be happy silence for ever.

While, then, all things were keeping the middle silence—rightly, all things: that is, not only those who despaired in petition, but also those who had failed in promise—and while the night in its course had reached the middle of its journey. In Sacred Scripture “night” is sometimes understood as the devil, sometimes as his members, that is, wicked sinners; sometimes as sin; sometimes as the present life. [Col. 0317D] Thus in this place the night signifies the passing course of this mortal life, just as elsewhere the day signifies the brightness of everlasting life. The present life, therefore, is night; but the life to come is day. This night has its evening; that day has its dawn. The evening of the present night was the decline of the first day; the dawn of that day is the decline of the present age. The evening of this night began when Adam sinned, until, having received the sentence of death, he was driven from Paradise and went out into the darkness of this world. The dawn of the following day extends from Christ’s resurrection to the end of the age. Therefore this life is night. But what is the course of this life? Let us see where it runs. Through mortality it runs toward death; through death, toward condemnation. Thus mortal life runs downward, [Col. 0318A] just as immortal life runs upward. The upward path is in heaven; the downward path is in hell. The middle path is the course of the present life: we enter it by being born, run through it by living, and leave it by dying. When, then, did the night in its course reach the middle of its journey, except when death drew down with itself to hell all whom it found in the course of this present life, and no mortal person could yet ascend to immortal life?

[Col. 0318B] Or “night” may be understood as sin: a night which began with original sin and ran on through actual sins. Thus, when, after the original transgression, first the transgression of the natural law and then the succeeding transgression of the written law had brought sin to its highest increase, the night, as it were, had reached the middle of its course. But when the true light appeared, this night immediately began to turn downward; and now, as though by a certain reciprocal exchange, it gradually diminishes and recedes, until the light, increasing, arrives at full day. Consider, then, the most ordered design of the divine dispensation. When every hope of recovering salvation had perished, when death was dragging all things downward with itself, and sin had reached its height, then the almighty Word is sent to liberate, so that the gift of divine grace may be commended all the more.

“He came,” it says. Who? From where? To where? The Word of the Most High, the Word of God, the Father’s only-begotten, king and son of the King, by the Father’s consent, came to endure suffering: from equality of majesty to the gibbet of the cross; from the royal seat to the workshop of sin; from heaven’s light down to [Col. 0318C] hell’s darkness. But did he therefore lose his kingdom? On the contrary: freeing those who were slaves of sin, he raised them up to reign together with himself. Perhaps, therefore, he came “from royal seats,” because in his Father’s house are many dwelling places (John 14), and they shall reign with him eternally when they receive the kingdom prepared from the beginning of the world. For he was the King’s only-begotten: he alone possessed the kingdom. But because he came to adopt brothers to reign with himself, he ought to come not now from a royal seat, but from royal seats, since the kingdom to which God’s elect are called was prepared from the beginning of the world.

## COLLATION II. That the Word, when made flesh, assumed a nature, not a person; and that the one person is both the assuming and the assumed.

[Col. 0318D] “The Word was made flesh” (John 1). What Word of God is this, which is also God? For a human being’s word is not a human being; but God’s Word is God. Just as the word of the heart is the heart, and the word goes forth from the heart, and the heart’s word is nothing other than the heart itself, so the Word of God cannot be other than God. Wisdom is the word of the heart; it is born from the heart and is not separated from the heart. The heart itself is wisdom, and wisdom is from the heart itself, and the heart and its wisdom are one wisdom. So God is wisdom, and wisdom is from God himself, and God and his wisdom are one wisdom. God’s Wisdom is God’s Word. That very Word was made flesh. What is flesh? A human being. It was made flesh; it was made human. How was it made human? By assuming humanity. For the Word assumed human [Col. 0319A] nature, not a human person. He did not assume a human person, but assumed humanity into person.

Understand what I say. The Catholic faith is firm: the personal Word assumed humanity—not a person, but a nature. Why do we not call the assumed a person, as we call the assuming Word a person? So that we may not proclaim two persons in Christ, nor appear to introduce a quaternity and so confuse the confession of the Trinity. Therefore we say that humanity, a nature and not a person, was assumed by the Word. What is a human being? Soul and body. Hence humanity was assumed, because soul and body were assumed. Hence an assumed person is not spoken of, because soul and body, before they were united to the Word in person, were not united to one another as a person.

[Col. 0319B] Consequently, because they were not assumed, they were not united, as an assumed person; but because in being assumed they were united, they were assumed into person. But you will say: if soul and body, before being united to the Word, were not a person because they were not united with one another, was not the soul nevertheless, even by itself, a person insofar as it was a rational spirit? But if the soul by itself was a person insofar as it was a rational spirit, how was a person not assumed when a rational soul was assumed?

But just as a rational soul and flesh were not assumed as a person because before the assumption they did not possess union, though they were assumed into person because they were united from the moment they were assumed, so the rational soul itself was not assumed as a person because before union with the Word it no more possessed personal existence than it possessed existence by itself. For from the moment it began to exist, it began to be united; and from the moment it existed, it was united. But from the moment it was united, it was one person together with that to which it was united. See what follows. If it was united from the moment it existed, and from the moment it was united it was a person, then was it a person from the moment it existed? But if it was a person from the moment it existed, how was a person not assumed, when that which was a person was assumed?

[Col. 0319C] But consider this. Do not let the entanglement of the language disturb you: faith is what is sought. Language causes much confusion. Attend carefully. It was a person from the moment it existed, because it was united from the moment it existed. Why, then, do we not say that a person was assumed? Attend. When it was assumed, it was united. From the moment it began to be united, it began to be a person; [Col. 0319D] yet not insofar as it existed, but insofar as it was united. Had it at any time possessed existence by itself, it would have possessed personhood from itself. But because it was always united, it was always one person together with him to whom it was united. Therefore we do not say that a human person was assumed, but that humanity was assumed into person, because human nature in Christ was not a person by virtue of its existence, since it did not exist by itself. Rather, by virtue of being united, it was one person together with him to whom it was united.

For “person” denotes distinction. Therefore that which was a person in itself was not a person from itself. Hence a person was not assumed, but a nature; because that which was assumed, being of rational nature, no more had personal existence outside the assumption than it had independent existence. [Col. 0320A] But you will say: why, then, is humanity said to have been assumed, if a person is not said to have been assumed, when that rational nature which was assumed was, before the union itself, neither human nor a person, since it never existed independently outside the union, for it was assumed from the moment it existed?

But consider that the rational nature which was assumed possessed human existence—that is, it was human nature—from the moment it existed. Therefore, because it was assumed in what it was, from the moment it was human, humanity was assumed. For what was assumed was humanity in and from the fact of being assumed. But that rational nature which was assumed was not a person in and from the fact that it existed, because it did not exist independently. Rather, it was united from the moment it was assumed; and from the moment it was united, [Col. 0320B] it was one person with the uniting Word. Therefore a person is not said to have been assumed, but a nature, because what was assumed had, from the moment it existed, both nature and humanity—that is, human nature; whereas it did not begin to be a person from the moment it existed, because it never existed independently, but from the moment it was united to the personal Word. Therefore humanity—that is, human nature—was assumed, not a person.

## COLLATION III. On the incarnation of the Word and its mystery with respect to the messenger and the Virgin.

All things were made through the Wisdom of God; but not all things were made for that Wisdom, except only those things which can enjoy wisdom. These are beings endowed with reason and possessing intelligence and perception for discerning [Col. 0320C] good and avoiding evil. One part of them was created above among the angels; another was ordered below among human beings. Thus humanity was made not only through God’s Wisdom, in order to exist, but also for God’s Wisdom, in order to be blessed: namely, that it might enjoy her by that faculty through which wisdom can be apprehended. But because, by sinning, it lost the faculty by which it ought to have enjoyed wisdom, it forgot to eat its own bread and exchanged that nourishment by which souls live for bodily pleasure. Thus immersed in earthly and bodily things in perception and affection, humanity could not raise itself to the thought or love of spiritual things; but savouring only what belongs to the flesh, it did not know the delight of spiritual things.

[Col. 0320D] Yet God’s Wisdom itself did not wish to lose the human being who had been made for her. Though she herself was above and humanity below, she came to where humanity was, in order to call humanity back to herself, whence it had fallen. The Word was made flesh so that he who was God above human beings might be human among human beings. And that bread was turned into milk, so that it could be taken by little children. Above, Wisdom was bread; below, that same Wisdom was milk. In divinity, bread; in humanity, milk. Thus little children, nourished by the milk of humanity, were strengthened for the bread of divinity, so that the same one might refresh them in both ways and, by refreshing them, restore the weak to incorruption. Therefore he gave those to be restored to incorruption the food of incorruption: for the little ones, the immaculate flesh which he took from his virgin Mother; but for the perfect, [Col. 0321A] the incorruptible divinity which he possessed from the eternal Father. To the former, that they might not fail meanwhile on the way; to the latter, that they might afterwards be perfected in the homeland. To the former, for consolation; to the latter, for glorification.

For this reason, then, the Son of God became human for the redemption of human beings: so that flesh might be liberated through flesh, and the price of redemption for the human race might be taken from its own substance; so that the remedy might arise from the source from which the defect had been contracted, and, in the same matter, both the physician’s skill and the redeemed person’s justice might be shown, when the remedy is found from what is to be healed and the price from what is to be redeemed. But because humanity was to be delivered from corruption, the price of redemption had to be incorrupt. Therefore a Virgin Mother was chosen, that the immaculate one might be born from the pure; so that, as in heaven the eternal God had [Col. 0321B] an immortal Father, so on earth the incorrupt one might have a Virgin Mother.

Thus in heaven, such as the Father is, such is the Son; and on earth, such as the mother is, such is the son. In heaven, eternal and immeasurable with the Father; on earth, immaculate and gentle with the mother. In heaven, incorrupt and exalted with the Father; on earth, virgin and humble with the mother. In heaven, the image of the Father; on earth, the imitator of the mother. The mother was a virgin and rejoiced in humility. The Virgin’s Son, himself a virgin, commended humility. Thus the Lamb was such as the Lamb’s mother: pure from the pure, incorrupt from the Virgin. Through a Virgin he came to us; through virginity he went before us. Through incorruption he came in order to take away sin; through virginity he went before us in order to show virtue. He came to confer a remedy; he went before us [Col. 0321C] to give an example. For a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, just as a bad tree cannot bear good fruit (Matt. 7; Luke 6), since every tree is known by its fruit: the root whole, and the branch incorrupt.

Accordingly, Gabriel the messenger was sent for this coming, to proclaim the new birth in the flesh of the Son of God, in which the form of a servant, joined to the Lord, powerfully overcame the enemy. The servant-form was strong in him, yet not violent in inflicting injury, but effective in obtaining justice. Therefore Gabriel was sent, since his name is interpreted “strength of God”; for that very weakness was strength, because in it the enemy was overcome and the spoil taken by the violent one was brought back. [Col. 0321D] For three had perished, and a fourth followed—namely, their Redeemer. The first was without male and without female; the second from a male, without a female; the third from male and female; the fourth without a male, from a female. Adam, indeed, was neither from male nor from female; Eve, however, was from a male without a female; but those descended from them were from male and female together. And the first male and female fell, and through them all who came after them, born of male and female, fell. Because the first author of sin was overthrown by a woman, a woman conceived and bore, without a male, the author of grace, so that the same sex which had been the origin of sin might become the beginning of grace.

Therefore he says: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you” (Luke 1). For Mary was truly full of grace, through whom grace descended upon [Col. 0322A] all the children of humankind. First grace was upon her, afterwards grace was in her, and then grace came forth from her: upon her, for overshadowing; in her, for fruitfulness; from her, for salvation. For grace came to visit human nature, and entered by the way by which it had gone out. It had gone out through a woman, and it entered through a woman. Grace came first into Mary herself, then descended into that which was from her, and took from the Virgin’s flesh a nature—a victim for nature—which it might offer free in order to liberate those in bondage; so that it might first pour out wholly into her what it would afterwards, through her, bestow upon all the redeemed.

Therefore she was full of grace, from whom the fountain of grace arose. And therefore, gracious Virgin, in some sense all that comes to us through him who was born [Col. 0322B] from you comes to us from you. Full of grace—so full that from your overflowing abundance the whole world may draw. For if the prudent virgins received oil in their vessels with their lamps (Matt. 25), you, most prudent Virgin and Virgin of virgins, had not merely one vessel filled with the oil of grace, by which you might nourish your lamp, burning unquenchably; but you bore another, overflowing and unfailing vessel, from which, by pouring out the oil of mercy, you might illuminate all lamps and fill everyone’s vessels to their utmost and perfection, without diminishing it in any respect. You were therefore prudent in providing for yourself, but not timid in helping others. You did not say, “Perhaps there will not be enough for me and for you” (ibid.); but, knowing that it would suffice both for you and for us, you retained sufficiently and gave sufficiently.

The light in the lamp was virginity in the flesh; the oil in the vessel was humility in the heart. And there was another vessel: the humanity of the Word in your womb, full of grace, from whose fullness you too received both the light of virginity in the flesh and the oil of humility in the heart. Afterwards, by your undefiled childbirth, you gave us that very unfailing vessel, so that from its fullness there might be poured forth that by which our extinguished lamps might be illumined and our empty vessels filled. You were full of grace when the fountain of grace burst forth from the soil of your flesh, [Col. 0322C] that it might flow over all the earth, water the dry land, and make the barren fruitful.

From this fullness of grace, she too received who, though barren, conceived; she recognized the fruitful Virgin coming to her and said: “How does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1). Rightly, “mother of the Lord,” because the Lord of majesty came in the form of a servant. For he who was born human was also God. In respect of what was assumed, he was the Virgin’s son; but in respect of what assumed, the Son of Majesty. Yet he was one and the same: both the Virgin’s son and the Son of Majesty. Therefore the human being who was assumed is the natural Son of God because of him who assumed; and he is the true son of man because of him whom he assumed. Let no one, then, call Christ an adoptive Son, since he is the natural Son; for the human being whom he assumed and the God who assumed are not two sons, but one Son: God and human, Jesus Christ. Therefore she who bore the form of a servant is the mother of the Lord, because the majesty of the Lord was in the form of a servant, and the form of a servant and the majesty of the Lord are one.

[Col. 0323A] Rightly, therefore, she calls her the mother of her Lord, since she believed that he who had been conceived as a human being and was carried in the Virgin’s womb according to the flesh was God—the one who by his divinity bore all things. Therefore she says: “How does this happen to me, that the mother of my Lord [Col. 0324A] should come to me? And blessed are you who believed, because all that was spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled in you.” Then Mary said: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (ibid.). An exposition on this was set forth earlier in the allegories on the Gospel of Luke.

[Col. 0323]

## ON JEPHTHAH’S DAUGHTER. (G)

[Col. 0323A] Concerning Jephthah’s daughter: because her father offered her to God as a whole burnt offering, having vowed in war that, if he won, [Col. 0323B] he would offer as a whole burnt offering whoever first came out of his house to meet him; when he made this vow he won, and, when his daughter came to meet him, he fulfilled what he had vowed. This is customarily a great and most difficult question to judge: some wish to understand what it means and inquire devoutly; while others, who truly oppose the holy Scriptures here with ignorant impiety, make this their principal charge—that the God of the Law and the Prophets was pleased even by human sacrifices.

To their calumnies we first reply that the God of the Law and the Prophets—or, to speak more explicitly, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—was not pleased even by those sacrifices in which burnt offerings of cattle were offered, but wished those sacrifices, because they were signs and certain shadows of things to come, to commend to us the realities which they signified. There was also this useful reason why those sacrifices were changed and are now not commanded to be offered, indeed are prohibited: lest we should suppose that God truly delights in such things according to a carnal affection. But whether future things ought also to have been signified by human sacrifices is rightly questioned.

Nor ought we to shudder and recoil in this matter even at the deaths of human beings, although dead, if those who willingly accepted these things being done to themselves were commended to God for eternal reward. But if this were true, that kind of sacrifice would not displease God. Yet the same Scripture testifies quite plainly that it does displease God. For when he wished and commanded that all firstborn should be consecrated to himself and be his own, he wished only the firstborn of human beings to be redeemed from him, lest they should believe that they must sacrifice to God those sons whom they had first received at birth.

Then Scripture speaks more openly as follows, showing that God disapproves human burnt offerings so strongly that he prohibits them, detesting them among other nations and commanding his own people not to dare imitate them: “Take heed to yourself,” he says, “that you do not follow the nations after they have been exterminated before you, and that you do not seek out their gods, saying: ‘As the nations do to their gods, so will I do.’ You shall not do so to the Lord your God. For they have done to their gods the abominations which the Lord hates, because they burn even their sons and daughters with fire” (Deut. 12).

What could be shown more clearly by these testimonies of Holy Scripture [Col. 0324A]—to omit others of the same kind—than that the Lord from whom this Scripture [Col. 0324B] was bestowed upon the human race not only does not love, but even hates such sacrifices in which human beings are immolated? He certainly loves and crowns those cases in which a righteous person, suffering injustice, contends for truth even unto death, or is killed by enemies whom he offends for justice’s sake, returning good to them for evil—that is, love for hatred. Such blood the Lord calls righteous blood, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. 23). Above all, he himself shed his blood for us and offered himself as a sacrifice to God; he offered himself, that is, by being killed by enemies for justice’s sake. Imitating him, many thousands of martyrs contended for truth even unto death and were immolated by raging enemies. Of them Scripture says: “He tested them as gold in the furnace, and accepted them as the victim of a whole burnt offering” (Wisdom 3). Hence also the Apostle says: “For I am already being sacrificed” (Phil. 2).

But Jephthah did not make a whole burnt offering to the Lord from his daughter in this way. Rather, he did so as cattle had been commanded to be offered and human beings had been forbidden to be sacrificed. What he did seems more like what Abraham did, which the Lord commanded specifically, not by a general law. He did command that such sacrifices should at some time be made for him; indeed, he also prohibited their being made. Therefore what Jephthah did differs from Abraham’s deed: Abraham offered his son because he was commanded; Jephthah did what was forbidden by the Law and was commanded by no special injunction.

Moreover, not only later in his own Law, but even then in Abraham’s own son, the Lord showed how little he delighted in such sacrifices, when he prevented the father—whose faith he had tested by commanding him—from killing his son, and supplied a ram, by which the sacrifice customarily and lawfully performed in accordance with the appropriateness of ancient times could be completed. But if anyone is troubled by this—how Abraham could devoutly believe that God delights in such sacrifices if they are unlawfully offered to God, and therefore thinks that Jephthah too rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God—let him first consider that it is one thing voluntarily to vow, another to obey one who commands. For if a servant is commanded by the Lord to do something unusual in the household, and does it in praiseworthy obedience, he is not therefore to be punished if he presumed to do it of his own accord.

Furthermore, Abraham [Col. 0325A] had grounds for believing that, because of the divine command, he should not spare his son—not because he believed that God gladly receives such victims, but because he believed that God had commanded this in order to raise his son after he was slain and to show something to him as the wise God. For this is also written of him in the Epistle entitled To the Hebrews, and his faith is praised because he believed of God that he could raise his son (Heb. 11). But Jephthah, though God neither commanded nor requested it, and contrary to God’s lawful command, voluntarily vowed a human sacrifice. For as it is written: “Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord and said: ‘If you deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, whoever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon, I shall offer him as a whole burnt offering to the Lord’” (Judg. 11).

[Col. 0325B] Certainly, by these words he did not vow some animal which could lawfully be offered as a whole burnt offering according to the Law. For it neither is nor ever was customary for cattle to come to meet commanders returning victorious from war. As concerns dumb animals, dogs are accustomed to run to meet their masters in fawning service; but he could not have been thinking of them in his vow, lest he seem to have vowed to God something not merely unlawful but contemptible and, according to the Law, unclean. Nor did he say, “Whatever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me, I shall offer it as a whole burnt offering”; rather he said, “Whoever comes out to meet me, I shall offer him.” There can be no doubt that he thought of nothing other than a human being—though perhaps not his only daughter, although who could have preceded her in such great paternal [Col. 0325C] glory, unless perhaps his wife?

For the fact that he did not say “whatever,” but “whoever comes out from the doors of my house” (ibid.), accords with Scripture’s custom of using the masculine gender for either sex, as it is said of Abraham, “rising from the dead” (Gen. 23), although his wife had died. Since, therefore, Scripture seems to have made no judgment about this vow and deed, as it made the clearest judgment about Abraham when he offered his son at God’s command, but has left it written merely for readers to judge—just as, concerning Judah the son of Jacob, when he unknowingly went in to his daughter-in-law, though, so far as it concerned him, he committed fornication because he thought her a prostitute, Scripture neither approved nor disapproved this, but left it to be weighed and judged after consultation with justice and God’s Law [Col. 0325D]—since, then, God’s Scripture has pronounced no judgment upon this deed of Jephthah in either direction, in order that our judgment might be exercised in judging it, we could now say that God was displeased by such a vow and that Jephthah was brought to this punishment, so that above all his only daughter came to meet him.

For if he had hoped for or wished this, he would not immediately, on seeing her, have torn his garments and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become an obstacle in my eyes” (Judg. 11). Moreover, although a long delay of sixty days was granted to his daughter, the Lord did not prevent him from killing his only and most beloved child, as he prevented Abraham, so that by fulfilling his vow he might strike himself with the gravest bereavement, while not in the least appeasing God by the immolation of a human being. [Col. 0326A] Therefore such a punishment seems to have been returned upon such a father, so that the example of such a vow might not be left unpunished, and that people might not suppose they vowed some great thing to God when they vowed human victims—and, what is more horrible, their children—or that such vows were not genuine but only feigned, in the hope, after Abraham’s example, that God would forbid their fulfillment.

[Col. 0326A] We could say this, I say, were we not especially recalled from this judgment by two testimonies of the divine Scriptures, so that we may investigate this event, recorded in books of such authoritative memory, more diligently, insofar as the Lord helps, and more cautiously, lest we rashly pronounce judgment in either direction. One testimony is that in the Epistle to the Hebrews [Col. 0326B] Jephthah is mentioned among such persons that we hesitate to condemn him. There it is written: “And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, performed righteousness, and obtained promises” (Heb. 11). The other is that, where these things are told of him—that he vowed and fulfilled such a vow—Scripture first says: “And the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and, going around Gilead and Manasseh, he passed through the watchtower of Gilead; and from the watchtower of Gilead he crossed over to the children of Ammon; and Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord” (Judg. 11), followed by the rest concerning the vow itself. Thus all that was done thereafter seems to be understood as works of the Spirit of the Lord which had come upon him.

[Col. 0326C] These testimonies compel us rather to ask why it happened than lightly to condemn why it happened. But first, with regard to the passage from the Epistle to the Hebrews which I mentioned: among those praiseworthy men there listed is not only Jephthah, but also Gideon, of whom Scripture likewise says, “The Spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon” (Judg. 6). Yet we cannot merely fail to praise Gideon’s deed in making an ephod, after which all Israel committed fornication, and which became a snare to Gideon’s house; rather, because Scripture has most plainly indicated this, we do not doubt that it condemns it. Yet no injury is thereby done to the Spirit of the Lord, who strengthened Gideon so that he might overcome his people’s enemies with such ease.

[Col. 0326D] Why, then, is he mentioned among those who through faith conquered kingdoms and performed righteousness (Heb. 11), unless because Holy Scripture, while truly praising the faith and justice of those persons, is not thereby prevented from also truthfully noting their sins, if it knows of any and judges it fitting to record them? For even in Gideon’s request for a sign, when he tested God by means of the fleece, I do not know whether he did not transgress the command which says: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Matt. 4). Yet even in his testing, the Lord showed what he wished to foretell: namely, by the fleece soaked with dew while the whole threshing floor around it was dry, he figured the first people of Israel, in whom the saints were chosen as though by spiritual rain; and afterwards, by the wet threshing floor and the dry fleece, he figured the Church spread throughout the world, possessing heavenly grace not in the fleece, as in a covering, but openly, while that former people had, as it were, been dried and estranged from the dew of the same grace.

[Col. 0327A] Nevertheless, because of his good and faithful life, in which he is to be believed to have died, he did not without reason deserve such a testimony in the Epistle to the Hebrews among the faithful and those who perform righteousness. Yet whether, because after the statement “the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah,” these events followed—that he vowed that vow and fulfilled what he vowed—all must be attributed to the Spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice should be regarded as if the Lord had commanded it, as he commanded Abraham’s, I would not readily say. For this difference could indeed be brought forward concerning Gideon: after the sin he committed in making the ephod, no subsequent prosperity of his is recorded; whereas after Jephthah vowed, there followed his remarkable victory, which he had vowed in order to obtain and, having obtained it, fulfilled what he had vowed.

[Col. 0327B] Again, however, we must consider that Gideon, although not after making the ephod, nevertheless after testing the Lord—which is certainly a sin—inflicted great slaughter on the enemies after defeating them and gained deliverance for the people. For it is written: “Let not your indignation be angry with me, and I will test once more with the fleece” (Judg. 6). He feared God’s anger because he knew that he sinned by testing him, which God most plainly forbids in his Law. Yet this sin of his was followed by the clear manifestation of a wonderful sign, great success in victory, and the people’s deliverance. For God had already determined to aid the afflicted people, and he made use of the mind of this leader, whom he had taken up for this work—not only when it was faithful and devout, but even when it was failing and erring—both to foretell what he wished and to accomplish what he had said.

For God bestowed many benefits upon his people not only through such persons as these, who, although they sinned, are nevertheless numbered among the righteous, but also through Saul himself, wholly rejected as he was. The Spirit of the Lord even rushed upon Saul, and he prophesied (1 Sam. 19), not when he acted justly, but when he raged against the holy and innocent David. For the Spirit of the Lord works through good and evil persons, through those who know and those who do not know, what he knows and has determined must be done. Thus even through Caiaphas, the Lord’s most bitter persecutor, who did not know what he was saying, he uttered the notable prophecy that Christ had to die for the nation (John 11).

For who acted, except the Spirit of the Lord, in bringing it specifically into Gideon’s mind—when the judge wished to test the Lord and did not believe what God had spoken to him through his hand about the people’s salvation—that the fleece should first be soaked and later dry, and the threshing floor first dry and later wet? Thus it may be reckoned to the weakness of his waning faith and to his fault. But the fact that God also used such a disposition of his for what needed to be signified to the human race is to be understood as belonging to God’s mercy and [Col. 0328A] wonderful providence.

But if anyone says that Gideon knowingly did and said all these things by prophetic revelation, so that such signs might be shown through him; that he did not fail in faith, and did believe what the Lord had promised him; but that he wished, under prophetic prompting, to test by means of the fleece, and therefore that his testing was blameless, just like Jacob’s deception; and that when he said to the Lord, “Let not your indignation be angry with me,” he said this not because he feared God’s anger, but because he trusted that God would not be angry when he did what, as a prophet, he knew ought to be done at the prompting of God’s Spirit—such a person may be heard, provided that he does not dare excuse from sin the matter concerning the ephod, which Scripture itself condemned, whatever it may signify.

For even the fact that three hundred men—whose very number pertains to the sign of the cross—took earthen jars and enclosed burning torches in them, and, when the jars were broken, suddenly displayed many flashing lights which terrified such a multitude of enemies, seems to have been done by Gideon on his own initiative. For Scripture does not say that the Lord instructed him to do this. Yet who inspired his mind and counsel to accomplish so great a sign, except the Lord, who prefigured that his saints would possess the treasure of Gospel light in earthen vessels? Hence the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). In the sufferings of martyrdom, as though those vessels were broken, the greater brilliance of their glory shone forth, and the unexpected brightness of Christ overcame the impious enemies of Gospel preaching.

[Col. 0328C] Whether, then, through those who knew or those who did not know, the Spirit of the Lord worked, in prophetic times, preaching and prefiguration of future things, it must not therefore be said that their sins were not sins, merely because God—who also knows how to make good use of our evils—used even their very sins to signify what he willed. Accordingly, if for that reason it was not sin either to vow or to render any kind of human killing, even a parricidal sacrifice, because it signified something great and spiritual, then God prohibited temporal things in vain and declared that he hated them; for those things which he commanded to be done are undoubtedly also related to some signification of great and spiritual realities. To whom, therefore, would he prohibit those things, since [Col. 0328D] they could nevertheless lawfully be done on account of the same signification of the same realities for which these things were lawfully done, unless human sacrifices, signifying nothing of that kind—as it is fitting to believe—were pleasing to God when a person is not killed by enemies for righteousness, because he wished to live rightly or refused to sin, but one human being is immolated by another as a chosen victim, in the manner of cattle?

“But what if,” someone says, “because animal victims, precisely because they were customary, although they too are referred by right understanding to the signification of spiritual things, nevertheless made people less attentive to the need to seek the great mystery of Christ and the Church, God wished to awaken the souls of men, as it were asleep, by something remarkable and unexpected? And especially because [Col. 0329A] he had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to him, he saw to it that something of this kind should be offered to him, so that astonishment itself might produce a great question, and a great question might raise the zeal of a devout mind to investigate a great mystery; and the human mind, devoutly searching the depth of prophecy, might draw up the Lord Christ like a fish on a hook from the depths of the Scriptures.”

We do not oppose this reasoning and consideration. But one question concerns the mind of the one making the vow; another concerns the providence of God, who makes good use of his mind, whatever it may be. Therefore, if the Spirit of the Lord, which came upon Jephthah, expressly commanded him to make this vow—which Scripture, indeed, does not disclose—yet, if he commanded it whose commands may not lawfully be despised, then not only is folly not to be blamed, but obedience is to be praised. For if a person kills himself—which certainly it is wicked to do by human will and design—then, if it is commanded by God, it must surely be understood as done obediently rather than criminally. This question has been sufficiently discussed in Book I of *The City of God*.

But if Jephthah, following human error, believed that a human sacrifice ought to be vowed, his sin was justly punished in the case of his only daughter. He himself seems sufficiently to indicate this by his words when he says: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become an offence in my eyes” (Judg. 11); and also by tearing his garments. Yet even here his error possesses some praise of faith: he feared God enough to render what he had vowed. Nor did he evade the sentence of divine judgment upon himself—whether hoping that God would forbid it, as he did in Abraham’s case, or resolving to do rather than despise the understood will of God, even if he did not forbid it.

Although here too it may rightly be asked whether it is more truly understood that God did not will this to be done, and that God would rather have been obeyed if it had not been done, since he had shown that he did not will it both in the case of Abraham’s son and in the legal prohibition. Yet if Jephthah had therefore not done it, he would have appeared to spare himself in the case of his only daughter rather than to follow God’s will. He therefore understood more fully in his daughter’s coming out to meet him that God was avenging himself; and he faithfully submitted himself to just punishment, fearing a harsher vengeance for evasion. For he believed [Col. 0329D] that the soul of his good and virgin daughter would be received well: she had not vowed herself to be sacrificed, but had not resisted her father’s vow and will, and had followed God’s judgment. For just as death ought not voluntarily to be inflicted by anyone either upon himself or upon another, so, when God commands it, it must not be refused, since by his ordinance it must be undergone at whatever time. Nor does anyone who declines to suffer it thereby strive to avoid it altogether, but only to postpone it.

Let us now briefly seek and unfold, so far as God helps us, what the Spirit of the Lord prefigured in this matter, whether through Jephthah’s ignorance or knowledge, through his imprudence or prudence, through obedience or offence, through faith. For this passage of the sacred Scriptures admonishes us [Col. 0330A] and in some manner urges us to consider one mighty in strength; for Jephthah is called such, and his name means “opening.” But the Lord Christ, as the Gospel states, “opened the understanding” of his disciples that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24).

Jephthah’s brothers rejected him and expelled him from his father’s house, objecting that he was the son of a harlot, as though they themselves had been born of a lawful wife. This too was done against the Lord by the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, who seemed to glory in observance of the Law, as though he were dissolving the Law and therefore were, as it were, not a legitimate son. And although he had assumed a body from the holy Virgin, as is known to believers, nevertheless his mother, in respect of his people, may also be called that Jewish Synagogue. Let whoever wishes turn over the prophetic books and see how often, and with how great severity of language and indignation of the Lord, that people is rebuked for its fornications as an unchaste woman.

Hence also comes what has just appeared in this book: either that all Israel is said to have committed fornication after the ephod made by Gideon, or that they went after the gods of the nations surrounding them. Therefore divine wrath was stirred against them, so that they were crushed for eighteen years by the children of Ammon. But were not those priests, scribes, and Pharisees, whom we have said were prefigured in them—the ones who, like Jephthah’s brothers, persecuted and expelled the Lord Christ as though he were not a legitimate son—also born from that same people of Israel? Yet the likeness is sketched in this: they, as apparent observers of the Law, believed that they had rightly expelled as illegitimate one who appeared to act against the commandments of the Law. For in this respect that people is said to commit fornication: by not keeping the commandments of the Law, it does not show faithfulness to its husband.

Thus it is written of Jephthah: “And the sons of the wife grew up and drove Jephthah out” (Judg. 11). The word “grew up” signifies figuratively “prevailed.” This was fulfilled in the Jews, who prevailed over Christ’s weakness, because he so willed that he should endure from them what was fitting in his Passion. Likewise Jacob, signifying this same thing, prevailed over the angel with whom he wrestled in order to prefigure him. They therefore said [Col. 0330D] to Jephthah: “You shall not inherit in our father’s house, because you are the son of a harlot woman” (ibid.). It is as though they said what the Gospel reports: “This man is not from God, because he thus breaks the Sabbath” (John 9). Yet boasting of themselves as legitimate sons, they said to the Lord: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8).

“And Jephthah fled from the face of his brothers and lived in the land of Thob” (Judg. 11). He fled because he concealed how great he was. “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). He fled because they saw the weakness of one dying but did not see the power of one rising. He lived in a good land, or, more expressly, a rich land. For what is called *agathon* [ἀγαθόν] in Greek is called *opimum* (“rich, fertile”) in Latin. [Col. 0331A] This is what Thob means, and in it I think his resurrection from the dead is to be understood. For what land is richer than an earthly body clothed in the excellence of immortality and incorruption?

Now it is said of Jephthah that, after fleeing from his brothers and dwelling in the land of Thob, robber-men gathered to him and went about with him (Judg. 11). Although before his Passion it was reproached to the Lord that he ate with tax collectors and sinners—when he replied that those who are well have no need of a physician, but the sick—and although he was numbered among the wicked when he was crucified between robbers and transferred one of them from the cross into paradise, nevertheless, after he rose and began to be, according to the explanation given above, in the land of Thob, wicked people gathered to him for the remission of sins. They walked with him because they lived according to his command. This does not cease to happen even now and hereafter, as long as evildoers flee to him so that he may justify the ungodly, because they turn to him and the unrighteous learn his ways.

Now, the fact that those who had rejected Jephthah—for he was a Gileadite—turned to him and sought him so that they might be delivered by him from their enemies (ibid.), most splendidly prefigures that those who rejected Christ, turning back to him, find salvation in him. This may refer either to those whom the apostle Peter, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, rebuked for that very crime and urged to turn to him whom they had persecuted; they were pierced in heart and desired from him the salvation from which they had estranged themselves. What is it to be delivered from enemies except to be delivered from sins? Thus he said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven you” (Acts 2).

Or rather, this signifies the renewal of the people Israel hoped for at the end. For this seems more apparent in the words: “And it came to pass after days,” which surely signifies after a time; and by this it indicates that what is meant is not what happened at the recent Passion of the Lord, but what will happen afterward. This also seems to be indicated by the elders of Gilead coming to Jephthah, so that by old age the later and final times may be understood. Gilead means “casting away” or “revelation.” Both meanings sufficiently suit this matter, because first they rejected the Lord Jesus Christ, and afterward he will be revealed to them.

The fact that Jephthah was sought as leader against the children of Ammon, after whose defeat those who wished to fight them under his leadership would be delivered, indicates—since Ammon means “son of my people” or “people of sorrow”—either those enemies from that very people who, persisting in unbelief, were foretold, or those altogether destined for Gehenna, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, as a people of sorrow. Yet “a people of sorrow” may not unsuitably be understood also of the devil and his angels, either because they procure eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves are assigned to eternal misery.

Very aptly, indeed, in order to express the prophecy more plainly, Jephthah answered the elders of Gilead: “Did you not hate me and drive me from my father’s house and send me away from you? Why have you come when you are distressed?” (Judg. 11). Something was prefigured from this in Joseph, whom his brothers rejected by selling him and to whose help and mercy they turned when distressed by famine. But here the meaning of future things shines out much more clearly, because the very brothers who expelled Jephthah did not come to him at all; rather, the elders of Gilead pleaded on behalf of that whole people. For the same nation is called Israel, whether in those then living who rejected Christ, or in those who later returned to his aid. Thus it is said to the hostile people—whether in its ancestors or its descendants, drawing out and retaining long hatred, and at last turning in those who are then to turn: “Did you not hate me and drive me from my father’s house?” For this is what those who persecuted him believed they had done: they cast Christ out from the house of David, “of whose kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1).

“And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah: We have not now come to you in this way” (Judg. 11), as though Jews converted to Christ were saying: “Then we came in order to persecute you.” They also confess that he will be their head against their enemies. He who will conquer their enemies also answers that he will be their prince, which Gideon refused when the Israelites desired it. For he answered them: “The Lord shall be your ruler” (ibid.). For the king is denoted by the name “prince,” whom that nation did not yet have in the time of the judges. They began to have Saul, and then his other successors, who are recorded in the Books of Kings.

For in Deuteronomy, when they are commanded what sort of king they should have if this pleased them, he is called there not king but prince. But because this Jephthah prefigured him who is the true King—whose title was also written and affixed to his cross, which Pilate did not dare erase or amend—it must be believed that he said: “I shall be your prince” (ibid.). But they said: “You shall be our head” (ibid.), because “Christ is the head of man,” and he is himself “the head of the body, the Church.” Finally, after Jephthah delivered them from all their enemies, he was not made their king; so that we may understand [Col. 0332D] that what was said belonged rather to a prophecy about Christ than properly to Jephthah himself. Scripture thus concludes its narrative about him: “And Jephthah judged Israel six years; and Jephthah the Gileadite died, and was buried in his city of Gilead” (Judg. 12). He therefore judged Israel like the other judges; he did not reign there as prince, as did those recorded in the volume of the kingdoms.

Moreover, after the same Jephthah had been appointed for them, he sent messengers to the enemies first bearing words of peace. This shows what the Apostle said, in whom Christ was speaking: “If it be possible, as far as depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12). To discuss in detail all the actual words which Jephthah commanded them is too long for us as we hasten to other matters. Yet, so far as concerns the signification of future things, they seem to me to be understood as Christ’s teaching. He admonishes us how we ought to walk—that is, live—among those “who are not called according to purpose” (Rom. 8). “For the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

Moreover, the fact that, when he was about to defeat the enemies, the Spirit of the Lord came upon him signifies the Holy Spirit bestowed upon Christ’s members. The fact that he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed through the cave of Gilead to beyond the children of Ammon, signifies the progress of Christ’s members toward victory over enemies. Gilead means “casting away,” and Manasseh, “necessity.” Those who are making progress must therefore pass beyond those who cast away—that is, those who despise—and necessity too must be passed beyond, lest perhaps the one who progresses, having passed on, yield to those who terrify.

The watchtower of Gilead must likewise be passed beyond; and Gilead also means “revelation.” A watchtower is a height for looking upon or looking down—that is, looking from above. The watchtower of Gilead therefore seems to me fittingly to signify pride in revelation. Hence the Apostle says: “And lest I should be exalted by the greatness of the revelations” (2 Cor. 12). Therefore this too must be passed beyond: one must not remain in it, because of the danger of falling. Once these things have been passed, the enemies are easily overcome. This is signified by the words: “And from the watchtower of Gilead he passed over to the children of Ammon” (Judg. 12), concerning whom as enemies enough has already been said:

“And Jephthah made a vow and said: If you deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then whoever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall be; I will offer him as a whole burnt offering to the Lord” (Judg. 11). Whoever Jephthah may have thought of in this place according to human thinking, he does not seem to have thought of his only daughter. Otherwise, when he saw that she had come out to meet him, he would not say: “Alas, my daughter, you have hindered me; you have become an offence in my eyes” (ibid.). For “you have hindered me” is said as though he judged himself to have been prevented from accomplishing what he had intended. But whom could he have thought would first come out to meet him, when he had no other children? Did he think of his wife? God did not will this to happen; and he did not leave it unpunished, lest anyone afterward dare such a thing; and by his great providence he also made the very event which occurred to prefigure the sacrament of the Church.

Therefore the prophecy is fitted together from both sides: from what the one making the vow thought, and from what happened against his will. For if he thought of his wife, the Church is Christ’s wife: “Therefore shall a man leave father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). “This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle, “but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5). But because Jephthah’s wife could not be a virgin, the fact that his daughter rather came out to meet him and did not remain unavenged prefigured the forbidden sacrifice, the rashness of the one making the vow, and the virginity of the Church. Nor is it alien from the truth that the same Church is signified by the name “daughter.” [Col. 0334A] For whose type did that woman bear, to whom the Lord said after she was healed by touching his fringe: “Daughter, your faith has made you whole; go in peace” (Luke 8)? And certainly, as none doubts, he himself called his disciples sons of the bridegroom, plainly judging himself to be the bridegroom. “The sons of the bridegroom,” he says, “cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them” (Matt. 9).

Therefore the Church will be a whole burnt offering, which the blessed Apostle calls a chaste virgin, when in the resurrection of the dead there shall come about universally what is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15). Then he will hand over the kingdom to God the Father. That kingdom is the Church itself, whose figure that man making the vow bore. But because this will occur when the sixth age of the world has been completed, a delay of sixty days was requested for lamenting virginity. For the Church is gathered from all the ages: the first is from Adam to the Flood; the second from the Flood to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation into Babylon; the fifth from that deportation to the Virgin’s childbirth; the sixth from then until the end of this age.

Through these six ages, as through sixty days, the holy virgin lamented her virgin state: for, although these were virginal things, they were nevertheless sins that had to be mourned, on account of which the whole virgin, spread throughout the world, says daily: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6). He preferred to call these same sixty days two months, I think, because of the two men, one through whom comes the resurrection of the dead; and because of them the two Testaments are also spoken of.

But what was established by command in Israel—“From days to days they came together to lament the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year” (Judg. 12)—I do not think signifies anything after the whole burnt offering has been fulfilled, which will be in eternal life, but rather the former times of the Church, in which “blessed are those who mourn.” Its universality is figured by the four days because it is spread far and wide through the four regions of the world. But as to the literal historical sense, I do not think the Israelites decreed this unless they understood that in this matter God’s judgment had been brought forth more to strike the father, lest anyone afterward dare to vow such a sacrifice. For why should mourning and lamentation have been decreed if that vow was a matter of joy?

Likewise, the fact that the people of Ephraim were afterward defeated by Jephthah himself must be referred to God’s judgment at the end, as the Lord himself says: “Bring here those who did not wish me to reign over them, and kill them before me” (Judg. 13 [citation as printed]). Nor are the forty-two thousand mentioned there as an idle number. For just as the two months signify, through the sixty days, the number six of the six ages, so there six times seven likewise figures the same thing, in relation to the six ages of the world. For six times seven makes forty-two. Nor without reason did Jephthah himself judge the people for six years (ibid.).

[Col. 0335]

# MIRROR OF THE MYSTERIES OF THE CHURCH. (G)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0335A]

Your affection has requested that I discuss the Church’s sacraments and explain to you their mystical sweetness. But since, by the right of custom, I turn over logical rather than theological opinions more willingly—because more easily and boldly—I began to doubt whether I preferred to contradict or rather to write. Yet soon, recalling that every good communicated shines forth more beautifully when it is communicated, I accordingly turned my pen to writing, invoking the aid of him who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3). Thus I offered to your understanding the desired little book, flowing with inward nectar like a honeycomb. And because in it one may behold what individual things in the Church mystically represent, I have thought it fitting to entitle it *Mirror of the Church*.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Church

The church building, therefore, into which the people assemble to praise God, signifies the holy Catholic Church, which is built in heaven from living stones. This is the firmly built house of the Lord. Christ, sent as the foundation cornerstone, is its foundation. Upon this foundation, and not apart from it, are the apostles and prophets, as it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 86). The superimposed walls are Jews and Gentiles coming to Christ from the four parts of the world. All the stones are polished and squared—that is, holy, clean, and firm—and are arranged by the hands of the supreme craftsman to remain forever.

Some are borne and do not bear, like the simpler members in the Church. Others are borne and bear, like the intermediate ones. Others only bear and are not borne, except by Christ alone, who is the unique foundation. For in this building, the more someone excels in distinction, the humbler he is and the more of the building he supports. One charity, like mortar, joins all together while living stones are bound in the framework of peace.

The towers are the preachers and prelates of the Church, its fortifications and defence. Hence the bridegroom speaks thus to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements” (Song 4). The cock placed above represents preachers. For the cock, wakeful in the depths of night, divides its hours by crowing, awakens sleepers, and announces the approaching day; but before crowing it arouses itself by beating its wings. Mark every detail mystically, for here nothing is without meaning. Those asleep are the children of this age, lying in sins; the cock is the company of prelates who preach strictly and awaken sleepers so that they may cast off works of darkness, crying: “Woe to those who sleep! Awake, you who sleep!” They announce the coming light when they preach the day of judgment and future glory. Wisely, before they preach to others, they awaken themselves from the sleep of sin through virtues and chastise their bodies. Hence the Apostle says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9).

They also turn themselves against the wind when, by reproving and rebuking, they fight or resist strongly against the rebellious, lest they be accused of fleeing when the wolf comes. The iron rod upon which the cock stands represents the preacher’s right word: he is not to speak from the spirit of man, but from God according to the Scriptures, in keeping with: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God” (1 Pet. 4). The fact that the rod is set above by means of the cross indicates that the word of the Scriptures was completed and confirmed through the cross. Hence the Lord said in his Passion: “It is finished” (John 19). And his title was written indelibly above him.

The dome upon which the cross is set signifies perfection by its roundness, because the Catholic faith must be preached and held perfectly and inviolate. Unless one keeps it whole and inviolate, one will without doubt perish eternally. Or the dome signifies the world redeemed by the price of the cross, for which reason the cross is placed above it. The cock set above the cross signifies that the preacher ought to affirm that Christ redeemed the world by his cross. The pinnacle of the tower represents the mind or life of the prelate, which tends toward heavenly things.

The bells, by whose sound the people are summoned to church, mystically signify preachers. Because they are necessary in many respects, they are designated by many names. The clapper, which produces sound on either side, is the preacher’s tongue, causing both Testaments to resound. The wood from which the bell hangs signifies the cross; the fastening, charity, through which charity the preacher, bound to the cross, glories according to the words: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6). The cord is the preacher’s life and humility. Hence the Apostle, who condescends for the sake of others: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5). The rings on the rope signify perseverance or the crown of reward.

The glass windows of the church are the divine Scriptures, which repel wind and rain—that is, they ward off harmful things—and, while transmitting the brightness of the true sun into the Church by day, illuminate its inhabitants. They are wider on the inside, because the mystical sense is broader and surpasses the literal one. Preachers frequent these windows, “who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows” (Isa. 60). Again, the five bodily senses are signified by the windows: they ought to be narrow outwardly, lest they take in vanities, and open inwardly to spiritual goods.

The door is Christ; hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “I am the door” (John 10). The columns [Col. 0337A] are teachers, who spiritually support the temple of God through teaching, as do the throne of God and the evangelists. Because of the resonance of their divine speech, they are called silver columns, according to the Song of Songs: “He made its columns of silver” (Song 3). The couches signify contemplatives, in whom God rests without offence. Because they contemplate the highest divinity and the brightness of eternal life, they are compared to gold. Hence it is said in the aforementioned Song: “He made its couch of gold” (ibid.).

The beams are those who spiritually support; the ceilings are those who adorn or strengthen. Since they do not decay through vices, the bride boasts of them in the same Song, saying: “The beams of our houses are cedar; our ceilings are cypress” (Song 1). For God built his Church for himself from living stones and imperishable timbers, according to: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon” (Song 3), that is, Christ made it from saints made white by chastity. The screen, lower than the rest of the body of the church, mystically signifies how great humility ought to be among the clergy, according to: “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3).

The altar signifies Christ, without whom no offering is made acceptable to the Father. Hence the Church customarily directs prayers to the Father through Christ. The garments with which the altar is adorned are the saints, of whom the prophet speaks to God, saying: “With all these you shall clothe yourself as with a garment” (Isa. 59). The steps by which one ascends to the altar spiritually represent the apostles and martyrs of Christ, who shed their blood for love of him. The bride in the Song of Songs calls the ascent purple (Song 3). The fifteen virtues are also expressed, signified by the fifteen steps by which one ascended into Solomon’s temple and continuously shown by the prophet in fifteen psalms; the blessed man has set these ascents in his heart. Jacob saw this ladder, whose top touched heaven.

The lights of the church are those through whose teaching the Church shines like sun and moon, to whom the Lord says: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5), and they are examples of good works. Hence he himself admonishes: “Let your light shine before men” (ibid.).

The fact that the Church is festively adorned inwardly, not outwardly, morally indicates that all her glory is from within. Though outwardly she may be contemptible, she shines in the soul, which is God’s seat; hence she says: “I am black, but beautiful” (Song 1). Hence she says: “Indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me” (Ps. 2 [citation as printed]). Considering this, the prophet says: “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house and the place of the dwelling of your glory” (Ps. 25). Faith, hope, and charity spiritually adorn her.

The triumphal cross is placed in the middle of the Church because the Church loves her Redeemer in the midst of her heart, who has spread his couch in the midst through love for the daughters of Jerusalem. Seeing it as a sign of victory, may all say, and may each say: “Hail, salvation of the whole world, life-giving tree.” Therefore, lest God’s love for us—he who delivered up his only Son in order to redeem a slave—ever be handed over to oblivion, the Church arms herself with this sign upon breast and forehead, signifying that the mystery of the cross is to be believed in the heart and openly confessed with the mouth.

Its figure came before in Egypt. When we sign ourselves from the forehead downward, then from left to right, we express the mystery that God bowed the heavens and descended in order to teach us to prefer eternal things to temporal things. By this sign the city of the devil is confounded. The Church triumphs, “terrible as an army arrayed for battle” (Song 6). “Terrible is this place,” it says; “this is none other than the house of the Lord” (Gen. 28). Of it is said: “The royal banners go forth; the mystery of the cross shines.” Heavenly hosts frequent it. Of it Scripture says: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” (Rev. 12 [citation as printed]).

For the Church fights here and reigns in the homeland: one part is on pilgrimage, and one part is glorified. The part on pilgrimage, ascending from exile through the wilderness, sighs for its homeland, from beside the rivers of Babylon toward the heavenly Jerusalem, which, continually beholding peace, keeps an unending feast. Blessed city Jerusalem, called the vision of peace: what a glorious kingdom! “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 68 [citation as printed]). Its guardians are the citizens of heaven: the hosts of angels, with the illustrious senate of apostles; prophets with patriarchs; purple-clad ranks of martyrs; virginal flowers; the flourishing choir of confessors; and the fellowship of saints, surrounded by universal variety—a chaste generation in splendour.

That heavenly court, admirable as it is, is wondrously adorned by that unique and incomparable jewel who is Mother and Virgin. No one like her was seen before, nor will she have a successor. But how great is the amazement of all at the sight of the King himself, and how harmonious are the voices in his praise, is known only to those who have deserved to be among them and to behold the mystery of the Trinity and the glory of Christ, before whom choirs of angels stand, upon whom angels always desire to gaze.

The Church now present prepares herself to see this immortal King face to face. While she celebrates temporal feasts here, she recalls the festive and eternal joys of her homeland, where the bridegroom is praised by angelic instruments. And all the saints, continually celebrating the day of great festival which the Lord has made, do not cease in wedding songs to praise the immortal bridegroom, “fairer in beauty than the sons of men,” who chose the Church for himself by free mercy. Of her, as he had foreseen from eternity, he says: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hills of Lebanon, and I will speak to my bride” (Song 4). For her he “rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18): his going forth was from the Father, his return to the Father; his journey extended to hell, his return to God’s seat, so that he might make all the elect from the beginning to the end of the world one kingdom in the vision of the supreme Trinity, in which one God is glorified through all ages.

## CHAPTER II. On the Dedication of the Church.

By what zeal and love Christ adorns and prepares his bride for the heavenly dedication is signified in part by the temporal dedication of a church. [Col. 0339A] The bishop circles the church to be dedicated three times, sprinkling it with blessed water, while clergy and people follow. Meanwhile twelve lamps burn outside and inside. Whenever they come to the door, which is closed on account of the mystery, the bishop strikes the threshold with his pastoral staff, saying: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, O everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23). The deacon replies: “Who is this King of glory?” (ibid.). To him the bishop says: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (ibid.). The third time, when the door has been opened, he enters with clergy and people, saying: “Peace to this house.” Then he performs the other rites belonging to the dedication.

All that is visibly done here God works in the soul by invisible power; for the soul is the true temple of God, where [Col. 0339B] faith lays the foundation, hope builds up, and charity brings to perfection. The Catholic Church itself, made one from many stones gathered together, is the temple of God, because many temples are one temple, having one Lord and one faith. Thus the house to be dedicated is the soul to be sanctified; the water is repentance; the salt, wisdom; the threefold sprinkling, the threefold immersion of one being baptized; the twelve lamps, the same number of apostles preaching the mystery of the cross; the bishop, Christ; his staff, power; the threefold striking, dominion over heavenly, earthly, and infernal things, so that the threefold structure of creation may bend the knee, now subjected; the question from within, the ignorance of the people; the opening of the door, the removal of sin. The bishop, entering, prays for peace upon the house; and Christ, entering the world, makes peace between God and human beings.

Then, prostrate, [Col. 0339C] the bishop prays to the Lord for sanctification; and Christ, humbled for the Passion, prayed for his disciples and for those who would believe, saying: “Father, sanctify them in truth” (John 17).
