Rising, he does not offer a greeting, but only prays, because those not yet sanctified are not to be applauded but prayed for. The writing of the alphabet upon the pavement is the simple teaching of faith in the human heart. A line drawn from the left corner of the east to the right of the west, and another from the right of the east to the left of the west, form a cross and signify the gathering of the two peoples, in accordance with the account that Jacob blessed Joseph’s sons with crossed hands (Gen. 48). For though Christ passes from the east, he left the Jews on the left because of their unbelief and came to the Gentiles; [Col. 0339D] although these had been in the west, he grants them to be on the right. Finally, passing from the east with the Gentiles placed on his right, he will visit the Jews in the left corner of the west; and it is evident that he will find them worse than the Gentiles had formerly been.

The *cambuca* [crozier] with which the letters are written mystically signifies the ministry of teachers, through which the conversion of the Gentiles has been accomplished and that of the Jews is yet to be completed. The bishop’s subsequent standing before the altar and calling upon God for aid signifies those who, having received faith, prepare themselves for battle. And because they are still in conflict, as though amid sighs, the Alleluia is not yet added. After this, water is blessed with salt and ashes, with wine also added and mixed with the water. The water is the people; the salt, teaching; the ash, remembrance of Christ’s Passion. Wine mixed with water is Christ [Col. 0340A] God and man: wine, divinity; water, humanity. Thus the people are sanctified through teaching of the faith and remembrance of the Passion, joined to their head, God and man. Therefore the altar and the church are sprinkled within, so that the spiritual Church may be shown to require sanctification inwardly as well as outwardly.

The sprinkler of hyssop is humility, by whose sprinkling the Catholic Church is cleansed. He goes around sprinkling, as though purifying it and bestowing care upon all. Meanwhile this is sung: “Let God arise, and let them be scattered” (Ps. 67), etc.; its responsory, with the antiphon followed by another: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High” (Ps. 90). The bishop sings: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21); and likewise: “I shall declare your name to my brethren” (Ps. 21). Since without God no work prospers, at [Col. 0340B] the conclusion he prays that the petitions of those entering there to seek benefits may be heard.

When these things have been done, he comes to the altar singing, “I shall enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. 42), with the entire psalm, etc.; and he pours what remains of the water at the base of the altar, entrusting to God what exceeds human strength in so great a sacrament. Then the altar is wiped with linen. The altar is Christ; the linen is his flesh, brought by the beatings of the Passion to the brightness and glory of immortality. Next the bishop offers incense on the altar, lit in the middle of the altar in the form of a cross, and with consecrated oil makes a cross at its four corners. Thereafter three crosses upon each wall of the church are anointed with the same oil; and, the consecration thus completed, the altar is covered with a white veil. Incense signifies prayers; oil, the grace of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0340C] Its fullness, “like ointment upon the head, which ran down upon the beard, Aaron’s beard” (Ps. 132), descends upon the apostles and their disciples, who, with the Lord working with them, preached the mystery of the cross through the four regions of the world. The white covering mystically signifies the joy of immortality, concerning which the Son rejoices before the Father, saying: “You have torn my sackcloth and girded me with gladness” (Ps. 29 [printed “XXVIV”]).

## Chapter III. On the offices of the canonical Hours

Ezra the prophet taught the Israelite people, returned from Babylonian captivity, to praise God four times in the night and four times in the day, because the prophet David declares that he gave praise to the Lord seven times in the day and rose at midnight to confess the Lord. Therefore the holy Fathers selected eight Hours above the rest [Col. 0340D] for praising God: namely midnight, daybreak, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline. For it is fitting that a human being, whose body consists of four elements, should strive to propitiate God four times in respect of the night and four times in respect of the day during the natural day. And although God is to be praised at every time, the Church praises him especially in the aforesaid Hours, in which he deigned to perform works more notable than the rest.

For at midnight he was born of the Virgin; at daybreak he rose; at Prime the Resurrection was announced to the women by angels; at Terce the Holy Spirit set the apostles aflame; at Sext the Lord, that is, the Redeemer of the world, was crucified; at None [Col. 0341A] he gave up his spirit for the salvation of the world. At Vespers we commemorate the Lord’s coming in the evening of the world. At Compline the joy of the saints will be complete on the day of universal recompense.

Rightly, therefore, we are instructed through the prophet to rise at midnight, because “while all things held the midst of silence” (Wis. 18), “a light arose in darkness” (Ps. 111), that is, Christ, to enlighten those sitting in darkness (Luke 1). He was born of the Virgin in the time of night. At the beginning of the office of this Hour, because we had previously kept silent while sleep prevailed, it is said: “Lord, you shall open my lips” (Ps. 50 [printed “V”]), because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15), unless he himself deigns to open the lips for his own praise. Then we invoke divine help; afterwards we glorify God in the Trinity of persons, as glory belongs to him eternally.

The invitatory follows in a loud voice, by which mother Church invites all, according to the saying: “Come, children, hear me” (Prov. 8). Its omission at Epiphany is because the Magi, the first fruits of the Gentiles, came uninvited to worship the King of heaven, according to the saying: “No one has hired us” (Matt. 20). Note that a humble voice comes first but is suitably raised for the invitatory, because the Church praises God secretly, as though behind a closed door, for herself; but publicly for others, so that fervour may rise in her neighbours. A hymn follows, which is praise of God with song, or a human voice metrically composed in praise of God; for after the invitation many accordingly praise God joyfully, according to the saying: “Zion heard and rejoiced” (Ps. 96).

[Col. 0341C] Then follow the psalms, signifying works: twelve or nine, so that, through the twelve hours of night, we may be protected by divine power from the business that walks in darkness; and so that we may deserve to be joined with the nine orders of angels and show that we are associated with those whose feasts we observe. By singing twelve psalms in the first nocturn on Sunday nights, we commend to memory the number of patriarchs, prophets, and apostles. By joining four psalms under one glorification of the Trinity, we signify that they possessed the four cardinal virtues in the one faith of the Trinity and gave examples of them to others: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

[Col. 0341D] The alternate singing of psalms indicates the saints’ reciprocal exhortation to do good works. Antiphons express charity, and they have the number of psalms for the causes already stated concerning the psalms. On non-festal days we sing twelve psalms for each of the night-hours in which God must be served, joining two psalms with each of six antiphons, because charity, necessary through the six ages, joins the work of God and neighbour. The fact that the antiphon is begun individually by one and sung jointly by the rest signifies that God first loved us, and that we should answer his love together. The *pneuma* at the end speaks of ineffable joy.

After psalms and antiphons, the Verse is exclaimed in a high voice, so as to stir the minds lest we ever grow sluggish in work or thought in divine love, and so that we may turn to the east and to God with the whole body. The Lord’s Prayer follows, for our hearts and bodies cleansed, and it is ended with common assent because of the communion of the saints. The reader, saying to Christ’s vicar, “Command, Lord, a blessing,” indicates the primacy of the Church and how abundant is the power of blessing entrusted to him to whom authority to command is given. But when the priest prays that the Lord may bless, he wisely blesses through Christ, who is the fountain of every blessing. Having received the blessing, each lesson is followed by its respective responsory. Thus we preach through the lessons; responsories are good works. They are aptly called responsories because we answer through them. For he answers preaching well who fulfils in work what he has heard. [Col. 0342B] Their number bears the same mystery as the number of psalms.

The three groups of lessons and responsories indicate that the saints of three times share in the glory of the Lord’s Resurrection, which is recalled on Sunday or festal night. The number three in each nocturn signifies faith in the Trinity in the three times. Among monks the number four expresses in the saints a stable, square, evangelical firmness; or the fourfold sense of Scripture because of the chariots of Amminadab: namely, historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical. Thus Jerusalem is understood as the earthly city, the Church, any faithful soul, and the heavenly homeland.

Then follows, in a loud voice, “We praise you, O God,” [Col. 0342C] by which it is shown how openly and wonderfully the Church praises God in the time of grace. Then the priest exhorts through the verse that they may remain in God’s praise. The matutinal office follows, concerning which the prophet says: “From the dawn I watch for you, O God” (Ps. 62). Through this office we recall how the Israelite people, as a figure of us, crossed the Red Sea and, after their enemies had been submerged, sang praises to the Lord; Exodus shows that this took place in the morning watch (Exod. 14). In it we also recall the Lord’s Resurrection and proclaim our own future resurrection, at the beginning of the brightness of the second robe. For these reasons this office is full of praises.

At its beginning we invoke divine aid; then we glorify God, confessing faith in [Col. 0342D] the supreme Trinity, which is the foundation of every good work. In this Hour we sing, as it were, five psalms to fortify the five bodily senses. Mystically, the first psalm also denotes the primitive Church from the Jews; the second, the secondary Church from the Gentiles; the third, which is another psalm joined under one *Gloria Patri*, mystically indicates that at the end of the world each people will confess under one faith. By the fourth, which the children in the fiery furnace sang, is figured the tribulation of Antichrist, which each people will endure for the faith of Christ. By the three psalms of Lauds, at last joined together as though one under one *Gloria*, are signified the three orders of the Church, expressed by Job, Noah, and Daniel, who will reign gloriously with the Bridegroom of the Church in bridal praise.

[Col. 0343A] Or the eight psalms signify eight orders, who are saved in the Church through baptism as eight souls were saved from the Flood in the ark. The first is indicated by the first psalm: the first Church, built by the apostles and living in Judaea. The second, by the second psalm: passing from Judaism to the Gentiles, as the apostles preached everywhere. The third is the believing Gentile world; the fourth, Judaea coming to repentance. But the third and fourth are joined under one glory, because Gentiles and Jews are joined into unity of faith before the persecution of Antichrist comes. Under him the fifth order blesses God as did the children in the furnace. The sixth, seventh, and eighth, gathered from Africa, Asia, and Europe, will enjoy peace after Antichrist. Therefore the final three psalms flow into Lauds; they are said and joined under one *Gloria*, because these three orders will exist simultaneously and be glorified together.

[Col. 0343B] After the psalms comes an exhortation through the Chapter, lest we fail on the way; assenting to this, the choir resounds with the hymn. Again roused by Zechariah’s prophecy, we bless God, remembering that he accomplished redemption as he spoke through the mouth of the saints and swore to Abraham our father.

Meanwhile the priest censes the altar with the thurible. The thurible is the human heart; the fire, charity; the incense, prayer, which smells sweetly to God when it burns with the fire of divine love. Hence the Prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). Every antiphon expresses charity, [Col. 0343C] without which works, signified by the psalms, are of no avail. The antiphon begun before the psalm and sung in full after it signifies that charity, begun here, will be brought to eternal perfection after this life, and this will be in unutterable joy. Therefore the *Pneuma* is added, indicating the ineffable joy of eternal life. It is so great that, while it is tasted here beforehand, it can neither be wholly expressed nor wholly kept silent. Hence, with subdued words, the Church leaps forth in wonder, rejoicing with the *Pneuma*, as though she said: “What voice, what tongue could unfold it?” Here words and understanding are insufficient, yet love does not allow silence.

Thus the Church, by uttering the *pneuma*, indicates more expressly in some way—wonderful though I say it—without words than through words, how great is the joy of heaven, where words will cease when all know all things. After the *Pneuma* follows the Prayer, so that our action, which begins through God, may end through him. The use, at the end, of the childlike voice in saying, “Let us bless the Lord,” signifies that all our praise is childlike in comparison with the God whom we praise, and that whatever can be said here falls short of God’s praise. [Col. 0343D] It is as though the Church said: “We praise, but do not suffice in praising; for the excellence of God surpasses our speech and understanding, because ‘man shall come to the deep heart, and God shall be exalted’” (Ps. 63). Therefore all subsequently say, “Thanks be to God,” because it is pleasing, as is devout, to be surpassed in the praise of God.

We rightly celebrate the office of Prime [Col. 0344A] because, when the women came to the tomb after the sun had already risen, the angels announced that Christ had risen. And because this Hour is the beginning of the day, in it we praise God because he enabled us to pass through the night safely. Therefore, having invoked divine help and glorified the Trinity of persons as is fitting, we render to God the hymn, “Now that the light’s star has risen.” Then in this Hour of Prime we sing five psalms every day, that our five senses may be divinely fortified through the day. To these we add an exposition of the Catholic faith, because “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5), and because it is an unconquerable shield against the ancient enemy. Hence Peter says: “Resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5).

In this Hour the Lord’s Prayer is said, in which there are seven petitions for obtaining [Col. 0344B] the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which we may deserve the seven virtues and, freed from the seven vices, attain the seven beatitudes. Then those cleansed through the Lord’s Prayer are armed by the Creed against every adversity. At this Hour general confession is also made, that we may be cleansed from venial sins, without which common life is not easily lived; and prayers are multiplied so that we may be defended during the day from impending evils.

The office of Terce is celebrated because at such an hour the Holy Spirit set the apostles aflame.

At Sext the office is celebrated in commemoration of the event that at that hour the Redeemer of the world was crucified.

At None, because then he gave up his spirit. For at the same [Col. 0344C] hour he chose to die for humankind at which humankind was expelled from paradise, and on the same day he was pleased to redeem humankind by the wood on which the enemy had deceived him by wood:

> Art, that it might deceive art,  
> And bring healing from that source  
> From which the enemy had inflicted harm.

In these three Hours and in the others, we first invoke divine aid—as must be done in every good work—glorify the holy Trinity, and render a hymn to God. We sing the psalms, which signify works, with a threefold glorification of the Trinity, because we must work in faith in the Trinity. By the antiphons, which express charity, we join the psalms, because we must confirm our works through charity and abide in it, as the Apostle says: “Rooted and founded in charity” (Eph. [Col. 0344D] 3); and again: “Let all your works be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16). By the Chapters is signified exhortation to good work; by the responsories, good work; by the verses, the fruit of good work. Hence it also has the *Pneuma*. In the Prayer the service is concluded, so that the divine grace which precedes our actions may itself follow them.

Vespers follow, in which we commemorate the coming of the Lord as the world declines into evening. In this Hour, because it is the end of the day and near to night, we sing five psalms, so that whatever venial offence we have committed in the day through the five senses may be forgiven by this psalmody to us who repent, and so that from this our senses may be kept through the night in what pleases God. Alternation in psalmody is the saints’ admonition. Antiphons, as has been said, signify charity. Through the Chapter [Col. 0345A] is suggested spiritual exhortation, that we may persevere in good. Hence the Apostle says: “We exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Cor. 6). The responsory signifies good work, through which we demonstrate that we obey the exhortation and that God is to be praised for good work.

The hymn follows, that we may give an example to our neighbours; then, after the Verse has been spoken to awaken minds, the hymn of the blessed Mother of God is sung with an antiphon. Through the example of her humility we are reformed, and the Incarnation of the Son of God—through which “he has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble” (Luke 1)—is recalled, that the devotion of our faith may be stirred. Meanwhile, as the Lord commanded Moses, the altar is censed, showing that the fragrance of prayer pleases Christ. Afterwards, once the antiphon has been sung [Col. 0345B] with the *Pneuma*, the Prayer follows; and “Let us bless the Lord” is said in a childlike voice, for the reasons previously mentioned.

Lastly Compline follows. It signifies the joy which, when the number of the elect has been completed, God will complete for his saints on the day of the general resurrection. In this final Hour is said, “Turn us, O God of our salvation,” to suggest that, after every perfection attainable here, where we often go astray, we must pray that God may turn us yet further away from error. Considering this, the Prophet says morally at the end of the psalm: “I have gone astray like a lost sheep” (Ps. 118). In this Hour, according to the four elements of our body in which we often offend, we say four psalms to propitiate God. In this Hour likewise the Chapter does not precede the Hymn, [Col. 0345C] by which it is typologically shown that those in whom the matters signified by the praise of what precedes have been completed outrun exhortation. Yet the Chapter is not omitted, because exhortation is always useful here.

Then the Verse is said in a high voice with the *Pneuma*. Thus awakened and made mindful of the ineffable joy that will be the reward of our labour, we sing the canticle of righteous Simeon, that, finding peace after his example, we may deserve to see the light which is Christ. Afterwards we fortify ourselves by the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed against nocturnal terrors; and we are cleansed by reciprocal confession, according to the saying: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5). And we are urged not to give rest to our times until we find a place for the Lord (Ps. 131). Nor indeed do we complete the office of this Hour without petitions and prayer, according to the apostle: “Pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 5).

Mystically, prayers signify humility, which should be at the end; for as humility is necessary at the beginning—signified by beginning the service in a very humble voice—so at its completion the same humility must be shown against pride, into which all workers of iniquity have fallen. Hence by this plague a rose is sometimes turned into a saltwort.

We pray facing east, although God is everywhere and there is no end to his greatness, remembering that he who is “the brightness of eternal light” enlightened those sitting in darkness when “the Dayspring from on high” visited us. Bending the knees in church signifies contrition of heart [Col. 0346A] and that every knee bends to Christ; we bend not one knee alone but both, lest we resemble the Jews. On the Lord’s Day and during the Paschal season it is not permitted to kneel, out of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection; rather, we should pray standing, with bowed head, as the devout women at the tomb, where they bowed themselves in reverence for the Lord’s body.

The three things involved in striking the breast—namely breast, sound, and hand—signify that we must repent of sins committed in mind, speech, and deed. With the psalms of the day office, “Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit” is said twelve times, for the twelve hours of day; and the bells are rung twelve times. At the first Hour they ring once, and at the last Hour once, because from one God are all things, and that same one will be all in all. But at Terce they ring three times for the second, third, [Col. 0346B] and fourth hours; and likewise at Sext for three—namely the seventh, eighth, and ninth. At Vespers, however, they ring many times, because preaching by the apostles was multiplied in the time of grace. Likewise at Matins, often, because there must often be the cry: “Awake, you who sleep.”

The divine office is celebrated at those Hours when the householder is remembered to have gone out to hire labourers for his vineyard. Likewise, the nocturnal time is from Adam to Noah; the matutinal time, between Noah and Abraham; Prime, between Abraham and Moses; Terce, between Moses and David; Sext, between David and the Lord’s coming; None, from the first coming until the coming when he will come to render recompense for hidden things. By Vespers, moreover, is understood the Sabbath, that is, the rest of souls after their departure from bodies until [Col. 0346C] the day of judgment. By Compline we recall the completed number and consummate joy of the saints, which will be completed on the great feast day when the blessed receive the kingdom.

For the three days before Easter signify the tropological sense of Scripture. The first is the day of repentance, the second the day of justice, the third the day of recompense, in which completion takes place. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Today and tomorrow I cast out demons and accomplish healings, and on the third day I am completed” (Luke 13). The day of repentance is signified by the day on which the Lord suffered; the day of justice, by the day on which he lay in the tomb; the day of recompense, by the day on which the Lord rose. Repentance torments, justice brings tranquillity, recompense brings joy.

Likewise these three [Col. 0346D] days are understood through the vigils, feasts, and octaves of saints; and again through the fiftieth psalm, the hundredth, and the hundred and fiftieth. For the fiftieth speaks of repentance, the hundredth of justice, and the hundred and fiftieth of the praise of God in his saints, when, their number having been completed, the Compline of the great festival will be celebrated forever. Moreover, singing in the Church signifies the joy of heaven, in which the saints rejoice in the Lord. Low, high, and very high voices indicate that the three orders of the Church must be preached to in three ways, because of the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit, or according to Solomon’s three books. Procession is the way to the heavenly homeland.

[Col. 0347A] The blessed water proceeding is purity of life. Lamps are works of mercy, according to the saying: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). The cross follows, the sign of triumph, because those who are pure and keepers of the law crucify the flesh and triumph. Then, for the reading of the Gospel, a cushion and the Gospel-book are carried. The cushion is sweetness and delight in the commandments of the Lord. Hence the Prophet says: “You have prepared in your goodness for the poor” (Ps. 67); and likewise: “How sweet are your words to my palate!” (Ps. 118). The Gospel is the confirmation of what has gone before. Once the Gospel has been read, the book is carried back upon the cushion, because the Church, when it heard the Gospel, received it sweetly in its heart and rejoiced, according to the saying: “Zion heard and rejoiced” (Ps. 96); and elsewhere: [Col. 0347B] “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5).

## Chapter IV. On the service of the whole year

At the beginning of Septuagesima, the Church begins the service of the whole year, and the Pentateuch is read. Septuagesima signifies the time of our captivity, from which we must mystically return to Jerusalem, as was figured of old by the Hebrews leaving Babylon. Therefore, that those who tend upward may remember their captivity, there is first read concerning Adam, made at the beginning of the world, and concerning his expulsion from paradise; then concerning the Flood, and how Abraham departed from his land, and concerning trials of this kind, as examples of patience.

And just as the Hebrews of old, carried captive into Babylon, were in sorrow almost until the end [Col. 0347C] of seventy days, the voices of joy are silent, having groaning with both “watering-pots” [*utroque irriguo*; wording uncertain in context], so that on the day of the Resurrection the Church may rejoice more festively when her citizens have been multiplied. On Holy Saturday we sing one Alleluia for the Lord’s Resurrection; and because here there is no joy except in labour, the Tract follows. But on the octave, that is, on the Saturday in White, a double Alleluia is sung, because on the day of judgment joy will be full, both for the Lord’s Resurrection and for our own, and because the just will shine in a double robe.

Fifteen days before Easter Jeremiah is read, because he clearly foreshadowed the Lord’s Passion. From the octave of Easter, for twenty days the Apocalypse is read and sung because of the mysteries of the Passion and Resurrection revealed to John [Col. 0347D] and preached by the apostles. Then, until the Lord’s Ascension, the Catholic Epistles and Acts of the Apostles are read, and psalms are sung, because David too prophesied concerning the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, and the apostles preached what they had learned from the Lord while enjoying his bodily presence until his Ascension. Between Ascension and Pentecost, the feast is sung, because the disciples, lifted up above, awaited the gifts promised by the Father.

After Pentecost until the Kalends of August, the books of Kings are read, and “God of all” is sung, because as Saul, Samuel, David, and others fought for God’s law, so we, after receiving in baptism the gift and power of the Holy Spirit, must fight against demons—formed, born, nourished, armed. [Col. 0348A] From the Kalends of August to the Kalends of September, Wisdom is read and sung, because August is the sixth month, and in the sixth age, since the Lord came, we ought to live wisely because of his presence, since Wisdom herself, who went forth from the mouth of the Most High, has been heard among us. Again, this month is hot and in the middle of the year; and in middle age, when each person is more inflamed by the heat of vices, Wisdom ought to give greater aid.

In September Job, Tobit, Ezra, Judith, and Esther are read and sung, because they patiently endured adversity, and the Church at the end of the world will endure every adversity for the Lord. From the Kalends of October until November the books of Maccabees are read, and responsories are sung from them, because this eighth month mystically signifies the joy of the Resurrection: just as the Jews, after battles had ended and the Temple had been restored, blessed the Lord in hymns and thanksgivings, so in the glory of the Resurrection and of the great festival, [Col. 0348B] with the Devil’s battles destroyed, the saints and righteous will rejoice festively in the Lord, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord” (Ps. 83).

From the Kalends of November until the Lord’s Advent, Ezekiel, Daniel, and the twelve prophets are read and sung, with the responsory “I saw the Lord.” For Ezekiel saw four living creatures as figures of the four Evangelists, who taught the Lord’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension, each of whom deserved his own form according to his principal intention. Daniel likewise prophesied that Christ would come, saying: “I looked in the vision of the night, and behold, [Col. 0348C] the Son of Man came” (Dan. 7).

Likewise the other prophets foretold that Christ would come; indeed, they are read before his Advent because they foretold his coming more clearly. From the Advent of the Lord until his Nativity, Isaiah is read, because, the more elegantly and openly he prophesied concerning Christ, the nearer he is read to Christ’s birth. Why, moreover, readings and chants concerning that same Nativity are used at the Nativity itself is obvious: so great a joy is then recognized as needing spiritual proclamation and heavenly manifestation.

The first Mass, celebrated on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, typologically signifies the time before the law of Moses. The second, celebrated at the appearance of dawn, recalls the time of the written Law and of the prophets, [Col. 0348D] because through the Law and the prophets the light concerning Christ appeared to the world like the herald of day. The third, more festively celebrated in the brightness of mid-day, refers to the time of grace, in which the great light descended from heaven, “which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Thereafter, at the individual feasts, readings and chants occur for the same reason.

From the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, chants are taken from the Psalms and the Epistles of Paul are read, because after the Law prophecy, and after the Gospel apostolic Scripture, moves us by sounding forth what we have heard. Likewise, from Septuagesima until Easter, the time from Adam to Moses is represented, in which death reigned. Therefore, since the fault opposed to righteousness is then commemorated, *Glory to God in the highest* (Luke 2) is silent—the song [Col. 0349A] heard as a testimony of peace when “truth sprang up from the earth and righteousness looked down from heaven” (Psalm 84). And because the punishment into which humanity fell through sin is recalled through the Scriptures, the Alleluia, the chant of joy, is omitted.

From Advent until the Nativity of the Lord is the time from Moses until Christ, in which sin reigned—not through ignorance, as death had previously done, but through the weakness of the flesh. During this time Alleluia is sung, because the fathers were under the Law; but *Glory to God in the highest* is silent, for it is the sign of peace and righteousness, which the Law could not give. The time from the first Advent until the second is that between Pentecost and the Advent of the Lord. In it the Church sings Alleluia in hope of the resurrection, and *Glory to God in the highest* for righteousness restored. She sings Alleluia daily, [Col. 0349B] because her hope is strengthened. *Glory to God in the highest* is sung not daily but only on feasts, because she sins daily. Yet in faith—that is, on the day which the Lord has made—she always holds fast to righteousness; for she praises always in faith, though not always in deeds.

The fourth time is between Easter and Pentecost and signifies the state of eternal blessedness. In it *Glory to God in the highest* is sung daily, and a double Alleluia; we also publicly open the doors of the Church to penitents, and do not bend the knee. But why do we observe this, unless we understand its mystery? *Glory to God in the highest* is then sung because in the resurrection righteousness—that is, charity—will be perfected, and peace will be fully granted. The Alleluia is called double because of the double robe at the *Albs*, since we shall be clothed in the glory of incorruption. The Church’s door is opened to penitents because [Col. 0349C] then no reproach for any sin will remain, since everything will be swallowed up by glory. We pray standing because there will then be nothing for which knees should be bent, but the house of God will be filled with glory.

But why is it that on ordinary weekdays we do not sing *Glory to God in the highest*, nor two Alleluias, except because we do not yet possess perfect righteousness or the glory for which we wait? Yet a single Alleluia is sung, because the Church already possesses the first resurrection. Hence Alleluia is always sung, except during Septuagesima. Since, therefore, this time is a figure of so great a joy, the Church sings it on Sundays and feasts. But because we are not yet in that state, she is silent on ordinary weekdays.

Thus through the Four Seasons the condition of the Church varies. The first brought in fault; the second uncovered it; the third erased it through righteousness [Col. 0349D] but reserved punishment; the fourth will perfect righteousness and swallow up punishment. The first was of fault and punishment; the second, of punishment and prophecy; the third, of punishment and grace; the fourth, of grace and glory. The subsequent order of the year mystically signifies that, in the resurrection, the first shall be last; likewise, this is signified by certain things done at the feast of the Circumcision. But we pass over many other matters which, though they may appear slight, are nevertheless performed with great mystery, because we hasten to the other subjects we have proposed.

## Chapter V. On the Orders of Clerics

It remains for us to consider the seven orders of clerics, which are the seven grades of the Church through which one who is a cleric ascends, becoming door-keeper, reader, [Col. 0350A] exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest.

The first grade, then, is that of the door-keepers, whose task is to discern whom they should justly exclude from the Church and whom they should worthily receive into it. It also belongs to them faithfully to guard the Church’s property; hence the keys of the church are handed to them when they are ordained. Afterwards they are promoted to the office of readers, whose duty it is to read in church the prophecies and apostolic Scriptures. When they are ordained, the book of divine readings is handed to them and they are told: “Receive it, and be proclaimers of the word of God; if you fulfil your office well, you will have a share with those who have faithfully ministered to the Lord.” Therefore one promoted to this grade ought to shine in knowledge of letters.

Third, they are promoted to the order of exorcists, so that they may have authority over [Col. 0350B] demons to be cast out. Those who must command the unclean ought to possess a clean spirit. When ordained, they receive the book of exorcisms and are told: “Receive it, and have authority to lay hands upon the possessed.”

When acolytes are ordained, they receive a candlestick with a candle, so that they may know that they are assigned to kindle and carry lights. They also receive a cruet for pouring water into the chalice in which the body of Christ is to be consecrated.

In the fifth place subdeacons are ordained, who draw near to the ministry of the altar. Their task is to carry the vessels of the body and blood of Christ. Hence the law of continence is imposed upon them, according to the saying: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52). For although chastity is a spiritual ray of light among clerics, it is nevertheless [Col. 0350C] the distinctive virtue, as it were, of those who approach these three highest orders, which by antonomasia—that is, by excellence—are now called the sacred orders. Subdeacons, moreover, minister in the offices of the Levites. It belongs to their office to lift or wash the corporal cloths and coverings. When ordained, they receive the paten and chalice from the bishop’s hand; from the archdeacon’s hand they receive the cruet with water in it, and a hand-towel, with which priest and Levite must cleanse their hands when they are about to handle the Lord’s sacraments.

In the sixth place come deacons, not without the mystery of the number six, which signifies perfection. This order took its beginning in the Old Testament from the tribe of Levi and was confirmed in the New Testament by the apostles, when the apostles chose seven men full of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0350D] for this office (Acts 6). Therefore the saints decreed that in every mother Church seven deacons should stand around the altar during the celebration of Mass, on account of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

In the Apocalypse these are called the seven angels sounding trumpets, because it is theirs to sound abroad, by divine inspiration, the lofty mysteries of God upon which they have attentively fixed their minds. They are called seven golden lampstands because it is theirs to show the light of the Gospel to others. They are the seven thunders because they ought to thunder fearfully: “Every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matthew 31). In the manner of a herald they openly call people to prayer and to bend the knee. They proclaim the Gospel and distribute the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. [Col. 0351A] Priests may not take up the Lord’s chalice unless it is handed to them by a deacon.

When Levites are ordained—which may lawfully be done from the age of twenty and above—they receive the *orarium* over the left shoulder, so that they may understand that they have received God’s yoke, by which they are to press down everything pertaining to the world, signified by the left shoulder. They also receive the text of the Gospels, so that they may understand themselves to be heralds of the Gospel.

The order of presbyters follows, which took its beginning from the sons of Aaron. When these are ordained from the age of thirty and above, while the bishop blesses them and holds his hands over their heads, all the presbyters present with him raise their hands with the bishop over them and invoke the Holy Spirit. After [Col. 0351B] the invocation, they receive the stole over both shoulders, so that they may understand that they ought to be armed with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, so that adversity may not break them nor prosperity exalt them. They also receive from the bishop’s hand a chalice with wine and a paten with a host, so that they may understand that they have authority to offer to God acceptable sacrifices—namely, the body and blood of Christ.

Great dignity, wondrous power, lofty and awe-inspiring office! No order is higher than this in the Church. Yet the ordination of clerics, dedication of basilicas, consecration of chrism, confirmation through laying on of hands, and general blessing over the people have been added to bishops, lest the same power of authority, if possessed by all and from all alike, dissolve obedience and generate scandal. [Col. 0351C]

Those exalted through the seven orders ought spiritually to fulfil the offices themselves. Therefore, whoever converts an unbeliever, or teaches the Catholic faith and thus spiritually brings someone into the Church, or justly casts someone out by excommunication, fulfils the office of door-keeper. Whoever corrects by teaching those who live badly in the Church, and instructs the lesser according to the authoritative Scriptures, is spiritually a reader. Whoever by prayers frees someone from diabolical vices performs the office of exorcist. Whoever supplies others with the light of good works is spiritually an acolyte. Whoever possesses such purity that by that person’s example and counsel others are washed from the stains of crimes fulfils and possesses the office of subdeacon. Whoever fittingly distributes the body and blood of Christ to worthy recipients, or by personal example [Col. 0351D] exhorts others to prayer and watchfulness, performs the office of deacon. Whoever worthily consecrates the Lord’s body and blood spiritually fulfils the office of priest.

Priests are successors of the seventy-two disciples, but bishops of the apostles. *Bishop* means “overseer”; *priest*, “one who gives sacred things”; *deacon*, “minister”; *subdeacon*, “subminister”; *acolyte*, “candle-bearer”; *exorcist*, “one who adjures.” That *reader* is named from reading, and *door-keeper* from a door, is not unknown to the Latin language.

We must now observe that all who possess these aforementioned grades spiritually are vicars of the bishop, who fulfilled these offices in himself. He showed himself to be a door-keeper when he expelled singers and sellers from the Temple—something which he does spiritually in the Church [Col. 0352A] every day. Hence in the Gospel the Lord says: “I am the door” (John 10). He showed himself to be a reader when, in the midst of the elders, he opened the book of Isaiah and read it distinctly so that it might be understood. He showed himself to be an exorcist by casting out demons; an acolyte by saying: “I am the light of the world” (John 8); a subdeacon when he washed the disciples’ feet; and a deacon when he distributed his body and blood with his own hands to the disciples, and again when he exhorted them to pray, saying: “Watch and pray” (Matthew 26).

He showed himself to be a true priest when he changed bread and wine into his body and blood, and commanded his disciples to do the same in memory of his Passion. Again, he fulfilled this office more manifestly when, himself both priest [Col. 0352B] and sacrifice, he offered himself to the Father upon the altar of the cross. He fulfils it still more gloriously when, seated at the right hand of the Father, he intercedes for us. Thus, making peace between what is in heaven and what is on earth, he makes the homeland of heaven and earth one commonwealth.

## Chapter VI. On Sacred Vestments

After this, let us briefly speak of priestly vestments, first recalling those of the Old Testament: two tunics, one of fine linen and one of hyacinth-blue; a girdle; breeches; an ephod; a mitre—which is also called a *cidaris* or tiara—and a golden plate placed above the mitre in front of the face. The girdle and ephod were varied in four colours: fine linen, purple, hyacinth-blue, and saffron, [Col. 0352C] by which the four elements are signified.

Upon the ephod the names of the twelve patriarchs were engraved on two precious stones, six on one and six on the other. On the breastpiece were twelve stones likewise bearing within themselves the engraved names of the twelve patriarchs. On the golden plate was engraved the name of God, called by the Hebrews ineffable.

The priests of the New Testament do not use all these ornaments, because they use only one tunic, except for bishops. They also have an amice in place of the ephod and breastpiece, since it is still customarily called an ephod. No one now uses a golden plate, because what was formerly shown on it is now shown in the sign of the cross. For, as Jerome says, the blood of the Gospel is more precious [Col. 0352D] than the gold of the Law. All priests now use the girdle and the stole, which the old priesthood did not use, so as to fulfil the Gospel saying: “Take my yoke upon you” (Matthew 11). It makes no difference that the girdle and ephod are no longer varied with so many colours, nor are those stones customarily placed on the ephod, since the Christian religion, serving truth, accomplishes mystically through economical things what the old observance did through costly ones.

Let us now briefly state what the vestments of the New Testament signify. The alb—that is, the tunic which in Greek is called *podērēs* (ποδήρις), meaning “reaching to the feet”—signifies purity in the soul. The girdle signifies chastity in the body, which pertains to temperance. The ephod, called *ephod* in Hebrew, signifies righteousness. The breastpiece, which the Greeks call *logion* (λόγιον), signifies wisdom; the amice contains the type of both, and therefore covers both shoulders and breast. The stole, also called the *orarium*, signifies fortitude amid prosperity and adversity, without which the other virtues are overcome and cannot be crowned. The length of the stole signifies perseverance, as does the tunic insofar as it is ankle-length: that is, souls are finally possessed through patience, which pertains to fortitude. That the stole is bound together with the girdle indicates that virtues are united to virtues.

To these aforementioned garments the chasuble is added, also called the *planeta* or *infula*. It expresses charity, which is placed in the position of prudence, because love is the fulfilment of the Law. The maniple, [Col. 0353B] which is placed on the left before the eyes behind the back, signifies vigilance, through which sloth—often arising in minds and frequently creeping in after the aforementioned virtues—is to be removed and wiped away from the eyes of reason or of the soul.

The dalmatic, too, used by Levites, signifies by its breadth the same thing as the chasuble, namely charity. By the two scarlet lines with which it is adorned in front and behind from top to bottom is figured the preaching of love of God and neighbour in both Testaments. The twelve fringes of the lines on either side express the twelve branches of charity enumerated by the Apostle:

> Charity is patient, is kind. Charity does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek what is its own, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice [Col. 0353C] in iniquity, but rejoices together with truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails.  
> —1 Corinthians 13

The third line, which is between the two and is marked with three fringes before and behind, shows charity adorned by faith in the Trinity. By the fringes on the left side is understood the concern of the active life with its many affairs; by the right side, which lacks fringes, contemplation of heavenly things without a multitude of disturbances.

That bishops use two tunics in addition to the *podērēs*, which the others use in common, shows that it is their particular duty to possess knowledge of the two Testaments, so that they may know how to bring forth new and old things from their treasury. For this reason each of the three tunics bears its own type. The *podērēs*, because it is of fine linen or linen, [Col. 0353D] indicates purity. For just as the whiteness of fine linen or linen, which does not come by nature, is attained through the effort of washing, so the purity which nature does not supply the saints acquire through diligence, aided by the grace of the Holy Spirit, while through the exercise of good works they mortify and cleanse the body.

The second tunic, of silk, which has its origin and is produced from worms that procreate without intercourse and are small, signifies chastity and humility. The third tunic, as formerly, is hyacinth-blue; its colour, like that of the hyacinth stone, which imitates the serenity of the ether, signifies saints who think upon and imitate heavenly things. This tunic is rightly [Col. 0354A] hyacinth-blue, because just as that stone changes colour with the air—for in clear air it is clear, and in dark air pale—so it spiritually and properly befits a bishop to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep.

The bishop’s horned mitre sets forth the two Testaments, by which he ought to overcome the Church’s enemies. The sandals used by bishops and cardinals are whole underneath, because they ought not to gape after earthly things; they are perforated above, because they ought to open the eyes of the mind to things above. Their being open in some places and whole in others openly shows that heavenly sacraments ought to be revealed to some and concealed from others. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of God, but to the rest in parables” (Luke 8). He considered the mysteries of these shoes who said: “How precious are the feet of those announcing peace” (Isaiah 52).

The bishop’s boots signify preparedness to set out and haste in preaching. The bishop’s ring is the seal of faith, because just as in ancient times the king’s name and image were impressed on a ring’s seal, so in Catholic faith the name and image of the heavenly King are declared. For example, his name is shown when it is said, “Lord Father, Lord Son, Lord Holy Spirit,” because “Lord” is his name. His image—that is, what he is like—is shown when he is called Almighty and Eternal and by similar names, although, strictly speaking, no quality or diversity is found in him. Therefore the bishop wears the ring for the Church, [Col. 0354C] which he must adorn by faith and present chaste to Christ, her heavenly bridegroom (2 Corinthians 11), so that the bride may sing: “My Lord Jesus Christ has betrothed me to himself with his ring.” That the bishop wears the ring on his hand teaches that he ought to show faith in action. By the gloves on the hands are understood the examples of the saints which should be present in works, and that works must be guarded against every defilement of nature, lest “a little leaven corrupt the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5).

The pastoral staff, by its straightness, signifies upright governance. Its one curved end and its other pointed end show that its bearer must preside over subjects and overcome rebels. Hence it is said:

> The curved part draws the gentle; the sharp part pricks the rebellious.

And again:

> The crook draws those whom the rod governs; its final part pricks.

And likewise:

> Draw by the curve; govern in the middle; prick with the lower end. And again: By the straight staff, bishop, teach right living; by the bend of iron hasten to show mercy.

The pallium placed above an archbishop signifies the collar and prize which those lawfully competing will receive; it also expresses the discipline with which they ought to clothe and constrain themselves from above for the example of their subjects. The scarlet *planeta*, with which the pope is vested wherever he goes preaching, [Col. 0355A] declares martyrdom. The cross now carried before him signifies that the saying is especially fitting for him: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

The tonsure of clerics teaches that every superfluity must be cut away, so that they may freely hear and see the law of God. The crown shows that clerics are in a special sense God’s kingdom. That priests’ hands are anointed with oil signifies that through the Holy Spirit they possess the power of consecration, and that their hands must be extended for giving, not dry and crooked for holding back. These aforementioned signs, therefore, are not the virtues themselves but emblems of virtues, by which their users are taught, as though by writings, what sort of persons they ought to be.

Let the prelates of the Church, who are custodians and stewards [Col. 0355B] of God’s mysteries, understand these sacraments. Otherwise they are blind and leaders of the blind (Matthew 5), like Jews carrying mysteries which they neither see nor understand, and deriving from them only as much as beasts that carry bread for the use of others take in. Unless there is this difference—which truly exists—that those entrusted with so much will deservedly be required to render an account for their negligence on the day of wrath and vengeance: when the cedars of paradise tremble, what will the twig of the wilderness do?

Yet God does not abandon his sacraments here, but fulfils them through ministers, even though unworthy, for the salvation of those who are called saints according to his purpose (Romans 8). Observe also that, although a sacrament is called the sign of a sacred thing or a sacred secret, here we take “sacraments” to mean signs. Therefore those who bear sacraments ought to shine with the virtues [Col. 0355C] signified through the sacraments, so that others may likewise be enlightened by their light. Each person ought in his or her own manner to shine with the same aforementioned virtues, though not all are figuratively marked by them. Anyone can indeed possess spiritually within themselves the effect of the sacraments.

For example, whoever belongs to the Lord’s portion, so as truly to be able to say, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15), and, “I have chosen to be cast down in the house of God” (Psalm 83), is spiritually a cleric, although not marked with the outward form—that is, the sign—of clerical status. For the Greek word *cleric* means one who belongs to the Lord’s portion: that is, the Lord has chosen that person as his portion, and that person has chosen God.

Whoever spiritually introduces others [Col. 0355D] into the Church—that is, teaches faith by preaching—is spiritually a door-keeper. Anyone teaching morals is a reader; anyone praying, an exorcist; anyone enlightening, an acolyte; anyone showing humility, a subdeacon; anyone exhorting others, a deacon; and anyone offering himself or herself to God as a holy sacrifice, a priest.

Let each, then, clothe shoulders and breast in a spiritual amice: that is, let each be fortified with the virtue of righteous works, clothed in the holiness of well-ordered thoughts. Let each be clothed in the purity signified by the alb. Let each be clothed, insofar as possible, in both tunics: that is, in understanding of both Testaments and of the letter—that is, in literal and spiritual understanding. Let each possess the girdle of chastity, the stole of fortitude, and fullness of knowledge—that is, charity, figured by the *infula*. Whoever is thus adorned [Col. 0356A] possesses the true and royal priesthood within the temple of God, which that person is.

It is therefore plain that the things signified without the signs—that is, virtues without the outward sacraments—sometimes justify; but these signs without the virtues do absolutely no good, indeed they condemn. When joined together, however, they seem to confer a greater good, because when something is added to something else, the whole becomes greater. But is it therefore a greater good when the two things taken separately are not both good? To this we reply that it is good, even though not separately so; nevertheless, when they are together both are good, and it is therefore evident that the whole is a greater good, as a brief but lofty example makes clear.

For the Virgin Mary to bear Christ bodily was a great thing when joined with love, though it would not have been so if separated from love; yet it was still [Col. 0356B] greater that through love she bore him spiritually. But because she merited to possess both together, she deserved to be incomparably blessed, because charity often burns more intensely within on account of outward gifts bestowed, and merit increases.

Here, if anyone says that charity alone is alone rewardable, this is indeed true if understood to mean that “alone” does not exclude other things, but removes comparison with other things; or that nothing without it and except on its account is to be rewarded. For charity is so great that it “never fails” (1 Corinthians 13): that is, it is lacking neither here nor in the life to come, but alone among the virtues remains forever. Therefore, according to what has been said, it may plausibly be stated that God rewards many goods in the saints besides charity—not as though without charity, but many things which are not charity itself.

Would we say that faith has no merit? Far from it! Yet faith itself is not charity, since it can exist without charity; but without charity it is not rewarded. Joined with charity, however, it increases merit. Thus God rewards his other gifts in those who preserve them with charity, gifts from which he works all things together for good (Romans 8); and for each of his gifts—whether virtues or sacraments—preserved through charity, he gives distinct crowns, yet by grace alone. “He gives,” I said, with regard to free will; “yet by grace alone,” I added, considering that every good is from above, descending from the Father of lights (James 1).

But having displayed these matters publicly thus far, as it were upon the plains of the valleys, let us now pass [Col. 0356D] to the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon.

## Chapter VII. On the Celebration of Mass

The holy Fathers and prophets, sighing for and proclaiming the Lord’s coming before his Advent, first offered desires, works, praises, and prayers. These are commemorated in the Introit of the Mass. For the choir of singing clerics signifies the choir of prophets and the multitude of saints who awaited the Lord’s coming. The Introit—called the *officium* because through it we begin the office of Mass—expresses the desires and proclamations of those awaiting him. The psalm verse signifies their works and prophecies; *Glory to the Father*, their praises. The repetition of the office indicates that they repeatedly uttered sighs and proclamations concerning Christ.

The *Kyrie eleison*, repeated three times threefold, signifies their prayers, which they multiply so that [Col. 0357A] the grace of the supreme Trinity, through Christ’s coming, might conform them to the nine distinct orders of angels. Meanwhile, while these words are said or these acts performed, the priest, clothed in sacred vestments, proceeds from the sacred building. This signifies that Christ, the expectation of the nations, so greatly desired, having taken most holy flesh from the incorrupt flesh of the Virgin, came forth from the secret dwelling-place of heaven into the world; or came forth from the secret sanctuary—that is, from the virginal womb—“like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Psalm 18). This pertains to the birth which he has from his mother; of the other birth it is said: “His going forth is from the Father,” etc. For he has two generations, one eternal and the other temporal; yet both secret and inexpressible, because he has the former without a father and [Col. 0357B] the latter without a mother. Hence the prophet says: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

The priest as he proceeds is preceded by two candle-bearers and a thurible-bearer; then come the subdeacon carrying the Gospel and the deacon who will read the Gospel. By the candle-bearers and thurible-bearer we understand the saints who preceded the New Testament; by the subdeacon carrying the Gospel-book and by the deacon, herald of the Gospel, the saints of the New Testament. By the two burning candleholders with candles we recall the Law and the prophets; by the Gospel-book, the New Testament. The candleholders fittingly go first, because the Law and the prophets preceded the law of grace.

Again, understand the human heart by the thurible; charity by its fire; and in the incense consider the example [Col. 0357C] of good works, or the most sweetly fragrant prayers. For just as incense smells sweetly and rises upward in the fire of the thurible, so a good work or prayer arising from charity gives fragrance beyond every balm, spice, and incense-offering. The thurible-bearer goes before, accompanying the candle-bearers and those following them, showing that the significance of the incense belongs jointly to saints of both Testaments.

The subdeacon and deacon go before the priest because the disciples were sent before the Lord, and preachers—that is, prelates of the Church—are still sent to prepare the way of the Lord spiritually before his face. When they arrive before the altar, the Gospel is placed upon it. The altar signifies Jerusalem, where preaching was first made to the primitive Church, and from there went forth publicly, [Col. 0357D] as it is written: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2).

Notice that, after the general confession has been made so that the breasts of those serving may be pure, the priest gives the kiss, signifying Christ, who first brought us peace. Then, coming to the altar, he likewise kisses it and the Gospel. The altar in this place signifies the Jewish people; the Gospel, the Gentile people, who believed through the Gospel. For Christ gave peace to both, when, made the cornerstone, he made both one. Notice also that the deacon or subdeacon presents the Gospel to the priest to be kissed because preachers reconciled and offered the Gentiles to Christ, to whom he himself did not preach in person.

That the priest first approaches [Col. 0358A] the right side of the altar indicates that Emmanuel, promised in the Law, came first to the Jews rather than to the Gentiles. The Jews, because of the Law, were then on the right side; the Gentiles were, as it were, on the left, because they worshipped idols.

After these aforementioned things have been completed, and while the choir is silent, the priest begins in the middle of the altar the angelic hymn, namely *Glory to God in the highest*. This signifies that, when God no longer required the shadow of the Law and when all things held the tranquil middle silence (Wisdom 18), the Messiah foretold by the prophets was born in the midst—that is, for all—at whose birth the angel said to the shepherds: “I announce to you great joy” (Luke 2). That the choir then cries out together and completes the hymn which the priest alone [Col. 0358B] first began signifies that immediately there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising and saying: “Glory to God in the highest” (ibid.).

When the hymn is completed, the priest greets the people, saying: “The Lord be with you.” He prays that God may be with them and remain in them. This greeting was heard in the Old Testament. But in the bishop’s saying, “Peace be to you,” it is understood that he is more properly Christ’s vicar, for Christ, announcing peace after the resurrection, greeted the apostles in this way.

The priest then, about to pray, exhorts others to pray, because the Lord instructed the disciples to pray and himself prayed. The Epistle which follows the Collect represents the preaching of John the Baptist, because, just as he was Christ’s forerunner, so the Epistle precedes the Gospel. [Col. 0358C] The Epistle also expresses the teaching of the seventy-two disciples, whom the Lord sent into every city and place where he himself was about to come, and to whom he said: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the labourers are few” (Matthew 9).

The Responsory which follows the Epistle signifies the assent which hearers gave to the admonitions of preachers. Hence it is fittingly called a *Responsory*. For in believing through preaching they responded according to the preachers’ desire, while fulfilling God’s law by holy living. Or it is called a Responsory because it is sung by a responding choir, and it signifies the active life, in which saints exhort one another to attain eternal life. Some also call it the Gradual, either because it is sung on the steps or [Col. 0358D] because of its mystical signification: active persons too sing upon the steps of virtues when they perform lofty works in virtues.

Alleluia follows, which is Hebrew. There are three languages that excel above others: Hebrew because of the Law, Greek because of wisdom, and Latin because of empire. In these three languages the triumphant title of Christ shone forth, and in these three languages God’s praise is sung in the Church. Therefore *Alleluia* is Hebrew, and in Latin it is interpreted: “Praise the Lord.” But let us continue on our way.

The Alleluia, which has a jubilus, expresses the joy and love of believers, and the great gladness and praise that followed faith upon hearing the preaching. For they did not merely give assent to the preaching, but rejoiced when they [Col. 0359A] heard it: “Zion heard and was glad, and the daughters of Judah exulted” (Psalm 96). Hence they say in the Song of Songs: “We shall exult and rejoice in you” (Song 1). And the bride says: “My soul,” she says, “melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5).

Alleluia also signifies the contemplative life; hence mystically it is sung on a higher degree than the Responsory. Further, when the Alleluia is repeated after the verse, it signifies the eternal joy which the saints receive after this life. Hence Alleluia is brief in words but abundant in *pneuma*, because that joy is greater than speech can explain; every language is too slight and imperfect to disclose its magnitude. For who could fully recount what has not entered into the human heart? (1 Corinthians 2.)

[Col. 0359B] Therefore, because this joy can neither be expressed fully in words nor kept wholly silent, the Church, as it were, laying words aside, leaps forth in jubilation, almost in wonder, as if saying: “What voice, what tongue, could unfold it,” etc. For here neither words nor understanding suffice, and yet love does not permit silence. Thus the Church, giving utterance through the pneuma, wonderfully to say, indicates in some way more expressly and more aptly without words than through words how great is the joy of God, where words shall cease. For by the pneuma, although the greatness of eternal joy is not narrated, it is at least shown to be beyond narration.

But when the Sequence follows, the latter Alleluia does not have a pneuma; rather, in its place the choir sings the Sequence, which signifies the same thing—namely, the joy and delights of eternal life. Therefore it [Col. 0359C] customarily has new and unusual words, because the joy of heaven is hidden and unknown to mortals. Or the Sequence mystically signifies the praises of eternal life. Hence it was said: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. LXXXIII).

The fact that the Sequence has praise-flowing words and sweet-sounding song well accords with this meaning, because there all things shall be full of praise, and the melody of the heavenly instrument shall abound in sweet-flowing gladness. For “the dwelling-place of all who rejoice shall be there” (Ps. LXXXVI). And because the praises of eternal life will not resound in human words, some Churches mystically pneumatize the Sequence without words. For no signification by words is necessary where each person’s heart shall lie open to every other, as they behold the book of life.

But the Tract, [Col. 0359D] because it expresses groaning and a tearful chant, represents the tears of the saints, whether in the active or in the contemplative life. Hence it is called a *Tract*, because the saints, sighing, draw a groan from the depths of the breast. Although they rejoice in hope, as the Alleluia teaches, nevertheless, while dwelling here in the valley of tears, they have the upper watering and the lower watering; and this the Tract mystically signifies. For they groan tearfully over the postponement of heavenly blessedness, sitting by the rivers of Babylon and remembering their native land. Again, they shed tears for their own sins and those of others when, from the nearness of Babylon’s river, they see themselves often sprinkled by it and others, wholly immersed, carried downward by the swiftness of that river.

But because this weeping is sometimes with reference to heavenly joy, [Col. 0360A] sometimes with reference to our misery, the Tract sometimes touches upon gladness because of the upper watering, as in *Jubilate* and *Laudate*, and sometimes sadness because of the lower watering, as in *De profundis* and similar chants. And because the joy of the saints is neither full nor unbroken, but is often interrupted, the Church sometimes inserts the Tract, as in the season of Septuagesima. And when she repeats Alleluia on Holy Saturday, the Tract follows Alleluia, because joy here is not fitting without weeping. On Saturday in Albis—that is, in the octave of Easter—Alleluia is doubled, because then in eternal life joy shall be perfect: the flesh glorified with the soul, and the resurrection of the saints completed together with Christ’s resurrection. Hence the Church sings: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Ps. CXVII), etc.

[Col. 0360B] Rightly, therefore, the Church, signifying eternal joy, as we said above, sometimes intimates joy through Alleluia; sometimes, living in sorrow, groans and weeps through the Tract. For, considering in the paradise of the divine Scriptures that she will arrive, through the paradise of virtues, at the paradise of heavenly riches, she exults; but seeing that she is still held in the valley of tears and that she fell from the earthly paradise, she weeps. But I shall explain this joy and this weeping more fully, separately, in two volumes, one of which will be called *Paradise*, and the other *Why Does One Who Rejoices Weep?*

Passing hence to another subject, let us consider the passage of the apostles from the Jews to the Gentiles, which the Church commemorates by transferring the Gospel from [Col. 0360C] the right side to the left and reading it there. For when Judaea rejected the word of God, the apostles passed to the Gentiles, when Gideon’s fleece had been dried and dew watered the threshing-floor. He who had first said, “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X), afterwards commanded, saying, “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark XVI). Therefore, because preaching reached even those who had been on the left side, the Gospel is rightly read on the left side; and not only on the left, but also toward the north, which signifies the wicked, according to the saying, “I shall set my throne in the north” (Isa. XIV), because preaching reached even such as had withdrawn far from the warmth of the true sun.

Or rather, it is read toward the north because the north wind, a cold wind, signifies the devil, who by the blast [Col. 0360D] of temptations freezes and chills human hearts away from the love of God. Hence, “From the north,” he says, “every evil shall be opened” (Jer. I). And the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “Arise, O north wind, and come, O south wind” (Cant. IV). That is: Depart, malignant spirit, who chill my garden; and come, O south wind—that is, O Holy Spirit—who, by breathing through it, make its spices flow forth. The Gospel is therefore rightly read toward the north, because the faith contained in the Gospel is our armor against the devil: “Resist him,” he says, “strong in faith” (1 Pet. V).

Now observe that the people here lay down their staffs, leave their kneelers, uncover their heads, make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads, and listen standing; that the Gospel is read on a higher step than the Epistle—note each point. To lay down [Col. 0361A] staffs indicates that it belongs to Christian perfection not to avenge oneself, but to reserve vengeance for the Lord; for he says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Heb. X). To leave kneelers signifies that we ought not to trust in princes or earthly supports, because “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” says Ecclesiastes (Ecclus. I)—understood in comparison with God, upon whom we ought to cast our care. The head is uncovered in order to show how attentively we ought to hear and understand the word of God. The sign of the cross is impressed on the forehead lest the ancient enemy, coming upon us through the tares of heresy, corrupt the seed of right faith. By our listening while standing, we are to consider the grave battle that remains: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI).

[Col. 0361B] The Gospel is read on a higher step than the Epistle because Christ’s teaching far surpasses the teaching of the apostles. After the Gospel, the choir sings the summary of our faith, showing that it gives assent to the word of the Gospel and declaring in whom, or in what, it believes. The order is right: the king calls; the soldiers answer, “We follow.”

Then the priest greets the people, saying, “The Lord be with you.” This greeting was received from antiquity: Boaz thus greeted his reapers, and the prophet in Chronicles greeted King Asa and those who were with him. Therefore the priest greets the people and exhorts them to pray that they may remain firm in the faith that has been recited. Promising him this, the choir begins the Offertory, as though saying: “I believe, and I shall fulfil in deed the faith which I have confessed.” [Col. 0361C] Hence the priest immediately offers the gifts to be consecrated; and afterwards the people offer their own gifts, signifying that they offer themselves to God.

Observe the order: the Gospel comes first, faith follows, and then gifts are offered. For it is necessary first to hear the word of God. Who, indeed, would believe unless he had first heard? “How,” he says, “shall they believe unless they are preached to?” (Rom. X). Then how can anyone who does not rightly believe offer a gift acceptable to God? For “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. X). Through the offered gifts we may also commemorate the abundant sacrifice offered by the people when King Solomon consecrated the temple and altar to the Lord. Following that example, the faithful people offer themselves and their gifts to the Lord.

Now let us look more carefully [Col. 0361D] to the fact that the priest, as we mentioned above, offers gifts for sacrifice—namely bread and wine. Melchizedek offered both figuratively; Christ gave both to his disciples at supper. But both were changed into body and blood. Whether both are changed into both is beyond me to determine. Yet I would more safely say that bread alone is changed into the body, and wine into the blood, rather than that each is changed into each—unless the fact seems to oppose this that we believe both are received under either species. But this too is not incompatible, if we look at the matter more subtly. For under the species of bread both can be present and received, not because perhaps bread has passed into both, but because where the one body is, there it is whole, and it is not separated or received in division as are the species under which it is received. Rather, both are received together, although we speak separately according to the different species: “This,” he says, “is my body,” and then, “This is my blood.”

[Col. 0362A] But someone says: Was it his own body that he gave, or did he speak figuratively, as when he called himself a door? It was indeed his own body and a true body which he then gave to his disciples and which is now received and eaten at the altar: the same body, I say, which was born of the Virgin and is now immortal in glory at God’s right hand. A wondrous thing! The flesh eaten below remains whole above. Why do you raise dialectical objections? What are you pondering here, sophist? Why do you seek arguments here? This is to scatter dust among the stars. Your dialectic does not rise so high.

[Col. 0362B] Look, then, and see where you are; understand that sense holds the first region of ascent, imagination the second, reason the third, in which your dialectic has learned to play. Above this is faith, loftier than dialectic, which has not been heard of in Canaan nor seen in Teman; human reason affords it no proof, especially concerning faith in the Trinity or in the body of the Lord, as this discourse now proceeds. But faith transcends understanding itself, through which the saints see the secrets of heaven, as Paul in the third heaven and John in the Apocalypse. Yet understanding will be perfected in the vision of eternal life, when we shall see God face to face, whom here we behold in a mirror, in an enigma (1 Cor. XIII). Let no one dispute arrogantly here; rather, let what increases the merit of faith be humbly sought, [Col. 0362C] and what cannot be examined without danger be firmly believed.

It may therefore be asked why the Lord willed his flesh to be received, and not flesh only, but flesh and blood; why he is not received under the appearance of flesh and blood, although he is flesh and blood; why he is received under a sacrament; whether only Christ’s flesh and blood are received, or the whole Christ; and, if the whole Christ, why we more commonly say that we receive the Lord’s body rather than Christ or the Lord.

Christ therefore willed his flesh to be received by the faithful in order that, through food of flesh, he might invite them to taste divinity; and that what we perform here in time we may attain in eternal joys—so that here it may be medicine, and there delight. He willed both to be received so that both our body and our soul might be glorified with him. He is not received under the appearance of flesh [Col. 0362D] and blood, lest the human mind recoil in horror and the senses be frightened by what is unfamiliar to them—as when, at the prayer of blessed Gregory, a little finger, bloodied with blood, was found and shown in the chalice. He is received under a sacrament and not under his own form, in order that faith may be confirmed, for faith concerns things not seen; or because mortal man could not behold the brightness that would be in Christ’s body, as the disciples experienced at the Transfiguration.

But he is received under such a sacrament—that is, under the species of bread and wine—because of this resemblance: bread strengthens and wine makes the human heart glad (Ps. CIII), and Christ is the strength and joy of human beings and angels. And although the same whole reality is received in either species, it is nevertheless received in both, to signify [Col. 0363A] that this sacrament has a twofold effect. For it is the redemption of body and soul; this would not be signified if it were received under only one species. Though under each species both are received, not both are signified under each. Rather, the species of bread signifies Christ’s body and the species of wine Christ’s blood, with respect to the resurrection; and reception under both species together signifies the redemption of the recipient’s body and soul.

Elsewhere, however, in another respect bread and wine signify Christ’s body, which is the Church: for as one loaf comes from many grains, and wine from many clusters, so the one Church—which is figuratively Christ’s body—is gathered into one from many persons.
