But here, that is, in the sacrament of the altar, Christ’s true body and true blood are truly received under each species, the species of bread and wine, after consecration. [Col. 0363B] Therefore, although both are under either species, they are received under both to signify, as we have said, the twofold effect. Nor is there a repetition of the sacrament unless it is received again under the same species.

That it should not be administered dipped [in the wine], we have from the decrees. And note that this sacrament is not consecrated from just any bread, but only from wheaten bread, because he says of himself: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone” (John XII). He fittingly calls himself a grain of wheat, because a grain of wheat is white within and red without. Christ is called white with respect to divinity, and ruddy in the flesh because of his passion. Hence the Bride in the Song of Songs says: “My beloved is white [Col. 0363C] and ruddy” (Cant. V). Of this redness is that voice of those who marvel: “Who is this who comes from Edom, dyed in garments from Bozrah?” (Isa. LXIII).

Christ’s blood is consecrated from wine so that we may understand that he is the true vine, truly gladdening his own. Hence the Bride sings: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Cant. I). And this sacrament is rightly consecrated from wheaten bread and wine, in which there is the principal refreshment, so that we may understand the principal refreshment to be in Christ’s body and blood through divinity. For Christ’s flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink (John VI), since the person who communicates in Christ’s body merits, in the reception of grace, the gift of inward and eternal refreshment.

[Col. 0363D] It remains to ask whether only flesh and blood are received, or the whole Christ. To this I answer that I, a son taught by Mother Church, have learned that the whole Christ is received undivided. But it is asked why his body is customarily said to be received, as though separately, when in the person of Christ there are three substances: Word, flesh, and soul. This should not be understood separately, as though only that which is body were received. Rather, the Lord’s body is said to be received in order that it may be understood that the Lord himself is truly received, in the kind of speech by which we say, “The king’s body was there,” that is, the king himself was truly there. Or we say that we receive the Lord’s body because the bodily substance, namely bread and wine, does not pass into an incorporeal substance but into a bodily substance, namely Christ’s body and blood.

[Col. 0364A] Or we name the body because of an excessive affection of love; or, since there are diverse natures in Christ, when we speak thus we name that which can properly be seen by bodily eyes: “This is the body.” But although Christ’s body is customarily said to be received, Christ is received whole: not one part under the species of bread and another under the species of wine, but wholly here and wholly there—not a part in a part, but the whole in a part. One part appears and seems, as it were, to be a part, yet the whole is there. Another part appears and seems, as it were, to be another part, and the same whole is there. The whole is here and the whole there: no less in the part than in the whole, no greater in the whole than in the part. And however many parts you make, the whole is in each. Do not wonder; it is God’s work. If one can be wholly in diverse places, why cannot he be wholly in each part? [Col. 0364B] Both are wonderful, but both are true. Nor are they wonderful in relation to their maker. For what is wonderful if the omnipotent and wonderful One performs wonders?

But you say: How can one body be in diverse places at the same time? It is upon the altar and it is in heaven; it is here and there, and it is whole wherever it is, as much here as there, and likewise wholly in many places. Do not wonder: he who made body and place makes each to be in the other as he wills, and always as he wills—he who knows and is able to act thus and otherwise, whose wisdom is without number and whose power commands the natures of things. But you wonder when you see or hear things that you are not accustomed to see or hear. Therefore, when you begin to wonder and your thought says to you, “How can this be?” [Col. 0364C] think of the Maker and look to the Almighty, and whatever it may be will cease to be wonderful. And if perhaps it does not cease to be wonderful, it will nevertheless not be incredible, because if the omnipotent Maker is considered, whatever may be will not be impossible to him.

But perhaps your heart says: Where is the Lord’s body after I have received and eaten it? Hear, then: Do you seek Christ’s bodily presence? Seek it in heaven. He willed to be with you in bodily presence for a time, when and as long as it was necessary. He displayed his presence for a time in order by it to stir you up and help you to find the spiritual presence. Therefore he came to you bodily so that the spiritual presence, which is not taken away, might be found through the bodily presence. He came [Col. 0364D] to you bodily not in order to remain with you bodily here, but spiritually.

Thus, through the flesh he assumed, he came hidden into the world, and according to bodily presence he lived among human beings in order to raise them to spiritual presence; and, his dispensation completed, he departed according to bodily presence but remained according to spiritual presence. Hence he says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). Thus he comes to you bodily in order to remain with you spiritually. When you hold his sacrament in your hands, he is bodily with you. When you receive it with your mouth and when you eat it with your mouth, he is bodily with you. Finally, in sight, touch, and taste he is bodily with you. And as long as your senses are bodily affected, his bodily presence is not [Col. 0365A] removed.

But once bodily sense fails in receiving it, Christ’s bodily presence is no longer to be sought; spiritual presence is to be retained. The dispensation is completed; it is perfect—the sacrament is perfect; its power remains. Christ passes from the mouth to the heart, not as food for the body but for the soul. He comes to you in bodily presence to be eaten, not consumed; to be tasted, not incorporated. But when Christ’s flesh is eaten, it is not the one eaten, but the one who eats, who is incorporated into him whom he eats. Augustine heard Christ saying from heaven: “I am the food of the mature. Believe, and you will eat me—not so that you may change me into yourself as the food of your flesh, but so that you may be changed into me.”

Therefore, once the sacramental dispensation is completed, if you seek [Col. 0365B] Christ’s bodily presence, seek it in heaven. Seek it there where it was before it began to be bodily with you through the sacrament, and from where it did not depart when it came to you. Therefore distinguish wisely what is presented to the senses in the sacrament of the altar and what is fitted to the spirit.

For three things are considered in this sacrament: one which is sacrament only; another which is sacrament and the reality of the sacrament; and a third which is reality only and not sacrament. The sacrament only is the visible species of bread and wine. The sacrament and reality are Christ’s body and blood: reality with respect to the species under which they are received; sacrament of another reality, because they are the sign of the grace and power received there—namely, the union of head and members. And this [Col. 0365C] union is reality, not sacrament, but the power of the sacrament.

See: we have considered three things. The first is a sign of the second; the second is the cause of the third; the third is the power of the second and the truth of the first. Thus one thing is the visible species that is seen; another, the truth of body and blood invisibly believed; another, spiritual grace, received invisibly and spiritually together with the body and blood. The visible species is the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; but the body and blood are the sacrament of invisible grace, without which the sacrament is of no benefit.

Since “sacrament” is said in two ways—either a sign of a sacred thing or a sacred mystery—the species of bread and wine is called sacrament, that is, a sign of a sacred thing, namely the Lord’s body [Col. 0365D] and blood. But the Lord’s body and blood are called sacrament because they are a sacred mystery signified through the visible species; because they are the sign of a sacred thing; because they signify spiritual grace, which is called Christ’s spiritual flesh. For, as Jerome says, Christ’s flesh is understood in two ways: either the flesh born of the Virgin, or spiritual flesh, of which the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink; whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him” (John VI).

Whoever is united, consecrated, and conformed to Christ through faith and love eats this flesh. For anyone who is made a member of Christ in baptism becomes a participant spiritually, though not sacramentally, in the Lord’s body and blood, as Augustine attests. Nor is the person in whom is found that which the sacrament signifies deprived of so great a sacrament: that is, of the efficacy itself, which is called the power of the sacrament and spiritual flesh, as we said above.

[Col. 0366A] Here you may observe that, just as Christ’s flesh is understood in two ways, as we have now said, so reception is twofold, sacramental and spiritual, because both good and evil receive the sacrament, but only the good receive the reality of the sacrament. In this place we call the Lord’s body the sacrament; the reality of the sacrament is that efficacy itself and spiritual grace which, as we said above, Jerome calls Christ’s spiritual flesh, and which only the good eat. Sacramental communion, however, is common to good and evil, and without spiritual [Col. 0366B] communion it is of no benefit. Hence the Lord says: “The flesh profits nothing; the spirit gives life” (John VI). As though he said: Receiving my flesh profits nothing unless it is received in spiritual grace. Indeed, whoever receives unworthily is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood (1 Cor. XI).

But spiritual reception, which is received through true faith, suffices without sacramental reception where there is no contempt for religion. Therefore, whoever eats worthily has both the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament. Whoever believes and loves, even if unable to eat under the sacrament, nevertheless has the reality of the sacrament, eats spiritually, and is truly incorporated into Christ. Thus some who eat do not eat, and some who do not eat do eat. For some who unworthily eat the Lord’s body do not receive spiritual grace.

[Col. 0366C] A person eats unworthily who remains in sin or receives irreverently, not discerning the Lord’s body. But some, although unable to receive bodily, nevertheless spiritually eat Christ’s spiritual flesh—that is, the efficacy of the sacrament—without which there is no spiritual life. Hence the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI). Thus the Lord’s body is for judgment to some and for salvation to others. But the power of this sacrament is for death to none, but for salvation to all who receive it; and it is increased through communion in the sacrament whenever this sacrament—that is, the Lord’s body—is received. “This is the living bread which came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever” (John VI).

[Col. 0366D] Therefore one must approach this great sacrament with true faith and a pure heart; this sacrament and immortal safeguard—the mystery and oblation to be celebrated—is the sacrament of sacraments, sanctifying all sacraments. Hence it is preeminently called Eucharist, that is, good grace, because not only is grace received in this sacrament, but also he from whom all grace comes. This Eucharist is called divine because it makes those who receive worthily divine and participants in divinity. This is the daily bread which the Church necessarily receives daily under the sacrament. For just as Christ’s presence in flesh was once necessary for us, so that he might be able to die, so his presence is necessary until the end of the world [Col. 0367A] in the manner in which the living bread that came down from heaven (ibid.) can be eaten. Therefore he who then offered himself from love alone in such a way that he could be pierced by the lance, now also, until the end of the age, offers himself in such a way that he can be eaten in the sacrament.

This sacrament is a stronghold against enemies, of which the Church says in the Prophet: “You have prepared a table before me” (Ps. XXII). This sacrament is provision for those ascending from exile to their homeland. For this was signified by manna: after the crossing of the Red Sea, it was given to the children of Israel as provision through the desert toward the land of promise. This spiritual manna of the Lord’s body is given after baptism to Christians, who have power to become children of God, so that, strengthened by this angelic bread, they may pass through the desert of this age [Col. 0367B] to the land of the living.

Man and angel eat the same bread. But man still receives it as medicine; the angel already as delight. It is customarily asked concerning the sacrament whether the Lord gave his disciples his mortal body before the Passion, or his immortal body—which we more readily believe—and how he could then give an immortal body when he himself was still mortal. Here one may ask how he could be born of a Virgin; how his body can now be wholly in diverse places at once; how bread and wine can pass into body and blood, not by union but by transformation; and many similar things which appear wonderful in this sacrament. For this sacrament is a mystery, full of miracles, and an inscrutable mystery.

Therefore, because when we discuss it we search above ourselves, [Col. 0367C] let the neighboring house be summoned to what remains. And if even it should not suffice, let what remains be burned with fire; that is, let it be entrusted to the Holy Spirit, who beholds all things subtly and fully, who breathes and teaches where he wills and as much as he wills.

But now let us return to the point that the priest, as we said above, offers gifts for sacrifice—namely bread and wine—but water is also added to the wine. You may perhaps wonder at this, but it too is a great sacrament. Since frail man is mortal, this water mixed with wine signifies the human being united to Christ with Christ’s blood. Whoever separates the water denies the union of Christ and the Church. Again, these must be joined because the font of baptism [Col. 0367D] avails nothing without Christ’s blood, nor the blood without baptism; both flowed from Christ’s side. Whoever removes one does not imitate the mystery of the Passion.

When about to begin the sacrament, the priest alone prays that the prayer of all may assist him. Therefore the Church also prays for him, saying: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke I). Or: “May the Lord send you help from the sanctuary, and defend you from Zion” (Ps. XIX). Or: “May he remember every sacrifice of yours, and may your burnt offering be made fat” (ibid.); or something similar. After this the priest, praying secretly, signifies Christ’s secret prayers when he said: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. XXVI).

After the prayers, the priest greets the people in a loud voice and exhorts them to lift up their hearts and give thanks [Col. 0368A] to the Father through Christ; and he declares that thanks are to be rendered through him before whom every power trembles. At last he consecrates the gifts to be consecrated. Note each point. Christ did all these things. After his prayers he came to the disciples, saying: “Watch and pray” (ibid.). Then he said: “Sleep now and rest” (ibid.). After this he was offered up. When he commanded them to watch, he greeted them, because salvation is present to those who watch. When he said, “Pray,” he exhorted them to lift up their hearts, because only what is above should be prayed for. When he calls them to rest, saying, “Sleep,” he exhorts them to give thanks. For the person who rests from evil becomes grateful to God; this is to give thanks to him.

And so that thanks may be fittingly rendered to God—that is, so that our life may accord with the heavenly citizens—the priest prays that our prayers may be joined to the voices of the angels, who through Christ praise, adore, and celebrate together the majesty [Col. 0368B] of the Father; who tremble; and who are certainly present at so great a mystery of the Mass, where things below are joined to things above and man is united to God. Then immediately the choir, grateful for gifts received and to be received, sings the angelic hymn which the heavenly host does not cease to cry. In it, as is found in the book of Isaiah (Isa. VI), the choir says *Sanctus* three times because of the Trinity of persons, and says “Lord of Sabaoth” once because of the unity of the divine *ousia*, that is, substance. It gives thanks to the Creator for his benefits when it says: “Heaven and earth are full of your glory.” It gives thanks especially for the benefit of redemption when it sings: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

Here the banner of the cross is made, because Christ triumphed through the cross [Col. 0368C] and makes us triumph. The choir repeats “Hosanna in the highest,” that we may be saved in body and soul among the angels. After this the priest begins the Secret. Some call this the Mass because in the early Church catechumens used to be present at the celebration of Mass until the consecration, and then the deacon cried out, saying: “Let the catechumens go out.” And because they were then sent out, this mystery was called *missa* [Mass]. It was called the Secret because it is performed in a secret voice.

[Col. 0368D] But in the early Church it was spoken aloud, until shepherds, retaining the words by memory through daily use, sang the same words in *camnis* [reading uncertain]. But they were struck there by divine vengeance. Therefore, out of reverence, the Church customarily performs so great a mystery in secret. It is also called the Secret because human reason cannot fully comprehend so great a mystery. To signify this, it is rightly celebrated in a secret voice. Let us touch briefly upon the substance of this great and most secret office.

The priest, therefore, when celebrating the Secret of the Mass, represents the acts once performed by the high priest, which those acts prefigured. Now, then, we must consider that the temple of God was formerly divided into two parts, with a veil placed between them; they called the first part the Holy Place, but the inner part the Holy of Holies. Thus, whatever is done in the office of the Mass before the Secret is, as it were, in the first sanctuary. But what is done in the Secret is within the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 0369A] Within the Holy of Holies there were, as the canons testify, an altar of incense, the ark of the covenant, a tablet above the ark, and above the tablet two cherubim of glory looking at one another face to face. The high priest alone entered this place once in the year, bearing the names of the Fathers inscribed on the breastpiece and shoulder-piece, and carrying blood and coals. Praying, he placed the coals with incense in a censer until the smoke overshadowed him. Then he sprinkled the tablet and the ark with blood; afterwards he went out to the people and washed his garments, and he was not called clean before evening.

These were signs, and they passed away after the things signified had come. The first sanctuary mystically signifies the present Church; the Holy of Holies, heaven; the high priest, Christ; the blood, the Passion; the coals, Christ’s charity; the censer, [Col. 0369B] Christ’s flesh; the burned incense, fragrant prayers; the altar, the hosts of heaven; the ark, Christ according to his humanity; the tablet above the ark, God the Father; the two cherubim, the two Testaments, which look at one another because they agree. The garment that is washed signifies the human being; evening, the end of the human being. Compare, then, what was formerly done with what Christ did, and see how the minister of the Church represents those things and performs these.

“*Te igitur*” through “*in primis*.” The high priest of old entered the Holy of Holies with blood once a year; and Christ, through his own blood, entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption (Heb. IX). Thus the minister of the Church enters with blood into the Holy of Holies whenever, bearing in mind the remembrance of Christ’s blood, he begins the mystery here; he recalls Christ’s Passion not only in mind but also by the sign of the cross, when at the first verse he makes the sign of the cross. Note that he calls them by three names: gifts, offerings, sacrifices. They are gifts because God gave them so that man might be sustained by them; offerings because by them man makes an offering to their author; sacrifices because they are sacrificed. By these three names, moreover, it is aptly intimated that this sacrifice fulfils what the threefold victim of the Law formerly promised.

“*In primis*” through “*Communicantes*.” The royal high priest, entering the Holy of Holies, prayed; and Christ before his Passion prayed that he might be glorified and that his disciples might be preserved. Now also, seated at the Father’s right hand, he intercedes for us. Thus our minister, following Aaron and Christ, makes supplication for the whole Church, then for prelates and subjects.

“*Communicantes*” through “*Hanc igitur*.” The high priest, as the Law commanded, carried with him into the Holy of Holies a golden censer full of living coals; and Christ bore to the stars the censer of his flesh, full of every virtue. Likewise, the priest under the Law carried the names of the Fathers inscribed upon the breastpiece and shoulder-piece, and Christ knows in mind and deed the names of the saints. Nor is it enough for the priest merely to commemorate them in words; he must himself represent the saints inwardly in love and outwardly in conduct, so that he may be inwardly warm [Col. 0370A] in love and outwardly radiant in conduct. This is signified by the *logion* [breastpiece] and the shoulder-piece.

Thus far, up to “Most humbly we beseech you.” The priest of the Law, while praying, was overshadowed and concealed by the smoke of incense, so that no one might see him while he burned the incense. And Christ, while interceding with the Father for us, passes beyond the gaze of angels, because it cannot be understood how much the presence of the flesh he assumed obtains from God the Father for us. Likewise, while the priest performs Christ’s office, he is in some manner veiled and hidden, because it can neither be conceived nor told how great a power and efficacy reside in the words of this mystery: for it is hidden from humans and angels how the words and mystical signs of the cross transform the gifts that have been offered. For when he asks the Lord graciously to receive the oblation, and, after inserting certain other words [Col. 0370B], asks that he may deign to make the oblation blessed—that is, advance it into something better—enrolled, that is, his own; ratified, that is, sufficient for salvation; reasonable and acceptable, that is, such that he may rightly distribute it and be able to appease the Lord, he makes this request. And all this is conferred in those words of the Lord uttered at the supper, which the priest then adds.

But before speaking them he begins thus: “Who, on the day before he suffered.” At these words he takes from the altar bread still common, and, having raised it, blesses it and makes the sign of the cross over it; and before setting it down, he represents the Lord’s words when he says, “He blessed it and broke it,” and what follows. Afterwards he takes the chalice and signs it, and represents the Lord’s words, saying: “And gave it to his disciples, saying: Take and drink from this, all of you” [Col. 0370C].

Here occurs that outstanding miracle. At these words the food of the flesh becomes food of the soul. Through these words and through the sign of the cross, nature is renewed: bread becomes flesh and wine blood. Therefore, rightly, when these words are reached, in which such great grace is given, the priest raises both high, signifying that this food and this drink are more excellent than all others.

“Most humbly we beseech you” through “Let us pray. Instructed.” The priest, as the Law commanded, sprinkled both the altar and the outer sanctuary with the blood of the peace-offering; and Christ sprinkles the Father with blood as often as he appeases him through the flesh he assumed. He sprinkles the altar while he restores the number of the angels. He sprinkles the outer sanctuary while he marks human beings and reconciles to the Father those things that are on earth [Col. 0370D]. The priest sprinkles them likewise, because through this sacrifice he appeases God and obtains pardon, and thus sprinkles it over us. For when he cleanses us, he increases the number of the citizens above.

When he names the sublime altar, he recalls the Holy of Holies. And when he enumerates the saints by name, he bears the names of the Fathers. But in order to possess both, namely the breastpiece (*logion*) and the shoulder-piece, he enumerates the names twice. In accordance with the beginning of the Canon and in this part, tropologically, he bears the breastpiece upon his breast and the shoulder-piece that covered the shoulders, while he imitates rational morals and works.

Then he says that God, through Christ, creates, sanctifies, gives life to, and blesses all these things [Col. 0371A]. For through the Word the Father created the nature of things; and through that same Christ he makes it wonderful, so that common food and drink become singular food and drink. Through the Word he signifies both, while he bestows upon things such great grace that the person who receives them is sanctified; he gives life, so that the one who receives worthily may be made alive; he blesses, so that the participant may receive eternal blessing.

“Let us pray. Instructed by saving commands.” The priest of the Law, returning to the people, washed his garments, and yet remained unclean until evening. Thus Christ, who entered the Holy of Holies, returns to the Church by suffering with it and helping it; he washes his garments—that is, he cleanses the saints—and yet certain stains adhere to his members until the end of the age [Col. 0371B].

The priest likewise returns to the people. When he again multiplies prayers in a loud voice, he seems to go outside; with prayers, as with waters, he washes and cleanses his garments—that is, the people—and yet is judged unclean, because until death there will be in every human being something that needs washing, and there is a spot on the moon. Therefore, being about to pray, he urges prayer, teaching that we may pray confidently as children to a father, as the Lord himself instructed us to pray, saying: “Our Father” (Matt. 6).

Thus seven petitions are set forth in the Lord’s Prayer, so that we may merit the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, through which we receive the seven virtues; through these, freed from the seven vices, we may attain the seven beatitudes. For there are seven principal vices [Col. 0371C], which are the source of all evils: pride, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. The first three strip a human being; the fourth scourges one who has been stripped; the fifth casts out one who has been scourged; the sixth seduces one who has been cast out; the seventh tramples underfoot one who has been seduced.

For pride takes God from a person; envy, one’s neighbour; anger, oneself. Once stripped of these, a person who is willing to rejoice piously neither in his own good nor in another’s, and who has nothing remaining in which to rejoice, is scourged by sadness. Avarice follows, casting out the scourged person, because, having lost inward joy, he is compelled to seek consolation outwardly. Afterwards gluttony comes, which lures the mind, greedy for external things, into excess. Lust follows, violently subjecting to slavery [Col. 0371D] the person who has been enticed and seduced.

Therefore, through pride the heart is swollen; through envy it dries up; through anger it bursts; through sadness it is crushed and, as it were, reduced to dust. Through avarice it is scattered abroad; through gluttony it is defiled and, as it were, moistened; through lust it is trampled down and reduced to mire, so that unhappy man may say: “I am stuck fast in the mire of the deep” (Ps. 68), he who “will be wiped away like the mud of the streets.”

Accordingly, the first petition is placed against pride, when it is said: “Hallowed be thy name,” that he may grant us to fear and venerate his name, so that through humility we may return to God, from whom we withdrew through pride. To this petition is given the gift called the spirit of the fear of the Lord, through which one comes to humility [Col. 0372A], which heals pride, so that the humble person may acquire the kingdom of heaven that the proud person lost. Hence in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

The second petition is against envy: “Thy kingdom come.” The kingdom of God is the salvation of human beings. Therefore, whoever petitions in this manner asks for the common salvation of all and thus rejects envy. To this is given the spirit of piety, kindling the heart toward benevolence, so that one may reach that same possession of the land of the living to which one desires others to attain, according to the saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5).

The third is against anger, when it is said: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For one who petitions in this manner does not wish to contend, but indicates that whatever pleases the divine will is pleasing to him [Col. 0372B]. To this is given the spirit of knowledge, so that, entering the heart, it may instruct and beneficially pierce it, in order that a person may know that whatever evil he suffers proceeds from fault, whereas whatever good he possesses proceeds from God’s mercy. Therefore, through compunction anger and indignation of mind are calmed; and through this virtue—that is, compunction—one comes to true joy, according to the saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5).

The fourth petition, against sadness, is that in which it is said: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Sadness is weariness of mind joined with sorrow, when the embittered mind does not desire inward goods. Therefore inward refreshment is necessary for the languishing soul. God accordingly gives it the spirit of fortitude, which raises the soul, so that it may become strong for the desire of eternal refreshment [Col. 0372C]. This gift of fortitude, therefore, kindles the human heart to hunger for righteousness, which leads to the full satisfaction and satiety of blessedness. Hence it is said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (ibid.).

The fifth petition is against avarice: “Forgive us our debts.” To this petition is given the spirit of counsel, which teaches one gladly to show mercy, so that we may obtain mercy, according to the saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (ibid.).

The sixth petition is against gluttony, concerning which it is said: “And lead us not into temptation.” To this is given the spirit of understanding, so that the inward refreshment of God’s word may restrain external appetite, and neither bodily want break a person nor the enticement of the flesh overcome him [Col. 0372D]. Therefore the Lord himself, when the tempter proposed to him, hungry as he was, a deceitful suggestion concerning outward bread, answered: “Man does not live by bread alone” (Matt. 4). By this he openly showed that, when the mind is refreshed with inward bread, it cares little if it suffers outwardly, in its throat, for a time the hunger of the flesh.

Therefore the spirit of understanding is given, that, entering the heart, it may cleanse the dreadful darkness of our mind and make the eye of our inner person so bright and clear that it may be found keen and pure for contemplating the brightness of divinity itself. For purity of heart is born from the spirit of understanding; and purity of heart merits vision, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. [Col. 0373A] 5).

The seventh petition is against lust, when we say: “Deliver us from evil.” Fittingly, the healed slave asks for freedom; to him is given the spirit of wisdom, which restores to the captive the freedom he has lost. For *sapientia* (“wisdom”) is so called from *saporem* (“taste”). It is given when the mind, touched by the taste of inward sweetness, gathers itself wholly inward through desire and is no longer dissipated outwardly through fleshly pleasure, because it possesses wholly within itself that in which it delights.

Thus inner sweetness is set against outward pleasure, so that the more the former begins to have taste and to please, the more freely and willingly the latter is despised; and finally the peaceful mind, desiring nothing outwardly, rests wholly within itself through love. Thus the spirit of wisdom, touching the heart with its sweetness, moderates outwardly the ardour of desire and establishes peace inwardly [Col. 0373B], so that, while the mind is gathered wholly toward inward joy, the human being may be fully and perfectly reformed into the image of God, according to the saying: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (ibid.).

Thereupon the minister asks to be delivered from evil through the intervention of the saints, and for peace in our days. For disturbance harms the weak.

The mystical breaking of the bread follows. For in the Law fine flour was commanded to be offered in pieces, and the Redeemer blessed bread, broke it, and distributed it, once broken, to the disciples. The priest likewise, following the Law and Christ, divides the most holy bread into three parts. One of these is placed in the blood for that part of the Church which still journeys as a pilgrim, exposed to sufferings. The other two are assigned to those parts of the Church of which one is cleansed by fire outside this life, while the other already glories with Christ [Col. 0373C], so that one part of the Church may be justified, another may be liberated more swiftly, and thanks may be rendered for the third.

But the minister, about to receive the Lamb whom the Law foretold, asks three things for himself and the people: first, that they may be numbered among those who are ashamed to live according to the flesh; next, that they may be glorified in God’s kingdom; finally, because the flesh resists the spirit, he requests peace, without which no human being is justified. Therefore the choir fittingly follows by singing aloud “Lamb of God” three times, in praise of the Holy Trinity, which sent the Lamb, the Ruler of the earth.

The Communion that is afterwards sung indicates that all the faithful share in Christ’s body, which the minister receives sacramentally for all, so that it may be received spiritually by himself and all. When these things have been completed, the priest returns to the right side of the altar, signifying that at the end of the world Christ will return to the Jews, whom he has already rejected, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter [Col. 0373D]. Then the remnant of Israel, according to the Scriptures, will be saved.

Finally follows the prayer at the end of the entire office, that the grace which goes before may follow through Christ, through whom all things were made; he who is Lord of all by creation became spiritually our Lord by assuming the nature of our humanity. Then, having greeted the people, he admonishes them to depart. For in this exile one must not sit or lie down, but must pass hence to the homeland, because the worthy victim has been sent, through whom hell has been shattered.

## Chapter VIII. On the hidden things of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments

[Col. 0374A]

Let us now come to the hidden things of the Scriptures, since they too are sealed in a mystical sense. Some are hidden, and are a sealed fountain, because they treat of hidden things and of matters exceeding human understanding, such as the mystery of the supreme Trinity, of the incarnate Word, or of the Lord’s body and blood. Others are hidden because they deal with certain things which, although easy in themselves, are less open to understanding because of brevity or difficulty of expression. Hence a person who cannot lack the desire to know the truth is stirred by frequent questions.

For as the eye seeks light, so the soul desires to see truth as its proper good, which makes it happy by knowing and loving it [Col. 0374B]. Yet it is deceived when it seeks to know some truth whose knowledge neither makes one happy nor helps happiness to be present. For there are different kinds of truth: the truth of curiosity, of covetousness, and of iniquity, none of which is good. There is, however, a kind of truth—for example, in the knowledge of all the liberal arts—which is indeed good, but is not the highest good, because knowledge of it by no means makes one happy.

Holy Scripture provides the knowledge that must be possessed of this truly good truth. It teaches a person to know himself and his Creator. To know oneself comes first and is the way; to know the Creator perfectly is the homeland: the one is merit, the other reward.

All sacred Scripture, therefore, consists of two Testaments. Each is distinguished by three orders. The Old contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa. In the first order are five volumes: the Pentateuch—Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. In the order of the Prophets are eight volumes: the book of Joshua, the book of Judges, the book of Samuel, which is First and Second Kings; Fourth Malachim, meaning “Kings,” which is called Third and Fourth according to the Latin reckoning; fifth, Isaiah; sixth, Jeremiah; seventh, Ezekiel; eighth, the book of the twelve prophets, called *Thareasra* [Col. 0374C]. These are called prophetic because they are the books of those who were called prophets by office, although not all of them are prophets.

In the order of the Hagiographa are nine volumes: the book of Job, the book of Psalms, the Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, Daniel, Paralipomenon, Ezra, and Esther. Furthermore, in the Old Testament there are other books which are read but are not written in the canon of authority: the book of Tobit, Judith, and Maccabees, and those entitled the Wisdom of Solomon and Ecclesiasticus [Col. 0374D].

The New, however, contains evangelists, apostles, and Fathers. The Gospel contains four volumes. The writing of the apostles contains four: the Epistles of Paul, the Catholic Epistles, the Apocalypse, and the Acts of the Apostles. The writings of the Fathers have no fixed number.

It should be considered that sacred Scripture, deeper than other writings, has a threefold sense: historical, allegorical, and moral. For in it not only words but also things have the power of signifying. Through the signification of words we understand the historical sense; through the signification of things, allegory and tropology. History is the signification of words referring to things. Allegory is when one event is understood through another event. If it concerns visible things, it is simple allegory; if invisible and heavenly things, it is called anagogy. Tropology is when through something accomplished another thing to be done is shown.

History is named from the Greek ἱστορέω, that is, “I see; I investigate,” because it belongs to historians to expound deeds done according to the primary signification of words [Col. 0375A]. Allegory is called, as it were, “speech about another thing,” when another reality is understood not through words but through an accomplished event; for example, through the crossing of the Red Sea is understood the passage through baptism to paradise. Tropology is called a “turning speech,” when what is said [Col. 0375B] is turned toward the building up of morals, as in moral interpretations. Anagogy is called an upward leading. Hence the anagogical sense is called that which leads from visible things to invisible things: for example, the light made on the first day signifies an invisible reality, namely the angelic nature created in the beginning.

Nevertheless, such a multiple sense is not found everywhere. Sometimes only the historical sense is present; sometimes also the allegorical or tropological sense, or both; and sometimes, though rarely, the anagogical is added. Thus Jerusalem is understood historically as an earthly city, allegorically as the Church, tropologically as the faithful soul, and anagogically as the heavenly homeland. Sacred Scripture, therefore, abounds beyond other writings in these senses.

In the books of the pagans, words alone signify things by means of concepts. In the divine page, not only concepts and things signify, but things themselves signify other things [Col. 0375C]. Hence it is clear that knowledge of the arts is very useful for understanding the divine Scriptures. For, since in the divine page both the signification of things and that of words are necessary, the arts serve it: the *trivium* supplies knowledge of words, the *quadrivium* knowledge of physical things.

Yet the signification of things is more dignified, because the allegorical sense is more acute and the tropological sweeter. Moreover, words signify by human institution, things by divine institution. For as a human being indicates his will to another through words, so God indicates his will through creatures. The signification of things is deeper than that of words, because words signify either one thing univocally or several things equivocally. But they signify few things equivocally, according to the institution made by human beings. Things, however, do so in a far different way: they have as many varieties of signification as they have figures by nature and properties.

Every thing signifies either according to its external form, as snow through whiteness, or according to its inner nature, according to the saying: “Your hair is like a flock of goats” (Song 4, 6), on account of subtlety of sight [Col. 0375D]. Thus it is evident how necessary knowledge of the arts is. Mathematics teaches about external forms; physics and theoretical science about inner natures.

To touch briefly upon the usefulness of the arts, we say that philosophy is divided into three parts or kinds: logic, ethics, and theoretical science. Logic treats of words, ethics of morals, theoretical science of things. Theoretical science is further subdivided into mathematics, physics, and theology. Mathematics treats of the invisible forms of visible things; physics, of the invisible natures of visible things; theology, of invisible essences and their natures [Col. 0376A]. Thus we are aided by the arts in the divine page when we attend to the signification of words for the literal sense and consider the signification of things in order to grasp the mystical meaning: through visible form, where mathematics helps; or according to invisible nature, where physics and theology serve.

## Chapter IX. On the subject matter of divine Scripture

The particular subject matter of divine Scripture is the work of restoration—that is, the incarnation of the Word with all its sacraments—just as the work of creation is the subject matter of pagan physicists. But they differ, because the latter was completed in six days, while the former is completed in six ages [Col. 0376B].

This subject matter is divided into an inner reality and an outer form. The inner reality is divided into truth and virtue; the outer form, into a sign of truth and a sign of virtue. Since the inner ear had become deaf, God spoke outwardly to human beings through signs. A sign of truth is one thing in an action, as when a thing signifies tropologically; another in a word, as: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). Faith is taught through a sign of truth; morality through a sign of virtue.

Thus the inner reality is called truth or virtue, the outward reality a sign. As in the sacrament of the incarnate Word two things are found, humanity and divinity, so in the sacrament of the Lord’s body the outward species is a sign, while the inner reality is truth and virtue—that is, the Lord’s body and the grace received only by the good [Col. 0376C]. Likewise, reality and sign are found here. Therefore every subject of the divine page is either a reality or a sign. Here “realities” are called those things which do not have the function of signifying; “signs,” those which do.

Of realities, some justify and some do not. Again, some realities are to be enjoyed, such as the highest good; others are to be used, by which we are assisted; others enjoy and use, such as human beings and angels. To enjoy is to love something for its own sake, so as to set one’s end in it. To use is to refer what comes into use to obtaining that which is to be enjoyed, although “enjoy” and “use” are often taken in another and improper sense.

Therefore we do not enjoy virtues but use them. Although they are to be loved and sought, they are not to be loved merely for their own sake, but ultimately for God alone, whom the saints enjoy here in hope and sometimes in actuality, because they already possess in some manner that which they will enjoy fully and perfectly in the future [Col. 0376D]. Thus virtues must be used, and through them the supreme Trinity—that is, the supreme and immutable good—must be enjoyed. We say the same of good will. Hence Augustine: “Will is that by which we enjoy.” Therefore we enjoy through virtues, not the virtues themselves—unless perhaps some virtue is God, as charity is.

God, however, uses us, not as we use other things. For he has mercy on us, not for his own benefit; whereas we have mercy on others for our own benefit.

Since, then, as has been said, all the subject matter of sacred Scripture is either reality or sign, and since we are concerned with hidden things, let us speak first of inner reality. And first let us begin with that which is called Truth—not with any truth whatever, but with the supreme Truth itself helping us—from the shadowy and dense mountain, which is signified by words when it is said: “God is one or three” [Col. 0377A].

Nor do words alone signify this Trinity, but things also: as when Abraham saw three angels in the figure of the supreme Trinity and worshipped one. The Trinity was likewise shown at Christ’s baptism and transfiguration. The soul in some manner represents its image; God has revealed himself to it through nature and grace—through nature, that is, through reason and creation; through grace, that is, through inspiration and teaching. Through inspiration he helps reason within; through teaching, creation without. The Apostle briefly embraces these four modes when he says: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. [Col. 0377B] 1).

Let us now see how far reason has been able to go by itself. Reason discovers that God exists, is one, and is three. For, considering that it has not always existed, it understands that it exists from another; and, lest this proceed to infinity, it proves that there is one which never began, and thus knows that God exists. Again, considering that, if there were more than one, either singularity would be imperfect or plurality superfluous, it proves that God is one: one not through collection, composition, or similarity, but in essence, because he lacks parts; and in identity, because he does not vary. Thus he is truly and supremely one essentially. A created spirit is truly, but not supremely, one essentially; it is not unchangeably so, as God is.

Let us now see how the rational soul apprehends that God is three [Col. 0377C]. Augustine, in his book *On the Trinity*, demonstrates a certain trinity in every thing, that through trinities in creatures one may more easily ascend to the Trinity of the Creator. But because this would be lengthy, let us return to the eminent likeness, namely the mind, which is the image of God. As through it we have known that God exists and is one, so through the same mind let us understand that he is three.

The soul therefore finds in itself a certain trinity: memory, understanding, and delight or joy; or, if we prefer, the natural power of understanding which is called mind, from which knowledge is born, and from these love proceeds. These three are the same in essence, though they differ in their properties. The three are also related to one another, and yet they are not accidents; they are substantially in the soul and one in essence, because they are one life, one mind, one essence. Whatever is said of each individually in relation to itself is said also of them together, not plurally but singularly. They are inseparable and equal to one another, because all and the whole are comprehended by each one [Col. 0377D].

In this sense these three are called one: according to Augustine, they exist substantially in the soul, not as in a subject, as colour exists in a body. Although each is said relatively, they are nevertheless substantial in their own substance. The mind, knowing itself, generates knowledge as offspring. The third is love, proceeding from both and embracing them both.

[Col. 0378A] From what it finds in itself, the soul investigates above itself and finds in God power, wisdom, and joy, though differently. In the soul these are so present that the mind comes first in time, from which understanding comes; joy follows. In God they are simultaneous, because eternal. Thus reason by itself finds that God exists, is one, and is three. But because it is weak unless aided, it consults creation to discover whether it contains some trace of the Trinity, and thus through creation recognizes what it perceived in itself.

For from the transience of things it knows that God exists, because that which passes away has its beginning from another. From the stability of things it understands that he is one, because ordered things agree among themselves, so that the highest accord with the lowest and the first with the last. Therefore, from their single harmony it does not doubt that there is one maker. It likewise knows that he is three, because through the immensity of things it investigates divine power; through their beauty, wisdom; through their usefulness, goodness [Col. 0378B].

Yet although reason and creation attest the same thing, this is the difference: the three things found in the mind are not merely signs but an image of the Trinity in God. The three things observed outside in creatures are merely signs, not an image. For although God’s power may be investigated through the immensity of creation, immensity is not power, nor beauty wisdom, nor usefulness goodness.

The things in the soul, however, are also an image, because as there is power in the mind, so there is power in God—but incomparably more so—and the power in the mind is its image. Likewise wisdom or joy in the mind is an image of the wisdom or joy in God, though these are more truly in God. For what are truly in God appear here as an image.

The judgment of reason is aided not only through the testimony of creation, but also through teaching and inspiration. When reason had found, as has been said, that God exists, is one, and is three, it also found in unity eternity and immensity; in eternity, immutability; in immensity, simplicity—that is, eternity without time and immensity without quantity [Col. 0378C].

I call eternity “without time” because God had no beginning. For that from which all things have being has being from none; nor will it have an end, because for it being and what it is are the same, and it receives no changeability whatever. It cannot be changed by any kind of change. For it cannot be changed in place, form, or time [Col. 0378D], by which modes bodies are changed.

A body changes in place when it is transferred as a whole from place to place. It changes in form—that is, in the arrangement of its parts—in three ways, when some part is added or removed so that it is otherwise. When a person blushes or grows pale, the blood is transferred, and there is change according to form. It changes in time when a thing is first in one state and afterwards in another.

Since bodies change in three ways—according to form, place, and time—the first entails the second and third; the second entails only the third; the third is entailed by either of the others and entails neither. Incorporeal beings likewise move in three ways: in knowledge, affection, and time. They change in knowledge in three ways: by increase, diminution, and succession [Col. 0379A]. A spirit changes in affection when it is now sad and now joyful. But whether it changes in knowledge or affection, it must change in time, for something is always earlier and something later for it.

Every one of these changes is excluded from God: he does not move in place, because he is everywhere; nor in form, because a simple essence lacks parts; nor in knowledge, because his knowledge neither grows nor diminishes, nor comprehends one thing earlier and another later. Likewise, he does not change in affection, because the supremely good receives nothing contrary to his goodness. Since, therefore, God is changed in none of these four ways, he is not changed in time. Thus, because he lacks beginning, end, and changeability, as has been said, God is eternal.

[Col. 0379B]

Reason likewise finds in the Trinity a communion of unity, coeternity of eternity, and equality of immensity: communion of unity without division; coeternity of eternity without succession; equality of immensity without diminution. In unity, all; in immensity, fullness; in eternity, perfection.

When the soul had discovered the Trinity in God through what it felt in itself, through creatures, teaching, and inspiration, faith assigned three names, as though proper names, in order that the Trinity might be discussed in certain definite and distinct terms. It calls Father the one who is from no one; Son, the one who is from him alone; Holy Spirit, the one who is from both. These terms were taken from human usage in order to signify what is eternal. But lest there seem to be complete similarity between divine and human things, it added the descriptions “omnipotent Father” and “wise Son,” so that he might not be thought to be as in other cases.

The one who is from no one is called Father because there is one who is from him; and the latter is Son, though in substance and nature he is the same as the former, not the very one who is the former. The one who is from both is the Holy Spirit, breathed forth from both. As Augustine says, Catholic faith found the term “person” for distinguishing the Trinity, not so that it might say what it is, but so that it might not be wholly silent about what it is [Col. 0379C]. By this term, as he says, it did not intend to signify diversity, but it refused singularity.

For when faith confesses persons in the plural, it does not thereby understand that there are three in essence; rather, it declares that the same person is not the other. And this is the only term which, although it is said of each individually in the highest reality, is nevertheless pronounced not in the singular but in the plural [Col. 0380A]. For plurality or distinction of persons does not posit something but removes something: it removes not unity of substance but solitude; for it denies solitude and singularity. Hence Hilary: “The confession of fellowship removes the conception of singularity.”

Therefore, when we say “several persons,” we remove solitude and signify that the Father is not alone. When we confess three persons, we proclaim that there is not only one, nor only two, but three together. And we confess three because whatever is truly said of God is referred to his power, wisdom, or goodness.

But it may be asked: since these three in God are called persons, why are the three things in the soul which are the image of this Trinity not called persons? We answer that, although they are substantially in the soul, they are not in every respect identical with it but vary in relation to it. [Col. 0380C] What is in God, however, does not vary but is truly identical with God in whom it is; and each is identical with God. God is one God and three persons, because one divinity is in the three [Col. 0380B].

But behold: while the true and supreme Trinity is investigated in its own image and likeness, which shines forth so beautifully and subtly, remarkable dissimilarities appear in the soul. For the soul, or human being, who is called the image of God on account of these three things, is nevertheless not these three things. God, however, is three persons, and these three persons are one God. Again, a human being possessing these three is one person. But the supreme Trinity is not one person, nor merely of one person, but three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Likewise, in the soul the mind precedes in time, and understanding and joy follow. In God there is nothing earlier and nothing later. The trinity of the mind, then, is a very slight image in comparison with the supreme Trinity, and in the greatest part unlike it; nevertheless, it is an image.

Augustine does not say this merely because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can remember, understand, and love God, by whom it was made. Whoever remembers through memory, beholds through understanding, and embraces through love, finds here the image and him whose image it is [Col. 0380D]. For one who loves finds more truly than one who disputes.

[Col. 0381]

# On Ceremonies, Sacraments, Offices, and Ecclesiastical Observances, by Robert Paululus, Apparently the Author. (G)

## Preface
I remember that some time ago, while I was writing a few small things for myself about the offices of the Church, in order to preserve them in memory, you, most beloved brother, found my little quire carelessly left outside the enclosure of my bookcase, and read certain things which seemed to please you. When later you repeatedly asked to have a copy of it, I refused—at one time saying that the work was unfinished, at another that it was uncorrected; and both were true. For the ecclesiastical offices themselves, in whose performance divine grace has willed that my insignificance should serve, did not permit me to write about ecclesiastical offices.

But lest perhaps, because of my excessive delay, you should suspect something else, I stole part of the night from sleep and did what I could. I have set down in restrained brevity those things which I had dictated to myself, together with certain other matters found in the treatises of the Fathers, so that they may be retained in memory and may not weary the reader. If you find anything praiseworthy in them, do not in any way suppose it to be mine. For I shall call nothing here my own, except that I transcribed in abbreviated form things found in various books, as best I could, gathering the grain while removing, as it were, the chaff. I have also taken care to add a few things—not devised by my own ingenuity, but received from the lips of teachers—which involve no difficulty and seemed very useful.

I judged it more fitting to explain the work in ordinary words and in terms akin to the matters under discussion than to entangle it in varieties of schisms, and to colour words by dimming matters which shine by themselves. For just as a very beautiful woman loses the value of her beauty precisely when, by making herself ugly, she acquires in human eyes a certain shadowy beauty, so other things are adorned with the white and purple pigments of rhetorical colouring, whereas things which possess their own splendour are darkened by the application of those same colours.

If you observe anything in this little work that is insufficiently treated or not correctly set forth, you, dearest brother, should not be reluctant to correct it, or to send it back to me for correction with some note. I have thought it good to mark the titles and numbers of the chapters, so that you may more easily find what you seek.
