## PROLOGUE

Among all the occupations of Jacob’s seekers after the face of God, I judge nothing equally worthy both of memory and of use as ecclesiastical sacraments together with ecclesiastical offices. The former, rightly considered, teach and instruct concerning faith and morals; the latter render daily tribute to the Author of things for his gifts, so that more ample benefits of divine generosity may be merited. On account of both, our smallness has endeavoured to gather into one place what we have been able suitably to draw out from the forests of Scripture, and first to treat, in brief words, of the consecration of the material church, which bears before it a figure of our sacraments.

## CHAPTER I. On Dedication

The dedication or consecration of churches is reserved to episcopal rank, as are also the consecration of virgins and the ordination of clerics. First, the bishop approaching the church to be consecrated blesses water and mixes blessed salt into it. Then, circling the church three times, he sprinkles its exterior. In this is presented a figure both of baptism and of the penance which accompanies baptism.

[Col. 0384A] For when a person is baptized, he is immersed three times in water on account of the three Persons, whose gift it is to remit sins. Through penance, moreover, God remits whatever human perversity commits in thought, speech, or deed. This is aptly signified by water and salt, because water cleanses from filth, while salt preserves the mind from the corruption of vices.

Meanwhile twelve lamps are lit at places within the church. By them is signified the burning and shining apostolic teaching, which is preached both in the material church and kindled by the Holy Spirit in the temple not made with hands. Thus also, when the tabernacle constructed by Moses at the Lord’s command had been dedicated, twelve leaders offered the same gifts, though on different days (Num. VII). By this the Holy Spirit signified that apostolic teaching, whenever it should be preached, would be harmonious and undivided in the Church.

[Col. 0384B] It should be noted that, before the pontiff enters it, the church bears the type of a people ignorant of God and enclosed in the darkness of unbelief. The pontiff circles it three times, sprinkling it with blessed water mixed with salt, as has been said, while clergy and people follow; for, just as the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour (I Pet. V), so the prelate of the Church ought to go about seeking whom he may rescue from that lion’s jaws, bringing such persons to repentance and baptizing them. Hence Peter also says: “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized” (Acts II).

## CHAPTER II. On the Bishop’s Threefold Approach to the Door of the Basilica

[Col. 0384C] To show that authority has been granted him, through the administration of the Church’s sacraments, to set free captivity and beneficially to make captive the captivity of the devil—of the Church it is said: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI)—at each circuit the pontiff approaches the door of the basilica and strikes the lintel with the pastoral staff. This bears the type of priestly authority, as did also the staff which the Lord permitted his disciples to carry on the road when he sent them out to preach.

While striking, he says the antiphon: “Lift up your gates, O princes,” etc. The princes of the people, signified by the unconsecrated basilica, are demons; the gates through which they enter human hearts are vices and evil deeds. He commands these to be removed, so that the gates through which one enters eternity—namely, the virtues—may be raised up, and that the King of glory may enter the hearts of those coming to faith.

[Col. 0384D] The archdeacon, who is inside and at the pontiff’s prompting asks in seeming astonishment, “Who is this King of glory?”, bears the figure of the aforesaid people. After the third striking, the door is opened, because the hostile party is overcome by the power of the Trinity.

Entering with clergy and people, the bishop says three times, “Peace to this house,” because Christ, by assuming flesh and entering the world, destroyed the wall of enmity and restored peace between heavenly and earthly things. Therefore, when the pontiff enters the basilica, he says, “Peace to this house,” because holy teachers intend that the people who had become estranged from God through sins should be reconciled to him through the practice of good works.

Having entered the church, [Col. 0385A] the bishop first prostrates himself in prayer with clergy and people, fulfilling what the Apostle says: “I urge, first of all, that prayers, supplications, intercessions be made for all” (I Tim. II), etc. Rising from prayer, he does not yet greet the people by saying, “The Lord be with you,” but invites them to prayer, because the newly formed people do not yet seem worthy of the pontiff’s greeting. Rather, prayer should be made for them, so that afterward they may be judged worthy of the greeting.

This is why the Lord commanded his preachers to greet no one on the road: that is, they should not flatter with empty hope a person who is still a human being in heart rather than in spirit, that is, one still desiring transient rather than spiritual things.

## CHAPTER III. On the Writing of the Twofold Alphabet on the Pavement

[Col. 0385B] When these things have been completed, the pontiff begins to write the alphabet upon the pavement from the left eastern corner to the right western corner, and from the right eastern corner to the left western corner. The alphabet signifies the rudiments of ecclesiastical teaching. It is therefore written in Greek and Latin, because these two languages agree in Christian teaching, and each people has been called to the rudiments of faith.

That it is written diagonally from corner to corner alludes to a twofold figure. The first is this: because a cross is represented in this form, the death of Christ is principally instilled in the Gospel teaching by which the simple are to be instructed. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians, still immature: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

The second is this: because the writing of the alphabet passes from the left corner to the right, and conversely, we should understand that through Gospel teaching and the cross the worthy people became unworthy, and conversely. This was also figured in Jacob’s blessing, when, crossing his hands, he put his right hand upon the head of Joseph’s younger son, Ephraim, and his left upon the head of the elder, Manasseh.

## CHAPTER IV. What the Bishop First Says or Does upon Entering the Basilica

[Col. 0385C] By the matters which our discourse has thus far explained, the church to be dedicated has been prepared so that it can and ought to be dedicated, that is, consecrated. The pontiff therefore approaches the altar and, as though beginning, says: “O God, come to my assistance” (Ps. LXIX), etc., without *alleluia*.

For this verse belongs to those labouring in this life and struggling against visible and invisible enemies, and thus calling upon God for their help. *Alleluia*, however, is the praise of angels, brought to human beings through John in the Apocalypse, where he testifies that he heard the voice of angels saying *alleluia* (Apoc. XIX). It is a cry of spiritual joy. Therefore it is not sung in the Church during the time of mourning, namely from Septuagesima until Easter.

[Col. 0385D] The pontiff, then, who is still striving against the ignorance of his subjects and who still, in a figure, calls to faith a Church not yet faithful, or calls the fallen to penance, indeed asks God’s help, but does not sing *alleluia* for those whose salvation he does not yet fully hope for.

## CHAPTER V. On Water, Salt, and Ashes Mixed Together

[Col. 0386A]

After this, water is blessed, and salt and ashes are mixed into it, and finally wine. Water signifies expiation, because things defiled are usually cleansed and washed by water. But expiation from sins is rightly accomplished if the salt of wisdom is applied, which preserves corruptible things from corruption. Hence it is commanded in the Law: “In every sacrifice you shall offer salt; nor shall you take away the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from his sacrifice” (Lev. II). That is: offer nothing to God rashly. For those works please him which are seasoned with the salt of wisdom.

Ashes signify the remains, that is, the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion; ashes of the heifer, sprinkled for the expiation of the people, likewise signified this, as is read in Deuteronomy. There is no expiation from sins without faith in the Lord’s Passion.

Or ashes, which are made from extinguished coals, signify the mortification and extinction of vices. Wine signifies spiritual sweetness, because sober minds are made drunk by the abundance of God’s house. One comes to this through the aforesaid things, as is promised in figure when wine is poured in after everything else.

[Col. 0386B] It may also be said that water and wine signify Christ’s two natures, faith in which cleanses from sins.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Crosses Made with Water upon the Altar

The pontiff dips his thumb in this water and makes a cross upon the altar which reaches across its entire length and breadth; then he makes a cross at the four corners of the altar. For the altar bears the figure of Christ. It extends through four corners because Christ is spread abroad in his members through the four quarters of the world: “You shall spread abroad to the east and west, north and south” (Gen. XXVIII).

It is fitting that the cross is made with water, both across the whole and in its parts, to show that both the universal Church of Christ and individual churches have been cleansed from the filth of sins through the washing of water and faith in the Passion.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Bishop’s Sevenfold Circuit around the Altar

He then circles the altar seven times and sprinkles it. By this number is signified the fullness of the Holy Spirit: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord [Col. 0386C] (Isa. XI). Everything that exalts itself against God gives way to this sevenfold Spirit, just as the walls of Jericho are read to have fallen at the seventh circuit.

The water is sprinkled with hyssop, a lowly herb which cleanses the breast and penetrates the hardness of rocks with its roots. It signifies the humility of Christ, who, by humbling himself even unto death, healed the swellings of our pride and softened the hardness of our hearts through contemplation of his humility.

Then he circles the entire church inside three times and sprinkles its walls with water. This sprinkling signifies the inward cleansing of the temple not made with hands, which takes place daily through true repentance. For just as the outward sprinkling of water signifies the washing of baptism—that is, the cleansing from sins which takes place in baptism—so the inward sprinkling signifies [Col. 0387A] that which takes place through true repentance. It is done three times because through repentance whatever is committed by evil speech, thought, or deed is remitted, as was said above.

The psalm “Let God arise” (Ps. LXVII) is sung with an antiphon, so that the enemies resisting this cleansing may be deprived of their strength. The antiphon “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High” (Ps. XC) is also sung, indicating that no one is protected by God unless that person, not presuming upon his own powers, has implored God’s help. When these things have been done, the pontiff turns to prayer, asking that all who enter that house may rejoice that they have been heard.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Depositing the Remainder of the Mortar at the Base of the Altar

When the prayer is complete, the pontiff turns to the altar, beginning the antiphon with the psalm: “I shall enter unto the altar of God” (Ps. XLII). And he pours at the base of the altar what remains of the mortar in which the relics of the saints were set, because he humbly entrusts to God what he himself cannot accomplish: namely, the cleansing of those subject to him through water and the honouring of the saints.

[Col. 0387B] Hence, in the sacrifices of the Old Testament, the priest’s finger was sprinkled with the blood of victims before God, or it was placed on the horns of the altar according to the different kinds of sacrifices; and what remained was poured at the base of the altar. This is because it belongs to priests to do whatever they can for the benefit of the flock committed to them, but what exceeds their powers they should most devoutly commend to the Lord.

The supreme Shepherd left this pattern to others when, approaching his Passion, he said to the Father: “Father, keep those whom you gave me” (John XVII). Paul, following the pattern of the Master at the final point of his present life, said to his disciples: “And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace” (Acts XX).

[Col. 0387C] This is also indicated by the antiphon. For he says that he will enter unto God’s altar, namely the altar signified by this visible altar, to which the eye of flesh does not penetrate, but the pure and devout intention of the mind does. This is what follows: “Unto God who gives joy to my youth” (Ps. XLII).

## CHAPTER IX. On Wiping the Altar with a Linen Cloth

Afterward the altar is wiped with linen. Linen, arising from the earth, is brought to whiteness with great labour. Therefore we wipe the altar not made with hands as though with linen when we preach that Christ entered into glory through the straits of the Passion, and invite those who belong to his body, which is the Church, to imitate him.

Then incense is offered, which signifies the prayers of the saints, because prelates ought to pray for those whom they invite to endure sufferings.

## CHAPTER X. What Is Signified in the Anointing of the Altar

When these things have been completed, the pontiff makes a cross with chrism in the middle of the altar, then at its four corners, just as he had previously done with consecrated water.

[Col. 0388A] The order is fitting: after cleansing by water and after the other things which have been mentioned, oil is applied, because the holy Church is first cleansed in the water of baptism and then marked by the anointing of chrism through the bishop’s hands. In this anointing the Holy Spirit is given for loving God and neighbour, just as in the anointing performed in baptism the same Spirit is given for the remission of sins.

The altar is therefore anointed, and the antiphon is sung: “The Lord has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV), so that in this anointing we may understand the fullness of grace which first went before in the Head and, when the Holy Spirit was sent on the day of Pentecost, shone forth in the apostles. Of this fullness, John testifies, we have all received (John I). Thus, once the altar has been consecrated, crosses are anointed with chrism everywhere upon the walls.

## CHAPTER XI. Why Is the Altar Covered with White Coverings?

Finally, once the consecration is completed, the altar is covered with white coverings. These signify both the newness in those baptized and foretell the glory of future incorruption, which will be in that glorious dedication already completed in the Head and awaited for fulfilment in the members.

## CHAPTER XII. On Ecclesiastical Sacraments

[Col. 0388B] Since we have treated the consecration of the church as briefly as brevity required, let us, under the same rule of concision, say something about the things done in the Church.

There are seven principal sacraments administered in the Church. Five are general, because neither sex, no age, and no condition is excluded from them: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, penance, and anointing of the sick. Two are particular, because they are not granted to all but to certain people: namely, orders and marriage.

I have judged it necessary to write of all these, so that I may retain in memory what I have received in them or administer, should it at any time happen that one of them is administered by my hands. Otherwise I carry bread for the use of others and do not taste it, though divine grace does not abandon the sacraments.

[Col. 0388C] It should be noted, therefore, that the five aforesaid general sacraments are remedies against sins, both original and actual. Baptism is for those entering the Church; confirmation for those standing, as though in battle; penance for those fallen but rising again; Eucharist for those remaining in the Church; and anointing for those departing this life.

Before the Law, these remedies were effected through sacrifices; under the Law, through circumcision as well as sacrifices.

“Sacrament” is used in two ways. Sometimes a sacrament is called a sign of a sacred thing, as in baptism the outward washing signifies inward cleansing. Sometimes sacrament is called, as it were, a sacred secret, as the sacrament of the Incarnation and such things.

A sacrament consists of three things: actions, words, and material elements. Its material elements are water and oil; its words are the invocation of the Trinity; its actions are immersion in water and breathing upon someone.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Baptism

The first sacrament is baptism. It is, as it were, the gate for all entering the courts of the Church. Baptism is the immersion of a human being in water, performed in the name of the Trinity. Baptism is interpreted as washing.

[Col. 0389A] The following questions concerning the sacrament of baptism seem worthy of inquiry: what its form is; by whom it is to be administered; what its efficacy is; and whence and when it began.

In baptism this form must be observed: that the person be baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For thus the supreme Master taught his disciples, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

Yet in the Acts of the Apostles the apostles are read to have baptized in the name of Christ (Acts X). In this, as Ambrose says, the Father is understood, by whom he was anointed; the Son, who was anointed; and the Holy Spirit, with whom he was anointed.

By institution, the administration of baptism belongs to priests. Yet if necessity presses, other ministers of the altar may baptize, observing the order of rank: thus, if a deacon is present, a subdeacon should not presume to baptize; and so in other cases. In the absence of ministers of the altar and of all clerics, and under urgent necessity, a layman may baptize. If no layman is present, a woman should baptize. If no other woman can be found, the mother herself should baptize. Nor for this reason shall she be separated from her husband, because necessity excuses her.

[Col. 0389B] The baptism of Christ and the blood of Christ give baptism its power and efficacy. For when Christ himself came to John’s baptism, he bestowed regenerative power upon the waters, so that they might have the efficacy of remission—not from themselves, however, but from grace working through the blood shed for sins. Since under the Law the blood of sacrifices was poured out as a figure of this, it too is believed to have had efficacy for remission.

The time of baptism began when it was said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Those who died without baptism before they could hear the apostles’ preaching did not therefore perish. But after the sound of their preaching went out into all the earth (Ps. XVIII), not only is the person who has not been baptized not saved, as Augustine says, but neither is the one who could not be baptized.

Yet concerning those who hasten to baptism and meanwhile die, it is asked whether they are saved. This seems to follow from the fact that sins are remitted through contrition of heart and the intention to confess, according to the saying: “I said: I shall confess my injustice against myself to the Lord” [Col. 0389C] (Ps. XXXI), etc.

For example: someone is contrite in heart and has confessed his iniquity before a priest; he also possesses love of God and neighbour, like Cornelius. Why, then, should he not enter the wedding, since he has been invited and possesses the wedding garment?

Some, however, have thought that such a person cannot be saved, since it is written: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of God” (John III). Augustine settles this dispute, saying: “How much, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, that of which the Apostle says, ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’ (Rom. X), avails, has been shown in the thief. But then it is fulfilled invisibly when not contempt for religion but a circumstance of necessity excludes the mystery of baptism.”

[Col. 0390A] By these words Augustine resolves the objection raised by the opposing side: “Unless one is born again.” His own words teach that it should be understood thus: “Whoever has despised being born again of water and the Spirit shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

That martyrdom supplies the place of baptism is doubted by no one. Those who had been baptized with John’s baptism are read to have been rebaptized, for they had not been born again of water and the Holy Spirit. But those baptized even by heretics in the form handed down by Christ, namely with the invocation of the Trinity, are not rebaptized. If they were baptized outside that form, they are rebaptized—indeed, they are truly baptized—for they had not been baptized before.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Words Pronounced Incorrectly, and Why Baptism Is Performed Only in Water

[Col. 0390B]

If a priest or another person, while baptizing, pronounces the words corruptly—for example, “in the name of the Fatherland and the Daughter and the Holy Spiritess”—yet does not intend error or heresy but does so from ignorance, the person need not be rebaptized.

Baptism was instituted to be celebrated not in wine or oil, but in water alone, so that the sacrament might correspond with the reality of the sacrament and the invisible reality might be understood through the visible sacrament. For outward washing signifies inward cleansing. Nothing more suitable than water can be found for washing.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Sponsors’ Response for an Infant

In the person of the infant, sponsors answer, “I believe”—that is, “I receive the sacrament of faith”—because here, as Augustine says, the sacrament of faith is called faith.

[Col. 0390C] When, in the person of the child, they say, “I renounce Satan,” etc., they promise that the child, if he reaches the years of discretion, will do this and that. By these words the child is bound for the future, so that unless he does so, he is held guilty of violating a promise.

No one can be baptized in the mother’s womb, for one not yet born cannot be born again. That Jeremiah and John were sanctified in the womb must be regarded as among miracles of divine power. Yet different people hold different opinions concerning that sanctification. Since sanctification cannot coexist with original sin, some say that they were sanctified in the womb—that is, cleansed from original sin.

[Col. 0390D] Without prejudicing the more authoritative opinion, it seems to me that they are said to have been sanctified in the womb because of signs of their future holiness. For we should not believe that they then possessed charity, in which the whole sum of sanctification consists, nor the sacrament of charity or of any other grace.

## CHAPTER XVI. What Is Remitted in Baptism

Through baptism guilt is remitted. But the punishment imposed for sin is not removed—namely, that temporal punishment which we experience daily in cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and the like. It remains in us so that eternal life may be sought by us more ardently.

The things preceding baptism, such as exorcism—that is, adjuration—and catechizing—that is, instruction—diminish the devil’s power; they do not confer remission of sins. Some things are also done there for the honour of the sacrament.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Day of Scrutiny

[Col. 0391A] It should also be noted that those to be baptized on Holy Saturday are brought to church on the Wednesday of the fourth week of Christian soldiery, that is, of Lent, in order to be exorcized and catechized.

The Wednesday of the fourth week has been assigned to this office so that those who are to be baptized may understand from the number itself that they are called not to idleness but to Christian soldiery—as though, in the fourth age, namely youth, which is suited for battle, they were chosen for military service.

Because on the aforesaid Wednesday they are questioned and instructed concerning faith, that day is called the day of scrutiny, and that office is called the scrutiny. On that day they are called by the reading preceding the Epistle, which itself concerns the waters of baptism. Likewise, for a similar reason, those to be ordained are called on the Wednesday of the Ember Days before the Epistle by the reading that concerns the Holy Spirit, by whom they are to be consecrated.

[Col. 0391B] Hence on that day they come to be questioned and examined concerning matters belonging to their office.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Preliminaries before Baptism

There are other matters to be considered concerning those to be baptized. First they are signed on the forehead, breast, between the shoulders, ears, and mouth with the sign of the cross. By its power all sacraments are completed and all inventions of the devil are frustrated.

Thus, when the firstborn of Egypt were slain, the Hebrew people were saved because the doorposts of their houses had been marked with the blood of the Paschal lamb, a type of the Lord’s Passion. Likewise in Ezekiel, those who were to be delivered from Jerusalem’s impending destruction are foretold as having the letter *Tau*—which represents the figure of the cross—marked on their foreheads.

Afterward blessed salt is given into the mouth of the person to be baptized, that he may be seasoned with the salt of wisdom. Not God’s creature in him, but the devil, in whose kingdom he was born because of sin, is breathed out from him. That is, through the Holy Spirit, of whom the outward breath is a sign, the devil is removed from him, while his power is diminished through the things done there, though not yet wholly taken away.

[Col. 0391C] For he has not yet been born again through baptism, but has only been conceived and nourished in the womb of mother Church through the sign of the cross and the other things done around him, so that at last he may be born again to Christ through the water of salvation.

Then the ears and nostrils are touched with saliva, which, because it descends from the head, signifies heavenly wisdom. By its touch the ears of the heart are opened to understand God’s word, and the nostrils of the heart to perceive the fragrance of Christ’s ointments, so that the heart, perceiving it, may say: “In the fragrance of your ointments we run” (Song I).

Christ handed down this form to the Church when, touching the mouth and ears of the mute and deaf man, he said: “Ephpheta,” that is, “Be opened” (Mark VII).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Threefold Immersion and the Anointing with Chrism

[Col. 0392A]

When these things have been done, the fonts are blessed, and the Creed is delivered to those beginning the way of new life. It was composed by the twelve apostles and contains twelve propositions. Afterward the candidate is asked whether he renounces Satan, etc. Then, after a threefold response, he is baptized by a threefold immersion, because there he is cleansed from sins by the power and grace of the Trinity.

Then he is anointed on the crown of the head with sacred chrism, so that he may understand himself to be advanced to be king and priest—not by ministerial office, indeed, but by the dignity of holiness—according to the saying: “You are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of possession” (I Pet. II).

And so that, through fellowship with Christ, he may be called a Christian and may be co-heir of the eternal King, the Holy Spirit is poured into him in this sacrament after the water of baptism, that he may be born again of water and the Holy Spirit—or rather, that the Spirit’s infusion may be shown. For the Holy Spirit grants remission of sins in the threefold immersion itself. But the sacrament of his presence could not be exhibited at the same time as the immersion.

## CHAPTER XX. On the White Garment and the Communion of Infants

Thereupon a white garment is given to the baptized person, signifying innocence; and the stole of everlasting joy is announced to him if he preserves innocence.

[Col. 0392B] Finally, a lighted candle is put into his hand, so that he may be taught to fulfil the Gospel saying: “Let your light shine before people, that they may see your good works and glorify, not you, but your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

By all these things the new human being is begun, advanced, and completed in the womb of mother Church, and is joined to the whole Church; that is, he becomes a member of Christ’s body. Therefore, if his health permits, he ought to receive the sacraments of unity, that is, Christ’s body and blood.

The same sacrament is to be administered to newly born infants in the species of blood, on the priest’s finger, because such infants are naturally able to suck. Augustine, in his work to Boniface against the Pelagian heresy, says: “In the Church of the Saviour infants believe through others, just as through others they contracted the sins which are remitted in baptism. Nor should you suppose that those who are deprived of the body and blood of Christ can have life, for the Lord himself says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood’” (John VI), etc.

[Col. 0392C] Therefore, if it can be done without danger, according to the primary institution of the Church, the sacrament of the Eucharist in the species of blood should be given to infants. Hence the ignorance of priests, still retaining the form but not the reality, gives them wine in place of blood. I would judge this entirely superfluous if it could be omitted without scandal to the simple.

But if danger threatens the child in reserving Christ’s blood or administering it, it seems better to refrain. Nor should the aforesaid words of Augustine frighten you. Elsewhere, as though defining them, he says: “No one should in any respect doubt that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body; nor is he separated from fellowship in that bread, even if, before he eats that bread and drinks the cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body.”

## CHAPTER XXI. That Infants, When They Reach a Suitable Age, Are Bound by the Promise of Their Sponsors
When he has reached the age of understanding, he must be instructed by the priests and by those through whose voice he renounced Satan and received the Creed, so that what he promised through the mouths of others he may now endeavor to believe in his heart, confess with his own mouth, and imitate in deed. Hence Augustine, in a sermon preached on the first Sunday after Easter:

> Above all I admonish you, both men and women, who have received little children at baptism, [Col. 0393B] that you should recognize that you have become sureties before God on their behalf. Therefore always admonish them to preserve chastity, love justice, retain charity, and do for all people what they wish done for themselves. Above all, both keep the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer yourselves, and teach them to those whom you have received, and love them in the Lord with fatherly affection.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Confirmation

Since in baptism full remission of sins has been effected, what does confirmation confer? In baptism the Spirit is given for remission; here, however, for strength. For through this we are armed against invisible enemies. A person can be saved without this sacrament, if he has not omitted it from contempt. Yet it is so necessary and effective that its administration [Col. 0393C] is reserved to episcopal rank, and that, if administered by another, it is held invalid.

We shall speak of the Eucharist in what follows, where there will be a treatment of the Mass.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Penance

Penance is to weep over sins committed and to be unwilling to commit things that ought to be wept over. And, as Jerome says, it is “the second plank after shipwreck,” because if anyone is endangered after the purity received in baptism, he can rise again and escape through penance. But for penance to be useful, three things are necessary: compunction of heart, confession of the mouth, and satisfaction.

Nevertheless, one must believe that sins are forgiven in contrition of heart before oral confession, because of that saying: “I said: I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety [Col. 0393D] of my sin” (Psalm 31). What, then, is the benefit of the subsequent oral confession? Much. For in contrition of heart the guilt and the debt of eternal damnation for grave sins are forgiven, but not the debt of temporal punishment. For God, being merciful and just, forgives sins in such a way that he nevertheless does not leave them unpunished; rather, he accepts temporal punishment in place of eternal punishment.

This temporal punishment is taught to be subject to the priest’s judgment in the saying addressed to the man cleansed of leprosy: “Go, and show yourself to the priests” (Matthew 8), etc. But if this confession is despised after contrition, either sins already forgiven return, according to some, or the person is held guilty, though all sins have been forgiven, of the equal sin of ingratitude, because he is found ungrateful for God’s grace.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Why Solemn Penance Is Not Repeated

[Col. 0394A]

Solemn penance—that is, penance performed publicly outside the church—is not repeated, even though the crimes for which it is undertaken are repeated; indeed, one who repeats the crimes is given another counsel. This seems to have been established in the Church so that repetition of sins after penance may be feared all the more. Such repetition is so detestable that it renders its author unworthy even of fitting penance.

Without consulting the bishop, a priest ought not reconcile excommunicated persons or public penitents, unless the necessity of a final crisis compels it.

## CHAPTER XXV. How a Priest Forgives Sins

God alone forgives sins. Yet authorities state both that priests forgive sins and that God forgives them through priests. But priests are said to forgive sins because they administer the sacraments in which and through which sins are forgiven by divine authority. Or priests are said to forgive sins because they absolve one who had been bound by the bond of excommunication on account of his sins. In this way they forgive sins, because they show that he need no longer be avoided on account of his preceding sins.

They retain sins, again and again, so that they may be avoided more strictly, by excommunicating; with the Lord approving both acts, as was said to the apostles: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20). Therefore, according to this [Col. 0394C] manner of forgiving or retaining, it does not seem that priests forgive or retain all sins, but only those for which a sentence of excommunication has been pronounced. According to the former manner, it may be understood of all sins.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Whether One Unjustly Excommunicated Is Bound

It is asked concerning one unjustly excommunicated whether he is bound before God. For if he is not, what is the meaning of the saying addressed to Peter as a figure of the Church: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16)?

But perhaps, seeking an answer, you will say: “Whatever you bind justly on earth shall be bound in heaven.” But how will one be said to have passed sentence unjustly if, being unable to know the truth of the matter, he has judged rightly according to what he heard? Again, blessed Gregory says: “The sentence of a pastor, whether just or unjust, must be feared.” Why, then, must it be feared if it does not hold?

On the other hand, it seems that a sentence unjustly pronounced is void. For the Decree, Cause 11, says: “If a sentence has been pronounced against you, put away the error, and the sentence is void.” By “error” it means the fault for which the sentence is imposed. Therefore, if, once the sin for which the sentence was imposed has been put away, the sentence itself is void, much more is void from the beginning a sentence pronounced not because of the sin of the person brought into the case, but from hatred on the priest’s part, or without canonical procedure, or for an unjust cause.

For three things must be weighed in a sentence of excommunication: the judge’s intention, [Col. 0395A] procedure, and cause. If any one of these is corrupted, the sentence is called unjust: sometimes in intention, sometimes in procedure, sometimes in cause. But since the aforesaid three are required for the justice of a sentence—namely, that it be imposed with an intention of correction rather than hatred, according to canonical procedure, and for a cause deserving such a sentence—the cause seems above all to decide the matter. Thus, if no cause preceded, the excommunication is not genuine, nor is one excommunicated without his own fault bound before God.

For how can anyone be bound before God without fault, when God alone examines the merits of cases without deception? For even among human beings it is held unjust for someone to be punished without deserving it. Finally, excommunication and absolution involve the same judgment, so far as this is concerned. Blessed Gregory speaks thus concerning absolution:

> The absolution of the superior is then true when it follows the judgment of the inward Judge.

This is well signified by the resurrection of Lazarus, dead for four days: the Lord called and gave life to the dead man, saying, “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11); and afterward he who had come forth alive was loosed by the disciples. From this consideration we must understand that through pastoral authority we ought to loose those whom we recognize our Creator has made alive through life-giving grace.

From these words it seems that neither excommunication nor absolution is true if it does not follow the sentence of the supreme Shepherd, who examines the merits of cases and condemns no one undeserving. Augustine, on Psalm 28:

> False testimony will prevail against you—but among human beings. Does it prevail before God, where your case must be pleaded? When God is judge, you will have no witness other than your conscience. Between the just Judge and your conscience, fear nothing except your own case.

So that you may be able to resolve this apparent conflict of arguments, observe when it was said to Peter, as a figure of the Church: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16). You will find that this was said when the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given. It is as if the Lord said: “Use these keys, and whatever you bind or loose in accordance with them shall be bound or loosed before me.” That is: “Whatever you do in accordance with these keys that I give you shall be ratified by me.”

These keys are understood as authority and discernment. Discernment is given as a key when its exercise [Col. 0395D] is granted, just as one is said to give wings to a bird who loosens those that were bound. Now discernment is of one kind in the matter itself, and another in action. Discernment in the matter is that by which truth is distinguished from falsehood without deception. Discernment in action is that by which one proceeds according to judicial order in a case and judges correctly according to what has been heard. This may occur both without deception and with deception. But the discernment called a key here embraces both.

Therefore, if one possessing the authority to excommunicate uses it discerningly—so that he proceeds according to judicial order and applies the diligence he can, distinguishing truth from falsehood without the cloud of deception—then he binds by the authority entrusted to him. And anyone thus bound by him among human beings is also bound before God; that is, God ratifies what his minister has done by using his authority with discernment. And just as he is bound on earth—that is, separated from the Church militant—so also he is separated from the heavenly court, so that, just as no human being has fellowship with him, so no angel is believed to offer him help.

Concerning one who has been bound according to judicial procedure, but for an unjust cause, we say that he is not bound before God unless he is found contumacious; yet the truth of the Gospel remains intact when it says: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” For by “heaven” the present Church is designated. In it, an excommunicated person is regarded and avoided as excommunicated; and though the sentence holds among human beings, it does not hold before God, and therefore deserves to be annulled. If someone has been excommunicated after an appeal to a higher hearing, [Col. 0396B] the sentence does not hold, but is invalid by operation of law.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Anointing of the Sick

The anointing of the sick was instituted by the apostles. Hence James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them anoint him with holy oil; and the Lord will raise up the sick person, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James 5). In this, the anointing is the sacrament; remission of sins is the reality of the sacrament.

To despise this sacrament is damnable. To die without it, apart from contempt, is not damnable. This sacrament may be repeated frequently, just as may the greater sacrament, that of the Eucharist. Augustine, however, says that a sacrament is not to be repeated. But this must be understood of the sacraments of baptism and confirmation, which were then under discussion; or perhaps it is not called repetition of a sacrament even if it is repeated in part. For although repetition occurs with respect to the person who receives the sacrament again, it is not repetition with respect to the sacrificial victim or the oil.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Marriage

Having dealt with those things concerning the five general sacraments which must by no means be unknown, let us proceed to two particular ones. Although the sacrament of ordination is the more worthy, we nevertheless wish to dispose first of marriage.

In marriage a certain trace of the Trinity is found. For the man is the principle from which the woman comes; from them proceeds a third, that is, offspring. The institution of marriage was made in Paradise before [Col. 0396D] sin, for the propagation of the human race, as the Lord said: “Increase and multiply” (Genesis 1). The same cause of marriage remains in the New Testament. But there is another cause as well: namely, avoidance of fornication, as Paul says: “On account of fornication, let each man have a wife” (1 Corinthians 7). Here it must be understood: whoever can lawfully have a wife. For those who have received holy orders or otherwise made a vow of continence are not to be included under this universality.

And it should be known that, whereas in the Old Testament every person was commanded to take a wife from his own tribe, so that each tribe’s own portion of the promised land might be preserved without confusion, in the New Testament it has been established that anyone may take a wife from another tribe, for the enlargement of charity, so that love which did not exist through blood relationship might arise through affinity. Hence those who descend from the same ancestors may be joined in marriage after the seventh degree, because from that point the affection of kinship fails, while personal acquaintance and the reputation of closeness of relationship cease. Isidore, however, sets only six degrees, because he does not call the first degree—namely, two brothers—a degree, but the trunk.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Goods of Marriage

There are three goods of marriage: fidelity, sacrament, and offspring. By fidelity is here understood fidelity to the marriage bed; by offspring, the welcome reception of children and their religious upbringing; by sacrament, that those joined by the marital union may aspire to Christ’s spiritual union, and that those who are one flesh through carnal union may, by cleaving to Christ [Col. 0397B] through charity, be one spirit. For marital union is the sacrament of the union of Christ and the Church, or of any faithful and devout soul with Christ.

## CHAPTER XXX. What Makes Marriage

Marriage is made by the consent of lawful persons concerning marital union, expressed by words in the present tense. Therefore, after consent of this kind, neither party may depart—whether by moving to another marriage, entering a cloister, or making a vow of continence—unless this occurs with the consent of the other, who likewise binds himself or herself by a vow of continence. But to enter another marriage is altogether unlawful.

That certain saints are reported, when they were already about to enter carnal union, to have fled their brides and the marriage bed, must be understood as having occurred after betrothal, in which there is a promise concerning the future, not after the aforesaid consent. For perhaps at that time consent was not customarily made in that form, or had not preceded.

The persons lawful for contracting marriage are those whom neither order, nor vow, nor status, nor inability to render the marital debt, nor blood relationship, nor affinity, nor spiritual relationship impedes. Order impedes the making of marriage and dissolves one already contracted, because a vow of continence is attached to holy orders, so that, although it is not made in words, it is nevertheless understood to have been made in the very reception of orders. Subdiaconate also is counted among holy orders, which was not the case in antiquity.

A vow likewise, expressed in words, impedes or dissolves marriage, [Col. 0397D] but not with respect to the judgment of the Church unless it has been public, because the Church does not judge hidden things. Status impedes, indeed, because if a free man marries a female slave and proves that he did not know this, they will be separated. But if he knowingly did so, they will not be separated.

Inability to render the marital debt arises sometimes from natural frigidity, sometimes from sorcery. In the case of natural frigidity, the marriage can be dissolved according to canonical procedure. But the frigid person shall not enter other marriages. If he alleges frigidity in obtaining a divorce and goes to another marriage bed, he shall be returned to the former union. But if he alleges sorcery and, after divorce, goes to other nuptials, according to the decree of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, he shall remain in the second union and shall not be compelled to return [Col. 0398A] to the former, as one who alleged natural frigidity as the cause of divorce would be.

For if the latter, after divorce, enters other nuptials, he shall be returned to the former union. Why? Because by his subsequent act he is judged to have lied in the cause of divorce by saying that he was naturally frigid, and the Church, so far as knowledge of the truth is concerned, is held to have been deceived. For in him there was no inability to render the marital debt arising from frigidity. For, as physicians say, natural heat once lost never returns.

But in a divorce obtained because of sorcery, the falsity of the claim cannot be discovered by a subsequent marital act. For it can happen through sorcery that a person is deprived of the ability to know this particular woman, while retaining the ability to know another. Therefore the Church does not rescind what was reasonably done regarding the former marriage.

Some nevertheless say that the same rule must be followed in divorce for natural frigidity and divorce for sorcery: namely, that someone who afterward, while the spouse is living, enters other nuptials should be compelled to return to the former union. They do not accept the decree of the aforesaid Hincmar, archbishop of Reims.

Yet in either case, whether of frigidity or sorcery, divorce is not to be permitted indiscriminately, but must proceed according to canonical procedure. Thus, in a case of natural frigidity, both man and woman must swear with the seventh hand of relatives that they have not known one another carnally and have been unable to do so. But if sorcery is alleged as the cause of divorce, they must first be admonished to persist in prayers and almsgiving and, by doing good deeds with God’s grace going before them, to render the powers of sorcery ineffective. If they cannot thus be freed, they must establish by the faith of the seventh hand of relatives that, with sorcery hindering them, they have neither known one another by carnal union nor been able to do so; and thus they may be separated.

In divorces of this kind, the oath used in a divorce for consanguinity is not to be made—namely, that they will not thereafter know each other by carnal union. For a person may be freed from a particular cause of sorcery, and, when the sorcery has ceased and the possibility of intercourse with her has been restored, be returned to that same woman. Up to what degree of descent consanguinity impedes marriage so that it cannot be made, or dissolves it when made, and why, has been said above.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What Impedes Marriage

[Col. 0398D]

Affinity also impedes the contracting of marriage and dissolves a marriage already contracted. There are three kinds of affinity. The first kind is contracted through first marriages—that is, through marriages preceded by none that generated affinity among the same persons. What I say of marriage, for the sake of a more honorable example, must be understood of any carnal union.

This affinity of the first kind proceeds in equal steps with consanguinity and extends in the same manner to the seventh degree. But they differ in this: consanguinity runs through the whole line, whereas affinity does not extend beyond the person through whom it exists. For example, because of the impediment of consanguinity you cannot take your sister in marriage, nor can your son take her daughter, nor your grandson her granddaughter, and so on to the seventh degree. In affinity it is not so. You are related by affinity to all your wife’s blood relatives, but your son, grandson, or even brother is not for that reason related by affinity to any of them.

And just as your wife’s whole kindred is related by affinity to you, so your entire kindred is related by affinity to your wife; but not through her kindred, because, as has been said, affinity does not extend beyond the person. The second kind of affinity is contracted through the second marriage of one who was already related by affinity of the first kind. This affinity extends to the fourth degree. The third kind of affinity is contracted by carnal union with one who was already related by affinity in the second kind. This proceeds only to the second degree.

Let us explain these three by three examples: your wife’s son by another husband is related to you by affinity of the first kind; his wife by affinity of the second kind; the second husband of the wife of your wife’s son is bound to you by affinity of the third kind. Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully should consult Gratian’s *Decretum*, Cause 35, questions 3 and 4.

Spiritual relationship, called compaternity, likewise both impedes marriage and dissolves it when contracted. Compaternity is either direct or principal, or indirect, arising, or accessory. It is direct between persons one of whom has received the other’s son or daughter from the sacred font. It is accessory when it is contracted through carnal union with one of such persons.

For example, your wife, without you, receives from the sacred font the son of another woman. Behold: your wife [Col. 0399C] is the direct comother of the woman whose son she lifted. But you, because you are one flesh with your wife, have through her become the compater of that same woman. Therefore, by indirect, arising, or accessory compaternity, you are her compater; and even after your wife’s death you cannot marry that woman.

Just as spiritual relationship is contracted by receiving anyone’s child at baptism, so it is also brought about by holding the child before the bishop for confirmation and by binding him or her after the sealing with chrism.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On Orders

After the other sacraments of the Church, it remains to speak of orders. There are, therefore, seven orders of ministers in the Church: doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, acolytes, subdeacons, deacons, and priests.

Therefore we, dearest brother, who have received all the orders, ought to know the ministry and significance of them all, and to conform our life and conduct to them, so that life may agree with the name and profession may appear in action. For first we are called clerics, from the Greek *klēros*, which is interpreted “inheritance” or “lot,” because we have chosen to be of the Lord’s lot and to receive God alone as our inheritance. Therefore we ought to present ourselves to him in such a manner that we may say of ourselves: “Lines have fallen to me in splendid places” (Psalm 15).

Let us therefore see to it that we do not wear the signs of holiness in vain—namely, the tonsure, the crown, and the vestments assigned to our offices—but that inward things worthily correspond to those that appear outwardly. For we cut off the hair first and free from it the instruments of the senses, so that by this sign we may learn to cut away from our hearts the enticing cares that frequently return and superfluous thoughts. We shave the top of the head in the manner of a crown, so that we may be taught to keep the mind, which is our highest part, free for contemplating and desiring things above.

Those thus disposed, who endeavor in conduct to be what they show themselves outwardly to be, ought to be promoted to the offices of the clerical soldiery. These, as has been said, are seven; the first of them is that of doorkeepers. It should be known that all these offices were taken from the legal rite and transferred to the Church with a certain imitation.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Doorkeepers

[Col. 0400B] Those who were called gatekeepers or temple attendants in the synagogue are called doorkeepers in the Church. Their office under the Law was to open and close the temple, receive the clean, and exclude the unclean. In the Church, however, doorkeepers have this office: to introduce catechumens who are to be baptized into the church, and to receive into the church penitents reconciled by the bishop.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On Readers

Those called singers in the temple are called readers in the Church. Their office was to make hymns and songs resound before the ark of the Lord. But in the Church their office is to recite the divine Scriptures and to sing Graduals, Alleluias, and such things to God’s praise.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Exorcists

[Col. 0400C]

Exorcists are called, as it were, adjurers. By certain incantations, which Solomon is said to have composed, these adjured demons and expelled them from possessed bodies. Our exorcists, however, exorcize catechumens in the exercise of their office, and expel demons or forbid them access to infants’ bodies.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On Acolytes

Acolytes are called, as it were, candle-bearers. Their office in the church, as also in the temple, is to light and extinguish lamps, prepare the censer with fire, assist in adorning the altar, and supply water from a pitcher or flask for the ministers’ hands.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Subdeacons

[Col. 0400D]

Because among the Hebrews they were called *Nathinnei*, that is, “those serving in humility,” by the Greeks *hypodiacones*, and by us subdeacons—that is, ministers—their duty was to receive sacrifices offered by the people and to carry water or whatever else was necessary for the services of the temple. In the Church their office is to read the Epistle and to offer the chalice and paten with the corporal cloth to the deacon at the altar.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Deacons

From Levi, son of Jacob, the Levites—meaning “those taken up”—are named; through them all sacrifices were administered under the priests. The Church calls these deacons, that is, ministers. Their office in the Church is to read the Gospel, arrange the sacrifice on the altar [Col. 0401A], distribute the body and blood of the Lord—though this is not observed everywhere—give the people leave to depart, and, if necessary, preach and baptize.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Priests

A presbyter is called an elder. This must be referred not to age but to understanding, because old age is venerable not for its length nor for its number of days. For the gray hairs of a human being are understanding. Through these the legal sacrifices of the people were offered. Their office in the Church is to celebrate Masses, distribute the Lord’s body, preach, baptize, absolve penitents, bury the dead, and administer all the sacraments of the Church not reserved to bishops. For certain things reserved to episcopal dignity are not granted to all priests.

## CHAPTER XL. On Bishops

The order of bishops is divided into three: bishops, archbishops, and patriarchs. A bishop is called, as it were, an overseer, because, seated as a watchman in a lookout over the Lord’s vineyard, he attends to the instruction and correction of those subject to him. He is also called a prelate because he presides over others in rank. He is also called an *antistes*, as one standing before, or as one standing against. For *anti* means “against,” because he ought to resist heretics as wolves in defense of the flock.

The same person is called pontiff, as it were, one made a bridge or making a bridge: namely, the bridge of doctrine by which one goes to the courts of life. That a pontiff is anointed with oil at consecration is taken from the Law, in which king, priest, and prophet were anointed with oil. That blessing is given through laying on of hands is believed to have arisen from the fact that Isaac laid hands on Jacob while blessing him; Jacob, when dying, laid hands on Joseph’s two sons; Moses laid hands on Joshua when he made him leader of the people; and the apostles laid hands on those to whom they gave the Holy Spirit.

When governance of the Church is committed to him, a staff is handed to him as to a shepherd. In it three things are noted that are not without symbolic meaning: the curve, the shaft, and the point. Their meaning is briefly explained by that distinguished versifying bishop of Le Mans in these verses:

> Gather, support, spur on: the wandering, the sick, the hesitant.  
> This is the shepherd’s task; this the staff of office signifies.

[Col. 0401D] And again someone says:

> I draw sinners back, govern the just, prick the wandering.  
> By this threefold office I serve the pontiff.

A ring is given to him as to the bridegroom of Christ’s bride, the Church, of which he is the head; and a mitre as to a bridegroom and teacher, according to the saying: “He bound a mitre upon me as upon a bridegroom.” His office is to ordain ministers of the Church, veil virgins, confirm the baptized, consecrate chrism and oil, dedicate churches, sanctify by blessing the vessels and vestments of the church, excommunicate the rebellious, and reconcile penitents.

## CHAPTER XLI. On Archbishops

An archbishop is called, as it were, the chief of bishops. He is also called a metropolitan because he presides over a city [Col. 0402A] called a metropolis, that is, the mother of cities. Their office is to consecrate bishops, convene a council, and restore rights that have lapsed. Beyond the other episcopal vestments, they are adorned with the pallium in the form of a collar, because if they fulfill their office rightly, a collar of eternal reward is promised to them as victors.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Patriarchs and Their Sees

A patriarch is called, as it were, chief of fathers or of a fatherland. Only three patriarchs are recorded to have existed, whose figure Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob bore. One of them presided at Antioch in Asia; another held primacy at Alexandria in Africa; the third possessed the rights of the Roman summit in Europe. The Church established these three sees as principal because the chief of the apostles consecrated them by making them his own possession. For blessed Peter himself presided over two, namely Antioch and Rome; the third, Alexandria, the Evangelist Mark dedicated to Peter’s name.

But after the Synod of Nicaea conferred on the Roman pontiff the privilege that, just as Augustus ranked above kings, so he should be held above all bishops and called both pope and Father of Fathers, the right of the Roman patriarchate passed to Constantinople. The reason the other two sees were moved is that those places, as their deserts demanded, were delivered into the hands of pagans. Thus the patriarchate of Antioch was transferred to Jerusalem, and that of Alexandria to Aquileia, because the Evangelist Mark first presided over this city and afterward presided at Alexandria. Their office [Col. 0402C] is to consecrate archbishops, convene councils of bishops, and renew the decrees of the canons.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Supreme Pontiff and His Office

He is called pope because he is Father of Fathers. He is called universal because he presides over the whole Church. He is also called apostolic because he performs the office of the chief of the apostles. He is also called supreme pontiff because he is the head of all bishops. His name is changed at ordination because Peter’s name was changed by Christ when he was placed over the Church. The keys also are handed to him, just as the keys of the kingdom of heaven were handed to Peter by the Lord, so that he may recognize himself as the gatekeeper of the kingdom of heaven.

His office is to order Masses and divine offices; also, as circumstances require, to promulgate or alter canons for the benefit of the Church; to consecrate the Augustus; to give pallia to archbishops and privileges to churches; and to govern the entire Church in Christ’s stead. Thus the pope holds Christ’s office and place; bishops, that of the apostles; priests, that of the seventy-two disciples; and the remaining ministers, that of the deacons appointed by the apostles.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Why Bishops Are Consecrated on Sunday

The pope and all bishops are consecrated on Sunday because the apostles, whose successors and vicars they are, received the Holy Spirit on Sunday; the Spirit is signified by the oil of anointing. Oil supplies light and heals wounds; likewise the Holy Spirit gives the light of knowledge and heals the wounds of sins. They are also consecrated on Sunday so that they may be reminded that they ought to have risen with Christ and walk in newness of life.

Priests and the other ministers of the Church are ordained on Saturday so that they may understand that they ought to rest from every servile work and devote themselves to God’s service. For Sabbath is interpreted “rest.” Virgins are veiled on the feast days of the apostles because the apostles first handed down to the Church the practice of virginity to be observed, and virgins are consecrated to Christ, the immortal bridegroom, through the apostles as bridegrooms’ attendants.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Priestly Dress, and First on the Humeral or Amice

These matters concerning the ministers of the Church have been related briefly. Now a few things must be added about the sacred vestments. For among the ancients it is also established that nothing in priestly dress is without rationale, as blessed Jerome testifies to Fabiola:

> Therefore, among us, the more worthy Christ’s priesthood is than the old priesthood, the more worthy are the reasons that we find in priestly dress.

For, relating their sacred vestments by the color, material, and position of each to the four elements of the world, the two hemispheres of heaven, and the divisions of the zodiac, they wished to signify that all things are subject to the authority of him whose person the priest represents when clothed in them. Although our own writers and blessed Jerome also wish to unfold the veils of spiritual understanding in those vestments, since even the old ones were not without rationale, let us, having surpassed the models [Col. 0403C] of heavenly things, contemplate rather the heavenly realities themselves in the true priesthood.

The Church took sacred vestments from the old Law. The humeral, which in the Law is the *ephod* and among us is called the amice, covers the head, neck, and shoulders—whence it is also called the humeral—and binds the breast with two bands. In the humeral, therefore, hope of eternal things is understood. Of this the Apostle says: “Take up the helmet of salvation” (Ephesians 6).

We cover the head with the amice so that we may serve God with all the senses, whose fullness is in the head, for hope of eternal things. We surround the neck, through which the voice passes, with it so that, in hope of eternal things, we may set a guard upon our mouth and utter nothing except what sounds God’s praise. We cover with it the shoulders, by which burdens are carried, so that we may be taught to bear the Lord’s yoke patiently. We bind the breast with the bands of the humeral [Col. 0403D] so that we may restrain in our breast wicked and useless thoughts.

## CHAPTER XLVI. On the Alb

The alb, which in the Law is called the linen or ankle-length tunic, and by the Greeks *podērēs*, signifies purity of life. It descends to the ankles, so that those who put it on may be admonished to preserve bodily purity until the end of their life. The alb and amice are made only of linen, which through much labor is turned white, because the things signified by these two are acquired through great labor and, once acquired, are preserved.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On the Girdle

By the girdle, which in the Law is called a *baltheus* and by the Greeks a *zōnē*, continence is understood, by which the heart is restrained from wantonness, lest it impede the steps of good works.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Stole
The stole, also called the orarium, encircles the neck and signifies obedience to the Gospel. For the Gospel is the Lord’s sweet yoke, while obedience is its strap. Thus the priest is, as it were, bound by a strap to the Lord’s yoke when his neck is encircled by the stole. In the diaconal order it is first taken upon the left shoulder. In the presbyteral order, however, without being removed from the left, it is also laid upon the right shoulder, because obedience to the Gospel is first undertaken in those things belonging to the active life, signified by the left shoulder, and is then extended through love to the contemplative life on the right.

It should be noted [Col. 0404B] that among the ancients it was not the orarium that was called a stole, but the alb—which, as we have said, signifies purity of life—was called a stole. Hence: “Those who have washed their stoles in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. XXII). And again: “We have the first stole in the font, and the ring, the seal of faith.” In both places purity of life was signified by the name *stole*, a purity conferred in baptism through the shedding of Christ’s blood.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the subcingulum

The subcingulum, called also the *perizoma* or cincture, signifies the practice of almsgiving. It hangs doubled, because everyone is commanded first to have mercy on his own soul by avoiding sins, and then upon his neighbour by supplying necessities.

## CHAPTER L. On the chasuble

[Col. 0404C] The chasuble, also called the *planeta*, is placed over all the vestments; it signifies charity, which is held to surpass all virtues. It is raised over the right arm, so that friends may be loved in God; and it is folded back over the left, so that enemies may be loved for God’s sake.

## CHAPTER LI. On the *favon*

Finally, the priest places the *favon* on his left arm. The ancients also called it the *maniple* and the *sudarium*, since formerly sweat and nasal discharge were wiped away with it. It signifies repentance, by which daily transgressions must be wiped away. It is borne on the left arm because repentance is necessary in the present life, signified by the left. [Col. 0404D] With all these ornaments the priest is arrayed.

## CHAPTER LII. On episcopal vesture

The bishop is adorned both with these and with certain other things: namely, a tunic, dalmatic, sandals, mitre, gloves, ring, and staff. Since the two last, namely the ring and staff, were discussed above in the section on bishops, let us speak of the others. The tunic has close-fitting sleeves and extends not to the ankles, as the alb does, but only to the middle of the shin; it signifies that the soldier of Christ ought to be free and ready for good works.

## CHAPTER LIII. On the dalmatic

The dalmatic takes its name from the province of Dalmatia, where it was first invented. The Church uses it, by the institution of Saint Silvester, in place of the apostles’ *colobium*, a hooded garment without sleeves. [Col. 0405A] This garment, made in the form of a cross, indicates that its wearer ought to be crucified together with his vices and desires. The two scarlet stripes signify the shedding of Christ’s blood for the two peoples. The fringes, which project like certain tongues from the dalmatic before and behind, are the words and examples of the preacher which he sets before us for imitation. The left side of the dalmatic has fringes, because the active life is hindered and troubled by many concerns. The right side has no fringes, because the contemplative life remains tranquil, and the queen standing at the right hand has nothing leftward in herself. The fullness of the sleeves signifies the cheerful generosity and liberality of the giver.

## CHAPTER LIV. On sandals

[Col. 0405B] Bishops use sandals, whole beneath but open above, signifying that the affections of prelates—designated in Scripture by the name of feet—must be withdrawn from earthly things and directed toward heavenly things.

## CHAPTER LV. On the mitre

The pontifical mitre has been adopted from the practice of the Law. In Greek it is called *tiara* and *mitra*; in Latin, *infula* and *pileum*. The mitre, which covers and veils the head, wherein lies the fullness of the senses, is the guarding of the senses against worldly enticements. Its two horns signify the defenses of the two Testaments, with which bishops ought to fortify both themselves and others against the world’s enticements and to put to flight the enemies of Christ.

## CHAPTER LVI. On gloves

[Col. 0406A]

The use of gloves was handed down from the apostles. Actions are signified by hands, and the concealment of actions by gloves. For as hands are sometimes covered with gloves and sometimes bared when they have been removed, so good works are sometimes hidden in order to avoid arrogance and sometimes disclosed for the edification of one’s neighbours. Gloves are put on when this is fulfilled: “Beware of practising your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI). They are again taken off when this is fulfilled: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER LVII. On the archbishop’s pallium

The archbishop shines with all these insignia, [Col. 0406B] and, besides, with the pallium by which he is distinguished from other bishops. It has two bands hanging from top to bottom, before and behind, and bearing the purple sign of the holy cross. This is the teaching of the two Testaments bearing witness to Christ’s Passion. The circle around the pontiff’s neck is the golden torque promised to those who contend lawfully. Among the ancients, it was customary for lawful competitors to receive a crown on the head and a torque about the neck. Hence theology, rich in realities but poor in words, often transfers the names “crown” and “torque” to signify the reward of eternal recompense. The pins by which the pallium is fastened are the goads of charity, by which the archbishop is spurred on in his care for those subject to him.

[Col. 0405]

[Col. 0405D] **CHAPTER XV.** On the chant “Glory to God in the highest.” **CHAPTER XVI.** On the Prayer: why it is called the Collect. **CHAPTER XVII.** On the Epistle and the reason for this name. **CHAPTER XVIII.** On the Gradual or Responsory, and the reason for each name. **CHAPTER XIX.** On Alleluia and the meaning of the *pneumata*. [Col. 0406C] **CHAPTER XX.** On the dispatch of the deacon to read the Gospel. **CHAPTER XXI.** On the Apostles’ Creed: when and why it should be sung. **CHAPTER XXII.** On the Offertory and the meaning of the Verses. **CHAPTER XXIII.** On the Secret Prayer; why the voice is raised at its conclusion; and how and by whom the paten is borne. **CHAPTER XXIV.** On the Preface. **CHAPTER XXV.** The overall sense of the whole Canon. **CHAPTER XXVI.** On the meaning of the outward altar. **CHAPTER XXVII.** On the meaning of the inward altar. **CHAPTER XXVIII.** On the mystical mercy-seat. **CHAPTER XXIX.** On the first action in the Mass. **CHAPTER XXX.** On the mystical *rationale*. **CHAPTER XXXI.** What the Prayer of the first action asks. **CHAPTER XXXII.** On the second action. **CHAPTER XXXIII.** What the Prayer of the second action asks. **CHAPTER XXXIV.** On the third action. [Col. 0406D] **CHAPTER XXXV.** On the Prayer for the dead. **CHAPTER XXXVI.** On the mystical shoulder-vestment. **CHAPTER XXXVII.** That the final signs of the cross differ from all those made previously in purpose. **CHAPTER XXXVIII.** What the elevation of the sacrament signifies. **CHAPTER XXXIX.** On the Lord’s Prayer, which is the Prayer of the third action. **CHAPTER XL.** Why peace is given before Communion. **CHAPTER XLI.** On Communion.

## CHAPTER I. On the Hour of Prime

[Col. 0407A]

Having dealt with the principal sacraments of the Church, the order of our undertaking requires that we add something concerning ecclesiastical offices, and first concerning the Canonical Hours. Canonical Hours are offices regularly celebrated in the Church at appointed times.

They are, indeed, praises owed to our Creator and, as it were, tributes of thanksgiving for his certain and great benefits. Among the Canonical Hours, that called Prime ought to hold first place. For it seems fitting to begin from the hour at which the householder hired labourers for his vineyard. The Lord’s vineyard is the Church, and its ministers are the labourers. They dig the vineyard when they bring to their own remembrance and that of others [Col. 0407B] the lowliness of our nature, and cause both themselves and others to humble themselves beneath God’s mighty hand. For these labourers belong to the vineyard. They manure the vineyard when, for the sake of greater fruitfulness, they call sins to mind.

In imitation of David, who says, “Seven times a day I have spoken praise to you” (Ps. CXVIII), they assemble seven times a day to confess the Lord: namely, at Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline, and at night for Matins, because it is written, “At midnight I rose to confess you” (Ps. CXVIII). Morning Lauds are added to these, although they are counted among the daytime Hours. Thus they meet seven times in the day to confess the Lord, and once in the night. At the aforesaid Hours they assemble to praise God in psalms [Col. 0407C] and hymns, and to give heed to divine readings. For readings are recited at all the divine Hours, and we call these readings *Capitella* in the divine Hours. They are called *Capitella* because they are the heads—that is, the beginnings—of the distinctions among the offices after the psalmody.

For example, on every day the psalmody of Terce and its hymn remain the same. After the psalmody, however, one thing follows on Sundays, another on ferias, another on the feasts of martyrs, and another on the feasts of confessors. The *capitellum* holds the place of beginning for this variation.

It should be noted, however, that at Prime and Compline there is no variation after the psalmody according to the differing days or feasts, in order to suggest thereby that we ought firmly and unshakably to attribute the beginning [Col. 0407D] and end of our works to God alone.

But let us return to our starting point. In the morning, when the sheep are gathered to Christ’s pastures of life, our shepherd, fearing the wolf who snatches and scatters the sheep, as we read in the Gospel (John X), and no less the lion who goes about seeking someone to devour (I Pet. V), begins thus: “O God, give heed to helping me; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. XXXVII). And because without right faith it is impossible for anything to please God (Heb. XI), the shepherd himself adds with his flock: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” This means: Let the glory of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit be believed to be one and the same, both now and always—that is, at every time—and unto ages of ages—that is, eternally after all times. [Col. 0408A] The phrase “ages of ages” is a circumlocution for eternity.

For just as an “age of years” is said to consist of one hundred years, so “an age of ages” would fittingly mean an age consisting of one hundred ages. But since this whole present age is not believed to endure for such a period, the phrase “through all ages of ages” signifies nothing other than the boundless duration of eternity. “As it was in the beginning.” Hence: “Glorify me, Father, with the glory which I had with you before the world was made” (John XVII).

Then follows the psalm which David sang when the Ziphites wished to seize him and hand him over to Saul. “Ziphites” is interpreted “flourishing”; by them are understood the devil and his own. For the devil promises the world its flower. Those who belong to him set their own flower and delight in worldly things. Against such Ziphites we pray that divine protection may be present to us through every hour of the day, so that neither the devil through suggestion, nor his members through open or covert persecution, [Col. 0408B] may prevail against us.

Afterward follow two octonaries of the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled” (Ps. CXVIII), with one *Gloria* as though they were a single psalm; and two others with one *Gloria* as though one. For the aforesaid psalm, “Blessed are the undefiled” (*ibid.*), is full of instruction in morals. Those whom God has delivered from the bonds and prison of enemies ought to stand before him with good and devout conduct.
