These, as it were three psalms, present our service to the Lord through three Hours, namely Prime, the Second, and Terce, so that in these three we may be guarded by the Lord. At each repetition “Glory be to the Father” is added, lest our office, because the psalms are from the Old Testament, be thought not to belong to the New Testament. Let this, once stated, be understood everywhere.

The devotion of the faithful added: “Whoever wishes to be saved,” so that we may forget the articles of faith necessary for salvation at no hour of the day.

Afterwards, according to the custom of our Church, follows a Reading taken from Isaiah: “Lord, have mercy upon us, for [in] you …” (Isa. XXXIII), etc., preserving, that is, the custom of the ancient people written in the book of Ezra. [Col. 0408D] For it says: “The children of Israel assembled in fasting and sackcloth, with earth upon them; and the seed of the children of Israel was separated from every foreigner. They stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers; and they rose up to stand; and they read in the book of the Law of the Lord their God” (Neh. IX). Hence Bede, on the book just mentioned:

> From their example, I think there has grown up in the Church a most beautiful custom: that at each Hour of divine psalmody one Reading from either the Old or the New Testament should be spoken for all who hear; and thus, strengthened by apostolic or prophetic words, they should bend the knee in earnest prayer.

Nevertheless, it is the practice of many Churches that at Prime no Reading be read, but that it be reserved until the *Capitulum* after Prime. The Reading is followed by the Responsory, as at nearly all the Hours: “Christ, Son of the living God,” etc.

Then comes the Verse, “Arise, O Lord” (Ps. XXXIII), etc. In other Churches, however, the Verse follows the psalmody without Reading and Responsory. A Verse received its name from “returning.” For we read in the book of Numbers that, when the ark of the Lord, signifying the Church, was set down in the tents, it was said: “Return, O Lord, to the multitude of the children of Israel” (Num. X). [Col. 0409A] The Lord’s return to Israel is nothing other than his causing Israel to return to him with all its heart. For God has no place from which he may return, since all things are present to him. In accordance with this custom, the holy Fathers ordained that a Verse should be spoken in every office, so that if our minds have wandered in unlawful thoughts amid the abundance of psalms, they may be stirred by the Verse to return to God.

## CHAPTER II. How and for what purpose prayers are made

When these things have been duly performed, we begin to implore God’s mercy, saying *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy.” We invoke the Father three times, the Son three times, and the Holy Spirit three times, that he may have mercy on us by hearing the prayers that follow. We invoke each of the three Persons three times, because the mercy of each of the three is the mercy of the Trinity, just as their honour is one and their majesty one.

The Prayers are said in the person of those who fall daily and strive to rise through repentance. Hence after the Lord’s Prayer follows: “My soul shall live and praise you” (Ps. CXVIII). It is as though one said: My soul was dead through my sins; but henceforth it shall live through conversion. [Col. 0409C] “And your judgments shall help me” (*ibid.*), because you said: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live” (Ezek. XVIII); and you judge it better to spare the penitent than to crush the sinner.

This office, like every other except the Nocturnal Office, concludes with a Prayer: “Lord God, Father, who [have brought] us to the beginning,” etc. All these things are said standing on Sundays and other feast-days, in memory of the Lord’s resurrection, with whom all the saints have risen in hope. On other days, however, we keep our knees fixed upon the ground while the Prayers are said, which are said for minor sins, and while the penitential psalm, “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Ps. L), is said, which is frequently used for grave sins.

Moreover, this office and every other except the Nocturnal Office concludes with a Prayer because, while we are in the present age—especially when we go out to external business—it is necessary that we be protected by the prayers of the saints; or because it is customary, when we have familiar conversation with the servants of God, to request a blessing at the end before we part from them, as an expression of religious affection. The Nocturnal Office, however, does not conclude thus, because there is no separation there: Matins is sung continuously with it.

After the end of this office, in the veneration of all saints, there is added: “Precious in the sight of the Lord” (Ps. CXV), etc. When the Prayer is finished, there follows a familiar observance for ourselves and for our household. Since we consider that we have sinned more than others, and in order that we may, by God’s help, wash away [Col. 0410A] past and present sins and avoid them hereafter, we say: “O God, come to my assistance” (Ps. LXXIII). And at the end of the Lord’s Prayer is added: “Look, O Lord, upon your servants and upon your works” (Ps. LXXXIX). This is done because we are both God’s servants and his works. “And guide their children” (*ibid.*): by “children” he means the thoughts born from the mind.

## CHAPTER III. On Terce, Sext, and None

At the Hour of Terce, having prayed for divine protection when gathered at the first hour, we again assemble in church, I say, at the third hour, to confess the Lord; and by three repetitions of the aforementioned psalm we present and offer ourselves to God’s service through the next three Hours, the fourth, fifth, and sixth. At Sext [Col. 0410B] we again assemble to sing psalms to the Lord; and through three repetitions of the aforesaid psalm we commend ourselves to divine protection for the next three hours, namely the seventh, eighth, and ninth. Again, at None we gather, and through three repetitions of the same psalm we station ourselves in God’s service through the next three Hours, or fortify ourselves against the enemy’s snares: namely the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth hours.

Each of these offices has its own Reading, which, as we have said above, is called a *Capitellum*. It is asked why a blessing is not sought for daytime Readings, as it is for Nocturnal ones. This is because a superior recites them, and it belongs to him to give the blessing; in the Nocturnal Office, however, it is sought because the Readings are read by inferiors.

But a no less important question arises: why are daytime Readings read by superiors, while Nocturnal Readings are customarily read by inferiors? This is because in the daytime offices the things preceding the Reading do not vary according to differing seasons or feasts, but always remain the same. With the Reading, however, the office begins to vary according to the variety of seasons and solemnities. Since superiors know this variation of the offices more certainly than inferiors, they customarily read the Reading.

In the Nocturnal Office, however, the Invitatory, Hymn, and psalms themselves make this distinction. Again, it is asked why in daytime Readings, and sometimes in Nocturnal ones, the author is not announced as in those readings used at Mass. [Col. 0410D] This is because herdsmen, swineherds, and almost all labourers come to Mass; but at the other Hours there come clerics and members of the church household, who, through their frequent habit of hearing authors’ words, know the authors well enough. The others, because they hear them rarely, do not know who the authors of the Readings are unless their names are announced.

It is also asked why daytime offices take their names from Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, rather than from other hours. This is because at these Hours we assemble for God’s service, and the Gospel recounts that labourers were brought into the vineyard at them; the vineyard signifies the Church.

## CHAPTER IV. When prayers are said at the Hours, when they are omitted, and why

In all offices except the Nocturnal Office, unless it is a feast-day, the Prayers and “Have mercy upon me, O God” are said. [Col. 0411A] The Prayers are for minor and daily sins; “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Ps. L), for grave sins. It should be noted that the Prayers retain the modes of prayer enumerated by Paul when he says: “I urge, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, and for those established in high position, that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity” (I Tim. II; Ps. XL).

Supplication is when we ask for deliverance from evils, as in: “I said, O Lord, have mercy upon me” (Ps. XL), etc. Prayer is when we ask that good things be given to us by God, as in: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy” (Ps. LXXXIV). Intercession is when we pray that all things contrary to our good—such as the stealthy attacks [*subreptio*] of demons or the troubles of suffering—may be diminished and overcome. Hence: “Return, O Lord—how long?—and be entreated” (Ps. LXXXIX). Thanksgiving is as in: “Let all your works confess you, O Lord” (Ps. CXLIV). We pray for those in high station, as in: “O Lord, save the king” (Ps. XIX), and: “Let us pray for our pontiff.”

While the Prayers are said, the priest, because he is a sinner, lies prostrate with sinners. But because he stands in Christ’s place, he says the Prayer standing, in order to recall the resurrection of him whose place he holds. On Sundays and feast-days Prayers of this sort are not made at the Hours, so that we may call to mind that in the future resurrection, where there will be true freedom and true fellowship of the saints with the angels, no entreaty for miseries will be necessary.

The salutation precedes and follows the Prayer because of the Lord’s twofold salutation to the disciples: “Peace be with you” (John XX). [Col. 0411C] After the Prayer follows “Let us bless the Lord,” and “Thanks be to God,” because, just as the Lord, after greeting the disciples, blessed them again, and they in return gave thanks and worshipped him, so the priest, who is his vicar, after again greeting his brethren, says to them: “Let us bless the Lord”—understanding, namely, him whose members we are and in whom we are all blessed. And the brethren give thanks, saying: “Thanks be to God.”

## CHAPTER V. On the evening office

[Col. 0411D] At the beginning of night, that is, at sunset, we offer God the evening sacrifice when we gather to confess the Lord. Isidore says in the book of *Etymologies*: “The evening office, at the beginning of night, is named from the evening star, which rises as night begins.” And Augustine, on Psalm XXIX: “Evening comes when the sun sets.” From this we may infer, when we observe feast-days and days of rest from servile work, that we ought to observe them from evening until evening: that is, from the setting of the sun until the following sunset.

Our daily practice maintains that we sing five psalms in the evening office. For who does not know, although we have commended ourselves to God through the four hours of the day, as has been stated above, how many hindrances and how many empty sorrows or joys [Col. 0412A] occupy even the righteous person’s mind during the day? The eyes bring alluring forms before it. Through the ears enter words of detraction or sensuality. Nor are the nostrils exempt from this deadly messenger. The mind is also polluted through the mouth when it speaks criminal or even idle words. Hands and feet undoubtedly touch these things, whence the soul becomes worse through thought. Thus we are assailed each day in these five senses. Therefore, at the beginning of night, when we approach sleep—which is a certain image of death and attended by many dangers—we sing five psalms, asking pardon for the sins of the five senses.

## CHAPTER VI. Whence the use of antiphons began

[Col. 0412B] We customarily sing these five psalms with antiphons. The use of antiphons began to be practised in the Churches from Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, as the *Tripartite History* relates. For it relates thus:

> It should be said whence the practice began of singing antiphons in the Church. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch in Syria, third after the apostle Peter, who also lived with the apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels singing hymns to the Holy Trinity antiphonally. He is shown to have delivered the pattern of that vision to the Church of Antioch; and from it the practice passed into all the Churches.

An antiphon is so called because, in accordance with its melody, one part of the choir sounds in response to the other, while the two parts of the choir chant the psalm alternately. After this follows a Reading spoken by the pastor, then a psalm. [Col. 0412C] Because that psalm has a sweet and pleasing melody, lest the heart, forgetful of itself through the pride that is apt to arise from sweet melody, should wander, there follows a Verse by which the mind is recalled and stirred to itself, so that it may attend more fittingly to what follows: namely, the hymn of blessed Mary, sung at the beginning of night to drive out the day’s enticements.

Let the person whom pride carries outside himself during the day return to himself on hearing, “He has scattered the proud” (Luke I). Let one whom the desire for temporal things delights be drawn back to himself by, “He has sent the rich away empty” (*ibid.*). Let one disturbed by a particular affliction consider that the Lord “has exalted the humble” (*ibid.*). If the power of this age steals upon anyone, let him suppress it with “He has cast down the mighty” (*ibid.*). The matter of the Prayer, and when Prayers are to be made or omitted, and why, has been discussed above.

## CHAPTER VII. On Compline

Compline is so called because in it are completed the things that must be done until the repose of sleep. Thus among monks, by the Rule of Saint Benedict, it is observed that from its office onward they should fortify the enclosure of their mouths and withdraw from common conversation until they return once more to their work. In this office four psalms are recalled as far as the Verse. In the four psalms we commend to God the four elements of our body. The very words of the psalms show this. In the first it is said: “In peace I shall at once sleep and rest” (Ps. IV). Although the Prophet understood this of the sleep of death, the founder of the office applied it to the sleep of slumber, [Col. 0413A] because sleep is a certain image of death, as we have said before.

In the second it is said: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII). Christ uttered this verse last before his death. Therefore we say nothing further from the same psalm. In the third psalm it is said: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High” (Ps. XC), etc.; almost all of which is full of prayer, although stated affirmatively. Fourth, that all these things may be granted us by God, we are admonished to bless and praise God.

Likewise, the Hymn commends our bodies to God, as is evident from the words of the hymns themselves. In the daily hymn you have:

> Let dreams  
> And harmful phantoms  
> Depart far away;  
> Restrain our enemy,  
> Lest our bodies be defiled.

In another hymn:

> Refresh our bodies,  
> Weary with labour,  
> With the repose of night.

And in another:

> We pray you, holy Lord,  
> Defend us in this night;  
> May we have rest in you;  
> Grant us a peaceful night, etc.

This is also made plainly clear by the Verse, which says:

> Guard us, O Lord, as the apple of the eye;  
> protect us beneath the shadow of your wings.  
> (Ps. XVI)

This is customarily done because dangers assail people more when they are sleeping than when they are awake. [Col. 0413C] For just as it is dangerous for a person, when passing from this age, unless he has commended himself to God, so it is dangerous for sleeping people unless they have been commended to God, either through these four psalms or through the sign of the cross, by which the Lord may guard our bodies, as we ask in the Hymn. In the Canticle of Simeon we pray with him that we may rest in peace from the turmoil of the age. Hence it is evident that those who sleep are conformed to those who have died in Christ. For Simeon prayed to be dismissed in peace through bodily death; we pray through the sleep of slumber.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the nocturnal office

In the Nocturnal Office we first say: “Lord, you will open my lips” (Ps. L), etc. [Col. 0413D] This is done because in Compline we commend ourselves to God and close our mouths. Each of us, as it were, has rested in his own tomb, standing before God alone, to whom words are not necessary because he knows every thought. But now, since we again gather to confess the Lord, we pray that he may open our lips by his guidance.

Then, through the Invitatory, all around are summoned to confess the Lord, as the second Verse of the Invitatory itself says: “Let us come before his face in confession, and rejoice before him in psalms” (Ps. XCIV). The Invitatory is followed by the Hymn, by which hearts still sluggish are stirred to the praises of God.

But it is asked why in this office and in some others—namely Prime, Terce, Sext, and None—the Hymn is placed before [Col. 0414A] the psalmody, whereas at Vespers, Compline, and Morning Lauds it follows the psalmody. The answer seems to be that at Matins, as has been said, the Hymn is placed immediately at the beginning in order to stir sluggish hearts by its melody. At Prime and the other daytime Hours, it does so in order to draw hearts occupied with daily cares back to the sweetness of divine love.

At Vespers, however, the Hymn is placed after the psalms in order to stir the hearts toward the Canticle of Simeon, taken from the Gospel, which follows immediately after the Hymn, though with a Verse first set before it. The same reason may fittingly be assigned for Vespers and Matins. At Vespers, by the melody of the Hymn we are stirred to understand the Canticle of the Virgin Mary: “My soul magnifies [Col. 0414B] the Lord” (Luke I). At Morning Lauds we are prepared for the Canticle of Zachariah: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (*ibid.*).

## CHAPTER IX. Why this office has three divisions

Psalms, Readings, and Responsories are sung on feast-days in three divisions. Morning Lauds constitute the fourth; the first three are called Nocturns, or vigils, in Roman usage. For by ancient custom the night is divided into four watches. The first is called *conticinium*, the second *intempestum*, the third *gallicinium*, and the fourth *antelucanum*. Each consists of three hours. Thus each of the three Nocturns has three psalms, through which we present ourselves to God’s service during the same number of night hours.

[Col. 0414C] Readings are recited according to the number of psalms, because at every Hour, especially at night, we must be fortified against spiritual wickedness. At lesser feasts, the number of psalms is retained for the same reason, but the number of readings is reduced to remove weariness, which must especially be avoided in matters in which desire alone is accepted.

On weekdays, that is, when no feast of a saint occurs, the psalms are paired and, as it were, six psalms are divided by *Gloria Patri*, so that the Psalter may be completed in each week and the mystery of the number preserved. For six psalms—or rather six pairs of psalms—refer to the six ages of the world or to the six days of our life, in which soul and body must labour in God’s service for the sake of the Sabbath, signified by the seventh age and the seventh day.

Some assign another mystery where the Nocturnal Office is celebrated in three divisions. The night to which this office belongs is compared to this age, full of the darkness of ignorance. The period that began with the world and will last until the general resurrection comprises three times: the time before the Law, the time under the Law, and the time of grace. These three times are expressed by the threefold Nocturn. Those who were before the Law and those who were under the Law, before true redemption had been found, offered different sacrifices to God for the expiation of sins, as the book of Leviticus shows. We express these different sacrifices offered to God when at one time we sing psalms, [Col. 0415A] at another Readings, and at another Responsories. Any psalm is sung by several persons; a Reading by one alone; a Responsory sometimes by one, sometimes by several. For some sacrifices were offered by the multitude of the people, some by the priest alone, and some by the priest with the people.

The third Nocturn expresses the time of the primitive Church, in which both Jews and Gentiles believing in Christ, because they did not know the true victim, still offered different sacrifices, or judged in their minds that they ought to be offered. In their person, as in that of those before them, the Psalmist says: “How long shall I devise counsels in my soul?” (Ps. XII). They sought different counsels because they had not found the one. But afterward the Church, seeking through the lanes and streets of the city him whom her soul loves, found the one counsel, the one way of life, Christ (Song III). [Col. 0415B] We express this after the third Nocturn by crying out, “We praise you, O God,” etc.

This office follows monastic practice. Like the others, it ends with a Prayer, in which they appear to preserve the original institution. Our custom, however, sparing human weakness and toil, joins Morning Lauds to the aforesaid office and closes two offices with one Prayer.

## CHAPTER X. On Morning Lauds
Morning Lauds claim for themselves the last portion of the night, namely the fourth watch, which extends until sunrise. In this office, as though the one way of salvation had been found [Col. 0415C], we sing manifold praises to the Lord. No longer do we offer and present to God’s service only three psalms, as in the three foregoing nocturns and in the daytime offices of the three remaining hours; rather, pouring out our hearts before him, we gather praises for our Redeemer from every quarter.

First we sing to him the psalm, “The Lord reigns” (Ps. 92). In it Christ is praised in many ways with remarkable brevity: first for beauty, second for strength, third for works, fourth for power [reading uncertain; *ptante*, perhaps *potestate*], fifth for the praise of the universe, sixth for the truth of his utterances, seventh for the holiness of his own house. The attentive reader may observe all these things in the same psalm and find them in the expositions of the saints.

The psalm follows: “Make a joyful noise unto the Lord, all the earth” [Col. 0415D] (Ps. 99). It summons not merely one corner of the earth to praise, but, just as blessing has been sown everywhere, demands rejoicing from every side. Hence its title reads: “A psalm for confession.” The third psalm is “O God, my God” (Ps. 62), pertaining to the praise of the Resurrection. There it is said, “At daybreak I watch for thee,” namely at that very dawn when Christ rose. For then prayer ought to be especially earnest, when Christ, rising again, gave mortals hope of resurrection. At its end it says: “The mouth of those who speak wickedness has been stopped” (ibid.). This was accomplished pre-eminently in the Resurrection, because then every uncertainty was trampled down.

But because Christ’s Resurrection is of no benefit to those unwilling to believe it, the psalm “May God have mercy on us” follows in consequence (Ps. 66), in which we pray that we may recognize the benefits [Col. 0416A] bestowed on us through Christ. No less does this psalm invite us to praise there: “Let the peoples confess thee, O God,” and repeats: “Let all peoples confess thee” (ibid.).

Here two psalms, and then three—namely, “Praise the Lord from the heavens” (Ps. 148) and the two following—are continued without inserting “Glory be to the Father,” so that, according to the number of our senses, as it were five psalms may be reckoned in this office, signifying that those who sing them to the Lord offer themselves to God in all their senses.

That Zechariah’s hymn, “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel” (Luke 1), and so forth, properly belongs to this office, in which we spiritually rejoice over our redemption, is declared by the contents of the hymn itself. On weekdays, in place of the first psalm in this office, the penitential psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” [Col. 0416B] (Ps. 50) is sung, because those days are days of penitence, whereas saints’ feasts are days of joy. In place of the canticle of the three youths another canticle is appointed according to the variety of days. That one, prompted by joy, calls all the elements and all creatures to praise; this one recalls the benefits of God’s mercy, so that penitents may not despair.

## CHAPTER XI. Whence the Mass took its beginning and whence its increase

But now, having run through the offices which the institution of the holy Fathers teaches, let us come to that which the Lord Jesus himself, priest according to the order of Melchizedek, instituted and commanded his own to celebrate in memory of himself [Col. 0416C]. First, then, it seems necessary to say whence the Mass took its beginning and whence its increase.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus instituted the celebration of Mass when, changing bread and wine into his body and blood, he commanded his disciples to do these things in commemoration of himself. The apostles enlarged the Mass when, over the bread and wine, they spoke the words which the Lord had spoken and the Lord’s Prayer. Then their successors ordained that Epistles and Gospels should be read. Some added chant, and others other things.

Moreover, Pope Celestine instituted the singing of psalms at the Entrance of Mass; afterward Pope Gregory composed antiphons to be sung at the Entrance from them. Hence even now some verse of that psalm is sung at the Entrance, whereas formerly the whole psalm was sung there [Col. 0416D]. The Nicene Synod composed “Glory be to the Father,” but Pope Damasus instituted its singing at Mass. Pope Sylvester took *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—from Greek, and Pope Gregory ordained that it be sung at Mass.

The chorus of angels first sang “Glory to God in the highest”; but Hilary of Poitiers composed it from the words “We praise thee” to the end. Pope Telesphorus instituted its singing at Mass, whereas Pope Symmachus decreed that it should be sung only on feast days. “The Lord be with you” was taken from the Old Testament, namely from the Book of Ruth; “Peace be with you” from the Gospel; “And with thy spirit” from the Epistles of Paul; and “Amen” from the Apocalypse. Pope Anacletus ordained that these be said.

Pope Alexander decreed that the Epistle and Gospel should be read at Mass. The presbyter Jerome compiled the lectionary as the Church has it today [Col. 0417A], but Pope Damasus instituted its reading as is now customary. He also decreed that on feast days the *pneuma*, called the *Jubilus*, should be sung. But Abbot Notker of Saint Gall is said to have composed Sequences in place of the *pneumata*; Pope Nicholas permitted these to be sung at Mass. Pope Anastasius decreed that no one should sit while the Gospel is being read.

The Synod of Constantinople is said to have composed “I believe in one God,” but Pope Damasus instituted its singing at Mass. Gregory composed the Offertory and instituted its singing at Mass. The apostles and their first successors celebrated Mass in ordinary clothing and with wooden chalices; but Clement, following the instruction of the apostle Peter, adopted from the Law the use of sacred vestments, and Pope Stephen instituted the celebration of Mass in sacred vestments [Col. 0417B].

Pope Zephyrinus ordained offerings in glass chalices; Pope Urban, however, in gold or silver chalices and patens. Pope Sylvester added the linen corporal, because Joseph wrapped the Lord’s body in a clean shroud. Pope Leo ordained that “Pray for me” should be said; he also composed the prefaces. Dionysius the Areopagite, however, is thought to have first composed the Preface, but Pope Gelasius instituted its singing at Mass. “Lift up your hearts” was taken from Jeremiah; “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God” from the Apostle.

Pope Sixtus composed “Holy, holy, holy,” one half from the Gospel and one half from Isaiah, and ordained that it be sung at Mass. Pope Gelasius composed the Canon; but Pope Gregory inserted the section beginning, “And dispose our days.” Pope Leo added “a holy sacrifice and an immaculate victim” [Col. 0417C].

The Lord himself taught the “Our Father,” but Matthew composed it; Pope Gregory decreed that it should be sung at Mass. He also added the preceding section, “Let us pray: Instructed by thy commands,” and the following one, “Deliver us, we beseech thee, O Lord.” Bishop Martial, a disciple of the apostles, handed down the episcopal blessing from the teaching of the apostles; the pious zeal of those serving God enlarged it, and this custom thereafter prevailed everywhere.

Ambrose began to say, “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” Pope Innocent ordained that it be said and that peace be given. Pope Sergius composed “Lamb of God” and instituted its singing at Mass. Pope Julius prohibited intinction of the Lord’s body into the blood [Col. 0417D], and Pope Gelasius excommunicated anyone who received the Lord’s body but did not receive—that is, scorned to receive—the blood. For the words of the decree must be understood thus; otherwise those who communicate on Good Friday would be anathema, because then Christ’s body is received without Christ’s blood under the species of wine. The wine is indeed consecrated by contact with Christ’s body, but is not changed into blood, since the words instituted for this purpose are not said.

Pope Gregory composed the Communion chant and instituted its singing at Mass. “Let us bless the Lord” was taken from the Psalter; “Thanks be to God,” from the Apostle. But Pope Leo ordained that these be said. From all these things Pope Gregory is said to have arranged the Mass as it is sung in the Church today.

## CHAPTER XII. That Mass is celebrated in three languages, and why

[Col. 0418A]

It should be noted that Mass is celebrated in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—because the title of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, of which the Mass is the representation, is recorded as having been written in these languages. For *Alleluia*, *Hosanna*, and *Amen* are Hebrew; *Kyrie eleison* is Greek; the remainder of the office is Latin.

## CHAPTER XIII. The rationale of singing in the celebration of Mass

Now we must approach the treasury of the highest sacrament, namely the sanctuary of the Mass. If the treasury of salvation makes itself accessible to me; if the key of David opens—which opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens (Rev. 3:7)—my soul may rejoice and sing that he has brought it into the wine-cellar [Col. 0418B].

For what was promised, prefigured, and greeted from afar in the Old Testament, but given, revealed, and openly manifested in the New, is here presented in its presence: not in shadow, but in truth; not in figure, but in reality. Here is enacted that in which our David seemed to play the madman before King Achish, when he beat the drum with his body stretched upon the wood of the Cross and struck against the gates of the city (1 Sam. 21 [the source reads XII]); that is, against hearts closed and unbelieving toward him; when he was carried in his hands, holding bread and wine and saying, “This is my body; this is my blood of the New Testament” (Matt. 26); when saliva ran down upon his beard—“beard,” that is, he seemed to speak childish things when he said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not [Col. 0418C] have life in yourselves” (John 6).

Yet, having received the kingdom over all Judah and all Israel, he now, according to the mystical sense in Chronicles, clothed in a robe of fine linen and wearing a linen ephod, as glorious precentor leads the choirs, sacrifices, and leaps before the ark of the Lord’s covenant. O king, O prince of sacred things! So great a dance belongs to so illustrious a head: he stretches the tabernacle for the ark of God; wearing the ephod, he offers a burnt offering and blesses the people in the Lord’s name. Yet, since he was of the tribe of Judah, the priesthood did not belong to him. But God rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh and chose the tribe of Judah; he chose David his servant.

Behold, the king of Judah joyfully hastens to perform with confidence those things which he knew were owed by his Lord to his Son, of whom he said: “The Lord has sworn to David and will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109 [110]). Behold, he commands the priests, orders the Levites to sanctify themselves, appoints singers, chooses some to sing the sacred mysteries, some to sing in octaves, some to sound trumpets, some to ring out with horns, some to strike lyres, cymbals, harps, and organs [Col. 0418D]. In all these things he looks toward the Son.

For all these things are daily performed through Christ in the Church before the spiritual ark of the Lord. The ark of the Lord aptly signifies the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, before whose consecration great cries of rejoicing are raised in the Church. This ark contains hidden manna, which no one knows except the one who receives it: namely, the sweetness of spiritual joy which pure hearts feel after receiving the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, and sometimes perceive in prayer. It also contains the tablets of the covenant inscribed with God’s law, because in Christ—whom the elect receive at the altar and by whom they are received, since they do not change him whom they receive into themselves, but are changed into him, so that with their head they may be one Christ—in Christ, I say, are hidden the treasures and knowledge of God [Col. 0419A]. In him, too, is Aaron’s rod: that is, the rod of priestly or royal power.

Therefore our David, having overthrown as it were Saul’s rule of death—that is, the devil’s kingdom—brings the ark of God into the Jerusalem of his present Church and places it in the tabernacle of faithful hearts, which he himself has stretched out. Thus the choir of the Church, like the whole multitude of Jacob, lawfully sings; and David strikes the lyre with the singers, which sounds from above when he kindles the hearts of those singing with heavenly desires and sings praises to God.

For whatever the Israel of God—that is, the Christian people—sings in praise of God, it sings under this precentor, under this teacher. Moved by him, the jubilation of the heart bursts into bodily voices and the harmony of the choir, now deep, now high and thin. The song of the great body of the Church, spread through all nations, because it resounds with one faith, is manifold and one; everywhere and from every side it rises jointly and together, and is sweetly heard by him [Col. 0419B].

Let us therefore now touch upon the order of the altar, the order of great and boundless meaning, and, he himself opening the way, come to know at least in part its imitation in the priests, who are members of his body, of those things which have preceded in the Head—namely, Christ, the prince of sacred things.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Entrance and the procession of ministers

When the priest is about to enter the altar, the entire Church present ought to enlarge its soul and, in the broad embrace of a fuller faith, hold the Incarnation in remembrance; it should remember the saints who awaited him from the beginning of the world and sought his coming with sighs, praises, and prayers; and, contemplating them, should burst into voices by singing beforehand the antiphon called “At the Entrance.”

For as the priest’s Entrance signifies the entry of the Son of God into this world, so the antiphon called “At the Entrance” presents the voices and expectation of the patriarchs and prophets. In the Procession, which most fittingly accords with the thing signified, burning candles go before [Col. 0419D], as a sign and reminder that, through Christ’s coming, light arose for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death (Isa. 9 [the source reads II]).

Two ministers go before the priest, not walking together nor matching their pace at his side, but with the subdeacon in front. These two signify the Old and New Testaments, or the preachers of each. The Law comes first in time, but second in dignity; the Gospel, later in time, comes first in dignity. These are the two feet of the angel who descended from heaven clothed with a cloud and placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth (Rev. 10).

The moral teaching of the Law was heard more calmly. But the dignity of the Gospel—such as, “I and the Father are one” (John [Col. 0420A] 10); “Before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8); and “Love your enemies” (Luke 6)—made unsteady and false hearts afraid, like the wondrous surges of the sea. The subdeacon carries before him the closed text of the Gospel, because the Law contains testimonies to Christ, but under the shadow of figures; for before the Lamb opened the seven seals, the sacrament of his Passion was shut up in the book of the Law.

The thurible precedes all these things, though as yet empty. It signifies hearts prepared to hear the Lord’s word and longing for the coals of the Lord’s word to kindle the incense of prayers and praises. In certain churches, however, the priest, on approaching the altar, immediately censes it. For the aforesaid angel, as we read in the Apocalypse, stood beside the altar of the temple holding a golden thurible [Col. 0420B] in his hand (Rev. 8), when the Son of God revealed himself before the Church as possessing a body altogether most pure from every stain; he filled it with fire, because the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit rested bodily in him.

Meanwhile the choir sings *Kyrie eleison*, “Lord, have mercy,” signifying the prayers of the universal Church, which are true incense. Of these it is there said: “Much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne” (ibid.). The acolytes hold lights until the *Kyrie eleison*, because doctors, the illuminators of the Church, ought to furnish the faithful with light by word and example until they themselves begin to imitate God in their conduct and recognize Christ as the true light enlightening every soul.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Angelic hymn

[Col. 0420C]

“Glory to God in the highest” follows (Luke 2), the priest beginning and the choir continuing. This hymn belongs both to angels and to human beings. First it is that of the angels rejoicing together that, at the Lord’s birth, the brightest lamp had now been kindled, by which the wisdom of God would find the lost drachma. Hence the angels, already anticipating the event, say: “And on earth peace to men of good will” (ibid.), because this maker of all things, God made man for humankind, was now about to make the peace between God and human beings which no person in heaven, on earth, or under the earth could make, after dissolving the wall of enmity.

Then, after the greeting, the priest says, “Let us pray,” where, being about to pray, he exhorts the others to pray with him. His prayer for us is most effectively received when our devotion is joined to it. Otherwise, even before an earthly judge, if someone were interceding for your offense while you, in that judge’s presence, gave your attention to trifles and laughter, would you not kindle his anger the more and cause your intercessor’s prayers to be of no benefit to you? Therefore, both in Mass and in the other offices, we must join our heart to the priest’s voice.

That one who is about to pray admonishes others to do likewise derives from Christ, who himself prayed and urged his disciples to pray: “Watch,” he says, “and pray” (Matt. 26 [the source reads XIII]). The choir answers, “And with thy spirit,” that he too may be granted to pray in spirit. For one prays only with the mouth who merely pronounces words [Col. 0421A]. One prays with mouth and spirit who understands in praying what one says. One prays with mouth, spirit, and mind who, through the words uttered by the mouth and discerned by the spirit, also understands something moral, allegorical, or anagogical. Hence the Apostle says: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14).

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Collect and the reason for this name

The Prayer follows, called the Collect because the priest, who performs the office of ambassador to God, gathers and offers the petitions of all. In the Roman Church only one Collect is said, unless the solemnity of some saint whose commemoration is being observed intervenes. Others multiply prayers in public celebrations of Masses for the diverse uses of churches, and in private celebrations according to personal choice.

In all these things the priest bears the person of the true and supreme priest, who, as the Apostle says, “in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5) [Col. 0421B]. At the end of the Prayer there is added, “Through our Lord,” because the splendid benefits of God flow to us through him. Through him we ask and obtain, just as through the intervening crystal stone we receive fire from the distant sun into food placed beneath it.

Thus far has been treated the beginning of the Mass called the Entrance, recalling for us the Savior’s entrance into this world, namely from his birth until John’s preaching, when he was baptized and, while praying, consecrated the forty-day fast.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Epistle and the reason for this name

[Col. 0421C]

The Epistle, bearing the person of the Law and the prophets, speaks the office owed by a forerunner before the Gospel. Although it is very often taken from apostolic letters, it nevertheless holds the same rank as if it were always from the Law and prophets. For even apostolic reading always teaches and administers morality and the active life rather than the contemplative life, which shines in the Gospel.

*Epistola* is called in Greek “sending over,” or in Latin “supermission” or “supererogation.” It is called “supermission” because, above the sequence of its account, the name both of the writer and of the person to whom it is written is prefixed. The name “supererogation” aptly suits apostolic letters because they are, as it were, added over and above Christ’s Gospel. This may also fittingly be understood as “supermission,” for one who does more than is required sends something beyond what is owed.

The apostolic order is that innkeeper to whom our Samaritan—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ, the guardian—committed the man whom he found stripped by robbers, giving him two denarii, that is, the Law and the Gospel, and saying: “Take care of him; and whatever thou spendest beyond this, I, when I return, will repay thee” (Luke 10) [Col. 0421D]. Therefore the Epistle differs from the Gospel as much as a servant from a master, a herald from a judge, an envoy from the one who sent him. Accordingly, when the Epistle is read, we rightly sit; but when we hear the Gospel, putting aside our looks with reverence, we stand as before our Lord.

In preceding the Gospel, the Epistle imitates John’s office. Rebuking the transgressors of the Law and preparing their conduct to receive evangelical faith, he fulfilled what the angel had foretold concerning him: “He shall go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1). And in Malachi: “Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way before thee” (Mal. 3).

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Gradual or Responsory, and the reason for each name

The following Responsory, also called the Gradual, shows that the hearers have assented to the preceding preaching. Because it is sung alternately, whence it is named a Responsory, and has a weighty and difficult chant—so much so that it is neither customary nor fitting to render it in high voices—it signifies the active life, in which the Church mutually exhorts itself to praise God and to good works [Col. 0422B]. Therefore it is omitted from the office during the days of Pentecost, since those days signify the Church’s future blessed state in God’s kingdom.

It is called the Gradual because it used to be sung on the steps before the altar, or because, by giving assent to the preceding preaching in the Epistle and exhorting one another alternately, we signify that we wish, step by step, to ascend as it were from virtue to virtue toward higher things. It is called a Verse because in it the melody of many returns, as it were, to one.

## CHAPTER XIX. On Alleluia and the meaning of the Pneumata

The following *Alleluia* signifies eternal glory, or the contemplative life, which the active life deserves but does not attain in this life. For what is that glory but the eternal banquet of angels and blessed spirits, which is always to praise God? The poverty of the present life cannot at all attain it. Yet to know where it is and to taste it beforehand in the joy of hope, to thirst and hunger for what one has tasted—this is what is called the perfection of the saints in this life.

Therefore this Hebrew word has remained untranslated, so that its foreign term might signify rather than express the joy foreign to this life. Since it is, as it were, the proper term of future blessedness, having fallen from heaven’s droplets into the mouths of the apostles, it is rightly used more frequently in that season when the risen Lord offered us hope of that same blessedness and sent the Holy Spirit promised to the apostles [Col. 0422D].

It should be noted that the *pneumata* occurring in *Alleluia* and other chants with few words signify the jubilation that occurs when the mind is sometimes so affected toward God and melts with a certain ineffable sweetness that it cannot fully utter what it feels. For this belongs properly to affection: the more fervent it is within, the less it can be explained outwardly. “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88 [89]), that is, the people that often experiences and tastes this sweetness beforehand, and is so moved inwardly that it can neither sufficiently express what it forefeels nor remain silent.

The Tract is so called from drawing out, because it is sung in a drawn-out manner. It expresses the toil of those in exile and, as it were, laments the long duration of their sojourning. The Sequence is so called because by the delightfulness of its chant it prepares for the things that follow.

## CHAPTER XX. On the sending of the deacon to read the Gospel

[Col. 0423A]

Until now the priest sat apart, while the ministers of the altar attended him as he sat: preparing the offering of bread and wine, placing a footstool under his feet if needed, and serving in every other matter that seemed necessary. This recalls the Lord Jesus, to whom angels ministered in the desert after the tempter had been overcome, as it is written: “The tempter left him, and angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. 4).

At last he rises and approaches the altar, so that we may remember that the Lord Jesus, returning from the wilderness to humanity after John had prepared the way, came and sent his disciples out to preach. For the priest sends the deacon to read the Gospel, giving the blessing requested [Col. 0423B]; he had not done this for the subdeacon, who was to read first. For, being invisible, he sent the Law and the prophets invisibly. But having become visible, he visibly taught and sent the apostles and evangelists, whose person the deacon bears; and, kissing his beloved—the Church—with the kiss of his mouth, he sent them visibly.

The deacon carries the text of the Gospel in his left hand, supported by his right, because in this life, signified by the left, the Gospel must be preached. Yet its preaching would fall and fail unless it were supported by hope of eternal life, signified by the right. The deacon ascends the lectern to signify the sublimity of evangelical doctrine, according to Isaiah: “Go up upon a high mountain, thou that bringest good tidings to Zion” (Isa. 40).

He sprinkles with incense—the sign of good repute—the place where the Gospel is to be read, because those who bear good news here confidently say: “We are the good odor of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2) [Col. 0423C]. The subdeacon places beneath the Gospel book the cushion which he had carried before his breast; this signifies that the words of the Gospel must be received with a humble and gentle heart.

When about to read the Gospel, the deacon turns toward the north, by which the people of the gentiles are signified. Hence: “God shall come from the south” (Hab. 3). To them this Gospel was first preached and will be preached at the end of the age. This is also commemorated in the office of Mass when the priest first stands toward the south, then toward the north, and a third time again toward the south.

The deacon, therefore, raises those standing by to listen, saying, “The Lord be with you.” In this he gains their attention [Col. 0423D] and goodwill. Therefore they respond, as attentive and well-disposed hearers, “And with thy spirit.” He makes them teachable by saying, “The continuation of the holy Gospel,” or “The beginning of the holy Gospel.” What rhetorical teaching accomplishes by its appeals for attention, the supreme nature of knowledge accomplishes in theological discourse.

They answer, “Glory to thee, O Lord,” glorifying God because the word of salvation has been sent to us, according to the saying: “And they glorified God, saying: Therefore God has granted to the gentiles also repentance unto life” (Acts 11). They also sign themselves upon the forehead, where is the seat of shame, to signify that they are not ashamed of the words of the Crucified One, or lest the devil’s hidden suggestion turn their hearts away from hearing the Gospel. For the sign of the Cross is greatly terrifying to the devil. They have uncovered heads, indicating by the very habit of their bodies that they are ready to hear [Col. 0424A].

## CHAPTER XXI. On when and why the Apostles’ Creed is sung

As, after the Lord’s preaching, greater gifts of charisms were poured out through grace than before, so greater sacraments are arranged after the reading of the Gospel. Then, if it is Sunday, Easter, or the solemnity of Pentecost, the Creed of faith is sung: “I believe in one God,” and so forth. For this joyful confession of faith looks especially to the sacrament of the Resurrection or Pentecost, when the new offspring of the Church, about to enter or newly entered into the washing of the life-giving font, professes the Creed of Christian faith which it learned when catechized.

It is also sung on the feasts of the Apostles because they composed it; likewise on every feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary, because she too is commemorated there, where it says, “Born of the Virgin Mary.” The apostles had her as their helper in their work; for they learned many things through her, since, as a mother, she had more attentively kept all the words, pondering them in her heart (Luke 2) [Col. 0424B].

Meanwhile the subdeacon carries the Gospel around for all to greet with a reverent kiss, because the Gospel brought temporal peace and announced eternal peace to Jews and gentiles, divided by differing observances: namely, peace for both peoples with God and his angels. Then the book is brought back to the altar and put in its place, so that, in imitation of the apostles, the ministers may indicate that whatever has been done ought to be ascribed not to themselves but to the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Offertory and the meaning of its Verses

The Offertory follows, taking its name from offering, because it is sung when we offer our Creator the sacrifice of praise. Here more and more the door of faith must be opened and the chambers of the soul spread wide, so that the woman—that is, the great Church—may believe everything that the angel cried with a loud cry of the Gospel. She is the woman seen in the Apocalypse (Rev. 12), clothed with the sun—that is, with him whom she put on in baptism—having the moon beneath her feet, that is, trampling all mutable things. For the moon is changeable and therefore signifies the mutable world. She bears upon her head a crown of twelve stars, that is, the choir of the twelve apostles [Col. 0424D], and is with child; and she cried in labor and was tormented to give birth.

The weighty and grand-sounding chant of the Offertory imitates the salutary travail of this woman who is with child, crying out and giving birth. Expanded by frequent *pneumata* and fruitful in its Verses, however long its jubilation may be, it cannot sufficiently express what it signifies. And why should one not cry to the Lord with the more urgent heart, when awakened by the words of the Gospel and seeing the mystery of one’s salvation being prepared?

With the aforesaid harmony, the prepared sacred offering of bread and wine is brought to the holy altar in this manner: the subdeacon hands it to the deacon, and the deacon carries it to the priest’s hand. For the Law, which, we have said, is signified by the subdeacon, prefigured the sacrifice of our salvation only in Melchizedek [Col. 0425A]; but through evangelical tradition it came to the altar, that is, to the Church’s solemn rite.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Secret Prayer and carrying the paten

Standing silently over the offerings, the priest says the Prayer, raising his voice at its end with the words, “For ever and ever,” so that the choir may answer, “Amen.” This is the confirmation of what precedes. For it is fitting that all who stand by pray in so great a mystery, as the priest exhorts them when he first turns toward them. In a manner they pray when they follow the priest’s prayer with this confirmation.

Meanwhile the deacon hands the paten to the subdeacon, and the subdeacon hands the same, wrapped, to the acolyte. This seems to be taken from the Old Law, where it is commanded that the sons of Kohath receive the vessels of the sanctuary only after they have first been wrapped by the sons of Aaron, and not touch them uncovered lest they die. For the mysteries are not to be revealed to everyone; yet those to whom they are not to be revealed must in some manner bear them—that is, they must observe them with reverence and veneration all the more because they are hidden [Col. 0425B].

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Preface

The priest, about to say something deserving attention, prefaces it with a greeting, wishing us to be such that we may be worthy to receive so great a sacrament. Thus he says, “Lift up your hearts”—that is, have them lifted up. Hearts devoted to earthly things are not worthy of heavenly food.

The choir, lest the priest be able to say to it, “We sang to you and you did not dance” (Luke 7), answers: “We have them unto the Lord”—that is, our hearts. Then the priest says that thanks ought to be given to God for the redemption of the human race through Christ, whose representation is present on the altar. Therefore, speaking of Christ, he adds: “Through whom the angels praise thy majesty,” and so forth.

For the angels praise God the Father for our restoration, accomplished by his dispensation through the Son. For the same reason the Dominations—another order of angels—adore him, because their number is completed by those redeemed through Christ. The Powers also tremble as they consider the depth of so lofty a counsel. Then, together with the praises of the angels, he asks that the praises of the servants may be admitted [Col. 0425C].

In humble confession—that is, humble praise—they say: “Holy, Holy, Holy,” on account of the persons of the Trinity; “Lord God,” in the singular and once only, on account of the unity of nature. *Hosanna* means “Save, I beseech thee, in the highest”; as though he said: I ask not to be saved here with that salvation by which thou savest humans and beasts, O Lord (Ps. 35 [36]), but in the highest, with eternal salvation. The priest ought to say this hymn together with the choir, since in the preceding Preface he has begged that both his own prayers and those of others might be admitted.

## CHAPTER XXV. Summary of the meaning of the whole Canon
But now, as we treat of the Canon itself, we shall endeavor, for the sake of memory, to observe brevity as far as may be possible in so great a matter. We call the whole following sequence, down to the final Prayer, the Canon according to Roman usage, because of the prescribed consecration of the sacraments. The diligence of the Fathers is found to have expounded it in many ways. Yet divine grace, providing for our weakness, [Col. 0426A] often bathes ancient chapters of meaning in newness, so that the lesser may perceive in them, through the inspiration of God’s wisdom, what the greater were unable to perceive. When new meanings therefore suddenly shine forth beyond all human measure, we wonder where they had lain hidden until now, and whence they have emerged so unexpectedly and without study. From this very wonder and unexpected exultation the heart is enlarged, as it is written: “Your heart shall marvel and be enlarged” (Isa. 50). And by this enlargement it is filled with devotion, love, and delight, according to the saying: “Open wide your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80). Yet at times, although clearer to sight than light and sweeter to taste than honey and the honeycomb, they are hidden while we pass through the same things, according to the saying: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30). [Col. 0426B]

For this very hiding produces dreadful fear; fear, grief; grief, groans, sighs, and unutterable inward complaints, so that we mourn no less at having lost the old things than we rejoice at having found the new. Thus, by both alternations—joy at the revelation of hidden things and sorrow at their concealment—as though crushed, ground, and milled between two millstones, we are transformed into the fine flour of God’s sacrifice. Those to whom these things are lacking are at least agitated between the millstones of fear and hope. For, remembering that “we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3), and knowing that he who receives unworthily the sacrament for which he prepares himself “eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11), they fear to approach. Yet, trusting in the mercy of God, who makes worthy persons out of the unworthy and righteous persons out of sinners, [Col. 0426C] and keeping in mind the saying, “He who eats me lives because of me; he abides in me, and I in him” (John 6), hope drawing them and fear holding them back, they approach the sacred mystery with a contrite and humbled heart. By this, as it were, collision of two millstones they make themselves into flour fit for God’s sacrifice.

Mixing that flour with tears of both kinds—that is, of compunction and devotion—and baking it in the oven of the heart, with the fire of grief or the ardor of love and desire, they offer themselves to God as loaves of presentation. They also crucify themselves inwardly with Christ before the Lord God, just as outwardly, in the extension of their hands, they show in themselves the form of the cross. Blessed are those who are thus often affected, who are thus visited from above. But because [Col. 0426D] we are least constant even to ourselves—for “the Spirit breathes where it wills, and you do not know whence it comes or whither it goes” (John 3), and a person cannot receive anything from himself, nor obtain it from another as he wishes, but only as it is given from above—the heavenly Craftsman has devised a way by which we and what is ours may together be offered to the Lord.

And, so that a column resting upon its base might stand more firmly and suitably, the heavenly Craftsman willed that both the form and material of sacrifice should be taken from the ancient rite of sacrifices. For two principal priests under the Law are said to have existed: Melchizedek and Aaron. From the priesthood of Melchizedek, taught by the Lord, the Church learned what it should offer. For he of whom it was said, “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109), consecrated at the Supper into his body and blood the bread and wine which Melchizedek had previously offered in figure, and commanded that the same be done in the Church. [Col. 0427A] From Aaron’s priesthood, moreover, the Church took the form of its priesthood.

For God’s tabernacle with human beings was so arranged in the wilderness that it had, outwardly in the court, a bronze altar upon which the flesh of animals was burned. Within the tabernacle was another, golden altar, called the altar of incense, upon which incense and other things producing fragrant smoke were burned. Beyond it, in the innermost and highest place, was set the mercy-seat, which was called the Holy of Holies. Between the mercy-seat and the golden altar a veil was stretched, which was torn in the Lord’s Passion so that the mercy-seat might be open. Between the golden and bronze altars, a veil divided them in the wilderness, but a wall in the Temple. [Col. 0427B] Of this wall the sinner, mystically moving through penitence toward righteousness, says: “In my God I shall pass over the wall” (Ps. 17).

In these three places Aaron offered the sacrifices appropriate to each. On the bronze altar in the court, animal sacrifices were burned. After this sacrifice, the priest took coals from the fire of that altar, carried them into the holy place, and kindled incense upon the golden altar. Then, placing coals from that same altar in a censer, he carried an exceedingly abundant smoke of incense beyond the veil into the Holy of Holies, so that, because of the obstructing smoke, he could not clearly see the mercy-seat or the two cherubim that stood above it and overshadowed it with outspread wings. The high priest alone entered before that mercy-seat once a year with blood. Thus the tabernacle in the wilderness was arranged [Col. 0427C] for this purpose, and according to that arrangement the Temple was made.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the meaning of the outer altar

But since, according to the Apostle, all these things cast a shadow of things to come, we understand the first, bronze altar to signify a contrite and humbled heart. Upon it, while through penitence we slay the beasts that we have lived as, and our irrational deeds, what else do we sacrifice to God but animals of various kinds? Such animals the compunction of the heart slays in the conversion of the sinner—who is indeed outside through sin and does not enter into righteousness except through worthy penitence; confession of the mouth flays them; discernment cuts them into pieces; and fitting affliction burns them. [Col. 0427D]

It is bronze—that is, dark and resonant—because the penitent places himself in darkness within himself, while his spirit is distressed within him and his heart troubled within him; and he must cry mightily “from the depths,” that his voice may be heard on high. We signify that this offering of such animals should invisibly be made to God upon this altar, and in some fashion visibly make it, when, after certain prayers or petitions have gone before with the incense of rams—that is, with the intercessions of apostles and martyrs—we offer visible victims of bread and wine upon the visible altar. All this is done, as it were, still outside, since what is done, and how it is done, is seen outwardly. Therefore these acts are known to belong to the servant “who does not remain in the house for ever” (John 8); accordingly, they are called an offering of servitude, as it is said: “This offering of our servitude.” [Col. 0428A]

We rightly call bread and wine an offering of servitude. For when man, taken from the earth by nature, had been made lord over the earth by grace, he departed through fault from the Author of nature and Giver of grace, and by justice was condemned beneath the earth. Hence the earth, which had freely served him, fertile for delight, now, softened by many and strange services and cultivated with many labors, scarcely yields what is necessary, as it is written: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. 3).

Since therefore bread and [Col. 0428B] wine are the chief things among the provisions without which animal life cannot continue, the servant who offers them kills that in which he lives animal-fashion; for he kills his life who deprives himself of his food. Hence the Wise Man says: “You have sat at a great table; carefully observe what is set before you. Put a knife to your throat, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Ecclus. 31; Prov. 23). The great table is the Lord’s altar. He is set before us for refreshment, who gave his body and soul for us for redemption. We must consider that we too ought to prepare such things for him: that is, to lay down, for him, our body and soul together and in like manner. Thus the Prophet, by the spirit of counsel, answers him: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation” (Ps. 115). [Col. 0428C]

Observe, moreover, how subtly and elegantly he expressed the form, saying: “Put a knife to your throat.” We put the knife of abstinence and fasting, as it were, to our throat when, having offered our food to God, we afterwards take of it sparingly and fearfully for necessity, as though from God’s altar. For God ordained that those who serve the altar should live from the altar (1 Cor. 9).

Otherwise, if after such an offering we again consume it luxuriously and extravagantly as though it were our own, we take away all that we offer and live, now worse, by robbery. We therefore have both what we should offer and how we should offer upon the first altar.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the meaning of the inner altar

[Col. 0428D]

The second altar, which was within and was golden, signifies the altar of faith in a heart cleansed through penitence, gleaming and bright with the testimony of a good conscience. This altar is also called the altar of righteousness, because righteousness comes from faith, as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gal. 3); and in Habakkuk: “My righteous one shall live by faith” (Hab. 2).

Upon this altar we offer the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and holocausts, “the calves of our lips” (Ps. 50), when we no longer, as before, lament our sins committed, but exult in divine things; when we no longer groan over the commission of crimes, but give thanks for the bestowal of virtues; when we ask that our life, works, and prayers may be made acceptable to God; when devotion pours forth tears and, longing for the delights of the homeland, [Col. 0429A] groans over the length of its sojourn. Upon the same altar the priest, now dead to the world through the offering of his sustenance but living to God—not now the old Melchizedek, born of flesh and therefore flesh, but a new man, born of Spirit and therefore spirit—offers the invisible victim of flesh and blood.

For what more fittingly may be said to be offered upon the altar of faith than that most holy sacrifice which is perceived by faith alone, benefits in faith alone, and is accepted through the merit of faith? This sacrifice is offered upon the altar of faith as an odor of sweetness; and prayer offered upon it is likewise received by the Lord as an odor of sweetness, as it is said: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). Coals taken from the other altar are placed upon the golden altar to burn the incense of prayers, because the heart is first kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit to weep for sins, and afterwards kindled with the same fire to send upward the fragrance of sweet prayers, when the person, now cleansed through penitence, desires to come and appear before the face of God. There the fire of the Holy Spirit draws tears of compunction as from green wood; here, tears of devotion. [Col. 0429B]

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the mercy-seat mystically understood

The third place, called the Holy of Holies, was divided from the holy place by a certain veil. Beyond the veil stood the ark of the covenant, and above it the mercy-seat: namely, a golden table of the same dimensions as the ark. It was so called because there the Lord, appearing to Moses, [Col. 0429C] was propitiated toward his people. The ark signifies Christ’s humanity, which is beyond the veil because Christ ascended beyond heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father—that is, amid his greater goods. The mercy-seat above the ark is God’s propitiation in Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “Whom God set forth as a propitiator through faith in his blood” (Rom. 3).

Or the mercy-seat is God’s mercy, through which he is propitiated toward his people. It is rightly said to be above the man Christ, because God’s mercy is divinity itself. To this ark, to this mercy-seat, the new priest strives to draw near after the sacrifice of animals upon the first altar and after the offering of Christ’s flesh and blood upon the second, with a censer full of fire from the altar: that is, with a lofty heart, as it is written, “A man shall come to a lofty heart” [Col. 0429D] (Ps. 63), kindled with the fire of the Holy Spirit and with an exceedingly abundant incense of prayers. This is so that what lies beyond the veil cannot be clearly seen, because the more devoutly we tend toward God, the more we understand that he cannot be comprehended. Hence: “Your eyes made me fly away” (Song 6); and, “A man shall come to a lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63).

Therefore the priest, directing his mind there but recognizing his insufficiency, sees with the eyes of his heart angels standing over the mercy-seat, ready, as it were, to help. He asks that his sacrifice may be carried thither, so that he himself may be joined and united to God and, adhering to the Spirit, may become one spirit with him. “We humbly beseech you.” But let us now attend to the words of the Canon and endeavor to explain how the aforesaid three things are fitted to it. [Col. 0430A]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Exposition of the Canon

The sacred Canon, which others have divided in various ways for various reasons, we divide into three actions. The first begins, “Therefore, you, O Lord,” and continues to “Who, on the day before he suffered.” In it we offer the chief elements of our sustenance—bread, which strengthens the heart of man, and wine, which gladdens the heart of man (Ps. 103; Ecclus. 40)—to the Lord in sacrifice.

We designate these by three terms. We call them gifts (*dona*) because they have been given to us by God; offerings (*munera*) because they are offered by us to him. A gift is what is given by a superior; an offering, what is given by an inferior. The added phrase, “these sacrifices,” specifies how God [Col. 0430B] may reward from them. The sign of the cross is made over them in remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, in which we make ourselves participants when, withdrawing the supports of our life from ourselves, we offer them to God.

We sign them three times because every consecration is accomplished by the power of the Trinity. In this first action prayer is made for all whose sacrifice is the same and who resemble it truly: namely, in that, though they are many, they are joined into the one body of the Church by one faith and one Spirit, just as that bread is made from many grains and the wine has flowed together from many grapes.

Then the Prayer proceeds particularly to the cultivators of the Church. The cultivators of the Church are those who cultivate her with the hoe of correction and holy teaching. In [Col. 0430C] the following tone of the Prayer it is said: “Who offer to you for themselves and for all their own.” Although the preposition *pro* (“for”) may be understood in the same way as in the other clauses, it may fittingly be understood in this sense: by offering these things—bread and wine, the principal elements in the sustenance of animal life—they are said to offer themselves and all that is theirs, that is, their entire sustenance. For these are its principal portion and represent the whole.

There follows: “In communion, venerating the memory.” Although writers make this seem like the beginning of a chapter, because on certain solemnities some variation occurs here, it is nevertheless joined to what preceded in this manner: “They offer for themselves and for all their own”—they, I say, “in communion,” remaining in the communion of the Church through faith.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the mystical breastplate

[Col. 0430D]

Then the names of the saints are recited, so that our sacrifices may be accepted with their intercessions, as though with the incense of rams. In signification of this Aaron wore inscribed upon the breastplate, which was upon his breast, the names of the twelve patriarchs. Both this commemoration of the saints and that inscription of names aim at this: that whoever approaches the Lord’s table should imitate in mind the purity of the holy Fathers.

## CHAPTER XXXI. What the Prayer of the First Action asks

“Therefore, this offering.” All these things, as belonging to the servant, are still performed, as it were, outside. Hence the previously mentioned gifts are here called an offering of servitude, [Col. 0431A] and the Prayer concerns matters in which the servant is affected: namely, that temporal peace may be granted him and that he may escape eternal punishments. He does not yet long for inheritance as a son, but fears stripes as a servant.

There follows: “Which offering.” This is preparation for the second Action. It is as though the servant says: “A higher counsel is needed. I have done all that I could, but I have not made satisfaction in all respects. I can do nothing more. I can kill myself; I cannot make myself alive.

“Therefore I shall raise myself by prayer to him who can do all things. I shall say to him: ‘Lord, I have done what I could. Command our offering to be made blessed, by advancing it to something better, so that what is food of the body may become saving food of the soul; enrolled (*ascriptam*), that is, appropriated to divinity in the person of the Son; ratified (*ratam*), so that you may hold as ratified what is performed by our [Col. 0431B] ministry, as though it were done by your own hands without us.’”

While saying these three words, we make the sign of the cross three times together over the two offerings; this is customary and familiar in all consecrations. For we believe that many things are accomplished through the power of the Lord’s cross. It is done three times because the Trinity acts together through the power of the cross.

There follows: “reasonable,” that is, offered reasonably, so that we who offer rightly may also divide rightly. Then he shows more clearly what the priest has implored beneath those three words. When he says, “that it may become for us the body,” and so forth, understand “this offering.” The meaning is: “May this offering of bread and wine become for us—that is, for our benefit—the flesh and blood of Christ.”

While saying this, the sign of the cross is made once over the bread [Col. 0431C] and once over the chalice, so that by the power of the cross the operation of the Trinity, whose memorial had been made in the three preceding signs, may be understood as one in both. Some, however, refer the five signs to Christ’s five wounds. With this prayer having preceded, the priest approaches the second Action, wavering in nothing through faith.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the second Action

“Who, on the day before he suffered,” and so forth. To these words belong power and efficacy, as it is written: “Behold, he shall give to his voice a voice of power” (Ps. 167). At these words, I say—“This is my body”—by divine power beyond all human reason, through human ministry, spiritual food is made out of bodily food. And by the power of the immeasurable Majesty [Col. 0431D] descending upon the bread and wine, we receive as true a divinity and humanity of Christ reigning in heaven as we may receive the true substance of fire from the sun by means of a small crystal sphere placed beneath it.

The rounded, golden hands, filled with hyacinths, of him who says, “Without me you can do nothing” (Song 5; John 15), accomplish these things through the priest’s hands, which are made most great by being conformed to his hands, because, that they may be able to accomplish these things with him and through him and with him, they have been sealed with holy oil.

Therefore, offering so sacred a victim upon the invisible altar of faith, the priest no longer speaks timidly as before, nor calls it a victim of servitude, but says with spiritual exultation and joy: “We offer to your supreme majesty from your gifts”—namely, those which you gave us for the sustenance of the body—“and from what has been given,” that is, what we gave you by sacrificing it to you. [Col. 0432A] For by your power we consecrate these into the body and blood of your Son: a pure and purifying victim; holy and sanctifying; immaculate and making us immaculate; that is, bread of holy life—not temporal, not animal, but spiritual and eternal—and the chalice which can save and satisfy for ever, and is therefore the chalice of eternal salvation.

It should be noted that the signing made over the bread and chalice before consecration is, as it were, a prayer that consecration may be completed; but the repeated signing after consecration is a certain testimony that the consecration has now been completed. Nor should it be passed over that in this chapter holy Church sets forth three marks of the Lord’s mercy: his blessed Passion, resurrection from the dead, and glorious ascension into heaven. The first wounds the Church with love; the second strengthens it with faith; the third gladdens it with hope.

We ought first to be conformed in the first Action; secondly, in the second Action, offering with devotion of prayers the mystery of faith; thirdly, in the third, contemplating Christ the Lord crowned with glory and honor at the right hand of the Father. For he says: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). [Col. 0432B]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. What the Prayer of the Second Action asks

There follows: “Upon which, look with a propitious countenance.” After offering the true and highest sacrifice upon the same altar of faith, he offers the sacrifice of prayer and asks for something still higher, [Col. 0432C] for nothing suffices him until through Christ’s body he is united with God in heaven and through humanity joined to divinity. Since he has raised a ladder for himself, he strives to ascend it. Therefore, even after so great an offering, he still girds himself for prayer, saying: “Upon which, look with a propitious countenance,” and so forth.
