As though ascending by the steps of that ladder, he recalls the gift of the boy Abel, the sacrifice of the patriarch Abraham, and the offering of Melchizedek the priest, who elegantly expressed in bread and wine the figure of the true sacrifice, just as Abraham expressed its truth in his son and Abel the gift of innocence in the lamb. When he says, “As you deigned to accept the gifts,” and so forth, he does not ask that the offerings be accepted in the same way—for this offering is far more acceptable—but that the offerers be accepted. Relying on this prayer, he approaches the third Action with confidence. [Col. 0432D]

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the third Action

But because he is not yet able to ascend as he wishes to that highest and sublime invisible altar, the mercy-seat—namely, in the presence of the divine Majesty, where the supreme and eternal Priest stands before the face of God the Father—as he himself signifies by bowing before the visible altar, he asks that his sacrifice may be carried thither through the hands of the angel, namely his guardian angel. He asks this so that he may share in the power of that sacrament; so that, through Christ’s body, which is in heaven and received from the visible altar on earth, he may arrive at God’s supreme propitiation and merit union with him.

For this is the perfect blessing of which he says: “May we be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.” We understand the carrying of the sacrifice through the angel’s hands as nothing other than the angel’s cooperation with our devotion. He cooperates with us by praying for us and, in a wonderful and invisible way, suggesting good things to our minds. Or perhaps the singular is used for the plural: “angel” for “angels.” For blessed Gregory says in Book IV of the *Dialogues* that at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened, choirs of angels are present, the lowest things are joined to the highest, earthly things are united to heavenly, and one thing is made from the visible and invisible. [Col. 0433A]

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Prayer for the dead

There follows: “Remember also, O Lord,” and so forth. Just as in the first Action, when he offered the supports of animal life, [Col. 0433B] he prayed for the living, so in this third Action, when, forgetting what lies behind and stretching himself toward what lies before, he seeks union with God, he prays for the dead, who need the same food. By the merit of love, while praying for others what he seeks for himself, he obtains it both for himself and for others.

Knowing, however, that some of those who are to be saved—for he prays only for the saved—are held after their death in purgatorial punishments, he first asks that a place of refreshment be granted them; then light, that they may see God as he is; finally peace, of which it was said: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave to you” (John 14), namely peace upon peace. A little later, in the third repetition of “Lamb of God,” the Church also asks that this peace be given to her, saying: “Grant us peace.” This peace consists in the unity of head and members.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the mystical shoulder-piece

[Col. 0433C]

The following chapter also commemorates for us the names of the saints, through whose intercession the priest wishes to obtain what he asks. This too seems to have been taken from the Levitical priesthood. For, as the legal priest bore on his breast, in the breastplate, twelve precious stones engraved with the twelve names of the children of Israel, as said above, so in the shoulder-piece he bore upon his shoulders two onyx stones set in gold and marked with the same names. Six names were on one and six on the other.

But our priest, as we have said above, then bears in the breastplate of his heart the names of the saints whom he recalls in words, when he imitates them in holiness and purity of mind; [Col. 0433D] and he then bears them in the shoulder-piece upon both shoulders when, in the right hand of prosperity and the left hand of adversity, he imitates them as far as he can in the perfection of works.

There follows: “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things.” It is written: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). How then does he always create? He created all bodies together as regards their matter; but he creates daily—that is, makes them—by giving each its own form, according to the saying: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). In saying “all these things,” moreover, he means all things of this kind—for he would not say “all things” either of two according to species or of one according to the reality of the thing.

Observe the order. First, God creates bread and wine through nature. The same things, offered upon the altar, he sanctifies through grace by the words of the first Action. For already, before the consecration, they have been sanctified and set apart from common uses. Then, by the sacred words of the second Action, he quickens them by advancing what has been sanctified, when he transubstantiates them into Christ’s body and blood; and he blesses them by giving them the effect of the highest blessing, which is in the unity of head and members and is recalled by the third Action. The three signs of the cross now made show that the foregoing things have been done through the operation of the Trinity by the power of the cross. For the signs made after consecration up to this point do not effect consecration, but make commemoration or testimony of it, as we said above. [Col. 0434A]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. How the final signs differ from the rest in purpose

[Col. 0434B]

“Through him and with him.” The signs of the cross made here at the end are known to be made for a different reason than all those set above. For these are made neither for consecration nor as testimony or memorial of consecration already accomplished. Why, then, they are made; why five times; and why three times in the chalice and twice outside it, must be briefly explained.

The very words of the chapter plainly indicate for what purpose these signs of the cross are made. Since “the cross is a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1), lest the repeatedly made signing and its threefold repetition in memory of the Trinity should seem to produce disgrace rather than praise, the priest repeats the sign of the cross three times in the chalice for Christ, whose blood is there, and twice outside the chalice for the Father and the Holy Spirit. Thus he affirms that the cross belongs to the glory and honor of the whole Trinity.

“Through him,” he says—that is, through Christ, through whom the Father’s glory has become known—“and with him.” For Christ cannot be alien from the Father’s glory, since he and the Father are one God. “And in him.” For in him is the fullness of divinity. Hence glory belongs to God the Father, who begot such a Son, and to the Holy Spirit, by whose operation he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb. [Col. 0434C]

But when only one sign is made in naming the Father and only one in naming the Holy Spirit, what is the purpose of the three signs made in the chalice while naming Christ? [Col. 0434D] The sign of the cross is also tripled because the pronoun designating Christ is uttered three times. For since a pronoun, as the grammarian says, may refer to every subject, if the sign were made at the first utterance of the pronoun and not at the others, it would seem to refer to another person or other persons.

It should also be noted that, whereas the other signs are made with the priest’s hand alone, these are made with Christ’s body. For here Christ’s crucifixion itself is represented, as though Christ, whom we believe present, were thus stretched out for us upon the wood of the cross. At the end of this chapter the priest raises his voice so that its content may be ratified by all when they answer: “Amen.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the elevation of the sacrament: what it signifies

[Col. 0435A]

And so that the priest may show how glory has been acquired for the Trinity through Christ in the minds of the faithful, he expresses, so far as he can, the mystery of the Passion. After the signs of the cross, with both hands he elevates the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood and shortly afterwards sets it down; this signifies the lifting up of the body of Jesus Christ upon the cross and its burial. Therefore he covers the chalice with the corporal pall, signifying its wrapping in the linen cloth.

Thus, although the chalice has hitherto been covered for protection, it is now covered for the mystery. At times, as the priest approaches the Lord’s Prayer, so that in the presence of the teacher the petitions which he himself taught may obtain a better result, he says first: [Col. 0435B] “Formed by divine instruction,” because, as Matthew and Luke testify, Christ taught prayer in this manner. He fittingly adds: “We dare to say.” For unless Christ had taught this, how would a human being, knowing himself to be earth and clay, dare to call God his Father?

It should be noted that there are seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer, containing everything that ought to be asked. Much has been written by the holy Fathers in exposition of it; but because the mind of one praying cannot at that hour grasp so much, we wish to say a few things about each petition, so that one who prays may understand what he asks and, understanding, become more devout. For this is why we utter words in prayer: to stir up in ourselves the affection of devotion, not to instruct God, who knows all things, concerning what our mind asks.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Lord’s Prayer, which is the prayer of the third Action

[Col. 0435C]

Our Father, who art in heaven (Matt. VI). All this is, as it were, the prologue and appeal of the petitioner. In it great confidence of obtaining is also given. For what will he refuse to his children, to whom he has already granted that he may be their Father? But we who call God Father must beware of defilements, lest we be unworthy of so great a Father. “In heaven,” that is, in the saints. Although God is present in all creatures by essence, he is present in the good alone by indwelling grace.

The first petition follows: “Hallowed be thy name” in us, so that our Father may be glorified by the good and spiritual conduct of his children. Or, although the Father’s name is holy in itself from eternity, it is then held holy and venerable in us when, as good children, we avoid offending the good Father not from fear but from love.

How is the second petition, which says, “Thy kingdom come,” fulfilled in us? This may indeed be understood not only of the future kingdom, when we shall be wholly subject to him, but also of the present: for the kingdom of God will be brought about in us when we serve him alone and devotedly, having now been set free from the kingdom of sin and the dominion of the devil.

It follows: “Thy will be done,” not ours; “as in heaven,” that is, as among the angels, “so also on earth,” that is, in us human beings. We attain these things here only in part, but in the future fully. For these three things which we ask in the preceding petitions are begun here in the saints and increase daily, but will be fully consummated in the future. The four which follow, however, belong only to the present life. There no one will need to be fed, no debts will be forgiven to anyone, no one will be tempted, and there will be no evils from which anyone must be delivered.

The fourth petition is: “Give us this day our daily bread.” The bread which we daily need, lest we fail on this road of our pilgrimage, is the spiritual food of the soul: namely, an affection arising from the sweetness of God, and a certain most pleasant savour by which the soul is sometimes refreshed in prayer. Of this bread it is said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). With this manna the true Israel is inwardly nourished through the wilderness of this age, until, having entered the land of promise, it is satisfied by the very countenance of God’s sweetness. There, therefore, this bread will not be daily, as it is requested here, but one; that is, it will not, as here, now be absent and now present, but in one and the same manner will sufficiently and unceasingly satisfy for ever.

It should further be noted that, when you ask for bread, you comprehend everything necessary for the support both of body and soul, as provision for your pilgrimage, which you request from the Creator. And note that it says “this day,” as though meaning the day of the present life, that is, as long as we are in this life.

The fifth petition is: “And forgive us our debts,” that is, the penalties due for sins, “as we forgive our debtors.” For unless we forgive those who sin against us, neither will God forgive us our sins.

The sixth petition is: “And lead us not,” that is, do not permit us to be led and to fall into temptation. It is not evil to be tempted; rather, temptation is an opportunity of victory for the good. Therefore here alone we pray that we may not be led into temptation, that is, that we may not be conquered.

The seventh petition is what follows: “But deliver us from evil.” As though saying: Do not merely permit us not to be led in, but also deliver us from those temptations into which we have already been led.

This seventh petition is sung aloud by the choir, which thereby shows that it has prayed with the priest. For it had been invited to do so when the priest said before the Lord’s Prayer, “Let us pray.” Then the priest adds “Amen,” in confirmation of all the foregoing petitions.

When the priest says, “Graciously grant peace in our days,” he receives from the deacon the paten, which the deacon had held until “Our bread,” and places it upon the altar in order to make the fraction upon it. We, however, make this fraction over the chalice as a precaution. The third part, which is placed in the chalice, is propitiation for the living; and the work of blood and flesh expiates—that flesh mingled with the blood. One of the remaining parts is propitiation for the faithful departed, who need our prayers because they are still held in punishments; the other is thanksgiving for those already triumphant.

Pope Sergius, however, speaks differently on these matters. He wishes the mingling of the body and blood to signify the union of Christ’s body and soul effected in the resurrection. For he says thus: “The part of the offering placed in the chalice shows the body of Christ which has already risen; the part consumed, Christ walking upon the earth; the part laid upon the altar until the end of the Mass, the members of Christ—that is, the bodies of the saints—resting in graves until the end of the age.”

## CHAPTER XL. Why peace is given before communion

[Col. 0437A]

Peace is fittingly given before communion, because whoever presumes to communicate before being reconciled with a brother eats and drinks judgment upon himself (I Cor. XI).

“Agnus Dei” is sung three times, so that the true Lamb, whose flesh and blood we receive, may be gracious to us. First we ask that he have mercy on us by remitting sins; second, that he have mercy on us by making us devoted to him; third, that he may deign to grant us peace. This peace begins here in the saints and will be perfected in the blessed life. These three things are requested by the three preceding Actions.

As a sign of this peace, the priest first gives the kiss to the deacon, and the deacon to the subdeacon, and he to the others. For Christ brought peace to the world, which he first announced to the greater ones, namely the apostles, and then through them to the lesser. Hence: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people” (Ps. LXXI).

## CHAPTER XLI. On communion

The Communion chant, which we sing after the saving food, is thanksgiving, according to the saying: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord” (Ps. XXI).

[Col. 0438A]

The prayer at the end of Mass is said so that those returning to their own affairs may be fortified by the prayers of the Church, lest they be ensnared by the allurements of the world. When the deacon says, “Let us bless the Lord,” he invites the people to thanksgiving. Yet on feast days on which the splendid tokens of Christ’s mercy are recalled and “Glory to God in the highest” is sung, the deacon says, “Go, the dismissal is made,” expressing the dignity of the matter with a solemn utterance.

The sense is: Go, as though, return to your own affairs; but lest, just as you are free from earthly labours, so you also be free from honourable thoughts, the dismissal has been made which you have heard. “You have sat at the table of a rich man; remember to prepare like things for him” (Ecclus. XXXI).

From this sending, that is, dismissal, they say that the Mass is called *missa*; or from sending in the sense of an embassy,

[Col. 0438B]

because in it Christ’s embassy is represented; or because in it the priest performs an embassy to God on our behalf. Or it is called from sending because in it the catechumens and those who ought not to be present at the sacraments are sent outside.

# BOOK III. ON THE SPECIAL OBSERVANCES OF MASSES ACCORDING TO THE VARIETY OF TIMES AND OCCASIONS

[Col. 0437]

## CHAPTER I. On the office in the fasts of the Four Seasons

Having spoken, with such brevity as we could preserve, about the office of the Mass, we turn our pen to the special observances performed in the Mass according to the changing seasons.

It must therefore be known that, through the Four Seasons of the year—namely spring, summer, autumn, and winter—in which we all have sinned in many ways, the primitive Church established four fasts to be celebrated, so that, abstaining more or less according to the measure of their crimes, different persons might bewail their sins.

Each of these fasts is performed over a period of forty days. The rationale of these four fasts and of the forty days in each is gathered both from the Gospel and from the Law. From the Gospel, because the Lord fasted forty days; from the Law, because Moses twice abstained from all food for forty days. Likewise Elijah remained fasting for forty days. Behold four fasts, each of forty days. Therefore the Church celebrates fasts in each of the Four Seasons over the span of forty days, which are specifically called the fasts of the Four Seasons.

The Church customarily celebrates them for the ordination of ministers. Hence fasts are kept on the days of Pentecost themselves, when the festival of the sevenfold Spirit and of the newly baptized is celebrated.

[Col. 0439B]

Concerning these Bede says in his Homily: “That the discipline of fasting is repeated amid these things, we ought to believe is taken from the example of the apostles themselves. Having received the Spirit, by whom they enjoyed more perfectly the new sweetness of heavenly goods, they lifted their minds all the more above the memory of earthly delights. For now that time had come of which the Lord had foretold, when people asked why his disciples did not fast: ‘The days will come,’ he says, ‘when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they shall fast’” (Matt. IX).

Each of the Four-Season fasts has three days, on account of the three months belonging to each of the Four Seasons of the year. Thus one day is assigned to fasting for each month: namely the fourth, sixth, and seventh feria—that is, Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Wednesday, because on that day the Jews formed the plan to kill Christ;

[Col. 0439C]

Friday, when they killed him; and Saturday, because the fast is concluded in the Roman manner on account of the apostles’ sorrow over the Lord’s death, as Innocent relates in the Decretals:

“Reason most clearly demonstrates that Saturday ought to be fasted; for if, because of the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, we celebrate the Lord’s Day not only at Easter but also regularly through every cycle of weeks as an image of that day, and if we ourselves fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not omit Saturday, which seems enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time.”

## CHAPTER II. Why two Lessons are read at Mass on Wednesday, one on Friday, and four on the Saturday of the Four Seasons

[Col. 0439D]

On Wednesday two Lessons are read at Mass, because in the fourth age of the world, namely from David to the Babylonian captivity, both law and prophecy flourished; and those who are to be ordained ought to be admonished to possess knowledge of the law and the prophets. On Friday one is read, because law and prophecy are recapitulated in the one Gospel, which is read in the sixth age of the world.

On Saturday, however, when ordinations take place, four Lessons are read, because there are four orders of those who bless God, which the Psalmist enumerates, saying: “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord” (Ps. CXXXIV).

Augustine explains these blessings thus in his book on the Psalter: “‘Bless the Lord, peoples’: this is the house of Israel generally. ‘Bless, rulers’: this is the house of Aaron. ‘Bless, ministers’: this is the house of Levi. ‘You from the remaining nations who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.’ Therefore let us all say with one voice what follows: ‘Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem’” (ibid.).

Therefore in these four Lessons those to be ordained are invited to imitate the footsteps of the ancient Fathers, who are distinguished by the aforesaid four orders, if four are to be named; the first of these includes all, while the remaining divide them into parts.

After those four, the reading concerning the fiery furnace is read next before ordination, because no one can rightly approach consecration unless he has first passed through the furnace. “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. XXVII).

The Tract displays the gravity and humility which the ordained person ought to preserve. For the Tract, because it is customarily celebrated in a time of humility, is always set in a matter of humility. The Epistle follows, which is, as it were, the sixth Lesson. Among the ancient Romans these six Lessons were read both in Greek and in Latin, because not all knew Latin and not all Greek. Hence, according to the number of readers, they were said to perform twelve Lessons.

## CHAPTER III. On the Prayer over the People in the season of Lent

In the Lenten season, beyond those things inserted in the office of the Mass at other times, a final blessing is added, entitled the Prayer over the People,

[Col. 0440C]

because, if at every time it is necessary to be ready against the adversary, how much more so when battle is imminent? In the Lenten season, our adversary knows that the Church is preparing for conflict against him; and therefore he presses more fiercely to seize someone, should he perhaps find any person negligent.

But the priest, as a wise combatant, sees Christ’s soldiers to be in greater danger and therefore protects them with a more ample blessing. And because the greater the devotion, the more beneficial the blessing, the deacon cries out that we should humble our heads before God, and then the priest adds the blessing.

In the Lenten season Alleluia is not sung, since it always sounds joy, as the following verses of *Pneuma* clearly show; but in place of Alleluia the Tract is sung.

[Col. 0440D]

The Tract both in its wording and in its chant expresses tribulation and labour: for example, “Out of the depths”; “You have moved”; “He who dwells”; “To you I have lifted up,” and so forth. Yet because in the resurrection we shall rejoice with the saints if we now prepare ourselves by confession and penitence, after two Tracts of sorrow follows a third Tract sounding joy.

Or this is done for this reason: because in two periods, namely before the Law and under the Law, the human race was in sorrow; in the third, under grace, it breathed again in Christ in joy. “Out of the depths” and “You have moved” sound tribulation; “Rejoice,” however, sounds joy. Likewise, “He who dwells” and “To you I have lifted up” express sorrow; “Those who trust” offers the melody of joy. Similarly, “They have often assailed me” and “God, my God” express sorrow; “Praise” hymns joy.

## CHAPTER IV. Why songs of joy are silent in the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 0441A]

When the Advent of the Lord is celebrated, and in the Lenten season, we do not sing in church “Glory to God in the highest” or *Te Deum*, nor are the dalmatic and the subdeacon’s vestment worn. For all these display joy.

The season of Advent recalls that time in which the Messiah was awaited, and the living lamented the great delay of his coming, as did the dead who were held in hell. But the season of Lent, beginning with Septuagesima itself, recalls our captivity, in which the human race, expelled from paradise, lived in exile under the devil as prince, until through Jesus the great priest it was led back to Jerusalem in this figure of our redemption.

[Col. 0441B]

Since, therefore, both seasons are seasons of sorrow, in both we abstain from those things which display joy; yet not equally, because in Lent Alleluia is altogether silent, which is not the case in Advent.

Finally, all these things are omitted in the aforesaid seasons so that they may be embraced more festively at the Nativity of the Lord and on the day of the Resurrection, and so that the grace of the New Testament may be known to excel the Old. As often as “Glory to God in the highest” is not said at Mass, so often “Go, the dismissal is made” is silent, because in a time of mourning and penitence it is more fitting in the Church to remember miseries, bewail sins, and bless God, the author of grace. Thus at the end of Mass “Let us bless the Lord” is said, as though through him we hope to be delivered from the present misery.

## CHAPTER V. Why three Masses are celebrated at the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0441C]

Before the Law and under the Law, Christ was already sacrificed in figure, as is written concerning him in the Apocalypse: “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Apoc. XIII). But in the time of grace he was truly offered for the salvation of the world.

Therefore, that the truth may be considered more credible through remembrance of the figures, since, as it is written, “In this the saying is true: one is the sower and another the reaper” (John IV), the Church established that once a year, namely at the Nativity of the Lord, Mass should be celebrated three times within the course of the Nativity day: first in the night, second at dawn, third in the daytime.

The time before the Law was like night, illuminated neither by law nor prophecies nor by any other light of preaching.

[Col. 0441D]

The time under the Law was like dawn, neither entirely lacking light nor possessing it fully. The time of grace is compared to full day. The first Mass commemorates the time before the Law; the second, the time under the Law, because in both Christ’s sacrifice preceded in figure. In the third Mass the true light is shown to have come, when it is said, “A child is born to us” (Isa. IX), and so forth.

At other times Mass is prescribed to be celebrated only once a day, because, with the figures having ceased, the truth remains. But in the time of figures, indeed because of the figures themselves, the solemnities of Masses are commemorated at the Nativity of the Lord and not at another time, because the Lord’s Nativity was the beginning of the time of grace. Hence at the very beginning of the time of grace, the preceding times which bore Christ’s figures and signs

[Col. 0442A]

must be called to mind.

## CHAPTER VI. Why two Masses are celebrated in some churches on the feast of Blessed John the Baptist

It is read in the Gospel of Luke that Blessed John the Baptist was filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb (Luke I). Therefore at the beginning of daylight, as though at the beginning of his Nativity, sacrifice is offered to God in his honour, in praise of the Creator who deigned to honour him from his mother’s womb.

Blessed John the Baptist shone forth pre-eminently with three distinguished triumphs. For he came to prepare the way for the Lord by the example of his manner of life; this triumph is celebrated in the vigil. He shone conspicuously through the ministry of baptism. The triumph of this ministry is recalled in the first Mass.

[Col. 0442B]

Moreover, he remained a Nazirite from his mother’s womb. This gift is recalled in the second Mass of the day.

## CHAPTER VII. On the repetition of words in the verses of the Offertory, “There was a man”

In the Offertory, “There was a man in the land” (Job I), there is no repetition of words. But in the verses there is. The words of the historian are contained in the Offertory; the words of Job, sick and grieving, are contained in the verses. Therefore the author of the office, in order that suffering Job might be recalled to us with feeling, repeated the words in the verses after the manner of the sick.

## CHAPTER VIII. Why the song of joy is silent on the feast of the Innocents

At the solemnity of the Innocents we do not sing at Mass “Glory to God in the highest,” nor Alleluia, unless it falls on the Lord’s Day, so that in some manner we may conform ourselves to the mothers mourning the death of their children.

[Col. 0442C]

Or we abstain on this day from voices of joy because the souls of the Innocents descended to the lower regions, as did the souls of all who died before Christ’s Passion. Yet because that day falls within the days of the Nativity of the Lord, we do not omit the dalmatic and the subdeacon’s vestment.

## CHAPTER IX. Why ministers of the altar wear chasubles in Advent and Lent

In the days of the Advent of the Lord and of Lent, the ministers do not use such vestments but chasubles. Yet when they undertake their proper office, they remove their chasubles, because in their proper office—that is, in reading the Epistle or Gospel—they represent those sent by the Lord to preach.

The chasuble signifies such works as cannot be observed on the journey. For by its width it signifies the breadth of charity. This is required in speaking, for which reason it surrounds the neck; in acting, because it is folded over both arms; in thinking, because it covers the breast; and in bearing the burdens of others, because it encompasses the shoulders. But these things cannot be observed on the journey.

Hence Bede, in his Treatise on Luke: “But thirst, hunger, vigils, nakedness, reading, psalmody, prayer, the labour of work, teaching, silence, and so forth—if anyone thinks that such things must always be performed, he will not only deprive himself of their fruit, but will incur the reproach of indiscreet obstinacy, indeed of stubborn folly.”

[Col. 0443A]

Accordingly, stripped of their chasubles, the subdeacon and deacon perform their respective offices. First the subdeacon, in remembrance of those seventy-two whom Jesus sent into every town and place where he himself was about to come (Luke X); afterward the deacon, in remembrance of the apostles who were sent to preach the Gospel.

Hence, as a more notable sign of perfection, although the subdeacon performs his office without a chasuble, the deacon bears his chasuble folded over his left shoulder, so that in this life, which is signified by the left side, he may signify himself ready to bear the burdens of his brothers, and not wholly devoid, even on the journey, of the works signified by the chasuble.

But since we have undertaken to discuss the special observances of Masses, we have judged it fitting to insert something also concerning the observances of times with which those ecclesiastical observances accord.

## CHAPTER X. On Septuagesima

Septuagesima is reckoned from nine weeks before the Lord’s Easter and ends on the Saturday after Easter. It begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday. For it signifies the captivity of God’s people, who by sinning departed from God and by his mercy return to rest.

God’s people were held captive in Babylon under the number of seventy years; when these were completed, they returned to Jerusalem. Hence Jeremiah: “All these nations shall serve the king of Babylon seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will visit punishment upon the king of Babylon” (Jer. XXVII), and so forth.

[Col. 0443C]

This captivity of the Israelite people, however, signifies the common captivity of the human race, which began in paradise, as though on the Lord’s Day, and will have its end in eternal rest, understood under the name of Sabbath.

Therefore, because in Septuagesima both the captivity of the Israelite people and our captivity are signified—which is to endure throughout the whole time of the world through the sevenfold cycle of days—we, together with the Israelite people, omit the voice of joy and gladness, as though hanging our instruments upon the willows with them; and by abstaining from delights we show how the Christian ought to live during the whole period of the age.

For by seventy, just as by seven, the whole time of the age is understood, since it turns in the sevenfold cycle of days. For every number signifies the same as that from which it is named: thus fifty is the same as five, and seventy the same as seven.

[Col. 0443D]

It should be noted, however, that in the seventy years of the Jewish captivity the time of return is understood. Thus near the end of Septuagesima, namely at the feast of the Resurrection, through which we return to the heavenly homeland, we sing Alleluia and do not omit the Gradual, because we are still on the way and have not yet reached the homeland, and we are still advancing. On the following Saturday, however, we sing a double Alleluia, as though already established in the homeland and rejoicing in the twofold garment of body and soul.

The institutor of the offices wishes us in these days to be anxious through tribulation, not dissolved in joy. For he says in the Introit: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell found me” (Ps. CIV). Augustine on the Psalm: “In those who surrounded me

[Col. 0444A]

to destroy me there were pains of envy, which work death and lead down to hell. Because of these pains we may rejoice and be secure, but we must prepare ourselves for battle.” Hence the Apostle: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things” (I Cor. IX). And in the first prayer of the Mass it is said thus: “That we who are justly afflicted for our sins,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XI. On Sexagesima

Sexagesima runs within Septuagesima up to Wednesday of Easter week. This Wednesday recalls the fourth age, in which David and Solomon reigned. In that age, that people—renowned in faith, glorious in the kingdom of David and Solomon, and splendid in the height and beauty of the Temple—prefigured the future kingdom of Christ, in which living stones, polished in this valley as though of stone-cutters, will be placed in the one temple of the Lord.

Hence Wednesday of Easter week, in signification of this matter, has the office: “Come, ye blessed of my Father” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

[Col. 0444B]

Toward that kingdom one must strive through sixty, that is, through perfection of works, which is designated by six. For the number six, which is a perfect number because it consists of the sum of all its parts, signifies perfection. And because the Lord completed his works in this number of days, it also conveys the meaning of activity. Thus six, or Sexagesima, signifies perfect activity, through which we ought to tend toward our homeland.

But because of ourselves we are powerless, having been sold under sin from the beginning of our Septuagesima, we ask the Lord in the Introit of the Mass to deliver us through himself from our present exile: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII), and so forth. The following prayer accords with this: “O God, who perceivest that we subsist by no strength of our own,” and so forth.

The Apostle in his Epistle strengthens us not to yield to evils: “You gladly bear with fools,” and so forth (II Cor. XI). The Tract, “You have moved,” shows the earth shaken by consciousness of sins. After the earth has been shaken, seed is introduced in the Gospel: “A sower went out,” and so forth (Luke VIII). In Septuagesima we were rebuked because we stood idle; in Sexagesima we sow the seed.

## CHAPTER XII. On Quinquagesima

[Col. 0444D]

Quinquagesima follows, ending on Easter Day itself, because through the works of the five senses one must strive toward the glory of the resurrection. Since our senses can easily be seized by the various enticements and pleasures of the world, and the instruments of the senses themselves are as it were windows through which death enters the soul unless a guard is set, therefore in Quinquagesima, as in a campaign, we anxiously say in the Introit of the Mass: “Be to me a protecting God and a place of refuge,” and so forth (Ps. XXX).

We pray to him as the leader of our warfare, saying: “And for thy name’s sake thou wilt be my guide and nourish me” (ibid.). The Apostle in the Epistle teaches us how we ought to be loved, and says: “But now remain faith, hope, charity,” and so forth (I Cor. XIII).

God is the victor of our warfare, to whom we say

[Col. 0445A]

in the Responsory: “Thou art the God who dost wonders” (Ps. LXXVI). And again: “Thou hast delivered thy people by thy arm” (ibid.). The Tract commands us to serve God, not him to whom we sold ourselves.

In Sexagesima we sowed; in Quinquagesima, in the Gospel, we gather the fruit. For we are that blind man who received from the Lord what he devoutly requested.

Three stages, therefore, should be noted in these three Sundays. The first Sunday contains the lament of captives unwilling to remain under the dominion of vices. The second shows the will to flee, while they think the Lord asleep, not yet secure in his assistance, and say: “Arise; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. XLIII). As though saying: Unless you arise and come to us, we shall flee. The third Sunday takes counsel as to how they may fortify themselves; in it they no longer address the Lord as though asleep, saying: “Be to me a protecting God” (Ps. XXX).

## CHAPTER XIII. On Lent

Lent, which begins on the following Sunday, ends on the Wednesday before Easter, which is called the Lord’s Supper. If you add the two following days to these forty days, there will be forty-two days up to the solemn baptism. For by so many stages the children of Israel reached the land of promise. Likewise, by the reckoning of so many generations in the Gospel of Matthew one reaches Christ, with Jeconiah counted twice.

[Col. 0445C]

In Lent, those who fight manfully should place confidence in God’s help. Hence he whom we invoked as protector in Quinquagesima says to us: “He shall call upon me, and I will hear him,” and so forth. The first Epistle says: “In an acceptable time I heard thee, and in the day of salvation I helped thee” (II Cor. VI). In the Responsory: “May the angels of the Lord guard us.” In the Tract: “We are surrounded with the shield of truth.” In the Gospel we press toward triumph, so that we may say to the enemy: “Get behind me, Satan.”

The number forty signifies the whole time of our life, on account of the four seasons of the year in which we live, or on account of the four elements by whose harmony we live. But it is asked why the Lord began his fast soon after baptism, while we defer the Lenten fast, which we observe in commemoration of his, until a time adjacent to Christ’s Passion. This is done so that by the observance of Lent we may be made more worthy for receiving the Paschal Lamb, which whoever receives unworthily, according to the Apostle,

[Col. 0445D]

eats and drinks judgment of condemnation upon himself (I Cor. XI [source reads II]).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the beginning of the Lenten fast

On Wednesday between Quinquagesima and Lent we begin the fast that extends to the Lord’s Easter. Until this day we were in expectation. On this day we join battle. This is shown by the first Collect of the Mass, which says: “Grant us, O Lord, to begin the safeguards of Christian warfare with holy fasts.”

Joel shows with what weapons we ought to fight: “With fasting and weeping and mourning,” and so forth (Joel II [source reads VI]). And the Gospel: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,” and so forth (Matt. VI).

There is no other variation on this day, except that until this day Mass is celebrated at the third hour; on this day and thereafter until Easter, except on Sundays, at the ninth hour.

[Col. 0446A]

Some hold that the Lenten fast is begun on this day because, with Sundays subtracted, only forty days remain from the aforesaid Wednesday until Saturday. But there is another, perhaps stronger, reason. Since in fasting we labour to prepare ourselves as a temple for the Lord to dwell in, we abstain from the customary pleasures of food for the same number of days as the number of years in which the Temple in Jerusalem was built, namely forty-six.

For construction of the Temple was begun in the first year of King Cyrus and completed in the sixth year of Darius. These are, according to the account of the Chronicles, forty-five years: Cyrus reigned thirty years; after him his son Cambyses, eight years; after him the Magi who killed him, one year; after them Darius, six years up to the completion of the Temple. These are, as we have said, forty-five years.

[Col. 0446B]

Yet in the Gospel the Jews are found saying: “This temple was built in forty-six years” (John II), although no more than forty-five are found. But if we follow the history of Josephus, in which he adds three more years after the completion of the Temple, during which the *peribolus*, that is, the defensive construction surrounding the Temple, and certain other things that remained were completed, we shall see that a total of forty-six years can rightly be reckoned in the building of the Temple, during which the more prominent buildings were completed.

There is no variation in the office of the Mass from the aforesaid day until Wednesday of the fourth week.

## CHAPTER XV. Why the scrutiny is celebrated in the fourth week and on Wednesday
On the Wednesday of the fourth week of Lent the solemn scrutiny is celebrated, which is the approach to baptism. On this day those to be baptized are instructed as catechumens. Catechesis contains a twofold instruction: namely, concerning faith and morals. Hence in the Mass, in the first Lesson, which is read from Ezekiel, it is shown how God gathers the catechumens into the unity of Christ’s body, rescuing them from their former life and causing them to believe in Christ. For thus it is read there: “I will take you from among the nations and gather you from all lands, and I will bring you into your own land; and I will pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed [Col. 0446D] from all your defilements, and from all your idols I will cleanse you; and I will give you a new heart,” etc. (Ezek. 36). Jerome explains this passage from Ezekiel as follows: “For I am the Creator of all things; I spared them and sanctified them, and restored them to their former glory, so that upon those who believed and were converted from error I might pour the clean water of saving baptism, cleanse them from all their abominations and from all the errors by which they had been occupied, and give them a new heart so that they might believe in the Son of God.” Thus the first Lesson treats of faith. The Responsory agrees with it: “Come, children, listen to me” (Ps. 33 [34]).

But the second Lesson discusses morals, in which it is said: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good; [Col. 0447A] seek judgment; assist the oppressed” (Isa. 1). And its conclusion is: “Come, and rebuke me, says the Lord” (ibid.). That is: if you do these things and I do not render you your reward, you will rightly rebuke me. The following Responsory shows that catechumens ought to pass over to the Christian name: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as his inheritance” (Ps. 32 [33]). The verse shows the good morals of the elect: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (ibid.). The Gospel is not at variance with this office. Augustine says in his commentary on John: “Therefore the blind man washed his eyes in the pool which is interpreted ‘Sent’; he was baptized in Christ. Thus, when he in some manner baptized him in himself, he then gave him sight; when he anointed [Col. 0447B] his eyes, perhaps he made him a catechumen.”

This office is celebrated on the Wednesday of the fourth week so that the fourth age of the world may be recalled. As Bede attests in his Chronicle, the fourth age of the world extended from David to the Exile. That age, illustrious through the reigns of David and Solomon, prefigured our glory in Christ. In it too the promise of our glory was made, when the Lord said to David: “From the fruit of your womb I will set one upon your throne” (Ps. 131 [132]). In it the building of the Temple from marble and precious stones foreshadowed the establishment of the Church, gathered from all nations through Christ. The scrutiny is rightly celebrated on the Wednesday of the fourth week, and those to be baptized at the holy Sabbath of Easter are instructed concerning faith and morals, [Col. 0447C] because the fourth age of humankind is suited to labours. Those who wish to enter God’s service must devote themselves to labours. Hence Solomon: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). From the day named above until the Saturday before Palm branches, no variation is to be shown.

## Chapter XVI. Concerning the Office of the Saturday Entitled “Saturday Is Free”

Concerning the Saturday before Palm branches, whose heading is found in ancient antiphonaries—“Saturday is free; the lord pope also gives alms”—books of our own age, for brevity’s sake, simply read: “Saturday is free.” The founder of the Church’s office assigned no proper office to this day [Col. 0447D] in order to show that he devoted himself on this day to almsgiving and invited posterity to do the same. On this day in particular the apostolic man willed that both he and we should devote ourselves to charitable giving, in memory of that most devout woman, so that we may endeavour to render to the members what she did on this day for the head.

John the Evangelist says: “Six days before Passover, the Lord Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been dead, whom he raised. They made him a supper there” (John 12). And a little later: “Mary therefore took a pound of costly genuine nard ointment, and anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the scent of the ointment” (ibid.). When Judas the traitor objected, the Lord, according to Matthew, approved the woman’s deed thus: “Why do you trouble [Col. 0448A] this woman? For she has done a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me” (Matt. 26).

Therefore let us too anoint the Lord’s feet: that is, let us give the poor of Christ consolations through compassion. For the poor are called the Lord’s feet because they are his members in a still lowly position; and by ointment may quite properly be understood the consolations which soothe minds. Likewise, to wipe the Lord’s feet with one’s hair is to assist the poor from what is superfluous to us. For hair appears to be a superfluity of the body.

## Chapter XVII. Concerning the Office of the Mass on the Wednesday after Palm Sunday

On the Wednesday after Palm Sunday there is variation in the office of the Mass through the addition of one Lesson and one Responsory with five verses, [Col. 0448B] because on that same day the Jews took counsel to put Jesus to death. Therefore, just as their act is recalled on Friday, so their counsel is recalled on Wednesday. Thus on this weekday, as also on Friday, two Lessons are read, because Christ by his single death destroyed our twofold death, namely that of body and soul.

The Introit is: “At the name of the Lord let every knee bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). This means: let every rational creature recognize itself as subject to Christ, “because the Lord became obedient,” etc. (ibid.); that is, because Christ by obedience and humility deserved to possess the same glory as the Father—not receiving it as something due to himself without merits, but accomplishing a work worthy of so great a reward. When it says, “at the name of the Lord,” this is to be understood as “in veneration of the name,” that is, of the thing designated by the name. Similarly, the Psalm says: “I will give thanks for ever because you have acted, and I will await your name, because it is good,” etc. (Ps. 51 [52]). [Col. 0448C] Ambrose, in his Epistle to the Philippians, testifies that by the name the thing named is understood. He says: “It is evident that ‘name’ does not mean a word, but some reality acquired by him, as in what is written: ‘Let them know that your name is Lord’” (Ps. 82 [83]); that is, “that you are Lord.”

In the Collect the Lord’s Passion is recalled, because on that day the Jews took counsel concerning his death. The following Lesson openly proclaims the Lord’s Passion, saying: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open [Col. 0448D] his mouth” (Isa. 53). And shortly afterward: “If he lays down his life as a sin-offering, he shall see a long-lived seed” (ibid.). Isaiah says of this seed: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we should have been like Sodom” (Isa. 1). The seed consists of the apostles and apostolic men, through whom, as though seed had been sown, the harvest of the Church is multiplied. This seed is called long-lived through succession, or in itself, because the righteous shall live forever.

The Responsory is: “Do not turn your face from your servant” (Ps. 68 [69]), words of Christ to the Father. The Psalmist calls Christ a servant because of his simplicity and innocence. The verse reads: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul; I am fixed fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground” (ibid.). By the name of waters he signifies the multitude of peoples, as also in Revelation: “The waters which you see are peoples and nations” (Rev. 17). These waters entered as far as the soul of Christ in order to take it away, by Christ’s own will, when they killed him. He calls these same people the mire of the deep, in which Christ says that he is fixed fast, preserving the metaphor of mire: that is, that he is held fast in the body. [Col. 0449A]

The second Lesson, like the first, treats of the Lord’s Passion. The following Responsory should not be called a Tract, as some suppose, but a Responsory, because after each verse the choir responds. It has five verses, to indicate that the sins committed by the five senses of the old Adam were destroyed by the Passion of the new Adam. For it is the voice of the old Adam that sounds in those verses.

## Chapter XVIII. Concerning the Office of Thursday before Good Friday

[Col. 0449B]

On Thursday before Good Friday there are many variations, not in the office of the Mass but in the Office. On it oil is consecrated in three ways. On it the Lord’s body is reserved until the following day. Oil for the sick is consecrated in the very office for consecrating the body and blood of the Lord. For illnesses are inflicted because of sins. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel to one who asks for healing: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2). For when sins are forgiven, that which had been inflicted because of sins is also driven out. The sacrament of the Lord’s body drives out sins, whereas consecrated oil drives out illnesses—that is, by divine grace through anointing with oil. James therefore says: “Is anyone among you ill? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and prayer shall save the sick man, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him” (Jas. 5). And in the consecration itself you have: “For removing all pains, every infirmity, and every sickness of the body.” [Col. 0449C] Their consecration is therefore fittingly performed in a similar way, since their effects are joined together in many respects.

Yet both—the sacrament of the Lord’s body and consecrated oil—have both effects, although because their sacramental forms differ, we distinguish them in words. For in the old Law flesh and blood were offered for sins, whereas oil was used to heal weary and sick limbs. But the Apostle, speaking of Christ, says: “He died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (1 Cor. 15). Thus he divided the effects, assigning to each sacrament what it signifies, although Christ did both for both purposes.

The consecration of oil for the sick is thus performed in the very office of consecrating the Lord’s body, before the words of the Canon, “Through whom, O Lord, you always create all these good things”; and these same words are the conclusion of that consecration. We therefore understand that there is an embolism—a supplementary prayer—of the aforesaid office after the *Agnus Dei*, when the sign of peace is usually given; on this day it is not given because of the kiss of Judas the traitor.

Chrism is consecrated, and afterwards the oil of catechumens follows, because by these two a human being is restored to the peace and concord of the angels. The exorcism of the oil causes the devil to withdraw from the catechu- [Col. 0450A] men; the anointing with chrism sanctifies him and gives him graces, or increases those already possessed. The consecration of oil is celebrated on Thursday because whatever is committed by the five senses—namely sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—is erased through God’s grace in anointing with oil.

## Chapter XIX. Why the Altars Are Stripped on the Same Day

On the same day the altars are stripped and left so until evening. This, unless I am mistaken, signifies the flight of the apostles. For the altar signifies Christ, while the apostles and other disciples are Christ’s garments, concerning whom it is written: “And leaving him, they all fled” (Matt. 26).

## Chapter XX. Concerning the Office of Friday, Why It Is Called *Parasceve*, and Why the Altars Are Washed with Water and Wine on This Day

[Col. 0450B]

*Parasceve*, as Bede says, means “preparation.” By this name the Jews living among Greeks called the sixth day of the Sabbath, because on that day they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath. This Friday corresponds to the sixth day of creation. For it was fitting that on the day on which God created man, he should recreate and redeem the one who had been lost.

On this day the Lessons concerning the sacrifice of the Lamb are read. For on this day we recall Christ’s Passion and offer the imitation we owe him when we pray, on behalf of humankind, for human beings, as he did for those who crucified him. It should be noted that just as the body of the Lord Jesus, which he assumed from the Virgin, was signified by the spotless lamb, so his body—which we are—is signified by the kid. Both are mentioned by the Lesson. The Lamb was sacrificed on the cross; the kid is daily sacrificed in the mortification of vices.

The Tract, “He who dwells in the aid of the Most High” (Ps. 90 [91]), is long because what the preceding Lesson from Hosea sets before us must be held in hope, though it is far off before we possess it in reality. The words of the Lesson are: “After two days he will visit us; on the third day he will raise us, and we shall live in his sight” (Hos. 6). The resurrection itself is mentioned at the end of the Tract: “With length of days I will satisfy him, and I will show him my salvation” (Ps. 90 [91]). [Col. 0450C]

It is asked why Mass is not sung on this day, but the body of Christ reserved on the preceding day is received. The answer, from a decree of Pope Innocent, is that Mass is not celebrated during these two days, so that the condition at that time of the apostles may be shown in the pastors of the Church: as the prophet foretold, when the shepherd was struck, they were scattered (Zech. 13). Hence neither “The Lord be with you” nor “O God, come to my assistance” is said on these days, nor anything else belonging to the office of presbyters.

It is asked again why Christ’s blood is not received on this day, as his flesh is. I answer that both are received under either species. But since the perishable species of wine cannot safely be reserved, it was ordained that Christ’s body should be reserved without it; or this may be because the Lord said at supper: “I shall not drink henceforth of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in [Col. 0451A] my kingdom” (Matt. 26). The Church is not accustomed, from the day of the supper until Easter Day—which begins in the evening, whence it is said in the blessing of the candle, “This is the night which [delivers] sinners,” etc.—to drink of this fruit of the vine.

Moreover, Christ was speaking of his own blood which he was offering his disciples; in respect of its species, he called it “fruit.” After his resurrection he himself drank it new with his disciples in his kingdom, that is, in royal splendour, because in the resurrection the whole Christ was renewed in respect of his bodily substance. But he said that he would drink it with his disciples, not because he bodily drank it after the resurrection, but because he delighted in the offering of his disciples when they partook, as he had commanded, of his body and blood in remembrance of him. Yet what he said—“I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” etc. (Mark 14)—may be understood simply of wine, so that the demonstrative pronoun does not point to what Christ held, but to the species: as if he said, “I shall not drink of fruit of the vine of such a kind,” such in species. Hence another Evangelist, without the demonstrative pronoun, says: “I shall not drink of the produce of the vine until the kingdom of God comes,” etc. (Luke 22). For after the resurrection we read that he both ate and drank with his disciples. Thus Peter says: “We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead” (Acts 10). [Col. 0451B]

It should be noted that on this day, in the prayers which the Church offers in imitation of Christ, we bend the knee one by one, to show—or rather, to increase—the humility of the mind, except when we pray for the faithless Jews, who did this in mockery before the Lord. When we mention them, we wish to be unlike them in every respect in what they did to Christ on this day. On this day the altar is washed with wine and water, because Christ on this day sent forth water and blood from his side.

## Chapter XXI. What the Candle Set Up before Baptism on Easter Night Signifies

At the beginning of the office belonging to Easter night, on which Christ is believed to have risen, a candle is blessed. The candle recalls to us the pillar given by God to the people of Israel in the wilderness, which was to them a cloud protecting them from the heat by day and a pillar of fire giving light by night (Exod. 13). [Col. 0451D] That pillar and this candle are figures of Christ, who both protects from the heat of vices and imparts the light of wisdom. This benefit of Christ is promised to those being baptized and is not withdrawn from the baptized while they are on the way.

Thus the pillar was given to the people who were to cross the Red Sea as a figure of baptism, and our candle is raised and lit in the Church before the catechumens are baptized. Nor should this be passed over: just as the aforesaid pillar was given to the people at the third stopping-place after their departure from Egypt, so the candle is lit for us on the third day of our deliverance, which was accomplished in Christ’s death. For, as we have said, that evening belongs to the following day, and truly the ancients celebrated this office when the Sabbath day was now almost ended. [Col. 0452A] But the weakness of modern people, hurrying to festive meals, anticipates the appointed time. Therefore for us, departing from spiritual Egypt, the first day is Christ’s Passion; the second, the day on which he descended into hell; the third is the day of resurrection.

## Chapter XXII. Concerning the Office of Mass on Easter Night

On the night mentioned above, four Lessons are read at Mass. For catechumens are called to the Lord’s table, that is, to Holy Scripture, which was signified by the four-legged table placed in the Lord’s tabernacle. The four feet of the table are the four interpretations of Holy Scripture: historical, allegorical, moral, and anagogical. If you examine them closely, you can find these four in the four Lessons of this night.

The first, according to [Col. 0452B] history, recalls the dignity of our creation. Since we fell from it through sinning, no canticle follows. The second Lesson, according to allegory, concerns our deliverance from the exile into which we came through sin. For it deals with the liberation of the people of Israel from Egypt, in which our liberation from spiritual Egypt was prefigured. The third Lesson is moral: “Seven women shall seize one man on that day,” etc. (Isa. 4). For the seven women are the seven graces that are spiritually called the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence he is also called the sevenfold Spirit. The same Lesson also treats of the washing away of defilements; all this pertains to morals. It is a proper order that, after they have been instructed concerning baptismal cleansing, they should be instructed concerning morals.

The fourth [Col. 0452C] Lesson says: “Hear, you who hear me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in richness” (Isa. 4). Jerome explains this in his commentary on Isaiah: “The divine word promises not goods of the flesh, but of the soul.” This Lesson therefore has an anagogical sense, because under the names of bodily goods it promises heavenly goods. Hence Bede: “Anagoge is a sense leading upward; that is, a discourse which treats, in either mystical or open language, of future rewards and the future life which is in heaven.”

Let us hear what the catechumens say after the teacher’s admonition: “As a servant longs,” etc. (Ps. 41 [42]). Hence Augustine: “And indeed it is not wrongly understood as the voice of those who, being catechumens, hasten toward the grace of the holy washing.”

## Chapter XXIII. What the New Fire in the Candle Signifies

[Col. 0452D]

The candle is lit with new light, to signify Christ’s new teaching, which is in the New Testament, or the new grace by which that night—the night of the Lord’s resurrection—was preeminently illuminated.

## Chapter XXIV. Why the Titles of the Lessons Are Omitted on This Day

The titles are omitted at the beginnings of the Lessons lest the Lessons should become contemptible to catechumens coming from paganism when they hear the names of Hebrew authors or books; for there has always been, as it were, a natural hatred between Jews and Gentiles.

## Chapter XXV. Why the Litanies Are Performed Three Times

The litanies performed around the consecration of the baptistery [Col. 0453A] are the intercessions of the saints for those being reborn. They are performed before and after because, as is read in Revelation, “There was a rainbow around the throne of God” (Rev. 4). Bede explains this thus: “The throne of God is in the Church; the rainbow, which appeared after the Flood as a sign of propitiation, signifies the intercession of the saints.”

Seven antiphons are performed before baptism, so that the Holy Spirit, whose grace is sevenfold, may come into the water of baptism. Five are performed while the catechumens are baptized, so that God may deign to guard their five senses, lest they be captured by worldly allurements. Three are performed after baptism, so that they may keep with all their heart, all their mind, and all their strength the faith of the holy Trinity which they have professed.

## Chapter XXVI. That Infants Are Saved in the Faith of the Church

[Col. 0453B]

If those baptized are of an age to possess the use of reason and know how to speak, they themselves ought to profess their faith, and they are saved in their own faith. But if they are infants, they are believed to be saved in the faith and confession of those who offer them for baptism, or in the general faith of the Church; just as the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman is recorded as having been delivered from a demon through her mother’s faith and humble confession, when the Lord said: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Mark 7). And, as Matthew says, her daughter was healed from that hour (Matt. 15).

## Chapter XXVII. Why Easter Week Is Celebrated in White Garments

From this Saturday until the following Saturday, that is, for eight days, white garments are worn, to show [Col. 0453C] what sort of bodies we shall receive in the octave of the resurrection, and what sort we ought to be in the New Testament. For as seven days belong to the Old Testament because of the Sabbath, so eight belong to the New because of the eighth day of the resurrection. Hence Solomon: “Give portions to seven, and also to eight” (Eccles. 12). He was already teaching his people not always to cling to the Old Testament, but at some point to pass over to the New.

## Chapter XXVIII. Why the Introit Is Not Sung at Mass on Holy Saturday

The Introit is not sung at Mass on this day because the Lessons and the other things which precede take the place of the Introit—indeed, they are more than an Introit. “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2) is sung because of the joy [Col. 0453D] of the Lord’s resurrection. It should be noted that everything up to the Gospel pertains to the neophytes. In the Collect the priest says: “Preserve in the new offspring of your household the Spirit whom you have given.” The Epistle says: “Since you have risen with Christ, seek the things which are above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God” (Col. 3).

## Chapter XXIX. Why a Tract Is Sung after “Alleluia”

In the same Mass, *Alleluia* is first sung because of the joy of the Lord’s resurrection, in which hope of our own resurrection has been given to us. But because our resurrection, which we possess in hope, is still far off in reality, and we must strive toward it through difficulties, the Tract follows.

## Chapter XXX. Why Candles Are Not Carried before the Gospel

On that night no light is carried before the Gospel, [Col. 0454A] because the women went secretly and without a light to the tomb in order to anoint him, as the Gospel relates; or because of the blindness of their hearts, in their ignorance of the resurrection.

## Chapter XXXI. Why the “Agnus Dei” Is Not Sung in the Same Mass

On the same night the *Agnus Dei* is not sung, in commemoration of those women’s unbelief: because they did not believe him to be God, nor did they believe that he could take away the sins of the world. Yet the priest meanwhile performs his office, because while the women and even the disciples doubted the resurrection, Christ both rose and made himself manifest.

## Chapter XXXII. Concerning the Office of Holy Easter

On holy Easter Day, in the Introit Christ presents himself through the mouths of the prophets, risen from the dead, to his Father in his Church, saying: “I have risen, and I am still with you” (Ps. 138 [139]). [Col. 0454B] On this day and on the five following days, we sing a gradual at Mass because we still advance toward the glory which the Lord’s resurrection promises, and while advancing we praise God. Yet we rejoice in the attainment which we possess in hope, and therefore sing *Alleluia*.

But on Saturday we sing a double *Alleluia*, because the end of Septuagesima signifies the rest which will be the end of pilgrimage, when, adorned with the twofold robe of body and soul, we shall praise God for both. Likewise, on Sundays and feast days until the octave of Pentecost we sing two *Alleluia*s, in remembrance of the Lord’s resurrection and of our own, a figure of whose attainment has preceded [Col. 0454C] on the Saturday mentioned above. On other days we sing one *Alleluia* for the joy of our redemption.

## Chapter XXXIII. Why No Responsory Is Sung from Easter until Pentecost

From the octaves of Pentecost until Septuagesima, on Sundays and feast days, the Responsory and *Alleluia* signify the deeds and joy, praise, or thanksgivings of those who persevere in the holiness which they received in baptism. For they possess the future kingdom already in hope, so that amid laborious works they give thanks to God. Or, as others say, by the Responsory we understand the active life, and by *Alleluia* the contemplative life. People must be instructed in the goods of the active life—almsgiving, reading, visiting the sick, and the like. They must also be instructed in the goods [Col. 0454D] of the contemplative life—contemplation of eternal things and praise of God.

But in those days from Easter Saturday until the octaves of Pentecost, no Responsory is sung because that period prefigures our resurrection, when all shall be taught by God and every work of the active life shall cease; only *Alleluia* will be sung, that is, there will be joy of souls over immortality received and bodies recovered. The number fifty signifies the same joy, and among the Hebrews it is called the Jubilee.

## Chapter XXXIV. Why “Alleluia” Is Not Sung at Mass on Fast Days

Penitential days, vigils of the apostles, and other days on which we ought to confess our sins, humble ourselves, and fast, so that we may merit to attain the joy celebrated in the ensuing feast, are marked without *Alleluia*, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). [Col. 0455A]

## Chapter XXXV. Why Baptism Is Celebrated on the Vigil of Pentecost

Baptism is celebrated on the vigil of Pentecost because the Lord, about to ascend into heaven, promised his disciples, saying: “You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1), namely after ten days; and this was done. For this reason the Church celebrates baptism on the tenth day after the Ascension, so that our catechumens may be baptized in the Holy Spirit, just as the apostles themselves were.

The days of Pentecost begin on Easter Day itself and end on the fiftieth day, which is commonly called Pentecost Day. Hence on that day itself the Antiphon at Vespers is sung: “Today the days of Pentecost are fulfilled, Alleluia,” etc. On the vigil of this day, because of the catechumens, four Lessons are read. The first belongs to history, proposing Abraham’s obedience as an example. The second Lesson is: “Moses wrote the canticle.” But the singer immediately shows which canticle is meant here, namely, “Give ear, O heaven.” Both the Lesson and the canticle are to be expounded allegorically concerning Christ and the Church. The third Lesson is moral, in which the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit make of those who obey one man, of whom Paul said: “Until we all attain to the perfect man” (Eph. 4). [Col. 0455B] The fourth Lesson has an anagogical sense, inviting only to heavenly things. Behold the four feet of the Lord’s table to which the catechumens are called.

The litanies around baptism have been discussed above. *Alleluia* is sung because of the joy of the cleansing which the neophytes receive in baptism. But because the complete cleansing—namely from punishment as well as guilt, toward which one strives through this—is far off, and cannot be attained except through immense difficulties, the Tract follows.

## Chapter XXXVI. Concerning the Office of the Masses during Pentecost Week

[Col. 0456A]

What we ought to do throughout the whole week which begins on Pentecost Day, Bede declares in his Homily, saying: “But let no one suppose without due discernment and fitting reason of the mystery that this also is done: immediately after the fiftieth day has been completed, we do not bend our knees in prayer, but throughout that week still pray to the Lord standing; and although we resume the fasts which had been interrupted, nevertheless we daily resound with *Alleluia*. Since the grace of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold, the solemnity of his coming is rightly commemorated for seven days with the due praise of hymns together with the celebration of Masses.”

## Chapter XXXVII. Concerning the Office of the Mass for the Dead

[Col. 0456B]

In the Mass for the dead, neither “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2) nor *Alleluia*, which signify sweetness and joy, is sung, because songs of rejoicing do not suit those grieving the passing of a neighbour. For ministers of the altar ought, just as they rejoice with those who rejoice, also to weep with those who weep (Rom. 12). The kiss is not given here because, where we are accustomed to say, “Grant us peace,” in this office, being mindful as it were more of the dead than of ourselves, we say: “Grant them eternal rest.” For here we strive earnestly to assist those whom we know can merit nothing further in this life.

The anniversary day is repeated for the dead because we do not know what their condition may be in the other life. Hence, just as the anniversary day of saints is repeated in their honour, so the anniversary day of the dead is recalled for their benefit, should they perhaps be in need. Mass for the dead is customarily celebrated for thirty consecutive days, so that whatever they have sinned against in the Decalogue of the Law may be erased through the mercy of the Holy Trinity. For ten multiplied by three makes thirty.

[Col. 0455]

# Little Book on the Canon of the Mystical Libation and Its Orders, by, Apparently, John of Cornwall. (G)\*

## Chapter I. Concerning the Power of the Lord’s Cross

[Col. 0455C]

In the power of the holy cross and in the sacrament of the altar there is great correspondence and great efficacy, since through each contrary things are excluded, and the Church is renewed and sanctified. We are renewed in a twofold way [Col. 0456C]: first, that we may be stripped of oldness; then, that we may be clothed with newness. For it cannot happen that, while remaining in oldness, we are clothed with Christ’s newness; nor could what Paul said in the person of the weak be fulfilled: “We do not wish to be unclothed, but further clothed” (2 Cor. 5). Hence, when the sons of Zebedee asked that one might sit at the right hand and the other at the left, it was said: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20). As though he said: First, by suffering with me and dying with me, you must be stripped of oldness, so that afterwards you may be able to sit at my right or at my left—which is to be clothed with newness. “This is not mine to give to you,” that is, to those still old, “but to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (ibid.), that is, to those renewed.

Therefore the Lord Jesus himself first chose to suffer upon the lower wood, and then to be glorified upon the upper wood: that he might first strip us of oldness and then clothe us with his newness. For first he is read to have been crucified, then the title was set above him. Thus it is written: “Bearing his cross for himself, he went out to the place called Calvary [Col. 0457B], where they crucified him. Pilate also wrote a title and placed it upon the cross” (John 19).

For our oldness is sevenfold; and the power and efficacy of the holy cross are likewise sevenfold. There are four abominations of the body and three corruptions of the mind. Hence the prophet says: “They have been corrupted and made abominable” (Ps. 40). They have been corrupted in mind and made abominable in body. For they misuse the four elements in the body: fire in the eyes through curiosity; air in the tongue through loquacity; earth in the hands through wrongdoing, when we wickedly strike a brother with the fist; water in the emission of seed through lust. These are the things that cast a brother out of the cloister. Hence the prophet “went in to see” (Ps. 40): behold curiosity; “he spoke vanity” (ibid.): behold [Col. 0457C] loquacity; “his heart gathered wrongdoing to itself” (ibid.): behold wrongdoing; “he went out abroad” (ibid.): through lust.

We are also corrupted in mind by a threefold corruption: in natural reason, through pride; in desire, through avarice; in anger, through envy. Now the cross has four dimensions—breadth, length, height, and depth—and the title has three distinctions: “Jesus,” “Nazareth,” “King of the Jews” (John 19). Breadth of mercy was in Christ’s Passion; length of life in the Resurrection; height of glory in the Ascension; depth of wisdom in the hidden power by which he did all these things and by which he will also judge at the last day.

The depth of the cross was hidden, while the other things lay openly manifest. So too the power by which the Lord Jesus did all the things stated above is still hidden; but when he judges at the end, it will be manifest, as it is written: “The Lord shall be known as one who executes judgments” (Ps. 9). Hence, in the fourth order of the Canon, remembrance is first made of the three manifest things. But the fourth, that is, the depth, is passed over in silence because it is hidden. The fourth order is: “Wherefore, O Lord, we also, thy servants, etc.”

Likewise, in the Passion there was contempt of self; in the Resurrection, contempt of the world; in the Ascension, love of God; in the hidden power, fear. Contempt of self excludes loquacity; contempt of the world, curiosity; love of God, wrongdoing; fear, lust.

In the three parts of the title, faith is understood in “Jesus,” without which no one is saved; hope in “Nazarenus,” for Nazareth is interpreted “flower,” from which fruit [Col. 0458A] is hoped for; and charity in “King of the Jews,” charity being the more excellent way, which makes kings and priests. Faith illumines reason, which pride had blinded, and excludes pride. Hope lifts up the desire for eternal things, which avarice had bent down, and excludes avarice. Charity moderates and orders anger, which envy had corrupted, and excludes envy.

Thus, by the power and efficacy of the holy cross, we are stripped of our oldness and clothed with Christ’s newness. Therefore the Lord Jesus gladly bore his cross, through which he triumphed over the prince of this world, through which he destroyed the kingdom of death and sin, and transferred grace and blessing to the Church. Hence Jacob, when about to bless Joseph’s sons, with the elder placed on his right and the younger on his left, crossed his hands, placing his right hand upon the younger and his left upon the elder [Col. 0458B], signifying in the Holy Spirit that the grace of the Holy Spirit would pass to the Church through the power of the holy cross.

Likewise, the Church is renewed and sanctified by the sacrament of the altar. Seven matters are usefully considered in the sacrament of the altar: what the cause of the Mass is, what its distinction is, what its end is, what its power is, what its order is, what its rationale is, and what its usefulness is.
