The cause of the Mass is threefold: the honour of the saints, the salvation of the living, and the repose of the dead. As it were a prologue, the prayer and invocation of the Trinity is set beforehand, in which the cause of the Mass that follows is anticipated and shown: “Receive, O holy Trinity.” For there it is contained that it may benefit the saints unto honour and us unto salvation, etc.

The distinction is threefold [Col. 0458C]. In accordance with the distinction among the three parts of the Church, there are three kinds of Masses: one is said of the saints; another of the season, that is, for the living; another for the faithful departed. There are indeed three parts of the Church. One part is in exultation, one in pilgrimage, and one in expectation. In exultation are the saints who have followed Christ’s footsteps. In pilgrimage are the living, who are subject to time, that is, to vanity. Hence the Apostle: “The creation was made subject to vanity, not willingly,” etc. (Rom. 8). In expectation are the faithful departed, who await repose.

In accordance with the distinction of these three parts, there are three distinctions of Masses, endings, and offices. For the Mass for saints has one ending—“Go, it is the dismissal”; the Mass of the season another—“Let us bless the Lord” [Col. 0458D]; and the Mass for the faithful departed another—“May they rest in peace.”

At the end of Mass for saints, we are invited to that glory in which the saints already rest: “Go, it is the dismissal,” as if to say: The victim has been sent from the Father to us, or has been sent back from us to the Father; therefore, go—that is, hasten—as the Apostle says: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest” (Heb. 4).

But the ending of the Mass of the season exhorts us, who are in time, to bless the Lord in adversity and prosperity—that is, at every time. Hence David: “I will bless the Lord at every time” (Ps. 23); and elsewhere: “To declare thy mercy in the morning and thy truth by night” (Ps. 9). Morning is prosperity, which is given not from our merits [Col. 0459A] but from mercy alone. Night is adversity, which is rendered in truth according to merits. At the end of Mass for the departed, we wish them repose; and at the beginning we ask: “Grant them eternal rest, O Lord,” etc.

The power of the Mass is Christ’s cross, which consecrates and sanctifies the sacrament of the altar and all the Church’s sacraments. There are seven orders of the cross in the sequence of the Canon, which the Holy Spirit has arranged with wondrous wisdom. The first order is from *Te igitur* to *Quam oblationem*; the second, from *Quam oblationem* to *Qui pridie*; the third, from *Qui pridie* to *Unde et memores*; the fourth, from *Unde et memores* to *Per quem omnia*; the fifth, from *Per quem omnia* to *Per ipsum*; the sixth, from *Per ipsum* to *Pax Domini*; the seventh, from *Pax Domini* [Col. 0459B] to the end. In each order are profound causes and rational explanations which prompt reasonable questions; the Holy Spirit, as he wills, closes them to whom he wills and opens them to whom he wills, as it is written: “To him the gatekeeper opens” (John 10).

## Chapter II. On the First Order of the Canon

In the first order of the Canon, we place three things; we pray for three things; we ask for three things; and therefore we make three crosses. We place three things: bread, wine, and water. The question arises why these three are placed rather than others. The reason is threefold.

The first reason is that, among all things necessary for sustaining human life, these three are cleaner, more useful, and more necessary. Therefore they ought rather than other things to be placed and transferred and transformed into that which is purer, more useful to all [Col. 0459C], and, above all else, more necessary for attaining eternal life: namely, into Christ’s body and blood.

The second reason is that in these the reality itself and the power of the sacrament are understood; without these, one approaches this sacrament unworthily and receives it unto judgment rather than salvation. In water is understood faith, which lies hidden and is nourished in the waters of baptism. In wine, which rises and gladdens, hope is understood. In bread, which strengthens, charity is understood.

Or, in the strengthening bread the Father is understood, who is the strength of all things; in the gladdening wine, the Son, who is our joy, which no one shall take from us; in the water, which cleanses and washes, the Holy Spirit, as it is written: “I will pour upon you clean water, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). And again: “Rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” But he said this concerning the Spirit which those who believed in him were to receive (John 7).

Or, water signifies the purity of chastity; bread, strength and works of piety; wine, which rises and kindles, uprightness of intention, which is not bent down to earthly things but lifted up to heavenly things. These three are so necessary to those approaching the altars that no one can approach with salvation without them. Hence the Lord in the Gospel: “When you enter the city, a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him and say to the master of the house: ‘Where am I to celebrate the Passover with my disciples?’ And he will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it there” (Luke 22).

Therefore the altar is prepared in the more elevated [Col. 0460A] place of the Church, so that those who are to ascend may endeavour, by these steps and ascents of virtues, to prepare and test themselves. Hence the Apostle: “But let a man test himself,” etc. (1 Cor. 11). In the upper room is height; in its being large, breadth; in its being furnished, fitness, since it was prepared and cleansed. Thus in what is furnished is the purity of chastity; in what is large, breadth and works of piety; in the upper room, uprightness of intention.

Hence, in the fourth order, before we say, “the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of perpetual salvation,” we necessarily first offer “a pure victim, a holy victim, an unspotted victim.” But these matters must be discussed in what follows.

The third reason why we place the three things mentioned above—bread, wine, and water—is that every blessing of the patriarchs, in the figure of this sacrament, consisted in these. Hence Abraham, when Melchizedek, in figure of this mystery, offered both bread and wine, received blessing from the greater and was called blessed by God Most High. With this blessing he afterwards enriched his son Isaac. Isaac too invoked these same goods upon his son Jacob in prophetic speech, saying: “May God give thee of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, abundance of grain, wine, and oil,” etc. (Gen. 27). Again, when Esau wept in complaint against Jacob, he said: “I have established him with grain and wine; and after this, my son, what more can I do for thee?” (ibid.) As if to say: I have established him with the grain of Christ’s body and the wine of Christ’s blood; and likewise with oil, which is understood through water.

## Chapter III. On the Three for Whom We Pray, and What We Ask

[Col. 0460C]

We pray for three groups: first, generally for all; second, for our absent familiars; third, for those standing around. Generally for all, where we say: “Above all, which we offer unto thee for thy holy Catholic Church,” etc. For our absent familiars, where we say: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids.” For those standing around, where we say: “And of all who stand around.”

We ask for three things: first, that our days may be ordered in peace; second, that we may be delivered from eternal damnation; third, that we may deserve to be numbered in the Lord’s flock. We have all these where we say: “And order our days in thy peace, and command that we be delivered from eternal [Col. 0460D] damnation and numbered in the flock of thine elect.”

Therefore, because we place three things, pray for three things, and ask for three things, we make three crosses: namely, that by the power of the cross, first the things placed before God may be blessed; secondly, those for whom they are placed; thirdly, that we may obtain what we ask. Thus the second question which might be raised is answered: why three crosses are made in this order when we say, “These gifts, these offerings, these holy unblemished sacrifices.” These gifts, namely, of nature; these offerings, namely, of our devotion; these holy unblemished sacrifices for the divine majesty: so that these gifts refer to nature, these offerings to grace, and these sacrifices to the glory of incorruption.

[Col. 0461A] Reasonable questions arise as to why this sacrament is repeated; how it is rightly received; what it accomplishes when rightly received; and why, under this sacramental species, the reality lies hidden and veiled.

The cause why this sacrament is repeated is threefold. The first cause is that, because we fall daily, we may daily be cleansed through it. The second is that, just as in the midst of paradise there was the tree of life, so Christ’s body may continually be in the midst of the Church, from which those who sin mortally may be barred until, making satisfaction through penitence, they return reconciled to it and through it. The third is that through this we may become one with Christ and, through Christ as mediator, become one with God. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my body and drinks my blood abides in me and I in him” (John 6).

It is rightly received if one prepares for it through these three things: whole faith, pure confession, and fitting penitence. Rightly received, it accomplishes three things: first, it cleanses sins; secondly, it strengthens virtues; thirdly, it raises one to eternal life. Hence he says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day” (ibid.).

The cause why the reality lies hidden and veiled under this sacramental species is threefold. The first cause is the testing of faith; the second, the increase of merit; the third [Col. 0461C], the weakness of the infirm. First, he tests faith so that by testing he may prove and distinguish. Secondly, he endows one who has been proved through faith with greater power and grace. Thirdly, to spare our weakness, he does not reveal himself in the brightness of his majesty, but conceals himself as it were beneath a certain veil.

Hence this miracle occurred in the church of Viviers of the Premonstratensian Order. While Mass was being celebrated in the aforesaid church, a certain brother, looking from the choir toward the altar, saw above it a circle of immeasurable brightness and, in that brightness, a dove of wondrous whiteness above the chalice. He began therefore to marvel and, marvelling, to gaze; suddenly, stupefied and terrified, he lost his sight and fell prostrate in the choir. The brothers led him out of the choir by the hands [Col. 0461D] and, seeking the truth of the event, persisted so long in prayers until God restored his sight. And let these remarks on the first order suffice.

## Chapter IV. On the Second Order of the Canon

In the first order we ask that the things set forth may be blessed; in the second, however, we ask that the things already blessed in the first may be transferred into the true and highest sacrifice. Therefore we make five crosses, because we ask that the things blessed may be transferred into that which surpasses all things in five respects: by a threefold prerogative and a twofold charity.

Therefore we say: “Blessed,” by the fullness of every grace; “enrolled,” by supreme dignity and honour; “ratified,” by supreme and eternal power. Concerning the first prerogative [Col. 0462A], namely the fullness of all graces, it is written: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1); and: “For God did not give the Holy Spirit to the Son by measure” (John 3). Concerning the second prerogative, namely supreme dignity and honour, it is written: “Having written upon his garment and upon his thigh: King of kings and Lord of lords” (Rev. 19). Concerning the third prerogative, namely supreme and eternal power, it is written: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away” (Dan. 7).

But because this threefold prerogative would profit us little unless it displayed twofold charity, therefore we say: “that it may become for us the body and blood of thy most beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.” His twofold charity was that which he had toward the Father and toward the flock: obeying the Father and dying for the flock. Or his twofold charity was that by which he laid down body and soul, or by which he poured blood and water from his side.

Or we make five crosses so that from the five things mentioned we may obtain the five things necessary to us: from participation in the blood, forgiveness of sins; from participation in the body, unity in the fellowship of saints; from supreme and eternal power, fear and concern for the commandments; from supreme dignity and honour, uprightness of life and maturity of character; from fullness of graces, fullness of rewards. For this reason, then, we make five crosses in the second order.

## Chapter V. On the Third Order of the Canon

In the third order, as we ask in the second, the things blessed in the first are transformed into the true and highest sacrifice [Col. 0462C], that is, into Christ’s true body and blood. Since this order is indeed brief but profound and full of great wisdom, two reasonable questions arise in it. The first question is why only two crosses are made; the second, why in this order rather than the others the substance of bread and wine passes into Christ’s true body and blood.

The solution to the first question: no nature other than the twofold nature of human beings—body and soul—needed redemption. In this order our redemption and restoration are celebrated, by which human nature is liberated. The reason why only a twofold cross is made here is thus manifest: namely, because of the redemption of the twofold nature.

The solution to the second question: there are three orders—the order of nature, the order of justice, and the order of grace. In the order of nature, the flower precedes the fruit, sound precedes song, and matter precedes the thing made from matter. In the order of justice, punishment follows sin and reward follows virtue. Hence it is written: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Exod. 21), etc.; and: “There is laid up for me a crown of justice, which the Lord will render to me on that day” (2 Tim. 4). In the order of grace, grace abounds beyond measure where sin has abounded; and the humble sinner precedes the proud righteous person, as the publican precedes the Pharisee; and mercy is bestowed where no merit precedes. Hence in the Gospel: “Publicans and harlots shall go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21).

But neither could nature nor ought justice to make bread and wine become flesh and blood. Divine grace alone both could and willed to do this; it both did and does it. Therefore, just as there are three times—the time before the Law, the time under the Law, and the time of grace—and the Lord Jesus came and celebrated and instituted this sacrament in the time of grace alone, so in this third order of the Canon, more fittingly than in the others, he comes daily and consecrates and makes his flesh and blood from bread and wine. And let these remarks on the third order suffice.

## Chapter VI. On the Fourth Order of the Canon

In the fourth order, with the supreme and true priest present, our petitions are now made known before the Father; with the supreme and true victim present, a longer delay is now prolonged. Then remembrance is celebrated of the great works which he did [Col. 0463B], so that the Father’s mercy may be moved and obtained both through him and through the deeds which he performed.

Therefore we make five crosses, not in order to sanctify him who is present, the Holy of Holies, but that through his presence and the efficacy of the cross we may obtain fivefold grace, by which we may worthily offer and receive the saving victim, and, conformed to him, may deserve to be admitted to the fellowship of the saints.

The Lord Jesus was a pure victim in his Passion, a holy victim in his Resurrection, and an unspotted victim in his Ascension; the bread of eternal life for those hungering, the chalice of perpetual salvation for those thirsting after justice. We must therefore be made like and conformed to him, when we approach to offer him. But because this cannot happen unless we strive to imitate his Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension [Col. 0463C], therefore we first make remembrance of these three when we say: “Wherefore, O Lord, we thy servants, and likewise thy holy people, mindful of the same Christ, thy Son, our Lord God, of his blessed Passion, and also of his Resurrection from the dead, and likewise of his glorious Ascension into heaven.”

Thus, by imitation of the Passion, through purity of chastity, we may be and offer a pure victim; by imitation of the Resurrection, may obtain strength and works of piety, and be and offer a holy victim; by imitation of the Ascension, may obtain uprightness of intention, and be and offer an unspotted victim; by participation in the holy bread of eternal life, may obtain unity and strength of charity; and by participation in the chalice of perpetual salvation, may obtain the multitude and greatness of exultation, as it is written: “And how excellent is my inebriating cup!” (Ps. 22).

We have already said something of these matters in the first order, and recalled why, in this fourth order, the three precede the two. Thus we necessarily first offer the three things, so that we may worthily approach the holy bread of eternal life and the chalice of perpetual salvation—that is, the sacrament of the altar. For the sacrament of the altar is comprehended in these two and, in a manner, comprises these things. In the first, then, is prudence; in the second, fortitude; in the third, justice; in the fourth—that is, in the sacrament of the altar—temperance.

Therefore the Apostle said: “But let a man test himself” (1 Cor. 11): that is, let him prepare himself in these things and through them, and, by testing, make himself fit—namely, through purity of chastity, through the strength [Col. 0464A] and works of piety, and through uprightness of intention. And thus let him eat of that bread and drink of that chalice: that is, thus tested and thus prepared, let him approach the sacrament of the altar.

Therefore the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands,” etc. (Luke 12). “Let your loins be girded”: behold purity of chastity. “And lamps burning in your hands”: behold works of piety. “And be yourselves like men waiting for their lord” (ibid.): behold uprightness of intention. For this alone truly waits and rejoices: it rejoices in waiting and waits in rejoicing. Hence the Apostle: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3), as though he said: Our intention is upright and raised toward the glory of God and the joys of heaven. “Whence also we await the Saviour,” etc. (ibid.), so that, when he comes and knocks, we may immediately [Col. 0464B] open to him (Luke 12): behold the sacrament of the altar.

For in this sacrament the Saviour truly comes also by the presence of his body. He knocks when he tests faith. He tests in order to distinguish. He tests in order to approve and reprove: to approve the faithful person, to reprove the unfaithful. “For the Lord tests the righteous and the wicked” (Ps. 10). Did he not test faith when he said concerning his body and blood: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6)? Did he not, by testing, distinguish, and by distinguishing approve and reprove, when, the twelve remaining, many went back, saying: “This saying is hard” (ibid.)? And truly then we receive him when he comes with whole and devout faith.

Or we make five crosses because we offer five things, pray for five things, and ask for five things. We pray for five: first, generally for all living faithful people; second, for those who share in the altar; third, for departed familiars; fourth, generally for all; fifth, for ourselves, sinners. Generally for all the living, where we say: “Upon which look favourably,” etc. But what does “upon which” mean, when it seems that “upon whom,” that is, upon Christ, ought rather to be said? It should therefore be understood thus: “upon which,” that is, upon whose members or upon whose gifts. For those who share in the altar, where we say: “That as many of us as shall receive from this participation of the altar,” etc. For departed familiars, where we say: “Remember, O Lord, thy servants and handmaids who have gone before us,” etc. Generally [Col. 0464D] for all the faithful departed, where we say: “To them and to all who rest in Christ,” etc. For ourselves, sinners, where we say: “To us also, thy sinful servants, hoping in the multitude of thy mercies, grant some share,” etc.

We ask for five things: two for ourselves who are living, and three for the faithful departed. For ourselves: first, that we may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace; second, that we may deserve to be admitted within the fellowship of the saints. For the faithful departed: a place of refreshment, the blessedness of rest, and brightness of light; which is there: “We beseech thee to grant them a place of refreshment, light, and peace.” Therefore we make the cross five times, by whose power and love we both obtain the things we offer, are heard for those for whom we pray, and gain the things we ask.

## Chapter VII. On the Fifth Order of the Canon

[Col. 0465A]

In the fifth order, so that we may obtain the effectiveness of our petitions, we seek favour and commend both persons: that of the Father and that of the Holy Spirit. We commend the Father’s person through ineffable charity, when we say: “Through whom, O Lord, thou dost always create all these good things,” etc. We commend the person of the Holy Spirit through the wondrous depth of wisdom by which he arranged the Canon so that we do not make the sign of the cross at the word “create,” but do make it at the three words which follow: “sanctifiest,” “givest life,” and “blessest.”

And why? The cause is this: human nature, from the state of its first creation, had neither progress in virtue nor stability in blessedness. From its first creation it possessed natural reason and rejoiced in freedom of will; but of itself it could neither stand nor advance, without assisting grace and without the power of the cross. Thus, in itself it is unstable and perishable; but through the power of the holy cross and assisting grace it becomes stable and blessed.

Therefore we do not make the sign of the cross at the first word, “create,” but make it at the three words that follow. “Sanctifiest”: by faith, hope, and forgiveness of sins. “Givest life”: by the sacraments of faith and the power of good works. “Blessest”: by the fullness of graces and the consummation of good things. Therefore we make the cross three times, because through its power and love we obtain these three things, which we need above all things.

We commend the person of the Son through manifold, that is, fourfold, power, showing him first as God of nature; secondly, as giver of pardon; thirdly, as Lord of power and grace and source of life; fourthly, as King of glory. Hence it is written: “The Lord of powers, he is the King of glory” (Ps. 23). The first power is that by which he can create all things from nothing; the second, that by which he can forgive sins; the third, that by which he can increase grace and virtue; the fourth, that by which he can crown those cleansed with glory and blessedness. “Through whom, O Lord, thou dost always create all these good things”: behold the God of nature. “Thou sanctifiest”: behold the giver of pardon. “Thou givest life”: behold the source of life and Lord of the power of grace. “Thou blessest”: behold the king and crown of eternal glory.

## Chapter VIII. On the Sixth Order of the Canon

In the sixth order, through him who came in the sixth age, and through the power of his cross, we now know all truth more fully, and through the same one honour and glorify the Father [Col. 0465D]. Hence, taking greater confidence and boldness, that we may attain the highest peace, we gather the sum of all petitions into a brief form, saying: “Our Father,” etc. (Matt. 6).

We make five crosses so that, through the power and love of the holy cross, we may ascend five steps in the knowledge of truth, without which we cannot be saved. This does not mean that there are stages in the Trinity of the Godhead or in the Godhead of the Trinity, but in faith in and love for it. Hence the Apostle: “From faith unto faith” (Rom. 1). The first step of faith is the eternity of the Son with the Father; the second step, equality; the third, unity of the same substance; the fourth, the same mode of existence of both; the fifth, the unity of the Holy Spirit with both, that is, with the Son and the Father.

[Col. 0466A] It should be noted that the Lord’s Prayer is contained in this order; therefore three reasonable questions arise in this order. The first is why such diversity is shown in making the crosses; the second, why the Lord’s body is held entire in the hand while the same crosses are made; the third, why the Lord’s Prayer is contained in this order rather than the others. It should also be noted that some things are understood through what is done, others through what is said.

But what is the diversity shown in the crosses? The first cross is extended on either side beyond the chalice. The second is level with the chalice. The third is confined below the chalice. The fourth is the same as the first. The fifth is traced before the chalice. In the first cross, therefore, is understood the eternity of the Son with the Father; in the second, equality [Col. 0466B]; in the third, unity of inner and identical substance; in the fourth, the same mode of existence of both, both before the world’s foundation and after the world’s consummation. Hence it is written of the seraphim that with two wings they covered the head, with two the feet, and with two they flew (Ezek. 1). In the head is the beginning, in the feet the end. For what was before the world’s foundation, or what shall be after the world’s consummation, is hidden and veiled. With two wings they flew: that is, they conveyed to human knowledge the things in the middle which pertained to human salvation.

In the fifth cross is understood the unity of the Holy Spirit with the Father and the Son. In the phrase “through him” creation is understood; in “with him,” operation; in “in him,” consummation. For through the Son the Father created all things; with the Son he works, and the Son with him, governing and disposing the things created. Hence in the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5). Finally, in him all things will be consummated.

But after the world’s consummation, when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father and is subject to him who subjected all things to him (1 Cor. 15), and when the person and nature of the Holy Spirit are perfectly known by all, then through the Son there will be all honour and glory to God the Father. In the creation and operation of things, God the Father indeed has honour and glory through the Son, but not all honour and glory, until after the consummation, just as inheritance returned from the Father to the Son, so it returns from the Son to the Father. Therefore the fifth cross, when it is said in the power of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0466D], is traced before the chalice—that is, it is made manifest before the eyes of all.

For after the world’s consummation, not only how the Son is one with the Father, but also how the Holy Spirit is one with both and proceeds from both, will be fully known by all the righteous, as it is written: “They shall all know me, from the least even to the greatest” (Jer. 31). Therefore all honour and glory is deferred until the end. Therefore we make five crosses, that through the power of the holy cross we may attain this fivefold knowledge of truth.

The first question—why such diversity is shown in making the crosses—is resolved in the matters set forth above. The other two questions remain to be resolved.

The solution to the second question: in the sixth age the Lord Jesus appeared a whole and perfect human being, and offered himself whole and perfect for us. Therefore, in the sixth order, we hold him with the whole hand: that is, we ought to imitate him with whole faith and perfect work; and thus we make crosses—that is, we share in his sufferings.

The solution to the third question: when the Lord Jesus came in the sixth age, he instituted and taught the Lord’s Prayer; therefore it was more fittingly placed in the sixth order than in the others.

## Chapter IX. On the Seventh Order of the Canon
The seventh order begins with peace and tends toward peace. Three things are required for the love of the Creator: mind, hand, and tongue; and these work together in this matter. The tongue forms the voice, the hand traces the cross, and the mind moves both—that is, the tongue to form the voice and [Col. 0467B] the hand to trace the cross. These three, therefore, are necessary: the voice of prayer, the power of the holy cross, and the faith of the mind, so that we may attain the height of peace. “The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

Not every peace is the Lord’s peace. There is disordered peace, feigned peace, defiled peace, and wicked peace. Disordered peace is the peace of the proud, who, despising a superior, obey an inferior—as Adam obeyed his wife—and thus lost both his superior and inferior self. But the second Adam preferred obedience to God the Father over obedience to the Synagogue, his mother; and therefore he recovered himself when he rose from the dead, preserved his Father, and will receive his mother at the end. In compassion for that mother, the Synagogue, he said to the Father: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26). Yet he neither feared the passion [Col. 0467C] nor wished to evade it; rather, because he knew that the Synagogue would perish through his passion, he grieved with an affection of compassion.

Feigned peace belongs to traitors, who speak with their mouths but not with their hearts; defiled peace belongs to fornicators and adulterers; wicked peace belongs to rebels and schismatics, who resist and contradict the authority of the universal Church. Hence Samuel says: “To resist is the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15). Augustine sets forth three authorities: first, the holy Scriptures; second, general councils; third, the custom of the universal Church, saying: “Everything not confirmed by any one of these authorities, I judge must be entirely cut away from the Church.”

But the Lord’s peace is ordered, [Col. 0467D] because it loves order. It is true, because it deceives no one. It is pure, because it avoids every defilement. It is chaste and eternal, because it knows neither strife nor end.

Within this order many questions arise which, by the revelation of the Holy Spirit, are resolved. The first question is why, according to the custom of the Church, three crosses are made; the second, why two suffice according to a certain rationale of faith; the third, why these crosses are made not above or outside the chalice, but only within the chalice. The fourth is why the third particle of the Lord’s body is held in the hand while the crosses are being made. The fifth, why that same particle descends into the chalice after the crosses have been made. The sixth, why two parts remain outside the chalice. The seventh, why, when *Agnus Dei* is said, the first two invocations agree, but the third differs by saying, [Col. 0468A] “grant us peace.”

Resolution of the first question: There are three lives of human nature: the first, of the soul together with the body; the second, of the soul after leaving the body; the third, of the soul after resuming the body—which will be at the resurrection. In the first life, peace is necessary, so that it may keep one far from sin. In the second, peace is necessary, so that it may keep one far from terror; hence at the burial of the dead it is said: “May no penal fear torment him; may no nearby chain of the accused bind him,” etc. In the third life, peace is necessary to keep one far from both, that is, from sin and terror, in the consummation of glory and blessedness. Therefore we make three crosses, so that through the power of the cross we may attain this threefold peace. Therefore too we always say it—that is, in this threefold life we implore peace for others.

Resolution of the second [Col. 0468B] question: No nature required redemption or restoration to peace except the body and soul of man alone; therefore, according to this rationale of faith, only a twofold cross seems to be required.

Resolution of the third question: In the seventh age, which will be succeeded by the eighth age of consummated peace, there will be nothing outwardly to grieve over, but rather something inwardly to rejoice in. Therefore the crosses are made not outside, but within the chalice.

Resolution of the fourth question: The third part of the Lord’s body, which we hold in the hand when making the crosses, is that part of the Church which is in exultation and rejoices with Christ in eternal blessedness. Therefore we ought to hold this part—that is, the saints—in the hand; that is, we ought to imitate them in faith and works, so that we may thus make crosses, that is, share in Christ’s passions.

[Col. 0468C] Resolution of the fifth question: The Lord’s chalice, which signifies toil and imitation of the Lord’s passion, has its exterior and its interior: externally, pressure and tribulation; inwardly, joy and consolation. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I have spoken these things to you, that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have tribulation” (John 16). Hence Isaiah: “My secret is for me” (Isa. 24); and David: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30); and again: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93). That secret of joy and consolation, and that hidden sweetness, are the interior of the chalice. Therefore [Col. 0468D] that third particle of the Lord’s body descends into the chalice, because after toil it will receive everlasting rest with Christ. Hence in the Gospel: “My children are already with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you” (Luc. II).

Resolution of the sixth question: The two parts of the Lord’s body which remain outside the chalice are the two parts of the Church: the part in pilgrimage and the part in expectation. Since these two parts are subject to penitential labors and still await and desire, and do not yet possess, the desired rest, those two parts of the Lord’s body remain outside the chalice.

Resolution of the seventh question: There are three times; two are times of mercy, while the third will be the time of peace and justice. Since mercy is hoped for [Col. 0469A] and awaited in the time of pilgrimage and in the time of expectation, but in the time of resurrection peace and justice will be consummated, therefore, when *Agnus Dei* is said, the first two agree, while the third differs.

## CHAPTER X. On the Three Orders of Saints Placed in the Canon

Finally, one must carefully observe and seek out by watchful investigation why three orders of saints are placed in the Canon: namely, three saints from among all the Fathers who lived before the Law—Abel, Abraham, and Melchizedek; then a greater number from the New Testament, namely twenty-five, of greater authority before the consecration; and a smaller number, namely fifteen, of lesser authority after the consecration.

The three aforesaid alone, out of all the Fathers who lived [Col. 0469B] before the Law, are especially placed in the Canon because in their persons and sacrifices the person and sacrifice of Christ were most fully prefigured. Abel offered a lamb from the flock and was slain by his brother through envy. Abraham, in obedience, departed from his land and kindred and offered his only son. Melchizedek, who is called king of peace and of righteousness, without father, without mother, made like the Son of God, remains a priest forever; and, as a figure of Christ, offered bread and wine to Abraham.

The greater number of saints of the New Testament—five times five, and of greater authority—are placed before the consecration because, in order that the thing may be wondrously accomplished through our office and ministry, namely that the substance of bread and wine may become the true body and [Col. 0470A] blood of Christ, we need more and greater aids, and we must be multiplied and perfected by the fivefold perfection of the senses. After the consecration, the smaller number of saints—fifteen, and of lesser authority—are arranged so that by their merits and prayers we may ascend through the fifteen degrees of charity and, united to the company of the saints, pass over.

Indeed, it is far more wonderful and greater for the substance of bread and wine to become the true body and blood of Christ than for us to be admitted to the fellowship of the saints. Therefore, Abel signifies true innocence; Abraham, true and perfect obedience; Melchizedek, devout and complete faith. These three virtues truly give forth their fragrance in those who faithfully offer to almighty God the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood.

[Col. 0470B] The holy Fathers, with great and subtle consideration, ordained that in the Canon of the Mass no confessors or virgins should be named unless they had been purified by the martyrdom of blood, since concerning martyrs there is no doubt that, immediately upon departing from their bodies, their souls ascended into the kingdom of heaven. But concerning the rest, who departed in the peace of the Church, it is uncertain whether they may still have something to expiate in the other life. Thus blessed Gregory relates concerning Paschasius the deacon that, even after death, he performed miracles, and yet was found by Saint Germanus doing penance for a very slight fault, which he had not even believed to be a fault and therefore had not extinguished by tears. We shall deserve to be delivered after death by the saving sacrifice if, before death, we ourselves have been a sacrifice to God.

[Col. 0469]

# MISCELLANEA. (G)*

## BOOK ONE. VARIOUS MORAL EXPLANATIONS OF SCRIPTURE

They are called *Miscellanea* because they proceed in a mixed and confused fashion. Some judge that these were collected by Hugh himself, so that he might apply them to his purpose wherever he saw fit. Others judge that they are not by Hugh, but excerpts from Hugh’s works, as little flowers of sayings, because they have found very many of them inserted into his writings. If I find them printed, I shall indicate only the title and the place.

## TITLE I. On the Spiritual Person Who Judges All Things, and on the Judgment of Truth and Goodness

[Col. 0469C]

“The spiritual person judges all things” (1 Cor. 2). The Spirit makes a person spiritual. That Spirit is the anointing which, when it has touched the mind, teaches concerning all things. It is one, and it teaches concerning all things. Nor is it surprising that it teaches all things, since it contains all things. Wisdom is one, and all things are in it; and all things in it are nothing other than itself. There, one is all things, and all things are one. Nor are they not one because they are all things, nor are they not all things because they are one. Greatness and simplicity alike; unity and universality.

There is one good, and in that good is every good. If you desire to see it, it is light and form. It is light because through it [Col. 0469D] you see; it is form because you see it itself. And what is it to see it itself? He sought to deserve to see it, saying: “If I have found favor before you, show me yourself.” And he said: “I will show you every good” (Exod. 33).

[Col. 0470C] See: he asked to see God himself, and God promised that he would show him every good. He seems to offer something other than what had been requested; but it is not something else, but that very same thing. He himself is every good, and to see him is to see every good. What then do you suppose is the form in which all beauty is seen?

This bodily light is of great service to you when you see through it, yet it does not give you everything; for you see something else, and you do not see everything in the light itself, because what you see is something other than the light itself, though you see it through the light. But through this light you see everything, and you see everything in it; and everything that you see in it is itself what you see. Such is spiritual light: when it offers itself to those to be illumined, [Col. 0470D] those who see it see everything.

Thus that very good which is light and form to spiritual eyes is song to spiritual ears. The eyes seek their joy; this good comes and says, “I am light.” [Col. 0471A] The ears seek their joy; this good comes and says, “I am song.” A certain new song was heard, so that both sweetness and novelty might increase delight: sweetness for pleasure, novelty for wonder. And joy was poured into the ears, and this good says: “Seek me: this is what I am.” The throat cries out, and flavor says, “I am”; the nostrils cry out, and fragrance says, “I am”; touch cries out, and sweetness responds, “I am.” I am wholly present; and all that I am is good; and whoever has me has everything.

Bodily nature could not emulate spiritual perfection by containing everything in one. Therefore it was necessary for many bodies to be made, so that all things together might accomplish what individual things could not accomplish by themselves. If white alone had been made, black would not exist. But one body [Col. 0471B] could not be white and black at the same time. And whatever things were contrary could not exist in one thing alone. Thus, if any one thing alone had been made, everything that exists besides that one would not exist.

But the principle of contraries is not itself contrary; and therefore the spirit, insofar as it contains the principle of all things, contains all things through reason. Though one and simple in nature, wisdom is nevertheless manifold, stable in truth and mobile in subtlety. Therefore, when this Spirit pours itself into the heart through grace, as in itself the truth of all things is contained, so through it knowledge of all things is supplied, as and insofar as it wills; and in some manner all things begin to exist in the one who receives it, just as all things exist in the one who gave it.

For whoever sees with the eye of contemplation sees God and the things that are in God. [Col. 0471C] Whoever sees with the eye of reason sees the soul and the things that are in the soul. Whoever sees with the eye of the flesh sees the world and the things that are in the world. But whoever sees the things seen by the eye of contemplation also sees the things seen by the eye of reason and the things seen by the eye of the flesh, because lower things are known in higher things. Whoever sees with the eye of reason indeed sees the things seen by the eye of the flesh, but does not in the same way see the things seen by the eye of contemplation. But whoever sees with the eye of the flesh sees neither the things seen by the eye of contemplation nor the things seen by the eye of reason.

Therefore the spiritual person judges all things, because, just as through the eye of contemplation that person sees the things that are in God, so through the eye of reason enlightened by contemplation that person sees the things that are in the soul, and through them and in [Col. 0471D] them also the things that are in the world. Whoever sees all things can judge concerning all things, because nothing is withdrawn from the judgment of one from whose knowledge nothing is hidden.

Thus the spiritual person judges all things. What does “all things” mean? Every truth, by wisdom; every goodness, by experience. By wisdom one judges every truth; by experience one judges every goodness. Truth and goodness are two things, and every good consists in these two. Just as this bodily light has two things in itself, brightness and heat, and by its brightness can illuminate, while by its heat it can kindle or warm, so the highest good, when it fills the mind, both illumines it for knowledge of truth and inflames it for love of goodness.

[Col. 0472A] The one Spirit supplies both, namely knowledge and love. Knowledge provides judgment of truth; love provides judgment of goodness. Human beings err in both. Some err in judgment of truth, blinded by ignorance; others err in judgment of goodness, blinded by wickedness. What is wickedness? An evil will. In an evil will is evil love. For just as good love illumines the mind, so evil love blinds it. To every person, that which one loves seems good.

Scripture says: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isa. 5). Those who love evil call evil good; and, conversely, those who hate good call good evil. What is it to love? To approve. Whoever approves praises, and judges good what he or she approves. What is it to hate? To disapprove and judge evil. [Col. 0472B] This is false judgment, in which both evil is called good and good evil. One says, “It is good”; another says, “It is evil”; and people, blinded by their errors, contend because they do not have the Spirit through whom they ought to judge every truth and every good.

“He made all things good in their time, and gave the world over to their disputation” (Eccles. 3). Therefore people dispute in their contention over judgment and cannot rightly judge concerning good, because they have known neither the good in truth nor the true in goodness. Since they do not truly know what good is, they cannot rightly judge concerning good. For everyone who judges something judges it by reference to something. Otherwise nothing can be judged unless there is something else certain and known, by comparison or collation with which the doubtful matter itself may be discerned.

[Col. 0472C] That by which something else is judged is, as it were, a rule to which that thing that is to be judged by comparison with it is somehow brought and fitted. Everything judged according to what is straight is judged by right judgment, because it is found either to agree with that standard and to be straight, or to differ from it and to be crooked. But what is judged according to something crooked must immediately be judged by a judgment that is not right, because just as what disagrees with the crooked is always found straight, so what agrees with it is undoubtedly crooked.

Therefore certain judgment exists only in rectitude, because what agrees with it must always be straight, and what disagrees with it can never [Col. 0472D] be straight. If, then, rectitude is the rule of every judgment, all things are most rightly judged according to that rectitude by which and from which all things that are straight are formed so as to be straight and are tested whether they are so. And what is supreme rectitude if not supreme truth and supreme goodness? Supreme truth is the rule of every truth; supreme goodness, the rule of every goodness.

Every good, therefore, is judged according to the highest good: what kind of good it is, and how great a good it is. There is a certain highest good that is truly highest and truly good; and everything that is good in relation to it is truly good. There is likewise a certain highest good that is neither truly highest nor truly good; and therefore everything that is good in relation to it is [Col. 0473A] not truly good. Yet all goods are good only insofar as they are good in relation to a highest good.

What is truly the highest good is highest universally. But what is not truly the highest good is highest not universally, but only in its own kind. Thus there are, in a sense, two highest goods: one truly highest and truly good; the other highest in its own kind and good only in its own kind. But what shall we say? Is not God the highest good? If, then, there are two highest goods, there are surely two gods. Perhaps the Apostle intended to signify precisely this when he said: “Indeed, though there are many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8): in a certain respect, something is not inappropriately called “god” when it is found to be highest in the good of its own kind.

[Col. 0473B] But he says to us: “There is one God” (ibid.). What does “to us” mean? To those tending toward the highest good. For to those tending toward the highest good, there is one God. To those tending toward the true good, he is the true God. For lower beings, to whom it is not granted to reach the true good, there are certain other highest goods which are not truly highest and therefore are not true, though they are established as highest in their own rank and order. What is highest for each thing is its god.

“See,” he says, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7). See: two gods—indeed, three: Moses in Egypt, man in the world, the Creator in heaven. And each has a Pharaoh of his own. What is Pharaoh? One who denies and contradicts. *Pharaoh* means “denying him,” that is, denying God. [Col. 0473C] “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5). In this he is called one who denies him.

What is it to deny God? To deny the highest good; for God is the highest good. “Whoever denies,” says the Apostle, “that Christ came in the flesh, this one is Antichrist” (1 John 2): that is, one opposed to Christ. If, then, whoever denies Christ is Antichrist, whoever opposes and is contrary to the highest good denies the highest good and is Pharaoh—that is, one who denies him. What is contrary to the true good but true evil? And what is contrary to a good that is not true but evil that is not true?

Let us therefore set three Pharaohs against three gods. The Egyptian tyrant opposes Moses, the world opposes man, and the devil opposes God. The first sets cruelty against him, the second adversity, the third wickedness. The first [Col. 0473D] sets ferocity against him, the second punishment, the third malice. Wickedness attempts to extinguish the inner life in the soul; mortality attempts to extinguish the outer life in the body. Pharaoh’s cruelty attempts to extinguish Moses’ life.

In all these there are contradictions. Thus there are two highest goods, each in its own order. Among spiritual goods God is the highest good, since he himself is a spiritual good. Among bodily goods man is the highest good, insofar as he is body and has been created above all bodily things, and all bodily things that were made were made for his sake. Therefore, just as all spiritual goods are referred to that good which is highest in its kind, so also all bodily goods are referred to that good which has been placed highest among all bodily things.

[Col. 0474A] But among spiritual goods God is the highest good; among bodily goods man is the highest good. Accordingly, bodily goods are referred to man as to their highest good; spiritual goods, consisting in knowledge of truth and love of goodness, are referred to God as to their highest good. Bodily goods are good in relation to man because they are goods belonging to man. Spiritual goods are good in relation to God, not because they are God’s goods, but because they are good from God. These are not good from man, but good for man; those are good from God.

Whatever is good outside God is indeed good from him, but it is not good for him, since he alone is his own good. Nevertheless, every good is good because it is good in relation to its highest good, and it is good insofar [Col. 0474B] as it is good in relation to that good. Therefore judge all other things by the highest good, and establish it in judging all things as the very rule of justice.

What is good? That which is good in relation to the highest good. What is truly good? That which is good in relation to the true good. What is it to be good in relation to it? To be useful toward it. That which converts and leads to it; and if it does not lead, nevertheless it assists. If it benefits toward it, it leads; if it benefits it, it assists it. Spiritual goods lead to their highest good because they are beneficial toward it. Bodily goods assist their highest good because they are beneficial to it.

What is evil? That which is evil in relation to the highest good. What is true evil? That which is evil in relation to the true good. What is it to be evil in relation to good? To harm it, or to harm toward it. What is it to harm toward it? To cause it to be lost, or to cause it not to be attained. Therefore all bodily goods and evils are good or evil because they benefit or harm the good that is highest in relation to them. But all spiritual goods and evils are good or evil because they benefit or harm, in relation to them, the good that is highest. Each is good or evil only insofar as it benefits or harms either that being or movement toward that end.

Whatever is called bodily good is called good insofar as it is good for man. Whatever bodily goods are good for man are so according to the perception of the five senses, through which there is commerce between the soul and the world, and between the world and the soul. All forms, shapes, colors, and appearances of things are called good in relation to sight, because they nourish sight and please man in relation to sight; and those which delight sight more are called better, just as those which torment it are called evil.

[Col. 0474D] Likewise, among sounds and songs, those which delight hearing are called good, and those which torment it evil; and those which delight or torment more are more good or more evil. In the same manner, among smells, those which delight the sense of smell more are called better; those which cause pain and torment are called evil. The same is found in taste and touch.

Thus whatever is called bodily good is called good on account of the human body, for whose benefit all things were made. If, then, all bodily goods are referred to the human body, how great must be considered the excellence of the rational soul, which is found superior to the body itself by an inestimable dignity?

[Col. 0475A] Four kinds of good are distinguished: true goods and true evils, non-true goods and non-true evils. Man does true evils; man suffers non-true evils. True evils lie in fault; non-true evils lie in punishment. It is written: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3). What pertains to fault in man, man does; what pertains to punishment in man, God does. Thus man causes fault; God causes punishment. Fault is true evil; punishment is non-true evil.

[Col. 0475B] Observe the unlike agents. God makes true good; man makes non-true good. Again, man makes true evil; God makes non-true evil. Just as there is no inward evil of fault that man does not make, so there is no outward evil of punishment that God does not make. But when man does evil, he does it to himself, and thus he does evil. When God does evil, he does not do it to himself but to the human being who does evil; and therefore he does not do evil. Man speaks foolishly inwardly by sinning; God answers the fool outwardly according to the fool’s folly, by punishing sin.

Thus there are four: true good and true evil, and non-true good and non-true evil. All these are judged, by comparison with the highest good, whether they are good or evil and, if so, how great they are.

There are, however, three kinds of good. There is a good which is good in itself and not in relation to anything else. There is another which is not good in itself but is good in relation to something else. And there is another which is good both in itself and in relation to something else. [Col. 0475C] The first is the lowest good, the second the middle, the third the highest. For just as that which is good both in itself and in relation to another is the best, so that which is good only in itself is the lowest; for better than it is that which, although it may not be good in itself, is nevertheless good in relation to another. Since from it comes a greater good, its being is better, because what comes from it is better.

Sometimes true good arises from a good thing, as when one virtue produces another virtue. Sometimes true evil arises from true good, as when the mind is puffed up through pride on account of virtue. Again, true evil arises from true evil, when one vice produces another. Likewise, true good arises from true evil, as when humility arises from fault.

[Col. 0475D] There were two men, a Pharisee and a publican: one righteous, the other a sinner. From the Pharisee’s righteousness arose exaltation; from the publican’s unrighteousness, humiliation. There true evil arose from true good; here true good arose from true evil.

Likewise, non-true good arises from non-true good, as when bodily health is acquired through the nourishment of the body. Again, non-true evil arises from non-true good, as when the stomach is burdened by excessive eating because the throat has been irritated by the sweetness of food. Non-true evil arises from non-true evil, as when bodily weakness is generated from bodily punishment. Likewise, non-true good arises from non-true evil, as when bodily health is generated through bodily punishment. For if punishment is evil in the bitterness of the potion, health is good in the attainment of healing.

[Col. 0476A] Likewise, from true good arise non-true good and non-true evil: for example, when, through the mind’s self-control, the body, restrained from excessive eating, is preserved in health, while the flesh, worn down by abstinence, is also afflicted by the very performance of a good work. Similarly, from true evil arise non-true good and non-true evil, when avarice brings about, either in bodily health or in the mortification of flesh, the very thing which we say self-control accomplishes.

From non-true good arise both true good and true evil, as when the mind is inflamed by bodily nourishment either toward virtue or toward vice. Likewise, from non-true evil arise both true good and true evil, when by bodily punishment the mind is either trained toward righteousness or inclined toward wickedness.

[Col. 0476B] Since, then, both good and evil alike result from both good and evil, when good arises from good and evil from evil, the nature of good and evil itself is at work. But when evil results from good, or good from evil, this is caused either by another’s wickedness or by another’s goodness: in the former case, by one abusing good; in the latter, by one using evil well for good—especially if what is done is true good or true evil, whether that from which it is done is true or non-true.

Since, therefore, for true good to result from true evil is not a work of human power but of divine goodness, a human being is never permitted either to do or to suffer true evil in order that good may result from it. Therefore, when the Apostle had said: “Where iniquity abounded, grace abounded still more” [Col. 0476C] (Rom. 5), and some tried to take this as an occasion, as though human beings ought therefore to do evil so that good might afterward result from it, he added concerning such people: “Their condemnation is just” (Rom. 3).

For if a human being acts wickedly, and afterward God acts beneficially from that person’s evil, the human being is justly condemned because of acting wickedly; but God is justly glorified because he makes good from evil. What is evil belongs to man; what is good from evil belongs to God. Therefore avoid evil, because, if you do evil, you cannot make good from it.

[Col. 0476D] Likewise, although true evil sometimes arises from true good, you should not therefore avoid good lest evil result from it; for even once good has been done, it still lies within your power to prevent evil from occurring. For this reason, do not do evil for the sake of good, because it is not in your power to make good arise from evil; nor abandon good for fear of evil, because, even once good has been done, it still lies in your power to prevent evil.

This, indeed, must be understood concerning true good and true evil. But with respect to non-true good and non-true evil, a person must exercise this caution: because these are in one’s power, and one can either abuse them toward true evil or use them toward true good, one should accept them, whether for doing or suffering, according to time and cause, so as always to turn them toward either the fruit or the use of acquiring good: toward the fruit of true good, with grace cooperating; toward the use of non-true good, [Col. 0477A] with nature cooperating.

The death of the flesh, because it is punishment, is always evil, but it is not always evil in a moral sense. Likewise, the life of the flesh, because it is natural, is always good, but it is not always morally good. A good life is one in which there is good merit; a good death is one after which there is a good reward. An evil life is one in which there is feeling without virtue; an evil death is one in which punishment comes without recompense.

Since neither the life of the flesh nor death, nor the things belonging to life or death, are true goods or evils, one ought to use all these things so that, whether the things endured are good or evil, one may direct them all to the use of goodness. Non-true good or non-true evil is directed toward the use of true good when a person either exercises virtue in life or earns the reward of virtue in death. Non-true good or non-true evil is directed toward the use of non-true good when the pleasant or bitter things of life are arranged for preserving or restoring bodily health.

[Col. 0477B] But when do all these things benefit a person in relation to true good? They benefit with grace cooperating; in relation to non-true good, with nature cooperating.

## TITLE II. On the Food of Emmanuel, concerning which it is written: “He shall eat butter and honey,” etc.

There is a great question concerning the food of Emmanuel: why he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good (Isa. VII). Butter is, as you all know, fat derived from flesh; honey is sweetness descending from the dew of heaven. What, then, are we to understand by butter, if not the refreshment of good work expressed through the body [Col. 0477C]? And what by honey, if not that sweetness of contemplation which is poured in from above by the gift of grace?

He, therefore, eats butter and honey who, in the assumed humanity, received from above the fullness of the Spirit, and who, as a man below, displayed through the flesh works of virtue. To eat butter and honey is to exercise the heart in the affection of piety, outwardly through good works and inwardly through contemplation. But one person eats for refreshment, another for delight. He who suffers deficiency through not yet possessing, or through having lost, the fullness of virtue needs food, that, strengthened by refreshment, he may be made firm. But he who suffers neither deficiency nor diminution in his fullness does not require food for refreshment.

We, therefore, who are mere human beings and advance through the passage of time toward increase in virtue, eat butter and honey, because of the need caused by our deficiency, not only for delight but also for refreshment: butter, so that love of neighbor may be exercised outwardly in us through works of piety; honey, so that love of God may be nourished inwardly through contemplation. But that man did not need butter and honey for refreshment, in whom, from the beginning of his conception—from the moment he began to be man—there was always the fullness of every virtue. Yet he ate as man in time, who had himself been food as God from eternity. He ate, not to refresh himself when hungry, but so that, being full, he might not disdain those who were hungry. He ate butter, not to increase in himself the virtue of charity through works, but to pour its affection into us. He ate the sweetness of heavenly things [Col. 0478A], neither seeking it through ignorance nor desiring it through want, but always beholding it as present in the fullest knowledge and enjoying it in most perfect charity.

Therefore, he who possessed fullness and was himself perfection ate not for refreshment but for delight. He ate butter when he fulfilled what had been foretold of him through the Psalmist: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season; and its leaf shall not fall; and whatever he does shall prosper” (Ps. I). He ate honey when he fulfilled what is written: “In his law he shall meditate day and night” (ibid.). “That he may know how to reject evil”: “Who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” [or, “of scoffers”] [Col. 0478B] (ibid.). “And choose good”: “But his will is in the law of the Lord” (ibid.).

Therefore, he shall eat butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good. Perhaps he shall eat butter in order to know how to reject evil, and honey in order to know how to choose good. Thus Christ learned, by eating, to reject evil and choose good. For if he had not eaten, he would not have tasted; if he had not tasted, he would not have known by experience. Therefore he ate and tasted; by tasting, he felt and recognized.

What did he eat? Butter and honey. In the butter something of bitterness was mixed; in the taste of honey no bitterness could be found. Therefore, in the former there was found something which deserved to be rejected; in the latter, nothing except what ought rightly to have been chosen.

Let us now consider the bitterness of butter. The Son of God, coming into the world through humanity, performed many works of piety for the human race: he taught by word and stirred men by example. Finally, in order to establish beyond doubt that he was the Savior of the world, he disclosed to human minds, by continual mighty works and miracles, the majesty of his divinity hidden in the flesh. All this was butter; but where is the bitterness? Thus, in doing all these things, he ate butter. But because, together with human nature, he had also assumed weakness, while doing these things with the affection of piety he endured, in hunger and thirst, cold and heat, labor and weariness, and the other punishments and deficiencies of our mortality, the bitterness of suffering.

For at one time Jesus, wearied from his journey, sat by the well; and when the Samaritan woman came, he asked for a drink [Col. 0478D], saying, “Give me to drink” (John IV). Behold the bitterness. Afterwards, when the disciples came, bringing the food they had bought, they wondered that he was speaking with a woman (ibid.). But he, wishing also to show what he chose in butter and what he rejected, said when they urged him to come and eat: “I have food of which you do not know” (ibid.). Then immediately he said: “My food is to do the will of my Father” (ibid.). Here he showed the butter. “The food,” he says, “of which you do not know is butter. The food of which you do know is bitterness. But because the former is not taken without the latter, I came to eat the former in the latter, and in the former to reject the latter.”

Let us consider elsewhere butter containing a greater bitterness. At another time, while he was teaching the crowds of Jews, he said: “Amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death for ever” [Col. 0479A] (John VIII). Behold good butter. But bitterness is present. And they said: “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; and you say: If anyone keeps my word, he shall not taste death for ever” (ibid.). But Jesus, removing the bitterness and turning himself to the eating of butter, said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” (ibid.). The Jews, however, again sprinkling on bitterness, took stones to throw at him (ibid.). And the rejection of evil follows: “But Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple” (ibid.).

Let us look elsewhere still. He walked in Solomon’s portico. They surrounded him, saying: “How long do you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” [Col. 0479B] (John X). And he: “I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works which I do in my Father’s name, they bear witness concerning me”—behold butter—“but you do not believe” (ibid.)—behold bitterness. The rejection follows: “Because you are not of my sheep” (ibid.). And again: “I and the Father are one” (ibid.)—behold butter. It follows: “The Jews took stones to throw at him” (ibid.)—behold bitterness once more.

But he could not be turned from his desire for sweetness by the taste of bitterness. For it continues: Jesus answered them, saying, “Many good works have I shown you from my Father” (ibid.); this is butter. Bitterness follows: “For which work do you stone me?” (ibid.). And elsewhere still, one thing upon another: “They sought to seize him” (John VII). But he, rejecting evil, went out of their hands [Col. 0479C].

Why recount each instance? We rarely find that Jesus ate butter without bitterness. Finally, who would not marvel as he considers that last and great bitterness, the sweetness of butter, and the rejection of evil? The Lord Jesus hung upon the cross in order to taste the cup of bitter death for the sweetness of piety; and while enemies surrounded him and, after inflicting dreadful wounds, hurled blasphemous cries against him, he, not forgetful of the sweetness of his food, said: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII). Behold the best butter, indeed outwardly sprinkled with great bitterness, yet preserving its sweetness within unharmed.

Therefore, to show that he had voluntarily accepted bitterness without corruption of his sweetness, he cried out: “I thirst.” But they offered him vinegar mixed with gall; and when he had tasted, he would not drink [Col. 0479D] (John XIX). He tasted and rejected, because he endured and cast it away. He suffered and overcame. Is it not now plainly evident how our Emmanuel eats butter in order to know how to reject evil? For God, displaying a work of piety in man and enduring the persecution of the ungodly, experienced how deserving of rejection their perversity was—a perversity which, through foreknowledge, he himself had already rejected.

Now let us gladly consider how this Emmanuel eats honey, in order to know how to choose good. In the taste of honey, indeed, no bitterness is found; and therefore everything that is there is chosen by the one who experiences it. Thus he eats honey in order that he may know how to choose good. But what are we saying? What sort of praise is this—if, indeed, it ought to be called praise—that God made man learned good by experience, he who was always himself goodness? Yet this is praise of his piety and a proclamation of his mercy: that he deigned so to bend down for us as to be able, in that which he assumed, to receive what he always possesses in that which he was.

For God made man tasted by experience in time what he, man made God, was by nature from eternity. Therefore the humanity of divinity ate honey when majesty poured itself into weakness and united itself to it. There human nature began, with the full taste of satiation, to drink in heavenly sweetness, where it received, united to itself by ineffable grace, all that God is. Yet eating belonged to the man; being food belonged to the divinity [Col. 0480B]. Therefore Emmanuel, who eats honey in order that he may know how to choose good, is true man. Emmanuel, who was honey—not learning by experience, but knowing by nature that he himself is good—is true God. Yet he is one and the same: knowing through himself and by nature, and learning through experience. For the same man received through experience what he himself, as God, was by nature.

O good Emmanuel, God with us: therefore you were able to eat butter and honey, because you became Emmanuel, God with us. For as God you could neither receive what you already were nor endure what you were not. Therefore you became Emmanuel, God with us, so that, humbled in what is ours, you might in that same assumed nature receive from above what was yours and unite to yourself below what was ours. Therefore you became Emmanuel, God with us, in order that you might be able to eat butter and honey, and while eating might learn, choosing good, to reject evil.

But what am I saying? Who is wise enough to understand these things? What kind of God, then, were you from the beginning, you who in the beginning divided light and darkness, if you did not know how to choose good and reject evil? Or perhaps not to know even this was a matter of power, and to learn it a matter of condescension, because choosing did not belong to the divine nature, which was not capable of either alternative? Thus Emmanuel learned to choose and reject because he who, in his own nature, was not subject to condition, assumed free choice in ours. To this free choice, established in himself, he granted the ability not to be able to fail into evil, and the free, uncoerced choice of good by the will [Col. 0480D]. It is no less free because it can voluntarily suffer no alternative, nor be compelled unwillingly toward another; rather, it is truly and supremely free because it cannot either suffer anything other than what it wills, will anything other than what it can, or be able to do anything other than to will well.

Thus Emmanuel eats butter and honey, that he may know how to reject evil and choose good, because in the human nature which he assumed he abandoned evil and chose good by the rational judgment of a holy will, as it is written: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV). In a similar manner of speaking the Apostle says of him: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things which he suffered; and, having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him” (Heb. V) [Col. 0481A].

For Christ learned obedience from the things which he suffered, because he who was the Son, equal by nature, assumed by grace what was possible to that which is lower, so that he might be subject. For it was, as it were, to learn: to take into use from another what he did not possess in his own nature. There remains only this: perhaps we may find our Emmanuel eating butter and honey not for refreshment but for delight, so that what he did may be will rather than necessity. “They offered him a piece of broiled fish and a honeycomb” (Luke XXIV). He had already been made immortal and impassible and had no need of bodily food; yet, in order to show what he was, he ate by will, not necessity.

Everything, therefore, would fit well if they had offered him butter and a honeycomb—unless perhaps the fish itself signifies to us that butter is not taken without frying. For we too daily still find bitterness mixed in butter and perceive pure sweetness in honey, because in the work of piety we are wearied by labor, while in the joy of contemplation we are refreshed by sweetness [Col. 0481B]. And all this occurs that we may know how to reject evil and choose good: namely, that in this very experience we may learn how much the present life, in which not even good can be done without pain, ought to be fled, and how much the future life, in which there is no pain, ought to be desired. Through our Lord.

## III. A Fable Demonstrating That Every Heart Is Inclined to Commend Itself and Its Own

A fable says that all the beasts presented their offspring to Jupiter for approval. Among them, a monkey dragging along her deformed young could not be restrained, despite everyone’s laughter, from preferring her own to all the others [Col. 0481C]. For it is inborn in every living creature to love what it has begotten. A thought is born from the heart, and hearts love their offspring so greatly that a perverse mind often does not blush, in the sight of the highest truth, to commend its own crooked and depraved thought, worthy of everyone’s laughter.

## IV. On the Fool Who “Changes Like the Moon,” and the Just Person Who Is “One Man”

“The fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII). The fool is personally one, but through instability and changeableness he is many. Just as the moon is one and is called first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and so on, and many variations arise in one body, so the fool—now weeping, now laughing, now sad, now cheerful—displays many forms in one person, as though increasing and decreasing and passing from one thing to another. By contrast, in praise of the just person it was said: “There was one man” (I Sam. I). For the just person is one, not only in person but in life, because, since he is not divided by diverse errors of living, he is found as though abiding in one countenance of truth [Col. 0481D].

## V. That a Human Being’s Good Does Not Lie in Sensation

By sinning, man brought it about that he should be compared with beasts; yet he could not bring it about that, in the very respect in which he was compared with beasts, he should be made their equal. For he who ceased to be superior in reason found himself inferior in sensation. If you consult sight, lynxes surpass him. If you inquire into smell, dogs prevail. And whatever is praiseworthy in bodily sensation, you will find it more excellent in them, so that you may seek your good elsewhere and not rest it upon that in which you are compared with beasts and yet not their equal [Col. 0482A].

## VI. On Threefold Peace

There is one peace which a human being ought to have toward God, another toward himself, and another toward his neighbor. For the human spirit was placed by this law between God and the flesh: if it rendered the obedience due to God, who is above, the flesh subject to its rule would never oppose it. Therefore, so long as man kept peace with God, he found no troublesome contradiction in his flesh. But after he began through pride to rebel against his Creator, immediately the flesh, separating itself from harmony with him, refused to be subject. From this point man, distracted by the various desires of his concupiscence and desiring what belonged to others and what had not been granted to him, crossed the bounds of justice against his neighbor. Thus peace there also having been disturbed, he began to be restless and troubled on every side [Col. 0482B].

The condition now proposed for restoration is this: if he wishes to have peace with God, he should strive to have peace with his neighbor. But when the spirit has been fully subjected to God, grace will also reform into peace the contradiction which it bears in its flesh.
