Thus the human being will be wholly at peace: outside himself with his neighbor through brotherly charity, within himself through a good conscience, and above himself through divine grace. Therefore, while the saving sacrifice by which we ought to be reconciled to God is offered, we first offer the sign of peace by a kiss, so that, once the peace which exists among ourselves has preceded, we may deserve to obtain that peace which is toward God.

But when this saving sacrifice is offered for the faithful departed, those who remain alive do not receive the kiss of peace from one another, since those for whom the life-giving offering is made have been removed from this life and can no longer maintain or display the peace or concord of human fellowship [Col. 0482C]. There, therefore, only that reconciliation which is toward God is sought, where those who have once departed hence are no longer subject to the condition of the present life. The living, however, through peace with their neighbor merit peace with God, and through peace with God merit peace with themselves—not that peace which is between the soul and the world, but that which is between the soul and the spirit, through that which is between the spirit and God.

For there is a certain peace between soul and world among those who live pleasantly and badly; there is a certain peace between soul and spirit among those who live pleasantly and well; and there is a certain peace between God and spirit among those who live happily and blessedly. Similarly, there is war between soul and world among those who live unpleasantly and badly; there is war between soul and spirit among those who live unpleasantly and well; and there is war between spirit and God among those who live unhappily and badly. For blessed Job testifies concerning wisdom that those who live pleasantly and badly do not know the true peace in which wisdom is found in the time of good leisure: “It is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII) [Col. 0482D].

## VII. On the Dignity and Freedom of Rational Creatures

The rational creature alone was so created that it was not itself its own good, but belonged to him by whom it was made. Its dignity, therefore, is great, because no good beneath the highest can suffice for it; and its freedom likewise is great, because it cannot be compelled toward its good [Col. 0483A].

## VIII. On Three Kinds of Exercise, and the Names by Which Active and Contemplative Life Are Figured

The condition of mutable life is such that it cannot remain long in the same state; moreover, what has been sought for consolation is turned again into labor and pain. Thus it fluctuates in its exercises and passes from one thing to another, so that it is never at rest until it comes to true stability.

There are three kinds of exercises: some for the advancement of virtue, others for the consolation of weakness, and others for the inflaming of wickedness. The first build up; the second sustain; the third overthrow. Therefore God introduced the building exercises, permitted the sustaining exercises, and forbade the overthrowing exercises. He divided times and distinguished places for building and sustaining exercises: when and where those which can suitably be done together should be done. For, occupied with sustaining exercises, we are not sufficient to maintain the building ones; and, turned toward building exercises, we ought not to become entangled in sustaining ones. The six days belong to sustaining exercises; the seventh to building ones. Thus all places are allowed for sustaining exercises, while few are reserved for building ones, except for those who have consecrated themselves to building exercises and serve them in every place and at all times [Col. 0483B].

For there are two kinds of human beings according to these two lawful exercises: builders correspond to the contemplative, sustainers to the active. These are the two lives, the two peoples, and the two testaments: Leah and Rachel, Jacob and Israel, Zion and Jerusalem, Peter and John, Martha and Mary, left and right, wool and flax, barley and wheat, water and wine, and so forth [Col. 0483C].

## IX. That “Element” Is Said in Two Ways

An element is the first matter of a bodily composition. An element is a material representation of an invisible subsistence and the beginning of knowledge for those passing from bodily things to incorporeal things. In the former sense, an element is the beginning of subsistence for things proceeding toward an invisible act; in the latter, it is the beginning of understanding for those entering into invisible truth.

## X. On the Trinity of the Universe

Truly, the universe subsists in a single trinity. There is one thing which is neither from another nor according to another: the creating nature. There is one thing which is from one and according to one: the rational creature, from God and like God. There is one thing which is from one and according to two—that is, from one through one: bodily nature, created by God and ordered according to uncreated and created wisdom [Col. 0483D]. The first is exemplar only, not image; the second is both exemplar and image; the third is image only, not exemplar.

## XI. That in Original Sin There Were Three Vices, Two Disobediences, and One Sin

In original sin there were three vices, two disobediences, and one sin. The three vices were pride, avarice, and gluttony; the two disobediences were against nature and against discipline. In pride and avarice there was disobedience against the natural command; in gluttony there was disobedience against the command of discipline, an added command. Since all these were completed in one act, they are called one sin [Col. 0484A].

## XII. That Christ and Wisdom Are Sought in Various Ways by Different People

Some sought Christ and did not find him. Some sought and found him, but did not keep him, because they did not seek him in order to possess him but in order to sell him. Some sought Christ, found him, and kept him, because they did not seek him to sell him but to possess him.

To the first he said: “Where I go, you cannot come. You shall seek me and shall not find me, but you shall die in your sins” (John VIII). To the second he said: “I am he. If you seek me, let these go away.” And they laid hands on him and held him (John XVIII) [Col. 0484B]. To the third he said: “Greetings.” And they came and took hold of his feet (Matt. XXVIII). The first sought and did not find. The second found him alive and killed what they had found. The third sought him dead and found him alive.

Thus many seek wisdom and do not find it, because they are judged useless and cast away. Others seek wisdom and find it, but do not love it, because they display and prostitute it in order to obtain profit and human praise. These find Christ alive but kill him, because wisdom dies in them precisely because they enjoy its sweetness with no feeling of love. They are taken up in order to be judged and cast down more grievously. Others seek wisdom as dead and find it alive, because, since they do not desire it for the use of this life, they attain more truly within to its sweetness and delight. These are taken up in order to be raised and glorified [Col. 0484C].

## XIII. That in Scripture God Speaks Outwardly to Man Through Commands, Prohibitions, Promises, and Threatenings

So long as man could hear God speaking within, he had no need of outward instruction. But after he was no longer able to behold the book of life with his inward eye, Scripture is set before him outwardly, so that at least by looking upon it he may be renewed unto the knowledge of truth. In this Scripture there are prohibitions of evils, that he may flee them, and commands of goods, that he may seek them. Threats are attached to prohibitions, because man could not be restrained by hatred of evil alone; promises are joined to commands, because he could not be moved to good by love of good alone.

These four things are generally distinct throughout all Scripture: commands and prohibitions, promises and threats. The first two pertain to the shaping of life; the latter two to the instruction of faith. In the former merit consists; in the latter, reward. Right faith and good action make a person perfect. At first, however, carnal threatenings and promises, temporal punishments and rewards, are given to carnal persons; then spiritual and eternal ones to spiritual persons. Finally, for those who have been exercised, hatred of evil and love of good suffice for exhortation. Thus salvation grows by its stages and virtue advances.

In all Scripture either knowledge of truth or a pattern of virtue must be sought [Col. 0485A]. The first is presented through the study of history and allegory; the second through tropology. Within tropology itself there are likewise two kinds of reading: the first instructs morals by straightforward narration; the second kindles in the minds of hearers desires for virtue by impassioned exhortation.

## XIV. That God Is with Man in Four Ways

God is with us in four ways: through the presence of majesty, through participation in humanity, through the bond of charity, and through the protection of truth. In the first, he knows our evils; in the second, he has experienced them; in the third, he has compassion on them; in the fourth, he removes them. And he is Emmanuel—that is, God with us.

Again, God is with some through the favor of grace, though they are not with God through the merit of their life. With some, God is through the favor of grace, and they themselves are with God through the merit of their life. With some, God is not through a manifest favor of grace, and yet they themselves are with God through the merit of their life. With some, God is not through the favor of grace, and they themselves are not with God through the merit of their life [Col. 0485B].

## XV. On the Stages of Knowledge

There are five stages of knowledge: the first in sensation, the second in imagination, the third in reason, the fourth in understanding, the fifth in intelligence. Through sensation, one is in these things and according to these things. Through imagination, one is not in these things but is according to these things. Through reason, one is neither in these things nor according to these things, but is in and concerning those things which are according to these things. Through understanding, one is not in those things, but is concerning them. Through intelligence, one is neither in those things nor concerning them [Col. 0485C].

## XVI. That the Mind Considers What Is to Be Done in Four Ways

We consider things to be done in our mind in four ways: by thinking, willing, deliberating, and vowing. Thought pertains to knowledge, will to desire, deliberation to resolve, and a vow to promise. If we do not do what we resolve, we are untruthful. If we do not do what we promise, we are both untruthful and deceiving. In the former case only falsehood is charged; in the latter, both falsehood is charged and what was promised is exacted.

One vow is secret, made to God and before God; another is manifest, made to God and before human beings. A secret vow broken is a sin; a manifest vow broken is both sin and scandal [Col. 0485C].

## XVII. On God’s Unequal Working

“If these things had been done in Tyre and Sidon,” etc. (Matt. XI; Luke X.) The Lord, wishing to show that both the gift of knowing truth and that of reverencing truth once known with due devotion are from him, preached truth to some whose hearts he did not soften toward love of the truth. But he softened the hearts of others with the affection of goodness, while not enlightening them with recognition of the truth.

In the former he ploughed but did not sow, breaking hardness but not scattering the word. In the latter he sowed but did not plough, scattering the word without breaking hardness. Thus we may know that both come from him and learn to ask both from him, since we recognize that neither is sufficient for salvation without the other [Col. 0486A].

In this way is resolved what people commonly raise from the Gospel: why God, coming in the flesh, preached the Word to those whom he foreknew would not receive that very Word, while he did not confer the word of preaching upon certain others whom he knew would have believed had they heard him teaching. Rebuking the hardness of some to whom truth had been preached, he says: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; woe to you, Capernaum! For if these things had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in ashes and sackcloth” (ibid.).

This seems astonishing: why Jesus, who possessed knowledge of all future things, preached in Capernaum when he foreknew their hardness to be so great that they would not receive the truth even when it was offered. And why, likewise, he did not perform in Tyre and Sidon the things which he performed in Capernaum and Bethsaida, when he knew that these people were such that they would readily receive truth if they could hear and know it [Col. 0486B]. For just as it seems impious to abandon the obedient, so it seems foolish altogether to teach rebels.

But the former was an act of judgment, the latter an example. Lest a person should suppose that the affection of good alone suffices without knowledge, and therefore, feeling in himself an affection for goodness, should not seek the word of truth, he pierced those persons but did not teach or save them. And lest, again, he should suppose that recognition of truth alone is sufficient for salvation, and that hearing the law without doing it is consummate righteousness, he taught these persons, did not pierce them, and condemned them. Thus, when the reprobate are seen to possess each in turn one without the other, the elect may understand that both are necessary for them; and whoever recognizes that he possesses one should not presume upon his own strength, but should humbly ask from him what he lacks—from him from whom it did not benefit some to receive one thing because he did not grant them the other, which is strictly required in judgment [Col. 0486C].

For a person does not deserve to receive what he lacks if he thinks that he possesses from himself what he has. Therefore, of the two, one is in turn granted by God and the other withdrawn, so that where both are together it may be shown that both are from him.

## XVIII. On Faith: What It Is and What Belongs to It

Before we begin to examine the matters which pertain to faith, we ought to consider what faith itself is. The Apostle defines faith thus: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not apparent” (Heb. XI).

For things of any kind subsist for us either through actuality, when they are present and grasped by the senses; or through understanding, when they are absent or even nonexistent but are grasped in their likeness and in imagination; or through experience, when we ourselves feel the things that are within us, such as joy and sorrow, fear and love, which subsist in us and are felt by us. None of these ways enables us to grasp within ourselves the invisible things of God, which are believed by us alone. For they are neither present through actuality, nor capable of being grasped in any likeness, nor are they like those things which are within us and are felt by us.

Therefore, they subsist in us by faith alone, and their subsistence is the faith by which they are believed, because they are understood to exist but not understood as they are [Col. 0487A]. Thus they subsist in us by faith alone and are proved to us by faith alone; nor can we have any other evidence except that we believe those things by faith which we do not comprehend by reason. This description of faith shows what faith does, but does not define what faith is.

The definition of faith is this: faith is a voluntary certainty concerning absent things, placed above opinion and below knowledge. It should be known that knowledge of faith is one thing, faith another. When the same discourse is heard by many people, all understand equally what is said; but they do not all believe equally. All have knowledge of what is said, but not all have faith. Knowledge of faith can exist without any faith at all; but faith cannot exist without any knowledge at all [Col. 0487B].

Yet many believe and do not have knowledge of all that they believe, because they believe those who believe and know, and do not themselves know everything which they believe, but those whom they believe know it. Such is the faith of simple persons in the Church, who are saved by believing and adhering to more perfect persons, as it is written: “The oxen were ploughing, and the she-asses were feeding beside them” (Job I). For these believe more fully in the faith of the perfect than they know by their own believing.

Faith grows in two ways: through devotion or steadfastness, and through knowledge. The increases of faith through devotion proceed in three stages. The first stage is assent; the second is judging or supposing; the third stage is certainty. Corresponding to these three stages are three kinds of people.

There is one kind of people in the holy Church for whom believing consists only in not contradicting the faith. They live as they were born, neither loving nor approving what they were born into; had they been born elsewhere, they would not be faithful. They hold the faith by custom of living, not by love [Col. 0487C].

There is another kind of people, more attentively considering the condition of human life and beginning in some measure to waver in faith because they see many turned away and alienated from faith. Yet, led by the piety of faith, they choose, of two uncertainties, that which they have learned from Catholic teaching. Peace is necessary for these, and tribulation dangerous, lest perhaps those who judge or suppose become deniers.

There is another kind of people who are certain and established in their faith, whom God has either confirmed by outward miracles or taught through inward inspiration. These are not overthrown by tribulation, but exercised by it. It should also be known that, just as there are three stages through which faith grows, so there are three stages through which knowledge of faith grows.

The first stage of knowledge of faith is that than which faith could never have had less: namely, to believe that God exists and to await him as Savior and rewarder. This knowledge of faith could suffice for salvation for simple persons before the incarnation of the Word: that they should believe in God and await a Savior, although they did not know the manner and time of that salvation. For there are only two things in man: nature and fault [Col. 0488A]. The Creator relates to nature; the Savior, to fault.

Under the written law knowledge increased, when open discourse began already to be made about the person of the Redeemer, when the Savior was promised through the law, and, after being promised, awaited. Under grace knowledge increased still further, when the Savior himself was manifested not merely as man, as many had formerly supposed, but also as true God; and when it was shown that the manner of redemption consisted not in the height of earthly power, but in the Savior’s death.

## XIX. On Charity, Faith, and Hope
As the other virtues are goods of nature, so charity is the good of all virtues: whoever has it has every virtue in some respect. For even those virtues which [Col. 0488B] he does not possess in act he possesses in their effect. To possess virtues in affection, through grace, zeal, and human merit, belongs to man; but to possess them in effect is a divine gift. For willing belongs to man, but power to God. Thus man’s good will is from God, his evil will from man. God’s power, in evil, is good to man for evil; in good, it is good to man for good. Therefore whoever has charity has everything; and whoever does not have it has nothing, or has nothing usefully. Hence the Apostle said of charity: “Charity believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. XIII). Faith points out the good; hope lays hold of it; endurance defends it. By faith good things begin to belong to us; by hope they become ours; by endurance they remain with us. Faith directs, hope draws, endurance brings us through. And all these are in charity, [Col. 0488C] because, where something is loved and pleasing, love readily persuades one to believe, to presume much, and not readily to desist.

## TITLE XX. On the Four Debtors

There are four debtors: God, spirit, flesh, and world. God owes the spirit that He should both enlighten it with knowledge of the truth and inflame it with love of virtue. The spirit owes God that, in all things which are to be done, it should be instructed by Him and act according to Him. The spirit owes the flesh that it should both restrain it from evils and exercise it in goods. The flesh owes the spirit service in doing good, and moderation in seeking what is advantageous. The flesh owes the world that it should take from its abundance what necessity requires, and employ what virtue requires. The world owes the flesh aid in necessity and, in its exercise, [Col. 0488D] encouragement.

But the spirit does not pay its debt to the Creator, because, either puffed up by pride, it despises seeking from Him knowledge of the truth, or, bound by sloth, it scorns to put into practice the understanding it has received. Therefore the Creator Himself justly withholds His debt from the spirit: He neither enlightens it to know the truth nor inflames it to love the good. For He casts the proud man inwardly away from knowledge of the truth; but He afflicts the slothful man outwardly in action.

Again, because this same spirit does not pay its debt to the flesh—namely, by restraining it from evil or exercising it in good—it follows that the flesh itself, by God’s just ordering, does not render to the spirit what it owes: namely, service in doing good or moderation in seeking what is advantageous. [Col. 0489A] Likewise, because the flesh, loosened through the spirit’s negligence, does not render its debt to the world, but turns its abundance toward the luxury of pleasure and does not employ its provision for the stirring up of virtue, the world too, in just recompense for multiplying the spirit’s misery, both breaks it by adversities and dissipates it by prosperities.

Since the spirit alone is the author of this discord, it must itself first return to peace and then, successively after it, restore the rest to peace. For if it endeavors both to render due subjection to the Creator and just governance to the flesh, perfect and complete justice follows; and, justice restored, perfect concord and peace are restored as well. For just as through its injustice the peace and concord of all are dissolved, so through its [Col. 0489B] justice all things are reconciled.

The spirit could lose this justice when it possessed it; but it cannot recover it by itself when it has lost it. For it is deceived by ignorance and thus fails to pay its debt to the Creator; it is hindered by concupiscence and thus fails to pay its debt to the flesh. And even if, perhaps, enlightened in part, it begins to recognize the truth, and, strengthened in part, to accomplish the good, it nevertheless cannot here attain that which is perfect. Rather, as it is written, it begins to hunger and thirst for justice tasted in part, but does not attain satiety through its fullness as though it had been possessed.

## TITLE XXI. On the Hindrance to Knowledge

As fine moisture is drawn upward from the earth by exhalations, so the understanding of the human heart, made subtle through meditations and investigations, is raised to things on high. [Col. 0489C] And just as moisture rising upward is congealed by cold and falls back whence it came, so many fall from understanding of the highest things into ignorance, because they grow numb through sloth in doing the goods which they were able to understand.

But the fall of snow neither makes a noise nor causes harm; the fall of hail both makes a noise and harms by its weight. Thus many are numb toward good and harmful in evil; others are numb but not harmful.

## TITLE XXII. On the Three Motions in Man

There are three motions in man: the motion of the mind, the motion of the body, and the motion of sensuality. The motion of the mind lies in the will; the motion of the body, in action; the motion of sensuality, intermediate between them, in pleasure. Free choice exists only in the motion of the mind. The motions of the body and sensuality follow free choice.

For such was the original disposition of nature: the motion of the mind is a voluntary appetite. In what is voluntary there is freedom; in appetite, choice. Thus the mind moves of itself and is the first motion of the will. The motion of the body follows the motion of the will. The mind, therefore, as I have said, has the power to move itself, but according to the will of its Creator, which is its form, exemplar, and proposed rule to follow. Therefore, if it moves according to God, this is justice; if it moves apart from God or against God, this is injustice.

Thus the motion of the mind is always either justice or injustice; but the motion of the body is always obedience. For when the mind moves, it moves in freedom, because it moves voluntarily [Col. 0490A] and of itself; and its motion belongs to it, either for merit if it moves well, or for fault if badly. But when the body moves, it moves by necessity, because it is moved by another, namely by the mind; nor does its motion belong to itself but to that by which it is moved—whether for merit, if rightly, or for fault, if wrongly. Thus the motion of the mind rules the motion of the body, which is subject to the law of nature; and when it misuses it, the fault is the ruler’s, while obedience is the subject’s due. The person led is not blamed, because he is led by necessity; rather, the one who leads is blamed, because he misuses his freedom over what is subject to him.

Moreover, if the will had retained justice, it would have possessed not only the obedient motion of the body but also the consenting motion of sensuality. But now, because it did not itself retain its rectitude, it still has, through the Creator’s indulgence, the obedient motion of the body, but through punishment it has the contrary motion of sensuality. [Col. 0490B] Sometimes, weakened, it follows this violence; at other times, strengthened, it restrains and moderates it. But if the motion of sensuality rules the motion of the mind, it also rules the motion of the body, which is subject to the mind; and then sin begins to reign in our mortal body. But if it does not rule, the mind uses the service of its body and presents its members as weapons of justice. Thus the motion of the mind and that of the body are together, while the motion of sensuality is separate; justice is accomplished and iniquity restrained.

## TITLE XXIII. On the Instruments of Knowledge

[Col. 0490C] In sounds there are two things: melody and meaning. In things likewise there are two: form and essence. In minds, similarly, there are two: affection and knowledge. In the human body there are two instruments: ears and eyes. Through the ears sounds enter, so that through melody they generate affection and through meaning knowledge. But things enter through the eyes, so that through form they likewise generate affection in the mind, and through essence knowledge.

## TITLE XXIV. On Man’s Carnal and Spiritual Sense

There are two senses in man, one carnal and the other spiritual; and each has its own good, in which it rejoices and delights. The carnal sense rejoices and exults in the serenity of the air and brightness of the sun, [Col. 0490D] in the sweetness of foods and drinks, in the pleasantness of places and delightfulness of rivers. This sense is animal-like, for it belongs to beasts and birds.

The spiritual sense, however, exults in divine light poured in from above, as befits contemplative persons. It also rejoices in the exercise of virtues and the cultivation of justice. When the external—that is, carnal—sense enjoys its own good, the inward sense of the mind, as it were, falls asleep. Hence one who is captivated by the delight of such goods does not even recognize the goods of the inward sense. For one despises external things who is carried away by the sweetness of the goods of the inner sense. Thus it is that most religious men appear foolish to the world.

## TITLE XXV. On Divine Lights

God’s lights are good, and He Himself, the author of gifts, [Col. 0491A] is the Father of lights, “with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. I), because neither is He changed when He enlightens, nor darkened when He does not enlighten. For He who begets does not degenerate, and He who does not beget does not grow dim, because He is neither diminished by going forth nor made darker by remaining hidden.

When His lights come to us, they do not depart from Him; and when they return from us, they shine brightly with Him. When they descend to us, they do not fail in us; and when they withdraw from us, they do not suffer diminution on our account. Therefore they are not changed into us when they come to us to be shared; nor are they overshadowed in themselves when they return from those whom they illuminate or overshadow, and remain in themselves.

## TITLE XXVI. On the Conception and Birth of Wisdom

[Col. 0491B] “The depths were not yet, and I was being brought forth” (Prov. VIII). God had conceived wisdom in foreknowledge of the future; He was bringing it forth in the will to create; He gave birth to it in the production of the thing accomplished.

## TITLE XXVII. On the Threefold Kind of Inspirations

The origin of inspirations is threefold: from God, from the devil, and from nature. Those which are from nature have a preceding cause of necessity. Those from God or the devil arise suddenly and unexpectedly: from God, good ones; from the devil, bad ones. Sometimes things come that seem good but are not; these too are from the devil, and their origin is proved by their outcome. This is the meaning of: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John IV).

## TITLE XXVIII. On the Five Yokes

There are five yokes: the yoke of iniquity, the yoke [Col. 0491C] of mortality, the yoke of the law, the yoke of one’s own will, and the yoke of charity.

## TITLE XXIX. That Nothing Can Be Disordered to God

“In Babylon one does not seek another; but owls answer one another in her shrines” (Isa. XIII). It is a small thing that all things should be ordered in heaven; the wonderful thing is that divine Wisdom does not even leave worldly confusion unordered. For there even works of darkness answer one another, and there is no need for one to seek another, because just ordering leaves nothing disordered, gives to each what is its own, and that which is confused for itself cannot be without order and arrangement for Him.

Even that inward confusion of evil hearts does not escape His ordering: there light-shunning thoughts and dark desires, drifting in secret, answer one another, because just judgment, as it understands all things through wisdom, so through equity leaves nothing without recompense.

## TITLE XXX. That God Is Not Changed

[Col. 0491D] God is not changed from what He Himself is; what is in Him does not undergo alteration. For what He Himself is is unchangeable; what is in Him is eternal. He is not changed so as to become another; He does not undergo alteration so as to be otherwise.

## TITLE XXXI. On the Mystery in the Form of Heaven and Earth

“As is the earth, such are the earthly; and as is heaven, such are the heavenly” (1 Cor. XV). Above, all things are equal. Below are mountains and valleys, heights and depths, low places and high, and all things are variously constituted. [Col. 0492A] Mortal life cannot indeed have a level road, but it exalts and humbles; now it displays evenness, but then presents a precipice and threatens a fall. Therefore the earth is such as the earthly are.

Above, however, there is nowhere to stumble or fall headlong, or to walk unevenly; all is level, equal, harmonious, and measured. Therefore heaven is such as the heavenly are.

## TITLE XXXII. On the Course of Times and the Proper Objects of Love

Past, present, and future make, as it were, one body of eternity. To love the past is the part of the unwise; the present, of the foolish; the future, of the prudent. Piety belongs to past things, covetousness to present things, charity to future things.

## TITLE XXXIII. On the Fruit and Desire of Justice

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst after justice” (Matt. V). [Col. 0492B] Therefore it is not those who are satiated, but those who hunger, who are blessed. Yet they are not blessed because they hunger, but because they shall be filled. For if desire were always present and attainment never came, this would be punishment and misery rather than blessedness.

But the mercy of our God has promised an assured fulfillment to holy desires. Therefore those who desire are blessed, because this is the first good, and the only one which mortal life, subject to punishments, can attain: to will the good. For possessing and enjoying it He has reserved for the life to come. Therefore He does not call the righteous blessed, but those who hunger and thirst after justice. For if He called only the righteous blessed, who would claim this for himself? Thus He had regard for our imperfection, that He might console our weakness: since, although we cannot be this, with His help we can at least will and desire to be it.

And again, those are called blessed not for desiring glory but justice, because many say that they love their homeland but are unwilling to keep the road. Glory and blessedness are the homeland, but justice is the road; and those who do not keep the road cannot come to the homeland. Who does not seek advantage? But not all wish to be just.

## TITLE XXXIV. On the Sacrament of Christ’s Body

The Lord Jesus Christ, in order to show that His divinity is the refreshment of our souls, set His flesh before us as food; and again, lest human weakness should shrink from receiving it, He veiled it under the appearance of familiar food.

## TITLE XXXV. On the Glory and Punishment of the Human Body

[Col. 0492D]

How great is the dignity of the soul, if the body’s glory is so great! For how much more excellent than all things seen is proved to be the human spirit, when all bodily things were created for the service of the human body? Hence, rightly, what had been established higher and more sublime by its condition has been made more contemptible than all things through punishment and misery. But when it has been restored, corruption removed from its midst, it will receive what is better than all bodies; and then, free from misery, it will be joined to the spirit for glory, to which it is now joined in misery for punishment.

## TITLE XXXVI. That Moses Was a Type of Christ, the Future Mediator between God and Men

It is written that the people could not speak with [Col. 0493A] God and asked for Moses as mediator. The Lord approved this and said that He would raise up a Prophet who would be Mediator, and through whom He would give commandments to the people (Exod. XX). For carnal hearts could not perceive the invisible things of God; and God adapted Himself to us through the humanity of His Son, so that through it as mediator we might perceive divine things.

The terror of majesty would overwhelm weak minds, and brilliant light would blind weak-sighted eyes, unless the cloud of flesh intervened, received contemplation, and gently soothed timid hearts by the pleasantness of the vision.

## TITLE XXXVII. That a Creature Cannot Be Well without Its Creator

“Woe to him who is alone! For when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccles. IV). There are two: the one who made, and that which was made. [Col. 0493B] But that which was made cannot be well without Him who made it. What was made has within itself the capacity to fall, not the capacity to rise. But He who made what was made cannot fall, and can lift up what falls. Therefore it is better for two to be together than for one to be alone.

## TITLE XXXVIII. On Division through Iniquity and Union through Charity

Iniquity first divided God and man; then it divided man himself. Afterwards charity came and reconciled and united first God and man, then man himself. Iniquity badly divided what was well united. Charity well united what was badly divided. Likewise, iniquity badly united what was well divided, and charity well divided what was badly united. Therefore iniquity divides [Col. 0493C] and unites, and charity divides and unites.

Finally death follows, dividing—and it does so because of iniquity—but uniting by its condition unto charity. Death divides body and soul. Iniquity divides God and the soul. Charity divides spirit and concupiscence. Death divides the unity of condition. Iniquity divides the unity of reconciliation. Charity divides the unity of alienation.

## TITLE XXXIX. On the Threefold Operation of Philosophy

The natural operation of philosophy acts through the senses upon things subject to it, and descends to particulars; without the experience of the senses it is weak, relying upon them as upon a supporting staff, unable to walk by itself. The rational operation of philosophy acts outside the senses upon universals, flourishing by reason alone. The technical operation has the rational as its instrument and tests the natural.

## TITLE XL. On the Threefold Instruction and the Twofold Operation of the Spirit

Some are instructed from within; others draw understanding from without. In the former the spirit of wisdom is stable; in the latter, mobile. Meditation belongs to the former; contemplation to the latter. The former penetrate hidden things by keenness of understanding; the latter fly swiftly to distant things by agility. Those who do not discern spirits think the lingering of meditation sloth and the movement of contemplation frivolity, although the body receives its quality from the soul.

As the spirit enlightens, so it kindles; and those whom it enlightens, it enlightens with knowledge of the truth; those whom it kindles, [Col. 0494A] it kindles with love of virtue. Its operation in both is often not discerned: stable persons are called slothful; those powerful in mind and effective in comprehension, frivolous; the contrite, sad; those joyful in spirit, wanton. Thus judgment of the spirit is made without the spirit, and people err in judgment, since each thinks good only what he loves.

Meditation and contrition have a similar outward expression; likewise contemplation and exultation resemble each other, because bodily movement is formed by the quality of the soul. Thus in one person there is gravity without heaviness, in another lightness without instability. Meditation and contrition belong to John; contemplation and exultation to Christ. One says: “We have mourned to you, and you have not wept” (Luke VII). The other says: “We have danced for you, and you have not stood up.” John came neither eating [Col. 0494B] nor drinking, and you said: “He has a demon.” The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you said: “Behold, a man who is a glutton and a drinker of wine, and a friend of sinners” (Luke VII; Matt. XI). Thus to the perverse all things are perverse.

## TITLE XLI. That the Faint-Hearted Must First Be Cherished by Consolation, That They May Rise; Afterwards Strengthened by Terror through Rebuke, Lest They Fall Again

“A scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. XIII). The new things are consolations; the old things, rebukes. For the old law set forth punishment, by which it might terrify; the new law, mercy, by which it might cherish. Why, then, new things first and old things afterwards? Because mercy speaks: it first caresses, then strikes.

For the faint-hearted must first be cherished by consolation, that they may rise; afterwards they must be strengthened by terror, lest they fall again. The obstinate and hard must first be rebuked, that they may fear; afterwards cherished by consolation, lest they despair. Therefore, when mercy speaks, it speaks new things and old; when severity speaks, old things and new. Or old things follow, rather than precede, because what is harsh ought to be additional and superabundant; and greater charity has punishment.

## TITLE XLII. That Fraternal Concord Must Not Be Broken for the Abundance of Temporal Things

Joseph forbids his brothers, whose asses are laden, to quarrel on the way (Gen. XLV), because Christ, if at any time He grants us abundance on the journey of this life, nevertheless does not permit us to break and violate peace and concord with one another for its sake.

## TITLE XLIII. That Virtue and Truth Wish to Be Together

[Col. 0494D]

“In wisdom there is a spirit of understanding, sure, gentle, loving the good, keen, which hinders not beneficence” (Wis. VII), etc. Virtue and truth, when they concern the same thing, do not impede one another. Hence, after it had been said of the spirit of wisdom that it is keen (Wis. VII), it was immediately added that it “hinders not beneficence” (ibid.).

Among the philosophers of the Gentiles there was keenness of spirit, but this very thing hindered beneficence; for the more their attention was moved by keenness to know things external, the more it was hindered by preoccupation from considering what was their own. True wisdom, however, always has virtue as its companion, because it desires above all to know what is most fitting to be. Hence it is further said of it: [Col. 0495A] “Sure, gentle, loving the good” (Wis. VII). Sure, namely by experience; gentle, by taste; loving the good, because it cannot hate in action what it truly loves in knowledge.

## TITLE XLIV. On the Twofold Love and Superstructure

“But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold” (1 Cor. III), etc. There are three kinds of people. There are those who love God alone: these build upon the foundation gold, silver, and precious stones—gold in love of virtue, silver in knowledge of truth, precious stones in the completion of good work.

There are others who love something besides God, yet nothing against God and nothing more than God. In them the foundation remains, because love of God is not destroyed; but from the affection of things loved alongside Him, because a certain corruption is contracted, wood, hay, and stubble are built upon it. In wood is the sin of unlawful action; in hay, sin of wrongful pleasure without action; in stubble, the fault of unlawful thought.

There are others who love certain things against God, and in them the foundation is utterly destroyed, because the love of God cannot exist where He is neither the sole nor the supreme object of love. Therefore the first are to be praised and saved; the second rebuked and delivered; the third reproved and condemned.

## TITLE XLV. On the Flesh as Beast of Burden and the Spirit as Rider

The flesh is a beast of burden; the spirit is its rider. It applies spurs when it arouses the flesh when sluggish, and a bridle when it moderates and restrains it when impetuous.

## TITLE XLVI. On What Is Hidden and Manifest of Man and to Man

[Col. 0495C] Some things are manifest of man and manifest to man. Some things are hidden of man and manifest to man. Some things are hidden of man and hidden to man. Therefore man ought first to be instructed in those things which are manifest and exercised so as to attain knowledge of hidden things.

For truly to know evils is to disapprove them and know that they are evil—not to call evil good or judge good to be evil—and to distinguish darkness from light, night from day, night from night, day from day, and to judge every day.

## TITLE XLVII. On the Twofold Life and Death, Joy and Pain

There are two things, life and death; and after these two others follow: joy and pain. From life comes joy; from death, pain. There is a good life and a bad life, a good joy and a bad joy; there is a good death and a bad death, a good pain and a bad pain.

The body lives from the soul; the soul, from God. At first He blessed both; afterwards the soul died through iniquity, then the body was struck with mortality and dissolved in death. Afterwards the soul was made alive through justification, then the body through resurrection. Thus now the old man, that is, the flesh, is on the cross; but the new man, that is, the soul, is in resurrection. Therefore in our resurrection is our joy; in our cross is our obedience: here, patience; there, gladness. Whoever is not crucified in the flesh has not risen in soul; and he feels where he lives, and where he feels, there he has his taste.

## TITLE XLVIII. On the Two Cities, Two Peoples, and Kings

[Col. 0496A]

There are two cities, Jerusalem and Babylon, and two peoples: lovers of God, citizens of Jerusalem; and lovers of the world, citizens of Babylon. There are also two kings: Christ, king of Jerusalem, and the devil, king of Babylon. Between these cities, two peoples, and two kings there is unceasing war, discord, and conflict. Each marks his soldiers—Christ His own and the devil his own—so that each may recognize his king and be recognized by him, and may follow him.

Jerusalem is a city above, in heaven; Babylon below, on earth. Likewise Christ is now above and the devil below. Christ’s soldiers follow their king, and the devil’s soldiers follow theirs. Christ showed us by three examples [Col. 0496B] the way in which we ought to follow Him; likewise the devil proposed three things by which those who follow him may rush headlong after him. For the way to Christ, because He is above, is steep, narrow, and lofty in its length. The way to the devil leads downward; it is broad, short to the depths, and easy for plunging headlong.

Therefore Christ left an example of poverty, that, freed from the burden of earthly possessions, we might lightly ascend the steep way; an example of humility, that, being small, we might pass without difficulty through the narrow way; and an example of patience, that we might not fail along the lengthy way. He gave the example of poverty when He said: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matt. VIII). He gave the example of humility when He said: “Learn from Me, [Col. 0496C] for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. XI). He gave the example of patience when, struck, He did not strike back, and when put to death, He endured.

Again, He gave the example of poverty because He did not wish to possess riches in this world; of humility because He despised glory; of patience because He endured evils. When praised, He did not rejoice; when cursed, He was not saddened; when oppressed, He was not broken. Someone said to Him: “Good Master.” And He answered: “Why do you call Me good?” (Mark X). Behold humility. Others said: “You have a demon”; and He said: “I do not have a demon, but I honor My Father” (John VIII). Behold patience. And when the people sought Him in order to make Him king (John VI), He fled, leaving an example [Col. 0496D] of humility and despising glory; and there are many other examples relevant to these matters.

Poverty, then, comes first, that we may cast away what weighs us down, in which there is an occasion of sinning. Because poverty is despised, humility follows, by which even lowliness is loved for God’s sake. And because one who is lowly is in turn injured without respect, patience is necessary after humility, by which all adversities may be borne courageously for God’s sake. Poverty makes one light and unencumbered; humility, small; patience, strong and robust.

Conversely, the devil first burdens his followers with the weight of riches, in love and anxiety, so that they may fall downward. Second, he puffs them up through pride, so that they may walk on the broad way. Third, he breaks them through impatience, so that they may quickly fail.

These two peoples built the two cities from their beginning [Col. 0497A]: Babylon, which took its beginning from Cain, and Jerusalem, from Abel. For the first man begot two sons, the beginning and sign of division, because that mass of human nature which in him was at first wholly created by its condition for glory was afterwards, through transgression, wholly bound over to punishment, so that it might be shown that mercy and truth had already then begun to be divided into vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath.

And the firstborn of earth was cast away, as the firstborn of heaven had fallen—if indeed he was firstborn who had not been begotten. For it was said of him: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job XL). And the first things were rejected, to show that the end is better than the beginning: for the things made by God at the beginning were indeed made good, but good in their beginning [Col. 0497B]; whereas the things to be made at the end were to be made good and good in their consummation.

For this reason, in the very creation of things, He first made matter and afterwards added form, to show that similarly in the rational creature being had first been made, but afterwards beauty and comeliness were to be added as something better; so that it should not glory too much in the first good it had received, but should rather hasten toward that better good which it was later to receive. But the firstborn loved the first thing in order to destroy the last, and was therefore rejected—both that one in heaven and this one on earth.

But the former, cast down from heaven, through envy tripped up man on earth; the latter, made reprobate on earth, killed his brother out of jealousy. For because his brother’s life was burdensome to him, he hastened toward [Col. 0497C] his death. His wicked conscience was tormented, daily seeing the life of the just man bear witness against itself; and the one whose presence condemned his wickedness was, as it were, grievous for him to behold. Therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst, so that he might not see, to his own shame, the one whom he had been unwilling to see for his own amendment and correction. Perhaps he supposed that God would thereafter not be the avenger of iniquity if the just man, the witness of truth, did not remain alive.

Thus Cain, murderer of his brother, laid the foundations of Babylon. But Abel, slain, consecrated in his own blood Jerusalem’s beginnings on earth. Thus Ishmael, the firstborn, was reprobate, while Isaac was chosen. Esau also was rejected from the lot of inheritance and the gift of blessing; Jacob was loved and chosen. And when [Col. 0497D] Eliab, the firstborn, was rejected, David the younger was raised to the height of kingship (1 Sam. XVII).

But the devil’s soldiers have always fought in fury, while Christ’s soldiers have conquered through patience, following their king in love of poverty and zeal for humility, and reaching Him through patience.

> [Note: [Col. 0497] The same may be seen in St. Ignatius, in that much-praised passage of the *Exercises*: “On the Two Standards.” —ED. PATROL.]

## TITLE XLIX. On the Office and Power of Prelates
Consider, brethren, the merciful dispensation of God. He alone can take away sins and justify sinners; yet, in order to assure the human conscience of his mercy, he granted to man the power to remit sins and the discretion to pardon, so that one person might approach another, as one like himself, more familiarly and confidently: one whom he could see when seeking forgiveness, and hear when receiving it. For God can see a person praying, but a person cannot see God granting pardon. Therefore God willed that one person should speak with another, should confer with him concerning salvation and ask forgiveness, and should receive pardon.

But lest salvation from a human being should perhaps be uncertain, God became man—one who could neither be mistaken in judging nor deceive in showing mercy. Thus all judgment was given to the Son (John 5), divine authority having been conveyed into participation by humanity, so that a human being might forgive sins—yet according to divine judgment, since that same human being was God. Christ himself, as he had become a participant in our nature, likewise willed you to be participants in his honor; and therefore he first gave you of the Holy Spirit, so that you might first be participants in truth and then sharers in dignity.

See, therefore, to your ministry, brethren: judge with the judgment of the Lord, since you have been appointed judges of the world. Hear what was said: “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth” (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 2). For this reason the Lord deferred his own judgment until the end: that you might first judge for correction, lest, when he afterward begins to judge, he judge for condemnation. For you have not been appointed as judges of crimes in order to strike, but as judges of diseases in order to heal.

See, therefore, the sick person in your hands, whom that merciful Samaritan entrusted to you, and for whom you have already received payment from him, so that that person’s cure may cost you nothing of your own. You have two coins in the twofold Testament: one of the old coinage and one of the new, so that from the Old may be purchased medicines that bite, and from the New medicines that soothe: the former to cleanse what is rotten, the latter to strengthen what is alive. These are the two obligations: namely, that of precept and that of vow. The obligation of precept, by which instruction is supplied; the obligation of vow, by which an example is formed.

These too are the two swords which Peter had prepared for defense at Christ’s Passion (Luke 21): one, namely, bodily, which under the old law inflicts punishment on sinners; the other, which under the new law strikes faults spiritually and heals people. This is your sword, by which you ought to strike the vices of people while loving the people themselves. Peter left it to you, provided that you have become heirs of his zeal and wish to be his imitators. Christ was not yet being crucified, and yet Peter could not restrain his zeal; but, drawing his sword, he struck the servant of the high priest (John 18), fearing neither the crowd nor authority. And unless Christ had restrained him, perhaps Peter would have done still greater things. Yet at that time Peter could not say, “Those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (4 Kingdoms [2 Kings] 6).

Consider, therefore, and see what you are doing. Christ is being crucified before your eyes, and you still keep the sword in its sheath, although the multitude with you is greater than that with them. What would you have done at Christ’s Passion, you who are now slow to strike? Behold, Christ is being killed before your eyes. For what is a Christian but Christ’s body? For he himself said: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matthew 25). Therefore Christ is killed in the Christian, and Christ is afflicted in the Christian. What, then, are you doing? Why are you sluggish? Why are you fearful?

Perhaps because you do not stand as Phinehas did, you cannot appease wrath so that the plague may cease (Psalm 105 [106]). Perhaps because you recline beside Pharaoh’s pots and love rich fare, you are too sluggish to rise for battle. Perhaps because you love wool and milk rather than sheep, you feed yourselves rather than the sheep, and flee when the wolf comes, because you do not care for the sheep. At least, if you consume the sheep’s milk, do not eat their flesh. If you seek profit in return for guarding the sheep, preserve the sheep themselves alive. The good shepherd even gave his own flesh for his sheep to eat, that he might restore them; but you seek payment for guarding them not merely as hired shepherds: having become wolves, you also kill the sheep themselves for your own nourishment.

Woe to evil shepherds who feed themselves rather than the sheep! And would that they merely did not feed them, if they did not also devour them! But now both the hired servants flee and the wolves kill. The hired servants flee (John 10), not by changing their place, but by withdrawing help. The wolves kill, because the visible ones tear bodies apart and the invisible ones destroy souls. If, therefore, you are shepherds, keep watch over your flock (Luke 2); do not permit Christ’s sheep to be torn apart in your hands. Go up into the breach, make yourselves a wall for the house of the Lord, and, like good dogs, bark around the sheepfolds of the Church with confident voices, so that they may fear, and so that you may deserve to receive the reward for good guardianship.

## TITLE L. On the Three Crosses

“But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Galatians 6).

In Christ’s cross there is glory; in the cross of the thief on the right, consolation; in the cross of the thief on the left, shame. In Christ’s cross, punishment without guilt and glorification after punishment; in the cross of the thief on the right, punishment for guilt and remission after punishment; in the cross of the thief on the left, punishment for guilt and condemnation after punishment.

When people suffer punishment, they say: “If we had deserved it, we would not be ashamed; but now it is shameful for us to suffer unjustly and without guilt.” Blind eyes! Rather, if you suffer for guilt, be ashamed; if you suffer without guilt, glory. Do you wish to be more a thief than Christ? And perhaps the thief on the left—a blasphemer rather than a confessor. For you suffer on account of guilt, yet do not acknowledge your guilt or reverence the judge. If only you were the thief on the right: you would humbly acknowledge your guilt, patiently endure punishment, devoutly implore pardon; you would neither presume because of punishment nor despair because of guilt—as do some who boast of their endurance, murmur at their punishment, and despair because of their guilt.

## TITLE LI. On the Twofold Oil, Namely That of God and That of the World

[Col. 0500A]

“Give us some of your oil, because our lamps are going out” (Matthew 25).

God has oil, and the world too has oil. Vessels fail for God’s oil; the world’s oil fails in the vessels. God’s oil is the sweetness of eternal things; the world’s oil is delight in present things. The former suffices; the latter fails. Therefore the vessels of the foolish virgins were empty, while the vessels of the wise widow were full (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 4). The vessels are hearts; the oil is joy.

## TITLE LII. On the Falsity of Worldly Consolation

“Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation now!” (Luke 6).

If the rational soul were truly wise, it would savor nothing except the true good. For its good is nothing other than the true good. This alone, therefore, is that in which it ought to rejoice in its abundance and in which it ought to be consoled in its poverty. And certainly, whether abounding or needy, it would rejoice well in that good and be well consoled by it, if it did not suffer lack of it either in abundance or in poverty.

But now its first evil has come about: when that good has been removed, it suffers its absence, so that it does not possess it. Then a second evil is added: it consoles itself in another good, so that it does not seek that good. Thus, having lost the good that was within, the soul has gone out to goods outside itself, goods belonging to another; it has made a pact with the delights of the world, and, returning, has brought them into itself to commit fornication with them in the hidden place of its heart, to rest upon them, to find consolation in them, and not to look to the absence of its own good because it sees its abundance and consolation in alien goods.

Now, therefore, the soul, desolated of its own good, does not recognize its desolation, because it has with itself the alien company of this world’s delights, entering it through the senses of its flesh or encountered when it goes out to them. But when these gates of bodily sense begin to be closed, there will no longer be an open way for passing to and fro. Then the fellowship of vanity will be separated: the world will be shut out outside, lest it enter, and the soul shut in within, lest it go out. The soul will come to the gates of the eyes and find them closed, so that it cannot go out through sight; it will turn to the gates of the ears and find them blocked, so that it cannot go out through hearing; then it will pour itself forth through the entrances of the remaining senses, and there will be no passage at all, because the bars of everlasting death, with unyielding severity and immovable bolts, close forever the doors of the senses—the avenues of its former commerce.

Then the wretched soul, in this sorrowful separation, will find itself alone. Turning upon itself, it will begin to seek that companion who is within and cannot be shut out; but it will be unable to have fellowship with him in its desolation, because it did not seek him in its consolation. Then that unhappy soul will fall, through despair, into itself and, through condemnation, beneath itself; and the abyss will open itself before the falling soul. When it has received it, it will immediately close above and open below, so that it may fall without end and never rise to an end. Then it will first recognize as true what had been said: “Woe to one alone! For when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4).

Therefore he said: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath” (Matthew 24). For what is winter except the numbness of death? And what is the Sabbath except the time of perpetual inactivity after death? Winter takes away the power of walking; the Sabbath denies permission. So too, a person bound by the numbness of impending death is hindered from correction; but after death repentance is not accepted. Here one is weighed down so as not to perform the first works; there one is bound so as not to escape impending condemnation. Here correction is burdensome; there cleansing is impossible. Therefore it is good to flee the wrath to come before you begin to feel it impending, lest either the will be too ineffective without action or sorrow be useless without correction.

Let the soul, then, now placed in the company of strangers, reflect that it cannot remain with them forever; meanwhile, let it choose that companion who, when all things have been taken away, alone keeps faith with those who love him and does not depart in the time of distress. And if it seems hard now, for his love, to reject all the world’s blandishments, let it hear him console it and say: “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 1). What then? Is the world sweet, and God not sweet? Far from it! “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclesiasticus 24). Therefore, brethren, if you begin to taste this sweetness, you will neither love false sweetness nor experience true bitterness.

## TITLE LIII. On the Fourfold Recollection of Past Evils

There is a fourfold recollection of past evils.

The first bends the mind to consent to wickedness; the second affects the memory with unlawful pleasure; the third softens the heart to penitential compunction and contrition; the fourth kindles the mind, through confidence of pardon, to thanksgiving. The first belongs to the wicked, the second to the foolish, the third to those making progress, and the fourth to the perfect. God imputes the first as guilt, pardons the second, rewards the third, and glorifies the fourth. The first is of iniquity, the second of weakness, the third of virtue, and the fourth of blessedness.

## TITLE LIV. From What Does Vice Take Its Origin?

Every vice takes its origin from nature, because vice is nothing other than a natural affection apart from order and beyond measure: transgressing order when it is moved toward what it ought not; exceeding measure when it is moved more than it ought. In the former case it desires because of need; in the latter it boils over because of vehemence. There it is perverse; here it is excessive.

In David, because of need, desire was moved toward what it ought not when, being hungry, he desired the consecrated loaves (1 Kingdoms [1 Samuel] 21). In Amnon, his son, because of vehemence, it was moved more than it ought when he indulged love for Tamar, his sister, to the point of fleshly lust (2 Kingdoms [2 Samuel] 13).

## TITLE LV. On the Various Ways of Humankind

The way of life is the commandment of righteousness. For the first human being the way to life lay open, short and easy. But now, to those returning to life, ways are shown: many instead of one, long instead of short, laborious instead of easy. For it was fitting that, while the human being was still one, he should have a single way; being near, a short way; being righteous, an easy way. But now, divided, he has a manifold way; being distant, a long way; being a sinner, a burdensome way.

Desire divided the human being, iniquity alienated him, mortality weakened him. Therefore the first way now is that he return to himself and, from many, become one; then let him proceed to him who is above him. The first way is one out of many, from many to one, and is manifold. The second way is one from one to unity, and is simple. The first is from vices to virtue; the second from truth to blessedness. On the first way the frail human being must leave behind what he loves; on the second the weak human being must grasp what is unfamiliar.

At first, one commandment was given to the one human being, easy to do and brief in its effect. First he was told to abstain from one thing outside himself; afterward, to conquer what was within him. This was neither easy to do nor brief to accomplish. There one thing had to be done; here many things oppose the doer. Pride meets one on the way of humility; envy troubles one on the way of piety; anger agitates one on the way of gentleness; lust on the way of chastity; avarice on the way of mercy; gluttony on the way of self-restraint; obstinacy on the way of obedience. To conquer all these is as difficult as it is natural to possess them.

## TITLE LVI. On the Two Ways in the Gospel

There are two ways: one broad, leading to destruction; the other narrow, leading to life. The broad way has many who travel on it; the narrow way admits few. For in every kind, what is precious is rare, while what is cheap abounds in number. The broad way is to go wherever one wishes and do what pleases one. The narrow way is to be governed by commandments and restrain unbounded desires by the rule of fairness.

There are, therefore, two ways: one of death, the other of life; two peoples, of the evil and of the good; and two kings, the devil and Christ. Each leads his own army: one to death, the other to life. Christ leads by humility; the devil by exaltation. Christ by purity; the devil by impurity. Christ by obedience; the devil by obstinacy. And whichever leader each person follows on the way, that person will have as king in the homeland.

> [Note: [Col. 0501] On mercy and truth, and how they disputed with one another, see near the beginning, among the exegetical works on Holy Scripture.]

## TITLE LVII. On Virtue and Justice

The difference between virtue and justice is this: virtue seems rather to be an affection of the rational will, well formed or rightly ordered; justice, however, is its form or ordering. The affection of the mind is well ordered when it is moved according to God’s will.

## TITLE LVIII. On Active and Passive Justice

Justice is of one kind according to the obligation of the agent, and of another according to the merit of the sufferer. Justice according to the obligation of the agent is justice of power; justice according to the merit of the sufferer is justice of equity.

Justice of power is that by which, without injustice, the agent may do, if he wishes, what is due to his authority. Justice of equity is that by which there is rendered to the sufferer, even if he does not wish it, what is due to his merit. Therefore, when God punishes the sinner, he acts justly, because it belongs to his authority that he may do this if he wishes; and the person who suffers suffers justly, because according to his merit there is rendered to him what is due to his merit. There is there a just power, by which God acts justly; and he himself is just. Here there is equitable recompense, because the sinner suffers justly—yet he himself is not just, but his punishment is just.

But when God justifies the sinner, he acts justly and is just by the justice of power, through which he is permitted to do this. The one who is justified is just by the justice which he receives; but not in respect of receiving it contrary to his merit. Yet he is not unjust, because he does not himself do what he receives. The one who acts is just, and so is the justice by which he acts; the one who receives is just by the justice which he receives, yet not because he receives it, since without justice of his own he receives justice by grace alone.

## TITLE LIX. On Solomon’s Bed and Litter

Solomon is Christ; Solomon’s bed is the heart of the contemplative person; Solomon’s litter is the heart that bears and exercises itself through good works. When Scripture spoke of Solomon’s bed (Song of Songs 3), it did not say from what it was made, because the breathings of contemplation that enlighten the heart are ineffable. But concerning Solomon’s litter it says what it is made of and describes its material (ibid.), because the exercises of virtues that build up the active person’s life can be narrated and spoken.

## TITLE LX. On the Same

Solomon’s litter is the heart exercised in the pursuit of virtue; the litter of wisdom is the word, carried from mouth to ear. The bed is the contemplative mind. This litter must first be made of the woods of Lebanon, through the purity and incorruptibility of truth; of silver, in commandments and promises. In the brightness of silver is a clean manner of life; in its sound, a sweet promise. It has gold through heavenly wisdom, which does not rust in eternity but glows red in charity. It has purple when it preaches the Passion; an ascent to glorification. In its midst charity is spread out for the daughters of Jerusalem, being set before the tender and weak for the attaining of salvation. Who is so tender that he cannot love? For if you cannot do the other things, you can nevertheless love, so that you may belong to Solomon’s litter.

## TITLE LXI. On the *Ferculum*, That Is, Solomon’s Litter or Vehicle, So Called from Carrying; and on Pharaoh’s Chariot

[Col. 0503D]

“King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon” (Song of Songs 3), etc.

Scripture mentions two kinds of vehicles: Solomon’s litter and Pharaoh’s chariot. A good heart is Solomon’s litter; a perverse heart, Pharaoh’s chariot. Since a chariot is drawn along the ground, the chariot fittingly signifies a heart clinging to earthly desires. For just as a loaded chariot emits a creaking sound, while an unburdened one makes a clatter, so the hearts of the wicked in adversity emit, through impatience, a kind of creaking; in prosperity, through boastfulness, they make a clatter. Pharaoh—that is, the devil—rides over these, and they are plunged like lead into the depths, because those whom he urges here toward vices he finally accompanies as they descend to torments.

But Solomon’s litter does not touch the earth; rather, it rises above it. It indeed moves, but has neither clatter nor creaking, because the heart lifted to heavenly desires and despising earthly pleasures, although still subject to mutability by its condition, neither creaks through impatience in adversity nor clatters through boastfulness in adversity.

There is something further that may be joined to the distinction just given. Let us therefore posit three things: Solomon’s bed, Solomon’s litter, and Pharaoh’s chariot. Let us understand Solomon’s bed as the heart resting in the sweetness of contemplation; Solomon’s litter as the heart applying itself to the exercise of good works; Pharaoh’s chariot as the heart resting in the desire for carnal things.

## TITLE LXII. On Solomon’s Litter and Bed

> [Note: [Col. 0503D] The same material, with a few changes, is read in Title 60.]

Solomon’s litter is the heart exercised in the pursuit of virtue. The litter of wisdom is the word carried from mouth to ear. The bed is contemplation of the mind. This litter must first be made of the woods of Lebanon through the purity and incorruptibility of truth; of silver in commandments and promises. In the brightness of silver is a clean manner of life; in its sound, a sweet promise. It has gold through heavenly wisdom, which does not rust in eternity but glows red in charity. It has purple when it preaches the Passion; it has an ascent to glorification. In its midst charity is spread out for the daughters of Jerusalem, set before the tender and weak for the attainment of salvation. For who is so tender that he cannot love? If you cannot do the other things, you can nevertheless love, so that you may belong to Solomon’s litter.

## TITLE LXIII. On the Four Ways in Which Knowledge of God Is Manifested to Humankind; or, on Nature, Grace, and God

Knowledge of God is manifested to the human heart in four ways: two inwardly and two outwardly; two through nature and two through grace. Inwardly, through reason and inspiration; outwardly, through creation and teaching. Reason and creation belong to nature; inspiration and teaching to grace.

Thus nature and grace were both given together—not nature alone, nor grace alone—lest, if nature could do everything, grace would not be sought; or, if nature could do nothing, guilt would be excused. The Jews said that nature could do everything and did not seek grace. Some Gentiles thought nature could do nothing and excused guilt. Both were mistaken.

Of the four, reason is first, creation second, teaching third, inspiration fourth. Reason investigates; creation proves; teaching explains; inspiration confirms faith. There are three witnesses proving that God exists: affection, deficiency, and effect. Affection comes first; deficiency follows; effect meets it. Affection seeks, deficiency demands, effect bestows—which would not be if there were no providence.

There are yet three other witnesses in creation proclaiming the Creator’s divinity: the greatness of power, the beauty of wisdom, and the usefulness of goodness. Then Scripture explains what creation proves: first, that God exists; then, that he is one; and then, that he is also three. God himself bears witness to faith, lest human testimony should be less firm.

Before the Law, he said that he is; under the Law, that he is one; under grace, that he is three, so that knowledge of truth might grow gradually. Before the Law he said: “I am” (Exodus 3); and again: “I am who I am” (ibid.); and again: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’” (ibid.). Under the Law he said: “Hear, Israel: your God is one God; you shall worship him and serve him alone” (Deuteronomy 6). Under grace he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28). The one who receives it knows the confirmation of inspiration.

## TITLE LXIV. On Pride and Humility

When God formed and created the human being in judgment, he placed in him certain lowly things and certain glorious things. Pride came and found certain excellences and adornments, beautiful for desire; but the lowly and weak things it found shameful for confusion and disgrace. Thus one is pressed down where one swells and put to shame where one glories.

But humility comes and considers the beautiful without desire, the weak without disgrace; and the Creator is pleasing in both. In the one case, because he demonstrates his own power; in the other, because he moderates our presumption, so that in the one we may see how much we can presume concerning him, and in the other how humbly we ought to think of ourselves.

## TITLE LXV. On the Threefold Contemplation and Instruction

The first contemplation is of visible things. The second proceeds from visible things to invisible things. The third is of invisible things. So the first instruction is in the letter; the second proceeds from the letter to meaning; the third is in meaning.

## TITLE LXVI. On the Three Degrees of Faith

There are three degrees of faith. The first is to choose, through piety alone, the things that are said; the second, to approve through reason the things that have been chosen; the third, through purity, to apprehend the things that have been approved.

There is a fourth class of people for whom merely not contradicting is faith, merely believing. Yet they are called faithful more by their customary way of living than by the truth of their belief. The faithful first make their choice through piety; afterward, from reason, they form an estimation; finally, through purity, they grasp certainty.

Knowledge of faith likewise grows by three degrees. Some accept as worthy of belief what they have heard without examination. Others examine by reason what is to be believed, and believe it. Others apprehend in experience what they have examined and believed. The first possess knowledge of faith; the second, the assertion of knowledge; the third, the assertion of reason.

Thus faith grew through the ages. Before the Law, God the Creator was believed in, and salvation and redemption were expected from him. But by whom, and in what manner, that same salvation was to be fulfilled and accomplished was not known even by other faithful people, except for a few to whom knowledge of this had been singularly granted as a gift. Under the Law, the person of the Redeemer to be sent was foretold and awaited as one who would come; but what that person himself was—whether human, angel, or God—was not yet revealed. Only those knew this who had been singularly illumined for this purpose through the Spirit.

Under grace, however, both the manner of redemption and the nature of the Redeemer’s person are now openly preached and believed by all. Yet in the Church of God there has always been, from the beginning, faith in Christ’s incarnation and Passion, because from the beginning there were never lacking those who knew this. Others were saved because, with simple faith, they joined themselves to the perfection of these people and followed them by good works.

Likewise, it must be understood that the disposition of mind by which one believes is one thing, and the knowledge by which one perceives what is believed is another. Faith resides in the disposition; those things that belong to faith reside in knowledge. Faith, therefore, is one thing and knowledge of faith another. Such knowledge can indeed exist without any faith at all; but faith absolutely cannot exist without knowledge. Yet it can sometimes exist above knowledge, since faith is also concerning faith.

## TITLE LXVII. That Charity Never Fails

“Hugh, a sinner, to his beloved son R.,” etc. See above among Hugh’s letters.

## TITLE LXVIII. Why Human Consciences Are Veiled
