For this reason God did not will that human consciences should be manifest to one another in the present life: lest those who saw should be provoked to evil, and those who possessed such evils should be put to shame. For the evils that dwell in the human heart are so great that, if they lay open, they would both be mutual incitement to guilt for those seeing them and testimony to disgrace for those possessing them. For this reason the hidden things of hearts are veiled, so that there may be a place for the future judgment. The veil of the heart, however, is the bodily condition, whether manifest or uncertain, whether good or bad.

## TITLE LXIX. On the Service and Fear of God

“My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

First observe how far the human being is from God when he is commanded to come near in order to become a servant. How far is he from the place where he is a son, who has not yet begun to be where he is a servant? Nor is this surprising. For a servant, though a servant, is nevertheless in the house: a member of the household and known. Though he will not remain, he is nevertheless within, knowing and known. One who is outside does not know what is done within. Outside are dogs and sorcerers; inside are sons and servants. The servants will depart; the sons will remain.

“My son, when you come”: he is still outside, yet is called a son; he is not yet a servant, yet already a son. Thus Israel, placed in Egypt, is called the firstborn son. For grace anticipates merit. Therefore: “When you come to the service of God, stand in fear.” Stand, not so as not to advance, but lest you fall away. Stand by remaining in what you have begun, not by returning to what you were. Stand in fear. Let fear fasten down the slippery impulses of the flesh, lest they flow out into guilt while foreseeing punishment.

“And prepare your soul for temptation.” Strengthen it by purpose, exercise it in virtue, fortify it with caution: strengthen it so that it may refuse to yield; exercise it so that it may be able to resist; fortify it so that, where it cannot conquer, it may know how to avoid.

## TITLE LXX. That a Good Mind Is a Garden of Delight

“Before him the land is like a garden of delight, and behind him a deserted wilderness” (Joel 2).

The king of the north is the devil; the garden of delight is the rational and good mind. God is the cultivator and guardian of this garden; the devil is its ravager and desolator. For when the seed of God’s word falls upon this rational ground, it is received through understanding; then it is covered, for nurturing and for prudence against danger.

It is covered for nurturing so that it may first take root before it sprouts; first descend for strengthening before it rises for display; first take root through hidden purpose, then sprout through manifest example. It sprouts upward, advancing toward fruit; it takes root downward, advancing toward stability. Upward through charity, downward through humility. It is covered for prudence so that it may not be brought forth into action before it has been directed by circumspection. First you conceive what must be done; afterward you nurture it by reflecting on how it must be done. It is covered against danger so that, even when it has gone forth to action, it may not lie open to display.

Thus God’s word, falling upon good ground, takes root, sprouts, and bears fruit; it becomes a garden of delight, producing every tree beautiful to see and pleasant for food, and breathing forth fragrant spices. The devil, king of the north, comes to this garden and finds it full of pleasantness; entering, he devastates, lays waste, and departs, leaving it dreadful in its desolation.

## TITLE LXXI. On Putting On Conformity to Christ

“Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13): that is, Christ’s form, Christ’s likeness. Put this on; assume this. To conform is to be measured together.

Wisdom proceeds upward and downward, from end to end: upward in majesty, downward in humility. If you look to height, no one is higher than Christ. If you consider lowliness, no one is humbler than Christ. See how far he descended in humility. He was a Son and became a servant; he accepted not merely the condition of a servant, so as to be subject, but also that of an evil servant, so as to be beaten; and, still more, to pay by punishment what he had not taken by guilt.

Thus he was humbled. How? From equality to subjection; from righteousness to suffering; and not to just any suffering, but to death; nor to just any death, but to a shameful one. Who can thus glory? Who can thus be humbled? Humbled to the lowest, he was exalted to the highest. In descending he left no further depth to which he could be humbled; in ascending he left no further height to which he could be exalted. Descend after Christ by enduring the deepest humility; ascend after Christ by desiring the highest charity. Go on with him, that you may grow in him. You can imitate him; you cannot equal him.

## TITLE LXXII. That Knowledge of Truth Is Natural

The desire to know truth is so natural to the soul that, however perverse it may be, it cannot wholly lack it. Daily questions show that we all desire to know what is true. The whole of human life consists in questioning. So long as one lives, one seeks. No one wishes to be deceived, even though everyone may wish to deceive. In this the human heart demonstrates that nothing belongs to it more properly than truth. But the perverse seek truth where salvation is not: truth because they are human beings; where salvation is not because they are perverse. Truth, but not good; therefore they do not find the true good.

One seeks for iniquity, another for greed, another for curiosity. One seeks how he may injure someone he hates; perhaps he finds what he seeks, and it is true that the other can be injured in this way. But this truth leads to wickedness, not goodness. Another seeks how he may multiply money, increase riches, and heap up profits; sometimes he finds what he seeks. It is wholly true that this can be done and managed in this way; but this truth has no good joined to it. Truth is indeed good, but it is not the true good when joined to no good, because greed is not goodness.

Curiosity draws another to seek truth. He pursues rumors, snatches at novelties, searches hidden matters, in order to provide food for his vice. Here too there is truth without the companion of good, so that in all these things the true good is not found. Others seek truth and love to possess it because it is true. These are indeed rightly directed, because they seek truth for the sake of good; but they are not brought to the goal, because they do not seek it for the sake of the highest good. Such are those who investigate the secrets of nature and are borne along with great desire merely to know what is true in created things. Even there is something that ought rightly to delight, provided that the human heart, through what it loves below, is kindled to love him who is supremely good.

Therefore that teaching is better by which a person is first taught to know himself: what he is, in order that he may correct it; and what he ought to be, in order that he may strive to become it. Then let him seek his Creator as one already known, and, having found him, rest in him.

## TITLE LXXIII. Why the Son of God Asks the Father
“I will ask the Father concerning you” (John 16), etc. The Son asks the Father to send the Holy Spirit to the disciples. He who asks is God; he whom he asks is God; he for whom God asks is God. God asks God for God. A wonderful thing! There is one good, and it makes itself known to us so that we may learn to seek it. For it wills to be desired, and accommodates itself to us in order to stir us up [Col. 0508D] to the love of seeking. He asks while teaching; he is asked while showing the value of the gift; he promises while consoling. Unless he asked, the need of the one in want would not be shown; unless he were asked, the worthiness of the gift would not be understood; unless he promised, the delay endured by the one who waits would not be confirmed. God bends himself to prayer for humankind’s sake: with great love, great necessity, and great benefit. With great love, by which the ungodly person is so greatly loved. With great necessity, by which the lost person is sustained, not saved. With great benefit, by which the one who has turned away is thus recalled. “I will ask the Father.” Why does he ask who has the power to give? He shows what you ought to think of him: namely, that you may understand your good, and perceive there the source from which you should seek.

## LXXIV. On the Great Consolation of the Sinner, and the Resolution of Doubts Concerning Conscience

[Col. 0509A]

You, though learned, ask advice from one who is foolish. You ask what you ought to do because, although you are established in the religious habit, you do not have works worthy of your profession. Rightly indeed, dearest one, are you troubled when you consider your imperfection. Your grief is just, provided that it is not excessive. We do an injury to mercy if, in whatever misery of ours, we despair of mercy itself. When you sin, you take your goodness from yourself; but when you fear that perhaps God will not forgive you, you take his goodness from him. This is the greater iniquity. You make yourself more ungodly if, because of your own iniquity, you think something less of his goodness.

Let us therefore give confusion [Col. 0509B] to ourselves by confessing our sins; let us give glory to him by never distrusting his mercy. If our works were sufficient for us, what would grace do? Grace is necessary precisely because a human being is not justified before him by his own work. Therefore, let us not grieve over our imperfection in such a way that we breathe or hope less in the divine goodness.

You also said that this troubled your soul: the forgetfulness which followed upon past sins you committed has obscured many things, so that you cannot remember, as would have been fitting, those matters in which you grieve that you offended God. And these things are indeed more suspect to you the more hidden they are. This is true, nor can it be contradicted. In all these matters [Col. 0509C] a human being is in danger and subject to judgment, unless mercy mitigates justice. But our God is merciful: he spares those who pray, and never abandons the humble.

It was certainly a great fault not to guard against sin; and another fault followed: after wickedness had been committed, not to fear the danger, and to turn one’s eyes away lest a person see his own evil and understand what he must suffer. Yet, after all this, eternal mercy still lives, to whom that man cried: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18). And again: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, because he himself will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24). Therefore I look to him who sees what I cannot see [Col. 0509D], that he may cleanse me even from those stains by which I am defiled through guilt but not enlightened through knowledge. For I confess my fault to him, not only because I have done evil, but because I have neglected even to consider and know my evil. Therefore I direct myself toward him, imploring mercy, that by the hand of his compassion he may wipe away the stains of my ignorance. Even if I do not know what I have done, I nevertheless do not fail to know that I have done wrong.

You further said that you are often disturbed by certain thoughts of past evils, reappearing in the mind through an illicit kind of pleasure; and that you are deeply saddened by this, because you are sometimes assailed and harassed by them even at the time of prayer. I answer briefly: if there were no battle, there would be no victory [Col. 0510A]. You added that you would rather be burdened by another kind of struggle, in which there would be labour but not so much danger. To this I answer likewise: if there were no pleasure in the thought, there would be no labour at all in resisting it, because the mind would easily reject everything that did not please it. But here the labour is to fight against what pleases: that is, at once to love and to disapprove. Yet if the mind’s purpose in goodness is firm, this pleasure not only does no harm but even benefits, because, in wearing out the one who resists, it crowns the one who conquers.

Finally, as to what you added concerning movements of disturbance which sometimes, when occasions arise, shake the mind’s peace, I answer in the words of the Psalmist: “Be angry, and do not sin. What you say in your hearts, be compunct in your beds” (Ps. 4). If anger comes into the mind, let the act not proceed to sin; and because the mind is inwardly disturbed by anger, let the conscience be pierced by repentance. This is the remedy: if disturbance comes, it must both be restrained lest it grow, and be pierced so that it may cease; and let what is said be fulfilled: “I was troubled, and I did not speak” (Ps. 76). It is no wonder if a human being is disturbed, because he is human; but if he does not govern his disturbance, that is remarkable, because he is rational. Therefore, if he is disturbed, let him not speak; let him curb his tongue and shut in his conscience, so that what has arisen inwardly through weakness may be restrained outwardly through discernment, until it is extinguished within.

## LXXV. That Sacred Scripture Is the Chair

[Col. 0510C]

Sacred Scripture is the teacher’s chair, in which he ought continually to preside over the people, both by the authority of instruction and by the example of his conduct. The rear part of the chair is contemplation, which lies hidden in secrecy; the front part is preaching, which is set forth openly. The two posts standing in the rear are fear and love: for, while through contemplation of mind we look toward the ineffable majesty of God, fear is born; but while we consider his inexpressible goodness, love is produced. Contemplation rests upon those things which are, as it were, behind and cannot be seen, supported by fear and love.

Then from these two things [Col. 0510D] which belong to hidden contemplation, two others proceed into the openness of preaching: terror and consolation, as if two posts supporting the front of the symbolic chair. Thus terror proceeds from fear, and consolation from love. On the left side fear is placed behind and terror in front; on the right, love is placed behind and consolation before it. Hence the posts which stand behind extend upward toward those in front and are, as it were, fitted to their knees; for fear and love, through contemplation, conceive more fully in either respect, whereas terror and consolation, in preaching, are brought forth not in all the measure in which they exist, but in the measure expedient for the little ones. They accommodate themselves to those who are still carried, as it were, upon the knees of mother Church.

What is beneath the one sitting signifies earthly things. Beneath him is necessity; on his right is prosperity; on his left, adversity. The first bears him and is pressed down. The second stands near and is despised. The third presses upon him and is overcome. What is beside the one sitting is the edification of the present life; what is above, the expectation of the future. What is on the right beside him signifies the caution of good work. What is on the left signifies the defensive watchfulness against evil. What is above is behind, because the things to come are not seen.

[Note: [Col. 0511] On the mutability of temporal things. See among the Homilies, Homily 13 on Ecclesiastes.]

## LXXVI. How Wisdom Conquered Malice

Wisdom conquers malice. “Therefore she reaches mightily from end to end, and disposes all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). As the Apostle testifies [Col. 0511B] (1 Cor. 1), the Wisdom of God is Christ. Therefore this Wisdom conquered malice when, through the passion of the flesh, triumphing over the devil, it snatched the human race from his power. Wisdom conquered malice because the Redeemer’s grace had greater power for our salvation than the seducer’s malice could have for our destruction. It reaches mightily from end to end, because first it cast the proud one out from the heights, and afterward mightily despoiled the greedy one in the depths below. It disposes all things sweetly because it displays patience together with counsel, and judgment together with reason.

## LXXVII. On the Five States of Human Life

Human life has five states through which—because it can never remain long in the same state—it changes without interruption, either advancing toward better things or failing and declining toward worse: the joy of vanity, the sorrow of confusion, the joy of consolation, the sorrow of discipline, and the joy of blessedness.

The joy of vanity is delighting in temporal gains. The sorrow of confusion is grieving over temporal losses. The joy of consolation is resting from the assault of vices. The sorrow of discipline is enduring the troubles of temptations. The joy of blessedness is tasting the delight of inward sweetness.

Through the joy of vanity the soul withdraws farther from God, because it recedes farther from him who is within in proportion as it more eagerly pours itself out toward external pleasures. The sorrow of confusion cuts off evil pleasure, as it were, outwardly, and compels the soul to return within [Col. 0511D]. Yet because it is driven back upon itself not willingly but in some sense under compulsion, it neither wholly abandons vice nor is truly restored to the integrity of virtue.

The joy of consolation already, in some measure, cherishes and orders the mind from without, persuading it to choose to remain with itself and not to deign to seek outside what it can possess more truly and securely within. Moreover, the sorrow of discipline so excludes from the mind every memory of outward pleasure that, while it is compelled to attend to its inward pain, it scarcely remembers what outside may be pleasant.

Finally, the joy of blessedness makes a person forget even himself [Col. 0512A], because, while the mind, raised above itself, wholly longs for the sweetness of heavenly joys, it not only does not remember the lowest pleasure but in some sense happily passes even out of its own remembrance.

Thus the joy of vanity scatters the mind; the sorrow of confusion gathers it; the joy of consolation orders it; the sorrow of discipline binds it; the joy of blessedness heals it. Yet it sometimes happens that the joy of vanity is turned in some persons into the joy of consolation, and conversely that some abuse the joy of consolation as a joy of vanity. Again, in some the sorrow of confusion is turned into the sorrow of discipline, and likewise in others the sorrow of discipline into the sorrow of confusion.

## LXXVIII. On the Six Modes of Working

There are six works. The first work is to make something from nothing. The second work is to make several things from one thing, increasing according to essence. The third work is to make one thing from several things, decreasing according to essence. The fourth work is to make several things from one thing without increase. The fifth work is to make one thing from several things without decrease. The sixth work is to make nothing from something.

The first work is creation. The second is propagation. The third is union. The fourth is separation. The fifth is conjunction. The sixth is destruction. The first, second, and third works alone are good. The fourth and fifth are sometimes good and sometimes evil. The sixth is only evil.

The first, second, and third works are possible to God alone. The fourth [Col. 0512C] and fifth are shared by God and the creature. The sixth belongs to the creature alone [the printed text reads “to the Creator”].

For God alone can make something from nothing. Likewise, God alone can make more from one thing according to essence—that is, cause one essence to increase into several. Likewise, God alone can make one thing from several according to essence—that is, cause several essences to return into one. There are those who deny that anything can increase unless something is either externally added to it from elsewhere or newly created; but they do not observe that this is not truly increase, where neither what is added nor that to which it is added is shown to grow. For the things united are not other than they were when disjoined.

But perhaps it seems impossible that several essences should proceed by increase from one simple essence, because they suppose that what is simple can neither be less than it is nor greater than it is. What then do we say? Is there more difference between nothing and something than between something and more? Therefore, since we confess that in creating God made something from nothing, why should we deny that in propagating he extends something into more?

So it is in the work of union, when several essences become one. Although this is remote from the senses, nevertheless it is rash to assert that it sometimes happens among the elements in the hidden bosom of nature—and foolish to deny it. Something was made from nothing when, in the beginning, God created heaven and earth (Gen. 1). More was made from something when woman was made from the man’s rib, and when five thousand people were fed from five loaves [Col. 0513A].

Do not, in the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, several essences daily unite with the substance of bread and wine? Before the words of blessing, these are truly other in essence than the essence of Christ’s body; through that blessing, by the wonderful working of the Holy Spirit, they are converted into the substance of Christ’s body itself, so that after consecration Christ’s body alone is what had previously truly been the substance of bread and wine. Nor do these things come to Christ’s body from without as an increase, or become incorporated into it while remaining essentially different; rather, they are changed into it, so that they become altogether one in essence.

Yet, whether this work of divine power is elsewhere carried out in nature in some hidden and unknown way, it ought neither to be asserted nor stubbornly denied, since the matter is very doubtful. But that these things truly occur must not be doubted at all. These three works therefore pertain to God’s power alone.

The fourth and fifth works—namely, to make several things from one thing, neither with increase nor decrease—are, for example, when several things are combined into one and the components are equal to the composite, or when one thing is divided into many and the divisions are equal to what was divided. These two works, which the creature alone can perform—that is, either joining things that are separate or separating things that are joined—are shared by us with God. Therefore, when God performs them without us, they are his good works. When we perform them without God, they are our evil works. When God performs them with us, or we with God, they are both his good works and ours.

The sixth work is to make that which is something to be nothing [Col. 0513C]. God cannot do this in himself; he does not will it in the creature. Angel and human being cannot do it in the creature. In themselves they sometimes can and will, sometimes can and do not will, never will and never can. Yet all this concerns not essence but justice.

Thus in Genesis God is said to have worked for six days; and similarly, in the Gospel six works of mercy are numbered, because in the number six the fullness of perfection—having neither more nor less than is right—is both signified and contained. Therefore he will not contain his mercies in his wrath, because goodness extends as far as five works, whereas malice spreads itself only through three.

## LXXIX. On Flight from Vices and Their Occasions

“You who inhabit the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” (Isa. 21). Why, brothers, does sacred Scripture so strongly urge flight upon us, unless because it considers both our weakness and the greatness of the danger? But what is this flight? What ought we to flee? How, or when?

There are three who wage war against us: the devil, the flesh, and the world. The devil leads against us ranks of vices; the flesh, ranks of evil desires; the world, prosperity and adversity. It would be happier indeed to fight well against all these things and conquer; but for one who is weak, it is more expedient to flee and be saved than to fight badly and be overcome.

We flee vices when we avoid occasions of sin—for example, the sight of the flesh in lust, and contention in anger. We flee desires when we guard against their incitement, lest we cast oil [Col. 0514A] upon the fire and what is warm burst into flame. We flee prosperity and adversity when we neither seek what delights us, fearing through covetousness to be dissolved, nor fling ourselves into what torments us, fearing through presumption to be broken.

We have said what we ought to flee and how. Now let us consider when we must flee. Truth says: “See that your flight does not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24). In winter, frost either makes roads harsh or rain makes them slippery. What, then, is winter but the numbness of approaching death, when pain constricts the bodily limbs through suffering and compassion dissolves strength? And what is the Sabbath but the time following death, when, for those led out from this life, freedom to act is removed and every possibility of turning aside from what is fixed is altogether denied?

Therefore, if you wish to flee the wrath to come, flee while you are well, because flight is difficult in death; after death it is entirely impossible. For the evils which you refused to flee in life, even if you wish to do so afterward, you will be unable to avoid after death. There they will follow as recompense for what is committed here in pleasure. Therefore flee here while you can. But lest you fail on the way, hear consolation: loaves will be offered to you. You will be refreshed, lest you fail. Nor will you wait until the end of the way; they will meet you, lest you fail on the way.

Those who inhabit the land of the south will meet you with loaves if they see you fleeing. They will meet you with compassion; they will refresh you with consolation. You will have good comforters: those who inhabit the land of the south. In the south there are brightness and heat: brightness of knowledge [Col. 0514C], heat of love. Those inhabit the land of the south who rest in the knowledge and love of truth. They abound in the loaves of God’s word and run to refresh those who labour. For this is the bread that strengthens the human heart, because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4).

Although this bread is one, it is presented under various appearances. Sometimes it is called bread baked under ashes; sometimes it is named barley bread or wheat bread. Elijah, fleeing in the desert, is refreshed with bread baked under ashes. The children of Jerusalem, who dwell in peace, are filled with the fat of wheat. But those who recline upon grass eat barley bread.

Bread beneath ashes is refreshment beneath lowliness. There are certain places in sacred Scripture which display lowliness in the appearance of the letter but preserve sweetness in the depth of spiritual understanding. This is bread beneath ashes, refreshment beneath lowliness. Would you have me show you bread baked under ashes? You read in sacred Scripture how Rachel and Leah, two sisters, contend for the one husband Jacob, which of them should more enjoy his embrace. Here is a great appearance of lowliness, a great heap of ashes, a great mass of earthliness. Turn over the ashes; search within: bread lies there, refreshment is hidden.

See, the bread uncovered: the two sisters signify the two lives. Leah, whose name is interpreted “laborious,” signifies the active life, fruitful in the produce of good work but seeing little in the light of contemplation. Rachel, whose name is interpreted “the beginning seen,” signifies the contemplative life [Col. 0515A], barren outwardly in work but penetrating in contemplation. In these two lives there is, as it were, a contention of the holy soul, striving alternately for the embrace of its Bridegroom—that is, Christ, the Wisdom of God—who makes the holy soul fruitful in offspring of virtues.

Contemplation and action therefore contend for the embrace of wisdom. The one in contemplation sighs for the barrenness of work; the one in work sighs for the joy of contemplation. Each laments that he is, as it were, rejected in comparison with the other, and a contention of desires arises, with hope and fear stirring both. See, you have found bread beneath ashes, able to refresh and delight. Attend not to what appeared outwardly in ashes, but to what lay hidden within in refreshment.

Would you still see bread beneath ashes—while it lay hidden, lowly; once revealed, sweet? Christ beneath mortality is bread beneath ashes. You see outwardly the weakness of one being born, crying, weeping; the confinement of the cradle and the bindings of swaddling clothes. All this is ash: earthly and weak. Yet beneath these ashes lay hidden the Word, refreshment of angels and human beings. You see him weary, hungry and thirsty, weeping, compassionate and suffering, dying and failing in the flesh. And what were all these things but ashes: indications of corruption, signs of mortality? Beneath them lay hidden the power of the Godhead, which those who could uncover it deserved to enjoy to the full.

See how Scripture sets before you bread baked under ashes. Elsewhere you see sacred discourse, hard upon the surface of the letter [Col. 0515C], as though it possessed tough chaff, so that one can scarcely penetrate to the marrow of spiritual understanding: this is barley. Chaff is indeed threshed out with labour; but when you reach the interior, you find strengthening sweetness. Elsewhere you find sacred Scripture pleasing both by the lightness of its words and by the sweetness of its meanings: this is wheat, in which sweet refreshment is prepared for gently nourishing minds.

These three kinds of bread are set upon God’s table for three kinds of persons to be refreshed. Bread baked under ashes is given to the poor; barley bread to servants; wheat bread to children. The poor at God’s table are those who, despising themselves, feed upon the example of humility and self-abasement. The servants at God’s table are those engaged in the practice of spiritual discipline, who, as though threshing out the chaff, uncover the stronger and more obscure passages of Scripture and through labour attain the savour of the marrow of spiritual understanding. The children at God’s table are those who rest in the sweetness of eternal delight.

Of the poor it was said: “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21). Therefore, if the poor eat—those nourished by the merit of piety alone—much more do the servants and children, who are refreshed according to the merit of good work by the reward of love’s recompense. Bread beneath ashes is set before the poor, to refresh them through an example of conduct. Barley bread is set before servants, to refresh them through the form of faith. Wheat bread is set before children, to refresh them through the incentive of love: the poor for consolation [Col. 0516A], servants for strengthening, children for exultation.

## LXXX. That Christian Faith Must Be Held Not Only in the Heart but Also Confessed with the Mouth, to the Archbishop of Seville Who Had Denied It with His Mouth

HUGH, servant of Christ, to JOHN, bishop of the people of Seville, etc. See above among Hugh’s letters.

## LXXXI. On the Text, “When Jesus Was Twelve Years Old”: How the Word Made Flesh Provides Us Both Remedy and Example; on Jerusalem Descending from Heaven; on Confession and Truth Arising from the Earth; and on Their Benefit

“When Jesus was twelve years old,” etc. (Luke 2). Just as this world serves humankind in two ways, namely for the sustenance of the body and the instruction of the mind, so the Word made flesh provides both remedy and example: remedy in that it was offered for redemption; example in that it acted for imitation; remedy in what it became; example in what it did. His imitation is his likeness.

“I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven” (Rev. 21). It descends from heaven and is built on earth. Its form is from heaven; its matter, from earth. Thus the form of a human being is human, and the form of Christ is Christ. Hence the saying: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13), that is, put on the form, the image of Christ. The image itself is also imitation. For this reason he was made an example for you, so that by imitating him you might put him on [Col. 0516C]. He acted bodily; you must imitate spiritually. “Even if,” he says, “we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5). In the example we knew according to the flesh; in imitation we no longer know according to the flesh.

Christ was born in the world according to the flesh; truth is born in your heart according to the spirit. Christ is born in Judaea from the Virgin, and truth is born in confession from purity. “Truth has sprung up from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84). When you confess your sins, truth springs up from the earth; but when God forgives the one confessing, justice looks down from heaven. Do you wish God to be with you? Confess what you are. When you begin to be truthful, truth begins to be with you. Say: “I am evil.” It is a short word, but true. Truth will make you truthful. If truth is with you, God is with you, because God is Truth. See how Christ is born in Judaea, truth in confession.

The Virgin Mother is purity of heart, when you believe with the heart what you confess with the mouth. In the confession of sin, purity is without wrinkle; in the confession of praise, purity is without stain. If you do not pretend goodness, you have no wrinkle. If you hate evil, you have no stain. Thus truth is conceived in you by desire, born by work, and nourished by zeal, so that it may advance in age through the passage of time, in wisdom through the increase of knowledge, and in grace through the growth of virtue: before human beings in reputation, before God in conscience; before human beings, that it may be known, and before God, that it may be glorified.

At twelve years of age he goes up to Jerusalem, because after perfection of work and the doubled virtue of love [Col. 0517A], he advances to the peace of contemplation. Jesus’ parents return from Jerusalem after a journey of one day, because the sense of the flesh, which through the practice of good work had nourished inward truth, when drawn back by external pleasure cannot long remain in inward peace. One day, one brightness, one joy, one blessing, which Esau receives because he could not deserve the double garment. This is that one day in which a child of one day could not be without sin upon earth, because the sense of the flesh, which as far as itself is concerned always seeks childish things, loving only the brightness of this life, never abides in it without the stain of sin. For it does not come to the other day of which it is said: “Announce day unto day” (Ps. 95). And again: “You will add days upon days to the king” (Ps. 60).

Therefore the journey of one day belongs to those withdrawing from Jerusalem, because delight in present things makes minds withdraw from contemplation of eternal things. Jesus is found in the temple after three days, because truth is perceived in a clean heart after the correction of thought, speech, and deed. He is found among teachers and wise persons, because truth is known in the Law, the Prophets, the Evangelists, the Apostles, and the teachers of the sacred word.

## LXXXII. On the Marriage Celebrated at Cana of Galilee and the Typology of the Water Jars

“Fill the water jars with water” (John 2). Galilee is interpreted “migration.” Therefore the present life is Galilee, passing from present things to future ones. In Galilee a marriage is celebrated, because in the passage of time the enduring union of the Church’s love with Christ, and of the soul’s love with God, is sanctified [Col. 0517C].

The six water jars are the six ages of the world: the first from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the Babylonian migration; the fifth from the Babylonian migration to Christ; the sixth from Christ to the end of the age. In human life, the first is infancy, the second childhood, the third adolescence, the fourth youth, the fifth mature adulthood, the sixth old age.

The first, infancy, is overwhelmed as by a flood of slippery forgetfulness, so that it is not seen afterward and leaves no trace of itself. The second, childhood, first emerging from the flood of forgetfulness into consciousness, is lifted up through pride, and divided and scattered through desire. The third, adolescence, is first circumcised through the restraint of discipline, then formed by precepts and governed by counsel. The fourth, youth, is now compelled to serve and subjected to rule, in order that through human fear it may learn divine fear. The fifth, mature adulthood, comes to divine fear after human fear. The sixth, old age, as though soon about to depart from here, is drawn by desire for future things.

Thus the human race was first overwhelmed by the flood. Second, it was raised up in the building [of Babel] and scattered in the division of languages. Third, it was circumcised in Abraham, instructed by precepts in Moses, and governed by counsel under the judges. Fourth, it was subjected to domination under kings. Fifth, it obeyed religion under high priests. Sixth [Col. 0518A], under grace, it was enlightened by true goodness.

These six jars, whether in the course of the present age or in human life, are all filled with waters because the world is full of judgment. “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 35). God has done many things from the beginning of the age and will not cease to work until its end; likewise, concerning a human being, from his beginning to his end. All these things are judgment, and nothing occurs without cause. But so long as a person cannot say, “Your judgments are pleasant,” the water has not yet been changed into wine.

When the old wine fails, the jars are filled with water, because when carnal pleasures fail in human life, divine consolations succeed. These bring less savour to those who minister, but grow sweeter to those who advance; for waters are changed into wine when God’s work, which at first did not taste good to one labouring, becomes sweet in the mind of one enlightened by spiritual understanding.

## LXXXIII. On the Multiple Theophany, and in What Things the Chief Divine Appearance Exists

Theophany is divine appearance. It is the divine likeness in which God appears and is made manifest. If anyone calls all creation a theophany, he is not mistaken. Theophany of power is the magnitude of creatures; theophany of wisdom, the beauty of creatures; theophany of goodness, the usefulness of creatures.

Every creature has some likeness to God. The first likeness of a creature to God is that it exists. The second is that it is one, because everything that exists is, in this respect, one [Col. 0518C]. But among those things which exist and are one, some are from one thing, as naturally simple things are; others are from several things, as composite things are. Those, however, which exist, are one, and are from one thing, are more like God—especially if they do not diffuse into many things the unity which they do not gather from many things.

Such are spiritual natures, which come nearer to the likeness of God. They are neither from many things, because by nature they are simple, nor do many things come from them, because they cannot be matter. In these God placed two things with respect to matter, and two with respect to form: life and sensation with respect to matter; knowledge and love with respect to form. Knowledge belongs to life; love, to sensation. These two are highest, nearest to God, and the expressed image: knowledge of truth and love of virtue.

## LXXXIV. On the Three Wills in Christ

[Col. 0518D]

In Christ the weakness of the flesh shrank from suffering. But there was a spirit intermediate between God and the flesh, which subjected the will of the flesh to the will of the Father. Therefore, when Christ said, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26), he professed what he felt in the flesh. But when he said, “Not my will, but yours be done” (ibid.), he professed what he had determined in the spirit.

The Father’s will was that Christ should die; the flesh’s will was to be delivered from death; the intermediate spirit ruled the flesh and obeyed the Father. The Father’s will was dispensation; the flesh’s will was nature; the spirit’s will was virtue. Therefore the Father’s will was honoured, the flesh’s will was directed [Col. 0519A], and the spirit’s will was crowned.

## LXXXV. That Christ Presented Himself to Human Beings in His Humanity, Since They Could Not Comprehend Him in His Divinity
Divine Wisdom, through whom the human being had been made in order to be blessed in her, did not will to destroy fallen humanity; and although she was above in majesty while humanity lay below in weakness, she descended to where it had fallen, so as to raise it to that from which it had fallen. Wisdom, therefore, was bread above and was transformed into milk below: bread in divinity, milk in humanity. And the infant understanding was nourished by the milk of humanity, so that, growing and strengthened, it might be able to receive the food of divinity. Christ, therefore, is bread in heaven and milk on earth. Christ [Col. 0519B] in heaven, God from the Father without a mother; Christ on earth, man from a mother without a father. In heaven, as is the Father, so is the Son; on earth, as is the mother, so is the son. In heaven, eternal and immeasurable with the Father; on earth, incorrupt and gentle with the mother. In heaven, incorrupt and exalted with the Father; on earth, virgin and humble with the mother. In heaven, the image of the Father; on earth, the imitator of the mother. The mother was a virgin and rejoiced in humility, and the Virgin’s son, himself a virgin, commended humility. She, a virgin, declared that her humility had been regarded by God; he, a virgin, showed himself humble and gentle. Such, therefore, was the Lamb as was the mother of the Lamb: pure from one who was pure, incorrupt from a Virgin; coming to us through virginity and going before us through virginity. Through incorruption, therefore, he came in order to take away sin [Col. 0519C]; through incorruption he went before us in order to display virtue. He came incorrupt in order to bestow a remedy; he went before us incorrupt in order to give an example. Therefore, if we cannot come by the way by which he came, let us follow by the way by which he went before, so that we may deserve to attain what he promised: that we may receive the food of milk in Christ’s humanity with a pure body, and the food of bread in Christ’s divinity with a pure heart—pure in body through virginity, pure in heart through humility—so that he who had an incorrupt origin in both may find a clean dwelling-place in both.

## LXXXVI. How Christ said: “My Father.”

One man said: “My Father” (John 5). He would not have said this had he not been more than a man. For insofar as he was man, he had brothers and ought to say, “Our Father”; but insofar as he alone was above humanity, he could say, “My Father,” and “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6).

## LXXXVII. Why he is both God and man.

God became man so that the Redeemer might be the same as the Creator; so that humanity might be liberated from what was its own; so that God, appearing in the likeness of a human being, might be loved more intimately by humanity; and so that both faculties of perception might be made blessed in him—the eye of the heart refreshed in his divinity and the eye of the body in his humanity [Col. 0520A]—so that created nature, whether entering or going out, might find pasture in him.

## LXXXVIII. Mystery concerning Mary’s purification.

Simeon’s old age is the failing of the old human being; his carrying of the child Christ, the assumption of the new; Simeon’s joy, the offering of the Savior; the Virgin’s purification, the devotion of the mind, the presentation of the work, the consummation of virtue.

## LXXXIX. Concerning the assertion by God, the woman, and the devil regarding death to be incurred.

The Lord said: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 3). The woman said: “Lest perhaps we die” (ibid.). The devil said: “You shall by no means die” (ibid.). The Lord affirmed; the woman doubted [Col. 0520B]; the devil denied. Therefore she who doubted departed from the one affirming and drew near to the one denying. If the woman had not doubted, perhaps the devil would not have denied. But she who began wickedness gave him boldness.

## XC. On God’s repentance and his varying love for creatures.

“God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was intent upon evil at all times; and he repented that he had made humankind upon the earth. And, touched inwardly by grief of heart, and taking precaution for the future [Note: [Col. 0519D] The Vulgate does not contain “and taking precaution for the future.”], he said: ‘I will destroy from the face of the earth the human being whom I created’” (Gen. 6).

First consider that mercy is not easily provoked to anger or vengeance unless our wickedness has become great. But when we begin to be changed away from the good in which we were made by him [Col. 0520C], then he repents concerning us, lest we attain the good for which we were made. His repentance, however, is not a change of intention from his original purpose, but a change of action from his original ordinance.

Observe also that, when humanity perishes, God is said to be touched inwardly by grief of heart. For grief was there where love was; since God loves all things that he made. Yet, although all other things are loved by him, they are not loved in order to possess him. But the rational creature is loved by him both because it has been made and for that for which it was made. In the case of perishing humanity, grief touched the Creator inwardly in the heart, where love had been for humanity standing firm and walking rightly.

For there are three kinds of things: one, of those fallen from their condition; another, of those standing in their condition; and another, of those advanced beyond their condition. The first are loved because they were made, but are, as it were, not loved with the heart because they afterward became evil. As it is written: “He has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart” (Luke 1). The second are loved because they were made, and are loved with the heart because they are good. Yet their love is, as it were, outside the heart, because they are loved insofar as they are good from him, but are not loved so that they may be blessed in him. The love of humanity, therefore, was within the Creator’s heart, because humanity was loved by him so greatly as to be both good from him and blessed in him. Thus humanity’s love was inward, and grief was there [Col. 0521A] where love was.

But what is meant by the words, “taking precaution for the future”? Was God ever incautious, so as to make things that ought not to have been made, and then afterward, considering what he had not done well, repent of what was done and take care regarding what was to be done? Rather, it must be understood that, just as God’s repentance is not a changed will regarding the approval of making, but a changed order in the establishment of what is made, so his precaution is not the foresight of one presiding, but the correction of those subject to him. For in doing evil, one who threatens so that it may not be done takes as much precaution as one who fears so as not to do it.

## XCI. “Go forth from your land and from your kindred.” A sermon to the brethren.

“Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you” [Col. 0521B] (Gen. 12).

For, brethren, since we speak to those who know God’s law, our discourse to you is not instruction but exhortation. For you know the Scriptures and their power. The power of the word is experience of the reality; the efficacy of speech is the performance of the work. You therefore do not err through not knowing the Scriptures or their power. You know the Scriptures through the practice of reading; their power through the discipline of action. You know the Scriptures by hearing Christ speak; their power by imitating him in action. In his sayings you have found the understanding of the Scriptures; in his deeds, their power. Therefore you know Christ not only by hearing but also by experience. You know him not only according to the flesh, but also according to majesty. “And even if we have known Christ,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0521C] “according to the flesh, now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5). You have experienced Christ in both respects, and know Christ according to the flesh and according to majesty. Formerly you knew Christ according to the flesh; now you know Christ according to majesty. Christ according to the flesh is Christ in his Passion. Christ according to majesty is Christ in the Resurrection. You have experienced Christ on the cross through compassion; you will experience Christ in majesty by rising with him.

For you are that bride and beloved one who knew her beloved and said from experience: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Song 1). This is Christ according to the flesh. And again: “My beloved is to me a cluster of henna [Cyprus]” (ibid.); this is Christ according to majesty. The bundle of myrrh is Christ in the Passion; the cluster of henna is Christ in the Resurrection. The bundle of myrrh is the bitterness of the Passion; the cluster of henna is the sweetness of the Resurrection. The bundle of myrrh is the multitude of sufferings; the cluster of henna is the abundance of joys. There he makes bitter; here he makes drunk. Yet you have placed the bundle of myrrh between your breasts, because you received Christ’s Passion with joy and love. You bear Christ suffering not only in your body but also in your heart, because you have embraced in the spirit of love the imitation of his Passion.

Therefore, what you knew of Christ according to the flesh you now no longer know, because what belongs to the Passion is transitory, while what belongs to the Resurrection will remain. [Col. 0522A] You knew, therefore, and now no longer know, because the pain of the Passion—which you received in the flesh by sharing his suffering—is at hand to pass away; and the joy of the Resurrection—which you received in spirit by rising with him—is at hand to be consummated. The pain of the Passion is at hand to pass away, but the love of the sufferer is not at hand to pass away. The Passion passes from the flesh, but love does not pass from the heart. Therefore “the bundle of myrrh shall remain between the breasts” (Song 1). For there is the heart; and where the heart is, there is love; and where love is, there is the dwelling of the beloved.

Therefore, brethren, you who are Christ’s beloved bride, have the bundle of myrrh, Christ suffering, and the cluster of henna, Christ rising. Thus you have no need to be taught concerning him, since you are taught by him, because his anointing teaches you concerning all things [Col. 0522B] (1 John 2), as does his word, which sounds in your ears and is sweet in your hearts.

Our words, therefore, do not suffice for our instruction; rather, let his own word pass through us to you, so that his grace may overflow from you even to us. For this is his word to you, which was spoken on your account: “Go forth from your land,” etc. It had been spoken long ago, and he willed that what had been spoken should be said to you, so that you might know that what was spoken pertains also to you. There was indeed one person then to whom it was spoken; but he belonged to that one bride in which you are one, of whom it is written: “One is my beloved, my dove, my perfect one” (Song 6).

And he was then an outsider because he was in what was foreign, and he was called so that he might go out from there and become near, beloved, and a friend. Even then he was beloved, because he was loved by him who called him; but he was not a friend, because he did not love him whom he did not know. Thus he was not loved because he was an outsider, but because he was to become near and a friend. For he was then in Ur of the Chaldeans, that is, in the fire and burning of demons: namely, the concupiscence and delight of earthly things. This very burning had darkened and blackened him, so that he was not lovable. Therefore he was called, so that he might leave the fire and come into refreshment, that he might be whitened and become bright, lest he remain hateful forever.

For this reason he said: “Go forth from your land, and from your kindred, and from your father’s house, and come into the land that I shall show you.” To go out from one’s land is to leave earthly goods that are possessed outwardly. To go out from one’s kindred is to renounce those vices that have arisen within us and with us. To go out from one’s father’s house is, after all things have been despised for God’s sake, finally to deny oneself. For the house of our father is our very heart, because our father dwells in us. Our first father was the devil, according to the birth by which we were born; our second Father is God, according to the birth by which we have been reborn. Each father wishes to dwell in his own children: the devil in the children of wrath, God in the children of grace.

Therefore, when we were in Ur of the Chaldeans, our heart was the devil’s house [Col. 0523A], because he then dwelt in us and we were all children of Beor, a name said to mean “one dwelling in skin.” For this father can dwell only in skin, because he loves the hearts of carnal people and rests only in them, since they relish the things that belong to the flesh and walk according to the flesh (Rom. 8). This is the skin—the house of our first father—from which we are commanded to go out: that is, to leave our very heart and its evil desires. For this is to go out from the heart: to withdraw from its desires and become a stranger to them, so that we may not be where they are by consent, but through a purpose of holiness may strive toward the land which God will show us, once first for God’s sake we have cast aside our possessions and then left even ourselves.

Thus at last the land of vision will be shown to us by the Lord—the land in which the Lord himself will be seen, which he set as a promise to his children, flowing with milk and honey: milk in the contemplation [Col. 0523B] of humanity, honey in the contemplation of divinity. For God was glorified in this way, that he might make the whole human being blessed in himself: that the whole conversion of humanity might be toward him and the whole love of humanity might be in him. For if God were the Creator of humanity, but God were not man, there would be in him what might be seen by the faculty of the mind, but there would not be what might be perceived by the faculty of the body. The sense of the flesh would endure the perpetual reproach of the Creator’s absence, always wandering vainly among creatures and not reaching its Creator.

Therefore, lest the carnal sense in humanity should bear this reproach forever and it should always rightly be said to it, “Where is your God?” (Mic. 7), if it were never admitted to contemplation of its Creator, the Creator assumed flesh—flesh that might be seen in him by the faculty of the flesh through flesh—so that the food of the flesh might be milk in contemplating the flesh, and the food of the mind honey in contemplating divinity. Thus it might go out and come in and find pasture (John 10): pasture outwardly in the Savior’s flesh, pasture inwardly in the Creator’s divinity. And Savior and Creator might be one, one joy both in the milk of flesh and in the honey of divinity. And so forth. Amen.

## XCII. On the soul’s twofold life.

The soul has a twofold life: one by which it lives in God, another by which it lives in the flesh. Where it lives, there it feels; there it suffers when injured and rejoices when cherished, because the place of joy and of pain is one. Nor is there pain except where joy [Col. 0523D] and love have been; for there is no pain except when you are injured where you rejoice, joy having been taken away.

But those who live in the flesh feel in the flesh, and bodily pain is grievous to them because its joy was sweet. Yet they do not feel the soul’s pains, because they are dead within, where they ought to live in God. Therefore, when the flesh is injured, they consider it grievous and flee its pains as far as they can. But they are utterly ignorant of the soul’s wounds and seek no remedy for them, because there they have no sense of pain.

But when the faculty by which the soul lives in the flesh has died, then that faculty by which it feels itself will begin to be brought to life. Then it will know its wounds and begin to feel its pains all the more heavily because they are nearer; for what is more inward harms more greatly when evil and benefits more greatly when good. Hence he says: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49).

## XCIII. On conscience and reputation.

There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience is oil in the vessel; reputation, light in the lamp. For conscience we go in; for reputation we go out. Within, we are refreshed by our own salvation; without, we are refreshed by another’s edification. Within: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 2). Without: “To remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (ibid.). Conscience is the upper spring; reputation, the lower spring (Judg. 1). Meditation pertains to conscience; preaching, to reputation. Silence pertains to conscience; speech, to reputation. By silence you sow your own field; by speech you sow your neighbor’s field. When you advance in your own edification, you reap your own field [Col. 0524B]; when you reflect on another’s advancement, you reap your neighbor’s field.

In time of leisure, reading first supplies material for knowing truth and practicing virtue; then meditation supplies form. In time of labor, work first provides an example, and afterward speech offers instruction, as it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). Therefore comes first the time of leisure, afterward the time of labor.

## XCIV. On the twofold oldness.

There were two old human beings in us: the inner one through iniquity, the outer through mortality. Christ, however, assumed flesh with mortality, but a soul without iniquity. He ordered the oldness of his flesh through the cross in this sequence: first he was bound [Col. 0524C], afterward crucified. So too must we destroy the oldness of the inward human being—that is, iniquity—in this sequence: first binding it outwardly through discipline, so that it cannot act; then crucifying and killing it wholly inwardly, so that it may no longer exist at all. Thus, first, through our effort, with God’s grace cooperating, iniquity must be destroyed in us; then, through that same grace, mortality itself must afterward be destroyed in us without our cooperation.

## XCV. On the three places of the children of Israel: Egypt, the wilderness, and the land of promise.

“At Israel’s going out from Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people” (Ps. 113). There are three places: Egypt, the wilderness, and the land of promise. In Egypt we are slaves and wretched. In the wilderness we are wretched. In the land of promise [Col. 0524D] we are free and blessed. In Egypt we are filled and beaten. In the wilderness we hunger, yet are not scourged. In the land of promise we are not scourged and are filled. Yet a noble soul meanwhile chooses want with freedom rather than abundance in slavery.

In Egypt we sin; in the wilderness we labor; in the land of promise we rest. In Egypt there is transgression; in the wilderness, training; in the land of promise, Sabbath-rest. At the beginning of the world God first created confusion, then wrought order, and afterward undertook rest. The ancient people wrought iniquity in Egypt, received training in the wilderness, and found rest in the land of promise. In secular life there is confusion; in spiritual conduct [Col. 0525A], training; in heavenly life, rest. In the flesh, sin; in the spirit, exercise; in God, Sabbath. Egypt is secular life; the wilderness, spiritual life; the land of promise, heavenly life. Egypt is flesh; the wilderness, the mind; the land of promise, God. Egypt is Jericho; the wilderness, the inn; the land of promise, Jerusalem. Egypt is the world; the wilderness, the Church; the land of promise, eternal life.

In Egypt we serve Pharaoh, that is, the devil—Pharaoh meaning, namely, “denying him, that is, the Lord,” who said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5). We serve him in Egypt, in mud and straw. Mud is the concupiscence of the flesh. Straw is worldly display. The former defiles through impurity; the latter flies away through changeability and instability. Therefore, as we leave Egypt and pass through the Red Sea—that is, baptism reddened by Christ’s blood—on the way to freedom, we renounce Pharaoh’s service, renouncing the devil and all his works and all his pomps: works in mud and pomps in straw.

Leaving Egypt for the wilderness, we leave evil behind so that we may not consent to it. Leaving the wilderness for the land of promise, we escape evil so that we may not feel it. In Egypt there is struggle without victory, or slavery without struggle. In the wilderness there is struggle without victory, or victory with struggle. In the land of promise there is victory without struggle. In Egypt there are evil and many pleasures, though not these alone. In the wilderness there are good and few pleasures, though not none. In the land of promise there are pleasures that are good, many, and alone [Col. 0525C].

## XCVI. An epistolary response concerning the two disciples running to the Lord’s tomb.

You ask what is signified by the passage written about the two disciples, John and Peter, running to the tomb: namely, that the one who came first entered later. For it is written: “The two were running together; and the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter and came first to the tomb; and, having stooped down, he saw the linen cloths lying there, yet he did not enter” (John 20). Then Simon Peter came following him, entered the tomb, and saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth which had been upon his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but separately wrapped up in one [Col. 0525D] place. Then the disciple who had come first to the tomb also entered.

John, therefore, who came first and entered later, may fittingly signify the Synagogue; Peter, who came later but entered first, the Church of the Gentiles. For the former first received in the Law the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation and Passion, but would not believe in one dead; while the latter afterward followed the Mediator between God and humanity, knew him dead in flesh, and believed him living God. It is fittingly said that John entered only after Peter had entered, because when “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered” (Rom. 12), then Judah too will be gathered in its remnant to faith. John, therefore, first saw the linen cloths and afterward entered, because the Synagogue first received in the Scriptures, as has been said, prophecy concerning the one who was to come, yet refused to believe that he had come until nearly the end of the age [Col. 0526A]. Peter, however, first enters and afterward sees the linen cloths, because the Church of the Gentiles comes not to faith in Christ through the prophets, but through faith in Christ to an understanding of the prophets.

Brother, I would have thought that this brief explanation was enough for you at present, had I not doubted that you were still seeking in the figure of this event something pertaining to the reformation of morals—especially because you had no need to seek from me this exposition, which you could sufficiently find elsewhere in the explanations of the Fathers without my instruction. I shall say, therefore, what seems to me to be morally signified in this event.

These two chosen disciples, who upon hearing of the Lord’s Resurrection [Col. 0526B] run together to the tomb but do not arrive together, seem to me to represent two affections of the soul: desire and counsel. For what else is it that the disciples run to the tomb on hearing of the Resurrection, except that the mind, upon hearing of the glory of the Resurrection, longs to imitate the Passion? And what is it that the other disciple ran ahead faster than Peter, except that, inflamed with love for the Savior, we desire more through longing than we presume through deliberation? Desire therefore runs ahead of the reasoning of counsel, because one who would wish, through charity, to suffer everything for love of the Redeemer is in some way delayed through consideration of his own weakness, lest he rashly dare boast of his own powers.

Thus we come first to the tomb through desire, but, having seen the linen cloths, we do not presume to enter before counsel: because although our mind offers itself willingly through charity to sufferings, nevertheless, considering the difficulty of those same sufferings, we see how unequal our weakness is to their endurance. This, in some manner, is to stop after seeing the linen cloths: after seeing the difficulties of the sufferings, to judge oneself unequal to enduring them. But after counsel, coming later, has entered first, desire too follows; for after the mind has deliberated that confidence must be placed in him who conquered first, then love is encouraged through hope in divine help to endurance in all things. And now it fearlessly enters the tomb, because, willingly despising the present life for his sake [Col. 0526D], it offers itself to death all the more readily as it has learned more certainly, through the Resurrection of its head, that death of the flesh is an entrance into life.

That when they have entered the tomb they find the cloth that was upon Jesus’ head separated from the other linen cloths, what else does this signify except that we, who are sinners, even if we are able to suffer death for love of him, nevertheless know that our death cannot worthily be equated with his death, since he suffered without sin? Most dear brother, kindly receive this Paschal dish sent to you, and pray for me for the Lord’s mercy, that by the abundance of his grace in these Paschal feasts the old human being may die in me and the new may rise. Amen.

## XCVII. On the two disciples running to the tomb: another letter.

[Col. 0527A]

If you do not wish to have a negligent writer, brother, do you think it fair that I should love a timid reader? We are now celebrating a festival; I should like, with serious matters laid aside for a little while, to take delight with you, to play with you in discourse, and at the same time to drive you out of sleep so that you may awaken.

You complain, then, that when I was speaking of the two disciples, John and Peter, running to the tomb (John 20), and, wishing to satisfy your request, was explaining what their action showed ought to be done by us, I maintained that the one who came first to the tomb and entered later—that is, John—signified desire; and that the one who came later but entered the tomb first—that is, Peter—signified the counsel of the mind [Col. 0527B]. Yet, as you assert, I did not show why the former rather than the latter signified desire, or the latter rather than the former counsel. Thus, you say, while expounding the meaning, I ought not to have kept silent concerning the reason for the meaning.

I gladly accept that this complaint of yours, while admonishing one person, teaches both of us: first, me, not to pass over what should be said, so that I may strive to be careful in writing; then also you, not to misunderstand what has been said less fully, so that you may be attentive in hearing. Yet, lest your complaint should seem altogether justified to itself, I shall show you how you could have found in the very place where its meaning was explained the reason you seek.

For when it was said there that John, who ran ahead and arrived first at the tomb, signifies the soul’s desire, while Peter, who came later, signifies counsel, does not the manifest reason why desire is signified by the former and counsel by the latter follow from their very action? If you ask why John signifies desire, the reason is evident: because he went first. And if you ask why Peter signifies counsel, this too is evident: because he came later. Thus the diversity of action plainly shows what diversity of meaning is maintained in the distinction of their persons.

But if perhaps you think that the force of the signification must be gathered not only from the quality of their actions but also from the distinction of their persons, I do not judge even this to be rejected. For the alertness and ardor of love are aptly expressed by John [Col. 0527D], the younger; while the gravity and delay of counsel are represented by Peter, old and slow. Your assertion that Peter loved more, and that therefore it seems right to you that desire or love should rather have been signified by him, is irrelevant to the present question. For in the present discussion the issue is not what Peter was inwardly, but what signification he presented to us by outward appearance or action—especially since we must always observe that, when we draw something by way of signification, we ought to seek it not in what is hidden but in what is manifest. A sign must not be hidden but manifest, since what is itself hidden cannot disclose hidden things. As you see, your tablets found me idle: with no one attacking me, I quarrel with myself and, as though I had no enemy, pour my strength out into the wind.

## XCVIII. On the love of Peter and John.

I know that the question is thought by some to be laborious, since it seems an unjust recompense that Peter, who loved Christ more, should be loved less by Christ, and that John should be more loved although he loved less. But when I examined the Gospel, from which the source of this question seems to flow, I found neither that Peter loved more nor that John was more loved. For when the Lord, after his Resurrection, asked Peter whether he loved him, and said, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” (John 21), he said this not by affirming but by asking [Col. 0528B]. Nor did Peter himself dare to say, when asked, “Lord, you know that I love you more than these”; rather, he said, “Lord, you know that I love you” (ibid.). John also, speaking of himself, said: “This is that disciple whom Jesus loved” (ibid.). He did not say, “whom Jesus loved more than the others,” but “whom Jesus loved.”

Thus Peter did not presume to claim that he loved more, nor John that he was loved more; rather, the one asserted that he loved not before the rest, but with the rest, and the other that he was loved not before the rest, but with the rest. But grant that Peter loved more and was nevertheless loved less: did he thereby suffer any injustice, provided he was loved as much as he deserved? Is this not the complaint of those who murmured against the householder in the Gospel, saying: “These last have worked one hour, and you have made them equal to us, who have borne the burden of the day and the heat” (Matt. 20)? But we have heard what the householder answered one of them, and in him all: “Friend, I do you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I will give to this one also as to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (ibid.).

Let us suppose, then, that Peter brings forward a complaint and alleges an injury in Christ’s love for him, saying: “Lord Jesus, you seem to do me wrong: although I love you more, you love me less.” Could not the Lord rightly answer one who says this: “Friend, I do you no wrong” [Col. 0528D] (ibid.). You are loved as much as you love; you are loved as much as you deserve. Take what is yours and go. I will give this man more than you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I will? Or is your eye evil because I am good? For you suffer no injustice if you receive less than he; you suffer injustice if you receive less than you deserve. But if you have everything, what do you complain of?

Receive me, brother, reasoning thus, so that you may know that your mind ought not to incline precipitously to any assertion. Yet there are some who strive to resolve this question more gently. They say that Peter both loved more and was loved more. John, however, because of the chastity in which he excelled, was simply received into more familiar intercourse with Christ the Lord than all the others [Col. 0529A]. Peter was loved more by Christ in respect of the effect of charity; John was received more affectionately in intercourse in respect of intimate familiarity. Peter was dearer; John more familiar: for charity was rewarded in Peter and chastity praised in John. John loved more tenderly, Peter more steadfastly.

## XCIX. On gratitude for God’s benefits, and on judging oneself and one’s neighbor.

“My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab planned, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim as far as Gilgal, that you may know the righteousness of the Lord” (Mic. 6). Balak king of Moab hired Balaam the diviner for payment, that he might curse the children of Israel [Col. 0529B]. But the latter was not permitted by the Lord to curse his people, to whom blessing had been promised as an inheritance. And although a human being’s curse could not harm one whom God had blessed, nevertheless, when the prophet’s curse is turned into a blessing, it plainly shows what God’s grace now accomplishes spiritually in his elect. For the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, for those who are called saints according to his purpose” (Rom. 8).

The wicked prophet, therefore, desiring to curse the people of God, is compelled, though unwillingly, to bless them; for the evils which the reprobate inflict upon the good cooperate, by the Lord’s ordering, toward the salvation of the latter. Therefore the Lord now speaks of His people through the prophet [Col. 0529C] and recalls His earlier benefits to their memory, saying: “My people, remember, I pray, what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam son of Beor answered him, from Shittim to Gilgal, that you might know the righteousness of the Lord.” Blush, wretched man. You ought never to have forgotten that you were so greatly loved by God that He not only would not permit the curse of your enemies to harm you, but even changed it into a blessing for you. But now, when the very Giver of good things asks you to remember these benefits, what else does this show except that, after receiving such great benefits, you have nevertheless remained ungrateful and forgetful?

[Col. 0529D] And if the ungrateful Jew refused to remember God’s benefits, take care at least, Christian, lest you ever forget the good things bestowed upon you. Take care, I say, and take all the more care because it is worse if you persist in ingratitude, since you are known to have received greater benefits from God than he. For you too have your enemy Balak, who persecutes you without ceasing and continually devises wicked counsels against you. Fearing also that perhaps he is not sufficient in his own strength to overthrow you, he invites an iniquitous and avaricious prophet, offering a reward, to curse you. For Balak, whose name is interpreted “one who crushes,” is Satan himself, our adversary and most evil enemy. The Lord heals and raises up those cast down and crushed by him; as is sung in the Psalm: “The Lord raises up the crushed; the Lord loves the righteous” [Ps. 145].

[Col. 0530A] This Balak is king also of Moab, which is interpreted “from the father”: that is, of those to whom the Lord says in the Gospel, “You are from your father the devil” [John 8]. He devises evil against us, as the Apostle Paul says to certain of his disciples: “That we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his devices” [1 Cor. 2]. But to this one devising against us and seeking a plan for our overthrow, Balaam answers—Balaam being interpreted “vain people,” namely, the whole people of the wicked. He answers by complying with Satan’s will and agreeing unanimously with him as he rages for our overthrow and ruin.

[Col. 0530B] This Balaam, that is, the vain people, is the son of Beor, a name which means “dwelling in skin,” that is, by imitation the son of the same devil, oppressing us with him and pursuing us in wicked hatred. The devil dwells in skin, that is, in the carnal heart, because he finds rest only in those whom the inclination of carnal desire, loosening them from the constancy and rigor of virtues, softens through shameful longings. But the place where Balaam son of Beor answers Balak while he devises our destruction is shown when the text adds: “From Shittim unto Gilgal”—understand, circling about, ensnaring, and seeking a place from which to curse. Shittim is interpreted “thorn”; Gilgal is called “a rolling-place.”

This, then, is the way of the vain people and the circuit of error: thorn and rolling-place, that is, care and pleasure. Care, by which one labors to acquire the transitory things of this world; pleasure, by which one defiles oneself through immoderate and unlawful enjoyment of things acquired. Thus, from Shittim to Gilgal, the vain people, responding to the malicious king, persecute the faithful, because all wicked people, both acquiring temporal goods through avarice and using what they have acquired through incontinence, are stirred up, while serving the devil, to persecute the good.

[Col. 0530C] The wicked are permitted to rage against the good in order that they may be shown unable to prevail; and the more vain their malice is shown to be, the more manifest God’s grace and mercy toward us become. This is what follows: “that you might know the righteousness,” or mercy, “of the Lord.” As though He said: They were allowed freedom in part, that you might recognize the danger; they were restrained, that you might understand whence your protection came. [Col. 0530D] Therefore, after receiving such great benefits, what remains for you now except to give thanks and respond with worthy recompense to your Savior and Protector? For if the vain people answer their king as he plots the destruction of the good, what should the faithful and chosen people do?
