Should they not much more answer their King, who frees and saves the good, by obeying and serving Him?

But perhaps you will say: “What worthy thing shall I offer to the Lord? Shall I bend the knee to God Most High? Shall I offer Him burnt offerings and year-old calves? Can God be appeased by thousands of rams, or by many thousands of fat he-goats?” [Mic. 6]. For all these things are external to me, and therefore cannot be a worthy recompense for my salvation. Yet perhaps I shall make satisfaction if I give “my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my womb for the sin of my soul.” But even these are outside me, although they proceeded from me; and I who have taken myself away from God, even if I gave everything besides myself, would not yet have fully repaid the debt. What, then, shall I do? What shall I give? What shall I render? “What shall I repay to the Lord for all that He has repaid to me?” [Ps. 116].

[Col. 0531A] “I will show you, O man, what is good and what God requires of you: namely, to do judgment, to love mercy” [Mic. 6], and to walk attentively with your God. These are the three things that you must offer, because God, who is Trinity, can be worthily pleased only by a threefold sacrifice. Offer judgment to the Son, the Judge. Offer mercy to the Holy Spirit, who is charity. Offer attentiveness to the Fatherhood. Discernment belongs to wisdom; compassion to charity; attentiveness to fatherhood. [Col. 0531B] Yet offer in such a way that neither in distinguishing the gifts do you divide the unity of the Trinity, nor in sharing the gifts do you confuse the Trinity of the unity; rather, render what belongs to each one severally, and each thing simultaneously to the one God. If you judge justly, you honor the just Judge. If you love mercy, you worship Him who is merciful with an acceptable sacrifice. If you always walk attentively in the fear of God, you appease for yourself the heavenly Father, whom you had offended by your sins.

Now hear what kind of judgment you are commanded to make. First you must make judgment concerning yourself; then between yourself and your neighbor; finally concerning your neighbor. In the judgment by which you judge yourself, you must be strict. In the judgment by which you judge between yourself and your neighbor, you must be just. In the judgment by which you judge your neighbor, you must be merciful.

[Col. 0531C] You must judge yourself in this manner. Carefully consider what you do and what you do not do; what you ought to do and what you ought not to do. Then, comparing these matters with one another, weigh whether what you do is the same as what you ought to do, and whether what you do not do is the same as what you ought not to do. If you find this to be so, rejoice. But if you perceive that what you do is what you ought not to do, or that what you do not do is what you ought to do, be afraid.

You must judge between yourself and your neighbor in this manner. See what you do to your neighbor, and what your neighbor does to you. If he does you good and you return good to him, you are not evil. If he does you evil and you return evil to him, you are not good. If he does you good and you return evil to him, you are evil. If he does you evil and you return good to him, you are good.

[Col. 0531D] You must judge your neighbor in this manner. Consider whatever he does: whether it is certainly good, doubtfully good, certainly evil, or doubtfully evil. If it is certainly good, judge a small good great and a great good greater. If it is doubtfully good, suppose it true. If it is certainly evil, judge a great evil small and a small evil smaller. If it is doubtfully evil, suppose it good. This is true judgment, good judgment, judgment pleasing to God. If you offer it to Him as a sacrifice, not only by discerning but also by doing it, you will appease His wrath and obtain grace.

[Col. 0532A] Then follows: “to love mercy.” Not merely to practice it, but to love it, because one who has compassion through an affection of piety does more than one who shows mercy merely from the obligation of a command. You must therefore first do judgment, so that you may fulfill in deed what you rightly discern; then love mercy, so that you may do the good you perform not from fear but from love. Finally, walk attentively, lest you fail to deserve to receive the good that you do not yet possess, or lose the good that you possess.

[Col. 0532B] Moreover, in these three things you cooperate with the Trinity at work within you. Wisdom enlightens you to the knowledge of truth; charity inflames you to the desire of goodness; fatherhood preserves within you what it created, lest it perish. Therefore, through enlightening wisdom shining upon you, you discern rightly; through inflaming charity burning together with you, you show mercy; through provident fatherhood watching over you, you guard yourself. Thus, by cooperating through the Trinity with the Trinity, you are made an image of the Trinity; and then you offer yourself as a true sacrifice to God, when you are re-formed in His likeness. Which, etc. Amen.

## TIT. C. On Christ’s appearance to the two disciples going to the village called Emmaus

Jesus hid His face from those walking on the road [Luke 24], intending to show it in the homeland. Therefore, at the end of the road, when they began to recline at table, Jesus broke bread so that His inner reality might be revealed; and there they recognized Him. For after the course of this life, reclining in the kingdom of heaven with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and eating and drinking at His table in the eternal banquet, they will see the brightness of Jesus.

[Col. 0532C] For the present, however, He appears on the road as a stranger, so that we may recognize our exile and know that our homeland is elsewhere. In speaking, He inflames hearts to love, but does not yet open eyes to contemplation. Therefore, those who on the road conceive in their hearts the fire of love from the words of Jesus will see His brightness at the journey’s end. Thus tongues of fire come to us, and every day we hear Christ speaking to us in flaming words; for whoever does not burn while hearing the words of Christ does not have the Spirit of Christ. The Holy Spirit appeared over Christ’s disciples in tongues of fire, and Christ Himself, by speaking, inflamed the hearts of those walking on the road. He joined Himself to them not as though from the head, but as though from the side, because in the way of this life He has been given to us as companion not by nature but by grace. [Col. 0532D]

## TIT. CI. On Christ, the sheep and the good shepherd

Christ was first a sheep and afterward became a shepherd. A sheep is a gentle and clean animal. Gentleness signifies humility; cleanness, chastity. Humility is twofold: first, not desiring to be over others; second, loving to be under others. For many do not wish to preside, fleeing labor rather than honor; yet they disdain to be subject. When they grumble under the command of obedience, they kick back as though being led to suffering. Such people are certainly not sheep, nor imitators of Him who “was led as a sheep to slaughter and did not open His mouth” [Isa. 53].

[Col. 0533A] Likewise, chastity is twofold: one kind outward, through purity of body; the other inward, through purity of heart. Purity of body is abstaining from evil action; purity of heart is freedom from evil delight. Therefore, whoever possesses purity and gentleness is a sheep. And whoever is a good sheep can in due course become a shepherd, having first learned in subjection of oneself how one may preside over others.

Some are shepherds, some hirelings, and some wolves. Shepherds are those who love the sheep; hirelings, those who receive wool and milk; wolves, those who eat flesh. Shepherds guard in prosperity and defend in adversity. Hirelings guard in prosperity, but do not defend in adversity. Wolves do not guard in prosperity and kill in adversity. Shepherds seek salvation; hirelings pursue gain. [Col. 0533B] Wolves, by giving sheep the material or license for sin, kill them. The first are loving, the second negligent, the third destructive.

## TIT. CII. On the words written: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come”

“Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come” [John 16]. Christ withdrew His bodily presence from the disciples so that they might learn to love Him spiritually. For He Himself had formerly been, according to that same bodily presence, a paraclete—that is, a comforter—and this consolation was like milk flowing from flesh for little children. Therefore the milk was withdrawn, so that they might grow strong unto the perfection of spiritual love. He ascended into heaven in order to draw hearts after Himself, and that love might go after the Beloved.

[Col. 0533C] To this day Christ comforts His friends through Holy Scripture, the sacraments of the Church, and other visible exercises of virtues, as though by a certain bodily presence. When, by His dispensation, He sometimes withdraws their use, He seems to remove a certain humanity of His from the eyes of those who behold Him, so that they may perceive the sweetness of spiritual love more purely, inasmuch as they have less outwardly, even in the work of virtue, upon which to expend their mind through attentive application.

## TIT. CIII. On the Spirit of God and the spirit of the world, through whom all things were consummated

“The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world” [Wis. 1]. What wonder is it if the Spirit of the Lord could fill human hearts, since He fills the whole world? [Col. 0533D] Now, therefore, has been fulfilled what the Lord Jesus Christ foretold in His Passion: “It is finished” [John 19]. Before the Holy Spirit came to human hearts, it could not be said, “It is finished.” For this is why all things were done by Him who did them—whether in the birth, Passion, Resurrection, or Ascension of Jesus Christ, or in all the other works visibly performed by the incarnate Word for the restoration of humankind: that humanity might receive that good for which it had been created, without which nothing was of use, and with which nothing was lacking. Therefore in this all things were consummated, because all things had been done for this end.

[Col. 0534A] For the cluster of flesh had been carried to the winepress of the Cross, and, once it had been pressed, the new wine of divinity began to flow. He willed that the vessels of hearts should be prepared, so that, when new wine was poured into new wineskins, they might first be cleansed, lest what was poured in be defiled; and afterward bound up, lest what was poured in be lost. Let them be cleansed from the joy of wickedness; let them be bound against the joy of vanity. For good joy cannot come unless evil joy has first departed. Evil joy is joy in wickedness, and evil joy is joy in vanity. The joy of wickedness defiles; the joy of vanity spills out. The joy of wickedness makes the vessel filthy; the joy of vanity makes the vessel cracked. Joy in wickedness is when sin is loved; joy in vanity is when transitory things are loved. Cast out, therefore, what is evil, so that you may receive what is good. Pour out bitterness, that you may be filled with sweetness.

[Col. 0534B] The Holy Spirit is joy, and the Holy Spirit is love. Cast out the spirit of the world and the spirit of the devil, that you may receive the Spirit of God. The spirit of the devil produces joy in wickedness, and the spirit of the world produces joy in vanity. These joys are evil, since one contains guilt and the other an occasion of guilt. But when evil spirits have been cast out, the Spirit of God comes, enters the dwelling of the heart, and produces His own joy and love—not like the spirit of the devil, nor like the spirit of the world, but good joy and good love. First comes the joy of truth, in which righteousness is loved; afterward, the joy of blessedness, in which one exults in having received the reward of righteousness. The joy of truth is opposed to the joy of wickedness; the joy of blessedness, to the joy of vanity. Good joys expel evil joys. And when they begin to fill the heart, then for the first time a person recognizes that the former joys were not true, because they could neither be full in the joy of wickedness nor lasting in the joy of vanity.

[Col. 0534C] But now true joys have come, full and eternal, as the Savior promised: “that your joy may be full, and no one may take your joy from you” [John 16]. This joy itself is love, and the same Spirit produces both joy and love: love when we seek it, joy when we possess it. Yet desire itself cannot exist without joy, nor attainment itself without love. Thus joy itself is love, and love itself is joy, because we rejoice in what we love and love that in which we rejoice. There is good joy and good love, and likewise evil joy and evil love.

[Col. 0534D] For there is love of God, love of the world, and love of sin. Some love God alone. Some love something besides God together with God, yet nothing against God. Others love certain things against God, and these do not love God. Those who love God alone build upon the foundation “gold, silver, and precious stones” [1 Cor. 3]. In gold is understanding; in silver, speech; in precious stones, incorruptible action. Those who love something besides God, and yet love God more, build upon the foundation “wood, hay, stubble” [ibid.]. In wood is affection for kindred; in hay, affection for possessions; in stubble, affection for familiar associates. [Col. 0535A] Although in all these there is no sin, an occasion of sin is nevertheless present. Those who love anything against God do not build upon the foundation but destroy the foundation, because the love of God cannot be in a heart where it is neither alone, as in those who love God alone, nor supreme, as in those who love something else together with God but not against God.

In the love by which something else is loved together with God there is joy of vanity. In the love by which something is loved against God there is joy of wickedness. There love of the world taints; here love of sin defiles. “The world passes away, and its desire” [1 John 2]; but “the word of the Lord remains for ever” [Ps. 119]. Whoever believes in His word and possesses His Spirit abides for ever, just as He Himself abides for ever. [Col. 0535B] For whoever is unstable through joy in wickedness, or clings to what is unstable through joy in vanity, cannot abide for ever, nor possess true joy—since it is false through wickedness and transitory through vanity. But whoever has the abiding Spirit of God has joy that is true, full, and eternal, because he loves what endures, clings to what is stable, and possesses the perfect good. For the whole good of humanity is to know and love its Creator.

[Col. 0535C] For this reason tongues of fire were given to the apostles: in tongues is knowledge of truth; in fire, love of virtue. For in the tongue is the word, and in fire the flame. The word belongs to knowledge, but fire to love. Therefore the word came with fire, wisdom with love, so that one might enlighten and the other inflame: the one against ignorance, the other against concupiscence. These gifts could come only to those gathered into one and lifted upward: gathered by concord and lifted by desire; gathered through love of neighbor and lifted through love of God. Therefore, if we wish to receive such gifts, let us be such persons. Which, etc. Amen.

## TIT. CIV. On the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament of repentance

[Col. 0535D] The sacrament of repentance is the outward performance of the work; the reality of the sacrament is true contrition of heart. If you receive the sacrament, perform works of repentance; possess the reality of the sacrament in true contrition, lest you display an appearance without truth in vain. Your repentance is as great as your contrition is, as great as your devotion is. Contrition is for the evil you have done; devotion is for recovering the good you have lost. Therefore do not say: “I have fasted so much, kept vigil so much, performed such great works of mercy.” In all these matters you have done only as much as you have advanced through them. Do not count leaves, but fruit. Do not weigh straw, but grain. Work without contrition is a flower without fruit; contrition without work is fruit without ripeness.

## TIT. CV. On the power of repentance

Do you wish to know, O man, how great the power of repentance is? Attend: I shall say what I can. It wholly takes away what damnation threatens; it wholly bestows what salvation promises. How great do you think this is? Consider well. It takes away eternal evils; it bestows eternal goods. Such and so great is the fruit of repentance. Repentance confers this fruit: if you produce fruit in it, you will obtain fruit from it. The fruit that you produce in it is merit; the fruit that you receive from it is reward. If you produce in it fruits worthy in merit, you will receive from it eternal fruits in reward.

[Col. 0536A] What is repentance? Sorrow for sin. What is the worthy fruit of repentance? Satisfaction for an offense. “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” [Matt. 3]. Consider these three things: repentance, fruit, and worthy. If you grieve over an error, that is repentance; show your grief through fruit. If you have changed your will, pursue iniquity. After repentance, the sorrow of the heart should be followed by the mortification of the flesh, which is its fruit.

## TIT. CVI. On the three things that are in repentance

There are three things in repentance: sorrow for the past, guarding against the future, and satisfaction for an offense. Guarding against the future prevents the penitent from being condemned in the future; satisfaction for an offense prevents punishment. [Col. 0536B] Therefore, if you wish to be secure, beware of future things and correct past things. Sorrow appeases guilt; satisfaction heals the vice; guarding preserves health. Among these, guarding against the future holds the first place, sorrow for the past the second, and satisfaction for the offense the last. The first accomplishes as much alone as the other two accomplish together.

Therefore the Savior enjoined only this—namely, guarding against the future—as the chief thing, and that in which the whole fruit of repentance consists, upon those confessing to Him: “Go, and sin no more” [John 8]; and: “Go in peace” [Mark 5]. Again: “See that nothing worse happen to you” [John 5]. These three things must be weighed so that sorrow may be full, guarding perfect, and satisfaction adequate.

## TIT. CVII. On wisdom in doing good and patience in enduring evil

[Col. 0536C] God is served in two ways: by doing good and by enduring evil. In confessors, good action is rewarded; in martyrs, suffering. Wisdom is necessary for doing good; patience is necessary for enduring evil: wisdom, that good may be done well; patience, lest one who endures evil become evil. For one who does good works in good material; but if one does not do good well, good material is deformed by a bad form. The form is good where there is neither more nor less than is just. If there is more than is just, it is sin; if less than is just, it is an offense. Therefore one who does good well impresses a good form upon good material.

For the endurance of evil, however, patience is necessary, because whoever yields to evil through impatience departs from good. [Col. 0536D] For just as evil which is guilt ought not to be done, so evil which is punishment ought to be endured. Punishment is pain; and pain is nothing other than the loss of what is loved: whether in renouncing guilt, when sin that formerly delighted is abandoned; or in renouncing one’s own possessions, when worldly property possessed outwardly is forsaken; or in renouncing worldly delight, when the wantonness of carnal senses is mortified. In all these there is labor, and none of them can be done without pain.

This, then, is the patience of the saints. Those who abandon endurance become apostates. After the last renunciation, first through vanity, because they return to worldly pleasure for delight; after the second, secondly through cupidity, because they seek superfluous worldly riches [Col. 0537A] which they had set aside; after the first, thirdly through wickedness, because they presume to repeat sins already committed and forgiven. Therefore patience is necessary for endurance, so that a person may not be in the counsel of the ungodly through vanity, nor stand in the way of sinners through cupidity, nor sit in the seat of pestilence through wickedness.

Job had not looked toward worldly pleasure when he said: “If I looked upon the sun when it shone, and the moon advancing brightly in its order” [Job 31]. David forbids us to become apostate after worldly riches, saying: “Do not envy him who prospers in his way” [Ps. 37]. The Lord Himself forbids apostasy after forgiven sins, saying: “Go, and sin no more” [John 3]. And the prophet says: “I will keep myself from my iniquity” [Ps. 18]. [Col. 0537B] Therefore let the person who comes to the service of God stand in his place through patience, so that he neither yields nor retreats. Let him do good in order to fulfill the first obligation; let him endure evil in order to expiate the first offense. For human beings were made in order to do good; human beings made themselves such that they must endure evil. Therefore, because of what they were made to be, they do good; because of what they did, they endure evil.

For the first human being was so made that he might advance from the good of innocence, through the good of obedience, to the good of glory. But changing his place and abandoning innocence, he began to decline and to proceed from the evil of wickedness, through the evil of mortality, to the evil of damnation. But the Savior came and showed another way by which humanity might return to its homeland: through the good of righteousness and the evil of punishment, to the good of glory.

## TIT. CVIII. How each person should prepare himself as food for God

[Col. 0537C] “You have sat at a great table. Consider what is set before you, and know that you must prepare similar things” [Ecclus. 31]. Behold, brothers, the Lord has prepared a meal for you through the examples of His saints, now refreshing you toward merit, until afterward He prepares a supper in the joy of the saints, satisfying you through reward. He has killed His oxen and fattened beasts, so that you may be nourished for action and contemplation through those whose flesh bore the yoke on earth in the labor of good work, while their minds had been raised to heaven by the flight of contemplation. You eat these meats at God’s table, so that, refreshed by bodily things, you may advance to spiritual things.

Nevertheless, you ought to know that God’s table does not receive boiled meat—that is, meat cooked in water. [Col. 0537D] For you have heard how the Paschal lamb is commanded not to be boiled in water but roasted [Exod. 12], and how after the Resurrection Christ eats roasted fish with a honeycomb [Luke 24]. Water softens meat compacted within itself; and therefore perhaps roasted meat is commended because God does not love soft and yielding flesh. Soft flesh says: “I cannot bear it; I am unable to endure; I melt away; I fail.” God does not love this flesh, but flesh scorched by the fire of suffering and strengthened by endurance of tribulation. Therefore, if you are refreshed by flesh, give refreshment in flesh. If God makes a feast for you, make a feast also for Him. If He grants you joy in Himself and in His own, give Him joy in yourselves: this is what it means to prepare similar things.

## TIT. CIX. On Elijah’s flight from the face of Jezebel

[Col. 0538A] Elijah, fleeing the impious Jezebel, hides in a cave [3 Kings 19], because the soul sometimes turns aside in order to avoid the foulness of the flesh, yet is not yet strengthened to abandon the dwelling of that same flesh. Jezebel, whose name is interpreted “dung of the earth,” signifies carnal concupiscence. The servant of God flees her persecution and lurks in a cave because, although he is encouraged to trample down filthiness, he is not yet strengthened for the endurance of sufferings. Hence the divine voice rebukingly says to him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” [ibid.]. For you were not made in order to linger beneath the shelter of the flesh, but to go forth to contemplate the face of the Creator.

[Col. 0538B] “Rise, therefore, and stand at the entrance of your cave” [ibid.]. Rise: lift yourself to higher things. Rise, lest you cling wholly to the earth. Rise, desiring the things above. Stand at the entrance of your cave: stand in perseverance; stand in patience. In perseverance, that you may not go backward; in patience, that you may not hasten to the end before the time. Stand; wait until you are called. Stand ready through the desire to depart. Stand fixed through obedience in enduring. Stand at the entrance of your cave, so that you neither enter through concupiscence nor go forth through impatience. Stand at the entrance of your cave, and behold, the Lord will pass by.

How can a person who clings to the flesh through concupiscence see God, when even one who longs with all desire for departure from the flesh can, while still placed in this corruption, see Him only as He passes by? [Col. 0538C] Therefore, amid this darkness of mortality, God’s coming to the soul occurs in passing; for what is here shown of His sweetness to those living changeably cannot be retained long by the soul itself, even though enlightened, since it falls back again into the darkness of its corruption. “Behold, the Lord will pass by. A great and strong wind, overthrowing mountains and breaking rocks; the Lord was not in the wind. After the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake. After the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire. After the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” [ibid.].

Behold the forerunners of God: wind, earthquake, and fire. The Lord does not come to you unless these first come. The wind is terror at eternal judgment; if it strikes the sinner’s heart, it casts down the mountains of pride and dissolves the rocks of hardness. But this is by no means called God, [Col. 0538D] because the soul still afflicted by fear of perdition does not yet feel the sweetness of perfect charity. After the wind comes an earthquake, because the mind shaken by terror of judgment is immediately moved from its stability. After the earthquake comes fire, because after anxiety concerning the age to come, the soul raging against itself is inflamed with the ardor of compunction. Finally, after the fire comes the whisper of a gentle breeze, because, after long burnings of compunction, the purified mind, breathed upon by the Spirit, feels the refreshing of consolation.

It should be noted that, although the Lord is said not to be in what precedes, He is by no means said not to be in the whisper of the gentle breeze. For only that mind perceives His sweetness which, after the labor and anxiety of repentance, [Col. 0539A] receives the refreshment of consolation and rests in hope of divine propitiation.

## TIT. CX. On the two messengers sent to us

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John” [John 1]. God sent two messengers into this world: a servant and the Son. First the servant, to threaten; afterward the Son, to console. The servant brought fear; the Son, love. The servant announced what we should fear; the Son revealed what we should love. For two things, dearest brothers, were hidden from human eyes: eternal evils and eternal goods. Humanity foresaw neither those evils, in order to avoid them, nor those goods, in order to seek them. Its eyes were open only to present things; and therefore, because people did not see where they especially ought to see, the things they did not know had to be shown to them.

[Col. 0539B] John came crying: “Brood of vipers, who will show you how to flee from the wrath to come? Produce fruits worthy of repentance” [Matt. 3]. He announces danger, urges caution, and shows counsel. A good servant, a good messenger: piously fierce, merciful in pursuing; the servant strikes so that the Lord may heal. Behold the two messengers: “John came neither eating nor drinking” [Matt. 11], an example of repentance; “the Son of Man came eating and drinking” [ibid.], an example of mercy. The one on account of human evils; the other on account of divine goods.

## TIT. CXI. On the wilderness that is the human heart; on the rod of smoke, the perfumer, and spices
What is this that comes up through the desert like a slender column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and incense and every [Col. 0539C] powder of the perfumer? (Song of Songs 3). It sleeps and rises, because it rests outwardly and rises inwardly. The desert is the world, because of the abundance of evil and the scarcity of good. The desert is an evil heart, because it is uncultivated, produces harmful growths, and beasts dwell in it. For because Christ the husbandman is not in it, and his Father does not sow his word there, shoots of vices arise: nettles of desire, thorns of anxiety, and things of that kind. Demons rest there because there is no one to frighten them away.

Likewise, the desert is a good heart, because it is far from noise and tumult and is not trampled by the crowd of earthly thoughts; rather, it remains green and flowering, produces the shoots of virtues, and there the dove, the Holy Spirit, sings; and no human voice, nor a voice belonging to man, is heard there. [Col. 0539D]

A slender rod is straight, thin, and extended in length. Since it tends only upward, it must be straight; because the way is narrow, it is thin; and because it is long, it is extended. Again, it is not a rod of unfeeling, hard wood, but of smoke: it has an appearance but no substance. When it is seen, it seems to be something; when the hand is applied, nothing is found. So every good person seems to be here by the appearance of the flesh, but is not here in love. Again, smoke rises from fire, because desire comes from love.

And what kind of smoke? “From the spices of myrrh and incense and every powder of the perfumer.” Christ is the perfumer; his perfumes are spices and virtues; myrrh is the mortification of the flesh; incense, the devotion of the mind. “Every powder of the perfumer” is the multitude of all virtues [Col. 0540A], just as a multitude is found in vices also. It is said in the book of Job: “From afar it smells the battle, the exhortation of the commanders and the shouting of the army” (Job 39). For the multitude of vices has a king or queen; it has commanders; it has peoples and an army. Pride is the queen; the capital vices are the commanders; the entire host of evils that follow is the army.

Thus the commanders of vices first, as though in battle, give exhortation, because they deceive a person in the deliberation of action. Then the army rushes in, as though with a shout, because after the first suggestion has been accepted, the following crowd of vices attacks the deceived mind with violence and tumult. So too, humility is queen among the virtues; the principal virtues are commanders; the totality of good things is the army. And after the first virtues are received by a person with a certain rational deliberation, the whole company of good things soon follows of its own accord. Therefore here he first placed the commanders, myrrh and incense; afterward the army, every powder of the perfumer. [Col. 0540B]

## TITLE CXII. On the three feasts—of virgins, confessors, and martyrs—and on the good of confession

A feast is joy. Great joy is a great feast; good joy is a good feast. There are three feasts: the feast of virgins, the feast of confessors, and the feast of martyrs.

The person who gladdens his conscience by the observance of chastity keeps the feast of virgins. The person who, although unable to glory in the integrity of virginity, nevertheless finds consolation in the purity of confession, keeps the feast of confessors. Though he has not done good from which to rejoice, he has accused and condemned the evil he did, so that he may find consolation. [Col. 0540C] The person who, under the pressure of tribulation, rejoices in hope of recompense keeps the feast of martyrs.

Consider your consciences, brothers. He who rejoices in purity keeps a great feast; nor is he excluded who finds consolation in humility. Purity belongs to virginity; humility to confession. Therefore, you who have not preserved virginity, embrace humility. Humility is a great virtue. I say boldly that virginity itself does not please without humility. Humble yourself, then, and acknowledge what you are.

Confession of sin indeed has a preceding punishment in shame; but the feast of joy and consolation in a good conscience follows. A good recompense has been set before you. You tell your sin to a human being so that God may be silent. You judge yourself so that he may not judge you. You confess before one [Col. 0540D] person in order to be justified, lest you be accused and condemned before heaven and earth, before all God’s angels. Therefore let the one who confesses rejoice, lest he be condemned.

## TITLE CXIII. On commemorating the feasts of the saints

Dearest brothers, it is an act of the great mercy of our Savior that we are commanded to recall the merits of the saints with festal gladness; for in this God both exhorts us to imitate their virtues and admits us to share in their joys. He does so for the imitation of virtues, that our wickedness may be corrected; and for participation in joys, that our misery may be consoled.

These are our two evils: one which we have done, the other which we suffer. One evil is in the soul, tending toward corruption through fault; the other is in the body, tending toward correction through punishment. Against each evil our Savior provides the remedy of remembering his saints. For when we consider what they did, we are stirred to imitate good works; when we consider what they received, we are consoled through participation in their joys. [Col. 0541A]

The first instruction comes when, through their patience, we are strengthened for endurance; the second, when, through their temptation, we are instructed in caution; the third, when, through their correction after sin, we are raised to hope. For when we see that they rose again after falling into sin through repentance, and are now taken up with the Lord God into such great glory, we recognize that even we, though fallen into grave sins, must by no means despair of God’s mercy. And when, again, we read that the ancient enemy dared something even against God’s elect, we do not doubt how watchfully we must guard against his snares. Finally, when we recall that those who did good suffered such great evils for God’s sake, it is openly shown to us how patiently we who have done evil ought to bear adversity. [Col. 0541B]

There is also another fruit which the remembrance of the saints yields to devout minds. For while we behold their joys in congratulation, we too are consoled in our misery by the joy which charity brings forth in us. First, indeed, we rejoice for them, in order that afterward we may also rejoice with them. First we rejoice for them through [Col. 0541C] love of neighbor, in which our merit is placed; then we shall rejoice with them in the love of God, where our reward is kept. For it is fitting, as we have said, that those who now rejoice for them should afterward rejoice with them also: so that the first joy may be consolation on the way, and the second joy full exultation in the homeland.

This joy, therefore, is our feast, in which, after the labor and pain of our works, we now take breath in part at certain intervals of time, until we receive it in the fullness of eternity. Here we commemorate certain saints at fixed times; there we shall always have the vision of all the saints without any interval of time. Here consolation is instilled by portions, as into little children who are being nourished, when we distinguish the feasts of individual saints by intervals of time; there the whole fullness will flow in all at once upon those made perfect, when, with all present, God will be all in all. [Col. 0541D]

Therefore, brothers, take care that, just as God has deigned to refresh you through the examples of the saints, so you may refresh him through imitation of the saints. May he himself deign to grant this, etc.

## TITLE CXIV. That Christ is the end of the law, and on the good of an end

Brothers, “Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness for everyone who believes” (Romans 10). Whoever has not reached the end is not yet complete. For whatever exists, so long as its end has not come, is not yet whole. Are you running a course? However far you go, if you stop before the end, you do not arrive. Are you doing a work? If there is no end, you do not complete it. Therefore the end is completion; the end is perfection; the end is arrival; and nothing is full without an end.

Let nothing, then, suffice you before the end; let nothing apart from Christ suffice you, because Christ is the end. Do not rest until you possess Christ; do not fail until you arrive at Christ. Christ is truth, and Christ is wisdom. If outwardly you have assumed the habit and likeness of virtue, you have begun. If inwardly you possess truth, you have been perfected and possess Christ as your end, because Christ is truth. If you are truly wise and know what ought to be known, you possess Christ and possess wisdom, because Christ is wisdom; and you have reached the end because you have found Christ. [Col. 0542A]

For Christ is your light, by which you are enlightened to love virtue and know truth. [Col. 0542B] It is not true wisdom to investigate what belongs to others while being ignorant of one’s own affairs. Therefore neither worldly wisdom nor secular prudence attains true wisdom, because the former investigates what belongs to others and the latter gathers things of no profit—things which Christ’s truth does not approve and Christ’s wisdom does not teach.

Therefore, brothers, seek that wisdom which is true, so that you may know what concerns your salvation; for Christ is in it, and it is in Christ, and whoever possesses it possesses Christ. Strive, then, to possess truth and true wisdom, and you will possess Christ as your end, in whom you must be completed. Christ is your whole good: he is your strength, your wisdom, your example, your help, your victory, your crown. Love him, desire him, embrace him with the soul’s love, and render in return the due of recompense. Whatever you do will be less than what he endured for you. For you have not yet resisted unto blood. [Col. 0542C]

Remember his Passion; remember his patience; remember his gentleness and humility: “When he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten” [the source has *criminabatur*, “did not accuse”] (1 Peter 2); when he was praised, he did not boast; when he was despised, he was not indignant. Consider these things, therefore, brothers; and if you cannot equal them, strive to imitate them. Strengthen your minds for patience. It is great to suffer with Christ, and glorious to suffer for Christ.

Hear what he promises those who suffer for him: “You are those [Col. 0542D] who have remained with me in my trials. And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22). Keep these promises before your eyes, therefore, brothers, whenever you suffer anything heavy or burdensome, whenever some temptation troubles you, whenever some affliction weighs upon you; so that you may not fail in spirit in tribulation. For if you now remain with Christ in temptation, afterward you will be with Christ in glorification. May he grant this, etc. Amen.

## TITLE CXV. On the twofold rest and unrest

There is peaceful rest, and there is restless rest; there is peaceful unrest, and there is restless unrest. Rest is freedom from outward things; unrest is occupation with outward things.

Peaceful rest is when we are outwardly free from work and inwardly rest from the tumult of thoughts. Restless rest is when a person outwardly rests from work but inwardly resounds with thought. Peaceful unrest is when one is outwardly occupied in work and yet inwardly rests within oneself in the bosom of tranquility. Restless unrest is when one is outwardly occupied with work and inwardly resounds with thought. [Col. 0543A]

## TITLE CXVI. On what is written: “My lips are a dripping honeycomb”

“My lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Song of Songs 4). The honeycomb is the Word made flesh in the Virgin; “dripping” signifies abundance. Of him alone, because he was full of grace, it could not be said: “I rained upon one city, and upon another I did not rain. One part was rained upon, and the part upon which it did not rain dried up” (Amos 4). For he himself, wholly overflowing and pouring out grace, was medicine in what he was, and doctrine in what he did and said. One thing was example, another remedy; and “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1). Therefore he is “dripping,” because he pours grace into each according to the measure of grace. [Col. 0543B]

## TITLE CXVII. On the twofold glory of Christ, the true Solomon, from father and mother

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song of Songs 3). Go forth, daughters of Zion. Go forth and enter in, and see King Solomon. Go forth and see in him what his mother gave; enter in and see in him what the Father gave. For what his mother gave is outward; what the Father gave is inward.

The mother gave weakness [Col. 0543C]; the Father gave majesty. The mother gave the substance of flesh; the Father gave fellowship in majesty. The mother gave that by which he conquered; the Father gave that by which he reigned. The mother gave that in which the victor is crowned; the Father gave that in which the reigning one is adored. In that which he has from the Father, he cast down the proud one in the heights; in that which he has from his mother, he despoiled the greedy one in the depths. There he is praised by angels as victor; here, conquering and triumphant, he is glorified by human beings.

Go forth, therefore, daughters of Zion, and see Solomon. Go forth and see what is outward, and praise it; enter in and see what is inward, and adore it. Go forth through compassion; enter in through contemplation. Go forth, visiting the one who suffers; enter in, admiring the one who is glorified. Go forth and cherish in his members one still weak; enter in and see him exalted in himself. If he has felt the devout as humble, he will show himself devout as exalted. [Col. 0543D]

## TITLE CXVIII. That general predication befits God, particular predication human beings; likewise, how God is everywhere; and on dialectical subtleties

The logician [or “localist”; the text reads *Logicalis [localis]*] says: “Follow the course of the argument: whatever is everywhere is here. God is everywhere. If he is everywhere, what shall I say? Shall I infer what is unfitting? Here is a place containing something filthy, and my thought said to me: If God is everywhere, he is there.” Again: if God is not everywhere but is somewhere, there is a place where he is and a place where he is not. But if there is a place where God is and a place where he is not, God is local. For who would say that he is nowhere?

Again, another argument: God wills every good thing; but taking a wife is good; therefore, the localist infers, God wills to take a wife. Such are the absurdities of fools who depend upon the sounds of words. Again: “God loves every creature of his”—Scripture says this: “You hate none of the things you have made, Lord” [Wisdom 11:24; the source cites “Sap. X”]—therefore God loves this creature of his. But consider how many unfitting things may be inferred from this. So it seems to those who judge the sounds of words without their meaning. “Drunkards,” they say, “love strong wines,” and other things of this sort. Many such statements could be made in this manner. [Col. 0544A]

What then? Do we deny everything, or affirm everything? One alternative appears contrary to truth; the other, contrary to purity. If everything is denied, something that belongs to God is taken from him. If everything is asserted, something that does not belong to him is imposed upon him. [Col. 0544B] But observe the distinction. General possession belongs to God; therefore general predication befits him. But particular expressions suit human beings, to whom portions have been given.

For this reason I rightly say of the Creator of all: “He loves all.” But of you, whose love is directed toward a part and whose possession is owed to a part, I rightly say: “You love this or that”—that is, you love gold, silver, money. Why do I not say this in the same way of God? Because of you. I could indeed say it correctly, if you could understand it soundly. But you are accustomed to understand this expression as said of yourself. Therefore I do not say it of God because of you, lest, hearing it, you think that the same thing is said of him which has been said of you. Thus I spare you and distinguish the expression, lest you suppose the thing to be common. Your love is one thing; his love another.

Accordingly, when I have said, “You love this,” I take care not to say, “He loves this,” lest you think he loves as you love. Yet I could say it correctly, if you could not understand it wrongly. So I say, “He is everywhere”; nevertheless, I refrain from saying of certain places, “He is there,” lest you think that he is there in the manner in which something is there according to your understanding—a manner unbefitting God. So I say, “He wills every good”; nevertheless, concerning some particular thing of which I say, “This is good,” I refrain from saying, “He wills this,” because of you, lest you suppose that he wills as you will and wills for the end for which you will. [Col. 0544C]

## TITLE CXIX. How we are not debtors to the flesh, etc.

Brothers, “we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh” (Romans 8). The human spirit, established as it were in a middle [Col. 0544D] place, has above itself its Creator, to whom it ought to be subject; and beneath itself its flesh, over which it ought to preside. It therefore owes one thing to the Creator because of subjection, another to the flesh because of governance. It owes the Creator, because of subjection, never to move itself apart from his will. It owes the flesh, because of governance, to order it according to the judgment of reason illumined by God.

For the justice of the human will is to be conformed in every respect to the divine will, and to gain by movement and the desire of a good appetite what that will possesses in steadfastness: so that it may neither overflow beyond it by presumptuously seeking things it ought not to seek, nor remain beneath it by languishing from things it ought to seek. This, then, is the spirit’s debt to the Creator: to be moved in every respect according to his will. Its debt to the flesh is not to allow the flesh’s appetite either to overflow beyond its own judgment or to remain beneath it.

For since the spirit is the rider and the flesh the beast of burden, it owes it a bridle, to restrain it when it rushes headlong toward evil; spurs, to exercise it by stirring it when it is sluggish toward good; and fodder, to sustain its weakness so that it does not fail. In the stable, fodder; on the road, spurs and bridle: that is, in rest, nourishment; in exercise, restraint and encouragement. [Col. 0545A]

The bridle is fear; the spurs are love. For when the desire of sin drives it headlong toward pleasure, foresight of punishment restrains from pleasure the one who fears. In seeing that punishment follows sin, whether in correction or condemnation, a person is restrained from sin, whether in act or [Col. 0545B] in delight. Fear, then, is the bridle: fear itself checks and tightens the overflowing mind and holds it to endurance, showing that it is easier to conquer evil desire than to bear an evil conscience; and it chooses what is hard in order to escape what is harder.

Then love comes and, by rousing it, spurs on the sluggish soul to the practice of good work, showing that the labor of the work should be endured gladly because of the recompense of so great a reward. For what we do is transient and has an end; but what we await is eternal and has no end. The reward is life without death, joy without sorrow, delight without pain. Therefore, if this life, which ends in death, is loved so greatly that for love of it one willingly despises whatever may be desired for its sake, lest life alone be lost, with what desire ought we to hasten there, where life is not ended by death, joy is not corrupted by any sorrow, and delight is not afflicted by pain? [Col. 0545C]

This consideration therefore makes the mind run gladly, through love’s desire, toward the endurance of suffering, so that whatever can end in time may not be burdensome, since afterward there will follow things that abide in fullness and perfect goods in eternity. This is, therefore, what is said: “Brothers, we are debtors, not to the flesh.” For we are debtors to the flesh in order to restrain it from wickedness, exercise it in virtue, and sustain it in weakness; but we are not its debtors in order to live according to it. For to live according to it is to live according to its lusts and desires: to flee what [Col. 0545D] it abhors and seek what it loves. If we did this, we would neither turn away from evil nor do good.

## TITLE CXX. On the twofold, and likewise threefold, contemplation of God

A devout mind is refreshed by continual contemplation of its Creator, and the more it considers his goodness, the more it is inflamed by his love. It marvels at the compassion that bends such great majesty to sympathy with us; it marvels at the majesty that does not permit itself to be affected or disturbed by sympathy and providential care for us despite such great compassion.

For if there were such goodness but not such majesty, our evils would rebound upon God. But if there were such majesty and not such goodness, his goods would not descend to us. Therefore we congratulate goodness on such great majesty, for his sake, lest he be affected on our account; we congratulate immensity on such great goodness, for our sake, that he may have compassion upon us. [Col. 0546A]

In all these things there is great admiration and astonishment for the mind, when God does not disdain our lowly and weak condition. His compassion makes him not deem himself unworthy of what our misery makes necessary for us. As a mother’s affection does not shrink from a dirty child, but in some way delights in touching and kissing it, and does not consider it dishonorable to endure unworthy things, because love makes beautiful whatever the need of the beloved demands—so the devout mind contemplates its God, and is sweetly refreshed by that contemplation itself; it is always sweet to it to consider what is always sweet to love and praise. [Col. 0546B]

The mind contemplates God in three ways: in himself, in his works, and in his judgments. In himself, as good; in his works, as great; in his judgments, as just. In himself, lovable; in his works, wonderful; in his judgments, to be feared.

## TITLE CXXI. That the soul torments and exercises the human being in this life

The human being is born in misery and for misery. This would not have been so had man not sinned. For at first he was in great delight and ought to have arrived from it at supreme blessedness; but because he did not keep obedience, he could neither retain what he had nor attain what he was to have.

Therefore, cast down into misery and reserved for misery, he began in the same state to be tormented and exercised: tormented, that he might acknowledge his sin; exercised, that he might be restored to mercy. Thus in pain he might feel the good he had lost, and through exercise might advance toward the good he was to possess. Everything, therefore, that had been created for delight was turned to torment, so that he might find pain and labor in all things and, in his own affliction, recognize both his present misery and his lost blessedness. [Col. 0546C]

## TITLE CXXII. That the Word of God alone is the soul’s good

A human being consists of two substances, soul and flesh, and each has its own good. The good of the flesh is the world with the abundance of its pleasures. The good of the soul is God with the abundance of his sweetness. If, then, the goods of the flesh are so great, how [Col. 0546D] great must the goods of the soul be thought to be? For as much as the soul is better than the flesh, so much better must the soul’s good be than the flesh’s good.

But all things that are visibly good are, as has been said, goods only of the flesh, and can in no way reach the good of the soul. Whatever is sweet to taste, fragrant to smell, pleasing to hear, soft to touch, or beautiful to see, flatters the flesh and is pleasant to the flesh; in all these things there is no good for the soul.

First consider visible light itself, which is pleasant to all visible things and without which nothing is visible. It is itself a great good, and among other visible goods a better and more pleasant good; yet it cannot be the soul’s good. For this light illuminates only the eyes of the flesh. If it illuminated the eyes of the soul, everyone situated in this light would recognize truth. But now truth is seen without this light. Therefore this light does not illuminate the eyes by which truth is seen. [Col. 0547A]

Just as visible light cannot illuminate the eyes of the mind, so bodily food cannot satisfy the mind’s hunger. Those things which are external and cling from without are like straw, fodder for beasts of burden; but those good things which are within are like bread from the fat of wheat, food for human beings. Therefore the children of Jerusalem do not eat straw but are satisfied with the fat of wheat, because all who have begun to taste inward sweetness despise whatever outwardly gives transient delight and seems sweet according to the flesh.

Thus the flesh has its food by which it is refreshed, and the soul has its food by which it is fattened. The food of the soul is the Word of God; and that same Word is both the light by which it is illuminated and the food by which it is refreshed: light, by which it becomes bright for knowledge of truth; food, by which it grows rich and joyful for love of goodness.

The Word of God first pours itself forth and then pours itself in. It pours itself forth that it may be seen; it pours itself in that it may be received. If it did not pour itself forth, it would not be known; if it did not pour itself in, it would not be tasted. First, therefore, it poured itself forth and made itself perceptible through creation; second, through assumed flesh; third, it still daily pours itself forth through a human voice. [Col. 0547B]

After the first outpouring, it was poured in and conceived through sight. After the second infusion, it was poured in and conceived through [Col. 0547C] faith. After the third outpouring, it is poured in and conceived through knowledge; and everywhere it feeds and refreshes. First, for manifestation; second, for salvation; third, for instruction. First, lest the wicked be without excuse; second, that the predestined may be saved; third, that the instructed may be formed.

## TITLE CXXIII. That knowledge and care are attributed to God in two ways

Knowledge or knowing is spoken of in one way according to contemplation, in another according to imparting. Likewise, God’s care is spoken of in one way according to providence, in another according to precept. According to contemplation he knows the number of all things; according to imparting he is said not to know, because he does not grant knowledge. Likewise, according to providence he has care for all things; according to Scripture and precept, he has no care for oxen. [Col. 0547D]

## TITLE CXXIV. On the two parts of worldly desire

The desire of the world has two parts: honorableness and usefulness. When both are present together, they are more moderate, because they temper each other in turn; those who restrain themselves from one toward the other pour themselves out more immoderately. Some seek honorable things because they want to appear praiseworthy. Some seek honorable things because they are ashamed to appear contemptible. Some flee honorable things out of humility. Some flee honorable things out of pretence. Usefulness should be sought so that nature may be sustained and sin extinguished.

## TITLE CXXV. On the three degrees of abstinence

[Col. 0548A]

The first degree of abstinence is to be content with what is given; the second, to be moderate in those things; the third, to exclude something from them.

## TITLE CXXVI. That many seek truth from curiosity alone

Pilate asked Jesus, “What is truth?” (John 18), and immediately went out into the praetorium. He therefore asked a question and did not await the answer. Thus many, turned toward God by a passing fervor, begin to desire true goods; but, through the same mutability of mind, they pour themselves out again toward transient things and do not persist in their mind’s purpose. Thus, turned toward God, they seek through desire for truth; but, turned away, they do not await the answer through appetite for vanity.

## TITLE CXXVII. On the twofold pride

[Col. 0548B]

There are two kinds of exaltation: one inwardly through pride, the other outwardly through the form of self-exaltation. Pride is inward; boasting outward. One kind of pride is that by which the mind swells in considering itself; another is that by which, in comparing itself with others, it despises others. Likewise, there are two kinds of outward boasting: one by which a person, in displaying himself, pretends to be gentle; another by which he shows himself to be cruel and fearsome. In the first he strives to please; in the second he disdains to please.

Thus from the first kind of pride, in which a person is pleased with himself, arises first the kind of boasting in which he desires to please others. From the second kind of pride, in which he despises others, arises the second kind of boasting, by which he endeavors to show himself to others not as lovable but as someone to be feared. [Col. 0548C]

## TITLE CXXVIII. On the twofold humility

There are two kinds of humility: the first toward oneself, the second toward others. Humility toward oneself is that by which one thinks little of oneself. Humility toward others is that by which one commends the good things of others without envy and malice. Through the first humility, one does not desire to rule; through the second, one does not disdain to be subject. Humility causes a person not to excuse his own evils; devotion causes him not to aggravate the evils of others.

Again, humility causes one to judge truthfully those things that are hidden in oneself; devotion causes one to incline toward the better interpretation of things not evident in others. Hence holy men judge themselves so strictly and think that all ought deservedly to be preferred to them. For they see their own things, both those that are manifest and those that are hidden; of others, however, only what is manifest.

Since, therefore, they do not presume to judge the hidden things of others, except insofar as compassion moves them to think them good, they see more evil things in themselves—where they see both manifest and hidden things—than in others, where they see only manifest things. For even if they sometimes infer certain hidden things of others from what is manifest, they nevertheless judge their own things strictly according to truth; while they do not presume to judge those others, excusing them through compassion. Thus it happens that they consider themselves inferior to all, and it is sweet to them to feel that they can aggravate their own evils and lighten those of others. [Col. 0548D]

## TITLE CXXIX. What a human being truly is

There is one thing in a human being which alone comes under judgment with God: the consent of reason. This is truly the human being himself; all else belongs to the human being and is in the human being. If this alone is good, nothing in the human being—whether good or evil—is counted toward evil; and if this alone is evil, nothing in the human being—whether evil or good—is counted toward good.

It should also be known that, just as in good persons after a good purpose there are certain stirrings of evils which are not culpable but are nevertheless sometimes an occasion of sin, so in evil persons with an evil purpose there are certain stirrings of goods which are not meritorious but nevertheless often become an occasion of repentance. [Col. 0549A]

## TITLE CXXX. On the three spirits

There are three spirits: the Spirit of God, the spirit of man, and the spirit of the devil. The Spirit of God and the spirit of the devil are immovable, the one in good, the other in evil. The human spirit is turned now here, now there; and with whichever it joins itself, it is sometimes a servant and sometimes a companion.

For it is written: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 14 [probably 10:20]; Mark 13). And of the other: “You know that when you were Gentiles, you were led away to dumb idols, as you were led” (1 Corinthians 12). If the human spirit is sometimes led and sometimes drawn: “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezekiel 1). [Col. 0549B]

## TITLE CXXXI. On the twofold lover and beloved

“Tell me whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs 1). There is one beloved of the soul and one lover of the soul; another beloved of the flesh and lover of the flesh. Christ is the beloved of the soul and its lover. The world is the beloved of the flesh and its lover. The lover is the one who loves; the beloved is the one who is loved.

That Christ is the soul’s lover is proved by this: in his eyes, where the soul is beautiful, it makes no difference what the appearance of the flesh is. And he is the beloved of the soul because the soul delights in enjoying him. For wisdom is such a good that no nature but the rational can enjoy it. Just as flesh enjoys and delights in the world, and the bodily eye loves what it grasps, so one who loves appearance also loves the things that commend appearance. [Col. 0549C]

## TITLE CXXXII. “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened”

“Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11). Wearied by labor, weighed down by burden, wasted by hunger, come to me. Like to like: the shut in to the door; the sick to the physician; the shipwrecked to the harbor. To the door of light, to the harbor of rest, to the physician of health. To the door, that, having gone out, you may see truth; to the physician, that, having been healed, you may regain strength unto health; to the harbor, that, gathered in after labor, you may rest.

Empty, that you may be filled with the light of truth; burdened, that you may be relieved of the weight of sins; laboring, that, having obtained rest, you may be consoled. [Col. 0549D]

## TITLE CXXXIII. On the two gates of death

Let those who sin through desire take David as an example, that they may rise again. Let those who sin through fear take Peter as an example, that they may rise again. Each fell, and each rose again, because Christ looked upon each: one in person, the other through his prophet. These are the two gates of death: desire and fear. If these are closed to anyone, there will be no entrance through which the world may enter. [Col. 0550A]

## TITLE CXXXIV. How the evil person lives beside the good person, and that being good and persevering in goodness are not from man

There is an example of every thing under heaven. There are evil persons who never become good. There are good persons who always remain in good. The former never rise; the latter never fall. Others, when they have fallen, do not rise again; others fall and rise again. Those who never rise, or never rise again, are evil. Those who never fall, or who rise again when they have fallen, are good.

Thus there are two kinds of evil persons and two kinds of good persons; and everywhere the evil person lives alongside the good person. Those who never become good are examples to the good, that they may understand that their goodness is not from themselves; for if being good came from man, every human being would be good. Again, those who fall from good and do not rise again are examples to the good, that they may know it is grace not only that they received good, but also that they persevered in good. For if perseverance belonged to man, no one would fall. [Col. 0550B]

## TITLE CXXXV. On the twofold end and the middle
Mortal life is set in the middle, and has eternal life on its right hand, but perpetual death on its left. From eternal life it has that it is life; from eternal death, that it is mortal. The way by which one goes to the right is righteousness; the way by which one goes to the left is fault. And this mortal life—or living death—is turned at one time through fault toward death, at another through righteousness toward life. What reaches life falls no more; just as what reaches death rises no more. For each end is immovable; the middle is movable and fluctuates until it is made firm. “In whatever direction the tree falls, there it will remain, whether toward the south or toward the north” (Eccles. XI).

## TITLE CXXXVI. On the twofold judgment of the proud.

Clouds rise from mountains, because swollen hearts grow dark against the light of truth. Again, lightning strikes mountains, because the powerful will receive a greater judgment.

## TITLE CXXXVII. That fellowship in the present life is unstable, and separation sorrowful.

[Col. 0550D] This is one of the great evils of the present life: those who share both one origin and one mind are divided from one another and cannot be together. Thus fellowship in union is found the more praiseworthy in proportion as love is more grievously wounded in separation.

## TITLE CXXXVIII. On the praise of compassion.

O blessed soul that can possess compassion! All suffer; few suffer with others. Yet how much more praiseworthy it is to suffer with another than merely to suffer! For the impious too can suffer, but none except the devout can suffer with another.

## TITLE CXXXIX. Why beasts are afflicted though they bear no guilt.

If punishment is owed to guilt, why do those who have not sinned suffer? Human punishment is just, because man has sinned. Why then are the other things punished, which have not sinned? But things made for man are punished for man. Further still: if man had not sinned, the things made for man would suffer for man, so that man may know how highly God values his salvation—for whose sake all things labour, lest he alone should labour—and so that, seeing the punishment of those who suffer in punishment, he may learn to fear punishment.

## TITLE CXL. How man departed both from God and from himself, and how he returns.

Man first departed from God through pride; afterward he departed from himself through concupiscence. Through pride he became a devil. Through concupiscence he became “like horse and mule, which have no understanding” [Col. 0551B] (Ps. XXXI). Now through humility he returns to God; through purity he returns to himself. Through humility he merits glory. Through purity he merits incorruption: the glory of divinity, the incorruption of immortality.

## TITLE CXLI. That man loves himself and what is his wrongly.

There is a certain love of man for himself and for what is his: for his life and for his concupiscence. He loves his life because he wishes to be here; his concupiscence, by which he wishes to be here with these things. He loves his life, by which he loves the world; his concupiscence, by which he loves the things that are in the world. He loves his life, by which he neglects God; his concupiscence, by which he forgets God. He loves his life, by which he flees adversities; his concupiscence, by which he seeks prosperity.

[Col. 0551C] He flees through fear and seeks through covetousness; and the members of man that have not been mortified upon earth live on. They live and feel. They live through discernment and feel through delight: through discernment concerning good and evil; through delight in good alone; through discernment in the things they hate and love; through delight in the things they love.

The eyes flatter themselves toward enticing sights, that they may be opened for seeing. The ears flatter themselves toward melodious songs and idle words, that they may be opened for hearing. The nostrils flatter themselves toward sweet scent, that they may be opened for smelling. The throat flatters itself toward sweet flavours, that it may be opened for tasting. The hands flatter themselves toward soft touches, that they may be stretched forth for touching. And the whole mass of nature luxuriates in the leaven of malice and wickedness: malice in what is manifest, wickedness in what is hidden; malice in deed, wickedness in thought; malice lacking sincerity, wickedness lacking truth.

[Col. 0551D] Man perversely loves himself and what is his; he nourishes these shoots and presents his evil members as weapons of unrighteousness. Casting off discipline and hating goodness, lest he distress his members, he loosens the reins for eyes and ears, that they may enter and go out to their pleasures and with their pleasures; and for all the senses, that they may rejoice and enjoy their delights—foreseeing no future pains, first through negligence and afterward through contempt.

## TITLE CXLII. On the journey of three days and three nights; and on approach to God and departure from him.

“We shall go a journey of three days into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to our God” (Exod. III). There is a certain approach and departure of the soul toward God or away from God: an approach to God, a departure from God.

For one departing, the journey is through night; for one returning, the journey is through day. By as many nights as it departs, by so many days it returns. For the one departing, the journey of the first night is through pride, by which it abandons God. The journey of the second night is through concupiscence, by which it desires things other than God. The journey of the third night is through obstinacy [“obstination”], by which it rests in alien things outside God.

In pride there is vanity; in concupiscence, delight; in obstinacy, consent. Thus through vanity it goes away, through delight it stands still, through consent it sits. Departing from God through pride, it goes to itself, that it may rest in itself. Through concupiscence it descends beneath itself, that it may rest in the flesh. Through obstinacy it is drawn outside itself, that it may rest in the visible appearance of bodily things and remain [Col. 0552B] in delight.

First, it goes to glory in its own strength; second, it goes to delight in its vices; third, it goes to find consolation in transient things. First: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. XVII). Second: “Who makes flesh his arm” (ibid.). Third: “Who trusted in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. LI).

For one returning, however, the journey of the first day is when the soul turns its intention from what is outside itself to that which it itself is. The journey of the second day is when, from what it is, it is led in mind to what it ought to be. The journey of the third day is when, from the apprehension of illumination, it is carried away to the fountain of light. The first return is from alien things to one’s own. The second is from evils to goods. The third is from the pursuit of virtue to the apprehension of inward and eternal [Col. 0552C] sweetness.

## TITLE CXLIII. How God is called food through knowledge and drink through love.

Our God is both food and drink: food when received through knowledge, drink when received through love. In this twofold sense the blessed soul enjoys God, namely by knowledge and love, because it lives by knowing and by loving.

There seems to be some labour in knowledge, in which, as with food, nothing is received unless it has first been chewed. Thus one comes through the labour of investigation to the taste of knowledge. The drink of love has no difficulty, and love of the good enters the soul more easily than knowledge of what is hidden.

## TITLE CXLIV. On the threefold refreshment of the soul.

God feeds the faithful soul with a threefold refreshment: through [Col. 0552D] word, sacrament, and spirit. When he refreshes us through his words and sacraments, he sets before us a honeycomb to eat. But when he refreshes us inwardly through his Spirit, he pours out honey for us to taste.

## TITLE CXLV. That the things of God are incomparable.

The excellence of the divine nature is shown to be so wholly incomprehensible that time cannot equal its eternity, place its immensity, work its power, or sense its wisdom.

## TITLE CXLVI. That God orders both his own things and those of others.

The divine ordering displays the power of its operation in all things. In good things it does so in two ways, since in them it brings about both their existence and their ordered condition. In evil things, however, it does so simply: it does not indeed bring about their existence, but only their being ordered.

## TITLE CXLVII. That God has received human beings in seven ways.

[Col. 0553A]

God has received human beings in seven ways: first for suretyship, second for protection, third for support, fourth for reconciliation, fifth for approval, sixth for consolation, seventh for reward.

First, when about to fight against the devil, he receives their cause as though he were standing surety for them, when he places confidence in them; just as he undertook to defend the cause of blessed Job, as of one of his own combatants, against the devil. But he receives some, as timid and feeble persons fleeing from battle, for protection, lest they fall; others who are collapsing in battle, for support, lest they be crushed; others rising after ruin, for reconciliation, that they may be restored; others already doing well, through [Col. 0553B] approval, that they may be rewarded; others after good works, through reward, that they may be glorified; and others, wearied amid their works, through inward inspiration, that they may be refreshed and consoled.

## TITLE CXLVIII. On human exercises and progress.

Some labour and do not advance; others labour and advance; others advance without labouring. Those who labour without advancing are to be pitied. Those who labour and advance are to be praised. Those who advance without labouring are to be declared blessed.

Those who labour for the glory of the world have labour but no progress. Those who labour for eternal life do indeed have labour, but in their labour they also have fruit [Col. 0553C]. Those who receive the gifts of virtues freely have progress where they have no labour.

## TITLE CXLIX. On the threefold fruit of reading.

The first fruit of reading is that you may be instructed for knowing truth; the second, that you may be stirred to love virtue; the third, that, occupied by the purpose of reading, your heart may not wander.

## TITLE CL. On the twofold fruit of fasting, labour, and prayer.

The first fruit of fasting is the mortification of fleshly delight; the second, that through the affliction of the flesh you may be pierced in heart.

The first fruit of labour is occupation; the second, exercise.

The first fruit of prayer is the obtaining of the request; [Col. 0553D] the second, the exercise of devotion.

## TITLE CLI. Why those who have not sinned are condemned.

“Why,” you ask, “are those who have not sinned condemned? Show how it is just that one who has not committed guilt should bear punishment.” Who is this person? “An infant,” you say, “who dies newly born and is therefore said to be condemned because he could not be reborn.” “This one,” you say, “did not commit guilt and yet bears punishment.”

Therefore you could not say, “He has no guilt.” For he has guilt, although he did not commit guilt; for by being born he contracted a guilt that he did not perpetrate by acting. Therefore he is punished for a guilt that he has: it is his own because he has it, and another’s because he has it from elsewhere. Yet he is altogether punished for his own guilt, which being born brought upon him and being reborn did not remove.

“But,” you say, “why is the soul itself, which has guilt neither through creation, because [Col. 0554A] it was created clean, nor through birth, because it is not from propagation, nor through action, because it is not yet capable of doing either good or evil—why is it judged guilty and condemned for guilt?”

Thus you press the argument in order to prove that punishment exists without guilt, and therefore that the punishment itself is not just when inflicted without guilt. You say, then, that no punishment can be just unless it has been inflicted for guilt. Say, therefore: why are brute animals punished when they have not sinned? Since man alone has sinned, why are the other creatures afflicted? All things labour lest he alone labour who rather ought alone to labour, because he alone sinned.

If the Creator cannot, according to the good pleasure of his almighty will, use the service of his creature—even with its labour and punishment—to fulfil his dispensation, tell us how it is not unjust that he punishes things that have not sinned. But the creature owes its Creator its labour even without guilt, if this pleases him, when reason requires it for completing his dispensation. Nor is it unjust when it pleases him to whom nothing unjust is pleasing. For as everything that it is is owed to him, so also everything that it can do is owed to him, so that, as much as he wills and as he wills, it may serve him from itself.

[Col. 0554B] By the same rule of justice God uses the labour of his creature for the service of man, so that man himself may understand from it how much has been bestowed upon him and how much he owes God, for whose sake all things labour lest he alone should labour.

“But,” you say, “it is one thing to discuss the punishment of brute animals, another the punishment of rational beings, to whom alone, just as it has been granted to do good that they may be glorified, so it is by no means just that they should be punished unless they have done evil.”

What then? Has a human being never been punished without guilt? Say, then: what did that man blind from birth do, that he should be born blind? Of him it is written: “Neither this man sinned nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John IX). What guilt did Job deserve the scourge for, he who says: “I have not sinned, and my eye remains in bitterness” (Job XVII)?
