Therefore, since even the righteous sometimes bear punishment which they did not merit by sinning—one who did not deserve to bear it, but rather bears it that he may merit—why do we so zealously accuse God of injustice in the case of those who have committed nothing besides original sin, because we see punishment and find no actual guilt? Especially [Col. 0554D] since it has been said that the punishment of those who have committed nothing besides original sin is most mild.

Therefore, if God, in order to display his glory, wills that among the vessels of mercy some who have actually sinned should be afflicted in punishment, while others held guilty only originally should be excluded from glory, so that in the former he may show his elect how great a misery they have escaped, and in the latter how great a glory they have attained—who can say to him, “Why do you act thus?” He who, when he wills, can justly inflict punishment without guilt, just as he can justly forgive one who is guilty so as not to inflict punishment.

But perhaps exclusion from the glory of blessedness is not thought to be the only punishment of those condemned for original guilt alone, unless they are also afflicted by the torments of punishments. But if there is another punishment, I do not know what or of what kind it is. One thing I know: it is a great punishment and a great misery not to possess that good without which no one can be well, since one received existence from it in such a way as to possess blessed existence in it.

## TITLE CLII. How wisdom conquers malice.

“When a strong man armed guards his court, the things that he possesses are in peace. But if one stronger than he comes upon him and conquers him, [he takes] all his weapons in which he trusted,” etc. (Luke XI). The court is the heart; the armed strong man, malice; the stronger one coming upon him, wisdom; the weapons, the members.

Wisdom first captures malice by detecting it through knowledge; afterward it binds it by restraining it from action. Then it scourges it, because a perverse affection is beaten as it were with certain hard scourges when, through the pursuit of discipline, it is restrained from what it desires. Finally, as though the limbs had been stretched out upon a cross and fixed apart from one another with nails, it is crucified: when its vices have been divided from one another, the soul is pierced by the fear of God.

For all vices are strong together, because they fortify one another mutually: gluttony supports luxury, ostentation supports pride, and so forth. Divide them, therefore, and separate them from one another; and thus nail your flesh with the fear of God, so that malice may die within you. Do not wonder, however, if wisdom does to malice what wisdom itself first endured from malice. Malice first crucified wisdom; afterward wisdom, prevailing, crucifies malice.

## TITLE CLIII. On dispensation.

What cannot be done without guilt ought not to be done; and if it is ever permitted, it is not itself evil. It requires indulgence because it is not without evil. For this reason the Apostle cries out, after speaking of sin: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (I Cor. VII)—which indeed would not be a sin if it could be done without sin. Now, therefore, because it cannot be done without guilt: if it is not done, it is merit; if it is done, it requires indulgence.

Thus the uncorrected person is denied the authority to correct. You wish to rebuke your brother who sins: see whether you can do so without guilt. What is “without guilt”? Purely, peaceably, without malice, without anger. Otherwise, if you grow angry while rebuking one who is angry, you fall into the vice that you condemn and become a witness against yourself. If you are such a person, leave it alone; do not touch it, lest it be said to you: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV). And: “Let him who is without sin cast a stone at her” (John VIII).

He indeed must be rebuked, provided that [the fault] is not in you. If you wish to stone the adulteress, hear what was said: “If anyone is without sin, let him cast a stone at her.” I do not deny that she is to be judged, but I do not want you to be the judge. Therefore always fear lest you rush to rebuke.

## TITLE CLIV. That God first gives temporal existence, and afterward eternal existence.

The Creator willed time to exist before eternity, so that in time a creature might first begin, as it were, to possess some existence, and afterward might be perfected more fully in eternity. Therefore he first gave his creature temporal existence, intending afterward to give eternal existence.

## TITLE CLV. That Scripture sometimes displays, and sometimes imparts, good morals and virtue.

Some Scriptures display good morals; others impart good morals. The former instruct the mind in the knowledge of virtue by teaching; the latter pierce it toward the effect of virtue by exhorting.

## TITLE CLVI. On the twofold perfection of charity.

Charity is called perfect in two ways: by constancy and by devotion. Charity is perfect in constancy when it is strong for enduring every adversity; it is perfect in devotion when it is fully kindled for desiring things that are right. It is perfect in constancy when it thrives so that it cannot be overcome; it is perfect in devotion when it burns so that it ought not to be inflamed further.

The first perfection is sometimes granted in this life; the second is reserved for the future. Constancy is in Peter, ardour in John. To the steadfast man it is said: “Strengthen your brothers” (Luke XXII); but of the tenderly devoted one: “Thus I will have him remain until I come” (John XXI).

## TITLE CLVII. On God’s terror and gentleness.

God’s wisdom sometimes threatens us in divine speech, that we may fear majesty; sometimes it speaks gently, that we may love mercy. Terror is in John, gentleness in Christ. Fear through the servant; love through the Son.

## TITLE CLVIII. What is signified by the words written: “The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman,” etc.

“The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. XLII). If, mystically, we wish to understand woman as sensuality and man as the contrary, reason, perhaps the saying of Scripture will be explained by the fact that, when the first man had newly been formed and a helper was sought among all living creatures, none like him could be found.

For this reason woman was afterward made as his helper—certainly a helper of likeness, which had not been found in all the other creatures. And so that she might possess the same likeness as he, she was made from him, because every likeness is either imitation or origin. Therefore let us seek two like things: first, one within one; afterward, two from one. When the man alone existed and the woman was still within the man, there were as it were two in one, and the two were one. But when the woman was made from the man, the one became in some manner two, and unity divided itself, so that one likeness might subsist in two.

Therefore let us seek two in one—or rather two from [Col. 0556D] one in one likeness—“in which one male and female are one in Christ Jesus.” What, then, is that one in which, and from which, two exist in one likeness? Let us look to the inward man.

There is there something directed toward heavenly and higher things, and this is called wisdom; and again there is something looking toward transient and perishable things, and it is called prudence. These two are from one reason and subsist in one reason; reason divides itself in two, upward and downward: upward in wisdom, downward in prudence; upward in the male, downward in the female—so that the male is superior and rules, while the female is inferior and ruled.

“The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (I Cor. XI; Eph. V). Wisdom rules prudence. Wisdom, moreover, is the Word of God; and the Word of God is from him whose Word it is. Prudence, like a woman managing the household, is occupied with the things of the flesh. Wisdom, like a man extending his acuteness toward distant things, ranges abroad through the breadth of spiritual contemplation.

[Col. 0557A] Hence that adulterous woman, who, through the absence of discipline and continence, had set modesty aside, declares that her husband has gone abroad; she testifies that she has spread out her house and bed for her lovers in painted tapestries, to entice pleasure (Prov. VII). This is because prudence, oppressed in earthly and transient things, when it is not governed by the presence of higher wisdom, serves the desires of its flesh as though to certain lovers, through the alluring appearances of visible things, unto unlawful delight.

But that strong woman whom Wisdom commends, because she ordered her house well, was praised by her husband, receiving fruit from the works of her hands (Prov. XXXI). This, then, is the beneficent woman; yet she cannot be compared with the iniquity of the man, so that it may be clearly shown by this how far the woman who does evil is from equality with him, if not even the beneficent woman can be made equal to his iniquity.

Consider now when the woman does good, and in what she does good. She does good when she does what she ought to do. What ought she to do? She is called prudence because she ought to provide, namely, what is necessary and suitable for her flesh, since its care has been entrusted to her.

But when does the man do good, and in what does he do good? When wisdom directs itself upward, seeking and desiring [Col. 0557C] only those things pleasing to God, then the man does good. Therefore the man does good when wisdom directs itself toward its higher object with love and desire. But the woman does good when prudence bestows care and concern upon its lower, infirm charge.

Have you seen a man carefully and shrewdly seeking out the comforts of his flesh, and persistently exerting effort and attention to satisfy its pleasure? This was the beneficent woman. Have you again seen a man strengthened by the taste of inward savour, afflicting his flesh and, for the prospect of the heavenly reward, withholding not only superfluities but even necessities? This was a man acting iniquitously.

For if it is equity to render the flesh what belongs to it, it is not improperly called iniquity when you do not give it what is owed to it. Yet the iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman, because one who, inflamed by heavenly desire, afflicts his flesh even by withholding necessities is better than one who, relaxed by fleshly affection, strives to satisfy its desires in every way that is convenient for it.

A woman does evil when, bound by imprudence or sloth, she neglects her flesh, or when, distracted by vain concern, she lavishes herself upon seeking superfluities. Therefore when the woman does good, it is not virtue; but when she does evil, it is fault. The man’s iniquity, however, is desire for righteousness; his goodness is the attainment of glory.

Therefore, if the man is iniquitous toward righteousness, while the woman is good toward nature, surely the iniquity [Col. 0558A] of the man is better than a beneficent woman: for if nature is good in creation, righteousness is better in recompense.

## TITLE CLIX. On the eternal generation of the Son of God.

When the Father begot the Word coeternal with himself, then he said, “You are my Son” (Ps. II). In the word “said,” he begot; and in the words “You are my Son,” [he begot]. But because the generation is not transitory, “today” is said; and because it is complete, “I have begotten” is said. Thus the past tense is used lest it be thought incomplete; and “today,” which is present, lest it be thought past.

## TITLE CLX. On the three things in God’s speech.

There are three things in God’s speech: elements, beginnings, and completions. In elements there is an utterance of sound, but no understanding; in the beginning of speech there is understanding, but it is not perfect; in the completion of speech there is perfect understanding.

The figures of the Old Testament were elements of God’s speech. The commandments of the Decalogue were the beginning of God’s speech. The commandments of the New Testament are the completion of God’s speech. The prohibition of swine’s flesh was an element of God’s speech. The prohibition of carnal adultery was its beginning; the prohibition of spiritual adultery, its completion.

Again, in the Old Testament, when it was said, “You shall not eat flesh with blood” (Gen. IX), this was an element; when it was said, “You shall not kill” (Exod. XII), a beginning; when it was said, “Whoever is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V), a completion.

In the Old Testament there was voice; in the New, understanding; in eternal life, reality. In the Old Testament there was way; in the New, truth; in eternity, life. Hence it is said: “I am [Col. 0558C] the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). For he was way there, is truth here, and will be life there.

## TITLE CLXI. On the twofold food and drink of the Scriptures.

In refreshment there are two things: drink and food. Drink is easily received just as it is. Food cannot be received unless it is chewed with some labour. Those things found in the Scriptures that are easy to understand are drink; those difficult and obscure are food.

Things easy to understand and pleasant to do are milk, that is, sweet drink. Things easy to understand and burdensome to do are wine, that is, austere drink. Things difficult to understand and burdensome to do are bread of sorrow. Things difficult to understand and sweet to do are [Col. 0558D] bread of exultation. Therefore four things refresh: sweet drink and bitter drink, bitter food and sweet food.

Likewise there are four kinds of persons to be refreshed: some who are nourished by milk alone; some for whom food is broken and chewed; some for whom it is not chewed but broken; some for whom it is neither chewed nor broken. Those who in God’s commandments willingly hear only what is easy to understand and obediently do what is easy to perform are nourished as though by milk.

Others, however, are capable of solid food because they can both do difficult things and understand obscure ones in God’s commandments—provided, however, that obscure matters are opened by being broken through exposition, and hard matters are softened by being chewed through exhortation and consolation. For difficult commandments are broken by explaining the reason for doing them, and chewed through encouragements and consolations, so that they may nourish the weaker persons.

[Col. 0559A] Others do not need food that has been chewed but only broken, because they are ready in will once they recognize the reason for acting. Others, however, think it unworthy to seek the reason for acting in a commandment of obedience, because they believe that they owe obedience on the command alone. These break and chew the food that is the word of God, because, strong in faith, they do not importunately demand a reason even in hidden matters; and, fervent in charity, they do not seek exhortation in difficult matters.

Milk is given to infants. Food is broken and chewed for children. For youths it is not chewed but broken. For grown men it is neither chewed nor broken, since they have senses trained so that they can use solid food.

## TITLE CLXII. On the twofold faculty of the soul: understanding and wisdom.

[Col. 0559B]

The soul has a twofold faculty. For the faculties of the soul are understanding and wisdom. The faculty of understanding pertains to knowledge; the faculty of wisdom, to virtue. The faculty of understanding is exercised outwardly through reading and inwardly through meditation. The faculty of wisdom is exercised outwardly through action and inwardly through temptation.

The faculty of understanding is to know the good; the faculty of wisdom is to love the good. Some live inwardly through the faculty of understanding, but are dead through the faculty of wisdom. Some live inwardly through the faculty of wisdom, but have not yet been fully made alive through the faculty of understanding. Others perceive the faculty neither of understanding nor of wisdom. Others live through the faculty both of understanding and wisdom.

[Col. 0559C] In some persons, the faculty of wisdom and understanding is sharpened through the practice of use; but in others it is dulled still further by the very practice of its exercise. Thus in some, dulled through frequent hearing, the word of God turns to weariness; others are increasingly inflamed to the love of the word by daily hearing. Thus the children of Israel in the wilderness grow weary of manna through familiarity, while the two disciples on the road burn in heart at the words of Jesus speaking.

Thus a sword is sharpened by the rubbing of a whetstone, while a knife is dulled by continual cutting of soil. A ploughshare, worn by the furrow, shines; a pot is blackened by the continual burning of the licking flame. But woe to those who become worse through what is good!

## TITLE CLXIII. On the twofold divine permission and prohibition.

[Col. 0559D] God is said to permit something in two ways: either by removing an obstacle or by not setting one in the way. Likewise he prohibits in two ways: namely, either by not removing an obstacle or by setting one in the way.

## TITLE CLXIV. That God softens the heart in three ways.

God softens the heart in three ways. First, through inspiration, by creating a good will; afterward, through breathing upon it, by arousing it; then, through an outwardly supplied occasion, by opening, as it were, a way and urging it toward perfection. Through inspiration he places; through aspiration he impels; through occasion he draws. He places it so as to will, impels it so as to desire, draws it so as to bring to completion.

But in the hearts of evil people God neither creates perverse wills through inspiration nor arouses them through aspiration. Only according to his dispensation—sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but always just—he at times casts them down by a just judgment through providing an outward occasion.

Therefore in the hearts of the good, he first himself makes righteous wills inwardly; then he directs those same wills outwardly, wherever and as far as he wills, toward their effect. But he does not himself produce perverse wills inwardly; rather, he bends them, already inwardly corrupted by themselves, according to the choice of their own will, so as to fulfil the order of the hidden dispensation.

Therefore God works good wills, but does not work evil wills; nevertheless, through both good and evil wills he works not evil but good. Thus he does not give either kind its origin, so that it may exist; but he opens a way for both, so that they may be brought to completion. Therefore, even if the will is evil, the power cannot be evil, because although what we will comes from us, the ability to fulfil the will comes from him.

Therefore God does not harden the hearts of evil people through inspiration or aspiration, but only through an outwardly supplied occasion. Thus he is said to have hardened Pharaoh and the Egyptians, as it is written: “He turned their heart, that they might hate his people,” etc. (Ps. CIV). Not by perverting their wills so that they might be evil, but by opening a way for those bent outwardly toward perversity so that they might rush headlong.

For when he increased his own people, namely the children of Israel, in their sight both in number and in riches, he thereby bound the hearts of their adversaries, jealous of the prosperity of his own, with the corruption of envy. From the very source from which he exalted his people, he hardened them—not indeed breathing inwardly an increase of malice, but provoking them outwardly by the sight of perverse rivalry.

[Col. 0560C] Even now daily, when an outward occasion suited to the inward motions of human minds is set before them, those who are filthy become still more filthy, and the righteous are made still more righteous (Apoc. XXII).

## TITLE CLXV. On the freedom and servitude of charity.

“Through charity, serve one another by the Spirit” (Gal. V). Note both servitude and freedom in charity. Charity is, as it were, free when, without receiving a command, it voluntarily exercises itself in certain private works of charity. But it is, as it were, servile when, setting aside its own wills, it wholly adapts itself to fulfilling the wills of neighbours, restraining itself in respect of its own affairs but expanding and exercising itself in respect of others’ affairs.

Yet this is much more free, because what makes it free is precisely that it freely subjects itself to the service of all.

## TITLE CLXVI. On Paul’s words: “Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

“Through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI). There are some to whom the world has been crucified, while they themselves have not been crucified to the world. There are others who have been crucified to the world, but to whom the world has not been crucified. There are others who both have been crucified to the world and have had the world crucified to them.

For the world has been crucified to those who are held in contempt by the world, and whom the world does not pursue. Those are crucified to the world who are held fast as though nailed to it and do not follow the world, but utterly reject it. The Apostle, however, had utterly rejected the world, and the world had rejected him. Therefore he says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

## TITLE CLXVII. On the essence and form of the soul.

There are two things in the soul: essence and righteousness, which is its form. It is created according to form, but renewed according to essence. For the form can wholly perish; the essence does not wholly perish, but is deformed when its form is lost.

One saying is: “Renew a spirit within my inward parts” (Ps. L). And, concerning righteousness to be created: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and [renew] a right spirit,” etc. (ibid.).

## TITLE CLXVIII. On the threefold meaning of nature.

Nature is understood in Holy Scripture in three ways. It is understood as that excellent state of the first creation in which the first human being was made [Col. 0561B], according to which all things are said to be naturally good. It is also understood as that remainder of the former state which survives after the Fall and remains active in the human mind, as in the Epistle to the Romans: “Will the uncircumcision which is by nature, fulfilling the law, judge you who through letter and circumcision are a transgressor of the law?” (Rom. II). That is to say: the Gentiles who fulfill the law through the power of reason implanted within them, which lies in the desire for the good—such persons will judge the Jews. In the third sense it is understood as the state of corruption into which we are all born. Hence the Apostle: “We are by nature children of wrath” (Eph. II).

## TITLE CLXIX. That the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.

[Col. 0561C] “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V). This statement seems contrary to what the Son himself says of himself: “I judge no one” (John VIII). But we must understand divine words in such a way that the testimonies of truth do not disagree. Therefore let us distinguish for a little while the kinds of judgments, lest a confused interpretation restrict our understanding.

There are, then, four judgments: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, according to operation, and according to recompense. We were judged according to foreknowledge before we existed; we are judged according to cause from the time when we begin to be good or evil. For what is judgment but discrimination? Those whom foreknowledge first distinguished [Col. 0561D], cause subsequently discerns.

But we cannot say of the Son either that he alone, apart from the Father and the Holy Spirit, has foreknowledge of future things, or that he alone discerns the hidden causes of human beings. Therefore, when it is said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” we cannot understand this of those judgments which we know to be common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Let us therefore seek the meaning in the two judgments which remain. These two—judgment according to operation and judgment according to recompense—are referred to the Son alone. One of them, judgment according to operation, he now administers through the ministries of human beings; the other, judgment according to recompense, he will later render [Col. 0562A] through himself.

Judgment according to operation occurs when human actions, not persons, are judged; judgment according to recompense occurs when human beings are judged for their actions. The one concerns the present time, the other the future. The one has been granted by God to human beings who are servants of God, God judging through them and in them; the other the God-man will fulfill through himself, with his servants present and bearing witness. For a human being can judge the actions of other human beings under God; but to judge human beings for their actions belongs not to a human being but to God. A person may, according to his capacity and office, approve a neighbour’s work if it is good, or disapprove it if it is evil, provided it is manifest and subject to judgment. Yet he must not presume to judge those whose works he approves [Col. 0562B] or disapproves, because we see people whom we sometimes observe acting perversely attain a good end; and we often see those who do many good things in human sight turn back at last and close their lives with an unhappy end.

Therefore, as I have said, people who cannot foresee the future can judge only present matters, so that they may not presume, with rash boldness, to condemn even those whose acts they judge worthy of condemnation. This is the judgment which Christ granted to Peter and, with Peter, to all who act in his stead, saying: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI); and, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (ibid.).

But concerning the judgment of recompense the Apostle says: [Col. 0562C] “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own Lord he stands or falls” (Rom. XIV). He plainly shows that only he who gave the price of his own blood for them and redeemed them from the slavery of the devil has authority to judge human beings either to death or to life, and to subject them to his own service.

Therefore the Father gave all judgment to the Son, so that in the present the Son may judge human actions through his servants acting in his stead, but in the future may judge human beings for their actions through himself. In the judgment of foreknowledge and cause, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together judge and examine righteousness. In the judgment of operation and recompense, the Son alone, either through himself or through his servants whom he chose to appoint for this purpose, pronounces the sentence of judgment. Thus the Son alone judges, because he alone administers all judgment [Col. 0562D]: either, as we have said, in the present, when through his vicars he conducts cases of equity; or in the future, when he visibly manifests himself for judgment according to the form of his humanity.

From these things it can sufficiently be gathered how the Son received all judgment and yet judges no one: for, just as in the form of a human being he received the office of pronouncing the sentence alone in every judgment, so he does not derive from his human form, but from the majesty of divinity, the power to declare righteousness not alone but together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, speaking elsewhere according to the form of the humanity he assumed, he says: “As I hear, I judge” (John V). He judges as he hears because he draws every judgment that he administers outwardly from inward disposition.

But there is something further that we may consider in these words: [Col. 0563A] “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” God the Father had a case against the human being whom he had created, in order to exact the penalty for contempt of himself. He had a case against the devil, so that the devil might answer for the assault and plunder he had committed by deceiving the human being. But because the Son alone, through the mystery of the Incarnation, both conquered the devil and snatched the human being from his power, he alone fulfilled the judgment, as though received from the Father.

He is said to have received all judgment from the Father because he was sent first to judge on behalf of humanity, then concerning humanity, and finally humanity itself. He judged on behalf of humanity when he snatched it from the devil’s power. Hence he says: “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John XII). Now he judges concerning humanity: calling some by grace, rejecting others by justice; among those called, advancing some by the growth of virtues, while leaving others who fall away from grace. But in the future he will judge humanity, since, rendering to each according to his works, he will appoint some to glory and others to punishment.

## TITLE CLXX. On what is written: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI). Forgiving debts is less than loving enemies. Yet the Christian is commanded, for the perfection of virtue, not merely not to hate enemies, but even to love them. But because not all can rise to the height of this command [Col. 0563C], lest those who are less perfect lose confidence in prayer—although perhaps for them it may suffice not to hate their enemies—the very form of the prayer has been thus moderated.

Yet those who desire to be heard in their prayers must take the greatest care: if they are not yet able to bestow the affection of charity upon their enemies, at least they must permit no trace of fraternal hatred to remain in their hearts, so that they may confidently say: “Forgive us our debts,” and so forth. For, by the logic of the condition, if they do not forgive perfectly, they bind themselves more tightly by their own prayer. There are indeed people who forgive in such a way that they do not exact revenge for an injury, yet do not banish hatred of their enemy from their heart. If we ask that our debts be forgiven in this manner, what else are we shown to be asking except that God should hate us and punish us? Therefore all bitterness [Col. 0563D] and rancour must be excluded from the heart, so that a pure conscience may more swiftly obtain the effect of its prayers, if nothing remains in our soul that may offend him whom we cannot deceive.

## TITLE CLXXI. That the love of God is the life of the heart.

Love is the life of the heart; therefore it is altogether impossible for a heart that desires to live to be without love. Consider what follows from this. Since the human mind cannot be without love, it must necessarily love either itself or something other than itself. But because it does not find perfect good within itself, if it loved itself alone, its love would not be happy. Therefore, if it wishes to love happily, it must seek something other than itself to love.

But if it begins to love something imperfect outside itself [Col. 0564A], it disappoints its love indeed, but does not exclude misery. Therefore it does not love happily until it turns, through the desire of love, toward the true and highest good. Since God is the highest and true good, only the person who loves God loves happily; and the more he loves, the more happily he loves.

This, then, is the true rest of our heart: when it is fixed through desire in the love of God. It desires nothing further, but delights with a certain happy security in that which it possesses. For that which neither desire urges further onward nor fear drives away rests, as it were, in untroubled delight. But because the weakness of the human mind is scarcely ever—or rather, not always, but hardly ever able—to remain fixed in that sweetness of divine contemplation, it must meanwhile be trained by a certain discipline toward that stability which it cannot yet attain [Col. 0564B]. That is, if we cannot always think of God, at least let us restrain our heart from unlawful and vain thoughts and hold it in contemplation of the works and wonders of God; so that, while we strive always to be less unstable, we may nevertheless at some time, by God’s gift, become truly stable.

To offer you an example of this progress: this whole world is like a flood, because all things in this world pass onward in fluctuating uncertainty of events, like water. But true faith, which promises not transitory but eternal things, raises the soul from the desire of this world toward higher things as if from certain waves. It can indeed be carried by the waters, but cannot be submerged, because it uses this world for necessity but is not entangled in affection by its desires.

Whoever, therefore, not believing eternal things, desires only what passes away, is carried along by the rushing force of the water, like one struggling in the waves without a ship. But whoever believes eternal things and loves transient things suffers shipwreck beside the ship. Whoever both believes and loves eternal goods crosses safely, placed in the ship, through the waves of the fluctuating sea. And because through the desire of faith he does not go beyond the ship, he already, in some fashion, imitates the stability of land amid the waves.

Therefore, if we wish to cross this great sea unharmed, let us first build a ship, that we may possess whole faith. Then let us dwell in the ship of faith through charity [Col. 0564D], so that we may both believe what we ought to love and love what we believe. Thus let the law of God be in our heart through the knowledge of right faith, and let our heart be in the law of God through love.

But that you may more easily know how and from what materials you ought to build in your heart the ship or ark of which I have spoken, by which, drawn out from the shipwreck of this flood, you may reach the harbour of rest, consider two works of God: namely, the work of creation and the work of restoration. The work of creation is the creation of heaven and earth and all that they contain, accomplished in six days. The work of restoration is the Incarnation of the Word, and all things which from the beginning of the world to its end either preceded it in order to foretell it or will follow it in order to confirm it. All these occur in six ages [Col. 0565A].

But the works of restoration pertain more particularly to Catholic faith; the saints love them more because in them they recognize the remedies of their salvation. God has performed these works partly through human beings, partly through angels, and partly through himself, so that in the spiritual ark the first dwelling is the works of human beings, the second the works of angels, and the third the works of God. God, the author of all things, is the uppermost cubit.

## TITLE CLXXII. That humility is attacked in two ways.

The devil attacks humility in us in two ways: namely, through insult and through reverence. At times he incites people to inflict injury upon us, and thereby strives to draw us into indignation, anger, and impatience. At times he causes them to show us reverence, and so attempts to incline us to empty glory [Col. 0565B] and vain delight.

But if, against these wars of the enemy, we wish to preserve our humility unharmed, let us strive continually to keep our evils before our eyes. By evils I mean not only inward evils, pertaining to wickedness and fault, but also outward ones, pertaining to disadvantage: such as lowliness of birth, want—which is the mother of poverty—bodily weakness, and any similar things that humble a person. For if we are willing to examine our faults and miseries carefully and attentively, then perhaps we shall judge neither that we are unworthy of injury when it is inflicted on us nor that we are worthy of reverence when it is shown to us.

But the devil often tries to trip secretly by means of reverence those whom he cannot overthrow by an overt thrust of injury. [Col. 0565C] The human mind is more quickly deceived by praise of itself, because what it receives more gladly it repels with greater difficulty. When it sometimes hears its good qualities praised outwardly and, returning in a sense to itself, considers again that it is what is said, it judges that it may now freely and, as it were, without fault delight in its own flattery. And when it thinks that it is merely assenting to the testimony of truth, it is not truth itself but flattery that delights it.

Moreover, in order to appear altogether innocent of the vice of self-exaltation, it disguises itself with still greater cunning. After it has agreed that what was said about it is true, so as not to seem to attribute it to itself in any way, it immediately turns to thanksgiving. Yet this confession, in a remarkable manner, contributes not to humility but to an increase of pride [Col. 0565D], because it now exalts itself within itself all the more confidently inasmuch as it more openly confesses that its good comes not from itself but from God.

Such was altogether the pride of the Pharisee who said: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of humankind—robbers, unjust persons, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. I fast twice in the Sabbath; I give tithes of all that I possess” (Luke XVIII). Observe how the poison of this pestilence gradually spreads. At first, perhaps, one single good quality in us had been praised; but while the mind is incautiously lifted up by it, all the other good qualities immediately come to memory, so that it may be inflamed more intensely toward self-exaltation.

It carefully reviews all its past good deeds; and, heaping them all together, while it deceitfully strives, as though by remembrance of the past [Col. 0566A], to enlarge its present thanksgiving, it truly swells in its own eyes through consideration of so many virtues. And while it remains fixed, occupied in admiration of itself, it gradually begins even to forget him from whom it has these things. As though what it is were already sufficient for itself, it no longer deigns to recall its evils to mind.

Then, after the enemy sees the heart swollen within and the person made great in his own eyes, he immediately brings reproaches and injuries from without. He knows that the deceived mind will now endure them all the more impatiently in proportion as it recognizes nothing in itself except what deserves praise.

Therefore, if we desire to preserve humility whole and perfect, we must turn the mind away from recognition of ourselves; and, when an insult has been received, learn not to be angry with the offender but to have compassion on him, and judge that what we suffer from him should be attributed not to his malice but to our own deserts. Finally, there are three means by which humility defends itself against an inflicted insult. First, that we consider our fault, by which we deserved to suffer such things; next, that we reflect that whenever our neighbour is stirred up to injure us, it is as though not he, but God in him, works this by his just judgment, either commanding or permitting it for our testing; lastly, that we should not be angry with one doing evil but compassionate toward him, just as toward one bodily ill or bearing a wound or injury. [Col. 0566B] No person of sound mind would think that such a one should be met with anger rather than compassion.

For sins are like wounds of souls; and everyone who does evil should be patiently borne in pity, not as acting from strength, but as failing from strength and suffering, as it were, from the disease of frenzy. The first consideration commends justice to us, the second reverence, the third mercy.

But humility should defend itself against reverence and praise by the same remembrance of its evils in this way. Whenever it senses itself outwardly assailed and tempted by the flattery of those who praise it or show it reverence, it should not attend to or consider whether what is said of it is true, or whether what is shown to it is deserved. Rather, lest the deceived mind receive inwardly, through empty glory, the praise that strikes it from without, it should immediately take care to set against this very vice something in itself by which it may rather be ashamed, saying with the Psalmist: “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ immediately be turned back ashamed” [Col. 0566C] (Ps. LXIV).

For whoever, having been praised, approaches conscience in order to consult it about the truth is thereby shown already to consent to flattery; for he would not seek an occasion for its approval unless from the beginning he preferred to retain it rather than reject it. Therefore it sometimes happens that God, by a just judgment, because he considers the perversity of such a person’s intention, does not permit him to discern the truth; and the testimony of conscience then answers him not concerning what he pretended to seek, but concerning what he desired to find.

Thus Balaam, when he was invited by Balak, king of the Moabites, with a reward offered for cursing the children of Israel, asked the Lord whether he ought to go and received permission to go; yet afterward, when he was going, the angel of the Lord met and opposed him on the way [Col. 0566D] (Num. XXII). What is this? If the way was good, why did the angel oppose him? Or, if it was bad, why did God grant him permission to go? Surely the perversity of his mind deserved that God should answer him rather what he himself more desired to hear. For because, blinded by greed, he wished to go, even before he asked whether he ought to go, when permission to go is granted him he is merely allowed to carry out what he desired. He is not led to do this by the Lord’s command, but, by the Lord’s permission, the ability is granted to one who wishes it. For even if the Lord had answered something different to his inquiry, he would not have instructed one who wished to go not to go, but compelled one unwilling to remain to stay.

So indeed a mind corrupted by delight in its own praise consults conscience concerning the testimony of truth [Col. 0567A], not because it loves to find truth, but because it desires to establish by a stronger attestation what it more desires to be the case.

## TITLE CLXXIII. On the natures and kinds of fire.

There are three natures of fire: that which comes into being, that which is fed, and that which feeds upon something—that is, that which arises, that which is nourished, and that which consumes. According to these three natures, fire has eleven kinds.

The first is that which exists by removal [of these properties]: it neither comes into being, nor is fed, nor feeds upon anything. Such is the fire of the sun and of Gehenna. It does not come into being because it has no origin outside itself; it is not fed because it needs no nourishment; it does not feed upon anything because it does not burn in a material subject.

The second kind is that which merely comes into being: it is neither fed nor feeds upon anything. Such is lightning emitted from clouds [Col. 0567B], which neither burns nor splits, and is immediately extinguished.

The third kind is that which is merely fed: it neither comes into being nor feeds upon anything. Such is the fire of the eyes, which is fed by green things. It does not come into being because it is natural; nor does it feed upon anything because it is not consuming.

The fourth kind is that which merely feeds upon something: it neither comes into being nor is fed. Such is the fire of the sun. For it feeds upon things externally. Hence no impurities can approach it; it consumes them not by incorporating them into itself, but by reducing them to nothing. This is the difference between the fire of the sun and the fire of Gehenna: the fire of the sun feeds externally; but the fire of Gehenna destroys neither externally that upon which it burns nor internally that in which it burns.

Therefore they have in common that they do not come into being, because they do not arise from elsewhere; they have in common that they are not fed, because they are not nourished by some material but live from themselves; they have in common that they do not feed inwardly, because they do not consume their own substance. But they differ in that the fire of the sun feeds externally, whereas the fire of Gehenna does not. These are the four simple kinds of fire.

There follow three kinds, each compounded of two properties. The fifth kind of fire is that which comes into being and is fed, but does not feed upon anything. Such is heat in an egg: it both arises from and is nourished by the body of the brooding creature, but does not consume the substance of the egg. Such also is the ray of the sun in the moon: it arises from and is nourished by the sun, but does not consume the lunar body. Likewise is the sunbeam shining in dry ground.

The sixth kind is that which comes into being and feeds upon something, but is not fed: such is lightning emitted from clouds [Col. 0568A]. It comes into being when it emerges from colliding clouds, and consumes what it burns; but it is not fed because it immediately vanishes.

The seventh kind is that which is fed and feeds upon something, but does not come into being: such is natural heat. It does not arise in the body because it is natural; but it is fed by food and clothing, and consumes the bodily humours.

Then follow the remaining four, each composed of all three properties. The eighth is that which separately comes into being, while at the same time it is fed and consumes: such is fire struck from flint and received into wood. It arises from flint, is fed in wood, and consumes the wood.

The ninth is that which is separately fed, while at the same time it comes into being and consumes: such is fire produced from ice and received into sulphur. It arises from ice [Col. 0568B] and consumes the ice, but is fed by sulphur.

The tenth is that which separately consumes, while at the same time it comes into being and is fed: such is the ray of the sun shining in moisture. It arises from and is fed by the sun, and consumes the moisture.

The eleventh is that which at once comes into being, is fed, and consumes: such is fire coming out of wood and burning in wood.

These are the eleven kinds of fire, which may perhaps signify something from which benefit may arise, if there is someone who knows how to draw from visible fire the fire of wisdom. The fire of the sun, which neither comes into being nor is fed nor consumes, signifies the eternal charity of God. Existing naturally in him, since it is perfect it cannot increase, and since it is eternal it cannot be extinguished. Because the ungodly did not wish to burn inwardly with this fire [Col. 0568C], they came to be burned outwardly with the fire of Gehenna, receiving in some manner like for like: so that the flesh might find outwardly in punishment such a fire as the mind had lost inwardly in conscience.

Consider, therefore, these three fires: the fire of the sun, the fire of charity, and the fire of Gehenna. The visible fire of the sun shows you the invisible fire of charity and warns you to seek it. But the visible fire of Gehenna threatens you with punishment if you lose the invisible fire of charity. Each resembles charity; each serves charity: the one by showing, the other by avenging.

That kind of fire which merely comes into being, like lightning, signifies the pre-passions (*propassiones*) of vices, which suddenly issue from the heart through thought. But because the mind, with reason opposing, does not receive them by consent, they immediately vanish. For they are not fed while they pass, nor do they consume while they do not burn the soul by consent.

That kind of fire which is merely fed, like the fire of the eyes, can signify created wisdom—that is, the understanding of the human heart. Like an eye in green pasture, it is fed inwardly by contemplation of uncreated wisdom, namely the Word of God, which never withers but is always new and green. This is the inward pasture in which we are nourished by contemplation, just as in the outward pasture, namely Holy Scripture, we are refreshed by reading. Therefore, whether we enter through thought, we find pasture: Catholic doctrine, in which both forms of understanding of our heart shine clearly like an eye amid greenery [Col. 0569A].

That kind of fire which merely consumes, like the fire of the sun externally, can signify the power of the divine nature. No corruption can approach it; it renews every creature and burns away in us the rust of vices, not by incorporating it into itself, but by making it nothing. Its power is so great that nothing worthy of being consumed can endure its presence. Hence it is said: “Your God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV).

That kind of fire which comes into being and is fed but does not consume, like heat in an egg or brightness in the moon, can signify charity in the perfect. It arises from and is nourished by the Holy Spirit, who both illumines them by inward light, as the sun does the moon, and, warming them by the heat of charity, makes them fruitful in virtue as a hen does an egg. But because they are good, he finds in them nothing to burn away [Col. 0569B]; therefore he does not consume—that is, he does not destroy—but illumines. For as a ray of the sun shines in dry ground, so the Holy Spirit shines in a pure heart. The evil spirit finds no rest in this dry ground (Luke II), because “under the shadow, in the hiding-place of the reed, in moist places, he sleeps” (Job XL).

That kind of fire which comes into being and merely consumes, but is not fed, like lightning, can signify the passing compunction of a sinful soul. It arises either from remembrance of sins, contemplation of torments, or in some other way; by a sudden fervour it consumes evil delight, but because, as soon as it has arisen, it passes away, it is not fed—that is, not nourished. This fire can also signify preliminary passions which reach the point of consent and so, in a sense, burn the soul through unlawful delight; yet they are not nourished, because the soul soon recovering its senses expels them through compunction.

That kind of fire which is fed and consumes but does not come into being, such as the natural fire in the body, signifies the natural ardour of the soul by which a human being is angered against sin. Because this ardour is natural, it does not come into being. It is fed by zeal for the love of God, and through natural strength it consumes the softness of the soul’s disposition, when it is indignant at vices and despises and rejects them [Col. 0569C].

But before I discuss the remaining four kinds, certain matters must first be stated. There are seven capital or principal vices, from which all other vices arise: pride, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust, or fornication. Some of these have the source of their arising from one place and the occasion of their arising from another. For example, lust has from the outward appearance of the flesh an occasion for arising, but has in the soul its source of arising: for it is conceived inwardly and stirred outwardly. Thus these vices arise inwardly and outwardly in different ways: inwardly through their source, outwardly through their occasion.

Yet there is this difference: vices are not always in their occasion, whereas they must always be in their source. Thus, when a beautiful and chaste woman unknowingly draws the eye of a lustful person to desire, the vice is in the mind of the person desiring, but not in the mind of the person furnishing the occasion of desire. Sometimes, however [Col. 0570A], it is found at once in both the source and the occasion, as when an adulteress entices an adulterer.

Therefore vices are in their source—that is, in the soul from which they arise—as fire is in that which it consumes, that is, in that in which it burns. They are in their occasion as fire is in that from which it is fed, that is, that from which it burns.

Therefore, that kind of fire which at once comes into being, is fed, and consumes signifies pride. It arises inwardly; it is fed inwardly by immoderate delight in one’s own virtue, because, in a manner of speaking, as virtue grows wonderfully, this vice is not diminished but increased; and it consumes inwardly, because it destroys the virtue from which it arises.

That kind of fire which separately consumes, while simultaneously coming into being and being fed, signifies vainglory. It consumes the soul inwardly, but arises and is fed outwardly from display [Col. 0570B]. Such also is envy: it arises and is fed outwardly from another’s happiness, and inwardly consumes the soul. Such is anger: it arises and is fed outwardly from injury inflicted, and inwardly consumes the soul. Such is avarice: it arises and is fed outwardly from the sight of money, and inwardly consumes the soul. Such is lust: it arises and is fed outwardly from the appearance of flesh, and inwardly consumes the soul. Such is gluttony: it arises and is fed outwardly from delicacies seen, and inwardly consumes the soul. This kind of fire can also signify the charity of God in penitents, which arises from and is fed by the Holy Spirit, and consumes sin.

That kind of fire which separately arises while simultaneously being fed and consuming signifies sadness. It arises outwardly from immoderate anger, is fed inwardly by silence, and consumes the soul [Col. 0570C]. This also sometimes applies to lust: it arises outwardly from the appearance of flesh, is fed inwardly by thought, and consumes the soul. At times it both arises inwardly from thought and is fed through thought, and consumes the soul.

That kind of fire which is separately fed while simultaneously arising and consuming signifies lust when it arises inwardly from thought, consumes the soul inwardly, and is fed outwardly by what is seen. It also signifies avarice when it arises inwardly from *acedia*, that is, weariness and sadness, consumes the soul inwardly, and is fed outwardly by contemplation of riches.

When we say that avarice arises from sadness, this is what we mean: after a person has lost inward joy, he immediately disperses his mind outwardly in an immoderate appetite for external things, so that one who has no ground for joy inwardly may seek joy outwardly. Avarice is the immoderate desire to possess. For a person would never seek false joy outwardly unless he had first lost true joy inwardly. Hence it is clear that, just as vainglory arises from pride, envy from vainglory, anger from envy, and sadness from anger, so avarice arises from sadness, and lust from gluttony [Col. 0570D].

These things have been stated briefly concerning the nature of fire and its meanings. But there is a profound intelligence that investigates all things. The Spirit of wisdom penetrates all things. Yet among all visible things from which a likeness of invisible realities is drawn, fire, as it holds the highest place, so too holds the foremost place in significance [Col. 0571A]. For in it is found a likeness of virtue and vice, so that the mind’s gaze, touched outwardly through an image, may return inwardly to contemplate truth.

For love is fire. There is good love, good fire—namely, the fire of charity; and there is bad love, bad fire—the fire of cupidity. Good fire consumes fault; bad fire destroys nature. Good fire is kindled by the Holy Spirit; bad fire is inflamed by the devil. Good fire is charity, the source of virtues; bad fire is cupidity, the root of vices (I Tim. VI). The Lord Jesus sent good fire onto the earth and wished it to be kindled (Luke XII). Bad fire is that of which the prophet says: “And still there is fire in the house of the ungodly” (Mic. IX). From this Abraham and Lot are delivered; for *Ur* is interpreted thus, “fire” or “conflagration,” from which Abraham is reported to have been led out [Col. 0571B].

But let us now see how these two craftsmen, so to speak, work within us: the Holy Spirit through his fire, and the devil through his fire. We must understand, therefore, that the Holy Spirit kindles us in one way, and the devil in another. For the Holy Spirit is himself fire, and by breathing upon us creates fire within us; whereas the devil is not fire but cold, and stirs up fire within us not by breathing upon us, but, so to speak, by blowing into it. The one creates a virtue that did not exist; the other rouses a corruption that had lain dormant. Therefore in Sacred Scripture we find the Holy Spirit signified by the south wind, and the devil by the north wind, because the south wind is warm and the north wind cold. And we know that a warm wind, by breathing from itself, imparts warmth [Col. 0571C]. A cold wind cannot warm from itself; yet it kindles fire. Thus the Holy Spirit possesses within himself the love by which he inflames us; but the devil finds in us the corruption which he awakens. The one gently breathes inwardly by secret suggestion; the other, striking from without with the blasts of temptations, shakes us. The one, proceeding inwardly from the hiddenness of his divinity, invisibly visits the human heart and ineffably consoles it; the other, roaming without and wrapping himself in the windings of his heat, always lies in wait for ruin. This is that prince of the world whom Christ, triumphing through his death on earth, cast out from human hearts; this is the Paraclete, whom, seated in heaven at the right hand of the Father’s Majesty [Col. 0571D], he sent down upon the apostles in tongues of fire. Therefore the Holy Spirit was sent to that place from which the evil spirit had been cast out: that the former, dwelling within, might guard, while the latter, striking from without, might exercise us. When this one blows from without, we are shaken; but when that one breathes within, we are not opened [i.e. laid open or overthrown; wording uncertain].

But behold: while we observe the contrary-blowing breaths of two craftsmen, we see four works proceeding from them: two works of the devil and two works of the Holy Spirit. The devil’s first work is when he burns the mind with unlawful pleasure and, by licking it from without in the manner of a flame, makes it in some way black. The devil’s second work is when, through consent to sin, he sets the mind ablaze to its marrow; then the harmful flame no longer blackens it by licking from without, but reduces it to ashes by burning within. The Holy Spirit’s first work [Col. 0572A] is when he finds a sinful soul and, through compunction, burns away the rust of sin. His second is when, the soul having been tested and cleansed, he immediately kindles it with desire for eternal goods and, as it were, melts it by the fire of love, so that it begins to run through desire, whereas formerly, being cold, it sluggishly languished in evil. And as melted metal is poured through a tube into coinage and takes on a form, so the mind, dissolved by the fire of love, hastens through the ray of contemplation even to the image of the divine likeness. Amen.

## TITLE CLXXIV. On the rational and sensory powers of the soul

The contemplative soul is called Jerusalem because with the inward eye of its purified heart it contemplates true peace, that is, God. In this Jerusalem there are two pools [Col. 0572B], one higher and one lower; both are mentioned in Isaiah. “Go,” says the Lord to Isaiah, “to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub, your son who is left, at the conduit of the upper pool in the fuller’s field” (Isa. VII). Of the lower pool he later says: “You gathered,” he says, “the waters of the lower pool, and numbered the houses of Jerusalem; and you made a space between wall and wall, and collected the waters of the old pool, and did not look to him who made it” (Isa. XXII).

If, then, Jerusalem is the soul, the soul’s two powers are its two pools. The upper pool is reason, through which it apprehends heavenly things. The lower pool is sensuality, through which it seeks earthly things. The upper pool has a conduit in the fuller’s field. The fuller is Christ, who treads his cloths because he cleanses his elect through tribulation, so that, whitened beyond snow, he may make them a garment for himself [Col. 0572C]. This valley of tears is the fuller’s city, that is, the present world, into which we have been cast to be trodden down. Yet while we are trodden, we are united and cleansed, because the pressure of tribulation both kindles charity and washes away fault. This is the fuller who made those Gospel garments of which it was said that they were white as snow, such as no fuller on earth can make (Mark IX). But this heavenly fuller can do what an earthly fuller cannot.

This fuller, therefore, has a field where the finest flowers are found for dyeing cloths. The field is Sacred Scripture, where God’s animals pasture; there are found the commandments of diverse virtues, like flowers for adorning souls, and also the thistles of corruptions for stripping away superfluities. We run in this field when we read divine Scripture; we gather flowers when we learn its commandments; we dye cloths when, by fulfilling the commandments, we adorn our souls with virtues. Patience is in the rose, chastity in the lily, charity in the crocus, humility in the violet, purity in the sapphire. Fittingly, moreover, the conduit of the upper pool passes through the fuller’s field. For the upper pool, as has already been said, is the higher power of our mind, namely reason. The conduit of the upper pool is the ray of contemplation. Through the study of divine reading, a path is opened to our heart for contemplating the light of divinity, so that from there, as from a fountain [Col. 0573A], the living waters of spiritual gifts may descend through the ray of contemplation to water and fill the bosom of our mind.

The lower pool is the lower power of the soul, namely sensuality. It has five conduits: the five senses of the body, through which the delights of this world flow in like waters to fill the appetite of our carnality. For the world is the fountain; the waters are the world’s delights; the conduits are our senses; and the pool is our sensuality. These five water-channels are the five porticoes in which a multitude of the sick lie, because, while through the body’s five senses we contract the corruption of sin, we lie sick, as it were, in the five porticoes. But “an angel of the Lord went down into the pool at a certain time, and the water was stirred” [Col. 0573B] (John V), because when divine inspiration touches the sinner inwardly, the carnal conscience is immediately disturbed by fear of judgment. And whoever goes down into the pool after the stirring of the water is healed of whatever infirmity holds him, because the sinner, anticipated by divine grace, if he truly humbles himself in repentance and, seeking a pure conscience, judges his past evils by strictly punishing them, deserves to obtain pardon for any offense.

But now let us examine the very words which we set forth above concerning this pool. “You gathered,” he says, “the waters of the lower pool” (Isa. XXII). It is not a fault to drink the waters of the lower pool, but it is a fault to gather them; for we may use transitory goods for necessity, but not love them unto excess. For he gathers the waters [Col. 0573C] of the lower pool who accumulates temporal goods not for the use of necessity but for the fulfillment of greed.

Next he says: “You numbered the houses of Jerusalem” (ibid.). If we call Jerusalem souls, we may fittingly call the houses of Jerusalem bodies. To number the houses of Jerusalem, then, is, upon considering the multitude of people, to fear a lack of resources, to calculate the body’s expenses, and not to trust in the generosity of the Giver. Thus he immediately adds: “You collected the waters of the old pool, and did not look to him who made it” (ibid.). It is as if he said: You greedily collect temporal goods that pass away and grow old, and refuse to look to their eternal Giver; yet you fear that souls created for everlasting life will fail in time.

What he says—“You made a reservoir between wall and wall” [Col. 0573D] (ibid.)—must be referred to the same greed. For the soul has both an outer and an inner wall. The outer wall is the body, by which the soul is enclosed and in some sense held captive. The inner wall is the natural power of anger in the soul, by which it is angry against vices and fortified against temptations; for this power was given to the soul so that through it the soul might fortify itself against vices and repel every temptation, as though they were missiles of the enemy. Fortified by the inner wall, the soul wishes, if possible, to reject everything belonging to the flesh; but pressed by the outer wall, it sometimes descends even to the filth of carnal allurements [Col. 0574A]. Yet it is between wall and wall when it neither rejects the flesh in its necessities nor loves it in its pleasures. Therefore it is not a fault to make a reservoir between wall and wall to collect waters, because it is not a fault to sustain nature in its needs by temporal goods; but it is a fault to admit desires in the place of necessities.

## TITLE CLXXV. Definitions of time and free will

Time is the number of mortals succeeding one another in order.

Free will is the capacity of the rational will by which, with grace assisting, it can advance toward a good which it does not possess or possesses to a lesser degree; or, with grace permitting it [in justice], it can of itself fall away from a good which it either possesses or ought to possess.

Again, free will is the spontaneous desire for good in the rational will, which can neither be given to one under compulsion nor taken away from one unwillingly [Col. 0574B].

## TITLE CLXXVI. That only the person who is not inclined to consent to sin commendably punishes another’s sin

No one can be both an accomplice in the same fault and its avenger. For it is unworthy that one who has not yet been willing to chastise himself for sin should presume to accuse another of sin. For it is written: “Phinehas stood and made atonement” (Ps. CV). By standing, he pierces those cast down in the foulness of fornication and appeases God, because, as has been said, only he commendably punishes sin in another who, raised up within himself by love of justice, is not inclined to consent to sin.

Conversely, this explains why the children of Israel, when they assembled in battle against the children of Benjamin to avenge the crime of the Gibeonites, stirred more by confidence in their numbers than by zeal for virtue, were struck down by so great a slaughter that twenty-two thousand are read to have fallen on the first day, and eighteen thousand on the second (Judg. XX) [Col. 0574C]. There are some who, by the authority through which they are set over others, wish freely to rebuke the faults of their subjects, yet do not cease, through wicked presumption, to foster the same faults in themselves. But such avengers of another’s guilt are destroyed by those very persons whom they ought to punish, because, when the latter are arrogantly rebuked, they openly reproach those vices and show their accusers themselves to be guilty. Yet the children of Israel at last obtain by tears the victory which they could not obtain by numbers [Col. 0574D], because superiors, often humbled by the reproaches of their subjects, learn not to provoke sinners’ minds by proud and swelling invective, but rather to correct them by gentle and humble admonition. For sinners readily grant reverence to the rebuke of one who is known both humbly to lament his own sins and mercifully to reprove the sins of others; nor then does the sinner dare to rise up against the words of the reprover when he finds nothing in that reprover’s life which he can rightly blame.

> [Note: [Col. 0573] On the seven deadly sins and their effects, see volume I on Matthew, *On the Lord’s Prayer*.]

## TITLE CLXXVII. A mystical description of the nature of the hind

It is said of the hind that, when it has been wounded by a hunter, if the violence of the wound is so great that it cannot run, weakened and delayed, it is caught and killed. But if the pain of the wound has not yet altogether taken away its strength, it escapes by running and, fleeing through deserted places, carries the embedded arrow with it. Then it wanders about groaning and in pain, and, finding no hand to draw the deadly weapon from its body, at last goes and seeks dittany, and eats it. When the juice of this plant has been received into its inward parts, it penetrates all things by its power and, reaching the wound, forcefully expels the iron and causes it even to emerge from the depths of the entrails [Col. 0575A].

The hind is the chaste and pure soul. The arrows are evil desires. The hunters are demons, who, whenever they introduce wicked desires into our hearts from outward things—through sight, hearing, taste, smell, or touch—send deadly arrows into the soul, as hunters do from afar. If the soul is weakened through pleasure in a wicked desire so far as to consent to the deed, it is, as it were, caught and killed. But if it flees and turns aside from carrying out the wicked deed, yet nevertheless cannot cast out the embedded iron of unlawful pleasure, it has, as it were, escaped the author of death. Yet it has not fully escaped the peril of death [Col. 0575B]. What it can do in order not to die is go into solitude and seek dittany—that is, the Word of God. When it has found this, whether through sacred reading or through conversation with holy persons, let it take and eat it eagerly; and by its sweetness let it expel all the corruption of deadly pleasure and restore itself to the wholeness of its former health, all danger having been escaped. For nothing excludes evil pleasure more quickly than good pleasure; when the mind begins to taste the latter, it immediately abandons the former of its own accord [Col. 0575C].

## TITLE CLXXVIII. On the fourfold distinction between the healthy and the sick

Physicians who customarily cure bodily diseases define four conditions of human life: health-producing, healthy, disease-prone, and sick. From these arise four kinds: health-producing and healthy; disease-prone and sick; health-producing and sick; disease-prone and healthy.

The health-producing are those whose nature is not corrupted inwardly by any hidden defect. The healthy are those troubled by no manifest pain [Col. 0575D]. The disease-prone are those who have hidden corruption within. The sick are those tormented by manifest pain. The health-producing and healthy are those whose nature is inwardly sound from corruption and outwardly free from the vexation of pain. The disease-prone and sick are those who endure both inward corruption from a hidden defect and outward pain, whether the pain has arisen from inward corruption or has been inflicted by some external injury. The health-producing and sick are those whose nature has no inward corruption but endures outwardly the pain of some injury. The disease-prone and healthy are those who feel no manifest pain but inwardly bear, all the more dangerously because more secretly, the wound of hidden corruption [Col. 0576A].

Of these four grades of persons, the best are the health-producing and healthy; the worst are the disease-prone and sick; intermediate are the health-producing and sick, and the disease-prone and healthy. Yet the health-producing and sick are better than the disease-prone and healthy, because in the former an uncorrupted nature easily recovers health violently disturbed, while in the latter a corrupted nature easily loses a health weakly and doubtfully granted. In the former, health has not been extinguished but violently aggravated; in the latter, sickness has not been removed but only lightly lulled to sleep. Therefore, just as the latter easily returns to its old corruption upon any slight occasion, so the former is restored by an easy remedy to its former soundness.

I have made this distinction because from the condition of bodies the character of minds may be understood. For there are likewise four differences in the soul: virtue, justice, vice, and sin [Col. 0576B]. What is health-producing in the body is virtue in the mind; what is healthy in the body is justice in the mind; what is disease-prone in the body is vice in the mind; and what is sick in the body is sin in the mind. Thus not everyone who possesses some virtue is just, but the one who does justice; nor is everyone who has some vice a sinner, but the one who commits sin.

For even the righteous, although unwillingly, sometimes feel the stings of vices because of the weakness of the flesh which they bear as corruptible; but because they do not incline themselves to these by consent, the movement itself, arising from the vice of corruption, is not imputed as sin to those who feel it but do not consent to it. Therefore there is vice there, yet there is no sin [Col. 0576C]. Again, there are many whose nature is not so strongly affected by the passions of vices, yet who often fall into sins through negligence. The guilt binding such sinners is greater in proportion as the necessity impelling them to sin was less.

Therefore those whose nature is more corrupted by the affections of vices fall more easily and rise more laboriously; yet, if they keep themselves from sin, they merit more, while if they sin, they obtain pardon more quickly. Those, however, whose nature is stronger fall more slowly and rise more quickly; and therefore, if they persevere in virtue, they merit less, but if they fall into sin, they are held more guilty.

## TITLE CLXXIX. On the text: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes”

“They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Rev. XIV) [Col. 0576D]. The Lamb came to us through humility and virginity; through humility and virginity he went before us. For he himself, a virgin and humble, was born from one who was humble and a Virgin. The humility of the Virgin and the virginity of the humble woman were the way by which he came. We cannot, therefore, come by the way by which he came; yet we can follow where he went, because, if we cannot have virgin parents, we are not forbidden to remain virgins. Whoever is a virgin but not humble, or humble but not a virgin, follows the Lamb, but not wherever he goes. Only that person follows the Lamb wherever he goes who preserves virginity together with humility, and humility together with virginity.

Certainly, of the two imperfect conditions, it is better to follow the Lamb through humility alone than through virginity alone [Col. 0577A], because humility without virginity can save a person, whereas virginity without humility cannot.

## TITLE CLXXX. On three kinds of compassion

There are three kinds of compassion. One compassion comes from vice, another from nature, and another from virtue. Compassion from vice occurs when one’s affection is touched by some blameworthy grief in a matter where it was previously held by unlawful love. Compassion from nature occurs when the mind, from an inborn affection of pity, grieves with others in their miseries whenever it sees them oppressed or afflicted contrary to the measure of piety or humanity. Compassion from virtue occurs when, for God’s sake, we suffer with the pains of others—namely, when we see justice oppressed or innocence afflicted.

Compassion from vice is blameworthy; compassion from nature is not blameworthy; compassion from virtue is praiseworthy [Col. 0577B]. The first is reproved and the third praised; the second, however, has neither fault, because it comes from nature, nor reward, because it does not come from virtue. Therefore, in this life, as long as mortal flesh can be wounded by suffering, so long can the mutable mind be touched by compassion. But where both are truly incapable of suffering, then surely neither suffering can reside in the flesh nor compassion in the mind. Now each rightly uses its mutability if the flesh does not abandon patience in suffering and the mind does not exceed the measure of justice in compassion.

If, therefore, you seek the time for compassion: as long as we can suffer, we ought to suffer with others [Col. 0577C]. If you seek its place: the mercy of compassion ought to be shown where the misery of suffering is not yet beyond hope. David shed tears while his son was ill; when he was dead, he washed his face (II Kings XII), showing that the mercy of compassion must be borne as long as the misery of suffering is not yet hopeless.

There is, nevertheless, a kind of compassionate feeling which pursues even fallen nature with pity. According to this feeling, in the likeness of our own kind, as we are angry at guilt which ought to be corrected, so we pity nature which ought not to be destroyed. At present mortal life, subject to mutability, endures in part the misery of both; but later, translated to incorruption, it will lay it aside. At present it suffers in both: in suffering in the flesh and in compassion in the mind [Col. 0577D]. Then it will be healed in both, so that through the immortality of the flesh it may be established against bodily suffering, and through the immutability of the mind against mental compassion. For as bodily sickness is to suffer, so mental sickness is to suffer with another.

Therefore God made man, who came to remove both, endured both. He assumed suffering in the flesh; he assumed compassion in the mind. He chose to be sick in both for our sake, so that he might heal us, sick in both. He was made weak through suffering in his own punishment; he was made weak through compassion in another’s misery. He endured suffering so far as to die for those who were to die. He assumed compassion so far as to weep for those who were perishing. Because of misery he gave his flesh over to suffering; because of mercy he disturbed his soul to compassion [Col. 0578A]. In his flesh he grieved, suffering for us; in his mind he grieved with us, having compassion. And just as the weakness of his flesh, according to the affection of nature, did not will his own punishment, so the piety of his mind, according to the affection of mercy, did not will another’s misery.

For just as, according to the will of the flesh, he asked that the cup of suffering be taken away from him—though he foreknew that it would not be taken away—so, according to piety, he prayed that the sentence of condemnation might be softened for others, though he foresaw that it was unchangeable. Piety did what belonged to it by showing mercy, and reason followed what belonged to it by obeying the divine ordering. Therefore there was no contradiction if Christ as man, according to the affection of piety which he had assumed in his humanity [Col. 0578B], willed something which, according to the divine will by which, together with the Father, he ordered all things, he foreknew would not come to pass. For it belonged to true humanity to be moved by pity, and to true divinity not to be moved from its own ordering.

Accordingly, in both respects he did what he ought.
