Nor was he thereby contrary to himself if, according to piety fitting to humanity, he willed what, according to justice owing to divinity, he did not will; for he willed both to will this and not to will that. For it is written: “Jesus groaned in spirit and troubled himself” (John XI). Attend here: “He troubled himself.” How did he trouble himself? What was this disturbance by which Jesus troubled himself? Piety itself, compassion itself, was the disturbance [Col. 0578C]. It was a good disturbance. He was rightly disturbed who was moved by piety. “He troubled himself.” Compassion disturbed him, and he himself troubled himself, since he voluntarily assumed compassion.

Just as he gave himself up when Judas gave him up, so he troubled himself when compassion troubled him. This is well known and proved by common usage: when a person suffers something, one says to him, “You have troubled yourself; you have done this evil to yourself.” Thus Jesus troubled himself when the compassion which he had voluntarily assumed troubled him. And he gave himself up when the man to whom he had granted power to betray him gave him up.

Thus Jesus, in the humanity he assumed, as long as he chose to bear it as capable of suffering, bore, according to the property of humanity, both suffering in the flesh and compassion in the mind [Col. 0578D]. Yet now, having been translated to immutability, he can neither suffer unto corruption nor suffer with another unto disturbance. When we knew Christ according to the human being, we knew him as both suffering and compassionate. “My days vanished like smoke, and my bones dried up like a firebrand” (Ps. CI). His days vanished because of suffering; his bones dried up because of compassion. His flesh died because of suffering; his soul dried up because of compassion. The pain of compassion was like a kind of frying of the soul, by which it was burned with pity, pressed by compassion, and dried by despair—by despair, I mean, not on its own account, but for those who were neither to be corrected in evil nor delivered from evil [Col. 0579A].

In all these things we know Christ according to the flesh, when we know that he bore true mortality in true humanity. But now we no longer know him according to the flesh (II Cor. V), since, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him. For in that he lives, he lives unto God (Rom. VI).

## TITLE CLXXXI. The mystery of the number of those proceeding to battle with Gideon

“And the number of those who lapped with their tongue was three hundred men” (Judg. VII). Most Latin codices do not have “with their hand,” but only “with their tongue,” because they understood the preceding words, “like dogs,” in this way. But the Greek has both “with their hand” and “with their tongue,” unless it is understood that they threw water snatched up by hand into their mouths. This was like dogs drinking, who do not draw in the water they drink by putting their mouths to it as oxen do, but catch it with their tongues into their mouths. This, too, is understood to have been done by these men: namely, that they threw water into their mouths with the hand, which they caught with the tongue [Col. 0579B].

For the translation from Hebrew states it more plainly in these words: “Thus the number of those who, with hand casting water into mouth, lapped water was three hundred men.” People do not normally drink in such a way as to draw water with the tongue like dogs without the use of the hand. But these men were commanded to do this; yet when they went down to the water to drink, many drank with bended knee, which could be done more easily and with less labor. But the few who did not bend their knees and stoop to drink as dogs did, but received water cast into their mouths—their number, because it was three hundred, suggests the sign of the cross because of the Greek letter tau. By this number it was also prefigured that the Gentiles would be more ready to believe in the Crucified One, because it is a Greek letter. By the name “Greek,” the Apostle signifies all Gentiles when he says, “To the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Rom. II), and “to Jews and Greeks” (ibid.), often thus referring to circumcision and uncircumcision, since among the languages of the nations Greek so excels that all may fittingly be signified by it [Col. 0579C].

This number should also be observed in Abraham’s household servants, through whom he rescued his brother from enemies, when Melchizedek blessed him in a great mystery (Gen. XIV). The fact that eighteen were added to them—for they are reported to have been three hundred and eighteen [ibid.; Col. 0579D]—seems to me to signify the time at which this would occur, namely, the third age, which was to be under grace. For the first age is before the law, the second under the law, and the third under grace. Each age, moreover, is signified by the number six because of perfection; for three times six is eighteen. Thus that woman had been infirm for eighteen years, whom the Savior, finding her bent over, raised up and, as the Gospel indicates, released from the devil’s bond (Luke XV [probably XIII]).

That these approved men, through whom Gideon was to conquer, were said to resemble dogs in drinking signifies that God chose “the contemptible and the ignoble” (I Cor. I) [Col. 0580A]. For dogs are held in contempt. Hence he says: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. XV).

## TITLE CLXXXII. Why the land rested forty years after Gideon’s sin

The question ought not to be omitted: how did the land rest for forty years after Gideon’s sin (Judg. VIII), when, after the victory by which he delivered the Hebrews, he made an abomination from the gold of the spoils, and after this all Israel committed fornication with it, and it became a stumbling block to him and his house? How then, after so great a crime committed by both Gideon and the people, did the land rest for forty years, when Scripture customarily shows that, when the people committed fornication against the Lord God, they then lost peace rather than gained it, and were subjugated to enemies rather than protected from hostile attack [Col. 0580B]?

But it must be understood that Scripture, as is its custom, spoke by prolepsis—that is, anticipation—when it said that Gideon made an ephod contrary to God’s law from the gold taken from the conquered enemies. It wished in one place to say both where the gold came from and what was done with it. But this sin occurred later, at the end of Gideon’s days, when the evils which Scripture subsequently relates also followed; after it had mentioned how many years the land rested in Gideon’s days, it recalled those years by recapitulation—that is, returning to the order which it had previously disturbed by first speaking of that scandal which happened last.

> [Note: [Col. 0579D] On the two schools, see volume I near the beginning. — On the fact that God’s commandments are signified by many names, [Col. 0580D] ibid. — On those who walk, stand, or turn aside in the law, ibid. — On the three ways, ibid.]

## TITLE CLXXXIII. What the perverse cry daily on account of God’s foreknowledge and predestination

[Col. 0580C]

It is not the carefulness of prudent people but the complaint of fools: “Leave me alone; I shall live as I shall live. Whoever is predestined to life cannot perish. Why should I strive? What is to happen will happen.” Yet no wounded or sick person says: “Leave me alone; if I am going to live, I shall not die. What can a physician do? What is to happen will happen.” And they do not fear to prescribe a rule for their souls which they refuse to prescribe for their bodies.

The perverse cry this daily: “Do not admonish us; do not correct us. If God wills, he will justify us.” Yet no one says: “Do not prepare food; do not provide clothing. If God wills, he will feed and clothe us.” And he says: “We cannot be good unless God does this.” Therefore you cannot possess those good things without God [Col. 0580D], but can you possess these things? Indeed, God rather requires your effort in those things which you cannot possess unless you will to possess them, not in those things which are so far outside your control that often you cannot have them when you desire them, and have them when you despise them.

## TITLE CLXXXIV. On the wisdom of God and of man, and on its twofold character, higher and lower

Wisdom proceeds from the heart and goes out through the mouth; it enters through the ear and rests in the heart. It does not depart from where it goes out, yet it arrives where it had not been. Wisdom ought to be veiled and adorned when it comes forth to us. When God’s wisdom first went forth to us in the creation of things, it did not go forth naked, but appeared to us clothed in the form of created things [Col. 0581A]. The second time, the same wisdom—that is, the Son of God—when he manifested himself to us, assumed the garment of flesh and thus appeared visible. The third time, clothed in the sacred veil of words, the same wisdom presents itself to our understanding. For because of our weakness we must ascend from visible things to invisible.

In the same way, our own wisdom always goes forth veiled. For it has the rule of a beautiful woman: if she walks in costly clothing, she appears more beautiful; but if in cheap clothing, her beauty is diminished as though worn away. So too wisdom shines when clothed in an elegant arrangement of words; when clothed in something cheap, it is demeaned. Hence it is said: “The tongue of the wise adorns wisdom” (Prov. XV).

The heart is a field; understanding is a root; thought is a branch; the word is a cluster; the ear is a winepress; wisdom is wine; memory is a storehouse [Col. 0581B]. Understanding is the capacity for understanding—that is, knowing—and proceeds from the heart; from it proceeds thought; from thought, word; and from word, wisdom, which enters through the ear. The ear, like a winepress, separates the meaning from the sound which enters through it.

Wisdom is twofold: one lower, the other higher. Lower wisdom is found in the natures of things; higher wisdom in invisible essences. The philosophers of the Gentiles were enlightened in lower wisdom, for they effectively grasped truth in visible things according to the elements of this world; but they could not apprehend the highest truth. Hence it is said: “They became vain in their reasonings” (Rom. I). For when, from visible things, they ascended to the divine essence and wished to affirm certain things about it, they became vain in that assertion through the likeness of created things and according to the grasp of human reason [Col. 0581C]: for example, when they said *peri agathou kai nou* (περὶ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ νοῦ), that is, “concerning the Good and Intellect and the Soul of the World,” asserting that these were three principles and yet unequal; when they said that *noun* (νοῦν, “Intellect”) was inferior to *to agathon* (τῷ ἀγαθῷ, “the Good”), and the World-Soul inferior to both. Yet it is not denied that they spoke rightly in some matters, as when they said that the original causes of things subsist in the divine mind, and other such things.

## TITLE CLXXXV. On obedience: to whom it is to be rendered
Some things are so evil that they can never lawfully be done; some so good that they can never be omitted without fault. In the former, obedience must never be rendered so that they are done; nor in the latter, so that they are not done. But there are certain intermediate matters which, according to time, place, and cause, are now good because they are done well, and now evil because they are done badly. In these, therefore, the command of obedience has a place—whether that they be done or not done—when it may properly be either done or not done.

Of these, some are commanded from reason, some according to reason, and some beyond reason. Those are commanded from reason whose cause is manifest: why they ought to be commanded and done. Those are commanded according to reason which, although they have no manifest cause why they ought to be commanded, nevertheless have a manifest cause why they are good and reasonable if done. Those are commanded beyond reason in which neither does any cause appear why they ought to be commanded, nor is there any evident reason why they ought to be done; yet, if they are done, neither reason is harmed nor justice violated. [Col. 0582A]

A command from reason is given, for example, when criminals and public sinners are ordered to keep away from the thresholds of the church. A command according to reason would be given if someone were ordered to distribute to the poor all that he lawfully possesses in this world. A command beyond reason is such as we read that certain holy Fathers imposed upon their subjects—many things ridiculous and foreign to human reason—for the testing of the virtue of obedience: namely, to water dry sticks until they put forth shoots; to soften hard rocks by pouring water upon them; to tame fierce creatures by the command of a word; and other things of this kind.

In those things commanded from reason, obedience is a duty; disobedience, a punishable fault. In those commanded according to reason, obedience is merit; disobedience, a venial weakness. In those commanded beyond reason, obedience is perfection; disobedience, goodness less worthy of praise. In those things commanded from reason, disobedience destroys obedience; but in those commanded according to reason and beyond reason, disobedience harms obedience. Therefore, in the latter two cases the merit of one who disobeys is diminished; but in the first case punishment is owed to the disobedient.

## TITLE CLXXXVI. On the highest good and the non-highest good, and on the manifold nature of evil, sin, and fault

God alone is he whose good is identical with what he himself is. Therefore he alone cannot himself be evil, because he cannot be deprived of his good. All other things, however, are other than their goods. Therefore all other things either are evil or can be evil, because they either lack their goods when these have been lost, or can be deprived of goods which they possess; and those which cannot be deprived cannot be deprived by grace.

Thus every other thing is other than its own good; it can naturally exist apart from its good; when it has its good, it is good; and when it does not have it, it is evil. It should likewise be known that above there is indeed one good, but every good is in it, and every good is itself that Good. Therefore it can neither be increased, because it is perfect, nor diminished, because it is eternal. Therefore it is always what it is.

But all other goods, because they are partial, can be increased; and because they are changeable, can be diminished; and because they are other than that whose goods they are, they can be lost. Since, moreover, in the totality of things there are only two natures, namely corporeal and incorporeal nature, and since they differ from one another, their goods likewise cannot be altogether the same. Therefore the good of incorporeal nature is one thing, and the good of corporeal nature another. Each, when it has its own good, is good; but when it does not have its own good, this is its evil, and it itself is evil. [Col. 0582D]

The good of incorporeal nature is knowledge of truth and love of virtue; the good of corporeal nature is the beauty of comeliness and the wholeness of health. Yet there is likeness, on either side, among the goods themselves; and things which are different from one another are not thereby unlike one another. Knowledge of truth is, as it were, a certain beauty of spiritual nature; love of virtue is, as it were, a kind of health. There is beauty without and beauty within, health without and health within.

When beauty is taken away, foulness and ugliness succeed; this is evil, yet it does not as yet cause pain or inflict torment. But when health is taken away, corruption and pain succeed, and a great evil results. Hence it is clear that not to love the good is a greater evil than not to know the true. The deprivation of bodily goods is evil, and only evil; but the deprivation of spiritual goods is evil, and not only evil but also sin. The latter, therefore, is fault; the former, punishment.

Ignorance follows the deprivation of knowledge of the true; desire for evil follows the deprivation of love of the good. These are the two evils from which all evils arise. Ignorance causes us not to do what ought to be done; desire causes us to do what ought not to be done. Not doing what ought to be done is a fault (*delictum*); doing what ought not to be done is sin (*peccatum*). [Col. 0583B]

It should be understood, however, that “evil,” used substantively, signifies only the deprivation of good itself; used denominatively, it denotes an evil act, or its effect, or its manifestation. Thus malice too is called evil, and the action of evil is called evil; but the one is substantive, the other denominative.

Every sin belongs to the will and is sin in the will alone; nevertheless, the action of sin is called sin because in it sin is completed, fulfilled, and manifested. Sin and the action of sin are not two sins, but one sin: it begins in a movement of the mind and is afterwards completed by a movement of the body. Every sin takes its beginning from a movement of the mind and thence grows to completion, either when it is fulfilled in bodily action or, if it cannot have a bodily effect, when it is confirmed by full consent.

Consent is twofold: one kind is not resisting evil; the other is doing evil. For every movement of the mind is either toward God by conversion, when it is good; or, when it is evil, by turning away from God. That very turning away is evil and sin. Since the mind turns away from God in many ways, many kinds of evil and many kinds of sin are said to exist. Yet the beginning of turning away is always the beginning of sin, and that turning away itself is sin.

That crooked movement of turning away grows, overflows into worse things, and comes first to delight, then to consent not to resist evil—which occurs through passion—and then to consent to do evil, which produces full passion; and then sin is completed in itself. Yet it sometimes proceeds as far as the performance of bodily action. This action, indeed, although it is not essentially sin in itself, nevertheless adds as much to sin as it inflames that movement of sin which is in the mind. [Col. 0583D]

For the movement of the body is not added to the movement of the mind so that the latter grows within itself; rather, from that bodily movement a cause is taken for the spiritual movement of the mind, so that it receives in itself an incentive—just as a bellows, when it kindles a fire, increases it not by adding fire to fire, but by stirring up the same fire from the fire itself so that it burns and heats more intensely.

Thus, even in those who will wrongly, the movement of the mind is sin; the movement of the body is the manifestation of sin. For in the mind’s turning away from God through its own movement we recognize fault; but in the body’s movement following the movement of the mind we find nature alone. The movement of the will is first, in itself, in thought; then it passes through bodily movement into action. An evil movement flows downward of itself, like a mass of molten lead: wherever an opening is made, it rushes downward by itself. A good movement, because it is upward, cannot proceed by itself.

## TITLE CLXXXVII. On the two denarii

“On the next day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper,” etc. (Luke 10).

The two denarii spent upon the care of the wounded man are the debt of command, in which is doctrine, and the debt of vow, in which is example; or the two Testaments, or the two swords, or the two judgments. The Old Testament judges crimes like an avenger and strikes with the bodily sword in order to punish. The New Testament judges diseases like a physician and strikes with the spiritual sword in order to heal. If anything is spent beyond what rigor or gentleness requires, it is repaid; if nothing is spent beyond it, nothing is demanded. [Col. 0584B]

## TITLE CLXXXVIII. On one who does evil or good badly and afterwards repents

For one who does evil and does it badly, when he afterwards repents, both are forgiven: both that he does evil and that he does it in this bad manner. For one who does good and does it badly, when he afterwards repents, what he does badly is forgiven; what he does well is retained, and the added good intention designates the work as good.

## TITLE CLXXXIX. On the attestation of human nature

A human being is born naked; a beast clothed. Nature therefore grants more to those who have no foresight. A human being is thus left unprovided, so that the dignity of his nature may be demonstrated and his reason exercised. [Col. 0584C]

## TITLE CXC. On Wisdom’s going forth and return

“I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16).

Wisdom’s first going forth is from the bosom of the Father to the human heart. Its second is when, clothed in voice, it goes out through the mouth and comes to the ear; there, stripping itself, it enters the heart through hearing, so that, leaving the world again through the heart’s contemplation, it may return to the Father. It takes root in the heart, sprouts in the mouth, is pressed in the ear, and is again received into the treasury of the heart.

Voice is the garment of wisdom, as it is written: “The tongue of the wise adorns knowledge” (Prov. 15). Wisdom does not go forth except clothed, nor return except stripped. Likewise, the visible form of creation is the garment of wisdom, by which it goes forth veiled and is seen, as it is written: “You have put on confession and splendour; clothed with light as with a garment; stretching out the heavens as a skin,” etc. (Ps. 103). [Col. 0584D]

## TITLE CXCI. Why God is called the Father of lights

“Every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights,” etc. (James 1).

The gifts of God are lights, and the author of gifts himself is the Father of lights: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning” (ibid.), because neither does he who illumines change, nor does he who does not illumine grow dark. For one who begets does not degenerate, and one who does not beget does not become dim, because neither is what goes forth inferior nor what remains hidden darker.

His lights, when they come to us, do not depart from him; and when they return from us, they do not become brighter with him. When they descend to us, they do not fail within us; and when they depart from us, they suffer no diminution on our account. Thus they are not changed in us when they come to us to be shared, nor are they shadowed in themselves when they return from those illumined and those cast into shadow; rather, they remain in themselves. [Col. 0585A]

## TITLE CXCII. How Wisdom was brought forth

“The deeps were not yet, and I was being brought forth” (Prov. 8).

God had conceived Wisdom in foreknowledge of the future; he was bringing her forth in the will to create; he gave birth to her in the production of the accomplished effect.

## TITLE CXCIII. On the four fears

[Col. 0585B]

There are four fears: worldly, servile, initial, and filial. Worldly fear, to avoid an impending punishment, disguises the good while retaining the will for the good; servile fear, to avoid an impending punishment, feigns the good while retaining the will for evil; initial fear, to avoid a future punishment, even changes the evil will; filial fear, out of reverence for the Creator, freely confirms the good will. Initial fear has the necessity of good; filial fear, its will. The first three are concerned with punishment and have punishment; the fourth is neither concerned with punishment nor has punishment.

## TITLE CXCIV. On the three kinds of persons in conflict with vices

[Col. 0585C]

Among persons struggling with vices, some stand firm, some waver, and some wander. Those standing are established; those wavering are not yet rooted; those wandering are scattered. Those standing are those who have conquered; those wavering, those who fight; those wandering, those who have been conquered. Those standing are at peace, concerning whom it is said: “He has made your borders peace and satisfies you with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 147); those wavering are in struggle; those wandering, in alienation. Those standing possess; those wavering desire and pursue; those wandering flee and are drawn away—first toward unlawful deeds, then toward shameful ones.

*Dispute between God and the devil. In the first volume, folio XXXIX, D.*

## TITLE CXCV. On the three tyrants

There are three tyrants who draw up their battle-lines against us: the devil, the world, and the flesh. In the devil’s army the vices serve; in the world’s camp, prosperity and adversity; in fellowship with the flesh, earthly desires. Of these three, two have conspired with the third for our overthrow. For the world and the flesh bring the devil aid against us: one is a neighbour, the other a member of the household. The world is near us; the flesh is with us. Therefore the devil places greater confidence in the flesh’s assistance, because the enemy of one’s household does greater harm.

We conquer the devil when we resist his suggestions; we conquer the world when we neither desire prosperity nor fear adversity; we conquer the flesh when we neither destroy its desires in things necessary nor relax them toward things lawful. [Col. 0585D]

## TITLE CCXVI. On the heart, delight, and thoughts

[Col. 0586A]

The heart is a pot; delight, the fat; thoughts, the flies. Therefore, where desires abound, thoughts too abound. Yet it sometimes happens that, after the heart has been cleansed of evil desires, wicked thoughts still return—now as intrusive as they were formerly unclean. There they defile; here they disturb. There is mud; here, dust.

## TITLE CXCVII. On the wisdom of God and of the world

It is written: “Because the world, in the wisdom of God, did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1).

The world had a wisdom through which it could not know God, who was set within his own wisdom. The wisdom of the world was human reason, shaped according to the nature of visible things and the elements of this world. The wisdom of God was his ineffable majesty and incomprehensible goodness. There was also the prudence of the world: a careful concern for the conveniences of the flesh.

Therefore the wisdom of the world, which proceeds by human reason, rejects faith; but worldly prudence, which teaches one to seek only the conveniences of the flesh and avoid its inconveniences, destroys good action. Therefore God reckons the wisdom of the world foolish and judges its prudence hostile, because the former opposes truth and the latter love. Therefore God destroyed both: wisdom through foolishness, prudence through madness. [Col. 0586C]

For it was, as it were, a certain foolishness of God according to human understanding that he humbled himself to things lowly and unworthy of himself. It was reckoned madness that he endured such harsh things without necessity. Yet he who could not be known in his wisdom was recognized, as it were, in foolishness; for he who could not be comprehended while remaining in his own exaltation began to be known in his humiliation.

God was, as it were, in his wisdom when he remained in that which seemed fitting to him; but there he was not recognized until he, as it were, became foolish and accepted unworthy things. There he destroyed the world’s wisdom, where he showed himself in what appears foolish to the world, so that humanity might learn that what it saw in human nature—God appearing—was above the reason of the world.

Then, as it were through madness, God nullified the prudence of the flesh when, acting against its judgment, he exposed his flesh without withdrawal to punishments and torments and thus led it forth to the incorruption of resurrection, showing that the flesh must be preserved not by sparing it but by chastising and persecuting it. [Col. 0586D]

Thus, because in its wisdom the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (1 Cor. 1). The things said appeared foolish; yet by them the things approved and loved were shown to be still more foolish: those approved by reason were foolish, and those loved by affection were mad—the former without truth, the latter without usefulness. For it was foolish stubbornly not to receive the truth of God beyond the understanding of the flesh; and it was madness patiently to endure the soul’s loss for the sake of the flesh’s advantage. [Col. 0587A]

## TITLE CXCVIII. On the soul’s threefold nourishment

God feeds the faithful soul with threefold nourishment: through the word, through the sacrament, and through the Spirit. When he refreshes us through his words and sacraments, he sets before us a honeycomb to eat; but when he refreshes us inwardly through his Spirit, he pours out honey for us to taste.

## TITLE CXCIX. On inducing contempt for the world

The first aid toward contempt of the world comes when a person begins to recognize why he was created and seeks his Maker, God. Then he will begin to repent of the things he committed during the time of his negligence. And then the gracious God gives him sorrow for his sins. After this, again through his goodness, he gives him bodily affliction: in fasts, vigils, persistence in prayer, contempt for the world; that he may gladly endure injuries inflicted upon him, hate every bodily comfort, and love weeping more than laughter. [Col. 0587B]

After this God will grant him desire, tears, lamentation, humiliation, and humility, so that he may consider the beam in his own eye and not strive to remove another’s speck; and so that he may always say: “For I know my iniquity, and my fault is ever before me” (Ps. 50). He should remember the end of his days, how he will meet God’s presence, and set before his mind the judgments and punishments, as well as the rewards deserved by the saints.

But one who knows that his heart is firm in the fear of the Lord, who does not waver from his place but stoutly resists his adversary, shall be called a perfect monk and soldier of Christ. For as a ship burdened with excessive weight is overwhelmed by the striking waves, so a monk possessing much is hindered on the way; possessing nothing, he flies like an eagle to the heights, descending only for food when necessity compels him.

A prudent monk will not flatter the rich for the pleasure of his belly. Possessing nothing, like a light runner he will swiftly reach the prize of God’s heavenly calling. After moderate work, the true monk gives himself to prayers and readings. The monk who possesses nothing stores treasure in heaven and sings praises to God day and night in the fear of God.

A monk’s glory is when he desires to possess none of the things of this present life. A monk’s glory is vigils and tears in his prayers. A monk’s glory is gentleness and faith. A monk’s glory is when he loves God with his whole heart and his neighbour as himself. A monk’s glory is abstinence from foods and from much speaking with the tongue. A monk’s glory is when his words accord with his deeds. A monk’s glory is when he remains in his place and does not wander here and there. A monk’s glory is long-suffering together with humility and grace. [Col. 0587D]

As a shining lamp in a dark place, as the radiant sun is splendid, so is the perfect monk in sobriety, chastity, and a wakeful heart during the time of the psalms. As the weight of the sun pressing upon a weak person, so is sleep upon the monk’s eyes. As thorns and briars in an excellent field, so are shameful thoughts in a monk’s heart. As a moth destroys a garment, so detraction destroys a monk’s soul.

Do not go to converse with a woman, lest you be separated from the kingdom of God. And do not wish to say: “I speak with a woman and am pure.” The wise monk works with his hands, acquiring his daily sustenance for himself, and thereby has gained his prayers and fasts. But if he receives sustenance from another, what profit is it that he prays and keeps vigil like an evil and harsh hireling? For it is written: “It is better and more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20).

An abundance of wood kindles a great flame; an abundance of food gives birth to disobedience and death. One in need keeps the belly wakeful in prayers and acquires the soul’s crown; but one filled induces the heaviness of sleep. The vainglorious eye searches out banquets; the eye of the wise meditates upon the self-restraint of martyrs. A fearful soldier dreads the trumpet that signifies battle; and the gluttonous monk, if he hears abstinence mentioned, does not heed the preacher. [Col. 0588B]

When a flame wanes, it shines again if it receives wood; and desire, once lulled, is kindled again by fullness of food. Do not spare the body if it fails through fatigue. A compliant horse, needing the body, never fails its rider. Desire is the mother of lust; oil nourishes the shining lamp, and conversation with women kindles the fire of sensuality.

For a woman’s face is a cruel arrow: it inflicts a wound and poison upon the soul. Flee conversation with a woman if you wish to be chaste. Poison is hidden in them. Approach a burning fire rather than a woman. Do not wish, while you are young, through desire in conversation with a woman to experience the impulses of lust. Whoever fills his belly and promises chastity lies to himself. Beautiful appearance sinks one worse than a storm. If you have once conceived a woman’s appearance in your mind, it persuades you to despise life itself.

For as fire lingering in straw kindles a flame, so the abiding memory of a woman inflames desire. Woman has become the sting of sin. Every association with women is the glue of faults, and, as with birdlime, binds by its song—on which the devil feeds—whether it is dissolved in laughter or delights in singing. It is more useful to hear a basilisk hissing than a woman singing. [Col. 0588D]

And what will you say? “Nothing? How did Elijah live with the widow?” You who call yourself Elijah’s disciple, do what Elijah himself did. Take for yourself a period of so many days of fasting that you may reign in heaven for ages of ages.

## TITLE CC. On the resolution of four questions proposed by Ranulf of Mauriac

HUGH TO RANULF OF MAURIAC, etc. See above among Hugh’s letters, *Works*, vol. II.

# BOOK TWO. ELUCIDATORY NOTES ON CERTAIN PSALMS OF DAVID

[Col. 0589]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0589A]

For you, dearest brother, I have tasted beforehand certain verses of the Psalmist, drawing a small drop from the deep abyss.

## CHAPTER I. On the construction of the seat of pestilence, and the matters pertaining to it

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence” (Ps. 1).

So long as the soul cleaves to God through contemplation, it remains in its homeland; when it bends its thought toward earthly and transitory things, it goes from its homeland into exile. First it departs through vanity; then it stands through delight; then it sits through consent. Through the deed it builds; through despair it dwells. One who performs evil constructs a seat; one who persists in evil sits in the seat.

The instruments of evil action are the five bodily senses; the material is that in which each person fulfills the purpose of a perverse will. The manner of construction is this: sight chooses; speech cuts; service fits together; experience arranges. Sight pertains to the eye, speech to hearing, service to the hand, experience to smell and taste.

One whom the action itself delights in a wicked deed for its own sake tastes in acting: such are gluttony and lust. But when the act itself does not please in itself, and through what is done a person wishes to attain some other object of desire, that person smells from afar: such are robbery and theft. For the robber is not delighted to kill a human being, but to possess the spoils; nor is the thief delighted to undermine a threshold, but to obtain money. [Col. 0589C]

These five instruments do not operate in every sin; nevertheless, there are sins in which all are found together, as, for example, lust. When someone has first conceived in the mind the burning of desire through thought, he then chooses through the eyes the material for fulfilling his perverse will, when he seeks a partner in shame—the one who can please him more. Then he cuts the material through speech, because by harmful persuasions he draws the person he has found from the state of uprightness to consent in perversity. Then he fits it by service, because by unceasing attendance, as though by caressing, he confirms that person in wicked consent.

When the material has been fitted, he constructs the structure because, after common consent has been obtained, he comes to the act of shamefulness. Thus these four—choosing, cutting, fitting, constructing—are the four little supports of the seat. That seat becomes a seat of pestilence when a wicked deed comes into the open and corrupts more people.

## CHAPTER II. On those who have the law in their heart, but not their heart in the law

“But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night” (Ps. 1).

Many have the law in their heart, but do not have their heart in the law. Those have the law in their heart who know the truth; those have their heart in the law who love the truth. But those who have the law in their heart, not their heart in the law, carry the law but are not carried by the law. They are burdened, not helped, because knowledge, where charity is absent, weighs down rather than lifts up. [Col. 0590A]

## CHAPTER III. On the four kinds of persons subject to God’s judgment

“Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the council of the just” (Ps. 1).

There are four classes of persons: those judged and condemned; those to be judged and condemned; those judged and saved; and those to be judged and saved. Those judged and condemned are those whose condemnation is already certain; those to be judged and condemned, those whose condemnation is not yet certain; those judged and saved are those whose salvation is already certain; those to be judged and saved, those whose salvation is not yet certain. [Col. 0590B]

## CHAPTER IV. On Christ’s eternal generation

“The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2).

When the Father begot the Word coeternal with himself, he then said: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” In the phrase “You are my Son” he said that he had begotten him; and because the begetting does not pass away, “today.”

## CHAPTER V. That by nature a human being was created in God’s image, but can rejoice in the Lord by grace alone

[Col. 0590C] “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4): this is reason. “You have given gladness in my heart” (ibid.): this is inspiration. The light is marked by nature; you have given gladness by grace. Therefore he says “upon us,” not “upon me,” because nature is common; and afterwards, “in my heart,” not “in our heart,” because grace is particular.

## CHAPTER VI. That God destroys a human being in two ways

“You will destroy all who speak falsehood” (Ps. 5).

God destroys a human being in two ways: first, when a person departs from God by sinning; second, when God rejects a person in judgment.

## CHAPTER VII. That here sin ought to be expelled through confession, lest one be compelled into judgment for shame

[Col. 0590D] “According to the multitude of their impieties, cast them out” (Ps. 5).

The sinner is within so long as he conceals his iniquity; but when he confesses his iniquity, he comes out. Therefore God now calls Lazarus and commands him to come forth, because he admonishes the sinner not to be ashamed to reveal his sin. But whoever refuses voluntarily to come out in this life will be cast out unwillingly in the life to come. For one who here neglects to reveal his sin for salvation will there, whether willing or unwilling, have that sin revealed to his shame, as is said in another psalm: “I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. 49). [Col. 0591A]

## CHAPTER VIII. On the cause of litigation between God, humanity, and the devil

“Because you have accomplished my judgment and my cause” (Ps. 9).

Three come into the case: the devil, the human being, and God. The devil is convicted of having wronged God because he both fraudulently led away God’s servant—that is, the human being—and held him by force. The human being is convicted of having wronged God because he both despised God’s command and, placing himself under another’s hand, inflicted upon God the loss of his own servitude.

Likewise, the devil is convicted of having wronged the human being because he first deceived him by promising good things and afterwards injured him by bringing evils upon him. Therefore the devil holds the human being unjustly, but the human being is held justly: the devil never deserved to oppress a human being subject to himself, but the human being deserved through his own fault to be oppressed by him.

For although the human being did not know that what the devil promised was false, he nevertheless knew that, even if it were true, he ought not to desire it against the will of the Creator. Therefore the human being is justly subject to the devil insofar as his own fault is concerned, but unjustly insofar as the devil’s fraud is concerned. [Col. 0591B]

If, therefore, a human being had such an advocate that the devil could be brought to trial by the advocate’s power, he would rightly dispute the devil’s lordship, because the devil had no just cause for claiming a right over the human being. But no such advocate could be found except God. Yet God was unwilling to take up the human being’s case because he was still angry with the human being for his fault.

It was therefore necessary first for the human being to appease God, and then, with God’s advocacy, confidently enter litigation with the devil. But he could not reasonably appease God unless he both restored the loss he had inflicted and made satisfaction for his contempt. Yet the human being had nothing with which worthily to compensate God for the loss inflicted: if he gave anything from irrational creation in return for rational creation taken away, it would be less. Nor could he give a human being for a human being, because he had taken away the just and innocent person and found no one except a sinner.

Thus the human being found nothing by which he could appease God, because whether he gave what was his or gave himself, it would not be worthy compensation. God, therefore, seeing that the human being could not escape the yoke of condemnation by his own power, had mercy on him. First, by mercy alone, he freely came before him, in order then to free him through justice. That is: because the human being had in himself no justice by which to escape, God through mercy gave the human being justice. [Col. 0591D]

For the human being’s deliverance would not have been wholly rational unless it occurred justly on both sides: that is, as God had justice in demanding the human being, so the human being had to possess justice in escaping. But the human being could never have possessed that justice unless God bestowed it upon him through mercy. Therefore, so that God might be appeased by the human being, God freely gave the human being what the human being should return to God as a debt.

He gave a human being to the human being, whom the human being might give back for a human being; and, in order that the recompense might be worthy, this man was not only equal to the former but greater. Therefore, in order that a human being might be given back for a human being, a human being greater than a human being was made: God became man for the human being; and man gave himself to man, that he might receive himself from the human being.

God the Son was incarnate, and Christ, God and man, was given to human beings, as Isaiah says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Mighty God,” etc. (Isa. 9). Therefore, that Christ was given to the human being was God’s mercy; that Christ was given back by the human being was human justice. [Col. 0592B]

For in Christ’s birth God was justly appeased toward the human being, because such a man was found for humanity—a man who, as stated, was not only equal but greater than humanity. Therefore at Christ’s birth the angels announce peace to the world, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2).

But it still remained for the human being: as he had appeased wrath by restoring the loss, so also, by making satisfaction for contempt, he had to become worthy to escape punishment. This could not fittingly occur unless he voluntarily and obediently underwent a punishment which he did not owe, so that he might become worthy to be delivered from the punishment which he had earned through disobedience.

But the sinful human being could not pay this punishment, because whatever punishment he underwent, he would endure it deservedly and justly on account of the guilt of the first contempt. Therefore, in order that the human being might justly escape the punishment owed, it was necessary that one should undergo punishment for humanity who owed no punishment. But none such could be found except Christ.

Therefore Christ, both by being born, paid the human being’s debt to the Father, and by dying expiated the human being’s guilt. Thus, since he endured for humanity the death which he did not owe, humanity might justly escape, for his sake, the death which it did owe; and the devil would no longer find ground for accusation, because the devil himself ought not to rule over humanity, and humanity had become worthy to be freed. [Col. 0592C]

Accordingly, he accomplished both our judgment and our cause: our cause, because by being born he paid the debt to the Father for us and by dying expiated guilt; our judgment, because, descending into hell and breaking the gates of death, he led out free the captivity that was held there. [Col. 0592D]

## CHAPTER IX. How God is said to have a right and a left eye
His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the children of men (Ps. IX). God is said to have eyes because he continually beholds the ways of the good and the evil. And he has, as it were, a left eye when he foresees the wicked for condemnation; but he looks with the right when, in his foreknowledge, he ordains the good for salvation. These eyes have eyelids, which are sometimes opened. When in this life God grants prosperity to the good and adversity to the evil, he raises, as it were, his eyelids, because by present recompense he makes manifest that he sees human deeds, good and evil. But when [Col. 0593A] he permits adversity to befall the good and prosperity the evil, he closes, as it were, his eyelids, because, while he recompenses the merits of individuals in seemingly dissimilar ways, he appears to disregard what he has seen. These eyelids examine the children of men, because through this God tests the human heart: by sometimes recompensing human merits similarly, sometimes dissimilarly, yet always justly.

Again: His eyes look upon the poor. There are two: a shepherd and a wolf; both look upon the sheep, the one in order to snatch it away, the other in order to guard it. Again: His eyes look upon the poor; the wolf lies in ambush in hiding, like a lion in his den. He lies in ambush in order to seize the poor person (ibid.). His eyes—that is, the shepherd’s—look upon the poor in order to preserve him. On this side is the wolf, on that side the shepherd. The sheep is the poor person in the middle [Col. 0593B]; the shepherd is God, the wolf the devil. Here is the shepherd, there the wolf. They never meet from one and the same side. If the shepherd is at the right, the wolf is at the left: He is at my right hand, that I may not be moved (Ps. XV). If the shepherd is at the left, then let the devil stand at his right; and the wolf watches: when the shepherd withdraws, the wolf approaches; when the shepherd returns, the wolf retreats. The devil shall go out before his feet. Yet every judgment proceeds from the sheep. The fearful [or swollen/proud] one is abandoned; the fearful one is visited: abandoned, lest it presume; visited, lest it despair. Hence: Do not turn away in anger from your servant (Ps. XXVI). And: Hear me speedily, O Lord (Ps. CI); My spirit has failed (Ps. LXXVI).

## CHAPTER X. That speech exists in voice and deed; who has vanity in the heart, who speaks it, and who speaks it to his neighbour.

[Col. 0593C]

They have spoken vain things, every one to his neighbour (Ps. XI). Speech may fittingly be understood not only as vocal utterance, but also as action, because the evidence of the heart is not merely the voice but also the performance of a deed. Now we know that everything which passes away is vain. The person who loves transient things has vanity in his heart. The person who, labouring without restraint for this passing life, shows by his very zeal and action that he loves it, speaks vanity. But the person who by his example encourages his neighbour to seek transient things speaks vanity to his neighbour.

## CHAPTER XI. Who have the fear of God and believe in Christ, and how Christ is known as the way of peace.

[Col. 0593D]

They have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes (Ps. I). Those unwilling to have the fear of God before their eyes cannot recognize the way of peace. But if they had the fear of God before their eyes, they would undoubtedly recognize the way of peace. Thus the Lord himself, speaking to the Jews in the Gospel: If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me (John V). For what should we understand in Moses but the law, and in the law but the fear of God? And what do we receive in Christ but grace and truth? What, then, is it to believe Moses except faithfully to observe the commands of the law which has been received? And to observe the command is truly to fear God, as it is written: Whoever fears God neglects nothing (Eccles. VII). And as it is said in [Col. 0594A] the Psalm: Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he takes great delight in his commandments.

But what is it to believe Christ, except to confess and acknowledge the grace and truth of God—that is, that the redemption of the human race and the salvation of all are accomplished and established through Christ—and to receive this with love and devotion? In this grace, indeed, the way of peace is recognized, because an entrance of reconciliation with God is opened to humankind. Therefore let it be said to the obstinate and transgressors of the law, who did not have the fear of God before their eyes and therefore did not recognize the way of peace—that is, Christ—let it be said: If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me. As though he said: If you had kept the law, you would understand the truth. If you had listened to the teacher, you would know the Saviour.

I know [Col. 0594B] indeed that the one not enlightened by me cannot know me as God. And therefore you do not believe, because you have not been enlightened by me. Yet I do not enlighten you to know me for this reason: I know your obstinacy and transgression; and it is fitting that you should now fail to recognize me when present, whose commands, formerly sent to you through Moses, you were unwilling to keep. Let those hear this who do not keep God’s commands and yet presume that they can comprehend God’s mysteries. Let them hear what is said: If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me. This is plainly to say: Obtain experience of virtue, if you wish to attain knowledge of truth. For one cannot perfectly know the good who has not [Col. 0594C] yet attained an experience of the good.

This is the same as what is said elsewhere: Search the Scriptures (John V). It is as though each person were told: “Experience and learn; do and understand.” That is, by doing, rather than by speaking, you investigate more effectively; once you have experienced, then you judge faithfully. Therefore, if we desire to know things not yet known, we must not be sluggish in those things which we already know. Whoever does not preserve the fear of God by doing the good that he can, is not only unworthy to receive greater gifts, but even deserves to be deprived of what he has already received. If, then, the Jews could not recognize the way of peace—that is, Christ—because they were unwilling to have the fear of God before their eyes in keeping the commandments, it is plainly shown to us that through the experience [Col. 0594D] of good work one comes most clearly to knowledge of the truth.

But we still wish to adapt the testimony of the Psalmist, set forth above, to a moral interpretation, in order to show that it contains an order not only of doctrine but also of discipline. “They have not known,” he says, “the way of peace. There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Ps. XIII). The soul has two ways, one good and the other evil, along which it walks not with the steps of its feet but with those of its desires. One way is charity; the other, cupidity. Cupidity is love of this world; charity is love of God. The soul which loves God runs toward God by certain steps of love through charity. Carnal affection [Col. 0595A] draws through cupidity the soul which loves this world toward what it loves.

Charity, however, is the way of peace, because the mind running in love of its Creator finds nothing to wound it. Cupidity is not the way of peace, because it distracts the mind through many labours and pains. The gates of this way are the bodily senses, because through them desire leads the soul outward. But among these gates sight is first, because the eyes are leaders of the other senses and in nearly every action precede them toward desire. For when you wish to taste, you first stretch out your hand to take; but before taking, you direct your sight in order to choose. In this order the first sin also was committed: The woman saw the tree, that it was beautiful to look upon and pleasant for eating; and she took of its fruit and ate (Jer. III). First she saw [Col. 0595B], then she touched and took, and finally tasted. Had she not seen, she would neither have touched nor tasted.

See how sight was before the other senses in desire, even in the act of seeing itself. For when it is said, “she saw that it was beautiful to look upon,” behold desire to see in sight. When it is said, “and pleasant,” behold desire to touch in sight. When it is said, “for eating,” behold desire to taste in sight. Therefore sight not only precedes the other senses in desire, but all the other senses in the desire of seeing precede themselves; and, in a manner, everything is first performed in sight through delight which is afterward committed in action by the other senses. Therefore the Lord said: Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matt. [Col. 0595C] V), because the mind, in seeing, delightfully imagines everything which subsequently delights it in acting.

If, therefore, the gate of the eyes is well fortified, the whole inner city of our heart will be at peace from the assaults of vices. But no guardian can be better for this gate than the fear of the Lord: it fastens and restrains the slippery carnal mind in the resolve of discipline, lest it return to former delights. The Psalmist desired this guard when he said: Fasten my flesh with your fear (Ps. CXVIII). And Wisdom admonished us to possess this guard when, prescribing the rule of discipline to one entering upon the pursuit of virtue, it said: My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear [Col. 0595D], and prepare your heart for trials (Ecclus. II). Stand in fear, lest the blandishments of the flesh seduce you. Prepare your heart for trials, lest adversities that come upon you break you. Restrain the wantonness of the flesh through fear; overcome the pressure of tribulation through patience.

For these are the two things especially accustomed to shake the resolve of beginners: the distress of pressing temptations and the memory of past pleasures. The former, when they come with greater than usual severity, often cast down the faint-hearted through impatience. The latter, when they return with their habitual wicked sweetness, lead the unwary away through lack of self-control. Therefore let us place the fear of the Lord before our eyes as the best guardian, so that, since it guards the leaders of the other senses, the whole body of consequent actions [Col. 0596A] may remain sound and whole.

Because Ish-bosheth was unwilling to set this guard over his household, he received a mortal wound in the groin (II Kings IV). Thus whoever neglects to fortify his senses with the fear of the Lord has the life of his soul extinguished by a suddenly creeping-in delight of the flesh. Rightly, therefore, it is said: They have not known the way of peace; there is no fear of God before their eyes. For whoever does not restrain his outward senses from the delight of the flesh through fear of God will be unable to taste the sweetness of inward love.

## CHAPTER XII. What God, having become man, found in the world that was his own; what belonged to the devil; and how each contended for his own right.

The measuring-lines have fallen to me in splendid places; indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me (Ps. XV). God came into the world through a human being in order to redeem the world, and found the devil ruling over the entire world. God, visiting the world through a human being, came unto his own (John I); and the human being through God, not loving the world, had nowhere to lay his head. God as man commanded the elements in this world, and God as man said that he did not have his kingdom from this world. Thus, in one respect all belonged to God, and in another respect all belonged to the devil. All belonged to God because he had made it; all belonged to the devil because he possessed it. God had created the world in the beginning, and the devil had possessed the world from the beginning.

Therefore a contest arose for God and a contest for the devil. God said that he ought to receive back what was his; the devil said that after so long a period of neglect he ought not to be deprived of his possession. God said that the devil had fraudulently seized what belonged to another and held it by force; the devil said that God had neither opposed him when he took it nor ever demanded it back when he held it. God said that, if he wished, he had power to use force to recover what was his; the devil said that he ought not to use force against justice. God said that it would not be just if he allowed what he had created in love to perish; the devil said that it would not be unjust if he did not restore what had perished of its own accord. God said that he wished to show mercy by his own kindness; the devil said that he was unwilling to suffer loss through another’s power. God said that it was just for those repenting of sin to be received unto salvation; the devil said [Col. 0596D] that it was not just for those persisting in sin to be compelled to salvation. God said that he had come not to compel the unwilling but to help the willing; the devil said that, for the present and for a time, he would patiently endure the loss of those who were willing, provided he retained the unwilling. God said that he would not lay a hand on what belonged to another for Gehenna if what belonged to him were restored; the devil said that he was prepared to restore what belonged to another if his own were not taken away. God said that he could reject no one from mercy; the devil said that he could not patiently endure it if he should lose everyone. God said that he urged people to withdraw wholly from another’s jurisdiction; the devil said that he requested that, at least in reverence for his former dominion, he not be denied some partial respite. God said that, since he had first chosen the more valuable things, he would afterwards concede the more worthless to him; the devil said that if he could not have a choice by right, he would at least make a division. [Col. 0597A] God said that by the privilege of lordship he claimed power over both; the devil said that, since he could no longer do more, he asked nothing by right but only by permission. God said that he would permit him only so much as could satisfy even the hunger of an avaricious man; the devil said that he would not accept so little that he would not desire more, if possible.

After saying this, God ordered measuring-cords to be stretched out for the division. He found green and well-watered places in the low valleys, smaller in extent but greater in value, and commanded these to be set apart on the other side. But he ordered the deserts and dry places in the fields and high mountains—broad, open to view, great in extent, and of little value—to be assigned to the other portion. Then he commanded the devil to be present; and, as he stood there, said to him: “Lest you should perhaps be able to complain either of violence by the judge or greed by the giver, whatever your eye sees I shall give you.” Then the devil, who beholds every lofty thing and cannot look upon lowly things, lifted his eyes and looked at the high mountains, projecting rocks upon the crags, and spreading deserts; and, glorying as though nearly all had fallen to him, he despised what God had chosen.

Then God, rebuking him and mocking the blindness of the proud one, said: “The measuring-lines have fallen to me in splendid places” (Ps. XV). You praise what you see, and I praise you for what I see. You are below, and therefore your eyes do not range except over what is high and prominent. From above I contemplate how lovely the lowly things are. Indeed, my inheritance is splendid to me (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XIII. What it is always to set the Lord before one’s sight.

[Col. 0597C]

I was setting the Lord always before my sight (Ps. V). One sets the Lord before oneself who, placed in tribulation, has hope in the Lord. For, as it were, to set before oneself is to await future help amid present tribulation. But if, wearied by prolonged waiting, the soul abandons its hope once begun, it turns, as it were, its sight away from the Lord. But the person always sets the Lord before his sight who, established in affliction, trusts that divine help will sometime be present for him and does not abandon his hope once begun until the end.

## CHAPTER XIV. To whom, and when, the Lord and the devil are at the right and at the left.

For he is at my right hand, that I may not be moved (Ps. XV). The Lord is at the left when he grants outward temporal prosperity. The Lord is at the right when he guards the virtues of the soul inwardly. The devil is at the left when he attacks outwardly through adversities. The devil is at the right when he tempts inwardly through vices. Hence Scripture speaks of the reprobate, saying: Let the devil stand at his right hand (Ps. CVIII). For “devil” is interpreted as “flowing downward,” because he fell through pride from the glory of his first condition.

The devil therefore stands at our right when he who fell from heaven, subjecting us to himself through consent to sin, rises up within us. For when we fall, the devil is raised; when we rise, he is cast down. Hence Jeremiah laments, saying: See, O Lord, my affliction, because my enemy [Col. 0598A] has been raised up (Lam. I). This left side is also spoken of in the Gospel: If anyone strikes you on the left cheek, offer him the other also (Matt. V). For one strikes the left cheek when one inflicts outward harm. We offer that person our right cheek if, against outward losses, we set the virtues of the soul, so that we fear outward danger the less as the inward defence in which we trust is the more secure.

## CHAPTER XV. Where fullness of joy is granted.

You will fill me with joy in the presence of your countenance (Ps. XV). In this mortal life we can sometimes rejoice; we cannot be filled with joy, because, although there are some things that make us glad, there are many that make us sad.

## CHAPTER XVI. What God’s right and left hands are, and where delight endures to the end.

[Col. 0598B]

Delights are at your right hand unto the end (Ps. XV). God’s left hand is temporal goods; God’s right hand is eternal goods. In temporal goods there are certain delights, but they do not endure unto the end, because in this life sorrow always follows joy and every delight ends in bitterness. But at God’s right hand delights endure unto the end, because in eternal life neither joys can be changed into sadness nor delights into pain.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the three kinds of those who pray.

Receive my prayer with your ears; it is not from deceitful lips (Ps. XVI). He asks to be heard because he prays not only with his lips but also with his heart. There are three kinds of those who pray: some pray with their lips alone, some with the heart alone, and some with both lips and heart. Those who pray with lips alone are deceitful, because they do not possess in their heart what they utter with their mouth. Those who pray with heart and lips are truthful, because they feel as they speak. Those who pray with heart alone are devout, because they desire their prayer to be heard by God alone.

Therefore, whenever in prayer we utter words, if we think about what we say, we do what we ought. But if we pour forth the words of prayer while turning over in the heart some other matter—even a good matter—we are nevertheless not wholly free from fault, since it is not ordered, provided that we are able to understand what we say. But if a person utters the words of prayer without understanding and is unable to understand what he says, yet says them with good intention, he will not be without fruit. If, however, while praying we think vain thoughts, then—even if we speak truth—we are made vain by thinking vanity. But if, while the mouth speaks truth, obscenity occupies the heart, we are now accounted not only vain but even abominable before God. Yet it is one thing when a person suffers these things unwillingly and another when he delights in them deliberately.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the testing of the very good and the very bad, but not of the mediocre.

You tested me by fire, and iniquity was not found in me (Ps. XVI). The test on the balance is that upper point by which it is weighed to which side the separate weight inclines. Therefore the righteous person is tested by the fire of tribulation, because perfect virtue is recognized in adversity. The thoroughly wicked [Col. 0599A] have already been tested, because through the weight of iniquity they have inclined themselves to the left side. The thoroughly good have been tested, because through the weight of steadfastness and perseverance in virtue they have turned to the right. Those of middling character have not yet been tested, because human judgments cannot yet discern to which side they belong.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the hard ways of this life, and who keep them for the words of God’s lips.

Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways (Ps. XVI). In this present life we are on a way, because through it we pass to another life. But because human weakness cannot remain long in the same condition, we enter upon as many, as it were, ways as the various actions in which we are engaged. And because in this life we can do nothing [Col. 0599B] without labour, we have hard ways, as it were, when walking. But those do not keep these hard ways who seek delight in this life. Those, however, who voluntarily humble and afflict themselves here keep hard ways.

But who can say to God: Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways? What are the words of his lips? The words of our lips are our sins, as it is said in the Psalm: The words of my offences are far from my salvation (ibid.). The words of God’s lips are his commandments. Whoever, conscious of past offences, voluntarily afflicts himself through repentance keeps hard ways because of the words of his own lips. But whoever labours not to transgress God’s commandments and, in order to fulfill his will, does violence to his own wishes, keeps hard ways because of the words of his lips [Col. 0599C]. The former pays a debt; the latter fulfills a command. For God commands a person not to fall; but once he has fallen, God no longer commands, but admonishes him to rise. A command applies only to those who obey; but one who still remains in sin is not obedient. Yet when, through repentance, he returns to obedience, he becomes worthy to receive a command.

## CHAPTER XX. On God’s ways and paths.

Perfect my steps in your paths, that my footprints may not be moved (Ps. XVI). God’s ways are easy commandments. God’s paths are stricter commands, in which few can walk. The person walks in God’s way who does no evil to his neighbour. The person walks in God’s path [Col. 0599D] who loves even one who does him evil. But the person who does not yet know how to walk in the path often departs from the way, because one who has not yet learned to love except the person by whom he is loved is often compelled to abandon charity.

## CHAPTER XXI. What God’s right hand is, who resist it, and how the righteous person desires to be guarded from them.

Guard me from those resisting your right hand, as the pupil of the eye (Ps. XVI). God’s right hand is Christ, because through him God the Father wrought our propitiation. Or God’s right hand is his more excellent works, that is, eternal goods. Therefore those resist God’s right hand who contradict Christ either by believing wrongly or by living wrongly. Those resist God’s right hand who, loving earthly things, disdain to seek eternal goods. From all these [Col. 0600A] the righteous person desires to be guarded, lest, provoked by their evil example, he fall into iniquity.

But how does he wish to be guarded? Hear how: “as the pupil,” he says, “of the eye.” The one who wishes to be guarded as the pupil of the eye wishes to be guarded with great care. The pupil is indeed a small and delicate part of the eye, yet precious. It is carefully guarded because it is greatly guarded. Mystically, the eye of God is the Church of the saints; the pupil of the eye is Christ’s humanity. Through the pupil an animal directs its gaze in order to distinguish things outside; and God the Father gave all judgment to the Son and judges no one except through the Son, distinguishing the righteous from the unrighteous as light from darkness. What, then, does it mean that the righteous person wishes to be guarded as the pupil of the eye? Christ suffered many adversities in this world [Col. 0600B], but through the pressure of tribulation came to the glory of the resurrection. Therefore we ought to pray that we may be guarded like the pupil of the eye: not, of course, that we suffer no evil in this world, but that through present evils we may pass to eternal joys.

## CHAPTER XXII. What are God’s wings, beneath which we are protected.

Protect me under the shadow of your wings (Ps. XVI).

God has two wings: mercy and charity. Through mercy he protects sinners; through charity, the righteous. Thus the person who asks to be protected not under the shadow of one wing but under the shadow of wings acknowledges that in some respects he needs mercy and hopes in other respects to be worthy of love.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What it means to oppose face and side to one who is running.

[Col. 0600C]

From the face of the wicked who have afflicted me (Ps. XVI). The enemy opposes, as it were, his face to us when a perverse delight obstructs the soul as it runs in desire for God. The enemy is at the side when temptation wearies the runner, but perverse delight does not retard him in his course.

## CHAPTER XXIV. What it is to forestall and to trip up.

Arise, O Lord, forestall him and trip him up (Ps. XVI). To forestall belongs to one who is running; to trip up, to one who is wrestling. For the person who tends toward the completion of the work he has undertaken runs, though not with the steps of his feet, yet with the advance of his actions. Therefore the devil ran in Christ’s passion, because he wished to lead to condemnation, through betrayal to suffering, through suffering to death, and through death to condemnation, him whom he believed [Col. 0600D] to be a mere human being. God likewise ran, because he intended to advance him through betrayal to suffering, through suffering to death, and through death to resurrection. Therefore both God and the devil ran; but the devil was forestalled, because he was impeded by divine power lest he could arrive at the end he intended.

“And trip him up,” he says. In Christ’s passion the devil wrestled with God. The devil wrestled outwardly in order to cast him down; God wrestled inwardly in order to sustain him. But the devil was tripped up because, by a certain hidden power and wisdom of God, he was suddenly and unexpectedly overthrown.

## CHAPTER XXV. That Christ’s soul is the sword which cut off a portion from hell.

[Col. 0601A]

Deliver my soul from the wicked man, your sword from the enemies of your hand (Ps. XVI). Christ’s soul is the *framea*, that is, God’s sword, because, when through Christ God redeemed his elect, he cut off, as it were, certain members from the devil’s body. Hence it is said elsewhere: I shall be your death, O death; your bite, O hell (Hos. XIII). For God, as it were, bit hell when, descending to hell, he took some persons from there and left others there. Therefore he says: “Deliver my soul from the wicked man by your sword.” As though he said: “If you do not first preserve the sword with which you are to fight, how will you be able to free those who are to be saved through the sword?”

## CHAPTER XXVI. How our God is our deliverer, refuge, stronghold, strength, God, helper, hope, protector, horn of salvation, receiver, and so forth.

[Col. 0601B]

I will love you, O Lord, my strength: the Lord is my stronghold, my refuge, and my deliverer; my God, my helper, and I shall hope in him; my protector, the horn of my salvation, and my receiver (Ps. XVII). Christ’s humanity speaks in the resurrection: “I will love you, O Lord.” In dangers there is fear; after dangers, love. “I will love you, O Lord.” It adds the causes of love: because you are my strength, because you are my stronghold, because you are my refuge, because you are my deliverer. It recounts them in reverse order, as the mind returns to the very beginning of divine grace. First, deliverer, because he snatched the human being from the devil’s power; then refuge, because he kindly receives for protection the one who distrusts his own strength; then stronghold, [Col. 0601C] so that one standing may not fall; then strength, so that one fighting may conquer. Deliverer through baptism, refuge through repentance, stronghold through patience, strength through victory. See in what order he escaped evil.

Then comes the second verse: how he attained the good. “My God,” because he enlightens through faith. “My helper,” because he helps toward good action. “I shall hope in him,” because he kindles the heart in love for himself. “My protector,” because he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear. “The horn of my salvation,” because he makes us despise even the devil who persecutes us. Finally, “my receiver,” because, when their course is ended, he opens heaven to those who arrive. Strength is signified in a horn. The horn of confusion is pride; the horn of salvation is good confidence.

## CHAPTER XXVII. What the sorrows and snares of death and hell, and the torrents of iniquity, are.

[Col. 0601D]

The sorrows of death surrounded me, and torrents of iniquity troubled me. The sorrows of hell surrounded me; the snares of death came before me (Ps. XVII). The sorrows of death are passibility and mortality. The torrents of iniquity are the vanity of this world. The sorrows of hell are eternal punishment. The snares of death are original guilt. The sorrows of death and the sorrows of hell surrounded humankind because before Christ it could not escape them. The torrents of iniquity troubled it because the vanity of this world impelled human beings toward actual sins. The snares of death came before them, because original guilt was in a human being before that human being could actually commit sin.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How human and divine salvation are bestowed upon a person.

[Col. 0602A]

And you gave me the protection of my salvation (Ps. XVII). Human salvation is health of the flesh; divine salvation is soundness of mind. A human being loves the former; God grants the latter. A human being preserves the former by fleeing hardships; God confirms the latter by bringing hardships upon him—provided, however, that the mind is guarded inwardly, so that it neither rushes into impatience through the harshness endured by the flesh nor grows soft into wantonness through pleasures. Therefore God grants us the protection of his salvation when, while the flesh suffers outwardly, he preserves our soul inwardly unharmed, so that the pressure which the flesh bears outside does not reach inwardly to corrupt the mind.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whom God’s right and left hands receive.

[Col. 0602B]

Your right hand received me (Ps. XVII). God’s left hand is temporal goods; God’s right hand is eternal goods. And it often happens that God more abundantly fills with spiritual goods those whom poverty of temporal possessions constricts outwardly. Thus those who, as it were, fall outwardly through want but are strengthened inwardly by the riches of virtues have been abandoned, as it were, by God’s left hand and received by his right.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the good and evil end, and the discipline of the Lord correcting unto the end.

And your discipline corrected me unto the end (Ps. XVII). There is a certain good end and a certain evil end. The evil end is the depth of sins; the good end is the consummation of virtues. God’s discipline corrects unto the end [Col. 0602C] because it leads even those who have fallen into the depth of sins to the consummation of virtues. O good, O sweet discipline of God! Would that we knew it! Would that we received it! Would that we endured it! For it enables us to see it, desire it, grasp it, and hold it.

It consists in three things: commandments, temptations, and scourges. In commandments God tests your obedience; in temptations, your steadfastness; in scourges, your patience. Receive commandments obediently, resist temptations steadfastly, endure scourges patiently. Yet these three—obedience, steadfastness, and patience—cannot be absent from one another, because all are necessary in each. In commandments, you must first receive them obediently [Col. 0602D], then carry them out steadfastly, and finally await the time of recompense patiently.
