In temptations you must be obedient, so that, if perhaps God wishes you to be assailed by an onrush of vices and wearied for a time, you do not resist in pride; steadfast, lest delight cause you to lapse into consent; patient, lest at last you grow weak through the troublesome persistence or insistence of temptation.

We say this particularly because of certain persons of insufficient discernment who, ignorant of the method of spiritual endeavour, desire after the first beginnings of good conduct to be so free from the temptation of vices that, if they perceive themselves assailed even slightly by unlawful delight, they immediately, with a swollen heart and forgetful of their own weakness, murmur against God; and, if they are wearied even a little, enfeebled by the vice of inconstancy and [Col. 0603A] impatience, they incline to consent to iniquity. But these persons do not know how merciful God’s dispensation is: he permits us still to feel in temptation, though unwillingly, evils which we have already abandoned in will, so that what was formerly committed in them when they delighted us may now be expiated in them when they torment us; and so that, mindful of our weakness, while we are always compelled to remember what we were, we may not be puffed up by what we are.

Moreover, when we overcome our evils with such great difficulty, we may fear sinning all the more. Since, therefore, so many benefits result from temptation, whenever we are tempted we ought to receive God’s dispensation obediently, oppose perverse delight steadfastly, and endure the violence of temptation patiently, so that our weariness may be acceptable to us, yet [Col. 0603B] perverse delight may not attain consent.

In scourging, moreover, the person preserves obedience who, even if ignorant of the reason for his own chastisement, nevertheless does not murmur against God. He is steadfast and patient whom neither the weight of tribulation oppresses nor its duration breaks. The first stage of God’s discipline, then, is the keeping of the commandments; the second stage is the battle of temptations. Hence it is clear that those who do not keep God’s commandments have not yet begun to be under God’s discipline. But the one who is not under God’s discipline cannot attain the inheritance of God’s children.

Let no one, therefore, despise God’s discipline: if one is a sinner, it is necessary for correction; if righteous, it is necessary for instruction. Therefore this man, who had received it for correction, affirms that it remains necessary to him for [Col. 0603C] instruction: so that, as one corrected, he has expiated past sins, and, as one instructed, may have caution against future sins. Therefore let him say: Your discipline corrected me unto the end; your discipline itself will teach me (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXI. What is beneath us and what is above us; and whose footprints are not weakened.

You have enlarged my steps beneath me, and my footprints have not been weakened (Ps. XVII). Beneath us is everything transient and perishable; what is eternal is above us. Therefore the mind of the righteous has steps enlarged above itself, because the higher it is directed through contemplation into love of eternal things, the more it is enlarged by desire for the sweetness it has tasted. [Col. 0603D] But when, in thought, it walks beneath itself among transient things, the very burden of its occupation in some fashion constricts it; and it is tightened within itself as often as it is impeded outside by adversities that meet it.

Yet it sometimes happens that a mind inflamed by divine love has enlarged steps even beneath itself: for while it keeps itself wholly within through desire, although it is occupied outwardly in action, no adversity of trouble constricts its freedom. Hence, rightly, when he had said, “You have enlarged my steps beneath me,” he immediately added: “And my footprints have not been weakened.” For when a step is set on slippery ground, even if the foot remains strong, its footprints are nevertheless weakened. So too, whoever has placed even slight confidence in perishing things, although he does not languish through shameful desires, nevertheless does not become stable because what he loves is transient; and when that on which he leans begins to slip, the footprints of the one leaning are at once weakened from their own stability. But when the whole desire of the mind is fixed in eternal things, as though the foot were planted on firm ground, its footprints are not weakened.

## CHAPTER XXXII. What spiritual enemies are, and how we pursue them

I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them; and I shall not turn back until they fail (Ps. XVII). We have certain spiritual enemies who lie in wait for us; the more hidden they are, the more they can harm us. These are fleshly impulses, which arise in our heart and, because they proceed from hidden desires, often deceive the unwary under the appearance of virtues. We surely pursue them when we carefully investigate the very root from which they spring, so that, when we feel them assailing us as an unlawful impulse arises, we immediately strive to discern from what affection it was born and toward what end its appetite tends.

Perhaps how this may be done will be understood more quickly if an example is set forth. For instance, there is someone who, thinking of himself more highly than he ought, suffers from hidden pride. If he should sit among others, either to converse or to give advice, then, because he considers himself uniquely wise, he thinks that he ought to be heard uniquely. But if he perhaps sees others less attentive to his word, [Col. 0604C] and perceives that his counsel is at times rejected, he immediately swells through the vice of impatience and judges that everything done contrary to his own will is done as an injury to himself. And because he believes that they have been stirred to despise him not by reason, but rather by hatred or envy, he now determines altogether to withdraw his conversation from them as from ill-disposed persons. And while he immoderately restrains his tongue from speech, his mind grows cold toward charity.

Therefore, when we feel that we are heard too little, whether we are speaking or giving counsel, and that our heart is perhaps touched by some sudden pain because of this, we ought to restrain the impulse of our mind and earnestly pursue this pain as an enemy leaping out from an ambush at our side. By searching out its hidden lurking-place, from which it came—that is, pride—and the encounter toward which it tends—that is, brotherly hatred—we may, when we see the snares, avoid the danger. The enemy has been overtaken, because, when we foresee the end of a perverse desire, we withdraw the mind from consent. For as we pursue vices by investigating them, so we overtake them by finding them; and we do not turn back until they fail, if we are not slackened from the urgency of good work before the vices are subdued.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On servile fear, the keeping of the divine law, and vain delight; on the earth, the firmament, the eye, and various necessities; and on humility

The Lord is sweet and upright; therefore he will give the law to those who sin in the way (Ps. XXIV). Fear is not servile where the establishment of the law takes place through the choice of the will. First we fear; then we choose the way; then the law is set before us by which we may walk in that way. By keeping the law, we receive a reward: in the present, joy of the soul; in the future, blessedness alike of soul and body. This is what follows: “His soul shall abide in good things”—this concerns the present—“and his seed shall inherit the earth” (ibid.)—this concerns the future.

And he expresses spiritual delights with sufficient elegance when he says: “His soul shall abide in good things.” Whatever is sweet in a fleshly way indeed affords those who enjoy it an experience of its pleasure, but it cannot remain with them long; for while it provokes appetite by its taste, it disappoints desire by passing away. But spiritual delights, which neither pass away when tasted, nor diminish while refreshing, nor produce weariness while satisfying, can remain long with those who enjoy them. It follows:

His seed shall inherit the earth. He shall receive as an inheritance in the future the land of the living, in return for his good works, which are signified by seed. Or the flesh may be understood by “earth”: whoever exercises it in works of virtue in the present will receive it in the future immortal and incapable of suffering. But how will he arrive there? The Lord is the firm support of those who fear him, and his covenant that it may be revealed to them (ibid.). He promises a reward to those who conquer and grants help to those who fight. The reward is such because God’s covenant—that is, his attested promise—is that he himself will be revealed to the one who sees him. The help is such because the Lord is a firm support—that is, a protection—to those who fear him.

Therefore, secure concerning the promise, I run with confidence. My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will pull my feet out of the snare (ibid.). The eye of actions is intention. He always has his eyes toward the Lord who, by intention, directs to the love of God everything that he does. The feet of such a person are indeed pulled out of the snare, because an action whose source is love of God cannot be evil. For the path of actions is run without danger when the intention of the mind is governed by charity as its guide.

But who can always look toward God unless God always looks toward him? For the love of God both awakens human love by going before it and preserves it by following it. This is what follows:

Look upon me (ibid.); as though he said: “That I may be able to love you, love me; and that I may be worthy of your love, have mercy on me” (ibid.), by forgiving my sins. “For I am alone and poor” (ibid.). Therefore look upon me, because I am alone; therefore have mercy, because I am poor. An only child is loved more; a poor person is pitied more. “The troubles of my heart are multiplied; deliver me from my necessities” (ibid.). What is your poverty? “The troubles of my heart are multiplied.” Bodily affliction is not dangerous when the constancy of the mind is not broken. But when pain touches the inmost parts, there is greater danger, even if outward tribulation is absent.

“Deliver me from my necessities” (ibid.). There are many necessities in which good people are endangered; perhaps we shall understand them better if we distinguish them. The necessity of the saints is twofold: one which they endure within, the other without; one from their neighbors, the other from themselves. So long as they live in this corruptible flesh, they cannot wholly avoid the troubles and temptations arising from corruptible flesh. These carry such danger along with toil that they must be felt daily; yet no one can consent to them without grave loss.

There is another necessity of the good: while they live among evil people whom they cannot avoid, their life is afflicted by a kind of daily persecution arising from those persons’ wicked conduct. They must endure them in such a way that they neither hate people because of their iniquity nor become partners in iniquity because of love for people. But no one can do this without humility and labor: humility, lest through pride he separate himself from the fellowship of vanity and, while scorning to associate with the wicked, swell more ruinously as though because of a singular righteousness; labor, that, while he does not abandon their company, he may continually strive, as far as he can, to flee their manner of life. This is what follows: “See my humility and my labor” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That God’s mercy and truth are necessary for penitents

For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been well-pleased in your truth (Ps. XXV). God’s mercy is that by which he spares; his truth, that by which he corrects. Through mercy he does not reject penitents from pardon; through truth, in punishing sins, he regards the cause, not the person. Therefore whoever desires to attain salvation must not despise these two remedies of God’s healing. For without mercy he does not obtain forgiveness; without truth he is not amended.

There are some who, while by a rash presumption seek to have their faults forgiven by God through mercy, refuse patiently to endure the scourges of divine correction. And if they perhaps learn that they have suffered any adversities for their sins, they immediately raise themselves by the stamp of pride; and they judge God’s mercy to be less necessary in proportion as they suppose themselves more fully cleansed at the divine judgment by their own doing. Let us hear what this man says against them. “Your mercy,” he says, “is before my eyes, and I have been well-pleased [Col. 0606D] in your truth” (ibid.). As though he said: “I see that your mercy is necessary for me everywhere; yet I not only do not reject the strokes of your correction, by which you strictly punish my sins, but gladly receive them; indeed, I recognize that your mercy is not absent even in them.”

“I have been well-pleased,” he says, “in your truth” (ibid.). Elegantly spoken, praiseworthily spoken, most worthy of imitation: “I have been well-pleased in your truth.” As though he said: “I please myself only in your truth, because what displeases you in me, I myself also condemn. I please myself in your truth because, while you pursue my sins by scourging, you make me glad through love of correction. For why should I not please myself in your truth, when I had previously pleased myself wickedly in my own falsehood? For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been well-pleased in your truth.”

## CHAPTER XXXV. On knowledge and love of truth

That I may see the delight of the Lord and visit his temple (Ps. XXVI). To see the delight of the Lord is to know truth; to visit his temple is to love truth.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the tabernacle of God

For he has hidden me in his tabernacle (Ps. XXVI). The tabernacle of God is the Catholic Church, in which the faithful labor and keep watch, prepared to fight in a kind of spiritual warfare against the powers of the air. In this tabernacle God hides those in whom, by inspiring the love of quiet, he makes them seek seclusion from the noise of this world. But those who refuse to live quietly in a place of quiet are not protected in the hidden place of the tabernacle.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. That God is the strength and refuge of those who fight

For you are my strength and my refuge (Ps. XXX). He seems to speak contradictory things. For if he fears, how does he say that he possesses strength? And if he does not fear, why does he seek refuge? But the human mind, placed between hope and fear, when it considers the strength of its helper, confidently presumes victory and willingly challenges the enemy. But when it calls its own weakness to mind, fearing defeat, it seeks refuge.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the vanity of temporal things

[Col. 0607C]

You hate those who observe vanities in vain (Ps. XXX). This is the voice of a righteous person despising present happiness. Above, he had commended his spirit to God; and as if you now asked what he wished to be done with the flesh, he replies that he has no concern for the flesh, because all flesh is vanity. For even those who guard it with every care and diligence by loving it unlawfully and excessively cannot preserve it from corruption. God surely hates them because, while they love a corruptible thing too much, they do not rise to the love of the incorruptible God.

“You hate,” he says, “those who observe vanities in vain.” Well said: “in vain.” For although we seek transient things for necessity, we must never love the flesh for excess; and the flesh destined to die should not be cherished in luxuries, but chiefly defended from those inconveniences that seem less conducive to the soul’s salvation.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Reproof of luxury, avarice, and pride

The Lord scatters the counsels of the nations; moreover, he reproves the thoughts of the peoples, and reproves the counsels of princes (Ps. XXXII). By “nations” sinners are understood; by “peoples,” fools; by “princes,” the proud. The counsel of the nations is the lust of the flesh; the thought of the peoples is the lust of the eyes; the counsel of princes is the pride of life. God reproves all these because the world passes away, and its lust. Yet the peoples fittingly have “thoughts,” not “counsel,” because fools are signified by peoples.

## CHAPTER XL. That the hidden enemies of the righteous are reserved for judgment, while manifest enemies are sometimes punished even in this life

[Col. 0608A]

Judge, O Lord, those harming me; overcome those attacking me (Ps. XXXIV). Those who harm are persons who lie in wait with a purpose of malice. Those who attack are persons who persecute openly. Therefore the righteous man asks only that his hidden enemies be judged—that is, reserved for future judgment—but that the manifest enemies be overcome—that is, punished even in this life—so that their manifest punishment may draw others back from iniquity, whom their malice had previously encouraged toward iniquity by example.

For this reason almighty God often avenges the public injuries of his servants even in this life: that it may be openly shown how great a worth righteousness has with him, and that this may kindle others to the love of righteousness—that the very author of righteousness makes it manifest that he loves it so greatly.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the weapons of wisdom and the shield of patience

Take up weapons and a shield, and rise to help me (Ps. XXXIV). We fight with weapons; we are covered by a shield. For the world fights against the elect in two ways, by word and by sword. We overcome the word of falsehood through wisdom; we resist the sword of adversity through patience. Thus in wisdom we receive weapons, and in patience a shield. But why is it said to God, “Take up weapons and a shield,” unless because he who fights in us arms us against our adversaries? For just as we have received his gifts from him, so without him we cannot use his gifts for salvation.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the manifest and hidden snares of the devil

[Col. 0608C]

Delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the destitute and poor from those who plunder him (Ps. XXXIV). The devil oppresses some by open temptation; he seduces others by hidden snares. Thus in Holy Scripture the devil is sometimes represented by a lion, sometimes by a dragon. By the lion his open confidence is signified; by the dragon, his hidden cunning. Accordingly, the Psalmist, expressing these two kinds of temptations, says: “Delivering the needy from the hand of those stronger than he, the destitute and poor from those who plunder him.”

For who is needy except one who does not possess the riches of virtues? And who is poor except one who has already deserved to receive certain gifts of virtue but has not yet reached the perfection of virtue? The hand of those stronger oppresses the needy, but the hand of plunderers afflicts the poor. For the ancient enemy violently subjects to himself, through consent to iniquity, those who are fortified by no virtue; but from those who have already begun to gather some goods of spiritual gain, he steals the gifts of virtues by hidden plunder. Thus, for those whom he destroys by open savagery he is a robber; for those whom he deceives by hidden fraud he is a thief. Hence the former need strength, that they may conquer their openly attacking enemy; the latter need vigilance, that they may avoid the enemy lying in wait secretly.

Therefore, when divine mercy preserves some by strengthening them against the enemy’s open savagery, and others by enlightening them through vigilance against his hidden snares, what else does it do but deliver the needy from the hand of those stronger than he and the poor from plunderers, so that the former may escape domination and the latter may avoid loss?

## CHAPTER XLIII. That the temporal prosperity of the wicked is testimony for the elect of eternal happiness

Unrighteous witnesses rose up; they questioned me concerning things I did not know (Ps. XXXIV). All unrighteous persons who prefer temporal goods to eternal ones, when they prosper in this life, rise as though in testimony against the elect. For while, by their very happiness, they bear witness about visible things not by speaking but by prospering, they endeavor to refute the judgment of the good concerning eternal and invisible goods. Hence he rightly says: “They questioned me concerning things I did not know.” The wicked question the good concerning present happiness because, since it is sweet to them, they wonder why the good do not incline themselves toward desiring it. But because this happiness is bitter, not sweet, to the good, whatever the wicked offer in praise of it is not known by the good through experience.

## CHAPTER XLIV. That the righteousness of the good is hidden for a time, until it is brought forth for judgment concerning its reward

And he shall bring forth your righteousness as the light, and your judgment as the noonday (Ps. XXXIV). The righteousness of the good is now hidden, because they strive to be justified where they cannot be seen by people. And although in them the example of good work already shines, the power of intention is nevertheless hidden. But in the future their righteousness is brought forth as light, because those who now hide their good works from human praise will, when the Judge comes, safely glory in eternal brightness on their account.

Thus it is also said in another psalm: “It is vain for you to rise before the light” (Ps. CXXVI), that is, to be exalted before the brightness of future judgment; “but rise after you have sat down” (ibid.), because your exaltation there will then be fruitful if you have first, of your own will, humbled yourselves for God in the exile of this life. It follows: “And your judgment as the noonday” (Ps. XXXIV). The righteousness of the good is the work of virtue which they do; their judgment is the reward of virtue which they choose. Therefore God brings forth the righteousness of the saints when he reveals the works of virtue which they performed; he brings forth their judgment when he reveals what reward of good work they chose. Therefore righteousness is brought forth as light, but judgment as noonday—that is, clear light—because every brightness of good work is less than the brightness of eternal recompense.

## CHAPTER XLV. On beneficial submission to God and rightly waiting for him

[Col. 0609D]

Be subject to the Lord, and pray to him (Ps. XXXVI). Here a perfect pattern of life is prescribed for us. Hear, then, O human being, what is said to you: “Be subject to the Lord, and pray to him.” First be subject, lest by acting wrongly you despise his commands. Then be subject, that you may not presume upon your own strength for doing good. For even one who presumes that he can do anything by his own virtue refuses to be subject to God.

“But,” you say to me, “if this belongs to obedience, that I understand that nothing comes from myself, why do I strive in vain? I will rather rest and wait for the Lord to do what belongs to him.” You have spoken very well. Wait for the Lord—but see how you wait. Mountains also wait, and human beings wait; but mountains do so in one way, human beings in another. Mountains wait by enduring; human beings ought to wait by desiring. Mountains wait for rain, human beings for grace; mountains, lest they dry up; human beings, lest they perish. As is read in the psalm: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me” (Ps. XXXIX). Whoever waits by enduring but does not wait by desiring does not wait while waiting. But whoever perseveres and desires, that person waits while waiting.

Therefore wait, and do not merely wait, but wait while waiting: that is, persevere in desiring, and desire in persevering. You will not be disappointed of your desire, just as he was not disappointed who waited while waiting for the Lord. For he says: “Waiting, I waited for the Lord, and he attended to me. And he heard my prayers; he brought me out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth” (ibid.). See, therefore, how he waited. He waited with prayers; he waited with desire. And what he then did, he now commands you to do. For after he had said, “Be subject to the Lord,” he immediately added, “and pray to him,” so that you may both be subject to God, not presuming upon yourself, and pray, seeking his aid.

For what else is praying to God but always looking with a humble and devout mind toward his mercy? He did not tell you, “Pray to him for this or that,” but merely, “Pray to him,” because he who knows your need even when you do not speak requires from you nothing but a good disposition. Therefore, when you pray, let it be sweet to you to consider whom rather than what you ask; and he whom you ask will provide whatever you ought to ask. As the Psalmist likewise testifies in another psalm: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will pull my feet out of the snare” (Ps. XXIV).

## CHAPTER XLVI. On four kinds of human beings in respect of wounds and scars; on true wisdom and the memory of the past

My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my folly (Ps. XXXVII). To one considering the force of this verse, what has so often been proved by suffering cannot now be unknown as he reads. But would that either experience had not given me knowledge, or, if I could not have known otherwise, that this knowledge itself had rather not been given. But if this was necessary, and I could not be instructed without a strong hand, would that now at least my knowledge might so give me wisdom that the experience of past pains might restrain me from future iniquity. But because I see that I have so often acted foolishly after experiencing evils, I still dread those very tastes of bitterness.

Nevertheless I shall say it—and not without pain: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my folly.” Although the exposition of these words is not necessary for me, since many more happily do not know it, it ought not to be wholly passed over for their instruction. “My scars,” he says, “have become putrid and corrupt.” Four kinds of human beings present themselves here to a careful observer.

The first are those who have never been wounded. The second are those who have been perfectly healed after wounds. The third are those whose wounds have indeed closed over, but scars still remain—that is, marks of wounds. The fourth are those in whom the wounds themselves are still gaping and have not yet begun to close. Therefore, if we understand sins by wounds, those who remain in the desire for sin have, as it were, open wounds. But those who abandon sin and yet have not been wholly cleansed by satisfaction from the guilt of sin still have, as it were, certain marks of wounds remaining in them. But from those who, after perpetrating crimes, both abandon the inclination to sin and close over the guilt of sin by full satisfaction, even the traces of wounds have departed.

Such was Saint Paul, who after so many evils said: “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. IV). For he could find in himself not even the marks of past wounds, since his conscience did not accuse him of former wickedness.

These are followed by those who, although they cannot lead a life without sin, have nevertheless never received the wound of a criminal fault. The first kind is that of sinners; the second, that of penitents; the third, that of those corrected through penitence; the fourth, that of those not corrupted through iniquity. The first are sick; the second have turned toward health; the third are healed; the fourth are healthy. From these things it can sufficiently be gathered to what kind of people this person belongs who laments that his scars have returned to corruption. For he had already begun to repent, and had already abandoned sin in will; but the guilt of sin had not yet been fully healed in him, and before he reached the complete healing of the wound, he was corrupted by a repetition of iniquity.

Hence it is rightly said first, “They have become putrid,” and then added, “My scars have become corrupt.” For perverse desires first return to the mind, and so the closed scars in some manner rot inwardly. Then, when the evil will is allowed to proceed as far as action, the scars themselves become corrupt as though through an excess of discharge. The cause of corruption is also explained when it is said: “Because of my folly.” A wise person is so called from *sapere*, “to have taste,” not one who perceives flavors with the palate of the mouth, but one who comprehends truth by the judgment of the mind. Hence even a heart devoid of truth may not improperly be called foolish.

It should be noted, however, that not every knowledge of truth is properly called wisdom, but only that which is acquired not by hearing alone but through the experience of things themselves. For we know what we have experienced in a more familiar and more perfect way than what we have heard; and experience completes the knowledge of truth which teaching begins in us. Nature herself, instructing us through things, has also taught that we judge the quality of anything more perfectly through experience of its opposite. For we embrace every good more pleasantly and delightfully when, wearied after long misery, we breathe again.

For this reason we love God’s mercy all the more in our deliverance, the more sharply the misery from which we have been rescued is tasted close at hand. And when we are sometimes abandoned, we learn through tribulation better how strictly grace ought to have been held, grace which perhaps we loved less in a time of peace. Therefore Scripture, admonishing us in one place, says: “My son, in the time of evils do not forget good things; and in the time of good things do not forget evils” (Ecclus. XI). For the memory of good things in a time of tribulation raises the mind through hope; and the memory of evils in a time of prosperity makes it cautious in guarding itself. And when, having tasted each in turn, it has come to despise both, neither does adversity cast it down through despair nor does prosperity dissolve the mind through empty joy.

For this reason Moses says to the people of Israel in rebuke: “A nation without counsel and without prudence. Would that they were wise, and understood, and foresaw their last things!” (Deut. XXXII). Since they could neither recognize God’s present benefits nor foresee their own future dangers, they had, as it were, no taste of prudence upon the palate of the mind.

Therefore there are two things which must always have taste for us: the evils which we have escaped, and the grace of God which we have obtained. For when a foolish mind does not remember the toil of evil pleasures, if it is at any time struck by temptation, it does not fear to repeat those same pleasures. Just as a woman oppressed by the distress of childbirth abominates the pleasure of fleshly desire, but when the memory of pain has left her mind she again desires the enticements of the flesh and is carried with all eagerness toward experiencing them, because she does not remember how much pain is mixed with them. For if the pain which follows evil pleasure had a true savor in memory, the unbridled mind would by no means be so drawn toward its appetite.

Likewise, if the mind did not become foolish by losing remembrance of grace received, that grace alone could restrain us from an injury to our Creator, even by shame. Therefore, because the scars of our sins would never be opened in action unless they had first become putrid through desire, and because the mind would by no means rot within through evil desires unless it had first become foolish by losing remembrance of its past miseries and consideration of God’s present benefit, let this man lament his folly and say: “My scars have become putrid and corrupt because of my folly.”

But it is still worth considering why he did not simply say, “because of my folly,” or “on account of my folly,” but “because of the face of my folly”: whether he intended by this addition to signify something for us. First, the manner of speaking itself must be considered. For a similar expression is often found in divine speech, when it says, “from the face of the Lord,” or “from the face of the enemy” (Ps. XLIII); and also, what is more obscure, when “face” is mentioned in treating matters lacking human form, whether bodily or sometimes even incorporeal—a usage which is now known not to exist in ordinary speech, though that it once existed is beyond doubt, as may sufficiently be gathered from so frequent a Scriptural usage.

Since we cannot everywhere avoid the face of one who confronts us, Scripture appropriately signifies by “face” presence, pressure, and importunity. What, then, does it mean that the scars are said not merely to have become putrid and corrupt through folly, but through the face of folly, except that God’s grace would by no means abandon us as far as a fall into sin unless our folly had first been importunate for a long time toward God dwelling in us? When he is unwillingly compelled to withdraw from us because of our prolonged negligence, the scars of our wounds at once become not only putrid through evil desires but corrupt even into evil action.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the twofold vanity of human beings

Every living human being is wholly vanity (Ps. XXXVIII). There is one vanity which we see in these visible things; another which we feel invisibly within ourselves. These outward things are vain because, when they fall into corruption, they lose their form. But the soul which declines through iniquity loses, in a more pitiable vanity, the beauty of righteousness. Therefore every living human being is wholly vanity, because outwardly he passes away through mortality and inwardly through iniquity. If he persisted at least in one of these, he would not be wholly vanity.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Since human life is short, evil, and uncertain, what should be said to God

Make known to me, O Lord, my end (Ps. XXXVIII). This present life is short, evil, and uncertain. Because it is uncertain, say to God: “Make known to me, O Lord, my end.” Because it is short, say to God: “Behold, you have made my days measurable.” Because it is evil, [Col. 0613C] say to God: “My substance before you is as nothing.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the multitude and depth of God’s wonders

You have done many wonders, O Lord my God; and none is like you in your thoughts (Ps. XXXIX). God made all things that exist; and yet God is said especially to have made those things through which humanity is brought back to God. Therefore God made, as it were, not his own those wonders whose admiration turns the human mind away from love of him. But those wonders which bring human beings back to the love of God can, because they make us his own, be called his by a certain singular privilege.

Therefore, because above the Psalmist had called blessed the person who does not look to the vanity of this world, he next adds, where admiration may be fruitful: “You have done many wonders, O Lord my God”—namely, works of our restoration. They are many in number, lest you fear weariness in them; and profound in mystery, lest you despise their accessibility. For after he had said, “You have done many wonders, O Lord my God,” immediately wishing to display their very depth, he added: “And none is like you in your thoughts,” so that the multitude of wonders may bring delight through variety, and their depth, exercise.

## CHAPTER L. On the evil of the curious and suspicious person

And if he entered in to see, he spoke vain things; his heart gathered iniquity for itself (Ps. XL). Curiosity is a great evil, and whoever readily inclines his mind to suspicion shows that he is not free from vice. For suspicion of another’s sin would not burn in his heart unless the inclination toward the same sin had first taken root in him. Therefore, by a just judgment, while from the wickedness of his own heart he draws a false opinion about another, he is more inflamed into an inclination toward wickedness by that same opinion; and from that source from which another’s action is falsely accused, his own mind is truly corrupted.

Accordingly, the Psalmist says against persons of this kind: “And if he entered in to see, he spoke vain things.” For every curious person enters, as it were, in order to see when he investigates another’s secret with eager diligence. He speaks vain things because, in order that he may be less suspected, he pretends to love those whom he does not want to be on guard against him. Then he gathers iniquity, because when he has been freely admitted, he fraudulently heaps up in his heart whatever blameworthy thing he can discover. He gathers small matters little by little so that, after a long silence, all things alleged together may do more harm—things which would injure reputation less if each had been brought forward separately.

But because the wicked person does this not from a desire to correct but to wound, he gathers things that will harm himself more. For, as has been said, from the source from which another’s action is falsely darkened by slander, his own mind truly wastes away through wickedness.

## CHAPTER LI. That the highest good is signified by the name “fountains”; that it is supremely desirable; and the matters treated throughout the whole psalm
[Col. 0614C] “As the stag longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41). The waters are God’s gifts; the spring of waters is the author of the gifts. He longs for the spring of water, whose longing is not fulfilled until he comes to God. Those who do not love God’s gifts for God’s sake long, as it were, for the waters and not for the spring. The highest good is expressed by the plural name “springs” because, although it is one in itself, the origin of all good things is contained in it. A living spring, because it gives life; a living spring, because it endures without failing. Therefore it is longed for as the stag longs, because one desires to restore the decay of old age. But the longing is deferred so that it may grow. Yet because every delay is long to one who longs, he cries: “When shall I come, [Col. 0614D] when shall I arrive, when shall I appear before the face of the Lord?”—not in order to be seen, but in order to begin to see him whom, while seeing previously, I did not see.

But this can now be longed for; it cannot be possessed. What then in the meantime? “My tears became my bread day and night.” I shall feed upon sorrows; I shall seek with weeping; I shall call with sighs. Tears nourish longing until presence satisfies affection. I shall weep because what I desire is absent; I shall weep because what I do not love is present. I do not love present unhappiness; I desire future blessedness. The upper waters, because my soul longs for the living spring; the lower waters, because it is said to me, “Where is your God?” This belongs to present misery: that I endure the reproaches of evil men because I do not love earthly prosperity. And because they see me abandoned in present prosperity, [Col. 0615A] they mockingly say that I have no God.

Crushed, then, by these insults, he had begun to grow weary. But immediately returning to himself and considering the condition of the present life, he rebukes himself for such grief, saying: “I remembered these things, because I shall pass through the tabernacle to the house,” that is, through toil to rest. It is as if he said: When I was saddened by the trouble of the present life, I did not remember what the condition of the present life is. But now I have remembered that no one can arrive at rest who has not first been willing to endure toil with equanimity. “Because I shall pass through the tabernacle to the house.” The tabernacle is the present Church; the house is the heavenly homeland. In the tabernacle there is a place, because outside faith there can be no secure dwelling.

Nor shall I merely pass [Col. 0615B] through the place of the tabernacle, but into the place of the tabernacle: that is, from unbelief to faith, and from faith to blessedness. “Into the place,” therefore, so that I may not merely begin to hold the right faith, but may remain in it until the end. Nor should the labor of struggle terrify us, because the tabernacle is wonderful and already many examples of virtue shine within it. And because I have recognized that the passage through the tabernacle to the house—that is, through toil to rest—must be made, I no longer poured out my soul outside myself, but poured it out within myself. As anguish constricts the mind, so joy expands it. Whoever therefore seeks to rejoice in transient things pours out his soul outside himself. But whoever, considering all earthly things vain, seeks joy more securely in a good conscience pours out his soul within himself. Above [Col. 0615C] itself, however, the soul is poured out when, through the joy of contemplation, it is enlarged in love for its Creator.

But when the soul is poured out within itself, the animal nature, which loves outward pleasure, is immediately saddened. Every faithful person must correct it by the motion of reason, saying: “Why are you sad, my soul? Why do you grieve at losing what you cannot retain? Why do you trouble me?” For since I am joined to you by natural affection, I cannot remain undisturbed when you are troubled. “Hope in God,” because if you now voluntarily reject transient pleasures for his sake, you will afterward, through his gift, obtain pleasures that endure: “For I shall yet confess him.” When I have obtained what I hope for, then I shall praise him and confess him, concerning whom there can be no doubt, because he is “the salvation of my countenance,” [Col. 0615D] that is, of my likeness—that is, man—and he is my God. There is no doubt that he will grant eternity promised to mortals, since he is known to have assumed mortal things for the salvation of mortals; and he who willed to suffer our death for us will much more give us his own life. He can do this because he is God: therefore do not doubt either his will, since he became man for us, or his power, since he is God.

“My soul was troubled within me.” That my soul was troubled must be referred to me alone, because unless my sin had first preceded, the flesh would not have been corrupted outwardly. Thus its corruption is rightly traced back to my disturbance, because its corruption first arose from my fault. Or “[Col. 0616A] within myself,” that is, in myself: for even if the soul finds no outward disturbance, the corruption of its own condition troubles it. That is, although the outward incentives to sin may cease, nevertheless the vices arising from natural corruption trouble me.

What remedies, then, must be applied against recurring sin? We cannot be baptized again; yet in place of baptism, against daily sins, we have the daily spring of tears. And although we are forbidden to be baptized repeatedly by water, we are never forbidden to be baptized by repentance. Thus the grace of the first baptism follows us in repentance, as water from the rock followed the people of Israel as they passed through the desert, so that whenever we dry up through sin in the desert of this life, we may be refreshed through repentance. Therefore, because every day our soul is troubled within [Col. 0616B] us, let us be mindful of God from the land of the Jordan: that is, let us still seek in repentance the remission that we formerly received in water, and do so with greater confidence inasmuch as we know more plainly that we have been marked with his sacrament.

For what is more rightly understood by the Jordan than baptism? And what by the land of the Jordan, except human nature washed in the spring of baptism? Thus we are mindful of God from the land of the Jordan when we seek in repentance that same washing which we remember having once received from him in water.

It follows: “And from Hermon, from the little mountain.” Understand: “I shall be mindful of you.” Hermon is interpreted “anathema” or “separation by anathema.” In baptism we anathematized the devil together with all his works and pomps; and, made conformed to Christ, we were separated from the members of the devil. Thus a person separated from the devil through baptism becomes Hermon, a mountain through virtue, little through humility. Therefore, when through repentance we seek from God the gifts of virtues lost through sin, we are mindful of him as though from the little mountain of Hermon, because we remember that he once separated us from the devil, raised us through virtue, and tempered us through conformity to Christ. We are mindful of him from the land of the Jordan when we offer to him for washing through repentance that same nature which he first washed from sin through the water of baptism. We are mindful of him from the little mountain of Hermon when we pray that the gifts of virtues may be restored to us with humility, [Col. 0616D] gifts which we remember having formerly received from him. Both are called remembrance because we ask again for what we recall having received before.

And repentance is necessary because “deep calls to deep”: that is, the judgment of damnation calls in confirmation of itself the judgment of mortality. If we see to be true what you threatened to the first man when he sinned—death—let us also believe to be true what you now threaten to those who sin and persist in sin—damnation. Thus the deep, that is, the judgment of damnation, calls to the deep, that is, the judgment of mortality, because the latter confirms the former. Or the future judgment of fire calls to the past judgment of water; or the New Testament, which commanded repentance, calls on the Old Testament to confirm this. Or the deep of divine wisdom [Col. 0617A] calls to the deep of human conscience, because God, who subtly penetrates our secrets through his wisdom, condemns them while our own conscience accuses them. Accordingly, it is very necessary for us now to seek his mercy in repentance, in whose judgment no external witness is required, because each person is condemned by the accusation of his own conscience.

We have learned all this “in the voice of your cataracts,” that is, in the preaching of your preachers. These preachers are called cataracts because, as they drip the rain of doctrine, the soil of the human heart is watered. Therefore, in the voice of the cataracts we have heard that, just as the threat of death to sinners was not empty in former times, so the threat of damnation to those persisting in sin will not now be empty either. [Col. 0617B] How, then, do we know that the ancient threat was not empty? We have all already learned by experience how exceedingly true was what God once threatened to sinful man. How have we learned it? “All your heights and your waves have passed over me.” Just as successive masses of waves pass over and overwhelm a shipwreck, until they sink it, shattered and broken, to the depths, so the punishments and sufferings of this life, ever one after another shattering and breaking mortal man, pass over him and at last sink him, exhausted, into the depth of death.

The waves are common and daily penalties; the heights are increasing and exceptional adversities, which do not happen alike to all, nor always to the same persons. Yet all occur to some, and some occur to all. Therefore, because I feel the present judgment to be so severe, I rightly dread the future judgment. And so, that I may escape it while time still remains, I must repent. How do you know whether your repentance will be accepted? I know because “in the day the Lord commanded his mercy.” God’s mercy is that he punishes human sin in the present life so that a person may escape eternal damnation. God commands this mercy to man through preachers, so that, recognizing the benefit of present mortality for his future deliverance, he may willingly receive these penalties. But he commands this mercy “in the day,” that is, in prosperity, because a person placed in tribulation would receive less readily whatever he heard concerning the usefulness of tribulation.

[Col. 0617D] It follows, as another translation has it: “And at night he made it known”—understand, this same mercy. For what he taught by word in the day, that is, in prosperity, concerning the usefulness of this common misery, he made known by example at night, that is, in adversity, through certain particular tribulations. For what fruit patience will have in the future was sufficiently made known when he showed, even in the present life, how necessary tribulations are. Thus what he commands in the day, he makes known in the night, because what is said in words is proved by experience.

Or, as another translation has it: “In the day the Lord commanded his mercy, and at night his song.” This may be understood thus. He commanded—that is, he promised his mercy through his messengers, namely heralds [Col. 0618A] of truth: that he would free us from the misery of this life—“in the day,” that is, when the brightness of eternal life should dawn after the darkness of mortality had been driven away. And therefore, meanwhile, in the night of this life, he commanded his song, that is, his praise, so that if we wish to receive his mercy in the future day, we may not depart from his praise in present adversity. For it is fitting that, if we wish to have him favorable in his glory, we should proclaim him just in our misery. Therefore, since we have sinned, since we endure the scourge, and since we await deliverance: in sin let us confess our fault; under the scourge let us praise his justice; in deliverance let us hope for his mercy.

“With me is prayer, for iniquity, to the God of my life in corruption; I shall say to God: You are my protector in mercy.” With me is prayer—in secret, in concealment. It is in concealment because through it I desire to please not human beings but God alone; the God of my life, because while he mortifies me outwardly by scourging, he breathes life into me inwardly by giving life. I shall say to God, in the future, when I have been received securely into glory: “You are my protector”—something which, still placed in uncertainty, I do not yet presume to say. Or I shall say it in the present, presuming upon the promise which I already have in hope, because I already hold as though accomplished what I await without doubt will be accomplished. “Why have you forgotten me?” The mind of one who loves and fears is drawn in different directions: now it glories in the promise; now it complains of delay; now it thinks itself abandoned because of the weight of tribulation; now it rejoices that it is received because of confidence in the promise.

[Col. 0618C] “Why have you forgotten me?” A cherished little child becomes angry with a loving father, and because he does not answer every wish, accuses him of forgetfulness. He also recounts the evils he suffers: “Why do I go about sorrowful?” And lest his sadness seem superfluous, he says, “while the enemy afflicts me.” And because it is often more appropriate to rejoice than to grieve, he heightens the cause in the affliction of the body, adding also the losses of virtue: “while my bones are broken,” that is, while virtues are destroyed. Finally, adding the sum of evil, he says: “Those who trouble me, my enemies, reproached me.” In this not one person alone is injured, but the whole community is darkened by disgrace. I suffer all these things “while I go about,” that is, while I advance by walking in the straight way; where he implicitly indicates his merit in saying that he both does good and suffers evil.

## Chapter LII. On judgment according to the cause, and according to recompense; on God’s light and truth; on the mountain and the tabernacle; and on the gladdening of our youth

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 62). Judgment according to the cause is one thing; judgment according to recompense another. Therefore the good, who are among the evil in the present life but are not joined to them in their cause, pray that God may first distinguish their cause and then judge them. For then he judges us beneficially in recompense, if he has first here distinguished our cause from the unholy nation. “For you are my strength.” Therefore I ask to be separated from them through you, because although I bear their malice grievously, I do not separate myself [Col. 0619A] from their society through pride and confidence in my own strength. But what is asked is deferred; therefore he cries: “Why have you cast me off? Send forth your light and your truth.” By faith enlighten me; by truth reward faith: merciful in enlightening, true in rewarding. These two led me away from my evils and brought me to your goods.

What goods? “To the mountain, to the tabernacles.” I was led to the mountain through faith; I was led to the tabernacles through action. “I shall enter to the altar” through love. To the mountain, that I might believe lofty things; to the tabernacles, that I might do strong things; to the altar, that I might sacrifice myself. The mountain and tabernacles belong to the present; the altar to the future, where charity is complete. Therefore he says, “I shall enter,” that I may sacrifice myself and contemplate at the altar—that is, God—who gladdens my youth.

[Col. 0619B] And rightly he gladdens youth; for he does not gladden old age, but makes it sorrowful. “To God, who gladdens my youth.” “Though our outward person is corrupt and old, our inward person is renewed day by day.” Our flesh, which is dissolved by death, is not renewed in the present life. But the spirit begins to renew its youth in this life when, through God’s grace, it casts off old desires by virtues made new. Therefore God gladdens not our old age but our youth, because the more the flesh is worn away outwardly, the more the mind is consoled inwardly with spiritual joy. Therefore, he says, “I shall confess you on the harp.” Because you love the joy not of old age but of youth—that is, not the joy of the flesh but of the spirit—therefore I too shall afflict the flesh and praise you [Col. 0619C] in the mortification of the flesh. Conversely, because animal nature murmurs at this, he chastens it by rebuke, saying: “Why are you sad, my soul?”

## Chapter LIII. Which paths the Lord has turned aside

“You turned aside our paths from your way” (Ps. 43). By coming in a human being, you laid out the way for us by example, and from that way you have derived through imitation whatever good is in us. Or, “our paths,” that is, our tangled and laborious paths in which we formerly walked according to the flesh, you turned aside from your good life—that is, you removed them—because we no longer run along them after we have been directed onto your way.

## Chapter LIV. On the dust of thoughts and the earth of useless desires

[Col. 0619D]

“Our soul has been humbled in the dust; our belly has been glued to the earth” (Ps. 63). Dust is vain thoughts; earth, however, is depraved desires. The soul is rightly first humbled in dust and the belly then glued to earth, because unless the soul had first subjected itself to vain thoughts, unclean desires of the flesh would never bind it. But because the soul is first conquered by vanity, the flesh is afterward glued to uncleanness.

## Chapter LV. On form, grace, and blessing from God—“for this” and “because of this,” etc.

“Fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 64): uprightness of action. “Grace has been poured out upon your lips”: purity of preaching. “Therefore God has blessed you [Col. 0620A] forever”: blessedness of recompense. First he blessed “for this”; afterward he blessed “because of this.” “For this,” in time; “because of this,” in eternity. He blessed for this, that good might be accomplished; he blessed because of this, that good might be rewarded.

## Chapter LVI. How and when God assists the blessed mind joined to him through peace and love

“God is in her midst; she shall not be moved. God will help her early in the morning” (Ps. 45). Blessed is the city that has God as king, because though it suffers wars outwardly, its peace is not disturbed within. Happy is one who has such a soul, so firmly established in the love of God that whatever troubles may resound outside, they nevertheless do not break through as far as the silence of inward rest. For God, who is a lover of peace, cannot dwell in a troubled heart. Yet because God would not find so peaceful a dwelling unless he himself made it, “God will help her early in the morning.” Morning: seasonably; dawn: in the light. Morning, because he is a helper in opportunities; dawn, because he does not know how to work in darkness. He helps one who is willing, because no one does good unwillingly. He helps the city, builds the city, rests in the city, and protects the city.

## Chapter LVII. What are the works of the Lord that we must see, and the wonders that he has placed upon the earth

“Come and see the works of the Lord, the wonders which he has placed upon the earth” (Ps. 45). “Come,” he says, “and see the works of the Lord.” First come, then see. For you are in darkness, and there you cannot see the works of the Lord. Come, therefore, to the light and see by the light what the light has done in light: see the works of the Lord. What works of the Lord? Heaven and earth, perhaps? No: but the things placed from above heaven upon earth.

For God first made heaven and earth; then from heaven and earth he produced certain things in heaven and on earth. But because these are earthly, they can be seen everywhere on earth; nor are people invited from one place to another in order to see them. There are other things which he produced neither from heaven nor from earth, but which, bringing them with him from above heaven, he placed upon earth—not casting them down, but bending them down; not pressing earth down with them, but lifting it up. What are these works of the Lord? “O Lord, I heard your report, and I feared. O Lord, you will make your work known in the midst of the years” (Hab. 1), namely, when you are known in the midst [Col. 0620D] of two living creatures. How were they placed upon earth? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). How are they wonders? “A little child has been born to us, and a son has been given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9).

They have been placed upon earth because they order earthly things toward peace; they are wonders because they foreshadow the joys of the age to come. They are wonders because he is the Father of the age to come. They have been placed upon earth because he is the Prince of Peace, removing wars, making a human being peaceful within and without, and utterly subjecting the earth of the flesh to the soul’s rule. “He will break the bow and shatter the weapons,” annihilating the devil’s deceptions and machinations. “He will burn the shields with fire,” softening hard hearts with the fire of the Holy Spirit. When these things have been accomplished and full peace restored, an exhortatory voice follows, by which all who are willing are invited to the true good: “Be still, and see that I am the Lord.”

## Chapter LVIII. How one should pray to obtain remission of sins from God, after David’s example

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy” (Ps. 50). Hear, sinners, a sinner praying, and learn that among yourselves you ought to pray for your sins. Hear what he says: “Have mercy on me, O God.” For an accused person brought before a court considers that his judge cannot be deceived, because he is wise; cannot be corrupted, because he is just; cannot be overcome, because he is almighty; and cannot be avoided, because he is everywhere. See, then, that there is absolutely no room for excuse or defense, and therefore he turns to seeking mercy alone, saying, “Have mercy.”

Oh, how great is the force of this word, “have mercy”! It is as if he said: “O Lord, I acknowledge my fault; I understand my guilt; I know what I have done; I know what I have deserved; I do not fail to know with whom my case is being heard; I do not fail to know what is owed to me for my fault. I want to hide my sin, but you know all things. I want to resist, but you can do all things. I want to escape, but you encompass all things. Therefore the one thing remaining is this: from you I flee to you. I flee from wrath; I flee to mercy. Have mercy. I do not want you to enter into judgment with your servant, because ‘every living person shall not be justified in your sight’ (Ps. 142)—how much less I, a sinner and guilty of crime. I do not ask that you judge with me, but that you have mercy on me. Have mercy on me.”

“Who are you? Declare who you are. Perhaps I may be bent more quickly to mercy if I recognize the person.” “No, Lord,” he says, “no. Yet for the time being I wish to remain hidden, though I cannot remain hidden. I want you for the time being not to know me, although I know that you do all things. For I fear and at the same time am ashamed to state my name, to identify my person; and the more familiar I was to you before my fault, the more I am now ashamed to be recognized after my fault. Therefore I do not say to you, ‘Lord, have mercy on David,’ as elsewhere I said: ‘Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness’ (Ps. 131). Nor do I say, as I once used flatteringly to say, ‘your child,’ not even ‘your servant’ or ‘the son of your handmaid,’ because all these are names of familiarity; and thus, the more clearly uttered, they would recall the benefit of greater grace, [Col. 0621D] and the more grievously they would accuse the guilt of the fault that followed.

“Therefore I pass over all these things; I am silent, conceal, and hide them, lest by perhaps recalling any of them I make you angrier and show myself more guilty. For the time being I wish not to be recognized, that you may the more quickly be appeased. Therefore do not ask, Lord, who I am; only have mercy on one confessing his sin, condemning his fault, and seeking your mercy. Have mercy on me, O God. For I dare not say, ‘My God’; I acknowledge only ‘God’ and do not presume to call him mine. For by sinning I lost you; by following the enemy I withdrew from you; by loving evil I went far from the good.

“Therefore, like a leper, like one cast out, like one separated, like one unclean, like a stranger, [Col. 0622A] I do not dare to draw near; I do not presume to approach. But standing only at a distance and lifting my voice to you, with great devotion and great contrition of heart, I cry and say: ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’ Let those who are good say, let those who are clean say, let those who are pure say, let those who are familiar say, let those who are children and heirs say: ‘My God.’ I, who am unclean, polluted, rejected, far away; who deserted my Father, sold myself to the enemy, went into a far country, lost my inheritance, and squandered my substance in luxurious living—I shall not say ‘My God’; I shall not say ‘My Father’; but only, ‘Have mercy on me, O God. Make me as one of your hired servants, because I am not worthy to be called your son’ (Luke 15).

“Have mercy, therefore, [Col. 0622B] on me, O God, according to your great mercy—not according to my great misery, but according to your great mercy. For although my misery is great, your mercy is greater. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. I do not wish to seek a small mercy, because it does not befit you to give a small mercy. For I would no longer be worthy of an answer if I sought something small from one who is great. Have mercy, therefore, on me, O God, according to your great mercy. In no way, Lord, do I trust in my merits while asking for great things; rather, I honor your magnificence. Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy. Because of your great mercy, and according to your great mercy. Have mercy on me, O God, [Col. 0622C] according to your great mercy.”

## Chapter LIX. That God is wonderful in the saints—that is, inwardly—more than outwardly

“God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. 67). Why do you wonder at what is outward? God is wonderful inwardly. For if what was made for servitude is wonderful, how can that which was made in the image not be wonderful? “God is wonderful in his saints.” Therefore do not look at them outwardly. What is outward is not wonderful; what is inward is wonderful. Look inward, then, and you will not wonder at whatever appears outwardly.

## Chapter LX. That it is always good to cling to God and place hope in him

“But for me it is good to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God” (Ps. 72). People have their own goods. For some, in need, their counsel is a good; for others, in prosperity, their counsel is a good; for others, in prosperity, their joy is a good. But for me there is one good: to cling to God and place my hope in the Lord God. If rivers of temptations overflow, it is good for me to cling to him lest I be dissolved. If the winds of adversity blow, it is good for me to fix the anchor of hope in him, lest I be shattered or scattered. But for them their counsel is not good even in adversity, because it does not deliver; nor is their joy good in prosperity, because it does not preserve. Therefore one rejected counsel, another joy: “How long shall I put counsels in my soul?” (Ps. 12). And I said to joy: “Why are you deceived in vain?” (Eccl. 2).

## Chapter LXI. On the three evils by which a human being is afflicted, and the four goods by which he is consoled

[Col. 0623A]

“Will he restrain his mercies in his wrath?” (Ps. 76). There are three evils by which a human being is afflicted, and four goods by which he is consoled. One evil is outward, beneath the human being; another is outward, in the human being; a third is inward, in the human being. The outward evil beneath the human being occurs when he suffers losses in the things he possesses outwardly. The outward evil in the human being occurs when his flesh is weakened. The inward evil in the human being is the worm of conscience.

Four goods are opposed to these three evils, so that wrath does not restrain mercy, but the benefits of the one who is favorable surpass the scourges of the one who is angry. For there is an outward good beneath the human being in the tranquility of temporal things; and there is an outward good in the human being, the security of consciences; and there is an inward good above the human being, the sweetness of heavenly joys. Therefore the favorable one bestows more than the angry one has taken away, because first we who sin are struck in what is ours, but afterward we are consoled even in things that are above what is ours.

## Chapter LXII. On the fourfold peace which the Lord speaks to different persons

“For he will speak peace to his people and to his saints” (Ps. 84). There are four kinds of peace: the world gives two, and God gives two. The world gives peace in the tranquility of temporal things and in bodily health. God gives peace in tranquility of mind and in the joy of contemplation. But the peace that is in tranquility of mind is within the human being; the peace [Col. 0623C] that is in the joy of contemplation is above the human being. God speaks the former to his people because he gives it to those less perfect; the latter he speaks over his saints, because he grants it to the more perfect.

## Chapter LXIII. How mercy and truth came to meet each other in dispute, and justice and peace kissed

“Mercy and truth have met each other; justice and peace have kissed. Truth has sprung from the earth, and justice has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84). God was above and man below. Truth was in heaven with God the judge, and mercy on earth with the human being who was to be judged. For where would mercy be if it were not with the miserable? Perhaps mercy had descended without truth’s knowledge, because truth knew that mercy would come to the human being and feared her arrival. Mercy therefore descended first, lest, if truth came first to the human being, she herself might afterward find no place.

Thus, after truth had been assumed, God descended in order to enter into an account with the human being. When mercy saw this, not ignorant of the divine purpose, she hastened to meet him, wishing to soften God and bring him appeased. But seeing truth proceeding with a stern countenance, she first met her, asking her to halt her step and not hurry too much, until she had poured out her prayer to the Lord. There, therefore, mercy and truth met each other.

Then mercy set forth a complaint before God with gentle pleading, saying that she took it grievously that she had not been summoned as a companion for this affair, especially since God had never been accustomed to undertake any journey without each of these two companions. “For,” she says, “since it is written: ‘All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth’ (Ps. 26), how, content with truth alone, did my Lord not summon mercy? Especially when Scripture everywhere recalls that mercy ought to be not only equal, but even prior. For it is not written, ‘Truth and mercy,’ but ‘Mercy and truth are all the ways of the Lord.’ Why, then, who ought to have been first, do I now come last—and, what grieves me more, approach your company without having been invited?”

Conversely, truth replied that on this journey mercy could neither be nor ought to be the Lord’s companion: first, because the plan of his will had been ordained otherwise, and consequently mercy herself could not be present in his work; and second, because she had not set out with him. Truth also said that mercy herself ought rather to give an account of why she had not been present when the Lord set out, and that the Lord had been injured more by her absence, so much so that he had been compelled to undertake the journey with only one companion.

To this mercy replied that she had neither gone out with an evil intention nor been occupied in an evil work. Rather, she was providing for the honor and advantage of her Lord, since she sought not to lose and destroy, as truth did, but to save. Truth, rather, ought to be censured and accused, since she wished the Lord’s servants and ministers to be diminished so completely that, once all had gone away, she allowed none to be raised and recalled by any indulgence.

Truth replied that it was not fitting that the good and just Lord should have wicked and unjust servants. Mercy said that the Lord ought not to be without servants altogether. Truth affirmed that evil people ought deservedly to be condemned. Mercy replied that they ought also to be recalled by free compassion, so that they might become good. Truth said that God ought not to spare evil persons at all. Mercy said: if God spared no one, he would never have good persons. Truth said that she neither wished nor could endure so many human crimes. Mercy replied that the Lord’s grace abounds for pardoning. Truth said: “Let each receive according to what he has done in the body.” Mercy said: “Let every human being rather turn to the Lord and live.”

[Col. 0624D] Thus, while these two opposed one another and desired to incline God’s will in different directions, God, seeing that such divergent opinions could not both proceed to their effect, said: “It is written: God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. XXIV). Therefore, those whom he loves he wishes always to be present with him; and since it is again said of God, “His place is made in peace” (Ps. LXXIII), he cannot endure them in discord. Yet there can be no harmony where the will is so divergent. For Truth wills that everything be charged against the offender; Mercy, however, that everything be forgiven. These cannot happen together. Therefore, lest I, who am a lover of peace, be compelled to leave your company, you must both endeavor to bend your wills toward a single agreement.

To this Truth replied [Col. 0625A] that she would be less praiseworthy if anything were left unavenged. Mercy said that she would be less lovable if not everything were remitted through gratuitous compassion. Then God asked whether they both wished to submit their wills to his judgment and, without contradiction, to assent to whatever he should decide concerning the matter. Both agreed, insofar as this could be done without diminution of their name and dignity. God said that it seemed equitable to him that human sin should be punished in part on account of Truth, and in part forgiven on account of Mercy.

When both had agreed to this, Truth added, saying that it was just that, just as Mercy had formerly been with humanity while Truth herself remained in heaven, so now Truth herself should remain on earth with humanity and Mercy should ascend to heaven with God. [Col. 0625B] For it is written: “Mercy and truth shall go before thy face” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Therefore, if Mercy went before first and Truth remained behind, it is just that Mercy should now remain and Truth go before.

Then Mercy, asking Truth to remember their common agreement—namely, not to devise anything against humanity beyond what had been granted—ascended with the Lord. But Truth, entering the human heart, found there every evil thing and things deserving punishment; and she began to cry out from the earth, accusing humanity. Mercy, meanwhile, did not cease in heaven to pray to the Lord and plead for humanity. Humanity, spurred on upon earth by Truth, confessed its sin; and God in heaven, moved by Mercy, had compassion on the one confessing. Humanity made confession with its own mouth unto salvation, and Mercy [Col. 0625C] by her prayers constrained the Lord toward humanity’s justification. Truth sprang from the earth through humanity’s confession, and justice, looking down from heaven through God’s mercy, was sent to earth.

Truth said that the one who had first done evil must first be punished. Mercy said that afterward the one who, by confessing evil, had done good must be justified and saved. Through Truth humanity was accused, and through Mercy, because of Truth, justified: because “truth sprang up from the earth, and justice looked down from heaven.” Therefore, because Mercy was with God for humanity, while justice and Truth were from God with humanity, there was now peace between God and humanity for the sake of justice. Justice ascended from humanity to God, asking for peace; and peace descended from God to humanity, [Col. 0625D] embracing and kissing justice.

Then Justice said to Peace: “Is it sufficient for the supreme Good merely to remit evils, unless he also endeavors to bestow good? He has released sins by pardon; now let him grant the gifts of virtues by grace.” Peace replied and said: “The Lord will give goodness, and our land will yield its fruit. But meanwhile justice shall walk before him and shall set his steps in the way.” Hearing this, Justice ran ahead and returned to humanity, so that she might not depart from it until the Lord should set his steps in the way and come.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the twofold confession, and on the Lord’s gentleness and sweetness

“It is good to confess to the Lord, and to sing praises to thy name, O Most High” [Col. 0626A] (Ps. XCI). Confession is twofold: one is confession of sin, the other confession of praise. Confession of sin is the conversion of the sinner; confession of praise is the glorification of the Creator. Confession of sin consists in detestation of evil; confession of praise, in the exaltation of good. Fear gives birth to confession of sin; love gives birth to confession of praise.

Therefore it is good to confess to the Lord, because he is gentle; and it is good to sing praises to his name, because he is sweet. An example of his gentleness was that he did not drive away sinners coming to him. An example of his sweetness was that those who tasted him could not grow weary of him. An example of gentleness was that he had compassion upon the weak. An example of sweetness was that he accommodated himself to the imperfect. He had compassion on the weak by granting pardon to those who confessed, [Col. 0626B] and by imposing no penalty upon those who repented. He accommodated himself to the imperfect by sowing spiritual things and reaping bodily things: sowing the word, the food of the mind, and reaping provision, the food of the body.

A sinful woman came to him and poured tears at his feet in confession of sin. He, in order to show his gentleness and to give the faint-hearted confidence to approach, promptly granted pardon and imposed no penalty. But he said, “Go, and sin no more” (John VIII). Elsewhere it is also said that Jesus had a money-box and received what was given (John XII), accommodating himself to the imperfect, so that those who preach the Gospel may live by the Gospel (1 Cor. IX). Paul, however, was unwilling to receive support from the Gospel, but became a minister of the word without charge (ibid.). Thus Paul is found [Col. 0626C] to have done something greater than Christ. Yet Christ chose to be found among the imperfect, lest those who do not receive support should presume upon themselves, those who receive it should be ashamed, and a person doing what Christ chose to do should be thought not to be a Christian. Therefore let us approach the gentle one with confidence, and not abandon the sweet one.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the spiritual harp

“With a song upon the harp” (Ps. XCI). In a harp there are two pieces of wood, one lower and the other upper. The lower piece is hollow; the upper is solid. Between the two pieces strings are stretched by pegs, some running downward and some drawn upward. A plectrum turns the upper pegs; but at the lower pegs the strings, struck by the fingers, [Col. 0626D] sound forth.

The two pieces of wood are two crosses: the lower wood is the cross of the flesh; the upper wood is the cross of the mind. The cross of the flesh is bodily affliction. The cross of the mind is compassion in the heart. The lower wood is not solid, because whatever suffers in the flesh, if the joy of a good conscience is removed, has the appearance of suffering outwardly but no reality within. The upper wood is solid, because the pain of the mind, penetrating to the inmost parts, can be displayed but cannot be feigned.

The string is the body, stretched and worn down between bodily punishment and pain of heart. The lower peg is fear, the upper one love: for by fear the flesh is fastened, and by love the spirit is wounded—the former so that it may not be moved toward evil, the latter so that it may be made sensitive to good. The plectrum [Col. 0627A] is grace, which, laying hold of the heart’s affection, draws it to itself and makes it ascend to higher things. The string is dried and stretched so that it may give sound; and the human flesh is first cleansed from evil, then stirred up toward good—there dried, here stretched. Dried by abstinence; stretched by patience. The lower pegs are round, the upper solid, because fear ought to be circumspect and love perfect.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On faith, action, and the reward of the good

“A light has risen in darkness for the upright in heart: the Lord is merciful, compassionate, and just” (Ps.
