CXI): this is faith. “Happy is the person who has compassion and lends; he shall order his words in judgment, because he shall never be moved” [Col. 0627B]: this is action. “The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance; he shall not fear evil tidings”: this is reward.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the two schools of virtue and truth, and the two kinds of learners; and on the fact that all desire to be blessed, but few strive to be undefiled

“Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies; they seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). There are two schools and two kinds of learners. Some seek virtue; others, truth. Yet those who seek either one in truth despise neither, since virtue is not hateful to lovers of truth, nor truth contemptible to lovers of virtue.

There are, however, people who seem to seek truth; but because they seek it not in truth and for truth, but for vanity, [Col. 0627C] they wish to possess truth without virtue. Yet truth is not without virtue, nor virtue except in truth. Some say: “We wish to be good, but we do not wish to be wise”; and these are not justified, because virtue is called wisdom. Just as those who say, “We wish to be wise, but we do not wish to be good,” are not instructed, because wisdom is established through virtue.

The school of virtue is: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” The school of wisdom is: “Blessed are those who search his testimonies; with their whole heart they seek him.” So also in the first psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence”: this is the school of virtue. “But his will is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he shall meditate day and night”: this is the school of wisdom.

[Col. 0627D] Yet in both cases the pursuit of virtue is put first, because many wish to know, but few to do; so that the conscience may first be cleansed by the pursuit of a good work, and afterward wisdom may be sought with a pure heart. First learn what you should do; afterward seek what you should know. Therefore, “Blessed are the undefiled” comes first, and then “Blessed are those who search.”

“Blessed are the undefiled.” All gladly hear “blessed,” but not all gladly hear “undefiled.” But if you wish to be blessed, be undefiled. Who is undefiled? One who has never been defiled, or one who has been washed. The holy undefiled person, and the sanctified undefiled person: first, the one who has not turned away; second, the one who has returned. The former, because he has not transgressed; the latter, because he has been reconciled.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the names of God’s precepts contained in Psalm CXVIII, and their reasons

[Col. 0628A]

God’s precepts are denoted by many names: way, law, testimonies, commandments, justifications, judgments, sayings, utterances, wonders, equity, words, truth, justice (Ps. CXVIII). They are called ways because by doing them we arrive at life. They are called law because, with a prescribed rule of observance, they bind. They are called testimonies because they clearly admonish, bearing witness through punishments, promises, rewards, or gifts. They are called commandments because they indicate what must be done. They are called justifications because, when fulfilled, they free from guilt. They are called judgments because they declare to each person the recompense due according to merit. They are called sayings because they instruct by narration. They are called utterances because they plainly [Col. 0628B] signify. They are called wonders because they command unfamiliar things and promise unknown things. They are called equity because they are made according to justice. They are called words because they are God’s signs to human beings. They are called truth because things are as they say. They are called justice because they contain nothing disordered.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On the three ways

“O that my ways might be directed!” etc. (Ps. CXVIII). There are three ways: the way of God, the way of humanity, and the way of the devil. The way of God is truth; the way of humanity is necessity; the way of the devil is iniquity. The ways of God and of the devil can never be bent so as to tend toward something else, because God’s way can never be evil, nor the devil’s way ever good. The human way is changeable and bends in different directions: that is, either toward God’s way or toward the devil’s way.

For if [Col. 0628C] necessity is bent toward desire, and desire toward iniquity, humanity’s way is bent toward the devil’s way. But if they are directed toward measure, and measure toward justice, humanity’s way is directed toward God’s way. Therefore he says: “O that my ways might be directed!” etc.

## CHAPTER LXX. Who are those walking in the law of the Lord, those standing in it, and those turning aside from it

“Blessed are those who walk in the law of the Lord,” etc. (Ps. CXVIII). Some walk in the law, others stand in the law, and others turn aside from the law. Those walk in the law who advance in good. Those stand in the law who do not retreat from good. Those turn aside from the law who venture upon things that ought not to be done.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the directing of the human heart

[Col. 0628D] “I will confess to thee in uprightness of heart” (Ps. CXVIII). The human heart is directed when the human will is conformed to the divine will: that is, when a person hates what God hates and loves what he loves. We are instructed toward this by God’s law, in which God’s will is shown to us; and that will is the rule of our will. Therefore humanity’s ways—that is, its works—are first directed toward keeping God’s justifications; afterward a person confesses to God in uprightness of heart.

Who is the one who confesses to God? The one who approves what God does confesses to God. Such a person is one whose will and heart are directed, so that he does not differ from God’s will either in approving or disapproving, hating or loving, neither stopping short nor going beyond.

## CHAPTER LXXII. Who seek God with their whole heart; what it is to seek God and how he is to be sought; and how one is repelled from God’s commandments

[Col. 0629A]

“With my whole heart I have sought thee; do not repel me from thy commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). Pagans and unbelievers do not seek God, since they render divine honor to a creature. Likewise false believers, who love something other than God more than God, do not seek God. To seek God is to seek him beyond all things: by faith, so that he is believed to be other than all things; by love, so that he is loved more than all things. One seeks with the whole heart who desires to find him alone.

“Do not repel me from thy commandments.” A person approaching God is often repelled by himself, often by the world, often by the devil, and sometimes by God. He is repelled by himself either through his own will or through the desire of the flesh. [Col. 0629B] He is repelled through his own will because what God wills sometimes becomes burdensome to him, since by his own will he wills something other than what God wills; and this cannot exist together with what God wills. He is repelled through the desire of the flesh because, when the flesh has desired something else, the will of the spirit does not proceed to its effect without difficulty. He is repelled by the world when he is either oppressed by adversities or ensnared by prosperities. He is repelled by the devil when he is harassed incessantly by the importunity of the devil’s suggestions. He is repelled by God when, rising to contemplate his majesty, he is struck back by the rays of incomprehensible light.

Yet this repulse is not wrath but exercise, because a person is for a time repelled from the heights so that through humility he may be trained more effectively in lesser things. [Col. 0629C] Hence it is said: “Do not turn away in anger from thy servant”; that is, if you turn away, turn away so as to return. Remember, therefore, Jacob’s ladder. Angels ascend and descend. Some know how to ascend but do not know how to descend. For descending is one thing; falling headlong is another. It is not for a human being always to go upward. If you know how to ascend through devotion of mind, know also how to descend through the exercise of good work. If you do not know how to descend, you do not know how to ascend; and after an undiscerning and immoderate intensity of ascent, you will eventually begin to fall.

When you descend, God, who is above, seems to draw away. But it is written: “The Lord is high, and he looks upon the lowly” (Ps. CXXXVII). It is therefore better for you to be humble and be seen than to be exalted and ignored. Birds take flight and descend upon [Col. 0629D] the earth to rest. But some love clean places, while others seek muddy and polluted ones. Therefore, if you descend, let your resting-place be clean. What is contemplation but heaven? What is action but earth? In contemplation you fly; in action you sit. But choose clean places—good works in life—and flee muddy places, where there is defilement for the one who touches them. These are works of uncleanness that pollute the one approaching them. Therefore you are now repelled when you are restored, because if you settle well, you will rise again stronger.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. How the Lord’s utterances are to be hidden

“In my heart I have hidden thy utterances, that I may not sin against thee” (Ps. CXVIII). A person hides God’s utterance in the heart [Col. 0630A] when he receives it through love, retains it through memory, and covers it through humility. If it were never covered, it would not be warmed; if it were never revealed, it would not be multiplied. The heart is a nest, the word an egg, the work a fledgling. Warm and nourish it. It is not made alive unless it is nourished. You sin if you do not receive it; you sin if you reject it once received; you sin if you expose it before its time once retained. The first is hardness, the second negligence, the third pride. Therefore hide it, lest you sin.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. That justifications come about through works

“Blessed art thou, O Lord; teach me thy justifications” (Ps. CXVIII). “Not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers” (Rom. II). Therefore God justifies through good work. One knows God’s justifications who understands it to be just that a person who committed evil with pleasure [Col. 0630B] should not be able to do good without pain and labor; nor does one who is humbled for guilt complain under punishment.

## CHAPTER LXXV. What impedes speech, and what are the judgments of heart and mouth; likewise, on the four ways in which judgments are made

“With my lips I have declared all the judgments of thy mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). This is a good order: first the humility of silence, then the pursuit of good work, and finally the confidence of declaring the word. “In my heart”: silence. “Teach me thy justifications”: work. “With my lips I have declared”: word.

There are two things that seal a person’s lips so that he cannot speak: ignorance, when he does not know; and an evil conscience, when he is ashamed. Therefore, against ignorance: “In my heart I have hidden thy utterances”; against [Col. 0630C] an evil conscience: “Teach me thy justifications.” “I have declared” signifies confidence in speaking. “All the judgments of thy mouth”: “I have hidden nothing,” that is, “I have said everything.” What you said to me I have declared: I hid nothing of yours and added nothing of my own, lest I either preach falsehood or deny truth.

The judgments of the heart are hidden; the judgments of the mouth are manifest. The judgments of the mouth are those you have set forth; the judgments of the heart those you have concealed. The judgments of the heart are where the sentence is devised; the judgments of the mouth where the sentence is uttered. Therefore what is manifest is declared; what is hidden cannot be known. To be silent concerning the former would be sloth; to presume concerning the latter would be arrogance.

There are four ways in which judgments are made. Sometimes God gives evil for evil unto good, as he gave Saul punishment for guilt for correction. [Col. 0630D] Sometimes he gives goods for good unto evil, as he gave a rich man abundance of goods for righteousness, for recompense. Sometimes he gives evil for evil unto evil, as he gave Herod, Antiochus, and Judas punishment for guilt unto condemnation. Sometimes he gives good for good unto good, as he gave Abraham and Job abundance for righteousness unto salvation.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. Who is exercised in God’s commandments

“I shall be exercised in thy commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). One is exercised who, by present application, is trained toward better and future goods. Therefore one is exercised in God’s commandments who so continually considers the good things he does that through them he believes himself to be prepared for the good things still to be done, [Col. 0631A] considering himself not as already perfected, but always as one beginning.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the manifold way of God, and who consider it

“I will consider thy ways” (Ps. CXVIII). The way of God is that by which inward inspiration comes to us. The way of God is that by which we go to him: good action. Therefore one considers God’s ways who watches attentively over the pursuit of practicing good works. One also considers God’s ways who carefully observes his inward coming to himself—when he comes, and to what sort of persons he comes—so that he may recognize the time of his visitation.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. How he calls the Lord’s utterances sweet to his throat; whether by eating them, and, if they are food, what sort of food they are

[Col. 0631B] “How sweet are thy utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). Do you suppose, brother, that this man was accustomed to eat God’s words, so that he said, “How sweet are thy utterances to my throat”? Who indeed would eat words? If God’s words are eaten, they are certainly food. But what kind of food? I think not food for the belly, but for the mind. In that saying there is both the fasting of the belly and the food of the mind: “Man does not live by bread alone,” Scripture says, “but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV).

Yet there is some likeness between the food of the belly and the food of the mind, and for this reason God’s words are called food: as bodily food refreshes the flesh, so wisdom feeds the mind. Bodily food has three things in it: flavor, nourishment, and bulk. Flavor delights; nourishment sustains; bulk burdens. Flavor pertains to the palate, nourishment to nature, bulk to misery. The throat receives flavor; the stomach receives nourishment and bulk: one for refreshment, the other for burden. It receives nourishment to convey it into the body; bulk to cast it out. Flavor is in some manner spiritual and therefore only delights; it does not burden.

Hence hunger can never be satisfied in the throat, because there desire has no measure and delight no end. But in the stomach hunger receives satiety, because there the appetite for eating has a fixed measure and delight an end. For since the stomach does not receive the nourishment that sustains without the bulk that burdens, lest it begin to crave without measure that which benefits, [Col. 0631D] the bulk which it receives at the same time restrains it by weighing it down. For when the weight which it bears unwillingly begins to burden it and, as it were, suffocate it, it then voluntarily ceases to desire the nourishment that refreshed it.

Therefore, brother, when you eat, do not ask your throat whether it has had enough. For if you follow its judgment, before you fill it with delight you will suffocate your stomach with burden. Rather consult your belly concerning the measure of eating, and before it begins to hurt, restrain your throat’s greed.

Yet understand this to have been said concerning bodily food. With regard to the refreshment of spiritual food, however, it is the throat rather than the belly that must be consulted. By throat I mean not the carnal but the spiritual throat; and by belly I mean not the carnal but the spiritual belly. For just as we know spiritual food, [Col. 0632A] so we must understand throat and belly spiritually. Spiritual food—that is, God’s word—likewise has its own flavor, which delights the spiritual throat; its own nourishment, which feeds and quickens the spiritual substance; and its own bulk, which in some manner presses and burdens weakness.

We call the spiritual throat the palate of the heart. The flavor of God’s word is the taste of inward sweetness. The soul itself is the spiritual substance. The nourishment of God’s word is the practice of virtue; its bulk, however, is the weight of labor. Therefore, since that flavor of inward sweetness is received without distaste, the throats of the heart, as though tasting a certain spiritual food, receive delight but cannot be filled. But since the practice of virtue, by which the soul is fed, is not received without the weight of labor, by which the flesh is burdened, the stomach, as it were, of our sensual nature, while receiving the food of good work by practicing it, is chastened by the very labor of the work that presses it, lest it desire beyond measure the virtue by which it is refreshed.

[Col. 0632B] By now, I think, you understand sufficiently what this man meant when he said: “How sweet are thy utterances to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” He did not say, “Sweet to my belly,” but “to my throat”; not “to my stomach,” but “to my mouth.” As though he said: “Indeed, Lord, through thy word the belly of carnality is pressed down, but inwardly the palate of the heart is delighted by the flavor of sweetness; for although the labor of work burdens weakness outwardly, inwardly the sweetness and taste of delight nevertheless feed desire.”

This is why that beloved and dear John, who was accustomed so frequently and so gladly to eat the word of God, testifies concerning himself, saying: “I received the book from the angel’s hand and devoured it; and it was sweet as honey in my mouth; but when I had devoured it, my belly became bitter” (Rev. X). Thus you too, brother, devour the book of life; eat God’s word. And do not merely eat it, but eat it eagerly; and do not on account of its sweetness abandon it if you feel some bitterness in your belly.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. How Christ is a lamp to us

“Thy word is a lamp to my feet” (Ps. CXVIII). A lamp is light in an earthen vessel; light in a vessel is divinity in humanity. The vessel is humanity; the light is divinity. Life is the way; darkness is ignorance. Christ went before bearing the lamp; the Christian follows, keeping to the path of the example. [Col. 0632D] He set forth shining humanity; from divinity he raised up the lamp, so that we may see by faith, walk by action, and be directed by imitation: one goes before, many follow.

## CHAPTER LXXX. How the eyes of the good are directed toward the Lord, etc.

“As the eyes of servants are upon the hands of their masters” (Ps. CXXXII). Where the staff is, there the eye is. For a servant is one who fears the whip. The eye of a child is upon the face; the eye of a servant upon the hand. “So our eyes are upon the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.”

## CHAPTER LXXXI. What is both good and pleasant

“Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in one” (Ps. CXXXII). In this world some things [Col. 0633A] are good but not pleasant; again, some things are pleasant but not good. To dwell together in one is good and pleasant: this is charity. It means in one mind, not in one place. For to be one in place yet not in mind is punishment. Goodness is unity in mind, not in place; happiness is unity in place and mind. The first unity is that the members adhere to the head; the second, that they do not depart from one another. By the first they live; by the second they are one.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Why the Lord reserved his judgment until the end

[Col. 0634A]

“The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth.” The Lord reserved his judgment until the end, so that justice may be fulfilled (1 Sam. II). Justice is not brought to perfection in human judgment; and therefore human judgment comes first, so that the human being may be tested, then God’s judgment follows, so that he may be rewarded. If humanity judged everything, God would have no judgment.

# BOOK THREE. NOTES ON SCRIPTURE, SERMONS, FRAGMENTS OF SERMONS, ETC.

[Col. 0633]

## TITLE I. On what follows the sacrament of baptism

[Col. 0633B]

In the crossing of the Jordan—note what is said—“the people hastened and crossed the Jordan” (Josh. IV), because when we come to baptism we must not act sluggishly, but hasten and press on, so that we may pass through all things. For to pass through is to fulfill everything commanded. First, as it is written, we must be blessed poor in spirit (Matt. V); then we must hunger and thirst for justice (ibid.); but neither then may we stand still. Rather, we must pass through, so that in this world we may mourn, and so forth, as follows: we must press on until, as children of God, we pass through even the burdens of persecution.

Moreover, note what is said: “They crossed girded” (Josh. III), lest, in walking too carelessly, our steps should be spilled in some fall. For diligence in preserving virtues ought to be no less than in gathering them. This girdle, however, is made from truth: for if we speak falsely, we are ungirded from Christ’s soldiery and unfastened from the belt of truth. Therefore note that Scripture adds, “Girded in the Spirit of the Lord,” because it is not enough to preserve truth before human beings unless you preserve it also before God: it must be on the tongue and in the heart, where God looks.

By this girdle Jericho is conquered after the crossing of the Jordan. For we cross over to battles; and we should seek these on no field other than that of our own heart, from which, according to the Gospel, evil thoughts, murders, thefts, and other sins proceed (Matt. XV). Do you see how great an army comes out against you? Let us therefore go forth to this war, so that the first city of this world—wickedness—may be besieged by us, and its proud [Col. 0633D] walls utterly destroyed, so that nothing revives, breaks forth, or breathes in our thoughts.

Then through Jesus there shall be given to the victor that rest, each under his vine and fig tree, so that there is no one to terrify him. After these things a second circumcision is performed with a stone knife, so that one who departs from the Law and the Prophets may come and receive in the Gospel a second circumcision through Christ the rock. Thus may be fulfilled what God said: “Today he has taken away the reproach of Egypt from the children of Israel” (Josh. V).

The reproaches of Egypt are the vices and sins of the enticements of flesh and soul. But where the second circumcision is given, when not only bodily but also spiritual vices have been abandoned, the reproaches of Egypt are removed, so that one is now neither Egyptian nor Jew, but Christian and a member of Christ. Therefore, if the enticement of desire strikes, meet this enemy born from your own flesh and say: “I am not my own. I was bought at the price of Christ’s blood and made a member of Christ. It is not lawful for me to take his member and make it the member of a prostitute” (1 Cor. VI). And say with the holy Idumaean: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not even think about a virgin” (Job XXXI).

For this is one of the reproaches of Egypt: that, thus purified in heart and body, guarding against a stain even upon that body which is the Church—for from one defiled member the stain spreads through the whole body—we may glorify God with pure hands, lips, and minds. To him be honor and glory for ages of ages.

## TITLE II. On the circumcision of every evil, and on the threefold food given to the Israelites

The circumcised children of Israel rested a second time in the same place until they were healed (Josh. V). For it is not enough to be circumcised by abstaining from evil works and thoughts, unless first, having been thoroughly cleansed of vices and having undertaken works of virtue, we are healed even as the marks of the scars are covered over. After this it may then be said that the reproach of Egypt has been taken away; and on the fourteenth day the Passover may be celebrated—which an unclean and uncircumcised person cannot celebrate—and they may eat the fruit of palms.

In this, three kinds of food given to the children of Israel should be noted. The first, for those departing Egypt, was flour mixed with water. The second, in the wilderness, was manna [Col. 0634D] from heaven. The third, in the Holy Land, was the fruit of the palm. The first belongs to beginners through repentance; the second, to those advancing through the Eucharist; the third is for the perfect and blessed through grace: Christ, the son of Mary, is displayed to them as the reward and fruit of victory—that is, eternal blessedness—in triumph over their enemies.

## TITLE III. On the trumpets of Holy Scripture, and on how attentive reading of it produces contempt for the world
Jericho, which is overthrown by the trumpets of the priests (Joshua 6), is the world. Therefore Jesus son of Nun—that is, Christ appearing in the flesh—sends the apostles bearing hammered trumpets, namely the magnificent and heavenly teaching of preaching [Col. 0635A]. The first of these are Matthew and Mark, Luke and John; each sounded his own trumpet. Peter sounded the trumpets of two Epistles; James and Jude, each one; John, three; and that last one who said, “I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last” (1 Cor. 4), and who thundered against the walls of Jericho with the trumpets of fourteen Epistles, overthrowing the engines of idolatry and the walls of vices. Thus, at the trumpet, the whole people, according to another translation, might cry aloud with a great shout for the destruction of the city, when the whole world now assents to preaching by abandoning idolatry: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. 88 [89]).

This jubilation is a certain disposition of harmony and unity; when it comes upon two or three, the heavenly Father grants them whatever they ask [Col. 0635B]. But if the blessedness is so great that even the people remain harmonious in one mind and judgment, let the people rejoice aloud, and the city of the world will utterly fall. Yet each person ought to accomplish this within himself. Through faith you have Jesus as your leader; he is priest, for you are “a royal race, a holy priesthood.” Make for yourself hammered trumpets from the Scriptures—for this is why they are called hammered—and sound them in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. And if you thus sound the trumpets and carry the ark around seven times—that is, if you do not separate the mystical precepts of the Law from those of the Gospel; if you also require from yourself the agreement of jubilation, that is, if the people of your thoughts and perceptions who are within you bring forth a voice harmonious in good—then Jericho is destroyed for you [Col. 0635C], the world is destroyed, so that none of the things belonging to the world may be retained.

For it is declared to be an anathema when it is said: “Keep yourselves from the anathema, lest you make the camp of the children of Israel an anathema.” John sounds this trumpet in his Epistle when he says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2). For those who bring worldly things into the Church defile God’s camp and cause it to be conquered by enemies, as the Apostle says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). Let us see what the theft of the anathema is (Joshua 7). The golden tongue [or: golden rule; *lingua*, Vulgate: *regula*] of the poets is their reading, which weaves together gods and goddesses in measured verses and glittering speech. Do not introduce into the tabernacle of your heart the golden tongue which he placed in his tent, nor the two hundred shekels of silver—perhaps, pure ornaments for the right hand [*ducentos siclos argenti*, perhaps *pura dextralia*]—that is, the sweetness of this eloquence [Col. 0635D]. Do not have a golden tongue, lest you become like Basilides and Valentinus; nor, perhaps, [do not have] right-hand ornaments, that is, works alone in which nothing divine is mingled, but everything is done according to man.

Likewise, because of the sin of the anathema, those inhabiting Ai killed very many of Israel. But Jesus son of Nun, coming against this enemy, divides the people into two parts, so that, when the first group flees and afterwards springs back into the midst of the enemies, he kills them on both sides; and he hangs the king of Ai upon a double piece of wood. Ai is interpreted “chaos,” which is the dwelling-place of demons; their king is Zebul. By them, because we have sinned, we have been conquered and cast down. But when our Jesus comes, he divides the people into two parts [Col. 0636A]. The two parts are the Jewish people and the Gentile people, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Glory and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2). The Jew, as though the former group, appears to flee when he withdraws from the burden of the Law and the observance of the Sabbath. But he turns back against the enemies when, through observance of the Gospel, he rises against those pursuing him. And when the latter people, that is, the Gentiles, pursue as though from behind, the army of evil ones is crushed, and their king Zebul is hung by Jesus upon the double wood. For upon the wood of the cross, which was twofold, according to the Apostle, he triumphed over the devil, fastening him to it.

For Christ’s cross was twofold in its wood, and this is established by a twofold reason. Visibly, the Son of God was crucified; invisibly, Zebul was fastened upon it. The first [sense is that] in which, according to Peter’s saying, Christ was crucified, “leaving us an example” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 0636B]; the second, that that cross was a trophy over the devil. The Apostle shows this twofold meaning of the cross when he says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6). He says that two contrary things have been crucified: himself, a righteous man, and the sinful world. We are crucified to the world when it finds nothing in us; the world is crucified to us when we do not receive sins.

## TIT. IV. On the altar built from stones and Deuteronomy written upon them

After the overthrow of Ai, Jesus builds an altar, according to what Moses did with stones (Joshua 8), namely whole stones upon which iron had not been applied. For after demons and vices have been overthrown, one altar is made from many whole persons, because they are without the corruption of vices [Col. 0636C], and upon them iron has not been applied: that is, they have not received the fiery darts of the evil one, namely lust. It is one altar because of unanimity; one altar because upon it, as upon a certain altar, a whole burnt offering is made in the case of those who devote themselves wholly to divine services, and a sacrifice in the case of those who, though still using lawful things in the world, nevertheless refrain from unlawful things.

And he wrote Deuteronomy upon the stones of the altar, that is, the second Law. If you wish to see how Jesus, after the first Law has been weakened, writes the second, hear him himself saying: “It was said to those of old: You shall not kill. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother is a murderer. It was said to those of old: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. It was said to those of old: You shall not swear falsely. But I say: Do not swear at all” (Matt. 5). You see how Jesus writes the second Law upon stones—not upon stone tablets, but upon the tablets of the heart; not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.

## TIT. V. On the threefold condition of the Canaanite

“Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite?” and so forth (Judg. 1). The account of the Canaanite is found in three parts. First, among Ephraim, under tribute, until Pharaoh should come, advance upon the city, kill the Canaanite, and give it as a dowry to his daughter. Second, when the children of Israel grew strong, they made the Canaanites subject and servants, but did not utterly destroy them. Third, it is said to the children of Ephraim—among whom they had previously been only under tribute—that they should exterminate them [Col. 0637A].

The Canaanite, then, whose name is interpreted “mobile and unstable,” is our flesh, always present with us, however much we bear fruit. For Ephraim is interpreted “fruitfulness.” The flesh, therefore, is stirred against those beginning to bear good fruit, because everyone who wishes to live devoutly suffers persecutions from the flesh, the world, and the devil (2 Tim. 3). For at first the flesh is only under tribute, because it renders a certain service in acting to the soul; and unless the soul subjects it, there is reason to fear lest Pharaoh kill both the city, that is, the soul, and the Canaanite, that is, the flesh, and assign them as a dowry to his daughter, that is, to the law of sin.

Second, when the children of Israel become strong, they make it a servant and obedient, when the flesh serves and obeys the will of the soul [Col. 0637B]. Although it resists as long as it fights against the spirit, it is not utterly exterminated. But if, thirdly, by the command of Jesus, according to the Apostle, we put to death our members—fornication, impurity, and the rest—so that they may no longer rise against us, bearing about in our body the death of Christ, then the Canaanite is said to be wholly exterminated.

Let us therefore take care to subject to ourselves the Canaanite that is with us, to make it obedient, and even to exterminate it. For if we neglect this, Pharaoh will come from Egypt and give our place to his daughter, namely, the law of sin. Far be it from the Israelite tribe, which God brought out of Egypt, to serve again Pharaoh, whom he drowned in the Red Sea! Let us prevail against the Canaanite, lest, if he prevails, he make us Canaanites from Israelites [Col. 0637C], as happened to the one to whom, overcome by the enticement of the flesh, it is said: “The seed of Canaan, and not the form of Judah, has deceived you” (Dan. 13). It follows: “And Canaan was cursed, a servant.”

## TIT. VI. Teaching that a judge of the Church should not always employ the sword, that is, severity, but sometimes the share of the plough, that is, gentleness, toward those subject to him

Ehud, ambidextrous, having nothing left-handed, girded with a sword upon his right thigh, killed the prince of Moab. But Shamgar, son of Anath and his successor, killed the Philistines with a ploughshare, as it were with the plough-handle, that is, with the foot of the plough (Judg. 3). By these things Scripture teaches that a judge of the Church should not always draw the sword and employ the sharpness and severity of correction; but should sometimes plough the soil of the soul [Col. 0637D] and, by gentle admonition breaking it up, prepare it to receive suitable seeds. For often vices are driven from the souls of hearers like Philistines no less by rustic and simple admonition than by sharp correction.

And you yourself, hearer, use this plough: become the farmer of your own soul; and when you have put your hand to it, do not look back.

## TIT. VII. On the defeat of the Midianites and Gideon’s fleece and its dew, etc.

The Midianites set up camp in the valley of Jezreel to attack Israel (Judg. 6). They do so in the valley because the Midianites, whose name is interpreted “outside judgment,” that is, demons [Col. 0638A] already judged, do not dare to approach those who are on the mountains. But [they camp] in the valley of Jezreel, which is interpreted “seed of God.” They did not dare to go where there are fruits, but only where there is seed, from which the fruit has not yet arisen.

Gideon, about to fight against them, consulted God after the sign of the wet fleece and then of the threshing-floor. The dew first in the fleece is the divine word in Judea, namely in the Law and the Prophets; afterwards [the dew] in the threshing-floor, that is, among the Gentiles, namely in the apostles and the Gospel. Hence it descends “as rain upon the fleece” of the Jews, and “as drops upon the earth” of the Gentiles (Ps. 71 [72]).

Gideon squeezed the fleece into a bowl and filled it with dew. This is the Savior, who places in a basin the water of the word from the fleece of the Law and Prophets, like the dew of heavenly grace, in order to wash the disciples’ feet. Hence he says: “You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” [Col. 0638B] (John 15). But if we too offer our feet to the Lord, that is, the feet of our soul, he is ready to wash them with the grace of the Holy Spirit and the word of teaching, and to say: “I have washed your feet, that you too may do likewise” (John 13).

Let us receive water from the springs of Israel; and, squeezing it from the fleece of the books of Kings, Judges, and the rest, let us put it first into the basin of our own soul, receiving the meaning in our heart. Then, taking the feet of our brothers, let us wash the feet of their souls as far as we are able, fulfilling the Lord’s command, so that hearers may be cleansed from the filth of sins by the word of teaching and may have clean feet, with which they may rightly walk toward the preparation of the Gospel of peace. By this Gospel God cleanses all together in Christ through the word of God [Col. 0638C].

Let us not be cast out from the bridegroom’s chamber because of filthy garments; but in white garments, with washed feet and a clean heart, let us recline at the banquet of our bridegroom Jesus Christ. To him be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

## TIT. VIII. On the three hundred who, while drinking the water of the stream, did not bend their knees

After receiving the sign, let us see in whom our Gideon conquered. For he conquered in those who are tested when led to the water: those who do not bend their knees to drink, but lap with hand or tongue (Judg. 7). For those who, coming to the water of baptism or repentance, fall down to the earth while seeking the earth, bend their knees and yield to temptations, having lowly affections [Col. 0638D], loosened knees, and not making a straight path with their steps. They are excluded from this battle and victory.

But those who stand and, according to the Apostle’s admonition, do not again cling to the yoke of slavery, but lap the water with hand and tongue—that is, like soldiers of Christ, work by word and hand, fulfilling in deed what they say—these, like a dog that preserves love for its master unto death and is not driven back by any injuries, overcome enemies by lanterns, lamps, and trumpets. The task must indeed be performed by bright works and words. And the likeness of the enemies is taken from the likeness of locusts. For the multitude of demons is compared to locusts, which have no dwelling either in heaven or on earth.

## TIT. IX. On the sevenfold leprosy of human pride

[Col. 0639A]

Elisha commanded Naaman the leper to be immersed seven times in the Jordan (4 Kings 5). For the leprosy of pride takes hold of us in seven ways: in possessing property, in the glory of garments, in bodily pleasure, twice in the mouth, and twice in the heart.

From the first, by which we wish to be rich in this world, one is cleansed in the first descent into the Jordan—which is interpreted “descent.” For in Christ’s descent, that is, in the humility of his manner of life, by which, though rich, he became poor: if one immersed [there] sees that he had nowhere to lay his head, when will he seek the riches of this world?

From the second leprosy, that of garments, by which we understand all the pompous vanity of the world, we are cleansed on emerging from the Jordan, where we find Christ wrapped in cheap rags, made “the reproach of men and the rejection of the people” [Col. 0639B]. From the third leprosy, that of the body, we are cleansed in the Jordan itself if, rightly reflecting upon the Lord’s passion, we are ashamed to follow bodily pleasure.

From the twofold leprosy of the mouth, which is the fourth and fifth—when amid adversities we pour forth a murmuring word like the discharge of leprosy, and amid prosperity contract the evil of boasting like the corruption of another leprosy—we are cleansed when immersed in the Jordan, as we attend to him who, “like a sheep led to slaughter, did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53), and imitate him who did not seek his own glory (John 8). Thus he commanded demons not to call him the Son of God (Matt. 8).

There is also a twofold leprosy in the heart: namely, one’s own will, which follows neither the will of God nor the benefit of one’s neighbor [Col. 0639C]. This sins in three ways, by willing that God either cannot, or will not, or does not know how to punish sins; and so it wills that God not exist, when it wills him to be either powerless, unjust, or foolish. From this most unclean leprosy we are relieved when washed in the Jordan, as we imitate him who came not to do his own will, but that of the Father who sent him.

[The other is] one’s own counsel, by which the obstinate person who does not yield to the counsel of others divides unity, tears peace asunder, and lacks charity. Let a person drenched in this leprosy be washed in the Jordan, considering how the Angel of Great Counsel, though he chose the counsel by which he would sit in the midst of the teachers, hearing and questioning them, nevertheless set it aside in submission to the counsel of his mother and father and his other parents [Col. 0639D] (Luke 2).

## TIT. X. On the sevenfold humility of Christ

In the Jordan—that is, in the descent of Christ’s humility, which possesses sevenfold power—if you wash seven times, you will be cleansed. The first power was that, though rich, he became poor; the second, that he added extremity to poverty by being laid in a manger; the third, that he was subject to his mother; the fourth, that today he bent his head beneath the hands of a servant; the fifth, that he endured a disciple who was a thief and betrayer; the sixth, that he stood so meekly before an unjust judge; the seventh, that he prayed for those persecuting him.

You are washed seven times in this Jordan, as though in certain footprints, although following the giant from far behind [Col. 0640A]: if you love poverty; if you love the lowest estate among the poor; if you are subject to the disciplines of the monastery; if you endure the rule of one lower than yourself there; if you patiently bear false brothers; if you overcome by meekness when judged; if you return charity to those from whom you suffer justly.

This is the second baptism, in which what is accomplished in the one baptism in figure is fulfilled in truth: it repeats Christ’s death, but restores the mortification and burial of sins. Whoever is washed in this is cleansed, so that his heart and flesh become like those of a child, possessing within innocence of mind and outwardly purity in the members.

## TIT. XI. On the illness of King Hezekiah and its moral cure

“Hezekiah was sick unto death,” and so forth (Isa. 38) [Col. 0640B]. Hezekiah is sick whenever any person sins. The prophet enters to him and says: “You shall die and not live; set your house in order” (Ezek. 18), when the word entering the sinner’s mind says: “The soul that sins shall die” (ibid.). “Every tree that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down,” and so forth (Matt. 3). Therefore, set your house in order, that is, order your conscience.

Struck by compunction at these words, he turns his face toward the wall when he sets before his eyes the wall of sins that is built as sins are added to sin, and that separates the sinner from God. Previously he had had it, as it were, behind his back, when he took no care of those sins; now he attempts to destroy it, striking it with tears as with so many blows. Just as the prophet had threatened death to the negligent man, so the same prophet promises life when he says: “Whenever a sinner groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities” (Ezek. 33); and: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18) [Col. 0640C].

And this is not merely any life, but a life of fifteen years. The number fifteen contains seven, the number consecrated because of the sevenfold Spirit, and eight, which prefigures rest after the future resurrection. The prophet promises this life when Scripture sets before converts, meanwhile, perfect righteousness through the sevenfold Spirit, and in the future the full restoration of body and soul.

Then, because the sun turns back ten lines as a sign, God is recovered through the observance of the Ten Commandments. The sinner had received its shadow, as it were, by as many lines as the commandments he had violated through the darkness of sins. Therefore, when we are sick, let the prophet enter to us; and, pierced by his words, let us turn the face of our mind toward the wall of our sins. And, according to the prophet who says, “Dig through the wall and see the abomination” (Ezek. 8), let us pierce it with tears, saying: “Every night I will wash my bed” (Ps. 6) [Col. 0640D]. It is as though he said: “I will destroy my wall stone by stone.”

This must be done through humility, which God especially requires in repentance. For Solomon speaks “from the cedar that is in Lebanon even unto the hyssop that grows out of the wall” (3 Kings 4). The cedar, incorruptible and taller than almost all other trees, is the righteous person who neither here decays through vices nor in the future through punishments, and who, stretching toward heaven, can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Hyssop, a lowly herb that cleanses and reduces swelling, signifies humility, which purges vices and casts out pride.

Our Solomon, then, speaks from the cedar to the hyssop that grows out of the wall, because the Word of God reaches from innocence and righteousness to the humility of the penitent [Col. 0641A], which is born amid the close-packed mass of sins. The penitent person, however, who regains strength only when God strengthens him, bears the king’s name Hezekiah, which is interpreted, “The Lord has strengthened.”

## TIT. XII. On the embassy sent to Sihon, that is, the devil; on who his sons are; and on the royal road by which we must pass

The people sent to Sihon, king of the Amorites, saying: “I beg that I may be allowed to pass through your land,” and so forth (Num. 20) [Col. 0641B]. Sihon is interpreted “temptation,” and therefore signifies the devil, who tempts us daily. He is called king because he is king “over all the children of pride” (Job 41). What benefit is it to say that Christ is our prince if we are convicted by our affairs and works that the devil holds dominion in us? Is it not plain under which prince the greedy person, the unchaste person, and so forth, act? Where Christ exercises dominion, vices have no place.

We, therefore, are those who send to this king in order that we may pass through his land to the holy land. Let each of us remember how, when he first came to the waters of baptism and afterwards to ecclesiastical profession, we did all these things and declared that we would not remain in the devil’s land [Col. 0641C], nor turn aside into his vineyard or field—that is, neither toward devilish thoughts nor toward his works; that we would not drink water from his pool—that is, acquire a devilish mind—but from the springs of Israel; and that, renouncing all his pomps, we would pass along the royal road, that royal road which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14).

This especially provokes the king: that we have said we do not wish to remain with him. Thus he immediately gathers his army against Israel, that is, spirits of every vice. But what did Israel do? It came to Lasa [Saar]. Lasa is interpreted “fulfillment of the commandment.” If we come to this place so as to fulfill the commandments, even if Sihon comes against us with his entire army, even if he arrays all his demons and men against us [Col. 0641D], we overcome him and trample down all his powers, according to the saying: “Behold, he gave you power to tread upon scorpions and upon every power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke 10).

## TIT. XIII. On Jacob’s fourfold struggle and supplanting

Jacob set up a stone as a pillar (Gen. 28). Jacob struggled four times: with his brother while still in the womb; in youth with the same brother in the house; in Mesopotamia with Laban his father-in-law; and finally with the angel at Bethel. First, by the exercise of supplanting; second, by the counsel of supplanting; third, by the conflict of contention; fourth, by the sleep of a night vision.

Jacob, then, struggling four times and four times victorious in struggle, signifies the person strong in virtues who overcomes four kinds of temptation. These are: the strength of lions in tribulations; the poisons of dragons in heresies; the sweetness of hares in movements of the flesh; the cunning of foxes in false brothers [Col. 0642A].

The stone set up is Christ, cut from the mountain without hands and growing into a great mountain (Dan. 2), made a wondrous cornerstone between the two walls. Upon it, in four corners, is inscribed the title *Em-ma-nu-el*, which is interpreted “God with us.” For God is with us in four ways: through the presence of majesty, through participation in humanity, through the bond of charity, and through the protection of truth. In the first he knows our evils; in the second he has experienced them; in the third he has compassion on his brethren; in the fourth he removes them. Thus he is Emmanuel, God with us.

And so that you might know what God is called, on the second four-sided figure he arranged in the four corners four words: “Wonderful God, Counsellor, Mighty,” because God works in us by four things: justice, in the glorious recompense of the good, in that he is called God; power, in the eternal condemnation of the wicked, in that he is called Wonderful; wisdom, in complete knowledge of things, in that he is called Counsellor; patience, in the necessary persecution by the wicked, in that he is called Mighty [Col. 0642B]. Of the first it is said: “The Lord is righteous and loves righteousness” (Ps. 10 [11]), rewarding the good; of the second: “Great is the Lord and great is his power” (Ps. 146 [147]), punishing the wicked; of the third: “To whom every heart lies open and every will speaks,” every thought being revealed; of the fourth: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter” (Isa. 53), amid the contradiction set before him.

But although on the second [side] he placed a definition, because knowledge of things perishes without a name, on the third side he inscribed the title *Hia, he, vau, het*, which is the Tetragrammaton, because there are four quarters of the Word, that is, of the preaching of our Lord and Savior. The first is that we ought to believe in the heart; the second, that we ought to confess with the mouth what we believe; the third, that we ought to fulfill in work what we confess; the fourth, that we should not cease to teach what we have fulfilled.

Therefore, the first is in the heart by conception; the second in the mouth by confession; the third in work by performance; the fourth in teaching by preaching. The first justifies, because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness” [Col. 0642D] (Rom. 4); the second grants salvation, because confession with the mouth is made unto salvation (ibid.); the third gives eternity, because a good work opens heaven; the fourth gloriously crowns, because teaching adds to merit.

On the fourth [side] a title is inscribed through four names: God, spirit, flesh, world, because these four are found mutually indebted to one another in a certain reciprocal relation. God owes the spirit both illumination by knowledge of truth and kindling by love of virtue. The spirit owes God that it be instructed by him in all things that must be done, and that it do according to him what it can. The spirit, moreover, owes the flesh that it restrain it from evils and exercise it in doing good. The flesh owes the spirit service in doing good and moderation in seeking what is pleasant [Col. 0643A]. The flesh likewise owes the world that it receive from it what necessity requires and exercise what virtue requires. The world owes the flesh help in necessity and an incentive in exercise.

## TIT. XIV. On the bronze altar and the things offered upon it

Under the bronze altar is a pit containing perpetual fire, before which the flesh of animals is sacrificed (Lev. 16). The altar is obedience; it is bronze because obedience is so strong that neither death nor life can separate us from it. Beneath it is the pit of humility, containing the fire of charity; before it are sacrificed the bull, the ram, and the goat: the proud bull, the wanton ram, the foul-smelling goat. In the bull is pride; in the ram, anger; in the goat, lust.

Before this altar we sacrifice the bull when by humility we tame pride [Col. 0643B]; and this must necessarily take place in the soul before perfect obedience is present. We sacrifice the ram and the goat when by patience we restrain anger and by chastity curb lust. These too take place in the soul before perfect obedience is present.

## TIT. XV. That the Lord is the portion of the Lord’s priests; earthly possession, the portion of Pharaoh’s priests

Joseph leaves land to Pharaoh’s priests, but the Lord does not grant it to his own; rather, he takes it away, saying: “I am your portion” (Gen. 47). Take heed, priests of the Lord, and see that those who have power in the land and occupy themselves with earthly affairs and cults seem to be priests not of the Lord but of Pharaoh. Hasten to pass from the priests of Pharaoh to the priests of the Lord, for whom not the Lord’s land but the Lord himself is their portion [Col. 0643C].

Let each examine his conscience and scrutinize himself by inward reasoning, whether he serves God or Pharaoh. To serve Pharaoh is to be subject to demons, vices, and fleshly desires.

## TIT. XVI. On not changing one’s garment and not feigning one’s character through hypocrisy

“A man shall not put on a woman’s garment, nor a woman a man’s, because such a person is abominable before God” (Num. 18; Deut. 22). Here it is not a change of clothing, but the feigning of virtue, that makes a person abominable. For when the hypocrite, pretending to be righteous, becomes a woman in strength and pleasures, he wears a man’s garment: outwardly a sheep, inwardly a wolf. Likewise, if a holy man outwardly displays the softness that is not within him, he uses a woman’s garment.

## TIT. XVII. The three testimonies of the saints in confirmation of the Christian faith

[Col. 0643D]

“Your testimonies have become exceedingly trustworthy” (Ps. 92 [93]), namely in the martyrs. There are three things by which the saints have contributed most greatly to Christian religion: instruction, testimony, and example—instruction by preaching, testimony by confession, example by suffering. Because faith, hope, and charity are especially required, the instruction of preaching has contributed most greatly to building faith; the testimony of confession, to raising hope; the example of suffering, to stirring charity.

## TIT. XVIII. On the twofold circumcision necessary for those who wish to sing a new song to the Lord

“He put a new song in my mouth” (Ps. 39 [40]) [Col. 0644A]. And elsewhere: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. 97 [98]). In order that we may be renewed and able to sing a new song, we must be fortified with a twofold circumcision, as we read concerning the ancient people that it was circumcised twice. Let us be circumcised by the twofold circumcision of flesh and mind, as the Apostle says: “Providing things good not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12).

The circumcision of the flesh consists of three things: dress, action, and speech. And because these three are assessed outwardly, they are said to belong to the circumcision of the flesh. Let us beware of being conspicuous in dress, blameworthy in action, or contemptible in speech. This will be so if each of these is shaped by a threefold quality. Action [must be shaped] by purity, piety, and chastity. Action should be pure, so that it displays cleanness; pious, so that it breathes mercy; chaste, so that it injures neither God nor neighbor [Col. 0644B]. Speech, however, ought to be adorned by truth, usefulness, and humility: by truth, without the paint of pretense or admixture of falsehood; by usefulness, so that it builds up hearers; by humility, so that it does not swell with the beauty of rhetorical ornament. If we have been adorned in this manner, we shall not be conspicuous in dress, speech, or action. See how the circumcision of the flesh ought to be made and in what parts it consists.

The circumcision of the mind, however, consists in three things: thought, affection, and intention. Thought moves within memory as in an ark; for memory is an ark in which we must preserve what we wish to have ready at hand. Its servant is thought, which brings in whatever is brought into it and brings out whatever is brought out. But if anything dishonorable is brought in, let the recollection of our profession arise, and let us recall that we are clerics, that is, those pledged to chastity, cultivators of righteousness, admitted into the number of Levites, so that we may offer sacrifices pleasing to God [Col. 0644C]. If we offer these sacrifices, whatever disorderly thing thought has brought in will be repelled.

Likewise, if affection wishes to introduce something shameful contrary to honor, let the memory of the heavenly homeland come to meet it, where there is life without death, light without cloud, day without night, peace without end; where are the praiseworthy number of angels, the choir of apostles, the army of martyrs, and the assembly of confessors and virgins.

Likewise, if intention devises to introduce anything contrary to reason, so that God is excluded and the devil introduced, let fear of the punishment of hell meet us. Let the fear of that unquenchable fire be recalled to memory, where there is continual hunger, thirst never relieved, unbearable torment of cold and heat, countless misery from worms, the horror of darkness, the gnashing of teeth, and everlasting terror dwelling there [Col. 0644D].

The first things, therefore, are to be thought upon; the middle things embraced; the last fled from, so that thought may be clean, affection holy, and intention pure. Thus we must be circumcised in flesh and mind; and if we are thus circumcised and renewed, we shall be able to rejoice and sing the new song which no one knows except the one who sings it.

## TIT. XIX. On the Ziphites trying to betray David to Saul, just as the devil tries to deliver the elect to death

David hides among the Ziphites, by whom he is betrayed to Saul; but Saul, entering a cave, is delivered into the hands of David, who is fleeing [Col. 0645A] (1 Kings 23–24). The Ziphites, whose name is interpreted “flourishing,” signify those who flourish today and tomorrow are cast into the furnace. David hides among them: the saints, dead to the world, whose life is hidden in glory. Saul is death, by which the devil is signified. The saints are betrayed to him by the Ziphites when they strive to draw them into the kingdom of death. Yet while he wishes to send suggestions of his own foulness into the cave, that is, into the bodies of the saints, he is delivered into the hands of the saints, being overcome by them through his own temptation.

## TIT. XX. On the fourfold siege and capture of Jerusalem, in its moral sense

“They set up their signs, signs,” and so forth (Ps. 73 [74]). “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” [Col. 0645B] (2 Tim. 3). Hence Jerusalem, a city full of people, mistress of nations, ruler of provinces, sits alone as a widow under tribute: first conquered by the Assyrians, second by the Chaldeans, third by Antiochus, fourth by the Romans.

Jerusalem has a fourfold meaning. First, it is this earthly city; second, the Catholic Church; third, the faithful soul; fourth, our mother who is above. The aforementioned men attack the earthly city; idolaters and false Christians, the second; vices, sins, and demons, the third. The prophet laments the siege of this latter, exposed to vices, trampled by sins, oppressed by demons, saying: “They set up their signs”—specifically the Assyrian, Chaldean, Antiochus, and Roman.

“Assyrian” is interpreted “one directing,” in whom pride is denoted. He sets up two signs: arrogance [Col. 0645C] and presumption. The Chaldean is fierce, in whom is disobedience; and he has two signs: boasting and impatience. Antiochus is opposed to chastity, in whom fornication is signified; and he has two signs: gluttony and drunkenness. The Roman has the flavor of exaltation, which is avarice. He is like a solitary wild beast; in order to devour everything, he sets up five signs: robbery, simony, ambition, license for sin, and despair of pardon. These spirits of vices, therefore, princes of darkness, surround Jerusalem, that is, the soul; they set up the aforesaid standards and guard the gates.

## TIT. XXI. On the perfect city and the things necessary to it
“They have cut down her gates with axe; with hatchet they have cast her down” (Ps. 73). Above he spoke of the siege; here [Col. 0645D] he treats of the overthrow of the city itself. Four things belong to the condition of a perfect city: the first to health, the second to stability, the third to beauty, the fourth to necessity. So also, for the condition of the soul: commandments of life belong to health; exercises of discipline to stability; gifts of grace to beauty; counsels of glory to necessity.

The first door or gate of this city is repentance; its gatekeeper is compunction. At this gate the commandments are kept. The second gate is obedience; its gatekeeper is the mortification of the flesh; here are found the exercises of discipline. The third door is steadfastness; its gatekeeper is devotion; there are the gifts of grace. The fourth is eminence of purity; its gatekeeper is the remembrance of heavenly joy; here it keeps the counsels of glory.

The love of the world therefore attacks the first gate [Col. 0646A]; self-love the second; presumption the third; pride the fourth. Each has an axe and a hatchet. Love of the world comes with the axe—that is, freedom to sin—and with the hatchet of flattery. Then repentance is broken, compunction is slain, and the keeping of the commandments is taken away. For it says: “By my strength I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood. I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. 5).

But self-love approaches with the axe—that is, the wantonness of the flesh—and the hatchet of ambition. Alas! Fasting is scattered, continence is trampled down, silence is destroyed, and every exercise of religion perishes. For it says: “All things were created for use. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let not the flower of time pass us by. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” [Col. 0646B] (Wis. 2).

Presumption, meanwhile, assails the gate of steadfastness with the axe of boasting and the hatchet of foolish merriment. Then the beauty of heavenly gifts perishes: the word of wisdom, the salt of teaching and divine revelation, and honour of this kind. Finally, pride comes to storm the gate of purity with the axe of presumptuous indignation and the hatchet of empty glory. Alas! At once the purity of the mind is destroyed; the banquets of paradise are trampled underfoot; the kisses of bridegroom and bride are severed; and the counsels of every joy are broken apart. Then love is destroyed and contemplation taken away, so that the prophet may truly say of them: “Her gates are sunk into the ground; he has ruined and broken her bars,” and has plundered everything (Lam. 2).

“Serve the Lord, brothers, in fear, and rejoice before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). For [Col. 0646C] if you glory against God in the brilliance of counsel, he is the one “who brings counsellors to a foolish end”; if in the power of judgment, he reduces them to astonishment; if in the height of holiness, he “leads priests away without glory”; if in the splendour of eloquence, he “takes away the teaching of elders.” Of such persons he says through the prophet Amos: “There shall be no flight for them” (Amos 9), because “there is none who can hide from his heat” (Ps. 18). Fear your deeds, knowing that he will by no means spare the offender. Supply virtue in your faith; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, patience; in patience, brotherly love.

## TITLE XXII. On manifold vision

“I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high [Col. 0646D] and lifted up,” etc. (Isa. 6). There are three visions. The first is from the creation of the world, concerning which the Apostle says: “The invisible things of God from the creation of the world,” etc. (Rom. 1). The second is from the purity of faith, concerning which he says: “Now we see through a mirror,” etc. (1 Cor. 23 [probably 13]). The third is from the splendour of God and of the Bridegroom, concerning which he says: “But then face to face” (ibid.).

In another sense, the first vision is revelation with matter and form, and is made under the appearance of an angel to the holy Fathers. The second is inspiration without matter but with form, and is made through the sweetness of ointment to holy minds. The third is an outpouring without matter and form, and is made in an ecstasy of the mind amid the Bridegroom’s embraces. In the first vision the soul becomes a throne and surpasses the state of the world; in the second, lofty, and surpasses its own affection and the will of its inner faculties by self-contempt; in the third, lifted up [Col. 0647A], and surpasses the office of an angel, the understanding of a creature, and the capacity of nature, in the Bridegroom’s embrace.

## TITLE XXIII. On the three enemies, and the three things difficult according to Solomon

“I brought you out of the land of Egypt,” etc. (Mic. 6). When they left Egypt, God delivered them from three kinds of enemies: in Egypt, from the pursuing Egyptians; in the middle of the journey, from the Amalekites; at the entrance into the land of promise, from the Amorites who came to meet them. Thus there are three kinds of enemies: behind, at the side, and in front. The first are at conversion; the second in one’s manner of life, as it were in the middle; the third at the dissolution of flesh and soul, and thus at the end.

These are the three things difficult according to Solomon: “the way of a serpent upon the earth” (Prov. 30), that is, suggestion; “the way of a ship in the midst of the sea” (ibid.), that is [Col. 0647B], the temptation of human life upon earth in bitterness; “the way of an eagle in heaven” (ibid.), that is, the intention of someone concerning the end—namely contemplation—by which the soul of the righteous person flies like an eagle to heaven on the wings of virtues.

## TITLE XXIV. On the seven crimes or sins

“For three crimes of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn him back” (Amos 3). There are seven crimes: three are in the soul and four in the body. The three in the soul are pride, vain glory, and envy. They arise from the soul’s three corrupted powers, when rationality is turned into pride, concupiscence into vain glory, and irascibility into envy.

The four in the body are curiosity in the eyes, talkativeness in the tongue, cruelty in the hands, and pleasure in the loins. For [Col. 0647C] when a human being, composed of four elements, receives light from fire, speech from air, bodily solidity from earth, and an abundance of natural humours from water, curiosity arises from the insolence of sight; talkativeness from the lightness of the tongue; cruelty from the solidity of the body. Thus brute animals, being more devoted to the body, are more cruel. From natural moisture comes the flow of lust. Thus the three vices in the soul and the four in the body make three and four corruptions, over which the sinner becomes obstinate and is not converted.

## TITLE XXV. Who should be called one, and who many

“There was one man” (1 Kings [1 Sam.] 1). None of us is one, but many. How is he one who now has a cheerful face, now a sad one, now an angry one, now a gentle one; now an avaricious heart, now a lustful one? You see [Col. 0647D] how one thought to be a single person is not one but many, in whom there are as many persons as there are dispositions; for according to the Scriptures, “the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27). Although it is one in substance, in its changes it is always different from itself.

But he is one—and all who imitate him who is truly one are likewise called one—who remains the same and unchangeable: not divided into pairs, not rent by schisms, always alike in wisdom. Nor are they merely “one,” but “a unity,” like the multitude that had “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). This is what the Apostle means: “One receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9). Therefore, because the righteous person is called one by not becoming other than himself, it is said in his praise: “There was one man from Mount Ephraim, named Elkanah” (1 Kings [1 Sam.] 1). [Col. 0648A] Ephraim means “fruitfulness”; Elkanah, “possession of God.” For whoever is one is not from low places but from a fruitful mountain; and he is the possession of God, not of a demon. Indeed, one possessed by demons is not one but many, as they themselves say in the case of the man whom they possessed: “Legion is his name” (Mark 5).

This one has two wives (ibid.): Hannah, at first barren and afterwards having such a son as might stand before God, Samuel; and Peninnah, who has many children. Hannah means grace; Peninnah, conversion. Everyone who wishes to be God’s possession must unite these two wives to himself. He must join grace to himself first through faith, because, as the Apostle said, “By grace we have been saved through faith” (Eph. 2); and he must also be joined to the second, that is, conversion [Col. 0648B], because after the grace of belief there should be the commendation of morals and the confession of life.

This is the order of marriage; but the order of begetting is different. Peninnah indeed bears the first children, because we bring forth the first fruits of conversion and the first shoots of righteousness from our deeds. Unless we are first converted from evil, we cannot become fathers by Hannah, that is, grace. Peninnah’s children are many; and although they receive portions, they do not stand before God, because there are many works of righteousness in the present life, for which a reward is received in the future. Hence it was said to Martha: “You are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10). But they do not stand before the Lord, because these works will cease.

First, therefore, one must turn from sin and bring forth fruits worthy of repentance. Then Hannah—that is, grace—roused by the emulation of good things, gives birth through prayers [Col. 0648C] to a son who may sit beside God and persevere, of whom it is said to Mary that she “has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (ibid.). For the son of grace is free for God and for the word of God. He is called Samuel, which means, “Where is God himself?” For God is truly in such a son of the Church, who always calls upon his name. Hence: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. 98).

## TITLE XXVI. On the four orders of human beings, and the threefold place of the world

“Fire has devoured the beautiful places of the wilderness; flame has kindled all the trees of the country; and even the beasts of the field have looked up to you like a threshing-floor thirsty for rain, because the fountains of waters have dried up” (Job 1). In these words of the prophet [Col. 0648D] four orders of human beings are indicated. By the beautiful places of the wilderness are meant religious persons; by the trees of the country, rulers of the world; by the beasts of the field, common people; and by the fountains, preachers.

Religious persons are called beautiful, because nothing is more beautiful to God and human beings than religion. Rulers are trees, because like a tree they shelter others beneath their branches. Common people are beasts of the field because, setting aside the reason they received for service, they live bestially. The fountains of waters are preachers, because they contain the streams of the word of God.

By wilderness, country, and field this world is understood. Hence wilderness is assigned to religious persons, because, having forsaken the world, they appear as though abandoned; trees to rulers, because although [Col. 0649A] they are higher than others, they have fixed the root of their mind in this age; and field to common people, because they devote their whole minds to rural work.

But fire, which is often found lurking among trees, devours the beautiful places of the wilderness when the fire of desires and vices secretly kindles religious persons within, not publicly. For though they do not dare openly to fall into vices and shameful acts, nevertheless the hidden furnace of vices burns within them. Flame, however, which gives light of itself, kindles rulers—that is, the rich of this world, who neither fear God nor respect human beings—because they sin not secretly but before the eyes of all; they burn in themselves and set others aflame by their example.

The beasts of the field look up to God like a threshing-floor thirsty for rain, when common people, who lie beneath like a threshing-floor barren in good things compared with the mighty who stand higher, by the very manifestation of their dryness silently cry, as it were, that they need the rain of God’s words. We have heard that the beautiful places of the wilderness—that is, those who wear the habit of religion—are consumed by fire; that the trees of the country—that is, the powerful—are kindled by open flame; and that the beasts—that is, disorderly human beings—by the manifest evidence of their need desire rain. Let us hear the cause of this calamity: “Because,” says the prophet, [Col. 0649B] “the fountains of waters have dried up”—that is, the tongue of preachers has fallen silent, and understanding withers, while, with a dry breast, they either despise their subjects or are unable and do not know how to nourish them.

## TITLE XXVII. On the three orders of contemplatives, and the threefold ground of Jacob’s ladder

[Col. 0649C] “Jacob saw a ladder” (Gen. 28). The ladder is the universal Church, which partly fights on earth and partly triumphs in heaven. In it are various ranks of steps. Some are beginners, others are advancing, others have arrived. Again, among these, some are at the mill, some in the field, some in bed. At the mill are followers of the world; in the field, teachers of the word; in bed, friends of the Bridegroom.

This ladder is said to stand upon earth; but earth is threefold: the earth beneath a human being, the earth which is a human being, and the earth above a human being. A human being treads the earth beneath him; bears the earth which is himself; desires the earth above him. Of the first it is said: “The earth is the Lord’s” (Ps. 8); of the second: “You are earth, and unto earth you shall return” [Col. 0649D] (Gen. 3); of the third: “If you do what I command you, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. 1).

Beneath this ladder are the weak; in the middle are the active; at the top are contemplatives placed in heaven. The weak eat earth and become weak. The active reject it and are healed. Contemplatives feed on the dew of heaven and are satisfied. The active have compassion on the weak, and thus descend. Contemplatives rejoice with them, and thus ascend. For these are the angels ascending and descending by the ladder: descending by the compassion of mercy, ascending by the contemplation of heavenly things. The active person is afflicted, and the weak person is afflicted; but the former by the compassion of mercy, and so he ought to descend; the latter by the sickness of sin, and so cannot ascend.

## TITLE XXVIII. On priests and prelates, and their threefold office

[Col. 0650A]

“The elders and guardians of the daughter of Zion sat upon the ground and kept silence” (Lam. 2). It is the voice of Jeremiah mourning Jerusalem’s desolation through the negligence of its elders; and also of the Saviour lamenting the Church’s ruin through the slothful guardianship of prelates.

“They sat,” he says, “upon the ground.” The office of priests is threefold: to walk about, to sit, and to teach. They must walk from sheep to sheep, from the sick to the broken, from the broken to the wandering, and from the wandering to the healthy. They must strengthen the sick, bind up the broken, call back the wandering, and preserve the healthy, lest they incur the saying of the prophet: “What is broken you have not bound up,” etc. (Ezek. 34). As Christ taught, they must: “Go,” he says, “preach, and walk upon [Col. 0650B] the sea.” They must also, after his example, sit in the little boat and teach the people from it.

There are three degrees of sitting: the first, lower and general; the second, higher and particular; the third, supreme and spiritual. The first is to sit beside the rivers of Babylon; the second, at the rich man’s table; the third, in Simon’s boat. In the first sit the faithful; in the second, young men; in the third, elders. To sit beside the rivers is to restrain the flow of desires; to sit at the rich man’s table is to persevere in meditation on Sacred Scripture; to sit in Simon’s boat is to hold the place of prelacy in the Church and, like Jesus, teach the people by word and example.

But those against whom the prophet complains have contrary sittings. When they ought to sit beside the rivers of Babylon, they sit beside [Col. 0650C] pots of flesh; when they ought to sit at the rich man’s table, they seek chairs in the marketplace, attending to trifles; when they ought to sit in Simon’s boat, they sit upon the ground—that is, they turn all the priestly profit into earthly pleasure. It should be noted, however, that some sat in their own land and others in another’s land. The first serve their own carnal pleasure; the second make others’ riches their own, joining house to house and field to field.

It follows: “They kept silence,” that is, they lost the twofold part and threefold mode of speaking. The parts of speaking are life and teaching. The three modes are to teach, to admonish, and to pray: to teach about faith, to admonish about morals, and to pray for king and people.
