Of the first it is said: “Go, teach all nations,” etc. (Matt. 28); of the second: “Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms [Col. 0650D], to pluck up and to destroy and to scatter and to build and to plant” (Jer. 2); of the third the Apostle says: “First of all I urge that supplications be made,” etc. (1 Tim. 2).

Or “they kept silence,” that is, they had every cause for silence. There are three: ignorance, inability, and negligence. Ignorance is shameful: that you should begin to learn when you ought to teach. “An old man learning his alphabet is a ludicrous thing,” as the philosopher testifies. Inability is difficult, because sometimes a prelate wishes to teach but cannot, his conscience reproaching him and closing his mouth. This is the little branch thrown into the mouths of dogs which restrains their barking. If he wishes to fulfil his office by speaking, let it be said to him: “Why do you recount my righteousnesses?” etc. (Ps. 49). If he is found silent through negligence, he stands [Col. 0651A] opposed to his office, and the Lord cries: “I will require the blood of the perishing man from your hand” (Ezek. 3).

## TITLE XXIX. On what drew Christ to us, and on our hardness

“Because of truth, and meekness, and righteousness, your right hand shall lead you wonderfully” (Ps. 44). The Word of God, established on high, was invited to descend to us by his own kindness; drawn by mercy; compelled by the truth by which he had promised that he would come; received by the purity of the virginal womb; brought forth by power; armed by patience; and manifested by charity through words and miracles.

For your right hand, Lord Jesus, led you wonderfully because of truth, by which the promises were fulfilled; because of meekness, by which iniquities were forgiven; and because of righteousness [Col. 0651B], by which proud demons and human beings were condemned. The human race needed these three things; but only the Son of God and of the Virgin could accomplish them: namely, to forgive iniquities, fulfil promises, and condemn demons.

See how sweetly, in charity, Christ our God calls us to life. He came and promised eternal life, yet was not heard on the ground of truth, though he promised truth alone; and he said: “Let him who does not hear the one making the promise hear the one who is lovable.” He therefore came and showed himself in every meekness, so that he rescued the sinful soul—an adulteress possessed by seven demons—from the hands of those stoning her, and looked upon the weeping Peter: “merciful and compassionate Lord” (Ps. 110), merciful in affection, compassionate in effect.

The human being was hardened both against the truth of the one promising [Col. 0651C] and against the display of meekness, so that God, though labouring, was heard neither because of truth nor because of meekness. But seeing that he gained nothing, he threatened burning fire and eternal death, so that the one whom he could not draw by truth nor attract by meekness he might pull back by righteousness, and “affliction might give understanding to hearing.” This is like the three-pronged spear which the Lord sent into this great sea to catch souls; he is blessed for ever.

## TITLE XXX. On three holy things—God, a human being, and a place—and on threefold sanctification

“The place in which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 24). God is holy, a human being is holy, and a place is holy. God is holy not as sanctified but as sanctifying; a human being is holy as sanctified and sanctifying; a place is holy [Col. 0651D] as sanctified but not sanctifying. God, indeed, is holy from himself, not from us; a human being from God, not from himself. “You have no need,” says the human being, “of my goods” (Ps. 15); and: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1).

The human being who is holy is sanctified by him and holy from him; it belongs to the human being to labour outwardly, but to God to confer grace inwardly: he is the one who baptizes. But a sanctified place, whether without a human being or by means of a human being, does not sanctify. For just as an unholy place does not defile a holy person—as Sodom did not defile Lot—so a holy place does not sanctify an unholy one—as heaven did not sanctify the devil, nor paradise the first human being.

A human being, however, often sanctifies a place in two ways: by merit and by office. There is indeed a threefold sanctification [Col. 0652A]: the sanctification of sacrament, the sanctification of righteousness or merit, and the sanctification of glory or reward. Churches are sanctified when they are dedicated; people are sanctified when they are justified; the elect are sanctified when they are endowed with the rewards of eternal glory.

## TITLE XXXI. On the threefold labour, the three kinds of labourer, and the three crosses, deaths, and tombs

“The just God renders them the reward of their labours and leads them in a wonderful way,” etc. (Wis. 10). Labour is threefold: that of the flesh, of compunction, and of charity. The labour of the flesh is burdensome; that of compunction, affective; that of charity, effectual. Of the first it is said: “Their heart was humbled in labours, and there was none to help” (Ps. 106). For all who toil in the service of the devil [Col. 0652B] have no help from God. They are led through crooked paths: although their beginning may sometimes be recognized, their end is never found. Hence: “The wicked walk in a circle, and their labour is the head of their circuit” (Ps. 11): that is, their circuit always has a beginning, never an end.

Of the labour of compunction it is said: “I have laboured in my groaning” (Ps. 6). It is affective because one who begins to repent conceives a good affection, which the labour of charity brings to effect. Thus the labour of charity is called effectual, because it accomplishes what compunction suggests.

The first labour is punitive, because in seeking their own will people are punished even in the present life. Hence: “God gave them up to the desires of their heart, to uncleanness, so that they might dishonour their bodies among themselves” [Col. 0652C] (Rom. 1). The labour of compunction is remissive, because it obtains forgiveness. Hence: “At whatever hour the sinner groans,” etc. (Ezek. 18). The labour of charity is remunerative, because it merits recompense. Hence: “You shall eat the labours of your hands” (Ps. 127). And because this labour is remunerative, it follows: “You are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (ibid.).

The Lord calls us back from the first by presenting the pain contained in the commandment, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). In this three kinds of human beings are indicated. There are those who labour and are burdened: namely, those engaged in the labour of the flesh, serving the devil, whose yoke is unbearable and burden insupportable. Others labour but are not burdened: those who serve Christ, whose yoke is sweet [Col. 0652D] and burden light. A third kind neither labour nor are burdened; they are called not burdened but honoured, since they receive rather the honours of human beings.

Each labour has its own cross. The labour of the flesh has the cross of punishment, which it bears here and in the future. The labour of compunction has the cross of abstinence, because repentance requires abstinence. The labour of charity has the cross of glory, because one who loves God crucifies his flesh with its vices and desires; and this crucifixion is glorious. Hence the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6).

According to these three crosses, a person is called in three ways: carnal, animal, and spiritual. The carnal person hangs upon the cross of punishment. The animate person, frightened by fear of Gehenna and choosing rather to abstain from vices than to go into Gehenna, hangs upon the cross of abstinence. This is Lot, rejecting the mountain heights and saved in Zoar: unwilling to leave even permitted things, he pursues a middling life. The spiritual person is on the cross of charity, glorying in the cross through love alone.

The first cross is exacting, the second necessary, the third voluntary. Each has its own death: the first death is ruinous, the second propitious, the third precious. Hence: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115). It is also useful to hang upon the cross of the Lord, so that, set ablaze by God’s ardour, we may so chastise each member that neither hand may be allowed to perform barren works nor foot to stray upon the broad way of the lame.

Everyone who has died upon his own cross has his own tomb. The first is in hell; the second [Col. 0653B] in the wilderness; the third in the garden—that is, in paradise, the garden of delights. In the first lies the thief who scorns; in the second, the thief who confesses; in the third, Christ who pardons. The first is foul and swarms with worms that do not die. The second is purified, being swept in confessions, because “Judah,” that is, confession, “became his sanctification” (Ps. 113). The third is prepared with spices, guarded by divine powers, and visited by women bearing spices.

Each is anointed with his own ointment. The first, with the ointment of despair, because in hell there is no redemption; the second, with the ointment of recovery, because here is a time for mercy; the third, with the ointment of devotion, saying with the whole affection of the mind: “You have turned my mourning into joy for me” (Ps. 29). Mary Magdalene bears [Col. 0653C] the ointment of compunction; Mary of James, that of compassion; Salome, that of devotion. Compunction arises from the remembrance of sins; compassion from the evils of neighbours; devotion from consideration of rewards.

By Mary Magdalene, who was “a sinner in the city” (Luke 7), is understood the penitent soul that amends its crimes; by Mary of James, the one that supplants vices and works virtues; by Salome, the peacemaker who impresses a kiss upon the mouth with God, and who, her lips cleansed from guilt, dares to say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1).

## TITLE XXXII. On threefold confession, the three names of Jerusalem, and the three days of restoration to life

“Judah and Jerusalem, do not fear or be dismayed. Tomorrow go out against them, and the Lord will be with you” [Col. 0653D] (2 Chron. 20). Judah means confession, which is threefold: confession of sins, when one recognizes one’s own sins; confession of merits, when one considers one’s own weakness and the grace which helps; and confession of rewards, concerning which it is said: “They shall praise you for ages of ages” (Ps. 83).

The first confession says: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50), and hears: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5). The second prays: “Direct my steps in your paths” (Ps. 118), and receives the response: “Stand in righteousness and walk” (Ecclus. 2). The third sings a new song, and is promised: “You shall sit upon the throne,” etc.

Jerusalem was first called Jebus, afterwards Salem, and then Jerusalem. Jebus means “trampled”; Salem, “peace”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” We were first trampled in the mud and filth [Col. 0654A] of sin, from which we are stripped through repentance. From there we have peace through righteousness, such as can be possessed in the present life. Finally we shall come to the vision of peace which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4), where we shall know as we are known.

The threefold name of the city corresponds to the threefold Judah: Jebus, that is, trampling down, to confession of sins, since one who confesses tramples himself down; Salem, that is, peace, to confession of merits, which is possessed by one who attributes things to God and not to himself, because there is “peace to people of good will”; and Jerusalem, that is, vision of peace, to confession of praise: “They shall praise you for ages of ages” (Ps. 83).

Therefore, to Judah and Jerusalem—not to those who, through an impenitent heart, store up wrath for themselves; who do not know the way of peace; for whom, when they go out, prison, darkness, and hell are prepared—it is said: “Do not fear; tomorrow go out against them, and the Lord will be with you.” “Do not fear”: here fears must be relinquished. “Tomorrow go out”: here he speaks of departures. “Tomorrow go out,” as though he said: You indeed have many enemies—flesh, than which none is nearer; the wicked world; and those stationed in the air who besiege our way—but do not fear. “Tomorrow go out,” that is, after two days.

For there are three days of which it is said: “He will restore us to life after two days; on the third day he will raise us,” etc. (Hos. 6). One day is under Adam, the second in Christ, the third with Christ. Would that Adam’s day—the day of sin in which we are all born—might perish in us! This is the day cursed by Job (Job 3) and Jeremiah (Jer. 20). And when we depart, either here from sin may there dawn the day of redemption, the new preparation of the old; [Col. 0654C] or, when we depart from the world, may shine forth the day which knows no evening.

The Gospel marks these three days: “Behold, today and tomorrow I cast out demons; and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13). And because temptations are brought upon us on the first day of conversion, it is rightly said to these persons: “Do not fear.” But because on the second day healing is given through righteousness, he says: “Tomorrow you shall go out,” leaving behind, that is, vices or the prison-house of the flesh. And for the third day is added: “The Lord will be with you,” either through his birth and his sharing in human nature, or, in the future, through grace by the gift of blessedness.

Note that he does not say, “We shall be with him,” but “He will be with us.” For we are with him when we do not adhere to his will; but he is not with us, because he does not consent to our will. We desire to be dissolved, but he delays it. Then he will be with us, when in him the enjoyment of all that is desired will be granted to us.

## TITLE XXXIII. On God’s fourfold speech, and the response to be made to it

“God has spoken once,” etc. (Ps. 6). God speaks, as it is said, once and does not repeat it thereafter (Job 33), because here he speaks once: commanding, prohibiting, promising, and threatening. In the future, however, there will be no time for teaching, but for judging. Thus this word by which he speaks once is fourfold: he commands what is good, forbids what is evil, promises glory, and threatens punishment.

Yet this word is called one, because it is one for our correction. For the future word belongs only to recompense [Col. 0655A]. In this first fourfold speech of God two things are heard: power and mercy. Power, by which he promises and threatens; mercy, by which he commands and forbids, showing the way by which we may run toward the promised good and avoid the evil set before us.

This fourfold word must be answered in four ways: the command by obedience, that we may do good; the prohibition by temperance, that we may abstain from evil; the promise by love; and the threat by fear. He was ready to answer in these ways who said: “Speak, and I will answer you” (Job 13). He surely says: Since you have already spoken and do not repeat it, I shall speak and answer you through obedience, temperance, love, and fear; and you answer me.

For in the future God will answer the one who has answered in the present, and that fourfold. God himself will answer obedience with freedom; temperance with integrity—so that temperance may have free integrity and obedience entire freedom, neither of which happens here unless temperance fights and obedience labours. He will answer love with happiness, and fear with security, so that happiness may be secure. O how good, how desirable are these answers: entire freedom, secure happiness! To the one to whom God answers these things he will give, for his hearing, ineffable joy and gladness, by which the bones now humbled shall then exult [Col. 0655B] (Ps. 50). For merits are lowly now, but rewards lofty then. “For whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14).

## TITLE XXXIV. On the three languages of human beings

[Col. 0655C] “There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. 19). There are three languages: Egyptian, Canaanite, and Hebrew; and among these, Canaanite is more closely related to Hebrew. Angels speak Hebrew; evil human beings Egyptian; good human beings Canaanite. Canaanite means “moved.” Such a person is already moved by repentance to depart from the Egypt of vices, and by desire for the homeland to depart from the Egypt of his flesh. But a Hebrew is one who has already crossed over.

Thus in our Egypt the Egyptians speak: there are five cities among evil people, when their five senses perform the works of the flesh—that is, of Egypt. In Egypt the five cities of good people speak the Canaanite language when their five senses are moved to abandon the works of the flesh. The Hebrew sounds praises not in Egypt but in heaven [Col. 0655D], where “every spirit praises the Lord” (Ps. 150).

## TITLE XXXV. On the threefold coming of the Lord
“Behold, your King comes to you, meek and a Saviour” (Zech. 9). There are three comings of the Lord: to human beings in the flesh; into human beings in the Spirit; and against human beings in judgment. Between the first and the last coming there is a frequent coming in the intervening time, conforming us to the first coming and preparing us for the last. For in this manner he comes into us, lest he have come to us in vain in his first coming, or lest in his last coming he come against us in anger. By this coming he strives to reform the disposition of our pride, conforming it to the disposition of his humility, which he displayed when he first came, so that he may likewise reform the body of his humility, conformed to the body of his glory (Phil. 3), which he will display when he returns again.

This middle coming, therefore, is to be desired: it grants the grace of the first and promises the glory of the second. For, as a mediator, it shares in both. The first is hidden and humble; the last manifest and wonderful. This one is hidden indeed, but wonderful. That glorious soul, exulting, had received this hidden coming when she said: “My secret is for me; my secret is for me” (Isa. 24). But how wonderful it is, how it holds suspended in admiration the soul that contemplates it, and how all the bones of the inward person cry out to it, “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34), those know who have experienced it. And would that those who have not experienced it might desire to do so!

The first coming, therefore, is of grace; the last, of glory; this middle one, of grace and glory, in which, through consoling grace, the future glory is in some measure tasted beforehand. In the first, God was seen as contemptible; in the last, God is to be seen as terrible; in this middle coming, wonderful and lovable: so that, because of the condescension of grace by which he makes himself lovable, he may not be despised but admired; and because of the magnificence of glory by which he appears wonderful, he may not be a cause of terror but of consolation.

Of the first the Jew says: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53). Even the righteous man was terrified by the last: “And who,” he says, “will be able to stand to see him?” (ibid.). Of this middle coming the Apostle says: “Beholding the glory of the Lord, we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3).

Let us therefore go out to meet our Saviour. We must answer this good tidings from a far country—that is, from the land of the living, far from the land of the dying. The first coming must be met with affection and exultation of heart; the last with the movement and exultation of the body. And just as then, in our bodies, “we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so shall we always be with the Lord” (2 Thess. 4), so now there are clouds of apostles and prophets which lend their services if our minds are not sluggish and too firmly fixed upon the earth. For, as though in a cloud-borne vehicle, our minds are raised so far that they may deserve, however little, to behold the glory of the Lord; and thus may we be with the Lord even for half an hour.

Therefore, brothers, let us whom long experience does not yet console, so that we may patiently await the final coming of the Lord, meanwhile be consoled by sure faith and a pure conscience, which says with the Apostle: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve his deposit unto that day” (2 Tim. 2), that is, unto the coming of the great God. He lives and reigns, etc.

### XXXVI. On the rod and the flower, in a moral sense

“A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11). The rod is Mary, and the flower Christ. The rod chastises one who does not need rebuke, but correction and punishments. The flower is for one who does not need harsh correction, but instruction; or certainly for one who does not need punishments, but wishes to begin with the flower and be brought to the fruit.

Do you wish to see an imitator of Christ as rod and flower? Of the rod he says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod?” (1 Cor. 4). Of the flower: “Or in charity and a spirit of gentleness?” (ibid.).

### XXXVII. On shepherds and their office

“Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). Three things are necessary for shepherds of the Lord’s flock: good conduct, discernment, and preaching, so that they may be light, eye, and salt.

They must be the light of good conduct, shining by their example. Hence: “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5). They must be the eye of discernment, so that by distinguishing between leprosy and leprosy they may provide for those subject to them. Hence God says to Ezekiel: “I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3). They must be the salt of preaching and correction, so that by preaching they may instruct their subjects, lest the worms of sins consume them. Hence: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5).

But among shepherds there are some who are neither salt, nor light, nor eye: that is, they preach badly, act badly, and discern badly. Of these it is said: “The priests have despised my law; they have defiled my sanctuaries” (Ezek. 22), because they have not understood the distinction between holy and profane, knowledge and ignorance, filthy and clean. Others are salt but not light. Of these it is said: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23). Others do not have the salt of preaching. Of these it is said: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56).

These three things, then, are necessary for us, that we may be light, eye, and salt. If even one of them is lacking, we guard the Lord’s flock dangerously. For if we are not light, although we may be eye and salt, we handle the body of the Lord at our peril; we are unworthy of the office, becoming like those who possess a key, open for others, but do not enter themselves. Thus we must greatly fear lest we, who are gatekeepers of heaven, after admitting others, may ourselves fail to enter; and, when the door is finally shut, cry in vain: “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matt. 2).

May it also come to pass that, when Jesus has driven from the temple those buying and selling (Matt. 21), the blind and lame may approach him and enter. But if they lack the eye of discernment—which ought to be that of doves, not ravens; hence, “Your eyes are doves” (Song 1)—then “the blind lead the blind, and both fall into the pit” (Matt. 15). If they lack the salt of preaching, the fasting people of God may faint on the way, and their blood will be required at the preacher’s hand.

Therefore let each consider his burden, so that by salt he may be a cloud, pouring rain; by light, flying toward heavenly things, showing by example what he preaches in word; by eye, a dove at the windows of Scripture, that by seeing God through them he may provide for his sheep. Rejoicing in such persons, the prophet says: “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” Consider, then, what you are and to what ministry you have been called in the house of God.

Hosea cries out to those who act otherwise: “Hear, O priests, for judgment is for you” (Hos. 5). And he shows why when he adds: “For you have become a snare to watchfulness and a net spread out” (ibid.). It is as though he said: Since you, who ought to set others free, entangle them by a bad example, judgment of condemnation is upon you. Hence you are also guilty of another’s blood.

### XXXVIII. On the two fawns of the roe, the three shadows, and the various days

[Col. 0658A]

“Two fawns of a roe feed among the lilies” (Song 4). The roe is the Church: keen of sight for penetrating the mysteries of Christ; agile in leaping over the obstacles of this age; mighty in suppressing the poisons of the ancient serpent. Her two twins are Peter and Paul, brothers in faith, equal in merit and virtue, joined in the same passion and death. They feed among lilies, among the virtues and advances of the pure and humble. They feed them with words; they themselves feed upon their works. Hence one of them said: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thess. 3); the other, when he was hungry, saw heaven opened and was commanded to kill and eat the flesh of unclean animals (Acts 10).

They do this, labouring in the heat, until the day breathes and the shadows incline (Song 2). There are three shadows and three days. The first shadow is the earth: it is the shadowy spirit of demons and human beings. The second is the darkness of errors. The third is the obscure signification of the ancient sacraments. The shadow of significations inclines toward sunset and its end; the shadow of errors inclines day by day toward diminution; the shadow of dark spirits will at last incline toward hell and death.

The first occurred when the eternal day breathed forth, appearing in the flesh. The second occurs daily, when the same day breathes forth by illuminating us with truth. The third will occur at the end, when he breathes forth in majesty.

There are also two other shadows which, within us as in a kind of mirror, overshadow us or overshadow things for us. Those which overshadow us freeze and blind us. Those which overshadow things for us refresh and illumine us. The first are from below, heavy and harmful; the second from above, pleasant and health-giving. For the human soul is placed in the middle: beneath it is the world, made for its sake; above it is God, from whom, for whom, and toward whom it was made. For as the body exists for the soul, so the soul’s house—that is, the world—exists for the body.

Therefore, when the soul bends down toward bodily and worldly things, shadows from below rise into it. When it goes forth toward divine things, shadows from above incline over it. For of the thing it thinks upon, it forms for itself a shadow. Though this shadow be luminous and glorious, it is nevertheless a shadow, however keenly the day of knowledge may shine, until that heavenly day breathes forth; just as, in the clear and bright face of a mirror, the image of a splendid object is reflected. “For now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13).

Note also that a shadow is not seen unless the day is inclining and breathing forth. For our humanity cannot grasp anything through a mirror and in an enigma, however much it be drawn from visible to invisible things, unless the majesty bends itself toward us through the favour of grace—when he who dwells in inaccessible light deigns to incline toward us and to show himself through the shadow of his image. Hence Moses went up the mountain (Exod. 9), and “the Lord bowed the heavens and came down” (Ps. 17).

But alas! This winter has days so brief and dark, and nights so long and laborious, that the prophet, labouring in his groaning and washing his bed every night with his tears (Ps. 6), rightly laments, saying: “My days have declined like a shadow” (Ps. 101). But if one asks why shadows are spoken of in the plural when there is one thing of which they are shadows, the answer is that the power of the Most High now overshadows less and now more, and so forms shadows differently. Hence the Apostle: “We are transformed from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3)—that is, from a lesser to a greater glory, because present glory is a shadow in comparison with the glory to come.

Note that, when shadows from above incline over us, shadows from below incline beneath us. For when we draw near to divine things, we overcome worldly things: to the degree that we approach the shadow of light, we escape the shadow of death. For light and life are in heaven; death is in hell; the shadow of death is in this Tartarean and dark place.

Now, brothers who labour, bearing “the burden of the day and the heat” (Matt. 20), draw near to these shadows of light. May it please you to imitate those upon whom the eternal day, breathing forth the dew of mercy, desires to incline relief amid the heat. Hear the day itself inviting you to the refreshment of shadows: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). Whoever obtains that shadow rightly glories and says: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat” (Song 2). In it there is sitting for rest and refreshment for satisfaction. Hence he adds: “And his fruit is sweet to my throat” (Ps. 83).

Breathe, therefore, upon our throat, O day of days, you who are in your courts above thousands (Ps. 139). Overshadow our head in the day of battle. Incline over us the shadows of salvation and refreshment, and let the shadows of blindness and death incline beneath us. Though shadows arising from thoughts of earthly things touch us, let not darkness—that is, denser shadows arising from love of those things—reach us; but may we always breathe in the luminous love of the true and eternal light.

### XXXIX. On gold, frankincense, and myrrh

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams. Bring to the Lord glory and honour,” etc. (Ps. 28). Since it is better to bring offerings to the Lord than to the leech—that is, concupiscence—whose two daughters, pleasure and vanity, give no rest day or night, saying, “Bring, bring” (Prov. 30), what then must be brought? “Bring,” he says, “glory,” namely the glory of gold, “and honour” of frankincense. “Bring to the Lord glory to his name”: myrrh for his burial.

Myrrh in your heart is sorrow; myrrh in your body is labour—provided that both are penitential. Myrrh is most bitter in taste, but in effect resists corruption. What is more bitter than the sorrow by which the sinner recalls his years “in the bitterness of his soul” (Isa. 38), saying to God: “Do not condemn me” (Job 10)? And what is more health-giving than that which protects both from the corruption of the lusts in which he decayed and from the immortal worms which he deserved?

The labour of the body, however, is not so much myrrh as a bundle of myrrh, in which the rule of fasts and vigils, the harshness of garments, and all bitter things are gathered, as it were, into one bundle to be borne. Hence the saying: “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning,” etc. (Joel 2), so that it may truly be called a bundle. Bitterness of heart ought to be mitigated by outward bitterness, just as bile in the stomach is treated with a draught of wormwood, so that one corrupted by the use of sweet things may be cleansed by a bitter drink.

For to the sinner must be given the myrrhed wine of the Lord’s Passion (Mark 15), which Jesus refused to drink because he had committed no sin for which the crucifixion could be imputed to him. After this frankincense is offered, because after the sacrifice of a contrite spirit and humbled body follows the sacrifice of praise with the frankincense of devotion. When you have offered this to the King, place beneath it the fire of charity, so that the prayer of devotion may rise straight as incense before God (Ps. 140). And, having smelled from this sacrifice an odour of sweetness, may he say to you: “The smell of your garments is like the smell of frankincense” (Song 4).

After these two, gold is offered. Myrrh is the offering of beginners, frankincense of those progressing, but gold of the perfect: this is wisdom, which no one knows except the one who receives it. This gold is more precious than all riches, even than myrrh and frankincense. He is rich in all things who can offer this last gift in contemplation and prudent administration. This indeed is true wisdom: wisdom in the contemplation of eternal things and the administration of temporal things. He who knows himself to be king and another, nevertheless does not neglect to offer frankincense in devotion to the divine work and myrrh in the mortification of himself.

Therefore, brothers, for the glory of the child-King who was born to us, let us offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh, which preserves from worms. For the worm of the flesh is lust: it enters by flattering, bites while smiling, pierces by delighting, and kills through voluntary consent. Sorrow also is a worm, because, as moth harms a garment and worm harms wood, so sorrow harms a man’s heart. Bodies and hearts breed worms from these and similar worms unless myrrh daily drips from the hands.

Therefore let our hands cause myrrh to drip over the whole of our body, forestalling it by anointing the body for its burial. For our body is Jesus, when it is buried by being withdrawn from all vices. One who is anointed in this way, as has been said, does not fear the worm that does not die, because he is already dead. Let us also offer the frankincense of devotion and the gold of wisdom. And if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it from him who gives generously to all, namely from the Father of lights, who gives “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1).

### XL. On meditating upon death while we still seem strong, and on acting well

“Remember your Creator in the day of your youth” (Eccl. 11), says the Wise Man, so that, according to the Apostle, “while we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. 6). He continues: “Before the silver cord is broken” (Eccl. 12), that is, before the body is dissolved and golden life—that is, the soul, released from the bonds of the flesh—returns to God who made it, to be punished or saved.

The body is called a cord because by certain laws of nature it binds the soul to itself, before the dust—that is, the human being made from earth—is crushed upon the fountain, that is, the world, so that he can no longer draw water from it; and before the wheel of thoughts, which go forth from the heart and roll and revolve over the cistern of the body, ceases, because “in that day their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 145).

He states the same thing in other words: “And the dust returns to its earth, from which it was” (“You are dust, and to dust you shall return,” Gen. 3), “and the spirit returns to him who gave it” (Eccl. 12), to receive punishment or glory.

### XLI. On the threefold opening of the heart, the sixfold command, and the threefold warfare and peace

“May the Lord open your heart in his law and in his commandments, and make peace,” etc. (2 Macc. 2). There is a threefold opening of the heart: the first toward penitence, the second toward righteousness, the third toward perfection. This opening comes through the law of the Lord when it is meditated upon day and night. Hence he adds, “in his law,” which consists of six things: prohibitions, threats, commands, promises, counsels, and exhortations.

The first opening occurs through prohibitions and threats, when a person, considering his transgressions and the punishments which follow from them, is pricked by fear of God toward penitence. For this is “the law of the Lord converting souls” (Ps. 18). The second is through commands and promises, when the penitent person, considering in God’s law the divine will and its reward, advances toward the righteousness of good works, because “the testimony of the Lord is faithful” (ibid.), giving the things promised. The third is through counsels and exhortations, when the righteous person delights in good things, burning toward God, and God—whom he desires alone to love—says to him: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have,” etc. (Matt. 19). Thus he seizes perfection, seeking nothing besides God, who gives wisdom to little ones.

But because love alone is the mark of religious life, as God says: “By this people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13), it is added: “and in his commandments,” which are love of God and neighbour, to be observed more than the other elements of God’s law, since on these hang the law and the prophets.

“And make peace.” We have a threefold warfare: from conscience, which never ceases to accuse the sinner; from flesh and demon, which pursue even the righteous; and from brother and neighbour, who attempt to disturb even the perfect. But God, who opens hearts in his law and in his commandments, establishes a threefold peace in a person. First, through penitence: when sin is blotted out, conscience cannot accuse him. Second, through righteousness: when the righteous person, by exercise in good works, has tamed the flesh, according to the Apostle, “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude” (1 Cor. 9), and has thus quenched all the arrows of the enemy (Eph. 6). Third, when, holding God alone, one is exalted by no prosperity and moved by no adversity, receiving prosperity and adversity alike, so that it may truly be said: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118).

When conscience has ceased from the first warfare, and flesh and demons from the second, a person is so perfect that, if someone causes offence, he does not receive offence; but, so far as lies within him, even when another gives offence, he has peace, possessing his soul in patience (Luke 21).

### XLII. On God’s kindness and severity toward the sinner

[Col. 0662A]

“Return to the Lord your God, for he is kind and merciful, patient and greatly merciful, and ready to relent concerning evil” (Joel 2). See how he magnifies God’s mercy concerning pardon to be granted the sinner if he is willing to return. He is kind in bestowing what is not owed; merciful in forgiving what is owed; patient in enduring for a long time; greatly merciful in accepting a brief affliction of penitence in return for long iniquities; ready to relent concerning evil, forgiving all evils even to one who persists without bodily affliction, if he turns his heart toward him.

Therefore let no one despair of pardon because of God’s justice. Let no one persist in evils because of his mercy, since the Lord is strong and patient, sweet and upright, merciful and true: patient, sweet, and merciful toward penitents; strong, upright, and true toward the impenitent. Therefore, brothers, if we love the patience, sweetness, and mercy by which he saves, let us fear the strength and uprightness by which he judges and condemns; and let us pray that he may withhold from us the severity of judgment and bestow the kindness of mercy. He, etc.

### XLIII. On the three goods of the human being, the three scourges of God, and their causes

“Many are the scourges of the sinner; but mercy shall surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Ps. 31). There are three goods of the human being which we enjoy in this life. Some are in the soul, such as virtues and other gifts of both nature and grace; some are in the body, such as health; and some are outside both, such as children and riches. Therefore there are three scourges by which, in God’s just judgment, one is struck. One is sometimes scourged in outward possessions, sometimes in one’s own flesh, sometimes in conscience.

In the first two, good and evil persons alike are scourged; in the third, only the reprobate. Job was scourged in the first two, but not in the third. Hence it was said to Satan: “Preserve his soul” (Job 2). Pharaoh was scourged in all these ways. For God had scourged him in outward possessions, in his own flesh with swelling blisters, and also in conscience through obstinacy.

People are scourged for four reasons: some for ruin, as Pharaoh; some for discipline, as David; some for preservation, as Paul; some for a crown, as Job.

### XLIV. On the seal of God impressed upon us

[Col. 0662D]

“The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us” (Ps. 4). It says “upon,” not “beneath,” because in the higher nature there are three things: the one sealing, the seal, and the thing sealed—by whom, with whom, and in whom. The one sealing is God, who first impressed his image upon the angelic nature and then upon the human, so that the angelic nature might be as it were the seal, and the human nature as it were the thing sealed.

Hence it is said to the first angel: “You are the seal of likeness, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God” (Ezek. 28). But the human being says of himself: “The light has been sealed upon us,” etc. Just as in a signet or seal the king’s image is first engraved and afterward impressed upon the thing placed beneath it, so the image was first impressed upon the angelic nature and afterward, as though beneath it, stamped upon the human nature; and also, in their own manner, upon other things, because by their ministry they are formed and governed.

### XLV. On the seven streams of sins issuing from the first parents

“We pass through the river on foot” (*pertransimus*; [variant] *pertransibunt*, “they shall pass”) (Ps. 65). What follows? “There we shall rejoice in him” (ibid.). Isaiah says of this: “The Lord will strike the river of Egypt into seven streams, so that they may cross through it shod” (Isa. 11). Egypt is the world; the river is the flow of the human race, which, bursting forth from the first parents in an unhappy vein, flooded the whole breadth of the world with an impetuous torrent. It is divided into seven streams and has overlaid valleys and plains with a deep abyss, threatening even the mountains with inundation. One of the more exalted cries out concerning them: “The torrents of iniquity have troubled me” (Ps. 17).

The first stream of this river is evil thought: a swelling stream, receiving frequent rain through the windows of bodily senses, which supply it more abundantly with deadly showers from worldly cataracts. The shape-shifting twister fashions likenesses, paints images, arranges colours, in order to draw forth consent and infect affection. He stirs everything up and, in the bedchamber of the mind, offers horrible things concerning divinity, terrifying things concerning faith, astonishing things concerning the institution of the faith; into the channel of the mind he pours poisonous draughts which the sinner, relieved in confession of sins, shudders to vomit out.

Why say more? The enemy of virtue uproots devotion in the chamber, drawing it in different directions; he uproots chastity in the chamber, unfolding perceptions of many-formed lust. Would that, even when he attacks with such powerful weapons, he might not conquer; when he pricks, might not wound! In the cloister, he cuts off reading and remembrance of the Scriptures, tearing books from the hands and moving one from this book to that. In the duties of silence, he destroys its strength by making himself companion to the wanderer, until he either opens or breaks the discipline of silence. Even at the altar of the Lord, these spirits of powers flutter about before the very eyes of the mind as it hangs around the sacrifices of the Crucified. The great patriarch scarcely drove these birds away from his sacrifices (Gen. 15). You see how turbulent this torrent is. Who denies that he is immersed or submerged in it?

The second stream is perverse speech. “No one can tame the tongue,” says the Apostle: it is “a restless and deadly member” (Jas. 3). One kind of speech is false. Hence: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5). Another is vain: “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbour” (Ps. 11). Another is abusive: “Neither revilers,” etc., “shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). Another is indecent: “Put away shameful speech from your mouth” (Col. 3); and, “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4). Another is self-excusing: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140). Another is deceitful: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips” (Ps. 11). Another is idle, of which the Lord says: “For every idle word that people have spoken, they shall give account on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12).

The third is wicked action after thought and speech, when the members are offered to sin as instruments of iniquity, so that they inflict dishonour upon our bodies. Far be it from any of us to serve this idol, to receive the Virgin’s Son in Venus’s temple, to place the ark of the Lord beside Dagon, or to embrace filth after having been nurtured amid saffron!

The fourth stream is the defence of sins, than which nothing more provokes the anger of the Godhead. For when is a person healed who scorns the physician and tramples the medicine underfoot? The prophet introduces for us, from the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, one who denies on this subject: “There,” he says, “the hedgehog had its den” (Isa. 34). When it thinks it has obtained solitude, it puts forth head and feet. If anyone comes near, immediately it draws them in and fortifies itself with spines, so that you first hold your blood upon its spines before you hold its body.

Thus the sinner’s head and feet—that is, intention and actions—are perceived by the shepherd; yet, though seen by everyone, as is the vice of almost all sinners, he thinks that no one sees him. But if you wish to catch, with hands of correction, the entrance of his intention together with the exits of his actions, this new dialectician excuses himself with a Cicero’s tongue to such an extent—denying what you saw, and turning back upon you faults which he himself has not seen in you—that you feel resentment before you remove the fault, and incur hatred before you correct him.

The fifth stream is rejoicing in sins. O detestable joy, that people should dare to mutter thanks even to God for evils! “They rejoice when they have done evil and delight in the worst things” (Prov. 2). “Coals shall fall upon them, and they shall be cast into the fire” (Ps. 139).

The sixth is teaching others toward evil: the person who proceeds from the chair of pestilence, for whom it is not enough to perish for ever and ever unless he draws others along with him, and who will receive a double punishment.

The seventh is to persevere in all these things. Over one so submerged and swallowed up the pit closes its mouth. Since he does not lift his eyes to heaven or remember the judgment of the righteous, he is dead and buried in the tomb of conscience. For confession perishes from one thus dead, so that, “when he comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18). This is the farthest point of Egypt’s rivers. The multitude of the Lord’s mercies is taken away from his eyes.

The Lord struck this river into streams when, shod with the footwear of flesh—whose strap that great man was unable to loosen (Matt. 3)—he crossed it through immunity from the aforesaid plagues; and in crossing it he freed us from the waters described above. Come then, brothers: if any moisture from these streams of the river of mortality is in you, wipe it away, and wipe it away with the snow-white garment of confession. Strike these streams by grieving for your sin, restraining the tongue, turning from evil and doing good, confessing your injustices against yourselves to the Lord, keeping your sorrow always before your eyes, teaching the wicked the ways of the Lord, and always bearing his praise in your mouth.

And so that you may cross shod, sew something from the shoemaker’s art: make shoes thick and finely stitched, able to keep out the waters that meet you. Make the flesh firm and fixed with the fear of the Lord, so that it excludes the moisture of lust; and, baked by tribulations and made dense, may it become a new wineskin to preserve new wine, so that you may say: “I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Ps. 118).

### XLVI. On how fearful to the devil is the harmonious common life of religious persons

“You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and fair, like Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in order” (Song 6). Sweet to human beings, fair to heavenly powers, terrible to demons. Why? Because she walks as an army arrayed in order—not scattered through envy, but closely united through charity. She is an army by gathering, a camp by readiness, ordered by agreement. Penitence creates the gathering; watchfulness establishes readiness; concord supplies agreement.

Certainly the devil fears little those who fast, keep vigils, and are continent, since he has cast many of them into the snare of ruin. But those who are concordant and dwell with one mind in the house of the Lord cause him pain, fear, and envy. When he finds them concordant, he knows especially that they are in the hand of God and that the torment of death will not touch them (Wis. 3). “By this,” he says, “people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13). The devil dreads charity among human beings, which he refused to preserve in heaven with God and the angels.

### XLVII. On the fourfold sickness from which Christ’s coming delivered us

“Say to the fainthearted: Be strengthened and do not fear. Behold, our God will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed. Then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. 35).

Before the coming of Christ, the human race was in great darkness, so that people refused to know God, hear his words, act well, and confess their sins. Therefore, to console them in such sicknesses of misery, God was pleased to entrust the medicine of salvation to his ministers, saying: “Say to the fainthearted,” etc. Behold, our Lord—our medicine, our salvation, and our Jesus—will come.

Truly they were fainthearted, lying in pains and despairing in a fourfold infirmity. For they were blind, deaf, lame, and mute: blind by not knowing God; deaf by scorning to hear him; mute by not confessing their sins; lame by neglecting to act well. This infirmity began with the first parent. He was blind when, from the serpent’s words, he supposed that he would become God, not seeing from God’s word that, if he did not obey him, he would become wretched. He was lame when he limped in one foot. For the spiritual human being has two feet, love of God and love of neighbour; whoever lacks one of these limps. Adam, wishing to comply with his wife, limped badly when he placed love for her before love for God. He was deaf when he did not hear God through obedience. He was mute in confession of sin when he cast the blame upon his wife.

He condemned his descendants to these vices: blind through the worship of idols; deaf in the likeness of the asp, because the people of God did not hear his voice; lame, because they limped from the paths of God; mute in confession of sin. For, “because I kept silence, my bones grew old” (Ps. 31).

Wishing to free us from this fourfold infirmity, he says in consolation through the prophet: “Behold, our God.” For then he opened the eyes of the blind, opening their understanding so that they understood the Scriptures; and their ears when he cried: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13). He directed lame steps when he bent them toward the way of heaven. The feet were made straight, unlike Origen, who trusted too greatly in mercy. Nor were they cast down to the left, like Cain, Judas, and the devil, who turned aside in despair. The middle path must be kept, so that one neither despairs nor, trusting in mercy, sins freely. Thus the cows carrying the ark for sins turn neither right nor left.

On this path we must leap as a stag leaps, so that we may leap over the thorny things of riches and the muddy things of lust. The stag leaves valleys and climbs mountains. You: leave the earth and ascend to heaven. The stag devours the serpent, thirsts for the spring, and sheds its old skin. You, sinner: kill the devil, run to Christ, and put off the old man—that is, pride.

He opened the mouths of the mute because, when he cried, “Do penance” (Matt. 3, 4), they confessed their sins. It is clear, then, brothers, that there is a fourfold remedy for the fourfold sickness. Let us not despise the medicine. Let us open our eyes here through faith, so that in the future we may see God face to face. Let our ears be open to God’s word, lest it also be said to us: “You do not hear the words of God because you are not of God” (John 8). Let us leap like the stag with the foot of love for God, so that we may be able to ascend to the heights of heaven. Meanwhile let us open our tongue in confession, going before God, so that there we may open it in that confession of praise by which every spirit shall praise the Lord (Ps. 150).

### XLVIII. On the fourfold state of the human being
Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of him who struck you has been broken. For from the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk, and his offspring a devouring flying creature, etc. (Isa. XIV). In these words four states of humankind are indicated: namely, before sin, its fall, redemption, and the destruction of the devil. The rod is the uprightness of the first parent before sin. The striker is that parent himself, by whose envy the devil himself was struck. But this rod was broken, because through sin the uprightness of man was lost [Col. 0666D]. Therefore, because the rod—that is, the uprightness—of the devil’s striker was broken, the devil rejoiced. But the prophet, showing that he had no cause for joy and wishing to console the human race, over which the devil exulted because he held it captive in prison, says in insult against that enemy of humankind: “Do not rejoice,” etc. Philistia, which is interpreted “drink,” signifies the devil, who, drunk with the draught of pride, fell from his native perception and heavenly glory. That he ought not to be exalted because he holds the human race is indicated when it is said, “From the root of the serpent shall come forth a basilisk,” etc.

The serpent is the human race, to which death was brought through the serpent. This is the serpent of which it is read that the rod cast from Moses’ hand was turned into a serpent; when Moses seized its tail, the serpent returned into a rod (Exod. IV) [Col. 0667A]. The rod is the human race, which before sin was like a rod because of the uprightness of its good will and action; concerning it Scripture says: “You redeemed the rod of your inheritance,” etc. (Ps. LXXIX). Before sin, the rod clung to the hand of Moses—that is, to Christ’s hand—because of the uprightness in the first parents. But immediately, on account of sins, cast out from God’s hand, it was changed into a serpent, because then the human race became both mortal by nature and crooked through wickedness. But because in the last days it returned by grace to immortality and goodness, as though its tail had been seized, the rod is changed back to its former uprightness.

From the root of this serpent—that is, from the beginning of the human race—comes forth the basilisk, that is, Christ; for Christ was so superior among mortals as the basilisk is said to be king of serpents. His offspring—that is, the apostles—devours the flying creature, that is, the devil. Of these flying creatures it is said: “And the birds of heaven ate it” (Luke VIII) [Col. 0667B]. Therefore let the devil be confounded and afraid, because the offspring of the basilisk—that is, Christ’s apostles—devours the flying creature: it will scatter the devil in the Lord’s members, the Lord saying to him, “Kill and eat” (Acts X). Let man rejoice because, through the midwifing hand of the Lord—that is, the healing Son of God—the serpent has been drawn out of the cave, that is, the devil out of human hearts; so that, rejoicing in their deliverance and giving thanks to their victorious consoling Savior, they may say: “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V).

## TITLE XLIX. On the Three Dwellings of Egypt

[Col. 0667C]

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Cant. III). Scripture, wishing to call back to the vision of the true Solomon weak minds that it grieved to see lying in carnal desires—minds created to see God—says: “Go forth.” Go forth, therefore, from the stench of the stable to the fragrance of the bridal chamber; from Egypt’s onions to the manna of the desert; from, that is, the three dwellings of Egypt, to the three visions of our Solomon.

There are three dwellings of Egypt: the outer, the inner, and the higher. The outer dwelling lies in desire for the things of the world; the inner, in delight in things of the flesh; the higher, in glorying in evils. Abraham is commanded to leave these dwellings when he is told: “Go out from your land”—this is the first—“and from your kindred”—this is the second—“and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII)—this is the third [Col. 0667D]. “Land” denotes curiosity about earthly things; “kindred,” the allied delight of the flesh; and “father’s house,” glorying in evils, after the example of him who, wishing uniquely to glory, said: “I will sit upon the mountain of the covenant” (Isa. XIV). He is here called the father of evils by imitation.

In the first dwelling live those who delight in honors and riches; in the second, those who serve fleshly desires; in the third, those who are proud of and glory in their own evils. These are the three evils enumerated by the apostle John when he says: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John II). Therefore, by a journey of three days—so that we may not sin grievously in thought, speech, or action—let us leave these three dwellings with Abraham, in order that we may see Solomon [Col. 0668A]. Otherwise he will not be seen.

His vision, however, is threefold, and it is reached from the threefold vision already mentioned: the first in this exile, the second at judgment, the third in the kingdom. Of the first it is said: “Because you have seen me, Thomas, you have believed” (John XX); of the second: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke III); of the third: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. XXVI). In the first he appeared gentle; in the second, a just judge. Hence: “When I receive the appointed time, I shall judge justly” (Ps. LXXIV). In the third he is glorious, because “the Lord crowned him with glory and honor” (Ps. VIII). In the first vision he enlightened the blind; in the second he will loose those in bonds; in the third he guides the righteous [Col. 0668B]. In these he is lovable, terrible, and wonderful. The first vision produces hope, lest adversity cast us down; the second, fear, lest prosperity raise us up; the third, love, that we may see face to face (1 Cor. XIII).

In the first vision he was a corrector of morals; in the second he will be a discerner of merits; in the third, a giver of rewards. Corresponding to these three visions, three names belong to him: Solomon, Ecclesiastes, and Idida. Solomon means “peaceful,” which he truly was in the first. Ecclesiastes means “preacher,” which he will be in the second, when he summons heaven from above and earth, saying to the evil: “Go, accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), and to the good: “Come, blessed,” etc. (ibid.). Idida, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” which he will be in the third vision, in the homeland, when he will be all things to all [Col. 0668C] (Col. III).

In the first vision good and evil people saw him, but not all. In the second good and evil people, and all people, will see him. In the third, all the good and they alone. Scripture invites sinners to the first vision, in which the gentle one waits, saying: “Go forth and see King Solomon, declaring the precepts of peace, that you may preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” See, I say, not the crown with which his stepmother crowned him, but that with which his mother crowned him. His stepmother, father, and mother crowned him. The Synagogue is the stepmother, the Virgin the mother, and God his Father. His stepmother crowned him with a crown of thorns and misery; his mother, with a crown of justice; his Father, with a crown of glory.

The thorny crown outwardly pierced him materially and inwardly spiritually, not for his own crimes but for ours [Col. 0668D], so that we should not disdain to be pierced for our thorns. His mother’s crown adorned him with four precious stones. These are the four principal affections of the soul: joy, love, sorrow, and fear. As blessed Augustine says, when these affections are ordered, they are justice; when disordered, injustice. Therefore, because our Solomon assumed them from the Virgin in ordered form, that aforesaid crown of justice crowned him. But that you may attain full knowledge of the third diadem, with which God the Father crowned him with glory and honor, go forth from vices; behold, by faith, action, and imitation, him crowned with the crown with which his mother crowned him, so that by his example you may have the aforesaid affections in ordered form—he himself granting it. Who, etc.

## TITLE L. On God’s Threefold Speech

[Col. 0669A]

“I will hear what the Lord God may speak in me” (Ps. LXXXIV). God speaks to a human being in three ways: through the written law, the natural law, and hidden inspiration. The written law is both the Old and New Testaments. The natural law is: “What you wish done to yourself, do to another”; and: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another.” The written law is set before the ears; the natural law is implanted in hearts. Neither is observed in works unto salvation unless God speaks to a human being in the third manner, namely, by hidden inspiration. This is God’s third speech: not talkative but effectual; not sounding outwardly, but teaching and penetrating inwardly.

It drives away the flies of Egypt, which pursue those sacrificing in the desert. The first fly is softness of the flesh; this contaminates the sacrifice of mortified flesh [Col. 0669B]. The second is worldly curiosity, and this stains the sacrifice of a contrite heart. The third fly is the devil’s malice, and this defiles it. Likewise, Egypt has just as many talkative frogs. The speech of divine inspiration extinguishes these frogs, by making one cease from the voice of fleshly delights, the noise of worldly curiosity, and the voice of the devil who suggests evil.

This speech also speaks peace within. Peace is twofold: temporal peace, which causes rest from vices; and eternal peace, which grants endurance in glory. Of both the prophet says: “Sabbath after Sabbath he will give you” (Isa. LXVI), that is, eternal rest in exchange for temporal rest. God speaks the aforesaid peace to his people, over his saints, and to those who turn to the heart (Ps. LXXXIV). In these three are indicated three orders in the Church [Col. 0669C]: married people by “his people”; prelates by “his saints”; continent persons by “those who turn to the heart.” Or they are the three orders of cloistered persons: beginners, who still fight against carnal desires; the perfect, who cling to God alone; and prelates, who provide for themselves and for others. Although they go out for the care of others, through what is their own they return to their heart.

## TITLE LI. On the Steps of the Heart’s Ascent to God

“He arranged ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII). This ascender is in Holy Scripture sometimes called the lost sheep, sometimes the prodigal son departing from his father. For he departed from his Shepherd and Father into the desert of this world, a region far from God by three steps of descent. The first was to depart from God’s teaching will and establish his own will as his teacher, preferring his own to the divine will; the second was to descend from his own will into fleshly pleasures, making provision for the flesh in its desires; the third was to flow down from himself beneath himself into earthly things, seeking the world and what is in the world. First he withdrew from God inward to himself; second, from within outward beside himself; third, outside himself [Col. 0669D]. The first stage made him distant, the second more distant, and the third most distant. The first is the perversion of the will, the second fleshly delight, the third ambition for earthly things. By these steps he descended through the desert to the far country, as far as Babylon.

But because, according to the prophet, even there he is sometimes delivered, we must consider how by a threefold ascent he returns from this threefold descent to God; for he begins to ascend where, in descending, he arrived [Col. 0670A]. The first step of ascent is to despise earthly things, desiring that poverty by which one poor in a cell becomes richer in conscience. The second is wholly to crush the delights of the flesh, taming carnal desires by vigils, fasts, and prayers. The third is to subject one’s own will to God and to one’s prelates, showing humility in the heart, patience in the mouth, and perseverance in action. For these three are necessary to true obedience, after the example of him who became obedient to the Father (Phil. II)—gentle and humble of heart (Matt. XI; Isa. LIII)—and who, like a sheep led to slaughter, did not open his mouth, persevering unto the death of the cross (Phil. II).

## TITLE LII. Sabbaths That Are Mocked

[Col. 0670B]

“Enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I). For enemies to mock Sabbaths is to draw even the works and leisure of rest from vices into unlawful thoughts.

## TITLE LIII. What Is Meant by: “You Will Make Them Like a Furnace of Fire”

“You will make them like a furnace of fire at the time of your countenance,” etc. (Ps. XX). A furnace burns inwardly; fire burns flesh outwardly. Therefore, at the time of the Lord’s countenance, conscience burns inwardly in the unjust, and Gehenna tortures the flesh outwardly.

## TITLE LIV. On the Meaning of the Name Jerusalem According to the Fourfold Sense

“Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. CXXI). Jerusalem is understood in four ways: historically, as this earthly city [Col. 0670C]; allegorically, as the holy Church; tropologically, as every faithful soul; anagogically, as eternal blessedness. Of the first it is said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets,” etc. (Luke XIII). Of the second and third: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem,” etc. (Isa. LX). Of the fourth: “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother” (Gal. IV). To it it is said: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem” (Ps. CXLVII).

This is, as the Church sings, a certain blessed city, namely Jerusalem, called “vision of peace,” according to the interpretation of its name. It is built upon mountains, because it is in heaven; from living stones, that is, angels and human beings; prepared from the foundation of the world, so that, betrothed through the prophets in time, it may at last be joined to the Lord in eternity. It is built as a city [Col. 0670D]: with living and rational buildings; angelic orders as though ramparts; apostolic strength as though defensive towers; the confessions of martyrs as walls; the chastities of continent persons as honorable houses; and the duties of married people as streets exercised in commerce. With such buildings it is constructed until, completed, it is dedicated. It is built during seven days and dedicated on the eighth.

Yet it is not a city but is built *as* a city: not by reason of its name, but by reason of resemblance. For three things occur in construction. First, stones are violently drawn out with hammers and iron levers, with much labor. Second, they are polished, rough-hewn, and squared with chisel, axe, and rule. Third, by the hand of the craftsman they are arranged in their places to remain there. In the construction of the heavenly homeland, three corresponding things are considered: separation, polishing, and placement [Col. 0671A]. Separation is violent, polishing purgatorial, and placement eternal. The first is in distress and affliction; the second in patience and expectation; the third in glory and exultation. By the first a person is sifted like wheat; in the second tested like silver; in the third placed in the treasury. For they are living stones whom God foresaw would be made conformable to the Son of his glory.

While they are in the body, they are as though in a mass of stone. For the weight of the body presses and confines them most tightly, because “the corruptible body weighs down the soul,” etc. (Wis. IX). He who said, “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. XV), desired to be withdrawn from it. We must be shaken by many blows so that we may be drawn out from it fit for use. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV). Hear one who had experienced them saying: “In many vigils, in labors beyond measure, in hunger and thirst,” etc. (2 Cor. XI) [Col. 0671B].

But concerning the distress of separation, hear the Psalmist: “The groanings of death surrounded me” (Ps. CXIV). How intolerable this separation is, when natural knots and proportional bonds are loosed, is read in the book of experience concerning one who did not wish to be raised by Antony, since he would have to die again. After this separation, those immediately found fit—as blessed Benedict, to whom the way to heaven was shown, which is rare—are lifted up. But those who pass through with wood, hay, and stubble are polished in purgatory (1 Cor. III). Hence: “If anyone’s work which he built upon it shall burn, he shall receive a reward” (ibid.) [Col. 0671C]. After polishing they are lifted up and fitted to their proper places by the hand of the craftsman, *d. p. i. e.* [so printed].

The Church indeed represents these three things every year: separation on the vigil of All Saints; placement on the feast itself; polishing in the commemoration of the dead. For the day of fasting is a day of affliction. Hence: “On the first day of the seventh month you shall afflict your souls” (Lev. XXIII). But the solemn day which follows signifies fullness of joy, on which the saints celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles (*scenopegizant*) for the Lord. Third, the commemoration of the dead is observed so that those polished in purgatory may obtain release from punishment, or mitigation of punishment.

Thus the Church represents three things concerning the hope of the blessed: whence they pass, by what they pass, and whither they pass [Col. 0671D]. Whence they pass: from this misery; by what they pass: through punishment and purgatory; and whither: to the heavenly Jerusalem, whose “participation,” that is, dwelling, “is in the same” (Ps. CXXI), that is, in the unchangeable. For everything under the sun is changeable; but the dwelling of the heavenly Church is in that which is “the same.” In whose, etc.

## TITLE LV. On the Names of the Daughters of God and of the Devil, and Their Going Forth to Their King

Just as a perverse soul is called daughter of the sea, daughter of Tyre, daughter of Sidon, daughter of Babylon—given over to vanity, pleasure, curiosity, and every vice—so a faithful soul is called daughter of Judah, daughter of Zion, daughter of Jerusalem. Because of the humility of compunction, the sublimity of contemplation [Col. 0672A], and the blessedness of the heavenly vision, these daughters are told: “Go forth to your Creator, because to one who sees the Creator every creature is narrow. Go forth to the Savior, because he says: ‘Behold, I make all things new’” (Rev. XXI). “Go forth to glorification, because it is said: ‘I shall be satisfied when your glory appears’” (Ps. XVI).

It continues: “And behold with the eye of reason the power of your Creator; with the eye of faith the mercy of your Redeemer; with the eye of contemplation the glory of the heavenly Bridegroom”—namely, King of nature, lest the times of grace be reduced to nothing, so that the gifts of grace and glory may succeed in due order: here tasted beforehand, though only a little; elsewhere consummated in full. King in the world, king in hell, king in heaven. In hell he ordains torments; in the world he distributes merits; in heaven he repays rewards [Col. 0672B]. Therefore behold, daughters of Zion, your King’s terror in the lower regions, his love in the world, and his honor in heaven. In the lower regions his justice oppresses the ungodly; in the world his mercy governs penitents; in heaven glory makes lovers blessed.

## TITLE LVI. On the Interpretation of Holy Scripture

“If you enter your neighbor’s grainfield, you shall pluck ears and rub them in your hand; but you shall not reap with a sickle” (Deut. XXIII). That is, you shall pull out sentences with the hand of understanding, rub the grain from the ear, separating spirit from letter. But “you shall not reap with a sickle” means rapidly and easily running through a book. It is enough to gather a few sheaves each day. There are those who reap with a sickle: reading an entire book at once, they understand nothing.

“Having entered your neighbor’s vineyard”—that is, the Scripture of your God—“you may eat grapes,” that is, sayings, as much as pleases you; “but you shall not carry them out with you” (ibid.) [Col. 0672C], because what is holy must not be given to dogs, nor pearls cast before swine (Matt. VII).

“With grain, wine, and oil I have established him” (Gen. XXVII). In some places divine Scripture is eaten with difficulty like bread; in others it is easily drunk like wine; in all places, when received, it heals the soul like a medicine and oil.

## TITLE LVII. How Firstborn Things Belong in Different Ways to God and to Priests

All firstborn things in the law belong to the priests. Unclean ones are redeemed; clean ones are not redeemed, but offered. Their blood is poured upon the altar; the breast and shoulder belong to the priests (Num. XVII) [Col. 0672D], because faith is offered to God through the ministry of priests. No one is baptized otherwise than when the faith, which is the firstborn, is first offered to the priests. The unclean is redeemed because a violated soul is restored at the cost of repentance. The clean are not redeemed because what is free has no need of redemption. Blood is poured upon the altar. The breast and shoulder belong to the priests because it belongs to them so to proclaim the lives of their people that they may be able to give counsel and bear burdens.

## TITLE LVIII. On the Purification and Offices of the Levites as a Type of the Christian Clergy

The Levites are commanded to be taken from the midst of the children of Israel, purified, sprinkled with water of purification, and to shave all the hair of their body (Num. VIII). By this it is signified that the life of our Levites and clergy ought to be separated from lay life [Col. 0673A], purified and washed from every filth of vice, and cleansed of superfluous thought. Hence it is added: “And the children of Israel shall lay their hands upon them” (ibid.), that they may understand how great a burden is laid upon those who must labor for all, whose hands they bear; and that what the hands of all should have done in the tabernacle, those alone should do who have taken the hands of all upon themselves.

The Levites, moreover, placed their hands upon the heads of two oxen, understanding that they ought to tame their body and soul. Their tamer was he who said: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. IX). If they have been tamed thus, then Moses—that is, the Savior—offers one ox for sin, the other as a burnt offering: by the one sins are forgiven, by the other God’s grace is received [Col. 0673B]. Thus purified, they enter the tabernacle to minister, because such persons are worthy of the tabernacle of the Church and of heaven.

## TITLE LIX. On Lifting Up the Ox and Ass—That Is, the Foolish and the Rustic—When They Fall

“If you see your brother’s ass or ox fallen on the way, you shall not despise it, but lift it up” (Exod. XXIV). We are on the way of God’s commandments, on which the Psalmist, weary from it, said: “I ran the way of your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). Our brother is Christ and every human being. For it is certain that we are children of one Father. His ass is some foolish, lazy, or lustful person. The ox is one who ought to labor in his field. If we see such persons fallen by sin on the way, we must lift them up. Therefore let us help, so that we too may be helped.

Within us is a garden in which is the Lord’s tomb. If we fall into it, we are raised up, just as the body carried away by robbers, when it fell into Elisha’s tomb out of fear of its pursuers, rose again alive (4 Kings XIII) [Col. 0673C]. But a stone is often placed before the door, lest we enter. Yet if holy women—that is, good thoughts—frequent the tomb, the angel removes the stone; and those who enter, even if they have been dead, shall live.

## TITLE LX. On Those Who Love and Fear God, and Those Who Confess God

“The upright love you” (Cant. I). Some people are lying down, others bent, others upright. Those lying down are people who neither fear nor love God; the bent are those who fear but do not love; the upright are those who both fear and love. Some confess God because he feeds them well. Hence in the Psalm: “He will confess you when you do good to him” (Ps. XLVIII). These, lying in the mire of sin, neither fear nor love God [Col. 0673D]. Others confess God because they know that he has power to cast body and soul into Gehenna; these fear and do not love. Others confess God for God’s own sake, because he alone is good, sweet, and of great mercy; not from fear, not from desire, but they confess because he is good. The first are hirelings, the second slaves, the third sons. The hireling desires for himself; the slave fears for himself; the son loves. Each has his own law: the hireling, desire, by which he is bound; the slave, fear, by which he is restrained; the son, love, which he embraces.

## TITLE LXI. On the Three Chambers into Which We Are Led

[Col. 0674A]

“The king brought me into his storechambers” (Cant. I). In moral discipline there are three chambers, as it were, in a true storehouse; hence he says “storechambers” in the plural. The first is that of discipline, the second of nature, the third of grace. In the first you learn to be below; in the second, equal; in the third, above—namely, to be subject, to live together, to preside. First, therefore, learn to be a disciple; second, a companion; third, a teacher. In the first evil habits are tamed; in the second good ones are assumed; in the third others are taught to tame and assume them.

## TITLE LXII. Again on the Interpretation of Jerusalem
