“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble together.” Jerusalem is spoken of in four ways: historically, allegorically, morally, and anagogically. Historically, it is the city established [Col. 0674B] upon Mount Zion, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where King David constructed a clouded tower. Allegorically, it is the city established on the mountain that is Christ, “its foundation in the holy mountains,” where Christ reigns eternally. Morally, it is the faithful soul devoted to contemplation, which lays its foundation upon the height of virtues. The Word, uttered from the Father’s heart, dwells in it. For we are God’s Word in him. Anagogically, it is that superheavenly court, the archangelic company, which is daily satisfied while glory appears to them, because it is believed to be continually established in the contemplation of eternal delight.

Earthly Jerusalem rejoices in earthly things. Jerusalem the Church rejoices in manifold gifts. Jerusalem the faithful soul rejoices in the varied dispositions of the mind. Jerusalem the divine court rejoices in diverse rewards [Col. 0674C]. The joy with which the Church rejoices is twofold: forgiveness of sins and attainment of gifts. Therefore, for these benefits received, the Holy Spirit invites it to exultation: “Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble together.” Let virtues assemble to resist vices. Let preachers assemble to resist heretics. Let martyrs assemble to resist tyrants. “For they have devised unanimously; together they have set a covenant against her: the tents of the Edomites and Ishmaelites.”

## TITLE LXIII. On Guarding a Person’s Way in Speech, and on Not Revealing Mysteries

A person’s way is not only guarded but also corrected by guarding speech. “By what shall the younger man correct his way? By keeping,” he says, “his words” (Ps. CXVIII) [Col. 0674D]. Because these words must sometimes be kept silent, he adds: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart” (because of swine and dogs), “that I may not sin against you” (ibid.): “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII). It is a vice to reveal the secrets of mystery to the unworthy. This is done either through flattery, to please the person to whom one reveals them; through avarice, to profit thereby; or through boasting, to seem to know much.

But that they must sometimes be spoken is shown when he says: “With my lips”—in harmony with the heart—“I have proclaimed”—to others, when I saw the time was right—“your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII). I do not say all, but those “of your mouth”: judgments which you have revealed to me through the apostles and others, by which the world is judged now and in the future, and which are a great abyss.

## TITLE LXIV. “He Shall Eat Butter and Honey,” etc.

[Col. 0675A]

“He who became a child for us eats butter and honey in us” (Isa. VII), when he makes us eat them; because when the Holy Spirit pours grace into us, he fills us with honey and butter together. Honey falls from above; butter is gathered from the milk of oxen or cows. Honey therefore comes from the air; butter from flesh. The Only-Begotten of the highest Father, though he is God above all things, became man among all things. Since he filled us with the sweetness of his divinity and the mystery of his incarnation, he nourished us with honey and butter together, so that he may know—that is, make us know—how to reject evil—namely, vices and punishments—and choose the good—namely, virtues and rewards.

## TITLE LXV. On the Five Cities of Egypt Speaking the Language of Canaan

[Col. 0675B]

“On that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. XIX), not Egyptian or Hebrew. The five cities are the five bodily senses. Egypt is the world. In Egypt the cities speak Egypt’s language when the five senses seek worldly things in the world. They speak Canaanite in Egypt when, moved from vices to virtue, they do not seek worldly things in the world. For “Canaanite” is interpreted “movement.” But no one speaks Hebrew, a language that signifies passage, in the Egypt of this world; it is spoken in that life to which passage is made from death. Yet here he speaks Canaanite, which is akin to Egyptian and Hebrew and lies between them, who is moved from vices to virtues, though he does not pass over altogether.

It follows: “And swearing by the Lord of hosts” [Col. 0675C] (ibid.), that is, remembering God, not human beings. It adds: “One shall be called the city of the sun” (ibid.). This is sight, through which the light of justice is received, so that it may be seen as a city.

## TITLE LXVI. How God Speaks to a Human Heart

“I will speak to her heart” (Hos. II). God speaks to the human heart by enlightening it with his grace. A person speaks to his own heart by carefully reading his deeds in the book of his heart. This book has two leaves. Sinners read on one, penitents on the other. The sinner reads this: “I did these things; I remember and delight in them.” On the opposite leaf, the penitent reads: “I did these things; I remember and grieve.” Let us read on the penitents’ leaf, lest perhaps we pay the last farthing—that is, be punished [Col. 0675D] for the things we drew forth from the earth.

For there are two farthings: one of God, the other of the world. God’s farthing is love with the whole heart, whole soul, and all one’s strength. The world’s farthing is pleasure, curiosity, and vain glory. Every farthing indeed consists of three things. The first is paid, and glory received; the second is received, and punishment assigned.

## TITLE LXVII. On the Last Things and the Ancient Things Applied to the Incarnation of the Word

“You have known all the last things and the ancient things” (Ps. CXXXVIII). The last thing is: “The Word was made flesh” (John I); the ancient thing: “In the beginning was the Word” (ibid.). These are new things in relation to old things, and the most ancient of ancient things, of which Leviticus says: “You shall eat the most ancient of old things; and when new things come in, you shall cast out the old” [Col. 0676A]. The old things are the promises of the laws and prophets concerning Christ who was to come. The new things are the fulfillment of the promises, the manifestation of truth. The most ancient things are those belonging to the eternity of divinity.

Therefore, when new things come in, old things must be cast out and the most ancient preserved; because, when the truth of the Lord’s coming has been manifested, figure and promise ought to cease, and the new thing of the Incarnation and the most ancient thing of the Word’s eternity must be retained in faith and worship. Hence three Masses are celebrated at Christmas. The first concerns eternal generation: “The Lord said to me.” The second, the promise of the coming: “The light shall shine.” The third, the fulfillment of the promise: “A child is born to us.” Because he who is the Son of God became the son of man [Col. 0676B], in the office of that Mass in which Christ’s eternal generation is sung—“The Lord said to me”—the Gospel of Christ’s temporal birth is read: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matt. I). And in the Mass in which his temporal birth is sung—“A child is born to us”—the Gospel of his eternal generation is read: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I).

And because figures cease when the truth is manifested, on the days following not the office pertaining to promise but that pertaining to fulfillment is repeated, namely: “A child is born to us.” These are the last things and ancient things which the Father knows, and which the Son reveals to whom he wills.

## TITLE LXVIII. On Those Who Divide Their Days and Those Who Do Not, and the Place of Their Death

“You will lead them down into the pit of destruction, because men of blood and deceit will not divide their days” (Ps. LIV): that is, so that if they have spent some days in evil, they may complete the remainder in good. For some do not begin days anew, but persevere continually in evil. Others divide their days, while others fill their days with good, because some die in Egypt, others in the desert, others in the Holy Land [Col. 0676C]. In Egypt die those who remain in the darkness of vices to the end of life; in the desert, those who, departing from the confession of sin, amend themselves through repentance; in the Holy Land, those fill their days who persevere without crime in works of justice to the end.

These three kinds of people are found in that scroll in which song, lamentation, and woe are written. Those sing a song who have not experienced the fall of sin; those lament who rise from sins through the lament of repentance; woe belongs to those who sin and do not repent [Col. 0676D]. These do not divide their days.

## TITLE LXIX. On the Two Silver Trumpets and Their Use, Applied to Peter and Paul

“Make for yourself two beaten silver trumpets” (Num. X), whose varied sounds gather the people prepared for battle and are sounded at the feast. These silver trumpets are Peter and Paul, silver by the brightness of their eloquence, beaten out upon the anvil of the heart, fashioned by the hammer of the Holy Spirit. By them we, the peoples of circumcision and of the Gentiles, are gathered into the Church; we are taught to fight against and overcome the enemies of vices and demons; and we learn, by living well, ordering our morals, and running in the way of the commandments, how we are to offer [Col. 0677A] God sacrifices of praise and jubilation, celebrating a feast pleasing to God. By them we are exhorted in one way to assemble and in another to fight, because in the threefold manner already explained.

## TITLE LXX. On the Two Kinds of Labor—That of the World and That of God—and the Threefold Form of Each

“He honored him in his labors” (Wis. X). Some labors belong to the world, others to God’s service. Worldly labor is threefold. One kind is pleasant and delightful, such as work in gardens, fishponds, and the like. Another is foolish and useless, such as athletic contests, theatre, dancing at horse-races, and leaps of the feet. Another is wicked and burdensome, such as thefts, murders, and the like. All these are the labors of fools.

Labor in God’s service is likewise threefold. One kind is hard but fruitful: manual labor for the salvation of the soul and out of obedience, full of sweat [Col. 0677B]. Another is honorable and full of the grace of virtues: to exercise oneself in hymns and songs, the harmony of morals and voices alike, in praise of God. Another is sweet and delightful, known only to one who has experienced it: when the mind clings most ardently to God in a certain contemplation and is nourished by wondrous tears. In Job these are called “waters of snow”; although they may seem labors to one without experience, to one who has experienced them they are sweeter than honey.

## TITLE LXXI. On the End That Consumes and Completes, and on the Commandment That Is Exceedingly Broad
Every consummation I have seen has its end. Your commandment is exceedingly broad (Ps. 118). The end of consummation is the fullness of love: an end that consumes and brings to completion. [Col. 0677C] It consumes three things: the iniquity of vices of the mind and sins of the flesh; the vanity of the world; and the misery of the flesh. It brings to completion by three things: perfect purity, equality with angels, and eternal blessedness. This commandment is exceedingly broad because, once it possesses the inner person, vanity does not disturb thought, impurity does not stain affection, and iniquity does not constrain intention. Thus God desires to be loved by us. “Love,” he says, “the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul” (Deut. 6), so that thought may be sound, affection pure, and intention upright. You shall love him, first, because he created you; secondly, because he redeemed you; thirdly, because he will glorify you—namely, on account of the works of creation, redemption, and glorification. In the first, he created you from nothing and endowed you with reason. [Col. 0677D] In the second, he freed you from the curse and healed you from concupiscence. In the third, he joined you to the fellowship of angels and endowed you with a most limpid memory.

## TITLE LXXII. On the threefold bodily state possessed by the soul that loves God

“Eat,” says the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs, “my friends, and drink, and be intoxicated” (Song 5). The soul that loves has three bodily states: that of the weak, the dead, and the raised. The first is effective for the soul toward the fruit of penitence; the second, toward rest; the third, toward consummation. In the first, the body burdens and assists the soul; in the second, it does not assist but burdens it; in the third, it assists and does not burden it. The first state is laborious but fruitful; the second burdensome and wearisome; the third glorious.

Therefore he calls those laboring in the body to food; those resting after the body has been laid aside he invites to drink; and those resuming their bodies he invites to be intoxicated. These he also calls most dear—certainly, full of love. Hence there is a difference among them in other respects as well. Those still weighed down in the flesh are called dear because of the love which they possess. But those already released from the fetter of flesh are the dearer insofar as they are nearer and freer for loving. Yet above both are called most dear those who, having received the second robe, are borne more freely into the love of God because they possess nothing from the former state to trouble or delay them. [Col. 0678A]

Thus, first, the faithful soul in the flesh is fed with the bread of sorrow; secondly, released from the flesh, it is given the wine of love to drink; thirdly, admitted to Solomon’s banquet, it is intoxicated with the spice of love. Wisdom celebrates this threefold banquet from one love: feeding those who labor, giving drink to those who rest, and intoxicating those who reign. Here, first, before death, in mortal flesh, we eat the labors of our hands; after death, in spiritual life, we shall drink in sweetest rest; after the resurrection of the flesh, we shall be intoxicated by a certain boundless blessedness. Eat, therefore, before death; drink after death; be intoxicated after the resurrection. [Col. 0678B]

## TITLE LXXIII. On the threefold blessing, the two hands and the fingers of each, and threefold obedience

“Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labors of your hands: you are blessed,” etc. (Ps. 127). The end of this psalm is blessing. Blessing is threefold: material, spiritual, and intellectual. Material blessing belongs to bodily things. Hence: “With grain, wine, and oil I have established him” (Gen. 27). Spiritual blessing belongs to incorporeal things. Hence: “In faith and gentleness he made him holy” (Ecclus. 45). “All who see such a one shall know that he is holy, whom the Lord has blessed.” Intellectual blessing belongs to heavenly things. Hence: “Jesus, having summoned his twelve disciples, gave them power over all demons and to cure diseases” (Luke 9).

In the first, therefore, human nature is sustained by the work and fruit of nature; in the second, it is restored by the gifts and work of grace; in the third, it is raised up by the works and gifts of glory. The present psalm speaks of the spiritual blessing. But note who deserves to be blessed: the one who fears, walks, labors, and eats. In the first, note obedience; in the second, penitence; in the third, constancy; [Col. 0678C] in the fourth, patience. For true penitence is always fearful and guards against sins; devout obedience, with heart enlarged, walks in the commandments; manly constancy labors in temptation so that it may not fall; humble patience rejoices in tribulation, while it triumphs. Hence: “Count it all joy,” etc. (Jas. 1).

Here: “You shall eat the labors of your hands.” The first hand, the left, is action. The second, the right, is contemplation. The fingers of the left hand are these: the first, abstinence, cuts off lust and ministers chastity; the second, silence, removes falsehood and gives truth; the third, psalmody, removes curiosity and grants purity of flesh, mouth, and mind; the fourth, the labor of vigils, takes away the blindness of ignorance and confers the brightness of knowledge; the fifth, the exercise of works, removes vanity [Col. 0678D] and grants the freedom of grace.

The fingers of the right hand are these: the first is reading; the second, meditation; the third, compunction; the fourth, devotion; the fifth, prayer. Reading seeks the bride; meditation finds her when sought; compunction washes her when found; devotion clothes and adorns her when washed; prayer gives a pledge to her when adorned. It seeks her in the divine utterances, finds her in the ordinances of the holy Fathers, washes her in the health-giving fountain of tears, clothes her in the varied warmth of virtues, and gives her a pledge through faith and vow, stability and purpose.

The wife of this man is regular and perfect obedience, like an abundant vine. From it wine is pressed, which is known to have a threefold power: it warms, gladdens, and intoxicates. The kinds of obedience likewise are threefold. The first concerns stable commands; the second inviolable commands; the third unchangeable commands. [Col. 0679A] The first is of human ordering and kindles; the second, of divine institution, gladdens; the third, of heavenly instruction, intoxicates. The first kindles with zeal for righteousness; the second gladdens with purity of conscience; the third intoxicates with fullness of grace.

Therefore the wife of the aforesaid rich man is “like an abundant vine” (Ps. 127), because her obedience kindles toward righteousness, gladdens through virtue toward grace and rest, and intoxicates toward glory and salvation. “At the sides of your house” (ibid.) are conscience, fear, and hope. The wife abounds at the sides of the house, because perfection of life cannot otherwise be attained unless fear is anxiously watchful below and hope raises one upward. Between these two sides the household of virtues rejoices, because watchful fear strives to hedge in the ways so that vices may not enter; hope bears upward, lest the rewards of contests [Col. 0679B] be overlooked; fear prevents a rival from entering; hope coaxes so as to please the bride.

Her children—that is, her works—are like young olive shoots. Oil nourishes, anoints, and gives light. It anoints through works of mercy, nourishes through works of righteousness, and gives light through works of grace. Works are called young olive shoots of works.

## TITLE LXXIV. On the rewards of flesh dried up and mortified through religious obedience

“O dry bones, hear the word of God. Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bring spirit into you, and you shall live,” etc. (Ezek. 37). By these words the Holy Spirit speaks to those to whom the Son said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you a kingdom,” etc. (Luke 22). He praises in them the rigor of mortification through contempt for sin, the world, and self. He praises the beauty of strength through love of what is right, of the Father and God, of what is equitable, just, and honorable.

But lest their constancy should waver, he raises their hope from the love of resurrection, saying “bones” because of the strength of love, and “dry” because of the leanness of mortification. “Hear the word of the Lord,” etc. In these consists the whole beauty of the soul. In the first, everything indecent and useless is removed; in the second, everything beautiful and honorable is prepared; in the third, everything healthful is established. In the first, it ceases to act perversely; in the second, it learns to act well; in the third, it seeks peace and possesses it.

Such were those to whom the Apostle said (Col. 3): “You have died”—behold, dry; “and your life is hidden with Christ in God”—behold, bones. [Col. 0679C] “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also shall appear with him in glory”—behold, the resurrection. Of such persons it is said in the psalm: “Myrrh and stacte and cassia from your garments,” etc. (Ps. 44). And elsewhere: “In a desert land, trackless and waterless, thus I appeared to you in the sanctuary,” etc. (Ps. 62).

There are three kinds of mortification: first, that of iniquity through penitence; second, that of the flesh through abstinence; third, that of the will through obedience. By penitence, iniquity is mortified; by abstinence, the flesh; by obedience, one’s own will. The first presses out the poison of malice; the second burns away the incentives of lust and gluttony; the third removes the unlawful and unsuitable impulses of self-will. Therefore the land becomes desert through penitence, trackless through abstinence, and waterless through spiritual obedience. In the first is found myrrh, [Col. 0680A] which expels the poison of iniquity; in the second, stacte, which casts out the blood of impure will; in the third, cassia, which presses out the natural vigor of just necessity.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My bones were dried up like firewood” (Ps. 101). Firewood is so for three reasons: first, through the power of salt; second, through human labor; third, through the nature of blood. This one—the member of Christ, bride of the Lamb, co-heiress of the Only-Begotten—dries the flesh from the act of sin by confessing iniquity; restrains the senses from the cause of wandering by excluding curiosity; and preserves the mind from the desire to sin by banishing vanity. Thus, first, they are dry from iniquity through confession; secondly, lean through the rigor of frugality; thirdly, arid through spiritual submission.

This is the bride who first ascends “like the rising dawn” (Song 6); secondly, through the desert “like a column of smoke” (Song 3); thirdly, “abounding in delights” (Song 8). She is dawn, raised from the darkness of vices through confession and recognition of truth; she passes through the desert of abstinence, having cut off occasion for curiosity; she abounds in riches—that is, spiritual exercises—under the purity of obedience. [Col. 0680B]

Thus dry, yet bones, they have fourfold strength: first, against the assault of vices; secondly, against worldly prosperity; thirdly, against its storms; fourthly, against the devil’s cunning. Therefore bones of truth are the Savior’s friends and disciples, contemptuous of the world, of their own sin, and of the devil. Hence: “All my bones shall say: Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 34). In the body of the Church, the skin is the carnal, the flesh the animal, the bones the spiritual.

Thus, when they have been dried by fear and parched by sorrow, the author of mercy promises a reward for labor in the glory of resurrection. Hence follows: “I shall put sinews upon you, flesh, and skin” (Ezek. 37). In the skin is signified the immortality of the body; in the flesh, the blessedness of the soul; in the sinews, the eternity of both. Great, therefore, are the consolations of affliction, precious the joys of mourning, glorious the rewards of struggle. A wonderful exchange. Hence the prophet: “On that day there shall be for you a crown instead of ashes, oil of joy instead of mourning, a garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow” (Isa. 61). In the last is the immortality of the body; in the middle, the blessedness of the soul; in the first, the eternity of both is indicated. [Col. 0680C]

Hence the Apostle: “What is momentary and light in tribulation works in us beyond measure a weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4), “as we look not at what is temporal, but at what is eternal.” Therefore manly compunction of mind, affliction of flesh, constancy in temptation, and patience in tribulation are fitting, because from compunction comes delight; from affliction, joy; from conflict, victory; and from battle, the crown is won. [Col. 0681A]

## TITLE LXXV. How God is exalted in us, and on the height of our heart

“Man shall approach the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). God is exalted in three ways: through that which he has from us, namely the human nature in which he was exalted above the heavens of heavens; according as he dwells in us, namely through faith and love, because whoever loves more is found more worthy of love; and likewise according as he is grasped by us through knowledge, because the more his knowledge grows in us, the greater his eminence is found to be.

It is like a mountain: the farther away you are from it, the smaller it appears; the nearer you come, the greater and higher it seems. The heart is deep, broad, and high: deep through despair, broad through love, high through contemplation. If, therefore, you wish God—who cannot be exalted in himself—to be exalted in you, approach from the depth of the heart to its breadth through faith and love, and from the breadth to its height through knowledge. And God will be exalted in us, because insofar as the affection of the human heart, suspended from desire for lower things, is advanced into love of eternal things, so the love of God, greater from great virtues and higher from the highest virtues, is exalted in that person.

## TITLE LXXVI. On threefold discipline

[Col. 0681C]

“Lay hold of discipline” (Ps. 2). Discipline is threefold: that of correction, instruction, and conduct. The first and second belong to the teacher; the third, to the disciple. Of the first and second the prophet says: “Your discipline corrected me unto the end; your discipline itself will teach me” (Ps. 17). Of the third, the Book of Wisdom says: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. 1). The discipline of correction occurs in two ways, by admonitions and punishments; the discipline of instruction is delivered in two ways, by precepts and examples; the discipline of conduct is practiced in two ways, by habits and studies.

## TITLE LXXVII. On the four contests of Christians

“Let the enemy pursue your soul” (Ps. 7). There are four contests in Christian warfare: wound, flight, assault, and triumph. Sometimes the enemy pursues a person, overtakes him, and strikes him with a great wound. Sometimes he pursues and overtakes, but the person escapes in flight. Sometimes, with the situation reversed, the person pursues but does not overtake the enemy, because his assault is indiscreet. Sometimes he pursues and overtakes him, and this is triumph. “I shall pursue my enemies,” he says, “and overtake them” (Ps. 17).

As long as a person is stretched out in the world, the enemy pursues and overtakes him; when he flees from the world, the enemy pursues but does not overtake him; when, in novice zeal, a person imprudently disciplines the body in order to be delivered from vices, then, with the situation reversed, the person pursues the enemy but does not overtake him; when, with perfected understanding, he so slays vice that he does not indulge it at all, he pursues and overtakes it. [Col. 0681D] Of the first the prophet says: “The wound of an enemy has struck you” (Jer. 30). Of the second, the Lord says: “See that your flight does not occur in winter or on a sabbath” (Matt. 24). Of the third: “Whoever is hasty stumbles with his feet” (Prov. 19). Of the fourth: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4). For to have resisted in temptations is to have conquered. [Col. 0682A]

## TITLE LXXVIII. On the wrath, face, and presence of God; on smoke, flame, and coals

“Smoke rose in his wrath, fire blazed forth from his face, and coals were kindled by him” (Ps. 17). Wrath in God is one thing, face another, presence another. Wrath denotes remembrance of judgment; face, knowledge; presence, enjoyment. Remembrance is good, knowledge better, enjoyment best. Moreover, smoke, flame, and coals signify different things. Smoke is the bitterness of penitence; flame, the ardor of love; coals, the holocaust of consummation. “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, and holocausts” (Ps. 50).

Remembrance of judgment therefore arouses compunction by instilling fear, and leads from fear to penitence. “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118). For after death one is thereby affected with love. Knowledge causes affection to burn, because the more God is known, the more he is loved. Thus, in the present life he is not loved fully by one who does not know him fully. Enjoyment, however, grants consummation, because, when after death the glory of contemplation is granted to be enjoyed through majesty, the fullness of love will be brought to completion.

[Col. 0682B] But when compunction is aroused from remembrance of judgment, then smoke rises from God’s wrath; when love grows warm from thought, fire blazes from his face; when knowledge is given from present enjoyment, coals are kindled by him. First he sets smoke, second flame, third coals. When fire touches raw and moist material, it does not immediately send forth flames or consume it all into coals. The raw and moist material is the conscience of sinners, infected, as it were, with certain dyes by the flux of the flesh and carnal vices. In this material, the *spanli* [reading uncertain] of divine indignation rises from the heart even to the eyes, and the smoke of compunction flows out in tears.

But when the material of the body has been stirred by abstinence, contrition, and penitence, it begins to shine through knowledge and to burn through love, having been released from the diverse darknesses of ignorance; and love becomes more ardent the more penetrating the wisdom of God has become. Or rather, fire blazes from his face when, from knowledge of him, love is kindled—able to inflame the human heart while life is here, but never able in the present life to consume or reduce all the material into coals, so long as “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9). For, like something still possessing moisture, the material can have flames of love but can never be converted into coals, until that which is perfect comes and that which is partial is abolished (1 Cor. 13), so that the fire of love may transform the whole person into itself and reduce him once more into coals; [Col. 0682C] so that nothing further may hinder the flesh and the fire of love may no longer have to struggle.

For when one has arrived there, it has made smoke into flame and flame into coals. Thus, after the fire that burns in Zion, there is a furnace of kindled coals in Jerusalem. The prophet says: “The Lord comes, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31). Zion is called contemplation; Jerusalem, the vision of peace. Here is contemplation in labor; there is the vision of peace. Therefore in contemplation there is fire, but in vision a furnace, because here fire blazes from the face, while there, in the furnace, coals are kindled by him. [Col. 0683A]

## TITLE LXXIX. On the threefold place of God

“His place was made in peace” (Ps. 75). The place of God is threefold: the world, the Church, and the faithful soul. In the world he is as an emperor in a kingdom; in the Church, as the master of a household in a house; in the soul, as a bridegroom in a bridal chamber. In the world he is present by creating and ruling; in the Church, by calling to participation in the sacraments and reception of faith; in the soul, by dwelling through love.

If you are in God’s house by creation, the devil too is with you. If you are in God’s house by faith, demons too are with you, for “the demons believe and tremble.” If by hope, chaff too is with the grain on the threshing floor and in the granary. But if you are there through love, you are blessed, because you have begun to be not so much in the house of God as the house of God, so that you may enter and dwell where peace is, and he whose place was made in peace may deign to dwell there. [Col. 0683B]

Make this place or house an ark of the flood, a tent of warfare, and the ark of the covenant. In the house let the son venerate his father. In the flood let the shipwrecked person weep for governance. In the tent let the soldier honor the king. In the covenant let the follower listen to the teacher. [Col. 0683C]

## TITLE LXXX. On the open and hidden fountain, namely Christ our Lord

“On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13). The hidden fountain is the Only-Begotten of the invisible Father. The same fountain, open, is God incarnate; and it is called an open fountain for the house of David because the Redeemer came to us from David’s line. He dwelt in Jerusalem, because he dwelt in the inward vision of peace.

The sinner and the menstruous woman signify the sinful mind; or, the sinner signifies one who sins in deed, and the menstruous woman the mind which slips through evil thought. For just as a menstruous woman is defiled, though she touches no alien flesh and is contaminated by her own, so the soul, even if it commits no evil deed, is nevertheless made foul and defiled by an impure thought. Hence: “All who seek her shall not fail; in her menstruation they shall find her” (Jer. 2), because evil spirits are repelled in her when she is established in the rectitude of good thought, whereas, when she is set in polluted thoughts, they easily draw her toward perverse thought.

“On that day,” therefore, etc., because now the fountain of mercy has been opened to us: our Redeemer, incarnate in the house of David, washes the sinner from perverse action and cleanses the menstruous mind from foul thought. Therefore, the Father being the fountain, let us run with tears and wash in this fountain of mercy. In this fountain David, washed by penitence from the grave stain of guilt, sought this fountain when he said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50), that is, of Jesus. [Col. 0683D] In this fountain of mercy Mary Magdalene, Peter, and the thief were washed.

Why, then, are we sluggish? Why do we remain lethargic and cold, when we know that so many have washed themselves in this fountain of mercy? Shall we then despair of our cleansing, when we hold so many examples of mercy as a pledge? We ought to seek the fountain of mercy if it were closed; but now it is open, and we neglect it. Let us cast the eyes of faith over the whole world; let us consider how many today are washed in this fountain and how many return to purity after tears. Let us run with such people to the water of life; let us consider how greatly we have sinned; and, that we may appear clean, let us wash our heart for him as a holocaust, with the help in these very things of the grace of our Lord Redeemer, who lives and reigns, etc. [Col. 0684A–B]

## TITLE LXXXI. On threefold humiliation

“It is good for me because you humbled me” (Ps. 118). Not all who are humbled are humble, because some are humbled with resentment, others patiently, others willingly. The first are guilty, the second innocent, the third just. For although innocence is a part of righteousness, its consummation lies with the humble. God does not give grace to one who murmurs inwardly, nor to one who murmurs less, but to the humble—not to those merely humbled.

## TITLE LXXXII. On the shameful transformation of man

“Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them” [Col. 0684C] (Ps. 48). A shameful transformation: he whose task formerly was to penetrate the heavens in meditation, to traverse the heavenly dwellings in mind, to greet the Fathers and apostles in devotion, to admire the choirs of prophets and the triumphs of martyrs, and to marvel at the most beautiful orders of angels, now shamefully enslaves himself to bodily servitude—to obey the flesh, to satisfy gluttony and the belly—so that the flesh, a servant, may command the spirit, its master, as though she were a mistress.

“Streams of waters shall lead down the eyes” (Ps. 118) over such a soul—one that, though once nourished in saffron, now embraces dung. “She feeds the barren woman who does not bear, and does not do good to the widow.” “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand” (Ps. 48). “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3). “When he was in honor, he did not understand,” he says. Where did he dwell? In paradise, in a place of delight, crowned with glory and honor, and set over the works of the Creator’s hands; his fellowship was with the host of angels and the whole army of the heavenly host. Yet he “changed this glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay” (Ps. 105).

Hence the bread of angels became hay laid in a manger and set before us like beasts. This hay, the flesh of Christ, has not dried up; it is for the life of the world. It is assuredly that hay—our flesh—which dries up and whose flower falls, not he who rises from the root and rod of Jesse. The food of man changed itself into fodder for cattle, when man was changed into cattle. Behold the sad and tearful transformation: man, inhabitant of paradise, lord of earth, citizen of heaven, member of the household of the Lord Sabaoth, above the ranks of blessed spirits, by a sudden transformation lies as cattle in a stall and needs hay. [Col. 0684D]

Recognize, O ox, your owner, and you, O ass, the manger of your Lord. Know, O beast, him whom you once knew; O man, adore in the stall him whom you fled in paradise, and eat hay, because you despised the bread of angels, because, when you were in honor, you did not understand either God your Creator or that you had been created blessed. [Col. 0685A]

This twofold ignorance is condemnable.

The first makes a person equal to beasts; the second places him behind them. Hence: “If you do not know yourself, go after the flock of your companions” (Song 1). Truly after them, because reprobate human beings, not cattle, are consigned to eternal fire. It would have been better for him if he had not been born a human being (Matt. 26), but a beast. Because of the first ignorance he had beasts as companions; he became like them in enjoying earthly goods. Because of the second, he is not with them but behind them in enduring the torments of Gehenna. For here he is more beastly than beasts themselves: endowed with reason and yet not living by reason. [Col. 0685B]

## TITLE LXXXIII. On the field of the cloister, in which are grapes, roses, lilies, violets, and olives

“Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. 27). The field is the world, or any religious community. In these, grape, rose, lily, violet, and olive give forth fragrance. The grape is divine love, which, pressed in the winepress of tribulation, is stored in the storehouse of eternity and jubilation. The rose gives fragrance from the blood of martyrdom. The lily is white from the incorruption of virginity. [Col. 0685C] The violet holds the lowest place through humility, while holding the purple of the heavenly kingdom in its mind. The olive, after the manner of oil, refreshes and gives light through the work of mercy.

## TITLE LXXXIV. On the greenness of the reed and rush

“In it shall arise the greenness of reed and rush” (Isa. 35). One writes with a reed and with a rush. The first is the preacher; the second, the hearer. Both grow from the same water, because both doctrine and the hearer’s progress come from God. Their greenness of works is born in the Church from the water of wisdom which proceeds from the mouth of the Most High. Therefore it is the grace of the Holy Spirit which both opens the teacher’s mouth and inwardly inspires and illumines the hearer’s mind and progress.

## TITLE LXXXV. That man’s sweetness is worms

“The sweetness of man is a worm” (Job 24), namely, a worm of the earth. [Col. 0685D] Whoever in this world desires to surpass others in possessions and swell with honors, for such a one worldly care is delight and repose is labor. Therefore, since it is the nature of worms to move and gnaw at every moment, worms signify the restlessness of the mind and the wasting of thoughts, by which a person continually feeds and consumes himself.

Or flesh is signified by the name worm. Therefore, when it is said, “His sweetness is a worm,” the blindness of the luxurious, devoted to fleshly pleasures, is shown. For what is flesh but decay and worm? Whoever pants after carnal desires, what else does he love but a worm? Tombs testify what the substance of flesh is. Who could touch the flesh of even a much-loved parent when it teems with worms? [Col. 0686A] When flesh is desired, consider what it is when lifeless, and you will understand what is loved. It greatly helps to subdue desire if one who loves the living considers what it will become when dead.

## TITLE LXXXVI. Let oil not fail from the head

“Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccl. 9). Oil on the head is love in the mind; oil fails from the head when love departs from the mind. Therefore let us shear the head of its hairs, lest they cast away the oil—that is, let us remove from the mind evil thoughts, through which love is lost.

## TITLE LXXXVII. That each person should visit his own likeness

“By visiting your likeness you shall not sin” (Job 5). A person’s likeness is another person. Therefore whoever visits his own likeness approaches with the steps of love toward the person whom he sees as like himself by nature; and, considering his own condition in another, he gathers from himself how he should condescend to another in weakness. In order that he may restore another in himself, he weighs himself in the other. Hence Moses: “The earth brought forth a tree bearing seed according to its own kind” (Gen. 2). I mean the blessed earth before sins; for after the curse it produces thorns and thistles. [Col. 0686B]

## TITLE LXXXVIII. What it means that priests must not shave their heads, yet must not grow their hair

“Priests shall not shave their heads, nor grow their hair long, but shall cut it” (Ezek. 44). Priests are those who preside in order to provide sacred leadership. The hairs on the outer head are thoughts in the mind. Since they ought to have concerns for the lives of their subjects, yet not be excessively occupied with them, they are forbidden to shave the head or grow the hair: they must neither cut off those concerns completely nor let them grow again too freely. Let them grow as much as necessary, yet let them be quickly cut back lest they grow too excessively; let them remain on the priest’s head to cover the ears, but be cut so that they do not close the eyes. [Col. 0686C]

## TITLE LXXXIX. On the pierced and whole bag

“He who has gathered wages put them into a pierced bag” (Hag. 1), from which what is put in at one side goes out at another. A pierced bag is one who, while living blamelessly, carries hatred in the heart. Consider how clean in deed yet cruel in mind is one who loses through hatred the reward that he stores up by a good work: what enters through the opening of good work goes out through the hole of harm done to heavenly love.

You, I say, be a whole bag to preserve good things, and pierced and torn through the contrition of penitence to cast out evil things, so that you may be encompassed by joy. Hence: “You have cut apart my sackcloth and encompassed me with joy” (Ps. 29). [Col. 0686D]

## TITLE XC. The eyes of the wise person are in his head

“The eyes of the wise are in his head; the fool walks in darkness” (Eccl. 2). For the wise person fixes the eyes of the mind on Christ the head through imitation, whereas the fool, placing the effort of his intention in outward things rather than within himself, walks in darkness as though without light.

## TITLE XCI. On one who hides grain

“He who hides grain is cursed among the peoples” (Prov. 11). To hide grain is to keep the words of preaching to oneself. Such a person is cursed among the peoples because, in knowledge alone, he is condemned for the fault of the many whom he could not correct. Hence: “Cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. 48), that is, who withholds the words of preaching from the slaying of the carnal life. [Col. 0687A]

## TITLE XCII. On destroying a neighbor’s vices

“Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join himself to me. Let every man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbor” (Exod. 32). A neighbor is a person’s fellow human by the condition of common origin. He is also a friend by love and a brother in spirit or flesh. Whoever wishes to kill such persons when they sin, in their vices, with the sword of rebuke, must first put the sword upon his own thigh—that is, he must first strive to tame in himself unlawful suggestions; and then he must go from gate to gate, that is, run in rebuke from vice to vice through which death enters the mind, through the midst of the camp, with such impartiality that he turns toward no one’s hatred or favor in judging the fault of sinners. [Col. 0687B]

## TITLE XCIII. On destructive flattery

“Woe to those who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand and make pillows under the head of every age, to catch souls!” (Ezek. 13). Cushions and pillows are placed so that one may rest more comfortably. Whoever flatters those acting wickedly sews cushions under another’s head and hand. Hence again: “He was building a wall, and others were plastering it” (ibid.). The wall is the hardness of sin. The one who builds it erects against himself the obstacle of sin; the one who plasters it flatters the person committing sins. [Col. 0687C]

## TITLE XCIV. On contempt for riches

“When the rich man sleeps, he shall take nothing with him; he shall open his eyes and find nothing” (Job 27). For when the sinner sleeps in death, he sees and recognizes that what he saw in life was nothing, because he is snatched from life into death. Hence it follows: “The burning wind shall carry him away,” that is, the evil spirit, who draws the living toward vices and the dying toward torments. Here the love of concupiscence kindles him; there the flame of Gehenna tortures him. Here, by the wind and breath of evil suggestion, it kindles the hearts of the wicked toward earthly desires, as Jeremiah testifies: “I see a seething pot,” that is, a human heart boiling with the ardors of vices, “and its face is from the face [Col. 0687D] of the north” (Jer. 1). For they were inflamed by the suggestions of him who said: “I shall sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north” (Isa. 14).

From the heat of this burning one, the prophets promise that the righteous will be freed by the Lord at Christ’s coming. “Instead of the saltwort,” he says, “the fir tree shall grow; instead of the nettle, the myrtle shall grow” (Isa. 55). Instead of the casting aside of earthly thought, there shall be the height of earthly contemplation; and instead of the itching and burning of vices, there shall grow the moderation of virtues and the tranquility of mind. This desire is promised to Mary: “The power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1), although by this expression Christ’s incarnation is denoted. For shadow is formed from light through a body. In matter, the light of divinity received a body of humanity.

## TITLE XCV. That the righteous may flourish like a palm tree

[Col. 0688A]

The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree (Ps. 91). In three respects. For the palm grows slowly, but remains green for a long time; below, it is rough to the touch, wrapped in dry bark; above, it is beautiful to behold and fruitful. Other trees are broad near the ground and become slenderer above. The palm is slender from its lowest part, but grows broader toward its summit. Such is the righteous person. At first, he advances toward the state of faith, as it were slowly, amid many difficulties; but he endures longer in the glory of faith. Despised below beneath many barks of tribulation, above he is glorious in the fruit of recompense. And while the other trees—that is, evil people—are stronger below, enduring many labours for lower things, yet are weak above, since they grow weary after serving the Lord [Col. 0688B] for the brief span of a single hour, the palm alone—that is, the righteous alone—is stronger in heavenly things and weaker in earthly things. Thus, as much as others shine in earthly matters, so much do the righteous shine in heavenly ones, so that, just as they presented their members to serve iniquity, they may present those same members to serve righteousness (Rom. 6). They are not like the other trees, which set out stronger purposes at the beginning and end feebly as time increases. For the conversion of the righteous, like the palm, accomplishes more at its end than it proposed at its beginning.

### TITLE XCVI. On the threefold dwelling-place of God

“This is nothing other than the house of God” (Gen. 28). God dwells in three things: the world, the Church, and the faithful soul. He is in the world as an emperor is in his kingdom, through essence and power; [Col. 0688C] in the Church as a householder in his house, through present righteousness, because he is the one who justifies her. “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1). He creates, re-creates, and preserves in the soul through spiritual grace.

### TITLE XCVII. On the fire always burning upon the altar

“The fire shall always burn upon the altar; the priest shall feed it, placing wood upon it each day” (Lev. 6). For the fire always to burn upon the altar is for the flame of charity to be kindled unceasingly toward God. To lay on wood lest it fail is to supply, in the practice of charity, the examples of the Fathers who have gone before, as certain kindlings. For because, on earth, novelty itself grows old daily through the course of this life, the fire of charity must be nourished and revived by the aforesaid wood. [Col. 0688D] This is done in the morning, because charity is extinguished only in the night.

### TITLE XCVIII. On bread baked under ashes

“Ephraim has become bread baked under ashes, which is not turned” (Hos. 7). By his well-created nature, a person possesses an intention by which he may rise toward God. From intention comes a sincere delight that presses the world below. Bread baked under ashes is cleaner below, but bears ashes above. Therefore, one who neglects the intention by which he ought to seek God presses the cleaner part downward and, willingly bearing the care of the world, carries as it were a heap of ashes above. But it is turned if, casting off the ashes of desires, he reveals above the good intention which he had been suppressing.

### TITLE XCIX. On the comparison of the sentence of the supreme judgment to a woman in labour

[Col. 0689A]

“I shall speak like a woman in labour” (Isa. 42). A woman in labour painfully brings forth what she has long carried, with weight, in hidden places. So God, who now silently endures within himself, makes manifest in the vengeance of judgment, as it were with prolonged pain after silence.

### TITLE C. Going down into hell with weapons

“They go down into hell with their weapons” (Ezek. 32). The weapons of sinners are the bodily members by which they carry out the perverse desires they conceive; with these they endure eternal torments with their prince, the devil. Hence: “There is Asshur and all his multitude; his graves are round about him” (ibid.). Asshur is the devil; his multitude is the angelic spirits whom he drew [Col. 0689B] into sin. He suffered death when he abandoned the life of his Creator. Their hearts are, as it were, the graves of this dead one, for they bury him within themselves through evil desires. They will be around him, because then graves with the dead will burn, where there is fire that is darkened, death without death, end without end, failure without failure: fire grows dark, death lives, the end always begins, and failure does not know how to fail.

### TITLE CI. By iron a hard but transitory punishment, by bronze an eternal one, is signified

“He shall flee from weapons of iron and fall upon a bow of bronze” (Job 20). Since the necessity of poverty torments life with the wound of sorrow, it is denoted by iron. Hence of Joseph when sold: “Iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104). Brotherly judgment, to which the mind of the greedy person does not [Col. 0689C] attend, is suggested by the bow. Therefore, if amid these iron weapons he does not enjoy necessity, but, fleeing it, seizes much through avarice, the bow of final and hidden judgment strikes him more severely. Note that it is called bronze, more durable than iron, because the punishment he flees is temporary, whereas that which he incurs is eternal.

### TITLE CII. The necessities of this life are not to be abhorred

“You shall not abhor an Egyptian or an Edomite” (Deut. 22): that is, although the Egyptian things—namely, one’s former manner of life—must be left behind, by not thinking of superfluities, they are nevertheless not altogether to be abhorred, so that we should not think even of necessities.

### TITLE CIII. Let us measure ourselves and our neighbours by one balance

“You shall not have a greater and a lesser weight” (Deut. 25), so that you measure one way for yourself and another for your neighbour, imposing [Col. 0689D] burdens that you would not wish to move even with a finger.

### TITLE CIV. Disputing from the cedar to the hyssop

“Solomon discoursed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that comes forth from the wall” (3 Kings 4). Solomon is Christ. By the cedar is understood the loftiness of glory in the elect; by the hyssop, a lowly herb clinging to the rock, the humility of Christ. Solomon discoursed from the cedar to the hyssop when Christ, descending from the lofty glory of heaven to the humility of the flesh, came thus far. The cedar also signifies the pride of the wicked. Hence: “The voice of the Lord breaking cedars” (Ps. 28). Therefore Christ disputes from the cedar to the hyssop because he judges the proud and the humble. [Col. 0690A] He disputes concerning trees because, hanging upon the cross, he cries out as the beetle from the wood; and then he brought the pride of the cedars down to humility, when he bent them toward the humility of the cross and its folly through the contemptible preaching of faith: “For the word of the cross is folly to those who perish, but to believers it is the power of God unto salvation” (1 Cor. 1).

### TITLE CV. On Elijah’s concealment at Cherith

“Elijah was hidden at the brook Cherith” (3 Kings 17), which is interpreted “bald”; and there he drank from the brook, while a raven fed him morning and evening with bread and flesh. Elijah, whose name is interpreted “God is strong,” is Christ, who, in the place of Calvary, where his glory was hidden, drank from the torrent of our immortality. He is fed morning and evening—that is, from the beginning of grace until the end of the world—by the raven, that is, by the human race blackened by sins, with the bread of faith and the flesh of resurrection. For the raven, as it were, offers flesh and bread to Christ, who thirsts for our salvation, when the sinner orders his life through faith and offers to God in sacrifice flesh subdued through penitence, in the hope of resurrection.

### TITLE CVI. On the threefold spirit that Elisha asked from Elijah, and on Christ’s generosity

When Elijah said, “Ask what you wish” (4 Kings 3), Elisha answered: “I pray, let your spirit be double in me” (ibid.). Elijah signifies the head; Elisha, the body, which is the Church. Our Elijah makes room for the petitioner when he says: “Ask, and you shall receive” (Luke 11). With this confidence Elisha—that is, the Christian—asks that his spirit may become double in the acquisition of virtues and the remission of sins. The spirit conferring these things was single in Christ, [Col. 0690C] who had no sins and therefore did not require remission of sins. Yet he performed works of virtue in the Spirit. Rightly, therefore, does the Church ask for a double spirit, because she needs both remission of sins, which Christ did not need, and the bestowal of virtues, which Christ grants from his fullness to one who places his hope in him.

Hence Elijah says to Elisha: “If you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so; if not, it shall not be” (4 Kings 2). For unless a person fixes the eyes of faith upon him, believing in the resurrection, ascension, and the other things to be believed, he will not receive the fruit of his petition. Elijah struck the river with his cloak because Christ, through the incarnation with which he clothed himself as with a garment, destroyed the river of our mortality; he himself crossed over and gave us passage [Col. 0690D] into life. But Elisha struck the river with the same cloak, and it was not divided. Then he said: “Where now is the God of Elijah?” (ibid.), and then it was divided, because the Church can perform no virtues except through the invocation of Christ, as he himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). For human effort can do nothing unless divine help is present.

### TITLE CVII. What it means to be eaten by dogs and birds

“Those of Jeroboam who die in the city, dogs shall eat; those who die in the field, birds of heaven shall devour” (3 Kings 14). For even one who is weak in faith and is situated in the Church, if he dies in mortal sins, is rebuked, accused, and condemned by the dogs that have surrounded the city—that is, by the judgments of the saints. These are those who cast unbelievers and thieves outside, drive them away, and [Col. 0691A] guard the holy sheepfolds. But one who dies in vices outside the churches is devoured by those birds that eat the seed scattered beside the way; that is, laden with sins, they take him with themselves, incorporated into them, to eternal destruction.

### TITLE CVIII. On the widow’s son raised by Elisha

Elisha takes from her bosom to the upper room the son of the widow, who had fallen ill and died in her bosom, in order to raise him, and lays him upon a bed; there, measuring himself over him three times with his body, he raises him through prayer (4 Kings 4). The son dies in his mother’s bosom when the spirit dies in the pleasure of a wicked manner of life. Thus Samson too is blinded in his wife’s bosom. For him to live, he is first removed from his vain way of life, because evil must first be abandoned. Then he was carried to the upper room [Col. 0691B] of the Church—that is, the monastery—where God dwells. There, laid upon the bed of contemplation, he perceives God as lying over him three times, when in mind, speech, and deed he receives God, thinking, saying, and doing nothing except what belongs to God. Thus he may now live in virtues and rest, not in the field or in the mill, but in the bed of that peace which begins here and is consummated in the future.

Likewise, it should be known that this widow signifies the soul, of whom it is said: “He fed the barren woman and did not do good to the widow” (Job 24). This means nourishing the flesh, barren of the fruit of good work, and making no provision for the soul, whose husband, Christ, is dead. The bosom of this widow is the flesh; the son is the work. He dies in the bosom, that is, in the pleasure of the flesh, but Elijah raises him in the manner described above.

### TITLE CIX. On the mystery of the altar built by Elijah and his actions around it

[Col. 0691C]

Elijah built an altar of twelve stones. Around the altar he made a water-channel, as it were of two little furrows [*arenuculas*, perhaps *aratiunculas*, “small plough-furrows”] (3 Kings 18). He places wood beneath; he divides the ox upon the wood; and first, second, and third, he has water poured over it, until the channel around the altar is filled. The altar is the faithful, or any congregation of those who follow the faith of the twelve apostles. The water-channel of two little furrows [*arenucularum*, perhaps *aratiuncularum*] is the streams of tears from a contrite heart, arising from fear of Gehenna and desire for eternal life. Upon the altar are arranged the wood—that is, the sayings and deeds of the saints, offered as an example to believers. The ox is also placed upon it, that is, Christ, who is set above all his acts as an example. [Col. 0691D] Water is poured three times over both, when a person imitates Christ and the saints, and the water of compunction cleanses words, thoughts, and deeds; nor does it cease until the first and second ditch—that is, through present death and future joy—is filled. Then God’s fire devours the burnt offerings and the wood, when, examining sayings and deeds, he receives the person into eternal life.

Let us therefore examine, brothers, whether we are at God’s altar by following apostolic teaching. Let us have around us both fear of Gehenna and desire for our homeland, like two ditches, so that, pierced by compunction, we may abstain from evil through fear of punishment and do good through love of our homeland. Let us set before ourselves the examples of the saints, like wood by which we are pressed lest we [Col. 0692A] go beyond bounds, and at last imitate the acts and words of Christ himself. Let us cleanse first our thoughts, then our words, and afterward our deeds with the water of penitence, so that we may deserve to be taken up by the divine fire, which burns by consuming vices and gives light by bestowing eternal brightness. After such a sacrifice, rain of divine grace follows upon Elijah’s prayer over the earth, which had been dry for three years and six months, the length of time Christ preached, when through evangelical preaching we are dissolved into tears of compunction and desires for eternal consolation.

### TITLE CX. On the incarnation of the Word, figured by the new vessel into which Elisha put salt

The waters of Jericho were very bad and the land barren. Therefore, when asked to heal them, Elisha put salt into a new earthen vessel [Col. 0692B] and cast it into the stream; and the bad waters and barren land were healed (4 Kings 2). Jericho signifies evil peoples, dry and barren of the fruit of good work. The new earthen vessel is either the holy Virgin, a new vessel through virginity and earthen because terrestrial; or it is the flesh of Christ, new flesh, created without sin by a new generation—that is, from a mother without a father. It is the fourth and new generation, and earthen because mortal. Salt is wisdom, namely the Word of the Father. When this salt is sent by God the Father into the new vessel—that is, into the womb of the Virgin, or into flesh assumed from the Virgin, where divinity lay hidden as in a vessel—the waters are healed: that is, the nations that received the vessel in which is salt, namely Christ in whom is divinity. For salt is in the vessel as divinity is [Col. 0692C] in the flesh. The vessel containing salt in the water is Christ, God and man, among the nations.

Likewise within us are vices and sins, bitter waters that make our land—that is, our soul—barren and sink it into the depths of hell. Therefore, for our waters, namely our works, to be healed, and for the land to become fit for the fruit of life, let us put off the old person with his deeds; and, having put on the new and become a new vessel cleansed from vices, let us receive the salt of true wisdom, by which we were made, and be preserved uncorrupted in the new person, who does not die.

### TITLE CXI. On the duty of prelates to shoot at and destroy vices

When the king of Israel held the bow, Elisha placed [Col. 0692D] his hands upon the king’s hands and commanded him to shoot an arrow through the eastern window; and when he had shot it, he said: “The arrow of the Lord’s salvation against the Assyrians” (4 Kings 13). In King Joash, who held the office of governing the people, are signified those who hold the office of governing souls. They take up the bow and shoot arrows—that is, they bring forth Scripture, the judgments of Scripture, and words—to wound souls in vices against the devil. For in the bow, the hardness of the Old Testament, from horn, is stretched by the string of the New and bent toward spiritual understanding, and directs arrows of salvation against the ancient enemy. Hence it is said of holy teachers entering the Gentile world: “They shall enter there with arrows and a bow” (Isa. 7). When we weigh the sayings of Holy Scripture, we stretch the bow; when we give words of teaching, [Col. 0693A] we release arrows. That this may be done, Elisha places his hands upon the hands of the king, because by his examples and grace the Lord directs and protects the actions of rulers.

It should be noted that the arrow of salvation—that is, holy preaching—is commanded to be shot through the eastern window, because those who must send forth the darts of words ought first to receive the light of knowledge and teaching. Again he commands him to strike the ground with the arrow. When he had done so three times and stopped, Elisha was angry with him because he had not struck five, six, or seven times. For carnal persons must not only be instructed in faith in the Trinity, but also taught to rule their five senses, to render the fruit of good works expressed by the number six, and to meditate upon the knowledge of the sevenfold Spirit. For faith without these [Col. 0693B] is dead (Jas. 2).

### TITLE CXII. On showing the virtue of patience through adversities, and its comparison to a mustard seed

Ointments, unless stirred, and spices, unless burned or ground, do not know how to diffuse their fragrance more widely. So saints, fragrant with virtues, become known through tribulations. Hence their faith is compared to a mustard seed, which does not know how to display its power unless crushed. Therefore, if you are moved by adversities, if you are inflamed by tribulations, then you show outwardly in works what warmth of charity you bore and savoured inwardly. For if our faith is like a mustard seed, and you say to the mountain, “Move yourself,” it shall be moved (Matt. 17).

### TITLE CXIII. On the twofold peace

There is peace begun, and there is peace complete. Truth gave the begun peace to the disciples, saying: “I give you my peace” (John 14); Simeon sought the complete peace: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2). The first is freedom from vices, not from punishments; the second, freedom both from vices and from punishments. Peace, therefore, begins through desire for the Creator and is perfected through his manifest vision.

### TITLE CXIV. On the sinner’s capture and blinding

The king of Babylon killed the sons of King Zedekiah before his eyes, and afterward put out his eyes so that he might go down to Babylon and not see Babylon (4 Kings 25). So the devil kills good works, which are the offspring of the one who works, so that the captive person may see and grieve that he is losing them. Yet, overcome by the pleasure of sin, he willingly and knowingly loses the good things he had produced, like one bereft of mind. But when he is struck while seeing, lest he raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon, he loses his eyes immediately after all his sons have been killed. Thus, with the very intelligence of light taken away, he no longer sees, in the Babylon of vices, even his own confusion.

### TITLE CXV. On hypocrisy and the simulation of virtue

“You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen” (Deut. 22). Wool is innocence; linen, subtlety. The garment of malice conceals linen within and displays wool without. Therefore, one wears a garment of wool and linen who hides within the subtlety of malice and shows outwardly the simplicity of innocence.

### TITLE CXVI. On avoiding murmuring and preserving concord, especially in cloisters

“The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel” (Ecclus. 33). A cart carries hay and creaks, as do brothers who dwell together in body alone—though it is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together as one—like the ointment of unity that is upon the head, Christ, and descends as far as the beard, that is, to the greater and stronger persons. This beard is indeed Aaron’s, that is, Christ the true priest. When he found no other worthy victim, he offered himself, becoming both victim and priest. From the beard it comes down to the hem of the garment. The garment is the Church, stretched upon the cross, so that it may have neither the stain of sin nor the wrinkle of duplicity. The hem is understood as the end or perfection. It descends therefore to the hem (Ps. 132), because the Church bore monasteries. Through this hem the head enters, because Christ enters through brotherly charity.

### TITLE CXVII. On the comparison of the Church to a vine

[Col. 0694B] A vine, in imitation of our life, fastens its root, is weighed down by its shoot, raises itself by clasping with its arms whatever it encompasses; some of its branches are cut off, while others are tied lest they bend back. So the Church takes root, takes root in faith, and is weighed down by the shoot of flesh. This is the woman bent by illness who cannot look upward (Luke 13). But Jesus looked upon her and arranged her earthly burdens, so that she might raise herself upward with the arms of charity, embrace her neighbours through charity, and, lifting herself to the top of the tree, bring herself into heaven. The barren growths of vices are cut away; the rest are bound with precepts and examples.

### TITLE CXVIII. On Noah and Christ mocked by his own people

“Noah planted a vineyard” (Gen. 9). Christ planted the Jewish people. For “the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel.” He drank its wine in the cup of death. Drunk with such a cup, he fell asleep, because he gave up the spirit. Ham—that is, the Jewish people—saw this in mockery: namely, that we adore as God one who died by the disgrace of the cross, so shamefully crucified. This is still cast in our teeth today. But the two faithful brothers, Greek and Latin, cover this disgrace with the testimonies of the prophets. When Noah awoke—that is, when Christ rose from the dead—he cursed the former and blessed the latter.

### TITLE CXIX. On Christ and his faith, prefigured in David by the slaughter of Goliath and his weapons

Goliath is the devil; David is Christ; pride challenged humility. Against Goliath David—that is, Christ—is clothed with weapons (1 Kings 17), namely [Col. 0694D] circumcision, the figures of the temple, and manifold sacrifices. But because these were pressing weapons, not helping ones, they are laid aside. Five stones are taken up. The law is laid aside and the law is taken up. The figurative law is laid aside; the reality figured is received. What concealed is abandoned, for at the Lord’s death the veil of the temple was torn (Matt. 27), and what had been veiled is received. Five stones—that is, the books—from the stream of the former people are taken up, where they had always lain idle and useless; the stream passed them by in transgression. They are put into the shepherd’s bag, that is, into the fold of Christ the good shepherd, where the sheep abound in the milk of grace; for without grace the law could neither be understood nor fulfilled. Mother Church labours to give this milk, but the unbeliever does not seek to receive it; she grieves if [Col. 0695A] she finds none to whom to give it. Armed with the five stones of the torrent of grace, he struck him down with one, because the five books have been opened, but in them the unity of charity conquers. For many sick people lay in the five porticoes, but one was healed. For unless charity, from which come the law and the prophets, prevails, it cannot conquer.

Then he cut off his head with his own sword. The sword of the devil consists of evil people, namely his members, by whom he fights against God and God’s members. Our David draws this sword out of the devil’s sheath when Christ tears his members from the power of the wicked. But through it he cuts off the devil’s head when, through the preaching of the Gospel, he drives the devil himself out from his own members.

### TITLE CXX. On the bush Moses saw that was not consumed

[Col. 0695B] When God sent Moses to a people whom he foreknew would never burn with the fire of charity, he showed him a flame in a bush, by which the bush was not consumed. The flame in the bush is the law in that people full of the thorns of sins. The bush was not consumed because their sins were not consumed by the word of God. The flame inflaming but not consuming the bush is persecution purifying but not consuming the Church. In it God speaks only to Moses—that is, only to believers—and one is forbidden to approach it unless he first takes the sandals from his feet, that is, unless he first casts away vices from his affections. With these, as with feet, one goes either toward the good of ardour or toward evil.

And you, O human being, are a bush conceived and born—a bush conceived and born in vices and sins—daily bringing forth the thorns of vices, [Col. 0695C] however much you may advance, since not even a child of one day is without sin. But let the flame of God’s word arise in you, so that it may redden within you and consume the thorns of sin. Do not be a bush that is not consumed. For there is one good bush and another bad bush; each has a flame. Both the good and the bad receive God’s word with the ear of the body, but the evil one does not at all consume evil within his wickedness. There is likewise a flame of persecution in both the good and bad bush. It consumes the bad bush, which falls away in the time of temptation. The good bush is not consumed but purified, and through tribulations it becomes known what it proves to be. For a furnace burns wood but purifies gold: tribulation makes the good purer and reveals the bad as worse.

If you wish to approach the bush of virtue through imitation, take the sandal from your foot (Exod. 3). [Col. 0695D] But there is one sandal which the person approaching takes off in order to hear and heed God speaking in the bush; another, which the departing person takes off when he fails to heed the neighbour who urges him to raise up his brother’s seed. The first is the vices that one abandons when approaching the righteous and holy; the second is the office of preaching that one loses by abandoning care for one’s neighbour. There is also a third sandal, with which Christ came into the world: the dispensation of his incarnation. Therefore prepare yourself with every effort to abandon the first sandal; strive with every care to bring forth the second; and judge yourself unworthy with John to loosen the strap of the third (Mark 1; Luke 3), so that you may lay aside vices, care for your neighbour, and not dare rashly to scrutinize the mystery [Col. 0696A] of Christ’s incarnation.

### TITLE CXXI. On Solomon’s litter

“King Solomon made himself a litter of the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold, its ascent of purple. He paved its midst with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3). Solomon is Christ, our peace, who made both one. The litter is the Church, or any congregation of saints, carrying souls to the eternal banquet. The silver columns are those who, by strength of work, support others by example and illuminate them by the light of preaching. The golden backrest is the splendour of eternal blessedness, in which one reclines and rests from every labour. The ascent is purple because one comes to the brightness of that rest only through tribulation [Col. 0696B].

What then shall we miserable people do? In this world we cannot be columns, since neither strength of work nor the light of preaching shines in us. We do not possess the golden backrest, because we do not yet behold the spiritual king in the mind. We are not the purple ascent, because we cannot shed our blood for Christ. Yet there is sure consolation for these things: let us love God, let us love our neighbour, and together we shall reach God’s litter, because it is written: “He paved its midst with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem.” For by the feminine sex divine speech called weak persons in mind. Therefore charity is said to be in the midst, between the silver columns, the golden backrest, and the purple ascent, because if you possess charity, you will undoubtedly reach the place where the column [Col. 0696C] is raised, the purple ascent held, and the golden backrest found.

Hence in the prophet: “Between the chambers are five cubits” (Ezek. 40), because among the perfect are lesser persons, who, still weighed down by the five bodily senses, are compelled to think something of the world. Thus our king made a litter for himself because he gathered the Church, out of the woods of Lebanon, which are cedar wood—that is, out of strong fathers, incorruptible in mind—and made it for himself, because it was for glorifying himself.

### TITLE CXXII. On changing priestly clothing

For the order of priests, it is very necessary to change one’s disposition according to the persons who come. Hence it is said through the prophet that, when the priest ministers within, [Col. 0696D] he should use linen garments (Ezek. 44); but, when he goes out to the people, these should be put away in the treasury of the sanctuary (ibid.). For when a priest goes within, he should employ the more subtle works of contemplation, as if wearing a linen garment. But when he goes out to the people, he should employ coarser things, because for their benefit he must also adapt his conduct to bearing earthly matters.

### TITLE CXXIII. Why bells formerly hung on the priest’s garment, and pomegranates among them

Bells are attached to the priest’s garments, lest he die if the sound of him entering and leaving is not heard (Exod. 28). For the priest’s works must proclaim the way of life with the sound of preaching, both to those who within have hope in a stricter life [Col. 0697A] and to those who are outside in secular dress, lest he die by provoking God’s wrath against himself. Pomegranates are also joined to the bells. In the pomegranate, in which many seeds are contained beneath one outer rind, is signified the unity of faith, because the unity of faith outwardly covers so many in the Church while diversity of merits is retained within. Therefore, that words may be joined to works, bells are attached to the garments; and, so that through all they say they may preserve this unity, pomegranates are joined to the bells.

### TITLE CXXIV. On spiritual and natural water

Spiritual water serves the person who from day to day is renewed by the spirit of the mind. Water is used for washing, drinking, and cooking food; and so spiritual water both cleanses the unclean from the filth of sins [Col. 0697B] and becomes, for the thirsty, a fountain of water springing up into eternal life, which whoever drinks shall never thirst (John 4). Divine utterance also cooks the foods of the mind with the fire of the Holy Spirit and transforms them into spiritual senses.

### TITLE CXXV. On the mystical queens, concubines, and young women of the true Solomon

The true Solomon has many queens, many concubines, and young women without number (Song 6). For there are many dwelling-places with the bridegroom: one holds the place of queen, another of concubine, another of young woman; and each receives a rank according to merits, insofar as, advancing, she is permitted to enter into the joy of her Lord and search out the sweet secrets of the bridegroom.
