For the contrite woman found a place at the feet; the righteous one at the head; the devout one [Col. 0697C] in the whole body. Thomas attained grace in the side of faith, John in the breast of abundant charity, Peter in the bosom of the Father—that is, in the light of truth—and Paul in the third heaven, that is, in the innermost secret of wisdom.

The sinful person, lying in misery and the mire of dregs, weeps and cries out in supplication to his Maker and Saviour: “Deliver me from the mire of dregs” (Ps. 68). And because he had rotted in the dung of his sins, he says, in order that he may be raised up to be washed, and that, while being washed, he may not fall and be defiled: “Set me upon my feet.” These feet are faith and action. With these, the one who has been washed walks, stands, and is raised up. Know that these three things are necessary for you, whoever you are who desire to be converted and return to God: namely, that you may walk, stand, and be raised up. The first you owe to your neighbour, the second to yourself, the third to God. You must walk [Col. 0697D] in order to help your neighbour; you must stand in the temple lest you fall back into the mire from which you were delivered; and at last you must be raised into heaven, from which you were cast out. Your neighbour must be taught: this is to walk, to make a passage from oneself to another, not only by word but also by example; so that you do not neglect to do what you have taught, which is to stand—not to depart from care of yourself—so that through this, thirdly, you may be raised into heaven: that is, ascend to God as the reward of merits. Hence the holy living creatures are read to walk, stand, and be raised up; and the wheels are likewise read to follow them (Ezek. 1).

### TITLE CXXVI. Jacob wrestling with the angel

When Jacob was returning to his parents, he wrestled with an angel on the way; and while he held the angel, he himself was held and touched in the thigh [Col. 0698A] and became lame (Gen. 32). Our parents are the holy angels and holy persons established in life and in the heavenly homeland. The angel is God; Jacob is any righteous person journeying from this exile toward the homeland of his parents. On this way he wrestles with the angel because, while he strives to contemplate God, he is placed as it were in a contest: in the manner of combatants, at one moment he overcomes when he tastes something of God by understanding it; at another he yields, when, unable to penetrate the unbounded light, he fails as one who had ventured too rashly. The angel is conquered when God is grasped by inward understanding; yet, conquered, he makes the conqueror lame in one foot.

One foot is love of God; the other, love of the world. Therefore, one who had formerly walked on two feet, while seeming to seek God and yet holding the world, when he grasps the angel becomes lame in one foot: because after the sweetness of divine knowledge, the strength of love for God increases in a person, while the strength of love for the flesh weakens. One remains sound, the other lame, because, when love of the world has been weakened, love of God alone grows strong. He stands on this one alone because he carries suspended from the ground the foot of love of the world which he had been accustomed to place upon the earth. And if we wish to return to our homeland, let us grasp the angel on the way by apprehending God, so that, with the foot of worldly love raised from the earth, we may be led by the one foot of love for God. This does not happen unless the proud king is killed. Hence Isaiah says: “In the year in which Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a lofty and exalted throne” (Isa. 6); and the house was full of his majesty, etc.; because, when the devil is killed out of the desire of the mind, the mind contemplates God’s glory.

### TITLE CXXVII. Doing penance in ashes and sackcloth

[Col. 0698C]

“They would have done penance in ashes and sackcloth” (Matt. 12). Sackcloth signifies the harshness and pricking of sin; ashes, the dust of the dead. Both are customarily employed in penitence, so that in the pricking of sackcloth we may recognize what we have done through fault, and in ashes what we shall become through judgment. Let us consider in sackcloth the piercing incitements of vices; in ashes, the punishment that follows. In the harshness of sackcloth let a person see what he did through pride; in ashes, what he came to through sinning.

### TITLE CXXVIII. On the arising and defence of evil thoughts and sins

[Col. 0698D] “Thorns and nettles shall arise in his houses, and brambles in his strongholds,” etc. (Isa. 34). Nettles are the itching of thoughts; thorns, the pricking of sin. Therefore in the house of Babylon arise both the desires of thoughts that irritate and human sins that pierce; but those who do these things have more wicked defenders. Hence it adds: “Brambles in his strongholds.” The bramble grows so thick with a surrounding mass of thorns that it can scarcely be touched because of its harshness. Thus nettles and thorns grow within, but both are fortified outwardly by brambles, because lesser evildoers commit wicked acts, while the very wicked among their superiors protect them. Hence Job says: “The shadows protect his shadow” (Job 40), because sinners protect others in that in which they themselves are confederates.

### TITLE CXXIX. On the threefold kiss

[Col. 0699A]

There are three kisses: at the feet, at the hands, and at the mouth. The feet are mercy and judgment. From mercy comes hope; from judgment fear is born. This fear claims the beginning, hope the advance, and charity the completion. If you are pierced with compunction through fear of judgment, you have pressed your lips to the foot of judgment; if you have tempered fear with hope in mercy, you have embraced the foot of mercy. At times it is not expedient to kiss one without the other, because remembrance of judgment alone is despair, while remembrance of mercy alone produces empty security. The hands are generosity and strength, because God gives abundantly and powerfully protects what he has given. The person who is not ungrateful kisses both, acknowledging God as giver and preserver. But the mouth is divinity itself: [Col. 0699B] for the head of Christ is God. He kisses this mouth to whom the eternal vision and knowledge of the Trinity are granted.

In the first kiss we offer the repentance of a contrite and humbled heart, and receive remission of sins, when we hear: “Many sins are forgiven you.” In the second we offer, with thanksgiving, fruits of repentance worthy of it, and receive perseverance in good works; and it is said: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV). In the third we present completion and receive glory, [Col. 0700A] and hear: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. XXXIII). By this kiss the Son kisses the Father, because “No one knows the Father except the Son” (John X). “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV). The kiss of the Holy Spirit has been given to us, because, as the Apostle says, “God has also revealed [it] to us through the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. II). Upon those to whom he reveals, he shines and kindles: he shines for knowledge and kindles for love. For “charity has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (Rom. V), who, like a bee bringing wax and honey, kindles in us the light of knowledge and pours in the sweetness of grace.

## TIT. CXXX. On the Praise and Usefulness of Psalmody

When the spirit of prophecy was lacking to Elisha, he ordered a psalmist to be brought to him, so that through the praise of psalmody [Col. 0700B] the spirit of prophecy might descend upon him (IV Kings III). When the voice of psalmody is directed to almighty God through the attention of the heart, a path is prepared to the heart, so that the grace either of prophecy or of compunction may be poured into the attentive mind. Hence: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me, and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIII). Therefore, in the sacrifice of praise a path is made for the manifestation of Jesus. For Jesus is called Savior. Thus in psalmody grace from heaven is always poured into the devout mind.

# BOOK FOUR. SERMONS, FRAGMENTS OF SERMONS, LETTERS, ETC.

[Col. 0699]

## TIT. I. On the Annunciation and Incarnation of the Word; on the Spiritual Paradise and What Is in It

[Col. 0699C]

“Return, virgin Israel; return to your cities. How long will you be dissolved in pleasures, wandering daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI). As though he said: “The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. XXXII), because “truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV). Christ was born from the Virgin Mary. The earth, formerly cursed through the sins of the first man, is now blessed through the grace of the second man, and will finally be blessed in the glory of God the Father. Hence: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land” (ibid.). Formerly it brought forth thorns and thistles; today, because “the Lord has given goodness, our earth has given its fruit” (Ps. LXVI).

O how great is the kindness that the sent Gabriel said to the Virgin: [Col. 0699D] “Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke I). And Elizabeth: “Blessed is the fruit of your womb” (ibid.). Truly the Lord gave the great kindness of the angelic salutation and divine blessing, because likewise our earth gave its fruit: that is, Mary brought forth Christ her Son, no longer, as before, thorns and thistles, as it is written that God said to disobedient Adam: “Because you have obeyed the voice of your wife more than mine, cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III). “When you cultivate it, it shall not [Col. 0700C] give you its fruit, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you.”

Even to this day Adam obeys the voice of his wife. The earth is cursed and brings forth thorns and thistles. Every person has beside himself and within himself, in paradise, the serpent, Eve, Adam, the earth, the paradise of God, and the rest. Paradise is any community; the serpent is the devil; Eve’s voice is the delight of the flesh; Adam is the spirit. The earth is the flesh itself. At the serpent’s suggestion Adam obeys the voice of his wife when, through the devil’s prompting, the spirit consents to the delight of its flesh. Then the earth of our flesh is cursed and brings forth not the fruit of eternal life, the fruit of everlasting glory, but the thorns of sins and the thistles of punishments.

There are two kinds of thorns: one of the flesh, the other of the spirit. The thorns of the flesh are sins performed and enacted through the flesh, such as lust and gluttony. The thorns of the spirit are vices committed through the spirit, such as anger and envy. These are the thorns which, according to the Prophet, produce the buckthorn (*rhamnus*) (Ps. LVII). From these thorns are received the fruits of life; but there are two thistles of punishment. One thistle is the fire overcoming the flesh, which is never extinguished; the second thistle is the worm gnawing the soul, which never dies.

Therefore, brothers, we must be greatly afraid lest perhaps the serpent which goes about in the paradise of the community [Col. 0701A] seeking whom it may devour should so deceive our Eve that Adam obeys the voice of his wife; that is, lest our spirit consent to the delight of our flesh, making provision for the flesh in its desires. For Eve cries daily within us to Adam; if he consents, the earth is cursed and brings forth the thorns of sins and the thistles of punishments. Therefore, before our thorns produce buckthorn, let us search out our way, lest through a path of thorns we generate for ourselves thistles of punishment; and let us return to the Lord, who calls us back through the prophet when he says: “Return, virgin Israel.”

A virgin is a soul created pure and whole by God. But of virgins, one is prudent and another foolish: the foolish one, who having received lamps did not take oil with her; the prudent one, who took oil in her vessels together with her lamps (Matt. [Col. 0701B] XXV). The lamp is the flesh, which both the prudent and foolish virgin received. But the prudent one took oil in her lamp—that is, mercy. For as oil excels other liquids, so mercy excels other works of charity.

Every person must first anoint himself with this threefold mercy, and then his neighbor. First let him anoint himself threefold by having mercy on his own soul: through contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed. Of this mercy, to be applied first to oneself, it is said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Ecclus. XXX). Toward one’s neighbor it consists in forgiving him if he has injured one; teaching him if he has sinned; and supplying necessities if he is in need. The foolish virgin does not take this threefold oil of mercy for herself and her neighbor; and so, when she comes and knocks, [Col. 0701C] she will be shut out and thrust into outer darkness.

Therefore the Lord, the door of life, calls her back from her crooked way, saying: “Return, return, virgin Israel.” As though he said: O foolish virgin, if you wish to be a wise virgin, be a virgin of Israel—that is, one who sees God; for that is the interpretation of Israel. Return, and return again: for he calls her back in two ways, first from evil to good, from vices to virtues; second, from good to reward. The evil from which he calls her back is the place of misery and the mire of filth, in which the sinful human being, lying down, ought to weep and pray.

Let everyone who belongs to the Lord therefore walk by teaching his neighbor, stand by correcting himself, and be raised up by awaiting and receiving from God the reward of his works. Hence the holy living creatures following the wheels are read in Ezekiel to have walked, stood, [Col. 0701D] and been lifted up (Ezek. I), because holy teachers, following the wheels—that is, the holy Scriptures—walk in teaching, stand in chastising themselves, and are lifted up in striving toward God. With these spiritual feet, therefore, dearest brothers, let each of us return to God, as he himself calls us to him: “Return, return,” etc.

First, let us return from Egypt to the desert, that there in the way of three days we may sacrifice to our God; second, that from the desert we may return to the promised land. We have now left the Egypt of this world and have reached the desert of the monastic profession. For the cloister is solitude and desert, where we have renounced not only our possessions but even ourselves. In it let us take every care that we do not return in mind to Egypt [Col. 0702A] and long for the fleshpots of Egypt. Let us know, however, that we must proceed to the land of the living not by the broad way leading to death, but by the narrow way leading to life.

Hence the Lord commands the children of Israel: “You shall pass through the land of Sihon king of the Amorites,” and the other matters said above, as far as the king, the devil, who seeks to shut us up in the three cities situated on this side and beyond Jordan, while we are making for the land of milk and honey. Let us return. For this is what follows: “Return,” etc. Where? “To your cities,” he says (Jer. XXXI).

There are three spiritual cities to which we are called back. The first is the mind; the second, the earthly Church; the third, the heavenly city. Into the city of the mind virtues are gathered; into the city of the Church good and evil persons are gathered; into the heavenly city only the good are received. In each, particular goods are given. In the first, faith, hope, and charity, to the good alone. In the second, sacraments such as baptism, to good and evil alike. In the third, glory to the blessed alone.

Of the first it is said: “In the morning I slew all the sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (Ps. C): that is, that I might destroy from the mind all unclean spirits which work vices and sins in it. Of the second: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly praiseworthy in the city of our God,” etc. (Ps. XLVII). This is the Church established upon the holy mountain, in which the Lord is great in forgiving sins, exceedingly praiseworthy in promising rewards. Of the heavenly city it is said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI). This is the city [Col. 0702C] of which truly glorious things are spoken and in which they are given, because “what eye has not seen,” etc. (I Cor. II): where there is light without cloud, life without end, fullness without disgust, glory without limit. O how glorious it is to be present in the choirs of angels, the companies of patriarchs, the senate of apostles, the troops of martyrs, and the fellowships of confessors and virgins, and with them to reign while praising God!

Therefore, that we may reach this city, let us now return to the city of the mind and of the Church. But because it is “not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. IX), the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth. As though he said: “Return, virgin Israel,” because, to help you, God the Father caused his Son to be incarnate, he who created a new thing upon the earth. What is this new thing? “A woman shall encompass a man.” The Virgin Mary shall conceive Christ in [Col. 0702D] her womb. Truly this is new, begotten by a new generation.

Three other generations preceded it; for there are four. The first, without father and mother; the second, from a father and without a mother; the third, from father and mother; the fourth, from a mother without a father. By the first generation Adam came into the world; by the second Eve was brought forth; by the third a human being is born; the fourth is unheard-of and new. For Christ came into the world, was born, and redeemed the world. Great indeed is the new thing the Lord created upon the earth. This is that new thing by which Elisha healed the bitter water of Jericho. Therefore a woman shall encompass a man. This man is said to have been encompassed by a woman just as Moses is said to have been enclosed by a basket of reeds. This, however, is the blessed Virgin, who [Col. 0703A] conceived as a virgin and gave birth as a virgin to the Savior, as we shall explain more fully elsewhere.

## TIT. II. On the Stature, Height, and Terrifying Appearance of Scripture

“The wheels had stature and height and a terrifying appearance” (Ezek. I). Stature is the practice of a good life; height, the promise of the heavenly kingdom; terrifying appearance, the fear of Gehenna. Stature lies in the uprightness of commandment; height, in the loftiness of the heavenly promise; terrifying appearance, in the threats and terrors of the punishment to follow.

Holy Scripture, therefore, which is like a wheel, as it turns from the lower level of history to the higher level of allegory, has stature, because it directs morals toward upright standing, so that the hearer’s mind may not bend down toward lower things. It has height, because it promises the joys of eternal life; [Col. 0703B] a terrifying appearance, because it threatens the reprobate with the punishments of Gehenna. It stands upright in its commandments when it says: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). And Paul: “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. III). It is lofty in its promises when it says: “There shall be month after month and Sabbath after Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI), that is, perfection of glory from perfection of life, and the repose of heavenly recompense from cessation of wrongful work. It is exceedingly terrifying when it says: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (ibid.).

Holy Scripture, therefore, is upright in admonishing, lofty in promising, and terrifying in threatening. The Apostle briefly includes these three in four, saying: “That you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. III). Breadth and [Col. 0703C] length belong to stature: breadth because of the works of charity extended even to enemies, and length because of perseverance. Height is the loftiness of eternal things which “eye has not seen,” etc. (I Cor. II). Depth is the inestimable terrifying appearance.

## TIT. III. On the Lamentations, Song, and Woe Written in the Book of Ezekiel

In the book of prophecy lamentations were written, because repentance for sins is written in it; song, because the rewards and glory of the righteous are foretold there; and woe, because the condemnation of the reprobate is there made explicit (Ezek. II). Therefore, if you wish to punish your sins, read the lamentations written in it: “Rend your hearts,” etc. (Joel II). And again: “Be miserable and mourn” [Col. 0703D] (Jas. IV). “Your mourning shall be turned into the Lord’s joy, and your joy into sorrow.” If you wish to rejoice in the promise of the joy to come, learn what eternal songs are written in it: “All its streets shall be paved with precious and pure stone, and alleluia shall be sung through all its lanes” (Tob. XIII). Those who cried together, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II), came to announce this heavenly song to us.

But if your mind still clings to the world, if you delight in earthly pleasures and cannot love the eternal joys of which you hear, know also what is written in it: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII). There is the woe of the reprobate; it is written: [Col. 0704A] “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” (Isa. LXVI). There it is said to the condemned and rejected: “Go, cursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV).

All instruction is contained in these things. Have you sinned and do you repent? Do you wish to do penance? You will find there lamentations to teach you. Do you desire the hope of heavenly joys to be revealed? There you will find a song for your consolation. But if you have committed evil deeds and incline neither to any lamentations of repentance nor to any heavenly joys, whether you wish it or not you will hear the woe written there, so that one whom neither fear humbles to repentance nor hope raises to heavenly rewards may fall into the punishment of his condemnation which he foresees. Therefore let us punish through repentance the evils we have committed, that through lamentations of compunction we may reach the song of life, lest, if [Col. 0704B] we refuse to be afflicted in repentance, we afterward experience woe without end.

## TIT. IV. On the Comparison of Noah’s Ark to the Church

The ark, which is three hundred cubits long, sixty broad, and thirty high, and terminates in one cubit (Gen. VI), is the Church: broad below and narrow above. Broad for carnal persons, like animals; narrow as it gathers into a single cubit in the few spiritual persons—namely, in the one man who is without sin.

We see many in the Church dissolved by the pleasure of the flesh, torn apart by the quarrels and hatreds of anger. Since the Church tolerates them in order to convert them, it bears them as beasts dwell below in the breadth of the ark. We see others content with what is their own, committing no injury and harboring no hatred; but because such people are already few, the ark grows narrow. We behold others who even disdain permitted things, love their enemies, subdue the flesh from all pleasures, and are raised on the wing of contemplation to the heights. But because such people are very rare, the ark is now drawn toward the cubit where human beings and birds are contained.

The margin [or ledge] which the prophet saw before the chambers belongs to this single cubit (Ezek. XLVI). The margin is faith; the chambers are the hearts of the elect, burning in the love of God. The margin is before the chambers: faith before charity. For no one can love what he does not believe. It is of one cubit, undivided by schisms but enduring in unity; it leads to the chamber of charity and eternal rest.

## TIT. V. Why Christ Is Compared to a Lampstand

“Make a hammered lampstand of purest gold, with its shaft and branches, cups, small spheres, and lilies dependent from it” [Col. 0704D] (Exod. XXV). The lampstand is Christ, who in the nature of humanity shone with the light of divinity, so that he became the lampstand of the world, by whose light the sinner might see in what darkness he lay. It is made of purest gold because he is without sin; hammered because, led through the Passion, he came to the glory of the Resurrection.

Its shaft is the Church, which is his body and which stands upright amid prosperity and adversity in the light of divinity. The branches are preachers, who give forth a sweet sound as they sing the new song. The small spheres signify the mobility of preaching, which, like a sphere, is delayed by no obstacle. Hence: “The word of God is not bound” (II Tim. II). After these [Col. 0705A] lilies are placed, which are the green country and the land flowering with eternal blossoms. The country pertains to labor; the lilies to recompense.

## TIT. VI. How Gideon Bore the Type of a Penitent

When Jerubbaal—that is, Gideon—was threshing grain from chaff (Judg. VI), that is, when the penitent was separating virtues from vices, he saw an angel. For each person merits inwardly to see God only in proportion as he purifies himself from outward things. The angel commanded him to kill a kid—that is, to sacrifice every appetite of our flesh—and to place the flesh upon the rock—that is, to crucify his own body in imitation of Christ, who is called the rock—and to pour the broth of the flesh over it: that is, to empty out thoughts of the flesh in imitation of him.

For he himself said: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Col. 0705B] (Matt. V). The rod immediately touches these things, because divine help is granted to our intention; and fire comes forth from the rock and consumes the unleavened loaves and the flesh, because the spirit breathed forth by the Redeemer burns up our heart with the flame of compunction and consumes every unlawful thing of thought and deed.

## TIT. VII. How Job Represents the Penitent

Job, sitting on a dungheap, scraped away his discharge (Job II); that is, the righteous person grieving over his sins—for this is the interpretation of *Job*—removes by the harshness of repentance the double discharge of sin, namely, that of thought and of deed. Or Job signifies Christ, made sorrowful for us, who by his flesh taken from the clay of our substance removed the discharge of our sin.

Job sat not on a mountain but on a dungheap, because the truly penitent person, abandoning pride, performs repentance in humility. When by weeping he sees his evils, he recognizes how greatly the dung of sin defiles him by departing from it; for he does not perceive its stench before he has withdrawn from it.

## TIT. VIII. On the Blindness by Which the Wicked Are Struck

When the Sodomites wished to use violence against Lot and break down the door, Lot was brought by an angel into the house, the door being shut; those men, struck with blindness, could not find the door (Gen. XIX). For when the righteous person endures the snares of the wicked, he is recalled to the house of the mind. But the wicked, struck with blindness, go about in circles: though finding [Col. 0705D] the holy Scriptures which they examine, they do not find the door, because corrupters of minds can find no opening for accusation against the life of the righteous.

## TIT. IX. On Repentance in the Sacrifice of the Heifer

In Moses, when a heifer is killed for sacrifice, it is commanded that hyssop, cedar wood, and twice-dyed scarlet be offered with it (Num. XIX). We kill the heifer when we extinguish the flesh from the wantonness of its pleasure; with hyssop, cedar wood, and twice-dyed scarlet, because with the mortification of the flesh we offer the sacrifice of faith, hope, and charity. Hyssop cleanses our inward parts, and Peter says: “Purifying your souls in obedience to charity, in brotherly love” (I Pet. I). Cedar wood is impaired by no decay, because no end consumes the hope of heavenly things. Hence Peter: [Col. 0706A] “He has regenerated us to a living hope” (ibid.). Scarlet shines yellow-red, because charity both fills and kindles the person whom it possesses. Hence the Lord: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). It is called twice-dyed so that charity may color the heart before God with the love of God and neighbor.

## TIT. X. On the Guarding of Our Mind, Figured through the Guarding of Ish-bosheth

Ish-bosheth, who in his house had not a male doorkeeper but a female doorkeeper, who fell asleep while cleansing wheat (II Kings IV), was killed by enemies entering then, carrying away ears of grain, and striking him in the groin. The female doorkeeper cleanses the wheat when the guard of the mind separates virtues from vices. If she falls asleep by ceasing from the care of discernment, she opens a path to malignant spirits for killing the Lord. Having entered, they carry off the ears of grain—that is, they take away the sprouts of good [Col. 0706B] thoughts—and they strike in the groin when, piercing life through the delight of the flesh, they take it away, because they appoint a soft guard to the guarding of the mind.

For the guard of our mind ought to be twofold if we do not wish to be Ish-bosheth, that is, a “man of confusion”: strong and wise, so that neither bodily sleep may oppress it nor the error of ignorance deceive it. Hence Solomon: “Keep your heart with all guarding, because from it life proceeds” (Prov. IV).

## TIT. XI. How the Oxen Supporting the Bronze Sea Signify Priestly Shepherds

Before the doors of the temple, for washing the hands of those entering, twelve oxen bear the bronze sea—that is, the basin. Their faces project outward, but their hind parts are concealed (II Kings VII). The oxen are the order of shepherds. Hence: “You shall not muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain” (Deut. XXV). Before the doors they bear the basin for washing the hands of those entering, when they make ready the patience of their condescension for cleansing their neighbors’ confessions, so that whoever strives to enter the gate of eternity may disclose his temptations to the mind of the shepherd and, as it were, wash the hands of thought and deed in the oxen’s basin.

Let such shepherds therefore present themselves that those subject to them may not be ashamed to disclose secrets, so that when little ones suffer waves of temptation, they may flee to the shepherd’s mind as to a mother’s breast and wash the filth of their sin in its consolation. Their faces are seen but their hind parts are hidden, because we see their works, but he knows what remains afterward.

## TIT. XII. That through Repentance the Sinner Will Be Preserved in the Unity of Faith

[Col. 0706D]

If someone goes with a friend into the forest to cut wood—that is, to rebuke vices—and the iron slips from his hand—that is, preaching inconsistent with his conduct departs from him—and he strikes his friend by an evil example and kills him in soul, he shall flee to one of the three cities (Deut. XIX), so that he may be saved in one of them. That is, converted through the lamentation of repentance, let him be hidden in the unity of the sacrament, under faith, hope, and charity, lest, when the kinsman of the slain—that is, the strict Judge—comes, he may kill him with eternal punishment at the judgment.

## TIT. XIII. On the Teachers of the Church Signified by the Bars

Bars of setim wood (Exod. XXI), clothed and covered with gold, placed in four golden rings at the four corners of the ark, carry the ark itself. The ark [Col. 0707A] is the Church; the bars are strong and persevering teachers who, adhering to the four rings—that is, to evangelical teaching—carry the Church through the four quarters of the world, just as the bars carry the ark through its four corners. The bars are commanded to be covered with gold, so that while they sound forth speech to others, they themselves may also shine with the splendor of life.

Of them it is added: “They shall always remain in the rings,” so that when an occasion requires carrying the ark—that is, teaching the Church—no delay may arise in inserting the bars. For when a pastor is asked by those subject to him about some spiritual doubt, it is highly shameful if he then seeks to learn when he ought to resolve the question. Hence the chief Shepherd says to shepherds: “Always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the [hope] faith that is in you” (I Pet. [Col. 0707B] III).

## TIT. XIV. On the Power of Speech through the Harp

When an evil spirit assailed Saul, David’s harp calmed his madness (I Kings XVI). For when the mind of the powerful is turned by pride into fury, it is fitting that it be recalled to salvation by the calmness of our speech, as by the sweetness of a harp. A hard diamond does not admit the cutting of iron, but is softened by the gentle blood of goats. A rich person must be appeased by gentle exhortations, for hard wounds are softened by mild poultices, and the rage of madmen is healed when a physician speaks gently.

## TIT. XV. What the Life of Secular People Who Live Well Is: Though Not Excellent, It Is Nevertheless Safe

Lot, who left burning Sodom and found Zoar, a small [Col. 0707C] city, did not immediately ascend to the summit of the mountain (Gen. XIV). To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the unlawful fires of the flesh; to climb the summit of the mountain is to seize the height of a perfect life. But since there are many who abandon certain crimes but have not yet ascended to the perfection of the mountain, they find in the middle Zoar—that is, the good life of secular people—in which they save their souls. For although this life is not remarkable in virtues, it is nevertheless safe from punishments.

## TIT. XVI. How We Must Veil Our Face through Humility, after the Example of Elijah

Elijah, in order to hear the voice of God speaking with him, stands at the entrance of his cave and veils his face (III Kings XIX). For when the voice of higher understanding arises in the mind, the whole person is no longer within the cave, because in mind he does not possess concern for the flesh; but he stands at the entrance, because he meditates upon leaving the miseries of mortality. Yet such a person must veil his face, because the more we are raised to understand higher things, the more humbly we ought to press ourselves down through the humility of repentance, lest we attempt to know more than we ought.

## TIT. XVII. That Avarice Is Not to Be Sought in God and the Holy Church

Laban, furiously pursuing Jacob, who had taken his daughters as wives, seeks his idols with him (Gen. XXXI). So, when the world in its members pursues Christ, who took the Church as his bride, it sought avarice in her—for avarice is the service of idols—and tempted God himself concerning avarice. The daughter covered it, not found with him, by her seated posture of repentance, so that it might not be found in her either.

## TIT. XVIII. Salt of Discernment, Not the Honey of Flattery or Pleasure, Must Be Used in Sacred Offerings

“No leaven or honey shall be burned in sacrifices; but in every sacrifice you shall offer salt” (Lev. II). Honey is forbidden to be offered in sacrifice because nothing pleasurable and sweet of this world pleases God, nothing that does not have something of biting truth. Hence the paschal lamb was eaten with wild and bitter lettuces. But salt is offered in every sacrifice because all things ought to be seasoned with the salt of reason and discernment.

## TIT. XIX. On Avoiding Schism

[Col. 0708B]

“If you make an altar, you shall not build it of cut stones” (Exod. XX). For one divided from unity and heavenly fellowship by hatred does not receive Christ in his body, nor can a sacrifice acceptable to God be offered in such persons. Hence it adds: “If you raise a tool upon it, it will be defiled,” that is, it will be defiled by a malignant and fiery stain.

## TIT. XX. On Avoiding Superfluity of Words and Things

“You shall not plant a grove or any tree beside the altar” (Deut. XVI). And to Gideon: “Cut down the grove which is around the altar” (Judg. VI). A grove is forbidden to be planted beside the altar because unfruitful words are not to be admitted around the Lord’s sayings.

## TIT. XXI. How the Sun of Justice Still Stands in Aid of the Good; and That Demons Are More Troublesome at Death

[Col. 0708C]

When battle was waged against five kings, the sun and moon stood still (Josh. X), because, while we fight against the five senses, the sun of justice does not abandon us, he who says: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). The five kings flee to the cave of the body; but while Jesus fights—that is, while the Gospel is preached and the word of God enters within us—all are killed together within the cave of the body.

When Abraham offered sacrifice at sunset, he endured birds settling upon it (Gen. XV), because near the end of life unclean spirits strive more intensely to defile what we offer upon the altar of the cross. He drives them away as commanded, lest they carry it off, when he does not allow that which the mind considers itself usefully offering to God to be defiled by unclean thoughts.

## TIT. XXII. What Water of Wisdom Demons Endeavor to Take Away

The Philistines fill with earth the wells which Abraham dug (Gen. XXVI), because unclean spirits inject earthly thoughts into those who penetrate to the heights through the hidden meanings of divine Scripture, and thus, as it were, take away the water of divine knowledge that has been found.

## TIT. XXIII. On Giving Counsel and Planting One’s Foot

To give counsel to a fool is an act of charity; to give it to a wise person is ostentation; to give it to Wisdom itself is rashness. The surge of the present life drags along the person whom it lifts up. But he is exceedingly foolish who is rolled about in the wave and tries to plant his foot firmly.

## TIT. XXIV. On the Soul’s Departure from God and Its Recall to Him

[Col. 0709A]

“Dinah went out to see the women of the land” (Gen. XXXIV). The soul goes out through the ears and through the eyes, to play with the daughters of perdition. The Lord calls it back, saying: “Return, return, O Shulammite,” etc. (Cant. VI). He says “return” four times, as though saying: Return from my things, because they are wonderful; from your things, because they are crooked; from yourself, because all flesh is grass; to me, because I am the highest good.

Thus God turns his face away from me because I turned my back upon him. Therefore, he says, “that we may look upon you,” as though he said: You cannot see me unless we first look upon you. I do not know what stain you have on your face; you are ugly and bear another’s image. Cleanse it, therefore, that we may look upon you.

## TIT. XXV. What It Is to Be Afflicted in Straw, Clay, and Brick, and to Build Cities for Pharaoh

[Col. 0709B]

Pharaoh afflicts the children of Israel with straw, clay, and brick (Exod. I and V). Straw is carnal delight. Clay is made from dust and water. This occurs when evil will is joined to action. From these bricks are made, when wicked works are baked into the hardness of wicked habit. From these are built Rameses, which is interpreted “the stirring of a moth,” and this is avarice; also Pithom, which is interpreted “mouth of the abyss,” that is, of hell or of all vices—for avarice is the root of all evils; and Heliopolis, which is interpreted “city of the sun,” namely good works done for empty glory, which is hypocrisy. He builds these three cities who introduces greed, falsehood, and hypocrisy.

## TIT. XXVI. On Beginnings, Middles, and Ends

[Col. 0709C]

“Son, remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7). There are first things, middle things, and last things: first shame, second sorrow, third fear, which is stronger than the others for resisting sin. Shame takes counsel from the crowd, from any consolation of the world; fear finds no comfort. Therefore, son, consider whence you have come, blush at where you are, groan at where you are going, and fear the “last things,” in the plural. These are bodily death, the strictness of judgment, and infernal punishment. Bodily death is harsh, because what someone possesses with love, he does not leave without pain. The examination is dreadful, where angels and archangels tremble. For if the cedar of Lebanon is shaken, what will the little wisps of smoke or of the desert do? [Col. 0709D] When the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly appear? (1 Pet. 4.) Punishment is perilous, where “the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Isa. 66).

Death, however, comes through infirmity, necessity, or violence. The first occurs neither by skill nor by strength; the second by the dagger; the third amid concern for boasting. Hence: “You showed me many tribulations”—many in quantity, evil in quality. The strictness of judgment occurs in three ways: through the revelation of sins not confessed here. Therefore do not blush to confess here. Through confusion; but there is a confusion which brings another’s glory, and a confusion which brings one’s own sin, namely that by which confession is hindered. Confusion over another’s glory is that by which the sinner is punished, when he sees the glory of the saints and says: “We fools accounted their life madness,” etc. [Col. 0710A] “Behold how they are numbered among the children of God” (Wis. 5).

Against these confusions, the first remedy is contrition of heart, the second confession of the mouth, the third affliction of the flesh. These are the three fountains by which the soul is washed: contrition through anguish, confession through humility, affliction through harshness. The first is that which waters the surface of the earth; the second, that which was placed outside the city; the third, that upon which Jesus sat. Infernal punishment follows, in which there is grim gnawing by worms and dreadful burning by fire, because there “the worm does not die and the fire is not quenched” (Isa. 66). From these two arises despair: first, the conscience is gnawed; second, bodies are burned; third, misery is heaped up. The first punishes the sin of thought, the second the guilt of speech, the third the practice [Col. 0710B] of action. These are the last things. But great is the mercy of God, who, against the path of error set before us, preaches the path of truth, recalls the wandering son, and mercifully chastises the one who persists.

## TITLE XXVII. What it is to be buried in the double cave

Abraham buried his dead wife in the double cave (Gen. 23), because the wayfarer hides his soul, dead to the activities of the world, under the rule of good action and contemplation. For the active life is a tomb, in that it buries those dead to wicked works; but the contemplative life covers more perfectly, because it utterly separates from all worldly desires those received into the inner places—such as those of whom Paul says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in glory” (Col. 3).

## TITLE XXVIII. What it is to flee from Jezebel to the cave, and to recognize the Lord in the gentle spirit

[Col. 0710C]

Elijah, fleeing Jezebel, hides in a cave (3 Kings 19), because at times the mind avoids disgrace, yet is not as yet strengthened to abandon the dwelling-place of the flesh. It flees concupiscence, but lurks in the cave, because it is not made strong for enduring sufferings. Hence the divine voice reproves him: “What are you doing here, Elijah?” (ibid.). As though it said: You were not made in order to make your dwelling beneath the shelter of the flesh, but to contemplate the form of the Creator. Therefore arise; stand in the entrance of the cave (ibid.). Arise—that is, do not cling to the earth; lift yourself to higher things; seek the things above. Stand in perseverance, [Col. 0710D] stand in patience, stand ready through the desire to depart, stand fixed through obedience in enduring. Stand at the entrance of the cave, so that you neither enter through concupiscence nor go forth through impatience.

“Behold, the Lord will pass by: a great and strong wind, overthrowing mountains and crushing rocks. The Lord is not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake. The Lord is not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, fire. The Lord is not in the fire; and after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (ibid.). Behold the forerunners of God: wind, earthquake, fire. The wind is the terror of eternal judgment; if it strikes the sinner’s heart, it casts down the mountains of pride and dissolves the rocks of hardness. But God is in no way said to be in this, because the soul still afflicted by fear of perdition does not yet feel the sweetness of charity. After the wind follows the earthquake, [Col. 0711A] because the mind stirred by the terror of judgment is enkindled with the love of compunction. Finally, after the fire comes the whisper of a gentle breeze, because after the long fires of compunction the purified mind, breathed upon by the Holy Spirit, feels the cooling refreshment of consolation. Nor is the Lord denied to be present in that whisper, because surely only that mind perceives sweetness which, after the labor and anguish of penitence, having received the refreshment of consolation, rests in the hope of divine enlargement.

## TITLE XXIX. How the iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman

“The iniquity of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42). In the inner human being there is something directed toward heavenly and higher things, and this is called wisdom; and again something looking toward transient and perishable things, [Col. 0711B] and this is called prudence. This power of the soul divides itself in two, upward and downward: upward into wisdom, downward into prudence; upward into the male, downward into the female, so that the male may be superior and rule, and the female inferior and ruled. “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ; the head of Christ is God” (Eph. 5). Let wisdom rule prudence. Wisdom, moreover, is the Word; and the Word is from him whose Word it is.

Prudence, like a woman attending to the care of the house, is occupied with the things of the flesh. The wisdom of God, like a man sending or extending his discernment into far-off things, ranges abroad through the breadth of spiritual contemplation. Thus the woman sometimes does well and sometimes badly. She does badly when prudence, either bound by sloth, neglects her flesh, or, distracted by care, pours herself out in seeking superfluities. [Col. 0711C] But she does well when she seeks what is necessary and the conveniences of her flesh, because responsibility for it has been entrusted to her.

Likewise, the man sometimes acts well and sometimes unjustly. He acts well when wisdom directs itself upward, seeking and desiring only what is pleasing to the Lord. He acts unjustly when, strengthened by the taste of inward savor, he cuts away not only superfluities but necessities as well. Have you seen someone carefully seeking the necessities required for his own condition? That was a beneficent woman. Have you, again, seen someone afflicting his flesh by the prompting or consideration of heavenly reward? That was a man acting unjustly. For it is injustice when you withdraw from someone what is owed to him; yet the iniquity of the man is better than the [Col. 0711D] beneficent woman. Better is one who, kindled by heavenly desire, afflicts his flesh by withholding necessities than one who, relaxed by carnal affection, strives to satisfy all its desires with conveniences.

Therefore the woman who does evil is far removed from the iniquity of the man. Yet even the beneficent woman cannot be compared with his iniquity. For when the woman does well, it is not a virtue; when she does ill, it is a fault. But the iniquity of the man is the desire for righteousness; his goodness is the perfection of glory. If, then, the man is unjust toward righteousness and the woman good toward nature, certainly the iniquity of the man is better than the beneficent woman, because, although nature is good in creation, righteousness is better in recompense.

## TITLE XXX. On the flight which Scripture urges upon us, and the bread which it supplies

[Col. 0712A]

“You who inhabit the land of the south, meet the fugitive with bread” (Isa. 21). Sacred Scripture urges flight upon us in many ways. But what ought we to flee, how, and when? There are three that wage war against us: the devil, the flesh, and the world. The devil leads against us the ranks of vices; the flesh, those of evil desires; the world, those of prosperity and adversity. It would be happier to fight and conquer, but for the weak it is more expedient to flee and be saved than to fight badly and be overcome.

We flee vices when we avoid occasions of sinning; for example, we flee the desires of the flesh’s luxury in the hope of inward contemplation, when we guard against their provocation, lest we cast oil [Col. 0712B] upon the fire and it blaze up as much as it can. We flee prosperity and adversity when we neither seek through desire even those things which delight us, fearing that we may be dissolved, nor cast ourselves upon those things which torment us, fearing that we may be broken. We have said what must be fled and how. Now let Truth say when: “See that your flight does not occur in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24).

Winter either roughens the roads with frost or makes them slippery with rain. Winter is the numbness of approaching death, when pain of the flesh binds the members by suffering and weakens strength by fellow-feeling. The Sabbath is the time after death, when, after departure from this life, the power to act is taken away. Therefore, if you wish to flee the wrath to come, flee while you are sound; for flight at death is difficult and after death impossible. But lest you fail on the way, [Col. 0712C] the inhabitants of the land of the south, if they see you fleeing, will meet you with bread that you may be refreshed. In the south are brightness and heat: brightness of thought, heat of love. Those inhabit the land of the south who rest in thought and love of truth. They abound in the breads of the word of God. They meet fugitives with compassion and refresh them with consolation.

Although this bread is one, it is set forth under diverse forms. For sometimes it is called bread baked under ashes, sometimes barley bread, sometimes wheat bread. Elijah, fleeing, is refreshed in the desert by bread baked under ashes. The children of Jerusalem, who dwell in peace, are filled with the fat of wheat; those who recline upon grass eat barley bread. Bread under ashes is refreshment beneath lowliness. Sacred Scripture, having lowliness in the appearance of the letter and preserving sweetness in the depth [Col. 0712D] of spiritual understanding, is bread under ashes.

Do you wish me to show you bread baked under ashes? You read that Rachel and Leah contend for intercourse with one man, Jacob. Great is the appearance of lowliness there, great the heap of ashes, and the pile of earthliness. Turn over the ashes; search within: bread lies there, refreshment is hidden. Understand the two sisters as the two lives, namely the active and the contemplative. Both contend for the embrace of the man: the one that she may have the usefulness of action, the other that she may receive the delight of contemplation. Behold, you have found bread under ashes.

Do you still wish to see bread under ashes? You see outwardly the weakness of the Lord at his birth: his crying, his weeping, the narrowness of the cradle, the bindings of swaddling-clothes. All this is ash, [Col. 0713A] earthly and weak; beneath this ash was hidden the Word, the refreshment of angels and human beings. You see him hungry and thirsty, weeping and suffering, showing compassion and being moved. What were all these things but ash—indications of corruption, signs of mortality? And beneath them was hidden the power of divinity; whoever could turn over these ashes deserved to be satisfied. Behold how Scripture sets before us bread baked under ashes.

Elsewhere you see sacred speech harsh on the surface of the letter, as though having tough chaff, so that one can scarcely penetrate to the marrow of spiritual understanding. This is barley. Indeed, the chaff is shaken out with labor; but if you reach the inner things, you find a sweetness that satisfies. Elsewhere you find sacred Scripture caressing both by gentleness of words and sweetness of meaning. This is wheat [Col. 0713B], in which sweet refreshment is prepared for minds to be gently nourished.

Among these three kinds of bread, bread baked under ashes is set before those who labor, that it may refresh those who despise themselves through the example of humility and lowliness; barley bread is for servants, who, by more earnest exercise, uncover the strong and obscure places of Scripture as though by shaking out chaff and arrive at tasting the marrow of spiritual understanding; wheat bread is for sons, that they may be refreshed in the sweetness of eternal delight unto exultation.

## TITLE XXXI. On the threefold base in Scripture, and on Samson and his riddle

There are three kinds of bases in the Scriptures: bronze, silver, and gold (Judg. 14). The first has strength; the second, brightness along with strength; the third, splendor along with strength and [Col. 0713C] brightness. Strength is in deed, brightness in speech, splendor in mind, because in these three a person preserves patience, which the bronze base signifies; clear truth, which the silver base signifies; and the splendor of conscience, which the golden base signifies, which bears the structure of all virtues. Moses employed these three.

“If you had not ploughed with my heifer, you would not have found my riddle” (Judg. 14). The heifer is wanton flesh; the riddle is an obscure saying. Samson, whose name means “their sun,” bears the type of the Sun of righteousness; his companions bear the type of students of wisdom. Thus he says: “If you had not ploughed with my heifer,” etc. As though he said: Unless the flesh is restrained and made sober, the mind cannot raise itself [Col. 0713D] to heavenly things. One ploughs with the heifer when the flesh is mortified. The riddle is found when contemplation of heavenly mysteries is opened.

Therefore Samson’s companions plough the heifer diligently, that they may understand the riddle, because the friends of truth, the disciples of Jesus Christ, soberly chastise the flesh and make the body lean, so that they may understand obscure matters of knowledge and be able to penetrate the mysteries of knowledge. Abstinence, then, is of great importance: by it vices are purged, pardon is obtained, grace is possessed, innocence is restored, and heavenly mysteries are opened. Abstinence is fourfold: from vices, from foods, from unclean occupations, and from desires. Concerning these Zechariah says: “The fast of the fourth, the fast of the fifth, the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth shall be to the house of Judah [Col. 0714A] joy and gladness and splendid solemnities,” etc. (Zech. 8).

## TITLE XXXII. On Absalom’s hair

Absalom was shorn once a year, because his hair burdened him; and then his hair was weighed at two hundred shekels by the common weight (2 Kings 14). The appetite of the flesh nourishes and produces hair, because it nourishes superfluous thoughts. This hair weighs down the mind when earthly habitation depresses the sense that thinks many things (Wis. 9). One who, when shorn once in the year, weighs two hundred shekels, is one who renounces worldly desires in the whole span of his life—and does so at its end. For then he is stripped of what he possesses, when at final death he is separated from earthly things.

Moreover, earth weighs more with him than heaven: he loves to be more in the house of clay [Col. 0714B] than in that not made with hands in heaven, more in transient things than eternal ones. And this is according to the common weight, not the weight of the sanctuary. Hear the weight of the sanctuary, the weight of Paul: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1). Hear the common weight: “Woe to those who dwell upon the earth” (Rev. 8). Not those who dwell there in body, but those who dwell there in heart.

## TITLE XXXIII. On the good things of the good born with the Lord, and the terrors of evil things

Manna came down from heaven: let the hungry rejoice. “The vine gave its fruit from heaven” (Zech. 8): let the thirsty be glad. “Oil has been poured out” (Song 1): let the sick exult. “The expectation of the nations” has come (Gen. 49): let those who wander come to their senses. “A stone was cut from the mountain” (Dan. 2): let the proud fear. “A fountain was made open to the house of David for the washing of the sinner” (Zech. [Col. 0714C] 13): let transgressors return. “This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes” (Ps. 117). “There is no God like our God, who alone does wonderful things” (Ps. 71).

## TITLE XXXIV. On the ointment descending from Christ to the hem, etc., that is, to his elect

“The ointment descended from Aaron’s beard to the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132): from Christ—who is the mountain of strength, as Aaron is interpreted—in whom is the fullness of grace, it descends to his own, when grace (John 1), which is in his beard, descends to the apostles, who are denoted by the beard, which signifies strength; and through them it reaches even to the least, who are at the hem of the garment.

## TITLE XXXV. On the child who was born and crushed: morally applied to feigned religion

“A child has been born to us” (Isa. 9). You, I say, martyrs: a child has been born for you and in you, because you have conceived the fear of the Lord and brought forth the spirit of salvation. Watch, O mother, over the care of the newborn until the spirit of life is formed in him who has been born to you; for the more newly born he is, the more easily he can perish for you—though he will never perish for himself. Watch, I say, remembering that your rival, while asleep, crushed the son who had been born to her (3 Kings 3).

For what is the rival but the carnal soul, which extinguishes the spirit? Such negligence touches those who, though they have lost the fervor of religious life, nevertheless arrogate to themselves its name and glory. Hence arise the contentions of carnal [Col. 0715A] persons against spiritual persons, even in chapters over which our Solomon invisibly presides as judge. “My son,” say the carnal persons, “is alive; yours is dead” (3 Kings 3): that is, they vie with one another for the authority of religious life, whose observances they judge according to their own desire. And truly the mother wishes to give the living and whole child to her rival, not begrudging her glory, provided that she may possess the truth. But the other says: “Let him be neither mine nor yours, but let him be divided” (ibid.), because she desires to retain for herself the honor of holiness and leave the labor to others.

But the judge does not err, even if for a while he conceals his judgment. Solomon’s sword discovers the mother to whom he awards the child undivided: as it grants the disposition of charity, so it grants the effect of authority; as the fervor for working, so the favor of working. Therefore, brothers, you in whom faith working through love [Col. 0715B] has been born from the Holy Spirit, guard it. Seek a nurse for it, like the infant Jesus, until the child may be formed in us—the child born to us, who gave us the pattern into which we are formed not only by being born, but by living and dying.

## TITLE XXXVI. On driving demons and vain thoughts away from the sacrifice of the mind

[Col. 0715C]

At Abram’s sacrifice the bodies of the other animals are divided; the birds are not divided (Gen. 15). When carnal persons are divided by diverse desires, they are divided like animals; and when spiritual persons maintain the bond of unity, they are undivided like birds. Birds descend upon the divided bodies, because demons seek food for themselves in the division of carnal desires. There are also other troublesome birds, thoughts which intrude themselves during the sacrifice of prayer and stain the offering; but Abram drives them away, because by the hand of holy discernment he drives away within both unclean spirits and vain thoughts. Flies, which return quickly, are driven away with greater difficulty than birds. Hence the coming of birds is not so grave as the importunity of flies, nor is the repeated driving away of demons as difficult as that of thoughts. “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you”; resist thoughts, and unless we are cautious and fortified, they will soon return again.

## TITLE XXXVII. On the functions of reason and sensuality, under the figure of Abraham and Sarah

Abraham meets the three angels outside the entrance; [Col. 0715D] Sarah remains behind the entrance (Gen. 18). For our spiritual understanding ought, in the knowledge of the Trinity, to rise beyond the flesh. But care for the flesh does not appear outside; rather, as though behind her husband’s back, under the discernment of the spirit, intent only upon necessities, she hears God’s promises and laughs when she is told not to presume of herself. Laughing, she is rebuked; rebuked, the old woman is now made fruitful, because, abandoning confidence in herself, she received from the Promiser, contrary to hope, what she had doubted she would have by human reason. Hence the child born is called Isaac, that is, “laughter,” because the mind trusting in God gives birth to joy. Therefore let care for the flesh not exceed the bounds of necessity, nor presume of itself in what it carries out moderately.

## TITLE XXXVIII. On the trees vainly seeking a king for themselves, and on evil monks seeking a superior

[Col. 0716A]

When the trees of the forest sought the olive as king, they said to it: “Rule over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my fatness, which gods and men use, and come to be promoted among the trees?” (Judg. 9.) Because the Holy Spirit, signified by the olive, says to religious persons negligent in profession but barren in works: “The richness which I offer appears among spiritual persons and those who seek me; but you, because you are barren, are unworthy of my grace.”

When they come to the fig tree, that is, to the Law, the same Law says in Isaiah: “Blind the heart of this people” (Isa. 6). And the Lord shows that the Law is understood to accomplish this, saying: “A certain man planted a vineyard” (Luke [Col. 0716B] 20), and planted a fig tree in it: that is, Christ made the Jewish people and gave it the Law. Hence Jeremiah also says: “He saw very good figs and very bad figs” (Jer. 24). Carnal observances are very bad figs; spiritual understandings are very good ones.

They also come to the vine, that is, Christ; but “what agreement has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6). As though Christ said: “I became obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. 2). But you are Belial, that is, “without a yoke,” and therefore you cannot be joined with me. Rejected by these three—the Holy Spirit, the understanding of the Law, and Jesus Christ—they come to the bramble, that is, Antichrist. For just as the bramble is first soft in its shoot, but later produces dense and sharp thorns, so Antichrist will flatter at the beginning and afterward persecute cruelly. “He shall be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path, biting” (Gen. 49). He invites them to rest beneath his shade: that is, to desire the things of this world and rest in works of the flesh. “Otherwise, let fire go out from the bramble” (Judg. 9), namely when Antichrist is struck down; it will devour not only the simple but also “the cedars of Lebanon” (ibid.), that is, his greater and lesser followers.

## TITLE XXXIX. That Christ is dew and rain; heaven is the blessed Trinity; the clouds are the prophets

“Drop down dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down the Just One” (Isa. 45). Dew descends from heaven to earth without sound; rain comes from clouds with noise. Christ is dew; Christ is rain. In this life Christ is the dew [Col. 0716D] of grace, placing sinners in the bosom of mercy. On the day of judgment he will be rain, raging noisily over the ungodly. Christ is dew: O sinner, rise to hope. Christ is rain: O proud one, descend from the tribunal of your heart.

“Drop down dew, O heavens, from above.” Heaven is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, three and one. Let the heavens therefore drop dew. As though it said: Let the Father cooperate, that the Son may come to us; and let the Holy Spirit cooperate, that the Son may redeem us. “Let the clouds rain down the Just One.” The clouds are the prophets. In these clouds the Just One was bound and suspended, because Christ was enclosed in the words of the prophets before the incarnation. But the human race asks that the clouds rain down the Just One, because it is time to act, that before the sight of the nations he may reveal his righteousness in the clouds as rain.

## TITLE XL. How the contrite, the beggars, the devout, and the contemplative return to God

[Col. 0717A]

“Transgressors, return to the heart” (Ps. 48). The terms are: the contrite, beggars, devout persons, and contemplatives. The contrite fall at the feet, watering them with tears and crying for their sins: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50); “Be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 7). These, with Mary our Magdalene, fallen at the feet because of the menstrual flow of vices, hear: “Many sins are forgiven you” (ibid.). Humble satisfaction redeems in them what proud transgression committed, and they experience the mercy of heavenly sweetness. The demon is cast out from the contrite person: “The devil shall go forth before his feet,” it says (Hab. 3). Thus, at the feet, the dead become living, the disinherited become heirs, the earthly become heavenly.

The beggars approach [Col. 0717B] the hands. Although they have obtained pardon for sins, they nevertheless feel themselves unable to restrain themselves and act well; therefore they ask and receive grace. “Behold, he shows to whom the kindly king extends the golden scepter of mercy” (Esth. 4): “You open your hand and fill every living thing with blessing” (Ps. 144). The devout remain and stand about the breast. These are those who have lived innocently or have wiped away crimes through penitence. They are not said to fall at the feet, because they are now washed; nor do they reach the head, because they are not yet contemplatives. They are in an intermediate advance, occupied in works of piety and ministering temporal and spiritual things to those in need. They do not possess from themselves the knowledge of this action and the grace of this ministry, but draw them from the very living fountain, namely from the breast of Jesus, which is the spiritual sanctuary of the heavenly treasury in which all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. 2).

Such ought to be prelates standing in the court of Jesus—that is, in the reading of Holy Scripture, wherein is the seat of wisdom—receiving and drawing peace from Christ’s bosom, in order to proclaim it to the peoples. There, after the example of John, they draw abundant fullness of spiritual teaching, so that, being more fully filled, they may pour out drops falling upon the earth, that, the Lord giving goodness, our earth may yield and render its fruit in its season. One must draw and offer to drink. This is not done by running about in a worldly way, but by preserving spiritually and meditating diligently, since no one will belch forth who has not eaten. It is one thing to yawn from emptiness, [Col. 0717D] another to belch from fullness. Therefore from divine fasts he will announce nothing savory; nor can he have anything from himself, because a human being cannot have anything from himself unless it has been given him from above.

Contemplatives or justified persons approach the head. “The head of Christ is God.” These are they who, by God’s grace and the privilege of merits, raise themselves above themselves with the Apostle, hearing things “which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Cor. 12). Therefore the contrite, at the feet, obtain forgiveness of sins; beggars, at the hands, the power to abstain from evil and act well; the devout, at the breast, moral knowledge for the instruction of subjects; contemplatives, at the head, a holier indulgence concerning heavenly things. The fearful, made in some manner harsh on account of their crimes, find a place of pardon with Thomas in the wounds and piercings of the nails. The rich, suffering from a flow of blood, find the grace of healing at the hem. Thus Christ, made man for us, stands in the midst of the Church, ready to aid all. Let us therefore approach him, lest it be said to us: “There stands one in the midst of you whom you do not know” (John 1). The Jews saw him in whom they did not believe. Let us see him by faith working through love, lest we someday fear him seated. For when seated, he will judge. Hence thrones were set and books opened, and the Ancient of Days sat. Let us therefore anticipate the face of the Judge in confession (Ps. 94), judging ourselves. For if, according to the Apostle, we judge ourselves, we shall certainly not be judged (1 Cor. 11).

## TITLE XLI. On applying to monks the office of Moses—that is, the lawgiver—Aaron—that is, the priest—and Samuel—that is, the prophet

[Col. 0718B]

“Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. 98). Let us recognize a certain living temple of God, if we believe the Apostle of God writing about it: “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3). It must not be believed that this temple of God ought to exist without priests or without those who call upon God’s name, but rather with Moses and Aaron among his priests and Samuel among those who call upon his name. Let us ask who these Moses, Aaron, and Samuel are. Through Moses the Law was given; through Aaron the priesthood was instituted; to Samuel the gift of prophecy was granted.

[Col. 0718C]

Therefore Moses’s office is to command what is to be done and forbid what is to be left undone. Aaron’s office is to implore the Lord’s help for those things which Moses commands, and through prayer and offering to render the true God propitious concerning transgressions. Samuel’s office is to foretell what reward those who keep the Law may hope for, and what punishment those who transgress the Law may expect.

If, therefore, you see someone recently come from the world and occupied with meditation, so as to make satisfaction for past offences and keep himself guarded against future ones; considering how he ought to regulate his countenance, compose his clothing and bearing, determine what and how much he should eat, how much he should keep vigil, and how he should resist anger, oppose gluttony, trample pride, extinguish lust, how prompt he ought to be in obedience and patient in endurance—know that Moses has risen in him [Col. 0718D] who is of such a heart, and is, as it were, establishing a new law.

If likewise you see him afflicting his body with nakedness and cold, subduing his flesh by labor and blows, slaughtering many victims on the outward altar, and, after first drawing fire from it, entering into the Holy of Holies itself, not without the blood of a slain calf; and if, after first slaughtering the calf of pride and many other victims on the outward altar, he habitually offers to God on the inward altar groans, sighs, prayers, and tears—do not doubt that Aaron is beginning a new priesthood in him. The outward altar is the carnal sense; the inward altar, the affection. Thus on the inward altar groans and tears are offered, and those things which move the heart’s affection; just as on the outward altar are offered [Col. 0719A] vigils, fasts, labor, and the other things that pertain to the sense of the flesh. Fire is drawn from this altar when one passes into inward things, because from bodily affliction the force of sorrow is transmitted to the heart; from this, afterward, the incense of compunction is kindled.

But that the office of the priesthood may be more fully understood, two things especially belong to it: to instruct the people in the Law of the Lord and to make the true Lord propitious for the people. Of these, Moses performs the one, Aaron the other. Hence it is said: “Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name.” In Samuel the gift of prophecy is eminent. Why then is he among those who call upon God, rather than among those who prophesy? Samuel gladly prophesies, and those among whom he prophesies gladly call upon God. The new prophecy of Samuel is to act, to call truly, and to incite those praying. For the more frequently someone considers what rewards are laid up in heaven for the righteous and what torments in hell for the wicked, the more truly he calls upon God and the more attentively he prays. But if Samuel ceases to prophesy, the priests cease to invoke and pray, because the rarer contemplation of future things becomes, the colder prayer returns and the more sluggish invocation arises.

Therefore, that Moses may be discerning in commandment, that Aaron may remain devout in prayer, Samuel must necessarily persevere subtle and diligent in contemplation. To reduce to a summary what we have said more diffusely: to Moses belongs prudently discerning what must be done; to Aaron belongs imploring divine assistance for those things which we cannot accomplish through ourselves; Samuel is charged with cautiously foreseeing what benefit and danger can arise from each matter. Therefore Moses signifies discernment, Aaron devotion, Samuel circumspection. It belongs to discernment to regulate morals, to devotion to supplicate God, and to circumspection to provide against what is coming.

If, therefore, you find your life discerning in action, devout in prayer, and provident in circumspection, then you may also say with the prophet: “Moses and Aaron,” etc. For since it belongs to priests to form the people by precepts and make God propitious through prayers, it is clear that without discernment and devotion—as though without Moses and Aaron—they cannot fulfil the office of their priesthood. And when Samuel makes them fearful concerning future things, he renders them devout in prayer and assiduous in invocation of God.

## TITLE XLII. On the seven rivers of Egypt—that is, the vices of the world—and on the fly—that is, the soul infected by them—and the whistle of God by which it is torn away from them; and on the bee—that is, the hypocrite—also driven away by the Lord; and on the twofold land, good and evil
On that day the Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the farthest end of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria; and they will come and all rest in the torrents of the valleys and in the hollows of the rocks (Isa. VII). Egypt is the world, wrapped in the darkness of error, sin, and ignorance. In Egypt there are seven rivers from one spring; in the world, seven vices from the single root of pride. “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” Though they come from one source, they are nevertheless of different colour, and inflict destruction in different ways.

The first river is vainglory: bright, pleasing through a kind of superficial gleam, yet suddenly drawing the unwary into itself and drowning them. The second river, envy, is livid, suspect because of a certain dreadful depth. The third, anger, is hot and turbulent. The fourth, sadness, is gloomy and clouded, altogether dangerous. The fifth, avarice, is a rapacious Scylla or Charybdis, drawing everything to itself, swallowing and engulfing it. The sixth, gluttony, is a kind of abyss and gulf, producing from itself foul vapours and corruptions. The seventh, lust, is muddy and viscous.

Therefore the fly is our soul: restless, filthy, and shameless, which, wandering about, stings this person, stains that one, corrupts another with the poison of malice—just as a fly, restless, filthy, and wanton, is troublesome and hateful to all wherever it settles, stings, or stains. And this fly, moving out from the spring of pride and running through all the rivers, comes to the river of lust, which is the last river of this Egypt. After it has passed through all the rivers of vices, our fly is caught, takes pleasure, becomes filthy, and is so entangled that neither threats, nor promises, nor blows, nor preaching or exhortation can move it from there. It could more easily be killed than torn away; nor indeed is it ever torn away except by the whistle of God.

This whistle is the sweet, pleasant, gentle inspiration of the Holy Spirit. If, therefore, the merciful Lord deigns to whistle to the fly and to pour in the grace of compunction, it cannot be held in the river. Thanks be to God, who has not driven even such flies from his mercy: “[he] has mercy on all, and hates nothing that he has made,” because he is kind and merciful, etc. [Col. 0720C]

He whistles also to the bee that is in the land of Assyria. Assyria is interpreted “lofty.” This is the devil, the head of pride; his land is accursed. But there is another land, blessed: “You have blessed, O Lord, your land” (Ps. LXXXIV). God commands his clouds to rain upon it; and it, receiving the rain, brings forth the green herb of devotion, nourished by good waters. But the accursed land produces thorns and thistles: “Cursed is the earth in your work,” etc. (Gen. III). This is the land of Assyria.

In it dwell bees—that is, hypocrites—who, like bees, have honey in their mouths but a sting in their tails. Of them the Lord thus complains: “They surrounded me like bees” [Col. 0720D] (Ps. CVII). The Jews come with the Herodians, saying, “Master, we know that you are true,” etc. (Matt. XXII). See how they form honeycombs and gather honey; but because they seek to catch him in speech, they have a sting in their tail. Of them the prophet says: “They speak peace with their neighbour” (Ps. XXVII). Here is honey in the mouth; but evil is in their hearts—here is the sting in the tail.

Therefore the bee dwelling in the land of Assyria is the hypocrite, dwelling with all his desires in the world. If, then, God whistles to this bee and to the fly, they will come by the steps of faith and love, and will rest in the hollows of the rocks—better than at the farthest end of the rivers of Egypt or in the land of Assyria—“because tribulation and distress [come] upon every soul that works evil” (Rom. II). For the end of that repose is occupied by mourning.

## TIT. XLIII. What servants, hired labourers, and sons ought to offer to God

[Col. 0721A]

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII). As under the Law one sacrifice belongs to rulers, another to priests, another to the poor, so one offering is fitting for a son, another for a servant, another for a hired labourer.
