For the servant it is enough, through fear of Gehenna, to repent of evil deeds; for the hired labourer, to abstain from evil for the sake of a reward; for the son, it is too little merely to lay down his soul for the Lord who is his Father.

Repentance, therefore, belongs to servants; abstinence to hired labourers; patience is fitting for sons. If anyone, then, “is led as a sheep to the slaughter and does not open his mouth before the one shearing him,” he is numbered among the sons, who offer sons of rams. For the servant who is unequal to so great a sacrifice, it is enough to offer a turtledove or a dove, making satisfaction by weeping and groaning, as though with a dove’s song. The hired labourer, though he slaughters the kid of unruliness and affection lest he lose his pay, does not readily attain the burnt offering of the spotless Lamb.

If, therefore, you long for the adoption of sons, offer to the Lord lambs of patience. Yet he does not say “lambs,” but “sons of rams,” which amounts to the same thing: whenever we desire to possess perfect works, we should have recourse to the prophets and apostles, the leaders of the Lord’s flock; and if we strive to imitate and foster, duplicating in our own deeds and words, desires such as they had, we sacrifice sons of rams.

“Bring,” therefore—or “bring to the Lord”: *bring* is stated twice, so that the sacrifice may be doubled, for the twofold robe. For the robe of the body, bring to the Lord the sacrifice of good action; for the robe of the mind, the sacrifice of devout devotion. Whoever does not double the sacrifice will be crushed by a double crushing. For it has been said: “Do not fear those who kill the body and have nothing they can do to the soul” (Matt. X). And so they are lords of the earth, not the Lord. “Fear him; bring gifts to him who can send the soul also into Gehenna” (ibid.).

Bring bodies to the Lord; bring spirit to God. First, to God, because he rules in eternity; second, to the Lord, because he rules in time. He is Lord because he gives temporal goods or evils to whomever he wills; Lord again because he will give eternal rewards or torments to the one who has pleased him. Notice also the fitting distinction of words: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God.” As *God* expresses goodness, so *Lord* expresses power. This distinction sufficiently indicates that we are sons, that we render the service owed, and that the benefit is owed.

“Bring to the Lord glory and honour.” In the first verse *bring* is used twice: first for our own sake, second for our neighbours’ sake; first for merit, second for example. Since some neighbours are good and others evil, “bring to the Lord glory,” and do this for the good; “bring glory to his name,” for the evil. If the good see your good works—namely, that you offer sons of rams and possess works of gentleness—they praise God and strive to act in the same way. You have offered glory and honour to the Lord. For God is glorified by praises and honoured by works.

For the good, therefore, bring to the Lord glory; bring to God glory and honour. For the evil, who refuse to change, bring [glory] to his name, so that they may find nothing to reproach. Thus among the good you have offered to the Lord not only glory but honour: they glorify him by praise and honour him by works. Among the evil, at least bring glory to his name: they praise his discipline, though they do not keep it. [Col. 0722A]

## TIT. XLIV. What it is to worship in the court of the Lord

“Worship the Lord in his holy court” (Ps. XXVIII). Above we are commanded to offer sacrifices; here we are commanded to worship within. First, lest we enter empty-handed; second, lest we stand idle. If you have entered the cloister with the vow of profession and renunciation of yourself, you have entered the court with sacrifices. But if there you have kept the institutions of the Rule, and, for God’s sake, have been subject to every human creature—not only to the good and gentle but also to the difficult, not only to superiors but also to inferiors—then in all things you worship humbly in the court of the Lord.

For to worship is to prostrate the whole body, even down to the feet and the lowest members. Therefore, as beginners on the narrow way and entering the strait gate, enter with sacrifices. Once entered, worship in the habit of religion, in the vow of profession, and in the institutions of the Rule; in the house of discipline, obey all. [Col. 0722B]

## TIT. XLV. Of the cedars of Lebanon broken in the religious good man, and of the twofold calf

“The voice of the Lord breaking cedars; and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon,” etc. (Ps. XXVIII). It is difficult, almost impossible, for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle—for a heart swollen with pride to penetrate the narrowness of obedience. Yet this is impossible with human beings, not with God, who “has done whatsoever he willed,” not only “in heaven” but also “on earth”—that is, not only in those whose heart, their understanding, is bright and directed toward heaven and whose mind is firm on earth, but also “in the sea and in all abysses” (Ps. CXXXIV): namely, in those whose heart is bitter and unstable like the sea, whose mind is dark as an abyss.

He has done what he willed: at his sight and at the thunder of his voice he has shattered every mountain of arrogance, bent down the hills of pride, and cast the mighty from their seat, because his is the voice breaking cedars, even cedars of Lebanon. There are other cedars on other mountains. Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” The whitening of the saints is justification. Hence John says: “For fine linen is the sanctifications of the righteous” (Apoc. XIX). Hence the voice of the righteous: “I shall be made whiter than snow” (Ps. L). And the Lord’s [voice]: “If your sins should be [as scarlet]” (Isa. I).

When such whitening has grown into a mountain and begun to rise above others—when, that is, someone thinks himself great and holier than the rest—know that a cedar has arisen in Lebanon. But if you have only recently come from the world, and still boast and exalt yourself on that account because of your learning or wealth, the nobility of your birth, or the dignity of the rank you held, such exaltations are certain cedars, but they are not cedars of Lebanon: they rise from the blackness of vanity, not from the whitening of holiness.

If, at the beginning of your good way of life, the cedars of worldly pomp are diminished, it is the voice of the Lord breaking cedars. And if perhaps later—as commonly happens—after settled practices, certain cedars of great self-exaltation arise, as though from perfect observance, the Lord will add the breaking of those too, because “the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon.” For this reason he uses the present rather than the future concerning the former, saying “breaking cedars,” whereas concerning the cedars of Lebanon he uses the future, “and the Lord shall break the cedars of Lebanon.” [Col. 0723A]

It is added: “And he shall crush them like the calf of Lebanon” (Ps. XXVIII). Truly this is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI): to break down the stiffness of the cedar into the likeness of the calf of Lebanon, and to bend every swollen heart to the image of Christ’s humility. How was that unique Calf first crushed for our crimes, coming from Lebanon, from the shadowy and thick mountain—that is, from the highest heaven, where the brightness of eternal light shines? How, I ask, was he crushed? Though he was in the form of God, he was humbled by the immensity of crushing; for nothing is more bitter than the torment of the cross, nothing more shameful than death.

Let one who desires to be crushed like the calf of Lebanon hear how he ought to be bent: let him willingly endure the harshest and most contemptible things, even without fault. He came to do his Father’s will; you, do the will of your superior. Behold, we have found the calf that we must slaughter as a burnt offering to the Lord. Nothing burns more pleasingly for the Lord than the slaughter of the calf of one’s own will.

But it matters whether it is from Lebanon or from Carmel. Those who have not yet abandoned their own will in carnal matters feed the calf in the pastures of Carmel. He feeds the calf on the summit of Lebanon who follows his own will in spiritual matters. The person who seeks richer food and softer clothing than others fattens his calf with the hay of Carmel. The person who, wishing to abstain from permitted things, avoids eating what others eat and arrogates to himself a rougher habit, feeds his calf in the pastures of Lebanon. Each seeks pasture for his calf; but one takes it from Carmel, the other from Mount Lebanon.

For whatever is done because of violence of mind or tenderness of flesh belongs to Carmel, because Carmel is interpreted “soft” or “tender.” Whatever, as though for holiness, is presumptuously undertaken above the institution of the order or the advice of the superior is counted among the herds of Lebanon. “But woe to you who trust in the bond of Samaria” (Amos VI), serving your own will with such zeal. You have come into Judaea, where the calf of one’s own will is slaughtered for the Lord. Why have you gone down to Samaria, where the calf is worshipped as God, preserving and following your own will? Do you not know that Jews do not associate with Samaritans? At first, when you came from the world, you condemned your own will. Now you seek to become Samaritans from Jews.

If you are in Judaea, you kill the calf for God in sacrifice; if in Samaria, you serve your calf. For if you make provision for the flesh in its desires, you feed the calf on the hay of Carmel. “For all flesh is hay” (Isa. XL). See, however, how the law treats the flesh of this calf: it crushes it and reduces it to ashes in flames. First it is slaughtered, when singularity is renounced through love of obedience. It is divided into pieces, when each act of singularity is distinguished, until every arrogant will is put to sleep, with only the ash of thought remaining, by which the conscience, humbled through remembrance, may be put to shame and may fear more greatly.

## TIT. XLVI. Of the twofold fire, and the manifold purity figured by the three youths

[Col. 0724A]

“The voice of the Lord cutting off the flame of fire; the voice of the Lord shaking the wilderness” (Ps. XXVIII). One fire is that which the Lord came to cast upon the earth; another is that which he came to extinguish. He brought the first with him, coming from heaven; he found the second. Every love is a fire, but not every fire is good. Therefore good love is a good fire, which the Lord came to cast upon the earth so that it might burn (Lev. X). The love of lust is evil, which he came to extinguish.

Thus through Moses he forbids alien fire to be offered upon his altar; he commands that his own fire always burn on his altar; he continually extinguishes the flame of alien fire. Hence the Angel of the Lord came down and shook off the flame of fire (Dan. III). It is extinguished in the youths, who are so called from purity.

There is one purity of heart, another of speech, another of action. In the heart, simplicity; in the mouth, truth; in work, sincerity. We have these three youths when what we meditate is holy, what we say true, and what we do just. Most happy and pleasing to God is the fellowship of these three youths, because of their single harmony in purity—in will, speech, and action.

The king of Babylon sees them and envies them, and desires them to worship the bronze statue, while he persuades them to rise from their holiness into pride. For to worship the golden statue is to devote diligent effort and service to these things. When he sees that they despise it, he prepares flames, so that those whom he cannot conquer through the glory of self-exaltation, he may kill through the flame of lust. For the flame is kindled when our flesh is inflamed with the burning of lust.

But the Angel of the Lord shakes off the flame, and makes the midst of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew, when, through the Holy Spirit’s breath, he drenches the depths of the heart with heavenly dew; and the cooled conscience turns the tongue of the youths to the praise of the Creator. When they are delivered, the flame consumes the Chaldeans, because the burning of envy and Gehenna scorches those who lie in wait for innocence. [Col. 0724C]

## TIT. XLVII. Of the qualities of the stag that should be imitated

“The voice of the Lord preparing the stags, and he will reveal the thickets,” etc. (Ps. XXVIII). The stag is a swift, timid animal, hostile to serpents. In the agility of its feet, swiftness of actions is signified. Do you wish to see a stag running eagerly? “I ran the way of your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII). Do you wish to see the voice preparing for stag-like swiftness? “So run that you may obtain” (I Cor. IX). Do you wish to hear the voice of the mind leading to stag-like fearfulness? “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. XXVIII), because “the wise man fears in all things” (Ecclus. XVIII). Do you wish to hear the voice moving the stag to the killing of serpents? “Mortify your members which are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness,” etc. (Col. III).

These three, therefore, seem to belong to the stag: to run swiftly through the way of the commandments; to regard the snares of demons with suspicion; and boldly to destroy the poisons of vices. Ready, fearful, and righteous action makes stags: insofar as it is ready, it imparts swiftness; insofar as it is fearful, it is usefully fearful because it makes one cautious; insofar as it is righteous, it extinguishes the poisons of vices.

Many, in running swiftly, do not kill serpents but nourish them, because in their vigorous action pride, vainglory, and other serpents grow strong. Others have a good intention in good works and endeavour to mortify the serpent-poisons of vices; but because they do not know how to observe measure and time, they fall into the snares of demons as into hunters’ traps.

Therefore it is the voice preparing stags, according to that saying: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II); and that: “Serve the Lord in fear” (Ps. II). Therefore, that they may belong to the number of stags, they must both run swiftly and fear cautiously.

To such prepared stags he will reveal the thickets of the Scriptures, the depths of allegories, the shadowed mysteries of sacraments, the secrets of mysteries. And he will grant them rest in thick and shady mountains, where they will find hiding places against hunters’ snares and refreshment against the heat of the sun. For the higher they attain to the understanding of the Scriptures, the more safely and quietly they will hide, as it were, in thickets and rest in shade. [Col. 0725B]

## TIT. XLVIII. What stands at God’s right and what at his left, and what it is to be clothed in charity’s variety

“The queen stood at your right hand in a garment embroidered with gold, clothed round about with variety” (Ps. XLIV). The Lord of hosts, as the psalmist says, is himself “the King of glory” (Ps. XXIII). Hence David says: “The queen stood,” etc. Charity is rightly believed to be called the queen of virtues, because any virtue that does not serve charity loses the name of virtue.

At God’s left are temporal goods; at his right, eternal goods. Charity is therefore said to stand at the right, because it is fortified by eternal, not temporal, goods. For charity reigns only in those whom love of eternal things inflames. Thus charity the queen stands, but at the right hand and in a gold-embroidered garment. She wishes to please the eyes of the highest King, she who wishes to possess such precious garments.

The proof of charity is the performance of work. Good works are its garments. “In a garment,” he says, “embroidered with gold.” By the garment understand works of righteousness; by gold, the brightness of wisdom. Golden garments, therefore, are discerning works. Perhaps you do everything vigorously, but not gently, because not wisely. Thus you have garments indeed, but not the brightness of wisdom, because “Wisdom reaches from end to end mightily, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII)—from the end of beginning to the end of completion.

You begin vigorously; you finish lukewarmly. Why? Because you do not order all things sweetly and do not know how to act wisely. You begin, run, hurry, tire, and are deceived. I shall not say that you reach the end: you do not even reach the middle. Charity, therefore, proceeds—indeed, stands firm—never departing from God’s right hand, in a gold-embroidered garment, clothed round about with variety.

It is surely fitting that she, being a queen, have a manifold and varied garment. You, whoever you are, always wish to remain in contemplation; as I hear, you do not know how to clothe yourself with variety. Another continually seeks to remain in prayer and does not notice that charity wishes to be adorned with variety. Whoever wishes to be adorned so exclusively in one precious kind of work that pleases him that he despises another equally useful work does not possess the adornment of charity, which is clothed with variety. [Col. 0726A]

## TIT. XLIX. Of reproach and contempt

“Take away from me reproach and contempt” (Ps. CXVIII). Reproach is guilt; contempt, punishment. Guilt is iniquity; punishment, mortality. Through iniquity I have become reproachable; through mortality, contemptible. Desire makes me abominable; misery, worthless. “Take away from me reproach,” etc. If you make me righteous, take reproach away from me; take away contempt.

## TIT. L. Of the end of the earth from which clouds, lightning, and rain are brought forth

“Bringing forth clouds from the end of the earth, he made lightning for the rain,” etc. (Ps. CXXXIV). The ends of our earth are the lowest sins and abject deeds. From such an end a cloud is brought forth, because from the remembrance of our foulness a darkness of shame is generated. When a cloud of this kind overshadows the mind, it provides refreshment against the heat of desire, as against the blaze of the sun. For the person who remembers that he has sinned and is ashamed that he has sinned renders himself more cautious for the future in proportion as he grieves more over the past.

“He made lightning for the rain.” Before lightning the cloud is brought forth; after lightning, rain follows. The cloud is the darkness of shame; the lightning, the terror of majesty; the rain, the fruit of compunction. Therefore, by the ordered mercy of God, first the memory of our foulness is brought before the eyes of the mind; then the mind is shaken by fear through remembrance of divine terror; finally, caught between shame and fear and wearied for a long time, it is pierced into tears.

I have seen a cloud over myself whenever “the shame of my face covered me” (Ps. XLIII); I receive lightning when the terrors of the Lord wage war against me; rain descends whenever I have been able to drench my bed with tears. [Col. 0726C]

## TIT. LI. Of the firstborn of Egypt

“He struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to beast” (Ps. CXXXIV). The firstborn of Egypt are diabolical self-exaltations and human presumptions. Some are proud of temporal things; others swell with pride in spiritual matters. Truly brutish and animal-like is the understanding when a person made in God’s image, bereft of mind, swells with things held in common with beasts.

Some, therefore, are proud of vanity; others, of holiness. The pride of vanity is the firstborn of the beast. The arrogance of holiness is the firstborn of man. Egypt, moreover, is the darkness of error. Such darkness produces these firstborn. But when the breath of the divine Spirit blows, the firstborn of Egypt, from man to beast, are struck down, because, when the spirit of the fear of the Lord breathes, every swelling of self-exaltation is cast down. [Col. 0726D]

## TIT. LII. Of the womb, children, and breasts

“What will you give them? Give them a womb without children and dry breasts.” The womb is studiousness; the seed is truth; good will. You ought to read for this purpose; you ought to understand for this purpose: that you may strive to fulfil [what you learn]. You have a womb when you have the desire to learn. If you love the truth conceived [within you] and fulfil it in work, you nourish children. Who are these children? Good and ordered affections.

For what does divine Scripture teach except to love religion, preserve unity, and possess charity? Yet I see many diligent students, few religious persons. They love reading, not religion; indeed, through love of reading they fall into hatred of religion. In them is fulfilled what is said: “I will give them a womb without children.”

Those wishing to be teachers and preachers, and seeking the first chairs and greetings among the people, are given breasts—that is, dry words. Speech ought to be clear in exhorting or explaining obscure matters, and useful in persuading. These are, as it were, two breasts: one of exposition, the other of exhortation. Many receive these breasts swollen indeed, but dry: they acquire knowledge that puffs up, but lack charity that builds up. Their breasts swell through knowledge but are dry, because they lack the sweetness of the Spirit. And today we see very many with an inflated tongue, few with a honeyed tongue. [Col. 0727B]

## TIT. LIII. Of the breasts attributed to the bridegroom

“Your breasts are better than wine” (Cant. I). The bridegroom has two breasts: innate gentleness and long-suffering, by which he patiently awaits the offender and mercifully receives the penitent. This twofold sweetness of pleasantness is in the breast of the Lord Jesus: long-suffering in waiting, and readiness in giving.

Would you see the breast of long-suffering? Hear the Apostle: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and long-suffering and patience? Do you not know that his kindness leads you to repentance?” (Rom. II). For this purpose he long delays the sentence of vengeance against one who despises him, so that at some time he may pour the grace of forgiveness into the penitent. For he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live (Ezek. XVIII).

Take an example also from the other breast, which is readiness to forgive. For it is written concerning it: “At whatever hour the sinner groans” (ibid.). It is also written: “Let the wicked man forsake his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him; and to our God, because he is abundant in forgiving” (Isa. LV). David beautifully comprehends both in few words, saying: “Long-suffering and very merciful” (Ps. CII). [Col. 0727C]

## TIT. LIV. Of chaste and pure thanksgiving to God, as to the spring from which all good things must be referred back

[Col. 0727D]

The Lord Jesus is the source of rivers and springs, the sea of virtues and knowledges; for, according to the song of Hannah, “The Lord is the God of knowledges” (I Kings II), giving chaste counsels, just judgments, and right desires. The streams of that spring are purity of heart, continence of flesh, and purity of speech. They flow from this source so that the rivers of graces may return to the place from which they issue, “that they may flow again” (Eccles. I).

Therefore let the heavenly outpouring be sent back to its own source. Let spiritual streams be returned to their proper fountain without deceit and without interruption, so that they do not cease to water the fields of minds and may be poured back again into the breasts. “How?” you ask. Hear the Apostle: “Giving thanks in all things” (Eph. V), so that whatever wisdom, virtue, and grace you have, you may attribute the whole to God’s power and God’s wisdom.

But not every thanksgiving is acceptable to God; only that which is chaste and pure. I call it chaste because of those who, glorying in their evils, are accustomed, when they have committed theft, murder, or adultery, to give thanks to God, as though God rejoiced in their conduct when they do evil and exulted, as they do, in most wicked acts. Such a person will hear: “You wickedly thought that I should be like you,” etc. (Ps. XL).

I call it pure because of hypocrites, who indeed glorify God verbally for their goods, but act deceitfully: “their iniquity is found unto hatred” in God’s sight. The former impiously turn their evils toward God; the latter fraudulently turn God’s goods toward themselves. Their voice is: “Our lips are our own” (Ps. XI). But what is your tongue except “the pen of a scribe” (Ps. XLIV)? You received even this on loan, to be demanded back from you with interest.

If you are found energetic in work and faithful in rendering back, you will receive the reward for your labour and hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant: because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many,” etc. (Matt. XXV). Otherwise you will be called a wicked and slothful servant. The praise is not the pen’s, but belongs to the writing well traced by it; nor is a good discourse the glory of tongue or lips, but of the mind—and of the God who gave it. [Col. 0728B]

## TIT. LV. Of the threefold cord

“A threefold cord,” “which is not quickly broken” (Eccles. IV), for drawing souls out of the devil’s prison and, after drawing them back, into the heavenly kingdoms, is to serve rightly, to speak profitably, and to fulfil effectively. [Col. 0728C]

## TIT. LVI. Funeral oration and lament for the death of a prudent and religious friend

“Grief commands much sadness” (Job VI). In my balance grief outweighs all, and the calamity that I suffer burns my sad breast like fire. Enclosed sorrow feeds upon my inward parts, spreads more widely, and rages more fiercely. What have I to do with joy, who am in bitterness? The force of sorrow carries away every joy. The indignation of the Lord has drained my spirit, taking away him whom my soul loved, and at the same time because my heart has abandoned me.

Why have you been torn away from me? Why have you been snatched from my hands, man of one mind with me, man according to my heart? Most bitter separation, and such as only death could accomplish. This is death’s work: so dreadful a divorce. Death, enemy of all sweetness, in snatching one away furiously kills two. You would have deprived me more gently, O harsh death, of the use of life than of its fruit, without which life itself is heavier than death.

For a brother in the flesh, if he loses dear ones, finds others dearer. But upon me, O death, your wrath has passed; your fury has been established over me, for you have removed friend and neighbour far from me. His presence was pleasant to us both, our companionship sweet, our conversation delightful. Yet I have lost so great delights belonging to us both; you have altered them beyond measure. And indeed, amid things altered, abundant requital meets me wherever I look: I turn to the dear place where I was accustomed [to find him], and he is not there.

Alas! How greatly I groan there, like a man without help. Whom shall I consult hereafter in uncertainties? To whom shall I entrust myself in adversities? Who will carry our burdens? Who will drive back the dangers that threaten? Moreover, my sorrow is multiplied above the snow. Shall I live? How long shall I live? And if I live long, I shall live in bitterness; I shall live in sorrow; I shall live in mourning. Shall I not spare myself and aid the hand of the Lord? For “the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX), when it cut him down; nor did it tell me that it would cut down the vine it had planted.

There I lie, a wretched portion in the mud, cut off from my own better part. It is useless to say to me, “Do not feel it.” For I feel it even unwillingly, since “the strength of stones is not my strength”—nor indeed is my sinew of horn—“nor is my flesh of bronze.” I feel it wholly and grieve: “and my sorrow is ever before me.”

The Lord struck me with the rod of his indignation: deservedly according to my merits, harshly beyond my strength. For my right hand, the light of my eyes, my breast, my tongue, have been cut off. In him, indeed, I worked, provided, perceived, and spoke; for “his mouth meditated wisdom and his tongue spoke judgment.” Now he, as I hope, enjoys everlasting glory according to his merits; and I, according to my deserts, have been left in this common misery. I have spoken. [Col. 0729B]

## TIT. LVII. Of the hunter and the snare of souls, and of the harsh word to monks

“He delivered me from the snare of hunters, and from the harsh word” (Ps. XC). Since “man, being in honour, did not understand: he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII), the hunter—the most cunning and wicked devil—has stretched out a snare for him. He spreads snares openly enough for worldly people who are wild and altogether beastlike, because he does not doubt that they are easily captured.

But for you, who are wiser like stags, kill serpents, and desire to flee to the living spring, he conceals subtler snares. Therefore, O new plantations, who do not yet have the senses of your hearts trained, do not abound in your own judgment; but humble yourselves beneath the mighty hand of your shepherd. Submit to the counsels of him who knows better the tricks of that hunter, lest the crafty hunter deceive you as inexperienced and unwary persons.

But we already know the hunters and the beasts. Let us hear what the snare is. Tell us, blessed Paul—you who are not ignorant of his devices—what is this snare? “Those who wish,” he says, “to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (I Tim. VI). Therefore the snares of the devil are the riches of this world. Alas for me, how few there are who wish to be set free from this snare! How many grieve that they are too little entangled in it!

But you who “have left all things and followed him who has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. XIX; Luke IX), rejoice and say: “He delivered me from the snare of hunters, and from the harsh word.” Beast, if you do not fear the snare, fear the hammer—that is, the harsh word: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). It is hard to repent, so that those who hear, “Repent” (Matt. III), say, “This saying is hard” (John VI). But if they reflect on this harsh word, they will find that “the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light” (Matt. XI).

But you who are winged, “before whose eyes the net is cast in vain” (Prov. I), slaughter whatever beast is in you; strip off its hide, lest at some time, when the hunter has caught the beast, he cry: “Take it away, take it away; put it on spits; bring it to the coals; bring it to the cauldrons.” For if you have been freed from the snare, you will not fear the harsh word.

Therefore hold your poverty more precious than the riches of this age, and from your labour feed and clothe Christ, so that on that day you may rejoice in thanksgiving and say: “He delivered me from the snare of hunters, and from the harsh word.”

## TIT. LVIII. Of the four kinds of sheep, their fold, and the fourfold guarding of the flesh
We are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand (Ps. [Col. 0730B] 94). There are four kinds of sheep: weak, pregnant, wandering, and strong. These are beginners, those making progress, those who stray, and the perfect. Each needs its own food: beginners, instruction, that they may progress further; those making progress, admonition, that they may reach the summit; those who stray, correction, that they may cast off sin; the strong, exhortation, that they may serve the crown. For these, as it were, a cloistered enclosure ought to be maintained: it is in some manner four-sided, like a cloister, so that individuals may not be excluded from their own proper spheres, but be content with their bounds. On the first side there shall be school-like submission, that humility may arise; on the second, moral reading, that discernment may be sharpened; on the third, spiritual correction, that wickedness may be uprooted; on the fourth, spiritual meditation, that truth may be known.

[Col. 0730C] Finally, a dog is necessary—that is, vigilance and the fourfold guard of the shepherd—so that, as a dog drives away wolves and thieves by barking, so the prelate may by threats forbid the devil and vices to draw near. As a dog makes itself its own physician with its tongue, so, if one has transgressed, let one heal oneself by confession of the tongue. As a hunting dog senses game from afar, so let one, by the power of faith, hope for life after death. And as a dog faithfully clings to its master, so let one not separate oneself from the unity of faith even unto death.

### TITLE LIX. On Solomon’s loaves, and the twofold love, evil and good.

There are three loaves of Solomon: contempt for the world, contempt for oneself, and love of God. He sets forth the first in Ecclesiastes, [Col. 0730D] the second in Proverbs, the third in the Song of Songs. For there are two evils which alone wage war most fiercely against the soul: namely, vain love of the world and excessive self-love; the first two loaves are known to oppose these two most evil things. But because there is one sole supreme good, which the bride desires to enjoy and embrace—namely God, the bridegroom—this is known to be broken in the third, that is, in the songs. Therefore, in the first we are taught, for our refreshment, to despise the vanity of this world; in the second, to know and follow the truth, namely to follow the Lamb wherever he goes; in the third, to enjoy the truth and attain him himself. And this is the fruit of the first two. When the friend who has come from the road has taken this third loaf, he will have nothing of which to complain. But who will break it?

[Col. 0731A] The master of the household is present, the Lord to be recognized in the breaking of bread (Luke 24). Let the poor and needy person knock at him, because he opens and shuts the door against no one.

### TITLE LX. On the threefold ointment of the good.

There are three kinds of ointment: that of contrition, devotion, and mercy. The first is pungent and produces pain; the second moderating and soothing pain; the third healing and driving out disease. The first is prepared by a soul entangled in many crimes, when it begins to consider its ways, so that it may gather, heap together, and crush in the little mortar of its conscience the many and various kinds of sins. Then, wonderfully boiling over, the sinner’s pot cooks all these together with a certain fire of sorrow and repentance, so that it may say: “My heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation a fire shall blaze” (Ps. [Col. 0731B] 38).

The second is prepared by a soul inflamed with many gifts of virtues, when holy devotion recalls the benefits of God with joy and thanksgiving, crushes them in the vessel of the breast with the pestle of frequent meditation, cooks them with the fire of holy longing, and then enriches them with the oil of gladness. Then it sings and understands in the undefiled way, so that it may say: “I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100).

The pious soul of a human being prepares the third for itself from the needs of the poor, the troubles of the sorrowful, the faults of offenders, and finally from all human miseries—even if they belong to enemies—because the person who has mercy and lends is pleasing to God (Ps. 112). Such a person is inclined to compassion, ready to help, easy to forgive, slow to anger and to take vengeance. Thus, having become all things to all, he becomes to himself [Col. 0731C] like a broken vessel, that he may be ready both to meet and to aid others. Finally, dead to himself in order that he may live, he takes care to enrich and anoint every sort of person, pouring upon the aforesaid needs of his neighbours, as with a certain spice, the oil of mercy, and cooking them with the ardour of charity; so that of such a brother, in the congregation of the saints, with a finger pointed at him, it may be said: “This is one who loves his brethren and the people of Israel; this is one who prays much for the people and for all the holy city” (2 Macc. 15).

With the first ointment the feet of Jesus are anointed; with the second, his head; with the third, his whole body, by good women. Jesus is called the head and bridegroom; the Church is called the body and bride. In it are good and evil persons: the breast signifies the good, the feet the evil; the body signifies both good and evil; but the head is God. Therefore the woman—[Col. 0731D] that is, the sinful soul—anoints these feet (Luke 7), by grinding wickedness in the mortar of the heart. The justified soul anoints the head, giving thanks and attributing to its head, that is, to God and not to itself, the benefits bestowed upon it. The pious woman anoints Jesus himself—that is, the whole body—by exercising her charity, bodily and spiritually, even toward enemies.

Although the first ointment is offered to the feet as to the extreme members, it is nevertheless not vile, since it was said of it: “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” (John 12). For it is a fragrance of life unto life. Although the penitent is said to be in the whole Church, so that the scent of the penitent reaches not only the earthly but also the heavenly Church; for Truth himself testifies that joy arises among the angels over one sinner doing repentance (Luke 15).

[Col. 0732A] We find the ingredients of this ointment in our own little gardens. For who does not have at hand, from his own resources, iniquities and sins, if he does not conceal them? But if the spices—that is, God’s benefits—have been received from afar and from the uttermost bounds, this is because “every good gift and every perfect donation is from above” (James 1). This ointment is the sacrifice of which it is said: “A sacrifice of praise shall honour me” (Ps. 49). Therefore this ointment is not that of a poor person: indeed, because such a person does not judge the venerable head unworthy to be touched, he judges it a mark of honour.

The third is preferred to these two; for it is healing, and concerning it the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). Therefore with it not merely the feet, nor merely the head, but also the whole body is anointed. Thus the first is good, the second better, the third best. For when the disciple said, “Why this waste?” (John 12), the Lord said: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work upon me” (ibid.).

Yet it may be said that this ointment signifies the preceding two. For when someone thought able to benefit many nevertheless lives only for himself, and, seated at the feet in recollection of sins, progresses toward the head in recollection of benefits, he is called to benefit and preside over others: what else is said but, “Why this waste? This ointment could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” But when such a person refuses the burden, and the Lord rejoices with him in such a calling, it is said: “Why do you trouble this woman? A good work,” etc. As if he said: “Not a man, as you suppose, [Col. 0732C] able to put his hands to mighty things; but let the woman remain in this good until she grows strong enough for what is better.”

### TITLE LXI. On the four ointments in whose fragrance the bride runs.

“We will run after the fragrance of your ointments,” etc. (Song 1). There are four ointments in whose fragrance our bride runs: the first, wisdom; the second, righteousness; the third, sanctification; the fourth, redemption. These four the bridegroom was made by God for humankind, as the Apostle says: “Who was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1). Wisdom is in preaching; righteousness in the absolution of sins; sanctification in the manner of life which he maintained among sinners; redemption in the passion which he endured for sinners. You see a fourfold [Col. 0732D] anointing.

### TITLE LXII. On God’s fourfold benefit toward us: illumination, justification, teaching, and redemption.

You sat in darkness and the shadow of death, bound by chains of offences through ignorance of truth; and the Teacher of truth came down to you and drove away the shadow of your ignorance by the light of his wisdom. Then, through the righteousness which is from faith, he loosed the bonds of sins, freely justifying sinners; and in these two respects “the Lord looses those in bonds; the Lord enlightens the blind.” He added sanctification: living holy among sinners, he handed down a pattern of life and a path by which a human being might return to the fatherland. He also joined redemption: [Col. 0733A] he delivered his soul to death and brought forth from his own side the price of sanctification, by which he might appease the Father, so that you might know that “with God there is mercy, and with him plentiful redemption” (Ps. 129).

### TITLE LXIII. On the three arrows to be sought.

There are three arrows: fear, the word of God, and charity. The first is sought by him who says: “Pierce my flesh with your fear” (Ps. 118). Of the second the Apostle says: “It is more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4). The third is she who was wounded when she said: “Sustain me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2). By the first arrow the pleasures of the flesh are pierced through; by the second the vices of the soul are slain; by the third every vice [Col. 0733B] or harmful thing is shaken from the soul itself. Then that peace of God which surpasses all understanding is attained (Phil. 4), and it brings it about that that in which the carnal sense consists no longer gives delight.

### TITLE LXIV. On the four temptations of one converted to the Lord.

“You shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying in darkness, the business that walks by day, and the noonday demon” (Ps. 90). These touch the four kinds of temptations experienced and still experienced by one converted to the Lord: terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business walking in darkness, and the noonday demon.

For the first beginnings of one converted are assailed by fear: terror of life and the austerity of an unfamiliar discipline. Hence it is said: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2). This fear is called nocturnal, either because night customarily signifies adversities, or because the purpose for which we undertake adversities is not yet revealed. For if that day shone by whose light labours and rewards were seen, there would be no fear of labours because of the desire for rewards, since “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). But because it is night, we are tempted by nocturnal fear in enduring things that appear adverse. Therefore those who are first entering must pray and watch against this temptation, lest suddenly overtaken by faint-heartedness of spirit and the storm of night, they recoil from the good they have begun.

When this has been overcome, [Col. 0733D] one must arm oneself against the arrow flying by day, which is the report of empty glory. It flies because it is light; and it is by day because it comes from works of light. But this is easily overcome as a breeze of vain glory. Third comes the business walking in darkness. One must fear it by day—that is, hypocrisy—and therefore the person who does not care for praise must take care not, being circumvented by the business that walks both by day and in darkness, to seek riches and dignities. For this business trades at every time, retaining a form of piety and claiming for itself a hidden virtue in order to purchase honours and prelacies. This business walks by day because it has the appearance of virtue and feigns virtue; but in reality it is in darkness, because its dwelling in darkness conceals what it is, and lies about what it is not.

[Col. 0734A] But whoever has overcome such favours and honours is finally tempted by the noonday demon: by him who transforms himself into a noonday being, that is, into an angel of light, while he is truly a demon and an angel of darkness. Joshua, suspecting deceit, did not accept the angel as a friend before he knew that he was a friend (Josh. 5). Likewise, when the disciples, tossed by storms, saw the Lord walking on the sea, they diminished the Lord’s power and mercy by open suspicion, thinking him a phantom (Matt. 14). Thus he came in the fourth watch of the night, urging that one should keep watch in the fourth place against this temptation. But you, O human being converted, according to the prophet, “shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the business walking in darkness, the assault and [Col. 0734B] noonday demon” (Ps. 90), if the truth of the Lord surrounds you with the shield of his protection and good will.

### TITLE LXV. On the two impulses of spirit and flesh.

“The rush of lightning gladdens the city of God,” etc. (Ps. 45). There are two impulses, one of the spirit and the other of the flesh. The first belongs to the blessed; the second to the wicked. The impulse of the flesh drives the mind toward hatred, anger, outward glory, and pleasure; the impulse of the spirit draws the mind toward charity, patience, faith in eternal things, and tears of contrition. Therefore one must take great care to consider which impulse leads us away from our thought. For when by an impulse we are driven to love earthly things, seek vengeance upon an enemy, or request temporal things not for necessity but for pleasure and excess, this is an impulse of the flesh.

[Col. 0734C] Conversely, to love heavenly things, forgive those who offend us, love enemies for God’s sake, and seek temporal things for necessary use, is an impulse of the spirit. Hence it is said of the holy living creatures: “Where the impulse of the spirit was, they went” (Ezek. 1). And because they tend toward good in such a way as not to return to evil, it is rightly added: “They did not turn back when they went” (ibid.). For one who has gone out from Egypt ought not in mind to return to the pots of Egypt. Yet the same prophet says that they “went and returned in the likeness of flashing lightning” (ibid.). For there is a twofold movement of the righteous: from evil to good, in which movement there ought to be no backward step; and from active good to contemplative good, from which there is a return to the active life in the likeness [Col. 0734D] of flashing lightning, striking vices and setting people ablaze with the love of God; for lightning strikes and burns.

### TITLE LXVI. On Job’s three daughters.

Job has three daughters: Day, Cassia, and the third named Cornustibii. These signify the human race, created, redeemed, and taken up again by Christ. For it was Day in its first creation, because it was created in innocence. But when the day of innocence was ended by sin and hidden in the night of sorrow, it became Cassia in the second, redemption; for it is bitter, like cassia, to be redeemed from vice through confession and mortification of the body. Therefore, that it may be restored to salvation, it must be given a bitter draught, but one fragrant with the fragrance of virtue through the grace of the Redeemer.

But because, thirdly, in the actual resumption of the flesh through Christ’s resurrection, we shall receive our renewed nature into eternal praise, the third daughter is called Cornustibii: in this name the song of those who rejoice is expressed. There our Creator receives the true songs of his praises, he who by creating made the human race Day, by redeeming it Cassia, and by taking it up Cornustibii. For we who were created light and day, and were redeemed Cassia, shall someday be Cornustibii, taken up into the exaltation of eternal praise.

### TITLE LXVII. On the door and windows of Noah’s ark.

There are two exits from Noah’s ark: one through the window, the other through the door. The window signifies an exit through thought; the door, an exit through action. The door is below and the window above, because action pertains to the [Col. 0735B] body and thought to the soul. Hence birds were sent out through the window, while humans and beasts went out through the door, which the Lord shut and opened. But man opened the window, because it is more grievous to sin in deed and thought than in thought alone.

### TITLE LXVIII. On the four ways of going out through action and the same number through thought.

One goes out through action in four ways. First, for the use of pleasure: these are unclean animals. Second, for the use of necessity: these too are animals, but clean. Third, for the care of government by the command of obedience: these are Noah’s sons, who, when he went out, offered sacrifice. Fourth, for the same care out of ambition, despising others: these were like Ham, who mocked his father’s shame.

There are four ways of going out through thought. First, by considering what one is from oneself; second, what one is by the Creator’s gift; third, how God uses creatures, speaking through these three voices: “Receive, repay, flee.” Receive the benefit, repay the debt, flee punishment. The first voice is that of one serving; the second, of one warning; the third, of one threatening. The earth, water, air, and fire say in the first voice: “Receive me as a benefit”; in the second: “Repay praise for the benefit”; in the third: “By me you shall be swallowed, burned, engulfed, drowned.” For whoever receives God’s benefits and does not return thanks shall deservedly suffer these things.

Fourthly one goes out through thought when one considers not the aid of necessity but the pleasure of lust. These are like Eve, who [Col. 0735D] saw that the tree was beautiful, etc., and like the raven, because it did not return to the ark of conscience. The first three are like the dove, which, sent out the first time, returned and brought nothing back; the second time returned and brought an olive branch; the third time did not return to the ark, but remained in the place purged by God from the waters.

From the first consideration it brings contempt for the world, because, after the world was despised and covered by the waters of the flood—that is, of pleasure—it returned to the ark. From the second, praise of God, because it brought an olive branch as a sign of peace. Peace is joined to God’s glory when the angels sing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace,” etc. (Luke 2). From the third, both love and fear of God, because it neither wished nor dared to depart from him any further. But from the fourth, if it should return, it brings an incentive to lust.

### TITLE LXIX. On the two girdles in the Old Testament.

[Col. 0736A]

We read of two girdles in the Old Testament. The leather girdle binds the loins; the golden girdle constrains the breasts. Elijah, girded with a leather girdle about the loins, is fear restraining the flesh from lust. The golden girdle about the breasts is love of virtue restraining the heart from lustful pleasure. This is the girdle of fear, which does not extend pardon but binds punishment; the golden girdle is where hidden pleasure is castrated in the heart. “Whoever looks,” he says, “upon a woman in order to lust after her,” etc. (Matt. 5). He is girded with the leather girdle who crucifies the flesh with its vices and lusts, who says: “Pierce me with your fear,” etc. (Ps. 117 [118]). He is bound with the golden girdle whose heart is not defiled by a foul thought, who has made a covenant with his eyes not even to think of a virgin (Job [Col. 0736B] 31).

He sought both who said: “Burn my loins and my heart” (Ps. 25 [26]): the flesh, against the flow of lust; the mind, against the passion of pleasure. If the leather girdle is torn, it is mended with thread and needle. The thread in the needle is almsgiving, which he performs with his hand together with the needle—that is, with repentance, which pricks.

### TITLE LXX. On the four mountains.

There are four kinds of mountains. Mounts Gilboa, where Saul’s sword is repelled: these are strong men in the Church, in whom the devil’s snares are repelled. The mountains of Israel, which stretch far abroad: these are the apostles, whose sound has gone out into all the earth. The mountains of Samaria, which rise into the air: these are heretics, who set their mouth in heaven. The fourth are the mountains of the world, concerning which the prophet says: “The everlasting mountains are broken” (Hab. 3). They are the rich and powerful of the world, whose powers are crushed in many ways.

### TITLE LXXI. On Pharaoh’s four bonds and four harmful garments.

There are four bonds of Pharaoh by which he binds the soul: luxury in stench, pride in fury, envy in pallor, avarice in heat. And, in order that this woman may not differ from Egyptian women, he clothes her in four garments like his own: the evil incentive of evil intention, through deliberation; the stumbling-block of evil action, through performance; the prison-house of evil habit, through display; the peril of evil expectation, through despair.

When the bridegroom wishes to raise her from these bonds, he says: “Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion” (Isa. 52). Then, if at his voice the bride says, “O God, attend to my help” (Ps. 69 [70]), the bridegroom is at hand and bursts the bonds, opposing to each its contrary: purity of bodily cleanness against luxury; the grace of spiritual innocence against pride; the truth of generous speech against envy; the practice of active righteousness against avarice. Once freed by these, she gives thanks, saying: “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. 115 [116]): blessed be God in his gifts.

### TITLE LXXII. On garments against harmful garments.

The bridegroom, drawing away the Egyptian garments for a blessing, applies their opposites: first, the holy affection of pious devotion in longing, against the evil incentive of evil intention; second, the holy progress of sacred religion in practice, against the stumbling-block of evil action; third, the holy effect of perfected virtue in unceasing study, against the prison-house of evil habit; fourth, the holy fruit of eternal blessedness by hereditary right, against the peril of evil expectation. Adorned with these, the bride says: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113 [115]). Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.

Immediately the bridegroom, holding her right hand, led her into the chamber of his mother; kindly placing his left hand beneath her head, he embraced her with his right and said: “You are wholly beautiful, bride; [beautiful, you are beloved], my beloved, and there is no stain in you” (Song 4).

### TITLE LXXIII. On the two spurs.

[Col. 0737B]

There are two spurs with which the prophet Balaam urges his she-ass: shame, lest it be defiled temporally; fear, lest it be tormented eternally.

### TITLE LXXIV. On the fourfold ordering of the house.

“Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live” (Isa. 38). This admonition was particular and given once to Hezekiah; it is general and daily for every faithful soul; and it is special and annual at this season of Lent. Hezekiah, being proud and not sick, is told to set his house in order by providing himself a successor, because, unless he repents, he will die in death. In general, the Holy Spirit cries to each one of us: “Set your house in order; for unless you do so, you shall die the death of the soul, and after eternal death you shall not live”—that is, you shall not be recalled to life anew.

But especially at this season of Lent it is said to each of us: “Set your house in order to receive Christ, to eat his flesh and blood worthily; for if you receive unworthily, you shall die the death, eating judgment to yourself.” For at this season the house must be cleansed and set in order: this is the preparation for Easter. But one must see to which master of the household, and concerning which house, he speaks.

Certainly four houses are read of: the house of the devil, the house of a human being, the house of the mind, and the house of God. The house of the devil is the children of distrust, concerning which it is said: “I will return to my house from which I came out” (Matt. 12). But since that master of the household is hardened like a stone, speech or admonition is not directed to him.

[Col. 0737D] The house of a human being is made by hands and visible; the house of the mind is a rational creature; the house of the Lord is to reign forever. A human being inhabits his own house, the mind administers its house, the Lord illumines his. Of the human being’s house the steward of unrighteousness said: “When I have been removed from my stewardship, they may receive me into their house” (Luke 16). Of ordering this house it is not said, “Set your house in order”; rather it is said, “Go out”—as God says to Abraham—“from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12).

The house of the mind is the human being himself, to whom guardianship has been entrusted and discipline commanded. Of it it is said: “Three things drive a man from his house: smoke, dripping, and a bad wife” (Prov. 27): that is, the sin of ignorance, of suggestion, and of one’s own conscience. Such things do not permit reason to rule in its own house, but compel it to serve as a handmaid.

[Col. 0738A] But the house of God is the mind. Hence: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. 9). Thus, in a wonderful manner, the mind is the house both of God and of the human being. But it is superfluous to admonish this master of the household concerning the ordering of his own house. For “who has helped the Spirit of the Lord?” Therefore it is said to the mind: “Set your house in order.”

Let it therefore search the Scriptures, and it will find attendants appointed for its ordering: some outward attendants, appointed for outward matters; others inward, who always stand before its face. The outward attendants are the five bodily senses. Scripture teaches their ordering often and in many places: “Turn away my eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118 [119]). “Keep your tongue from evil” (Ps. 33 [34]). Stop your ears, lest they hear against your neighbour. Restrain your nostrils, lest they seek delight in foreign scents. Shut your hands, lest they receive gifts. Put the feet of the innocent in the fetters of wisdom, lest they run to shed blood.

[Col. 0738B] The inward attendants are four: joy, sorrow, hope, and fear. Sorrow is door-keeper; joy, steward; hope, cupbearer; fear, chamberlain. For of fear it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110 [111]). It guards two gates, and between them is a little door; these are closed against flies seeking to rush in toward the sweetness of ointment. The first gate is deprivation of the vision of God; the other, the fire which is not extinguished. The little door is the worm of conscience, which does not die (Isa. [Col. 0738C] 66). Therefore let fear oppose the rushing enemies and say: “You shall by no means enter, lest because of you it be deprived of the vision of God and tormented in eternal fire, lest it perish with its own conscience as witness and accuser.”

### TITLE LXXV. On the two priestly tribes.

There are two tribes, Levi and Judah, from which priests are taken: Aaron and Christ, and their succession. How this corresponds may be inferred from the interpretation of the names.

### TITLE LXXVI. On the fourfold office of priests.

The priestly office is fourfold: to sacrifice the living victim of the flesh, which belongs to Levi; to offer God the gifts of virtues, which is to burn spices and belongs to Aaron’s sons; to enter heaven with the ardour of martyrdom, which is to enter the Holy of Holies with blood; and to convey to heaven the vows of thanksgivings and prayers, which is to offer bread and wine to God.

### TITLE LXXVII. On the three loaves by which we are fed.

There are three loaves by which we are fed in this life: the purgative loaf with bitterness, which the woman of Zarephath serves in famine (3 Kings 7 [1 Kings 17]); the consoling loaf with sweetness, which the angel sets before one resting in the shade (3 Kings 19 [1 Kings 19]); and the solid loaf with strength, which brings one to Horeb, the mountain of God (ibid.).

### TITLE LXXVIII. On the three streams from the Lord’s body.

Three streams of salvation flowed from Jesus’ body: the word of sorrow, in which is confession; the blood of sprinkling, [Col. 0739A] in which is affliction; and the water of cleansing, in which is compunction.

### TITLE LXXIX. On the three pools of Scripture.

Three pools are found in Scripture: the antiquity of error, which is behind two walls; the sensuality of the flesh, into which the sick descended; and the keenness of reason, which is on the road of the fuller’s field. In these sheep are watered and burnt offerings washed.

### TITLE LXXX. On the three fuels of fire.

There are three fuels of fire within us: straw of unclean thought, hay of perverse speech, and wood of unlawful action. These nourish us for the fire unless they are extinguished by higher fountains.

### TITLE LXXXI. On the three windows of contemplatives.

There are three windows of contemplatives: the originating one, [Col. 0739B] which faces east; the governing one, which turns south; and the consummating one, which looks west.

### TITLE LXXXII. On the four fountains of paradise.

Four fountains water the Lord’s garden: lamentation for one’s own guilt, which circles the land of Ethiopia; compassion for a brother’s transgression, which goes toward the Assyrians; consideration of bestowed grace, which cuts through the midst of Babylon; and the longing affection of charity, which circles the whole land of Ejulath [Havilah?]. These fountains have lower and upper irrigation, possessing waters of sea, spring, and snow.

### TITLE LXXXIII. On the three doors to life.

There are three doors through which one passes to life: the truth of faith, [Col. 0739C] after Sarah laughs; the firmness of hope, which is in the side of the ark; and the solidity of charity, which the cherub guards with a flaming sword.

### TITLE LXXXIV. On the threefold wine in the Lord’s cup.

The wine in the Lord’s cup is threefold: red in the long-suffering of the saints, which gladdens Isaac in sickness; white in the reward of the righteous, by which Noah is made drunk; black and sour in the condemnation of the wicked, which Jesus tasted but did not wish to drink.

### TITLE LXXXV. On the threefold garment of priests.

The garment which the priest ought to use is threefold: the coarseness of outward work, with which Aaron is clothed before the people; the condition of spiritual holiness, which Rebecca keeps hidden with herself, and which Aaron uses in [Col. 0739D] the tabernacle; and the beauty of contemplative sweetness, which is seamless, and which Jesus uses.

### TITLE LXXXVI. On the three tunics of religious persons.

There are three tunics with which we are clothed: the chastening subjugation of the body, which is of skin and clothes Adam; the length of steadfast perseverance, by which Joseph is recognized as beloved; and the abundance of rewarding grace, with which Jesus is clothed.

### TITLE LXXXVII. On the six wings of the Seraphim.

The Seraphim has six wings: two for the feet, shame for past things and dread of future things; two at the sides, by which it flies, fear pressing downward and hope lifting upward; and two for the head, humility advancing it and charity perfecting it.

### TITLE LXXXVIII. On the Lord’s two thrones.

[Col. 0740A]

God has two thrones: angelic substance, which is the high throne; and human nature, which is the exalted throne.

### TITLE LXXXIX. On the four feathers of the living creatures.

The four living creatures have four feathers: fear and repentance, which cover the body; love and hope, which are joined together and fly.

### TITLE XC. On the six wings of the animals of the new law.

The living creatures of the new law possess six wings: natural prompting, legal institution, prophetic affirmation, evangelical ordinance, apostolic command, and ecclesiastical custom.

### TITLE XCI. On the twofold house of God.

There are two houses of God: the external curiosity that ministers to things, [Col. 0740B] which is the tabernacle over which the glory of the Lord appears and departs; and devoted simplicity, free for and serving God, which is the temple, and is not removed from it.

### TITLE XCII. On the twofold ark of the old law.

There are two arks in the old law: the text of literal history, which contains human beings and beasts; and the spiritual sense of conscience, which contains manna and Aaron’s rod.

### TITLE XCIII. On the threefold chariot in Scripture.

Three chariots are found in Scripture. The first is the exaltation of temporal power; its charioteer is the swelling of presumption and audacity, and it has as horse the strength of self-confidence. Its wheels are the headlong mobility of vanity [Col. 0740C] and the fortunate succession of prosperity. This is Pharaoh’s chariot, in which Rechab dies.

Next comes the height of conversion and life; its charioteer is the word of divine admonition, and it has as horse the vow of perseverance. Its wheels are the dreadful terror of torments and the marvellous delightfulness of rewards. This is the chariot in which the eunuch read with Philip (Acts 8).

Next comes the loftiness of contemplation and grace; its charioteer is love of the heavenly homeland, and it has as horse blessedness. Its wheels are rejection of worldly glory and reverence for divine majesty. This is the fiery chariot in which Elijah is caught up into heaven (4 Kings 2 [2 Kings 2]).

### TITLE XCIV. On the rivers in which sinners bathe.

There are two rivers in which sinners wash themselves: the flood of corruption and lust, and the plague of flattery and [Col. 0740D] deceit. These are the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus (4 Kings 5 [2 Kings 5]).

### TITLE XCV. On the rivers in which the righteous are washed.

There are two in which the righteous bathe: the assault of correction and reproach, and the sweetness of consolation and grace. These are the rivers Jor and Dan of Judaea.

### TITLE XCVI. On the four songs of the faithful.

There are four songs of the faithful: the song of victory, sung when Pharaoh has been drowned; the song of exhortation, sung when they are about to enter the land of promise; the song of joy, which Hannah sings at the receiving of her son; and the song of strength, which David sings when delivered from Saul’s hand (1 Kings 2 [1 Samuel 2]).

### TITLE XCVII. On the feet and horses upon which we ought to rely.

There are two feet which we ought to use: nature and [Col. 0741A] habit. There are three horses by which we are borne up to heaven.

The first is sorrow arising from repentance, whose hoofs the serpent bites. Its saddle is presumptuous confidence in receiving pardon; its bridle and bit are the consolations of Scripture and the examples of the ancients; its spurs, shame at the enormity of guilt and fear arising from consideration of punishment; its pit is despair.

Next comes zeal arising from religious life, upon which Mordecai sits in royal apparel. Its saddle is the weight of moderating discernment; its bridle and bit, a wary appraisal of one’s bodily condition and a useful measuring-out of perseverance. Its spurs are desire to practise honourableness and eagerness for a brother’s benefit; the pit into which it may rush headlong is lack of moderation.

Next comes desire arising from love, to which strength is given and around which a neighing is placed. Its spurs are the fleeting [Col. 0741B] instability of present things and the stable eternity of future things; its guide is the longing to see God; its pit is indiscretion.

### TITLE XCVIII. On the three caves in Scripture.

Caves in the sacred books are found in three forms: the perverse ungodliness of the will, which is the cave of robbers in which Saul relieves himself; the solid firmness of even-mindedness, which is made in the altar and is one cubit in size; and the exercise of a twofold piety. This is the double cave in which the prophets are buried.

## TITLE XCIX. On the Three Heavens to Which We Are Carried Away

There are three heavens to which we are carried away: the dignity of ecclesiastical purity, to which Paul is carried away; the contemplation of heavenly things, to which Ezekiel is carried away in the Spirit, saying: “The heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God” (Ezek. I [Col. 0741C]); and the unboundedness of the supreme Godhead, to which the souls of the elect are carried away.

## TITLE C. On the Six Cities of Refuge

There are six cities of refuge: caution against forbidden transgression, obedience to the precept that must be followed, and desire to propitiate the Divinity—these are in the land of Canaan; contemplation of the world’s construction, continual consideration of the tyrannical city, and knowledge of the surpassing Word of God—these are beyond the Jordan and are of Levitical allotment.

## TITLE CI. On the Threefold Paradise

There are three kinds of paradise: the pleasurable sweetness of visible things, which is watered like a garden of delights; the sincere purity of spiritual things, which preserves the human being within itself [Col. 0741D]; and the delightful truth of things above the heavens, where Paul hears secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (II Cor. XII).

## TITLE CII. On Four Other Mountains

There are four kinds of mountains: the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul’s shield is cast away; the mountains of Samaria, which raise themselves too high; the mountains of Armenia, upon which Noah’s ark rested; and the mountains of Israel, which spread out their branches.

## TITLE CIII. On the Two Things That Call Us Away from Our Purpose

There are two things that call us away from our resolve: shame at the work begun, and despair of carrying virtue through. These are Rechab and Baanah, who kill Ish-bosheth on his bed (II Kings IV).

## TITLE CIV. On the Four Coverings of Our Nakedness

[Col. 0742A]

There are four coverings by which our nakedness is covered: the oldness of error and wickedness, which is the loincloth of shameful parts; the newness of conduct and life, by which Rebekah, descending from the camel, covered her face; the integrity of heavenly holiness, which Elijah left to Elisha and with which he divided the Jordan; and the brightness of eternal immortality. This is the sapphire mantle which Mordecai wears on the feast day.

## TITLE CV. On the Three Enemies to Whom We Are Handed Over

There are three enemies to whom we are handed over: the impurity of unclean desires, which are like mice gnawing the hind parts; the foulness of bodily passions, which are like locusts striking with the manner of a scorpion; and the stubborn perversity of reason and sense, which are fiery serpents [Col. 0742B].

## TITLE CVI. On the Four Thieves of Our Goods

There are four thieves who steal every good thing from us: the sluggishness of a blunted understanding, taking from us knowledge of the truth. This thief is called by the Psalmist “business in darkness” (Ps. XC). The unbridled wantonness of the flesh, snatching away the merit of integrity, is called “the midday demon” (ibid.); boastful ostentation seeking favor, taking away the fullness of holiness, is called “the arrow flying by day” (ibid.); and love and desire for this life, snatching away the reward of eternity, is called “the terror by night” (ibid.). These are the thieves of Syria.

## TITLE CVII. On the Three Kisses

There are three kisses: the reconciling kiss, by which the two feet of the Lord—mercy and justice—are touched; the rewarding kiss, by which the two hands—the work of creative justice and the bond of governance—are embraced [Col. 0742C]; and the contemplative kiss, which is received at the mouth and the Word of God, and joins the human being to him in wondrous unity.

They may also be called natural, when we are led to the good by spontaneous will; doctrinal, when we are invited to God by another’s admonition; and gracious, when we are drawn by inspiration to do good.

## TITLE CVIII. On the Threefold Rod in Scripture

There are three rods: the rod of Moses, which divides the Red Sea; the rod of Aaron, which confers the priesthood; and David’s shepherd’s rod, which drives away the adversary.

## TITLE CIX. On the Threefold Food of the Israelites

There are three foods of Israel: unleavened bread of secular knowledge in the departure from Egypt; manna of understanding in the desert [Col. 0742D]; and the palm of triumphant victory in the kingdom of promise.

## TITLE CX. On Three Delivered and Three Taken into the Priesthood

Three are delivered from among all the people: Noah, Daniel, and Jacob. Three are taken into the priesthood: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.

## TITLE CXI. On the Sword and Bow by Which the Lord Took Us as His Portion from the Hand of the Amorite

“We are your portion, Lord, whom you took from the hand of the Amorite with your sword and your bow.” Your sword is your word, living and effective; your bow is your incarnation. For there, as it were, the wood of wisdom is bent, the sinew of flesh is stretched out in a pious manner, and humanity is known to be ineffably exalted. Therefore we are your portion and the people [Col. 0743A] of your acquisition, whom you acquired by the word of your preaching and by the mystery of the incarnation.

## TITLE CXII. On the Mystery of Circumcision

In circumcision neither sinew is broken nor bone crushed, so that all that is strongest and firmest may remain unharmed. But the skin is opened, flesh is cut away, and blood is shed, so that seductive softness may be chastised.

Understand by the flesh the sin that remains in it. Moreover, in the skin is a covering, and in the blood an incitement. This, therefore, is the true circumcision: in spirit, not letter. Remove through compunction of heart and confession of mouth the veil of excuse and dissimulation; cut off through amendment of conduct the habit of sin; and finally, as is necessary, flee also the occasions of sin [Col. 0743B] and the fuel of desires.

## TITLE CXIII. On the Mystical Division of the Waters

Even to this day, among the citizens of Babylon, the outpouring of waters—that is, the confusion of thoughts—makes the earth empty and void. For while the whole thought floats about the flesh, no fruit of salvation is to be hoped for from it.

Let the waters, therefore, be divided from the waters, so that every soul, as has been said, may claim for itself its own portion of concern or meditation. Let the lower waters indeed be restrained within fixed limits, contained in fixed channels, and not exceed the bounds of necessity. Let the upper waters, accordingly, be extended more abundantly. From this the Lord gives blessing, and our land will yield its fruit.

## TITLE CXIV. On the Desire by Which Human Beings Are Judged Spiritual or Carnal, According to the Blessing of Jacob and Esau

[Col. 0743C]

Since among the people of God some are carnal and others spiritual, and yet the former do not wholly lack desire for eternal things, nor the latter desire for temporal things, they differ in this: each seeks some things more than others; and according to what they prefer, they are judged either spiritual or carnal.

Hence, in the blessings of Jacob and Esau, both the dew of heaven and the earth and its richness are named, but not in the same order in each case: “May God give you abundance from the dew of heaven and from the richness of the earth” (Gen. XXVII), Isaac says to Jacob. But to Esau he says: “In the richness of the earth and in the dew of heaven from above shall your blessing be” (ibid.). What each person prefers may easily be recognized [Col. 0743D] by one attentive to their pursuits and concerns.

## TITLE CXV. How Tabernacles, Courts, and Houses Differ

There are three kinds of dwelling: tabernacles, courts, and houses. In tabernacles are all the righteous who live and labor in the flesh, because tabernacles belong to those who labor and serve as soldiers. A tabernacle has a roof but lacks a foundation, and is portable, because the righteous are not founded in present things but seek the city above that has foundations. Their faith also, which is their foundation, is not in earthly things but in the Lord. It has a roof, that is, the defense of grace and protection.

Courts are spacious places adjoining a house. In them [Col. 0744A] are holy souls stripped of their bodies, which exist in spaciousness after laying aside the narrowness of the flesh. Courts have a foundation but no roof, because souls that are in the love of God do not fall. Hence: “Our feet were standing in your courts” (Ps. CXXI). Yet they have no roof, still hoping for an increase which will not be until the resurrection of their bodies.

After that resurrection, indeed, they will be with the angels in the house, which has both foundation and roof. The foundation is the stability of eternal blessedness; the roof is its completion and perfection.

## TITLE CXVI. On the Two Breasts of the Merciful

There are two breasts of the merciful: compassion, from which flows the milk of consolation, by which the weak are nourished; and rejoicing with others, [Col. 0744B] from which flows the milk of encouragement, by which the strong are sustained.

## TITLE CXVII. On Washing the Feet, That Is, Our Senses

“He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet” (John XIII). The feet are the senses of the body, which carry us outside ourselves and are stained within us. The gateway of sight opens toward a woman, and there it is stained: it needs washing. Hearing opens toward detraction, taste toward gluttony, and so with the rest.

Therefore, whoever has been washed in baptism and afterward stained should take care that these feet are washed; otherwise he has no share with God. For he said to Peter: “Unless I wash you, you will have no share with me” (ibid.).

## TITLE CXVIII. On the Two Denarii to Be Spent

The innkeeper receives two denarii when the preacher [Col. 0744C] and pastor possesses both doctrine by which to instruct and a life by which to encourage.

## TITLE CXIX. On Shepherds, Hirelings, and Wolves

Shepherds are those who love the sheep. They keep them in prosperity and defend them in adversity. Hirelings are those who keep sheep for gain. Wolves are those who eat the flesh: they do not guard; they do not defend, but kill.

The first preserve for those subject to them what they are and what they have. The second guard the persons themselves, not their goods. They sin because they restrain those subject to them from sins only in order to take away their goods. The third kill the persons themselves and seize their goods. The first seek salvation, the second profit, and the third kill by the means [Col. 0744D] and license of sinning which they grant.

## TITLE CXX. On the Fourfold Cross and the Cause and End of Crucifixion

In Christ’s cross is glory; in Simon’s cross, compulsion; in the cross of the right-hand thief, consolation; in the cross of the left-hand thief, confusion.
