In Christ’s cross there is punishment without fault, and glorification after punishment. In Simon’s cross there is fault with punishment, and after punishment the pursuit of praise. In the cross of the right-hand thief there is punishment for fault, and remission after fault. In the left-hand cross there is punishment for fault, and condemnation after punishment.

Some say when they suffer: “If we had deserved it, we should not be ashamed.” Alas, eyes that do not see! On the contrary: if you suffer for guilt, be ashamed; if without guilt, glory. Would you rather be a thief than [Col. 0745A] Christ, and a left-hand thief, so that you become a blasphemer rather than a confessor?

## TITLE CXXI. Why the Mount of Olives Was Called the Mountain of Three Lights; Why It Figures the Trinity; and on the Threefold Light in Us

The Mount of Olives was formerly called the Mountain of Three Lights: on the side of the Temple it had the light of a lamp opposite it; on another side, the light of the rising sun; and in itself, the light of the olive.

This mountain is the Divinity: namely, the lamp’s paternal light, the Son, who is “the true light, enlightening every person coming into this world”; and the light of the rising sun, the Father. Hence, “East” is his name (Zech. VI), by whose rays the mountain is illumined. The third light, that of the olive, is the Holy Spirit. Hence he is called an anointing: “His anointing,” says the Apostle, “teaches [Col. 0745B] you concerning all things” (I John II).

Likewise, in us there is a threefold light: of nature, grace, and doctrine. The first is common to good and evil alike, because all are according to the image and likeness of God. The second belongs only to the good, who live according to the image and likeness in which they were made. The third belongs only to those who, beyond others, have received knowledge of the divine law and truth.

## TITLE CXXII. On the Three Doors and the Gates of Discipline That Must Be Closed Against the Adversary

Following the example of the disciples, I admonish and exhort you who are gathered together—not indeed because of fear of the Jews, but because of fear of sins—“Close your doors.” For what good is it if you do not go out to your enemies, but allow them to enter you? Whether a sheep goes from the fold to the wolf, or the wolf enters it, [Col. 0745C] the death is the same.

Therefore be sober and watch in prayers, because your adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. “Resist him, firm in faith” (I Pet. V), and close your doors upon yourselves. For in this house of discipline there are three doors.

The first is regular observance, such as silence, abstinence, and the like. If these are loosened or opened, talkativeness, gluttony, and the other vices opposed to them enter; room is made for dissension, and peace is lost.

The second consists of the five senses, through which there is commerce between the world and the soul. If you open this one, death enters as though through windows.

The third is the will. Through it, when open, every evil and it alone enters; when closed, every good and it alone [Col. 0745D] enters it. This is surely the door concerning which the prophet says: “This gate shall be closed and shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it” (Ezek. XLIV).

Thus, to put it briefly, there are three enclosures into which Christ enters to his disciples when the doors are closed: the first is of the body, which is external; the second, of the soul, which is internal; the third, of the spirit, which is innermost. Each has its own doors. The first has certain observances and traditions of the elders; the second, the pleasures of bodily sense; the third, the presumption of one’s own will. When these are open, the devil always enters through them; Christ is received only through those that are closed, and, once received, he speaks peace: “Peace to you” (John XX).

This peace is [Col. 0746A], in the first enclosure, between a man and his brother; in the second, between soul and spirit; in the third, between spirit and God. Concerning these three enclosures Isaiah says: “Go, my people, enter into your chambers; close your doors over yourself, and hide for a little while, until my indignation has passed” (Isa. XXVI).

In the first chamber or enclosure—for it is written, “a monk in the city is a monster”—the flesh is hidden from the tumult of secular life. In the second, the soul is hidden from the flesh itself, lest it fulfill concern for it in its desires. In the third, the spirit is hidden even from itself, lest the presumption of its own will find it.

Of this the Lord says: “When you pray, enter into your chamber; and, having closed the door, pray to your Father in secret” (Matt. VI). The first enclosure is made by flight from this world and care for discipline and rule [Col. 0746B]; in it the neighbor is built up, the flesh is crucified, the lust of the eyes dies, and it admits a deceptive dispensation. The second is made by contempt for pleasure; in it a person governs himself, the soul is buried, the flesh’s desire dies, and it scarcely admits any dispensation. The third is perfected by the love of God; in it God is honored, the spirit rises again, the pride of life dies, and it admits no dispensation whatsoever.

## TITLE CXXIII. On the Allegorical Office of the Ploughman

The oxherd who ploughs with oxen ought to possess two things: sweetness of voice, by which he soothes the labor of those working well; and a sharp goad, by which he shakes sluggish people out of their torpor.

## TITLE CXXIV. On the Threefold Manner and End of Acting

The things we do, we do either in the light of the faces of human beings [Col. 0746C], that we may please people; or in the light of our own face, that we may believe we do well what is evil; or in the light of God’s face, that we may humbly ascribe to him alone whatever good is in us.

## TITLE CXXV. That Death Is Precious in Three Ways

Sometimes life makes death precious, as in confessors; sometimes the cause, as in martyrs; sometimes both life and cause, as in very many persons.

## TITLE CXXVI. On What We Bear on Our Forehead

At times we bear leprosy on our forehead, at times a *tau*, at times a golden plate. The leprosy belongs to the luxurious and wanton; the *tau*, to penitents; the golden plate, to those living gloriously for God, while our light so shines before people that they glorify the Father who is in heaven [Col. 0746D] (Matt. V).

## TITLE CXXVII. On the Cords by Which We Are Drawn

Placed in this world between paradise and hell, we are drawn by different persons toward different things and by different cords. By the Father of lights toward the glory of heaven, by a threefold cord: faith, hope, and charity. By the father of darkness toward outer darkness, by a threefold cord: unbelief, despair, and hatred.

The first asks to be drawn, whose “lines have fallen in pleasant places” (Ps. XV), and who says: “Draw me after you” (Song I). Of the second it is said: “Woe to you who draw a cord with the cord of iniquity, and make a long garment!” (Isa. V).

## TITLE CXXVIII. On the Contemplative Compared with the Active through the Male and Female Palm

The palm that produces dates, displaying an appearance of embrace, bends its branches toward the palm tree which they call male; and, received by it for the sake of the desired union, the female immediately restores herself to her former state. Thus the spiritual contemplative, sensing that he has produced the fruit of eternal life, bends himself through the active life toward lesser persons [Col. 0747A]; after he has received from them the fruit of preaching, he returns again to contemplation.

## TITLE CXXIX. On the Mattress, Pillow, and Covering of Conscience

Let the blessed soul have as a mattress the purity of its conscience; as pillow or headrest, tranquility; as covering, security. In this bed let it sleep pleasantly and rest happily.

## TITLE CXXX. On the Difference Between Those Who Govern and Those Governed

[Col. 0747B]

To know, to be able, and to be willing to govern is charity if they wish to benefit others; it is pride if they do not. To know, to be able, and not to be willing is humility if they decline; it is indolence if they withdraw altogether. Neither to know nor to be able, yet to be willing, is ambitious desire or folly. Neither to know nor to be able nor to be willing is discretion and prudence given from heaven for this purpose.

Four of these—folly, indolence, desire, and pride—produce negligence. The other four—prudence, discretion, humility, and charity—if nourished, eliminate negligence. Counsel belongs to prudence; judgment, to discretion; guardianship, to humility; diligence, to charity. The counsel of prudence separates the wicked from the good; the judgment of discretion [Col. 0747C] chooses what is better; the guardianship of humility avoids losses to the virtues; diligence avoids danger. In these negligence has no place.

But negligence possesses those who have the eyes of prudence open, yet are darkened by the gloom of folly; who, because they are lethargic in good works through indolence, are drawn away to pleasurable things through desire, and do not condescend to the humble through pride. Through folly negligence enters; through indolence it remains. It is fed by the desire of cupidity; through pride it reigns.

Let the negligent shepherd hear what the diligent Shepherd says to him: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X). He lays it down who, entering through the door, walks in the midst of all between the tongues of flatterers and detractors, subjecting himself to all; who consoles and strengthens the fainthearted and resists the proud. Such a person can say: “I know my sheep, and my own know me” (ibid.).

The evil sheep know the shepherd when he rebukes them; the good sheep know him when he consoles them. The shepherd knows the sheep by carefully examining their characters and deeds. Hence it is said: “Diligently consider the face of your flock”: their hearts by confession, their works by circumspection.

The Lord adds: “And they hear my voice” (ibid.). There are three voices of the shepherd: gentle, sweet, and loud. The gentle belongs to the weak, the sweet to the dying, and the loud to the deaf. One is weak who is tempted; one dies who despairs; one is deaf who does not hear. But the weak hear the gentle voice of consolation; those despairing, the sweetness of entreaty; and the deaf, the harshness of rebuke.

“And my own follow me” [Col. 0748A] (ibid.). Whom? The one who goes before. Where? To life, if he is diligent; to death, if negligent. For if a blind person provides guidance to a blind person, both fall into the pit (Matt. XV). How does he go before? By life and teaching.

“So there shall be one fold and one shepherd” (John X): one in himself, and one with the flock. One in himself, so that he fulfills in works what he teaches in words; one, so that he is not changed by prosperity or adversity; one with the flock, so that he is not divided from those subject to him by more costly food or dress, while he becomes one with the weak through compassion and with the delicate through dispensation, so that he may say with the Apostle: “I became all things to all people” (I Cor. IX), neither fleeing what they command nor imposing heavy burdens which they themselves are unwilling to move even with a finger (Matt. XXIII).

Such is the negligent shepherd, who is also called a hireling. Such are those [Col. 0748B] who do what is wrong and do not wish to be rebuked. “They take pleasure,” says Gregory, “that, when they do even unlawful things freely, none of those subject to them should contradict them; they think themselves wiser than all whom they see themselves able to surpass in power.” They love this: to seem wise and to be powerful. This is the cause of angelic and human ruin. When the angel wished to be more powerful, he fell; when the human being wished to be wiser, he became foolish.

There are three kinds of negligence in prelates. The first is that of those who live well and permit their subjects to live badly. The second is that of those who live badly and compel their subjects to live well. The third is that of those who live badly and wish their subjects to live badly.

The first are like Eli, whose sons slept with the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle; when people came to sacrifice at Shiloh, they did not permit them, but, before the flesh was burned for the sacrificial rite, seized it raw (I Kings II).

Those who sleep under prelates living well, or in reality join themselves with fleshly desires, are like Eli’s sons. They prevent those coming to Shiloh from sacrificing when, by word and example, they draw recent converts back from the good. They do not permit the priest’s right to receive the fat, because, once the fire of charity has been extinguished, they do not pour the sweetness of the heart into good action. They seek raw, unboiled flesh, because, fleeing the fire of tribulation, they withdraw themselves from poverty and labor. For the vices of the flesh are usually cooked in the furnace of poverty; they therefore desire raw flesh in order to cook it for themselves when, as, and in whatever quantity they wish. Such are those who do nothing in the cloister, as though in Shiloh [Col. 0748D], except what they wish, when they wish, or as much as they wish.

## TITLE CXXXI. On the Steadfastness and Hardness of Prelates

Good shepherds ought to possess such steadfastness and strength that they are neither bent away from truth by praise or flattery nor moved by insults. The Lord showed this in saying to the prophet: “I have made your face like a diamond and like flint” (Ezek. III). The hardness of both stones is great, but one—the diamond—is valued; the other is trampled underfoot.

Therefore, the shepherd of the Church is like a diamond when praised and honored by people, yet not turned aside from what is right by praise or flattery. The hardness of a good shepherd is also like the hardness of flint when, for the sake of justice, he is despised, trampled upon, and treated indignantly by the wicked [Col. 0749A], yet does not fail or grow weary, but perseveres in the defense of justice with unconquered strength.

Hirelings possess none of these qualities. They attend not to repelling harm from souls but to acquiring temporal goods; they do not resist wolves but sweat for profits. There are two kinds of wolves: visible and invisible. The visible are human beings; the invisible are demons. The former inflict harms; the latter inflict or suggest vices. Good shepherds oppose themselves to the first by office, to the second by teaching and prayer.

Therefore, brothers, in order that we may accomplish this blamelessly, let us chastise our body and bring it into slavery, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, we ourselves become reprobate. Let our works correspond before God and before people, so that our preaching may be useful, pleasing, and sweet [Col. 0749B], so that our sheep may gladly hear our voice and follow us more eagerly as we go before them on the path of justice. Watch, attend, and labor toward this, brothers, so that for the labor of the pastoral office you may receive an eternal reward, granted by the eternal Shepherd, our Lord.

## TITLE CXXXII. On the Threefold Oil, and on Faith and Charity

One oil is for pouring out, another for purity, another for exultation. The oil of pouring out is the word of preaching, in which good and bad alike share, for good or ill. The oil of purity is that by which the lamps of works ought to burn with the fire of divine love. It fittingly follows the first oil, because after receiving the divine word, a person comes to do good works. The oil of exultation is charity [Col. 0749C], by which a person is so kindled that he loves only what belongs to God and glories only in his God.

The first oil is the word of preaching; the second, the devotion of charity; the third, the love of charity. But concerning the pouring out of oil, we must see that we do not retain what ought to be poured out, nor pour out what ought to be retained. There is something in us that is ours, and something that is not ours but belongs to our neighbors. If we pour out what is ours, we are foolish and vain; if we retain what belongs to others, we are deceitful.

Ours are the things without which no one is saved: faith, hope, and charity. These must not be poured out so that they are lost in us for the sake of others. Faith makes servants, by which the punishments of hell are believed; hope makes hirelings, by which a reward is desired; charity makes children, by which the goodness of God the Father is loved. Faith makes the soul a handmaid; hope, a concubine; charity, a bride. Faith says: “It is so: fear.” Hope says: “You shall have it.” Charity gives glory to God.

Faith is knowledge, or at least belief, concerning good and evil things; hope is confidence in attaining an advantage and avoiding a disadvantage. Charity is grace for both. These must be received, so that we may be preserved beforehand, maintained, and saved. Faith preserves from sin; hope keeps us in good; charity saves us in blessedness.

Other things given in us by God belong to our neighbors, such as the word of knowledge, kinds of tongues, and the other gifts of God. These must be poured out. Yet sometimes we retain them lukewarmly, fearfully, or enviously: lukewarmly, when we distrust the understanding of our hearers; fearfully, when we despair of ourselves, believing that we cannot suffice for our hearers, although we should rather think [Col. 0750A] that it is not we who speak, but the Spirit of the Father; enviously, when we do not love our neighbor. In the first, faith is destroyed; in the second, hope is rejected; in the third, charity is condemned.

Therefore let us not retain what belongs to others, lest we be deceitful. But if it is poured out, care must be taken that it is not poured out rashly or incautiously, lest what is holy be given to dogs; nor ambitiously, for temporal advantage. See, then, how the gratuitous gifts of the Holy Spirit are to be retained and poured out; and if we impart what is ours to others in this manner, he will work his own things in us.

Oil has three properties: it nourishes, shines, and anoints. So the oil of God’s word—that is, charity—nourishes itself, shines for the neighbor, and anoints God. And through this well-ordered pouring out of oil, “the young maidens loved you, Jesus Christ, bridegroom of souls, because your name is oil poured out” (Song I) [Col. 0750B].

## TITLE CXXXIII. On the Fourfold Thirst Restrained by the Four Rivers of Paradise

There are four rivers of paradise against four kinds of thirst. The first thirst is for present possessions, thirsting for money; the second burns with wickedness in pleasures; the third thirsts for justice, desiring to turn back from sin and do good; the fourth is thirst for the Lord’s presence: it possesses it and yet still thirsts.

The first is the thirst of those falling, the second of those lying down, the third of those rising again, the fourth of those reigning. Against the first drink Pishon, which is interpreted “the mouth of the pupil,” so that you may stretch the pupil toward inward goods; outward things will immediately become cheap.

Has your thirst burned toward wickedness, so that you teach your tongue to speak falsehood [Col. 0750C] and labor to act unjustly? Come to Gihon, which is interpreted “breast.” Wisdom is denoted in the breast; hence those who are as if insane are called “without breast.” Drink wisdom, therefore, because wisdom conquers wickedness.

You have now driven out thirst for riches; the fierce poison of wickedness has now cooled; you have now conceived thirst for justice. To nourish this thirst for justice with perpetual food, come to the Tigris. *Tigris* is said to be as though *theogris*, that is, “God’s step”: this is humility. By this step he came to the virgin, walked upon the earth, and ascended the cross. And although there are three degrees of humility, he chose the lowest: namely, to be subjected to one lesser than himself. Christian humility is set before us like a yoke by which we are restrained.

Drink the Tigris, God’s step—that is, humility—so that from thirst for justice you may come to thirst for God’s presence, when he will satisfy you so that you do not hunger and kindle you so that you do not grow weary. Then [Col. 0750D] you will drink the Euphrates, which is interpreted “fruitful,” so that in the field of the divine presence you may gather the fruit of every joy. Thus the divine vision will be fruitful: joys will always be born from joy.

Pishon fittingly circles the land of Havilah, Gihon Ethiopia, and the Tigris passes around the Assyrians (Gen. II), because confession by the mouth relieves the afflicted, wisdom makes the black white, and humility resists the proud. But it is not stated through what region the Euphrates flows, because the goods of another are rightly inexplicable to us.

## TITLE CXXXIV. On the Things by Which Virtue Is Preserved

There are three things by which virtue is preserved: patience, humility, and charity. With these the soldier of Christ must arm himself: possessing patience as a shield, to bear and carry about [Col. 0751A] against every adversity; humility, by which to preserve the inward affections; and charity as a lance, by which, as the Apostle says, “having become all things to all people” (I Cor. IX), he may wage the Lord’s war.

He must also have the helmet of salvation, which is hope, fortifying and preserving the head and governing faculty of the mind. Let him also have the sword, the word of God, and the horse of good desire.

## TITLE CXXXV. On Threefold Long-Suffering

There is a threefold long-suffering: God’s toward a human being, a human being’s toward God, and a human being’s toward another human being. The first is the expectation by which God long-sufferingly awaits a person’s conversion. The second is the endurance by which the righteous person tirelessly awaits God’s promise. The third is that by which the spiritual father, instructing gently a child overtaken in some fault, even-mindedly awaits his promise.

Long-suffering, therefore, is a long expectation through patience—not long in the duration of the thing, but in desire. Concerning this twofold long-suffering of a human being toward God and toward another human being it is said: “Woe to those who have lost endurance!” (Ecclus. II) [Col. 0751B].

## TITLE CXXXVI. On the Various Modes of Prayer

There is a threefold prayer: of voice without devotion, concerning which the Apostle says, “If I pray, my tongue is without fruit” (I Cor. XIV); of devotion without voice, concerning which the Lord says: “Enter into your chamber, and, with the door closed, pray to your Father” (Matt. VI). Of this door it is said: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CIV [Col. 0752A]). To one praying thus the Lord says: “Why do you cry out to me?” (Exod. XIV).

There is prayer of voice with devotion, when, from the meaning of the spoken words, the affection of devotion is stirred up. Hence: “Sing to the Lord; sing a psalm to him” (Ps. LXVII). There is also a fourth form: devotion with voice, when from the innermost affection of the heart a person bursts forth into the voice of praise and prayer. Hence: “My heart exulted in the Lord,” etc. (I Kings II).

## TITLE CXXXVII. On the Three Graces for Doing Good

There are three graces for doing good: prevenient, cooperating, and subsequent. The first gives will, the second ability, the third perseverance. I judge that in Scripture they are called by the names of grain, wine, and oil.

## TITLE CXXXVIII. Who Is Full of Grace and Truth

[Col. 0752B]

“Full of grace and truth” (John I). There is grace without truth: popular favor. “Grace is deceptive,” it says, “and beauty is vain” (Prov. XXXI). There is also truth without grace, when it produces hatred. There is grace with truth, true grace; and truth with grace, gracious truth.

Therefore he showed himself full of the grace of truth and the truth of grace, who, seeking neither the truth of human discernment’s favor nor the favor of human truth, set aside favor for the salvation of human beings.

# BOOK FIVE. FRAGMENTS OF MORAL TREATISES, LETTERS, ETC.

[Col. 0751]

## TITLE I. On the Restoration of Names through the Double Trinity of Divine Persons and Theological Virtues

[Col. 0751C]

That blessed Trinity repaired the fall of our nature, mindful of its mercy and not unmindful of our fault. Sent by the Father, the Son of God came and gave faith. After the Son, the Spirit was sent and bestowed charity; and through these two, faith and charity, hope of returning to the Father came to be. This is the Trinity—faith, hope, and charity—by which, as by a three-pronged hook, the immutable Trinity drew back the mutable and fallen trinity from the mire of the deep to the blessedness it had lost: faith illuminated reason, hope raised memory, and charity purified the will. Therefore, when the Son of God came, like a good physician he gave commandments whose observance would restore lost salvation. [Col. 0751D] To produce faith in the commandments, he displayed signs; to show the usefulness of those commandments, he promised blessedness. Thus faith is of one kind in commandments, of another in signs, and of another in promises: that by which we believe in God, that is, love him; that by which we believe God, that is, believe that he himself knows and can do all things; and that by which we believe God, namely, that he truthfully fulfills whatever he promises. Likewise hope is threefold and proceeds from the aforesaid threefold faith. From faith in the commandments arises hope of pardon; from faith in signs, hope of grace; from faith in promises, hope of glory. Charity is likewise gathered under a threefold number: “From a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1). We owe purity to our neighbour, conscience to ourselves, and faith to God. Purity consists in this: that whatever is done should be done either for the neighbour’s benefit or for God’s honour. This must especially be shown toward one’s neighbour, for we are manifest to God. Two things produce a good conscience within us: penitence and continence. When by penitence we punish sins committed, and by continence do not commit sins that must be punished, we owe this to ourselves. After these comes unfeigned faith, which must be vigilantly shown to God, [Col. 0752D] so that neither for our own sake nor for our neighbour’s do we less fully carry out obedience to God’s commandments. It is called “unfeigned” in contrast to dead faith, which is without works.

There is therefore the creating Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—from which the created trinity fell: memory, reason, and will; the trinity through which it fell: suggestion, delight, and consent; and the trinity into which it fell: weakness, blindness, and uncleanness. The Trinity [Col. 0753A] which fell has in each of its elements a threefold fall. Memory fell into three kinds of affective thoughts: necessary thoughts, such as eating, drinking, and the like; burdensome thoughts, involved in arduous management of affairs, such as acquiring, preserving, and so forth; and idle thoughts, as when it thinks of a horse running or a bird flying. Reason fell into a threefold ignorance: of good and evil, true and false, advantageous and disadvantageous. The will fell into the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of life. There is a Trinity through which it rises again: faith, hope, and charity. Faith in commandments and signs; hope of pardon, grace, and glory; charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.

## TITLE II. What evils are found in hypocrisy.

Hypocrisy is a subtle evil, a hidden poison, a thief lying in wait, [Col. 0753B] consuming rust, a destroying moth, a pestilence to be shunned. From remedies it creates diseases; from medicine it produces sickness; it turns holiness into guilt, reconciliation into liability, virtue into vice, reward into loss, remission into sin.

Who am I that I should pour out my spirit before my fathers and the elders of Israel? To teach masters, rebuke elders, and command one’s superiors belongs to a proud spirit, one presumptuous concerning itself. For you are “the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5), “all sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81). But who am I? “The reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21). Yet, as though compelled to bear this cross, you say to your servant: “Do this,” and I do it.

## TITLE III. On the threefold knowledge arising from the vision of God.

The first knowledge is born from the vision of God, who is [Col. 0753C] the fountain and origin of all knowledge possessed by the person who beholds God. From it a threefold vision and knowledge arise: first, of God who is seen; second, of the one who sees; third, of the other things that are seen—that is, understood—in God, to whom they are present. Just as a mirror affords a threefold vision, by which we see the mirror itself, ourselves, and whatever is present, so in seeing God we behold even the hidden things of creation, including hell itself. Then the elect will have a threefold vision: bodily vision, by which bodies will be seen; spiritual vision, by which likenesses of bodies will be seen in the spirit, not in deceptive imagination—a vision enjoyed by the spirits of the righteous after their departure; and intellectual vision, by which, with the pure gaze of the mind, they behold God, their own souls, and the angelic [Col. 0753D] powers.

## TITLE IV. On the twelve degrees of virtues.

There are twelve degrees by which the saints ascend along the path of virtues. Hence: “They shall go from strength to strength, that they may see the God of gods in Zion” (Ps. 83). The first is confession. Therefore in John’s vision Judah is placed first; his name is interpreted “confession” (Rev. 7). Whoever desires to turn back after sins must first confess his sins. Since he weeps for evil deeds, he makes God, whom he had offended, gracious toward himself and turns God’s eyes of mercy toward himself, as it is said: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1). Reuben is placed after Judah, and his name is interpreted “son of vision,” when the sinner too is looked upon by God through confession. Since [Col. 0754A] by penitence he has obtained mercy through God’s regard, he must, lest he fall back, arm himself against every vice and temptation and cut off from himself the pleasures of the flesh. Third comes Gad, whose name is interpreted “girt.” To be girded belongs to a recruit; after he has subdued his vices, he begins to be blessed. Thus Asher, interpreted “blessed,” is placed fourth in the order, so that the person now made blessed in ascent may extend himself also toward the advancement of others and be enlarged through mercy: by pardoning those who injure him, sympathizing with sinners, and aiding those in need. Thus Naphtali follows Asher, interpreted “expansion.” When he has properly provided for his own salvation and that of others, he must forget all sins and all things of the world, following God alone; therefore Manasseh, [Col. 0754B] interpreted “forgetful,” is placed after Naphtali. God truly hears such a person for himself and for others. Hence Simeon is found in seventh place, interpreted “hearing”; and, having become such, he is added to the good and perfect. Thus Levi follows, interpreted “added”; and rightly he now receives a reward from God. Therefore Issachar follows him, interpreted “reward.” But we shall see the interpretation of this name more clearly if we set down what his mother Leah said at his birth: “The Lord,” she said, “has rendered a reward to me, because I gave my handmaid”; and therefore she called his name Issachar, that is, “reward” (Gen. 30). Our flesh ought to be our handmaid, and God our husband. We give the handmaid to our husband if we subject our flesh to God’s service, if we compel it to keep watch and abstain. Issachar is given to Leah [Col. 0754C] because reward is given to the soul that subdues the flesh and extinguishes vices, so that it may be enriched with virtues. Therefore Zebulun follows Issachar, interpreted “dwelling-place of strength.” Who is strong like our God? “The Lord,” says the prophet, “is strong and mighty in battle” (Ps. 23). The dwelling-place of strength is thus God’s dwelling. For God dwells in the person in whom are faith, hope, charity, chastity, and the other virtues. Since rewards of merits are increased by the practice of virtues, Joseph follows, interpreted “increase.” Benjamin is placed last and highest, interpreted “son of the right hand.” For the son is said to be at the father’s right hand; to it the saints, made sons of the right hand, will be placed when removed from this life and established in [Col. 0754D] heavenly dwellings, where there is nothing left-handed, but all is right and at the right hand. The number of these tribes is one hundred and forty-four thousand, namely twelve times twelve thousand, because those who follow the faith and works of the apostles will be counted among this number of the sealed and blessed.

## TITLE V. On the threefold conversion of the good.

Among good people, some are drawn, some are led, and some are caught up. The first say: “Draw me after you” (Song 1). Of the second it is said: “The king brought me into his storerooms” (Song 2). The voice of the third is spoken with the Apostle: “I was caught up even to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12). The first are happy: those who possess their souls in patience (Luke 21). The second are happier: those who willingly confess him. The third are happiest: those who, their own will now buried in the deepest [Col. 0755A] mercy of God, are caught up in the spirit of fervour into the riches of glory. Blessed is the one who has God as guide throughout all these degrees—he who is life, truth, and way (John 14): way in example, truth in promise, life in reward.

## TITLE VI. On the three mountains which the Lord ascended.

There are three mountains which the Lord ascended. On the first he was transfigured, and his glory is seen. On the second he ascended to teach. On the third he ascended alone to pray. Let us therefore ascend to him on the first, forming in our hearts the many dwelling-places of patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins, so that, having known the sweetness of God’s house and its glory, we may say: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17). Then, choosing to be there so that we may learn the way, [Col. 0755B] let us ascend the other mountain on which he teaches and raises a ladder marked out by eight intervening steps, whose summit touches heaven: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). We shall not find it burdensome to climb this mountain, where you may say to the Lord Jesus, “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6), if we have first ascended the mountain of his glory by unceasing meditation. For thus you will hear: “You know where I am going,” because of the first ascent, “and you know the way” (John 14), because of the second. On the first, then, he was transfigured so that you might know where you should tend, that is, the glory he promises you. On the second he spoke words of life so that you might know by what way you would arrive. On the third he prayed so that you might obtain a good will to go and arrive, and apply diligent effort.

## TITLE VII. On the twofold scandal and its instrument.

[Col. 0755C]

Scandal is twofold. The first is external, of which the Lord says: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18). The second is internal, and is itself threefold: first, of the eye; second, of the hand; third, of the foot. If therefore your eye, hand, or foot causes you to stumble (Matt. 5)—which is said to be ours, and yet is then left-handed when it seeks contrary things, draws you back toward evils, and drags your intention either from good works toward their opposites, or from the path of holy conduct, by which you would ascend from virtue to virtue along the rungs of Jacob’s ladder, down into the depths of hell—pluck out and cut off that eye, hand, and foot by turning away from it, and cast it from yourself by abandoning it.

## TITLE VIII. On the two keys of heaven.

There are two keys to the gate of paradise: charity and patience. Charity must first be embraced. And because one who wishes to love God is exposed to temptations, patience must be employed. These are the cherubim and the turning, flaming sword set to guard paradise. “Cherubim” is interpreted “fullness of knowledge”; but the fullness of the law, according to the Apostle, is charity (Rom. 13). Tribulation is understood by the flaming and turning sword: it is a sword when it divides; it is called flaming when it burns; turning because it is transitory. If therefore you wish to enter heaven, know that these two are necessary, because we can do nothing without charity, and “through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14). Charity and patience are the keys of paradise; without them entrance is impossible, and [Col. 0756A] they have been placed between us and paradise so that we may know we can enter only through them.

## TITLE IX. On the threefold state of the faithful soul.

There are three states of the faithful soul. In the first it is captive; in the second free; in the third blessed. As captive, it is oppressed by slavery to sin; as free, it fights under the leader Justice; as blessed, it rejoices in the enjoyment of joy. To the captive it is said: “Return, return, O Shulammite,” so that from captive you may become free (Song 6). To the free it is said: “Act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26), so that from free you may become blessed. To the blessed it is said: “Sing to the Lord in Zion; make joyful sound to him with a voice of exultation” (Ps. 48). In the first state it is a handmaid and fears; in the second, a daughter and loves; in the third, a friend and embraces.

## TITLE X. On the soul’s three enemies.

[Col. 0756B]

Three peoples are hostile to the faithful soul. The first are worldly people, who draw it away from good; concerning them the Lord says: “If your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it from you” (Matt. 5). The second are desires of the flesh, which suggest evil; concerning them the Apostle Peter says: “I beseech you to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Pet. 2). The third are thoughts, which compel one to sin; concerning them Job says: “My thoughts that torment my heart have been scattered” (Job 27). The first people is a friend of the world and an enemy of God, according to: “A friend of the world will be made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4). The second is a friend of the flesh and an enemy of the human being. Hence: “A person’s enemies are those of his household” (Matt. 10). The third [Col. 0756C] is a friend of the mind and an enemy of peace. Hence: “Dying flies spoil the sweetness of ointment” (Eccl. 10). The daughter is commanded to forget these peoples when it is said: “Forget your people” (Ps. 44).

## TITLE XI. On the three fathers of humankind.

There are three fathers of humankind. The first begets, the second seizes, the third requires. The first begets for the life of the flesh; the second seizes for the punishment of death; the third requires for the joy of eternity. The first father is man, the second the devil, the third God. Of the first: “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1). Of the second: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). Of the third: “Our Father, who art in heaven” (Matt. 6). Under the first we live carnally; under the second we sin mortally; [Col. 0756D] under the third we reign happily. The third commands that the first be abandoned and the second not imitated. The daughter is commanded to forget the house of the two former fathers when it is said: “And the house of your father” (Ps. 44).

## TITLE XII. On the four things to be overcome by the soul, and its threefold beauty.

The faithful soul overcomes four things: the world, the flesh, the mind, and the devil. The wars of the world are external; those of the flesh domestic; those of the mind internal; those of the devil deceitful. How difficult victory is to gain where such a host of opponents stands against us! Yet in victory the king desires the beauty of the victorious soul. This beauty is threefold: in voice, because it speaks beautifully; in face, because it performs good deeds; in heart, because it meditates on holy things. Therefore he says to it: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish [Col. 0757A] in you” (Song 4). Therefore rise from labour to rest, from the world to glory, from battle to reward, and come into the bridal chamber, in which you will be a bride with him without end.

## TITLE XIII. On the three things contained in penitence.

There are three things in penitence: sorrow for the past, guarding against the future, and satisfaction for the offence. Sorrow appeases guilt; satisfaction satisfies the vice; guarding preserves health. These three must be proportioned such that sorrow is complete, guarding perfect, and satisfaction fitting.

## TITLE XIV. On the two kinds of oil, namely God’s and the world’s.

There are two kinds of oil: God has oil, and the world too has oil. Vessels do not fail God’s oil; the world’s oil fails in vessels. God’s oil is the sweetness of eternal things; [Col. 0757B] the world’s oil is delight in present things. The former suffices; the latter fails. Hence the vessels of the foolish virgins are said to be empty (Matt. 25), while the vessels of the wise widow are full (4 Kgs. 4). The vessels are hearts; the oil is joy.

## TITLE XV. On the threefold peace and war.

Peace is threefold: toward God, toward oneself, and toward one’s neighbour. So long as man kept peace with God, he found peace within himself and no contradiction in his flesh. But now, if he wishes to have peace with God and thereby with himself, peace with his neighbour is set forth first, so that he may be wholly at peace: outwardly with his neighbour through fraternal charity, inwardly through good desire, and above himself through divine grace. Therefore, when the saving sacrifice by which we must [Col. 0757C] be reconciled to God is offered, we first offer the kiss of peace to our neighbours, so that, with the peace between us thus first established, we may deserve to obtain that peace which is toward God. When it is offered for the dead, the peace is not given, since, removed from this life, they cannot keep or offer the peace of human fellowship. Therefore only that peace which is toward God is sought. The living, however, ought through peace with their neighbour to seek God’s peace; and through God’s peace, peace with themselves—not that peace of the soul with the world, which belongs to those who live pleasantly, but the peace between soul and spirit, through that between spirit and God. For true peace—because wisdom is found in a time of leisure—is not in the land of those who live pleasantly (Job 18). There is a peace, then, between soul and world, of those who live pleasantly and [Col. 0757D] badly; another between soul and spirit, of those who live pleasantly and well; and a third between spirit and God, of those who live happily and blessedly. Likewise there is war between soul and world, of those who live unpleasantly and badly; between soul and spirit, of those who live unpleasantly and well; and between spirit and God, of those who live unhappily and badly.

## TITLE XVI. On the three modes of unity.

The universe of things subsists by a single Trinity. There is a unity which is neither from another nor according to another, as the creating nature. There is a unity which is from one and according to one, as the rational creature, from God and like God. There is a unity which is from one according to two—that is, from one through one—as bodily nature. The first is exemplar [Col. 0758A] only, not an example; the second is both exemplar and example; the third is example only.

## TITLE XVII. On the threefold kind of those seeking God and wisdom.

The kind of those seeking God is threefold. Some seek and find, but do not retain, because they do not seek in order to possess, but to sell. Others seek, find, and retain. To the first it is said: “You shall seek me and shall not find me, and you shall die in your sin” (John 7). Of the second it is said: “I am he”; and they laid hands on him and held him (John 18). To the third he said: “Hail”; and they came, embraced, and held his feet (Matt. 28). The first seekers by no means find. The second find him living and kill him. The third seek him dead and find him living. Thus some find wisdom [Col. 0758B] but do not love it, because they prostitute it for profit and human praise. These find Christ living and kill him, because wisdom dies in them precisely because they enjoy none of its sweetness with any feeling of love. Others seek it dead and find it living, because, while they do not desire it for the use of this life, they attain more truly within to its sweetness.

## TITLE XVIII. On three builders upon the foundation of faith, and three things built upon it.

There are three kinds of people building upon the foundation of faith. There are those who love God alone. These build upon it gold in the love of virtue, silver in the knowledge of truth, and precious stones in the splendour of good work. There are those who love things besides God, [Col. 0758C] yet not against God nor more than God. In them the foundation remains, because love is not destroyed. Yet because some corruption is contracted from attachment to the things loved, they build upon it wood through the sin of unlawful action, hay through the offence of delight, and stubble through the fault of unlawful thought. There are those who love certain things against God; in them the foundation is destroyed, because the love of God cannot exist where he is not alone or supreme. Therefore the first deserve praise and salvation; the second, rebuke and deliverance; the third, accusation and condemnation.

## TITLE XIX. On the four things that confer humility.

Four things confer true humility: the lowliness of the body, continual subjection, comparison with one better, and dread of God’s judgment.

## TITLE XX. On the threefold living together of brothers.

[Col. 0758D]

Brothers dwell together in unity in three ways: in place only, in place and disposition, and in disposition only. To dwell together in place only is punishment; in disposition but not place, goodness; in disposition and place, blessedness.

## TITLE XXI. On the shepherd, sheep, and wolf.

There are three: shepherd, sheep, and wolf. The first and last look toward the sheep in the middle: one in order to guard it, the other to seize it. Hence of the first it is said: “His eyes look upon the poor; his eyelids examine the children of men” (Ps. 10). Of the second: “He lies in wait to seize the poor,” etc. (Ps. 9). The sheep in the middle is the poor person; the shepherd is God; the wolf is the devil. Every judgment proceeds from the sheep: the proud one is forsaken, the fearful one [Col. 0759A] visited. The former is forsaken lest it presume; the latter visited lest it despair. Therefore: “Do not turn away from your servant” (Ps. 26). When the shepherd withdraws, the wolf approaches; when the shepherd returns, the wolf flees.

## TITLE XXII. On conscience and reputation.

There are two: conscience and reputation. Conscience has God in the vessel; reputation, a light in the lamp. For conscience’s sake we go inward; for reputation’s sake we go outward. Within, we are restored by our own salvation; without, by another’s edification. Within: “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1); without: “I judge it necessary to remain in the flesh for your sake” (ibid.). Conscience is the upper watering-place; reputation, the lower watering-place. Meditation belongs to conscience; preaching, to reputation. Silence belongs to conscience; speech, to reputation. By silence you sow [Col. 0759B] your own field; by speech, your neighbour’s field.

## TITLE XXIII. On the three examples given by God for life, and the devil’s three examples for death.

By three examples Christ showed us the way by which we should follow him. Likewise the devil sets before us three things by which those who follow him are hurled down. The way to God is upward, steep, narrow, and lofty in its length. The path to the devil is downward, broad, short, and easy toward the depth and precipice. Therefore Christ left us the example of poverty, so that, relieved of the burden of earthly things, we may climb lightly by the steep way. Hence it is said: “Foxes have dens and birds of the air nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8). Therefore he did not wish to possess riches in this world, that we might be unencumbered; and he gave the example [Col. 0759C] of humility, so that, made small, we may pass without difficulty through the narrow way. Hence he says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). He therefore despised glory as an example of patience, lest we fail along the long way. Hence: “When struck, he did not strike back; when killed, he endured” (1 Pet. 2). Therefore poverty must first be learned, that we may cast away what weighs us down and offers an occasion of sin; and because poverty is despised, humility follows, so that even lowliness itself may be loved for God’s sake; and because a lowly person is injured without respect, patience is necessary after humility, so that adversities may be courageously endured for God’s sake. Poverty makes one light and unencumbered; humility, small; patience, strong and robust. Conversely, [Col. 0759D] the devil first burdens his own with the weight of riches in order to cast them down; second, puffs them up through pride, so that they may walk along the broad way; third, breaks them through impatience, so that they may quickly fail.

## TITLE XXIV. On the particular inhabitants of heaven, earth, and hell, and the three witnesses in each.

The three places—heaven, earth, and hell—each have their own inhabitants. Heaven has only the good; hell only the evil; earth has evil people mingled with good. There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Three on earth: spirit, water, and blood (1 John 5). Three in hell: the worm that does not die, by which conscience is gnawed; the fire that is not extinguished, by which bodies are burned; and, third, despair, [Col. 0760A] which is understood in the statement, “is not extinguished, does not die” (Isa. 66). To those in heaven is given the testimony of blessedness; to those on earth, that of justification; to those in hell, that of damnation. The first testimony is of glory, the second of grace, the third of wrath.

## TITLE XXV. On the threefold labour of humankind and its threefold remedy.

The human race labours in a threefold place: at the beginning, middle, and end—that is, in birth, life, and death. Birth was unclean, life perverse, death perilous. Therefore the heavenly physician came and brought a threefold remedy against this threefold disease. He was born, lived, and died. His birth purified ours; his life instructed ours; his death destroyed ours.

## TITLE XXVI. On the three loaves with which the arriving friend must be refreshed.

[Col. 0760B]

An arriving friend must be refreshed with three loaves. The first loaf is continence, by which the body is restrained so that it may not dissipate itself through deadly pleasures. The second is humility, by which the soul is instructed not to be proud because of the body’s continence itself. The third is the fervour of charity, by which the spirit is kindled so that it may steadfastly preserve both—the body and the soul—in chastity and humility. By these three virtues the person of God is refreshed and strengthened so that, according to the Apostle, at the day of the Lord’s coming spirit, soul, and body may be whole (1 Thess. 5). Whenever these loaves fail, they must be sought from God. They are rightly sought in threes, because three beings are to be refreshed: the soul, as husband; the flesh, as [Col. 0760C] wife; and the spirit, as the servant belonging to them both. Note that he does not say “give,” but “lend” (Luke 11), because one ought always to acknowledge that the fruit of this grace belongs not to oneself but to God.

## TITLE XXVII. The four ways in which prayer is made.

Prayer is made in four ways. First, with a modest disposition. This occurs when the sinner does not yet dare to approach in person, but seeks in the Church a holy man who may be, as it were, a fringe on the Lord’s garment, through whom he may gain access. The woman in the Gospel who suffered from an issue of blood prefigured this prayer when she said: “If I touch the fringe of his garment, I shall be healed” (Matt. 9). Second, prayer is made with a pure disposition, when the sinner now approaches in person and confesses with his own mouth. [Col. 0760D] The sinful Mary prefigured this when she watered the Lord’s feet with tears and wiped them with her hair (Luke 7), and heard: “Your sins are forgiven you” (ibid.). Third, prayer is poured forth with a broad disposition, when it is made not only for oneself but for others, as the apostles prayed for the Canaanite woman’s daughter. Fourth, prayer is made when it is uttered with confidence of heart and without any hesitation. The Lord made such a prayer when he raised Lazarus. The Apostle calls these kinds of prayer—modest, pure, broad, and unhesitating—by other names when he says: “I exhort, first of all, that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people” (1 Tim. 2). For supplications are made with a modest, prayers with a pure, petitions with a broad, and thanksgivings with an unhesitating disposition.

## TITLE XXVIII. The two ways in which a sinner’s prayer is prevented from being heard.

[Col. 0761A]

A sinner’s prayer is hindered in two ways: either it is illuminated by no light, or it is overwhelmed by excessive light. It is illuminated by no light when the sinner neither sees nor confesses sins. Conversely, it is overwhelmed by excessive light when the sinner sees them so great that he despairs of forgiveness. Therefore the light must be moderated, so that the sinner sees and confesses sins and prays with hope of pardon that they may be forgiven.

## TITLE XXIX. On the three vices prefigured by the three horses in the Apocalypse, and innocence prefigured by the white horse.

These three vices—pride, luxury, and hypocrisy—are the red, black, and pale horses of the Apocalypse (Rev. [Col. 0761B] 6). The red horse carries its rider, namely the human spirit, toward wars, quarrels, and angers; the black toward luxury, gluttony, and drunkenness; the pale toward hypocrisy and pretence. The red goes through hard and rough places; the black through unclean and fetid places; the pale through steep and lofty places. The white horse is innocence. The one who rides it goes out conquering, that he may conquer. This horse is threefold because innocence has three parts. Hence Habakkuk also speaks in the plural: “You ride upon your horses,” etc. (Hab. 3).

## TITLE XXX. On the three dissolutions and the three girdles of human beings.

There are three dissolutions that utterly dissolve a human being and cause soul and body wholly to perish: avarice, luxury, and pride. Avarice produces envy, drawing a person outside himself by wandering abroad, so that he may go to find consolation in transient things. Luxury brings forth uncleanness, pressing a person beneath himself through defilement, so that he may go to delight in vices. Pride gives birth to injustice, snatching him outside himself through self-exaltation, so that he may proceed to glory in power. These three deserve three curses. The first is: “Cursed is he who trusted in the abundance of his riches” (Ps. 51). The second: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17). The first dissolution, namely avarice, harms by three loves: love of money, ambition for honour, and desire for damnation. From this we lose three things: love in Christ and the Creator, expectation of heavenly glory, and obedience to divine power. The second, namely luxury, also harms in three ways: by brightness of skin, [Col. 0761D] splendour of clothing, and exquisite savour of food. Through these three we lose the first robe, which would be owed at death; future incorruption in the body; and the refreshment of the divine presence. The third, namely pride, likewise harms in three ways: by unclean thought, superfluous speech, and impure action. Through these three we lose simplicity of mind, moderation of tongue or voice, and purity of hands. The first dissolution has removed many from good; the second has advanced many toward evil; the third has removed countless people into death.

Three girdles are opposed to these. The first is remembrance of bodily death. This is the leather girdle with which John was girded and which hermits use. It is shown by three signs—pain, pallor, and numbness—when one remembers bodily death. [Col. 0762A] This girdle confers three things: to be less proud, to hate no one, and not to seek great things. For it humbles the proud, pacifies the hater, and fills and satisfies the covetous. The second girdle is the worthiness and beauty of chastity: the belt with which Aaron was girded when about to go to God, and which priests and Levites pursuing chastity use. It is shown by three signs: inward joy in the heart, outward confidence in the mouth, and external cleanliness in the body. This girdle confers three things: gravity in the countenance, moderation in dress, and composure in gait. For chastity, established inwardly in the heart, is outwardly adorned by these goods. The third girdle is love of religion and justice: the golden girdle with which John in the Apocalypse was girded about the breasts, and which Jesus uses in seeking the integrity of all. [Col. 0762B] It is shown by three signs: caution against transgression in foresight; obedience to command in patience; and attentiveness to divine knowledge in constancy. This girdle confers three things: humility in prosperity, firmness in adversity, and moderation in all things. For by it justice renders to each person what is his own. The first girdle trains the hands of fighters for battle; the second increases strength with strength; the third adorns the victor with rewards. Because John possessed the first, namely remembrance of death, he did not fear to meet death. Because Peter possessed the second, it was said to him: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you” (Matt. 16). Because Christ possessed the third preeminently, standing at Lazarus’s tomb he confidently said: “I thank you, because you have heard me” (John 11). [Col. 0762C] The first girdle separates a person from evil, and with it David slew Goliath; the second strengthens with virtues, and lacking it Absalom did not escape his enemies. The third joins one to religion, and with it Christ alone redeemed the human race.

## TITLE XXXI. On the titles of praise of Blessed John the Baptist, to be applied to the person renewed and persevering.

From the titles of John’s praises, very many may be applied, just as to blessed John historically, so also morally and not inappropriately to a man reborn and persevering. These are: a miracle in conception, joy in birth, loftiness in manner of life, humility in confession, truth in preaching, constancy in death. For when someone, from the old Adam, through the fear of God—which, like a standard-bearer of the heavenly host, is accustomed to turn minds toward [Col. 0762D] God, deter them from evil, and bring transgressors back to themselves—becomes a new man, and from earthly becomes heavenly and spiritual: what else occurs than that, by a kind of new conception, he is transformed into the womb of the Church and conceived? And in this conception there is cause for joy. For here is the finger of God, working subtly, renewing gently, transforming beneficially. This comes about through three things converging into one: thought, because it is in spirit and mind; will, which is not without merit; and steadfastness of purpose, which is not without justice. Joy in birth follows.

Birth is twofold: the first is from the father, the devil, whose life is perverse and whose death, following in either respect, is perilous; the second is from the Father, God, whose life is religious and whose death, following in either respect, is precious. This birth occurs through three things: firm faith, sure hope, and strong charity. Loftiness in manner of life follows; it consists in bearing, action, and speech. Let us take care not to be conspicuous in bearing, blameworthy in action, contemptible in speech. Let our bearing be moderate, our action upright, our speech truthful. Humility in confession follows. Let him who stands take heed lest he fall through pride. This confession is made in three ways: if he confesses himself to be no greater than his inferiors, less than his equals, obedient to his superiors; a companion to inferiors, a friend to equals, a son to superiors. Truth in preaching follows; it consists in three things: faithfulness, usefulness, and humility. It must be faithful and true, not deceiving by the mist of pretence; [Col. 0763B] useful, instructing hearers unto edification; humble, not puffed up by the loftiness of eloquence. Constancy in death follows. “He who perseveres unto the end, he shall be saved” (Matt. 10). This is accomplished in three ways when one, placed under the necessity of denying the faith, scorns offered riches, despises the power of honour, and willingly endures torments, reflecting within himself what Scripture says: “To him who conquers I will give to eat of the tree of life which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2). For the steadfast man chooses to fight, that he may conquer; to labour, that he may rest; to die, that he may live. Who, therefore, doubts that he is John in whom these things are found? Assuredly the grace of God is in him: this is the meaning of John.

## TITLE XXXII. How we should live soberly, devoutly, and justly

“Let us live soberly, devoutly, and justly in this world” (Titus [Col. 0763C] 2). Soberly toward ourselves, justly toward our neighbour, devoutly toward God. Soberly in two respects: in avoiding the pleasure of the flesh and the curiosity of the world. Hence the Lord says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with surfeiting and drunkenness and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). Behold the fetters which bind and constrict surfeiting—that is, concern for the flesh—and the prison which shuts in and confines the curiosities of the world. Whoever conquers the first, though walking in the flesh, does not wage war according to the flesh; whoever conquers the second can say: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

Likewise, justly in two respects: that you harm no one and desire to benefit all. Hence: “What you do not wish for yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4); and, “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7). Devoutly with regard to faith, which [Col. 0763D] consists in two things: justification, by which it justifies us in the present, and beatification, by which it makes us blessed in the future. God requires this faith from us: that we believe that we are to be justified by him through mercy, and made blessed through truth. For he has promised to make the righteous blessed. Hence: “Those whom he will justify, them he will also glorify” (Rom. 8). And the Lord says: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3). Earthly justification occurs in the present; heavenly beatification in the future. Therefore let us live soberly, that we may have a good conscience; justly, that we may be able to benefit our neighbours. Hence the wisdom which is from above (Jas. 3) is first chaste, then peaceable; devoutly, that we may love God. For all these things must be done for God’s sake.

## TITLE XXXIII. On the four callings and the two elections

[Col. 0764A]

“Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 10). There are four callings and two elections. The first calling is that of nature, from the womb into the light; concerning it the prophet says: “The Lord called me from the womb” (Isa. 49). The second is that of grace, concerning which the Apostle says: “Consider, brethren, your calling, that not many are noble” (1 Cor. 1). And: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called” (Rom. 8). The third is that of release, concerning which the same Apostle says: “I press on toward the prize of the heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3). Hence also the day of death is called the day of calling. The fourth is that of recompense, concerning which the Prophet says: “He called heaven from above, and earth, to distinguish his people” (Ps. 49). Many, therefore, are called, but few are chosen. [Col. 0764B] Many are called to faith; few are chosen to justification. Many are called to labour; few are chosen to rest. Many are called to judgment; few are chosen to the kingdom.

## TITLE XXXIV. How God sets his throne in his chosen ones

“Come, my chosen one, and I will set my throne in you.” It is one thing for God to set his throne in his chosen ones, and another for him to place the chosen ones upon the throne. The former is to justify; the latter, to make blessed. To justify is through faith; to make blessed is through sight. For through faith Christ dwells in our hearts; and since Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, the soul of the righteous becomes the seat and throne of wisdom. Therefore God calls his chosen one, first from error to faith; second, from faith to sight, being chosen by predestination. He calls to faith one chosen and taken from all flesh. [Col. 0764C] First he calls her in order to set his throne in her; second, in order to establish her upon the throne: because first he calls in order that, dwelling within her and cleansing her heart by faith, he may justify her; second, in order that he may glorify her when justified and assumed.

## TITLE XXXV. On the three things in marriage, the threefold fornication, and its remedy

“When the steward of the feast had tasted,” etc. (John 2). There are three things in marriage: the sacrament of religion, concerning which the Apostle says, “This sacrament, I say, is great,” etc. (Eph. 5); the office of purification, whence: “Cursed is he who has not left seed upon the earth”; and the remedy for fornication, whence: “Let each have his own wife because of fornication” (1 Cor. 7).

Fornication, however, is threefold: slippery in deed; phantastical in thought. [Col. 0764D] Hence: “Whoever looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5); apostate in departure, when one returns from the way of holy conduct to the world and to vomit. Hence: “You have destroyed all those who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72). Hosea briefly comprehends this threefold form: “Fornication,” he says, “and wine and drunkenness take away the heart” (Hos. 4), calling apostate fornication “wine,” phantastical fornication “drunkenness,” and slippery fornication “fornication.”

To this threefold fornication a threefold remedy is applied: betrothal, concerning which the Lord says in Hosea: “I will betroth you to myself in mercy; I will betroth you to myself in justice; I will betroth you to myself in faith” (Hos. 2): in the mercy of reconciliation, in the justice of covenant, in the faith of the marriage-bed. The Lord, calling to himself her who has committed fornication far away from him, [Col. 0765A] reconciles her to himself by mercy alone; he justifies her when reconciled; and, having justified her, by a certain inward taste of his sweetness, as by the earnest-money of a pledge, makes her covenanted to himself and inflamed with the ardour of desire for him. At last, rescuing her from the exile of this pilgrimage, he brings her into the bridal chamber of glory that absorbs her and glorifies her with his embrace.

Thus betrothal is threefold: in mercy, in justice, and in faith. That in faith unites bridegroom and bride; that in mercy, Christ and the Church; that in justice, God and the soul. The first is lawful, the second mystical, the third spiritual. The lawful is the remedy for slippery fornication; the mystical for phantastical fornication; the spiritual for apostate fornication. For each person is permitted to have his own spouse because of fornication; and the Church, chosen by her [Col. 0765B] Christ, is freed from fornication. But the Christian beloved, after prolonged incontinence, returning to her former husband and cleaving to him with chaste love, becomes one spirit with him.

As a figure of the threefold betrothal, among the Jews at weddings a *triclinium* was prepared—that is, a reclining chamber with three couches, called from *tris*, “three,” and Greek *κλίνη* (*klinē*), “bed”—over which presided the master of the feast, called the *architriclinus*. A bridal chamber is a place where people embrace one another in marital love. On the first couch are bridegroom and bride; on the second, Christ and the Church; on the third, God and the soul. The first is lawful, the second mystical, the third spiritual. Indeed, the first is that material bed; the second is the virginal womb, of which the Prophet says: “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” [Col. 0765C] (Ps. 18); the third is a mind sincere, devout, and faithful. Hence the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds be corrupted and depart from the simplicity which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Cor. 11).

## TITLE XXXVI. That persecution occurs for three causes and by four swords

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5). Some suffer persecution because of injustice; others because of false and feigned righteousness; others because of true righteousness. The first are wicked, the second hypocrites, the third chosen. Persecution takes place by a fourfold sword: that of punishment, of the tongue, of human disturbance, and of diabolical suggestion. Of the first it is said: “Tribulation, or the sword?” (Rom. 8). [Col. 0765D] Of the second: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56). Of the third: “A sword shall pierce your own soul” (Luke 2). Of the fourth: “Deliver me from the evil sword” (Ps. 143). To these four swords are opposed the two swords of ecclesiastical defence. Hence Peter says: “Behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22); and the Lord says: “It is enough” (ibid.).

## TITLE XXXVII. What the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent to teach

“The hour is coming, and now is, when true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4). God is Spirit, who teaches those who worship in spirit and truth. For the Son and the Holy Spirit were sent to teach three things: whom, where, and how. Whom? God. Where? In the Spirit. How? In truth. [Col. 0766A] There are those who do not worship God but demons; there are those who worship God, but not in spirit; there are those who worship God in spirit, but not in truth. There are those who worship God both in spirit and in truth. The first are Gentiles or the avaricious; the second, Jews; the third, hypocrites or heretics; the fourth, Catholics and the chosen. In the first there is profane religion; in the second, vain religion; in the third, false religion; in the fourth, true religion. This last is taught by the Son, Truth, and by the Holy Spirit; this religion blessed James calls pure and undefiled (Jas. 1): pure, without the wrinkle of gilded intention; undefiled, without the poison of perversity.

## TITLE XXXVIII. What it is to love God “with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s strength”; and what three things may be loved in different degrees

[Col. 0766B] “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Deut. 6). He who loves the world for God’s sake, and casts upon the Lord every thought that arises from worldly concern, loves God with all his heart. He who loves himself for God’s sake—he for whom to live is Christ and to die gain, who can say, “I live, yet no longer I; but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2)—loves God with all his soul, that is, with all his life. And this in two ways: either by loving God in himself or himself in God. But he who, having tasted the sweetness of God’s delight, loves God for God’s own sake and is now one spirit with God, loves God with all his strength.

There are indeed three things that can be loved in this degree, although only one is worthy of love: the world, man, and God. For one may love the world for the world’s sake, the world for [Col. 0766C] one’s own sake, or the world for God’s sake. But because every good effect—and only such an effect—is one whose cause is good, he certainly loves rightly who loves for God’s sake; for nothing apart from God is rightly loved. In the heart is signified thought; in the soul, life; in the mind, understanding. Therefore he loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind who thinks, desires, and understands nothing apart from God.

## TITLE XXXIX. On faith: whom, and through whom, it saves or does not save, both now and formerly

“Your faith has made you well” (Luke 8). At times a person’s own faith, and not another’s, made him well: as in the case of the man with dropsy while the Pharisees watched the Lord. At times another’s faith, and not his own: as in the case of the paralytic, when certain persons lowered him through the tiles. When he heard their faith, he said: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 5). At times both his own faith and another’s: as in the case of the Canaanite woman’s daughter, when the apostles interceded for her (Matt. 15). At times neither his own nor another’s faith, but grace alone: as in the case of the man blind from birth, who did not sin so as to be born blind, but that the grace of God might be manifested (John 9). Grace alone saves many today, as Paul; another’s faith, as children; their own faith, as Cornelius and the righteous. Some, destined for condemnation, are saved neither by their own faith, since they do not have it living, nor by another’s. For without faith it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11).

## TITLE XL. On the fourfold peace of the cloister

“Jesus stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: Peace to you” (Luke 24). The disciples were gathered together because of [Col. 0767A] fear of the Jews. We are gathered together in the cloister because of fear of demons: when we feared to engage them on the field of the world, we fled to the stronghold of the cloister. There, if we wish Jesus to enter among us and say, “Peace to you,” as he said it to the disciples when he came to them after the doors had already been shut, let us shut the doors.

There are four kinds of peace, much needed by religious persons: peace without, peace between, peace within, and peace above. Peace without is toward the world; peace between is peace among brothers; peace within is toward oneself; peace above is toward God. The first is good, the second better, the third best, the fourth most excellent. Whoever desires to attain these should establish four cloisters for himself and carefully shut the gates of each. The first cloister is material; the second, that of discipline; [Col. 0767B] the third, spiritual—that is, of virtue; the fourth, that of contemplation and divine love.

If the material cloister is guarded and closed, peace toward the world is frequently acquired. If the cloister of discipline is enclosed, peace among brothers is preserved. For the cloister of discipline includes the regulation of all bodily movements. Thus, if silence is imposed upon the mouth against murmuring, detraction, idle speech, foolish speech, and false speech; if the hand is restrained from evil and the foot withdrawn from where it may not lawfully go: when the cloister of discipline is guarded, brotherly peace is preserved, through which God is possessed among brothers.

But one must still advance to the peace that is within us. Many have peace outwardly with people and inwardly among their brothers; but within themselves they are ravaged by the tumult of vices. Yet just as soundness of skin outwardly is useless if the inner parts are corrupted by the pestilence of humours, so peace with people is of no avail when internal peace with oneself and with the angels is absent. For, according to the Apostle, we have been made a spectacle both to angels and to men [Col. 0767C] (1 Cor. 4), to good and evil angels, not to men only. The good observe in order to help and relieve; the evil, in order to attack and mock. Men see our fall and our standing outwardly and inwardly; angels see outwardly, inwardly, and within us. Therefore peace without and within is necessary in relation to men; but much more necessary is peace within us, in relation to ourselves and the angels. Hence Solomon says: “With all vigilance guard your heart” (Prov. 4).

There are those who close these material cloisters with such diligence that no outsider has an open entrance [Col. 0767D] or exit, and no sign contrary to discipline breaks out externally; yet, neglecting what is within, they do not fear to be fed upon inwardly by demonic bites. Such people perish unless they wash away the stain of the heart by worthy satisfaction. There remains the supreme peace, which is toward God; and there remains the loftiest cloister of all. When anyone has entered it, secure in God, both God will delight in him and rest in him. There he hides his own in the hiding-place of his face from the disturbance of men (Ps. 30), that is, in the gathering of himself. This peace is hidden from many and scarcely revealed to a few.

## TITLE XLI. On the moral etymology of the little castle

“Jesus entered into a certain little castle” (Luke 10). The castle is the soul; the rampart, patience; the tower, the name of the Lord; the depth of the moat, true humility; the gates, [Col. 0768A] the bodily senses; the weapons, works of virtue; the watchmen and defenders, the spiritual senses. Some of these keep watch through circumspection in conduct; others fight by driving out vices; others rest through inward contemplation of heavenly things. Food is sacred Scripture; drink, a more ready understanding; the leaders are the four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance.

## TITLE XLII. On the prodigal son and the three loaves to be lent him as a friend coming from a journey

“Friend, lend me three loaves” (Luke 11). A friend is one who speaks to a friend and for a friend. Our friend coming from a journey is the prodigal son, who, returning from a distant country, must be refreshed with three loaves. For he says to his father: “Give me the portion that falls to me” [Col. 0768B] (Luke 15). Having received it, he departed abroad into a distant country, making a journey without end, labour without rest, movement without stability, a course without arrival.
