The portion was threefold: memory, reason, and will. Memory attended to those things which belonged to God alone. Reason examined their depth with a discerning eye. Will, triumphing over earthly things, sought heavenly things. Memory grasped true things in summary. Reason examined what was good, what better, what best. Will chose uniquely that which was best. Having received this substance, therefore, the son withdrew from his father, fleeing through three nights. The journey of the first night is that by which he abandoned God the Creator; of the second, that by which he desired something other than God; of the third, that by which he rested outside God in alien things. First, withdrawing from God, [Col. 0768C] he goes to himself. Second, descending beneath himself, he delights in the flesh. Third, drawn outside himself, he delights in the appearance of things. First he goes to glory in virtue; second, to delight in vices; third, to find consolation in transient things.

Thus, when he had completed his journey, in the first year he squandered the goods of memory in three ways: through affectionate, burdensome, and idle thoughts. Affectionate thoughts, through concern with domestic affairs; burdensome thoughts, through anxiety over external matters; idle thoughts, through wandering among matters irrelevant to the matter at hand. In the second year he dissipated the goods of reason in three ways: receiving evil as good, falsehood as truth, and what is harmful as advantageous. Evil as good, because he lost ethics; falsehood as truth, because he lost logic; [Col. 0768D] harmful as advantageous, because he lost natural philosophy. In the third year he dissipated the goods of will by living luxuriously: through the burning of hidden fire, through the wandering of the outward eye, through ambition for the passing world—that is, through lust in stench, pride in rage, avarice in heat.

“After he had consumed everything, there was a famine in that land, and he began to be in want.” In the fourth year, returning to himself, he said: “I will arise and go to my father” (ibid.). First he makes good the losses of reason through faith, the losses of memory through hope, and those of will through charity. Faith enlightens reason in three ways: by commandments, signs, and promises. Hope strengthens memory in three ways: by pardon, grace, and glory. Charity restores will in three ways: by natural love, by which he loves his neighbour; rational love, by which he loves [Col. 0769A] himself; and spiritual love, by which he loves God.

Thus he returns by the contrary path in three days, so that by the same stages through which the diseased pest grew, health may return by the same boundaries. On the first day of return, therefore, he turns aside to a friend in order to dine with him. But whom will he find as a friend in the distant country? He himself is his own neighbour and friend. Therefore, turning to himself, he finds in himself nothing to set before himself except sins; he grieves and groans, and seeks another friend, namely a priest, and says to him: “Friend, lend me three loaves; impose a measure of penance.” Rising, the priest gives him as many as are necessary (Luke 11): namely, the bread of love, of labour, and of sorrow. On the second day he goes down to another friend, to the examples of the Fathers through frequent reading of the Scriptures. They set before him three loaves: the bread of pardon, of grace, and of glory. [Col. 0769B] Thus the man ate and was abundantly filled. On the third day he came to his father, God merciful and compassionate, who set before him three most tender calves: a new calf, a calf taken from the herd, and a fatted calf. Thus he ate and was abundantly satisfied. The first return, therefore, is from alien things to one’s own; the second, from evils to goods; the third, from transient things to eternal things.

## TITLE XLIII. That anyone resembling the blessed apostle Peter according to the etymology of his three names will be delivered from the hostile hand

“Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod” (Acts 12). This is the voice of one who has three names, namely Peter. For he was first called Simon, that is, obedient; then Bar-Jona, [Col. 0769C] that is, son of the dove, namely humility; thirdly Peter, that is, firm. If you are such a person, you will be delivered from every expectation of the people of the Jews (Acts 12): every expectation, that is, threefold expectation. For it consists in three things: the bond of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. The bond of the flesh binds; the lust of the eyes defiles; the pride of life devours. The bond of the flesh is compared to slime, the lust of the eyes to mud, the pride of life to the deep of a storm. Slime is worse than mud. For mud, though it defiles, is not tenacious; but from slime scarcely anyone can easily extricate himself, because flesh binds the spirit in such a way that even a good person scarcely wishes to be separated from it, but rather to be clothed over. Concerning the deep you have: “Let not the storm of water overwhelm me, nor let the pit press its mouth upon me” [Col. 0769D] (Ps. 68).

But even a cloistered religious, if he bears three names through obedience, humility, and steadfastness, can escape the first and second guard and the iron gate. The first guard is the habit of the flesh; the second, the onset of temptation; the third, the appearance of truth. The habit of the flesh binds, the onset chokes, the appearance of truth torments. It is hard to pass from feasts to vegetables, from cushions to straw, to turn olive-lees into oil, chaff into grain, a log into a calf. Thus it is difficult to be converted to the Lord. That calf puts forth horns and hoofs which is wholly offered to God in burnt offering. This is truly “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 67), which no one passes through except by obedience.

But when you have passed this guard, the onset of temptation remains. When one sees a brother keeping every rule of strictness and says: “What does this man expect except the abbot’s death? He would like to be abbot himself,” and thus envies and slanders him—this is the worst guard. Certainly, unless you are a son of humility, you will not pass this guard. Hear what answer was given to Antony. For when he sought to have all temptations shown to him, and, when they had been shown, said: “Lord, who can ever pass through these snares?” the answer was: “Humility.” If anyone has passed the onset of this temptation, the iron gate remains—namely, the appearance of truth—which no one can pass unless he is Peter.

Four squads were set to guard Peter (Acts [Col. 0770A] 22); one above, another below; one before, another behind. Below is concern for the flesh, [Col. 0770B] which under the appearance of truth addresses the brother thus: “Brother, hear what the Apostle says: As the rod, so food ought to be given to the beast; no one ought to be deprived of that by which the string of the harp is broken, upon which he must sing with the brothers. But the food of cloistered religious is not healthy. Cheese is altogether bad; eggs are quickly changed into flesh; vegetables cause swelling; cold water is harmful. Seek other foods.” Behold how it deceives under the appearance of truth. Here you must answer the brother what the Lord said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan” (Matt. 16). Bread and water, blessed life. You wish to make me a disciple of Galen, not Augustine; a physician, not a canon.

But the upper squad, pride, attacks him thus: “Brother, you are a good speaker, devout, learned; you are noble by birth; you have easy entrance [Col. 0770C] to the royal court; with one word you can do more good than all the rest. Therefore you ought to preside.” Behold how it deceives under the appearance of truth. Therefore say what the Lord said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan.” It is better for me to imitate Christ seeking lowly things than the devil wishing to set his seat in the north.

The rear squad approaches, and through remembrance of the past tries to deceive under this appearance of truth: that he left his parents poor, to whom provision ought to be made; that he ought first to visit the place where the Lord’s feet had been and the thresholds of the saints. Therefore say to it what was said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan.” Do you wish to make me a wandering vagrant? “I have not seen the righteous forsaken by the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 36). Behold, if you are thus three-named—Simon, Bar-Jona, and Peter—you will be able to pass the first and second guard and the iron gate, despise the squads there, and say in thanksgiving: “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel,” etc. (Acts 12).

## TITLE XLIV. On the praises of the blessed Mary, ever Virgin

Those who remember the blessed Virgin are blessed. Yet happier are the angels who possess her presence, whose beauty the Almighty desired and in whom he set his throne. Concerning this the history says: “Solomon made a great throne” (1 Kgs. 10). Solomon has three names. For our Saviour is first Solomon, that is, peaceful toward us in this exile, lovable, compassionate, a corrector of conduct: therefore king. He will be Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher, at the judgment, terrifying to the unjust and distinguishing merits: [Col. 0771A] therefore king. He is Idida, that is, glorious in the kingdom, wonderful and distributor of rewards: therefore king. He made the throne, that is, the Virgin’s womb, in which sits that Majesty who shakes the world by a nod. This throne is like the sun in the sight of God. Hence that voice: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21). For through it old things are made new.

He made, I say, a great throne of ivory. Ivory is cool, hard, and white. What is greater than she who enclosed within the secret chamber of her womb the greatness of divinity? “He clothed it with gold” (Isa. 47), that is, he wholly and indivisibly flooded the entire Virgin with the fuller grace of divinity. There follows, “exceedingly golden” (ibid.), because he is present in creatures in four ways: in good and evil by essence; in the good by operation; in those whom [Col. 0771B] he ennobles by knowledge of future things, by illumination; in his mother alone by identity. For he dwells in angels, but not with angels, with whom he is not of the same essence. But in the Virgin he dwells and dwells with her. Hence the angel says: “The Lord is with you” (Luke 1).

There follows: “It was ascended by seven steps” (1 Kgs. 10). Choose to meditate on holy things, because perverse thoughts separate from God, and you have ascended the first step. Accustom your tongue to speak well, and you have stood upon the second. Do justly what is just, and you have deserved to ascend the third. Leave the world and what belongs to it, and you have flown to the fourth summit. Persevere, and you have manfully held the sixth, so that you now aspire to that glory in which, in the region of angels, glory reflects [Col. 0771C] her glorious dignity.

There follows: “At the back it was rounded,” because her end, understood by those “back parts,” is glorious; like a circle, it has neither beginning nor end. There follows: “Twelve stood upon the steps,” because the twelve apostles, standing beforehand upon the steps in the manner described, gaze at the Queen not without amazement and say: “Who is this that ascends,” etc. (Song 8). There follows: “Two hands held the seat on either side” (1 Kgs. 10), that is, the active and contemplative life. For if you remember how she nursed her Son and endured every act of the crying child, you will understand that she ministered greatly in the active life. But if you hear how she pondered all his words in her heart (Luke 2), you will recognize in her the contemplative [Col. 0771D] life.

There follows: “Two lions stood beside the armrests” (1 Kgs. 10). These are Gabriel and John, one assigned as guardian of the Virgin’s right hand, the other of her left. Gabriel guarded her mind; John, her body. They are fittingly lions because of the roar of their most exalted voice. One cried: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1); the other: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). They announced such things to the world that whatever is said of their work is as though mute.

Therefore, Virgin whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, aid us as we cry: “Return, return, Shulammite” (Song 4), that we may behold you, blessed threefold and beyond. Return first by nature. Surely, because you have been so exalted, have you forgotten our mortality? By no means, Lady. You know in what danger [Col. 0772A] you left us, where your own lie, how greatly your servants sin. Such great mercy, then, does not befit forgetting such great misery; for although glory withdraws you, nature nevertheless calls you back. You are not so incapable of suffering that you are incapable of compassion; and therefore you do not so remember the glory of God alone that you have no mercy.

Return second by power: “For he who is mighty has done great things in you.” What can be denied to you, who rescued Theophilus from the very jaws of the devil? How can that power of your power resist you which took from your flesh the origin of its own flesh? You approach that altar of reconciliation, not merely pleading but commanding. Therefore let nature move and admonish you; let power move and admonish you, because the more powerful you are, the more merciful you ought to be.

Return third by [Col. 0772B] love. I know, Lady, that you are most gracious and love us with invincible love—us whom in you and through you your Son and your God loved with highest love. Who knows how often you restrain the wrath of the Judge, from whose justice the power issues forth before the divine countenance? Return fourth by singularity. In your hands are the treasures of God’s mercy. Far be it that your hand should cease; for your glory is not diminished but increased when penitents are received into pardon and the justified are assumed into glory.

Return, therefore, Shulammite, that is, “despised,” who was called the wife of a craftsman, whose soul a sword pierces (Luke 2). For what purpose? That we may behold you. The highest glory is to see you after God, to cleave to you, and to remain under your protection. She has heard us, she whom her Son, refusing her nothing, honours.

## TITLE XLV. On the battle to be waged by us against devils with the aid of angels

[Col. 0772C]

“A great battle took place in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon,” etc. (Rev. 12). Heaven is the Church of the chosen; in it, from the beginning of the Christian faith until the end of the age, that great battle occurs, concerning which the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6). He arms us for this war who says: “Your adversary the devil goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith” (1 Pet. 5). But this war is called not only ours but also that of the angels. Hence: “At that time Michael, the great prince, who stands for the children of your people, shall arise,” etc. (Dan. 12). Again: “In this battle the angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him and shall deliver them” (Ps. 33). For according to the Apostle all are ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. 1). Let us therefore take up arms confidently, because we have the bravest and unconquered helpers of our homeland.

Hence it follows: “That great dragon, the ancient serpent, the devil and Satan, went down from heaven to earth” (Rev. 12). Dragon, because of malice; great, because of enormity; serpent, because of hidden snares; ancient, because of long duration. He falls daily from heaven to earth when, expelled from the hearts of the chosen, he flows downward [Col. 0773A]—which is what *diabolus* signifies—and attacks the reprobate, who are wise in earthly things. Having subjected them to himself, he turns accusation against those whom he abandoned. Hence he is also called Satan, because that name means “adversary.” Would that it not be said of us also what follows: “Their place was no longer found in heaven” (Rev. 12). For many go back after profession, and in them the devil sets his place and seat.

## TITLE XLVI. On mercy and faith cleansing sins
By mercy and faith sins are cleansed (Prov. 15). Solomon says this to the tender and delicate. For if they have no tears, shrink from labours, and do not know how to endure tribulations, how will they excuse themselves from faith [Col. 0773B] and mercy? What is sweeter than mercy? What more delightful than faith? The one is the better oil; the other, light for the eyes. Mercy anoints the affections; faith enlightens and directs the senses, so as to lead them from darkness to light. For one who bestows mercy repays debts; faith, moreover, obtains pardon freely, without works. Of mercy it is said: “Give alms; and behold, all things are clean unto you” (Luke 11). Of the second: “Go; thy faith hath made thee whole” (Luke 8). Therefore these two are rightly joined.

## TITLE XLVII. On the inevitable judgment of God, how dreadful it is unless we flee to mercy.

“The eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil in every place” (Prov. 15). You feared human eyes; you did not dread the eyes of the Most High, of whom the prophet says: “Behold, thou, [Col. 0773C] O Lord, hast known all things, the last and the ancient” (Ps. 138). Neither from east nor west, nor from the wilderness of the mountains, is there a place of escape, since God is judge. And so he does not arrogate judgment to himself while he is God; he cannot be corrupted, because he is just; he cannot be resisted, because he is strong; he does not judge impetuously, because he is patient. He saw your deeds and the course of your crimes, and restrained his wrath; heaven did not thunderbolt you, water did not drown you, earth did not swallow you up. And though the whole earth is full of God’s glory, you have vomited forth your misery into his glory, and did not reverence the God who is present, nor hesitate to practise your uncleanness before such purity. Yet he says: “But I as though not seeing.”

[Col. 0773D] Has he revealed your shame to any of his ministers, who are judges appointed for this very purpose of his wrath? Behold, he sees and is silent, lest he judge. He sees and does not judge; he sees and feigns not to see. He calls, and you do not hear; he promises, and you despise; he threatens, and you do not fear. “You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (Rom. 2). Although he is exceedingly patient, and his eye is not angry every day, but spares sinners, nevertheless he is a just and strong judge. Will he who has thus kept silence always keep silence? Have you not read that he will come for judgment, laying aside patience, knowing nothing of humility, disregarding mercy? You have attended to one patiently silent; attend also to one speaking impatiently. “Like a woman in labour,” he says, “I shall speak” (Isa. 42). You have seen him dissembling; see also him threatening on account of even the least things. “You have numbered the footsteps of my feet,” he says (Job 13).

[Col. 0774A] What place will there be for hope when the judge comes—he who stood beneath judgment—with trumpets sounding, accusers crying out, and the elements burning? To whose help shall we flee when fire will mingle heaven and earth in frenzied conflagrations? He will come with power and majesty, not with sweetness and humility, because there his right hand is full of justice (Ps. 47), he who here sowed and scattered mercy. Then that merciful eye will not spare nor have pity, but will strike and kill. But what of sinners? Seeing, they will be troubled by a dreadful yet remediable fear, on hearing that terrible thunder: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25).

Who then are you, who despise [Col. 0774B] the riches of God’s goodness and patience? Know, according to the Apostle, that you have not escaped God’s judgment (Rom. 2). Look therefore first to the abundance of your sins; secondly, to your negligence; thirdly, to God’s patience in these matters; fourthly, lift your eyes to his mercy. Though you have sinned, been negligent, and provoked patience to wrath, he is ready to have mercy when you wish to return. Strive to blot out and cover your sins, and cast them into the depths of the sea; nor will there be delay between the one confessing and the one forgiving, for he is kind and merciful.

There are people quick to anger and slow to mercy, who disdain not only to speak to, but even to look upon, one cast down at their feet. The Lord Jesus is not so. He speaks with me more willingly than with the person whom I find whenever I seek him. He meets the fugitive [Col. 0774C] with loaves; everywhere he is gracious, everywhere sweet, everywhere possessing the great abundance of his sweetness. He does not raise his eyebrow or turn aside his eyes; rather, he meets the returning person, rushes into embraces, commands that the first robe be brought forth, that a ring be placed upon the hand, that the fatted calf be killed for the remission of sins, and that the return to the joys above take place with music. You see how long God’s patience is, how swift his mercy: “Long-suffering,” says the saint, “and abundant in mercy” (Ps. 102).

Far be it, then, that anyone should abuse such mercy by walking in the passion of his desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God! You who either consecrate or minister the body of Christ, chosen to serve Christ’s body so that you may sit with the emperor: with what mind, with what conscience [Col. 0774D] do you approach the holy of holies, you whose life is notorious, reputation contemptible, and speech held blameworthy? Yet if anyone has folded up something of this kind in the chamber of conscience, let it displease him; let him erase it by confession and wash it away by penance. And I promise mercy to that same person, to whom a child has been born for us—provided, however, that it has been born to him and that, holding it in the basin of his heart, he has received water made warm by the fire of charity—so that the light of the world may be born in him; nor will he deny mercy to the wretched, mercifully born, the merciful and compassionate Lord.

## TITLE XLVIII. On the eye as the lamp of the body, in a moral sense—that is, on the prelate.

“The lamp of thy body is thine eye” (Matt. 6). The prelate is the light of the Church. If he is single-hearted and without [Col. 0775A] stain, the whole body of the Church is rightly governed. If he is wicked, if sexually immoral, if greedy, the whole body will be dark. It does not say “wicked,” but “dark”; for not all imitate his wickedness, although they are enveloped in darkness because their lamp has been extinguished. It is therefore necessary that the eye—that is, priest or bishop—be without stain, so that all the members may be enlightened by his character.

## TITLE XLIX. On Christ’s going out from the Father and return to the Father, and wisdom’s going out from the heart and return to the heart.

“I went out from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16). Wisdom’s first going forth is from the Father’s bosom; its second is to the human heart, when, clothed in voice, it goes out through them and comes to the ear. There, stripping itself, it slips through hearing into the heart, [Col. 0775B] so that, leaving the world again through contemplation of the heart, it may return to the Father. It takes root in the heart, puts forth shoots in the human being, is pressed in the ear, and is again received into the storehouse of the heart. Voice is wisdom’s garment. Hence it is written: “The tongue of the wise adorneth knowledge” (Prov. 15). It does not go out except clothed, nor does it go out except stripped.

## TITLE L. On four points to be noted in the election of the apostles.

“Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and appointed you that ye should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15). In these words note four things: dignity, where he says, “I have chosen you”; office, “that ye should go”; caution, “and bear fruit”; constancy, “and that your fruit should remain.”

There is dignity in election. For it is a great thing that he who does not err chose; greater still is the work for which he chose [Col. 0775C] the chosen person; greatest of all is that he pre-elected among the elect. The meaning is: “Ye have not chosen me”—that is, you have not chosen by any mode of election—but I have chosen you by every mode. For there are three modes of choosing.

The first is election, when the good are chosen out of a multitude of bad and good, as grain from a heap, oil from a press. By this mode the children of Israel were chosen from every nation as a peculiar people. The second is sub-election, by which better persons are chosen from among the good, as he chose the sons of Levi for the service of the tabernacle. The third mode is pre-election, by which the best are chosen from among the better; by this mode he chose Aaron’s sons as priests.

Accordingly, first he chose you through water and Spirit from the breasts of unbelief. [Col. 0775D] He sub-chose you when he called you into the lot of the saints; and, advancing you to the order of the clergy, separated you from lesser believers by a distinctive tonsure of the head. But he pre-chose you when he set you over the heads of human beings as stewards of his household, that you might give it food in its season. Great, therefore, is the fact that he chose; greater, that he sub-chose; greatest, that he pre-chose. For how great it is that, at the lifting of your hands, the heads of kings are bowed down; all confess you to be fathers. Kings and kingdoms offer gifts and await intercessors. But woe to them who, though they were stones of the sanctuary, are scattered at the head of the streets (Lam. 4). Woe to fishers of souls if they are cast out among the bad fish. Woe to labourers in the Lord’s harvest if they are to burn like chaff.

The office follows [Col. 0776A] in walking: “I have appointed you,” he says, “that ye should go.” There are four postures of human beings. The first is that of those lying down, all of whose part is at rest. These are the wicked, lying in the world, who place all their hope in the uncertainty of riches, or whose god is their belly (Phil. 3), and do not set God as their helper (Ps. 51); who say: “Soul, thou hast many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry” (Luke 12). Those who are such lie cast down.

The second is that of those seated, whose lower parts lie at rest while the upper labour. These are good married people, who use lawful things rightly and serve partly God and partly the world. The third is that of those standing. These are contemplatives, every part of whom labours in raising itself, although by nature it is directed toward lower things; their citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3). [Col. 0776B] They establish peace with God; on earth they endure pressures, for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain (Phil. 1).

The fourth is that of those walking, whose labour increases through movement. These are prelates, on whom, above other classes of people, rests the duty of going about and distributing now to these, now to those, now to others, rebuke, exhortation, and correction as the grain of God’s word. Jesus, walking by the Sea of Galilee to give an example, said: “Go into all the world,” etc. Therefore you have been chosen that you may go. To sit, then, is dangerous for you; to lie down is deadly. Go, therefore, awaken those who lie down, and say: “Awake, thou that sleepest,” etc. (Eph. 5), lest the thief suddenly come and dig through your house.

But if one weighed down by heavy sleep does not awaken at the touch of a hand, cry aloud, do not cease (Isa. 58), for the Lord too with a loud voice [Col. 0776C] raised the man dead four days. Apply threats by whose stings the lethargic may be awakened. A hard sting is the saying: “The fire shall not be quenched, the worm shall not die; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Mark 9). From these pass to those who are seated, exhorting them to make progress; and say: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered thee, Jerusalem” (Ps. 136). Stretch forth your hand to the poor, lest your right hand be given over to forgetfulness. If he cannot stand, place your hand under the wavering person and say: “Rise up after ye have sat down, ye who eat the bread of sorrow” (ibid.).

From these one must pass to those standing, to whom consolation is necessary. “Stand,” say to them, “in your ways; act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” [Col. 0776D] (Ps. 26), “who shall sit upon twelve seats judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19). Walk now in the way of God’s commandments: this is the labour of your office.

The caution concerning fruit-bearing follows: “And bear fruit,” he says. There are three fruits: the thirtyfold, the sixtyfold, and the hundredfold—the fruit of subjects, prelates, and virgins. It does not suffice for a prelate to be good unless, so far as lies in him, he also makes others good. I think it was not without reason that it was said: “And lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). One lamp in the hand suffices for subjects, because they will render an account only for themselves. For prelates it does not suffice unless they carry a lamp in each hand. Hence, when the lord pope ordains a priest, he causes the ordinand to hold a burning [Col. 0777A] candle in each hand, signifying beforehand that the ordained person will render an account to the supreme Shepherd for the care of himself and of his own people.

Constancy in continuance follows: “And that your fruit,” he says, “may remain”—that is, may persevere. For the end—that is, victory—not the battle, crowns. Hence the command to offer the tail with the head. For this also the priests’ altar-tunic was given. Behold how many steps of rank you have ascended; by so many bonds of accountability you are bound. For who is bound by as many bonds as a priest when he is vested for ministry? First, with the amice he binds his throat; then, with the sleeves drawn under the armpits, he girds his breast. Thirdly, he constricts his loins beneath the girdle; as if it were said to him: Bind your throat—that is, set a guard over your mouth; bind your breast—that is, let evil thoughts not arise in your heart; bind your loins—that [Col. 0777B] is, crucify your flesh with its vices and desires. Pray, moreover, to him without whom you can do nothing, that, as he chose you, so he may help you to bear fruit and that your fruit may remain. Amen.

## TITLE LI. On the twofold birth, etc.

“Everything that is born of God overcomes the world” (1 John 5). There are two births: one from God, the other from the world. In this observe four things: carnal desire, temporal abundance, natural reason, and spiritual grace. The desire of the flesh agrees with the world, follows it, and has peace with it, because the first two readily run together. Natural reason dissents, resists the world, and fights with it; but it is defeated, and thus a human being is born, by existing in the world. But when spiritual grace is given by God, [Col. 0777C] reason, which formerly alone could not resist the two, is helped; the world is overcome and desire restrained.

But the grace of God is, according to the Apostle, through faith in Jesus Christ, upon all who believe in him, the power to become children of God; those who are born of God overcome the world (1 John 2). Nature resists, faith conquers, peace reigns. Now it must be seen who conquer. There are two kinds of people who triumph over the world; a third is conquered by the world. Thus there are Mary, Martha, and Lazarus in one house. Mary chose the best part (Luke 10), because no one overcomes the world more safely, easily, and quickly than one who wholly abandons and despises it. But one who handles worldly affairs, ministers through pious activity, and is troubled about many things, like Martha, fights laboriously, dangerously, [Col. 0777D] and for a long time, yet triumphs gloriously. Mary therefore wisely avoids the enemy; Martha bravely attacks it. Mary conquers by flight; Martha by battle. Lazarus, however, who neither avoids nor fights, burdened by the mound of earthly abundance, is buried in the desire of the flesh, virtue—that is, Christ—being absent. For, as Martha says to Jesus: “Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11).

Now it must be seen what conquers and by what means. “Overcomes the world,” he says (1 John 2). By the name “world” he includes three things: the prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God; the wisdom of the age, which is foolishness with God; and presumption of spirit, which belongs to one apostate from God. These are overcome by chastity, humility, and charity. The prudence of the flesh [Col. 0778A] exhorts the soul, saying: “Soul, thou hast many goods laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, make merry” (Luke 12). Temperance overcomes this, chastising the body, bringing it again under the soul into servitude, and making the members of the body instruments of righteousness for God. The wisdom of this age seeks its own things and cares only for what is useful to itself. Charity tramples it down, for charity “seeketh not her own,” but the things of Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 13); it considers not what is useful to itself, but what is useful to others. Presumption of spirit, while seeking to rule over others, disdains to be subject to God. Humility rises above it; in order to be more fully subject to God, humility wishes to be set over no one. Everything therefore that is born of God overcomes the world (1 John 5), that is, the prudence of the flesh, the wisdom of the age, and presumption of spirit: by chastity, charity, [Col. 0778B] and humility.

## TITLE LII. On the three heavens, lands, and testimonies in them, again in another sense.

“There are three who bear testimony in heaven” (1 John 5). There are three heavens, three lands, and three testimonies. The first heaven is God. In this, power, wisdom, and goodness—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—give testimony of full and supreme perfection; and these three are properly and principally one (ibid.), from whom are all things, in whom are all things, through whom are all things.

The second heaven is the angels. Hence: “Drop down, ye heavens, from above” (Isa. 45). In this, power, truth, and charity give testimony of blessedness; and these three are one, because they are one from the One: power from the power of God, truth from wisdom, [Col. 0778C] charity from goodness. The third heaven is spiritual persons, who declare the glory of God; in them faith, hope, and charity give testimony of justification. And these three are one because they are from one source. Faith, from wisdom, enlightens toward truth; fire, from the Holy Spirit, kindles toward charity; and through these two we have hope of reaching the Father.

The first land is the penitent people, the holy land. In it spirit, water, and blood give testimony of remission—that is, compunction, confession, and remission. The Holy Spirit, searching hearts and loins, while convicting sinners concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, surely pierces them with repentance. Therefore the Spirit signifies that which he gives. Water signifies confession, because sins are washed in [Col. 0778D] confession, as the streams of the eyes often make evident. Good is the confession of the mouth; better, that of the eyes; best, that of works. Understand, then, the spirit as compunction and the water as confession. The blood of remission follows; for without blood remission does not occur. And these three are one, because they are from the one source from whom comes every good gift (Jas. 1).

But the middle land, cursed in Adam’s work, is ploughed by the share of threatening and watered by the dew of promise, bringing forth thorns and thistles. It has three witnesses of destruction: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. The last land, of eternal condemnation, has as witnesses unquenchable fire, the immortal worm, or the incorruptible flesh of the damned; and from these, despair. For if the material fire or worm [Col. 0779A] were finite, the punishment too could be temporal.

## TITLE LIII. On the three gifts of God in the human being.

“Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). There are three gifts of God in the human being: the first, of nature, by which one exists; the second, of grace, by which one merits him; the third, of glory, by which one is glorified with him. Yet all are gifts of grace. By the first gifts of nature we are human; by the gifts of grace, just; by the gifts of glory, we shall be blessed. By the first we were created free from sin; by the second, freed from sin; by the third, made secure against sin.

The gifts of nature are memory, reason, and will, by which we excel brute animals. The gifts of grace are faith, hope, and charity, by which we overcome demons. [Col. 0779B] The gifts of glory are eternal and true blessedness, blessed and eternal truth, true and blessed eternity, by which we are made equal to angels. Among the gifts of nature and grace, some are least, some middle, and some great. The first are bodily beauty, health, and the rest, together with those things which concern the body’s maintenance; if they are not abundant, it does no harm, and often helps. The second are gifts of the soul, such as reason, intellect, and will; when strong, they do indeed often profit salvation, but never unless we use them well. The third gifts are the good use of these endowments, which are called virtues. We sometimes use the first well without the second; the rest rarely without the second; never without the third. Every good is from God. Virtue uses good things well; vice abuses them.

These goods or gifts sometimes descend from God to [Col. 0779C] a human being, and then they are gifts; sometimes they ascend from a human being to God, and then they are merits. Sometimes a human being ascends to the gifts, and then they are rewards and the fruit of labour. Therefore God’s gifts are, first, second, and third: gifts, merits, rewards. Gifts and merits ascend to rewards, and we ascend to them. Yet all descend from God, because all are his gifts. From gift we ascend to merit; from merit to reward. A gift is a simple bestowal; merit is gift upon gift, descending from the Father of lights. For from him comes gift; from gift, merit; from merit, reward. God himself comes to you through the first; in the second he labours with you; in the third you rest in him. Therefore God is your gift, and your whole [Col. 0779D] good is his gift, descending from the Father of lights. You receive divisions; he is not divided. You partake of him within yourself, because he always remains whole and the same in himself: “With whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (ibid.). Thus he is varied in you who is not changed in himself.

## TITLE LIV. On the threefold form of the world, and the threefold oldness and its remedies.

“Be not conformed to this age, but be reformed in the newness of your mind, that ye may prove what is the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God” (Rom. 12). The world is threefold in form. By the first form it delights us with the flower of prosperity; by the second it kisses us with the honour of dignity through being set over others; by the third it embraces us with the love of power through domination. By the first it wearies us; by the second it conquers us; by the third it binds us when conquered.

The world’s kisses are like Judas’s kisses. Judas betrayed Christ by a kiss into the hands of the Jews; the world betrays its followers into the power of demons. Judas said to the Jews: “Whomsoever I shall kiss, that is he; hold him” (Matt. 26). The world says to the devil and his angels: “Whomsoever I shall kiss, that is he; condemn him.” The Apostle therefore advises us with salutary counsel: “Be not conformed to this age” (Rom. 12). But why? Because it is threefold, and we are conformed to it in three ways: through the pleasure of prosperity into luxury, through the ambition of dignity into pride, and through the abuse of power into violence. Prosperity softens; dignity exalts; power drives to ruin.

[Col. 0780B] These are the vices that he first uproots when he says: “Be not conformed to this age,” as though saying: “Turn away from evil.” Secondly, he plants virtues, adding: “But be reformed in newness” (ibid.), as though saying: “And do good.” When he says “in newness,” he indicates that oldness has preceded; and it is threefold. The first is in the heart: desires of the flesh through thought; the second is in the mouth: arrogance through speech; the third is in action: crimes through performance. If there were no oldness in the heart, he would not have said: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4). If there were no arrogance in the mouth, he would not say: “That every mouth may be stopped, and all the world made subject to God” (Rom. 3). If it were not in action, he would not say: “Ye have yielded your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity,” etc. (Rom. 6).

[Col. 0780C] Behold the threefold oldness in the image of the old human being. As we have borne it, let us bear the image of the heavenly one (1 Cor. 2), which is threefold: love of righteousness in the heart against desires of the flesh; confession of humility in the mouth against arrogance; innocence of simplicity in action against crimes.

## TITLE LV. On the threefold property of stone and love, and on the good and bad shepherd.

The Lord said to Peter: “Peter, dost thou love me?” (John 21). There are three properties of stone: stones are solid, rough, and suitable for building. Their solidity designates those who do not yield to vices; their roughness, those who live austerely; their suitability for building, those who advance in virtues. Thus that person is Peter who does not yield to vices, lives austerely, and advances in virtues.

Three things likewise are considered in love: that one does not neglect one’s neighbour; that one loves oneself; and that one chooses God as one’s portion, because he is good. Let one love one’s neighbour, oneself more than one’s neighbour, and God more than oneself. Whoever has these properties of stone and love truly confesses himself to be Peter. The Lord says for the third time: “Feed my sheep” (ibid.). Feed them by example; feed them by teaching; feed them by holy prayer.

Peter, made shepherd, follows the pattern of the good shepherd in three ways: he feeds servants by correction with the rod of penance; he feeds hired workers by consoling them with the reward of righteousness; he feeds sons by instructing them in the grace of obedience. But bad shepherds are designated by other properties. For they are hard, dry, cold stones: hard through cruelty, lacking the spirit of gentleness; dry through barrenness, not possessing the moisture [Col. 0781A] of grace; cold, not warmed by the fire of the Holy Spirit. When the Lord says for the third time, “Dost thou love me?” these cannot truthfully answer, “I love thee”—or “myself.” Such a person hates his neighbour from malice, neglects himself from sloth, and does not worship God from avarice: harmful to his neighbour through disdain; destructive to himself through deficiency; presumptuous toward God through contempt.

Hearing, “Feed my sheep,” these people perversely feed them in three ways: by the example of action, teaching them to live badly through transgression in deed; by the teaching of speech, teaching them cleverly to deceive through abuse in deed; by the work of prayer, teaching them to plead cases by contemplation of money. Thus bad prelates feed Christ’s sheep for themselves—or rather, so they consume them: they strip off the fleece, drink the milk, and gnaw the flesh.

But considering that a shepherd is so called from feeding, lest he be a shepherd in name only, he utterly neglects the flock and with every effort feeds his own belly, and does so in three ways: with food seasoned by a sweet taste, that it may please the palate; with a delightful aromatic scent, that it may please the sense of smell; with a marvellous desirable brilliance, that it may please the sight. Behold Nebuzaradan, Pharaoh’s cook, who threw down the walls of Jerusalem. For gluttony destroys body, soul, and mind, as though they were a city.

## TITLE LVI. On choosing the best part.

“Mary chose the best part” (Luke 10). “Best” is said in excess of two. Good is marital chastity; better, widowly continence; best, virginal purity.

## TITLE LVII. How one ought to be girded for the road, armed for battle, and apron-girded for the table; and on the belt with which we are to be girded.

[Col. 0781C]

“Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). We gird ourselves for going on a journey; we arm ourselves for fighting; we are belted for serving. These three are owed to three disciplines of ecclesiastical life: the road, the battle, and the table—the course of the road, the conflict of battle, and service at table. The road is that of works; the battle, that against enemies; the table, that of the sacraments. Therefore we must gird ourselves for the road with the belt of patience, arm ourselves for battle with the sword of penitence, and belt ourselves for the table with the linen cloth of continence. To the belt of patience pertains what is said to Peter: “Another shall gird you” (John 21). For the battle of penitence: “He who has no sword, let him sell his tunic and buy a sword” [Col. 0781D] (Luke 22); that is, let him leave the manner of life of the world and take up the fruit of penitence. For the linen cloth of continence there are the linen breeches of Aaron and his sons.

Paul both displayed these three things in himself—namely, the course on the road, battle, and service—and taught them to others. For he ran, saying: “I run, not as though uncertainly” (1 Cor. 9); and, “I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4). He taught others to run, saying: “So run, that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). He fought, saying: “So I fight, not as one beating the air” (ibid.); and likewise: “I have fought a good fight,” etc. (2 Tim. 4). He taught others to fight, saying: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9). He ministered, saying: “They are ministers of Christ, and so am I” (2 Cor. 11). He taught others to minister, saying: “That our ministry may not be blamed” [Col. 0782A] (2 Cor. 9).

Therefore, girded for the road, let us beware of its four impediments. For the road is rough, crumbling, steep, and muddy: rough with the stones of hardships; crumbling with the valleys of failures; steep with the hills of successes; muddy with the marshes of pleasures. We stumble over stones, fall in ruins, and are submerged in marshes. Come to the battle and “gird your sword upon your thigh” (Ps. 44); for “the life of man upon earth is a warfare” (Job 7).

This battle is against enemies who can be overcome, though they are immortal. They draw up a threefold battle-line against us: the first of suggestions, the second of occasions, the third of occupations. By suggestions they attack; by occasions they conquer; by occupations they bind. Suggestions disturb the affections and summon pleasure [Col. 0782B] and consent as auxiliaries. By these the first battle-line conquers and is not conquered unless it is met. Occasions obstruct the senses, and are considered in terms of place, time, and person. A solitary place affords boldness; nighttime, confidence; a lustful and shameless person, an opening. These must be fled, lest the second battle-line prevail.

Occupations confuse actions, and concern two kinds of activity: public acts, such as the external administrations of prelates, abbots, and the like; and private acts, such as writing, painting, and similar things. Whoever passes through these with uninjured foot triumphs over the third troop. By the first battle-line, namely that of suggestions, the troop was defeated (Gen. 32); by the second, that is, of occasions, Dinah was captured (Gen. 34); by the third, which is that of occupations, Tamar, Absalom’s sister, was violated [Col. 0782C] by Amnon (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 13).

By way of the road and battle you are summoned to the table, which is that of the sacraments. Since you approach it in order to minister, let your loins be girded with the linen cloth of continence; for by linen is signified purity of the flesh, and by the loins, lust. We read that these three expressions apply their force to this restraining of the loins: that we are commanded to gird ourselves, arm ourselves, and belt ourselves. “Having your loins girded with truth” (Eph. 6), says the Apostle; and the Lord says to Job: “Gird your loins like a man out of the whirlwind” (Job 40). And in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded.”

This linen cloth of continence is signified by that linen girdle of the prophet which he first put upon his flesh; then took and placed in the river Euphrates, [Col. 0782D] and, when he returned to retrieve it, found it rotten, so that it was fit for no use (Jer. 13). The girdle upon the flesh is continence restraining it; it is placed in the river when it is relaxed amid the flowing pleasure of the age. It rots there when continence is dissolved and perishes among fleshly delights. The girdle is no longer fit for any use, because it is acceptable neither to God nor to human beings.

This girdle is signified by the leather belt of John and Elijah. For each is read to have had a leather belt around his loins. There are two kinds of loins: permitted and illicit pleasure. Permitted pleasure belongs to married persons; illicit pleasure to the unmarried and to those devoted to God. The loins of married persons must be belted, lest they approach another woman; those of unmarried persons, lest they touch any woman unless they marry her; those of the devout, lest they touch or marry. These especially must be belted, because they serve [Col. 0783A] at the Lord’s table. “Be cleansed,” he says, “you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52).

Those who minister at this table should gird themselves with the belt of John and Elijah—that is, continence—which some have had and have, as virgins perpetually continent; some did not have before but have now, as penitents; while some neither had it nor have it, as those continuing in lust. Let the one who possesses it keep it, for blessed is the one who keeps it; let the one who has not possessed it buy it; let the one who has lost it redeem it. The seller is at hand, who offered his own skin for sale and made ample straps upon the cross from his own flesh, not another’s. The price of this belt will be small: only two denarii, prayer and fasting. “This kind of demons,” says the same seller, “is not cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9).

But let these denarii [Col. 0783B] be genuine, not counterfeit; for one who pays debased currency does not free himself. The genuineness of coins consists in three things: material, weight, and image. The material is charity, which is compared to gold; the weight, hope, which raises one from earthly things; the image, faith, which imprints the sign of the cross on our foreheads. The Apostle says that this currency has value: “Let all your works be done in charity” (Rom. 16). And he shows that what is fashioned outside this material is false, saying: “If I distribute all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body so that I burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Without the image of faith it is not genuine. “Without faith,” says the same Apostle, “it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11).

Therefore, if one of these is lacking from your fasting and prayer, you incur the crime [Col. 0783C] of counterfeit currency, which is the burning of the living. For if you offer false currency to God, you will be burned in everlasting fires. See, therefore, that your prayer is directed in the sight of the Lord and that your fasting is acceptable. One prayer is that of Tully, another that of the Pharisee, another that of the tax collector. Tully’s flatters; the Pharisee’s angers: “I am not as the rest of men,” etc. (Luke 18). The prayer of the righteous obtains what it seeks; and if it is continual, it is very powerful. Let your fasting be that which God chooses, not like that of the hypocrites, who make themselves sad in order to appear to fast; rather, anoint your head—that is, your mind—with the oil of joy, and wash your face with the tears of penitence (Matt. 6).

But the leather belt which you are commanded to redeem must be fashioned thus. First, it must be separated from the flesh by a vow, so that it may be cut by the sword which the Lord came to cast upon the earth, by which [Col. 0783D] each is separated from his household: son from father, daughter from mother, daughter-in-law from mother-in-law (Matt. 10). Second, it must be sprinkled with salt through fear, lest it rot; for salt drives away worms, and the fear of the Lord casts out sin. Third, it must be dried by the sun through desire, lest it dissolve; for the sun dries, and desire inflames. Fourth, it must be anointed with oil through joy, lest it grow cold; for joy of conscience makes one glad and cheerful. “This,” says the Apostle, “is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). Fifth, it must be scraped with iron through zeal, lest it become filthy; for zeal also destroys in others the filth of lust. Sixth, it must be colored with vermilion through good testimony, because the testimony of a good reputation makes it attractive and acceptable to people. Therefore, if with this belt, made from the strap [Col. 0784A] of the crucified flesh and bought with the two denarii already mentioned, you gird your loins, you will minister securely at the Lord’s table.

## TITLE LVIII. On the threefold deafness, death, and poverty.

“The deaf hear, the dead rise, and the poor have the Gospel preached to them” (Matt. 11). Deafness arises in three ways. Death gains strength in three ways. Poverty consists in three ways. Deafness arises from beginning at birth, from illness that supervenes, and from declining age; this deafness is natural. There is another, spiritual deafness, demonstrated in this: God has spoken in three ways, and we have not heard him. He has spoken through the law of nature, the figure of Scripture, and the word of the reality to come. The law of nature spoke in the heart, written in deed; the word of reality, in the human being.

[Col. 0784B] From this threefold deafness the Lord rouses us by a threefold call, crying three times: “Come, come, come.” The first call: “Come, children, hear me” (Ps. 33). The second: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). The third: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25). The first call removes the torpor of our deafness; the second restores to the ears the strength to hear; the third preserves what has been heard through perseverance.

Death gains strength in three ways: through necessity, infirmity, and savagery—naturally through old age, accidentally through fever, cruelly through poison and sword. Likewise spiritual death gained strength in three ways: through affirmation, doubt, and denial. The Lord affirmed it, saying: “In whatever hour you eat, you shall die [Col. 0784C] by death” (Gen. 3). The woman doubted, saying: “Lest perhaps we die” (ibid.). The devil denied it, saying: “You shall by no means die” (ibid.). Therefore death is threefold: wicked consent, wicked deed, and wicked habit. The cause of the first death is that Adam “went away in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1); of the second, that he “stood in the way of sinners” (ibid.); of the third, that he “sat in the seat of pestilence” (ibid.), corrupting others by his example.

From this threefold death the Lord raised us in three ways: by compunction, confession, and affliction—compunction through the bitterness of a contrite spirit; confession through the truth of speech uttered; affliction through the harshness of a body made lean. Poverty consists in three ways: one kind is feigned, another necessary, another [Col. 0784D] voluntary. Feigned poverty belongs to hypocrites; necessary poverty, to the needy; voluntary poverty, to the elect. The first brings condemnation, the second expiation, the third reward. The Lord consoles those enduring necessary poverty through the prophet: “Do not fear,” he says; “you shall not be confounded, poor little one, shaken by the storm” (Isa. 54). Hence it is clear that such a person escapes condemnation, yet does not merit a crown. Therefore he adds: “I have refined you, but not as silver” (ibid.). Voluntary poverty, however, has the first crown. This is poverty in spirit. Feigned poverty is of the will, but not of truth; therefore it is not in spirit either. A will without spirit is like a body without soul: it falls, rots, and is dissolved into dust.

But when a person is humbled in his spirit, so as to presume nothing of himself in anything, his own spirit begins to fail [Col. 0785A] and cleaves to God; then one spirit with him is made. For the Spirit breathes into and fills his will, and the will thus made spiritual is customarily called spirit. This is poverty in spirit: that is, poverty in a spiritual will.

Likewise, possession is threefold: one kind destructive, in the avaricious; another idle, in those converted only lukewarmly; another burdensome, in the devout. Of destructive possession the Apostle says: “All who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil” (1 Tim. 6). Idle possession belongs to those who outwardly possess nothing but inwardly set before themselves many possessions, as if dreaming. Of burdensome possession: “You cannot serve God and mammon,” etc. (Matt. 6).

### On three sorrows to be avoided or turned into joy.

[Col. 0785B] “Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16). Sorrow that is turned into joy is threefold. For it condemns past sins, judges present ones, and avoids those that are approaching: it condemns through penitence, judges through discernment, and avoids through foresight. Through penitence concerning the past it obtains pardon; through discernment concerning the present, protection; through foresight concerning the future, caution. Past things are erased through pardon, as though they had never existed; present things are overcome through displeasure, so that they can do no harm; future things are excluded through caution, so that they may never be.

## TITLE LIX. Why “Feed my sheep” was said three times.

“Feed my sheep” (John 21). It was said three times, as though he said: Feed servants, feed hirelings, feed sons. You shall correct servants with the rod of guidance; hirelings, consoling them [Col. 0785C] with the reward of justice; sons, instructing them by the grace of obedience—adding moderation in correction, abundance in consolation, and gentleness in persuasion.

## TITLE LX. On spiritual refreshment, the tree of paradise, and old leaven.

“Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are unleavened” (1 Cor. 5). The Apostle invites us to divine feasts and the refreshment of the soul. The bride of God, invited to these, rejoicing that she had received the shade which she desired, said: “I sat beneath the shade of him whom I desired, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2). For in the midst of paradise is the tree of life, giving shade, leaf, and fruit. This paradise is an assembly of religious persons, a congregation of monks.

[Col. 0785D] So also are we, if indeed we are gathered together in heart and not only in body, to glorify God. For if there is disagreement in minds, it profits nothing for bodies to be gathered together; indeed, we ought rather to be called a dissension than a congregation. But if it is granted from above by him who “makes those of one manner dwell in a house,” that exceedingly delightful gift—namely, that brothers dwell together as one in affection, charity, and unity—then we are truly paradise, that is, God’s garden of delight, in which God rejoices and takes pleasure; and then he dwells in us.

In the midst of such a paradise is the tree of life, that is, Christ giving life. He himself promised this: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). For “where two or three are gathered together in [Col. 0786A] my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. 18). This tree, that is, Christ, gives shade, leaf, and fruit: the shade of protection, the leaf of commandment, and the fruit of eternal recompense. He gives shade by protecting us round about: behind, by forgiving past sins; before, by guarding us from impending evils; at the right, by protecting us lest prosperity exalt us; at the left, lest adversities disturb us. After shade comes the leaf of commandment, which withdraws from evil and draws toward good. This is: “Do good and turn aside from evil” (Ps. 102). After shade and leaf comes the fruit of recompense, in which our desire shall be satisfied with good things (Prov. 13).

Thus the bride sits beneath God’s shade of divine protection, receiving through obedience the leaf of his commandment, and through hope awaiting the fruit [Col. 0786B] of eternal recompense. Yet she sits upon grass with the five thousand to be fed by the Lord in the desert; that is, she subdues the flesh, signified by grass, together with the five bodily senses. Or she sits upon the footstool, by which the world is signified, restraining it and its desires; or, with Rachel, upon Laban’s idols, restraining the deceits of the devil. These are the three worst persons, making up the old leaven of the wretched soul, from which the Apostle commands us to be cleansed: “Purge out the old leaven.” This old leaven consists in three things: pleasure, vainglory, and pride. The devil gives pride; the world adds vainglory; the flesh mixes in pleasure; and together they make the old leaven, that is, the old human being.

The first [Col. 0786C] part of this leaven is bad, the second worse, the third worst. Blessed is the one who casts away the devil’s pride; more perfect, the one who casts away the world’s vainglory; most perfect, the one who has subdued the flesh’s pleasure. Samson overcame the lion and defeated the Philistines, but the softness of his wife breaks him. The lion is the devil, who goes about as a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour. The Philistines are the world and secular life. The wife is the flesh. Samson kills the lion when any spiritual person renounces the devil. He conquers the Philistines who rejects worldly life; but he is deceived by his wife when he is overcome by the flesh. He sleeps in his wife’s lap who “makes provision for the flesh in its desires.” Then the Philistines rise up, the evil spirits come, and cut off his hair [Col. 0786D]—that is, take away his virtues; they pluck out his eyes—that is, remove the light of Christ; and put him to the mill—that is, into the circuit of transitory things—so that he may be among those of whom it is said: “The wicked walk round about” (Ps. 11). See where the first part of the leaven, the pleasure of the flesh, leads.

Let us see where the other two corruptions, vainglory and pride, lead. These two are Lot’s two daughters. After he left Sodom, abandoned his wife and Zoar, the little city in which he could have been saved, they follow him to the summit of the mountain and make him drunk. Drunk, he fathers sons who do not enter the Church of God. This Lot signifies the monk who abandons the flames of Sodom, and his wife—that is, the flesh—which looked back; and even the lawful secular life in which he might have been [Col. 0787A] saved, and ascends to the summit of the perfection of monastic profession. But in the state of perfection, the two daughters, from their father as though from himself, generate sons: that is, such works as do not enter the Church of God. See where the second and third parts of the leaven lead.

Therefore, brothers, lest through the flesh we lose our eyes and the light of Christ, and through pride and vainglory be excluded from heavenly glory, let us purge out the old leaven: subduing pride through humility, casting away vainglory through the purity of right action, and mortifying the flesh’s pleasure through abstinence. Thus may we be a new dough, a new unleavened bread, which is given to the people departing from Egypt and placed before Elijah fleeing the evil queen Jezebel (3 Kings [1 Kings] 19).

The evil queen is the flesh, which, given over to fleshly [Col. 0787B] desires, seeks to kill and rule over the virtues. She pursues Elijah and every spiritual person who lusts against the spirit. Elijah flees her by abandoning her concupiscence. He comes to Beersheba of Judah, to confession, where there is the well of the sevenfold grace of the Spirit; and there he leaves his servant—that is, in confession he leaves behind childish understanding and childish works, putting away, with the Apostle, the things that belonged to a child. He goes into the desert, that is, contempt of the world; sleeps beneath the shade of the juniper, that is, rests from vices; keeps watch beneath the hard works of penitence, and eats ash-baked bread. For while he rests from vices, he is pressed by the hard thorns of penitence; and while he watches, harsh and difficult things are set before him. Ash-baked bread is the life of penitence: in bread life is signified; in ash, [Col. 0787C] penitence.

After the first sleep he sleeps again, and then, awakening, walks to Mount Horeb, the mountain of God. The first sleep is rest from vices; the second is that in which saints rest from their labors when they die in the Lord and come to the height of glory through the strength of ash-baked bread—that is, a penitential life, by which they afflict themselves for sins. This bread belongs properly to monks. For nothing but hard and harsh things are prescribed for them. Bread is offered with ashes—that is, life with penitence—by which they ought to afflict themselves through the sacrifice of a contrite heart and the sacrifice of mortified flesh, so that they may come to the sacrifice of Christ’s body. That they may attain it, sacrifice of humility in the mind and affliction in the flesh must precede, so that [Col. 0787D] devotion may be present in the immolation of the living Lamb.

“For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). He is sacrificed because he is the Lamb who is commanded to be taken on the tenth day and sacrificed on the fourteenth. Why is he eaten neither raw nor boiled in water, but roasted with fire? (Exod. 12). He is taken in the number ten because of the Decalogue of the Old Testament, and in the number four because of the four Gospels. Therefore the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1) is taken on the tenth moon, because he is foretold as to come in the Old Testament; and sacrificed on the fourteenth, because he is crucified in the New Testament.

He is eaten in three ways by three classes of people: raw, boiled in water, and roasted with fire. The first class of people were unbelievers; the second, foolish believers; the third, good believers. Unbelievers eat him raw; foolish believers, [Col. 0788A] boiled in water; good believers, roasted by fire. He is eaten raw when he is believed to be merely human; boiled in water when he is also believed to be God, but it is investigated through human wisdom how he could be born of a Virgin and how God could become human. For then he is boiled in water when he is examined by human wisdom. He is eaten roasted with fire when Christ, God and man, is believed to have suffered and to have been conceived and born by the fire of the Holy Spirit. For the roasted Lamb is Christ suffering. Unbelievers swallow him, as it were raw and tasteless, when they judge Christ to be merely human; foolish believers receive him boiled in water, because they presume to investigate him by human wisdom; good believers incorporate the roasted Lamb into themselves, faithfully receiving Christ as God and human being through the operation of the Holy Spirit, and devoutly receiving his body and [Col. 0788B] blood.

## TITLE LXI. On the threefold migration and the cloud.

“Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, shall so come,” etc. (Acts 1). Galilee is interpreted “migration.” This is threefold: one migration is in the flesh, another in penitence, another in charity.

Migration in the flesh is threefold: from a good state into delight in sin; from delight into action; from action into habit. Migration in penitence is likewise threefold: from sin into contrition of heart; from contrition into confession of mouth; from confession into satisfaction in deed. Migration in charity is similarly threefold: from the good sorrow of penitence into the joy of justice; [Col. 0788C] from the good work of justice into hope and faith of glory; from contemplation in faith and hope to contemplation of the reality itself.

Penitence is indeed good, but so long as it speaks with itself in its bitterness it is not joyful. Yet when it begins to act, so that the fear of sins is consumed by desire for eternal things, it immediately migrates from the good of sorrow to the good of joy. Therefore the first migration in charity is from the good of penitence to the joyful good of justice; the second, from the good work of justice to contemplation in faith and hope; the third, from contemplation in faith and hope to contemplation of the reality.

The first of all these migrants are carnal, because they are in the flesh and walk according to the flesh. The second are rational, who are in the flesh but do not walk according to the flesh. The third [Col. 0788D] are wholly spiritual, whose “citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). To these latter two kinds of migrants it is said: “Men of Galilee,” etc. For they see God ascending; but the first see otherwise than the second, because God ascends in two ways: with the sound of a trumpet and with jubilation. He ascends to penitents with the sound of a trumpet, to those in charity with jubilation. He ascends with the trumpet to penitents when, at the terrible sounding of the fear of God, the sinner comes to his senses.

He ascends with jubilation to those in charity in three ways. For jubilation is one thing in the heart, another in the mouth, another in deed. That person jubilates in the heart who cannot express the conceived joy by speech, yet cannot suppress the voice. That person jubilates in the mouth who, considering subtle things concerning God, longs to advance in him and is forced to acknowledge his own failure. That person jubilates in deed who sighs with all his strength to love God, since he cannot fully do this in the present; for God is not loved as much in the vision of faith as in the vision of God. The Psalmist indicates these modes, saying: “Make a joyful noise to God, all the earth; sing, exult, and play psalms” (Ps. 97). Sing with the jubilation of the mouth; exult with the jubilation of the heart; play psalms with the jubilation of deed. Therefore, in charity God ascends with jubilation to be embraced. The true Galilean beholds him, so that the ascending God may make him rejoice in the cloud.

One cloud is good, another evil. The evil cloud is threefold: the first of pleasure, the second of iniquity, the third of fantasy. The first is muddy, because it defiles the human being; the second smoky, because when someone sets aside pleasures yet retains avarice and other wickednesses, he becomes worse and, as smoke blinds the eye, so it blinds reason. In the third cloud, namely that of fantasy, those who have escaped the cloud of pleasure and iniquity are disturbed in their prayers. Against these clouds the Lord ascends in a good cloud. This too is threefold: one cloud is of thunder, another of rain, another of day. The first is terrifying, the second moist, the third bright. The terrifying one frightens; the moist one waters; the bright one illuminates, showing how great the reward laid up for the righteous is, so that they may await perseverance. Therefore, against the threefold evil cloud the Lord ascends in a threefold cloud.

When, therefore, the man of Galilee, migrating in charity, contemplates God ascending, he grieves and is sorrowful because he does not fully grasp him as he vanishes from the eye of his heart. And behold, two men stand by in white garments, consoling charity. These are hope and faith: hope of the promises, faith of glory. They say: “O charity, why do you stand here in despair? Believe that God wills, knows, and is able to give what he has promised.” Faith says: “Hope that you shall be glorified.” Hope says: “For truly he shall thus come to give you glory, as you saw him ascending into heaven.” Therefore, brothers, let us migrate from evil Galilee to good Galilee, abandoning contrary clouds, and ascend to God in good clouds, so that when he who ascends comes for judgment, he may grant us the glory he promised.

## TITLE LXII. On the plank of penitence, the wings of the dove and raven, and the bronze laver which Moses made from the mirrors of women.

“Confess your sins to one another” (James 5). This is the second plank after shipwreck, by which we sail through the sea [Col. 0789D] of this world lest we perish. This is one wing—for the other is prayer—by which the dove flies from the ark of its heart to the olive-tree of God’s merciful heart, and from there bears back to the ark of Noah, that is, of the person placed in danger, a branch of divine compassion. The raven, whose cry is not to utter the groaning of penitence but, for the song of present joy, rather “tomorrow, tomorrow,” flies from the ark on the wings of false hope and flattery to the corpse of rotten pleasure. Nor does it return to the ark of its heart, so as to repent and be washed from the rottenness of the corpse and of flesh dead in its resolve.

Likewise, by the bronze laver which Moses made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle (Exod. 38), so that the priests about to enter the Holy of Holies might first wash in it (Exod. 30), Moses signifies the Law. The bronze [Col. 0790A] laver is hard penitence; the mirrors are divine commandments; the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle are holy souls, which, so long as they are in this life and cannot enter the eternal tabernacle, continually watch the entrance of the kingdom in love. These women have mirrors of commandments, in which, as they always look at themselves, they discover and correct the stains of their foulness; they recognize what in themselves pleases or displeases the heavenly bridegroom, and, as though correcting their countenances by the image reflected back, they order themselves.

Thus Moses makes from the mirrors of the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle a laver for the priests to wash in, because God’s Law provides a washing away of sins. Through it holy souls awaiting entry into the heavenly homeland both saw and corrected their stains by considering the divine commandments. For when the divine Law sets before us David recognizing his sin by a divine command and correcting it, what else does it do but make, through Moses, a laver of washing from those mirrors?

Therefore, brothers, we are those priests who ought to give sacred things of good works to you and to others. But for us who are about to enter the Holy of Holies—that is, the entrance into the inward dwelling—is set before us the laver made from the mirrors of women: namely, penitence through the example of the ancient Fathers. If, therefore, we wish to enter, let us first wash away the stains of the heart in this laver, which Moses makes for us—that is, that Law which says: “Confess your sins to one another” (James 5)—so that we may thus be made blessed to see God, who lives and reigns. Amen.

## TITLE LXIII. On despising the world and its snares.

[Col. 0790C]

“Do not love the world or the things which are in the world, since everything which is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). Brothers, the world does not cleanse but stains the beauty of the soul according to which we were created in the image and likeness of God. While the world overlays upon the image in which “the light of the Lord’s countenance has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4) the image of its earthly countenance, God rejects his own image when it has been disfigured; and then the hostile devil defiles the soul through the world, binds it with the world’s snares, captures it, and suffocates it. For whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God; through the world a human being is captured [Col. 0790D] by the devil and subjected to its lord.

Therefore, wishing to draw us back from love of the world and show its snares, Blessed John the Evangelist says: “Do not love the world,” because no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6), God and the world. One draws to life; the other draws to the snares of death. Hence he adds: “Because everything which is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the pride of life” (1 John 2). These are the three snares: the first, concupiscence of the flesh; the second, concupiscence of the eyes; the third, pride of life. Whomever the first does not hold, the second captures; and whoever by God’s grace has shaken himself free from the first two will scarcely leap over the third.

The concupiscence of the flesh is pleasure which the flesh seeks by unlawful motion, such as gluttony, drunkenness, and lust. Through this snare [Col. 0791A] the world binds all the more quickly as it applies the mind more closely to the flesh; and it is more dangerous because it is nearer. It overthrew Adam through gluttony, Lot through drunkenness, and Solomon through lust. Therefore let us meet gluttony, which was the beginning of our captivity, with abstinence; drunkenness with sobriety; lust with mortification of the flesh.

Yet there are many whom the devil does not hold through vices of the flesh, but draws through the snare of greed, the concupiscence of the eyes. These escape the first snare but are captured by the second, called concupiscence of the eyes. For while through the eyes one desires gold, silver, and other things, death enters the soul through the windows and binds it captive in external things. Of this person it will be mocked and said: “Behold the man who did not make God his helper,” etc. (Ps. 51).

[Col. 0791B] If consideration of the Creator, who ought to appear more precious than the creature, meets this snare, one must beware of the third, which rages through all things. There are people who subdue the flesh and reject the world; but while they become proud, as it were, of their perfection, they are held by the third snare, the pride of life.
