This vice is first among those departing and last among those returning. It is proper to the devil and therefore must be guarded against more carefully. It is one of Lot’s daughters, which overthrew him even at the summit of the mountain.

Everyone who is captured is captured by these three snares, because all vices are included in them. A person is bound either by external things, which are in the world; by nearer things, which are in the flesh; or by interior things, which are in the heart. The last snare lies hidden within us; the second lies or is spread outside us; the first is prepared beside us. By these three the first human being was tempted and overcome (Gen. 3). By these three the second human being was tempted and conquered. By these three every human being is tempted and, if willing, is aided and conquers.

Against the vice of gluttony, which is the snare of the flesh, Christ goes into the desert and fasts, answering the tempter that a human being does not live by bread alone (Matt. 4). Against the concupiscence of external things, he says that God must be preferred to creatures. Against pride, by which the tempter urged him to throw himself down, he likewise has recourse, as in the other instances, to the testimony of Scripture: “You shall worship your God and serve him alone” (ibid.). Therefore, following Christ’s example, who taught us to conquer, when tempted in these things let us run to Scripture for defense.

And because in the time of abstinence we are tempted more, let us also resist more. In the desert [Col. 0791D] of monastic profession, where, having left behind the prince of vanity, we fast with Elijah in the Judah of confession from foods, let us fast from vices also. Thus after victory we may receive angels here as ministering helpers, and in the future attain glory, where we shall receive liberty of glory.

For liberty is threefold: of nature, grace, and glory. The first was in paradise, in all; the second in the world, in some; the third in the good, only in heaven. In paradise liberty was granted from the necessity of sin and punishment; in the world, from the necessity of sin but not of punishment; in heaven, from both. Therefore liberty of nature from necessity was in paradise, when before the first sin no necessity of suffering or sinning lay upon the human being. Liberty of grace from sin is in the world, because through Christ we receive remission of sins, beneath whose yoke we were held as slaves. Liberty of glory will be in heaven, because then, freed from every sin and punishment, we shall rejoice in heavenly blessedness. But in all these things, “If the Son shall set you free, you shall be free indeed” (John 8), says the Lord, who lives and reigns. Amen.

## TITLE LXIV. On the manifold struggle of the faithful in this world.

Not ours is the wrestling, etc. (Eph. VI). The faithful person has manifold conflict in this world. For he fights against the flesh, against human beings, and against the devil. Against the flesh, as the Apostle says: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Gal. V). And again: “I see another law in my members, opposing the law of my mind” (Rom. VII). He fights against ungodly people [Col. 0792B], concerning whom the Lord says: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV). For the sinner watches the righteous person and seeks to put him to death. He has a third enemy, harsher in proportion as he is more cunning, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood” (as stated above only), “but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). Thus the first enemy, namely the flesh, harms by inciting unlawful impulses; the second, namely the tyrant, by inflicting tribulations; the third, namely the devil, by suggesting temptations.

The first must be overcome by fasts, vigils, and labours, by subduing the flesh. The Apostle taught this in word and example: in word, saying, “Mortify your members which are upon [Col. 0792C] the earth” (Col. III), because “we are not debtors to the flesh, to live according to the flesh” (Rom. VIII); by example: “I chastise my body,” he says, “and bring it into slavery” (I Cor. IX). The second enemy, however, must be overcome by suffering, as the Apostle says: “Do not defend yourselves, beloved” (Rom. XII); and as the Lord says: “Love your enemies” (Luke VI); and: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V). The third enemy likewise must be repelled by withholding consent, as the Apostle says: “Give no place to the devil” (Eph. IV). However many arrows of vices he directs against you, set against them as many protecting shields from the armoury of Holy Scripture. If he tries stealthily to strike you with the dart of adultery, oppose to him the shield by which it is prescribed to you [Col. 0792D]: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. XX); or that by which it is forbidden: “You shall not steal” (ibid.).

But, in order that we may conquer the first enemy, let us strip ourselves of delight in the flesh, for those who are in the flesh cannot please God. “For if you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. VIII). In order that we may gain the second, let us do what the Apostle says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him” (Rom. XII)—namely, with the word of God—so that you may pray for those who persecute you and bless those who curse you. By doing this, “you shall heap coals of fire upon his head” (ibid.), that is, the fire of charity upon his mind. So that you may not be conquered by the third, dwell “in the help of the Most High” (Ps. XC), because one who dwells in him “shall not be moved” (ibid.). Therefore, both to conquer the first enemy, to gain the second, and not to be conquered by the third, [Col. 0793A] we must rise beneath the wings of his protection—he who, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings from the face of the kite (Matt. XXIII), warms like a partridge children whom she did not bear, and like an eagle provokes them to fly.

## TITLE LXV. On Christ’s manifold entry

“Jesus, entering into the temple, began to cast out those who sold and bought,” etc. (Luke II). The entries of my God, my King, who is in the holy place, are many, as divine speech teaches: into a city, a fortified town, a house, and a temple. Of the first: “When the Lord entered the holy city” (Matt. XI). Of the second: “When he entered a certain fortified town, ten leprous men met him” (Luke XVII). Of the third: “He entered the house of a Pharisee” (Luke VII). Of the fourth: “Jesus entered into the temple” [Col. 0793B], and the rest, which we set forth above. He entered the city as king; the fortified town as defender; the house as master of the household; and the temple as priest.

Holy Scripture teaches that he himself is king, defender, and master of the household. Of the first, Isaiah says: “The Lord our king will come and save us” (Isa. XXXV). Of the second: “Send us a saviour and defender,” etc. (Isa. IX). Of the third: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who is a master of a household,” etc. (Matt. XX). Of the fourth: “You are a priest for ever,” etc. (Ps. CIX). A diadem befits a king, weapons a defender, the distribution of provisions a master of a household, and the administration of sacraments a priest. Therefore let us see, with the prophet, the king crowned with glory and honour (Ps. VIII). Let us understand the defender, while the prophet asks: “Take hold of [Col. 0793C] weapons and shield” (Ps. XXXIV). Let us observe the master of the household refreshing crowds with five or seven loaves (Matt. XIV). Let us recall the priest sacrificing himself (Isa. LIII).

The king makes himself wondrous in his diadem; the defender makes himself formidable in arms; the priest makes himself acceptable in sacrifice. The crowned king sits upon the throne of divinity; the defender, about to overcome the adversary, stands upon the stronghold of the cross; the master of the household, intending to fill the hungry with good things, gives his voice in the streets; the priest enters the temple to offer God a sacrifice of praise. There are two temples: one of Solomon and one of the Saviour. Solomon’s temple is built of gold, wood, and stones; the Saviour’s temple [Col. 0793D] of righteous people.

There are three temples of the Saviour. His temple is the body which he assumed from the Virgin; his temple is every faithful person; his temple is the universal Church. Of the first it is said: “Destroy this temple” (John II). Of the second: “If anyone defiles the temple of God, God will destroy him,” etc. (I Cor. II). Of the third: “Behold, he comes to his holy temple,” etc. (Mal. III). What he will do there is shown when he adds shortly afterward: “And he cleansed the sons of Levi” (ibid.). The sons of Levi are ministers of the altar and stewards of God’s ministries. He is in some sense reported to have cleansed them by the Gospel reading when he cast sellers and buyers from the temple—namely, lest ministers of the altar, attending to profit, should be corrupted by their example. This also prefigures the separation [Col. 0794A] that will be made between good and evil at judgment. For as sellers and buyers were cast from the temple, so the reprobate will be taken away from the midst of the righteous when the Lord comes to judge the living and the dead.

## TITLE LXVI. On the word of God sent to a village, a fortified town, and a city; and how they differ

The word of God is sometimes sent to a village, sometimes to a fortified town, sometimes to a city. Figuratively, Jesus turned water into wine in a village of Galilee (John II). Then he performed that celebrated miracle in a fortified town (John XI). Afterwards, in a city he is honoured by the Hebrews with mystical observances (Matt. XXI). A village is inhabited only by its own peasants and defended by no rampart. This is the soul strong only in natural virtues, fortified by no rampart of humility or by the added strength [Col. 0794B] of grace-given virtue. A fortified town is defended by a rampart or wall, but does not extend to the breadth of a city. It is the soul fortified by the rampart of penitence and humility, or by the wall of obedience rather than self-will; it is not yet enlarged by charity but restricted by fear. A city, surrounded with many defences, is enlarged and inhabited by its broad expanse and numerous population living under the equity of law and justice. This is the soul enlarged by charity through varied defences of uprightness and inhabited by an abundant and ordered host of virtues.

Thus the divine word comes to the village, so that water may be changed into wine: that is, so that it may be fortified from the insipid taste of rusticity toward the ardour of virtues, lest it be destroyed by attacking enemies. It comes to the fortified town so that, when the dead person has been raised and even the openings of fears have been loosened, it may instil hope of freedom from the bonds of sins. [Col. 0794C] It comes to the city so that the city itself may be preserved, and the same word may there be held in greater honour, lest the most beautiful walls of voluntary obedience, strengthened by diverse examples of the ancients, be secretly undermined by those lying in wait. Therefore in the village it is quickly overwhelmed; in the fortified town it is suddenly strengthened; in the city it is continuously honoured.

## TITLE LXVII. On the light of the divine countenance, the attributes of the Trinity, and the powers of the soul

The countenance of the Father is power; that of the Son, wisdom; that of the Holy Spirit, kindness. The light of the countenance is memory, understanding, and will. From memory man fell into forgetfulness; from understanding, into ignorance; from will, into the misuse of uprightness. But God sent his Son, who brought faith, hope, and charity. [Col. 0794D] By these this image, this countenance, is marked upon us—that is, impressed upon reason. Faith drives away forgetfulness by restoring memory; hope banishes ignorance by cleansing understanding; charity extinguishes the misuse of uprightness by raising up the will.

Thus the countenance of the Trinity, in charity, is power, wisdom, and kindness. By power he created all things; by wisdom he ordered all things; by kindness he governs and cherishes all things. But because we cannot approach to behold the countenance, we possess its light—that is, image and likeness. By the image we apprehend him, namely by memory, understanding, and will. By the likeness we express him in ourselves, namely by faith, hope, and charity, etc.

## TITLE LXVIII. On one who sows in the spirit or in the flesh

[Col. 0795A]

One thing is the sower, another that in which seed is sown. The soul sows; but if it sows in the spirit, it will reap life from the spirit. “For the fruit of the Spirit is joy and peace,” etc. (Gal. V). If it sows in the flesh, it will reap corruption. For the fruit of the flesh is luxury, avarice, etc. (ibid.). Therefore it is the soul that sows either in the flesh or in the spirit; the body follows whichever direction the soul assigns to it; the soul is a guide toward truth, if the body is willing to follow it.

## TITLE LXIX. On the two catches of fish

In the first fishing, the net breaks because of the multitude of fish. In the second, many fish are caught and the net does not break, because here too, at the first calling, so many reprobate enter the Church along with the elect that they tear it apart with heresies; but in the future only the elect will enter, [Col. 0795B] who will possess in the author of peace an indissoluble bond of peace. In the first, a fish escapes, because the Lord knows how to preserve his own even amid the scandals of persecutors. In the second, however, the good are selected into vessels, while the evil are cast out.

## TITLE LXX. On washing and folding nets

By the example of Peter sitting on the shore, the preacher’s nets must first be washed and then dried (Luke V): because after preaching the teacher ought to wash away the dust of sin which he may perhaps have contracted from preaching itself, and then fold them—that is, fulfil what he has taught.

## TITLE LXXI. On catching fish by the word of the Lord

The Apostles labour all night and catch nothing; but Peter lets down the net at Christ’s word and catches [Col. 0795C] fish (Luke V), because the preacher vainly casts the dart of his voice unless the nets have been let down by the word of grace.

## TITLE LXXII. On the commerce of those in the cloister

“Trade until I come” (Luke XIX). At the death of each person the Lord comes, either as a welcome rewarder or as a terrible condemner. Nothing is more certain than death. Therefore watch, because you know neither the day nor the hour (Matt. XXV). “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction shall come upon them” (Prov. XXIX). But so that we may always watch and avoid that day of calamity and misery, the master of the household has assigned five regions for trading. In them, as though running through fairs, people may cast aside what is useless and gather what is useful, and, like prudent merchants, bring back their packs [Col. 0795D] for themselves.

Their names are these. The region of dissimilarity is the present life, in which some people, loving it too greatly, have become unlike God and, compared with beasts of burden, have descended to the place of death. Hence the Prophet cries: “Man, when he was in honour,” etc. (Ps. XXXXVIII). A person trades prudently there if, whenever even a little of the world smiles upon him, he weighs and discerns how deceptive, brief, and uncertain life is, and how cheap and worthless temporal things are.

The southern region is the cloister or desert, in which Christ hides his own from the contradiction of tongues and afterwards will join them to the company of angels. For in Holy Scripture the south signifies the Holy Spirit, and the southern quarter a way of life characterized by spiritual goods. The cloistered person’s paradise, under the gentle mildness of the sweetly breathing south wind, flowers with as many blossoms [Col. 0796A] as it abounds in virtues.

The region of expiation is a place known not to human beings but to God, in which are the souls of certain persons who are to be saved and whom sacrifices and alms assist. But in this region the good merchant surpasses a marketable pack when he puts on the disposition of compassion.

The infernal region is the prison of the damned, from which and in which no redemption is open. There is also another prison, this world, in which we are held as exiles and captives, but only for a time. Thus the world is the prison of captives; hell, of the damned. A marvellous and severe matter, which must be heard not without the thunderclap of fear. We must have recourse to this region in careful reflection whenever the devil suggests evil, so that a person may thus be restrained from sin and may acquire hatred of sin for himself.

[Col. 0796B] The supercelestial region is Jerusalem, our mother. Into this region let one gather for oneself the sweetest thing—namely, the love of God. We ought to survey these five regions and bring back one pack from each: from the region of dissimilarity, contempt for the world; from the southern region, a pattern for living well; from the region of expiation, the disposition of compassion; from the region of hell, hatred of sin; from the supercelestial region, love of God.

## TITLE LXXIII. On the three states of Christian perfection

The Lord says: “Behold, today and tomorrow I cast out demons and perform cures; and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke XIII). And the Apostle says: “Until we all meet in a perfect man” (Eph. IV). Three states of Christian [Col. 0796C] perfection are signified in these words: one in the future, where we shall triumph; two in the present, where we merit reward. The first is in penitence, the second in righteousness, the third in glory. In the first he casts out demons; in the second he completes healing, when through mercy he makes one live justly; in the third he will perfect, when he crowns us. He showed these in his passion, sleeping, and awakening. Suffering on the cross, he triumphed over the devil; in the tomb he rested; in the resurrection he rejoiced. Thus penitence, by which we conquer the devil, afflicts us; righteousness, by which we rest from evils, brings tranquillity; eternal life, where God will be seen, will delight us.

Accordingly, the first of these three states concerns penitence. Its voice is: “Have mercy on me, O God” (Ps. L). The second concerns mercy [Col. 0796D] and judgment, and its voice is: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. C). The third concerns eternal life, and its voice is: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. CL). Accordingly, in the Old Testament three principal feasts are celebrated: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles (*Scenopegia*). At the first they ate wild lettuces and offered ears of grain roasted by fire; by these are signified the mortification of the flesh and the bitterness of penitence. At Pentecost new loaves from new crops are offered; by this is understood the state of righteousness, in which we walk in newness of life. At the Feast of Tabernacles an offering was made from all the crops of the year; by this is signified the state of glory, when “they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV).

These are the works of the Samaritan, who first poured wine, then oil, and afterward [Col. 0797A] said: “Go; you have been made whole” (John V). In the wine is the fervour of penitence; in the oil, the gentleness of righteousness; in the third is signified perfection.

## TITLE LXXIV. On fourfold sorrow and joy

“Your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John XVI). Sorrow is fourfold. The first is sorrow of affliction, of which it is said: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow; so you also now have sorrow” (ibid.). The second is sorrow of penitence. Hence: “I rejoice because you were made sorrowful unto penitence”; and: “The sorrow which is according to God works a steadfast penitence unto salvation” (II Cor. VII). The third is sorrow of despair. Hence: “The sorrow of the world works death” (ibid.). The fourth is sorrow of condemnation. Hence: “There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII).

Joy likewise is fourfold. The first is joy of dissipation. [Col. 0797B] Hence: “Woe to you who laugh” (Luke VI). The second is joy of presumption. Hence: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. II). The third is joy of conscience, concerning which he says: “We rejoice in our tribulations” (Col. I). “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). The fourth is joy of peace and glory. Therefore sorrow of affliction will be turned into joy of conscience. Sorrow of penitence produces joy of peace and glory. But joy of dissipation is sometimes turned into sorrow of distrust. Sorrow of despair, however, is completed in sorrow of condemnation; while joy of conscience is completed in the joy of the light of glory.

## TITLE LXXXV. On the threefold acquisition of the kingdom

“Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness” [Col. 0797C] (Matt. VI). The kingdom is threefold: of power, grace, and glory. Of the first it is said: “Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages” (Ps. CXLIV). Of the second: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII). Of the third: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John XVIII). The kingdom of power is in every creature; the kingdom of grace is in the present Church; the kingdom of glory is in eternal life.

The kingdom of power is sought in three ways: through pride, deceit, and hypocrisy. Through pride, as by him who is king over all the children of pride: “I will sit in the north,” he says, “and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV). Those who belong to his party imitate him; through deceit, as Herod did; through hypocrisy, as Antichrist does, and all hypocrites with [Col. 0797D] him. But the kingdom of grace and glory is sought through penitence and confession, as it was by the thief on the cross, who seized it by force.

Some do not seek this twofold kingdom of God at all, but worldly gain. Others do not seek God’s kingdom first, but the gain and enjoyment of things. Others seek both, but worldly gain first. Others seek God’s kingdom first. The first are carnal; the second are solitary or self-regarding (*singulares*); the third are animal or merely natural; the fourth are spiritual. On account of the first, who never seek God’s kingdom, it is said, “Seek.” On account of those who seek something else first, it adds, “first [the kingdom].” On account of those who seek a worldly kingdom, it adds, “of God.” On account of those who seek not God’s righteousness but worldly righteousness or their own, it adds, “and his righteousness.”

For there is righteousness directed toward the world, toward oneself, and toward God. A person seeks righteousness toward the world when he wishes to be justified by human judgment and gives precedence to heavenly things over earthly, so that he takes them for the use of necessity rather than for the fruit of usefulness. But one who renders to each what is its own—temporal things to necessity, eternal things to usefulness—hastens by the path of righteousness toward the kingdom of glory. To state the matter briefly: some seek neither the kingdom of God nor his righteousness, namely the carnal; some seek God’s kingdom but not his righteousness, namely the self-regarding; some seek God’s kingdom and his righteousness, but not first, namely the merely natural; some seek first both the kingdom of God and his righteousness, namely the spiritual.

## TITLE LXXVI. On the threefold state of the soul and the manner in which penitence is to be performed

[Col. 0798B]

There are three states of the soul: in the body, after the body has been set aside, and after the body has been received again. The first is given for performing penitence; the other two for receiving rest or punishment, according as one has done good or evil in the body (II Cor. V). But three things are necessary for performing penitence: time, place, and body. That time is necessary the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” etc. (II Cor. VI). Likewise, concerning place and body, he says: “We must all be made manifest before the tribunal of the Lord, so that each may receive according to the things proper to the body, according as he has acted” (II Cor. V). But Scripture speaks of this place when it says: “If the spirit of one having authority rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccl. X).

Moreover, time is divided [Col. 0798C] into three: past, present, and future. Whoever performs penitence rightly loses none of these. For he restores the past which he had lost, while in the bitterness of his soul he recalls all his years. He holds the present through the exercise of work, and the future through steadfastness in a good purpose. The Apostle speaks of sin when he says: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Eph. V). He exhorts us to work in the present time when he says: “While we have time, let us do good to all” (Gal. VI). The Lord admonishes us regarding the future when he says: “He who has persevered unto the end shall be saved” (Matt. X).

The body too is necessary for performing penitence. In the body we can suffer evils to purge offences we have committed [Col. 0798D] and do good works to obtain the rewards of eternal life. But how could a soul deprived of a body bring forth worthy fruits of penitence? It should be noted that penitence performed through the body is brief and light. It is brief because it is shortened by the death of the body; light because it is borne more easily through partnership with the body. Penitence would indeed be burdensome if the mind bore it alone. But when both the mind and its body share the burden, the more the body is burdened by it, the more fully the mind is unburdened.

A place for penitence is not necessary, indeed, but useful: it is the place of the Church. The time, however, is the lifetime of the penitent; for whoever neglects to perform penitence while living in the body will be able to have no remedy of salvation in the future.

## TITLE LXXVII. What is necessary for purity of prayer

[Col. 0799A]

For prayer to be pure, three things seem to me necessary, to which the intention of prayer must be firmly attached. The person who prays ought to consider what he asks, why he asks it, and the one whom he asks. In what he asks, he ought to attend to two points: that what he requests be according to God, and that he have this very thing as his highest desire. For example, if anyone asks in prayer for an enemy’s death or for the injury or overthrow of a neighbour, such prayer is not according to God, since he himself commands and says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you; pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. V). But if he seeks forgiveness of sins, the grace of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0799B] virtue and wisdom, faith, truth, righteousness, humility, patience, gentleness, and the other spiritual gifts, and desires them ardently in his thoughts, this is prayer according to God and truly deserves to be heard. The Lord speaks through Isaiah about prayers of this kind: “Before they call, I will hear” (Isa. LXV).

There are other things which, when absent and requested from God, are granted. In themselves they may either be from God or not be from God, depending only on the end to which they are directed: such as health of body, money, and abundance of other possessions. Even if they are from God, they ought not to be highly valued or possessed out of desire. Likewise, in the one whom he asks, the petitioner should consider two things: goodness, by which he may freely will to give, and majesty, by which he may fully be able [Col. 0799C] to give whatever is asked. But in himself, the petitioner must likewise attend to two things: that he think he will receive nothing for his own merits, and that he hope he will obtain from God’s mercy alone whatever he asks.

Therefore the heart is called pure when it reflects upon these three things that have been mentioned. Whoever prays with this purity and intensity of heart may know that he will be heard, because, as the apostle Peter testifies: “In truth I have found that God is not a respecter of persons; but in every nation, one who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

## TITLE LXXVIII. On the soul raised from death

The death of the soul is forgetfulness. A soul raised from this death is recognized in this way: through memory it feels; through [Col. 0799D] obedience it hears; through understanding it sees; through circumspection it smells; and through love it tastes.

## TITLE LXXIX. On the four wills of humankind

There are four kinds of human will: dry in the reprobate and earthly-minded, whose hearts are moistened by no dew of grace; right in beginners, who, leaving behind the crookedness of their former life, rise by a change of will to the rectitude of good work; devout in those making progress, who, by the practice of constant prayer, are raised from heaven to the love of doing good; perfect in those who are complete, who think of almost nothing other than God and place in him the end of all their desire.

Between dry and right will is a certain firmament, so that those wishing to cross may not be able to; namely, perverse intention is between right and devout will, [Col. 0800A] an ingrained habit of acting badly; between devout and perfect will, bodily refreshment. Since these three things oppose themselves like hard stones in the path of our body, they hinder us from ascending from virtue to virtue.

## TITLE LXXX. On the four whom we serve

There are four whose services we perform in this life: flesh, the world, the devil, and God. We serve the flesh by serving the enticements of gluttony and yielding to the spurs of lust; we serve the world by panting after the heats of avarice and aspiring to the height of honour; we serve the devil by envying the progress of good people and swelling against God with a spirit of pride; we serve God by humbly persisting in works of piety and assaulting the powers of the air by the strength of the spirit. Each of these rulers also has his own rewards. The flesh [Col. 0800B] grants its recruits momentary self-will; the world, transient eminence; the devil, everlasting captivity; God, endless blessedness. This alone outweighs all the rest.

## TITLE LXXXI. On the causes of the flesh’s arousals

The movement and arousal of our flesh arise from three causes. They arise from a preceding thought, which draws inward shameful and unlawful images, at the recollection of which the flesh is disgracefully stirred. They arise from fullness of the stomach, because when the belly is distended by an abundance of foods, the wanton flesh is very strongly incited to lust. They arise from the assault of an evil spirit, because the less he sees himself able to overcome the righteous, the more grievously he attacks them through the flesh’s arousals.

## TITLE LXXXII. How one must ascend from the valley and desert, and that the desert is threefold

[Col. 0800C]

As we are about to ascend from the valley of weeping, we must always strive and yearn for higher things. For this mortal way is like a kind of desert, concerning which it is said: “A desert land, impassable,” etc. (Ps. LXII). But there are three kinds of deserts. One desert is momentary vanity, which we must despise through moderation of life. We ought to ascend from this desert, as it is said: “Who is this who comes up through the desert, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII). We abound in delights when we abound in virtues; we lean upon the beloved when we ascribe to God whatever good we do.

There is another desert [Col. 0800D] of Christian simplicity: humility. It is called a desert because there is scarcely any Christian who makes it his aim to practise this good fully. Through this desert we must ascend. Hence it is said: “Who is this who comes up through the desert like a slender column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh, frankincense,” etc. (Song III). We ascend like a slender column of smoke from spices when, trained by the study and discipline of virtues, we incite our neighbours to imitate right action. There is also another desert: the simplicity or integrity of purer innocence. We must ascend to this, because we ought to yearn for the true healing, so that we may be holy in body and spirit. Therefore let us ascend from the desert of momentary vanity, through the desert of most humble simplicity, to the desert of most complete purity.

## TITLE LXXXIII. On the arrows used by the Lord

[Col. 0801A]

Our Lord has his own arrows with which he wounds his enemies and assails them with the arm of his power. There are three arrows by which enemies are wounded. The sting of lost money: for a person is greatly saddened when he remembers that he has lost the means of living, the attendants of pleasures, and riches. Next comes the plague of bodily suffering, which, in order to suppress his courses by the power of the mind, scourges with bodily affliction the one whom it sees hurrying toward sin. Next comes the hammer of infernal remembrance: for when a person considers himself surrounded on every side by the weight of bodily pains, he also turns his eyes toward that anguish which has no end and ponders within himself, with fearful reflection, the dreadful furnace of hell.

## TITLE LXXXIV. On the wine of drunkenness

[Col. 0801B]

Not all who are drunk are intoxicated in one and the same manner. One wine is the wine of malice, flowing from the vine of wickedness and originating with the devil, who offered the human race the bitterness of sin and death; the wicked who resemble Holofernes are intoxicated by it. Another wine is the wine of suffering, flowing from the wild vine of the human condition, which from itself has added the vinegar of iniquity. Whoever is intoxicated by this wine is shown to suffer punishment from God, not unjustly, but according to the desert of his sin. Another wine is the wine of grace, which runs from the cluster of *cyprus*—that is, from the generosity of the Creator. This is the new wine by which the bridegroom’s sons are intoxicated and which is also put into new wineskins.

## TITLE LXXXV. On the degrees of good condescension

[Col. 0801C]

Humility has seven degrees of descent: renunciation of possessions, after the example of the apostles; rejection of fine clothing, like Elijah and John the Baptist; the practice of compassion and cooperation, like Paul; lowliness amid prosperity, after the manner of David the poor king; patience amid adversity, like Job and Tobit; abhorrence of one’s own counsel and of the inclination of one’s own will.

## TITLE LXXXVI. On the five battles against sin

The battles of virtue by which the weapons of sin are overcome are these: full recognition of sin, which expels the darkness of pleasure; penitential affliction, against the sweetness of carnality; humble and true confession, against [Col. 0801D] the poison of iniquity which we have drunk; sufficient and worthy correction, against imitation of former pleasure; and a perseverance-filled continuance, so that perfect safeguarding of health may be substituted.

## TITLE LXXXVII. On the diversity of those advancing toward God

Not all advance toward God in the same manner. Some move with slow and sluggish step, like those so entangled in earthly cares that they scarcely ever take breath or look back in order to remember God. Some move with measured pace, like those devoted to God’s service: they serve God indeed, yet show themselves more indulgent toward themselves. Others hasten with swift and rapid course, like those who, looking down upon their flesh, despise both themselves and transitory things, and speedily advance toward [Col. 0802A] God, desiring only this: to rest together in peace.

## TITLE LXXXVIII. On the threefold fear of prelates

The fear of prelates is threefold: lest an apparatus of carefully sought words move the minds of their hearers; lest immoderate practices offend the eyes of the inward Judge; lest the recompense of justice be made to them in the present life.

## TITLE LXXXIX. On the threefold sorrow of the saints

The sorrow of the saints is threefold: because they are far from paradise, because they are held in exile, and because they are delayed from the kingdom.

## TITLE XC. What is in Christ, the mountain of mountains

“A mountain curdled, a fat mountain,” etc. (Ps. LXVII). In Christ, the mountain of mountains, were these two things: the curdling of suffering and the richness of holiness. Likewise: a young calf, a calf from the herd, a fatted calf.

## TITLE XCI. On various gates

The world has its gates through which it foolishly strives to enter toward God. These are corrupted sensuality and incestuous desire. Hence: “They drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. CVI). The gates of hell are blind dispensation and hard obstinacy: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against her” (Matt. XVI). The gates of heaven are humble power, which is the iron gate leading to life, and harmony of love, which is the eastern gate.

## TITLE XCII. On the three lamps

[Col. 0802C] There are three lamps: the rule of discipline in Christ, which is lit so that the lost drachma may be found; the form of truth, which is set in the Gospel upon a lampstand; and purity of knowledge in a good heart, which is illumined by the Lord.

## TITLE XCIII. On the ways in which God questions us

God questions us in three ways: by the promulgation of a command, so that our obedience may be known; by the infliction of a scourge, so that our patience may become known to our neighbours; and by the revelation of a secret, so that the virtue of humility may disclose itself to us.

## TITLE XCIV. On what must be set against adversity

Three things must be set against adversity: the struggles and distresses of the elect, which those who live piously endure; the afflictions and sufferings of the Redeemer, which most savage [Col. 0802D] rulers inflicted upon him; and the ordinance of governing justice, whose height, like the summit of Joseph’s rod, we ought not investigate but adore. These are the three gates, bars, and bounds by which the Lord surrounds the sea of human iniquity (Job XXXVIII).

## TITLE XCV. On the three things requested by the elect

The elect request three things to be accomplished in the future time: that what is mortal in them may be wholly swallowed up by life; that they may be enriched with the recompense of everlasting glory; and that they may contemplate God insatiably as he is.

## TITLE XCVI. On three desires sought in vain

The reprobate are said to desire three things: that bodily pleasure may be accumulated for them in abundance; that momentary glory may contribute to blessedness; and that their customs and works may be condemned by no judgment after them.

## TITLE XCVII. On the three things a Christian must do

An imitator of Christ must do three things: retain the disposition of simple innocence, so that he may become a child with Christ; love an abject and humble condition, so that he may be wrapped with Christ in the poor swaddling-clothes of infancy; walk simply in discipline, so that he may be found with Christ laid in a manger—by the vision of whose blessed Spirit they are satisfied and intoxicated with sweetness.

### TIT. XCVIII. On the Attributes of Christ

Christ is sometimes called the shoot or root, as in the saying: “On that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign to the peoples—the nations shall seek him” (Isa. 11). Sometimes he is called wood or a trunk, as there: “Wisdom is a tree of life” (Prov. 3). Sometimes a flower, as: “I am the flower of the field” (Song 2). Sometimes fruit, as was said above. Christ was raised upon the cross, as in the saying: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12). He was exalted from the earth in the resurrection, as in the saying: “Therefore God exalted him,” etc. (Phil. 2). He was exalted in the ascension, as in the saying: “Your magnificence has been raised above the heavens” (Ps. 8). He was exalted in the preaching of the apostles, as in the saying: “I shall be exalted among the nations, and I shall be exalted in the earth” (Ps. 44).

### TIT. XCIX. On the Difference between Rising, Getting Up, Rising Again, Rising against, Standing Up, and Rising Together

We rise from a seat; get up from sleep; rise again from death; rise against someone for vengeance; stand up in honour; and rise together to give assistance.

### TIT. C. On the Characteristics of Smoke in a Sinner

Smoke arises from fire, rises, and vanishes. A sinner, whether male or female, has these three characteristics. For the sinner arises from the flame of desire, as in the saying: “Fire rose up in his anger” (Ps. 17). The sinner rises, as in the saying: “I saw the wicked man exalted exceedingly” (Ps. 36). The sinner vanishes, as in the saying: “And I passed by, and behold, he was not” (ibid.).

But smoke fails in two ways: it fails from its very birth; sometimes it is dispersed through brightness and fails, and sometimes it vanishes altogether. The sinner fails in only one way: the sinner fails from sin when, swallowed up in Gehenna, he can no longer sin.

### TIT. CI. On the Meanings of a Cord

[Col. 0803D] A cord signifies virtues, as in the saying: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4). A cord also signifies sins, as in the saying: “The cords of sinners have entangled me” (Ps. 118). It also signifies temporal goods. Thus it is said: “Woe to you who draw the people with cords of iniquity!” (Isa. 5). A cord also signifies form, grace, or inheritance. Hence the Psalmist says: “The measuring-lines have fallen to me in splendid places” (Ps. 15).

### TIT. CII. On Faith and the Understanding of Faith

Faith is one thing; the understanding of faith is another. Even laypeople are bound to faith: they must believe the articles of faith, namely the nativity, passion, and so forth. Those of higher rank, such as prelates, are bound to the understanding of faith; for they are bound to possess both faith and an understanding of faith.

### TIT. CIII. On the Fourfold Sense of “Good”

[Col. 0804A]

“Good” is understood in four ways. Something is called good essentially, as God is; denominatively, as every creature is called good because it is from the highest good, as in the saying: “God saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1); by use, as a horse is called good because its use is good; and by effect, as justice and the other virtues are called good because they produce good.

God himself is called good in three ways: in his nature, for his goodness is deity itself, and he is good in himself and through himself; he is also called good because he gives good things and because he does good things.

### TIT. CIV. On the Difference between the Logician and the Theologian, and on the Threefold Intellect

The difference between a logician and a theologian is this: the logician understands before believing, whereas the theologian believes before understanding, according to the saying: “Believe, and you shall understand,” although, according to some, understanding ought to precede faith.

Moreover, for someone actually to possess faith concerning a thing, first one must know that it exists; second, believe; third, understand what it is. This will be complete in the homeland. One kind of intellect is pure, by which form and subject are grasped; another is purer, by which we comprehend angelic nature; another is most pure, by which we contemplate, in some manner, the divine nature. The first is called the low heart, the second the middle heart, the third the high heart.

### TIT. CV. On the Threefold Likeness

Likenesses are of equality, imitation, or contrariety. The first belongs to the Son of God. Hence it is said: “He did not consider equality with God a robbery” (Phil. 2). The second belongs to humankind, for humanity was created in the image of God. The third belongs to the devil: since God is the author and principle of good things, the devil, by a likeness of contrariety, is the author of all evils.

Although the first likeness is the best, it is to be desired by no one. Because man wished to possess it, he fell into sin. Though he was a servant, he did not wish to have a lord; believing the devil’s suggestion when he said, “In whatever hour you eat, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3), man wished to be made equal to God through knowledge. Thus, since the Son is the wisdom of the Father, he became, as it were, an occasion of humanity’s fall; therefore it was fitting that humanity should be redeemed by the Son.

Hence Jonah, speaking in the person of the Son, says: “Because of me the storm has arisen; cast me into the sea” (Jonah 1). Jonah signifies Christ; the sea, the world. For Christ was occasion­ally the cause of the storm arising in the world, when man, at the devil’s prompting, proudly wished to be equal to God. It was therefore necessary that Christ himself be sent into the sea—that is, into the world—and calm the storm, that is, restore peace between God and humankind.

### TIT. CVI. On the Threefold Baptism

There is a threefold baptism: of the river, of the Spirit (*flaminis*), and of blood. The baptism of the river is in water; that of the Spirit is in penitence; that of blood is in martyrdom. This is not to say that baptism is other than baptism in water, but that the latter two take the place of baptism.

Thus the Gospel saying is to be supplied or expounded as follows: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, that person cannot enter the kingdom of God,” that is, unless someone is reborn by that power through which those who are baptized in water and the Holy Spirit are reborn, that person shall not enter, etc.

### TIT. CVII. On the Fourfold Change

Change occurs in four ways: divine, physical, magical, and moral.

Divine change is twofold: one kind is alteration; the other, transubstantiation. The change of alteration occurred at Cana of Galilee, where water was made wine: the substantial elements were changed while the nature remained. The change of transubstantiation occurs in the Eucharist, for bread and wine are transubstantiated into Christ’s flesh and blood.

Physical, that is natural, change occurs when water becomes ice and ice becomes crystal. Magical change occurred when Pharaoh’s magicians changed rods into serpents. Moral change is that by which philosophers or poets say that some persons were changed into swine, such as the companions of Ulysses—that is, into the lustful; another into a stag, such as Actaeon, who spent all he possessed on hunting; and Lycaon into a wolf, because of his savagery.

### TIT. CVIII. On the Many Kinds of Obligation

“Obligation” is used in many ways. There is the obligation arising from commission, omission, merit, fittingness, vow, command, and promise.

By reason of commission, a priest owes the singing of Mass. By reason of omission, a monk ought to be beaten if he fails in his observance. By reason of merit, anyone ought to return a favour received to a friend. By reason of fittingness, one who is suited to bear arms ought to be a soldier. By reason of a vow, one who has vowed not to know his wife during Lent must observe this. By reason of command, we ought to have love for Christ and neighbour. By reason of promise, God owes us eternal life, provided that we observe his commands.

### TIT. CIX. On the Disposition of Those Awaiting God

Those awaiting God ought to be in suspense as to when he will come; uncertain whether he will abandon them; joyful and devout; more carefully adorned; despising earthly things; and earnestly desiring in him a nuptial presence, familiar grace, and generous bounty.

### TIT. CX. On the Three Marriages, and the Various Words of God

There are three kinds of marriage. The first is reconciliation through faith, in which there are three dishes: the washing away of sins, the acquisition of grace, and the restoration of nature. The second is adoption through hope, in which there are likewise three: the consolation of the divine utterance, communion in heavenly nourishment, and a foretaste of inward sweetness. The third is perfect glorification through charity, whose three dishes are eternal incorruption, true glorification, and the perpetual vision of God.

The words of God’s consolation are the washing away of guilt, restoration of grace, escape from exile, attainment of the kingdom, fellowship with divinity, and acquisition of eternity.

### TIT. CXI. On the Three Weapons of the Faithful

The faithful possess three weapons: wisdom, which is David’s sling, from which stones of authoritative sayings are discharged; the strength of patience, which is the staff by which the rage of wolves is driven back; and the breadth of charity, which is David’s bag, from which prayers are brought forth.

### TIT. CXII. On Three Things Necessary for a Prelate

Three things are necessary for prelates: the way of faith and purity of teaching, so that they may dwell in the same region; diligent zeal in doing good works, so that they may keep watch with the shepherds; and earnest concern for the salvation of their subjects, so that they may guard and preserve their flock.

### TIT. CXIII. On the Three Kinds of Penitence

There are three kinds of penitence: feigned and unfruitful penitence, exemplified in Esau and false believers; desperate penitence, as in Cain and Judas; and useful and complete penitence, as in Mary Magdalene and Zacchaeus. Its five parts are contrition in the heart, confession in the mouth, mortification in the flesh, amendment in deed, and perseverance in virtue.

### TIT. CXIV. On Three Things Marvellously Changed

[Col. 0806B]

Three things were marvellously changed: sublimity into humility, when the Word assumed flesh; contemptibility into majesty, when God-man was transfigured before the disciples; and mutability into eternity, when Christ, after the resurrection, ascended to reign in heaven.

### TIT. CXV. On Three Things Impeding Penitence

Three things overwhelm penitence: excessive anxiety; an exacting demand for sorrow equal to that of an innocent person; and the unworthiness of the one imposing it.

### TIT. CXVI. On the Threefold Ascent of the Lord

The Lord’s ascent is threefold: victorious, by which he ascends above the air; spiritual, by which he ascends above the heaven of heavens; and glorious, by which he ascends above the wings of the winds.

### TIT. CXVII. On Acquiring the Kingdom of Heaven

Some seize the kingdom of heaven violently, as do the poor in spirit. Some merit it, such as those who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity. Some steal it, as did the woman who secretly touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment. Some are compelled into it, as are the poor of this world.

### TIT. CXVIII. On the Instruments of Divine Vengeance

God employs three instruments in exacting vengeance upon enemies: the healing remedy of the laver, which overwhelms devils as the Red Sea killed the Egyptians; the exercise of fitting penitence, which destroys the stench of sins as sulphur does; and the judgment of utter strictness, which, like fire at Elijah’s word, envelops hardened idolaters.

### TIT. CXIX. On the Threefold Bed of the Soul

The soul’s bed, on which it rests, is threefold. The first is the heaviness of infirmity, in the arrangement which the sick person, now restored to health, lays beneath himself. The second is the tranquillity of a quiet conscience, in which, when David flees, his image is placed (1 Sam. 19). This is the bed beneath which two supports are placed: from the past, an enlargement of security and confidence; from the future, certainty of recompense and reward. The pillow placed beneath the head is the abundance of divine and familiar grace.

The third bed is humility free from vainglory: it is the flower-strewn bed surrounded by sixty mighty men (Song 3).

### TIT. CXX. On the Two Rivers in Which Sinners Wash Themselves, and Those in Which the Just Do So

[Col. 0807A]

There are two rivers in which sinners wash themselves: the current of elaborate self-presentation and wantonness; likewise, the pestilence of flattery and deceit. These are Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus (2 Kgs. 5).

There are likewise two rivers in which the just bathe themselves: the onset of elaboration and insult; the sweetness of consolation and grace. These are Korah and Dathan, sons of Levi.

### TIT. CXXI. On the Four Herbs or Flowers Growing in the Lord’s Garden

There are four kinds of herbs in the Lord’s garden: purity of bodily cleanness, which is like a lily; the special grace of innocence, which is like hyssop; the free truth of eloquence, which is like a violet; and the justice of continual action, which is like a rose.

### TIT. CXXII. On the Three Paradises

There are three kinds of paradise: the pleasurable sweetness of visible things, which is watered like a garden of delights; the sincere purity of spiritual things, which preserves the human being within itself; and the delightful truth of supercelestial things, where Paul hears secret words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12).

### TIT. CXXIII. On the Thieves of Our Possessions

There are four thieves who steal every excellent thing from us: dullness of intellect, and discord, which takes from us knowledge of the truth. This thief is called by the Psalmist “business in darkness” (Ps. 90). The unrestrained wantonness of the flesh steals the merit of integrity and is called the “noonday demon” (ibid.). Favourable boastfulness takes away the fullness of holiness and is called “an arrow flying by day” (ibid.). Love and desire for this life steal the reward of eternity and are called “the terror by night” (ibid.). These are thieves lying in wait without interruption.

### TIT. CXXIV. On the Three Loaves

There are three loaves which the friend arriving from the road seeks: charity, humility, and continence.

### TIT. CXXV. On the Assumption and Ten Praises of Mary Ever-Virgin

Mary was assumed into heaven. Blessed is this day, happier than days gone by, on which the Virgin of virgins, the Holy One of holy ones, the mother of mercy, is assumed; on which the aromatic chamber, paradise of delights, and glory of angels is raised to the height of the royal throne.

This is our Lady; this is the Virgin who, by a singular privilege and attended by angelic choirs, today comes to the right hand of her Son. For the King of all, who is both her Son and Lord of heaven, together with the whole heavenly court, meets her today, saying: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song 4).

Today our Lady, surrounded by a remarkable crown, displays to angelic dignity the privileges of her exalted rank, in which the court of the whole paradise rejoices.

The first privilege is that she conceived without defilement and without a man. In this she showed herself exempt at conception from that prophetic decree: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Ps. 50).

The second privilege is that she gave birth without pain. In this she overcame the curse given to the first woman: “In pain you shall bear a son,” etc. (Gen. 3). For she whom no man deflowers is not tormented and does not labour, etc.

The third is that she was virgin and mother, when nature altered its course and stood amazed in wonder. For it marvels that a pure virgin bears a son. No fecundity is proclaimed there by any natural arrangement where intact virginity is preserved.

The fourth is that she knew everything wholly and perfectly. For how could she have been ignorant of anything when she knew the One who knows all things, and in whom the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily?

The fifth is that she bore God.

The sixth is that she departed without the pain of death, for she was made as foreign to the pain of death as she had been removed from corruption.

The seventh is that she lives in heaven with her body, as we believe. Although blessed Jerome here presents opinions, he nevertheless does not deny the fact; rather, he has bowed the necks of all our faith beneath subtle reasoning, in which we say that it is not impossible for God that the singular dwelling-place of divinity should not be subject to corruption or worms. He who preserved unharmed the garments of the three boys in the furnace of fire both willed and was able to preserve incorrupt the body of his own mother.

The eighth is that she surpasses angelic sublimity.

The ninth is that she sits in a singular manner at the Son’s right hand, as the Psalmist testifies: “The queen stood at your right hand,” etc. (Ps. 44).

The tenth is the general one which is woven along the edge of the cloak: “She has been seen to have neither one like her before nor any successor after her.”

### TIT. CXXVI. On the Threefold Joy

[Col. 0808C] “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25). Joy is threefold: there is the joy of the world, your joy, and the joy of your Lord. The first comes from earthly abundance; the second from a good conscience; the third from the experience of eternity. Therefore, do not go out into the joy of the world; do not remain in your own joy; but enter into the joy of your Lord.

For the first is external; the second is indeed within you; but the third is far more inward. One goes out to the first; one begins to come to the second; one arrives at the third. Humanity went out to the first when it fell from paradise; it begins to come to the second when it is reconciled to God through faith. But it will arrive at the third when, seeing him as he is, it enjoys him forever.

The first is onefold, the second a hundredfold, the third eternal life. But whoever renounces all that he possesses shall receive a hundredfold and in the future possess eternal life.

### TIT. CXXVII. On God’s Exaltation in Us through a Heart That Is High, Broad, and Deep

“Man shall approach the high heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). God is exalted in three ways. First, by what he has from us, namely through the condition of human nature, in which he was exalted above the heaven of heavens. Second, through that by which he dwells in us, namely faith and love: for whoever loves more is found more worthy of love. Third, through that by which he is apprehended by us, namely through knowledge: for the more his knowledge increases in us, the greater his eminence is found to be.

This is like a mountain: the farther away one is from it, the smaller it appears; the nearer one comes, the larger and higher it seems. The heart, moreover, is deep, broad, and high: deep through despair, broad through love, high through contemplation.

Therefore, if you wish God—who cannot be exalted in himself—to be exalted in you, move from the deep heart to the broad heart through faith and love, and from the broad to the high through knowledge. Then God will be exalted in us: for the more the affection of the human heart is drawn away from desire for lower things and advanced toward love of eternal things, the more the charity of God is exalted before him, greater than the greatest and higher than the highest virtues.

### TIT. CXXVIII. On the Threefold Promotion of Humankind

[Col. 0809B] “Well done, good and faithful servant! Because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many things” (Matt. 25). There are three promotions: the first in virtues, the second in offices of administration, the third in rewards. The first is of merits, the second of stipends, the third of rewards. The first is meritorious, the second dispensatory, the third remunerative. The first works inwardly; the second outwardly; the third inwardly and outwardly. The first makes a person good; the second proves a person faithful; the third makes a person blessed. The first is set over oneself, the second over one’s neighbour, the third over human beings and angels alike. “Do you not know,” says the Apostle, “that we shall judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6).

Hence it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant, because you have been faithful over a few things,” etc. This first promotion is good in one’s own affairs. The second is faithful in things entrusted: good in conscience, faithful in stewardship. “Because you have been faithful over a few things, I shall set you over many things.” The third, however, is blessed in rewards; therefore it is added: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

### TIT. CXXIX. To Be “from God,” “by God,” and “of God”

“He who is from God hears God’s words” (John 8). It is one thing to be from God (*ex Deo*), another to be by God (*a Deo*), another to be of God (*de Deo*). To be from God is to have existence from him; to be by God is to be conformed to him through grace and justice; to be of God is to possess the nature of deity.

Nothing is of God except God; no one is by God except the elect. Both elect and reprobate are from God; but nothing is of God except God, for God alone possesses the nature of deity. The elect are conformed to him through justice. All things have existence from God, from whom, in whom, and through whom all things are.

Thus not all things are from God according to grace, but according to existence, because many things are from God by the nature of their creation, while they are from the devil through the wickedness of imitation. Hence the Lord says: “You are from your father the devil,” etc. (John 3).

Therefore those who have from God the nature of subsisting and the form of living and conquering are wholly from God; and they hear God’s words not merely with the hearing of the ear, but also with that of heart and deed. In the hearing of deed lies obedience. For one who hears only with the ear hears negligently; one who hears with the heart, intelligently; and one who hears in deed, obediently.

### TIT. CXXX. On the Office of the Good Shepherd

“I am the good shepherd,” etc. (John 10). Whoever bears the name of shepherd should so perform the office that he also possesses its merit: not merely good in name, but good in deed, good in nourishment both for himself and for the flock. Those whom he feeds with the word, let him shape by example. For this twofold goodness, according to the Apostle, he should be considered worthy of a twofold honour (1 Tim. 5).

For one may be good and not a shepherd; a shepherd and not good; neither good nor a shepherd; or both good and a shepherd. But whoever is a good shepherd must be good. Such a person, therefore, is endowed with a double goodness: by one he knows his own sheep; by the other he is known by his own sheep. For he would not be a good shepherd if he possessed one and not the other—if, that is, he either did not know his sheep or was not known by them.

Some shepherds know their sheep but are not known by their own. Others are known by their own but do not know their own. Others neither are known by their own nor know their own. Others both know their own and are known by their own.

The first occurs when prelates provide their subjects with necessary care but do not receive from them the obedience due. The second occurs when due obedience is rendered to prelates, but they do not extend to their subjects the necessary care. The third occurs when the former provide no care and the latter render no obedience. The fourth occurs when both the former render due care and the latter yield due obedience.

For the shepherd knows the sheep if he diligently provides for its need as for something known or entrusted to him. The sheep recognizes the shepherd if it obeys his voice immediately, not as that of a stranger but as that of one of the household.

## BOOK SIX. EXPLANATORY NOTES ON SCRIPTURE, FRAGMENTS OF MORAL TREATISES, ETC.

[Col. 0809]

### TIT. I. On the Fourfold Power Given to Christ and the Fourfold State of Creatures

[Col. 0809D]

“All power has been given to me,” etc. (Matt. 28). Our mind can rejoice with great and immeasurable joy if it takes care to consider by how exalted a grace human nature has been transferred from death to glory. For that which fell has been exalted more than twice over, if you consider from what state it fell and to what it ascended.

For it fell from the animate and mortal state into death. The first human being was made into a living soul—that is, an animate life; and if animate, then mortal as well. “The body is dead because of sins.” But restoration was made from death to immortality and spirituality, because the second human being became a life-giving spirit: that is, everything mortal in him was swallowed up by immortality.

I distinguish three stages in humanity: mortal, dead, and immortal. Sin cast the dead person from the middle stage to the lowest; grace raised the person from the lowest to the highest, so that there is no return from death to the animate state of the first human being, but rather an ascent to the immortal life of the second.

Four states of rational creatures are distinguished. The first is that of a miserable and mortal creature; the second, of a blessed but mortal creature; the third, of a miserable though immortal creature; the fourth, of a blessed and immortal creature. In the first stands the miserable and mortal creature; in the second, the blessed and mortal creature; in the third, the miserable and immortal creature; in the fourth, the blessed and immortal creature.

The first state—the mortal and miserable creature—is the unjust human being: mortal by the condition of creation, and utterly miserable through a perverse will and sin. For sin makes the human being miserable, so that it may fittingly be said: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30). It is as though the text said: Have mercy, although it is miserable, because it can be blessed.

The second state—the blessed and mortal creature—is the just human being: mortal by right of condition, blessed by the habit of justice. For David says that the blessedness belongs to the person to whom God reckons justice. Thus: “Blessed is the just man to whom the Lord has not imputed injustice.” So also: “Blessed are the poor in spirit; blessed are the meek” (Matt. 5), and the rest.

The third state—the miserable and immortal creature—is that of apostate angels, who possess immortal misery, like a creature assigned to misery forever. It is immortal by reason of the indivisible duration of its nature, yet miserable by reason of the unresolvable evil of its wickedness. Three things contribute to its misery: the torment of envy, by which it wastes away through envy at the success of another, namely the just human being; the torment of conscience, which, in bitter self-laceration because it has become such through its own fault, rages with fresh fury against itself; and the fear of impending Gehenna, which shakes them.

The fourth state—the blessed and immortal creature—is the angelic spirit, blessed by the contemplation of the Creator and immortal through the perpetuity of life.

Thus, in the first state, the miserable and mortal creature is the unjust human being; in the second, the blessed and mortal creature is the just human being; in the third, the miserable and immortal creature is the apostate spirit; in the fourth, the blessed and immortal creature is the angelic spirit.

Humanity likewise corresponds to the state of the fourfold creature. Fourfold is the power granted to Christ in glory. He received the power of justifying, by which he might make the mortal and miserable creature blessed; of giving life, by which he might make the blessed and mortal creature blessed and immortal; of judging, by which he might distinguish the blessed and immortal creature from the miserable and mortal; and of glorifying, by which he might make glorious and immortal the one distinguished by judgment.

Of the first it is said: “The Son has power to forgive sins” (Matt. 11). Of the second: “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10). Of the third: “Fear him who has power to cast body and soul into Gehenna” (Matt. 10). Of the fourth: “As you gave him power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17).

The first removes impiety from the miserable and mortal creature; the second excludes mortality from the miserable and mortal creature; the third grants to the creature separated from the miserable and immortal creature, which cannot change, the possibility of being changed for the better; the fourth presents to the creature already received into glory the brightness of inaccessible light.

The first heals inwardly; the second outwardly. The former removes guilt; the latter removes the bodily penalty consequent upon sin, not that eternal penalty which threatens after the body. For by the third power that follows, the judicial power distinguishes some as subject to that penalty through the present punishment of mortality by being born, and likewise removes others from it as though immediately.

It is therefore best and just that every being of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms should bend at the name of Jesus (Phil. 2), whom, because of his passion, we see crowned with glory and honour: the heavenly beings because of his power to glorify; earthly beings because of his power to justify; and the infernal beings because of his power to judge the dead and the living.

Because of the power to give life, let the miserable—or unjust—and mortal creature embrace and love the power of justification. Let the just and mortal creature faithfully await the power to give life. Let the miserable and immortal creature experience the power of judgment. Let the blessed and immortal creature happily enjoy the power of glorification.

### TIT. II. On the Silence of the Contemplative Soul

“There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8). There is a silence which is contemplation. Heaven is the soul of the just person. Hence: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66); and: “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Ps. 18). Therefore, when the repose of the contemplative life is practised in the mind, silence takes place in heaven. Because that repose is not perfect in the present life, it is said to occur not for an hour but for half an hour.

### TIT. III. On the Breast of Maternal Affection

“Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12). Maternal affections are briefly expressed, because little children cannot either grieve or rejoice without the one who bore them. For she has two breasts, from which she offers a double milk to her children. The first breast is rejoicing-with; the second, compassion. The first milk is exhortation; the second, consolation.

From the breast of rejoicing-with, therefore, the good shepherd draws milk of exhortation for those making progress; from the breast of compassion he offers milk of consolation to the fainthearted, shaken by the force of temptation.

How many today melt Christ’s reproaches, spittle, nails, lance, cross, and finally death in the furnace of avarice; hasten to enclose the price of the universe in their purses; and, though they are of the patrimony of Christ crucified, are excessively fattened, made gross, and enlarged, yet do not suffer compassion over the affliction of Joseph! But she who is a mother has breasts, and does not cease to draw from the breast of rejoicing-with milk of exhortation, and from the breast of compassion milk of consolation: that is, to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep.

### TIT. IV. A Response Is Received from a Threefold Spirit

“Simeon received an answer from the Holy Spirit” (Luke 2). At times a human being receives an answer from the Holy Spirit; at times from an evil spirit; at times from one’s own spirit. When received from an evil spirit, one is always deceived; when from one’s own spirit, one is often deceived; when from the Holy Spirit, one is never misled.

The evil spirit always deceives; the human spirit often deceives; the Holy Spirit always teaches and instructs rightly. For whenever he gives an answer, he bears witness to truth and makes himself both guarantor and witness of judgment concerning himself. “The Spirit,” says the Apostle, “searches the words of God” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore the Holy Spirit gives an answer through the inspiration that he suggests; testimony through the grace that he pours in; and judgment through the discernment that he bestows. But because suggestions are many and one should not easily believe every spirit, the grace of a certain excellent savour bears testimony to the good spirit. “The Spirit himself,” he says, “bears witness to our spirit” (Rom. 8), because knowledge of judgment distinguishes this taste from the affections of the flesh. “The Spirit judges all things” (1 Cor. 2), “reaching mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8).

Thus inspiration judges, grace commends, and the knowledge of discernment examines. Whoever is supported by these authorities and circumstances, you may safely trust.

### TIT. V. On the Sick Person, the Cause of Illness, the Physician, and the Remedy for Illness

[Col. 0813C]

“Unhappy man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). Here four things must be considered: the sick person, the cause of illness, the physician, and the remedy. God is the physician; humanity is the sick person; love of the world is the cause of illness; love of God is the remedy.

Their difference is this: love of the world is sweet at first and exceedingly bitter in the end; love of God begins in bitterness and ends in great sweetness. Hence the chief steward says to the bridegroom: “Every person first puts forward the good wine; but when they have become drunk, then that which is inferior,” etc. (John 2).

### TIT. VI. On the Threefold Edict and, Allegorically Applied to Christ, Moses Shut in a Basket

[Col. 0813D] “An edict went out from Caesar Augustus,” etc. (Luke 2). There are three edicts: the first for liberation, the second for purification, the third for salvation. The first issued from wisdom, the second from power, the third from glory. Unless wisdom had gone forth, power would not save us, nor would glory give us life.

The Son went forth, who had long lain hidden. As Scripture says, Moses lay hidden for three months in his father’s house (Exod. 2); Christ lay hidden for three periods in the bosom of the Father: before the flood, after the flood, and after the law.

For his going forth, a basket of reeds is woven. The basket is Mary; it is of reeds, being fashioned from fragile flesh without the knot of guilt. Fresh in the water through the dew of grace, it is smeared with pitch and bitumen, lest it dissolve or water enter it. There are two evils in the human being: one of flesh, the other of spirit—lust and pride. Against lust the bitumen of virginity is applied; against pride, the pitch of humility. Therefore the water of lust cannot flow in, because bitumen encloses the flesh; nor can pride dissolve it, because pitch seals the mind.

Hear the voice of bitumen: “Because I do not know a man” (Luke 1). Hear the flowing pitch: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (ibid.). The strong basket contains every good thing within; no evil approaches it from without. In such a vessel the Lord came into the Egypt of this world.

### TIT. VII. On Watches, Dreams, and When and by Whom One Must Rise
“Now it is the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13). He sets forth three things: the hour, sleep, and rising. There were, as it were, three watches of a certain dark night.

The first was in paradise, in which the devil tempts and overcomes in three ways: through avarice, vainglory, and gluttony. The second was under the law of nature, in which there are three things by which a conquered human being despairs: the enemy’s assault through suggestion; the malignity of the flesh through concupiscence and the prompting of frailty; and the mind’s ignorance through estrangement from truth. The third was under Moses’ written law, in which there are three things through which the dying person expires: misuse of bodily things, as they did with the manna, saying, “Let us return to the pots of meat”; transgression of spiritual commandments, when they became lawbreakers; and the obstinacy of evil hearts, for often, when corrected, they became worse.

Likewise there are three kinds of sleep. The first is drowsing in thought, in three ways: impurity, when one turns shameful things over in the mind; pride, when one exalts oneself over one’s neighbour; and concupiscence, when one covets one’s neighbour’s possessions. The second is sleeping in speech, in three ways: idle, slanderous, and flattering talk. The third is being sunk in slumber through action, in three ways: hypocritical, impious, and indecent work. Therefore he says: “Now it is the hour for us to rise from sleep.”

After the three watches of the night follows the fourth watch, which extends from the Lord’s incarnation to the end of the age. After it there is no night, but perpetual day: “For the night has passed; but the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13). The fourth watch of the night, in which the Lord came upon the waters, is threefold, principally distinguished by three hours. The first hour was in the time of the martyrs, while heretics clamoured; the second, in the time of the confessors, while hypocrites sprang up; the third will be when the charity of many grows cold.

In these and in those, just as through the three watches we drowsed, slept, and were sunk in slumber, so in the fourth watch we rise from sleep in three opposite ways, by the purpose of three watchful dispositions: spiritual purity against impurity; spiritual poverty against concupiscence; and custody of the mouth against the vice of the tongue. This too is threefold: a door of discretion against idle speech; praise proceeding from love against slanderous speech; and truth in the mouth against flattering speech. We are also stirred to watchfulness in the performance of works in three ways, through three instructors: actual truth against hypocritical work; maternal compassion against impious work; and bodily sincerity against indecent work.

## TITLE VIII. On the Threefold Sweet Yoke and Light Burden of Obedience and Disobedience

“My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11). The sweet yoke or burden is threefold. The first is that of fear of Gehenna; the second, of regular discipline; the third, of love and grace. The first is borne by those who, solely through fear of the punishment of Gehenna, restrain their hands from wrongful action. The second is carried by those who, through fear of temporal punishment and love of present advantage, keep their hearts from wrongful thought. The third belongs to those who, by love of God alone, turn from evil and do good.

The first are servants; the second, hired labourers; the third, sons. The first awakens servants; the second strengthens hired labourers; the third fortifies sons: for the first begin, the second advance, and the third persevere.
