But as obedience has a threefold yoke, so also does disobedience. The first is the yoke of iniquity and malice—that is, lust—under which Solomon was enslaved. The second is that of prosperity and abundance, under which the rich man is clothed in purple. The third is that of affliction and misery, under which Ahaziah, after falling through the lattice, consulted Baalzebub, the god of Ekron (4 Kings [2 Kings] 1).

## TITLE IX. On the Threefold Working of Divine Grace

“What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4). You are created, healed, and saved. Those who think rightly confess this threefold working of divine grace. The first is formation; the second, reformation; the third, consummation. First we are formed in God through Christ; secondly, we are re-formed through him; finally, through him and with him we shall be consummated.

For what did not exist had to be created in him; what existed but was deformed had to be re-formed by the Form; and the members can be perfected only by the head. This will occur “when we come to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4). “When Christ, our life, shall appear, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3). Creation, therefore, takes place without us; consummation concerns us, but neither proceeds from us. Reformation alone is in some measure accomplished with us, because of voluntary consent. Hence our fasts, vigils, works of mercy, and the other exercises of virtues, by which our inward person is renewed day by day, are counted among merits.

## TITLE X. On the Qualities of a Good Horse

Let a horse be sought for us with more exacting care: one whose very beauty commends it to the eye; one which careful inspection approves as free from every fault; one which moves over level ground and neither jolts its rider by any unevenness nor has its speed hindered by smoothness. Let no foot, ever thrown back, stumble upon a clod. There should be no need either to restrain it with the bridle or to urge it with spurs; rather, it should submit itself with such readiness to every service that it seems to explore the rider’s every wish. Finally, let it proceed with such pleasantness of gait that the rider seems not to move but to glide, and judges himself not so much to be carried by a horse as borne onward in a little boat.

All these things may be applied morally to the body, which the soul uses as a horse.

## TITLE XI. What a Ruler Should Be toward Those Subject to Him

Care must be taken that compassion shows the ruler to his subjects as a mother, and discipline as a father. Between these, careful circumspection must provide that neither severity be rigid nor compassion lax, so that there may be mercy that wisely provides with justice, and discipline that sternly chastises with piety.

Thus wine and oil are applied to the half-dead man: through wine the wounds are bitten, through oil they are soothed. Let there be in the wine the bite of severity, and in the oil the softness of compassion; let there be a certain tempering of both, so that subjects may neither be ulcerated by excessive harshness nor dissolved by excessive leniency.

Therefore, in the ark of the covenant, together with the tablets, there are both rod and manna: for in the ark of the heart, together with knowledge of sacred Scripture, there is both the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness. Hence David says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22 [23]). We are struck with the rod; we are supported by the staff. Let there therefore be the strictness of the rod that strikes, and the consolation of the staff that supports; let there be love, but not softening; rigour, but not embittering; zeal that does not rage immoderately; and compassion that does not spare beyond what is fitting.

## TITLE XII. On the Similar Office of the Cock and the Preacher

Before the cock crows, it shakes its wings and strikes itself, making itself more wakeful. So the preacher first exercises himself in good actions, lest, torpid in work within himself, he awaken others by voice. What they are about to say, they should proclaim both by work and by voice, and thus call others to vigils.

At the deeper hour of night they utter a stronger and more prolonged voice; toward morning, a gentler one. Thus they thunder terrors loudly to the wicked, but set forth gentle words about rewards to those drawing near to the light.

## TITLE XIII. On Four Matters to Be Considered

Four things present themselves for consideration: consider yourself; what is beneath you; what is around you; and what is above you. Let your consideration begin with yourself, lest you extend yourself fruitlessly to other things while neglecting yourself. For what does it profit you if you gain the whole world but lose yourself? If you are wise, everything will serve you for wisdom; if you do not belong to yourself, then—even if you know all mysteries, the breadth of earth, the heights of heaven, and the depths of the sea—if you do not know yourself, you will be like one building without a foundation, making a ruin rather than a structure.

The wise person will be wise for himself and will himself first drink from the fountain of faith. Therefore let your consideration begin with yourself and end in yourself; wherever it wanders, draw it back to yourself with the fruit of salvation. Take your example from the Father of all, who both sends forth and retains his Word. Your word is your consideration: let it go forth in such a way that it does not leave you.

This consideration of yours is divided into three parts: that you may consider what you are, who you are, and what sort of person you are—how kind, gentle, and the like. According to the philosophers, a human being is a rational and mortal animal. To one considering these two things there comes this benefit: let the rational element in you humble the mortal; and conversely let the rational element strengthen the mortal. Thus neither good will be neglected.

When you carefully consider what you are, the nature by which you are human comes before you. When you ask, “Who are you?” the name of your person comes before you, because you are either a simple monk, a pastor, or a bishop. Which of these chiefly belongs to you—what you have acquired or what you were born? Therefore consider most of all what you most truly are. Consider not merely that you were born, but how you were born. You came naked from your mother’s womb. Were you born wearing a mitre?

If you consider what sort of person you are, you find a suffering human being: blushing because you are human, ashamed that you are naked, weeping because you were born, murmuring because you were born for labour, not for honour. Thus take your pattern for yourself both from the condition of your origin and from the mystery of redemption: for the author of nature joins the highest and lowest in his own person; he tempers Light and Word. You who sit high, do not be high-minded; rather, think humbly of yourself and agree with the humble.

Therefore, if you consider how great you are, consider also what sort of person you are. It is especially monstrous when the mind is very great but weak; when the seat is first and lowest; when the tongue is empty yet speaks grandly; when the hand is idle, speech abundant, and fruit absent; when the face is grave but conduct frivolous; when authority is great but stability wavering.

Consider, therefore, what you are, so that you may hold yourself within yourself, “not walking in great matters nor in wonderful things above” yourself, nor sinking beneath yourself into the deep. Your place is the middle place; and virtue consists in this: that, recognizing what you have become, you consider not your dignity but the ministry entrusted to you.

When the prophet was likewise raised up, he heard: “That you may root up and destroy, and build and plant” (Jer. 1). The image is rustic: in the figure of sweat, a certain spiritual labour is expressed, not honour. For the work of a farmer requires a prophet’s hoe, not a sceptre. Give attention to governing, not as one about to command, but as one about to uproot vices. Content with that tenor, one will inherit care and labour, not glory; indeed, hardness instead of pleasantness. The episcopal chair is a watchtower; from it the one who watches over others—such is the meaning of the name bishop (*episcopus*)—signifies an office, not lordship.

To the third consideration must be added what sort of person you are in forgiving injuries, what sort in avenging them, how prudent an observer you are in both matters of place and manner; what you are in prosperity, what in adversity; how steadfast in injuries done to yourself, and compassionate in injuries done to others. Great is the person who, falling into adversity, does not fall even a little from wisdom; greater is the person to whom present happiness smiles, yet who does not smile back at it. For wisdom is more easily retained amid adverse fortune than amid prosperity.

## TITLE XIV. On the Three Principal Supplications, or Rogation Processions

There are three principal processions. The first is at the Purification of blessed Mary, with candles and lamps; the second, on Palm Sunday, with flowers and palms; the third, around the Ascension of the Lord, with crosses and banners.

The feast of our purification consists in two things: cleansing the conscience for God’s sake, and cleansing one’s reputation for one’s neighbour’s sake. Conscience must be cleansed from manifest and hidden sins. Hence: “Wash me yet more, O Lord, from my iniquity,” etc. (Ps. 50 [51]). This concerns manifest sins. And: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults” (Ps. 18 [19]). This concerns hidden sins. Reputation too must be cleansed and guarded from true and false disgrace.

For these things a lamp is needed—that is, abundant prudence—which in more secret and obscure places seeks out, finds, and cleanses the sins through which we have become blind, so that, thus enlightened, one may say: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles,” etc. (Luke 2).

Once purified, we make the second procession with flowers and palms. Trees first produce leaves, then flowers, and finally fruits. In the leaf is the beginning of good; in the flower, the promise of the first beginning; in the fruit, possession. We proceed with flowers if, through good beginnings and hope of reward, we tend toward the fruit of eternity. The palm does not bear fruit until its hundredth year, and the palm signifies victory. The hundredfold fruit signifies eternal life. One carries the palm in one’s hand who triumphs over the devil in good works and awaits the fruit of eternal life.

The procession with crosses and banners follows. In the cross is the affliction of the flesh; in the banners, the raising of the mind. We add banners to crosses when, from mortification of the flesh, we advance to magnanimity of heart.

The first procession goes from house to temple; the second, from village to city; the third, from earth to heaven. A house is a dwelling intended for private use; a temple is a house dedicated to divine things. An unclean conscience, therefore, is a house; a clean conscience, a temple. Thus the first procession begins from an unclean conscience and ends in its purification. A village is an unfortified habitation. Thus the second procession proceeds from faintness of spirit and tempest to the security opposed to it. The last goes from earth to heaven: from a place of affliction and misery to a place of joy and glory.

In the first procession, on one side there are a boy and a girl; on the other, an old man and a widow. In the boy are tears and sorrow; in the girl, modesty; in the old man, trembling; and in the widow, grief. Our feast of purification entirely needs worshippers such as these: weeping, blushing, trembling, and grieving in remembrance of sins. For such persons should lead the procession with an offering in the temple of loud acclamation.

In the second procession, on one side may be seen the gathering of disciples; on the other, a crowd of both sexes who had assembled for the feast day. It includes children, youths, and those mature in age. In the first is marked the beginning of virtue; in the second, its progress; in the third, perfection. One who wishes to enter the holy city must proceed with these.

The final procession receives only the perfect: on one side angelic men descending, and Galileans looking upward; in the middle, Jesus lifted from the earth, received by a cloud, and taken up into heaven. The first signify good teachers; the second, good hearers; the third, those who from both these groups are received into heaven.

In the second procession there is need of either a turtledove or a dove; each has groaning rather than song. In the turtledove’s song we recognize groaning for sins; therefore it loves solitude. In the dove’s song we recognize groaning from longing for the homeland; therefore it loves the assembly. Such is required in the procession of expiation.

In the second procession there are the colt and the she-ass, which are lesser kinds of mounts and pack-animals. In the she-ass is humility; in the colt, humiliation. Humility is that by which a person is inwardly despised in his own eyes before God; humiliation is its effect, by which one as it were outwardly casts oneself down in the neighbour’s eyes. For many are outwardly abased who are not truly humble. These sit upon the colt, not upon the ass. Others acknowledge their weakness, but, while they are ashamed of outwardly humble things, they possess the ass, not the colt. The Lord sits only upon these mounts, because: “To whom shall I look, except to the poor and contrite in spirit, and to the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66).

In the third procession there are trumpet and cymbal. The cymbal is for jubilation, the trumpet for wonder. Whichever side of the cymbal is struck, it gives the same sound. The striking is manifold; the resonance is one. So too, however and wherever we may be struck, let us sound nothing but the praise of God in well-sounding cymbals of jubilation, while directing our attention to the trumpet of wonder.

## TITLE XV. A Form for Beginning a Sermon

Before the ears of persons so prudent and so venerable, I fear to presume to deliver any discourse, since I possess nothing but a guilty conscience, slight learning, and imperfect eloquence. It would be more fitting for me to be silent than to speak, to be fed than to feed, to offer you my ears rather than my tongue.

But who am I that I should dare to resist the commands of my Lord? I have little confidence in myself; yet I turn to the holiness of him who commands and to your merits. I must obey according to the rule, and without delay. For the necessity of obedience opens my mouth; may your merits, by the grace of him who said, “Open [or: Widen] your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80 [81]), fill it.

## TITLE XVI. A Sermon to Pastors and Prelates on the Pastoral Office

“See to your ministry, brothers; judge the judgment of the Lord,” because you have been appointed judges in the world, not of crimes in order to kill, but of wounds in order to heal. Look at the sick man in your hands, whom that merciful Samaritan entrusted to you, and for whom you received payment from him, lest his cure be provided at your own expense.

You have two coins in the twofold Testament: one of the old currency and the other of the new. With the Old are bought medicines that bite; with the New, those that soothe. The first are for cleansing putrid things; the second, for strengthening living things. These are the two swords which Peter prepared at the Lord’s Passion. The first is rebuke; the second, exhortation. With one, putrid members are cut off from the Church; with the other, healthy members are defended from wounds.

Peter left this to you: strike the vices of human beings. But do so with Peter’s fervour, if you wish to be his heirs and imitators. Christ is crucified before your eyes, and you keep the sword in its sheath? What is a Christian, if not Christ’s body, when he himself says: “What you did to one of the least of these, you did to me” (Matt. 25)?

Why are you sluggish? Why are you timid? Perhaps because you do not stand as Phinehas did, appeasing the Lord’s wrath so that the shaking may cease. Perhaps because you have reclined beside Pharaoh’s pot and love rich food; it is burdensome to you to rise for battle. Perhaps because you love milk and wool: you do not feed the sheep but yourselves, and you flee when the wolf comes because you do not care for the sheep.

At least, if you eat the sheep’s milk, preserve their flesh. If you seek profit in return for guarding them, do not kill the sheep themselves. Do you not kill them? “If you do not announce their iniquity to them, I will require their blood from your hand,” says the Lord (Ezek. 3). Christ the good shepherd even gave his own flesh to the sheep to eat, in order to refresh them; and how is it that you, receiving payment for grace and becoming wolves, kill the sheep themselves?

Woe to evil shepherds, who feed themselves and not the sheep; who, like hired labourers, seeing the wolf come, flee—not by changing place, but by withholding help. If therefore you are shepherds, keep watch over your flock. “Go up against the enemy and make yourselves a wall for the house of Israel.” And, like good dogs, bark around the sheepfolds of the Church with voices of confidence, so that the ravaging wolves may fear, the sheep remain secure, and you may deserve to receive a fitting reward for good guardianship.

## TITLE XVII. On the Efficacy of the Word of God

“The word of the Lord is living and effective,” etc. (Heb. 4). The Lord’s word is living and manifold, because he speaks through human beings and also speaks through himself: through many human beings, but through himself as one. Let us behold a great mystery. The Word of God, clothed in human flesh, once appeared visibly; every day that same Word comes to us hidden in the repeated voice.

The wicked were able not only to see Christ’s humanity, but even to kill it. Every day the wicked hear the word of God and despise it. Yet just as those people would not have killed him had they known him, so these would never despise the heard words of God if they tasted their power by inward savour.

The word of God is living because life is in it and it gives life to the heart. What is outside passes away; what is within does not admit change. It is living, therefore, because it does not change; effective, because it does not fail. Its promise is not deceived in judgment, does not die through forgetfulness, and is not altered in purpose. Its operation is not overcome by difficulty; its judgment is not deceived by ambiguity. It truly permits, powerfully acts, and subtly discerns. It is living, that you may believe; effective, that you may hope. It is penetrating in judgments; living in commands and prohibitions; effective in promises and threats.

It is penetrating in judgments and condemnations, “sharper than every two-edged sword.” A human sword cuts only the human body; thus it is not two-edged. For that is called two-edged which cuts on both sides, because it can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna (Matt. 10). Or it judges, cuts, and discerns both: “reaching even to the division of soul and spirit,” when sacred discourse shows us what among fleshly things is opposed to faith; and also “of joints and marrow,” which is explained by what follows: “of thoughts and intentions.”

First, on the outside above everything, is something like skin; then delight, like flesh; then thoughts, like bones; finally intention, like marrow. As skin covers flesh, so works cover delight; as bones support flesh, so thoughts nourish desires; and as marrow is interior to bones, so intentions lie hidden in thoughts. Thoughts are called joints because, just as a joint is a bond joining middle and extremities, so thoughts, because they arise from desires and produce desires, in some manner join both—nourishing the former and producing the latter.

And fittingly, after “the division of soul and spirit,” that is, of fleshly wills, is set the division of joints, that is, of good and evil thoughts, as more intricate and difficult; finally, as the discerner of intentions, is placed at the end the division of marrow, deservedly hidden among all these. The word of God penetrates inwardly by judging, through its wisdom subtly understanding our secrets; outwardly, through its teaching usefully enlightening us and causing us to understand these same things.

Therefore, because it is living, let us believe that it promises true things; because it is effective, let us hope that it will accomplish what it has promised; because it is penetrating and cannot be deceived, let us grieve that we have offended it, and henceforth guard against offending it.

## TITLE XVIII. On Pharisaic Self-Admiring Persons and Hypocritical Secret Slanderers

Certain people, with Pharisaic boasting, despise all others because they judge themselves superior and better. They come to them in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves; indeed, biting fleas, or rather moths destroying the lives of good people. Since they do not dare act openly, they gnaw in secret; if they cannot utter the outcry of public attack, at least they emit the whisper of detraction.

What good to such people is so great a frugality in food, harshness and conspicuous poverty in clothing, vigils, fasts, and, finally, a certain more austere manner of life in all their distinctive conduct, unless perhaps they do their works in order to be seen by human beings? (Matt. 9.) But Christ says: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (ibid.). Such persons, according to the Apostle, hoping in Christ only in this life, are more pitiable than all human beings (1 Cor. 15).

One hopes in Christ only in this life who seeks from Christ’s service only temporal glory. Miserable little man, who with such labour and industry strives not to be—or rather, not to appear—like other people: less acceptable, indeed more grievously tormented, than any other human being. Is there then no way for hypocrites, so to speak, even somewhat more tolerable toward hell? Why do they not at least choose the broad way which many travel, the way that leads to death, so that they might pass as it were from joy, and not from mourning, into mourning?

“O how happily it is with those for whom there is no pain in their death,” and whose strength is in their affliction; “who are not in the labour of human beings, nor are they scourged with other people” (Ps. 72 [73]). Though sinners, and destined to everlasting torments for temporal joys, at least they obtained riches while abounding in the world.

Woe to those carrying the cross, not as the Saviour carried his own, but as Cyrenian [Simon] carried another’s. Woe to the harpists who play not like those in the Apocalypse on their own harps, but truly, like hypocrites, on the harps of others. Woe once, and woe again, to proud poor people, carrying Christ’s cross but not following Christ—those who share his sufferings but neglect to follow humility. Such people are crushed by a double breaking: here they afflict themselves for temporal glory, and in the future they shall be dragged to eternal punishments for inward pride.

They labour with Christ, but shall not reign with Christ. They follow Christ in feigned sorrow, yet shall not attain Christ in glory. They drink from the torrent on the way, but shall not lift up their head. They mourn on the road, but shall not be consoled in their homeland—and rightly so. For what has pride to do under the rags of Christ’s humility? Does human malice have no covering under which to cloak itself except that in which the Saviour’s infancy was wrapped? And how does feigned arrogance confine itself beside the Lord’s manger, and, instead of innocent cries, murmur the evil of slander?

Would not those supremely proud persons in the psalm, “whose iniquity has come forth from fatness,” be redeemed from iniquity and impiety much sooner than those who hide under another’s holiness? (Ps. 72 [73].) Certainly one who confesses impiety is less impious than one who feigns holiness, because by adding falsehood the latter doubles impiety.

## TITLE XIX. On the Growth of Seed Cast into the Earth, That Is, of Faith and the Other Virtues

“So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, and sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should germinate and grow while he does not know. For the earth bears fruit of itself: first the blade, then the ear, then full grain in the ear. And when it has produced fruit, immediately he sends in the sickle, because the harvest is present” (Mark 4).

In the ascent of the heart there are certain steps, concerning which the psalmist says: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Ps. 83 [84]). Hence Job says: “I shall declare him for each of my steps” (Job 31). For one declares him for each of one’s steps who gives praise to him who gave the increases of virtues that one receives.

There are not only steps from virtue to virtue; each virtue itself is increased, as it were, by certain steps and is perfected through increments. For the beginning of virtue is one thing, its progress another, its perfection another. If faith itself were not led to perfection by certain steps, the apostles would not have said: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17); nor would another, when asked whether he believed, have answered: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (Mark 9).

For if he knew that he possessed unbelief, how did he believe? But because faith grows by steps of merits, at one and the same time the one who did not fully believe both believed and was unbelieving. Thus Mark describes these steps under the name of harvest, saying: “So is the kingdom of God,” etc.

A person casts seed into the earth when he implants a good intention in his heart. Afterwards he sleeps—that is, rests in hope of good work. He rises by night and day, because amid prosperity and adversity the seed does not fail. It germinates and grows, although the person does not know, because even when one is not yet able to merit one’s own increase, virtue once conceived is led toward advancement. And the earth bears fruit of itself because, with grace preceding, the human mind rises spontaneously to the fruit of good work.

But this same earth first produces the blade, then the ear, then full grain in the ear. The very beginning of a good work has the tenderness of a blade; it reaches the ear when acquired virtue leads toward the perfection of work. Full grain bears fruit in the ear when virtue is brought to a strong and perfect work. When fruit has been produced, almighty God sends the sickle and cuts his harvest, because, when each person has brought forth his temporal life in perfect works, he cuts it down by his sentence, in order to bring his grain into the heavenly granary.

Therefore, when we conceive good desires, we cast the seed of life into the earth. When we conceive upright works, we are a blade. When we bring good work to perfection, we reach the ear. When we are strengthened by the perfection of the work itself, we produce full grain in the ear.

Peter was a blade. When he feared the words of the maidservant, the greenness was still in his mind: he believed Christ to be the redeemer of all, but, being pliable, he was trampled under the foot of fear. He had grown into his ear when he saw alive in Galilee the one whom he had feared to confess. He had reached full grain in the ear when, after the Spirit came from above, he was so strengthened that, though beaten, he despised the forces of his persecutors and preached God amid scourges.

## TITLE XX. On Empty and Full Water Jars

Water jars are sometimes empty and sometimes full. When full, they are sometimes filled with poison, sometimes with water or wine. They are empty when actions are done for empty glory or earthly advantage. They are full of poison when done with rancour of spirit or murmuring; full of water when done from fear—for water signifies a certain fear. Hence Solomon says: “The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life” (Prov. 14). They are full of wine when fear is turned into love, when charity excludes fear. The Lord does not will them to be empty or full of poison; he commands that they be filled with water; he causes the water to be turned into wine.

## TITLE XXI. On the Sluggish, the Struggling, and the Conquering

There are three: the sluggish, the struggling, and the conquering. Of the first it is said: “The sluggard hides his hands under his armpit” (Prov. 19). The struggling person hears: “Act manfully” (Ps. 30 [31]). And to the conqueror the Lord cries: “To the conqueror I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” (Rev. 2).

The sluggish person must therefore first be consoled; the second, sympathized with; the combatant, feared for; the conqueror, rejoiced with. The first has bound hands; the second, hands stretched out; the third, hands at rest. The first is sick without a wound; the second, healthy with a wound; the third, healthy from every wound. The first sleeps without hope; the second watches in hope; the third rejoices in possession.

The sluggish person keeps silence from good; the second from evil; the third from hardship. By hardship I mean what is harmful to body and soul—namely, sins and the punishment of sin. This silence will exist in the blessed life, where the servant will be free from his lord. For in this life the servant is not free from the Lord, because even though by repentance the sinner leaves sin, the assault of sin nevertheless still persists.

## TITLE XXII. On the Night, Its Course, and Its Paths

“The night, in its course, held the middle of its journey” (Wis. 13). Night is ignorance of the good. The course of night is directed toward preserving a period of goodness. There are three paths of night: first, to err through ignorance of the good; second, after the good is known, to love error; third, to persevere in error.

Therefore, when Christ came, all things held the middle of silence; immediately night held the middle of its journey in its course, because human beings were silent concerning the good and loved error.

## TITLE XXIII. On the Manifold Reception of the Eucharist, the Lord’s Body

He who was once given to the world in the form of flesh is given to the faithful every day and hour under the appearance of bread, namely in eating his sacrament; but more often, and at every hour, he is given to the devout in the tasting of his Spirit. The first is for redemption; the second for sanctification; the third for consolation.

The first requires right faith; the second, a pure conscience; the third, pure and ready devotion. This raises the mind to meet grace, opens the heart to receive it, and expands the affection so that it may receive from it more abundantly.

## TITLE XXIV. On Preparations for Worthily Celebrating the Purification of Mary
“Let your loins be girded,” etc. (Luke 12). Let our loins be girded, so that we may emulate Mary’s Purification; let lamps be burning in our hands, so that we may present in ourselves, even by a visible sign, the light which was the joy of Simeon as he bore it. Let us be chaste in body and pure in heart, that we may celebrate the Purification of the Virgin more expressly. Let us burn with devotion and shine in action, so that with Simeon we may bear Christ in our hands. Let there be a lamp in the heart, in the hand, and in the mouth. Let the lamp in the heart shine in us; that in the hand, for others; that in the mouth, for our neighbour. The lamp in the heart is purity of faith; the lamp in the hand, the example of action; [Col. 0824C] the lamp in the mouth, speech that edifies. We must shine not only before human beings through prayer, and before God through intention, but also before angels through action. Our lamp before angels is pure devotion, when we sing psalms wisely or pray fervently in the sight of angels. The lamp before God is a single-minded intention: that we may please him alone whom we have chosen to approve.

That faith is a lamp Solomon testifies: “Her lamp shall not be extinguished in the night” (Prov. 31), that is, her faith shall not fail in temptation. That a good work is a lamp the Lord shows: “Let your light shine,” etc. (Matt. 5). That the Lord’s word is a lamp David shows: “Your word is a lamp to my feet” [Col. 0824D] (Ps. 118). That prayer is a lamp Solomon observes: “The lamp of the Lord is the breath of a person’s life, which searches all the secret places of the belly” (Prov. 20). For the light opened to us from above while we pray or sing psalms is the breath of life, in which we breathe sweetly.

But when it is said to “search the secret places of the belly,” that is, of the mind, this must not be taken as the thing which the Lord threatens that he will search with lamps. For the former belongs to the cause of one who enlightens; the latter, to the judgment of one who examines. For the physician’s draught searches the secret places of the belly in one way, the executioner’s sword in another. Of intention it is said: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6). Therefore, for us, for whom so many lamps are burning, when the lamp of this life has been extinguished, the inextinguishable light [Col. 0825A] of life will rise; and, as the brightness of noon, it will rise for us at evening. “When you think us consumed, we shall arise as the morning star, and darkness shall be as noon.”

## TITLE XXV. On the threefold enrolment for marriage, continence, and virginity

“That the whole world might be enrolled,” etc. (Luke 2). There is a threefold enrolment: some are enrolled for marriage, some for continence, others for virginity. In these three consists Christ’s whole enrolment. Whoever is in none of them is not Christ’s, but rather belongs to the devil’s census.

Marriage is compared to carpets spread upon the ground. Continence is a curtain hanging on a wall. Virginity is the royal cloth upon which dishes are placed. The first is beneath the king’s feet; the second is before his eyes; the third [Col. 0825B] is beside or around the king. The first is for use, the second for delight, the third for dignity. The first is darkened in the earth by earth’s dust; the second is crowned above the earth; the third imitates heavenly things.

In marriage there is the bond of spirit for fellowship, the use of flesh for offspring, and moderation in carnal union for receiving the body of Christ and for prayer. Fornication is a fire that burns up; marriage, a fire that warms; virginity, a fire that shines, and by lightness sharpens and drives itself upward toward the heights. It is therefore ours either to perish in the blaze or to escape by the remedy.

## TITLE XXVI. On the calling of Lazarus in the tomb, first morally alluding to “deep calls to deep”; then on the thirteenth station of the Jews in the wilderness, and what follows

[Col. 0825C] “Lazarus, come forth” (John 21). In this calling we must see who calls, whom he calls, and how he calls. For these three matters must be considered in every calling: the quality of the caller, of the called, and of the calling—that is, the caller, the one called, and the call.

Historically, Christ called the material Lazarus out of a material tomb. Spiritually, deep calls to deep: the deep of God calls to the deep of man; the deep of wisdom, the deep of ignorance; the deep of mercy, the deep of misery. For God’s wisdom came to our ignorance; God’s mercy came to our misery; Christ, the exalted one, came down to our mud; the most high came to our depth, and was fixed in the mud of the deep, in order to draw us out of the deep.

Christ is the deep, [Col. 0825D] because “his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable” (Rom. 11). Hence, “I am breadth,” etc. (Jer. 17). The human heart too is a deep, wicked and unsearchable: “Who shall know it?” (ibid.). Hence Jonah, under the figure of Christ in the Passion, says: “The deep surrounded me; the sea covered my head” (Jonah 2).

The higher deep therefore calls the lower: Christ calls the human being, saying, “Lazarus, come forth.” As though he said: “O deep of Adam’s malice, deep of ignorance, deep of misery, come forth.” But from where, and from what tomb—or rather, from what tombs? For every sin is a tomb; therefore, as many sins, so many tombs. “Let the dead bury their dead” (Luke 9). A dead man buries a dead man when a sinner nourishes another sinner with flatteries. Dead and [Col. 0826A] buried in tombs of desire are those to whom the Lord gave the desires of their hearts.

At the thirteenth station after the departure from Egypt, the people murmured against their Lord and Moses; for they had returned in heart to Egypt, to the pots of meat, onions, garlic, and melons. For the thirteenth number, the first after the twelvefold doctrine of the apostles, denotes transgression. Accordingly, Christ, passing beyond the thirteenth, suffered on the thirteenth; at evening he made for us the evening sacrifice, so that from the evening of death he might lead us to the morning of life.

In such tombs the man dead four days was stinking. The first day of death is carnal birth, because man is born to labour, filled with many miseries. Hence: “Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). The second is transgression of the natural law; the third, of the written [Col. 0826B] law; the fourth, of grace given. “Behold, he already stinks.” Yet he calls him from the depths of the earth. Hence: “From the depths of the earth you brought me back again” (Ps. 70). First in the body, again in the soul; first from original sin, again from actual sin; first in you, our head, when you raised our nature from death; again in your members, when you freed us from the death of sin. Once in hope, again in reality, you brought us back from the depths of earth to the deep of heaven.

There are three depths of life: the first deep, the second deeper, the third deepest—sin in thought, action, and habit; the dead person in the house, at the gate, and stinking in the tombs. From this threefold deep the Prophet asks to be delivered: “Let not the tempest of waters overwhelm me,” he says, through wicked thought; [Col. 0826C] “nor let the deep swallow me,” through perverse action; “nor let the pit press its mouth upon me,” through obstinate habit (Ps. 68).

“Lazarus, come forth.” By what way? By me, because “I am the way” (John 14). To where? To me, because I am the homeland. Come through me as man, to me as God. From where is he called? From sins. By what way? Through Christ man to Christ God. Therefore the deep calls from the deeps, and through the deep.

## TITLE XXVII. That for many reasons Mary is called a rod, and Christ her flower

The Virgin Mother of God is the rod; her Son is the flower. Most fittingly, dearest brethren, is the blessed Virgin Mary called a rod. For she is a straight rod, an upright rod, and a rod extended even unto heaven. A slender rod, a fragile rod, a flexible rod, a leafy rod, [Col. 0826D] a flowering rod, a fruitful rod: straight through faith, upright through hope, extended through long-suffering; slender through humility, flexible through gentleness, flowering through virginal conception, fruitful through the birth of salvation.

Slender through self-abasement, fragile through contempt for the world, flexible through compassion for one’s neighbour, leafy through the grace of devotion, flowering through the grace of virginity, fruitful through the prerogative of fecundity. The prerogative of fecundity was that such a woman in such a manner gave birth to such a one. What kind of woman? A virgin conceived, a virgin gave birth, a virgin remained. In what manner? With an angel announcing, the Holy Spirit acting, and the power of the Most High overshadowing. To what kind of one? The Holy of holies, King of the ages, Lord of angels, indeed King of kings and Lord of lords, the only Son of the Virgin [Col. 0827A] Mother, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, God and Lord of majesty.

The Virgin Mother of God is a rod; her Son is a flower. How well and rightly is he called a flower, because he is produced from the virgin rod. What is thinner than a flower? What more tender? What softer to the touch? What lighter to carry? What more beautiful? What more fragrant? What more fruitful do we observe? In the flower, therefore, is honey-making; from the flower comes fruit-bearing; from the flower come honeycomb and fruit. In the honeycomb are honey and wax; in the fruit, drink and food. If these things are small, I add that medicines also are in the flower.

What is thinner than a flower when it is compressed? What more tender when it is crushed? What softer when it is handled? What lighter when it is carried? What more beautiful when it is seen? What more fragrant when it is smelled? What more useful if its effects are considered? Seven things, [Col. 0827B] therefore, we admire in a flower: thinness, tenderness, softness, lightness, beauty, fragrance, usefulness. From these, then, infer what the Virgin’s Son is found to be by those for whom he is changed into a flower. For he who is “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence” to unbelievers and transgressors (1 Pet. 2), is a flower to those who cleave to him in hope and love.

For them, therefore, he is a flower matchless in beauty and usefulness: a flower in which is the Virgin’s Son—thin in indignation, tender in compassion, gentle in meekness, light in dominion, beautiful through dominion, beautiful through moderation, fragrant through promise, useful through recompense. He is therefore thin in scourges, tender in mercies, gentle in gifts, light in commandments, beautiful in examples, fragrant in promises, fruitful [Col. 0827C] in rewards.

This flower has become medicine for us; for from him come honey and wax, and in him are drink and food. Medicine in redemption; drink and food in justification; honey and wax in glorification. From this medicine comes the health of everlasting incorruptibility; from his food, restoration of inward health; from his drink, the intoxication of eternal fecundity. From his food and wax comes the splendour of highest brightness; in his honey, the sweetness of unfailing blessedness.

## TITLE XXVIII. On the mother and child fleeing into Egypt, understood morally, and on the persecution of the children of the holy Innocents

“Take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt” (Matt. 2). The mother is purity of heart; the child is truth, [Col. 0827D] because from such a mother are born understanding, truth, knowledge of self, and knowledge of God. This is full understanding and full wisdom. Do you wish to know that such a son is born from such a mother—namely, knowledge of God from purity of heart? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5), that is, they shall know him.

Purity of heart is the earth that stands forever. For what is pure knows no corruption, and thus does not know how to perish. The fruit of this earth is truth, because “truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84). When such a child has been born, Herod is troubled, and all Jerusalem with him, because he does not wish the child who has been born to grow; indeed, he wishes to kill all the children. Herod is pride; Jerusalem is his kingdom.

Christ loves little Jews; Jerusalem loves great Jews. “Jews” is interpreted “those confessing.” [Col. 0828A] Do you wish to know what sort of confessors the proud king Herod has? “I am not,” he says, “like other men, extortioners,” etc. (Luke 18). The Jerusalem of such persons is troubled with him. Do you wish to hear what kind Christ has? “I am,” he says, “the least of the apostles,” etc. (1 Cor. 15). “The Lord on high looks upon the humble” (Ps. 137); he seeks little ones. “Allow the little children,” he says, “to come to me,” etc. (Matt. 19).

Proud Herod despises the humble, walking in great matters and in wonders beyond himself; he seeks to kill Christ’s little ones from two years old and under. Humble confession makes a Jew little and a child: insofar as it is humble, a little child; insofar as it is confession, a Jew. But one confession is of sin, another of praise. You perhaps find in yourself only evils, and are ashamed to confess them; [Col. 0828B] the other embraces certain good things and, recognizing them as God’s gift, gives thanks. Both are Jews and little children by humble confession; but you are a one-year-old, the other a two-year-old. Those who confess to the Lord because of sins arrive at the first year; those who confess because of gifts attain the second. Thus confession of sin makes one-year-olds; confession of praise, two-year-olds.

Herod, then, loves Jews who are great and swollen—not ready to praise God, but to stone Stephen—who have passed beyond not only the first but also the second year of devout or humble confession. He persecutes even to death, from two years old and under, the little children whom Christ loves, and the child himself: namely, the very truth of the purified heart. Herod persecutes the child when, after understanding of truth has been received, [Col. 0828C] the mind is attacked by the spirit of arrogance. For many, when they receive understanding of truth, seek things higher than themselves and abandon themselves. Now they dispute concerning the mystery of the Incarnation and Trinity, now concerning heavenly secrets and the charisms of the Holy Spirit; and while they investigate matters above themselves, unaware of their own weakness, they forget that they are human beings.

Therefore, whoever wishes to escape this Herodian impiety should obey the angel’s counsel: “Take,” he says, “the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt.” Egypt is interpreted “darkness.” Therefore, when we are attacked by the spirit of pride, we are commanded to go to consider our own darkness. The child is sometimes in Egypt, sometimes found in Judaea. He is in Egypt when he teaches me how great my darkness is, instructing [Col. 0828D] me to know true things concerning myself; he is in Judaea when he shows me the brightness of his wisdom, teaching me true things concerning God. In Egypt he gives knowledge of myself; in Judaea, knowledge of God, because “God is known in Judaea” (Ps. 75).

“Take the child and his mother”; flee with both. If you do not escape Herod, the child is killed, because if you do not turn aside from pride, the light of truth is extinguished. If you do not proceed with both, you will not be within. If you recall former errors and past pleasures, you have indeed come into Egypt and remain there, occupied in considering your darkness; but because you came there without purity, you are snatched away into shameful delight; and because truth is not with you, you quickly fall into error.

[Col. 0829A] If, through desire, you look back toward the former paths of pleasure, you proceed without the Virgin Mother. If you excuse your evils or pretend that they are not evils, you remain in Egypt without the child. Flee, therefore, and remain there with both until I tell you. Do not return before the time, but do not remain longer than is enough. For if you attend too much to your evils, you quickly cast yourself into the pit of despair; if before the time or beyond measure you trust in God’s mercy, you nevertheless raise yourself into presumption.

Therefore, when from excessive consideration of your darkness, as from too long a stay in Egypt, you are drawn into despair and swallowed by sadness, you follow the counsel of Satan’s angel. If you do the same from dwelling in Judaea, you will be carried away through empty joy into vain glory and hope. [Col. 0829B] If, therefore, you are discerning, do not merely flee, but “remain there until I tell you,” as the Angel of great counsel says. Thus Joseph rose and fled into Egypt with mother and child, and remained there until Herod’s death, until it was said to him: “Return to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child’s life have died,” etc.

Observe that he fled by night. Night, because of darkness, can sometimes signify ignorance; at other times, because of cold, sadness. Therefore he journeys to Egypt by night who looks back upon the paths of his former error with grave sorrow. Whoever views the darkness of his conscience with cheerfulness returns to Egypt in broad daylight. O how great the shamelessness: to have sins before one’s eyes and not groan; to behold shameful things and not be ashamed; [Col. 0829C] to see things that should grieve and not grieve at all! He was indeed preparing to go by night who said: “I shall recall my years in the bitterness of my soul” (Isa. 38). Whoever recalls the years of his past life in the pleasure of his soul recalls them for himself, O Lord, not for you.

Recall your years to him in the bitterness of your soul, not in sweetness, so that you may flee by night into Egypt: that God’s goodness may become sweeter to you in proportion as your iniquity becomes more bitter to you; and that, as injustice displeases you more, God’s mercy may please you more. For it is useful to flee to Egypt and look upon the darkness of our weakness, lest the mind become swollen. But perhaps you will say: “The darkness will trample me down if I go into Egypt.” Therefore hear: “Night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. 18). Therefore, only let the child [Col. 0829D] Jesus and his mother be with you, and you will be able confidently and truly to say there: “If I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils” (Ps. 137), because the child Jesus and the Virgin Mother—purity of heart and understanding of truth—are with me; indeed, “night has become my illumination in my delights.”

O good Jesus! What and how great are the divine mercies, when night is turned into day, darkness into light, bitterness into joy, ignorance into knowledge! Joseph also fled into Egypt and remained there until Herod’s death. Herod’s death is the failure of arrogance. If you go into Egypt and remain there, when you acknowledge the darkness of your weakness, all arrogance certainly fails. Once Herod has died, it is time to return to the land of Israel. Israel is interpreted “a man seeing God.” [Col. 0830A] That person is Israel whose mind is raised in contemplation. “I am a man seeing my poverty” (Lam. 3). Until today, because I see nothing but darkness, I am in Egypt; but whoever through contemplation beholds the glory of God remains in the land of Israel. For if anyone speaks wisdom among the perfect, and confesses with the mouth what he contemplates in the heart, that person dwells in Judaea. Each person is in Egypt through consideration of self; in the land of Israel through contemplation of God; in Judaea through the edification of one’s neighbour.

## TITLE XXIX. On the diversity of sacraments

Some sacraments consist in things, such as water for sprinkling; others in acts, such as the sign of the cross, striking the breast, and extending the hands; others in words, such as responsories; others in jubilation and gesture, such as [the] sprinkling of water, after the example of Elisha casting salt into water so that bitter springs might be sweetened. Water signifies repentance for the past; salt, discernment concerning the future. Joined together, these two turn a bitter conscience into sweetness and drive away demonic illusions and assaults. The sign of the cross is the power of Christ’s Passion; striking the breast, the expulsion of evil thought; extending the hands signifies charity; the responsory, good action. Alleluia signifies present joy; jubilation, future joy.

## TITLE XXX. On the wounded person, his wounds, the physician and medicines, and works of mercy

A person lying in sins is sick; vices are wounds; God is the physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit are antidotes; [Col. 0830C] virtues are healths; beatitudes are joys. Vices are healed through the gifts of the Holy Spirit; the healthy person acts through virtues; the one who acts is rewarded with joys.

There are six works of mercy: feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, taking in the stranger, clothing the naked, visiting the sick, and coming to the imprisoned and confined; the seventh, as is read in Tobit (Tob. 1), is burying the dead.

## TITLE XXXI. On the two gates, either supremely good or evil

There are two gates: love and fear. When they are good, they accomplish every good. For through fear evils are avoided, and through love goods are practised. But when they are evil, they are the cause of all evils. For through fear an evil person is cut off from good, and through evil love, evil things are done. Therefore they are gates through which death and life enter: death, when they are opened to evil; life, when they are opened to good.

## TITLE XXXII. On the fourfold fear

There are four fears: servile, worldly, initial, and filial. The first abstains from evil in order to avoid punishment, while retaining an evil will; the second abstains from evil in order to avoid punishment, having acquired a good will; the third abstains from a wicked deed in order to avoid punishment, and cuts off wicked thoughts; the fourth clings firmly to the good, unwilling to lose it.

The first seeks to please people, fearing the punishment inflicted by people rather than the guilt of conscience. The second, not seeking to please people but nevertheless fearing to displease them, is as deceitful in denying truth [Col. 0831A] as the other is deceptive in concealing truth; both offend against truth. The third, because it wishes to avoid the punishment threatened by God, who looks upon the heart, fears to displease him. The fourth, wishing to please God, fears the good appointed for it—that is, does not wish to lose it.

## TITLE XXXIII. On threefold vice, threefold sin, and threefold remedy

Threefold vice, threefold sin, threefold remedy: weakness, ignorance, concupiscence. These three vices belong to the power of the inward person; when they entice consent, they pass into sins. Some of these we commit through weakness, others through error, others freely from a perverse will alone. But the threefold remedy is understood in divine ordinances, threats, and promises.

Hence: “Every head is sick, [Col. 0831B] and every heart is sorrowful. From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it” (Isa. 1): behold the evils inborn. “A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore,” etc.: behold the evils inflicted. The first are inward, the second outward. But to the accumulation of evils is added contempt for remedies. “It has not,” he says, “been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil,” etc. Behold how many evils oppress us.

Therefore learn, O human being: and if you disdain to learn from a human being, learn at least from him who teaches a human being knowledge—learn such great misery, namely that you ought to fear inward things and dread outward things, so that you may seek more ardently the physician’s remedies and love the bindings, namely divine ordinances; the treatments, threats; and the fomentations, promises.

“Every head is sick,” says the physician in the prophet, [Col. 0831C] etc. The head is free will. For as the head stands above the body, so free will presides over every occasion. Nothing is more worthy than this, because it approaches immutable eternity more closely than other things and bears its image within itself more expressly. For no fault or misery can—not merely destroy it, but not even diminish it. And just as it has no superior and cannot have one, so free will endures no dominion and cannot endure it: for it neither befits the Creator to inflict violence upon it, nor is it possible for a creature to do so. Though all hell, all the world, and the army of the heavenly host should conspire together as one, not one consent proceeding from free will can be extorted against its will in any matter.

[Col. 0831D] Thus this head is called sick in a human being because it is sluggish toward love of the good. The one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15), showed the sickness of the head. For what good can a person do from himself, when he cannot even say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12)? Nothing, therefore, is more sickly than that which cannot gain strength for any good whatever, even the least, because “it is not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of God who has mercy” (Rom. 9). “Who can resist his will?” Hence, just as the dignity of free choice—that it cannot be compelled by anyone—is admirable, so its weakness is pitiable: in itself it is sluggish toward every good work.

It follows: “Every heart is sorrowful,” etc. Counsel is drawn out from the heart’s hidden place, found in secrecy, and from it a good intention proceeds, because through counsel [Col. 0832A] our corrupted life is corrected. For death and life proceed from it. If a good intention is corrupted through counsel, what good is it to beget offspring of good works and kill it through a wicked intention? Some corrupt works in the very purpose through an evil intention; others, after exercises of virtue, fade from good intention through vain praise. The first cause abortions to be born; the second kill those already born or grown. Is it not better not to give birth than to crush one’s child in sleep, or kill it by one’s counsel? Better is the barren woman who does not bear than the merciless murderess of children.

For what are dry bones without a soul except strong works without good intention? These are frustrated of the merit and reward of virtues; but, with the son of man prophesying, the spirit entered into them, and they lived. [Col. 0832B] Therefore, because intention receives from counsel the quality of being good, the spirit proceeds, as it were, from the heart; going forth to give life to the body, it spreads itself through the works of virtue, so that the saying may be ours: “Counsel shall keep you, and prudence shall preserve you” (Prov. 2).

But this heart was placed in the darkness of ignorance: at one time in discerning quantity, calling a greater evil lesser, and conversely; at another in examining quality, calling evil good and conversely. It does not judge between night and night, so as to distinguish worse evils from evil and worst from worse; nor between day and day, so as to separate better goods from good and best from better; nor every night, so as to weigh each vice by a worthy examination; nor every [Col. 0832C] day, according to the Apostle, so as to assess each virtue according to its proper worth.

For these are the five talents impressed upon thought, from which five others must be gained if they are also impressed upon affection, so that what it knows it may double by loving effectively. Otherwise, “it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2). We must love eagerly what ought to be loved, and we must hate its opposites. Nor is it enough to have ascended this far, unless we ascend further: namely, that among evils we pursue worse things with greater hatred, and among goods embrace better things with higher love; and from the second stage to the third, that we choose the best among better things and most greatly despise the worst among inferior things.

[Col. 0832D] And because we can do these three things in love of goods and rejection of their opposites, let us make every effort not to maintain the contrary mode, but to ascend through the fourth and fifth, so that in every good or evil we preserve a fitting measure of hatred or love. Yet in all these matters the heart is sorrowful, and from sorrow grows dim. For sorrow pours forth tears, and tears make the eyes grow dim. Rightly, therefore, is the heart sorrowful, because the heart is dull for every counsel of reason. Truly it grieves, and it ought to grieve, because we love evil; and, while it receives counsel, it neither fails to know this nor conceals it. For the more clearly it knows through counsel the evil it suffers, the more it grieves and is angry with its own perversities, because “he who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1).

Therefore, if we have a heart and are not wholly devoid of counsel, we must not conceal so great an evil. [Col. 0833A] Our sorrow ought to press us more keenly within and appear outwardly: inwardly for remedy, outwardly for example. For sorrow is pain raging more sharply within and bursting outward into tears. Therefore, if we are not a deceived dove without a heart, if we are not without prudence and counsel, let us prove in action how truly we grieve in heart; let what we suffer inwardly appear outwardly.

It follows: “From the sole of the foot,” etc. The foot denotes carnal desire. For as the foot lies lowest and the whole body is carried about by the feet, so carnal desire clings to the lowest things, and the mind is agitated and carried about by carnal desires. For as long as a human being lives as a wanderer and fugitive upon earth, so long, pursuing his desires, he is filled with miseries and never remains in the same state, seeking to grasp what he desires and to escape what he hates. Now he loves this, now that; what he formerly loved he again despises and loathes.

But why do we say that he loathes it, when, as Scripture testifies, they “finish their course in bitterness”? “All rivers enter into the sea” (Eccl. 1): that is, every carnal delight comes to an end in bitterness. Every stream and all sweet water, when it enters the sea, is changed into bitter water, because grief takes possession of the end of joy, and “laughter shall be mingled with sorrow” (Prov. 14). “And the sea does not overflow” (Eccl. 1), because divine equity observes measure in every blow that it inflicts for vengeance or correction; it does not exceed the bounds of justice. It does not surpass the desert of our malice or the measure of our misery.

[Col. 0833B] Therefore from foot [Col. 0833C] to crown there is no health, and so the foot suffers together with the whole body, because the evil of concupiscence burns everywhere, and each member’s own weakness forcibly produces pain. What is weaker than being unable fully to resist those things of which we are ashamed? To consent in the mind to the law of God, and to be made captive and conquered in the law of God?

These, then, are the three vices: sickness of the head, sorrow of the heart, pain of the weak body. These defects arise in us from inward things. By sickness of the head we understand the weakness of free will toward good; by the infirmity of the body, the restlessness of desire toward evil; by sorrow of heart, the darkness and uncertainty of judgment for discerning both. In sickness: incapacity for good; in the vexation of weakness: concupiscence for evil; in the cloud of sorrow: [Col. 0833D] ignorance of good and evil.

According to this threefold kind of vice, there is a threefold kind of sin. Hence it follows: “A wound, a bruise, and a swelling sore.” For some sins we incur through weakness, some through error, others through iniquity. A wound is sin committed through weakness. For what is a wound opened outwardly without swelling, except manifest fault without pride, accompanied by humiliation and shame? We commit such things through weakness in a certain sense unwillingly; for we are ashamed of none more and condemn none more.

A bruise is the sin of ignorance. For just as a wound is covered over with skin and, lest pus flow out, is held back by the skin that covers it, so sins of ignorance, lest they come out into the open, conceal themselves beneath the shadow of their ambiguity; and, lest the rot of their corruption burst forth through the opening of confession, they cloak themselves in the covering of false opinion.

[Col. 0834A] A swelling sore is the sin of malice, because the swelling pride of contempt for God is committed neither through weakness nor through ignorance, but through evil will alone. These are the three sins against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Or by these three we may understand the dead person outside the house, in the house, and in the tomb—namely, sin in thought, action, and habit.

A wound turned into swelling is sin overlaid by habit; an open wound, sin made manifest through action; a bruise rotting under the skin, sin hidden in thought. Or, by the wound without swelling, [Col. 0834B] sin which we accuse and do not defend; by the bruise, that which we cover through hypocrisy; by the swelling sore, that which we defend through obstinacy.

Thus in three ways the wound of sin is opened, in three covered over, and in three inflated: it is opened in the manner of a wound, covered in the manner of a bruise, inflated in the manner of a swelling sore. But the wound of sin is evident in one way to a person in himself, another to his neighbour, another to God: to himself through knowledge, to his neighbour through action, to God through confession. For, so far as lies in us, we hide from God that sin which we are unwilling to condemn before him by confession.

Likewise it is hidden in three ways after the likeness of a bruise. It is covered with skin differently for ourselves, for God’s eyes, and for our neighbour: for ourselves through error; for God through silence; for our neighbour through pretence. [Col. 0834C] Likewise it swells in three ways when it is distended after the manner of a swelling sore: in itself it rots through malice; before its neighbour through imprudence; toward God it swells through obstinacy. Through malice a person destroys himself; through imprudence he destroys or kills his neighbour; through obstinacy he attacks God.

This threefold evil is met by a threefold remedy: by bandages, medicines, and fomentations, although each of these may seem capable of being referred to the three evils. They concern the swelling wound in the present passage, when it says “bound up, treated, and softened.” We understand the bandages as commandments, the medicines as threats, and the fomentations as promises. The bond of commandments is threefold.

[Col. 0834D] First we are drawn, second we are drawn back, third we are bound fast. The attracting bond consists in precepts, that is, in matters which ought to be done; by these we are often urged because we do not direct the steps of good works without difficulty. Such are: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. (Deut. VI). The restraining bond consists in prohibitions, that is, in matters which it is not permitted to do; yet by these we are often drawn back from the course into which desire hastens us. Such are: “You shall not kill,” etc. (ibid.). The constricting bond consists in admonitions, by which we bind the incontinence of our hearts when we restrain our wills even from lawful things. Such are: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell,” etc. (Matt. XIX).

There is a threefold kind of treatment in divine threats: a threat of correction, of reprobation, and of [Col. 0835A] condemnation. Of the first it is said: “He chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII). Of the second: “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. VII); and: “He hardens whom he wills” (Rom. IX); and: “I shall add your corrections sevenfold, because of your sins” (Lev. XXVI); and: “I shall break the pride of your hardness” (ibid.). Of the third he will say to those at the left: “Go into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV); “Their worm shall not die,” etc. (Isa. LXVI). This is a bitter juice of herbs, but most effective for drying up the humours of vices. Excessively unrestrained is the person who does not strive to moderate or curb his desires, even though he observes that among the elect evils are punished sevenfold; that others are given over to a reprobate mind because of their sins; and that some are assigned to eternal punishment.

There are three kinds of oil in divine promises. The first promise is of [Col. 0835B] forgiveness, the second of grace, the third of glory. For the merciful and compassionate Lord will grant not forgiveness of sins alone, nor grace alone, but glory also. To the first belongs: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isa. I). To the second belongs: “There are diversities of graces” (I Cor. XII). To the third: “One is the glory of heavenly bodies, another that of earthly bodies,” etc. (I Cor. XV).

The first more healthfully softens wounds to be healed by serving for anointing. The second burns more brightly for preparing lamps, in the service of light. The third tastes sweeter for seasoning food, in the service of refreshment, because it is the oil of gladness, a participation in glory. These kinds of oil are remedies against a threefold sorrow. If you grieve from the wound of sin, and the consciousness of sins presses you too bitterly, receive the anointing of promised [Col. 0835C] forgiveness, and take consolation from that utterance: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live” (Ezek. XVIII). “Turn from your most evil ways” (Ezek. XXXIII). And: “Why will you die, house of Israel?” (Ezek. XVIII). What bitterness of contrition and repentance is so dreadful that the infusion of this divine anointing cannot soften it?

If you grieve because of your weakness and deficiency, anoint yourself with the oil of promised grace, and receive from him who “gives to all abundantly and reproaches no one” (Jas. I). “If,” he says, “you know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” etc. (Luke XI). Pour this into empty vessels at the command, because it does not know how to fail unless empty vessels that could [Col. 0835D] be filled are lacking.

If you grieve over tribulations, you have the oil of glory, by which you may lighten weariness and moderate pain, from that precious perfumer who says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come,” etc. (Rom. VIII). The Samaritan poured in the first anointing for the man who fell among robbers, and by it that sinful woman healed her wounds. The second was received by him who said: “By the grace of God I am what I am,” etc. (I Cor. XIII). This grace ought not to be empty: he taught this both by example and by word. By example: “His grace in me was not empty” (ibid.). By word: “See to it,” he says, “that you do not receive the grace of God in vain” (II Cor. VI). The third kind is possessed abundantly by the prudent virgins, entering into the joy of their Lord and reclining at the wedding feast of the Lamb (Matt. XXV).

Therefore we have three kinds of oil, useful and necessary:

[Col. 0836A] The first, against the threefold affliction of a wound, a bruise, and a swelling wound; the second, against the threefold pain of a sorrowful heart, an enfeebled head, and a sick body; the third, against the threefold weariness even of a healthy body—namely, that of labour, want, and persecution. You have the oil of divine mercy, with which to soothe the wounds of sins; the oil of grace, with which to moderate the diseases of vices; the oil of glory, with which to ease the weariness of struggles. The first, therefore, is for healing the wounds of sins; the second for treating the diseases of vices; the third for relieving the pains of weariness.

For the healing of sins we have the oil of mercy: that prophetic preparation, made from the first kind of oil: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven” (Ps. XXXI). It is that wondrous ointment [Col. 0836B] which not only makes the sick person well, but even makes the wretched person blessed. Against the diseases of vices receive another preparation from the oil of grace: “Blessed is the man whose helper is God” (Ps. LXXXIII); and: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord” (Ps. XLIII); and: “Blessed is he who trusts in the Lord,” etc. (Ps. II). Blessed, I say, is the one whom the Lord helps, instructs, and protects: he helps toward good, defends against evil, and instructs for discerning both. To help, to instruct, and to defend are wholly the work of grace.

The first is therefore against lack of strength, the second against lack of truth, the third against lack of virtue: all against a deficiency in natural good. The first is against the weakness of an enfeebled head; the second against the darkness of a grieving heart; the third against the anxious weakness of a sick body.

[Col. 0836C] We have yet a third kind of oil, from the promise of grace, against the threefold weariness of a body now restored to health. Against the weariness of labour you have this: “You shall eat the labours of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Matt. V). Against the affliction of want, this: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Against the tribulation of persecution, this: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). Amid so many struggles of tribulation, who would not merely cease to grieve, but even rejoice, when, on Scripture’s testimony, he learns that concerning which he dares not hesitate: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been tested, [Col. 0836D] he shall receive the crown of life” (Jas. I)? This is why the apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were deemed worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus (Acts V). Therefore the third kind of oil makes a person rejoice amid tribulation [printed *gaudentis*, perhaps *gandentes*], when he hopes [printed *speret*, perhaps *sperent*] amid the struggle for that which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man,” etc. (Isa. LXIV; I Cor. II).

Let us therefore strive, each according to his own need and strength, to soothe our weaknesses by these means, lest we be charged by that sentence of divine rebuke: “A wound and a bruise and a swelling sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil,” etc. (Isa. I).

## TITLE XXXIV. On the justification of the publican

He returned to his house justified by three virtues: obedience, by which he called himself a servant; righteousness, which [Col. 0837A] mercy produces; and filial love, which God begets in himself. For he says three things: “Lord, have mercy [Vulgate: ‘God, be propitious’] to me, a sinner.” In crying “Lord,” he calls himself a servant; in loudly pleading “have mercy,” mercy makes him righteous; in accusing himself as a sinner, God begets a son from an ungodly man.

## TITLE XXXV. On the counsel of the ungodly in four respects

“Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly,” etc. (Ps. I). The counsel of the ungodly consists in four things: malice, cunning, audacity, and imprudence. Malice directs in thought; cunning arranges in deliberation; audacity carries evil through in action; imprudence leads to repetition through habit. These lead the sinner to burial. But [Col. 0837B] if Jesus touches the bier of mortal sin through mercy, the bearers stand still.

## TITLE XXXVI. On the counsel of the godly, etc.

The counsel of the godly consists in four things: innocence, which removes the foul smell of vices; foresight, which endows one with the fragrance of virtues close at hand; constancy, which confirms one by the honour of virtues received; reverence, which adorns one with the beauty of recompense.

## TITLE XXXVII. On the three kinds of greetings in the Gospel

We find three kinds of greetings in the Gospel: the angel greeted the Virgin; the Virgin greeted Elizabeth; the Lord, after the resurrection, greeted the disciples. When we see those who have grown old in barrenness, ascending the mountains of religious profession, conceive, by ascending the heights of religious profession, the fervour of repentance as though a son, we ought to offer them the grace of remission in the word of God and in the voice of greeting. [Col. 0837C] Those whom we see serving God in holiness and chastity, we must encourage toward better things, permitting the fruitfulness of blessing. To those whom we observe, sound and placed in the inner chamber of a more secluded life, striving toward the height of apostolic imitation, we pledge through the ministry of speech the firmness of a twofold peace, when they also perceive within their own body certain preliminaries of it. But in the same Gospel we are forbidden to greet others who are set on the way of the world, because those who cling to the world deserve no salvation.

## TITLE XXXVIII. On four things that increase the grace of devotion and religion

[Col. 0837D] There are four things which increase the grace of our devotion: remembrance of sins, which makes a person humble in his own eyes; recollection of sin, which makes him diligent in doing good; consideration of pilgrimage, which urges him to despise visible things; and desire for everlasting life, which, inviting a person to perfection, compels him to suspend the pursuit of pleasure together with earthly affections.

## TITLE XXXIX. On the three ways in which the Lord instructs us

The Lord instructs us in three ways: by the abundance of a granted benefit, which softens hardness of mind and awakens it to love; by the severity of an inflicted loss and of a word, which, providing understanding to hearing, instils fear in us; and by the public usefulness of contempt, which, filling our faces with disgrace, produces in us shame, so that we may seek God and his name: [Col. 0838A] “Whose Egyptian servant is this?”—the one whom David found abandoned by an Amalekite when exhausted and restored with food (I Kings XXXIX).

## TITLE XL. On three things forbidden to us and three permitted to us

Three things are forbidden to us: evil thinking, evil speaking, and evil doing. For in evil thinking there is either uncleanness, when foul matters are turned over in the mind; or pride, when the mind raises itself above its neighbour; or ambition, when wealth or honour is unlawfully desired. In the evil thought of those who always wish to speak ill, speech must necessarily be either superfluous, lacking reason and usefulness; or slanderous, diminishing heavenly goods with envious and hateful corrosion; or flattering, soothing another’s head with the false anointing of oil.

[Col. 0838B] In evil doing, a work is either deceptive, when we intend one thing and display another; or impious, when we injure our neighbours; or shameless, when we defile ourselves. Conversely, the same distinctions may be observed in thinking well, speaking well, and doing well. The offering of our praise ought to be threefold: affectionate, so that the mind agrees with the voice; fruitful, so that it produces edification in the beholder; gracious, so that it pleases the Creator, who gave freely.

## TITLE XLI. Three necessities of repentance

Three things are necessary to repentance: abstinence, by which the pride of the flesh is subdued; reading, by whose fruit the mind, needing renewal in strength, is nourished; prayer, by whose protection the virtues are guarded within the soul.

## TITLE XLII. On the three respects in which we are bound to God

[Col. 0838C]

There are three respects in which we are bound to God: the seal of nature, by which we were made in God’s likeness; the talent of faith, which we must return intact to God through good work; and the title given through confession, by which we are bound to serve God with the bonds of a pledge.
