## TITLE XLIII. On the threefold way to death

The ways to death are divided in a threefold manner. One is miserable for the poor, who, swelling in spirit like the rich, are transferred from temporal poverty to an eternal state [the object is omitted in the source]; another is laborious for those in bitter circumstances, who, constrained by the straits of diverse cares, forget God and thus are carried from these straits into eternal ones; the third is delightful [Col. 0838D] for the rich, who after momentary sweetness find everlasting bitterness.

## TITLE XLIV. On the threefold narrow way

The narrow way which leads to life is threefold: blood-red in martyrs, who, washing their bodies in the blood of the Lamb, attain the throne on high; purple in confessors, who by abstinence have imprinted upon their own cross the footprints of manifold suffering; milky-white in virgins, who consecrating in themselves the whiteness of angelic purity fly thence to the embrace of the bridegroom through virtues.

## TITLE XLV. On the three respects in which we ought to imitate Christ

There are three things exemplified for us in Christ which we Christians, so called from Christ, ought to practise: reject the vanity [Col. 0839A] of the world, because Jesus too fled from the crowds lest he be made king; practise patience, because he too was slain as a lamb; possess twofold love, because Christ prayed even for his enemies.

## TITLE XLVI. That the ungodly are called sons in four ways

The ungodly are called sons in four ways: sons of strangers, of Belial, of iniquity, and of malice. Sons of strangers are those who lie; sons of Belial are those who do not know God; sons of iniquity are a brood of vipers; sons of malice are Canaan, and not Judah.

## TITLE XLVII. On the threefold good of tribulation

Tribulation confers three things: exercise, lest love of virtue grow cold through the lukewarmness of idleness; testing, so that the strength of our constancy may become known to people as an example; and reward, so that according to tribulation it may receive an immense [Col. 0839B] weight of glory.

## TITLE XLVIII. On the threefold exercise of the elect

The exercise of the elect is threefold: the austerity of fasts, by which the ground is cultivated so that it may bear fruit; assiduity in reading, by which it is refreshed so that it may grow rich; and persistence in prayer, by which the mind is strengthened so that it may rise more vigorously toward the desire for heavenly things.

## TITLE XLIX. On the three rulers within us

There are three rulers within us who must die within us so that Christ may live: worldly prudence, which is Joseph; spiritual eloquence, which is Moses; and abundance of temporal things, which is Joshua.

## TITLE L. On the three cups offered by the Lord

There are three cups which the Lord offers us: that of repentance and sorrow, which is full of *misto* [perhaps *musto*, “new wine”]; [Col. 0839C] that of repentance and labour, which John drank; and that of goodwill and love, which is intoxicating and splendid.

## TITLE LI. On the three garments of the elect

There are three garments common to God’s elect: heavenly wisdom, which is the ephod and covers the head; persevering righteousness, which is the *poderis* [a long priestly robe] and clothes the whole body; and bodily continence, which girds the loins.

## TITLE LII. On the three maidens who pervert the mind

There are three maidens who pervert our mind: tenderness of the flesh, which is Samson’s Delilah; the eye of curiosity for worldly glory, which is Jezebel and killed Naboth; and distrust of the life to come, which is Herod’s daughter and takes John’s head away on a [Col. 0839D] dish.

## TITLE LIII. On the fourfold office of priests

The priest’s office is fourfold: to sacrifice the living victim of his own flesh, which is the Levitical office; to offer to God the gift of virtues, which is to burn spices and belongs to the sons of Aaron; to enter heaven with the fervour of martyrdom, which is to enter the holy of holies; and to convey to heaven the vows of grace and prayers, which is to offer bread and wine to God.

## TITLE LIV. On the three kinds of people for whom the sea of this age is passable

This great sea, namely the present age, is passable for three kinds of people, so that they may cross and be delivered. These are said to be Noah, Daniel, and Job. In Noah, who governed the ark so that it should not perish in the flood, I understand the image of rulers; in Daniel, the man of desires, abstinence and chastity, devoted solely to God, I understand the order of penitents and continent persons; in Job, wisely dispensing the substance of this world in a feast, I understand the faithful people possessing earthly goods in faith.

[Col. 0840A] The first crosses by ship, the second by bridge, the third by a ford. The order of married persons crosses the great sea by a ford, having a laborious, perilous, and long journey, especially in these days, when wickedness has exceedingly increased [printed *involvit*, perhaps *invaluit*], amid the waves of this age, the whirlpools of vices, and the pits of crimes, to be avoided. The order of continent persons crosses by a bridge. This way is shorter and easier, but not altogether safe. For a threefold danger must be feared: perhaps someone may wish to make himself equal to another, or look back, or indeed stand in the middle of the bridge. The narrowness of the bridge suffers no straitening from any of these three difficulties; for “narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII).

[Col. 0840B] Against the first danger let us pray that the foot of pride may not come upon us, because there fell those who hate iniquity. For the sea at once covers the head of one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back. But one who wishes to stand still—not indeed abandoning his order, but failing to advance—must fall, thrust down and overturned by those who follow. For it is necessary to do one of two things: either progress or decline. Yet on this narrow path of the bridge one must have confidence, for it is made of timbers, so that the feet of those who rest upon them may not slip. These timbers are bodily punishment, poverty in worldly life, and the humility of obedience. For “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV); and: “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil” (I Tim. VI). And the person whom disobedience drove so far from his straight path returned through obedience.

[Col. 0840C] Once these are rightly arranged, you have avoided the sea’s three dangers: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. Prelates, however, “go down to the sea in ships, doing business in great waters” (Ps. CVI). They are not confined to the fixed path of bridge or ford, so that they may freely go about and come to the aid of each; and, as is necessary, direct those walking in orderly fashion along the path of bridge and ford, investigating and avoiding dangers. “They rise up to the heavens and descend to the abysses” (ibid.), now handling sublime matters and judging dreadful places.

[Col. 0840D] But what ship can be found that can endure such enormous waves without danger? This is “love, strong as death” (Cant. VIII), because, as you have elsewhere: “Many waters cannot extinguish love” (ibid.). It is built of these three sides, so that, according to the Apostle, there may be “love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I): so that they may desire rather to benefit than to rule, having a good intention; so that, being made an example to the flock, they may begin to do and teach; and so that, following the rule that teaches, whatever they have taught their disciples to be contrary to the word, they may show by their deeds not to be done—lest a subject murmur and say: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke IV). Thus they may confidently answer those who reproach them: “Which of you shall convict me of sin?” (John [Col. 0841A] VIII)—if not of a venial sin, at least of a grave one.

They must also have unfeigned faith, so that a prelate may be inwardly in secret thought what he is outwardly in conduct: not humble outwardly but proud within, trusting in his own virtue or wisdom, which is counterfeit faith. To these three things Peter’s threefold question is suitably fitted: “Do you love me? Do you love me? Do you love me?” That is to say: Do you love me from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith?

## TITLE LV. On fivefold obedience

Obedience ought to be fivefold: right, so that it is not contrary to God; voluntary, because God does not approve compelled service; pure, because the intention ought to be sincere: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke XI); discerning, so that there is no excess—for he who offers rightly but does not divide rightly sins; [Col. 0841B] and steadfast, so that it does not cease: “He who perseveres shall be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

## TITLE LVI. On the threefold good indicated to us by the Prophet

The good which every prophet indicates is threefold: to do judgment and righteousness, and to walk uprightly with the Lord. To do righteousness is to render to each what is his own: obedience to superiors, instruction to inferiors, gladness to friends, patience to enemies. One must also exercise judgment: one kind toward oneself, another toward one’s neighbour, another toward God.

Toward oneself it ought to be severe. “For if we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (I Cor. X). Toward one’s neighbour it should be merciful, so that whether you entreat mercifully or rebuke zealously, you do both in a spirit of gentleness. Toward God it should be pure and true. For a person considering himself ought to attend to God’s judgments in simplicity and purity of heart, saying in confession: “All God’s works are very good.”

[Col. 0841C] Let a person therefore be a strict judge toward himself through understanding of truth; merciful toward his neighbour through the affection of love; pure toward God through the consent of the will. But after a person has exercised judgment and righteousness, vigilance is necessary to him, lest he become slack through sluggishness or fall through [uncertain: *clationem*], so that he may walk diligently with his God, subject to him and praying to him.

## TITLE LVII. On the threefold state of souls

The state of holy souls is threefold. The first is in the corruptible body, the second without the body, the third in the body now glorified. The first is in warfare, [Col. 0841D] the second in rest, the third in blessedness. The first is in tents, the second in courts, the third in the house of God. “How beloved are your tents, O Lord of hosts” (Ps. LXXXIII). Much more desirable are the courts, according to the saying: “One day in your courts is better than thousands” (ibid.). “My soul longs for and fails in longing for the courts of the Lord” (ibid.). But because even in those courts there is some deficiency: “Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord; they shall praise you for ages of ages” (ibid.). “I was glad,” he says elsewhere, “at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI).

In the first state the Church is not without spot and wrinkle. “For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (II John I). In the second it is without spot. “They are without spot,” he says, [Col. 0842A] “before the throne of God” (Apoc. XIV). Yet it is not without wrinkle. For their longing for the house of God, in which they are to be clothed with double garments, is so fixed within them that their direct intention does not yet tend toward God; rather, it is in some way drawn back and makes a wrinkle as they cry, bowed down with desire: “Avenge, O Lord, the blood of your servants that has been shed” (Apoc. XIX). This is not because they desire vengeance, but because they desire resurrection, which must be deferred until the day of judgment. But in the third state the Lord presents the Church without spot and without wrinkle (Eph. V).

The person who works righteousness dwells in the tent; the person who enters without spot enters into the court. Hence, when the Prophet asks, “Lord, who shall dwell in your tent, or who shall rest on your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIX), the answer is: “He who enters without spot and works [Col. 0842B] righteousness” (ibid.). It is as though he said: He who works righteousness and enters without spot shall rest upon your holy mountain. Therefore, in the dwelling there is always some spot of oldness and some wrinkle of necessity. In the court the spot of sin is removed, while, as has been said, some wrinkle of constraint remains, while they receive only single robes and are not clothed with double garments until they receive their bodies and the number of their brethren is completed, so that we too may be clothed together, as the Apostle says concerning the patriarchs: “God having provided something better for us, that they should not be made perfect without us” (Heb. XI). In the house both spot and wrinkle are utterly removed, when heaven is stretched out and expanded like a skin (Ps. CIII), so that not even the least spot or wrinkle may be found in them.

We shall serve God in three ways: seeing [Col. 0842C] him in all creatures, possessing him in ourselves, and knowing him in himself as Three and One, while beholding glory without an enigma with the eye of a purified heart. Hence: “They shall give into your bosom a measure full, pressed down, and overflowing” (Luke VI): full in the totality of creatures, pressed down in the inward self, overflowing in God himself. How he comes to be seen in creatures and possessed in ourselves we can know, at least in part. For that wondrous knowledge has been made strong, and we cannot attain to it.

## TITLE LVIII. On the threefold hearer of the heavenly word

We read of three hearers of the heavenly word: the slothful, the active, and the contemplative. The slothful hear and despise what they have heard. [Col. 0842D] The active hear and obey what they have heard. The contemplative hear and fall asleep in an embrace. The slothful are idle, the active labour, the contemplative rest. Of the slothful it is written: “He hides his hands beneath his armpit” (Prov. XIX); of the active: “You shall eat the labours of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII); of the contemplative: “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I shall fly and be at rest” (Ps. LIV).

The slothful are weak, the active strong, the contemplative disengaged. The weakness of the slothful is threefold: they are blind in their eyes, contracted in their hands, and lame in their feet. Blind, because they see and do not understand; contracted, because they gather and do not distribute; lame, because, turning aside to the innermost wantonness of error, they do not take hold of the straight path of salvation. The slothful are idle toward God, not toward [Col. 0843A] the world, for by many labours they heap up worldly riches for themselves. The active are idle neither toward God nor toward the world, for they heap up for themselves the riches of heaven and the blessedness of God. The contemplative are idle, not toward God, to whom they devote themselves, but toward the world, which they despise.

## TITLE LIX. On the threefold life of man

Human life is spoken of in three ways: the life of nature, by which a human being lives; the life of grace, by which Christ lives in the human heart; and the life of sin, by which sin lives in a person. Two are from God; the third is from man. David speaks of them all: “O God, I have declared my life to you” (Ps. LV). For he declares to God even the lives of nature and grace, while confessing that he possesses them from God; and he declares the third, that of sin, while confessing it with the Apostle, so that he may not lie.

The life of grace is above [Col. 0843B] the earth, the life of nature is on the earth, the life of fault beneath the earth. Of the first the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). Of the second, Job: “Man is born for labour” (Job V). Of the third, the Lord: “He who does evil hates the light” (John III). And John: “He who hates his brother is in darkness” (John II).

## TITLE LX. On the three dwellings of human beings

There are three dwellings: heavenly, earthly, and infernal. To creatures set in the middle, the good Creator gives a choice, so that they may choose what they will and acquire by merits what they choose. The dwelling in which we are set in the middle has heaven above and hell below. The dwelling of hell is harder and harsher than can be expressed. There is the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched. There the wretched person finds no respite amid miseries, [Col. 0843C] because the human being has neither heart nor understanding by which he can express the boundless calamities of evils and pains.

But in the dwelling of heaven Wisdom sets a table: bread of life and understanding. She mixes wine that gladdens the human heart, so that they may drink in delight and be intoxicated by the abundance of the house, so that they may hunger and thirst no more, when the Lord, passing by, shall minister to them and reveal himself to them. Therefore, brothers, since we are placed in the earthly dwelling between these dwellings, let us raise ourselves upward toward the heavenly one. For blessed is he who is called to the supper of the Lamb (Apoc. XIX). “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XIV). And because we who are placed here have been called to this, let us possess that blessedness as an inheritance.

Let us hasten to enter [Col. 0843D] into that rest. But because nothing stained and unclean shall enter it, let all our effort concern our purification, so that, purified, we may deserve to be presented with the Son of the Virgin in that lofty temple not made by hands and to stand before the Lord. The Mother of the Lord observed days of purification though she had no need of them; the Lord was circumcised, though in him there was no sin. Let us, stained and ugly, observe days of purification; let us cleanse our consciences, purify our mouths, and assign the time that remains to purification. For our souls to be cleansed and washed, the fountain of divine compassion stands open in the washing of the breast and of the menstruating woman.

## TITLE LXI. On the threefold virginity

Virginity is threefold: the first is in the flesh while the mind [Col. 0844A] is corrupt; the second is in the mind, though the chastity of the flesh has been violated; the third is in mind and body. The first is a handmaid, the second a young woman, the third a bride. The first is foolish: prostituted in mind, she lives chastely in the flesh from fear or human praise. The second is prudent: after losing the virginity of the flesh, she prudently regains the virginity of the mind, subjecting herself in all things to the divine commandments. The third is faithful: she incurs no corruption of flesh or mind, but remains faithfully in the love of the bridegroom. The first is condemned, the second rewarded, the third crowned. Of the latter the bridegroom says in a most sweet voice: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no spot in you” (Cant. IV).

## TITLE LXII. On the three things received by the betrothed woman

The betrothed woman receives three things: a necklace on her breast, a ring [Col. 0844B] on her finger, and a dowry by hereditary right. By the necklace the breast is guarded, by the ring the hand is adorned, and by the dowry the marriage is consummated. In the breast is reason, with which thought is occupied; in the hand, action; in the dowry, the reward of both.

By the necklace, fashioned laboriously out of gold and gems, understand heavenly wisdom, illuminated by diverse disciplines. For, as Scripture says, “Wisdom is from above” (Jas. III): first indeed chaste, then peaceable, modest, persuasive, consenting to good things. This is acquired with difficulty, because it is poured only into minds disciplined in learning. “For wisdom shall not enter into a malevolent soul” (Wis. I). Therefore, once acquired, it guards the breast lest the secrets of the bosom be opened; lest the tender breasts of the bride be harmed by the blowing breeze of flattery; lest a suggestion be admitted by which [Col. 0844C] reason is darkened and chaste thought prostituted. Rather, being wholly intact and guarded on every side by the seal of wisdom, she is made worthy of the bridegroom’s praise when he says: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine” (Cant. IV).

By the ring, without which no woman is betrothed, is received the pledge of the Holy Spirit, without whom no one is joined to the embraces of the heavenly bridegroom. He adorns and loves every action signified by the hands, so that she may say: “My hands have dripped most choice myrrh; my fingers are full of myrrh” (Cant. V). Adorned with such great ornaments and endowed with gifts, she is made worthy of the heavenly dowry, which is eternal recompense. In the hope and love of this, the faithful soul is betrothed to the spiritual man of whom it is said: “The man—Rising is his name” (Zech. VI).

## TITLE LXIII. On the three bearers of Christ

Three principal bearers of Jesus are read of: blessed Mary, conceiving him in her womb; Simeon, offering him in his arms; and Joseph, carrying him on his shoulders. They signify three orders of the elect: Mary, preachers; Simeon, good workers; Joseph, defenders of the faith. For those who preach the word of God carry Christ as it were in the womb, in order that they may give birth with others or give birth to others. Hence Paul says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV). But the person who gives bread to the hungry and does the other works of mercy is rightly seen to carry Christ in his arms, to whom Christ will say at the judgment: “What you did to one of the least of these, you did to me” (Matt. XXV). And those who are [Col. 0845A] wearied by labours for Christ, who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, are said to carry Jesus on their shoulders; hence: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX).

## TITLE LXIV. Three things necessary for a preacher

Three things are commonly required in a preacher: holiness of conduct, perfection of knowledge, and graceful eloquence, so that his speech may be holy, prudent, and brilliant. Holiness is necessary because, when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching is held in contempt. “Why,” says the Lord, “do you recount my righteousnesses and take my covenant into your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX). Perfection of knowledge is necessary, so that he may have from his treasury the means of bringing forth new things and old. Eloquence is necessary, so that through knowledge he may have what to say, and through eloquence how to say it: so that elegance of speech may correspond to excellence of thought, and the dignity of words to the majesty of things; and so that things and words may come together as in a kind of harmony, that his speech may thus be worthy in a threefold—and therefore every—respect. Hence: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance” (I Tim. I).

## TITLE LXV. On the three things harmed by luxury

Luxury does harm through three things: the brightness of the skin, the beauty of clothing, and the refined flavour of foods.

## TITLE LXVI. On the three elements of confession

Confession consists in three things: frequent groans, many sobs, and streaming tears. Let groans be in the breast, sobs in the throat, and tears on the face.

## TITLE LXVII. On the three elements of contrition
[Col. 0845C] Contrition of heart is brought about by three things: shame, fear, and sorrow. By shame, because one has acted disgracefully; by sorrow, because one has offended God; by fear, because it will not go unpunished. First one is ashamed of having sinned; second, one grieves at having offended; third, one fears.

### TIT. LXVIII. On the three silences before grace.

Three silences preceded grace. The first was blind and deaf; the second deaf; the third mute. The first was before the Law, when man neither saw death by himself nor heard of it from another, and therefore sought no remedy. The second was under the Law, when he saw the disease through the Law, yet neither heard through the prophets nor demanded the remedy through grace. The third was in the prophets, when he both saw the disease and [Col. 0845D] heard through the prophets, but did not confess or ask for the remedy unto pardon.

In grace every silence departed; for, “while all things were holding the deepest silence” (Wisdom 18)—that is, while the final silence was in all things—and night, that is, the devil, or night amid the darkness of sins, was pursuing its mid-course, the almighty Word came (ibid.). In him, those who saw the disease heard also and had the remedy present. They began both to know inwardly the disease by knowledge, to hear with the love of the heart, and to entreat the physician by the confession of the mouth.

### TIT. LXIX. On three other silences.

Silence is threefold: of heart, mouth, and deed. A person is silent in heart who, never conceiving what ought to be said, never speaks inwardly in the heart. One is silent with the mouth who, although he conceives it, nevertheless restrains it outwardly in his mouth by the great force of silence. One is silent in deed who, although he conceives and utters it, nevertheless does not proceed to its effect.

He who is silent by not conceiving wicked things in his heart is good. He who breaks silence within, though outwardly restraining his tongue, is evil. He who breaks it in heart and tongue is worse; he who breaks it in heart, tongue, and deed is worst. For such a one not only speaks without restraint what he has conceived without restraint, but acts with yet greater abandon. Of him it is said: “He who lets out water is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. 17). To let out water is to bring the flow of the tongue into action; and it is the beginning of quarrels because there the source of discord is furnished.

### TIT. LXX. On the four watches of our life.

The four watches of human life, as it were of a certain dark night, are four states. The first watch of the night [Col. 0846B] is in the enclosure of paradise; the second, after sin, under the law of nature; the third, under sin, under the Law of Moses; the fourth, in Christ’s Law under grace.

In all these the devil is opposed to man. In the first state the devil fights with man and overcomes him, because man has cast aside the weapons of virtue. In the second there is no battle, because man, subdued and conquered through despair, lies defeated, when the tinder of sin has joined the victor as a companion. In the third he expires in dying, because through the commandment of the Law death revived. But in the fourth watch of this night the Lord comes walking upon the sea; and for the man sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, light has arisen (Luke 1). And, crying with a loud voice in the person of Lazarus, he says to each one lying in death: “Come forth” (Matt. 11).

Thus man revived, and fights again with the devil [Col. 0846C] and conquers, because grace has been added to free will. In the first state he fights badly through negligence; in the second he resists through ignorance; in the third he is slain through pride; in the fourth he is raised, fights, and conquers through grace.

### TIT. LXXI. On the threefold fragrance of life.

The fragrance of life is threefold: not to sin, which servile fear accomplishes; not to wish to sin, which filial fear accomplishes; not to be able to sin, which everlasting glory bestows. The first are servants, the second sons, the third blessed persons.

### TIT. LXXII. On the three degrees of pride and humility.

There are three degrees of pride and three degrees of humility. [Col. 0846D] The first degree of pride is to think that what one has, one has from oneself; the second, when one boasts that he has received the good he possesses by his own merits; the third, when, scorning the rest, he desires to appear singular and thinks that he can have no equal.

The utterance of the first is: “Our lips are our own” (Ps. 2). Of the second: “I give thanks to you because I am not like other men” (Luke 18). Of the third: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14). This is the highest degree, by which the first man refused to be subject to God, believing the serpent’s words: “You shall be like gods.” This highest degree of pride had to be healed by the highest degree of humility.

For the first degree is to be subject to one’s superior, and this is sufficient; the second, to submit oneself to one’s equal and companion, and this is abundant; the third, to submit oneself to one’s inferior, and this is [Col. 0847A] complete and superabundant. Concerning this Christ says to John: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all righteousness” (Matt. 3), that is, superabundant humility. The first is attained humbly, the second more humbly, the third most humbly.

By this higher kind of humility, God, who is above all things, becoming man among all things, healed the highest degree of human pride, so that the medicine of healing might increase in proportion to the sickness of the disease. Blush, therefore, O man, you who will not consent to be placed beneath one greater than yourself, when God, greater than all, did not disdain, for your sake, to be subjected to one inferior to himself. O pride worthy of condemnation! The Creator is subjected to his creature, while the creature is proud against its Creator.

But because everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled in Gehenna, “humble yourself, O man, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Pet. 5), that he may exalt you in [Col. 0847B] the time of that tribulation where there shall be fire that is not quenched and a worm that does not die, through him who grants it, who lives and reigns, etc.

### TIT. LXXIII. On the three girdles.

There are three girdles that bind and restrain us: remembrance of death, the beauty of chastity, and religious love. The first is the leathern girdle with which John was girded; the second, the belt with which Aaron approached God; the third, the golden girdle with which one like the Son of Man, clothed in a long robe, is girded at the breasts in the Apocalypse. By the first girdle are girded hermits pursuing austerity; by the second, priests pursuing chastity; by the third, angelic citizens intent upon charity. Hence the girdle is called golden.

### TIT. LXXIV. On the three camps, etc.

[Col. 0847C] There are three camps: of preachers, of those who practice continence, and of married persons. The first fight against heretics; the second against themselves; the third against those things that the world gives, because they are preoccupied with worldly matters and are compelled to please one another.

### TIT. LXXV. On the twofold compunction.

There are two kinds of compunction: one arises from fear, the other from love. The first comes from fear of punishment; the second from love of reward. Hence in the tabernacle two altars are made: one outside, the other inside; thus in the court there is one, and another before the ark. One is overlaid with bronze, the other with gold. On the first flesh is burned; on the second incense.

The altars are hearts, in which either, through fear of sins, the fire of compunction burns [Col. 0847D] and the flesh is consumed by the burning of wicked action; or, through love of heavenly things, from the fire of charity the incense of prayer rises. For many, while fearing punishments, daily burn up their vices with tears in the fire of compunction. There are others who, free from sins, are inflamed by the flame of love into tears of compunction and long, together with their fellow-citizens, to see the king in his beauty.

The first altar is outside, so that good works may be seen and God glorified (Matt. 5); the second is within, before the ark, so that recompense may be awaited from him alone who sees inwardly. It should be noted that between this altar and the ark a veil intervenes. The ark is he in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. The veil is heaven. Therefore the ark within the veil is our Redeemer in heaven. But the altar is before the veil, [Col. 0848A] because the hearts of the elect, which burn with love through holy longing, cannot yet see with unveiled face that which they desire to see.

So long, therefore, as we are outside in the court of the people, let us burn upon the altar of compunction the flesh of vices through fear. If we are inside before the veil—that is, before we enter heaven—through loving compunction we ought to weep for nothing earthly. Let him alone who made all things suffice us; let us transcend all things through longing; and, kindled not so much by fear of punishments or remembrance of vices as by the flame of love, let us burn with tears amid the fragrance of virtues, like her who “ascends through longing like a little column of smoke from aromatics,” etc. (Song 3).

### TIT. LXXVI. On the three senses in which “man” is used.

Scripture calls a human being in three ways: by nature, as in “Let us make man” (Gen. 1); by guilt, as in “You shall die like men” (Ps. 81); by weakness, as in “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jer. 17).

### TIT. LXXVII. On the three senses of sleep.

Sleep is understood in Scripture in three ways: for death of the flesh. Hence the Apostle: “I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep” (1 Thess.). For sinful negligence. Hence the same Apostle: “It is now time for us to rise from sleep” (Rom. 13). And for rest and the desires of life. Jacob slept this sleep when he laid his head upon the stone (Gen. 28).

### TIT. LXXVIII. On the twofold regard of God.

God’s regard is twofold: here, through mercy, by which he looks upon penitents; in the future, through justice, [Col. 0848C] by which he will condemn the reprobate. Hence: “Your eyes are upon me, and I shall not remain” (Job 7). And because there is no regard of mercy there, he adds beforehand: “The sight of man shall not behold me” (ibid.), that is, the sight of Christ; and because no one returns thence hither for amendment, he likewise says beforehand: “My eye shall not return to see good things” (ibid.). Because one also swiftly passes hence to that place, saying, “Remember, Lord, that my life is wind” (Prov. 18), he prays here to be regarded through mercy.

But because God does not spare you if you spare yourself, hear what Job himself says: “I will not spare my mouth” (Job 7). A person spares his mouth when he is ashamed to confess evil. But the righteous person, who “at the beginning of his speech is his own accuser” (Prov. 18), does not spare his mouth, because, forestalling the word of the strict Judge, he assails himself with the word of his own confession; as the Psalmist says: “Let us go before his face in confession” (Ps. 94).

### TIT. LXXIX. On the four ways of sinning.

Sins are committed in four ways in the heart, and are completed in as many ways in deed. In the heart they occur by suggestion through the adversary; by delight through the flesh; by consent through the spirit; by the boldness of self-defence through pride, when guilt, which ought to terrify the mind, instead exalts it. By these four blows the ancient enemy shattered the uprightness of the first man. For the serpent suggested; Eve took delight; Adam consented; when asked where he was, he refused through boldness to confess his fault.

This happens daily in man. The devil, like a twisting and slippery serpent, suggests; the flesh, like Eve, delights; the spirit, set over it like Adam, [Col. 0849A] consents, bent away from its own uprightness by the flesh’s delight. Like Adam when questioned, it is made more wickedly hardened by the boldness of self-defence.

These four are completed in deed. First the hidden fault is committed; afterward it is openly displayed without shame before human eyes; it is brought into habit; finally it is nourished by false hope or miserable despair. Job laments these stages, saying: “Why did I not die in the womb? Why, when I came forth from the womb, did I not perish at once? Why was I received upon knees? Why nursed at breasts?” (Job 3). He would have died in the womb if he had recognized himself as dying at the very suggestion. So likewise concerning the rest.

Yet it must be known that the first three stages are easily corrected; the fourth never is. Hence the Lord raises the girl in the house (Luke 8), the young man [Col. 0849B] outside the gate (Luke 7), and Lazarus four days dead (John 11). The girl in the house is the sinner in secret; the young man carried out beyond the gate is the sinner whose guilt is made public; he is weighed down by the mound of burial who is heavily burdened by habitual practice. Nevertheless, the merciful Lord calls these back to life through penitence. But the fourth is announced by the Lord, not raised, because the sin of despair is forgiven neither in this world nor in the future (Luke 12); indeed, he who reports the dead person hears: “Leave the dead to bury their own dead” (Matt. 8).

### TIT. LXXX. On the threefold coming of God.

There are three comings of God: to human beings, into human beings, and against human beings. The first and the last are not as desirable as the middle one, by which the wisdom of God, coming into a human being, [Col. 0849C] makes its dwelling there, building a house and hewing out seven pillars, in order to make itself a seat (Prov. 9).

The house is the human being; the seat is the soul; the seven pillars are the furnishings of the seat. “Righteousness,” he says, “and judgment are the preparation of your seat” (Ps. 68). Righteousness is the virtue that gives each person what is his own: to the superior, to the inferior, and to the equal. To the superior: obedience and reverence, one of which belongs to the body, the other to the heart. To the equal: counsel, by which ignorance may be instructed, and assistance, by which weakness may be helped—not only in word and service, but also by example, by which one is provoked to better things, and prayer, by which one is helped by the Lord. To the inferior: guardianship, by which future sin can be guarded against, and discipline, by which committed sin is punished.

If, therefore, [Col. 0849D] you render devotion and obedience to a superior, counsel and help to an equal, and guardianship and discipline to an inferior subject—or to yourself, who have your body subject to you, so that sins may not reign in it and that it may produce fruits worthy of penitence—the Lord will come into you.

### TIT. LXXXI. Why the soul is Christ’s bride.

There are four reasons why the soul is called a bride: the gifts of graces by which she was given an earnest in baptism; chaste love, by which she was joined to him in the anointing with chrism; the offspring of virtues, by which she was made fruitful through the doctrine of the divine Word; and the restful marriage-bed, by which she is to be joined to him eternally, with every enigma far removed.

Of the earnest-money, one kind is common and another special. The common is fourfold: by it we are born, feel, sleep, and discern. The special likewise is fourfold: [Col. 0850A] by it, through preceding mercy, we shall reign; through following understanding, we have obtained forgiveness; through superabounding grace, we are adorned with virtues; through abiding steadfastness, we are blessed in certain hope.

### TIT. LXXXII. On the fivefold vice of gluttony.

The vice of gluttony is fivefold. Sometimes, in some persons, the time of need is anticipated; these are like Jonathan in tasting honey. Sometimes they do not anticipate the hour, but seek more lavish foods; these are like the Jewish people in the wilderness, who, despising manna, demanded meat. Sometimes they demand that whatever is to be eaten be prepared more carefully; these are like the sons of Eli, who extort not meat cooked in the customary way, but raw meat to be specially prepared. Sometimes they conform to quality and time, but exceed the measure. Hence it is said: “This was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and abundance” (Ezek. 16). Sometimes food is rejected, and sin is committed more grievously through the heat of desire; these are like Esau, who sold his birthright for a dish of lentils.

For the fault lies not in food but in appetite. Hence the one lost his primacy through a lentil dish, while Elijah preserved his bodily strength by eating meat; and the devil tempted the first man not with meat but with fruit (Gen. 3), and the second with bread (Matt. 4).

### TIT. LXXXIII. On the three vices of priests.

There are three vices through which priests frequently sin in different ways: greed, incontinence, and negligence. Those sin through greed who celebrate divine offices in order to obtain temporal advantages; in their [Col. 0850C] intention lies not love of God but temporal profit. To these the Lord says through Amos: “Therefore I have heard and rejected your feasts, and I will not receive the smell of your sacrifices” (Amos 5). For sacrifices cannot be fragrant and pleasing to God when a person performs them seeking not God’s honor but his own gain.

But if he says, “I serve God in this, although I obtain an advantage,” it is said to him: “No one can serve two masters,” etc. “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6). Such persons set Dagon beside the ark (1 Kings 12), when they intend to accumulate money through the divine offices that they perform. From such persons both Dagon shall be taken away and they themselves shall be struck in their hind parts, because both temporal things are withdrawn and they are punished with eternal penalty.

[Col. 0850D] How greatly the Apostle pursues the second vice, incontinence, with hatred is known from his teaching that “God shall destroy the violator of God’s temple” (1 Cor. 3). But these two vices occur because of the third, namely negligence, when priests are so negligent toward their subjects and themselves that they are not roused to guard Zion and to pasture the land of Assyria with the sword, as the Lord says through the prophet: “We shall raise up against him seven shepherds and eight principal men, and they shall pasture the land of Assyria with the sword” (Mic. 5).

By the seven shepherds and eight principal men are understood all prelates, who ought to be seven and eight, that is, instructed in the New and Old Testaments. “I shall raise up shepherds,” that is, guardians of souls by both Testaments, so that they may know how to bring forth from their treasure new things and [Col. 0851A] old. They must vigilantly guard Zion, that is, the Church, and manfully resist Assyria attacking the people of God, that is, the devil; for as Assyria once persecuted God’s people, so now each day the devil persecutes the Christian people.

And they must pasture the land of Assyria with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God: so that those subject to the devil through love of earthly things may be recalled from evil by the food of sacred teaching, as by a two-edged sword—on one side frightening them through fear of Gehenna, on the other stirring them through love of the heavenly homeland—recalled from evils by dread of punishments and to good by the sweetness of rewards.

Such, dearest brethren, we ought to be: prudent and exercised in the sacred Scriptures, roused and girded with the sword’s sharpness over the flock entrusted to us, so that, restraining greed for temporal things, [Col. 0851B] we may attend to heavenly things alone; preserving continence of the flesh, appearing pure in the sight of God and men; casting away negligence, we may diligently devote care to guarding not only other souls but our own, so that this may not be our utterance: “They made me guardian of vineyards; my vineyard, that is, my own house, I did not guard” (Song 1). May we receive rewards worthy of our labors, through the Lord who lives and reigns, etc.

### TIT. LXXXIV. On the three things in which salvation consists.

Eternal salvation consists in three things. First, to renounce the world and join oneself to God; second, to despise earthly things and seek eternal ones; third, to trample down vices and devote oneself to virtues. By this three-day period a three-year-old heifer, a ram, and a bull are offered as a burnt offering. [Col. 0851C] By this three-day period the Lord, through his mercy, has compassion on the company enduring in the wilderness. By this three-day period the Hebrew passes from vices to virtues, from light to darkness.

On the first day he leaves Pharaoh, joined to God; on the second, he leaves the servile works of mud and brick, desiring freedom; on the third, departing Egypt, he makes for the land of promise. Of the first it is said: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72); of the second: “Seek the things that are above” (Col. 3); of the third: “Bring my soul out of confinement” (Ps. 141).

### TIT. LXXXV. On the three kinds of injury to be endured.

Injury is inflicted on a human being in three ways: by a demon, by a neighbor, and by the flesh. The demon lies in wait for charity, the neighbor for possessions, the flesh for chastity. [Col. 0851D] Isaiah briefly portrayed this as follows: “There the hedgehog had its den and nourished its young; kites gather together; the lamia lay down and found rest for herself” (Isa. 34).

Babylon is the human being, the child of confusion, whom the pleasure of sin, the bitterness of punishment, and isolation of life confound. In him are the three evils of Babylon, three kinds of confusion. Now concerning each.

The hedgehog—sluggish, thorny, hidden beneath the covering of its skin—is the devil: sluggish in effect, lest anyone run to penitence; covered with thorns, lest he receive glory or grace; concealed by the hiding-place of perdition, lest he come to mercy. The hedgehog is sluggish because the devil has no power against a human being unless the human being freely enslaves himself to him. An ant resists a lion; against consenting ants, the lion prevails. Do you wish to see an ant? “Lord, send us into the pigs” (Mark 5). [Col. 0852A] Here he gives the Lord a sword so that he may kill. At the beginning he is easy to repel; if he gains strength by striking root, he is not uprooted unless Jesus cries with a loud voice.

Therefore, while the enemy is still little, beware lest wickedness rise up in the seed. But if the sluggish one is repelled, he puts forth thorns. These are his many devices for doing harm. The devil plants the root of sin; unless it is immediately torn out, it sprouts and the tree of guilt is born. Through the eye the branches of wickedness spread; through the tongue man tastes of this tree and gathers the fruit of delight unto eternal damnation.

The hedgehog, therefore, is the sluggishness of weakness, the thorn of deceit, and the skin of concealment. Through the thorn he casts one headlong into open evils; through the skin, into hidden ones. He has his den there, that is, a dwelling in confused minds, and nourishes barking young, that is, vices.

[Col. 0852B] After the hedgehog come kites, because after the devil comes the malice of the neighbor: when he curses and injures us, he tears us with beak and claws. But if we escape the hedgehog and kite, the lamia follows. The lamia has a human face and a beastly body. This is the flesh; this is the domestic enemy. It must first be conquered, having roots in us against us, fighting by flattery as though rational for necessary things, and yielding as though bestial for superfluous things. It finds rest when one makes provision for the flesh in its desires.

These are the three wars of Babylon: the demon’s temptation, the neighbor’s calumny, and the furnace of the flesh. Against these God’s countenance rebukes, and they perish; it soothes, and it strikes. It soothes by patiently waiting; it rebukes by chastising correction; it strikes by justly condemning.

### TIT. LXXXVI. On the threefold coming of the Lord.

[Col. 0852C]

The first coming is in a cloud, the second in dew, the third in lightning. In the first he comes hidden; in the second, partly manifest; in the third, wholly manifest. In the first the hidden Lamb comes to the altar; in the second, the bridegroom to his beloved; in the third, the sword to guilt. These are the three descents: of presence, mercy, and vengeance. Of the first it is said: “Bow the heavens and come down” (Ps. 17). Of the second: “I have come down into my garden” (Song 6). Of the third: “Let us go down and confound their speech” (Gen. 11).

### TIT. LXXXVII. On the way of flesh and spirit.

There are two ways: one of the flesh, the other of the spirit. One separates from the Lord; the other recalls to the Lord. One is visible; the other invisible. On the first [Col. 0852D] lovers of the world wander; in the second despisers of the world rest. The first are Hebrews according to the flesh, who so pass through temporal goods that they incur eternal evils; the second are Hebrews according to the spirit, who pass through these things to eternal goods.

### TIT. LXXXVIII. On desiring wisdom in five ways.

Wisdom is desired in five ways. Some learn in order to know: this is curiosity. Some learn in order to appear learned: this is vanity. Others, in order to sell and make profit: this is Simonian wickedness. Others, in order to build up others: this is praiseworthy charity. Others, in order to be built up: this is pious humility. The first three abound fruitlessly in desiring. [Col. 0853A] They gather manna, but it rots in their mouths. The latter two reap fruit.

### TIT. LXXXIX. On three kinships.

There are three kinships: of nature, grace, and glory. In the first we are created as God’s noble creature; in the second, reborn as a new creature in Christ; in the third, translated as a creature perfected in the Lord. Through the first we excel among animals; through the second we overcome the flesh; through the third we conquer death.

### TIT. XC. On the three companions of disobedience and the three goods of obedience.

Disobedience has three companions: imprudence, in relation to itself; irreverence, in relation to God; and insult, in relation to one’s neighbor. [Col. 0853B] But that you may know the dignity of obedience, observe that outside Bethany—which is interpreted “house of obedience”—neither the tears of the penitent, nor zeal for good work, nor the leisure of holy contemplation is found pleasing to God.

At Bethany the man four days dead is raised; there, in Simon’s house, Mary is relieved of the burden of sins. Finally, from Bethany one comes to Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace, because through obedience the hundredth sheep is carried on the shoulders of the loving Father back to the king. Through obedience the found drachma is hidden in the king’s treasury. Through obedience the queen of the south is spoken of in connection with the true Solomon. Through obedience Bathsheba is presented to the embrace of the true bridegroom.

### TIT. XCI. On three things to observe in the cross.

Let us observe three things in Christ’s cross: nobility, [Col. 0853C] wisdom, and religion. Hence the title is inscribed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters. In Latin is marked the nobility in which the Romans excelled; in Greek, the wisdom which they seek; in Hebrew, the religion from which the Jews, who seek signs, proceed.

### TIT. XCII. On the three acts required of an imitator of Christ.

An imitator of Christ ought to do three things: retain the disposition of simple innocence, so that he may become a child with Christ; love a lowly and humble manner of life, so that he may be wrapped with Christ in the cheap cloths of infancy; walk simply in discipline, so that he may be found laid with Christ in the manger.

### TIT. XCIII. On the three pools—of the devil, the world, and God—and their porticoes.

[Col. 0853D] There are three pools: one of the devil, another of the world, and a third of God. The first is called confusion and torments mortally; the second, contrition, and washes potentially; the third, compunction, and cleanses healthfully. Of the first it is said: “They shall be cast into the lake of burning fire and sulphur” (Apoc. 19). Of the second: “What do you desire in the way of Egypt, to drink troubled water?” (Jer. 2). Of the third: “On that day there shall be an open fountain for the house of David,” etc. (Zech. 13).

The first has five dark porticoes of punishments: in the first is gnashing of teeth; in the second, unquenchable fire; in the third, the undying worm; in the fourth, excessive cold; in the fifth, despair.

The second pool also has five porticoes. The first is negligence, and there Saul lies with the disobedient; the second, curiosity about the world, and there Jezebel lies with curious women; the third, contempt for one’s neighbor, and there the rich feaster lies with all the greedy; the fourth, the depth of malice, and there Arius and Caiaphas lie with other malicious persons; the fifth, despair of forgiveness, where Cain and Judas lie with the rest who despair. In the first they hear: “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48); in the second: “Death has gone up through our windows” (Jer. 9); in the third: “He who does not love remains in death” (John 3); in the fourth: “Wisdom shall not enter a malevolent soul” (Wis. 1); in the fifth: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the future” (Luke 12).

The third pool has five porticoes. The first is fear of punishment, and in it lie penitents; [Col. 0854B] the second, sorrow for present exile, in which lie those who mourn and hunger for righteousness; the third, compassion for one’s neighbor, in which lie the merciful; the fourth, love of reward, in which lie those pure in heart; the fifth, love of marriage, in which lie the peacemakers. Although in these there is health of virtues, nevertheless, because it is not possessed fully in the present, a multitude of the sick are said to lie there. They await the angel’s descent; when the water of compunction has been stirred by him (John 5), the weakness of venial or mortal sins is wiped away by the grace of the descending Holy Spirit, and one alone is healed from every stain: namely, only the one who preserves the unity of charity.

### TIT. XCIV. On the threefold source of the faithful soul’s joy.

The faithful soul, Christ’s bride, has a threefold source of joy. The first is the glory of the bridegroom; the second, reverence for her own [Col. 0854C] betrothal; the third, the magnificence of her dowry.

The bridegroom’s praise is manifold: from form, because he is “more beautiful than the children of men” (Ps. 44); from lineage, because he descends from the Father of lights (Jas. 1); from riches, because “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness,” etc. (Ps. 23); from power, because he cannot be conquered; from wisdom, because he cannot be deceived; from justice, because he cannot be corrupted; from certainty of knowledge, because he cannot be avoided. He is wonderful in the goodness of life, counsellor in the usefulness of teaching, God in the uniqueness of power, mighty in the property of victory, Father of the age to come in gifts of grace, Prince of Peace in the blessedness of glory: “There is none like you among the gods, O Lord, and there is none according to your works” (Ps. 35). Therefore the bride is first happy in such a marriage. “She made fine linen and sold it,” etc.

[Col. 0854D] The reverence of betrothal is threefold: first, the sacraments of life; second, the righteousness of commandments; third, the discipline of counsels. First he betrothed her by washing her with sacraments; second, by clothing her with commandments; third, by adorning her with exercises. The bridegroom will receive her washed, clothed, and honored, so that he may be known among her peoples, according to the saying: “God shall be known among her peoples when he has received her” (Ps. 47).

These are in the ranks of clergy, laity, prelates, subjects, hermits, and despisers of the world. To prelates belongs reverence for the sacraments; to subjects, obedience to the commandments; to despisers of the world, the exercises of counsels. To prelates belong the sacraments of salvation, ordinations, and dispensations of commandments. Therefore he who consecrates ought to be holy; he who ordains, ordained; he who administers the commandments of life, righteous; he who weighs another’s life and orders human conduct, discerning and humane.

[Col. 0855A] Thus betrothed, she receives the magnificence of a dowry. Therefore the bride rightly rejoices: first, happy through the bridegroom’s glory; second, happier through the reverence of dispensation; third, happiest because of the magnificence of the dowry, so that it is rightly said to her: “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” etc.

### TIT. XCV. On the three endowments of flowers and souls.

Three things are considered in a flower: a pleasing appearance, a sweet touch, and a delightful scent. What appears more pleasing to a soul purified by spiritual understanding? What is more sweetly embraced by spiritual embraces? [Col. 0855B] What is sensed more delightfully by the fragrance of such a soul?

In such a soul pride, claiming nothing for itself in swelling arrogance, does not offend the sight; envy, introducing no rusty corrosion, does not roughen the touch; luxury, introducing nothing withered, does not disturb the smell. Rather, it is wholly green within, flowers for those present, and bears fruit for those absent: green within through a good conscience, flowering for those present through good example, bearing fruit for those absent through good action.

### TIT. XCVI. On the entry of God’s word.

The divine word enters the human soul in four ways. It enters the first soul, hardened and blinded by its own malice, with a rod in order that it may be punished—stern and cruel—condemning it and saying: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). It enters [Col. 0855C] the second, fallen and terrified by its own conscience, with a parable in order that it may be restored—terrible but saving—inviting it by healing and saying: “My son, do not delay to turn to the Lord from day to day” (Ecclus. 5).

It enters the third, justified and scourged for its testing, with a saying—consoling and loving—saying to that soul: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested he shall receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him,” etc. (Jas. 1). It enters the fourth, deserving of reward and worthy of heavenly recompense, with grace in order that it may be rewarded, graciously and joyfully inviting it to its reward and saying: “Hasten, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2).

In the figure of this mystical discourse Moses, [Col. 0855D] stern in speech, carrying in his hand the rod of most severe contrition, walks into the presence of hardened Pharaoh. In the figure of the second, terrible but saving, Nathan the prophet entered David, prostrate and bound by the guilt of his own conscience, with a parable of correction; by rebuking him, he raised the fallen man and, error abandoned, restored him to righteousness.

In the figure of the third, loving and consoling, the prophet Isaiah entered King Hezekiah, indeed righteous but sick with bodily weakness for the sake of his testing, with a saying of divine consolation. He healed him, already tested and instructed by patience, and promised to protect him from the hand of the king of Assyria.

In the figure of the fourth, gracious and joyful, the angel Gabriel—pleasant in appearance, comely in bearing, gentle in speech—entered [Col. 0856A] Mary, greeted her reverently, and promised heavenly fruit as, as it were, the reward of her virginity, saying: “Behold, you shall conceive in the womb and bear a son,” etc. (Luke 1).

### TIT. XCVII. On the three gifts bestowed at creation upon the human body and the corresponding three upon the spirit.

At creation we find three inducements of divine love bestowed upon the body: bread, sun, and air—food for one eating, light for one seeing, breath for one breathing. Moreover, upon the spirit, three: dignity, knowledge, and virtue. Dignity possesses a twofold gift: the prerogative of nature and the capacity for bestowal. Knowledge likewise is twofold: knowing this dignity itself, or knowing another dignity to be present in us and not from us. Virtue too is twofold: seeking the author, and, once found, clinging to him inseparably. Dignity without knowledge will not profit; knowledge, however, is even harmful if virtue is absent.

### TIT. XCVIII. On the three things in the redemption of man that incite him to love of God.

In redemption there are three incentives to love: time, manner, and fruit. In the time, three things are considered: the corruption of nature, the transgression of the law, and the fullness of wickedness. In the manner likewise there are three, because he emptied himself even unto becoming man, descended even unto the cross, and suffered even unto death. In the fruit likewise there are three: perfect truth, which cast off ignorance; consummate charity, which removed concupiscence; and secure eternity, which takes away forgetfulness. Therefore, in the time there is the consummation of evil; in the manner, [Col. 0856C] the self-emptying of God; in the fruit, our being filled from him. Who could conceive how great a mercy it was to destroy wickedness, erase guilt, and form nature anew? How great a humanity it was for the Lord of Majesty to endure death in the flesh and suffer on the cross? How great a condescension it was to restore to blinded reason the fullness of light, to defiled will an abundance of peace, and to troubled memory the continuance of bright eternity?

### TITLE XCIX. On the Fourfold Love

There are four kinds of love. In the first, a human being loves himself for his own sake; in the second, he loves God for his own sake; in the third, God for God’s sake; in the fourth, himself for God’s sake. The first mode is carnal and belongs to slaves, concerning which it is said: “No one ever hates his own flesh” (Eph. 5). The second is animal and belongs to hirelings, concerning which: “He will praise you when you have done well for him” (Ps. 48 [Vulgate]). The third is spiritual and belongs to sons, concerning which: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good” (Ps. 117 [Vulgate]). He who gives thanks to the Lord not merely because he is good truly loves God for God’s sake, not for his own; the fourth is intellectual and belongs to angels, concerning which: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1).

### TITLE C. On the Seven Degrees of Confession

There are seven degrees of confession: knowledge of sin, repentance, sorrow of heart, confession of the mouth, mortification of the flesh, correction of conduct, and perseverance in goodness. Three look inward and three outward; the seventh [Col. 0857A] looks inward and outward.

Therefore, for confession to be true and fruitful, in the first degree knowledge of sin is necessary. In it three things are necessary: first, that you see what you have done—namely, with how many insults you have afflicted your body, possessing your vessel for uncleanness and dishonour, not in sanctification and honour; second, what you have deserved, considering that fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25), and the other evils that accumulate and increase in places of punishment; third, that you examine what you have lost: surely those good things which eye has not seen, etc. (1 Cor. 2).

Terrified by reflection upon these things, pass to the second degree, which is repentance. This too is threefold: that you repent of having lain too long in the mire of the dregs and misery of sin; that you do penance and crush the body; and that, withdrawing the seeds of incentives from the raging little ass of the flesh, [Col. 0857B] you admit no more things to be repented of, lest, repeatedly doubling wound upon wound, you break the bones of your soul.

Thus, knowing and repenting, fly onward to the third degree, which is sorrow of heart. It too is threefold: sharp, sharper, and sharpest. The sorrow is sharp because you have offended the Creator, whose law, while heavenly and earthly things observe it in so great a commonwealth of God, you alone, a stranger, disregard, despising the right hand of imperial Majesty. It is sharper because, along with the Creator, you have provoked to anger even the Father, who supplies you with the courses of the stars and abundance of fruits. It is sharpest, piercing the soul, because you have scorned the benefit of him who endured the pain of the cross so that you might no longer endure the pain of hell.

Thus let the shoot of justice generated in the inward person [Col. 0857C] burst forth into a tree, and let the tongue speak what conscience holds, so that you may ascend to the fourth degree, which is confession of the mouth. This must be made in three ways: purely, humbly, faithfully. Purely, so that you conceal nothing, but vomit forth every rot of vices; humbly, so that what is in the mouth may be in the heart. For both kings, David and Saul, said, “I have sinned”; but Saul heard: “The Lord has taken your kingdom from you and will give it to your rival” (1 Sam. 15). David, however: “The Lord has taken away your sin, and you shall not die” (2 Sam. 12). For Saul’s confession, which was in his mouth, was not in his heart; while the humility that appeared in David’s mouth was rooted in his heart. Faithfully, so that in the faith of the Church one believes one’s sins to be forgiven. For Cain and Judas confessed purely and humbly, but not faithfully: the one, [Col. 0857D] despairing, ran to the noose; the other vomited forth that great crime: “My iniquity is greater than that I may deserve pardon” (Gen. 4).

The fifth degree follows: mortification of the flesh, which must be weakened by fasts and vigils, lest it fly back through fresh itching to a life of pleasure. This also must be done in three ways: with permission, because what is done without permission will be counted to vainglory, not reward; secretly, “so that your left hand may not know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6); and discreetly, so that it may be done according to the body’s capacity.

Thus enlightened, one proceeds to the sixth degree, which is correction of conduct, so that, restraining every sensual movement with the reins of continence, one may come to the seventh degree, which is perseverance in goodness. In this seventh degree the Lord will call you with Moses from the midst of [Col. 0858A] darkness, and will fix the inward eyes upon the very multitude of divinity. This perseverance is produced by expectation of rewards, remembrance of punishments, the firstfruits of the Spirit, and the heavenly gift. Of this sevenfold confession it is said in the first three degrees: “With the heart one believes unto justice” (Rom. 10); in the other three: “Confession of the mouth is made unto salvation” (ibid.). The seventh runs through every degree.

Four things hinder this confession. First, shame, by which we are ashamed to confess what we have committed. This must be opposed in three ways: by consideration of reason, which urges confession; by reverence for the God who beholds, from whom nothing is hidden; and by comparison with greater confusion, since in the future all crimes will be laid open to all.

Second, fear, which oppresses many lest they be struck by a grievous punishment and be unable to bear it. [Col. 0858B] This likewise must be met in three ways: by considering how grievous, how long, and how fruitless the punishment of Gehenna is; and, conversely, that present repentance is light, momentary, and fruitful. Truly, “upon those who fear frost snow shall fall” (Job 6).

Third, hope, which overwhelms many while, desiring present things, they refuse to open their consciences, lest, if they appeared to people as they are, they should attain none of the good things of the present. Against this it must be impressed how uncertain and momentary the goods of this age are, and how certain and eternal those to come.

Fourth, despair destroys many, because they fear that they cannot restrain themselves. Against this, the strength of confession, the grace of humility, and the constancy of that confirmation must be opened up.

### TITLE CI. That “Today” Is Said in Three Ways

[Col. 0858C]

“Today” is said in three ways, because one kind is transitory. Hence: “If the grass that flourishes today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, God so clothes it,” etc. (Matt. 6). Another is recurrent. Hence the Apostle: “Exhort one another every day, while it is called Today” (Heb. 3). Another is eternal. Hence: “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2).

### TITLE CII. On the Three States of Humankind and the Threefold Offering to Be Made in Each

There are three states of a human being: the first, repentance; the second, justice; the third, eternal life. In accordance with these three states we ought to offer three sacrifices. In the first state, the sacrifice of compunction; in the second, that of good works; in the third, that of praise and rejoicing. [Col. 0858D] We are commanded to offer ourselves to God by this threefold sacrifice when it is said: “Offer the sacrifice of justice, and hope in the Lord” (Ps. 4). For the beginning of justice is compunction, its progress is action, and its good consummation is the praise of eternal life. Each of these has its own richness: the first, the butter of humility; the second, the oil of discernment; the third, the balm of charity.

### TITLE CIII. On the Three Bearing Witness in Heaven, the Three on Earth, and the Three in Hell; Again

There are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Three are on earth: the Spirit, water, and blood (1 John 5). Likewise in hell, as we read in Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” [Col. 0859A] (Isa. 66). Fire and worm are two evils: by the one conscience is gnawed; by the other bodies are burned. A third is added, despair, which indeed is understood in the saying: “It shall not die, and it shall not be quenched.” To those who are in heaven testimony of blessedness is given; to those on earth, testimony of justification; to those in hell, testimony of damnation. The first is of glory, the second of grace, the third of wrath.

### TITLE CIV. How the Holy Spirit Rebukes the World

The Holy Spirit will rebuke the world concerning sin (John 16), which it disguises; concerning justice, which it does not set in order, since it attributes it to itself rather than to God; and concerning judgment, which it unjustly usurps, since it rashly judges both itself and others.

### TITLE CV. On the Christian Name, etc.

[Col. 0859B]

Christians received their name from Christ; and it is necessary that, as they are heirs of the name, so they may be imitators of holiness. Therefore there are three things which we must practise with all our strength, as displayed in Christ: to reject vigorously the vanity of the world, since Christ too fled when the crowds sought to make him king; to practise patience manfully, since Jesus too was slain as a lamb; and to possess double charity truly, since Jesus prayed for his enemies.

### TITLE CVI. On the Seven Degrees of Humility

Humility has seven degrees of descent: renunciation of possessions, after the example of the apostles; casting aside garments, as Elijah and John did; bodily discipline, [Col. 0859C] as Paul had; lowliness in prosperity, after the manner of David, poor man and king; patience in adversity, as Job and Tobias showed; and abhorring one’s own counsel and the inclination of one’s own will.

### TITLE CVII. On the Weapons of Virtue and Wickedness

The weapons of virtue by which the weapons of wickedness are conquered are these: full knowledge of sin, which drives out the darkness of pleasure; penitential affliction against the poison of iniquity; sufficient and fitting correction through a change of former will; and the full continuance of perseverance, so that perfect guardianship of health may be supplied.

### TITLE CVIII. On the Three Things Necessary for Repentance

[Col. 0859D]

These three are necessary for repentance: abstinence, by which the pride of the flesh is tamed; reading, by whose fruit the mind, to be restored to strength, is nourished; and prayer, by whose protection and defence the swarms of virtues are safeguarded.

### TITLE CIX. What Three Things Humility Has

The virtue of humility has these three things: to submit to one’s superior, so that no ambition or envy may seize upon equality with him; not to prefer oneself to one’s equal, lest one seem to wish to become superior through unlawful desire; and rather to submit to one inferior than to be set over him, so that the grace of humility may thereby be proved.

### TITLE CX. On the Unequal Progress of Those Going to God

Not all advance uniformly toward God. Some go with a slow step, such as those who, entangled in earthly cares, [Col. 0860A] scarcely ever take breath to remember God. Some go at a moderate pace, such as those devoted to the Lord’s service who indeed serve God, yet prove too indulgent toward themselves. Others go swiftly, that is, at a rapid course, such as those who look beyond their flesh and thus scorn transient things, advancing quickly toward God, desiring this alone: to rest together in peace.

### TITLE CXI. On the Three Things Awaiting the Elect

Three things await the elect in the future: inward satiety, eternal joy, and delightful pleasure. Of these it is said: “Let the righteous feast and exult before God, and delight in gladness” (Ps. 67 [Vulgate]).

### TITLE CXII. On the Threefold Desire of the Elect

The desire of the elect is threefold: to dwell [Col. 0860B] with one mind in the Lord. Hence: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26 [Vulgate]). To gain victory over the world. Hence: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7). To enjoy God in his presence. Hence also: “Having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

### TITLE CXIII. On the Threefold Fear of Prelates

The fear of prelates is threefold: lest an overly elaborate display of words move the minds of hearers; lest an excessive use offend the eyes of the inward Judge; and lest recompense according to justice be made to them in the present life.

### TITLE CXIV. On the Three Calves to Be Sacrificed to the Lord

There are three calves which we ought to sacrifice to the Lord: the affection of a new manner of life, like a young calf putting forth horns and hoofs; progress in sacred religion, which is a most tender calf from the herd; and the effect of consummate virtue, which is the fattened calf.

### TITLE CXV. On the Fourfold Affliction of Humankind

Our affliction is fourfold: the straits of corruptible flesh, which are the pains of death; the troubles of temporal oppressions, which are torrents of iniquity; the hidden snares of the secret enemy, which are the pains of hell; and the deceitful appearances of worldly glory, which are the snares of death.

### TITLE CXVI. On Smoke, Fire, and Darkness in Relation to God

Smoke is from God’s wrath (Ps. 17 [Vulgate]), because the elect are pierced with compunction in reflecting [Col. 0860D] on God’s wrath. Fire is from his face, because through knowledge and awareness of his presence they are kindled to love. Darkness is beneath his feet, because by his strict judgment the reprobate person is darkened by the clouds of despair.

### TITLE CXVII. How God Walks, Flies, and Dwells with Us

“The Lord walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. 103 [Vulgate]) when his elect attain his sweetness, even slightly. He flies when they perceive nothing of his unbounded substance. Hence: “Flee, my beloved” (Song 8). The Lord places the darkness of profundity and height as the hiding-place of his divinity; in the sun of manifestation and labour, the tabernacle of his flesh; in the light of purity and holiness, the dwelling-place of his abode.

### TITLE CXVIII. On the Gates of the World, Hell, and Heaven

[Col. 0861A]

The world has two impure gates by which we enter into it: corrupted sensuality and incestuous covetousness. Hence: “They drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. 106 [Vulgate]). The gates of hell are blind despair and hard obstinacy. Hence: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16). The gates of heaven are humble patience, which is the iron gate leading into the city, and concord in love, which is the eastern gate.

### TITLE CXIX. On the Fourfold Recompense

There are four kinds of recompense: two in this age and two in the future. The recompense of prosperity and abundance belongs to the wicked. Hence: “They have received their reward” (Matt. 6). There is also their recompense of damnation and ignominy; that of familiarity and grace for the righteous; and that of sweetness, [Col. 0861B] love, and glory. But there are two things which are rewarded: righteousness of deed and purity of heart.

### TITLE CXX. On the Three Lamps

There are three lamps: the rule of discipline in Christ, which is raised so that the lost drachma may be found; the form of truth in the Gospel, which is placed upon a lampstand; and purity of knowledge in a good heart, which is enlightened by the Lord.

### TITLE CXXI. On the Threefold Seed

The seed is threefold. The first is of truth and justice, which, cast into the earth, produces a hundredfold seed. The second is of iniquity and faithlessness, which is a brood of vipers. The third is of error and wickedness, which is the seed of Canaan and not of Judah.

### TITLE CXXII. That God’s Wisdom Is Like a Partridge, a Hen, and an Eagle toward Its Young, That Is, Its Hearers

[Col. 0861C]

The Wisdom of God, like a partridge, broods over children whom it did not bear; like a hen, gathers chicks beneath its wings; like an eagle, urges its young to fly.

### TITLE CXXIII. On the Threefold Garment of the Good

Our garment is threefold: penitential anxiety, which is the garment of widowhood; religious maturity, which is the garment of joy; and sincere integrity, which is the garment of virginity.

### TITLE CXXIV. On Esau’s Garment and the Kids’ Skins

Esau’s garments are uprightness of life and maturity of discipline. The kids’ skins are the casting off of harmful oldness and the mortification of one’s own will. The foods are cheerful obedience [Col. 0861D] and humble abstinence. The father touches the son by applying the hand of testing; he kisses him through the prompting of secret inspiration; he blesses him through progress in religion.

### TITLE CXXV. On the Three Things Necessary for Purity

Three things are necessary for purity: integrity of action, simplicity of intention, and tranquillity of devotion.

### TITLE CXXVI. On the Three Goods Bestowed by Purity

Purity bestows three things: the Spirit of liberty, the joy of sincerity, and the steadfastness of charity.
