### TITLE CXXVII. That the Reprobate Are Smoke, Dust, and Wax

The reprobate are sometimes like smoke, because they vanish away in their own height; sometimes like dust, because they produce no moisture of charity; and sometimes like wax, because they melt easily under heat—that is, under the onset of temptation.

### TITLE CXXVIII. On the Threefold Gates

[Col. 0862A]

The gates of Zion are the sacraments of the Church, without which we do not enter the Church. The gates of justice are the intermediate virtues, which we exercise in time. The eternal gates are especially those virtues which we shall possess also in the future.

### TITLE CXXIX. That Religious Persons Are Obligated to God in Three Things

There are three things in which we are obligated to God: the seal of nature, because we were made in God’s likeness; the talent of faith, which we must return whole to God through good works; and the title of profession, because we are bound by the bonds of a promise to serve God.

### TITLE CXXX. God Questions Us in Three Ways

God questions us in three ways: through the promulgation [Col. 0862B] of a commandment, so that our obedience may become known; through the infliction of the scourge, so that our patience may become known to our neighbours; and through the revelation of a secret, so that the power of humility may disclose itself to us.

### TITLE CXXXI. On the Three Goods of Tribulation

Tribulation confers three things: exercise, lest the virtue of love grow cold in the warmth of idleness; testing, so that the strength of our constancy may become known to people as an example; and reward, so that according to the measure of tribulation it may receive an immense weight of glory.

### TITLE CXXXII. On the Three Things to Be Opposed to Adversity

Three things are to be set against adversity: the struggles and hardships of the elect, suffered by those who live devoutly; the afflictions and troubles of the Redeemer, inflicted upon him by most cruel rulers; and the ordering of governing justice, [Col. 0862C] whose height, like the top of Joseph’s rod, we ought not investigate but adore. These are those three things—doors, bars, and boundaries—by which the Lord surrounds the sea of this age (Job 38).

### TITLE CXXXIII. On the Threefold Exercise of the Elect

The exercise of the elect is threefold: the austerity of fasts, by which the earth of the flesh is cultivated so that it may bear fruit; assiduity in reading, by which the mind is refreshed so that the inward person may grow rich; and persistence in prayers, by which the mind rises toward desire for heavenly things.

### TITLE CXXXIV. On the Three Marvels in Mary

God, the author of marvels, worked three wondrous things in Mary: he marvellously raised up integrity of purity, so that the ark of the covenant might be covered with purest gold; he powerfully made virginal purity fruitful, so that the burning bush might not be consumed; and he ineffably joined the lowest to the highest, so that, by means of Jacob’s ladder, earthly things might be united with heavenly.

### TITLE CXXXV. On the Benefits of Mary’s Fruitfulness

Mary’s fruitfulness bestowed three things upon us: it removed the yoke of ancient captivity; remitted the wrath of divine indignation; and erased the knot of human iniquity.

### TITLE CXXXVI. On the Three Things the Elect Await, and the Three Things the Reprobate Desire

The elect await three things in the future: that what is mortal in them may be wholly swallowed up by life; that they may be enriched by the recompense of everlasting glory; and that they may contemplate God as he is without satiety. The reprobate are said to desire three things: to heap up bodily pleasure for themselves in sufficiency; [Col. 0863A] to have momentary glory contribute toward blessedness; and to have their morals and deeds incapable of being condemned by any judgment.

### TITLE CXXXVII. That Those Awaiting God Are Fourfold, and What They Hope from Him Again

People awaiting God ought to be expectant: uncertain when he will come and what he will bring them; cheerful, devout, and more diligently adorned; hoping for three things in him: a nuptial presence, familiar grace, and liberal bounty.

### TITLE CXXXVIII. On the Three Spiritual Weddings

There are three kinds of weddings. The first are those of reconciliation through faith, in which there are three dishes: the washing away of sins, the attainment of grace, and the restoration of nature. The second are those of adoption through hope, in which there are consolation from the divine word, communion in heavenly nourishment, [Col. 0863B] and a foretaste of inward sweetness. The third are those of perfect glorification through charity, whose dishes are eternal incorruptibility, true glorification, and perpetual vision of God.

### TITLE CXXXIX. On the Three Weapons of the Faithful

The faithful have three weapons: fullness of wisdom, which is David’s sling, from which stones of sayings are cast; strength of patience, which is the staff by which the rage of wolves is repelled; and breadth of charity, which is David’s bag, from which prayers are brought forth.

### TITLE CXL. On the Three Things Necessary for a Prelate

Three things are necessary for prelates: the living sincerity of faith and doctrine, so that they may dwell in the same region; [Col. 0863C] diligent zeal in doing good, so that they may keep watch with the shepherds; and careful concern for the salvation of their subjects, so that they may guard their flock from wolves.

### TITLE CXLI. On the Kinds and Parts of Repentance

There are three kinds of repentance: feigned and fruitless, exemplified by Esau and Saul; cruel and despairing, as in Cain and Judas; useful and complete, as in the Magdalene and Zacchaeus. Its parts are five: contrition in the heart, confession in the mouth, mortification in the flesh, correction in conduct, and perseverance in virtue.

### TITLE CXLII. On the Threefold Change

There are three kinds of changes: loftiness into humility, when the Word assumed flesh; contemptibility into majesty, when the God-man [Col. 0863D] was transfigured before the disciples; and changeability into eternity, when, rising again, he ascended to reign in heaven.

### TITLE CXLIII. On the Threefold Refuge of the Ungodly

The refuge of the ungodly is threefold: the teaching of deceptive deceit, which is Python; the defence of worldly power, which is Rameses; and the appearance of feigned justice, which is the city of the sun. Pharaoh orders these to be built.

### On the Five Torrents

> [Note: [Col. 0863D] The title and number are lacking here.]

There are five torrents: that of cruelty and wickedness, which is the Kishon, beside which Jabin is killed; that of philosophical eloquence, which is the Kidron beyond which [Col. 0864A] Jesus goes forth; that of suffering and distress, which is the brook from which Jesus is said to have drunk on the way; that of heavenly wisdom, beside which Elijah is fed; and that of delight and joy, from which the elect are given drink in heaven. *Cison* means “their hardness”; *Cedron*, “of cedars,” and is a Greek genitive.

### TITLE CXLIV. On the Fourfold Kind of Earth

The kind of earth is fourfold: the flower and greenness of temporal goods, which is watered like paradise; the useful life and conduct of the elect, from which the bread of life arises; the loveliness of heavenly dwelling-places, which flows with milk and honey; and the situation of infernal places, which is a land of misery and darkness.

### TITLE CXLV. On the Fourfold Desert

There are four kinds of desert: the trackless solitude of worldly exile, concerning which David says: “In a desert land, trackless and waterless” (Ps. 62 [Vulgate]); the difficult height of Christian discipline, in which the children of Israel wander; the delightful expanse of heavenly Jerusalem, in which the ninety-nine sheep are left; and the terrible condition of infernal misery, which is the desert of desolation.

### TITLE CXLVI. On the Fourfold Chariot

There are four kinds of chariots: that of pride and dominion, in which Pharaoh is drowned; that of humility and study, in which the eunuch of Queen Candace sits; that of devotion and service, in which Joseph, seated, meets his father; and that of love and desire, in which Elijah is carried away.

### TITLE CXLVII. On the Threefold Ascension of the Lord

The Lord’s ascent is threefold: victorious, by which [Col. 0864C] he ascends above the west; beautiful, by which he ascends above the heaven of heavens; glorious, by which he ascends upon the wings of the winds.

### TITLE CXLVIII. On Acquiring the Kingdom of Heaven

Some seize the kingdom of heaven by force, like the poor in spirit; others purchase it, like those who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity (Luke 16); others steal it, like the woman who secretly touched the fringe of the Lord’s garment; others are compelled to enter it, like the poor of this world.

### TITLE CXLIX. On What Makes Death Precious

A precious death is sometimes made by life, as in confessors; sometimes by its cause, as in martyrs; sometimes by both life and cause, as in the many who, after a holy life, are crowned by martyrdom.

### TITLE CL. On the Fourfold Visitation of God

God visits us in four ways: through the giving of a commandment, for one commandment is carnal and another spiritual; through the severity of the scourge, which has five modes—so that he may correct someone from iniquity; lest someone grow proud of a virtue bestowed; so that virtue may become known to people; so that he may restrain others by someone’s example; and so that the crown may be accumulated and increased; through the novelty of a miracle, which is visible and invisible; and through subtle inspiration.

### TITLE CLI. On the Four Virgins to Be Taken in Marriage

There are four virgins whom we ought to join to ourselves in marriage: philosophical eloquence, which is Zilpah, [Col. 0865A] Jacob’s handmaid; judicial judgment, signified by Balaam; practical innocence, which may be called Leah; and spiritual contemplation, understood as Rachel.

### TITLE CLII. On the Three Lampstands

Three lampstands are found in the Scriptures: the obscurity of the Law, which has little globes and lilies; prophetic subtlety, which has two olive trees at its summit; and evangelical truth, which has in its midst one like the Son of Man.

### TITLE CLIII. On the Three Defences of the Soul

There are three defences by which the soul is fortified: diligent watchfulness, which is a hedge; the intercession of the saints, which is a most strong rampart; and divine protection, which is a wall defending against the assault of enemies.

### TITLE CLIV. On the Three Things Strengthening Hope

[Col. 0865B]

A threefold reason examines and strengthens our hope: the humility of imparted wisdom, which is to cook an egg in water; the firmness of steadfast wisdom, which is to roast an egg over fire; and the vigour of hidden inspiration, which is to fry an egg in a pan.

### TITLE CLV. On the Three Means by Which God Conquers Enemies

There are three means by which God inflicts vengeance upon our enemies: the healing remedy of baptism, which, like the Red Sea, kills the Egyptians; the fitting exercise of repentance, which, like sulphur, destroys sinners; and the judgment of utter strictness, which, like fire at Elijah’s word, envelops idolaters.

### TITLE CLVI. On the Threefold Bed of the Soul

[Col. 0865C]

The bed on which the soul rests is threefold: the burden of bodily weakness, which the sick man healed spreads beneath himself; the tranquillity of a quiet conscience, upon which, while David flees, a statue is placed. This is the bed beneath which two cushions are laid: with respect to the past, the fullness of security and confidence; with respect to the future, certainty of recompense and reward. The pillow placed beneath the head is the abundance of divine familiarity and grace. The third bed is humility before higher glory: the flowering bed surrounded by sixty mighty men (Song 3).

### TITLE CLVII. On the Three Panes of Glass

There are three panes through which the sun’s ray is poured: integrity of charity, through which forgiveness of sins is poured in; purity of humility, through which heavenly grace descended upon [Col. 0865D] Mary; and subtlety of understanding, through which the ray of wisdom illuminates the heart.

### TITLE CLVIII. On the Seven Lamps of the Mind

Seven lamps illuminate the throne of the chosen mind: the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the prophet treats more fully (Isa. 2), and which, as they consume by heavenly fire the oil of glory and the wine of fear and weakness, continually supply the light of truth.

### TITLE CLIX. On the Threefold Food Set Before Us

The food of the flesh set before us to eat is threefold [Col. 0866A]: a kid from the goats, in the fruit of repentance, which Jacob offered to his father Isaac that he might be blessed; a calf from the herd, in the act of justice, which Abraham expended as food for angels; and the fattened calf, in the abundance of glory, which the father is said to have slaughtered when the prodigal son returned.

### TITLE CLX. On the Threefold Garden of Souls

The garden in which chosen souls walk is threefold: the hardship of corruptible life, which is the garden of nuts in which Susanna washes; the loveliness of heavenly joy, which is the garden of delights in which Adam is placed to work it and keep it; and the sweetness and delight of the divine vision, which is the enclosed garden in which Joseph erected for himself a monument cut from rock. A clean conscience too, [Col. 0866B] according to its diversity, receives these gardens within itself.

### TITLE CLXI. On the Three Tables Set Before Us

Three tables are set before our hunger: the mystery of Law and Gospel, in which the feasts of wisdom are taken; the mystery of Catholic instruction, where a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb are received; and the mystery of eternal satiety, which is within the veil and contains the loaves of the Presence and of life.

### TITLE CLXII. On the Three Treasures to Be Stored Up

There are three treasures which we ought to store up: the desire of piety in the heart, which is hidden in a field so that the field may be bought; the teaching of truth in the mouth, which is the treasury of snow and hail; and persevering assiduity [Col. 0866C] in a person, which has wheat, barley, oil, and honey. These are the treasures of the Magi, who offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the Lord at his birth.

### TITLE CLXIII. On the Four Kinds of Bread

Four kinds of bread are found in the Scriptures, by which the various miseries of humankind are lamented: bread baked in human dung, bovine dung, ashes, and an oven. By these the differing dispositions of the human mind are expressed.

### TITLE CLXIV. On Placing a Vow upon Three Altars

There are three altars upon which we ought to place vows: the fulfilment of divine ordinances, which is made of shittim wood in the desert; the manifold invocation of the blessed, which is made of stones untouched by iron; and the humble incarnation of the Redeemer, which is made of earth.

### TITLE CLXV. On the Three Girls Who Overturn Our Understanding, Concerning Whom Much Has Been Said More Fully Above, as of Many Others

There are three girls who turn our understanding aside: the weakness of our flesh, which is Delilah, who tears out Samson’s eyes; the attractiveness of worldly glory, which is Jezebel, who kills Naboth; and distrust of the life to come, which is the daughter of Herodias, who takes away the prophet’s head.

# BOOK SEVEN: ON MISCELLANEOUS MATTERS

## TITLE I. On the Spiritual Ornament of Churches and Holy Buildings

[Col. 0867A]

“Our little bed is flowering; the beams of our houses are cedar, our ceilings cypress” (Song 1). The houses are the various assemblies of the faithful; the beams, the prelates who serve for defence, by whose word and example they are supported. These are of cedar, whose scent drives away serpents, because by the power of their word they are accustomed to expel poisonous doctrines, thoughts, and deeds. The ceilings, which serve only for ornament, are those who know rather how to adorn the Church with virtues than to reform it. These ought to be fastened to the beams, because those who desire to shine in the Church through their conduct should cleave with their whole mind to the sayings and examples of the highest Fathers. And they are cypress. Cypresses do not shed the beauty of their foliage when struck by winds, [Col. 0867B] expressing the constancy of those who adorn the holy Church with loftier ornaments of virtues, as it were with ceilings.

## TITLE II. On the Moral Construction of the Temple or Church from Wood, Gold, and Stone
The Temple of Solomon was made from three kinds of material; the Church consists of three orders. The three materials are gold, wood, and stone: stone is assigned to prelates, gold to contemplatives, wood to those in the active life. In wood, one part is raised upward and another lowered downward. Those in the active life, in order to attain heavenly glory, are occupied on earth with pious deeds. A man who finds gold hides it; and of contemplatives it is said: “You will hide them in the secrecy of your presence, from the disturbance of men” [Col. 0867C] (Ps. 30). In the stone written by God’s finger there are three things: writing, fire, and hardness. In a prelate there ought to be teaching, love, and correction. The writing signifies teaching, hardness correction, and fire love. Neither is love without correction, nor is correction useful without love. Both are necessary; yet it is better to be loved than feared.

Solomon teaches this mystically in the base of the Temple, which is applied to prelates, where together with cherubim he carved an ox and a lion. In the cherubim, knowledge is indicated; in the ox, gentleness; in the lion, fear. Knowledge pertains to teaching, gentleness to charity, fear to correction. Teaching produces virtue, charity nourishes it, correction preserves it. Teaching instructs the ignorant; charity consoles the faint-hearted; [Col. 0867D] correction restrains the obstinate. As Solomon’s Temple consisted of three materials, so Christ’s Church consists of three orders. Therefore these three things befit a prelate: teaching, lest the blind lead the blind; charity, that he may rejoice with the truth; correction, that he may not consent to the vicious.

The prelate, with Noah, governs the ark amid the flood. The contemplative, with Daniel, prays at the eastern window [Col. 0868A] in the upper chamber. The active person, with Job, gives pious assistance to all who suffer need. The prelate is in the field, that he may sow the word of God; the contemplative is in bed, that he may enjoy the sweetness of God; the active person is at the mill, that he may be troubled and occupied about many things for the love of God. And Christ, who was to be the model of these three orders, to whom they might conform, set himself forth; for the true master first acted and afterwards taught (Acts 1). As a devout contemplative he ascended the mountain alone to pray; as a diligent minister he came not to be ministered to, but to minister.

He also displayed this threefold material in the temple of his body. For not only does Solomon’s Temple signify the Temple of the Church, but also the temple of Christ’s body, concerning which he says: “Destroy this temple,” etc. (John [Col. 0868B] 2). This temple too consists of gold, wood, and stone. Thus it is written: “Gold of that land is excellent; there also is bdellium”—which, as Pliny says, is a fragrant tree—“and the onyx stone” (Gen. 2). That land is the blessed Virgin; the remaining things signify Christ, who consists of divinity, flesh, and soul. Stone corresponds to divinity because of its immutability; gold to the soul because of the suffering it endured; wood to the flesh because of its weakness. Of the first it is said: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3). Of the second: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 16). Of the third: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21).

[Col. 0868C] According to his divinity he worked miracles; according to his soul he suffered compassionately with us; according to his flesh he endured torments. In the first, he is a lion, because strong; in the second, a hen, because exceedingly merciful; in the third, a lamb, because exceedingly gentle and meek. Of these—that is, of the lion, hen, and lamb; of the Word, flesh, and soul—a union was made when God and man came together as one, so that by a wondrous exchange the high became lowly, the unknown visible, the ἀθάνατος (*athánatos*), that is, the immortal, passible and mortal.

## TITLE III. Allegorically, concerning Solomon’s Temple

In Solomon’s Temple, which signifies the universal Church existing in heaven and on earth, three things must be noted: the porch, or court, before the Temple; the Temple itself; and the oracle, called the Holy of Holies. There were three doors: of the porch, of the Temple, and of the oracle (3 Kings 6). The porch before the Temple [Col. 0868D] bears the figure of those who lived under the Law before Christ’s coming. The Temple denotes the whole Christ—namely, the head and the members that follow him. The oracle signifies the joys of the inner heavenly kingdom given to both. The door of the porch is the prophetic word, which first receives the rays of the sun. The door of the house is Christ himself, who says: “I am [Col. 0869A] the door” (John 10). The entrance of the oracle is the entrance of the heavenly kingdom.

In the Temple are slanting windows, that is, wider inwardly. These are the teachers of the Church, who through preaching pour upon others the light they have received; they are wider within because they hold more fully in practice what they preach outwardly. Or, the light they receive outwardly is small in comparison with that which they hold inwardly in hope of glory.

## TITLE IV. Concerning the same

Upon the wall of the Temple there are three stories (3 Kings 6): the first was seven cubits broad, the second six, the third five. These are the three orders in the Church: the married, the continent, and virgins; or laity, clergy, and monks. [Col. 0869B] The first and second are more extensive in earthly life; the third is stricter than the others. Or, the first upper chamber signifies the present state of the Church; the second, the state of souls after this life; the third displays the twofold glory of souls and bodies after judgment.

There was a door in the side of the Temple, from which a spiral passage rose inwardly through the wall to the middle story, and from the middle to the third, in which the Lord’s body is signified. In its side a door was made when, on the cross, one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and blood and water came forth (John 19): water by which we are washed in baptism, and blood by which we are consecrated in the holy chalice. Through this door, therefore, ascent is made to the [Col. 0869C] middle and third stories, because through faith and the mysteries of the Redeemer we ascend from the present age and the conversion of the Church to the rest of souls after death, and again, after judgment, to the rest of souls and the immortality of bodies, as it were into the third story.

This inward journey is by a spiral way because it occurs invisibly. No one knows it except one who, with the Lord as guide, climbs by these means to heavenly things; and those outside behold there only the celebrations of the sacraments. This story is called in the Gospel the pinnacle, where the Lord is tempted by the devil. Each story had surrounding ledges, lest anyone sitting upon them should slip downward. These signify the daily strength of divine protection, or the guard of humility, by which we are preserved upon the height of good works, [Col. 0869D] lest we fall to the depths in evils when deserted by God, or in goods when puffed up by ourselves—as Uzziah fell from the railing upon which, separated from the house of David, he had climbed.

For even if evil persons maintain the ascent of good activity, yet because they do not possess the unity of David’s house, they slip, as though the protections of the ledges were crumbling, toward the slopes of vices; deprived of divine help, they perish through their own arrogance. Moses commands that such ledges be made on every house, saying: “If you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you be guilty when another falls” (Deut. 22). If you build a new manner of life, the protection of humility must be applied, lest by falling therein through pride you become guilty both of yourself and of your neighbour, whom you have killed by your example.

## TITLE V. Concerning the same

[Col. 0870A]

“He covered the wall of the house, from the pavement to the top of the walls and up to the ceilings within, with cedar wood” (3 Kings 6). The stones of the wall were made living stones, which grow upon the foundation that is Christ into a dwelling-place of God, joined by the cement of charity, bearing one another’s burdens in the fear of God. These are clothed within with cedar. Cedar is an incorruptible tree, pleasant in fragrance and appearance, driving away and, when burned, killing serpents. Such indeed are the saints: invincible through patience, exalted in reputation and works, destroying the devil’s wiles, kindled by the fire of divine love. They are covered with cedar from the pavement of the house to the top of the walls; that is, from the beginning of faith to the completion [Col. 0870B] of good work, and to the ceilings, that is, to entrance into the heavenly homeland.

There were three ceilings: the first in the first story, the second in the second, the third in the third. By the ceilings, therefore, we understand the righteous: those in the present Church, those in the future state of souls, and those after judgment in soul and body. They adorn God’s Church and, set in the upper part of the house either here or in the future, protect it by their prayers. Thus the stone in the wall is covered up to the upper ceilings: it endures in firmness of faith until it enters among those who are at rest.

The walls themselves, like also the pavement—which is said to have been laid with precious stone upon stone, with fir boards upon the stones, and with golden plates upon the boards—are covered with gold after the cedar, in order that the whole life of the saints may be represented. [Col. 0870C] The living stones, both in wall and foundation, are the saints, cemented in unity by the strength of faith. The cedar or fir boards are saints who, by their exaltation, despise earthly things and strive toward those above through the virtue of patience, driving demons away by the fragrance of their virtues. The golden plates are charity possessing knowledge that surpasses all things; they are placed over marble and wood because, as gold surpasses other metals, so charity surpasses the other virtues: as the Apostle briefly indicates, saying, “In Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision avails anything, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5). Stone represents unconquered faith; cedar, fragrant action; gold, love transcending all things.

[Col. 0870D] The stone wall is covered with cedar boards when faith is adorned with works, lest it be idle or dead. Golden plates are added, that faith and work may shine with love of God and neighbour, so that in every work God alone may be sought. Therefore, because the Law was written on stone and the teaching of the Gospel was confirmed through the wood of the cross, the former people were marked in the foreskin by that stone, while we are consecrated on the forehead by the sign of the cross. The stones of wall or pavement may also, not incongruously, signify believers under the Law, and the cedar boards the righteous of the New Testament. Since one glory of heavenly recompense awaits both, golden brightness is added to stones and wood, signifying the radiance of eternal recompense.

## TITLE VI. Concerning the same

He also built the wall that divides the oracle [Col. 0871A] from the Temple, not reaching to the ceilings; rather, it had an opening throughout the lower part, like a door, through which the incense smoke, kindled for the Lord from the altar of incense before the door of the oracle, entered the oracle and filled the ark (3 Kings 6). The outer house, into which priests always entered to perform the offices of sacrifices, is the present Church, where, daily pursuing pious works, we offer to God sacrifices of praise. The inner house is the life promised to us in heaven, where are the ark of the covenant and the cherubim, where is Christ, in whom alone we have with the Father the covenant of peace, and where the solemn assembly of the blessed angels is held, into which they enter once a year, not without blood.

The wall dividing the two houses from each other is the enclosure of heaven, [Col. 0871B] for whose opening we sigh daily and knock until it may be opened to us and we may be permitted to enter. Although we are not permitted to enter before the dissolution of our bodies, we nevertheless possess, in the lower part, an open door of divine mercy, through which we send beforehand from the altar of the heart the incense and fragrant offerings of prayers, alms, fasts, and other good works. This altar is near the door of the oracle, signifying that the voices of prayers are sent through the door of divine mercy into the Holy of Holies, to Christ’s ears. For those still held only by the flesh, yet suspended in all desire toward higher things, receive from God more swiftly what they ask the nearer they are to the heavenly homeland.

It should also be known that all the nails by which the plates throughout the Temple were fixed were of gold, each weighing [Col. 0871C] fifty shekels. These are the commandments of charity, or the promises of blessedness, by which we are held fast lest we fail. They are weighed at fifty shekels because heavenly words promise forgiveness of sin—namely, grace and eternal rest—all of which are signified in Scripture in this manner. These are the nails of love.

There are also other nails, those of fear, by which beginners mortify the enticements of vices and of the flesh: namely, those sayings of virtue by which we crucify the flesh with its vices and desires, of which it is said: “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118). One who progresses again says concerning the nails: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72).

He made in the oracle two cherubim of [Col. 0871D] olive wood. In the cherubim is signified angelic ministry: in their praise of the Creator, their mutual love, and the service they extend to human beings. For their touching and embracing both walls with two wings, and their spreading wings over the ark as though to fly, expresses that they refer every good to the praise of God and are ready for divine service. Their being made from olive wood expresses that the angelic virtues are anointed with grace, so that they never wither away from the love of God. Set in the oracle, they turn their faces toward the outer house because, established in glory, they desire those in this pilgrimage to be delivered and to come to their fellowship. Or the two cherubim are the two Testaments: they touch both walls because they are given to each people, and they touch one another [Col. 0872A] because each is in the other and they venerate Christ himself with equal harmony.

## TITLE VII. Concerning the same

“At the entrance of the oracle he made two little doors of olive wood” (3 Kings 6). These are love of God and of neighbour, because no one enters through the door of life without love. They are of olive wood so that they may shine with works of mercy. At the entrance of the Temple, likewise, were two doors of fir wood; each was double and opened, enclosing itself. As the entrance of the oracle calls to entrance into the kingdom, so the entrance of the Temple is the beginning of conversion by which we enter the Church. The latter belongs to faith, the former to hope. These are love of God and neighbour, which contain each other: one is not without the other. Each is double because of the working of faith. [Col. 0872B] The oracle’s little doors are not double because there we shall see what we believe, and shall need no labor where we receive the reward of labors.

On the walls and doors he carved cherubim, palms, reliefs, and various pictures. He makes cherubim when he teaches them to imitate the purity of angelic chastity; palms when he impresses upon their minds the memory of eternal recompense; diverse pictures protruding, as it were, from the wall when he grants them various actions of virtues that stand forth from them—for example, bowels of mercy, humility, patience, and so forth.

It should be noted that the house was built from stones hewn outside, because, while the house was being built, neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house. For here we are struck by adversities and trained by disciplines, so that there, when chastisement has ceased, we may be placed in fitting locations according to merit [Col. 0872C]—or rather, filled with the Spirit, joined to God. It should further be noted that those wishing to enter the Temple first found in the court a sea, that is, a basin for washing. Water flowed from it through twelve oxen. Then in the same court, at the entrance of the Temple, stood an altar on which flesh was sacrificed. In the Temple, near the door of the oracle, was a golden altar on which incense was burned. In the oracle, behind the veil, was the ark beneath the wings of the cherubim. By these things it is indicated that whoever wishes to enter the Holy of Holies—that is, heaven, where Christ is, and the glory of the angels—must first wash himself through repentance, mortify his flesh on the altar of burnt offerings, and, advancing at the altar of incense, send forward works of perfection, [Col. 0872D] and afterwards deserve entrance into the Holy of Holies.

## TITLE VIII. Concerning the same

Solomon caused the images of cherubim, lion, and ox to be painted upon the bases of the basins in the Temple (3 Kings 7). The bases in the Temple are the high priests in the Church, who receive the care of government, like separate bases, in order that they may bear the burden. Cherubim means fullness of knowledge, and this is rightly impressed upon the bases, since it is fitting that high priests be filled with fullness of knowledge. By the lion is signified the terror of truth; by the ox, the patience of gentleness. Therefore lions are not impressed upon the bases without oxen, nor oxen without lions, because priests ought to have gentleness and anger: in anger they should know how to moderate wrath, and in gentleness how to rouse it.

## TITLE IX. Concerning the candle and what is mystically contained in it

[Col. 0873A]

The candle is Christ. For there are three things in a candle: wax, wood, and fire. Wax is remarkably gathered not through intercourse but from the varied beauty of flowers. It is set around the wood; the wood is kindled by fire so that it may give light. Thus the wax signifies that flesh which, through the work of the Holy Spirit, was conceived from the Virgin without intercourse; the wood clothed in wax signifies Christ’s soul clothed in flesh; the fire by which it shines is divinity itself.

Or the candle is faith and action. For the candle has light, and wax is made through the great labor of bees, in which action is signified. The light is faith itself, which illuminates action. We ought to offer these two things to Christ as a child, so that he, the true light arisen for the illumination of the nations, may kindle in us the light of faith and may reward with eternal recompense the good [Col. 0873B] work given to us, by the light that is himself.

## TITLE X. Concerning the canonical hours in which the Lord’s Passion is commemorated; and first, concerning Prime

At the first hour, the Lord was spat upon, mocked, struck with blows, afflicted with reproaches, and bound before Pilate for our sake. At the same hour, risen again and standing on the shore, in the catching of the great and many fish by which the nets were not broken, and in sharing a honeyed meal with the disciples, he signified the Church as it will be in the resurrection of the dead. Therefore, before every care of the body, let us offer the first hour of the day to our Creator and Redeemer, who “was delivered up for our offences and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4). For we must first seek [Col. 0873C] the kingdom of God, and all else shall be added to us (Matt. 6); since in the Law the Lord also commands that every firstborn be offered to him (Exod. 13).

## TITLE XI. Concerning the canonical third hour

The third hour shines illustriously for a twofold reason. At this hour Jesus was crowned with thorns and crucified by those tongues of the Jews whose teeth are weapons and arrows and whose tongue is a sharp sword; though Pilate judged him to be released, they established for themselves an evil word (Ps. 63), crying, “Away with him!” and “Crucify him!” (Mark 15; Luke 23). And because the Holy Spirit, who had not been given for the remission of sins before Jesus was glorified, was poured out upon the nascent Church in tongues of fire at about the third hour [Col. 0873D].

## TITLE XII. Concerning the canonical ninth hour

The ninth hour is rightly celebrated in praise of the Lord, when Jesus, crying with a loud voice, gave up his spirit (Matt. 27); when, with the thief admitted into Paradise, forgiveness is dedicated to those who repent truly, though late; when, with the veil of Law and Prophets torn, we began to behold the glory of the Lord with unveiled face; and when Christ’s side was pierced and the elements for forming the Church flowed forth—his blood by which we are redeemed and water by which we are washed. There are, therefore, four reasons why we should celebrate this hour.

## TITLE XIII. Concerning Vespers and Matins

The sacrifice of evening and morning praise is consecrated by great mysteries. [Col. 0874A] In the Law a burnt offering is commanded to be offered continually in the evening and morning. In the evening, the Lord took bread and wine, made them present in the reality of his body and blood, was borne in his own hands, made his testament for his heirs, commending humility and charity by washing the disciples’ feet; and then, being about to die, in the solemnity of a long discourse bade final farewell to his friends and little children. Likewise, appearing alive in the evening, he is recognized in the breaking of bread and kindles the doubting hearts of the disciples with the fire of charity.

In the morning the crowing cock reproves Peter as he denies him; the Lord looks upon him, and the denier flees to tears of repentance. When the Lord’s resurrection is announced by the holy women, the sorrow of the faithful is changed to joy, because he who was dead shows himself alive and deigns to be touched and adored. [Col. 0874B] Note that although the other Hours have seven parts—that is, the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” with the doxology, hymn, psalms, reading, and concluding prayer—an eighth part is added to these Hours, namely the Gospel canticle, because it is sung for the octave in the blessedness of the resurrection, by which they are marked, according to the sense of the Gospel: “On the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns toward the first day of the Sabbath,” etc. (Matt. 28).

## TITLE XIV. Concerning the hour of Compline

The hour of Compline recalls to us from the Lord’s Passion that, after Judas had gone out, the Lord began to fear and be distressed; that, entering into agony, he prayed more earnestly, and, as drops of bloody sweat, alone trod the winepress, foreshadowing [Col. 0874C] the blood of martyrs to be shed in the future for him. It also recalls from his resurrection that, after making peace between God and human beings, he returned as a faithful ambassador and preached the Gospel to us, standing in the midst of the disciples and saying: “Peace be to you” (John 20).

## TITLE XV. Concerning the canonical night vigils

The radiance of evangelical grace established the night vigils of which the Prophet says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (Ps. 118). For the Lord is born at midnight. Likewise, like Samson once besieged, he rose from the dead at midnight after breaking the gates of hell; and he is declared to be coming at midnight, after the manner of the Egyptian time, when Passover was celebrated, the destroyer came, the Lord passed over the tabernacles, and the doorposts were consecrated by the lamb’s blood as a type of our foreheads [Col. 0874D].

“Therefore, I think,” says blessed Jerome, “that the apostolic tradition has endured, that on the day of the Paschal vigil the people awaiting Christ’s coming may not be dismissed before midnight; and when that time has come, all may celebrate the feast day in confident security.”

## TITLE XVI. Concerning prayer before readings

We precede the readings with prayer because we ought to ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest and to open our heart in his Law and commandments, lest the seed of the word we are about to hear either be eaten by birds, choked by thorns, or uprooted by the hardness of rock, its root having been frustrated.

## TITLE XVII. Concerning the blessing to be sought by the reader before the reading

[Col. 0875A]

The reader, requesting a blessing, signifies that no one, unless sent, ought to assume the office of preaching: “For how,” says the Apostle, “shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10). His saying at the end, “But you, O Lord, have mercy upon us,” indicates that the office of preaching can scarcely be performed without the dust of some slight fault. Since the feet of the evangelist walk, as it were, on earth and are defiled, he needs mercy to be washed in this respect, even if he is wholly clean.

That the choir responds, “Thanks be to God,” concerns not the reader’s prayer but the whole reading. For we give thanks because he breaks for us the bread of his teaching, lest we perish through hunger for God’s word. [Col. 0875B] Likewise, at readings at whose end “But you,” etc., is not said—namely, the short readings of the Hours—we cry out “Thanks be to God,” because the word of God is that by which every human being lives.

## TITLE XVIII. Concerning the significance of bells

Bells, like the legal trumpets, signify the holy preachers of the Church, who invite and prepare the people for Mount Zion, the holy city Jerusalem, and the future judgment of God; and who strive to bend the understanding of the deaf hearer to hear the greatness of the matter by the greatness of their speech. The hardness of the metal represents strength of mind; the iron clapper by which the sound is struck out represents constancy of speech: “Behold,” says the Lord, “I have made your forehead harder than their foreheads, and your face like adamant and flint” (Ezek. 3).

He should flee earthly habitation, saying, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3); he should raise his heart on high and, hanging from the tower of strength which stands against the face of the enemy, know that he has been stationed as a watchman over the house of Israel. [Col. 0875C] He should bear upon the summit of his mind the wood of the cross, and extend from it to weak brethren, as it were to the earth, the rope bound thereto—that is, the bond of charity—so that, urged by it, he may not cease to sound forth and open his mouth widely, saying: “The charity of Christ urges us” (2 Cor. 5).

Likewise, appointed as a guard upon the walls of Jerusalem (Isa. 62), he should not be silent, pressing his message in season and out of season. Those who sleep upon ivory beds (Amos 6), who are drunk by night and revel in their beds, and those who sleep by night [Col. 0875D] and are drunk by night, should be roused, as it were forcibly, to the praise of God, lest they perish buried in sleep until morning—that is, the dreadful judgment of God. The evangelical choir of preachers should imitate the threefold ringing of a solemn day—Matins, Vespers, and that rung at the beginning of Mass—so that it always proclaims the lamentations of the present life, the song of the future, and the woe of Gehenna’s wrath.

## TITLE XIX. Concerning the Sundays of Advent and their offices

The first coming is commemorated in the person of the ancient Church, that is, on the third Sunday. The second coming is announced as now imminent to those who await and desire it by prophetic and apostolic trumpets. The second coming is therefore set forth on two Sundays because the Church preceding [Col. 0876A] the first coming alone awaited the promised incarnation of the Lord; the second Church, both preceding and following, heard it. The former was instructed only by prophetic proclamations; the latter by prophetic and apostolic ones. Accordingly, in the second Sunday the prophetic office resounds: “People of Zion”; in the third, the apostolic: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Phil. 4).

The fourth Sunday, which looks toward the approaching day of the Nativity, commemorates the time when the Virgin’s womb, already pregnant and swollen, held the Lord near; and when the Lord, clothing himself in the Virgin’s body, bound upon himself the sandal-strap of his incarnation, which John confesses that he is unable to untie (John 1). Therefore it is called the vacant Sunday: it is so vacant of an office that none of the saints—all of whom are the officers of this King, Christ—[Col. 0876B] has been believed able to unfasten this strap of the King, that is, to unveil the mystery of the holy incarnation. Only that Idumaea, that is, the Gentile world, which had heard the promise, “I will stretch out my shoe over Idumaea” (Ps. 59), stands and looks upon the time when the King who made this promise, having gone forth from the Father’s bosom, was shod in the womb; and seeing that no one possesses the office of investigating this mystery, it indicates only the office of prayer, crying in the Introit: “Remember us, O Lord, in your good pleasure” (Ps. 105)—that is, in the Son alone, in whom you are well pleased, among the thousands of your people; “visit us with your salvation” (ibid.), namely with that same Son, who like a physician visits the sick by gratuitous [Col. 0876C] condescension.

## TITLE XX. Concerning the office of the first Sunday of Advent

The first Sunday, looking toward the first coming, has this purpose in its office: that so great a salvation may come to those to whom the Lord has not yet come—that is, those who have not received faith in the incarnation—that they may lift up their souls to God, and, trusting in the Lord, may not be put to shame or mocked by enemies, that is, demons; but that he may show them his ways and teach them his paths. The Apostle shows them how to walk in these ways, saying: “Knowing that it is the hour,” etc. (Rom. 13).

## TITLE XXI. Concerning the office of the second Sunday of Advent

On the second Sunday, a little and orphaned [Col. 0876D] son is born to a mother in exile. He has never seen his Father; hearing from his mother’s report that he has gone to heaven, he mourns his Father’s absence, desires his presence as a deer desires springs, strikes heaven with groans and prayers, and the compassionate mother sings the office of the second coming, comforting him by announcing that the return of the Father whom he longs for is near, and saying: “People of Zion, behold, the Lord will come to save the nations, and the Lord will make heard the glory of his voice,” by which he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25). “In the joy,” she says, “of your heart”—which will be so great that we ought to lift up our hearts. Thus in the Collect we pray: “Stir up, O Lord, our hearts,” that is, lift them up and make them joyful, to prepare the ways of your only-begotten Son.

On the third Sunday, too, [Col. 0877A] the apostolic voice proclaims the same thing: even if anyone is torn apart and endures persecutions and groans at the Father’s delay, he should rejoice in tribulations; and again rejoice, because of the abundant reward laid up in heaven, and be anxious about nothing, because the Lord is near to reward him. Only let his gentleness be known to all people, and let his petitions be made known to God (Phil. 4).

Note that at this time the deacon and subdeacon do not wear dalmatic and tunic, because the subdeacon, as the Law before the incarnation, lacked the adornment of the Gospel; and the deacon, as the Gospel itself, lay hidden, its great radiance not yet appearing before the mysteries of the incarnation, Passion, and resurrection. They do, however, wear chasubles, which they remove when they are to read, chiefly declaring that these are not their own garments, but that for reverence toward the Lord’s Day or some feast they receive them as a loan, so that they may console their poverty and unseemly nakedness. [Col. 0877B] For the same reason, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2) and “Go, the dismissal is made” are omitted, signifying both the time when the joy of peace was still awaited and the time in which we now anxiously await the consummation of our salvation.

## TITLE XXII. Concerning the two Masses in the night of the Lord’s Nativity and the one in the day

Two Masses are celebrated in the night of the Nativity: so that the Church may appoint the first Mass in honour of the birth by which God the Father begot him from the secret of his own substance, and sing the second in remembrance of that birth by which the blessed Son was believed, before the incarnation [Col. 0877C], to be about to come through the Virgin’s womb. The third is celebrated in the day, when she rejoices that he is not about to come but has come, and proclaims: “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9). The office of the first Mass expresses his eternal generation; the office of the second his future temporal dwelling; and the office of the third plainly demonstrates that this has taken place.

That two readings are read in these Masses signifies that the incarnate Lord is designated or prefigured by the two cherubim which look upon one another with faces turned toward the propitiatory. Therefore, at every Mass of this feast, two readings are read: one from the Old Testament, the other from the New, so that, while the Old announces that this was to be done and the New proclaims it done, the cherubim may as it were look upon each other; and, while they narrate in harmony the mystery of Christ’s dispensation, they may turn their faces toward the propitiatory and, as it were, behold the incarnate Lord between themselves. [Col. 0877D] Thus for the cherubim to look upon one another with faces turned toward the propitiatory is for the two readings from the two Testaments—the prophetic reading, in which the Word is preached as to come, and the evangelical reading, in which our propitiatory, the Word now incarnate, is preached—to look toward one another in harmonious testimonies and one and the same meaning.

## TITLE XXIII. That Alleluia is not sung in Septuagesima, and why

The chant *Alleluia*, of ancient authority and dignity, is removed from the mouth of holy Church during Septuagesima. Whatever Jesus Christ—the everlasting music and glory of [Col. 0878A] the Father, born from the heart of that eternal musician, to whom also belong psaltery and harp, as is said to him, “Arise, my glory, psaltery and harp” (Ps. 56)—offered to his hearers from eternal joy, whose eyes were blessed because they saw and whose ears because they heard; whatever, I say, the Lord Jesus preached with his own mouth concerning heavenly joys, that is our *Alleluia*: a new song, sweet praise. Yet the ancient holy Fathers did not see this. Hence: “Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke 10). Nor can we see or hear it while we are pilgrims from the Lord in the body.

Therefore, when we commemorate the lamentable state of the ancient Church not yet redeemed [Col. 0878B] and bewail our own exile because it has been prolonged, *Alleluia* is fittingly removed from our mouths. For by that *Alleluia* is signified what had not yet come to them, has departed from us, and has been taken away: the bridegroom from the sons. But on the day of resurrection, when a new offspring is reborn and young lambs that have come to the springs are filled with brightness, the new Church proclaims to the whole world new joys by this name: *Alleluia*.

## TITLE XXIV. Concerning the meaning of Septuagesima and Paschal joy
We call Septuagesima the seven Sundays that follow. On the first of them, wretched humanity, cast out from the happiness of paradise and from the face of its Creator, cries: “The groans of death surrounded me” (Ps. 17). On the seventh Sunday from Septuagesima, to one returning from this pilgrimage and from the valley of tears it is said: “Rejoice, Jerusalem.” We call it Septuagesima because the offices intimate the same thing as was signified by that seventy-year captivity of God’s people, who literally sat and wept beside the rivers of Babylon. It is not called Septuagesima from the seventy days that end at the Saturday on which the white garments are laid aside, since nothing could be more unsuitable than for captivity to be marked by the number within which falls the day of resurrection—the nobility of the year, the glory of the months, the dawn of days—on which, having conquered the captor, the victorious Lord rose and set all his own free. The same is to be said of Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, and Quadragesima.

## TITLE XXV. On the Office of Sexagesima

[Col. 0878D]

On Sexagesima, he whom “the pains of death surrounded” (Ps. 17), considering his misery, now begins to cry for deliverance, saying: “Rise up; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. 43). Therefore the Redeemer, taking pity on his calamity, “went out to sow good seed” (Matt. 13) in the soil of his heart; and for this reason the station at Saint Paul is altogether fitting. For, rising at the cry of the praying wretch, when he seemed to sleep, the sower of God’s word hires his ploughmen of heavenly wisdom, the holy apostles, and especially Saint Paul, who laboured more than all the rest: a useful workman, leader in the word, and truly a sower of words. Through him all nations learned [Col. 0879A] the grace of God which he sent to the Gentiles; and, cleaving hard hearts with the sharp ploughshare of his tongue, he poured out abundant seed of faith and morals.

Thus, when the priest enters, he makes in the Collect the celebrated commemoration of the Doctor of the Gentiles. Further, the following Epistle belongs to this theme, in which that same most valiant cultivator and labourer of heaven enumerates his true labours and the dangers inflicted upon him by those who had invaded his Lord’s borders and would not allow them to be tilled—those who, rebelling against the ruler of the whole earth, broke his plough and slaughtered his innocent oxen.

Once the teacher’s word has been sown abroad, the Gradual sings: “Let the nations now know that your name is God”; and those who rejected it “were made like a wheel”: rising in things behind, that is, in carnal matters, they fall in things before, [Col. 0879B] that is, in intellectual matters; and, as before the face of the wind, they perished when the spirit of God’s wrath blew. In the Tract it gives thanks to the sower because the earth was shaken and troubled—that is, all sinners, perceiving their detestable cultivations, were stirred to repentance; and, beginning to fear through the signification of preaching, they flee from the face of the bow, that is, of the divine judgment. In that bow, with the two Testaments bent like two horns, rebels against the divine word shall be struck by the sentence of condemnation.

After the Gospel has been read, it prays in the Offertory: “Perfect my steps” (Ps. 118). For one must fear lest the seed of God’s word that has been received, if it falls beside the way—that is, among those occupied with outward things—be snatched away by the birds of unclean spirits; or be choked by thorny riches; or wither for want of the moisture [Col. 0879C] of charity; and so our steps may not be made perfect. In the Offertory itself God’s mercies are requested: that God may guard his seed as the pupil of the eye, lest it be pierced by choking thorns (Luke 8); may protect it beneath the shadow of his wings, lest it be dried by the sun’s heat, that is, by burning avarice; and may rescue it from the wicked one, lest he take the word from our hearts—so that the good ground, bringing forth fruit in patience, may say: “But I shall appear in righteousness before your countenance” (Ps. 16).

The Communion says the same. “I will go in,” it says, “to the altar of God” (Ps. 42). For God’s seed bears upward with itself to the barns of heaven our earth, in which that which is mutable has grown. Since we are earth, unless we are borne by the word of God, which is Christ, we do not ascend to heaven, as he himself says: “No one ascends to heaven except …” (John 3), and so forth. Raised up with him and through him, and bearing sheaves of righteousness, we shall rejoice, God renewing our youth by the vigour of eternal newness.

## TITLE XXVI. On the Office of Quinquagesima

On Quinquagesima, the one who, considering his calamity, had cried from the depths to the Lord on the preceding Sunday, that he might rise and not cast him away forever, sees his captivity and the devil stirring against him the whole army of vices—from whom everyone who wishes to live devoutly suffers persecution (2 Tim. 3). Hearing the words addressed to him, “My son, if you wish to turn to the Lord, prepare your soul for temptations” (Ecclus. 2), he implores the protection [Col. 0880A] of God his helper, saying: “Be to me a protecting God” (Ps. 30), and so forth.

And because he can do nothing without him—for it depends neither on one who runs nor on one who wills, but on God who shows mercy—that he, though blind, may himself see and do good, he prays for this same thing in the Collect. To the Lord saying to him in the Gospel, “What do you want me to do for you?” (Mark 10), he answers: “Lord, that I may see” (ibid.). In the Epistle also the Apostle undertakes the care of illuminating this same blind man, when he shows a way more excellent than all gifts, namely charity: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels,” he says, “but have not charity, I have become as sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 13).

For charity is the light and eye of the heart. Whoever lacks it is blind, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going. God also began to illuminate the blind human race by giving faith to the children of Israel. With this first eye-salve he anointed its eyes, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God,” and so forth (Matt. 22). The Gradual makes known among the nations the power of the illuminator for this illumination. For this reason also the Tract says: “Enter into his presence,” as though it said: “Draw near and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). For this reason likewise we give thanks in the Offertory, saying: “Blessed …,” and so forth. But because it is not enough to have received the illumination of knowledge unless we cast off carnal desires, we are fittingly frightened by the example of those of whom we say in the Communion: “They ate and were satisfied” (Ps. 77).

## TITLE XXVII. On the Office of Quadragesima

In Quadragesima the Church cries in the office as though in the person of the Deliverer saying to the one who calls upon him: “Behold, I am here”: “He shall call upon me, and I will hear him,” and so forth. Accordingly, throughout all that follows, it recounts that Christ, while fasting, overcame the snares of the tempter; that he walked upon the asp and basilisk, and trampled the lion and dragon underfoot—promising us, the body of that same head, the same victory.

But because the Scripture of the prophets who spoke these things was closed until the coming of Christ and the time of his passion—because there was “dark water in the clouds of the air,” that is, hidden knowledge in the prophets—until the Lamb of God, alone worthy to unseal the book, opened the prophetic utterances by fulfilling in his passion the things signified by them: for this reason, from this Sunday onward, veils are hung before the altars [Col. 0880D] of holy Church, so that the people may not see the Holy of Holies until, in the week before Easter, the removal of the veils reveals the same signification which was accomplished when the veil of the temple was torn as the Lord yielded up his spirit.

## TITLE XXVIII. On Ash Wednesday, at the Beginning of the Fast

At the beginning of the fast, there would be no need to sprinkle the head with ashes or to walk barefoot, if we all possessed knowledge of mourning and if all alike understood what the reproaching prophet says: “The crown of our head has fallen; woe to us, because we have sinned!” (Lam. 5); and if all were ready to do what is said: “Rend your hearts and not your garments” (Joel 2).

But now the greater part of us do not willingly remember what adornment of the head—that is, of the heart—they lost by offending God. Nor can lukewarm hearts easily be rent unless we are aided by outward signs. Therefore, that we may remember that we are dust, that our father forgot what we were when he cast away God, his crown, and thereafter perceived his nakedness, we sprinkle our heads with ash and bare our lowest parts. By this attire we confess that we are neither gods nor from heaven, but human beings, having our beginning from the earth; and that, stripped of our glory through sins and set naked among enemies, we need the adornment of God’s glory.

## TITLE XXIX. On Beginning Penance on the Same Day

At the beginning of the fast ashes and haircloth, the weapons of penitents, are set before us. In the haircloth there is a remembrance of pricking sins: so that sin may not delight us, but prick and strike us, and admonish us to punishment. It is therefore made from goats’ hair, because goats used to be offered for sin.

Ash signifies that the devil’s edifice, formerly built badly within us, ought to have been burned down, and that the heat of sin in us has grown cold. Therefore the unclean person in the Law who was washed with water was not completely cleansed until evening, that is, until the heat had subsided. Nor is it without reason that ash is customarily made from vine-branches, rather than indiscriminately from any woods. Branches of the vine are more valuable than any wild trees because they are fruitful and bring forth precious fruit. But unfruitful branches are more worthless than the rest, because they are fit for no construction, but only for the fire, to burn. So also Christians cut off from Christ the vine are punished all the more grievously, the more abundantly [Col. 0881C] they have abused God’s benefits.

## TITLE XXX. On the Office of the Second Sunday, Which Is Vacant

The Second Sunday of Quadragesima is vacant and has no office except what it borrows from elsewhere. This indicates that, after divine help has been implored and granted us, we are vacant from our own works, making no provision for the flesh in its desires; but, being free from vices, we abstain even from our customary uses, so that we may attribute this not to ourselves but to the mercy of our God.

For in the borrowed Introit we ask him to remember his mercies, lest our enemies ever rule over us; and in the Gradual, that he may deliver us from necessities: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 24); “Have mercy on me according to your word,” and so forth (Ps. 118). In the Offertory and likewise [Col. 0881D] in the Communion: “Understand my cry” (Ps. 5). These are borrowed from a day of fasting because the sufferings of evil desire, signified by the demon-possessed daughter of the Canaanite woman—for whom that great woman, the mother Church, cries aloud as for every sinful soul—are not cast out except through prayer and fasting.

## TITLE XXXI. On the Third Sunday of Quadragesima

On the third Sunday, the Church, now freed and intent only upon divine things, has her eyes fixed upon God, saying in the Introit to the Lord: “My eyes are toward the Lord” (Ps. 24). And in the Tract she rejoices: “To you I have lifted up my soul” (Ps. 85), glad because in the Gospel the unclean spirit has gone out from her, and the stronger one, Christ, coming upon the strong devil, has taken his goods—that is, the human beings whom he possessed in peace—and distributed his weapons (Luke 11).

Therefore in the Offertory she proclaims the Lord’s judgments to be righteous: because the demon cast out from her was permitted to return to the one from whom it had gone out, that is, the Jewish people. In the Communion she rejoices that, like a sparrow, she has found herself a house, and, like a turtledove, a nest (Ps. 83), so that she may be with the blessed who dwell in the house of the Lord and who will praise him for ages of ages; or as though celebrating the Sabbath after the work of six days.

## TITLE XXXII. On the Sunday “Laetare,” Which Is the Fourth

The Sunday on which “Rejoice, Jerusalem” is sung in the Introit signifies, from Septuagesima onward, the Sabbath of the world: that is, the rest in which the souls of the elect, having laid down the burden of flesh, rejoice in leisure like victors after battle who have laid aside their arms. Adorned with their single robes, that is, with the blessedness of the soul, they await the resurrection in which they will receive the twofold glory of soul and body.

There Jerusalem which is above, the mother of all, rejoices; keeping festival for the multitude of her children returning from the pilgrimage of this world, she spreads the feasts laid up in store and pours out from her breasts the milky delights of maternal consolation. In proclamation of this consolation, the rejoicing address of the Holy Spirit is first sent to her through the prophetic mouth: “Rejoice, Jerusalem,” and so forth. And the consolation sung here is: “You shall be filled from the breasts of her consolation.” In the Collect is sought the consolation that is God’s freedom; which the Apostle sets forth in the Epistle: “That Jerusalem,” he says, “which is above is free” (Gal. 4). This is “peace in your strength and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121).

Of it we sing in the Gradual: “Rejoicing in the things which were said” (Ps. 121) to us by the holy apostles and our teachers, “we shall go into the house of the Lord” (ibid.). When we have come there, what is said in the Tract will be fulfilled: “He who dwells in Jerusalem shall not be moved forever” (Ps. 74). For the rod—that is, the power—of sinners will be taken away; though the Lord permits it for a time as a trial, he will not leave it over the land of the righteous.

This joy also belongs to that life-giving banquet of the saints, at which the Lord in the Gospel satisfies five thousand people with five loaves and two fishes: that is, the banquet at which, from the books of Paul, Moses, and the prophets, the abundance of the divine blessing increases among the mouths of those eating—that is, among the studies of those expounding—and the world, formerly fasting from knowledge of God, is abundantly refreshed. With our storehouses filled by the abundance of sayings, we weary guests stand by. This banquet of divine knowledge begins here; it will be perfected in the everlasting glory of that Sabbath of which we speak. Hence the Apostle says: “Now we know in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13).

Therefore in the Offertory he blesses the guests rejoicing in feasts of praise, and the father of the banquet himself: the one blessed from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. Thus, beginning from the present Church which is called Zion—that is, “watchtower,” in which we now see through a mirror—we begin to sound forth the Lord’s praise, and may be perfected in that heavenly Jerusalem in which he himself dwells. According to the mystical sense of the Communion, that Jerusalem is still built as a city from living and chosen stones: “the tribes of the Lord went up,” that is, noble tribes, royal tribes, priestly tribes.

## TITLE XXXIII. On Passion Sunday

Having shown on the preceding seven Sundays how one ascends from the valley of tears and lamentation to the city of delights and glorification, the celebration of Passion Sunday begins, so that the greatness of the divine mercy by which this is attained may be set before the eyes of all; and so that the wounds and all the tokens of death endured for all by the one salvation, God and man, Christ, the Only-Begotten of the Father, may be impressed upon the devout minds of believers.

For we constantly meditate in nocturnal as well as diurnal chants upon the advancing standards of the cross and its radiant mystery: the vinegar, gall, reed, nails, and lance that pierced his body. Thus the hair of the Church’s head—that is, the thoughts of its heart—becomes like royal purple dipped in channels, while it meditates on the Redeemer’s passion in the authoritative Scriptures: that is, in the precious purple dyes which flowed, the Holy Spirit producing them, through the mouths of prophets and apostles as through certain channels.

He who commanded the children of Israel: “Whenever you go out to war or hold feast days, you shall sound trumpets over our holocausts and peace offerings” (Num. 10)—he, our King, about to go out to the warfare of his passion against the devil, prince of this world; he, our high priest, about to hold the banquet of his own body and blood and to celebrate with his disciples the feast of his holy resurrection—sounds the trumpet of the great miracle of Lazarus raised from the dead, by which he also encouraged devout hearts to believe. Hence they go out to meet him with palms and praises; while the enemies, namely the chief priests and Pharisees, disturbed, assembled a council against Jesus, saying: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him continue thus, all will believe in him” (John 11).

And because from that hour they were devising how to seize him, he no longer walked openly before them. When they took up stones to throw at him, “he hid himself and went out of the temple” (John 8), as the high priest of future good things, as is found in the Epistle—not for those who, as the Tract says, “often attacked him from his youth,” that is, from the beginning in the blood of righteous Abel; and attacked him again by killing the prophets and stoning those sent to them.

With our head withdrawing, we begin to restrain the voice of joy and praise, omitting “Glory be to the Father” in some—though brief—versicles. For the glory of the Holy Trinity is its proper praise. Therefore, by its not being said, it signifies the solitude and silence of our head, who no longer walked openly.

## TITLE XXXIV. On the Saturday of Palm Branches

The Saturday before Palm Sunday is vacant because the lord pope gives alms. This is the Sabbath on which the Lord came to Bethany and dined in the house of Lazarus, whom he had raised; there Mary Magdalene washed his feet and wiped them with her hair (Luke 7), as the Evangelist relates: “Six days before the Passover,” he says (John 12), and so forth.

There, by a celebrated mystery, the fragrant work of almsgiving was commended. Mary—that is, the Church—wipes the Lord’s feet, that is, the poor, the lowest members of Christ, with hair that is superfluous to the body: that is, she supports them with the riches that abound to the rich. Therefore, in order that the lord pope may present to the Lord the celebrated supper with Mary, on this Saturday he gives alms and is thus occupied about the Lord’s feet.

## TITLE XXXV. On Palm Sunday

Palm Sunday, on which the Lord entered Jerusalem to suffer, was the tenth day of the moon, because the Law commanded that on the tenth day the lamb should be taken and kept to be sacrificed on the fourteenth.

Observe that Moses struck Pharaoh and Egypt with ten plagues by means of the rod. Pharaoh was indeed afflicted by them, but was not conquered until the lamb was sacrificed. For Christ, by the discipline of the Law as by a rod, commands God’s people to resist their captor by the ten commandments, as though by ten plagues. The devil held captive in the Egypt of this world the people of God, who had been created in the freedom of paradise. But just as Pharaoh was not so conquered by ten plagues that he released the children of Israel, so neither was the devil so overcome by observance of the ten commandments that humanity returned to paradise.

But when Christ, the Lamb of God, was sacrificed, the firstborn of Pharaoh—that is, original sin—was destroyed; and in the Red Sea of baptism, made red by Christ’s blood, actual sins also, along with that other sin, were utterly swallowed up, and God’s people were set free. Thus Christ, the true Lamb, obedient to the Father’s command, was received into the city of Jerusalem on the tenth moon with palm branches, in order to suffer. Hence, after the procession of palms, his passion is read.

This procession foreshadows what benefit lies in his blood and what fruit of his passion comes from that mercy in the multitude of which he came blessed. From the Mount of Olives he first sends two into the village opposite them, so that, loosing the ass and colt tied there, they may bring them to him. For he was to ascend, crowned with glory and honour because of his passion, to the right hand of the Father: who is the God of peace, the source and origin of light, the Mount of Olives, the Father of mercies. From there, giving gifts to men, he was to send the apostles, who, having received the power of binding and loosing, would free the ass and colt—that is, both peoples—from error and the burden of sin; and, sitting upon the human race brought to him through faith, would lead it into the heavenly Jerusalem, while crowds of angels came to meet him in praise, raising victories symbolized by palms along with olive branches, the emblems of peace.

This must not be counted as one act with the Sunday procession. For we do not commemorate the joy of the Lord’s resurrection, by which he signified to us that we ought to go out with the apostles into Galilee—that is, into “transmigration”—to see the Lord, so that we may not be old but may walk in newness of life (Rom. 6). Therefore, in such a procession we always follow our prelates going before us, as though following the Lord into Galilee; and we rightly call Galilee the place at which we conclude the procession with the final station.

Hence also in these processions, in order that we may rejoice with the Virgin Mother at the resurrection of her only-begotten Son, who now dies no more—and in whose passion a sword passed through her soul—we commemorate her, singing at one station what is proper to her, even at the lodging customarily provided for her in the cloister; and, having greeted her, we thereafter complete the procession as usual.

The first procession of palms, however, presents not the joy of the resurrection but the sacrament of the fruit of the Lord’s passion; and, as has been said, that final procession of the Lord is prefigured by it. Since, therefore, the procession of palms is the sacrament of the fruit of that passion of the Lord, and on this day he came obedient to the Father to drink the cup of his passion, rightly his passion is first read with the same palm branches with which he was received; and there follows the whole office of the passion, in which God, in the uttermost humility of humanity, is mocked, spat upon, gives his back to the strikers, prays for his enemies, and patiently endures the rest in obedience to the Father. Paul openly sets these things before us for imitation in the Epistle, saying: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus,” and so forth (Phil. 2).

## TITLE XXXVI. On the Tuesday after Palm Branches

After Palm Sunday, the reading of the passion is preceded on Tuesday by that Lesson which displays the counsels of those plotting Christ’s death, saying: “Come, let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. 11). During these days, until Wednesday, their efforts burned more intensely, yet they feared lest an uproar should arise among the people.

For just as the most arrogant Haman, having erected the cross which he had prepared for Mordecai, sought an opportunity to suggest to the king that Mordecai should be seized and hanged, so the devil, having formed a counsel in his own house—that is, in the hearts of the Jews—saying, “Come, let us put wood into his bread,” sought an opportunity to deliver Jesus to Roman authority.

We therefore see his vengeance in being pierced upon that same wood. But we are Jews with Esther—that is, the Church—set free, as the Epistle says; and therefore “we ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6), which was raised from the punishment of criminals to the brow of the emperor. The remaining words that follow are those of Christ in his agony, praying for his own resurrection.

### On the Wednesday of the Same Holy Week

On Wednesday, when Judas went and agreed with the Jews to betray the head of the Church, she hears his passion, in which he is remembered to have prayed at greater length in his agony, having fallen upon his knees; and, trembling at his sweat flowing down like drops of blood, she, beholder of so great miracles, cries out as if astonished by a sudden cry: “At the name of the Lord let every knee bend” (Phil. 2). With this terrible cry she strikes human hearts, so that no one may dare to remain erect and proud when he sees the Lord of human beings and angels fall down and struggle in the sweat of his face.

Once the Introit has been spoken with a cry, Isaiah, the most eager spectator of this Lord’s passion, immediately runs up as if present. In the reader’s voice he summons us to behold that agony, saying: “Tell the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Saviour comes” (Isa. 62). To show the work of the passion upon which he was intent and the reward of glory with which he was to be crowned, he adds: “Behold, his reward is with him and his work before him” (ibid.).

Marvelling also at his appearance, he says: “Who is this that comes from Edom”—that is, from the bloody and earthly Jews—“with garments,” that is, members which are the clothing of the Godhead, “dyed crimson with blood, from Bosra” (Isa. 63), which is interpreted “strong,” that is, from the city of Jerusalem, which God had made strong more by his help than by walls. When he has answered: “I who speak righteousness” (ibid.), Isaiah asks again: if you speak righteousness, why is your garment red with the pressure of the cross? “I have trodden the winepress alone,” he answers (ibid.), for all people.

Having heard this, the choir, knowing its Lord’s agony, prays in its own person in the Gradual, saying: “Do not turn away,” and so forth.
