After the second Lesson is proclaimed, hearing that he had neither form nor beauty, was despised and the last of men, wounded for our iniquities (Isa. 53), and the other things there narrated, it comes about that, on no day except Friday in the Ember Saturdays, not Alleluia, which is used during the days of Pentecost, nor the Gradual, but the Tract follows.

For that musician who said, “We played for you and you did not dance; we lamented and you did not weep” (Luke 7)—to whose lamentation the Gradual corresponds as the weeping of penance, and to whose music the Alleluia corresponds as dancing—is heard in that utterance as taken away from us. Therefore there follows neither the Alleluia of joy nor the Gradual of any sort of mourning, but the Tract, with much sorrow. That the Tract rather than the Gradual is appropriate to mourning is shown by the fact that, in the days of Quadragesima in which we mourn that death entered the world through envy, it is sung not as Alleluia is sung in the Gradual, but in place of the Alleluia of the Gradual.

Further, it comes about that, with Good Friday, only one Lesson is read in all things, to express greater mourning: because on Wednesday only he was sold, while he remained with the disciples; but on Good Friday he is utterly taken away and crucified.

## TITLE XXXVII. On the Office at the Lord’s Supper, Especially on the Chrism Then Instituted

[Col. 0886D]

Among the mournful hours, in which we cut off the heads—that is, their beginnings—and hide their endings in silence, the celebrated and more solemn Mass of the day of the Lord’s Supper exults, as the sun sometimes glows red amid clouds. The reason is this: because on this day the high priest himself, himself the victim, handed down the true sacrifice and instituted the rite of sacrifice, taking bread and the cup and saying, “This is my body” (Matt. 26), and, “This is my blood” (ibid.). Offering himself first to God as the typical lamb, he inscribed the New Testament for his heirs in his own blood.

Rightly, therefore, amid the sorrow marked through all the hours, the Mass merits a solemn harmony and joyous adornment of the ministers of the altar, as on the day of its institution. And lest anything of beauty be lacking to the holy sacrifice, “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2) is sung, and all the vesture of the pontiff is completed.

Hence on this day the pope blesses oil, makes chrism, and reconciles penitents, signifying that the high priest, by the oil of mercy, loosens for penitents their sins as certain bonds, while by chrism he performs the role not only of comforter but also of protector. For chrism is oil with balsam: that is, the Holy Spirit, comforter and protector.

Formerly only kings and priests were anointed, by which Christ, the future highest king and priest, was prefigured. But after he came in person, anointed by God the Father above his fellows, not only kings and priests but the whole Church is consecrated by the anointing of chrism. In confirmation this was given only by bishops, as is clear from the Lesson in which the Holy Spirit was given through Paul’s hand to the baptized (Acts 19), and Peter and John were sent to Samaria so that the baptized might receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8). Hence it is understood that this is lawful only for bishops, the vicars of the apostles.

Yet, because of the contingency of death, lest the baptized depart without any anointing through the bishop’s absence, Pope Sylvester decreed that priests should anoint the baptized at the same time, but on the crown of the head, not on the forehead. Nor should you say: “What does the mystery of confirmation avail, as though we did not receive everything from the font, by the addition of a new kind?” It must not be understood thus. For what does it avail to provide a great inheritance for a little child and not give him a guardian?

The Paraclete, therefore, is for those reborn in Christ a comforter, keeper, and guardian. He comforts by forgiving sins with the oil of mercy, conferring virtues, and promising good things; he protects by driving enemies away with the fragrance of balsam and confirming them in good. With this chrism we are marked upon our foreheads, as on both doorposts, by the blood of the true Lamb, so that the destroying devil may possess no right to harm our soul or body.

Thus, fleeing the true Pharaoh and making our way to God through the sea of baptism, when Pharaoh has been drowned, we may celebrate in our homes, with the voice of Paschal exultation and confession, the feast of the Lamb, saying: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us feast” (1 Cor. 5).

That the flask of chrism appears only in the middle before it comes to the altar signifies Christ, in whom the sacrament of his body was then instituted, containing the fullness of the Holy Spirit: he concealed his beginning—that he was born of the Virgin—and his end—that by his death he would destroy death—before he came to the altar of the cross. Only the middle appeared, that is, the miracles he performed between beginning and end, in which it was proven that he was God. But upon the very altar of the cross his beginning and end appeared, so that it could now be said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15).

That the host is visibly saluted by the ministers of the altar but invisibly and veiledly by the rest signifies that after Easter he showed himself visibly to the witnesses of his resurrection. That he is saluted invisibly by the others signifies that Christ, returning to heaven from which he came, as he says, “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16), is not bodily seen by us, though we daily salute him in veneration.

## TITLE XXXVIII. On the Mystery in the Washing of Feet

The Lord instructs us in a twofold sense, namely moral and historical, when he rises from supper, lays aside his garments, girds himself with a towel, pours water into a basin, and washes the disciples’ feet.

Historically, by giving us an example so that we may do as he did, he humbles our pride. For how can we, who are dust and ashes, not blush to raise stiff neck and erect bearing in contempt of our equals, when we have heard that the Creator of heaven and earth bent his knees and stooped to the ground in order to wash the disciples’ feet?

Here too is a moral sacrament of piety: Christ rose from the supper of paternal glory, laid aside the purple of his dominion, emptied himself, girded himself with earthly flesh as with a towel—whose material springs from the earth—and poured the water of baptism or penance, or his own blood as water, into the basin. Whenever we receive it for the remission of sins, he daily washes our feet, that is, our actions. Though we have once been washed and are wholly clean through baptism by faith, if we disdain to have our feet washed in this manner, we shall have no part with him. For, he says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves,” and so forth (John 6).

The apostolic reading fittingly precedes this Gospel reading. In it, when it says, “When you come together,” and so forth (1 Cor. 11), it shows how we are washed by this sacrament: “Let a person first prove himself, and so let him eat” (ibid.). For from defilements we are purified by nothing better than by approaching this table in purity while hating our sins.

By this same act he prohibited the prelates of churches from ruling and being served after the manner of the kings of the Gentiles; rather, after the manner of servants, they are to wash feet and minister to others. But where subjects become like beasts, ancient authority permits prelates to rule over them. Where persons live rationally, even if they have soiled their feet with the dust of venial sins, the evangelical person is not to know himself as their superior, but humbly submits himself to wash their feet and offer them the kiss.

## TITLE XXXIX. On Performing the Twofold Mandatum

On the very day of the Lord’s Supper a person customarily performs two mandata: that of the poor and that of the community.

In the first, Mary, receiving Christ in Bethany, rose from supper for the banquet; taking a pound of ointment, she anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment. This woman bore the type of the Church, which, anointing the Lord’s feet—that is, nourishing the poor with alms—wipes them with hair when it supports them from what is superfluous.

This mandatum, therefore, is the Church’s act of service; and thus the whole community washes the poor’s feet. Like Mary, it invites Christ to supper in Bethany when it receives in the house of obedience the poor, in whom Christ is present, by rendering the office of charity. Rising from supper, as though breaking the fast, it brings a pound of ointment when, rising from the table after a small taste, it directs its intention toward almsgiving fragrant with Christ.

This is called the mandatum of the poor, belonging to the Church; the mandatum of the community, however, belongs to Christ. Therefore in the first the whole community serves; in the second only the prelates serve in Christ’s place. The Church beautifully goes before its Lord in its mandatum, so that before Christ washes the disciples’ feet, Christ’s disciples themselves may wash Christ’s feet—that is, the poor—and anoint them with the ointment of almsgiving; so that the house in which Christ is, at the hour when he has washed feet through our prelates, may be filled with the fragrance of this ointment.

## TITLE XL. On the Office of the Three Nights, Namely at the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, and on the Following Saturday
In the night of the Lord’s Supper, when Christ is betrayed; and on the night of the Preparation, when he is crucified; and on the night of the Sabbath, when he is in the tomb: canons and monks celebrate the vigils in the customary order of nine lessons, and complete them in darkness, signifying the offices of Christ’s three-day death and showing that the vigils themselves are assigned to mourning for Christ’s death, since they differ little or not at all from the Office of the Dead. Therefore, in all the Hours we cut off the beginnings and conceal the endings in silence, because he who is the beginning and the end, alpha and omega, has during these days been taken from us, handed over into the hands of sinners and cast among the wicked. The *Glory be to the Father* [Col. 0889C] is entirely omitted, for the same reason that in certain places it began to be omitted from Passion Sunday onward: because from then Christ began to be sought for death. The fact that the candles are extinguished one by one when each psalm or lesson has ended represents the deed of the Jews, who killed, one by one, the prophets who went before the Sun that was to rise and shone with prophetic speech, once they had fulfilled the offices of prophecy. But the candle which illuminated the Gospel while it was being read is extinguished last, though it is no larger than the others: for Christ, who preached the Gospel, was reckoned as one of the prophets, was the last to be killed, and, when extinguished, left them in the deep darkness of error and unbelief. Hence, when the Lord was crucified, darkness came over the whole earth (Luke 23).

## TITLE XLI. On the mystical rekindling of the extinguished fire during this period.

[Col. 0889D]

When the fire has been lost, during these same three days we resort to Christ the stone, so that, striking it, we may draw forth hidden fire; or we set a crystalline stone before the sun and place tinder beneath it, so that by the sun’s rays passing through the crystal the extinguished coals may revive. The struck stone gives forth fire when Christ, the cornerstone, struck by the blow of the cross, poured out upon us the Holy Spirit. This is sufficiently shown in the prayer for blessing that same fire. The crystal, placed between the sun and the extinguished coals, is the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), who, intervening between God and extinguished human beings, conveys to us from God the Father, through himself, the fire which, as he himself testifies, he came to cast so that it might burn (Luke 12). Therefore, if through sin we have lost Christ’s light, let us go out in solemn procession, for the blessing of the new fire, outside the camp, bearing his reproach, and believing in him whom the Jews extinguished in themselves from this present life.

## TITLE XLII. On the increasing sorrow of the Church as the Lord’s Passion draws near.

Then, as evening approaches, greater increments of sorrow follow: the altars are stripped, the bells fall silent, a mournful silence engulfs all the Hours except the nocturnal ones. The altar is laid bare, while Christ—that altar which Moses was commanded to make of earth—is set before our mind as without form or beauty, so that, seeing him stripped for our sake, we may say with the prophet: “Behold, we saw him having neither form nor beauty. Truly he bore our infirmities” (Isa. 53), etc. He who was “beautiful in form above the sons of men” (Ps. 44 [45]) emptied himself, stripped of every honor—not divine honor only, but also human honor, when he was spat upon and suffered other things. This altar is washed with water and wine by means of rough branches, because Christ is believed to have offered us the water of cleansing and the wine of redemption through harsh scourges. We impose silence upon the bells, signifying the holy heralds of Christ, who, fired by the flame of charity and formed by divine instruction, dwelling continually under God’s heavenly protection as in a tower of strength, are moved by a certain cord of heavenly love, so that throughout day and night they do not cease to praise the Lord’s name—namely, the holy [Col. 0890C] apostles, who then not only fell silent but also fled. Thus that mighty bell, Peter, whose voice saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16), went forth into all the earth, was then not merely restrained but fled, and sounded hoarsely in his denial.

When these signs cease, we signify Christ treading the winepress alone, and, stretched out bodily on the wood of the cross, sounding as on a drum by means of a wooden mallet suspended against a board, inviting the people to church. This silence also signifies the silence of the apostles in the Hours. The nocturnal offices, however, are sung not in silence but in a louder voice, because one time is signified by day and another by night. For in the daytime Hours we signify the presence of the Lord’s Passion; in the night Hours, the earlier events by which the prophets openly foretold that same coming Passion—five of whom were slain without keeping silent. As we prolong their voices, the candles are extinguished; the last candle, which is extinguished at the Gospel canticle, signifies the Lord himself, who was killed while preaching the Gospel, so that, once he is extinguished, we may thereafter be silent during the day in sorrow for his death.

## TITLE XLIII. Why the Preparation should be celebrated with grief rather than joy; and on the penance then to be performed, and on the Passion according to John.

On the day of the Preparation, we ought to glory in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (Gal. 6), and in the grace of so great a price given for our redemption; and with a pure and devout mind we ought to adore and venerate that cross [Col. 0891A]. But why do we refrain from the celebration of Masses and cease from public rejoicing, when the Lord’s Passion, accomplished on this day, is the beginning and completion of our salvation? For just as the day on which an individual martyr passed through suffering into glory is festive for us, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115 [116]), so this day, on which the King of all martyrs and saints opened paradise through his death to all saints, ancient and new, and shattered the bars of hell, ought rightly to be honored with still greater joys.

Yet certain profoundly painful matters overshadow this glory and exultation of ours: for the commanding love of the Holy Trinity, for our sake consigned to death a man of such reverence—who is one person with God the Word—an innocent man owing nothing to death, as the Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). Therefore we ought not so to rejoice in the grace of the one delivered up or in the love of the one dying that we do not grieve that we were the cause of torments to so great a Lord; and therefore we refrain from the joys of sacrifice. For not to grieve is recognized as ingratitude, while to rejoice beyond measure is cruelty. Therefore on this sorrowful day let us share sorrow unto repentance. Let the iron of the Lord’s spear pass through our soul; let the nails in his hands and feet pierce our flesh; let the cross suspend our desire. Let us suffer with him, that we may reign with him.

Today let us not offer sacrifice while the victim is taken from our hands; let not friends offer sacrifice while enemies slaughter him. Let it be deferred until that day when so great a victor, rising again, announces his victory to us. Meanwhile let us keep a profound silence friendly to grief, and, entering the inward solitude and taking off our shoes from our feet with Moses, let us hear him speaking as though from the midst of the bush: “Seeing, I have seen the affliction of my people, and I have come down to deliver them” (Exod. 3). For now he clings, as it were, to a bush of thorns, fastened with nails and crowned with thorns; and the shrub of the cross buds forth with the blood-red drops of death, so that, as Prudentius says:

> . . . . sorrowful faults may be cleansed by blood,  
> which the twisted bush brings forth amid dense torments.

(PRUDENTIUS, *Apotheosis*, vv. 69–70, *Patrologia*, vol. LIX.) [Col. 0891D]

On this day the Passion according to John is read, because he wrote last and was present—for, being known to the high priest, he was there when the others did not dare to be present. To him, himself a virgin, the Lord, himself a virgin, entrusted the Virgin Mother.

## TITLE XLIV. On the tasting of wine mixed with gall.

The fact that, when he had tasted vinegar mixed with gall, he would not drink, signifies his rejection of the vineyard of his own Jewish people, from which he expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes and at last mixed in bitterness. Having tasted it only slightly, he thereafter did not care to drink for three days from the fruit of that vine. For, rising from the dead, he dies no more (Rom. 6).

## TITLE XLV. On the purple or scarlet cloak.

[Col. 0892A]

The fact that he is clothed in a scarlet cloak, of the fiery color offered in the tabernacle and read of in the twice-dyed garment of the priest, signifies the twofold love by which, obedient to the Father, he drank the cup of suffering for us because of his exceeding charity; so that we too, following in his footsteps, may shine in this twofold garment of discernment, and whatever we offer, as though set aflame and richly colored, may please the divine gaze.

## TITLE XLVI. On the reed placed in Christ’s hand.

He did not refuse to receive the reed from those mocking him, so that he might write down the sacrilege of the Jews, destroy venomous creatures, and show that he had the rod in his hand—that is, his soul in his own power—so that he might lay it down and take it up again at will; and so that, as Moses’ rod [Col. 0892B] was changed into a serpent—that is, into death, which came through a serpent—it might take up the serpents of Egypt, that is, the deaths of sinners, and then return again into a rod, that is, into its former power.

## TITLE XLVII. On the crown of thorns and the blows; and on why the Lord’s legs were not broken, and on the blood and water flowing from his side.

He wears a crown of thorns, to make known that he himself bore our sins. Mocked, he is struck with blows, he who is most strong providing an example of humility, so that man may be ashamed to raise his neck and be proud when God and the Lord of all has been humbled by so many insults. His legs are not broken, and all his ways remained straight amid so many sufferings, so that in tribulation [Col. 0892C] we may not fail but persevere firmly. From his side flowed not blood only but water also, so that there might be something by which we could be washed from sins. Water alone could wash bodily stains; but joined to blood, which is the price of redemption, it received power to cleanse the invisible stains of sins. Thus it is rightly compared to the Red Sea, through which the people of Israel passed and were saved, while Pharaoh was drowned with his chariots and horsemen. For it conveys those fleeing the Egypt of this age, cleansed, into the land of promise; it utterly swallows up the pursuing devil together with his former deeds and pomp; and the Church is born from the side of Christ dying, just as Eve was formed from the side of Adam sleeping.

## TITLE XLVIII. On the prayers then made for all.

[Col. 0892D]

On this day solemn prayers are made for the condition of the Church, its ranks, dignities, and orders, because the high priest, praying for all, stood beside the altar of the temple with a censer, etc. That is, beside the altar of the cross, he raised up, as he hung upon the cross before God, the golden censer of his spotless body, in which he burned the incense of prayer to the Father. Rightly, therefore, we too offer common prayers with him, because to that passage is added: “and much incense was given.” But we do not bend the knee for the Jews, because the blindness that has happened to Israel cannot be driven away by the hand of any prayer. Yet we pray in some fashion, because this will come to pass; but we do not bend the knee, because, since we cannot oppose the divine judgments [Col. 0893A], we do not make intense prayer.

## TITLE XLIX. On the threefold water that flowed in Christ when he wept, sweated, and was already dead.

Christ set before us a threefold water and a threefold blood of his own. He weeps over Lazarus and over the holy city Jerusalem, and this is pure water. When he sweats as the hour of the Passion approaches, water mixed with blood flows not so much from his eyes as from his whole body, and this is water of bloody color. The third is that which flowed together with blood from his side. One who truly repents possesses the first if, in a spirit of humility and a contrite heart, he washes away the stains of his sins. Thus, by the Lord’s bounty, you will change the skin of the Ethiopian, lamenting in sorrow the long-established letters of death. You possess the second water if, in the sweat of your face, you wear down your body by the labor of repentance and restrain the flame of desire. But if you begin perfectly to flow, even to the surrender of yourself, into divine contemplation, you have drunk the third water from the Lord’s side.

## TITLE L. On the threefold dedication of the temple.

A threefold dedication of the temple is recorded: the first in autumn under Solomon; the second in spring under Zerubbabel; the third in winter under Judas Maccabaeus. Solomon built the temple and dedicated it on the seventh day of the seventh month. Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it; and after seventy years, under Zerubbabel, it was dedicated on the third day of the twelfth month. Later, after Antiochus had destroyed it, Judas Maccabaeus dedicated it in the ninth month. This threefold dedication, therefore, signifies the threefold order in the Church: married, widowed, and virgin. First comes the thirtyfold fruit, second the sixtyfold, third the hundredfold. These are the three men who are saved: Daniel, Noah, and Job. Daniel rests on a bed; Noah works at a mill; Job celebrates a wedding in a house.

Each person is also dedicated to God in three ways—that is, becomes God’s possession: first, through the regeneration of baptism; second, through the satisfaction of repentance; third, through confession of sins. For “the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (2 Cor. 6), and it must be dedicated by those three dedicators. Let Solomon dedicate the house of rest, Zerubbabel the house of [Col. 0893D] satisfaction, Judas the house of confession. God has no dwelling except either in those at rest, in penitents, or in those confessing. Rest belongs to peace; repentance to humility; confession to fear. Therefore Solomon dedicates rest in peace, Zerubbabel repentance in humility, Judas confession in fear: Solomon in the righteous person, Zerubbabel in the person made righteous, Judas in the person being made righteous.

So that this threefold cord may be dedicated in the tabernacle, it is founded upon a threefold foundation. Our peace must be grounded in goodness, lest it be hypocritical; satisfaction in discipline, lest it be erroneous; confession in knowledge, lest it be foolish. He sought to be grounded in these three when he said: “Teach me goodness, discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 118 [119]): goodness, lest my peace be false; discipline, lest satisfaction go astray; knowledge, lest confession become foolish. Knowledge is never more fitting than in connection with confession.

## TITLE LI. On the five things in which the dedication of the temple consists, explained morally.

There are, I think, five things in which the dedication of the temple consists: the sprinkling of water, to which three things are added—salt, ashes, and wine; the inscription of the alphabet upon the pavement; the anointing with chrism in twelve places; a twelvefold illumination; and the episcopal blessing which concludes everything. Sprinkling is the outpouring of repentance and lamentation, containing ashes, salt, and wine. Salt is fear. Hence salt accompanies every sacrifice through all its stages. For in all sacrifices which a Christian offers, fear ought to be before his eyes. Ashes are the remembrance of human frailty that runs its course. For our life [Col. 0894B] is like a line drawn in a circle and returning to the same point: beginning from dust as from a point, advancing through natural defects, and returning in a circle to dust. The hand of the Lord, driving us onward, has made this inevitable course, when he said: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Eccl. 3). Wine is the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, which is very apt to dissolve a person into tears when he recalls that, for his own sake, Christ was condemned to a most shameful death.

The inscription is the rigor of our order, handed down to us by the holy Fathers. The inscription is twofold, because it ought to be written indelibly from corner to corner both upon the tablets of the heart and upon the pavement of the body. A heart is called angular—that is, deceitful. Here, however, we call the two corners the humble heart and the exalted heart: humble heart, when someone considers in his mind the lowest things that are within himself; exalted heart, when he contemplates the highest things above. Or “from corner to corner” means that one may be formed by divine instruction from head to foot, or from beginning to end. The twelvefold anointing is apostolic institution. Now, therefore, sprinkled through repentance, inscribed through discipline, anointed through grace, illuminated through works, await the final blessing. For you know in whom you have believed, and are certain that the righteous Judge will grant you that blessing by which he will deem worthy to call the elect into his kingdom, saying: “Come, you blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25).

## TITLE LII. On the washing of feet at the Supper: another interpretation.

When Christ was about to pass from the world to the Father, he performed the commandment [Col. 0894D]: he laid aside his garments, girded himself with a towel, and poured water into a basin. This deed is full of mysteries and overflows with sacraments. Christ laid aside his garment when, leaving the purple of royal dignity, he emptied himself; and he girded himself with the towel of servile form, about to fight against the devil. He poured water into the basin when he poured out his precious blood upon the earth—upon that earth, I say, which opened its mouth and received Abel’s blood poured out by Cain’s hand, that is, Christ’s blood poured out by the hands of the Jews—that is, into the Church and into every faithful soul.

For a long time this basin was empty, for a long time this earth was dry and waterless, and our soul was like land without water. Christ came and poured [Col. 0895A] water into the basin, precious blood upon the earth—provided that we are the basin. A basin has two features: hollowness and resonance. Hollowness is within; resonance is without. So we too ought to empty ourselves of vices by the sound of confession, that we may receive the water from Christ’s side which washes the stains of sins. He dried them with a towel—that is, with his flesh. For he bore our sins in his flesh.

But why does he here wash only the disciples’ feet? Because in that part by which they are compelled to touch the earth in necessary matters, they cannot be without sin; and therefore in the perfect only the feet are washed, that is, venial sins. But we wretches, who sin not only by thought but also by deed and habit, should say with Peter: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and head” (John 23 [13:9]). Wash the feet of thoughts, the hands of deeds, the head of habit.

## TITLE LIII. On the threefold purification and the six water-jars.

“There were six water-jars set there according to the purification of the Jews” (John 2). There are three purifications suited to purifying true Jews, in the first Jews: the first, of reconciliation, by which we are reconciled from evil slavery into good servitude; the second, of adoption, by which we are adopted as children; and the third, of glorification, by which we are made heirs of God and fellow-heirs of Christ.

But six water-jars must be set forth. The first water-jar, that is, purification, is compunction. For “at whatever hour the sinner turns, I will remember none of his iniquities” (Ezek. 18). The second [Col. 0895C] is confession, for everything is washed in confession. Hence: “Declare your iniquities first, and the Lord will put them away” (Isa. 33). The third is the giving of alms: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). The fourth is forgiveness of injuries: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6). The fifth is affliction of the flesh: “I have been afflicted and greatly humbled,” etc. (Ps. 37 [38]). The sixth is obedience to God’s word: “You are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you” (John 15).

These jars are empty for those who rise to penitential lament with no fear of God. Jesus commands them to be filled with water, that is, with divine fear. For the fear of the Lord is water of life: though less pleasant to taste, it cools the person burning with harmful desires. This water can extinguish the enemy’s fiery darts. Water always seeks the lowest point, and fear descends to the lower things, surveying with a trembling mind the places of hell. For its voice is: “I shall go to the gates of hell” (Isa. 38). But by divine power it is changed into wine, because charity casts out fear (John 4 [1 John 4]). They are called stone jars not because of hardness but because of steadfastness. Each holds two or three measures, because fear is twofold: fear of being cast down into hell and fear of being excluded from eternal glory. But those who have put their hand to mighty things “will not fear for their household because of snowy cold” (Prov. 31), that is, they will not fear being deprived of spiritual wine.

At the first wedding, purified through the water-jars just mentioned, one passes on to the second wedding and purification, so as to be adopted and cease to be a servant; and from those to the third, so as to sit with the Father at table in his kingdom. Since he has invited us to these, let us meanwhile be like people awaiting their master when he returns from a wedding, so that when he comes we may open to him at once. For he will come to those awaiting him in truth as one returning from a wedding, drunk with the wine of charity and forgetful of our iniquities. But to those not awaiting him he will come as one returning from a wedding, yet like a powerful man overcome by drunkenness and as one intoxicated, forgetful of his mercies, because, with respect to them, God forgets to have mercy.

## TITLE LIV. On the fourfold purification instituted through Christ, on the day of Purification.

Christ, effecting four purifications from sins, [Col. 0896B] purifies the world by water, blood, spirit, and fire. “This,” says John, “is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ.” “This is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3). The first is contrition of heart; the second, affliction of body; the third, a work of piety and faith; the fourth, patience in tribulation. By these four days of our purification we are purified so that we may offer the newborn child with his mother and receive him with Simeon.

Accordingly, Christ was baptized in water and washed his disciples’ feet, consecrating the baptism of tears that flow from contrition of heart. He shed blood, so that we too, through the mortification of the body and participation in his Passion, may wash our garments in the blood of the Lamb. He gave the Spirit; hence love of neighbor “has been poured into our hearts” (Rom. 5), so that it may cover in us a multitude of sins (Jas. 5). If that love is less perfect and cannot cover so many and such great sins, then the Refiner applies fire, which burns the sons of Levi; and the fire of present and future tribulation burns away whatever rust remains, so that at last we may sing: “We have passed through fire and water” (Ps. 65 [66]), etc.

## TITLE LV. On the three tabernacles of which Peter said, “Let us make three tabernacles here.”

There are three tabernacles: the Synagogue, the Church, and heaven. The first belongs to Moses; the second to Elijah, of whom the Lord says: “Elijah is to come, and he will restore all things” (Matt. 17); the third is Christ’s tabernacle. The first tabernacle was made, as the Apostle says, in which were lampstands (Heb. 9), namely the patriarchs and prophets; and a table, the law; and loaves, the spiritual food of the commandments. The second was behind the veil of the law, in which the censer signifies the apostles, whose fragrance is to some “death unto death,” to others “life unto life” (2 Cor. 2); the urn containing manna signifies Christ’s humanity containing divinity; and the golden rod, and Aaron’s rod which flowered and produced an almond nut, signifies the Virgin Mary, who conceived and bore Christ against nature. But the third is the one “not made with hands,” into which, as the Apostle says, Jesus, made high priest, entered (Heb. 9). The first was in shadow and figure; the second in figure and truth; the third in truth alone. In the first life is shown; in the second it is given; in the third it is possessed.

## TITLE LVI. On the voluntarily undertaken Lord’s Passion, and the exaltation and fruit of the cross.

[Col. 0897A]

“I said,” says the Lord, “I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits” (Song 7). Three things are indicated by this saying: in the words, the purpose and will by which he suffered; in the ascent, the exaltation of the Crucified, by which he was exalted through suffering; in seizing the fruit, the benefit of redemption is shown, because he did not suffer without fruit. Thus he ascended the cross by will, triumphed upon it by power, and gathered its fruit by mercy. In one work alike he scorned the world, destroyed the devil, and redeemed the Christian. Therefore let those whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy say: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ!” (Gal. 6).

Upon it the Lord did three things [Col. 0897B]: by wisdom he made foolish the counsel of wickedness; by justice he destroyed him who had the power of death; by mercy he freed the captive. Therefore the one freed rightly glories in it—made alive by its triumph, justified by its ministry, strengthened by its example, fortified by its sign. Thus the consequence of right reason requires those who imprint the sign of the cross upon their foreheads for protection to imprint upon their conduct the example of the Crucified for justification, so that they may live by the law of him in whose faith they are armed. Otherwise a soldier deceitfully bears the king’s mark if he does not observe his command; he is not rightly protected by the sign of one to whose authority he does not submit. Such are those who, indulging in luxury, are enemies of the cross’s mercy. They will not be protected by it when, through the ministry of angels rather than of men, those who groan and grieve will be marked on their foreheads, that those to be saved may be distinguished from the multitude of the lost. He too distinguished them who said: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5).

## TITLE LVII. On the clean linen cloth and the crown of thorns in the Lord’s Passion.

“Joseph wrapped the body of Jesus in a clean linen cloth” (Matt. 27), because the Lord must be received in a clean conscience and pure heart, as in a new tomb. The crown of thorns signified a kingdom drawn from sinners.

## TITLE LVIII. On obedience, patience, and perseverance signified in Christ’s Passion.

“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2). In [Col. 0897D] Christ’s Passion, three emblems of virtue, as though for the beginning, progress, and completion of all the others, were displayed. First, obedience, by which he became obedient to the Father even unto death (Phil. 2). Second, great patience: great because he did not yield to sufferings and mockers; greater because he did not yield to honors; greatest because he prayed for his persecutors. Of this patience it was said: “You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19), because, as bones are the strength of the body, so patience is the strength of the whole religious life. Third, perseverance, because he dies upon the cross and is taken down not by himself but by another.

Obedience, therefore, undertook in Christ the war against the devil; patience and perseverance conquered it. Therefore, if you wish to follow his footsteps, so that as he whom you have chosen as guide in the way walked, you too may walk, undertake the conflict set before you obediently, seek patiently, persevere happily. For obedience begins every good work, patience endures it, perseverance completes it; because all run, but one receives the prize (1 Cor. 9).

## TITLE LIX. On the threefold will signified in Christ’s sorrow unto death.

“My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26).

In this sorrow three wills are considered: the will of the Father, the will of the spirit, and the will of the flesh. The Father’s will was to redeem the human race through Christ’s death. The spirit’s will was the same as the Father’s. The flesh’s will naturally recoiled from death, unless God’s will should at some time be changed: “Not my will,” he says, “but yours be done” (ibid.).

## TITLE LX. Why prophecies and Epistles in the divine office end in different tones of voice.

The prophecies end in a subdued voice, the Epistles in an elevated voice, because in the Old Testament temporal things were promised, beneath which Moses’ hands were heavy; but in the New, spiritual and eternal things, which are above and call us upward, are promised.

## TITLE LXI. On the three things which compelled the Lord to die for us by a kind of voluntary compulsion.

Three things especially compelled the Lord Jesus to undergo the disgrace of death and the cross by a voluntary compulsion: filial and pure obedience, by which the expiation of the earlier disobedience might be paid; compassionate and common misery, which desired to bend his inflexible justice and iron rod toward mercy; and that misery—weighty and grievous—which oppressed human necks by the power of the common enemy and the sentence of death: public and universal, binding just and unjust alike in the same sentence of obligation; continuous and everlasting, which, unless the grace of redemption were accomplished through Christ, would swallow the entire human race in the abyss of damnation through the unremediable bond of captivity. Moreover, the third thing which freely compelled him to death was the most celebrated and solemn victory, by the success of which the unavoidable power of the devil and death was gloriously and effectively to be diminished in a moment.

## TITLE LXII. On the fourfold handing-over of Christ.

“The Son of Man will be handed over” (Matt. 26). There is one handing-over of sending or permission, by which the Father hands over the Son; another of propitiation, by which the Son hands over himself; another of betrayal, by which Judas hands him over to the chief priests; another of condemnation, by which the governor, having scourged him, handed him over to the Jews. Of the first: “He did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us” (Rom. 8). Of the second: “He loved us and handed himself over for us” (Eph. 5). Of the third: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over” (Matt. 22 [26]). Of the fourth: “They will hand him over to the Gentiles to be mocked” (Luke 18), etc.

## TITLE LXIII. On the threefold shedding of Christ’s blood.

The Lord shed his blood for us in threefold fashion: from his hands, feet, and side. On the cross this was our price; on the altar, our cup; in exile, our provision for the journey; [Col. 0899A] in departure from Egypt, our guide; in heaven, our advocate.

## TITLE LXIV. On Christ’s various appearances, made in different places and manners; and on our appearance.

How did Christ appear, on the third day of the festival repeated three times, in three places and three modes? In a stable to the three Magi, on the first day; at baptism to a few disciples, on the second day; at a feast to many invited guests, on the third day. The first appearance took place in a lowly place, the second in a humble place, the third in an exalted place. The first appearance was made to the Magi through a star in an oracle; the second to the disciples through a voice heard openly; the third at the feast through wine made miraculously. In a lowly place the star was seen by the wise, so that the wisdom of the wise might be destroyed. The voice was heard openly by the simple, so that [Col. 0899B] simplicity might be instructed. Wine, transformed in miracle, was set before those doubting, so that unbelief might be confounded. Of the first it is said: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3). Of the second: “Be simple as doves” (Matt. 10). Of the third: “Everything not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14).

He appeared in three ways: in the stable, the Son of man; at baptism, the Son of God and conceived of the Spirit, because it was said: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 17), and the Holy Spirit was seen above him; at the feast, God, because no one could do this unless God were with him. The first appearance was in humanity, by which he is true man; the second in dignity, by which he is more than man; the third in power, by which he is equal [Col. 0899C] to God.

Likewise, let us too appear in three places and modes: beginning in the stable, advancing in baptism, persevering at the feast. Adam appeared as a beast in the stable: “I am fixed,” he says, “in the deep mire” (Ps. 68 [69]). Naaman the Syrian and the eunuch of Queen Candace appeared at baptism: “Behold water,” he says; “what prevents me from being baptized?” (Acts 8). Stephen appeared at the feast: “Behold,” he says, “I see the heavens opened” (Acts 7). In the first, the person cries from below: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40 [41]). In the second, the cleansed person prays: “Wash me still more, O Lord” (Ps. 50 [51]). In the third, the hungry person says: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matt. 6). In the stable we are healed by his bruise; in baptism we are washed by his blood; at the feast we shall be made drunk by his fragrance. Of the first it is said: “By his bruise we are healed” (Isa. 53); of the second: “You have been washed; you have been sanctified” (1 Cor. 6); of the third: “We shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1).

The stable is in the stench [Col. 0900B] of your sins; baptism in the beauty of gifts; the feast in the fragrance of merits. Likewise, one appears in three ways: in conscience, reputation, and righteousness. Conscience corresponds to the star; reputation to the voice heard; righteousness to the wine offered. The star signifies the conscience of shining thought; the voice, the reputation of one’s conduct; the wine, the righteousness of pleasing action. Conscience lies hidden in private; reputation flies abroad in public; righteousness is open in plain sight. Of the first it is said: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1). Of reputation: “Let your light shine” (Matt. 5), etc. Of the third: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake” (ibid.). Through conscience secular peoples appear; through reputation, regular clergy and monks; through righteousness, secular persons. The first appear walking with a slow step, the second with a hurried pace, the third in swift running.

## APPENDIX TO HUGH’S MYSTICAL WORKS.

[Col. 0899]

## ONE HUNDRED SERMONS. (G)*

## PREFACE.

With Scripture as witness, the word of God is “a lamp to our feet and a light to our paths” (Ps. 118), and therefore we ought, in every way possible, to devote ourselves to reading, meditating upon, hearing, speaking, and writing the words of sacred Scripture, insofar as we are able—especially we, dearest brothers and fellow members of the cloister, who have renounced the disturbances of active affairs and bound ourselves to the repose of contemplation alone. Blessed Mary, Martha’s sister, furnishes us with a most evident example of this virtue: while her sister was busied with much service, Mary sat at the Lord’s feet, with attentive ears thirsting for the words he spoke, and, as the Lord himself testified, is said to have chosen the better part. Yet many despise her praiseworthy and wonderful virtue.

Of these, we hear that some, though by a heaven-given understanding they might have taken delight in the Scriptures, have fallen into such foulness and enormity of vices and habits that, their souls nauseating the word of God and abhorring spiritual food, they drew near to the very gates of death; and they seemed to be reckoned rather among Egyptians than Israelites, and among citizens of Babylon rather than of Jerusalem. We have also seen others, by the diligence of their study, with Christ’s grace cooperating, arrive from depravity at such goodness of virtues and uprightness of conduct that there was recognized in them, more clearly than light, the fulfillment of what is written: “He sent forth his word, and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions” (Ps. 106).

Let us all, therefore, be urged to read the word of God; the more learned also to speak it, and the less learned to hear it, so that in us too may be fulfilled what is written: “Glorify the Lord in teachings” (Isa. 24). And because I once gathered for you certain teachings from the most flourishing field of divine Scripture, it seemed good to me to set them before you in this sermon, so that in them too you may exercise your understanding.

Yet it must be known that we ought not to devote all our time to reading, because, according to Solomon, all things have their season, and everything passes through its allotted intervals (Eccl. 5). Thus there is a time for reading and a time for meditation. There is a time for seeking truth, that the understanding may be instructed; a time for practising virtue, that the affections may be healed; and a time for performing good works, that one’s neighbour may be helped. There is a time for prayer and a time for singing; a time for attending the divine offices, and a time for attending to every necessary matter. From all these things, like bees gathering honey from different flowers, we ought to gather for ourselves the sweetness of inward delight and, by holy living, bring the honey-bearing comb of righteousness to completion.

## SERMON I. On the Dedication of a Church, in the Historical Sense

[Col. 0901A]

“The Lord has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. 45).

The tabernacle of the Lord—that is, the holy Church—has, dearest brothers, its stones; it has mortar; it has a foundation; it has walls; it has a roof; it has length, breadth, and height; it has a sanctuary, choir, nave, courtyard, altar, tower, sounding bells, glass windows, inner and outer whitewashing, twelve candles, and a bishop who dedicates it. All that has been mentioned is full of mysteries and bears spiritual teachings.

The individual stones are the individual faithful: square and firm; square through the steadfastness of faith, firm through the virtue of endurance. The mortar is charity, which fits, joins, and quickens each one, and, lest they be set at variance with one another through any discord, makes them equal in unity. The foundation is the prophets and apostles, as it is written: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone” (Eph. 2). The walls are contemplatives, who, abandoning earthly things and cleaving to heavenly things, adhere more closely to Christ their foundation, which is above their neighbour.

In this spiritual building the roof does not rise upward but hangs downward; in this it differs from a material building and is removed from such an arrangement in a contrary manner. The roof consists of those living the active life: they are near earthly actions, attend less to heavenly things because of their imperfection, and administer earthly goods for the needs of their neighbours.

The length of the holy Church is considered according to the duration of times; its breadth, according to the multitude of peoples; its height, according to the difference of merits. It extends in length as it is stretched from the first righteous person to the last righteous person through the three periods: the time of natural law, the time of written law, and the time of grace. It is spread in breadth as it is enlarged by the number of many peoples. It rises in height as it is elevated by the distinction between lesser and greater persons.

We may also say that the length of the holy Church is from east to west, its breadth from north to south. Of the length it was said: “They shall come from the East and the West, and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8). Of the breadth it was said: “I shall say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not hinder” (Isa. 43). Of both it was said: “Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise from your side” (Isa. 60).

Its height is also considered according to degrees of rank. For it is raised on high when the priestly order is placed above the laity, the episcopal order above the priestly, the archiepiscopal above this, and finally the pope, bishop of the Romans, above all.

The sanctuary signifies the order of virgins; the choir, the order of the continent; the nave, the order of married persons. For the sanctuary is more restricted than the choir, and the choir than the nave; and virgins are fewer than the continent, and the continent fewer than married persons. The sanctuary is also holier than the choir, and the choir than the nave. Thus the choir of virgins is worthier than the order of the continent, and the order of the continent worthier than that of married persons.

The courtyard consists of false Christians, who are sanctified insofar as they have been baptized, but are full of the rottenness of corpses because they are full of the corruption of vices. Of this courtyard it is written: “Do not measure the court which is outside, because it has been cast out and given to the Gentiles” (Rev. 11): for false Christians will be condemned with the Gentiles and handed over to demons for punishment.

The altar is Christ, upon whom we offer not only sacrifices of good works but also prayers, saying: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son,” and so forth. The tower is the name of the Lord, as it is written: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous shall flee to it and be saved” (Prov. 18). The bells are preachers, who speak the words of God. The glass windows are spiritual men, through whom divine knowledge shines upon us. The inner whitewashing signifies purity of hearts; the outer, purity of bodies. The twelve candles are the twelve apostles, who preached the banner of the cross and faith in Christ’s passion through the four quarters of the world.

Thus the holy Church has individual stones in the individual faithful; mortar in charity; foundation in prophets and apostles; walls in contemplatives; roof in those living the active life. It has length in the duration of times, breadth in the multitude of peoples, height in the difference of merits; sanctuary in the order of virgins, choir in the order of the continent, and nave in the order of married persons. It has Christ as altar; the name of the Lord as tower; preachers as bells; spiritual men as glass windows; purity of hearts as inner whitewashing; purity of bodies as outer whitewashing; and the twelve apostles as twelve candles.

There follows the bishop, who signifies Christ. He went around his Church: first, in the time of natural law, admonishing her through the patriarchs; then, in the time of written law, admonishing her through the prophets. Then, in the time of grace, he went around her and entered her in his own person, teaching her outwardly by doctrine and sanctifying her inwardly by grace.

On the first circuit he said: “You shall not eat flesh with blood” (Gen. 4). On the second he said: “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20). On the third he said: “Whoever is angry with his brother is liable to judgment” (Matt. 5).

Yet many are thought to be contained in this spiritual building by holiness who are far removed from it by depravity. Outside it are the unclean, fornicators, concubine-keepers, adulterers, incestuous persons, drunkards, usurers, the greedy, thieves, robbers, hateful persons, murderers, liars, perjurers, and those who say to their brother, “You fool” (Matt. 5), and those who look upon a woman in order to lust after her (ibid.). Nor are those its stones who do not partake in charity.

Therefore, brothers, let us lead such a life that we may be stones of God. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON II. On the Dedication of a Church, in the Tropological Sense

“The Lord has sanctified his tabernacle” (Ps. 45) [Col. 0903D].

The Lord’s tabernacle, according to the tropological sense, is the soul. This soul, called the Lord’s tabernacle, has its stones, its mortar, and all the other things belonging to the construction of the Church, as we set them out in the preceding sermon.

The stones of this tabernacle are the individual virtues, well polished through practice and stable against vices through immovability. Mortar is charity, by which the other virtues are embraced, united, equalized, and held together. The foundation is Christ, as the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3).

It has walls through contemplation of heavenly goods, through which, removed from earthly affections, it cleaves more closely to its foundation—that is, Christ. It also has a roof through good action, by which it administers temporal things to those in need for the sake of eternal things.

It has length through faith, by which it believes true all that God has done from the beginning, through himself, angels, and human beings, and all that he will do until the end. It has height through hope, by which it is raised from earthly to heavenly things, from transient to eternal things, from visible to invisible things, and from bodily to spiritual things. It has breadth through charity, by which it is extended to the right and to the left: to the right, in loving friends in God; to the left, in loving enemies for God’s sake.

It has a sanctuary because it was made in the image of God. For as in the church building nothing is worthier than the sanctuary, so in the soul nothing is holier, nobler, or more excellent than the divine image. It has a choir because it was made in the likeness of God. For as the choir is found first in a church after the sanctuary, so in the soul the divine likeness is understood as most exalted after the divine image.

It has its nave through sensuality. For as married persons stand in the nave of a church, so the five senses of our body are contained in sensuality. They are rightly called married, because in earthly things they have both the propagation of knowledge through exercise and the pleasure of natural delight through experience.

It has a courtyard through the flesh, in which the original incentives of vices are like corpses of the dead. It has an altar in its heart, of which it is written: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50). It has glass windows in the spiritual senses, through which it is illuminated by the ray of the true Sun and freed from the blindness of its ignorance.

It has the name of the Lord as a tower, of which it is written: “The name of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous shall flee to it and be saved” (Prov. 17). It has bells through preaching, by which it calls those who are far off to the worship of God. It has inner whitewashing through purity of heart, and outer whitewashing through purity of body. It has twelve candles, by which it is illumined according to the teaching of the twelve apostles, through which it is instructed in faith by good works.

It has the holy Trinity as bishop. The Father goes around it by power, the Son by wisdom, and the Holy Spirit by kindness. The Father by power instils fear; the Son by wisdom gives knowledge; the Holy Spirit by kindness gives consolation.

The Father says: “I made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them. I did not spare the angels when they sinned. I cast Adam out of paradise. I destroyed the primal race by the flood. I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. I drowned Pharaoh with his army. I punished the Israelite people when they sinned. Open to me, lest I do the same to you.”

The Son says: “I am the wisdom of God, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High. I reach mightily from end to end. I am the living and effective word of God, more penetrating than any two-edged sword. Open to me, lest perhaps I do not spare you.”

The Holy Spirit says: “I proceed from the Father and the Son, the love of both, the lifter-up of the fallen, the comforter of the sorrowful. Open to me, if you wish to be gladdened with spiritual joy.”

Yet these three, as they are one God, are also one bishop. Thus the Trinity sanctifies this Church—that is, the soul—within and without: within, from the defilement of the spirit; without, from the defilement of the flesh.

Therefore this Church, namely the soul, has stones through virtues; mortar through charity; foundation through Christ; walls through contemplation; roof through good action; length through faith; height through hope; breadth through charity; sanctuary because it was made in God’s image; choir because it was made in God’s likeness; nave through sensuality; courtyard through the flesh; altar through a contrite heart. It also has glass windows through spiritual senses; a tower through the Name; bells through preaching; inner whitewashing through purity of heart; outer whitewashing through purity of body; twelve candles through the teaching of the twelve apostles. Its bishop is the holy Trinity.

Let each one of you, therefore, dearest brothers—let each one, I say—strive to become, according to what has been said above, God’s tabernacle, so that God may deign to dwell in him. It is a great honour, great security, and great glory to have God dwelling within oneself. We must therefore take the utmost care that we are such inwardly and outwardly: inwardly through faith, outwardly through good works, so that the Lord of majesty may deign to come to us and make his dwelling with us.

But because we cannot be such without his grace, we must implore it without ceasing. For he will give grace, and not grace only but also glory: grace on the way, glory in the homeland; grace in the world, glory in heaven; grace in the present, glory in the future; grace in the journey, glory in arrival; grace in time, glory in eternity; grace in justification, glory in blessedness; grace in merit, glory in the reward of merit. In this glory he lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On the Dedication of a Church, in the Anagogical Sense

“Praise the Lord, Jerusalem” (Ps. 147).

Jerusalem, the holy city and the city of the Holy One, is the holy Church. Like a city, it is built; and, once built, it is adorned with diverse ornaments. This holy city—that is, the Church—has its stones, wall, towers, buildings, and gates.

It has stones, namely the faithful, who are joined to one another by charity just as stone is joined to stone by mortar. It has a wall in the protection of virtues, by which it is strengthened against vices, lest invading vices take spiritual goods away from it. It has towers in those who are exalted in contemplation. For towers, as it were, are raised in the holy Church when all the perfect, leaving earthly things behind, are lifted to heavenly things through contemplation.

It has smaller, larger, and greatest buildings. Its smaller buildings are the life of married persons, its larger buildings the life of the continent, and its greatest buildings the life of virgins. The life of married persons remains near lower things through earthly activity and the pleasure of begetting. The life of the continent raises itself higher through the practice of virtues and the performance of good works. The life of virgins lifts itself to heavenly things through purity of heart and integrity of flesh.

It has stone buildings and ivory buildings. It has stone buildings in those firm in faith, ivory ones in those resplendent in chastity. For stone signifies faith through firmness; ivory signifies chastity through the coldness of its nature.

It has diverse gates, through which it brings in people of different nations and ways of life, formerly far from it, and makes them its citizens and members of its household. It has gates: the Sheep Gate, the Fish Gate, the Old Gate, the Valley Gate, the Dung Gate, the Fountain Gate, the Water Gate, the Horse Gate, and the Judgment Gate. I shall briefly set down for you their mystical meaning, insofar as the Lord grants.

The Sheep Gate was where the Pool of Bethesda was—that is, the sheep-pool—because the flesh of sheep that was placed in sacrifice was washed there. The Sheep Gate, because a sheep is an innocent animal, signifies innocence. Through this gate the guilty are brought in and become innocent: guilty through fault, innocent through righteousness; outside through fault, inside through righteousness. Outside are wolves; inside, sheep: wolves through rapacity, sheep through simplicity. Oh, what a good gate, at which the right hand of the Most High has done such things!

The Fish Gate was the gate through which fish coming from the sea were brought in. This gate signifies repentance, which has, as it were, one pillar here in contrition of heart, another there in confession of mouth, and satisfaction in deed as its roof above. Through it are brought in those shaken by the unrest of this present world: made bitter by salt, corrupted by stench, puffed up by waves, rough with the scales of the old man, defiled by the mud of carnal pleasure, alienated from the light of the true Sun, drawn from worldly waves by the net of blessed Peter or those acting in his place, and brought into holy Jerusalem—that is, the Church—after the scales of sins have been stripped off.

Yet there are some who, like eels, constrict themselves in the skin of the old man, cling to the mud of vices, and often or always escape the Lord’s net; nor do they come upward to the light of truth, so that there they may die to themselves, be made alive, and live to God.

The Old Gate is charity. As it is written: “Beloved, I write to you not a new commandment, but an old commandment, which you had from the beginning” (1 John 2). Through this gate enter those who transfer themselves from love of the world to love of God. Blessed Mary Magdalene entered by this gate: after so many and such great scandals of the flesh, she was made from a cauldron into a cup, transferred from a vessel of dishonour into a vessel of glory.

The Valley Gate, which was opposite the valley of Jehoshaphat, signifies humility. Through it enter those who return from the pride of the devil to the humility of Christ. Outside they are lofty; within, humble. Outside they resemble cedar; within, hyssop: cedar through pride, hyssop through humility. Through pride turned away; through humility converted—that is, turned away from God and converted to God.

The Dung Gate, which was in the lower part of the city and through which refuse was cast out, signifies excommunication. Through it the profane are not brought in but cast out: they are dung through fault and are cast out through punishment; dung by their own deed, cast out by the divine word. For it is not fitting that a goat should lie down with a lamb, a sinner with a righteous person, an unclean person with a clean person, an adulterer with Christ, lest the righteous person, provoked by the sinner’s example, stretch out his hands to iniquity.

The Fountain Gate was so called because it stood opposite the fountain of Siloam. *Siloam* is interpreted “Sent,” and signifies Christ, whom the Father sent for the salvation of the human race. Oh, what a good fountain! This fountain is wisdom, the Word of God on high; by its stream the thirsty are given drink, the hungry are satisfied, the rejected are recalled, the sick are healed, enemies are reconciled, captives are freed, the ungodly are justified, and the wretched are made blessed.

Thus the Gate of Siloam is faith in Christ. Those outside this gate are unbelievers; those within are believers. Unbelievers are members of the devil; believers, members of Christ. The members of the devil, united to the devil through fault, are to be condemned with the devil through punishment. The members of Christ, united to Christ through faith, are to be made blessed with Christ through glory.

The Water Gate signifies contrition. Those who enter it are washed in it. Outside it they are filthy; within it, clean. Outside, black; within, white. Outside, goats; within, lambs.

The Horse Gate signifies restraint of vices. Those who enter through it check with the bridle of temperance the rush of anger, the gaping mouth of avarice, the greediness of gluttony, and the excess of lust.

The Judgment Gate signifies discernment. Those who enter through it distinguish between holy and profane, clean and unclean, true and false, good and evil, righteousness and fault, truth and falsehood, honourable and dishonourable.

Thus the holy Church has a wall through the protection of virtues; towers through those exalted in contemplation; diverse buildings through the different merits of those who live well; diverse gates through the diverse operations of heavenly grace: the Sheep Gate through innocence; the Fish Gate through repentance; the Old Gate through charity; the Valley Gate through humility; the Dung Gate through excommunication; the Fountain Gate through faith; the Water Gate through contrition; the Horse Gate through restraint of vices; the Judgment Gate through discernment.

Blessed are those who enter through these gates. Let us strive, dearest brothers, let us strive to be citizens of so glorious a city, and within it offer to the Lord our God a sacrifice of praise, offering him the calves of our lips. He lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On the Nativity of Blessed Mary

“Hail, star of the sea.”

This present age, dearest brothers, is a sea. For, like the sea, it stinks, swells, is deceptive, and is unstable. It stinks through lust, swells through pride, and is unstable through curiosity. Therefore, dearest brothers, if we wish to cross such a dangerous sea without peril, we must have a ship and the things belonging to a ship.

We must have a ship, mast, sail, and the two timbers between which the sail is stretched, the upper and the lower; a little vane, which we may call the cock that observes the wind. We must have ropes, oars, a rudder, an anchor, and food necessary for us. Let us also have a net, so that we may be able to draw out some fish. See what these signify.

The ship signifies faith. It began, as it were, in a single timber in Abraham, who was the first way of believing; and it was still greatly enlarged in Isaac and Jacob. Then this ship began to be extended according to the propagation of the ten tribes. The more the number of believers increased, the more it enlarged the ship of faith. Then, after the crossing of the Red Sea, when the children of Israel received God’s law and were later multiplied in the promised land, it was enlarged still further. Then, when Christ came and suffered for the human race, and the sound of apostolic preaching was heard throughout all the earth, after the fullness of the Gentiles began to enter, it enlarged this ship greatly. But in the time of Antichrist, as the charity of many grows cold and false believers are excluded, it will again be drawn up and narrowed; and as Adam was the first timber in the prow of faith, so the last righteous person will be its final timber in the stern.

Indeed, whoever from the beginning has beneficially crossed the sea of this present age, whoever has escaped its dangers, whoever has come to the harbour of salvation—all have sailed and crossed in the ship of faith.

By faith Abel offered God a more pleasing sacrifice than Cain, through which he received testimony that he was righteous; and by it, though dead, he still speaks. By faith Enoch pleased God and was taken up. By faith Noah prepared an ark for the salvation of his household. By faith Abraham, when called, obeyed in going out to the place which he was to receive. By faith barren Sarah received power to conceive. By faith Isaac blessed each of his sons. By faith Joseph, dying, remembered the return of the children of Israel to the promised land and commanded that his bones be carried there. By faith Moses was hidden at his birth. By faith he refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter. By faith he celebrated the Passover. By faith the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea. By faith the walls of Jericho fell.

And what more shall I say? For midday would fail me while I tell of the saints of old, who through faith conquered kingdoms, performed righteousness, and obtained promises. Some stopped the mouths of lions, as Daniel did. Others quenched the violence of fire, as the three youths did. Others recovered strength from weakness, as Job and Hezekiah did. Others were made mighty in battle, as Joshua and Judas Maccabaeus did. Women received their dead raised to life, as through Elijah and Elisha. Others were stretched upon the rack, refusing redemption from temporal death through transgression of the law, as the seven brothers are recorded to have suffered in the book of Maccabees. Others were stoned, as Jeremiah in Egypt and Ezekiel in Babylon; sawn asunder, as Isaiah; killed by the sword, as Uriah and Josiah; and wandered in sheepskins, as Elijah and other hermits (Heb. 11:4–38).

All these, and many others, crossed the dangers of the present age through faith, because they were found approved by the testimony of faith.

The planks of this ship are the sayings of sacred Scripture. For its construction, the Old Testament gives us some planks and the New Testament others. The nails by which these planks—that is, these sayings—are fastened together are the authorities of the saints, by which the things contained in the sequence of the two Testaments agree. These planks are cut by reading and smoothed by meditation.

The mast, raised on high, signifies hope, through which we are lifted up to seek and set our minds on heavenly things. As it is written: “Seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth; set your minds on the things above, where Christ is at the right hand of God the Father” (Col. 3).

The sail is charity, which is stretched forward, to the right, and to the left: forward through desire for future things, to the right through love of friends, and to the left through love of enemies. The upper and lower timbers signify reason and sensuality: reason above, sensuality below. Charity ought to be fastened above by reason and held immovably; but below, through sensuality, it should not merely be held but also moved, because through it charity must be exercised in good action. This is also the case in a material ship: the upper timber does not move, but the lower one does.

The little cock signifies discernment of spirits. For this purpose a little cock, or something else in its place, is set above the mast, so that one may discern which wind is blowing and from where. Of this cock—that is, the testing of spirits—it is written: “Test the spirits whether they are from God” (1 John 4); and again: “To another is given discernment of spirits” (1 Cor. 12).

The ropes are the virtues: humility, patience, compassion, modesty, chastity, continence, constancy, gentleness, goodness, prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. These ropes—that is, the virtues—must always be stretched through practice, so that through them the mast of our hope may be secured. For the mast of hope can have no support if the practice of virtues is lacking.

Next come the oars, which are extended from the ship and lowered into the waters. They signify good works, which proceed from faith and extend themselves into the waters—that is, toward neighbours. For waters are peoples: they rise by birth, flow by mortality, and flow out in death. We ought to have these oars not only on the right, doing good only to those who do good to us, but also on the left, doing good to those who do evil to us, as it is written: “Do good to those who hate you” (Matt. 5); and: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink” (Rom. 12).

The rudder by which the ship is directed signifies discernment, which guides us straight ahead, lest we be dissolved by prosperity on the right or broken by adversity on the left. Our anchor is humility, which is cast downward, by which our ship is made stable, lest, when the wind of diabolical suggestions blows and the sea of our thoughts is troubled, our ship be shaken and sink into the deep. Therefore the ship of our faith must be secured and stabilized through humility, so that in time of temptation it may have a firm position, although it cannot have a free course.

We must have food through the reading of the Scriptures. The wicked do not desire this food, as it is written: “Their soul abhorred all food, and they drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. 106). It is given to the good, as it is written: “He sent forth his word, and healed them, and rescued them from their destructions” (Ps. 106).

The net signifies preaching. We must use this net without ceasing, draw out by it people submerged in the waves of this present age, strip away the scales of their sins, and prepare them for our Lord Jesus Christ. We must also, like sailors, sing the *celeusma*—the rowing-song—by the melody of divine praise, as the Psalmist says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Ps. 33).

After all these things we need the wind, which signifies the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, so that through it we may be directed to the harbour of rest, to the physician of salvation, to the promised land, to the house of eternity.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we must have a ship through faith, a mast through hope, a sail through charity, a little cock through testing of spirits, ropes through the practice of virtues, oars through the performance of good works, a rudder through discernment, an anchor through humility, food through meditation upon and reading of the Scriptures, and a net through preaching; and we must sing the *celeusma* through rejoicing in God’s praise. But the Lord will give the wind through the inspiration of his Spirit. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). The lights are gifts; the Father of lights is the maker, giver, and distributor of gifts. The best gift signifies gifts of nature; the perfect gift signifies gifts of grace.

Thus he will give us a favourable wind—that is, the Holy Spirit—who has given us the other goods, whether those that belong to nature or those bestowed upon us through grace.

But, dearest brothers, that we may cross this sea safely, let us most often greet the star of the sea, blessed Mary; and, greeting her, let us invoke her, saying: “Hail, star of the sea.” Let us also, after the manner of sailors, always pour forth prayers to blessed Mary and to her Son. For our impediments are many, as an excellent poet has testified, saying:

> The sea rages, the winds roar,  
> The turbulent waves rise;  
> The ship runs, yet as it runs  
> So many obstacles meet it.  
>
> Here are sirens of pleasure,  
> A dragon, dogs, and pirates;  
> All these threaten death  
> To those nearly driven to despair.  
>
> After the abyss, now a raging wave  
> Bears the little vessel up to heaven;  
> The mast sways, the sail streams,  
> The sailors’ work comes to a halt.  
>
> In these evils our animal man  
> Wastes away;  
> You, our spiritual Mother,  
> Deliver us as we perish.  
>
> Jesus, fruit of the holy womb,  
> Amid the waves of the world  
> Be for us the way, guide, and convoy,  
> Setting us free toward heavenly things.  
>
> Hold the helm; steer the ship.  
> You who calm the heavy storm,  
> By your power grant us  
> A pleasant harbour.  
>
> Born from you and given to us,  
> He reigns as blessed God  
> Through unbounded ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. On the Coming of the Lord

[Col. 0911B]

“Be ready, Israel, to meet the Lord, for he comes.”

As every place is sacred, dearest brothers, insofar as it is a place, so every time is sacred insofar as it is time. Yet we sometimes say, in comparison with another place, “This place is good or bad”; and, in comparison with another time, “That time is good or bad.” We do not say this or that because of place and time themselves, but because of what happens in place and time.
