Thus, just as one place is called less sacred because of an offence committed there, and another more sacred because grace works there, so one time is called less sacred because some iniquity has been committed in it, and another is called more sacred because some religious observance is to be performed in it. Nevertheless, every time is sacred insofar as it is time, and every place is sacred insofar as it is a place.

Now, brothers, it is the season of the Lord’s coming, in which we ought to prepare ourselves through some spiritual observance. It is the time in which God comes as man to humanity for humanity’s redemption, liberation, justification, and beatification: redeeming from fault, liberating from punishment, justifying through grace, and making blessed through glory.

Therefore, in this most sacred time, we ought to practise the good more earnestly, so that through his grace we may deserve to be visited more abundantly. Certainly, if a king deigned to come to us and make his dwelling with us, we would diligently prepare both ourselves and our belongings for his reception.

Therefore, brothers, let us strive—those of us who perhaps still remain outside, occupied with servile works—to enter the house of our heart, open its windows, examine what is fitting there and what is not, take down the spiders’ webs, sweep the floor with brooms, cast out the mud and straw, cover the cleaned floor with fresh rushes, fragrant herbs, and sweet-smelling flowers, adorn the walls with varied hangings, put on festive garments, prepare a solemn banquet, and then rejoice in meeting him with glad songs. If we have been outside, intent upon servile works—that is, sins—let us return to our heart, as the prophet teaches, saying: “Return, transgressors, to the heart” (Isa. LXIV). The windows of this house are the spiritual senses, through which [Col. 0912A] divine knowledge shines upon us and illumines the inner chambers of our mind. Let us open these windows by careful self-examination, so that we may discern what is good there and what is evil: let us preserve the good and cast out the evil. The webs of spiders, thin and hanging on high, signify the pride of the human mind. One person is puffed up because of noble birth, another because of the bloom of beauty, another because of physical strength, another because of an abundance of possessions, another because of the arrogance of power, another because a greater prerogative of heavenly grace has been granted to him. But whoever is proud weaves empty spiders’ webs on high. Let us, brothers, take down these webs by humbling our pride, as the Apostle commands, saying: “Do not be high-minded, but fear” (Rom. [Col. 0912B] II). Let us also cleanse the floor of our heart, casting out straw and mud. Mud defiles; straw flies away. Thus mud signifies uncleanness, and straw vain glory. Let us cast out both this and that through contrition of heart and confession of mouth.

Finally, let us cover the floor of the heart, as it were, with rushes through the satisfaction of repentance, lest anything of our former earthly and carnal life appear in us, as David says: “Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI). Let us also possess fragrant herbs and sweet-smelling flowers through a good reputation, so that with the Apostle we may say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II). The varied hangings are the different virtues. We ought to spread them out through the exercise of virtues. [Col. 0912C] One hanging is green, another hyacinth-blue, another saffron-yellow, another black, another red, another white. Green signifies faith, because, just as in things growing from the earth greenery first meets the eye, so faith stands first among all virtues. First, I say, in order, not in dignity. For charity precedes all virtues in dignity; without it the others are of no benefit. Hyacinth-blue signifies hope for heavenly things, because it displays within itself the colour of the sky and of purer air. By the hanging of saffron colour charity is figured, since the saffron colour imitates flame. The black hanging suggests humility, which continually sets before itself the blackness of its own sins; the red, patience, which is sometimes reddened by the blood of suffering; the white [Col. 0912D] signifies purity, which always shines white without stain. More elegant garments, brothers, signify good works. For just as beautiful garments outwardly adorn people before other people, so good works commend and recommend the holy and righteous person. Therefore nothing about us is more glorious than these garments, nothing more precious, nothing more praiseworthy, nothing more useful. Let us strive to put them on, if we wish to be glorious at the Lord’s coming. We ought to prepare food by more frequent and more diligent reading and meditation upon sacred Scripture. By this food the soul is strengthened; by it it is made rich; by it it receives strength for good work and brings that strength to perfection without defect. We must also show the gladness of our heart at his coming by songs, as it is written: “Bless, O nations, our God, [Col. 0913A] and make heard the voice of his praise” (Ps. LXV).

Let us therefore take care, let us take care to open the windows of this house through examination of the mind; to take down spiders’ webs by humbling pride; to sweep the floor through confession of sin; to cover it with rushes through the satisfaction of repentance; to spread hangings along the walls through the exercise of virtues; to clothe ourselves in precious garments through the performance of good works; to prepare food through reading and meditation upon sacred Scripture; and to sing psalms through the chanting of divine praise. Let us take care to prepare ourselves thus for the Lord’s coming, so that we may deserve to be visited by him who lives and reigns as God.

## SERMON VI. On the Feast of Any Saint

Sacred Scripture, singing the praise of the righteous man at the beginning [Col. 0913B] of the book, says of him: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which will yield its fruit in its season” (Ps. I). We must inquire, dearest brothers, what these waters are; what the course of the waters is; what is the root of the tree, what the trunk, what the branches, what the bark, what the pith, what the leaves, what the flowers, and what the fruit. These waters are gifts of grace, by which God waters the righteous person so that he may grow and bear fruit. The course of the waters is the succession of inspirations. For it is written: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you do not know whence he comes or where he goes” (John III). Therefore the Holy Spirit flows to us and flows away, approaches and withdraws. He flows in for our justification; he flows away for our humiliation. He approaches so that we may grow; he withdraws lest we become proud—so that we may grow in virtue, [Col. 0913C] yet not be proud of virtue on account of abundant grace. Christ is the spring; the streams are the gifts by which the righteous person is enlivened, increased, and brought to completion through perfection. The root of this tree is faith, which is the origin and foundation of the other virtues and the root of good works. By this root the righteous person is planted in God; without it he produces no good fruit. As the Apostle says: “For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. II). O how good is this root, from which the life of the righteous person takes its beginning in good! The trunk signifies hope in heavenly goods, through which we are raised and strengthened as we ascend from transitory things to eternal ones. The branches suggest charity, which rises upward through love of God and spreads abroad through love [Col. 0913D] of neighbour. The pith, hidden within, signifies the secret intention of the heart; the bark, which is visible, the manifest surface of good conduct. The heart’s intention concerns conscience alone; the surface of conduct concerns reputation as well. God alone judges the former; one’s neighbour judges the latter also. Therefore the former benefits you alone, but the latter can benefit another too, if that person is willing to imitate you. The leaves with which the tree is clothed signify good action, by which the righteous person is surrounded and adorned. The greenness of the leaves expresses the perseverance and continuance of that action. Flowers, because of their fragrance, signify a good reputation. That leafy and fruitful tree, which raised its foliage to heaven, had these flowers, saying: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). [Col. 0914A] That tree, I say, possessed and gave forth the fragrance of these flowers when it said: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Cor. II). Of these flowers it is written: “A good name is better than precious ointments” (Eccl. VII). But of the wicked: “The name of the ungodly shall rot” (Prov. X). This tree also has fruit: fruit without, fruit within, and fruit above. Within, in the mind; without, before one’s neighbour; above, in God. In the mind through a good conscience; before one’s neighbour through teaching; in God through glory. Thus this tree—that is, the righteous person planted beside the health-giving courses of waters—has a root through faith, a trunk through hope, branches through charity, pith through intention, bark through the appearance of conduct, leaves through good action, flowers through good [Col. 0914B] repute, and fruit, as was said above: inwardly through conscience, outwardly through teaching, and above through glory. Such, dearest brothers, was this righteous man. For blessed is he whose feast we celebrate today, whose virtues we recount, whose holiness we commend, whose assistance we implore; by whose word we are enlightened, by whose example we are formed, and by whose patronage we are defended. Let us labour, brothers, to be such, and let sons imitate their father, disciples their master, servants their lord, soldiers their leader, sheep their shepherd. But because we cannot accomplish such things by our own strength, let us pray to the Lord, “who gives generously to all and does not reproach” (Jas. I), that he may deign to water the dryness of our heart with the river of his wisdom, “whose stream makes glad his city” (Ps. XLVII), so that from the womb of our mind there may flow [Col. 0914C] rivers of living water springing up into eternal life (John VII). For if he waters the garden of our heart with this water, the root of faith will flourish in us, the trunk of hope will be strengthened, the branches of charity will be raised and spread abroad, the leaves of good work will appear, the flowers of good reputation, and the fruits of justification and glorification: justification on the way, glorification in the homeland. At the entrance into that homeland God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his saints (Rev. XXI). And he will give what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—those things, namely, which God has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II), he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. On the Feast of the Apostles

[Col. 0914D] “Who are these that fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. LX). Brothers, we celebrate the feasts of the blessed apostles. In proclamation, praise, and wonder at them, the prophet, marvelling at their dignity and excellence and inspired by God, proclaimed with such an oracle, saying: “Who are these,” etc. Therefore, with ready devotion, we undertake to expound the words of this oracle, so splendid and divine: for the praise, honour, and glory of those of whom they were spoken, and for your benefit, to whom they must be spoken, insofar as the Lord God of knowledge grants; and we promise completion in hope. “Who are these,” he says, “who fly like clouds?” For rightly and fittingly, dearest brothers, the holy [Col. 0915A] apostles are compared to clouds and signified by clouds. For, as we gather not only from our own perception but also from the words of the saints, clouds possess four properties, by which the four chief virtues of the blessed apostles are signified. Clouds rain, shelter, flash, and fly. Thus the apostles rain, shelter, flash, and fly. They rained when “their sound went forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). They rain through preaching; they shelter through intercession; they flash through miracles; they fly through contemplation. Each rained where he preached: Thomas rained in Greater India; Bartholomew in Lesser India; Simon and Jude in Persia; Philip in Scythia; Matthew in Ethiopia; [Col. 0915B] Mark in Alexandria; John in Asia; Andrew in Achaia; Peter in Cappadocia; Paul in Greece; and finally Peter and Paul in Italy. Thus, at the beginning of grace, they poured out the rain of saving words with the mighty sound of preaching. The Psalmist desired this rain when he said: “My soul is like earth without water before you” (Ps. CXLII). Therefore the earth—that is, the human race intent upon earthly things—received this coming rain and bore fruit: the fruit of which it is written, “but the fruit [is] eternal life” (John IV). O how good are these clouds, whose rain so drenches the earth that it bears such fruit! Even now we are watered by the saving drops of these clouds when we read or meditate upon their writings. They shelter through intercession. For they set themselves in the middle [Col. 0915C] between God and us, lest God look upon our crimes in wrath and punish us in the heat of strict judgment. Thus Paul was a cloud, and he sheltered the nations converted through him and entrusted to him when he gave thanks for them and prayed without ceasing. Even now both he and the others shelter us when they pour out prayers to God for our salvation. They flash with miracles, raising the dead, cleansing lepers, giving sight to the blind, and healing other sick persons—not only while living in the flesh, but also now while reigning with Christ. Flight signifies contemplation. Had not he flown who said: “But our citizenship is in heaven”? (Phil. III). Truly they flew who ascended even to the palace of heaven, reigning with Christ. Therefore the apostles are clouds: raining through preaching, sheltering through prayer, flashing through power, flying through contemplation.

And “like doves to their windows.” The dove is a simple bird: it has neither the anger of gall within nor hypocrisy of deed without. It therefore signifies true simplicity. The windows are the bodily senses, through which inward things go out and outward things enter. Thus the holy apostles are said to be like doves at their windows because they are known to have possessed dovelike simplicity in their senses. There follows a verse in praise of them: “Whiter than snow, more lustrous than milk,” etc. (Lam. IV). By snow, which comes from heaven and is whiter than every white thing, we can understand virgins; [Col. 0916A] by milk, which is produced from the fruitfulness of the flesh, married persons of the New Testament; by ancient ivory, because the elephant is a most chaste animal, the continent persons of the Old Testament. By sapphire, because it displays the colour of heaven, we may rightly signify the spiritual men of that same Testament. But the holy apostles are whiter than snow, more lustrous than milk, redder than ancient ivory, and more beautiful than sapphire, because they surpass with marvellous dignity both the virgins of the New Testament, who imitate the angelic life through the honour of chastity, and lawfully married people; and the continent persons of the Old Testament, though red even with martyrdom, and spiritual men, or prophets, by singular excellence. For many prophets and kings of the Old Testament wished to see [Col. 0916B] what they saw and did not see it, and to hear what they heard and did not hear it (Matt. XIII). Hence Isaiah, contemplating in the Spirit Christ struck with blows, crowned with thorns, and hanging on the cross, said: “We saw him, and there was no appearance; we desired him, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows, knowing infirmity” (Isa. XXXIII). In the New Testament as well, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and indeed all other saints would gladly have seen Christ in the flesh and heard his saving teaching, if they could have done so. But this privilege was granted to apostolic dignity. Therefore the blessed apostles precede all the saints, for they saw Christ in the flesh and received the first fruits of the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Let us strive to venerate them with worthy praises, [Col. 0916C] to imitate them in good works, to pray that we may be governed by their direction and protected by their intervention. Finally, let us desire to be joined to their fellowship and to enjoy their joy, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father, etc.

## SERMON VIII. On the Feast of Any Saint

“Israel shall sprout like a lily.” Hence we sing: “The righteous shall sprout like a lily, and shall bloom forever before the Lord” (Hos. XIV). If anyone considers visible things, as many significations of spiritual and invisible things can be found as there are properties in those visible and bodily things themselves, whether within in their nature or outwardly in their form. [Col. 0916D] For not only the things themselves are, as it were, directions and exhortations to us for knowing and seeking the highest and eternal good, but also their natural qualities and formal arrangements. For a human being, whom the Lord teaches knowledge, is recalled to the true and unchangeable good not only inwardly through reason and inspiration, but outwardly too through Scripture and creation. The first property of the lily which presents itself to our senses is its greenness. We also see the lily grow upright and bend its upright stance neither here nor there. It is medicinal, and has fibres in its root most fittingly joined to one another. The stalk of its stem is clothed with its leaves. When it reaches the fullness of its growth, it is found divided into many parts above through its little branches. It has [Col. 0917A] a six-parted white flower, saffron-coloured within by certain grains, and sweetly fragrant. It is not only upright but also straight. All these things apply spiritually to the righteous person. The righteous person is green, grows upright, and all the other things we have already set forth are found spiritually in him. Greenness signifies faith, because faith is first among virtues just as greenness is first seen in sprouting things, as we showed in a previous sermon. Uprightness signifies hope, by which we are raised from this wicked present age to fellowship with heavenly spirits, to the fullness of true blessedness, and to the contemplation of the eternal God—to be hoped for, loved, desired, sought, and found. He is medicinal through preaching; for just as diseases and infirmities of bodies are variously cured by various antidotes [Col. 0917B] and medicines, so the illnesses of souls are cured by manifold preaching. Remedies and medicines heal abscesses; the word of preaching drives out sins. The righteous person also has inward fibres [dossas: reading uncertain] and roots united, when thought agrees with thought in him, perception with perception, will with will, affection with affection. Thus he agrees with himself and does not change himself from one thing into another, just as, conversely, it is written of the fool: “The fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII). For as the moon is now first, now second, now third, and without ceasing passes from one state to another, so the fool, carried away by carnal desires, is altered, so that he is found never in harmony either with himself or with another, but always at variance.

And it should be noted that the leaves of the lily rise upward, because whatever the righteous person outwardly performs in action is raised upward through intention. He is straight through justice, for he gives to each person what is that person’s due: to the faithful what belongs to the faithful, to the unfaithful what belongs to the unfaithful, to the just what belongs to the just, to the unjust what belongs to the unjust, to a friend what is owed to a friend, to an enemy what is owed to an enemy, “the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God” (Matt. XXII). He divides into many little branches through the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit. For, as he is variously suffused with diverse gifts, he is not unfittingly said to divide branches. He is white through purity: for, as he is cleansed from every defilement of mind and spirit, he imitates the lily’s whiteness through the beauty of purity. [Col. 0917D] He is six-parted through perfection: for the number six, because it consists of and is completed by its parts, signifies perfection. The parts of six are one, two, three, which together make six; and whether you say six times one, three times two, or twice three, you complete the number six. The grains in the flower displaying a saffron colour figure charity. For saffron colour seems to bear before itself the ruddy brightness of flame, as we have already shown elsewhere. Its fragrance likewise expresses a good reputation, as has been said in other sermons. Thus, after the likeness of the lily, the righteous person is green through faith, rises through hope, heals through preaching, is united to himself through unanimity, is clothed with his leaves through good action, is straight through justice, [Col. 0918A] variously divided through the manifold grace of the Holy Spirit, white through purity, six-parted through perfection, saffron-coloured through charity, and fragrant through good repute. There are also other properties of the lily—for example, that it is known to be of a cold nature, suggesting the extinction of vices—and certain others by which virtues and good works may be figured. But for the present, let this suffice concerning the properties of the lily. We should also note the four words which were spoken: “shall sprout,” “shall bloom,” “for ever,” “before the Lord.” In the lily, brothers, sprouting comes first and blooming last. Sprouting therefore signifies a good beginning, blooming completion. The phrase “for ever” expresses the righteous person’s perpetual perseverance in good; “before the Lord” denotes a good intention. Thus the righteous person sprouts by making a good beginning, blooms by reaching completion, abides for ever by persevering, and acts before the Lord by doing his good works with a right intention. Let us strive, brothers, so to sprout and so to bloom through the merits and intercession of the righteous person whose feast we celebrate today, that we may deserve to be carried into the glory of the heavenly kingdom, through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON IX. On the Feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin, but more particularly on the Betrothal of Any Faithful Soul

“You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV). Who, brothers, is speaking, and to whom does he speak? A friend speaks to a beloved, a bridegroom to a bride, the spotless one [Col. 0918C] to the chaste, the incorruptible one [Col. 0918C] to the intact one, God to the soul—and to one such as she was whose feast we celebrate today, by the examples of whose chastity we are illuminated. “You are wholly beautiful.” Beautiful within, beautiful without: within in the heart, without in the body; red within, white without, well-proportioned in both. Red through charity, white through chastity, well-proportioned through humility. Therefore, “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” Everything in you is beautiful, and nothing in you is unclean. Pleasing in every respect, displeasing in none; in every respect you please, in none do you displease. “You are wholly beautiful.” Beautiful by nature, more beautiful by grace, and most beautiful you will become by glory. What and how great, brothers, do you think are the ornaments by which the bride of God, the soul of the righteous person, can be adorned so that her beauty ought thus to be commended? We read that King Ahasuerus had the maidens brought to his bridal chamber prepared with great diligence, washed in baths, anointed with ointments, and adorned with everything suited to beauty (Esther II). Thus God—indeed, much more abundantly—prepares his bride for himself and enriches her with everything that adorns spiritual beauty. First he gives her washing through contrition and weeping for sins, so that, sprinkled as it were with hyssop, she may be cleansed from the filth of crimes and, washed, become whiter than snow. The ointments are spiritual gifts, by which, after she has been anointed following tears, she is soothed from the harshness of grief. Then follow ornaments: garments, a girdle, a ring, a breastlet, a comb, a veil, earrings, a diadem, a mirror, and shoes. Garments signify [Col. 0919A] the variety of virtues and good works by which the soul is adorned and made honourable inwardly and outwardly before God and neighbour. Of this manifold variety it is written: “The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, clothed about with variety” (Ps. XLIV). The girdle, by which the loins are bound, signifies chastity, by which the unchecked lust of human flesh is restrained, as it is written: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke XII). The ring expresses whole faith, through which the bride loves the absent bridegroom and longs to attain his presence through continual desire. The breastlet (*murenula*), which is fastened upon the breast lest an adulterer put in his hand, represents chaste love, which the devil is not permitted to violate through any wicked delight. The comb, because it separates hairs from one another, figures the virtue [Col. 0919B] of discernment. The veil, which keeps the hair from flowing loose, suggests sobriety and tranquility of thoughts. Earrings, because they are ornaments of the ears, express obedience. The diadem figures the glory of conscience, of which it is written: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience” (I Cor. I). The mirror signifies the reading of the Scriptures, in which the soul contemplates what in itself is good or evil, honourable or dishonourable. Shoes, which protect the feet by which we move through various places, figure preaching carried abroad everywhere.

Therefore this bride has washing through contrition; ointments through the reception of spiritual gifts; garments through good action; a girdle through [Col. 0919C] chastity; a ring through faith; a breastlet through chaste love; a comb through discernment; a veil through tranquility and sobriety of thoughts; earrings through obedience; a diadem through glory; a mirror through reading; shoes through preaching. Precious stones are also often added to all these, which, on account of their brilliance, signify miracles flashing far and wide. O blessed bride of God, soul of the righteous person, adorned with such ornaments and prepared for the bridal chamber of the eternal king! Such a soul can employ great confidence. Yet it sometimes happens that, enriched with divine gifts, she is shaken with great terror while contemplating divine judgments, and is affected by a profound stirring of fear. The history of Esther offers us an example of this matter. For we read that Esther, beholding King Ahasuerus sitting upon his throne opposite the basilica, holding a sceptre and showing the fury of his breast through his burning eyes, was almost overcome, so much so that, although the king and his attendants comforted her in person, she could scarcely raise herself (Esther V). What, brothers, does King Ahasuerus signify in this matter except God? What does Esther signify except the soul? What does the basilica signify except divinity? What does the throne signify except majesty? What does the sceptre signify except power? What does the burning of the eyes figure except the terror of heavenly judgment? Esther, seeing the king as described, was terrified and fell; likewise the soul trembles before the divine majesty as it contemplates God and the strict judgments of God. But let it recover strength, consider the gifts bestowed upon it and the consolations given, and say: [Col. 0920A] “Even if he kills me, I shall hope in him.” For “the Lord is good to those who hope in him, to the soul that seeks him.” He who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON X. On the Fear of God

“Fear God, and keep his commandments: this is the whole human being” (Ecclus. XII). Dearest brothers, we find many splendid authorities in the divine Scriptures concerning the fear of the Lord. For it is written: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. CXI); and again: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. CX); and: “One who is without fear cannot be justified” (Ecclus. I); and: “How great is one who finds wisdom and knowledge, yet not greater than one who fears the Lord” (Ecclus. XXV). Wisdom is called reflection upon heavenly and divine things; knowledge, reflection upon [Col. 0920B] earthly and human things. Great is proclaimed the person who finds either one or both. For, first to speak of the discoverer of knowledge and to ascend from lesser things to greater: when we see someone skilled in logic, we call him great. Certainly, if we saw someone learned in grammar like Priscian, in dialectic like Aristotle, in rhetoric like Tully, we would say: “This man is great.” If, however, we saw him learned in mechanics, we would say likewise: “This man is great.” But if we saw him educated in arithmetic, music, geometry, and astronomy like Boethius, or as any discoverer or translator of the arts, we would cry out all the more: “This man is great.” If we further knew him wise in physics like Hippocrates or Galen, and advanced in secular theoretical learning like Plato and Socrates, we would certainly cry: “This man is great.” And if we saw a man thus learned in secular knowledge, and most skilled in the wisdom of divine Scripture—learned, that is, in the Old and New Testament, in history, allegory, tropology, anagogy, and the threefold language of letters like Jerome; eloquent in reasoning like Augustine; in morality like Gregory; and, finally, wise like Solomon—we would in every way proclaim: “This man is great.” Yet, brothers, he is not greater than one who fears the Lord. For great indeed is one who finds wisdom and knowledge, but not above the one who fears the Lord. Wisdom here is understood as knowledge which makes a person not only learned [Col. 0920C] but also righteous, concerning which it is written: “Blessed is the man who finds wisdom” (Prov. III). Blessed, indeed, is the person who finds wisdom not only through knowledge but also through the savour of righteousness, because by such finding he begins to taste the inner good. But even if such a finder of wisdom were handsome as Absalom, strong as Samson, swift as Asahel, excellent as Alexander, rich as Croesus, powerful as Octavian Augustus, long-lived as Enoch, none or all of these qualities would profit him unless he feared God. For it is written concerning beauty: “Charm is deceitful and beauty is vain; the woman who fears God shall be praised” (Prov. XXXI). But concerning wisdom, strength, and riches, the Lord says in these words through Jeremiah: “Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man [Col. 0921A] in his riches; but let him glory in this, if he knows that I am the Lord” (Jer. IX).

Finally, from many passages of Scripture we learn how useless and transitory are all things whatsoever that can be acquired in the present age. Therefore only the one who fears God hastens to blessedness, provided that he so fears as to depart from evil and do good. Now there are two fears: one servile, the other filial. The servile fear belongs to servants; the filial, to children. The servile has dread; the filial, love. The servile arises from sin committed; the filial, from a gift received. The servile concerns punishment to be endured; the filial, reward to be received. The servile belongs to beginners; the filial, to the perfect. But there are eight things by which we are stirred and formed toward the fear of God: by the first three toward servile fear, by the last three toward filial fear, and by the two in the middle toward both. These are: sin, judgment, punishment, creation, Scripture, nature, grace, and glory. By sin, judgment, and punishment we are stirred toward servile fear; by nature, grace, and glory toward filial fear; by creation and Scripture toward both. Servile fear has dread of punishment; filial fear has love of righteousness. Servile fear sometimes quickly passes away; filial fear, which is called holy, remains for ever and ever. We are stirred toward servile fear by sin through consideration of divine judgment; by judgment, moreover, we are stirred through estimation of the punishment that follows. For while we fear being punished by punishment, we also fear being judged by judgment; and while we fear being judged by judgment, we shudder at sin, [Col. 0921B] which is the cause of evils. For in the damned there will be, according to the magnitude of sin, the weight of judgment and the misery of the punishment that follows. Thus “deep calls to deep” (Ps. XLI). The deep of sin calls to the deep of judgment, and the deep of judgment calls to the deep of punishment. And this is “in the voice of your cataracts, O Lord” (ibid.), that is, in the witness of your preachers. O how deep, how broad, how terrible are these deeps! Greatness makes their depth, multitude their breadth, and contemplation of both their terror. We dread punishment for its own sake. Yet how few turn their eyes toward the contemplation of fear, and how many turn them toward spectacles of vanity! Of the former it is written: “The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow” (Eccl. VII); but of the latter: “The heart of fools is where there is joy” (ibid.). Through the last three also—nature, grace, and glory—we are formed toward filial fear. Filial fear is this: that you should be unwilling to offend, for the sake of glory, the one whom you love; just as servile fear is this: that you should not dare to offend, for the sake of punishment, the one whom you fear. We are called to filial fear through nature, because, as we consider the dignity of our nature, we fear from great love to offend God through sin, since in love he deigned to imprint upon us his image and likeness.

Great indeed is the honor, great the dignity, of the human condition, to which the image of the creating Godhead has been naturally imparted. We are likewise led to this same fear through consideration of grace [Col. 0922A], because, when we reflect on what He has bestowed upon us, ungodly though we were, by grace and without merit, we shrink from provoking Him to anger by sinning. We are also moved to this fear by the future glory that shall be revealed in us; for when we hear what He has promised us—what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man (1 Cor. 2)—we already fear, out of exceedingly great love, to offend Him who has willed to promise us such things and is able to give them.

Through the two intermediate means as well, creation and Scripture, we sometimes arrive at both kinds of fear. We are compelled toward servile fear through creation, because, when we consider its greatness, we dread the immeasurable majesty of the Creator; nor are we ignorant that He who is almighty [Col. 0922B] can inflict punishment if He finds us transgressors of His law. Likewise we are impelled to this same fear through Scripture, because, when we frequently hear divine threats in it, we are greatly afraid to transgress God’s commandments. But through creation we attain filial fear, because, when we behold so great a fabric, we judge the Creator to be wonderful, worthy of praise, lovable, and, because of love, to be feared. In the same way Scripture advances us toward this chaste fear, when we read in it divine promises surpassing human merit, and, loving the Promiser, fear lest we offend Him.

There are therefore eight means by which we ascend to the fear of God, beginning with lesser things and reaching greater: fault, judgment, punishment, creation, Scripture, nature, [Col. 0922C] grace, glory. Let us fear God, brothers, each according to what he perceives in himself. If we are in evil, let us correct our errors; if in good, let us improve what we have begun and keep His commandments. What are these commandments? Love of God and of neighbor. How greatly ought we to love God? Above all things. How greatly our neighbor? As ourselves: by deed, word, and intention. In deed there is a good work; in word, sound counsel; in intention, a devout desire.

Let us therefore fear God and keep His commandments. Through these we go to glory; without them, to punishment. “This,” he says, “is every human being.” If everyone who fears God and keeps His commandments is a human being, it follows that the person who does not do this is not a human being. For if he knows God [Col. 0922D] and His commandments, yet neither fears nor keeps them, he is a despiser, and should rather be called a devil than a human being. But if he does not know God and His commandments, he is blind, and should rather be called a beast than a human being. If, however, he knows, fears, and keeps them, he is truly a human being and worthy to be called by that name. Let us therefore fear the Lord and keep His commandments, so that by such a way we may reach the heavenly fatherland, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns.

## SERMON XI. On Spiritual Health

“Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise” (Jer. 17). Brothers, the one who asks to be healed shows that he is sick. [Col. 0923A] But who is this sick person? The human race, in whose voice these words are spoken, was sick through original sin and through many actual sins, and sought a physician. The physician came, and the sick person was healed.

There are twelve things concerning the healing of the human race which we have undertaken to explain: the sick person, the physician, wounds, medicine, vessels, antidotes, diet, dispensers, place, time, healings, and joys over those healings recovered.

This sick person is the human race, concerning whose illness Isaiah testified, saying: “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no health in it” (Isa. 1). “A wound, a bruise, and a swollen sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” Another likewise cries elsewhere: [Col. 0923B] “My head pains me.” Another: “My belly pains me.” Another: “My loins are filled with mockeries” (Ps. 37). Thus the members of the human race cried out and made known the pain of their sickness.

But, as was said, the physician came, and the sick person was healed. Who is this physician? God, “who heals the broken in heart and binds up their bruises” (Ps. 146). The wounds are original sins, which each person contracted through ignorance in the mind and through concupiscence in the flesh by living lustfully, as well as actual sins, which he committed by living perversely. The former he has from his parents; the latter from his own deeds. The former from another; the latter from himself.

The medicine is grace, which is poured into our wounds in two ways: one bitter and the other sweet. Bitter through rebuke; sweet through consolation. Rebuke [Col. 0923C] is wine; consolation, oil. The vessels are the sacraments, in which and through which spiritual grace is contained and conveyed: such as the water of baptism, oil, chrism, holy water, and other things of that kind.

The antidotes are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord—so that through fear we may be humble, through piety merciful, through knowledge discerning, through fortitude unconquered, through counsel provident, through understanding cautious, and through wisdom mature. Fear expels pride; piety, cruelty; knowledge, indiscretion; fortitude, weakness; counsel, imprudence; understanding, incaution; wisdom, folly. O how good are these antidotes, by which such evil abscesses are cured!

[Col. 0923D]

Diet is Sacred Scripture, which is set before us in diverse ways when it is preached according to the differing capacity of its hearers. At one time it is set before hearers or readers through history; at another through allegory; at another through tropology; at another through anagoge; at another through the authority of the Old Testament; at another through that of the New; now veiled in mystical coverings, now pure, bare, and open.

Thus, by such modes and many others, this spiritual food is set before us, that through it our sick person may be strengthened and restored to health. Scripture is rightly called diet when we do the things which we read in it must be done, and avoid those which must be avoided. For thus we obey physicians’ prescriptions regarding food: [Col. 0924A] we eat some things and avoid others.

The dispensers are the priests, who handle the divine sacraments and wonderfully administer divine grace to us through the hidden dispensation of the supreme Giver. They are servants of the supreme physician and ought, at His command, to handle His vessels and medicines.

The place is this world, into which, as into a kind of infirmary, the human being was brought from paradise after sin, so that here he may strive to cure his sickness and receive health. The time which God granted to the human being for restoration to health is the present age. It is divided into three times: the time of the natural law, the time of the written law, and the time of grace. The time of the natural law was from Adam to Moses; that of the written law, from Moses to Christ; the time of grace [Col. 0924B] is from Christ’s birth to the end of the world.

It should be noted that this place in which the sick person is healed is harsh, the time long, and the remedy effective. The place is harsh so that the transgressor may be chastised; the time long, lest the one to be healed be cut off beforehand; the remedy effective, that the sick person may be cured.

The healings are virtues. For when a person is exercised in virtues, the vices are driven out and he himself is healed. Virtues drive out vices: humility, pride; charity, envy; peace, anger; joy, acedia; generosity, avarice; abstinence, gluttony; chastity, lust. Virtues, therefore, taking possession of the place of vices, are the healings of illnesses.

The joys over recovered healings are the beatitudes. A person is saddened when he falls ill and rejoices when he is healed. Thus in the present age [Col. 0924C] we grieve over the infirmity of our corruption; but when, in the resurrection, we rise to true health, we shall rejoice in eternal blessedness, having attained health.

Therefore, the human being is the sick person; God, the physician; vices, the wounds; grace, the medicine; sacraments, the vessels; the gifts of the Holy Spirit, the antidotes; Scripture, the diet; priests, the dispensers; the world, the place; the present age, the time; virtues, the healings; beatitudes, the joys: “Heal me, therefore, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me and I shall be saved, for you are my praise.” Heal me from infirmity; save me from destruction. Heal me from fault; save me from punishment. Heal me in time; save me in eternity, because you are my praise in both, you who live and reign.

## SERMON XII. On the Spiritual Mountains and Trees of Israel

[Col. 0924D]

“Mountains of Israel, spread out your branches, blossom, and bear fruit” (Ezek. 36). Dearest brothers, places have their meanings just as times do. For as by morning we understand knowledge of truth, by midday love of virtue, by evening ignorance, by midnight malice, by light justice, and by darkness fault; so by a plain we understand freedom, by a hill good action, by a mountain contemplation, by heaven blessedness, by a valley iniquity, by an abyss despair, and by hell damnation.

The plain, established in levelness, has three places above it [Col. 0925A] which signify: the hill, mountain, and heaven; and three below: valley, abyss, and hell. The plain signifies freedom, because just as one who is on a plain has the ability, without obstruction from any hillock, to turn forward or backward, to the right or left, or wherever he pleases, so one who is truly free has the power to do what pleases him most.

The hill, which rises a little from the flatness of the earth, expresses good action, through which we are lifted from earthly things. The mountain, which comes nearer to the clouds, signifies contemplation, which, lifting us upward, raises us to the vision of heavenly goods. Heaven, because it is the place of blessedness, suitably signifies blessedness itself. The valley, because it descends toward lower things, signifies iniquity, which draws the wicked to the depths. [Col. 0925B] The abyss signifies despair, into which the wicked descend from the valley of iniquity. Hence it is written: “When the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. 18). Hell, because it is the place of damnation, signifies damnation.

“Mountains of Israel,” etc. The mountains of Israel are righteous contemplatives, who spread out their branches—that is, holy and fruitful thoughts proceeding from the root of faith and the trunk of good will—through love of neighbor; they blossom through good beginning, bear fruit through completion, and put forth leaves through good action.

Three principal kinds of trees seem to me to be born, grow, spread branches, blossom, bear fruit, and put forth leaves in the mountains of Israel. [Col. 0925C] The first is the olive or olive tree; the second, the vine; the third, the fig tree. The olive signifies mercy, because just as oil surpasses other liquids, so mercy precedes other virtues. The vine signifies wisdom, because wine, taken moderately, sharpens the intellect. The fig tree, because it has sweet fruits, signifies inward sweetness.

Mercy is customarily assigned to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and sweetness to the Holy Spirit. Thus the Father plants the olive, the Son the vine, and the Holy Spirit the fig tree. It must nevertheless be understood that, although we make such a distinction in assigning these three virtues, no division is to be understood in the activity of the three Persons.

Lamenting the unfruitfulness of these three virtues in the reprobate, the prophet said: [Col. 0925D] “The fig tree shall not blossom, and there shall be no shoot on the vines. The work of the olive shall fail” (Hab. 3). The olive therefore signifies mercy, the vine wisdom, and the fig tree inward sweetness.

There are perhaps other trees in the mountains of Israel through which diverse virtues are figured: as faith through the box tree because of its greenness; hope through the cedar because of its height; charity through the pine because of its richness; right rebuke through the thorn; temperance through the myrtle. Let us spread out our branches, brothers, blossom, and bear fruit, lest the Lord find us unfruitful and cut us down and burn us. “For now the axe has been laid to the root of the tree” (Matt. 3).

Let us bear fruit like the olive, vine, and fig tree. For there are some who bear a most bitter fruit, of whom it is written: [Col. 0926A] “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32). But let us, like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord, hope in the mercy of God (Ps. 51). He who lives and reigns.

## SERMON XIII. On the New Year

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonderful things” (Ps. 97). The Lord has done wonderful things in the creation of the world; He has done wonderful things in the redemption of the human race. He did wonderful things in the creation of the world, creating earthly and heavenly things, lowest and highest, visible and invisible, bodily and spiritual. He also did wonderful things in created things: in elements and things composed of elements, in simple and composite things, in causes and agencies, in natures and forms, in figures and colors, [Col. 0926B] in the growth of things that sprout and the fecundity of things that generate.

He did wonderful things in the redemption of the human race: by assuming flesh, hungering, thirsting, working miracles, suffering, dying, rising again, ascending, granting the grace of the Holy Spirit, forgiving sins, justifying the ungodly, and making the wretched blessed.

“Sing to the Lord a new song, for he has done wonderful things.” A song is a life. A new song is a new life. An old song is an old life. New life is justice; old life is sin. Moreover, singing is distinguished in three ways: low, high, and very high. The low signifies the life of married persons; the high, that of the continent; the very high, that of virgins. One who lives well sings well; one who lives badly sings badly, because he is out of harmony.

Those out of harmony with this song are the avaricious, thieves, robbers, the unclean, fornicators, adulterers, effeminate men, men who lie with males, perjurers, liars, murderers. [Col. 0926C] Many also out of harmony with this song are those raised to sacred orders, who ought to dwell in ivory houses—that is, preserve chastity—such as subdeacons, deacons, priests, bishops, archbishops, and perhaps apostolic men, regular canons, monks, hermits, recluses. Some of all these are out of harmony with divine praise because, although Christians in name, they are nevertheless pagans in manner of life; and though they have right faith concerning God, it is dead because they have no works. Therefore they are out of harmony with the song of God’s praise, because “praise is not comely in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). All such sing an old song, which signifies sorrow rather than joy.

Of such praisers it is written: “What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me? says the Lord. I am full. I have not desired holocausts of rams, and fat of fatlings, and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you came before my presence, who required these things at your hands, that you should walk in my courts? Do not bring sacrifice any longer in vain. Incense is an abomination to me. The new moon, the Sabbath, and other feasts I will not endure. Your assemblies are iniquitous. My soul has hated your calends and your solemnities; they have become burdensome to me; I have labored in bearing them. And when you stretch out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you; and when [Col. 0927A] you multiply prayer, I will not hear, for your hands are full of blood”—that is, sin (Isa. 1).

And through the prophet Malachi: “Behold, I will cast an arm upon you, and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities, and it shall take you away with it, says the Lord” (Mal. 2). Through another prophet it is likewise said of such persons: “They thought themselves to have instruments of song like David” (Amos 6). For while they hiss the words of divine praise with subtle voices and sound out songs in double or triple modulation, they think that they possess instruments of song like David, because they judge themselves to be true praisers of God. But their voice does not please, because their life displeases.

Let us therefore, brothers, sing to the Lord as the Psalmist commanded: “God is King of all the earth; sing wisely” (Ps. 46). What does “wisely” mean? Let us not be devoted to depraved works; let us not, in psalmody, be intent on idle words; let us not be curious after empty sights, undisciplined in laughter, or wandering in running about and roaming. Let us sing as a certain versifier says:

> At all these hours, let the voice of heart and mouth be one and the same.  
> The choir’s voice is pleasing when the heart sings in harmony with the mouth.

Let us therefore sing to the Lord a new song, for He has done wonderful things—not only because He has done them, but also because He will do wonderful things. He has done two chief wonders: one in the creation of the world, the other in the redemption of the human race. And He will do two: one in the renewal of creation, the other in the glorification of the redeemed. For at the end of the age, when He makes all things new, He will then do wonderful things in the renewal [Col. 0927C] of creation. But when He says to the elect, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the origin of the world” (Matt. 25), He will then do wonderful things in the glorification of the redeemed. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to bring us to that glorification, He who lives and reigns.

## SERMON XIV. At a Synod, or on the Feast of Priestly Confessors: On Sacred Vestments

“Let your priests, O Lord, be clothed in righteousness” (Ps. 131). Dearest brothers, we who exercise the priesthood in the house of God must lead a righteousness worthy of the priesthood and be clothed in honorable vestments in our office—or rather, [Col. 0927D] we must exercise the virtues signified by priestly vestments. What advantage is there in being adorned with vestments unless we are adorned with virtues? Certainly, if we saw a priest celebrating Mass without priestly garments—without alb, stole, or mitre—we would be greatly astonished and would detest such a minister with extreme horror.

If, then, one who approached the altar without vestments would be detestable, how detestable, how dreadful is one who presumes to approach with vices and without virtues? As great as the difference between any vessel and food is the difference between the signifier and the thing signified. The vestments signify; the virtues are signified. Vestments adorn the minister outwardly before the people; virtues commend him inwardly before the Lord. Therefore, just as we do not dare approach the altar without vestments, so let us not presume to approach without virtues.

Let us see, then, [Col. 0928A] what these vestments are and what virtues they signify. The vestments are the inner linen garment, the outer garment—that is, the alb—the amice over the shoulders, which we may call a shoulder-covering, the girdle, the stole, the maniple, and the mitre. Before all else, the priest ought to lay aside his daily clothes, then wash his hands, and thus take up white vestments. The laying aside of daily garments signifies putting off the old man; washing the hands, confession of sins; putting on new garments, the exercise of virtues.

The inner linen garment is inward; the outer one outward. The former is in secret; the latter in public. The former is hidden; the latter visible. Therefore the inner garment signifies purity of heart; the outer, purity of body. The shoulder-covering, placed upon the shoulders where burdens are customarily laid, signifies endurance of present labors, which is necessary to us if we wish to be true priests. [Col. 0928B] Concerning those who have lost it, it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance!” (Ecclus. 2).

And the Lord says in the Gospel, in praise of patience: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

Let us therefore endure, brothers, whatever adversity befalls us, so that, just as we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, so we may endure evil things also (Job 2). The girdle, which surrounds the loins and binds the garments lest they hang loose, signifies the virtue of continence, which restrains the loose wantonness of our lust. The stole, placed about the neck, expresses the Lord’s sweet yoke, of which the Lord says in the Gospel: “For my yoke is sweet [Col. 0928C] and my burden light” (Matt. 11).

Next comes the maniple, which hangs on the left arm. It signifies nothing else sacramentally except that it is placed there as a safeguard, lest the priest do anything in his office incautiously or negligently, but accomplish all things carefully, as one standing in the sight of the Lord and the holy angels. It therefore signifies caution, through which we avoid what must be avoided and do what must be done.

Though the minister of the Lord is clothed and adorned with all these things, he is not yet fit for priestly office, nor does he presume to fulfill it, unless a seventh garment, called the mitre, is added to and placed above the rest. This vestment is more excellent than the others and stands out above all. What virtue, then, do we say is signified by it, if not charity, [Col. 0928D] concerning which the Apostle says: “I show you a still more excellent way. Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” etc. (1 Cor. 12–13), as your fraternity well knows. After he had shown other spiritual gifts and virtues, he finally introduced charity, saying, “Though I speak with tongues,” etc. O blessed virtue, charity! And blessed is the one alone who perseveres in it to the end!

Therefore, one who has charity together with the other virtues is a priest. One who has even the other virtues without it is not a priest. Let us therefore have, if we wish to be true priests, what we ought to be: let us have the inner linen garment through purity of heart, the outer garment through purity of body; the shoulder-covering through patience, the girdle through continence, the stole through obedience, the maniple through caution, and the mitre through fraternal charity. [Col. 0929A] Armed with all these, we shall devoutly and religiously complete the Lord’s holocaust, and it shall be said of us what is written: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2).

Such were the saints whose solemnities we celebrate today. Let us strive, dearest brothers, to be such, so that we too may be clothed in righteousness and, made participants with them in merits, may deserve to become companions in rewards. May He who lives and reigns deign to grant this to us through their merits and intercession, etc.

## SERMON XV. On Septuagesima: On the Lord’s Vineyard

“Go you also into my vineyard, and I will give you whatever is just” (Matt. 20). Brothers, concerning the Lord’s vineyard, to which the divine word invites us, we shall give you a brief [Col. 0929B] exhortation, lest we burden your love with overly lengthy words. Let us first see what is the field in which the planting is made; what the vineyard is; what digging, double-digging, and triple-digging are; what the shoots are; what pruning, bending, leaves, flowers, fruit, and the promised denarius are.

This field is the human heart, which we ought to break with the continual hoe of compunction, and in which, by divine grace, we ought to plant a vineyard or vines through good wills, so that they may grow in goodness and produce shoots, leaves, flowers, and fruit. We ought to dig this vineyard through compunction born from examination of our sins; to dig it a second time through compunction born from consideration of the gifts bestowed upon us from heaven; and to dig it a third time through compunction [Col. 0929C] arising from a foretaste of future goods.

The shoots are good thoughts proceeding in many ways from good will. We prune this vineyard when we cut away less useful thoughts and apply ourselves to cultivating more useful ones. We bend the shoots when we humble our thoughts, and, as it were, drive a stake into the ground when we remember our mortality and recall that we are earth and shall go into earth. Thus Abraham bent his vine when he said: “I shall speak to my Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Thus Jacob, when he said: “I am less than all your mercies” (Gen. 32). David likewise said: “I am alone and poor” (Ps. 24). Blessed Mary bent her vine [Col. 0929D] and said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). But blessed Paul had bent his shoot when he said: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15).

The leaves signify good action, which surrounds and adorns us, as we have often said in other sermons. Flowers, because they are fragrant and spread their scent far abroad, signify good reputation, through which we are fragrant to our neighbor whether near or far. Fruit signifies a good conscience from righteousness brought to completion. For we labor in order to have a good conscience, just as one who toils in cultivating a vineyard aims to receive fruit.

We therefore have, brothers, the field as our heart; the Lord’s vine as good will; the shoots as good thoughts. Let us dig, dig a second time, [Col. 0930A] and dig a third time, as has been written, through threefold compunction. Let us prune it by cutting off superfluous and less useful thoughts. Let us bend it through humility of mind, that it may produce leaves through good action, flowers through good reputation, and fruit through good conscience. If, dearest brothers, we labor thus in the Lord’s vineyard, we shall receive the promised denarius.

What is this denarius? This denarius is eternal life. This denarius is what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love Him (1 Cor. 2). This denarius is the highest good, in which is every good and from which is every good: every good in it through fullness, every good from it through liberality. This denarius is to see God and to taste Him: [Col. 0930B] to see through contemplation, to taste through love. May Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns, deign to help us labor in this vineyard and reward us with this denarius, etc.

## SERMON XVI. On the Feast of Martyrs: On Spiritual Agriculture

“Those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Ps. 125). Brothers, “the one who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly, and the one who sows in blessings shall also reap of blessings” (2 Cor. 9). Let us therefore sow what is good and abundant if we wish to reap what is good and abundant. Let us sow in merit according as we desire to reap in reward.

Let us seek the plough and the implements of the plough: the long piece of wood which country people call *hagia*, the forked piece of wood by which the plough is held with the hands, [Col. 0930C] and the rest, which, for brevity’s sake, I pass over in setting forth the explanation. The ploughshare-base, upon which the rest of the structure stands, is faith, the origin of the other virtues. The long beam that extends lengthwise, which we call *hagia* in the rustic tongue, signifies hope, concerning whose length it is written: “You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages, in the Lord God strong forever” (Isa. 26). The handle, which is forked and held with both hands, shows charity, which we hold with the right hand when we do good to friends, and with the left when we do good to enemies.

The ears of the plough signify the virtue of obedience, because with ears we hear and obey. The wheels signify knowledge of the two Testaments. The Testaments are fittingly figured by wheels: they touch the earth, as it were, below through history and are raised upward through allegory; are lowered below through the carnal sense and raised upward through the spiritual sense; below through the things signifying, above through the things signified. [Col. 0930D] The ploughshare and the blade, by which the earth is cut and opened, signify reason and understanding, through which we examine and turn over the hidden things of creatures and the obscure things of Scripture.

The yoke, which presses the neck, expresses the weight of divine fear, placed upon our minds so that our understanding may not rise in pride against God. The straps by which the yoke is fastened are the commandments of the divine law. Concerning the despiser of this yoke and these straps it is written: “From of old you have broken the yoke, you have burst the straps; you said: ‘I will not serve’” (Jer. 2). The oxen, [Col. 0931A] which labor in ploughing, are the bodily senses, which become ten because they are doubled for the two sexes. They are rightly called oxen because of maturity, not bulls because of unruliness; oxen because of continence, not bulls because of wantonness. The goad by which they are pricked is bodily affliction in vigils, fasts, and other things of that sort.

The earth which we ought to plough is ourselves. We ought to plough it through compunction born from examining our sins; to dig it a second time through compunction arising from consideration of heavenly gifts bestowed on us; and also to dig it a third time through compunction arising from a foretaste of future goods. We ought also to manure this earth by remembering our old and wicked ways of life. For, as it were, [Col. 0931B] we carry dung from each of the stalls of our animals onto our earth when we recall in grief whatever we did carnally and bestially in past conduct. And we scatter it, as it were, in portions when we examine each evil deed according to place and time, quality and quantity.

We therefore have, brothers: through faith, the ploughshare-base; through hope, the *hagia*; through charity, the handle; its right horn through love of friends, its left through love of enemies; the ears of the plough through obedience; the little wheels through knowledge of both Testaments; the blade and ploughshare through sound reason and sound understanding; the yoke through divine fear; the straps through the precepts of the law; the oxen through the five bodily senses; [Col. 0931C] the goad through affliction of the flesh; the triple ploughing through threefold compunction; manuring through recollection of sins.

But our seeds are divine gifts; the vessel in which we preserve them is spiritual understanding and sense. We commit these seeds to the earth when we devote them to affection and effect: to affection through love, to effect through action. We sow in tears; we shall reap in exultation. We sow in tears because “all who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3); we shall reap in exultation because we shall rejoice in recompense. May He who lives and reigns deign to grant this, etc.

## SERMON XVII. On the Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0931D]

“He shall live, and to him shall be given from the gold of Arabia” (Ps. 71). Who is the one who shall live, and to whom shall be given from the gold of Arabia? The child who has been born to us and the son who has been given to us, whose name is Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Strong, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace (Isa. 9).

Wonderful in glory; counsellor in wisdom; God in nature; strong in power; father in mercy; prince in justice. He is wonderful in glory because even the angels, gazing upon Him through excessive wonder at His glory, fail and sing, saying: “Heaven and earth are full of the majesty of your glory.” He is counsellor in wisdom because He is the Angel of Great Counsel, who brought back the human being wandering in the trackless place of unbelief and iniquity. He is God in nature because He possesses deity by nature and grants others to be gods by grace. [Col. 0932A] He is strong in power because He defeated the prince of this world guarding his court—that is, the world—and took as spoil his vessels—that is, souls in which he had placed iniquity, yet souls predestined to life. He cast him down and bound him (Luke 2), so that he might not according to his ancient custom rule in the human being, until, by God’s permission, he is released for a little while in the time of Antichrist and afterwards is consigned with his own to hell on the day of judgment.

He is father in mercy because He came to us in fatherly compassion, and redeemed, justified, and made us blessed. He came through humanity, redeemed through passion, justified through grace, and made blessed through glory. He is prince in justice because He will render to each what is his: good things to the good, evil things to the evil; glory to the good, punishment to the evil. Thus He is wonderful in glory, counsellor in wisdom, God in nature, strong in power, father in mercy, prince in justice. [Col. 0932B]

“He shall live, and to him shall be given.” What shall be given to Him? From the gold of Arabia—not gold only, but also frankincense and myrrh. Gold, because of the brightness of divine knowledge, signifies radiance—that is, faith. Frankincense, because of its fragrance, signifies good reputation. Myrrh, which preserves bodies incorrupt, signifies incorruption of the flesh.

But from myrrh, because of its bitterness, we can draw multiple meanings. There is myrrh of sorrow; myrrh of fear; myrrh of compunction; myrrh of confession; myrrh of satisfaction; myrrh of spiritual exercise; myrrh of labor; myrrh of submission; myrrh of compassion; [Col. 0932C] and also myrrh of suffering.

Myrrh of sorrow is when we recall past evils and grieve over them. Myrrh of fear is when we fear future punishment for the evils we have committed. Myrrh of compunction is when, compelled by sorrow and fear, we are pierced with remorse for evils perpetrated. Myrrh of confession is when, confessing the evils we have done, we are ashamed. Myrrh of labor, of satisfaction, is when, after confessing our transgression of the divine law, we make satisfaction to God, according to our measure, through the affliction of penitence. Myrrh of labor is when we labor in rendering the six works of mercy to our neighbor. Myrrh of spiritual exercise is when, vices having been expelled, we attain virtues through prolonged exercise. [Col. 0932D] Myrrh of submission is when we submit ourselves to one higher for God’s sake and sometimes endure bitterness as a result. Myrrh of compassion is when we have compassion upon another’s evils. Myrrh of suffering is when we endure our own evils.

We have, therefore, ten kinds of myrrh: the first through sorrow, the second through fear, the third through compunction, the fourth through confession, the fifth through satisfaction, the sixth through the exercise of virtues, the seventh through the performance of good works, the eighth through submission, the ninth through compassion, the tenth through suffering. Let us also, brothers, offer gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the Lord who has been born: gold through faith, frankincense through a good reputation, myrrh through the incorruption of our flesh, and [Col. 0933A] according to the manifold division of myrrh given above. And because we can do nothing without divine grace, let us always implore that grace, that through its help we may be able to offer this oblation and attain eternal recompense. May he deign to grant this to us who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XVIII. On the Annunciation of the Lord

“Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son” (Luke 1). Dearest brothers, as we are to speak on the Annunciation of the Lord, we shall give you a brief sermon, lest we burden your charity. And since, with many Scriptures explaining it, you know the manner of that most sacred conception, it seems fitting to pass over that inviolate manner and set forth something that may build up your conduct.

We ought, [Col. 0933B] brothers, ourselves to be mothers of Christ if we wish to be righteous, if we wish to be blessed: righteous by grace, blessed by glory. We ought to conceive Christ, to be in labour with Christ, to give birth to Christ, to possess Christ when he is born. In bodily generation, conception comes first; labour second; birth third; possession of the child when born fourth. In that possession there is joy, because “a human being has been born into the world,” and the mother remembers no longer the distress she has passed through (John 16). But in this spiritual generation faith comes first, good will second, good action third, eternal blessedness fourth.

In bodily generation, the first stage is the union of male and female, when the woman, retaining the seed, is made fruitful. Then comes labour—that is, preparation for birth: namely, the growth and development of the conceived fetus, the formation [Col. 0933C] and arrangement of its limbs, its endowment with sensation, and its completion as a human being. Finally birth follows—that is, the bringing forth of the fetus—in which the mother undergoes the greatest pain, distress, toil, and crying. At last follows possession of the child born; in this, because of her overwhelming joy that a human being has been born into the world, the mother does not remember her former distress.

So it is in spiritual generation, in which God is male and the soul female. When God himself is joined to the soul, the soul conceives Christ through faith. For faith is first among all good things, without which it is impossible to please God, just as it is impossible by nature for a human being to be generated without seed. Then labour follows, when knowledge of the good that has been conceived grows through good will, is endowed with feeling through affection, [Col. 0933D] and is, as it were, arranged limb by limb through the desire to act. Birth follows when the good is outwardly made manifest by action, which had previously been contained inwardly in good will. In this there is the mother’s toil and crying, because the soul is then weighed down by the weakness and murmuring of the flesh.

But as long as this labour lasts, as long as one lives, this fetus is always being brought forth; for as long as there is time to live, there is always time to act well. When a human being dies, however, then the child is perfectly born, because only on the day of death are the virtue and merit of the work perfectly made manifest. Possession of the child born is eternal blessedness, in which we shall see Christ and taste him: we shall see him through contemplation, and taste him through love. Of the joy and fruit of this birth it is written: “When he gives sleep to his beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord: children, the reward, the fruit of the womb” (Psalm 128). [Col. 0934A] Therefore we conceive Christ through faith, are in labour through good will, give birth through good action, and shall rejoice in the child born through eternal recompense.

But it must be understood that a fleshly soul cannot receive Christ, just as a wooden window cannot receive the sunbeam within itself. And just as a glass window receives the ray of the sun into itself, and that ray enters and penetrates it, so a spiritual soul, purified from the filth of vices and made bright by the sun of virtues, conceives Christ. For what is the wood in the window but the body? What is the glass but the spirit? The iron that binds the panes, because all things are subdued by iron, [Col. 0934B] signifies the rigor of severity; and lead, because of its heaviness, the virtue of gravity. The different panels are the different faculties of the soul: some are directed upward through contemplation of God; others downward through care of oneself; others to the right through love of friends; others to the left through love of enemies; others round about through watchfulness over one’s movements.

The natural purity of the glass signifies the virtues bestowed on us by nature; its added colours, the virtues granted us by grace. Painted images signify the examples of the saints, which we must diligently paint within ourselves by reflecting on their virtues: Abel’s innocence, Noah’s righteousness, Abraham’s faith, Isaac’s perseverance, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, [Col. 0934C] Joshua’s steadfastness, Samuel’s charity, David’s humility, Elijah’s zeal, Daniel’s abstinence, the outstanding humility of St John the Baptist, and the chastity of the Blessed Mary. We also paint the cross within ourselves by continually reflecting on the Lord’s passion, which he endured for us. Thus let us paint within ourselves the images of the other saints, reflecting upon and imitating their virtues and examples.

Therefore, brothers, in this mystical meaning of the glass window: the wood is the body; the glass, the spirit; the iron, severity; the lead, gravity; the individual panels, the individual faculties of the soul; the purity of the glass, virtues given us by nature; the added colours, virtues bestowed upon us by grace; and the painted images, examples of the saints. [Col. 0934D] Let us therefore, dearest brothers, be spiritual, that we may be illumined by the ray of the sun of righteousness and may spiritually conceive and give birth to Christ, the son of the Virgin Mary, so that we may thus attain the joy of eternal recompense, through him who comes and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XIX. On Any Confessor

“Behold, a great priest” (from the Common Epistle for confessors and pontiffs). Great in office, great in merit, great in reward, great in intercession. Great in office, because he is a bishop; great in merit, because he is worthy of heaven; great in reward, because he is blessed; great in intercession, because he is our patron.

Concerning his greatness Scripture adds, saying: “Like a star, like the moon, like the sun, like the rainbow, like the cedar, like the cypress, like the rose, like the lily, like frankincense, [Col. 0935A] like fire, like a vessel of solid gold.” A star is a light in heaven, and smaller than the others—namely, the sun and moon—and signifies a good beginning: a beginning because it is smallest; good because it is a light. The moon, because from its beginning it advances through moments, hours, days, and weeks to fullness, signifies progress toward perfection: from good to better, from beginning to completion. But the sun, because it is complete in its size and full in its circuit and never grows, rightly denotes perfection.

The rainbow—that is, the heavenly bow—because it is rainy and carries waters before it, expresses preaching, which waters us who, without it, are earth without water, so that, finding us barren, it may make us fruitful. The cedar is a tree of Mount Lebanon. “Lebanon” is interpreted “whitening,” and figures one who has been sprinkled with the hyssop [Col. 0935B] of grace and whitened beyond snow. But the cedar, a tree of Lebanon which rises high and lifts itself toward lofty places, signifies the hope of the righteous person, who stretches himself upward from earthly things to hope for heavenly things.

The cypress is a fragrant tree and expresses a good reputation, which, in the report of its sweet fragrance, pleasantly spreads itself everywhere, not merely through neighbouring places but also through distant ones. The rose, on account of its redness, figures martyrdom. One kind of martyrdom is inward, another outward: inward by compassion, outward by suffering. Lilies, because of their marvellous whiteness, fittingly signify chastity of the flesh. Frankincense, because it is customarily offered with the sacrifice of prayer, signifies prayer ascending to the divine ears. Fire signifies charity, concerning which it is written: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I will but [Col. 0935C] that it should burn?” (Luke 12). This is the perpetual fire which, in the Old Testament, was commanded to burn on the altar (Leviticus 6). For charity ought always to remain upon the altar of the heart, because without its flame no sacrifice of thought, speech, or action can be consecrated or made acceptable in the sight of the Lord.
