“Like a vessel of solid gold”: “vessel” signifies measure; “gold,” wisdom; “solid,” constancy. Therefore, dearest brothers, this priest whose solemnity we celebrate today was like the morning star through a good beginning; like the moon through a better perfection; like the sun through the highest perfection; like the rainbow through preaching; like the cedar through hope; like the cypress through a good reputation; like the rose through compassion; like the lily through chastity; like frankincense through prayer; like fire through charity; like a vessel of solid gold—vessel through measure, gold through wisdom, solid through constancy. [Col. 0935D]

Let us too, brothers, be priests, imitating this saint according to our capacity, adorned with the virtues named above and occupied in divine offices, so that it may be said also of us what is written: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2); and likewise: “You shall be called priests of the Lord, ministers of our God” (Isaiah 62). Our sacrifice is our soul, which we ought always to hold in our hands and offer undefiled to God, as the Psalmist says: “My soul is always in my hands” (Psalm 117). This sacrifice [Col. 0936A] is the cause of all sacrifices, because all the rest were made for its sake. Even Christ’s passion was the cause of the other sacrifices preceding it. Let us offer this first, because the others profit nothing without it, although they too are great. May he who lives and reigns bring us to fulfil this, etc.

## SERMON XX. On Any Faithful Soul

“The bee is small among flying creatures, and the beginning of sweetness is its fruit” (Ecclesiasticus 11). Just as even the smallest deeds of the saints in Scripture supply us with many and great lessons, so things that appear least among creatures sometimes offer us eminent examples of virtue. For although the bee [Col. 0936B] is small among flying creatures, by its nature and activity it nevertheless presents us with great encouragements to righteousness.

For the bee, as the present Scripture tells us, is small among flying creatures—that is, little. It brings water for the making of its work. It naturally possesses anger. It has a sting, through which it exercises vengeance. It is without sexual union; it makes wax and makes honey. It has feet and wings; it emits a buzzing sound. It follows a leader and is found swift in flight. All these things that we have said of the bee are fittingly understood spiritually of any faithful soul.

For that soul is small or little through humility, when it does not wish to think lofty thoughts but to fear; and the more it perceives itself to be exalted through righteousness, the more earnestly it strives to humble itself. It also takes water into its work [Col. 0936C] when it is moved to compunction either for its own sin or for the future reward. It has anger when it is justly angry against evil persons. It has a sting with which it pricks when it punishes evil not only in itself but also, as far as it can, in others. It is without sexual union when it restrains itself from unlawful pleasure. It makes wax when it shows others, by its holiness, the forms of righteousness. It also gathers honey when it accumulates the sweetness of charity in the inner chambers of the heart. It has feet when it passes from virtue to virtue, from good action to good action. It has wings when it flies by contemplation from low things to high. It emits a buzzing sound when it gives thanks to the Creator in all things. It follows a leader when it humbly imitates any superior. Finally, it is swift because it is ready in every exercise of virtue and [Col. 0936D] performance of good work.

Therefore, like the bee, the faithful soul has smallness—that is, littleness—through humility; water for its work through compunction; anger through righteousness; a sting through vengeance. It lacks sexual union through continence; has wax through the showing forth of good work, honey through charity, feet through good action, wings through contemplation, and buzzing through thanksgiving. It follows a leader through imitation of a superior; it is swift through readiness for every virtue and work. Let us, brothers, imitate the bee, that we may deserve to have the beginning of sweetness through the marrow of charity and through the sweetness of heavenly blessedness, through him who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XXI. On the Members of the Human Body

[Col. 0937A]

“Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed” (Jeremiah 17). As long as a human being persisted in righteousness, he was healthy; but after he fell through sin, he fell into grave sickness. And he who before sin possessed health in all his spiritual members, after sin suffers infirmity in all of them. Therefore he must cry: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.”

But should a human being be said to have spiritual members? He has spiritual members, namely virtues. For just as outwardly he is formed by members properly suited to one another, so inwardly he is wonderfully arranged and ordered by virtues harmonious with one another; and the members of the body themselves figure virtues of the spiritual substance. The head signifies [Col. 0937B] the mind. For as the head holds the highest place among the members, so the mind appears to be chief and supreme among the virtues of the soul. And just as hairs of diverse kinds rise from the head—yellow, red, white, black—so diverse thoughts proceed from the mind: kindly, malicious, clean, unclean.

The eyes denote contemplation. For just as we see outward visible things with the eyes of the body, so we examine invisible things with the rays of contemplation. By the nostrils we understand discernment. For we distinguish fragrances and stenches by the nostrils, and therefore we not inappropriately signify the virtue of discernment by the nostrils. The ears express obedience, since they are instruments for hearing and obeying. The mouth indicates understanding. For just as we receive food through the mouth, so by the virtue of understanding [Col. 0937C] we grasp the nourishment of divine reading. The teeth signify meditation, because just as we grind food received with the teeth, so through the work of meditation we more subtly examine and divide the bread received from reading. The tongue, too, because it forms speech, fittingly signifies the beauty of eloquence.

By the neck, shoulders, and back, because burdens are usually placed upon them, we rightly understand patience. By the arms, because great strength is in them, we understand the virtue of fortitude. The hands, because we work by them, signify action. Thus the breast, because by it we resist the adversary in struggle, figures steadfastness. The heart, too, because wisdom is contained in it, signifies wisdom. The breasts express teaching. For just as a mother nourishes her children with two breasts, so any devout teacher advances all imperfect persons to the perfection of righteousness through the teaching of love for God and neighbour. By the belly [Col. 0937D] let us understand memory.

For just as we transfer bodily food, received through the mouth and ground by the teeth, into the belly so that it may be digested there and distributed to all the members, in order that the members may be strengthened by it, so we store within memory spiritual food known through understanding, examined and refined by meditation, so that, cooked there by the fire of love, it may be supplied and apportioned to all the virtues, in order that they may be strengthened by it. But just as bodily food received into the belly does not benefit some people because, owing to an excess of it or weakness [Col. 0938A] of the digestive power, it is not properly digested but is expelled as though whole, so spiritual food received into the mind does not benefit some because, being weakened by excessive negligence, it slips suddenly from memory and is lost. But the person who keeps such food once received through memory and digests it through love is strengthened and fortified to avoid evils and accomplish goods.

The lower members—the legs and feet, by which the body is carried swiftly—signify the perfection of virtues and good works, and swiftness in that perfection. For by legs and feet we not only move, but sometimes run swiftly. The fingers of feet and hands, because they are the extremities of the members, figure the perfection of virtues and good works. [Col. 0938B] The nails, because they are the defence of the fingers, signify firmness of perfection. Therefore, whoever has fingers through perfection should desire to have nails through the firmness of perfection.

Accordingly, whoever has fingers should beware lest he ever be loosened from perfection and, gradually dissolving, be reduced to nothing. Therefore the members of the outward human being signify the virtues of the inward human being. The head signifies the mind; the hairs, thoughts; the eyes, contemplation; the nostrils, discernment; the ears, obedience; the mouth, understanding; the tongue, eloquence; the neck, humility; the back, patience and long-suffering; the arms, fortitude; the hands, action; the breast, steadfastness; the heart, wisdom; the breasts, teaching; the belly, memory. The lower members, by which the body [Col. 0938C] moves, signify the perfection of virtues and good works, and swiftness in that perfection. The fingers of feet and hands, which are the extremities of the members, signify the perfection of all good things. The nails, which are the protection of the fingers, signify firmness of perfection. The inner members signify hidden virtues; the outer, manifest virtues. The bones signify the inward vigour of good work; the skin, the surface of that same work.

But if anyone obtains the wholeness and health of these members—so that he has a sound head through incorruption of mind, white hairs through purity of thought, a ruddy face through fervour of charity, bright eyes through the radiance of heavenly contemplation, and, as stated above, possesses the beauty of the remaining members—he is truly healthy. [Col. 0938D] But whenever he is injured by the contagion of some vice, at once the beauty of inward loveliness is violated. Let us restore in ourselves, brothers, the beauty of the spiritual form, the divine image. But because we can neither heal spiritual sickness within ourselves nor obtain health without the aid of the supreme physician, let each of us cry out to him: “Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.” May he, etc., who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XXII. On the People and Land of the Lord

We read in the song of Moses, which he wrote concerning the ancient people, the people of Israel, that he said of that same people that God “set him upon a high land, that he might eat the fruits of the fields, that he might suck honey [Col. 0939A] from the rock and oil from the hardest stone” (Deuteronomy 32). For just as God, when creating the first human being, gave him the paradise of delight, that through that good he might know to hope for the good of heavenly glory, so, wishing after sin to lead his people back to glory, he gave the land of promise to those to whom he entrusted the mysteries of redemption, so that through the good received in time they might learn to hope for the good to be received in eternity.

This land is called high—that is, mountainous—as Moses says elsewhere when speaking with Israel: “The land which you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt from which you came out, where waters are drawn for irrigation; but it is mountainous, awaiting rains from heaven, which the Lord your God always visits, and his eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year until its end” (Deuteronomy [Col. 0939B] 11). The land of Egypt is said to be flat because the blindness of the present life reckons altogether lawful whatever the world, the flesh, and the devil suggest. The wicked person sets no obstacle before himself in the commission of evil; rather, everything that he desires, as though it were permitted, he pursues through the delight of perverse will and the accomplishment of the deed. It is irrigated by its rivers because it is drenched in vices.

But the land of Israel is called high because the spiritual life, through the eminence of virtues, is likewise exalted on high to contemplate heavenly goods. It awaits rain from heaven, that is, grace from God. The Lord God promised it and always visits it because he carefully observes what is done in it and mercifully grants it grace for accomplishing greater goods. And his eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year [Col. 0939C] until its end. For whatever good is done in spiritual conduct in the time of grace—which is the year of his favour—he always beholds; and for its crown, so that this land may bear more abundant fruit, he blesses it with the drops of heavenly gift.

But God set his people—not the old people but the new, not the Jewish but the Christian—upon this high land, that it might eat the fruits of the fields, suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone. The apostle Paul had established his dwelling upon this land when he said of himself and of those like him: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Philippians 3). For what is high land but spiritual life, holy life, honourable life?

Some boast of living in a city situated on the slope of some steep place, because such a city, when rains fall, is washed clean of its filth and thereby has not only cleaner streets but also healthier air. They also disparage cities situated in low places because of their filth, their foul smells, and the consequent corruption of the air, since, they say, cities of that sort devour their inhabitants by their stench. [Col. 0939D] But what benefits you to dwell bodily on high ground if by perverse conduct you live in the depths of vices? For the form of this world passes away, and nothing remains; rather, every good and evil of the present age flows away wholly and swiftly. Therefore it matters little where you dwell; instead, strive with all your strength to lead a life worthy of God.

“He set him,” it says, “upon a high land, that he might eat [Col. 0940A] the fruits of the fields.” What are these fields but the sacred books? What are the fruits of the fields but the meanings and senses of the books? The individual books are individual fields: namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and the other books of the Old Testament; Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, and the other books of the New Testament. For the former produce barley because of the roughness and hardness of the letter; the latter wheat because of the gentleness and tenderness of spiritual understanding.

If it displeases you to gather fruit by reading the former, let it at least please you to gather it from the latter—that is, if you shrink from reading the books of the Old Testament, at least strive to read and know the books of the New Testament. If you despise barley, reap wheat. Know that these fields, namely the divine books, have been well cultivated by excellent farmers through many labours—that is, corrected, well glossed, and expounded by perfect teachers through many afflictions, vigils, readings, meditations, and disputations. Others have laboured; and you, enter into their labours, reap the fruits of the fields, and read the teachings of the books. [Col. 0940B] If you are willing to heed my words, the Lord will shepherd you and nothing shall be lacking to you, because he will place you in a pasture-place (Psalm 22). But if you are unwilling, your soul, having abhorred every food, will draw near even to the gates of death (Psalm 106).

Beware also lest you eat the husks of swine—that is, lest you delight in the fictions of poets or in the filth of vices. Gather the fruits of divine books, and through them become rich and enlarged. There you will find, as we have already said elsewhere, the fruit of honourable occupation, the fruit of inward devotion, and the fruit [Col. 0940C] of heavenly contemplation.

There are also other books fertile in spiritual goods, offering abundant and health-giving fruits. For the whole universe of creation is like a certain bodily library. But just as, if an unlearned layman finds a new library well arranged, well written, painted and illuminated with gold and diverse colours, he opens it and looks at it, praises the lettering, commends the gold and colours, yet does not at all know what wisdom it contains; so a brutish person, blinded by the darkness of ignorance, considering this world only in its outward appearance, praises the height of heaven, the breadth of earth, the brightness of the heavenly lights, the greenness of growing things, the variety of every sort of living creature, the masses of mountains, and the courses of rivers, yet does not perceive what knowledge of God lies hidden within it. “A senseless man shall not know, nor a fool understand these things” (Psalm 91). He does not recognize in creatures the omnipotence of the Creator, which made so many and such great things from nothing; nor the wisdom that orders things so beautifully made; nor the goodness that gave things so useful. [Col. 0940D] But let us, brothers, delight in God’s creation and rejoice in the works of his hands.

When the text says, “that he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone,” it sets forth two things, the rock and honey, and again two, the stone and oil. According to the traditions of our teachers, a *petra* (“rock”) is smaller and more fragile than a *saxum* (“stone”); a *saxum* is greater and harder than a *petra*. The rock and the stone signify Christ. But the rock signifies Christ in his mother’s womb, while the stone signifies Christ at the right hand of God the Father. The rock is Christ in the world; the stone is Christ in heaven.

Do you wish to see Christ as the small rock? See him hidden in a cradle, or preaching only in Judaea. Do you wish to see Christ as the great stone? See him exalted at the Father’s right hand and, through faith, extended in the hearts of believers to the ends of the earth. This is the stone of which it is written: “A stone was cut from the mountain without human hand; it became a great mountain and filled the earth” (Daniel 2). [Col. 0941A] Do you wish to see Christ as the fragile rock? See him crying, hungry, thirsty, weary, cold, weeping, scourged, put to death. Do you wish to see Christ as the hardest stone? See that Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him, for in that he lives, he lives to God (Romans 6).

Honey from the rock signifies the grace of redemption; oil from the hardest stone, the glory of blessedness. For just as honey tastes sweeter to the palate than everything else eaten, so the grace of redemption becomes sweet in the hearts of the elect beyond all things that can belong to a human being in the present age. And just as oil surpasses all liquids, so the glory of blessedness, which is the highest good, surpasses and exceeds all goods. Therefore, brothers, we ought to be established upon high land through the eminence of virtues; to eat the fruits of the fields through reading the Scriptures; and, through contemplation of creatures, to suck honey from the rock by receiving the grace of redemption, and oil from the hardest stone by hoping for the glory of blessedness. May he who lives and reigns deign [Col. 0941C] to bring us to it, etc.

## SERMON XXIII. To Priests in Synod

“Go, swift angels, to a people torn away and rent asunder; to a terrible people, after which there is no other; to a people awaiting and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land” (Isaiah 18). Behold, dearest brothers, the divine office laid upon us; behold the care, solicitude, and labour of priests. Behold the pious yet perilous burden imposed on them: “Go, swift angels.”

This prophetic—indeed divine—utterance admonishes us here not to scorn the ministry divinely enjoined upon us, not to cast off the holy burden, not to neglect the people formed in the image and likeness of God, redeemed by Christ’s precious blood, and entrusted to us; lest through temporal sin it sink into eternal damnation; lest—God forbid!—sin be committed not only in that people because of its own offences, but sin beyond measure be committed also in us because of the offences of others. For we shall render an account not only of ourselves but also of the souls entrusted to us, unless we diligently proclaim to them the word of salvation.

Let us therefore listen more attentively to what is divinely said to us: “Go, swift angels, to a people torn away.” Priests are angels, as Scripture indicates in one place, saying: “The lips of the priest keep wisdom, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2). Therefore, if we are priests of the Lord, by virtue of our office we are also angels—that is, messengers—and we ought to announce to the people the things of God. “Go, swift angels, to a people torn away.” [Col. 0942A]

Human nature is shown to cleave to God and have its root in him in two respects: namely, as we have already said elsewhere, in that it was made in God’s image because it can know truth; and in that it was made in God’s likeness because it can love good. In these two respects not only the human but also the angelic creature is known to be joined to the Creator, while by knowledge it contemplates his wisdom and by love continually enjoys the blessedness of him. In these two respects it avoids evil: by knowledge of truth, which it possesses in the divine image originally implanted within it, it drives away error; and by love of virtue, which it possesses in the divine likeness, it hates wickedness.

But through diabolical suggestion ignorance entered into human nature and tore out in the human being the root of divine knowledge; and concupiscence came and uprooted the plant of love. [Col. 0942B]

Therefore every impious people, removed by sin from divine and heavenly goods, having first been planted in good through the two preceding goods, is rightly shown and called thereafter “torn away from good” through the two succeeding evils. Go therefore, swift angels, to a people torn away—and not only torn away, but also rent asunder: torn away from good, rent asunder in evil. For once human nature has been torn from good, it is immediately variously rent apart in evil, while different persons are dragged to damnation by different vices and sins: some by pride, others by envy, others by anger, others by sloth, others by avarice, others by gluttony, others by lust, others by usury, others by robbery, others by theft, others by false witness, others by perjury, others by homicide, others by looking upon a woman in order to lust after her, others by saying to a brother, “Fool”; and by whatever other vices or sins there may be, inward or outward, which, for the sake of brevity at present, we neither wish nor are able to enumerate. [Col. 0942C]

Go therefore, swift angels, to a people torn away and rent asunder, so that by your preaching you may gather together those rent apart in evil and replant those torn away from good. Go, angels; go swiftly; go to a people torn away and rent asunder, to a terrible people after which there is no other.

As long as a human being, dearest brothers, preserves through righteousness the nobility, elegance, and beauty of his created condition, he is proved fair in form. But when through sin he stains the beauty of loveliness within himself, he is at once found ugly and horrible, unlike God and made like the devil as well. Alas, how foul, how terrible is this people! Some among this people are hideously black through impure thought; others are blind through ignorance; others lack nostrils through indiscretion; others lack tongue or lips through harmful silence. In others the face is turned backward through recollection and delight in past sin; in others only the trunk of the body remains, the head having been cut off through derangement of mind; others likewise lack arms through the loss [Col. 0943A] of the strength of fortitude; others lack feet through the loss of perfection in virtues; others—and this is more grievous, more foul, more horrible, more terrible—having all their members scattered, that is, their virtues and good works torn apart, have come even to the gates of death, as the Psalmist says: “Our bones have been scattered beside hell” (Psalm 140).

What then, brothers? If anyone were to see a people bodily deformed in this fashion passing before him in a crowd—some black, others, as said above, without ears, without noses, without lips; others with their faces turned backwards; others with heads, hands, arms, feet, and legs cut off; mere trunks rolling before him; or scattered human limbs following one another separately—[Col. 0943B] if, I say, any one of you saw this, would he not at once fortify himself with the sign of the cross, or flee, crying out that neither he nor anyone else had ever seen such things? What then? On Sundays and feast days the people entrusted to your care, whom you ought to tend, flock to church; they arrange their bodily appearance and clothe themselves in finer garments dyed in varied colours. And as you behold men and women in so great a splendour, perhaps you glory that such persons are subject to you and that you are set over such persons. Your glorying is not good if you glory in this, while the people entrusted to you are found torn apart from the good, mangled in evil, and made dreadful by various vices and sins, brothers.

Therefore examine their life carefully, consider their conduct, and judge their beauty according to what pertains to the inward person, [Col. 0943C] not according to what pertains to the outward person. Be ashamed, and grieve for the people subject to you, if you see them such as you hear described here: namely, a nation convulsed and torn apart, a dreadful people after whom there is none other. For perhaps it is your fault—your negligence, your sloth—that it is such, because you have not proclaimed to it its sins and its crimes. Go therefore, swift angels, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other. Go, angels, because this is your office; go swiftly, lest your delay produce danger. Go to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other, that through your preaching it may obtain a remedy: “Do not sit with the council of vanity; do not go in with those who do iniquity. Hate the assembly of evildoers, and do not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. 25).

What then? Someone among you may silently think, or answer more openly, saying: “You forbid us, on the example of the Psalmist just cited, to go to such persons; and does not the Lord direct us to such persons when he says: ‘Go, swift ones, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other’?” Attend to this: where the Lord says, “Go, swift angels, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other,” there your office is imposed upon you, and a command is given to preach to the ungodly. But where we say, “Do not sit with the council of vanity; do not go in with those who do iniquity. [Col. 0944A] Hate the assembly of evildoers; do not sit with the ungodly,” there, I say, you are immediately forbidden the licence of sinning with the ungodly.

Go, therefore, angels, by preaching; do not go by sinning. Go to the dreadful people, that by the word of salvation you may make it beautiful in form; do not go so as to make yourselves like it through the deformity of its sin. Christ ate with sinners in order to join them to himself in goodness; but he did not eat with them in order to associate himself with them in evil. As Christ did, so do; as he did not do, do not do. Go, angels; go swiftly. How swiftly? So swiftly that “you greet no one on the road” (Luke 10), and if anyone greets you, you do not answer him (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4). This is not because salvation is not to be wished for all, but because by these [Col. 0944B] words the Holy Spirit indicates how swift, how unencumbered priests ought to be in preaching salvation. It is as though he said: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; rebuke, entreat, reprove in all patience” (2 Tim. 4). Do not defer the word from day to day, from Sunday to Sunday, from feast to feast. At least on Sundays and feast days, when the people gather in church according to custom, let it not suffice you merely to celebrate Masses; let it not suffice to offer a general prayer for the apostolic lord and for each order, or to announce the feasts of the following week. Rather, correct the people from evil, instruct and form them in goodness, and declare to them the punishment awaiting sinners and the glory reserved for the righteous.

[Col. 0944C] Go, angels. Go swiftly. For if you postpone preaching the word of salvation to the people from Sunday to Sunday, who, I ask, knows whether you will then be alive, healthy, and present? But even if it should happen that you are alive, healthy, and present, who knows whether someone will then be absent who was formerly present, and, no longer hearing counsel for his soul, may be overtaken by an unforeseen and sudden death and, without washing away his guilt, be snatched away to punishment? Will not God justly require the blood of such a person from your hands? Go therefore, swift angels, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other.

What does it mean that it is said, “after whom there is none other”? Is no people to be born, to live, to do good and evil after this people? Certainly there is. What, then, is meant [Col. 0944D] by “after whom there is none other”? It means: none worse than it before the supreme Judge; none more disgraceful through fault; none more dreadful. There are three peoples: Christian, Jewish, and Gentile. Therefore those who among the Christian people are Christians only in name, but serve the devil through injustice, are more dreadful than Jews or pagans, because through iniquity they are worse. For the more easily, aided by grace, they could have remained in righteousness if they had wished, the more gravely they offend when they refuse to abstain from sin. For “to whom more is entrusted, more will be required from him”; and the higher the rank, the more grievous the fall. The devil sinned more in heaven than man in paradise: “The servant who knows his master’s will [Col. 0945A] and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows; but the servant who does not know it shall be beaten with few” (Luke 12).

Therefore, just as the Lord reproached the cities in which he had performed very many miracles because they had not repented, saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Yet I say to you: it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you. And you, Capernaum, will you perhaps be exalted unto heaven? You shall descend unto hell. For if the miracles done in you had been done among the Sidonians, perhaps they would have remained until this day. Yet I say to you that the land of the Sidonians shall be treated more tolerably on the day of judgment than you” (Matt. 11). So also this people of false [Col. 0945B] Christians, corrupted by various impieties, made dreadful, and in some manner removed far from the divine likeness according to its wickedness—so, I say, it may be reproached, as though it were said to it: “Woe to you, wicked people, lying people, apostate people, who by living wickedly trample the Son of God underfoot; who count unclean the blood of the covenant by which you were sanctified; and who do outrage to the Spirit of grace! For it would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Pet. 2). For that true proverb also has befallen them: “A dog returns to its vomit, and a washed sow to wallowing in mud” (ibid.).

But how can this people be worse or more dreadful than itself, or than an evil people to come after us? We scarcely see this. For it seems also to have plunged into that very mass of evils uttered by the prophetic voice: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter! Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight! Woe to those who are mighty in drinking wine, and strong men in mixing drunkenness; who justify the ungodly for gifts, and take away from the righteous the righteousness due to him” (Isa. 5). Many things, dearest brothers, which could still be said about all these matters, we omit for brevity’s sake.

Go, swift angels, to the dreadful people after whom there is none other. It follows: “to a nation waiting and trampled down.” What does it await? Your word, your example, [Col. 0945D] your protection, and the divine help and gift through your care and administration. It awaits your word, that it may be instructed; your example, that it may be formed; your protection, that it may be defended; the divine help and gift through your care and administration, that it may be delivered from evil and justified in goodness. “And trampled down.” Who has trampled it down? All the demons, who continually say to its soul: “Bend down, that we may pass over you.” For the wicked, those who despise heavenly things and bend themselves toward earthly things, grant demons a path for trampling and passing over them. It follows:

“Whose rivers have plundered its land.” What are these rivers that plunder the land of those who live wickedly? They are the vices flowing violently and dragging the wicked to torments. What is the plundering of the land except the destruction of every virtue? Thus the rivers of evils plunder their land when vices take away their virtues. Pride takes away humility; anger, peace; envy, charity; sloth, spiritual exultation; avarice, generosity; lust, continence. Go, swift angels, to a nation convulsed and torn apart, to a dreadful people after whom there is none other, to a nation waiting and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land.

“At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts from a people torn apart and mangled; from a dreadful people after whom there was none other; from a nation waiting and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land.” [Col. 0946B] “At that time,” he says, “a gift shall be brought to the Lord” (Isa. 18). At what time? Namely, when you have gone to this people to whom you are sent and, through your preaching, have cured it of the evils mentioned above. What gift shall be brought? An acceptable gift, a rich holocaust, an inward vow; and it shall be brought to the place of the Lord’s name, to Mount Zion—that is, to the holy Church. Go therefore, swift angels, and preach to the dreadful people; fulfil your ministry. If you do this, you will gain for yourselves a good rank. May he grant to you and to us the grace of this matter, he who promises glory, Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. On the Nativity of the Lord

[Col. 0946C]

“Lord, have mercy on us, for we have waited for you. Be our arm in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation” (Isa. 33).

God, the fountain and source of every good, without whose aid we can neither possess good, nor escape evil, nor attain righteousness or glory, nor avoid guilt or punishment—he himself must continually be entreated by us, he himself continually invoked, that, with his grace aiding us, we may both be delivered from evil and established in good. We read in the words of Isaiah the prophet that Isaiah himself prayed for the Jewish people, who on account of their sins were besieged by Sennacherib within the walls of Jerusalem, saying: “Lord, have mercy on us; for we have waited for you. Be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation.” For the Jews feared that, [Col. 0946D] when morning dawned, Sennacherib himself would assault the city and that the city would thus be taken.

The Jewish people established in Jerusalem signifies the people of the elect, set in the vision of divine peace. Sennacherib and his army, the fierce enemy of God’s people, signify the devil and the multitude of demons and wicked persons. Sennacherib comes with his army and attempts to overcome the Jews dwelling in Jerusalem when the devil, with a multitude of evil spirits and perverse persons, attacks through many temptations the true confessors of the divine name who rest in the vision of divine peace, and strives to overthrow them, by any sin whatever, from the security of their rest and from the state of uprightness.

There were two [Col. 0947A] walls in Jerusalem: an upper or inner wall, and a lower or outer wall. So, in the spiritual way of life of the faithful, there are two chief defences, like two walls: love, namely, and action. Love is the inner wall; action, the outer wall. But the outer wall avails nothing for salvation unless the inner is carefully guarded. For what good is the performance of a work if love of heart is absent? What does it avail to offer bread to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, receive the stranger, cover the naked, visit the sick, go to one confined in prison, pour forth the words of various prayers, open one’s mouth in divine praises, celebrate Masses, administer and partake of whatever sacraments of God, and do any such things, if you neglect or despise the keeping of the commandment of love?

There are some who distribute much to the poor, visit many holy places as pilgrims, under the pretext of redeeming their own wickedness and winning blessed recompense, and do many other good things; yet by living wickedly they nonetheless entangle themselves in crimes. [Col. 0947B] These give their goods to God in vain as long as they take themselves away from God. For if you give what is yours to God but give yourself to the devil, the division is not fair. God made and redeemed the human being; therefore he ought to possess the whole person, and gather from that person the fruit of good thought, speech, and action. Therefore you ought not to give the devil what you owe to God.

Every wicked person, therefore, ought, just as he strives to give temporal goods to Christ in his members, so also to offer himself to Christ, by loving Christ above all things and his neighbour as himself. Thus their city shall be fortified by a double wall: the inner wall through love, the outer through action. But if the inner wall—that is, love—should be lacking, the outer wall—that is, action—cannot withstand the enemy’s assault.

“Lord, have mercy on us.” God has mercy on a person when he delivers that person from evil and establishes him in good; and thus, by delivering from evil and establishing in good, he justifies. Therefore, Lord, have mercy on us by justification. For we cannot possess righteousness unless you give it to us by grace. “For we have waited for you.” Whoever hopes in God waits for God through hope. Whoever does not hope does not wait; but through a wretched conscience flees the divine presence [Col. 0947D] and does not seek to be presented to God, because he fears condemnation by him. Lord, have mercy on us through justification, for we have waited for you through hope.

“Be our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation.” What he first calls “arm” and then adds as “salvation” has one meaning; and what he says “in the morning” and adds as “in the time of tribulation” has one meaning. Be, Lord, our arm and our salvation, that you may deliver us from evil and establish us in good. If you are our arm and our salvation, we shall be delivered from enemies attacking us and saved in good conduct, like those ancient people in the city of Jerusalem.

“In the morning, in the time of tribulation.” We may distinguish in three ways what is called “morning,” or “the time of tribulation.” The first morning, or time of tribulation, is after the passing of the night of the present feast; the second, after the hour of death; the third, after the course of the present age. But how can the morning of the present feast, the morning of the Lord’s Nativity, be called a time of tribulation, when it appears to everyone to be a time of exultation? Yet, if it is considered closely, it is for some a time of tribulation because it is a time of temptation, while the devil sets many snares of ruin through spectacles of vanity and excess of eating, drinking, and manifold dissipation. Therefore, the more eagerly the devil seeks an occasion on solemn days and the more readily finds an opportunity for temptation, the more cautiously and strongly each person ought to prepare himself to resist, lest, when the sons of God have gathered [Col. 0948B] together, Satan come upon them and corrupt one of them through sin, making him a son of damnation.

As we have said, therefore, when it is a time of feast, it is a time of temptation; and as long as it is a time of temptation, so long it is a time of tribulation. Be therefore our arm, Lord, and our salvation in the day of tribulation, lest the devil break the holy city through temptation and carry off your faithful people captured by iniquities.

The second morning, or time of tribulation, is after the hour, or even in the very hour, of death. As long as a person lives, he is in a certain sense in night, because he does not know many things that he will know after death. For Solomon says: “The righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God. Yet a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; but all things are kept uncertain for the future, since all things happen alike to the righteous and the wicked, to the good and the evil, to one offering sacrifices and one despising sacrifice. As is the good person, so is the sinner; as the perjurer, so also the one who swears truthfully” (Eccl. 9). And again: “A person does not know his end; but as fish are caught by a hook, so people are caught in an evil time when it suddenly comes upon them” (ibid.). And the apostle Paul: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified; the one who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4).

Therefore a person is covered by the night of great ignorance throughout all the days of life. But in death the day of that knowledge rises, because when the soul departs from the body it beholds both its reward and its merit together and clearly. [Col. 0948D] In the dawn of this day the human spirit must greatly fear lest it be attacked by cruel Sennacherib and carried away for its sins to the furthest land, namely to hell. For at death the devil is accustomed to surround the wretched soul with his attendants, hem it in on every side, and, if permission is granted him, cast it down to that land. Lord, be our arm in this morning, our salvation in the time of so great a tribulation.

The third morning, or time of tribulation, is the day of the universal resurrection. For as long as the human race remains in the present age, it is covered by the great night of ignorance. It cannot yet know how long the world will endure or when it will end; it does not yet know who are to be saved and who condemned; nor does it see the rewards of the good [Col. 0949A] or the punishments of the evil. Nor does the congregation of the holy Church yet contemplate by sight what it believes by faith, nor yet see the thing toward which it tends by hope. But in the general resurrection, when the night of present ignorance has departed, the day of perfect knowledge will dawn, when all rational creatures have been gathered and every eye shall see God, when God will illuminate the hidden things of our heart.

Then, when the Lord comes with all his saints, there shall be a great light: the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of their injury (Isa. 30). The sound of that day shall be bitter for the reprobate: “There the mighty man shall be afflicted” (Zeph. 1). That day shall be a day of wrath for those condemned, a day of tribulation and anguish, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and whirlwind, a day of trumpet and blast. On that day our King, our Saviour, shall kill and destroy from the holy city of David all sinners of the earth, when he says to them: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

From that evil hearing—than which no worse has ever been, or ever shall be, for the ungodly until that hour—the righteous will not fear, for to them it shall be said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (ibid.). On that day our Saviour, whose name is dreadful to the ungodly and holy to the saints, shall “sing of mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100): mercy by saving the good, judgment by condemning the evil. [Col. 0949C] And “the honour of the king,” by which he will save the good, “loves judgment” (Ps. 99), by which he will condemn the evil. And the two things which God has spoken once by one eternal word shall be fulfilled (Ps. 62): “power belongs to God” for punishing the reprobate, and “to you, Lord, belongs mercy” (ibid.) for glorifying the righteous, because you render to each according to his works (Rom. 2). Then, when the Son has delivered the kingdom to the Father, there shall be the end—that is, the consummation of all things (1 Cor. 15)—when he has abolished every rule, authority, and power (ibid.), so that spirit shall no longer rule spirit, angel angel, or human being human being.

Be, Lord, our arm in the morning and our salvation in the time of tribulation. In the first morning, that is, on the day of this present feast, deliver us from diabolical temptation; in the second, that is, at the hour of death, deliver us from diabolical assault; in the third, that is, on the day of resurrection, deliver us from everlasting damnation. Be everywhere our arm and our salvation, that you may deliver us from evil and save us in good, granting us the glory which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2), which you have prepared for those who love you, in which you live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. On the Feast of Any Saint, and Especially of Augustine

“Asperge me, Domine, hyssopo, et mundabor”: “Sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50).

David, king and prophet, was stained by three grave sins: adultery, when he sinned with Bathsheba; [Col. 0950A] betrayal, when he gave Uriah the letter of his death; homicide, when Joab, according to the king’s command, placed the aforesaid Uriah in the place where the battle was fiercest, and Uriah himself was struck down and died. This David, I say, after he understood that he had sinned, composed the penitential psalm in which this verse occurs, and in it humbly begged God to cleanse him from transgression: “Sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.”

The herb hyssop, from which in the Old Testament a sprinkler was made, by which whatever was to be cleansed was sprinkled and cleansed, bears as many spiritual meanings as it has properties. Therefore we have resolved to set out several of its properties in order, and thus explain their mystical meanings. We know that hyssop puts down its root in the hidden part of the earth, comes out from the earth, grows upward, multiplies its branches, produces leaves, is green, naturally warm, small, and cleansing; that it has grains of seed, little flowers of hyacinth-blue colour, and fragrance from these very flowers. All these things spiritually belong to this holy righteous man, namely Augustine, whose solemn feast we celebrate today.

The root, which is the beginning of a growing thing, signifies faith of the heart, the source of every virtue or good work arising from it. The emergence of the shoot signifies confession by the mouth. Thus the root signifies faith of the heart, and the emergence of the shoot confession of the mouth. For “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10). That hyssop grows [Col. 0950C] upward represents hope for heavenly goods, through which we savour and seek the good things above and hasten toward them in desire. The multiplication of the little branches expresses the multiplication of virtues proceeding from one faith as from one root. The leaves, which externally clothe the thing from which they grow, signify good works, which outwardly cover the righteous person honourably and fittingly. The greenness of hyssop signifies the unceasing preservation of righteousness in the righteous person, or love of heavenly eternity. Hyssop’s natural warmth represents love of God and neighbour, by which the righteous person loves God above all things and his neighbour as himself. For he is warm with a certain heat when he burns with both kinds of love. The smallness of hyssop expresses the humility of the righteous person. For the righteous person imitates hyssop’s humility when he does not presume to seek things higher than himself, but consents to the lowly.

It has cleansing power through preaching. For as hyssop cleanses the chests of those who use it, so a preacher, with the aiding hand of the supreme Physician, cleanses the hearts of his hearers. It also has grains in the words of sound teaching, which, sown in the hearts of hearers, produce, with grace cooperating, the shoot of righteousness and yield the fruit of glory. It has little flowers of hyacinth-blue colour when it practises virtues and displays works belonging to a heavenly manner of life. It spreads fragrance when, through a good reputation, it is the good odour of Christ in every place.

Thus our righteous patron, whose feast we celebrate today, has in the manner of hyssop a root through faith, [Col. 0951A] an emerging shoot through confession of faith, upright growth through hope, many branches through the multiplicity of virtues, leaves through good action, greenness through the persevering preservation of righteousness and perpetual love of the eternal homeland. He is warm through love, small through humility, cleansing through preaching. He has hyacinth-blue colour through heavenly life, grains through sound teaching, and fragrance through a good reputation. With this hyssop, as with a certain sprinkler, God sprinkles us as often as he instructs and kindles us by Augustine’s teaching and example. And we are cleansed, washed, and made whiter than snow when, purified from every defilement of flesh and spirit by his instruction and imitation, we are raised to the heavenly reward. Therefore the hyssop sprinkler is the life of the righteous person; the water, grace; the sprinkling, imitation; the cleansing, justification. May God sprinkle us in time with this hyssop, that we may glory with him in eternity, who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XXVI. On the Ancient People of the Jews and Present-Day Righteous Persons

The blessed apostle Paul, speaking in his Epistle of the Israelite people—namely, what good things and what evil things befell that people—adds as follows: “All these things happened to them figuratively; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10).

God gave that people many good things, dearest brothers; he bestowed many benefits. Without regard to merits he chose their fathers; through many great signs [Col. 0951C] and wonders he brought them out of Egypt, out of the iron furnace, out of the house of bondage. He went before them in a pillar of cloud and fire through the wilderness for a long time, during which their garments did not wear out. He fed them with heavenly bread and gave them water to drink from the rock; he led them about, taught them, and guarded them as the pupil of his eye. As an eagle stirring up her young to fly and hovering over them spreads her wings, so he took up that people and bore it on his shoulders. The Lord alone was its leader, and no strange god was with it. Before them he struck down great kings and slew mighty kings: Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. He gave them their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel his people, so that they might eat the fruits of the fields and suck honey from the rock and oil from the hardest stone; butter [Col. 0951D] from the herd and milk from the sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, sons of Bashan, and goats, with the marrow of wheat, and drink the purest blood of the grape. “He has not dealt thus with every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (Deut. 32; Ps. 134).

Then, as time went on, when the aforesaid people was scorning the commandments of the law, God raised up holy men among them and appointed prophets, that they might correct transgressors from sin, recall them to righteousness, and announce to that people the coming of his beloved Son. Finally, when the fullness of the sacred time had come, God sent his Son into the world to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, that he himself as shepherd might feed his flock, gather the lambs in his arm, lift them in his bosom, and himself carry those with young (Gal. 4).

These great works, and many others which we neither wish nor are able to enumerate, God did for them; and, as has already been said, these things happened to them figuratively, but were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10). For “whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope” (Rom. 15). According to the pattern of this figure, dearest brothers, God chose our fathers in faith—not by human merit but by gratuitous gift—namely, the holy apostles, whom he freely begot by the word of truth, that they might be a kind of beginning of his creation (Jas. 1).

He brought us out of Egypt when he brought us out [Col. 0952B] of paganism, when he brought us out of the darkness of Gentile unbelief into his marvellous light, so that we who once were not a people may now be the people of God; and we who had not obtained mercy may now have obtained mercy (1 Pet. 2). He feeds and carries us on the way and in the life of this present age by the sacrament of his body and blood.

In this life the pillar of cloud and fire goes before us, because, for the strengthening of faith, he sets before us the brightness and miracles of his divinity, and, as an example of good action, the gentleness and humility of his humanity. On this way our garments do not wear out, because our virtues and good works, if we wish it, are kept unharmed for us by his grace until the end. On this way God leads us about through good action, teaches us through the reading of the Scriptures, and guards us by the protection of his grace. As an eagle stirring up her young to fly, hovering over them, spreads her wings, takes them up, and bears them on her shoulders: so, when he stretched out his hands on the cross, he bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows (Isa. 53), and showed an example of suffering, so that through the suffering which is in time we may learn to fly toward the glory which is in eternity.

On this way God alone is our guide, and no strange god is with us, because he alone trod the winepress of human redemption by his passion, and among the nations there was no man with him. For the priest and Levite passed by the man stripped and wounded, and the Samaritan alone, moved by mercy, drew near; he bound up [Col. 0952D] his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, set him upon his beast, brought him to an inn, and took care of him (Luke 10). Having overthrown many great enemies, he gave us a most excellent land, because “he has delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1), regenerating us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, unto an incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading inheritance, kept in heaven for us, who are guarded by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time—when our faith, much more precious than gold tested by fire, shall be found unto praise, glory, and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ (1 Pet. 1); when we shall rejoice with inexpressible and glorified joy [Col. 0953A].

But even if we sometimes transgress the law, rulers and teachers have been appointed throughout the churches to correct us from evil and reform us in good. The Son himself also comes frequently to us, that, if we stray in any respect, he may lead us back to his sheepfold and guard us there by his protection. See how the patterns of truth correspond. See what great goods God bestowed upon them, and what goods upon us: great goods upon them, greater upon us.

But what does the divine Scripture say of them? It recounts in many ways their transgressions in Egypt, in the wilderness, and in the land of promise: the hardness of their heart and their unbelief, their disputes and murmurings against the Lord, and against Moses his servant, and against many others who after him taught that people. For when Pharaoh pursued them, the children of Israel lifted up their eyes and saw the Egyptians behind them, and said to Moses: “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, and therefore you brought us out to die in the wilderness. Why did you choose to do this, to bring us out of Egypt? Is this not the word which we spoke to you in Egypt, saying: ‘Leave us alone, that we may serve the Egyptians’? For it is much better to serve them than to die in the wilderness” (Exod. XIV).

Likewise, in the wilderness of Sin the whole assembly of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and said: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the pots of meat and ate bread to the full. Why have you led us into this wilderness, to kill the whole multitude with hunger?” (Exod. XVI).

[Col. 0953C] At Rephidim, where there was no water to drink, the people quarrelled with Moses and said: “Give us water to drink. Why did you make us leave Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our cattle with thirst?” (Exod. XVII.) At Horeb they made a calf and worshipped a graven image, and changed their glory into the likeness of a calf eating hay; they forgot God who saved them, who performed great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, and terrible deeds at the Red Sea (Exod. XXXII; Ps. CV).

After they had departed from the wilderness of Sinai, there arose a murmuring of the people, as though they were grieving over toil, against the Lord. For the mixed multitude who had come down with them burned with desire for meat; and sitting and weeping, joined by the children of Israel, they said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish [Col. 0953D] which we ate freely in Egypt. Cucumbers and melons come to mind, likewise leeks, onions, and garlic. Our soul is parched; our eyes see nothing else but manna” (Num. XI).

But ten explorers out of the twelve whom Moses sent to explore the land of promise disparaged the land which they had inspected before the children of Israel, saying: “The land which we surveyed devours its inhabitants. The people whom we saw are of very great stature. There we saw certain monstrous sons of Anak, of giant stock; compared with them we seemed like locusts.” Therefore the children of Israel wept and murmured against Moses and Aaron, saying: “Would that we had died in Egypt, and not in this [Col. 0954A] vast wilderness! Would that we might perish, and that the Lord might not lead us into this land, lest we fall by the sword and our wives and children be carried captive. Is it not better to return to Egypt? Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt” (Num. XIII–XIV).

Korah also, and his company, provoked Moses in the camp, Aaron the holy one (Num. XVI). At the waters of contradiction Moses was distressed because of them, for they embittered his spirit (Ps. CV). At Shittim the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor (Num. XXV).

Finally, having entered the good land, they defiled it with their idols and with all their abominations. For the beloved grew fat and kicked: he grew fat, became sleek, and enlarged; he forsook God his maker and withdrew [Col. 0954B] from God his saviour. They provoked him with foreign gods and stirred him to wrath by their abominations. They sacrificed to demons and not to God—to gods whom they did not know. New and recent gods came whom their fathers had not worshipped. They turned their backs upon God in withdrawal and most wickedly transgressed his laws (Zech. VII).

“Oholah,” that is, Samaria, “played the harlot against me,” and raved after her lovers, the Assyrians who came near, clothed in hyacinth-blue: princes and magistrates, young men of desire; and she was defiled by their uncleannesses. When her sister Oholibah, which is Jerusalem, saw this, she too raved after her lovers and exposed her prostitution to such a degree that she was more impious than the nations (Ezek. XXIII).

Therefore all turned aside; together they became useless; there is none [Col. 0954C] who does good, not even one (Ps. XIII), except for the holy seed which remained in that nation, which was not shaken off, because the blessing of the Lord was there.

And when the Lord sent his servants, the prophets, to receive the fruits of this vineyard, the husbandmen, having seized his servants, beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the former, and they did the same to them. Finally he sent his Son to them, saying: “They will respect my Son.” But when the husbandmen saw the Son, they said among themselves: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and we shall have the inheritance.” And they seized him, cast him outside the vineyard, and killed him (Matt. XXI).

And let us see, brothers, how that crooked and perverse generation, that foolish and senseless people, repaid evil for the benefits mentioned above; and let us beware lest, by transgressing the commandments of the Saviour, we be fashioned, made like, and conformed to them. Many are called in the holy Church; few are chosen. Many follow their example by living wickedly, walking in revelries and drunkenness, in beds and shameless acts, in strife and jealousy; they conform themselves, as the blessed apostle Peter says, to the former desires of their ignorance (I Pet. I)—those who walk after the flesh in the desire of uncleanness, despise condemnation, are bold and self-pleasing, and do not fear to introduce blaspheming sects (II Pet. II).

But woe to them, as the apostle Jude says, who have gone in the way of Cain, have poured themselves out in Balaam’s error for payment, and have perished in the rebellion [Col. 0955A] of Korah. These are those who feast early at their banquets without fear, feeding themselves; waterless clouds carried about by winds; autumnal trees, unfruitful, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, for whom the storm of darkness has been reserved for ever (Jude 11–13).

These are, according to the blessed apostle Peter, those who consider the pleasures of the day to be delights of defilement and stain; who abound in delights, luxuriating at feasts; whose eyes are full of adultery and unceasing sin; who entice unstable souls; who have a heart trained in greed; children of curse (II Pet. II). Of them Paul thunders terribly, saying: “It is impossible for those who have once been enlightened, have also tasted the heavenly gift, and have become partakers [Col. 0955B] of the Holy Spirit, have nevertheless tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again to repentance, crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to public contempt” (Heb. VI).

For by committing sin they lose the gift of grace and make themselves such that, with respect to them—not with respect to divine mercy and power—that it would, I say, appear necessary for the Son of God to be crucified again for their redemption and exposed to public contempt. For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of truth, no sacrifice for sins now remains. Rather, there is a certain terrible expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which will consume the adversaries (Heb. X).

“No sacrifice,” he says, “remains for sins when we sin deliberately [Col. 0955C] after receiving the knowledge of truth.” For there is one true, perfect, and sole sacrifice: the flesh of Christ, once offered in the Passion for the sin of the human race. It will not again be crucified or suffer for anyone’s sin, because Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more (Rom. VI).

Therefore, whoever sins criminally or damnably after receiving the grace of baptism loses the price of human redemption, and has nothing to offer for the sin of a redemption already accomplished and no longer to be accomplished, since its price has been lost. Just as the human race, after the sin of the first parent, would have had no original sacrifice which it might offer for that original sin or for its own actual sin, unless the Father of supreme mercy had freely given for offering the assumed humanity [Col. 0955D] of his beloved Son—cleansed from every stain of sin by divine power.

That humanity of Christ, offered once upon the cross, by the shedding of its blood washed away the guilt of all those predestined to eternal life, both preceding and following, and reconciled them to the eternal Father, paying Adam’s debt. Therefore there is one sacrifice of redemption; once it is lost, no other remains for us.

But although these matters are so grave and terrible for sinners, nevertheless with God no word is impossible (Luke I). For he can have mercy, and does have mercy, on one who falls; and even at this time, to those who return to him in repentance after losing baptismal grace, he remits their guilt. Yet although divine mercy is never far from repentant sinners, guilt after grace has been received must nevertheless be feared by all, because a terrible sentence hangs over those who despise grace, as may be understood from the words of the same Apostle. For he says: “Anyone who sets aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishments, do you think, will he deserve who has trampled the Son of God underfoot, counted as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?” (Heb. X.)

“If the word of the Old Testament, spoken through angels, became firm, and every transgression received a just recompense, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?” (Heb. II.) Therefore let us not be conformed to them in transgression, lest we become like them in condemnation, as certain people [Col. 0956B] in this age, imitating their depravity and despising the correction of the Scriptures, entangle themselves in so many and such great crimes that it can deservedly be said of them that upon them have come not only the ends of the ages but also the extremes of vices—not because there will be no vices after them, but because human viciousness can never break forth more gravely or more wickedly.

Nor do they understand how strictly and diligently holiness must be guarded, since it is written that even the thought of the ungodly shall be examined, and that peace was not brought at the birth of the Saviour except to people of good will (Luke II). For not only the stream of deed or speech must be purified in God’s sight, but also the spring of the inmost thought. But if we neglect to be corrected according to those rebukes which were written for our sake, let us fear to be condemned with those ancient despisers.

You know, brothers, that manifold punishments were inflicted upon them because of their iniquity. Some were killed by swords; others burned by heavenly fire; others swallowed up by the earth as it opened; others killed by the bites of serpents; others died when the Lord struck them in other ways. In the land of promise, transgressing God’s commandments, they were often subjected to servitude by the nations. Finally, uprooted utterly from their own land, they were scattered through many regions and subjected to continual slavery; and—what is more grievous than all—they were excluded from faith in the Saviour and assigned to everlasting damnation.

Therefore let us not become like them in guilt, lest we be tormented with them in punishment. Let us fear the Lord our God, who brought us out of the Egypt of unbelief [Col. 0956D] and gave us the delight of eternal sweetness; who gave us houses through good preservation, gardens, vineyards, and olive-groves through the fruitfulness of virtues and good works; and who satisfies us through the refreshment of spiritual grace. Let us serve him alone, that by his grace we may merit the glory in which God lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII. On the Paschal Feast and the Body of Christ

“These are days which you must observe. On the fourteenth day, at evening, is the Passover of the Lord; and on the fifteenth you shall celebrate a solemn feast to the Most High Lord” (Lev. XXIII).

Divine providence, intending to restore the human race to its lost blessedness, set before the people of the Old Testament many institutions of the sacred law, to which it entrusted the sacraments of the redemption to come; and it plainly taught how each should be observed. Therefore, among the other legal sacraments, it showed when they should celebrate the Paschal solemnity—which was special and pre-eminent because it was the sacrament of human redemption—saying: “On the fourteenth day, at evening, is the Passover of the Lord.”

We therefore, brothers, for whom the carnal prescriptions of the law are no longer to be kept, but rather the things signified by them—we, I say, must dig more deeply and seek the fountain of hidden good: beneath the shadow, the truth; beneath the figure, the reality; beneath the hardness of the bark, the tenderness of the pith; beneath the letter, spiritual understanding; beneath the covering of straw, the inner nourishment [Col. 0957B] of the grain. For in the field of the divine law lies hidden the treasure of wisdom; whoever finds it finds life and draws salvation from the Lord.

“On the fourteenth day, at evening, is the Passover of the Lord.” This number, composed of ten and four, bears a great and manifest sacrament. Ten signifies the completion and end of the law; four, the manifestation and perfection of evangelical preaching. For the law is contained in ten commandments, and the Gospel in four books. Therefore Christ, coming in the flesh, who is the end of the law, fulfilled the ten of the law; and, by assuming humanity and making known the light of evangelical teaching, as it were completed four days. And at the completion of the preaching of the four Gospels, as it were at the end or evening of the four days, Christ himself celebrated the Pasch, because through the nature of our frailty, by dying for us on the cross, he made a passage from the world to the Father.

We must, dearly beloved, always ponder this Pasch—that is, this passage of the Lord—in which he subdued the Egyptians, namely the dark demons, and freed us from their power; and we must spiritually observe in the New Testament those things written according to the letter in the Old Testament concerning this solemnity.

We must eat the flesh of the lamb, devour its head with its feet and entrails (Exod. XII). Yet there mention is made not only of a lamb but also of a kid. Christ is lamb; Christ is kid: lamb for the righteous, kid for sinners; the head is divinity, [Col. 0957D] the feet humanity. We devour his head when with sound faith and highest devotion we contemplate his divinity. We devour his feet when with the same faith and devotion we contemplate his humanity.

We devour his head when we contemplate his immensity without dimension, eternity without time, simplicity without diminution. We devour his head when we truly contemplate him as in every essence, in every place, and in every time: but in every essence without being defined; in every place without being contained; in every time without changeability. We devour his head when we contemplate that he who is everywhere cannot be changed by place; he who is eternal, by time; he who is most wise, by perception; he who is best, by affection; he who is immense, increased; he who is simple, diminished; he who is one, divided.

[Col. 0958A] We devour his head when we contemplate his power, wisdom, and goodness: his power, by which he creates all things; his wisdom, by which he governs all things; his goodness, by which he preserves the things created and governed. We devour his head when we contemplate him above all things, beneath all things, outside all things, within all things: above, not exalted; beneath, not laid underneath; outside, not excluded; within, not enclosed. He is above by presiding, beneath by sustaining, outside by containing, within by penetrating.

We devour his head when, intoxicated by the abundance of God’s house and drinking from the torrent of his delight, we contemplate him as the fountain of life from whom all good things proceed, and as the true light, in the true light and from the true light—yet not two lights, but one light. We devour his head when we contemplate the harmony of the blessed angels, the praises offered to the highest divinity by the saints already glorified in the first robe, and the heavenly goods which, insofar as it is possible through divinely bestowed goodness, we taste beforehand.

[Col. 0958B] We devour his feet when we contemplate his humanity. We devour his feet when we contemplate the Son of God incarnate for us, wrapped in swaddling clothes, crying in a cradle, nursing at the breast, hungering, thirsting, growing weary, weeping, seized, bound, struck, crucified, dead, buried, risen from the dead, ascended into heaven, seated at the right hand of the Father, and destined to come on the day of judgment and render to each according to his works.

We devour his entrails when we faithfully and devoutly contemplate his hidden and profound sacraments, by which Christ himself was prefigured from the beginning, as he was foretold by many oracles. We eat the flesh of this lamb at night, because now we receive the Lord’s body in a sacrament, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. But let us not eat anything of it raw, nor believe him to be a mere human being; rather, let us cook him through the understanding of his divinity—yet not in water, lest we presume to examine his mysteries by human wisdom, but roasted through the grace of the Holy Spirit. If anything remains which exceeds your understanding, it should be burned with fire, that is, faithfully entrusted to the Holy Spirit.

Let us gird our loins [Col. 0958D] by chastity. Let us have shoes on our feet through imitation of the deceased Fathers; staffs in our hands through pastoral watchfulness. Let us eat unleavened bread through simple teaching, wild lettuces through bitter repentance. Let us eat in haste, so that we may swiftly learn God’s commandments, the mysteries of redemption, and the joys of the heavenly country, and fulfil the commandments of life; for even if today we know what good we are permitted to do, we do not know whether it will be permitted tomorrow. Therefore let us eat in haste—that is, let us yearn for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland.

We have briefly touched upon these matters of spiritual understanding, so that from so great a sacrament we may gather what we can. Let us eat the Pasch, brothers, and not merely eat it, but perform it. Let us perform Pasch; let us make the passage. Let us pass from darkness to light, from falsehood to truth, from vice to virtue. Let us pass, insofar as we can, from pride to humility, from envy to charity, from anger to tranquillity, from sloth to exultation, from avarice to generosity, from drunkenness to sobriety, from lust to chastity. Let us pass from evil to good, from the world to God, so that we may die to the world and live to God.

[Col. 0959A] Let servants imitate the Lord and disciples the Master, so that, as Christ passed from the world to the Father, we too may pass from impiety to piety. “And on the fifteenth day you shall celebrate a solemn feast to the Most High Lord.” The fifteenth day signifies the entire age of grace, extending from the ascension of the Lord Jesus Christ and the sending of the Holy Spirit. In it we celebrate a solemn feast to the Lord, because by his grace we must restore to wholeness the fivefold number of our senses, corrupted by sin, and fulfil by good living the ten of the law.

Fifteen is also divided into seven and eight, because during this solemnity of grace we must live in such a way that, through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, we may deserve to attain the eight beatitudes of heaven. These are the days—the days, namely, of human redemption and of divine grace—which we must observe by ceasing from servile work, that is, from sinful work; and not only from sinful work but also from the will to sin. For the will is counted as the deed. Whoever wishes to observe these days [Col. 0959C]—and all of us ought to wish it—should diligently preserve himself from evil; for each person observes these days solemnly precisely insofar as he preserves himself from evil. And he offers praises to the divinity all the more festively insofar as, with a mind cleansed of dross, he tastes more tranquilly the delight of grace.

There is also another passage at the death of the righteous, when the soul, leaving the prison and bonds of the flesh and liberated from the temptations of the world, passes to the glory of the freedom of the children of God. Happy is that passage, by which the righteous person, after good action, receives the first robe; escapes misery and enters glory; and finds rest after labour. “Blessed indeed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on,” says the Spirit—that is, God—“that they may rest from their labours” (Rev. XIV).

For there, when the ten of the law and the four of the Gospel have been fulfilled, as it were completing the number of fourteen days, they celebrate the solemn fifteenth day with the angels before the Most High Lord. There, rejoicing with the blessed spirits in the joy of that solemnity, they happily await the glorification of their bodies. There, dwelling on high, they see the King in his beauty.

There is also another Pasch, or passage: when, on the day of judgment, in the general resurrection, the holy universal Church will pass from the misery of the world to the blessedness of heaven, from the mutability of time to the state of eternity.
