In this passage, this corruptible body will put on incorruption and this mortal body immortality; death will be swallowed up in victory, and death and [Col. 0960A] the sting of death will be taken away (I Cor. XV). God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his saints, and there will be no more mourning, crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away (Rev. XXI).

Thus we may distinguish five kinds of Pasch, or Phase, or passage. The first was in the striking of Egypt; the second in the Passion of the Lord; the third in the justification of the ungodly; the fourth in the death of the righteous; the fifth in the assumption and glorification of the whole Church, which is the mystical body of Christ. In the first, the children of Israel were freed from Pharaoh’s servitude; in the second, the elect were freed from the yoke of diabolical power; in the third, the person to be justified is freed from the dominion of iniquity; in the fourth, the righteous person is freed from the bond of the flesh; in the fifth, the holy Church in all her children will be freed from the corruption of mortality.

Then holy mother Church, having first in this age fulfilled the law through works of righteousness and perfected the Gospel, as though the circuit of fourteen days had passed, will celebrate on the fifteenth day of eternity a solemn feast to the Most High Lord. For there she will devote herself without end to God’s praises, and God will be all in all to her. But let us, brothers, meanwhile celebrate and observe these days, the days of human redemption and divine grace, according to what has been said above, so that through present merit we may come to the future reward, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVIII. On the Feast of All Saints

[Col. 0960C]

“Jesus, seeing the crowds, went up the mountain,” etc. (Matt. V). That the Lord, intending to teach the disciples the eightfold path through which one comes to the eight beatitudes, went up the mountain teaches us that one who dispenses the word of sacred doctrine ought not stand in the valley of depraved conduct or on the plain of unrestrained dissipation, but ought to ascend the mountain of spiritual conduct through the exercises of virtues and the performance of good works. As it is also written: “Go up onto a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion” (Isa. XL).

The ascent of the mountain, therefore, signifies exalted conduct; the Lord’s sitting, the authority of teaching; the opening of his mouth, the effect of preaching.

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Some are rich in spirit; others, in a certain manner, have nothing of spirit; others are poor in spirit. Rich in spirit are the proud; those who have nothing of spirit are excessively faint-hearted; the poor in spirit are the humble. The proud do what ought not to be done through self-exaltation; the faint-hearted omit what ought to be done; and the humble do what ought to be done through humility. Therefore poverty of spirit, having nothing of deficiency and nothing of excess, leads by the royal way to heavenly blessedness.

“Blessed are the meek.” The meek are gentle and patient: they injure no one and yield to wicked people. Yet there are some who wish to be so meek that they care nothing for another’s life, admonish no one toward good, and correct no one for evil. But such gentleness is not greatly to be praised, [Col. 0961A] because it permits a deficiency where it ought to exercise the efficacy of virtue. Therefore people ought to be meek in such a way that they harm no one, patiently endure evils inflicted upon them, and neglect neither their own life nor that of another; so that, where needed, they may offer exhortation to the good toward better things and correction to the evil concerning evil.

For there is a measure in things: just as a person ought not to be excessively harsh, so neither ought he be excessively gentle, but should reach the land of blessedness between right and left through discerning meekness.

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Mourning is customarily for the loss of loved ones—for example, when someone loses those dear to him: father, mother, child, or another relative. Alas, how many mourn their loved ones but by no means mourn themselves! How many mourn bodily losses who disdain to mourn spiritual losses! When someone grows ill or dies, friends mourn. But when he sins damnably, commits fornication, calls his brother “fool,” or looks at a woman in order to lust after her, no one mourns. O mad health! O blind sight! O dead life! They mourn things which should not be mourned, and they mourn gravely things which ought to be mourned little; but spiritual losses, which ought gravely to be mourned, they do not mourn, or even laugh at them.

[Col. 0961B] Of these things Isaiah prophesied, saying: “Woe to you who call good evil and evil good, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter” (Isa. V).

Let us mourn, brothers, the loss of loved ones, but mourn more the loss of good works and the loss of virtues. Let the corrupt person mourn the loss of virginal integrity. Let the proud person mourn the loss of humility. Let the angry person mourn the loss of inward tranquillity. Let the avaricious person mourn the loss of generosity. Let the drunken person mourn the loss of sobriety. Let the slothful person mourn the loss of spiritual exultation. Let the envious person mourn the loss of charity.

For blessed are those who now mourn through repentance, because they shall be comforted through pardon, then through righteousness, and finally through glory. We may say, moreover, that there are three kinds of people who spiritually and fruitfully mourn before the eyes of the Creator. Some mourn for the pardon of guilt; others mourn from the sweetness of grace divinely bestowed upon them; others, kindled by a more intense fervour, [Col. 0961D] mourn from desire for future glory. And in all these cases blessed are those who mourn, because “those who sow in tears shall reap in exultation” (Ps. CXXV). For God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of his saints, and there will be no more mourning, crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away (Rev. XXI).

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled.” All people hunger and thirst, but some hunger and thirst for evil, others hunger and thirst for good. Some hunger and thirst for gold, silver, costly garments, estates, lands, vineyards, houses, horses, and innumerable possessions. All these things are good in themselves; but they are in a certain sense called evil in that wicked persons hunger and thirst for them wickedly. So too the Lord called *mammon*, that is, riches, iniquitous—not because the things constituting riches were iniquitous, but because they were acquired through iniquity.

Others hunger and thirst for power and honours; others for pleasures; others for greetings in the marketplace, the first places at feasts, the first seats in synagogues, and to be called Rabbi by men. But such people cannot become blessed, because they cannot be filled. For the whole world would not be enough for a human being, who is lord of the world. The eye is not filled with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing, nor can a person be satisfied by the delights of the other senses.

[Col. 0962B] King David considered this well. Although he had food and drink not only for necessity but also, had he wished, in abundance, nevertheless he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI). Let us hunger and thirst not for transitory, earthly things, but for righteousness, because through hunger and thirst for righteousness we shall come to the fullness of eternal glory.

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Therefore, if you wish to receive mercy, show mercy: “Forgive,” he says, “and you shall be forgiven.” For according to the measure by which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you.

Blessed also are the merciful who stand by others in their miseries and, according to their means, protect and defend them.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Pure in heart are those who are defiled neither by the dust of useless thought nor by the mud of wicked pleasure. Pure in heart are those whom the cloud of earthly ignorance does not cover and the heat of concupiscence does not corrupt. [Col. 0962C] Therefore let us cleanse our hearts from every ignorance through the inquiry into truth, and from every perverse desire through love of virtue, that we may deserve to see God in the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Peacemakers are those who wish to make and preserve peace within themselves: who subdue opposing vices, raise up virtues, prudently and vigorously drive out whatever perverse thought, speech, or deed they discover in themselves, and permit no disturbance to remain within the kingdom of their own governance. And if adversity befalls them, they nevertheless preserve their peace and judge all things with tranquillity of heart.

Peacemakers are those who not only preserve peace in themselves but also bring others who are at discord back to the unity of peace. Peacemakers are those who, when evil is inflicted upon them by evil people, do not return evil, but are peaceable with those who hate peace (Ps. CXIX). These shall be called sons of God, because God is supreme peace and judges all things with tranquillity: sons of God, brothers of Christ. These are sons by grace; Christ is Son by nature. They are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Many suffer persecution, but some suffer it for guilt, others for righteousness and innocence. But someone may say: “No one can now attain blessedness through persecution, because everything now stands in peace and the holy Church suffers adversity from almost no quarter.” And I say that persecutions are everywhere, because daily in the inner places of the holy Church Cain persecutes Abel, Ishmael Isaac, Esau Jacob—that is, the wicked person persecutes the righteous; and if anyone does not suffer persecution from outsiders, he nevertheless suffers it from false brothers.

[Col. 0963A] “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III). Since persecutions therefore do not cease, patience is necessary for us, so that we may receive the promises (Heb. X). But woe to those who lose patience, for they lose the crown of patience as well. Therefore let us not murmur if we are troubled in a few things, because in many things we shall be well ordered (Wis. III).

Thus, through poverty of spirit one reaches the kingdom of heaven; through meekness or gentleness, the land of the living; through mourning, true consolation; through thirst and hunger for righteousness, the fullness of heavenly delight; through mercy exercised in time, eternal mercy; through purity of heart, the vision of God; through peace, sonship of God; and through present persecution, the everlasting tranquillity and rest of the heavenly kingdom.

Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth. Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution [Col. 0963C] for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are you when people curse you and persecute you, etc.

Above he spoke to all the elect; now he turns directly to the apostles, although these words also apply to the other elect, showing the apostles by these words how much they would suffer for his name. Oh, how few there are who direct the eyes of their heart to these words of the Lord and, through their admonition, seek blessedness. How many there are who, for a slight verbal injury, return blows if they can; and if they cannot accomplish what they attempt, nevertheless they attempt this and greater things. How well the holy apostles impressed these words upon their hearts: they went away from the presence of the council rejoicing because they had been counted worthy [Col. 0963D] to suffer insult for the name of Jesus (Acts 5).

But observe that he says, “lying” and “for my sake.” For if, when people curse us, they curse us justly, we no longer have merit. “Rejoice and exult.” In many things we are deceived, brothers. When worldly things smile upon us, when the crowd raises us up with vain praises, we rejoice and exult—when we ought rather to grieve and weep all the more, since prosperity brings greater danger than adversity, and praises more than reproaches. But let us hear what salutary joy, what salutary exultation, is shown to the apostles when they are told to rejoice and exult amid insults and persecutions.

He adds the reason, saying: “For your reward is great in heaven.” This reward, brothers, is great, exalted, precious, and lasting: so great that it cannot be numbered; so exalted that it cannot be comprehended; so precious that it cannot be valued; so lasting [Col. 0964A] that it cannot end—Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. On the man possessed by a legion.

As Jesus was leaving the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came out from the tombs to meet him; he had his dwelling among the tombs, etc. (Mark 5.) This demoniac, possessed by a legion, signifies the people of the Gentiles, long possessed by the whole host of demons. For the Gentile people was held in possession by all demons as long as, through the manifold worship of idolatry, [Col. 0964B] it served them all. For the Gentiles, as the Apostle says, “changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and serpents. They changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen” (Rom. 1).

The chains and fetters with which he was bound and which he broke signify the precepts of the natural law or the ordinances of Gentile laws by which he ought to have been restrained from evil. But the bound demoniac broke chains and fetters, because the more the Gentile people was bound by one or another of these precepts through the prohibition of evils, the more furiously it broke them through transgression. And he dwelt among the tombs because he lived amid [Col. 0964C] foul and dead works.

Concerning this breaking of chains and fetters Paul accordingly says: “Their women changed the natural use into that use which is against nature. Likewise also the men, abandoning the natural use of woman, burned in their desires toward one another—men committing shamefulness with men, and receiving in themselves the recompense that was fitting for their error. And because they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting: filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, covetousness, malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insulting, proud, arrogant, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, [Col. 0964D] senseless, disorderly, without natural affection, faithless, without mercy” (ibid.).

See how the legion possessed the man, how he broke chains and fetters, how he dwelt among tombs. He is rightly said to have cried out night and day among the tombs and in the mountains, and to have cut himself with stones, because both in adversity and prosperity the Gentile people shamelessly displayed itself in foul conduct and vain self-exaltation, and tore itself apart through the worship of stony idols.

The herd of swine which fed beside the mountain, into which the legion expelled from the man entered, and which it drove headlong into the sea, represents the multitude of unbelievers and of all unclean persons. They rightly feed beside a mountain: lifted up through pride, yet bent down to the depths after the likeness of swine, [Col. 0965A] they know nothing of things above and brutishly immerse themselves only in transient things. And while they defile themselves with the pollution of flesh or spirit, they seek food in the mud, after the manner of swine.

Alas, how manifold is this multitude of swine: that is, people living bestially and shamefully, imitating swine which seek their good only in the lowest things! To say nothing of pagans and Jews, who could count the multitudes of false Christians who, though they have received baptism, nevertheless insult the Spirit of grace and, by evil living, have driven him out of themselves and defiled themselves with dreadful crimes? Yet they may figuratively be called two thousand: two, because they are divided from the good; thousands, because they are perfected in evil.

Therefore the legion expelled from the man [Col. 0965B] enters the swine, because demons, driven away by the Redeemer’s grace from those predestined to eternal life, rule over the wicked, who live wickedly and attend to earthly things. Yet they do not do this unless Jesus first grants it, for they do not presume even to tempt the wicked unless divine power permits it. But the herd of swine is precipitated by the legion into the sea when, through demons, the whole company of the wicked is brought to infernal bitterness.

The people of that city saw the man freed from the legion sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and of sound mind, and they were afraid. Sitting at the Lord’s feet signifies humility and the imitation of good works; clothing, good conduct; soundness of mind, justification. And they asked Jesus to depart from their borders. [Col. 0965C] As Peter, mindful of his own frailty, said, “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5), so these persons too, still weak, were afraid and asked him to depart from their borders.

Jesus said to the man who had been freed: “Go home to your own people, and tell them how much the Lord has done for you and how he has had mercy on you.” By this example each person is taught first to proclaim to his own people the salvation granted to him and to urge them to receive salvation. For he seems to owe them more by reason of kinship of the flesh, and perhaps they will sooner believe him than a stranger.

But how many are contained within the bounds of holy Church who do not follow this example at all! How many ask concerning their relatives whether they are healthy in body, whether [Col. 0965D] they have food, clothing, houses, fields, horses, flocks, vine-cuttings, gold, silver, temporal peace, whether they possess the favor of the powerful and wealthy; and so they are concerned for their friends in matters pertaining to the body, but bear no concern at all for matters necessary to the salvation of souls! It is to be feared that such people have relapsed into their former vices and themselves now lack the salvation which they do not care to preach even to their own.

For those who are spiritual and perceive the things of the Spirit diligently inquire concerning their own people whether they are pure from vices, free from sins, enriched with virtues, full of good works, whether they have the peace of God with all, whether they do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith. These imitate the man who had been freed, [Col. 0966A] who, at the Lord’s command, made it his care to announce to others the salvation granted him and to preach throughout the Decapolis. The Decapolis, a region of ten cities, signifies holy Church, which keeps the Decalogue of the Law. And he proclaims throughout the Decapolis the salvation granted him who shows by words and good works to the faithful of holy Church that he has been delivered from the devil.

Let us also strive, if we have not yet been freed, to be delivered from the devil; and if we know ourselves already freed, let us preach to others the salvation which we rejoice to have obtained, mindful of what is written: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12; Luke 11). And again: “Let him who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22). Therefore let us now hear and speak in such a way on the way that we may deserve to be rewarded in our homeland. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, [Col. 0966B] he who is God, blessed for ever.

## SERMON XXX. On the feast of a confessor.

“A certain man, going abroad, called his servants and gave them his goods” (Matt. 25). This man is Christ; the servants are Christians; the departure is the Ascension; the goods are gifts; the five talents are outward knowledge acquired through the five senses; the two talents are understanding and good action; the one talent is understanding alone; the multiplication of talents is the exercise of virtues and the performance of good works for one’s own justification and the benefit of others.

The servant who hid his lord’s money in the earth signifies false Christians, who expend their received ability upon earthly and transient matters; who fear to enter the paths of a stricter life; who think little of multiplying, by preaching to others, the knowledge divinely received; who are ashamed and disdainful. “I reap where I have not sown; I gather where I have not scattered.” As though he said: I require the fruit of work and preaching not only from those to whom I have given the grace of acting and preaching, but I also condemn for unfruitfulness and barrenness those to whom I have given no grace.

“Wicked and slothful servant.” A servant, because you ought to have served me by acting and preaching; wicked, by doing evil; slothful, by ceasing from good. “You ought to have entrusted my money to bankers, and when I came I should have received what was mine with interest.” The bankers are those who, having heard preaching, strive by deed and word to multiply what they have heard. As though he said: You ought to have directed my grace received toward good action and preaching. Had you done so, you would have gained for me not only yourself but also many others by your example and speech. But because through your sloth, by which you ceased from good, and through your wickedness, by which you did evil, you brought me loss not only of your own justification but also of that of others, I therefore rightly rebuke and condemn you for your wickedness and sloth.

“Take the talent from him and give it to the one who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, more will be given and he will abound; but from him,” etc. To one who has merit, reward will be given: it will be given as recompense; he will abound in blessedness. “But from him who does not have, even what he seemed to have shall be taken away from him,” because every false Christian, [Col. 0967A] in condemnation, will not be permitted even to retain the name of Christian. As he is now stripped of the inward reality of the sacraments, so then he will be stripped outwardly of their external shadow.

Let human conscience therefore take heed now in time, that afterward it may rejoice in eternal reward. Let it so expend the talent of heavenly gift that in the end it receives not condemnation but salvation. Let no one say: “It is enough for me to attend to myself and provide for myself alone. I shall render an account of myself; I do not wish, by seeking another’s salvation, to put myself in danger. I am not learned in the Scriptures nor eloquent in speech; I know little. God will never accuse or condemn anyone because so small a thing is not preached.” For from as many persons as each person could benefit, so far as depends on him, by speech, he causes God loss by his silence; and for so many [Col. 0967B] you will not unjustly render an account at judgment.

Therefore, whoever knows much, let him say much; whoever knows little, let him say little; and whatever each person knows, let him say that much. Whoever knows even one Gospel or one example of virtue, let him give to others through preaching whatever he possesses by knowledge. Let him consider neither sex, age, status, time, nor place, but preach to all, always and everywhere: to men, women, old persons, young persons, rich and poor; in prosperity and adversity; by day, by night, morning, noon, and evening; in church, in the street, on the road, in the field, on land and sea. Let him always and everywhere tell all the good which he knows, if someone able to hear is present.

For there are many who always consider the more distinguished circumstances in all these matters and, confronted by the opposite circumstances, refuse to preach, as though God looked after higher things and did not care for lower things—although what seems lowest to human beings is sometimes regarded as highest before God. There are also some who preach at times to a more numerous people but never care to speak to a few. They bind themselves with greater guilt before God, because, whether from shame, pride, or the pomp of riches, they altogether refuse to utter the word of God.

Therefore whoever expends in preaching the talent of known good gains a talent for the Giver—even if not in another, at least in himself. For though the hearer does not abandon evil or do good, the speaker nonetheless, in what he says, delivers his own soul; ignorance does not excuse the hearer, and therefore the divine judgment more justly condemns him. [Col. 0967D] No one, however, can excuse himself from this disbursement of the talent, for there is no one unable by his own word to urge someone toward better things.

But many who have been marked out for the ministry of preaching, who receive the revenues of that ministry and live delicately and luxuriously from them—these, I say, who do not know the divine Scriptures, must be reproved for sluggishness, idleness, or contempt, because churches everywhere are filled with libraries, homiliaries, expositions, and treatises, while they themselves devote no effort to reading and meditating upon the Scriptures. Let the useless, ignorant, and slothful ministers of certain churches therefore be ashamed; let them shake off their torpor, read books, expend their talent, redeem the time, because the days are evil.

Finally, by every means through which we can amend ourselves or aid others, [Col. 0968A] we ought to distribute and, by distributing, multiply the Lord’s talent, since we shall render an account of it at the strict judgment. Thus, brothers, let us expend the talent in the world, that we may deserve to glory in the joy of the Lord in heaven. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. On the tabernacles of the children of Israel.

We read in the page of the Old Testament (Lev. CXXIII [i.e. Leviticus 23]) that the Lord commanded through Moses the children of Israel diligently to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles for seven days in the seventh month, so that by this observance their descendants might remember that their fathers, delivered from Egyptian [Col. 0968B] bondage, had dwelt in tabernacles in the wilderness for forty years, and might through this remembrance render more earnest thanks to God their deliverer.

Later observing this rite of the sacred feast, they ceased from every servile work, went up the mountain, cut branches of the most beautiful tree—the olive—myrtle, palm-fronds, willows from the stream, and branches of a leafy tree with thick foliage. On their roofs—that is, the flat roofs which the people of Palestine customarily made—or also in the courtyards of their dwellings, they erected tabernacles; they sacrificed victims to the Lord, sounded trumpets, refreshed themselves with a great and varied provision of feasting, and rejoiced before the Lord their God.

But we, who ought to hold not [Col. 0968C] figures but truth, and seek not the killing letter but the life-giving Spirit, should carefully consider what, by the example of the ancients, we must observe not carnally but spiritually. What then is this seventh month in which we are commanded to dwell in tabernacles, unless it is the time of grace, in which the sevenfold Spirit is bestowed upon believers throughout the world? What are the seven days unless they are the course of the present time, which turns within the cycle and succession of seven days? What are the tabernacles unless they are examples of holy and honorable conduct, constructed from diverse virtues and good works, as it were from various branches and their leaves?

Therefore, in the seventh month, for seven days, [Col. 0968D] we ought to dwell in tabernacles: in this time of grace, in the gift of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, and throughout all our life, which proceeds in the sevenfold division of days, we ought to exercise virtues and perform good works. Our fathers—that is, the apostles, whose children we are—delivered from Egyptian bondage in the blood of the Lamb, dwelt for forty years in tabernacles through the wilderness. For, redeemed in Christ’s Passion from the dark dominion of the world, they abstained from every unlawful delight in the spiritual life signified by the wilderness; they kept the Decalogue of the Law and the fourfold Gospel, thus, as it were, completing the number forty; they exercised virtues, performed good works, and by all these things showed that they had no abiding city here but sought the city to come.

We too ought [Col. 0969A] to resemble them, imitate their life, remember our pilgrimage, and, while dwelling in spiritual tabernacles, continually give thanks to God, the deliverer of all his own. But that we may build tabernacles fitting and worthy of the most sacred feast, let us strive to abandon fleshly affections, earthly desires, worldly vanities, and secular occupations; and, rising above the habit of general thoughts, let us ascend the mountain—that is, undertake a higher meditation upon the Scriptures and lofty contemplation of heavenly good. Let us pluck the leafy branches of virtues and good works, and hasten to erect tabernacles of honorable conduct, by which, while observing so great a feast, we may be protected against the heat of vices, the wind of temptations, and the rain of persecutions.

[Col. 0969B] We are commanded to cease from every servile work because consent to and affection for sin are forbidden us. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8). Sin is committed not only outwardly in deed but inwardly in the heart, as it is written: “Indeed, you work iniquities in your hearts upon the earth” (Ps. 57). And elsewhere: “There will be an examination concerning the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. 1). Nor was peace announced at the Savior’s birth except to persons of good will (Luke 2). From this consider how greatly we are commanded to cease from servile work, since not only the act but even consent to sin is reproved.

Among the spiritual trees—that is, virtues—charity is the most beautiful. Through love of God it rises to heaven; through love of neighbor it is extended [Col. 0969C] to the ends of the earth. Of its praise and beauty it is written: “Though I speak with the tongues of men and angels; though I have all faith and all knowledge; though I distribute all my possessions as food to the poor; though I give my body to be burned,” and the other things contained there, “yet if I do not have charity, I am nothing; it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore we ought to possess branches of this most beautiful tree, because we ought to shade ourselves with the inward thoughts and affections of charity.

The olive also yields oil surpassing all other liquids and fittingly expresses mercy, which surpasses many other virtues. Myrtle has a good fragrance and signifies a good reputation, fragrant far and wide. We ought to have this in the building of our tabernacle, because in every place we ought to be the good fragrance of Christ. Alternatively, myrtle belongs to the virtue of moderation, in that it restrains lax limbs by tempering them; and it therefore rightly signifies temperance. [Col. 0969D] The palm, which adorns the hand of victors, suitably represents victory. We ought to possess it, showing that we have conquered flesh, world, and devil.

Let us also have willows from the stream, that in this mortal life, which now runs like a torrent, we may be able to serve the Lord with chaste heart and body. For willows, which are fruitless and barren, can signify chaste thoughts and the functions of the flesh made barren of unlawful pleasure for the kingdom of heaven. We are therefore commanded to have willows by name, because without purity [Col. 0970A] we cannot worthily celebrate the Lord’s feast. Let us also seek branches of a leafy tree, or of thick foliage, that we may possess the multiplication of other virtues. From all these virtues and the leaves proceeding from them—that is, good works—we ought to erect tabernacles, that is, examples of holy conduct, by which we may show ourselves to be strangers and pilgrims in this world, like all our fathers, and plainly demonstrate that we have no abiding city here but seek the one to come.

Finally, following the example of the ancients, we must erect and dwell in these tabernacles upon our roofs and in our courtyards, because we ought to rise above every pleasure of this wretched flesh through desire for heavenly good, and leave behind even the world around us [Col. 0970B] through enlargement of heart, so that we may contemplate more loftily and perfectly the things above and the immeasurable goods there.

Let us also offer sacrifice to the Lord—not the blood of calves, but the fruit of lips confessing his name. For “a sacrifice of praise honors him,” and there is the way in which he shows his salvation. By doing this we shall also fulfill what the psalm says: “Your ordinances were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118). Let us sound the trumpets through the office of preaching, that we may preach what is right to others and summon them to the observance of so great a feast. For it is written: “Let him who hears say: Come” (Rev. 22). And the Psalmist says: “I will not restrain my lips, Lord; you know it. I have not concealed your righteousness in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation. I have not hidden your mercy [Col. 0970C] and truth from the great assembly” (Ps. 39).

Let us refresh ourselves with the provision of the feast, that through communion in the body and blood of Christ and participation in spiritual gifts we may make ourselves worthy to the extent of our strength. For by such banquets our inward person is nourished; in such feasting God delights. Let us rejoice not in the world but in the Lord, as the Apostle admonishes us, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). If we rejoice in the Lord, there will be a voice of exultation and salvation in our tabernacles, not the voice of exultation and destruction found in the tabernacles of the ungodly, whose expectation and exultation is rage, who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2).

[Col. 0970D] Therefore, if we wish worthily to celebrate the feast of Tabernacles, let us observe all these things not carnally but spiritually. Let us cease from servile work, renouncing sinful affections. Let us ascend the mountain through meditation on sacred discourse and contemplation of the good above. Let us gather branches of the most beautiful tree through brotherly charity; of the olive through mercy; of the myrtle through temperance; of palms through victory; of willows through chastity; branches of thick foliage through the manifold exercise of other virtues. Let us erect tabernacles through honorable conduct: upon our roofs, by rising above the corruption of our flesh through devotion of mind; and in our courtyards, by leaving behind the world itself through enlargement of heart.

Let us sacrifice—but the sacrifice of praise; [Col. 0971A] let us sound—but the trumpet of preaching; let us feast—but through participation in Christ’s sacraments and the sweetness of heavenly grace; let us exult—but with the joy of spiritual gladness. We perform all these things for seven days if we do not cease to do them throughout our whole life, which turns in the cycle of seven days.

Finally, we shall complete this feast, according to the commandment of the Law, on the eighth day, when on the day of resurrection death, swallowed up in victory, shall bring us from corruption to incorruption and from mortality to immortality. For if we now complete the seven days on the journey, then we shall celebrate the eighth upon arrival: when we shall possess joy and gladness; when sorrow and groaning shall flee away; when God shall wipe every tear from the eyes [Col. 0971B] of his saints; when he shall reveal to those who fear him the abundance of his sweetness, which he still hides from them, which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII. On the apostles, or other preachers.

“The righteous shall shine, and shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds. They shall judge nations and reign for ever” (Wis. 3). Great, wonderful, and precious, dearest brothers, is the praise of the saints in these words; great, splendid, and sublime are the merit and reward that shine forth in them. The proposed text sets forth four statements concerning them: they shall shine, run to and fro, judge, and reign. Shining belongs to virtue; running to and fro, to preaching; judging, to resurrection; reigning, to blessedness. Therefore the righteous shine through virtue, run through preaching, shall judge in the resurrection, and shall reign in blessedness.

“The righteous shall shine.” We know that different righteous persons have shone through different virtues. Abel shone through innocence; Noah through righteousness; Abraham through faith; Isaac through long-suffering; Jacob through endurance of labor; Joseph through bodily continence; Moses through meekness; Joshua through courage; Samuel through charity; David through humility; Elijah through zeal for righteousness; Daniel through the virtue of abstinence; Saint John the Baptist through outstanding holiness; [Col. 0971D] the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary through the special grace of humility and integrity. In subsequent times some likewise shone through faith, others through hope, others through charity, others through humility, others through the brightness of chastity, others through the shedding of blood, others through the exercise of whatsoever other virtues, and others through the performance of many good works.

But—what must be lamented grievously and cannot be said without great groaning—we see many, established in an order and profession of holiness, clothed in clerical or religious habit, apostatizing from their holy purpose, becoming sluggish in the exercise of works of righteousness, panting after secular honors, yearning for the desires of earthly things, sighing for the instability of worldly [Col. 0972A] curiosity, entirely forgetful of holy rest and inward contemplation, and shamelessly and tumultuously involving themselves in the conduct of outward affairs without any good intention. Those who ought to shine with the splendor of the virtues named above are sometimes found foul with the blackness of vices, so that we are compelled to cry out in prophetic astonishment: “How the gold has grown dim! How the finest color has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4).

We see Isaiah’s prophecy fulfilled in some persons: namely, that boys fail in labor and young men fall into weakness—that is, certain converts who have recently entered the path of good purpose, who, as their strength is not yet exhausted, ought eagerly to run, [Col. 0972B] act manfully, and zealously cleanse away the rust of their sins by bearing the burden and heat of the day. Yet we see them shamelessly seeking many occasions for idleness and wandering, displaying no fervor of the conceived spirit in the fruit of good work, but remaining barren through enervating lukewarmness.

In saying these things so sharply, we do not rashly blame the pious concern of those who serve the needs of their brothers; rather, we reprove the perversity of certain people who do not walk rightly in the path of their profession. Nor ought we merely to abhor, detest, and avoid evils in order to attain the splendor of the virtues named above; we should also choose better things among good things, so that one who serves a neighbor’s necessities in charity, if he sees that he can attain the hidden loftiness of inward [Col. 0972C] contemplation, may, according to the prophetic voice, sit alone and raise himself above himself: from Jacob become Israel, from Leah become Rachel, from Peninnah become Hannah, from Martha become Mary.

Encouragements to this—namely, that we should prefer contemplation to action—are given us not only by Jacob, who loved Rachel more than Leah, but also by Elkanah, who loved Hannah more than Peninnah; by Mary, who is said to have chosen the better part; and by the true Caleb, son of Jephunneh. Of him we read that, neither broken by old age nor wearied by labor, he asked Joshua to give him the mountain so that he might conquer the giants dwelling there and possess the mountain which God had promised him (Josh. 14). He also testified that the same strength remained in him [Col. 0972D] which he had possessed many years earlier, when he was sent to spy out that land.

But—what cannot be stated without great sorrow—few persevere, after the example of this man, in the same strength of virtue, despise low things, conquer demons, and attempt to ascend to things above. But let us, dearest brothers, gather in mind the outstanding examples of the Fathers spiritually, and, preferring better things among goods, always choose the higher, that we may in some measure attain the splendor of the virtues named above.

Let no one presume to undertake outward affairs contrary to the counsel or will of his superior, lest, deceived by the devil’s snare and struck down by the enemy’s sword, [Col. 0973A] he fall. For thus, as is read in the book of the Maccabees, “on that day priests fell in battle,” while they wished to act bravely and went out to battle without counsel (1 Macc. 5). So too the children of Israel, while Moses resisted and himself remained in the camp with the ark of the Lord, darkened by ignorance, went up the mountain through pride; and the Canaanite and Amalekite—by whom fleshly and spiritual vices are signified—pursued them as far as Hormah, which is interpreted “anathema.” In all this it is plainly shown that whoever presumes, against the discernment of elders, to undertake earthly affairs is slain by the sword of hostile suggestion.

Moreover, superiors themselves ought carefully to weigh the capacity of their subjects, lest, if they attempt what exceeds their knowledge or [Col. 0973B] strength, they succumb beneath a burden which they cannot bear. Let them employ the example and words of Moses, who, when the Lord promised that he would send his angel before the children of Israel, replied: “I beseech you, Lord, if I have found favor before you, that you yourself may go with us” (Exod. 34). And again: “If you do not come with us, do not lead us out from this place” (Exod. 33).

For Moses tends with the people of Israel toward the promised land when any superior advances those subject to him to ministries for carrying out some good work. He rightly asks the Lord not merely to send an angel ahead but to go himself, when he steadfastly prays that this should be done [Col. 0973C] or left undone not so much according to the counsel of some wise person, who may sometimes be mistaken, as according to divine providence, which alone perfectly knows what is beneficial to human beings. “I beseech you,” he says, “do not lead us out from this place unless you go with us.” For it is better for anyone to live and die in his own simplicity than to be advanced, without God as guide and fellow-worker, to the management of affairs in which he may take scandal to his own soul.

I say all these things, brothers, that you may see how carefully you ought to walk and not be wise in your own eyes; lest, while you imprudently seek the splendor of virtues, you fall into the foul darkness of vices and sins. It follows:

And they shall run to and fro like sparks among reeds. A spark is small in size, and has brightness and heat. Thus, by the name of sparks the holy apostles and the preachers who succeeded the apostles are rightly signified [Col. 0973D]: they are small through the virtue of humility, bright through knowledge of truth, and warm through love of virtue. They are rightly said to run to and fro like sparks among reeds, because, running through the Gentile world—resembling reeds, empty of every truth, filled with every vanity, barren and fruitless of every good work, shaken by every wind of doctrine—they consumed it by their preaching, stripping it of pride; and, showing it that it was ashes and would return to ashes, they reduced it, as it were, to cinders so that it might rise again as a good harvest. Saint Thomas made this course through Greater India; Bartholomew through Lesser India; Simon and Jude through Persia; John through Asia; Andrew through [Col. 0974A] Achaia; Matthew through Ethiopia; Peter through Cappadocia; Paul through Illyricum and Italy; and the other apostles and disciples of the apostles through the other places allotted to them by God.

Thus we see shepherds burning dry grasses in forests by setting fire to them; when these are burned, other grasses, green and suitable for the animals’ pasture, spring up. But—what cannot be said without sorrow—behold: in the places where fruitful harvests had sprung up through the labours of the apostles and their successors, after the reed-beds had been set aflame, reed-beds have grown again in those same places through our negligence and have now almost filled the Lord’s field. For what are the unclean, the fornicators, the covetous, thieves, robbers, and all who are separated from God by any other wickedness [Col. 0974B] and joined to the devil? What, I ask, are they but barren, fruitless reeds, driven by the suggestions of demons, as by certain winds, in every direction of impiety? Why then do we grow numb in idleness? Why do we not run to and fro in preaching? Why do we not set aflame by our teaching whatever evil persons there are, in order to make them good? But woe to us wretches, because many of us are travellers-about, few are preachers! We pass through cities, castles, and villages, but labour little in reproving sinners and converting souls. The world is full of priests; and if there is someone to hear what is good, there is no one to speak it.

We read in the book of the *Dialogues* that a certain holy man always carried with him books containing sacred words. Wherever he went, he watered the meadows of minds from those books [Col. 0974C]. Let us blush, brethren, for our laziness; let us consider the zeal of the holy Fathers. For we ought to imitate the life of those whose sons we ought to be. Let us set the reed-beds aflame; let us correct the wicked in their perversities. And he rightly said first, “They shall shine,” and then, “They shall run to and fro,” because we must first shine in virtues and then teach them to others, as it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). It follows:

“They shall judge nations.” With respect to judgment, there are four classes of human beings: those judged and saved; those to be judged and saved; those judged and condemned; and those to be judged and condemned. Those judged and saved are those whose salvation is already certain; those to be judged and saved are those whose salvation is still uncertain; those judged and condemned [Col. 0974D] are those whose condemnation is already certain; and those to be judged and condemned are those whose condemnation is not yet certain. Therefore, although at the end of the world, on the day of judgment, in the general resurrection, these four classes of people will exist, it is evident that only those whose salvation, by the merit of a more eminent life, will then be clear and manifest shall judge nations—the persons whose praise is sung here when it says: “They shall judge nations.”

Which nations will they judge? They will certainly judge those whose salvation or condemnation will not yet be certain: by their judgment some will be transferred to glory and others to punishment. For the devil and the thoroughly wicked, as already judged, will be thrust into torments without any examination. Let us strive, beloved, that on that day we may at least be among those to be judged and saved, even if we cannot be among those judged and saved who will judge others [Col. 0975A]. Yet great, desirable in every way, and to be sought is the glory on that day of the perfect saints, who will sit with the Judge himself and judge the world with him.

It is praiseworthy indeed to shine in virtue, to run to and fro in preaching, and to judge at the judgment; but what follows is unspeakably more praiseworthy, more excellent, and more sublime: namely, that they shall reign for ever. They shall reign for ever because they shall cleave eternally to the divinity that reigns. Since we cannot explain in more extended words, as we should wish, the glory of that kingdom—which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered into the human heart—we briefly urge you to desire and merit it with all your hearts [Col. 0975B]. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant us to merit it. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. On the Annunciation of the Lord

Brethren, few and small are the things we know about God; few and small are the things we set forth. For what, or how great, can we say about him whom no one has seen or can see? Whenever anyone speaks of God, it is as though one born blind were speaking of light. For “no one has ever seen God” (John 1; 1 John 4); and: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Hence the Lord said even to Moses himself, to whom these words were spoken: “I shall come to you in the darkness [Col. 0975C] of the cloud” (Exod. 19). And afterwards: “Moses approached the darkness in which God was” (Exod. 20). And Solomon says: “The Lord said that he would dwell in the cloud” (3 Kings 8). The Psalmist likewise says: “Cloud and darkness are round about him” (Ps. 96); and again: “Darkness is under his feet” (Ps. 17).

God’s feet are the holy teachers and preachers, who bear him everywhere to the hearts of their hearers. Sometimes they speak in their writings of the heavenly mysteries so obscurely that we can scarcely understand them. Hence it is rightly written in the Psalm: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17), because knowledge in the prophets is obscure (Dan. 7). Daniel too saw the divine vision in a vision of the night; and Eliphaz beheld someone standing [Col. 0975D] before him whose face he did not recognize, and he saw the terror of a night vision (Job 4). Moreover, King Belshazzar beheld not a body, arm, or hand, but the joints of a writing hand (Dan. 5), because the things made manifest to us concerning the mystery of the invisible Godhead are very small.

God indeed dwells in inaccessible light, whom no human being has seen or can see (1 Tim. 6). Even if we see anything of heavenly things, we see, as Solomon says, through openings (Eccl. 12), and, as the Apostle says, “through a mirror, in an enigma, not face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Therefore, because the things we know are very small, the things we preach are correspondingly limited. Thus the explorers of the land of promise left behind them the many and great goods of the land they had seen, and, returning to the children of Israel in the wilderness, brought only [Col. 0976A] one cluster and some pomegranates, figs, and other of its good things. So also we, brethren, have drawn a small drop from the abundance of spiritual good—from the sweetness, that is, of divine praise—which was sung this night in the sacred solemnity of the Lord’s Annunciation, and we have resolved to offer it to you.

We have therefore heard the Psalmist saying: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44). This utterance is the voice of the ancient righteous ones—the patriarchs and prophets, all who live rightly—who desired with every longing, sought with continual prayers, and at last obtained the incarnation of the Word, Christ’s coming, the expulsion of the ancient enemy, and the redemption of the human race. He [Col. 0976B] indeed heard them and girded himself with his sword upon his thigh, when he joined the power of his divinity to the frailty of our humanity. And, girded with the power of his divinity upon the thigh of assumed humanity, he came into the world to overcome “the strong man armed who guards his court” (Luke 2). The strong armed man is the devil; the stronger one who comes upon him is Christ; the court is the world; the vessels are human hearts. Christ snatched these from the devil’s hand, emptied and filled them: he emptied them of guilt and filled them with grace.

Samson, the leader of the Israelite people, prefigured this most mighty warrior—the Redeemer of the human race—in many ways. Samson’s conception and birth were announced through an angel; the Saviour’s conception and birth were announced through an angel. Samson [Col. 0976C] had strength in his hair; Christ in the gifts of spiritual grace. Samson drank neither wine nor anything that could intoxicate; and Babylon’s cup did not intoxicate Christ. No razor came upon Samson’s head; and malice did not enter Christ’s mind. Samson killed a lion and drew a honeycomb from its jaws; Christ conquered the devil and rescued the human race from his mouth. Samson took a foreign woman; Christ took the Church of the Gentiles. Samson overthrew the Philistines; Christ overthrew spiritual and bodily enemies. Samson ascended the summit of a mountain after breaking the gates of Gaza; Christ ascended into heaven after breaking the gates of hell. Samson destroyed far more of his enemies in dying than in living [Col. 0976D]; and Christ defeated the devil and his attendants far more fully by dying than while living.

Thus our Redeemer, not only foretold by prophetic oracles but also prefigured by types, came into the world girded with the sword of divine power upon the thigh of his humanity. He conquered the strong man—that is, the ancient enemy—showed us an example of conquest, and laid this duty upon us, saying: “Be strong in battle, fight against the ancient serpent, and you shall receive the eternal kingdom.”

Let us therefore take up the armour of God, that we may be able to extinguish all the fiery darts of the wicked one (Eph. 6): the shield through faith, the helmet through hope, and the breastplate and greaves through charity. These two, namely breastplate and greaves, just as they are of one fabric, may also be of one symbolic meaning. By the interlinking of their many rings they also signify the union of many virtues [Col. 0977A]. Let us also have a lance, raised upward to God and directed against the enemy through prayer; a bow and arrows through preaching; and the sword of the Spirit through the divine word, which is living, effectual, sharper than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, joints and marrow, discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in its sight, but all things are naked and open to its eyes (Heb. 4).

This sword is the sword of justice. The soldier of Christ ought to have it, draw it, and destroy the enemy battle-lines with it. There is another sword of warfare, which sinners draw. “They sharpen their tongues like a sword,” and “their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 63). Esau lives by this sword (Gen. 27). By it Simeon and Levi, brothers who are “weapons of iniquity, making war,” rage: “Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly. For in their fury they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, for it is stubborn, and their indignation, for it is harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. 49) [Col. 0977B]. This sword, brethren, should not be drawn, but kept in its sheath. For “all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26).

Let this sword, then, be set aside and let the sword described above be taken up. It is the sword that the Lord came to send upon the earth (Luke 12). The saints hold it in their hands—those who have the exaltations of God in their throat—in order [Col. 0977C] to execute justice among the nations and rebukes among peoples, to carry out among them the written judgment; and “this is glory for all his saints” (Ps. 149). Moses spoke of this sword when the Israelite people sinned by making the golden calf. He said: “Whoever belongs to the Lord, let him join himself to me.” When all the sons of Levi had gathered to him, he said: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each kill his brother, friend, and neighbour.” They did so, and about twenty-three thousand people fell that day. And Moses said: “Today each of you has consecrated his hands to the Lord in his son and in his brother, that a blessing may be given to you” (Exod. 32) [Col. 0977D].

Moses signifies any prelate; the assembly of Israel, the subject people; and the calf, sin. Moses ascends the mountain when any prelate, leaving lower matters behind, ascends to the inward contemplation of heavenly things. But Israel’s people makes a calf when the ranks of subjects sin by living wickedly. Moses descends when the prelate turns his mind from contemplation of heavenly things toward lower matters in order to consider the life of those subject to him. He crushes the golden calf when he carefully discerns, according to place and time, cause, person, and manner, a wicked action committed through carnal prudence or worldly wisdom. He throws it into water when, by the authority of sacred speech, he reproves that action as perverse. When the people drink this water, they have gold in their beards [Col. 0978A]: that is, in the very thing in which they gloried that they had acted wisely, it becomes plainly clear that they acted foolishly. And the transgressing people are pierced through with swords when, by the most severe rebuke, they are made dead to evil and alive to good, so that, dead to the world, they may live to God.

“If anyone,” Moses says, “belongs to the Lord, let him join himself to me.” As blessed Gregory says: “Whoever does not join Moses in avenging the sin of the people does not belong to the Lord.” “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh.” And again: “Go and return from gate to gate.” We must first place the sword upon our own thigh; then go and return and kill the guilty, because we must first punish our own vices and then those of others. We go and return from gate to gate when we carefully investigate what each person, from greatest to least, has committed [Col. 0978B]. Or we proceed from gate to gate when we consider the weight of a wicked action from its very beginning to its outcome. We also pass through the midst when we pierce through not only strangers or the less beloved, but friends and intimates too, with the rebuke of just reproof. And we kill, as it were, twenty-three thousand when we punish with the sword of most severe correction the reprobate who transgress the sacred law either in love of God or of neighbour, or who do not possess an entire faith in the holy Trinity.

Concerning this divine and spiritual vengeance it is written in Ezekiel that, while a man having a writer’s inkhorn at his loins went before through the midst of Jerusalem and marked with the letter *tau* the foreheads of men groaning and grieving over all the abominations committed in its midst [Col. 0978C], the Lord commanded six men, each having a weapon of slaughter in his hand: “Pass through the midst of the city after him, and strike. Let not your eye spare, nor have pity. Kill old man, youth, virgin, little child, and women, even to utter destruction. But do not kill anyone upon whom you see the *tau*; and begin from my sanctuary” (Ezek. 9).

The man who had the writer’s inkhorn is Christ, who joined the wisdom of his divinity to the nature of his humanity. He marks with the letter *tau*, in Jerusalem, the men groaning and grieving over all the abominations done in it, because within the holy Church he confirms to true salvation by faith in his passion his elect who grieve over the perversity of false Christians. The six men who follow him kill those not marked, because the five perfect prelates of the holy city, made imitators of their Redeemer, show that all reprobates who deny their received faith by wicked works are now dead through guilt and proclaim that they will be put to death in the future by the punishment of eternal condemnation [Col. 0978D]. They begin from the Lord’s sanctuary when they prove that even many of those who hold a holier rank in the holy Church sin damnably.

“Kill old man, youth, virgin, little child, and women.” The old man is one made old in evil days, polluted through long habit [Col. 0979A] and wrapped in the filth of his sins. The youth signifies one who increases by lasting growth an evil long since begun. The virgin is one who remains barren of the fruitfulness of virtues and good works. The little child represents one who has only recently begun his wickedness. Under the name of women are fittingly signified those who serve, womanishly, softer vices. The six men cut down all these with weapons of slaughter when they declare to them the punishment of future condemnation. Some of them, struck in this way, are brought to life, because, converted from their perversities, they are justified.

The prophet Jeremiah also terribly curses, in prophetic speech, those who are sluggish in this striking, saying: “Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully [Col. 0979B] and negligently; and cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). Behold, brethren, how one who does not, to the extent of his ability, avenge the divine injury is cursed. Let zeal for the Lord’s house therefore consume us, and let us not withhold the sword of the mouth from cleansing sin. And, to use not our own words but those of the eminent teacher, the priest Bede: “Let us be zealous for the house of God, and, so far as we are able, let us strive that no wrong be done in it.” If we see a brother belonging to God’s house swollen with pride, accustomed to detraction, enslaved to drunkenness, enfeebled by lust, troubled by anger, or burdened by any other vice, let us strive, insofar as our ability permits, to chastise what is defiled and correct what is perverse. And if we cannot amend anything in such persons, let us endure it only with the sharpest grief of mind; and especially in the house of prayer itself, where the body of the Lord is consecrated and where the presence of angels is never doubted, let us exert all our strength to prevent anything unseemly from taking place or anything that might impede our fraternal prayer [Col. 0979C].

Let us therefore take care to hear these most sacred words with attentive ears, and let us not neglect to correct whatever needs correction either in ourselves or in others. The Psalmist boasts that he possessed this diligence in cutting away vices, saying: “I have done judgment and justice; do not deliver me to those who slander me” (Ps. 118). Demons slander us when we depart from the body, just as we read in the life of Saint Martin that at the hour of his death the devil came to accuse his soul. If, therefore, we wish to escape this accusation, let us do judgment and justice. “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times” (Ps. 105). “My eyes have shed streams of water” (Ps. 118), when we see the wicked not keeping the law of the Lord. Let our zeal cause us to waste away, because our enemies forget his words (ibid.). Let us be valiant in battle, that we may deserve to be glorious in victory and blessed in glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. On the Nativity or Assumption of the Blessed Mary, Ever-Virgin

“Who is this who comes forth like the dawn rising?” [Col. 0980A] (Song 6). The Blessed Virgin Mary, dearest brethren, was the dawn, because she was the end of the preceding time, which was like night, and the forerunner and morning star of the true light of grace and of the sun of righteousness, who was born from her. For all the time that preceded from Adam to her birth was like night: a long, dark, cold, idle, sluggish, drowsy, silent—indeed mute—night. It was night through the absence of the true light; long through the length of time; dark through the darkness of unbelief; cold through the lack of charity; sluggish through failure to perform good works; drowsy through forgetfulness of blessedness; silent through lack of the voice of true confession; mute through lack of the song of divine praise.

Except for a few persons who in that earlier time rebuked that ancient people for its perversities and, like cocks proclaiming the day during the night, foretold the mysteries of the future Saviour and of the Church, nearly the whole world was oppressed by silence and sleep [Col. 0980B]. As it is written in the Book of Wisdom: “While all things held the middle—that is, the deepest—silence, and night in its course was pursuing its way, your almighty Word, O Lord, came from royal thrones” (Wis. 18). Yet certain stars illumined that time with their rays, because the holy patriarchs and prophets enlightened the ignorance of that people by their virtues. Their rays were in some sense dimmed when the dawn appeared, because the saints who came before had little brightness in comparison with Blessed Mary.

For what were Abel’s innocence, Noah’s justice, Abraham’s faith, Isaac’s long-suffering, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s continence [Col. 0980C], Moses’ meekness, Joshua’s strength, Samuel’s charity, David’s humility, Elijah’s zeal, Daniel’s abstinence, the outstanding holiness of Blessed John, and the virtues of the other saints, in comparison with Blessed Mary? Thus the Blessed Virgin Mary was truly a most brilliant dawn, which diminished the brightness of the preceding Fathers by its magnificent radiance. Certainly, whatever is praiseworthy in Scriptures or in created things is suitable for her praise. As dawn, therefore, she is so by her anticipation of the true light; as a flower, by beauty; a honeycomb, by sweetness; a violet, by humility; a rose, by charity or compassion; a lily, by sweetness; a vine, by fruitfulness; every fragrance, by good repute; a fortress, by security; a wall or tower, by strength; a shield or bulwark, by defence [Col. 0980D]; a column, by uprightness; a bride, by faithfulness; a friend, by love; a mother, by fruitfulness; a virgin, by integrity; a lady, by dignity; a queen, by majesty; a sheep, by innocence; a lamb, by purity; a dove, by simplicity; a turtledove, by chastity; every clean domestic animal, by pure and gentle conduct; a cloud, by protection; a star, by the beginning of every virtue or good work; the moon, by its increase; the sun, by its completion; and, finally, the heavenly paradise, by the fullness of heavenly good.

But to return to what we began: after this blessed Mary arose in the world like a radiant dawn, immediately after her rising the sun of righteousness, Christ our God, rose from her; and, driving away darkness, he illumined the whole world, so that the people of the Gentiles, who had walked in darkness, saw a great light [Col. 0981A] (Isa. 9). Christ illumined the world by his birth, preaching, working of miracles, passion, resurrection, appearance, ascension, sending of the Holy Spirit, dispersal of the apostles throughout the world, their preaching, and the distribution of heavenly grace in the holy Church.

Therefore, dearest brethren, since night has passed and day has dawned upon us, let us walk honourably as in the day (Rom. 13). Let us not walk as our Gentile fathers did (Rom. 1), of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is God blessed for ever. Therefore he gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things unfitting; being filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, covetousness” (Rom. 1), and the other detestable vices and sins listed there. But let us, brethren, cast off vices and sins, which are works of darkness, and put on the armour of light, which consists in virtues and good works; and let us walk honourably as in the day of grace (Rom. 13) [Col. 0981B].

All vices and sins are either carnal or spiritual. The Apostle forbids them all to us, either expressly or figuratively, where he says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in beds and shamelessness, not in strife and envy” (ibid.). All carnal sins either concern gluttony and are forbidden where it says, “not in revelries and drunkenness,” or concern lust and are forbidden [Col. 0981C] where it adds, “in beds and shamelessness.” Spiritual sins, however, are either committed outwardly and are forbidden where it says, “not in strife,” or are committed inwardly and are forbidden where it continues, “not in envy.” Strife is outward, in the mouth; envy is inward, in the heart. Finally, both spiritual and bodily goods are commanded where it adds: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid.). To put on Christ is to live holy and honourably in Christ.

Therefore, beloved, let us cast off the devil with his dark works by hating evil; let us put on Christ by loving good, practising virtues, and performing good works. Thus we shall walk honourably as in the day of grace and attain the glory of the heavenly homeland. Let us pray together [Col. 0981D] that, through the merits and prayers of the holy Virgin Mary, the Sun of righteousness may always shine upon us, always remain, and never set; that, after the example of Joshua, for whom the sun stood still at Gibeon until he had avenged himself upon his enemies (Josh. 10), he may be with us—as he promised his faithful ones, until the consummation of the age—until we too, our enemies having been slain, are granted the heavenly dwelling-places. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XXXV. On Any Confessor Who Is a Bishop, or Other Ruler of the People, and on His Necessary Office and Teaching

Solomon, wisest of the ancient kings, dearest brethren, and son of King David, whom the Lord chose as an ecclesiastical prelate and teacher, figuratively admonishes him in a certain passage to hasten to free himself from the danger in which he is daily engaged through the care of souls entrusted to him for instruction, by diligently correcting and teaching them. He says: “My son, if you have gone surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger. You are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own speech. Do therefore what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into your neighbour’s hand: run about, make haste, rouse your friend; give no sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber. Rescue yourself like a gazelle from the hand, and like a bird from the fowler’s snares” (Prov. 6) [Col. 0982A].

Our friend is our neighbour, whom, according to the divine command, we ought to love as ourselves. This stranger is Christ [Col. 0982B], who is a stranger to us both in his humanity and in his divinity. In his humanity he is a stranger to us because we did not see him in the flesh; in his divinity because no one has ever seen God. He is a stranger to us because he is righteous and blessed, whereas we are sinners and wretched. He is a stranger to all, because, although people may be righteous and wise and their works may be in God’s hand, yet no one knows whether he is worthy of hatred or love; all things are reserved uncertain for the future (Eccl. 9).

Therefore, the person who takes into the care of his providence the souls of others truly goes surety before this stranger for his friend; like a guarantor who must answer for repayment of a debt, he pledges his hand, is ensnared by the words of his mouth, and caught by his own speech. He [Col. 0982C] must therefore run about and make haste, and rouse his friend. Let him run and make haste by example; let him rouse by word. Let him run on the right and the left, in prosperity and adversity, and do good to friends and enemies, good and evil persons, the gentle and the difficult. Let him rouse his friend by admonition, that he may avoid evil and do good. Let him not sleep by avoiding greater negligence, nor slumber by avoiding lesser negligence. Let him be rescued like a gazelle and like a bird. The gazelle is a clean animal, most sharp-sighted; the bird seeks the heights in flight. Let the prelate or teacher be rescued like a gazelle, that he may be clean through honourable conduct and sharp-sighted through discernment. Let him be rescued like a bird, that he may seek lofty things through contemplation. For not only a prelate’s good action [Col. 0982D], but also his contemplation, benefits his subjects. Hence the Apostle says: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5).

At times, therefore, the ruler ought to take for himself the wings of a kite in rapacity—not of a raven in tearing apart, but of a dove in simplicity—and fly through contemplation; and rest, through a cessation from action, from faintness of spirit and storm—that is, from the anxiety of pastoral care. Thus Moses, having sent away the flock, went into the interior of the wilderness to see the great vision (Exod. 3). But when the apostles were weary and occupied by the crowd’s approach so that they had no time to eat, the Lord said: “Come apart into a deserted place and rest a little” (Mark 6). And, as blessed Gregory says: “A ruler ought not, because of concern for his neighbour, to put aside contemplation of God; nor, because of contemplation of God, to neglect concern for his neighbour” [Col. 0983A].

Therefore, in order to free himself, the ruler must run about through good action, make haste through the prompt performance of that action, rouse his friend through exhortation, be rescued like a gazelle through purity of honourable conduct and keenness of discernment, and like a bird through the loftiness of contemplation. Certainly, there are two principal means by which a prelate must free himself: example and word—example in action and word in preaching. First example, then word, so that he may imitate the Lord, of whom it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). But because it is certain that he must act well, if not for his neighbour’s sake, at least for his own; and because [Col. 0983B] we see many shepherds who, though they themselves are believed to live well, nevertheless refrain from speaking, either because they do not know how to speak or because they neglect it, let us pass over the example of action and speak of the word of preaching.

Every prelate owes fourfold instruction to the souls entrusted to him. First, he must teach his subjects the faith of the holy, undivided Trinity; second, how they are to rule and command the five bodily senses; third, that they should perform the six works of mercy; fourth, that they should practise the seven principal virtues. Let us treat each matter individually, beginning with faith.

There were three things: body, spirit, and God. The body was the world, the spirit the soul; and the soul itself was, as it were, in the middle, with the world outside it and God within it. It had received an eye by which it could see the world outside itself and the things that were in the world: this was the eye of flesh. It had received another eye by which it could see itself and the things within it: this is the eye of reason. Again it had received another eye by which it could see God within itself and the things that were in God: this is the eye of contemplation [Col. 0983C].

So long as the soul kept these eyes open and unveiled, it saw clearly and discerned rightly. But after the darkness of sin entered it, the eye of contemplation was extinguished within it, so that it saw nothing; while the eye of reason became bleary, so that it saw uncertainly. Only the eye that was outward remained in its brightness; and so long as it has clear light [Col. 0983D], it has no doubtful judgment. But the eye of reason, so long as its light is clouded, cannot have certain judgment, because it does not see clearly and discerns ambiguously. Hence human hearts agree with one another more readily about those things perceived by the eye of flesh than about those reached by the keenness of mind and the sense of reason, because where they are not obscured in seeing, they do not differ in judging.

Thus a human being who has the eye of flesh can see the world and the things that are in the world. Likewise, because he has the eye of reason only in part, he similarly sees the mind only in part and the things that are in the mind. But because he does not have the eye of contemplation, he cannot see God and the things that are in God. Faith, therefore, is necessary, by which things not seen are believed, and by faith those things that are not yet present to us in direct vision subsist within us [Col. 0984A].

Thus their substance is faith, because they are established for us by faith alone. For those who doubt them, we can adduce no greater proof than that the things believed by faith are not comprehended by reason. Faith is in us the source and foundation of virtues and good works. Hence, as the Apostle says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). Faith, if it consists in knowledge alone, is insufficient unless it is made alive through love and, if it can, works out of love. If it cannot work, provided it has love, love itself is its work. There are many who perform many works, but because they do not have love of God and neighbour, they do not attain the kingdom of God by their work. Therefore only that faith is to be called faith which has love as its companion and which, through love, works, if indeed it is able.

There are therefore two elements of faith: knowledge and affection. Some have great faith in knowledge but little in affection; others great in affection but little in knowledge. Some have faith great both in knowledge and affection; others have it small in both knowledge and affection.
