But the Lord plainly shows that great affection in faith is more praiseworthy than great knowledge, when he compared faith to a mustard seed (Matt. 13), which is small in size but not in ardour. Thus to the Canaanite woman, still little instructed indeed but greatly confident, it was said: “Woman, great is your faith” (Matt. 15). For that faith is reckoned great before God which, although less vigorous in knowledge, nevertheless shows itself strong through constancy. Therefore, when faith grows in knowledge, it is assisted; when faith grows in affection, it earns merit. Faith, then, is praised and rewarded not from knowledge alone, but from affection and action. For this is the faith which justifies, which, according to the Apostle, works through love (Gal. 5). The other kind is that of demons, of whom it is written that “the demons believe and tremble” (Jas. 2 [printed: Isa. 2]); or it is the faith of any ungodly person who has faith only according to knowledge and not also according to love. Of him it is written: “What the ungodly fears shall come upon him” (Prov. 10).

But let us, brothers, work through love, that we may be rewarded for love. The bodily senses are five: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch. Through these the soul proceeds outwardly toward visible things in its own way, just as inwardly it proceeds through reason and contemplation toward invisible things; and it does what is pleasant, convenient, useful, and necessary to the body. For as the human being is made of two natures, spiritual and bodily, and endowed with two goods, spiritual and bodily, so he is furnished and adorned with a twofold power of perception: inwardly, with rationality for contemplating invisible things; outwardly, with sense-perception for contemplating visible things.

Rationality has its fruit and delight in invisible goods, just as sense-perception has its own in visible goods. Among invisible goods are beauty, virtue, form, justice, sweetness, love, song, joy, the touch of the beloved, and the finding of the good for which one thirsts. Among the senses, sight is more excellent and more effective than the others, but far inferior to reason’s discriminating and contemplative power. For bodily sight, because it is narrow, does not comprehend the greatest things; because it is dull, does not distinguish the smallest; because it is slow, does not reach what is distant; and because it is not penetrating, does not pierce hidden things. Even among visible objects, in which sight ought always to seek what is useful, it is sometimes deceived by a misleading appearance and takes hold of harmful things; and while the unhappy mind delights in them in an unregulated way, inwardly it is defiled by the dust of innumerable pleasures and thoughts. Since worldly things, which we desire externally, are infinite, the thoughts which we draw inwardly from the delight or remembrance of those things cannot be finite. And as the eye feeds upon appearance, so the mind feeds upon thought.

Yet, so far as things themselves are concerned, there is no thing that cannot be thought of without sin; but so far as perverse affections are concerned, there is no thing in thinking of which we cannot sin. Since, therefore, this sense—that is, sight—has so great a defect in relation to good and so great an inclination toward evil, it must be guarded in every way, because through its corruption the mind is especially defiled. It must be guarded, I say, lest, according to Jeremiah, “our eye plunder our souls among all the daughters of our city” (Lam. 3); or, as is read in Job, lest “our eye follow our heart” (Job 31); but rather it should be turned away “lest it see vanity” (Ps. 118 [119]).

Hearing too is corrupted in various ways and must therefore be guarded carefully. Sometimes it is corrupted by empty talk, sometimes by flattery, sometimes by obscene songs, sometimes by detractions. Hence it is written: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Smell is corrupted whenever it takes disordered pleasure in varied fragrances. This sense seems purer and cleaner than the others, and therefore the soul is shown to be less corrupted through it. Taste follows it, through which unhappy gluttony experiences its unlawful appetites. Once this sense is corrupted, it delights insatiably in varied preparations of food and drink. Thus blessed Jerome, speaking in his own person, rebukes the shameless excess of certain people:

> “Born in a poor house and in a rustic hut, when I could scarcely satisfy my roaring belly with millet and coarse bread, I now despise fine flour and honey. I know the names and kinds of fish; I know on what shore a shell was gathered. By the flavours of birds I distinguish their regions, and the rarity of foods, and finally their very expense, delight me.”

But for us, brothers, according to the same teacher, let food be poor, plain, and taken in the evening: vegetables and legumes; and let us sometimes reckon a few little fish the height of delicacies. Last is touch, which is often defiled by the softness of various garments and the impurity of various obscenities.

It would take long, brothers, to enumerate everything through which the unhappy soul is weakened by its senses. These are the five porticoes of the pool mentioned in the Gospel, in which “a great multitude of sick persons lay” (John 5). For each sense keeps as many sick persons as it suffers corruptions of desire. But whenever the Holy Spirit descends into us and stirs up in us the grace of compunction, then our sense is healed from whatever infirmity of corruption holds it. Let us guard our senses, dearest friends, lest perhaps—may it not be so!—death enter through our windows into our souls.

Isaiah briefly sets forth the fruit of this guarding when he says: “Who among you can dwell with devouring fire? Or who among you can dwell with everlasting burnings? He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth; who casts away avarice gained by oppression, and shakes his hands free from every bribe; who stops his ears lest he hear of blood, and closes his eyes lest he see evil. He shall dwell on high; the strongholds of rocks shall be his lofty refuge. Bread is given him; his waters are sure. His eyes shall see the king in his beauty; they shall behold a land far off. Your heart shall meditate fear” (Isa. 33). [Col. 0986A–B]

There are six works of mercy: the first is to feed the hungry; the second, to give drink to the thirsty; the third, to receive the stranger; the fourth, to clothe the naked; the fifth, to visit the sick; the sixth, to come to the imprisoned and confined. Whoever attends to these in time shall be blessed in eternity. “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor; in the evil day the Lord shall deliver him” (Ps. 40 [41])—that is, in the day of judgment.

And observe—what is marvellous to say—that in the Gospel no other sins are said to be recalled or reproached to those condemned on the day of judgment, except this alone: that they neglected works of mercy. Conversely, those to be saved are not praised for any virtues whatsoever, except solely because they performed them. Hence Peter of Ravenna, in the fourteenth sermon of his *Book of Sermons*: “In the kingdom of heaven, before all the angels in the assembly of those who rise again, God is silent concerning what Abel suffered, what Abraham began in faith, what law Moses brought, what cross Peter mounted head downward; and he cries out only that the poor man ate” (Luke 11 [apparently a faulty citation]).

Therefore, brothers, let us give alms, and all things shall be clean for us (Luke 6). Let us give, that it may be given to us. Let us give, that those to whom we give may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16). Let us give freely, because we especially, who live from alms, have received freely. Let us cast bread upon passing waters (Eccl. 11), that is, upon peoples, because after many days we shall find it. We say these things, brothers, because even we who live in religion sometimes inhumanely shut our ears—indeed, our hearts—against the cry of the poor. But “whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother in need,” and so forth, “how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3). “The soul that blesses shall be made fat, and he who gives drink shall himself also be given drink” (Prov. 11).

Holy volumes, dearest friends, are full of such sayings; nor do we say these things in order to instruct you as though ignorant. Rather, perhaps it was not useless to recall them, because the performance of good works, or the exercise of virtues, confers eternal salvation. Having spoken of works, let us speak of virtues. [Col. 0986C–0987A]

Many virtues are enumerated in Scripture, but for the moment let us mention those which are arranged in the Gospel under the number seven. The first is humility; the second meekness; the third compunction of mind; the fourth desire for justice; the fifth mercy; the sixth purity of heart; the seventh eternal peace of mind.

Abraham had humility when he said: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Jacob likewise had humility when, speaking to the Lord, he said: “I am less than all your mercies” (Gen. 32). Blessed Mary too possessed this same virtue: when the angel called her Mother of God, she called herself the handmaid of the Lord (Luke 1).

David had meekness, saying: “I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you. You held my right hand, and by your will you led me” (Ps. 72 [73]). For *mansuetus* [“meek”] is so called as though accustomed to come to the hand or to be led by the hand, as domestic animals are. Such a person, like a beast of burden, is prepared not only for prosperity but also for adversity. Hence the same man says: “I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 37 [38]).

Third is compunction of mind. David also had this, as elsewhere he says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6). Fourth is desire for justice. He too had this, as he said in one place: “My feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was envious of the wicked when I saw the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72 [73]). And again: “In the morning I was putting to death all the sinners of the land, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all workers of iniquity” (Ps. 100 [101]).

Fifth is mercy. But because the matters said above concerning works of mercy pertain to it, we do not repeat them here. It shone outstandingly in blessed Job. Hence he says: “If I ate my morsel of bread alone, and the orphan did not eat from it,” and so forth (Job 31). Sixth is purity of heart, which the same holy man also possessed perfectly. Hence he said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I might not even think of a virgin” (Job 31). Seventh is eternal peace of mind. David possessed this, as it were, especially: “With those who hated peace I was peaceable” (Ps. 119 [120]). [Col. 0987B–D]

There is a very great deal that we could say concerning the ternary of faith, the fivefold number of the senses, the sixfold number of works, and the sevenfold number of virtues; but let us touch on each briefly, lest we burden you with too many words. Those, however, who think the teaching of faith alone sufficient are greatly mistaken. Elisha aptly rebukes them in a figure, when, speaking to the king of Israel, he says: “Strike the earth with the arrow.” When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God was angry with him, saying: “Had you struck it five, or six, or seven times, you would have struck Syria until its destruction. But now you shall strike it three times” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 13).

To strike the earth three times and stop is to instruct earthly hearts only concerning faith in the Holy Trinity and to add nothing concerning the holiness of good conduct. Therefore, dearest friends, let us—by speaking, you by hearing, and both by doing—strike the earth, that is, earthliness in ourselves, three times, by faithfully believing in the Holy Trinity. Let us strike it five times, by exercising strong governance over our senses. Let us strike it six times, by mercifully performing the six works mentioned above. Let us strike it seven times, by manfully exercising the seven virtues mentioned above. If we do this, we shall strike our spiritual enemies unto destruction, and shall possess peace in the world by grace and in heaven by glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord, God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI. On the Epiphany of the Lord

[Col. 0988B]

“The Magi offered the Lord gold, frankincense, and myrrh” (Matt. 2). Gold signifies the brightness of holy faith; frankincense, devout prayer; myrrh, the mortification of carnal affection. We offer gold when through faith we are inwardly illumined by divine wisdom. To show how great and magnificent the value of this offering is, we shall explain it in another’s words.

There are two certain things, and these two are in one, and one thing is these two: Creator and Saviour. They are two names, but one reality. Yet Creator signifies one thing, Saviour another. He is Creator because he made us; Redeemer and Saviour because he redeemed us. First we did not exist, and we were made; afterwards we had perished, and we were redeemed. Both were done by one, so that our whole good might be from one, wholly in one, and one. We owe the Creator that we exist; we owe the Saviour that we have been restored.

These, then, are the two things proposed to faith for belief: Creator and Saviour, together with the things that pertain to the Creator and those that pertain to the Saviour. The Creator and the things belonging to the Creator are one part of faith; the Saviour and the things belonging to the Saviour are the other. In the first part, faith distinguishes between the Creator and his works. In the second, faith distinguishes between the Saviour and his sacraments. The works of creation, which were made in six days, pertain to the Creator; the works of restoration, which are completed through six ages, pertain to the Saviour.

In the first part, faith requires confession that the Creator exists and that all things which have being were made by him. In the second, faith requires reverence for the one Saviour and belief that what had perished has been restored by him, for those to whom blessedness has been given or will be given. In the first part, right faith must distinguish Creator and creature in such a way that it gives to each what is its own and does not transfer the property of one to the other: it must neither attribute the Creator’s majesty to the creature nor ascribe the creature’s weakness to the Creator; neither confine God within time nor extend the creature through eternity. Thus faith, if it gives to each what is its own, offers rightly; if it distinguishes well between the two, it divides rightly and does not sin. But if it goes wrong in either matter, sound faith must necessarily suffer damage.

For those who, worshipping the creature as God, are deceived by a twofold error and believe either that the creature is eternal or that God is temporal—what else can they be said to have done except to attribute the excellence of the Maker to the work, and the weakness of the thing made, or creature, to the Creator? Again, the philosophers of the Gentiles, although they rightly distinguished between the Creator and his work, are by no means called faithful, because they did not have faith concerning the Saviour. [Col. 0988C–0989A]

There follow, then, the things which we set in the second part, where we first recognize redemption in the Saviour and preparation for that redemption in his sacraments. The first part of faith concerns the debt of nature; the second concerns the debt of grace. We ought to believe the former because we were created by nature; we ought to believe the latter because we were restored by grace. Let us offer, brothers, the sacraments and sound faith, because this pleases God beyond gold and topaz.

Frankincense signifies devout prayer. For as frankincense, burned by fire in a censer, rises upward in fragrant smoke, so devout prayer, kindled in the heart by the flame of love, reaches the ears of the Divinity with inward sweetness. The censer is the heart, the fire is love, and the frankincense is prayer. There are various kinds of this spiritual incense. For as many Christian souls as there are whose good, devout, or in any manner useful and fruitful affections are directed toward him, so many prayers may fittingly be said to be offered.

Sometimes we pray by fearing the punishment which we have deserved for our sins. Sometimes we pray by bewailing those sins. Sometimes by confessing them. Sometimes by placing very great confidence in pardon. Sometimes by humbling ourselves before the judge. Sometimes by seeking his goodwill. Sometimes by exalting his power. Sometimes by intensifying our prayers. Sometimes by calling down evils upon our enemies. Sometimes by making known our need. Sometimes by declaring our tribulation. Sometimes by accusing the malice of our enemies. Sometimes by urgently asking for divine help. Sometimes by giving alms.

We pray by fearing punishment when we say: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your wrath” (Ps. 6). We pray by bewailing it when, while praying, “we wash our bed every night and drench our bed with our tears” (ibid.). We pray by confessing it when, according to the same prophet, “we declare our iniquity and are anxious over our sin” (Ps. 27 [28]). We pray by placing good confidence in pardon, according to: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence; and hoping in the Lord, I shall not be weakened” (Ps. 25 [26]). And again: “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet confess him” (Ps. 42 [43]).

We pray by humbling ourselves before God, as in: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only speak the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8). And elsewhere: “I have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea, and I am not worthy to see the height of heaven because of the multitude of my iniquity” (2 Par. 37 [Prayer of Manasseh]). We pray by seeking his goodwill when, praising his mercy, we proclaim him gentle, kindly, and long-suffering, as in: “The Lord is merciful and compassionate, long-suffering and greatly merciful. He will not be angry for ever” (Ps. 102 [103]), and the rest which follows. We pray by exalting his power when we say: “Yours is the power, yours the kingdom, O Lord. Give peace, O Lord, in our days” (*Office of the Church*).

Sometimes we pray by magnifying our prayers before God, according to: “Hear, O Lord; be appeased, O Lord; attend and act.” We pray by calling down evils upon our enemies when we say: “Let those who malign my soul be confounded and fail” (Ps. 70 [71]). We pray merely by making known our need, according to: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11); and as blessed Mary, praying to the Lord at the wedding, said: “They have no wine” (John 2). We pray by declaring our tribulation whenever we say those words of David: “I pour out my prayer before him, and I declare my tribulation before him” (Ps. 161 [142]). We pray by accusing the malice of our enemies, as in: “Look upon my enemies, for they have multiplied, and they hate me with unjust hatred” (Ps. 24 [25]). We pray by urgently asking divine help when we say: “O God, attend to helping me; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Ps. 69 [70]). Finally, we pray by giving alms when we fulfil what is written: “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it itself shall pray to the Lord for you,” and so forth (Ecclus. 29). [Col. 0989B–0990C]

There are also many other ways in which we are accustomed to pray, which here, to avoid prolixity, we neither wish nor are able to describe. There is also another kind of incense, namely rustic incense, which in poorer churches is customarily burned around dead bodies, either for honour or to suppress their stench; it has a heavy and unpleasant smell. This fittingly signifies the prayer of sinners, concerning whom it is written: “God does not hear sinners” (John 9); and David says: “If I have regarded iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear” (Ps. 65 [66]). For prayer poured out to God must be clean if it is to be acceptable. But the prayer of those is clean who, cleansed from the filth of vices by true compunction and confession, can confidently say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6).

Myrrh, which is bitter, signifies the mortification of flesh and carnal affection. Its kinds too, as we set forth in another sermon, are various. One myrrh is that of sorrow; another, of fear; another, of compunction; another, of confession; another, of satisfaction; another also, of compassion. One is the myrrh of any virtue; another, of a good work; one is the myrrh of abstinence; another, of prelacy—or rather administration. For every prelate who presides with care is filled with the bitterness of manifold concern. Hence blessed Paul says of himself in one place: “Besides those things which are external, my daily pressure is concern for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). And in Job it is read that “the giants groan beneath the waters” (Job 26). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10). This disturbance, when God’s grace is at work, should be believed to have more merit than loss, since, according to Solomon, “by sadness of countenance the mind of the offender is corrected” (Eccl. 7).

Therefore the variety of spiritual incense and myrrh is as manifold as the usefulness of holy prayer and fruitful bitterness is diverse. So then, brothers, what the pagan Magi offered bodily, let us also offer spiritually, that through the grace of this offering we may deserve to attain glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord, God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen. [Col. 0990D–0991B]

## SERMON XXXVII. On sacrifices, holocausts, and offerings, and their differences

“My soul is always in my hands” (Ps. 118 [119]). Whatever precious thing we possess, whatever we love more, whatever we fear more to lose, we always or often have in our hands, or customarily keep before our hands. Yet there is nothing that ought to be dearer or more precious to a human being than his soul. “For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul? Or what exchange shall a man give for his soul?” (Matt. 16). Therefore “skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his soul” (Job 2).

Hence, dearest friends, the holy Psalmist said that he had his soul in his hands not often but always, as a holy offering worthy of being continually offered to God. He wished to guard it in every way and offer it to the Father upon Christ, who is our altar. Instructed by his example, we ought to hold our souls in our hands and always sacrifice and offer them to God.

In the Old Testament, *sacrifice* was the term used when an offering was made from animals; *offering* was the term for offerings of any other things. According to Old Testament custom, sacrifices have three kinds. Some are holocausts; others simple sacrifices; others peace offerings. A holocaust was that which, offered either by obligation or freely, was entirely burned. A simple sacrifice was that which, offered by the obligation of the ordinance, was partly burned and partly reserved. Peace offerings were those offered freely, whether in thanksgiving, for fulfilment of a previous vow, or from voluntary and spontaneous devotion.

A holocaust was sometimes made from cattle, sometimes from sheep and goats, sometimes from birds. An offering was sometimes made from fine flour, called an uncooked sacrifice; sometimes from an oven, sometimes from a frying-pan, sometimes from a griddle, and it was called a cooked sacrifice. Some sacrifices were for sin, others for offence. An offence is when what ought to be done is not done; a sin is when what ought not to be done is done.

For sacrifice or holocaust, sometimes a bull was offered, sometimes a heifer, sometimes a he-goat, sometimes a she-goat, sometimes a kid, sometimes a calf, sometimes a cow, sometimes an ox, sometimes a sheep, sometimes a lamb, sometimes a ram, sometimes a turtledove, sometimes a dove, sometimes a sparrow. An offering, however, was sometimes made from fine flour, sometimes oil, sometimes vinegar, sometimes wine, sometimes frankincense, sometimes incense, sometimes calamus, called aromatic. Hence the Lord says through Isaiah to the people of Israel: “You have not bought me calamus with your silver” (Isa. 43). [Col. 0991C–0992B]

Let us now see what these things signify, so that from their meanings we may understand in how many ways we can offer our souls to God. The bull signifies pride. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull” (Ecclus. 6). Therefore, whenever we humble and crush our pride, we sacrifice a bull to God. The heifer signifies lust. Hence, in the Book of Wisdom, it is said of the luxurious and impure: “The bastard offspring shall not put down deep roots, nor lay a stable foundation” (Wis. 4). Therefore, while we restrain our lust for God’s sake, we sacrifice to God as it were a calf.

The he-goat, she-goat, and kid customarily figure sins or repentance for sins. Some sins are mortal, others venial; some mortal sins are greater, others lesser. The greater are murder, incest, adultery, sacrilege; the lesser are theft and fornication; venial sins are laughter, slight and passing anger, and an occasional idle word. Thus we offer a he-goat when we repent of greater crimes; a she-goat when of lesser ones; a kid when of venial sins.

Thus in the calf, because of its tenderness, we understand the beginning of a good work; in the cow, because it has grown to greater strength, the perfection of that work; in the ox, because of its complete strength, the perfect and robust completion of a good work. In the sheep, because it is an innocent animal, we understand the innocence of good conduct; in the lamb, because at the beginning of its life it has a very clean fleece, purity of heart; in the ram, because it is leader of the flock, we receive a figure of the strong power of rational understanding, by which, with grace’s help, all our goods ought to be governed.

Therefore, brothers, let us sacrifice our souls to God: in the bull, by humbling our pride for his sake; in the heifer, by restraining our lust; in the he-goat, she-goat, and kid, by doing penance for our sins; in the calf, by beginning a good work; in the cow, by advancing in it; in the ox, by bringing it perfectly to completion.

We may also say that every victim signifies good conduct: the victim’s skin, the outward surface of that conduct; its head, the beginning; its tail, the end; its entrails, hidden virtue; the washing of the victim, the purity of an honourable life. We strip the skin from the victim and divide it limb by limb when, laying aside the outward appearance of our conduct, we carefully examine inwardly each of our works, with reason discerning according to place, time, manner, and intention, lest vice deceive us under the appearance of virtue, or guilt under the appearance of right action.

Sacrifices signify the imperfection of our good conduct; holocausts figure its perfection. Voluntary sacrifices or holocausts, of which it is written, “I shall sacrifice freely to you” (Ps. 53 [54]), signify either the devotion of a good will or the performance of a spontaneous work. And what we offer is, as it were, of the feminine gender when we are somewhat weak in some virtue; but we offer what is masculine when we act manfully, when our heart is strengthened, when boys grow faint and weary, and young men fall into weakness, but we hope in the Lord, take up wings like eagles, run and do not labour, walk and do not fail.

The turtledove is said not to seek a second mate after the first, and therefore ought to signify chastity. The dove too, which lacks gall and does not tear with its beak, signifies simplicity and concord. The sparrow, which nests upon the roof, figures heavenly contemplation. He had nested like a sparrow upon the roof who said: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Let us offer our souls, brothers, in the turtledove through chastity, in the dove through simplicity, in the sparrow through contemplation.

Fine flour, which was offered without leaven, signified simple teaching. Oil expresses mercy. For as oil rises above all liquids with which it is mixed, so a work of mercy surpasses the effects of all works. Hence, as we said elsewhere, setting other things aside, works of mercy alone will be recalled on the day of judgment. Vinegar and wine express a twofold compunction: one arising from sorrow for sins and fear of torments; the other arising from the reception of heavenly gifts and the foretaste of future goods. Vinegar signifies the first, wine the second. Frankincense, as we have often said, signifies prayer. But incense does not here mean the rustic incense mentioned above; rather, the sweet-smelling incense, because of its fragrance, signifies good repute. Hence Paul says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2). Finally, calamus, because songs are customarily made with a reed, signifies divine praise or thanksgiving. Let us offer our souls in these also: in fine flour through simple teaching; in oil through mercy; in vinegar or wine through compunction; in frankincense through prayer; in sweet incense through good repute; in calamus through the singing of divine praise and thanksgiving. [Col. 0992C–0993D]

It should be known, moreover, that when birds—namely turtledoves or doves—were offered, their heads were bent back toward the neck, and blood was poured out through the wound; the little pouch of the throat was removed, the feathers stripped away, and thus their flesh was burned. The bending back of the head signifies the humbling of the mind; the pouring out of blood, confession of sin; the removal of the pouch and stripping away of feathers, the removal of puffed-up pride and loose frivolity. Thus we must prepare our victim if we desire it to be pleasing to God.

Leaven and honey were not offered upon the altar of the Lord, and we too ought to avoid them spiritually. Leaven signifies heretical perversity; honey, worldly sweetness. Heresy corrupts faith; the sweetness of the world corrupts good action. Salt was offered with every offering. For thus it is written in Leviticus: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; you shall not take away the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice; in every offering you shall offer salt” (Lev. 2). Salt signifies wisdom. Therefore, whatever good we think, say, or do, we must do it all wisely. Hence in the psalm specially sung concerning the offering of divine praise, it is written: “Sing wisely” (Ps. 46 [47]). This salt is also commended in the Book of Wisdom, where it is said: “Though someone be perfect among the children of men, if your wisdom is absent from him, he shall be counted as nothing” (Wis. 9).

Therefore, because we cannot all do everything, and each has his own gift from God, and one walks in God’s way in one manner and another in another, let each of us abound in his own understanding. And as blessed Peter says: “Each one, as he has received grace, administering it to one another as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If anyone speaks, let him speak as the words of God; if anyone ministers, let him do so from the strength which God supplies, so that in all things God may be honoured” (1 Pet. 4).

Therefore he who does not have the ox of perfection should not stand before God without the calf of beginning; and he who does not abound in the fine flour of teaching should offer the oil of mercy. Let each excel outstandingly in the gift given to him as though individually, and in it live not for himself individually but also in common for others, so that through grace well administered in time we may deserve glory in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen. [Col. 0994A–C]

## SERMON XXXVIII. On Babylon—that is, worldly conduct—to be fled through the seven crimes

[Col. 0994D]

“Go out from Babylon; flee from the Chaldeans” (Isa. 48). That Babylon, glorious among kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, which of old was reduced to everlasting desolation because of the crimes of its citizens, signifies the present age by the interpretation of its name, by the cruel exaltation of its rulers, and by the perverse conduct of its inhabitants. This age is most rightly compared to wicked and impious Babylon, both on account of guilt, on account of punishment, and on account of both together.

For, according to the tropological sense, it has, like a city, its gates, its wall, its streets, and its lesser and greater buildings. The gate by which one enters is birth; the way through which one passes is mortality; [Col. 0995A] the gate by which one exits is death. Whatever miserable birth lays upon us, unhappy mortality carries wholly away with it; and whatever mortality carries away, insatiable death wholly devours. Its wall is the circumference of this world: we enter it by being born, but cannot leave it except by dying. Between the two gates—that is, birth, by which we enter, and death, by which we leave by the way, that is, mortality, through which we pass—we are continually occupied and tossed about, hour by hour and moment by moment, amid corruption and penal suffering, until, according to the judgment of the inward and eternal Judge, we come after merit to reward.

The streets of this spiritual Babylon are the seven principal vices. These streets are long and broad: [Col. 0995B] long through enduring habit, broad through unrestrained license. The first is pride; the second envy; the third anger; the fourth sloth; the fifth avarice; the sixth gluttony; the seventh lust. Pride has, on one side—or on one hand—the exaltation of the heart, and on the other the display of one’s works. Pride is inward; boastfulness outward. Pride consists in exaltation of heart, boastfulness in display of works. Pride is more hidden before God; boastfulness more manifest before one’s neighbour.

The devil first laid a stone for the construction of this street when he wished to set his throne in the north and be like the Most High (Isa. 14). He is the king of this Babylon; then and in this manner he began to build the city itself and its first street. In the second place, our first parents built this same street of the Babylonian city [Col. 0995C] when, by eating the forbidden fruit, they proudly sought the house of knowledge. On this street every proud person builds himself a house so much higher as he swells more arrogantly above others. The same must be understood of the other vices: those who were first in discovering and practising vices laboured first in building the streets of Babylon. And the more grievously each vicious person corrupts himself by any vice, the loftier a palace he prepares for himself in Babylon.

On this first street, which is pride, there are diverse furnishings and diverse ornaments; and things pertaining to praise are sought there more than things pertaining to pleasure. More is desired there that concerns worldly glory than what concerns the lust of the flesh. [Col. 0995D] Everything is arranged and adorned in imitation of a temple. There are purple and fine linen, wholly silken garments and Egyptian tapestries, ornaments for footwear, crescent-shaped ornaments, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, turbans, hair-ribbons, anklets, chains, scent-vessels, earrings, rings, gems, changes of clothing, cloaks, linen garments, pins, mirrors, fine linen cloths, and light shawls. Its inhabitants walk in pomp, with necks outstretched, clapping with signals of their eyes, proceeding with carefully composed steps. Its land is filled with horses, and its chariots are innumerable.

The second street of Babylon, which is envy, is constrained and pressed by the deepest poverty. [Col. 0996A] For even if its inhabitants sometimes possess goods, when they regard with envious eyes the pomp, riches, and glory which abound in the first neighbouring street, they imagine themselves utterly poor and as though deprived of all happiness, and groan and waste away inconsolably. Torments and pains shall seize its inhabitants, and they shall suffer as women in labour. On one side it has its own diminution; on the other, another’s increase. Between one’s own loss and another’s advancement—or indeed between one’s own disgrace and another’s glory—the whole world is tortured, as though through the middle of its street. The devil too is ruler on this street, because “through the envy of the devil death entered into the world” (Wis. 2). It has many citizens, but all are ruined: Cain, the scribes and Pharisees, [Col. 0996B] and the chief priests, whom Pilate knew had delivered Christ through envy.

The third street of the reprobate city is anger. On one hand it has mild and passing anger; on the other, hatred, that is, grave and continuous anger. Here you will see a splinter; there, a beam. Into this wretched street rush all the assaults of every storm. Here whirlwinds of dissension rage, crashes of threats resound, winds of contention roar, rains and hailstorms of persecution fall, lightning flashes from weapons, and thunder peals of blows and killings sound.

The fourth street of the accursed city is sloth. On one side it has sorrow; on the other, despair. It appears more terrible and more to be feared than the rest. For although it is serious to sin, it is more serious to fall irrationally into sorrow; but most serious of all is to hurl oneself through sorrow into despair. [Col. 0996C] On this street unhappy Cain first erected a house for himself when he said, “My iniquity is greater than that I should deserve pardon” (Gen. 4). Judas too, that most wicked trader, established a dwelling for himself on this same street when, despairing of pardon, he hanged himself with a noose. The Psalmist prayed to be delivered from its dwelling when he said: “Let not the storm of waters overwhelm me; let not the deep swallow me, nor the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. 68).

The fifth street is avarice. On one side desire establishes it; on the other, possessiveness. [Col. 0996D] Although it is filled with silver and gold and there is no end to its treasures, it cannot be satisfied, because the avaricious person—so far as the burning of his thirst is concerned—will not be filled with money (Eccles. 5). Rather, the more he acquires, the more he desires to possess. Hence the saying:

> Love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* XIV, v. 138.)

On this street the rich avaricious man buried in hell has a notable citadel (Luke 16).

The sixth street is gluttony. One part of it consists of voracity, the other drunkenness. The Lord prohibited us from dwelling on this street when he said: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by dissipation and drunkenness” (Luke 21). And the Apostle says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” (Rom. 15). [Col. 0997A] In the part called voracity are all kinds of breads made by the baker’s art, and dishes made by the cook’s art; various kinds of meat from four-footed animals and birds, marine and river fish, pepper, garlic, and cumin, for preparing flavours and seasonings. In the other part, which is drunkenness, are wines of differing colour, taste, strength, and smell, prepared with various herbs and spices, for those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening (Isa. 5).

The same prophet, whose words these are, elsewhere rebukes their shamelessness: “Through wine,” he says, “they have not known, and through drunkenness they have gone astray” (Isa. 28). “Priest and prophet have not known through drunkenness; they have been swallowed up by wine. They have gone astray in drunkenness; they have not known the seer; they have been ignorant of judgment. For all their tables are filled with vomit and filth, so that there is no place left” (Isa. 28). And elsewhere again, speaking in their person: “Come, let us take wine and be filled with drunkenness; and today shall be as yesterday, and much more abundant” (Isa. 56). If prophet, priest, and watchmen of the people were such—those whom the same prophet calls most shameless dogs, knowing no satiety—what, do you suppose, was the mixed and low-born multitude like? The Apostle Paul also, speaking of gluttons, says: “Many walk, of whom I often told you, but now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ; their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in [Col. 0997C] their shame, who savour earthly things” (Phil. 3).

The seventh street is lust. On one side it has impurity of thought; on the other, impurity of action. This is the last and lowest of all Babylon’s streets. Into it the impurities of the entire city seem to flow, and yet it cannot be sated by the river of its defilement. For, as sacred Scripture testifies, the mouth of the womb is insatiable (Prov. 30).

Many things, brethren, could be said about all these matters, which must now be omitted. For we are occupied almost the whole day with other affairs, and therefore do not have time to write as we would wish. What exceeds our capacity we leave for you to investigate and reserve for you to collect.

[Col. 0997D] And now, dearest brethren, let us shudder at and abhor the streets, and detest the dwellings, of Babylon—that is, all the crimes of secular life. Let us go out of Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans, and return to Jerusalem. Let us go out by abandoning our evils; let us flee by repenting; let us return by living well.

In turning away or descending from Jerusalem into Babylon, temptation comes first; delight second; consent third; action fourth; habit fifth; despair sixth. Through temptation we are moved; through delight we descend—or rather slip; through consent we enter Babylon’s gates; through action we build ourselves a dwelling; through habit we are brought into slavery; through despair we are thrust into prison and bound in chains.

[Col. 0998A] But in the return from Babylon to Jerusalem, first comes recognition of sin through divine inspiration; second, compunction of heart; third, confession by the mouth; fourth, satisfaction through penance; fifth, the exercise of virtue; sixth, the performance of a good work. Observe also that he says: “Let us flee from the Chaldeans.” For certain sins, especially those which become sweet to us, are conquered better by fleeing than by resisting. Thus the Apostle says concerning fornication: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. 6). The messenger who came to Eli likewise expresses this when he says: “I am he who came from the battle, and I am he who fled today from the line of battle” (1 Sam. 4). For it is better to flee and save one’s life than to perish in battle.

Let us go out, brethren, and flee. The road from Jerusalem to Babylon is short and easy; [Col. 0998B] but conversely—marvellous though it is to say—the road from Babylon to Jerusalem is great and difficult. We readily slip from good to evil, from virtue to vice, from spirit to flesh; but, weighed down by the body which corrupts and burdens the soul, we do not rise again from lower things to higher with equal ease. Hence the poetic saying:

> … Easy is the descent to Avernus;  
> But to retrace one’s steps and escape to the upper air—  
> This is the task, this is the labour.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, vv. 126, 128–129.)

Because spirit and flesh are neighbouring territories with a great common boundary, we slip easily and swiftly through fault; but because, after we have sinned, we are weighed down by the habit of sin, we are raised with difficulty through righteousness. Therefore this spiritual return is rightly said to involve a long, steep, and difficult ascent. [Col. 0998C] Hence the Saviour says: “Narrow and arduous is the way which leads to life” (Matt. 7).

If therefore we are on this path of return through repentance, or in Jerusalem itself through a good and perfect conscience, let us hold what we have, lest another receive our crown. If we stand, let us take heed lest we fall (1 Cor. 1), always on guard against the snares and attacks of our enemies, who led us away, took us captive, and questioned us concerning the songs of Zion (Ps. 136). According to Jeremiah’s statement, “They are swifter than the eagles of heaven; upon the mountains they pursue us; in the wilderness they lie in wait for us” (Lam. 4).

The eagles of heaven are made to signify prelates, who fly loftily toward heavenly goods and contemplate the rays of supernal brightness. Mountains signify the height of contemplation. The wilderness signifies the secrecy of spiritual life. Yet our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven, because cruel spirits strive much more keenly to pursue us than our prelates do to defend us. Even if we ascend to the heights of heavenly contemplation, or withdraw into the hidden recesses of intimate life, they never cease to pursue us or to lie in wait for us. [Col. 0998D] Therefore it is necessary, dearest brethren, that we proceed not only courageously but wisely. Against persecution we must be courageous; against snares, wise. If therefore we walk courageously and wisely, we shall escape our enemies, arrive in Zion in safety, and possess everlasting joy in Christ. [Col. 0999A] May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIX. On the holy city Jerusalem in the tropological sense

“Jerusalem, the holy city” (Rev. 21), and “the city of the Holy One” (Isa. 52). According to history, it is an earthly city; according to allegory, the holy Church; according to tropology, spiritual life; according to anagogy, the heavenly homeland. Leaving aside the other meanings, let us speak of that which concerns tropology, and let us endeavour to build good morals from its description.

Just as Babylon—that is, secular life—has its streets and the other things described above, so holy Jerusalem—that is, spiritual life—has a good ordering for its construction: namely, its wall, streets, buildings, and gates. [Col. 0999B] It has a wall externally all around, by which it is enclosed through the strict, continuous, and perfect discipline of good morals. It also has seven streets opposed to the seven streets of Babylon, through seven virtues opposed to the seven vices described above.

Thus holy and spiritual life has humility, opposed to pride; charity, opposed to envy; peace, opposed to anger; spiritual joy, opposed to sloth; generosity, opposed to avarice; [Col. 0999C] abstinence, opposed to gluttony; and continence, opposed to lust. It may perhaps be useful to describe the sides of these streets, whether those on one hand or those on the other.

The first street of the holy city, called humility, has on this side that humility which a person possesses and exhibits inwardly before God alone in secret; on that side, that humility which a person possesses and exhibits outwardly, for God’s sake, openly before his neighbour. The Lord shows the fruit of this virtue, or the good of this street, when he says: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14). The more anyone humbles himself for God’s sake in the present, the more exalted he shall be with God in the future.

[Col. 0999D] The second street is charity. On one side it has love of God, and on the other love of neighbour. On this side we are commanded to love God with all our heart, soul, strength, and memory; on that side we are commanded to love our neighbour as ourselves. The Lord himself makes known how great is the fruit and good of charity when he says that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon these two commandments (Matt. 22). Hence the Apostle says: “Love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13).

The third street of this spiritual Jerusalem is peace. One part consists inwardly in harmony with God; the other outwardly in harmony with one’s neighbour. The Lord commanded us to inhabit this peace on both sides and to have it between us when he said: “Have salt in yourselves [Col. 1000A] and have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9). Elsewhere he shows how great its fruit is when he says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5). Great is this fruit; great is this good. For if sons, then heirs: heirs indeed of God and fellow heirs with Christ (Rom. 8).

The fourth street is spiritual joy. One part consists in that exultation which is felt only within in the affection; the other in that which also appears outwardly in the senses. At times such great joy is infused into the soul from heaven that it is not only felt inwardly but also recognized outwardly, in expression, voice, gesture, and movement. Thus the Psalmist says: “My heart and my flesh have exulted in the living God” (Ps. 83). Hence sacred Scripture recounts that, when the people of God rejoiced and praised God, their voice was heard from afar. What wonder, indeed, if, when the father inwardly rejoices over the son who has returned to himself after transgression, the music of joy and the chorus are likewise heard together outside (Luke 15)?

Hence also, on solemn holy days, we are forbidden to grieve, Scripture testifying as follows: “The day is sanctified to the Lord your God. Do not mourn and do not weep. Go, eat rich foods, drink sweet wine, and send portions to those who have prepared nothing for themselves. For the day of the Lord is holy. Do not grieve” (2 Esdras 8). [Col. 1000B] For the joy of the Lord is our strength. Thus the Saviour says: “Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?” (Luke 5). That joy which believers possess or display in food or dress on holy solemn days is good for those who use it well, because it comes to them as God’s gift and is rendered by them to God’s honour.

Paul declares the usefulness and greatness of this virtue when, writing to the Corinthians concerning collections, he says: “Let each give as he has determined in his heart, not from sorrow or necessity; for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9).

The fifth street of the holy city is generosity. On one side it is constituted by just acquisition; on the other by prudent distribution. Just acquisition makes one side of it, because religious and honourable generosity disdains to live or give from wealth obtained by robbery, shameful gain, fraud, theft, or any other unjust means; it disdains to sacrifice praise from leavened material. [Col. 1000D] Prudent distribution builds the other side. For if it gave less than justice required, it would itself become avarice; if more than justice required, it would no longer be generosity but prodigality. The Saviour shows how great is the fruit of generosity in the Gospel: “Give, and it shall be given to you. They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6).

The sixth street of this Jerusalem is abstinence. On one side it has frugality; on the other sobriety. Frugality is opposed to voracity and sobriety to drunkenness. Many examples of fasting and abstinence are found in Scripture, of which the chief are the fasts of Moses, Elijah, and the Lord Saviour. How great is the fruit of fasting and abstinence is evident in the Ninevites, who by three days’ abstinence appeased [Col. 1001A] divine wrath and obtained pardon from the overthrow threatened against them (Jonah 3).

The seventh street of the holy city is continence, or chastity. On one side it has purity of heart; on the other purity of body. Or, on one side purity of thought; on the other purity of action. How great is the fruit and good of this virtue shines forth in widows and virgins, of whom widows possess a sixtyfold and virgins a hundredfold fruit.

We rightly call these virtues, dearest brethren, streets—that is, broad ways suitable for dwelling, spiritual walking and running, and every spiritual undertaking—because every way leading to life, although it seems narrow and arduous to beginners and even to those making progress, is found broad and level to those who have advanced [Col. 1001B] and become perfect. Hence the Psalmist says: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118). And again: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (ibid.).

For whoever has perfect charity, which casts out fear (1 John 4), finds sweet—indeed, regards as sweet—whatever temptations or adversities come to him, saying with the Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). Thus it is written in the Song of Songs concerning charity: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is hard as hell. Its lamps are lamps of fire and flame. Many waters cannot extinguish charity, neither shall floods overwhelm it. If a man gave all [Col. 1001C] the substance of his house for love, he would despise it as nothing” (Song 8). In this spiritual city there is also a most strong tower, of which it is written: “The name [Col. 1001D] of the Lord is a most strong tower; the righteous runs to it and shall be saved” (Prov. 18).

You know, dearest brethren, that persons defending a city place no such confidence in horses, arms, gates, walls, or even their own strength as in their city’s tower. For when they have been routed and driven back, the tower is their one refuge and sole protection. Likewise, for the faithful fighting against spiritual enemies, invocation of the divine name is the one hope and protection, not only in adversity but also in prosperity. For they know that whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved (Joel 2).

Therefore the holy universal Church has established that, when divine offices are begun, the name of the Lord should first be invoked, faithfully and confidently crying: “O God, incline unto my aid” (Ps. 69). This spiritual Jerusalem also has two gates: the first and lower is Catholic faith; the second and higher is divine contemplation. Of these two gates it is written: “He shall go in and go out and find pasture” (John 10). At the first gate he shall find the pastures of grace; at the second, the pastures of glory.

As may be understood from various passages of Scripture and statements of certain writers, earthly Jerusalem itself was situated, according to its ancient location, on a slope. Likewise, this city—spiritual life—is situated on a slope [Col. 1002A] and has its steps from gate to gate, by which one ascends from lower to higher things, so that those who go up the individual steps may be separated from earthly things and approach heavenly ones. Those who wish to live holy lives must first enter through faith, and then ascend through the growth of righteousness to contemplation of heavenly things.

Thus the first step at the first gate—or rather, the gate itself—is the first step or ladder of ascent. Raised from earthly things, we must first set our foot upon the first ladder, that is, faith. Second, from faith we must rise to hope. Third, from hope we must rise to charity. Fourth, from charity we must rise to the exercise of the other virtues, especially to the seven [Col. 1002B] principal virtues described in the Gospel, which sevenfold series begins where it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Fifth, we must rise from the seven principal virtues to the six good works, which begin where it is said: “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25). Sixth, we must rise from the six good works to preaching. For it is judged just and fitting that one who does good should speak of it to others, so as to imitate the Saviour, of whom it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1).

Preaching is sometimes fulfilled in two ways, namely by words and by miracles. Hence it is written of the first and greatest preachers: “They went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord cooperating and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark 16). [Col. 1002C] Seventh, we must rise from preaching to contemplation. Of these ladders or steps of ascent it is written: “The tribes went up there, the tribes of the Lord, the testimony of Israel, to confess the name of the Lord” (Ps. 121). And elsewhere: “Blessed is the man whose help is from you: he has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place which he has appointed” (Ps. 83).

Whoever has ascended through these steps to the gate of contemplation, which is situated at the summit and, as it were, at the exit of this city, shall spiritually go out of and surpass himself: Jacob shall become Israel, Leah Rachel, Phenenna [Peninnah] Anna, [Col. 1002D] and Martha Mary. The one who was a performer of good works shall become a contemplator of divinity. Hence Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone, because he shall raise himself above himself” (Lam. 3). Hence it is written in the Song of Songs: “Go out, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and in the joy of his heart” (Song 3). Hence the Psalmist says: “There is Benjamin, the young one, in ecstasy of mind” (Ps. 67).

Let us hasten, brethren, after the labours of action, to go out into the rest and freedom of contemplation, so that we may be able to behold the King in his beauty and our land, though still from afar. Let us ascend from strength to strength, as salvation requires, so that through the aforesaid sevenfold ascent [Col. 1003A] we may be able to reach the eightfold series of beatitudes. May he grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XL. On the guardians of Jerusalem, the holy city

“Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all day and all night, forever, they shall not be silent. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and give him no silence until he establish and make Jerusalem a praise in the earth” (Isa. 62).

Jerusalem, the holy city and city of the Holy One, is the holy Church. Its king, departing into a far country, set over it guardians and watchmen, that they might guard it day and night and defend it from evil. There are therefore diverse watch-posts and diverse watchmen—indeed, ranks of watchmen—who preside in diverse [Col. 1003B] places in the holy city, repel enemies, and guard citizens.

At the first watch-post sits the apostolic lord [the pope], who, as he presides over all, ought also to provide for all. At the second watch-post are the patriarchs; at the third, archbishops; at the fourth, bishops; at the fifth, archdeacons; at the sixth, archpriests, or, as they are called in certain places, deans; at the seventh, priests. And in all these ranks, whoever are higher in dignity are more obligated to guard the city.

The office of each is his watch-post. For example: the watch-post of priests is their priesthood; that of archpriests, their archpriesthood; that of archdeacons, their archdeaconry; and likewise with the others. Yet, brethren, according to the testimony of sacred speech, because the sins of the people demand it, a hypocrite sometimes ascends the watch-post of sacred rule; he oppresses the people rather than guarding them. [Col. 1003C] This is cause for deep sorrow and deep lamentation.

For what beauty or honour, dearest brethren, could be spoken of if a monkey climbed the pinnacle of God’s temple and sat upon it? Would not the whole city run together at so monstrous a sight, clapping their hands and laughing aloud? A monkey, so called, they say, because it has certain similarities to human form, is a small and hairy animal, without speech, agile, ugly, wanton, and fond of climbing the heights of mountains or buildings. Although it is a most vile, ugly, and horrible animal, secular people, deceived by their errors—who take pleasure in birds of the sky and beasts of the earth, and, alas, especially clerics—are accustomed to keep it in their houses and place it in their windows, so that before foolish passers-by they may boast, by its appearance, of the glory of their riches.

By this monstrous little beast the hypocritical watchman is most rightly represented. He is a monkey through simulation, small through contemptibility, hairy through excess, without voice through harmful silence, agile through fickleness, ugly through shameful conduct, wanton and lewd through lust, and seeking heights through pride. [Col. 1003D] He seeks heights through pride because, if he holds one dignity, he always longs for another—that is, a higher one. For example, if he sits in the priesthood, he desires the archpriesthood; if in the archpriesthood, [Col. 1004A] the archdeaconry; if in the archdeaconry, the episcopacy; if in the archiepiscopacy, the patriarchate, which dignity we also call the primacy; if he is in the patriarchate, he would rather possess the apostolic office.

But since among ecclesiastical dignities there is nothing higher than this office, here God has set a limit to the sea—that is, to human thought, surging and swelling—and here he breaks its swelling waves. For “the wicked are like a raging sea which cannot rest.” Concerning watchmen of this sort, the venerable and praiseworthy Bernard of Clairvaux writes in his book *On Consideration*:

> A monkey on a roof; a foolish king on a throne. A monstrous thing: the highest rank and the lowest spirit; the first seat and the basest life; a grandiloquent tongue and an idle hand; much speech and no fruit; [Col. 1004B] a grave countenance and a frivolous manner; vast authority and unstable stability.

Hence the Lord says through Hosea: “They have reigned, and not through me; they have become princes, and I did not know them” (Hos. 8). Hence he complains through Isaiah of such persons, saying: “Their watchmen are all blind; they all have no knowledge; mute dogs, unable to bark, seeing vain things, sleeping and loving dreams. And most imprudent dogs, they know no satiety. The shepherds themselves have not understood; all have turned aside into their own way, each to his own avarice, from the greatest to the least. Come, let us take wine and be filled with drunkenness; and today shall be as yesterday, and much more abundant” (Isa. 56).

Now, leaving aside those whom the Lord did not send but let go, let us turn to those who govern well [Col. 1004C] and consider what kind of persons they ought to be, and how they ought to preside or to benefit others. But how, brethren, shall we find a suitable watchman, when the Lord himself scarcely finds one, saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” (Isa. 6). And again in the Gospel: “Who, do you think, is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household?” (Luke 12).

Yet the Lord himself, speaking in the Apostle, teaches us through the Apostle what sort of watchman he ought to be: “A bishop,” he says, “must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, well ordered, chaste, hospitable, a teacher; not given to wine, not a striker, but gentle; not quarrelsome, not covetous; one who rules his own household well, having children subject with all [Col. 1004D] chastity. But if anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how shall he take care of the Church of God? Not a neophyte”—that is, a novice—“lest, lifted up by pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3).

But what he says, “the husband of one wife,” and what he says, “having children,” belonged to that time, not to this, and ought not to belong to this. If a watchman, whom we may call a shepherd or prelate, is vicious, however, he is by no means to be reproved by his subjects. Hence Isidore says:

> There are those who perversely judge their superiors when they see them more occupied with earthly pursuits, if they themselves have already learned even a little about spiritual matters.

Rulers, therefore, are to be judged by God, but are not to be accused by their subjects. The Lord provides the example, for he himself [Col. 1005A] overturned with his own scourge those selling doves and the tables of the money changers. Or likewise, as it is said: “God stood in the synagogue of gods, but in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81). But if a ruler departs from the faith, then he is to be rebuked by his subjects. For reprehensible morals, however, he should be endured by the people rather than sternly censured.

It should also be known that, just as he is not to be reproved by his subjects for reprehensible morals, so neither is he to be despised in matters which he teaches and commands well. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ chair. Observe what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23).

But now, dearest brethren, let us see what the guardians of earthly and worldly cities are accustomed to do in their watch, and then perhaps we shall see more clearly what the spiritual guardians of the holy Church [Col. 1005B] ought to do. The guardians and watchmen of cities, especially in times of war, are accustomed to sit in high places, keep watch, go around the whole city—especially at night—sound trumpets, blow pipes, play the cithara, and sing.

Yes, yes, most beloved, this is what the watchmen of our city ought to do. They ought to sit on high through spiritual conduct, so that their manner of life may be not on earth but in heaven, not in the flesh but in the spirit; so that their soul may not be humbled in the dust, nor their belly cling to the earth, but that those who proclaim good news to Zion may ascend the lofty mountain, and that the feet of those announcing peace, preaching salvation, and saying, “Zion, your God shall reign,” may be beautiful upon the mountains (Isa. LII). They ought to keep watch [Col. 1005C] through vigilance, turning their gaze to the right lest prosperity deceive them; to the left lest adversity break them; backward, through a useful remembrance of things past; forward, through foresight of things to come. They ought, while keeping watch, to look around lest the enemy arrive unexpectedly, break down the gates or burst through the wall, set houses on fire, overthrow towers, kill citizens, carry off spoils, destroy the city, and lead the people away into Babylon. They ought to make the circuit of the whole city—that is, of the people entrusted to them—and examine whether, through the displacement of any stone of virtue, the wall of discipline may have been weakened even a little; and, if they find this has happened, repair it as quickly as possible. He well fulfilled this who said: “Apart from the things that are outside, my daily pressure: concern for all the Churches” [Col. 1005D] (II Cor. II). They ought to sound trumpets through awe-inspiring preaching. Of trumpets, one is wooden, another earthen, another horn, another bronze. A wooden trumpet is easily burned when fire is applied; a horn trumpet is easily broken by a blow; a horn trumpet proceeds from flesh, yet surpasses flesh; a bronze trumpet is strong and does not readily yield to blows. Therefore the wooden trumpet fittingly signifies the preaching of those who are easily overcome by temptations; the earthen trumpet, the preaching of those broken by adversities; the horn trumpet, the preaching of those who overcome temptations; the bronze trumpet, the preaching of those who endure invincibly amid adversities. They ought to blow pipes through gentle consolation. For it is fitting that the soothing charm of consolation should follow the harshness and [Col. 1006A] severity of fear, so that the preceding harshness may be tempered by the sweetness that follows. Preachers are commanded to possess these pipes where it is written: “Say to the faint-hearted: Take courage” (Isa. XXXIII). They ought to play the lyre through good works. For the lyre, which is touched with the fingers in order to give forth sound, fittingly represents good works. This lyre has six strings: namely, the six works of mercy: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. XXV). They ought to sing through praise and thanksgiving. For they ought always to give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things.

Therefore holy watchmen ought to sit on high through spiritual conduct, to keep watch through vigilance, to make the circuit through solicitude, to sound trumpets [Col. 1006B] through preaching, to blow pipes through consolation, to play the lyre through good works, and to sing through thanksgiving. And they ought to do all these things by day and by night, that is, in prosperity and adversity. Thus Isaiah himself, whose words we have set before us, said of himself: “Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day, and at my post I stand throughout the nights.” Until, he says, he establishes and sets Jerusalem as praise upon the earth (Isa. XXI). First God sets the praise of the holy Church in the world through grace; afterward he sets for her praise in heaven through glory. But until he sets for her praise in heaven, her holy watchmen must keep watch on guard in the world. But because “unless the Lord guards the city, the watchman who guards [Col. 1006C] it watches in vain” (Ps. CVI), let us beseech the Lord to guard us himself as the pupil of his eye, so that through the grace bestowed on us in time we may be able to reign with him in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed, deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON XLI. On the Purification of Blessed Mary Ever-Virgin: on the purification of the mind.

“The Lord whom you seek shall come to his temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom you desire” (Mal. III). Brothers, “the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (I Cor. III). The Lord comes to this temple in diverse ways. He comes through contemplation of created things; he comes through reading the Scriptures; [Col. 1006D] he comes through the working of miracles; he comes through the preaching of his commandments; he comes through inward inspiration; he comes through adversity; he comes through prosperity; he comes by threatening evils; he comes by promising good things; he comes by taking evils away; he comes by conferring good things; he comes through knowledge of truth; he comes through love of virtue. He is indeed in his temple through grace, but he comes to that same temple through greater grace, in order to give grace for grace, so that “the righteous may yet do righteousness, and the holy may yet be sanctified.” For “to everyone who has, more shall be given, and he shall abound” (Luke XIX). But when, after receiving grace, we sin deliberately, the house is left to us—as the Lord himself says to the Jews—not now his house but ours, desolate [Col. 1007A] (Matt. XXIII). And, as he says through Jeremiah, “His inheritance becomes to him like a hyena’s den [like a lion in the forest]” (Jer. XII); and his house—which we were—which ought to be a house of prayer, because in our hearts we ought to worship and fear him, becomes “a den of thieves” (Matt. XXI), that is, a dwelling-place of demons, who through stealthy suggestions defile us and draw us toward unlawful pleasures. But when the Lord rises again to have mercy upon Zion, “for it is time to have mercy upon her, for the time has come” (Ps. CI), then he sends a vigorous servant of his household to prepare his way before him, so that, once the temple which had been defiled and profaned has been cleansed and sanctified, the Lord whom we seek, and the Angel of the covenant whom [Col. 1007B] we desire, may immediately come to it. Lord by power, Angel by grace: Lord in that he deigned to create us; Angel in that he deigned to redeem us.

Therefore, before all the servants and officers of the heavenly court, there is sent as it were the first guardian, stewardess, ruler, and cleanser of the Lord’s temple: consideration of sin, so that it may cleanse that temple of every defilement and, by cleansing it, fittingly adorn it as the bedchamber of the truly heavenly King. When consideration, or knowledge, of sin has entered, it sees nations entering the sanctuary of God—nations concerning whom he had commanded that they should not enter his Church. It sees the temple and all its vessels stained and wrapped about, defiled and profaned; its roof above, with beams, rafters, and ceilings, covered everywhere with cobwebs [Col. 1007C]—that is, it sees the mind, with its senses, affections, and powers, wholly veiled by the vanity of swelling pride. It sees the floor below—that is, the flesh—spread with the mud of lust; the middle walls—that is, words and actions—dunged and fouled from top to bottom with the filth of vices. There beasts rest; ostriches dwell; shaggy creatures dance there and answer one another. There are owls in its houses and Sirens in its shrines of pleasure (Isa. XIII). Thorns, nettles, and the paliurus have sprung up in its strongholds. And the house of the Lord has become a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches. Wild oxen descend with them, and bulls with the mighty. No one passes through it, because pelican, hedgehog, ibis, and raven dwell there. Demons [Col. 1007D] meet onocentaurs, and a shaggy creature cries to another. There the lamia lies down and finds rest for herself; there the hedgehog has its burrow, brings up its young, digs around, and broods in its shadow. There kites gather one to another. There is a raven on its threshold, and burdock and thistle upon its altars (Isa. XXXIV; Zeph. II).

By all this nothing other is meant than that a sinful Christian has been corrupted inwardly and outwardly, whether by the cruel promptings of demons or by the counsels of reprobate people, and has been made subject no longer to the Lord’s dwelling but rather to a demonic habitation. Considering this, knowledge or consideration of sin groans and wastes away, having no comforter and finding no consolation. Nor does it presume alone to undertake [Col. 1008A] the burden of so great a task, remembering Solomon’s words, where he says: “Two are better together than one, for they have the benefit of their companionship. If one falls, he will be supported by the other. Woe to one alone, because when he falls he has no one to lift him up. And if two sleep together, they will keep one another warm. How shall one alone become warm? And if someone prevails against one, two will resist him” (Eccl. IV). For all these reasons this first virtue, sent before the others, which we call consideration of sin, invokes God, ruler of all, asking him to deign to grant her aid for carrying out so great a service. There is therefore sent down from heaven to her a certain attendant, who, whenever such business is being rightly conducted, is accustomed always to accompany her: namely, consideration of punishment. She is commanded to hasten the work and speedily prepare [Col. 1008B] the house of the Lord for his coming. Entering the human heart from heaven, she sees the wages which the sinner has earned and which are now on the very point of being paid—for “the wages of sin is death,” and eternal death. She sees cruel torments, the heat of fires and the cold of snows, hunger and thirst, terrors and tormentors, darkness, worms, and whatever things are similar. Therefore, while consideration of sin on this side and consideration of punishment on that side apply themselves diligently everywhere to the tasks to be done, each according to her office, they wisely perceive that their strength alone is by no means sufficient for properly accomplishing this undertaking. Two vigorous and powerful attendants of the heavenly court are therefore sent to them—namely, sorrow and fear—accustomed not only to follow them but also to serve them in completing this labor. [Col. 1008C] Consideration of sin enjoins sorrow for past sin, while consideration of punishment enjoins fear of future torment. Recognizing that arduous labor lies before them, they take up poles and brooms and rage with such frenzy—if it is permissible to say so—within the walls that, unless the moderating and governing discretion of all things runs swiftly to them, they will not merely overturn the whole house in seeking what was lost, but rather destroy it so as to lose what still remained saved. For while they ought to effect the sinner’s amendment, he, unable to endure their onslaught, is sometimes almost hurled into despair. Therefore discretion is sent, and flying in more swiftly than speech, checks, moderates, directs, and governs the raging ones with the bridle of her restraint.

[Col. 1008D] While all these, therefore, labor together and assist one another in turn, all the filth of the Lord’s house that had arisen through thought, speech, or action is gathered into a single dung-heap in the middle of the heart, so that, with divine counsel and aid still to be received, it may somehow be dealt with. Then, as God renews ancient miracles, the rock of the heart is struck and waters flow in abundance. For sixth in order, signifying the perfection of the work, contrition is sent into the human heart. Rising from the depths of the heart, she lifts and dissolves by her force that detestable and dreadful mass; and, as the others lend a hand with all their strength, it is driven to the door [Col. 1009A] to be expelled. Finally, to show that the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit is present, seventh in order the gatekeeper is directed—that is, confession. When she comes and opens the mouth long mute and barred by the devil, that whole accursed heap is cast out. When this has been accomplished—that is, when vices and sins have been expelled—virtues and good works succeed by hereditary right. With all these the Lord’s house is adorned; cleansed and most becomingly furnished, it is made ready for his entrance. And immediately the Lord whom we seek comes to his holy temple, and the Angel of the covenant whom we desire. Thus the holy feast of the Purification is celebrated with such joy that there is joy in heaven not only among human beings but also among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke XV). Come then, most beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we may be without spot and wrinkle, and so that, through our good conduct and through the still better conduct of conversion, we may do in time those things in which we shall rejoice in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ages, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XLII. On the Purification of Blessed Mary: on the purification of the Church.

“He is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb. He shall sit refining and cleansing silver; and he shall purify the sons of Levi. He shall strain them like gold and like silver, [Col. 1009C] and they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness” (Mal. III). Our Savior, most beloved, coming to his temple—that is, visiting the holy Church through the dispensation of his incarnation—in order to present her to himself without the spot of lust and without the wrinkle of malice, cleansed her from every defilement of flesh and spirit through the grace of redemption and the effect of justification.
