This grace or effect is most clearly indicated, comprehended, and expressed here, where it is proclaimed through the Prophet: “He shall sit refining and cleansing the sons of Levi.” Where it is said, “He shall sit,” his diligent attention in saving us is shown. Where “refining” is added, the distress of our tribulation is shown; and where thereafter “he shall purify [Col. 1009D] the sons of Levi” is introduced, the effect of our justification is shown. “He is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb.” The Lord is like a fire consuming wood, hay, and straw, because he severely punishes grave sins. He is also like fullers’ herb because, by more lightly punishing lighter sins, he restores cleanliness to those who have been washed. “And he shall purify the sons of Levi, and strain them like gold and like silver.” By the sons of Levi the priestly dignity is understood. And if priests are to be strained and purified, what is to be said of the rest, when judgment begins at the house of God? “And he shall strain them.” After metal has been melted in a furnace, as we often see, it is conveyed and transferred, by whatever implement serves as a strainer, into an earthen mould—which in the vernacular may be called a *coclear* [ladle]—into which and through which it is to be poured and shaped by the craftsman into a vessel or any other implement; the strainer being interposed lest the coals pass through with it [Col. 1010A]. All this is perfectly fulfilled in this spiritual purification. For it is written of spiritual refining: “Tribulation produces patience, and patience proof” (Rom. V). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “In the world you shall have affliction” (John XVI). But straining pertains to what he says: “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII); and again: “Strive to enter through the narrow gate” (Luke XIII). For no slight constriction is experienced by one who hears on one side: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV); and on the other: “Whatever you wish to do” [reading uncertain; the text appears defective] (Tob. IV); and on the other: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII). He is led by the narrow way and strained through the tight aperture to whom it is forbidden even to think anything that gives pleasure unless it is according to [Col. 1010B] God. Concerning shaping or conforming, the Apostle says: “We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. III). Refined through tribulation and strained through strict discipline—which at present seems to be not of joy but of sorrow—we receive in ourselves the integrity and beauty of the divine image, which we had miserably corrupted in ourselves by living wickedly; and the dignity of our creation is transferred from a vessel of dishonor into a vessel of glory.

“He shall strain them,” he says, “like gold and like silver.” Whatever in gold—that is, in our understanding—and in silver—that is, in our speech—is mixed with bronze, tin, [Col. 1010C] lead, is cooked out in God’s furnace and strained through the strictness of discipline (Ps. XI), so that it may be “tested by fire, proved in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ezek. XXVII). Yet it happens, most beloved, quite often that those who are cast into the furnace of holy purification in order to be proved are not proved but reproved. Hence Isaiah says to the people of Israel: “Your silver has become dross” (Isa. I). Hence Ezekiel says: “Son of man, the house of Israel has become dross to me” (Ezek. XXII). “All these are bronze and tin and iron and lead; in the midst of the furnace they have become the dross of silver.” Hence the Lord says to Jeremiah: “I have given you as a strong tester among my people, and you shall know and test their way. All these are rebellious princes, walking deceitfully; [Col. 1010D] bronze and iron: they are all corrupt. The bellows have failed; the lead has been consumed in the fire; the refiner has refined in vain, for their evils have not been consumed. Call them reprobate silver, because the Lord has rejected them” (Jer. VI). Yet bronze, iron, tin, and lead can sometimes be understood in a good sense. Bronze, because it is resonant, aptly signifies the sound of preaching. Iron, because justice is customarily exercised through it, signifies the power of severity. Tin, although it is not silver, nevertheless, because from afar it seems by its color or sheen to bear a likeness to silver, can represent the imitation of any virtue or good work. For when someone sees the radiance of a virtue shining in another and cannot equal that person in the same [Col. 1011A] virtue, yet endeavors to imitate him as far as possible, he seems like tin: though far distant from silver in likeness, still adorned by some imitation of it. Lead, because it is heavy, signifies gravity. But in this passage all these may be taken not in a good but in an evil sense. Bronze, therefore, because of the melody of its ringing, can signify pleasing flattery. Iron, because cruel and unjust killings are often committed with it, represents cruelty. Lead, through its heaviness, denotes sloth. Tin expresses a pretence of virtue. Dross, which is the refuse of metal, signifies every kind of vice.

Brothers, let us not be bronze through flattery, nor iron [Col. 1011B] through cruelty, nor lead through sloth, nor tin through pretence; nor dross through any kind of vice. Let us fear with dread what is said: “The bellows have failed; the lead has been consumed in the fire; the refiner has refined in vain, for their evils have not been consumed. Call them reprobate silver, because the Lord has rejected them.” All these things are terribly to be feared by us. For we who are in religious life are especially in the refining furnace. The monastery is indeed our refinery, in which, like gold in a furnace, through weariness, silence, reading, meditation, prayer, fasts, vigils, and the rigor of discipline, we ought to be cleansed from our sins and proved. Our superior is the refiner, who labors continually to amend us. His word and example are the bellows [Col. 1011C]. Let us fear, most beloved, that his labor upon us may be frustrated, while, by remaining incorrigible, we despise amendment through him. Let us fear being called reprobate silver. Let us fear being rejected by the Lord. Hence it is said concerning the reprobate and proud person: “God gave him a place for repentance, and he abuses it for pride” (Job XXIV). Let us therefore fear to be proud in a place of humility, because “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X). Let us set before the eyes of our mind the words of today’s prophetic reading contained above, where it is said of the Lord: “Who can contemplate the day of his coming? And who shall stand to see him? For he is like a refining fire and like fullers’ herb” (Mal. III). For he who comes and refines and purifies his elect through [Col. 1011D] mercy in time will, at the end of time, come and refine those less purified through judgment. Hence it is written: “I shall sing to you, Lord, of mercy and judgment” (Ps. C): mercy now, judgment then. For imperfect elect persons, less purified before judgment, will be perfectly purified in the judgment. Hence the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid” (I Cor. III). But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold and silver and precious stones—that is, thinks only of the things that are God’s, as the perfect do—or wood, hay, and straw, while divided in mind he thinks of the things of the world, which he cannot surrender without pain, as the imperfect do, each one’s work [Col. 1012A] will be made manifest. When? On the day of judgment. For the day of the Lord—that is, the day of judgment—will reveal it, because it will be revealed in fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work remains—understand, intact—he shall receive the reward of perfection. If anyone’s work burns, in that namely he thought partly of worldly things, he shall suffer loss: both the loss of imperfection and the loss caused by burning. Yet he himself shall be saved, but only as through fire (I Cor. III). Let us strive, most beloved, and labor according to our strength to be perfectly corrected now by the Lord through mercy, lest the coming Judge, who will judge the world through fire, find something that must be burned by his judicial sentence—through which even certain elect persons must pass and be purified and strained—but so that, for perfect merit, we may then deserve to be crowned by him with a perfect reward. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XLIII. On Septuagesima, or another time of penance: on planting nurseries of virtues within us and casting out the roots of vices, using the parable of the delights of paradise.

“The Lord God took the man whom he had formed and placed him in the paradise of delight” (Gen. II). Speaking tropologically, that is, morally, most beloved, we say that a human being is formed by God when he is justified, and is placed in paradise when he is established in the secure delight, or delightful security, of a good conscience. For what do we understand more fittingly by a paradise full of delight than the human mind [Col. 1012C] full of security through confidence in a good conscience? For a secure mind is like a continual feast (Prov. XV). Therefore nothing is more rightly understood by that earthly glory of paradise than the good conscience of a righteous person. Of this the Apostle also says: “Our glory is the testimony of our conscience” (II Cor. I). What could I also say is more fittingly represented by that supreme rest than tranquility of mind and inward peace? Of this peace Baruch says to a people not walking in God’s way but wandering in the trackless way of the devil: “If you had walked in the way of God, you would certainly have dwelt in peace upon the earth” (Bar. III). For if our first parents had kept the Creator’s command in paradise, they would have rested forever in his peaceful dwelling. So also now, whoever keep God’s commandments with a perfect heart rest, with fear of evils removed, in the security of inward peace. Not only, however, does earthly paradise, by its delight, security, peace, and glory, signify the spiritual goods of our good conscience; its spring and the outflow of its rivers, its multitude of swimming, walking, and high-flying, sweet-singing creatures, the abundant fruitfulness of its diverse trees, and the beauty of all its blooming flowers fittingly signify them as well. The spring of paradise in us signifies spiritual grace; the four rivers, the exercise of the four principal virtues; swimming creatures, because fish labor in swimming while tossed about by waves here and there in the waters, the laborious performance of good works; walking creatures, [Col. 1013A] the growth and perfection of our righteousness; flying creatures, divine contemplation through flight, and praise and thanksgiving through song. Trees, too, through their abundant fruitfulness, and flowers through their varied beauty, represent in us the useful beauty and reputation of virtues. The olive tree signifies mercy, as may be understood from diverse pages of sacred Scripture. *Olea* is the name of the tree itself, whose fruit is called *oliva*. Hence the couplet of a certain versifier:

> *Olea* is the name of the tree; *oliva* [olive] is the name of its fruit.
>
> Hence *oleum* [oil], the expressed liquid; *amurca*, its dregs.

The vine signifies wisdom. For Christ, who is the wisdom of God, said: “I am the true vine” (John XV). Wine also, taken moderately, sharpens the intellect. The fig tree, because of the sweetness and pleasantness of its fruit, signifies inward sweetness and pleasantness. Of this it is written: “O how good and sweet, Lord, is your spirit in all things” (Wis. XII). And Wisdom says: “My spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ecclus. XXIV). And the Psalmist, concerning pleasantness: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your pleasantness” (Ps. XLIV); and concerning sweetness: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey to my mouth” (Ps. CXVIII). The tree of the knowledge of good and evil represents obedience. For in obedience, if we keep it, we experience good; if we transgress it, evil. The tree of life, however, is charity. For the tree of life would always have preserved human life sound, whole, and immortal if the human being had been able always to eat of it [Col. 1013C]. Hence also, after Adam sinned, it is written concerning him: “Lest perhaps he put forth his hand and take also from the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.” “The Lord God sent him out from the paradise of delight” (Gen. III). Therefore, just as the tree of life, as stated above, would have kept the human body immortal, so charity, while it is possessed, keeps the human spirit immune from the death of sin. A palm branch was customarily carried in the hands of victors and therefore signifies victory. Any tree, moreover, fragrant with its aromas signifies good repute. Likewise, the rose through its redness signifies suffering or compassion; the lily, through its whiteness, chastity; the violet, through the bending down of its small flower and head toward the ground, represents humility. Do not be surprised [Col. 1013D] if the trees mentioned above, or indeed any animals or birds, are said to have existed in earthly paradise. For of the trees it is written: “The Lord God had planted from the beginning a paradise of delight, in which he placed the man whom he had formed. And the Lord God brought forth from the ground—namely, of paradise—every tree beautiful to look upon and sweet to eat, also the tree of life in the middle of paradise, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. II). Where every tree beautiful to look upon and sweet to eat is said to have been in paradise, no tree seems to have been absent. And concerning animals and birds, after the Lord had placed Adam in paradise, it is written: “The Lord God, having formed all animals of the earth and birds of heaven, brought them to Adam, to see what he would call [Col. 1014A] them” (ibid.). For it does not seem credible that Adam would have had to seek them far away outside paradise if he wished to make use of their service, but rather that he would have received them from nearby. Thus the mind of the righteous is known to be interwoven, filled, and crowned with the mystical riches and delights described above. Very unlike it is the mind of the wicked, without conscience. For, as Paul says, “Their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus I). Hence Solomon says: “I passed by the field of a sluggard and by the vineyard of a foolish man; and behold, nettles had filled it all, thorns had covered its surface, and its stone wall had been destroyed” (Prov. XXIV). It is as though he said: I considered the life and mind of a negligent person, which nettles and thorns fill, because in the negligent heart itching earthly desires and the pricks of vices spring up, and it has lost the fortifications of virtues. Yet not only nettles and thorns, which are here specifically named and described, arise in the sluggard’s field and the fool’s vineyard, but many useless shrubs and harmful herbs as well: namely, caltrops, brambles, blackberry bushes, burrs, hemlock, and many similar things. Caltrops, therefore, because they have less hard thorns and do not greatly wound in hurting, rightly signify the affliction of any evil bitterness. Thorns, which have harder pricks and sting more sharply, fittingly represent a graver rancor of the heart. Brambles, too, because they wound by tearing, aptly signify the aggravation and rending of quarrels and contentions. Blackberry bushes also, which have most hard thorns and wound and draw blood most severely, express the monstrosity of cruelty. The nettle, because it often burns the fingers of one touching it, [Col. 1014C] signifies lust. The burr, because when it attaches itself to clothes or hair it clings tenaciously to them, represents tenacity. Finally, hemlock, because it is hollow and empty inside and foul-smelling outside, expresses empty glory and bad repute. By the nettles and thorns, however, which Solomon above alone named expressly, all vices of flesh and heart are signified. For lust, represented by nettles, can signify all vices of the flesh; rancor, understood by thorns, all vices of the heart.

Let there not be, most beloved, in the garden of our delights—let there not be, I say—caltrops through any, even the slightest, affliction of evil bitterness; no thorns through rancor; no brambles through exasperation; [Col. 1014D] no blackberry bushes, which some also call scorpions, through cruelty. Let there be no nettles through lust; no burrs through tenacity; no hemlock through foul repute; nor, finally, any useless shrub or harmful herb through any kind of vice. Rather, let there be in our paradise an olive tree through mercy; a vine through wisdom; a fig tree through inward sweetness; the tree of knowledge of good and evil through obedience; the tree of life through brotherly charity; a palm through victory; and every aromatic tree through good repute. Let there be in it a rose through suffering, or at least compassion; a lily through chastity; a violet through humility; finally, every good tree and most beautiful flower through the fruitfulness, beauty, and reputation of every virtue. [Col. 1015A] Let us cultivate this paradise, most beloved, with all our strength; let us guard it with every diligence. Let us cultivate it through action and guard it through vigilance, because it is written: “That he might work it and guard it” (Gen. II). For we must fear lest the serpent come, offer the fruit, deceive Eve within us, corrupt Adam, and cause us to be cast out of paradise. Hence the Apostle says: “I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted and fall away from the simplicity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI). The serpent is the devil; Eve, the flesh; the fruit, pleasure in earthly things. Just as the serpent deceived Eve with the fruit, so the devil entices and seduces the unreasoning flesh through earthly pleasure. And just as Eve induced Adam to eat the fruit, so sometimes the flesh draws the spirit into consent [Col. 1015B] to sin; and so both are cast out from paradise—that is, from the state of their good—because the spirit is afflicted through an evil conscience and the flesh is punished through penalty. Therefore, most beloved, let us not only cultivate our mind and conscience, but also guard them. For the tempter will not be lacking, nor will temptation be lacking. Let us therefore work and keep watch in time, so that we may glory in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ages, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV. In the middle of Lent: on Jerusalem, understood allegorically as the holy Church.

Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her. (At the Introit.) Jerusalem, beloved, is a holy city, and the city of the Holy One is the holy Church, which is the bride of God, as Holy Scripture testifies, saying in the Apocalypse, with the angel speaking to Saint John: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.” And he carried me away in the spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city Jerusalem descending from heaven from God, having the glory of God (Rev. 21). And the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself for her, in order that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word of life, in order that he might present her to himself as a glorious Church, having neither spot nor wrinkle nor anything of the sort, but that she might be holy and without blemish. So husbands also ought to love their wives as their own bodies” (Eph. 5). And a little later: “This is a great mystery” [Col. 1015D]. “But I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (ibid.).

The holy Church is rightly said to descend from heaven, because every good gift and every perfect gift by which her bridegroom, Christ, sanctifying her, makes her righteous, cleansing her from every spot and wrinkle, comes down from above, from the Father of lights (James 1). She is also said to possess the glory of God, because the glory which her bridegroom possesses by nature he grants her by grace—not in its fullness, but by participation in that fullness. The holy Church herself is partly in heaven, partly in the world: there as in her homeland, here as in exile; there reigning, here a pilgrim. The wedding is celebrated in both places: here in faith, there in contemplation; here in hope, there in reality. For now we see [Col. 1016A] through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now we know in part; then we shall know as we are known. For when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be abolished (1 Cor. 13).

Here, at the wedding, the wine of grace is served; there the wine of glory is served: the wine of grace for justification, the wine of glory for blessedness. And although we distinguish the holy Church according to these differing states—namely, faith and sight, hope and reality, justification and blessedness, grace and glory—so that she is daughter in exile and mother in the kingdom, as it is written: “But that Jerusalem which is above, free indeed from temptations, tribulations, and mortality, is the mother of us all” (Gal. 6); although, I say, we distinguish her thus, nevertheless she is one wife of the Lamb, the bride [Col. 1016B] of Christ, as it is written: “My dove, my perfect one, is one” (Song 6). One in predestination, not yet one in glorification; a dove by the purity of simplicity, perfect by the completion of virtue.

Therefore these words which we placed at the beginning—“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and assemble, all you who love her”—words of consolation, seem not to be addressed to her who above, in the kingdom, already glories with the bridegroom, but to her who still journeys far from his vision amid the misery of this present age.

“Rejoice, Jerusalem.” It is as though consolation were spoken to the pilgrim: Jerusalem, you who still journey in the world, are wearied by temptations, tested by adversities, exercised by persecutions, oppressed by mortality: rejoice amid adversities, as knowing that, although [Col. 1016C] “the outward person is perishing, yet the inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4). For this present, momentary and light affliction works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high, while we look not at what is seen but at what is unseen (ibid.). Rejoice, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8). Rejoice, therefore, for the days in which you are humbled and the years in which you see evils, because the graver the conflict, the greater the crown.

“And assemble, all you who love her.” Brethren, whenever an assembly is formed for a good purpose and in a good manner, it is material for exultation, an occasion of joy, and an incentive to gladness—especially in this place and undertaking, where children are urged to assemble [Col. 1016D] and rejoice with their mother: the mother, I say, who gave them birth in baptism and nourished them with the sweet milk, as it were, of her breasts—the teaching of the divine covenants.

But where an assembly is made in order to perpetrate evil, it often becomes the cause and result of many evils. Paul says of such an assembly: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes beforehand his own supper to eat; and one is hungry while another is drunk” (1 Cor. 11; the source’s “II” is evidently an error). And a little later: “Do I praise you in this? I do not praise you” (ibid.). Hence the Lord says through the Psalmist concerning those who assemble wickedly: “I will not gather their assemblies of blood” (Ps. 15 [Vulgate numbering]).

It belongs to the wicked to separate themselves from the assembly of the righteous and make of themselves [Col. 1017A] a little faction, or little factions: so that, gathered two or three together, they study nothing but to gnaw at the lives of the absent with their words, or to devise some evil against others, or even to their own destruction. Such factions are made in many ways—or rather, these factions are of many kinds. Some are factions of vanity, such as gatherings of players; others, of talkativeness, such as those who utter idle, superfluous, jesting, and obscene words. There are also factions of detraction, of contention, of sedition, of feasting and drinking, of lust and shamefulness, and finally of every kind of wickedness.

Therefore, most beloved, let us by no means form factions as the wicked do; for if we make assemblies of blood—that is, for perpetrating sins—we are not gathered by the Lord, as you have heard [Col. 1017B]. Rather, let us make an assembly, so that, according to the Apostle, we may consider one another for the provocation of charity and good works, “not forsaking our gathering together, as is the custom of some” (Heb. 10). Let us make an assembly, that we may all be together in one faith, one love, one exercise of virtues, one performance of good works.

But since assemblies of this kind are in some measure required generally of all Christians, including laypeople and married persons, let us who belong to a religious congregation make our assembly more diligently and more particularly, so that we may surpass their merit—as is just—and receive a more excellent reward from the Lord.

There are, therefore, six places in which we ought to make and maintain [Col. 1017C] an assembly: namely, the refectory, work, the cloister, the choir, the dormitory, and the chapter house.

When we assemble in the refectory, we gain a double fruit, because there both body and spirit are refreshed: the body by food, the spirit by the divine word. In work we gain a threefold fruit. There we have the fruit of honourable occupation, the fruit of exercise, and the fruit of usefulness. We have the fruit of occupation because, while we attend to labour, we wander toward no useless things; there too we receive the fruit of exercise, by which we become healthier. We have the fruit of usefulness because “our labour is not in vain in the Lord.”

In the cloister we receive the fruit of peace and silence. Of this it is written: “The work of righteousness shall be peace, and the cultivation of righteousness silence, and security for ever; and my people shall sit in the beauty of peace, in tabernacles of confidence, and in abundant repose” (Isa. 32) [Col. 1017D]. We also have in the cloister the fruit of reading and meditation, the fruit of devotion and prayer, the fruit of contemplation and compunction. There we are instructed by the precepts of our elders, formed by their examples, and stirred by their admonitions.

In the choir, through the recitation of lessons, we have the fruit of instruction. In psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, we have the fruit of divine praise. Indeed, by the fruit of divine praise we are joined in fellowship with the angels, while we perform on earth the office which they fulfil in heaven; and through them and us together is fulfilled what is written: “His praise is above heaven and earth” (Ps. 148).

In the dormitory we receive the fruit of bodily rest [Col. 1018A]. There are also those who receive there not only rest for the body, but a taste of spiritual good. For sometimes, while sleeping there, their mind perceives an inward sweetness which it cannot perceive while awake. Some also receive other fruits and benefit there while awake—keeping vigil, praying, weeping for their sins—and in them is fulfilled that saying of David: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 6).

Finally, we assemble in chapter in order to correct our negligences and transgressions.

Therefore all who wish to submit to correction and amendment ought to attend chapter. Yet there are certain religious who are like fattened, wanton breeding-stallions [Col. 1018B], unable to endure the hand of the stableman who wipes away their dung and tends them; they cannot bear even a mild rebuke for the smallest matters. Instead, like untamable horses, they rage with utterly unbridled madness against the masters who ought to chastise and correct them, or cleanse them from sins. Seized by the furies of impatience, they rail against them with the biting threats and insults.

What the holy prelate, who is the Lord’s stableman, should do concerning such people, the Psalmist declares where he says: “Constrain their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31 [Vulgate numbering]). By the bit and bridle are signified the lesser and greater commandments of God. Therefore those who do not reasonably and voluntarily submit to reasonable chastisements must be constrained more tightly by the authorities of divine commandments, like horse and mule with bit and bridle. For, as the Apostle says, “All Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting, for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3) [Col. 1018C].

Some horses, however, are of such wildness and impatience that, while they are being shod or treated, they can in no way be held by bit or bridle. A *broie*—that is, an iron implement—is placed on the lip of horses of this kind, in order that they may be kept quiet by its restraint. This is fittingly done in a figurative sense in the case of certain persons: because of their excessive insolence, their food or drink is reduced, or continual silence is imposed on them. For the obstinacy of the proud must be struck by a severe sentence, lest, “if we show mercy to the wicked, he should not learn to do justice, and, acting wickedly in the land of the saints, should not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26); unless rather he be “delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Cor. 5)—that is, to a most severe sentence, hostile and contrary to him in his fleshly disposition—so that, even by affliction alone giving understanding to his hearing, his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (ibid.) [Col. 1018D].

If he refuses to bear that sentence, even if he has not departed, let him be cast out of the community. This is done not cruelly but mercifully, lest he destroy very many by a pestilential contagion. Nor do we say these things, brethren, in order to deny that the weakness of the less perfect must be borne; but in the house of God judgment and justice must be exercised in such a way that the pride of the insolent is not tolerated without limit, nor the weakness of the imperfect unduly weighed down.

There are others, by God’s grace, in religion like work-horses or burden-bearing, industrious asses [Col. 1019A]. Rebuked by others, or even voluntarily prostrating themselves, they freely ask pardon for their negligences and humbly and patiently correct them. There are others in God’s house, enriched with heavenly grace, who, even when rebuked unjustly, gladly prostrate themselves and silently bear injuries for Christ. To those who freely amend their faults, as well as to those who patiently bear injuries, that saying of the Psalmist applies: “But I am ready for scourges” (Ps. 37 [Vulgate numbering]); and elsewhere: “I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you. You have held my right hand and led me according to your will” (Ps. 72 [Vulgate numbering]).

Yet only those who, unjustly scourged, silently bear injuries acquire glory before God. Hence Peter says: “This is grace, if on account of the consciousness of God someone endures sorrows, suffering unjustly. For what grace is it if, when you sin and are struck, you endure it? But if, when doing good, you patiently endure, this is grace before God. For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten. But he gave himself over to the one judging unjustly” [Col. 1019B] (1 Pet. 2).

The first, therefore, so long as they persist uncorrected, hang upon the cross of the blaspheming thief; the second, while they are corrected, upon the cross of the thief asking pardon; the third, who suffer for God alone, upon the cross of Christ suffering innocently. To the first, if they refuse correction, fault is imputed on account of pride; to the second, pardon is granted on account of humility; to the third, grace is increased on account of innocence.

Therefore, most beloved, let us assemble in chapter so that we may correct our faults—indeed, that we may receive injury. Let us avoid factions; let us make an assembly. Let us make an assembly so that we may be of one mind in faith, charity, and action: believing rightly, loving sincerely, living holily. Let us assemble in the refectory, eating together; in work, carrying out together what pertains to it; in the cloister, sitting together; in the choir, singing together; in the dormitory, resting together; in chapter [Col. 1019C–D], correcting our faults. Let us assemble in time, so that we may deserve to be joined in eternity to the heavenly assembly of the blessed. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XLV. On the wine-cellar, allegorically understood as the Church

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered charity within me” (Song 2). The wine-cellar, most beloved, is for us the holy Church; individual faithful souls are individual casks.

A cellar seems to be so called from hiding (*celando*). For in it things necessary or useful are hidden from the eyes and reach of outsiders or thieves. The holy Church is therefore rightly called a cellar, because in her and through her the divine mystery and heavenly sacrament are concealed from the unclean multitude, as it is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not scatter pearls before swine” [Col. 1020A] (Matt. 7).

A cask (*dolium*), too, is rightly named from hewing (*dolando*). Thus any faithful soul is fittingly called a cask, since it is prepared and fitted, through the hewings of temptations and persecutions, to contain the liquid of heavenly grace. The staves or boards from which the cask is constructed fittingly signify the virtues given to us by nature; and the hoops added over them, by which the boards are bound together, aptly signify the virtues given to us by grace. For just as those boards do not hold wine unless they are bound by hoops, so natural virtues cannot contain heavenly gifts unless they are aided by virtues added to us through grace.

The two heads, front and back, also signify sensibility and rationality. The front head, since it faces the light and is exposed, signifies sensibility; the back head, which customarily faces the wall and is hidden, signifies rationality, which is concealed and hidden [Col. 1020B]. Further, the upper opening through which wine is poured in is fittingly understood as the mind’s understanding; the wine drawn out is grace. Finally, the spigot—that is, the opening through which wine is drawn out to be distributed and served—is eloquence or good action. And just as some casks contain harsh and austere wines, while others contain sweet and pleasant wines, so some faithful and holy souls are more severe and strong in word and deed, while others are gentler and more yielding.

Indeed, four things may especially be discerned in wine: taste, scent, beauty or colour, and vigour. Thus the taste of the spiritual wine of which we speak is perceived and known in teaching; its scent in reputation; its beauty in the attractiveness of a good example; its vigour in the firmness of right judgment.

Taste pertains to what the Psalmist says: “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118 [Vulgate numbering]). Scent pertains to Paul’s statement: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2). Beauty pertains to what he says elsewhere: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near; let us walk honourably as in the day” (Rom. 13) [Col. 1020C]. Vigour pertains to the Psalmist’s song: “I have done judgment and justice; do not hand me over to those who slander me” (Ps. 118 [Vulgate numbering]).

Wine, moreover, is sometimes the better and more readily acceptable the stronger it is. So too, the stronger holy men are in goodness, the more biting they become toward sinners. Wine, then, is good, but vinegar is more precious: the gentleness of meekness is good, but the vigour of severity is sometimes more salutary. Hence Wisdom says: “Those who rebuke shall be praised” (Prov. 24). Elsewhere: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep” (Eccl. 12).

Hence too, after the Spirit of God lifted the prophet on high, he went away “beloved” (*amatus*, sic) in the inquiry of his spirit: for the more highly someone is raised by God’s Spirit, the more he is angered against sinners. Hence, finally, vessels of vinegar are described as having been in the tabernacle of the Lord (Exod. 34), because rebuke is necessary in every way on account of sinners [Col. 1020D–1021A]. If rebuke is withdrawn, the moth of sin gradually corrupts and destroys the whole body of goodness.

But by new wine, which ferments in the cask until it is made ready and purified, what can more rightly be understood than the grace or life of neophytes and penitents? They are agitated by the heats of diverse thoughts and affections until, their conscience purified, brightened, and pacified, they rest. For although heavenly grace is divinely poured sweetly into the cask of the human mind like sweet wine, and is gratefully and joyfully received by that mind, nevertheless the grace received wondrously burdens the mind itself: either by making it bitter through the remembrance of sins, or by goading, pressing, and urging it to make satisfaction and live well. Thus we read of blessed John that the book which he received from heaven to eat was sweet as honey in his mouth, but made his belly bitter (Rev. 10). For, as Solomon says: “In much wisdom is much indignation; and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1) [Col. 1021B].

The anguish and fervour of a soul repenting and striving with all its strength toward amendment are therefore rightly signified by the fermenting heat of bubbling new wine. But by iron-bound casks or vessels, what do we understand more fittingly than the life or mode of living of those who, after conversion, are committed to the bonds of cloistered discipline, so that, restrained by its strictness, they may become stronger thereafter in virtue and deed? Shut up there, they are constrained like new wine without a vent, because they are not permitted to go out, even for a little while, toward things which may please according to the flesh. For what opening for air can one have to whom even the thought of worldly things is forbidden?

Some of these—as must be said with grief—because their sins demand it, break their bonds and pour out the wine: through their impatience they lose grace. Hence the Lord fittingly said through the prophet to the Jewish people: “You have shaken off the yoke, broken the bonds, and said: ‘I will not serve’” (Jer. 2) [Col. 1021C]. Others, afflicted by no lesser madness, endeavour to waste themselves with so many and such great fasts and vigils that they cannot maintain their undertaking of discipline; and, their strength both of mind and body broken, they are unable to perform any good works or virtues. While they afflict themselves without discernment, they lose the sweetness and fruit of heavenly grace. We have heard of, and have even seen, some who after such abstinence fell into such gluttony that they could not be satisfied.

But those who fly between the two extremes and walk by the royal road—who neither break the bonds of discipline nor destroy themselves by unreasonable affliction—often attain the summit of highest perfection. From their strength they also sometimes confer the vigour of goodness by word or example [Col. 1021D].

Sometimes wines are prepared with aromatic herbs or spices so that they may become more pleasing to drinkers. This truly occurs in the elect when their holiness is seasoned and strengthened with certain special and excellent gifts, so that their saving cup may be full of mixed wine (Ps. 7 [citation as printed]), intoxicating and splendid (Ps. 22 [citation as printed]) [Col. 1022A].

There are also some casks containing weak wine. Since such wines do not rise to the strength of robust wines, they rightly signify the life of the weak and less perfect. Wines of this kind are also easily spoiled by the impact of certain accidents, so that they are often thrown away; for the weak and imperfect are quickly broken and overcome by persecutions and temptations—sometimes to such an extent that they are not approved, but rejected. Yet this must not be attributed to divine grace but to human malice.

Finally, the dregs which settle beneath the wine at the bottom of the cask signify the tinder of sin. Although in this mortality it cannot be wholly emptied out, it ought always to be pressed downward, lest it rise upward and corrupt the virtues of the soul by its foulness [Col. 1022B].

Indeed, just as the righteous are casks containing God’s grace, so the unjust are casks of the devil, containing guilt within themselves. Of them Scripture cries: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32). Do Simeon and Levi, Jacob’s sons, not seem to you to have been casks of the devil? Of them Jacob himself bears witness, saying: “Simeon and Levi are brothers, vessels of iniquity in warfare. Let not my soul enter into their counsel, nor my glory be in their assembly; for in their anger they killed a man, and in their self-will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their anger, because it is obstinate, and their indignation, because it is harsh. I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. 49).

For there are certain pestilent people, joined to one another by a kind of fraternity in evil, who sometimes disturb the whole city of God. Seized violently by the fury of their anger, they kill a man: that is, as much as they can, they overthrow a prelate who acts manfully and speaks perfectly. Then, when the man has been slain, they undermine the wall: the prelate being suppressed, they strive with the swords of their malice utterly to destroy the fortifications of virtues and good works in the holy congregation [Col. 1022C].

Brethren, may our soul not enter into their counsel, nor our glory be in their assembly. Let their anger be cursed, because it is obstinate, and their indignation, because it is harsh. Jacob himself indicates what should be done regarding such people in order to escape danger, saying: “I shall divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” [Col. 1022D]. For nothing is done better regarding such people, in order that danger may be avoided, than that they be separated from one another, lest they be able to carry out the iniquity they have conceived and begun.

It should also be carefully noted that the slaughter which Simeon and Levi accomplished by boldness they began by deceit. For first, when Hamor and Shechem spoke deceitfully with Jacob’s sons about circumcision, and when circumcision had been performed, on the third day, when the pain of the wounds is most severe and they could not resist, Simeon and Levi carried out the slaughter (Gen. 34). So too, most beloved, certain persons who malign the prelates of the Church, or even friends and brethren, often offer them deceitful counsels, in which they later wickedly entangle them.

But what reward is owed or repaid to those who give deceitful counsels the prophet Habakkuk testifies, saying: “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, sending forth his gall and making him drunk in order to look upon his nakedness. You have been filled with shame instead of glory” (Hab. 2) [Col. 1023A]. “Drink also yourself and fall into stupor. The cup of the Lord’s right hand shall surround you, and the vomit of shame shall be upon your glory.” Hence Solomon says of the deceitful: “They lie in wait for their own blood, and devise frauds against their own souls” (Prov. 1). For the trap which they hide catches them, and they themselves fall into the snare which they have hidden (Ps. 34 [Vulgate numbering]). Therefore not only must the boldness of such people be broken, but their deceit must also be prudently guarded against.

The devil also has other casks containing other kinds of wines. For he fills not only the malicious with wickedness, but also the lustful with impurity. Hence that notorious harlot Babylon is read to hold a golden cup in her hand, by which she intoxicates the kings and nations of the earth (Jer. 51). It does not suffice the devil to fill some with spiritual vices unless he also fills others with carnal vices. Sometimes, moreover, in order to make a mixture, he defiles some people with both sorts of vices.

Let us not, brethren, be casks of the devil, filled with vices. Rather, let us be casks containing God’s wine: wine through true holiness; vinegar through just rebuke; iron-bound wine through the strictness and discipline of justice; spiced or honeyed wine through the sweetness of inward delight; or at least weak wine through the moderation of human imperfection [Col. 1023B–C]. We have said these things thus, brethren, because outward life reveals what kind of wine each person contains within himself. For it is written that “the clothing of the body, the laughter of the teeth, and a person’s gait proclaim what he is” (Eccl. 19).

Therefore, the wine-cellar is the holy Church; any cask is any faithful and perfect soul; the boards from which casks are constructed are the virtues which we possess through grace; the back head is rationality, the front head sensibility; the opening through which wine is poured in is the mind’s understanding; the wine is grace; the opening of the spigot or little fountain through which it goes out is eloquence or good action.

“The king brought me into the wine-cellar; he ordered [Col. 1023D] charity within me” (Song 2). These words, most beloved, belong to every faithful soul which rejoices that, under Christ’s guidance, it has been brought into the holy Church, and rejoices that it has been imbued with heavenly grace through the words and examples of perfect saints—such as he whose solemn feast we celebrate today.

Let us also enter, brethren, into the holy Church. Let us enter, I say, not only by faith but also by love: that is, not only by belief but also by action; not only by visible participation in the sacraments, but also by the invisible reception of spiritual gifts.

“He ordered charity within me.” Every virtue and good work has its order. The order of almsgiving, indeed, is that first you give yourself to God and then give your possessions for his sake. For if you give your possessions to God and yourself to the devil, it is not an equitable division [Col. 1024A]. Therefore first “have mercy on your own soul, pleasing God” (Sir. 30). For “he who is evil to himself, to whom will he be good?” (Sir. 14). First clothe yourself in good works; then clothe the poor in garments. First receive Christ in your heart; then receive the poor into your lodging. When you desire to go on pilgrimage, first remove yourself from your vice, then from your village.

Thus charity too has its order according to the divine commandment: first love God with all that you can, and then love your neighbour as yourself. Let us enter, brethren, into this wine-cellar and approach the larger casks containing stronger wines—that is, the more perfect saints, more perfectly abounding in heavenly grace—so that through them we may be intoxicated from the abundance of God’s house and drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35 [Vulgate numbering]), and through them draw salvation from the Lord (Prov. 8). Let us enter, I say, so that we may now be intoxicated by grace and, with charity divinely ordered within us, may afterward deserve to be intoxicated by glory [Col. 1024B]. May Jesus Christ our Lord, God blessed above all things for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI. On the Assumption of Blessed Mary

Among the other glorious miracles, most beloved, which in the Assumption of the most blessed Virgin Mary we recite in reading or singing, in order that her praise may be exalted and commemorated throughout all ages, we are accustomed most devoutly to sing that she is purple as a violet. As we briefly indicated in an earlier sermon [Col. 1024C], whatever things in the Scriptures, whatever things in created nature, are lovely, pleasant, sweet, beautiful, fragrant, delightful, precious, or praiseworthy, are fitting for her praises.

But, leaving all else aside, let us speak of the violet alone, in order to show how it plainly signifies the most blessed Virgin not only by its purple colour but also by certain other properties. Natural philosophers affirm in their books, and physicians demonstrate in their preparations, that the violet has a cold nature and is therefore good against hot diseases. It therefore rightly signifies the extinguishing of carnal vices. Carnal vices are like hot diseases, because they set aflame with their heats the wretched soul that they hold. Thus, as it were, the violet is applied to bodily members that burn wrongly, in order that they may be healed, whenever heavenly grace is poured into us so that the heats of vices may be mitigated within us [Col. 1024D].

The violet has two colours, green and purple. Teachers commonly understand by greenness the hope of heavenly and unfading good works. For heavenly goods are ever green, as it were, and never wither, since they do not fall from the perpetual state of their goodness and beauty through any drought of changeability. When we hope for them firmly, steadfastly, and without ceasing, we are coloured, as it were, by their unfading green. We may also understand by greenness the beginning of any virtue or good work. For in shoots emerging from the hidden bosom of the earth, green first appears. Thus, as it were, we produce in ourselves the green of a new shoot when we adorn ourselves with the beauty of a virtue or good work being born in us and from us. We may also understand by greenness the unfading permanence of virtues and good works. For they are always green in us, as it were, when they abide in us without failure [Col. 1025A].

Purple belongs to kings. Hence Alexander, king of Syria, sent Jonathan purple and a golden crown, honouring him with a royal gift. And when this same Jonathan met the aforesaid king and Ptolemy, king of Egypt, at Ptolemais, the aforesaid king ordered him to be stripped of his own garments and clothed in purple, wishing to glorify him with royal adornment. Purple therefore fittingly signifies royal dignity.

Thus the blessed Virgin Mary was truly purple, shining forth above all saints in royal dignity as Lady of the world and Queen of heaven; she conducted and ruled herself more royally than all others. She cast down vices and raised up virtues: she cast down pride in herself and raised humility; cast down anger and raised peace; cast down envy and raised charity; cast down worldly sadness and raised God’s exultation; cast down miserliness and raised generosity; cast down gluttony and raised moderation; cast down lust and raised chastity—indeed, outstanding virginity [Col. 1025B]. Therefore, because she cast down evils and raised up goods, or because, according to the prophet’s statement, she rooted out and destroyed the former, and built and planted the latter (Jer. 1), she was truly purple, truly adorned with royal dignity.

The violet also has a good scent, by which it signifies good repute. For not only a good conscience but also a good reputation is necessary. Hence chrism has two liquids within itself. *Chrisma* is called “anointing” in Latin from Greek. Chrism is oil mixed with balsam; the heads of kings and pontiffs are anointed with it, and a priest also anoints the baptized on the crown of the head with it, just as a bishop anoints on the forehead those who are to be confirmed by the laying on of hands. In chrism the Paraclete Spirit is principally bestowed.

Accordingly, by the abundance of grace it contains two mixed liquids, oil and balsam: oil of conscience, balsam of reputation; oil by which the conscience is anointed within, balsam by whose scent neighbours are sprinkled without; oil within for peace with God, balsam without for an example to one’s neighbour [Col. 1025C–D]. The most blessed Virgin therefore possessed not only inward holiness for conscience, but also outward repute for holiness.

For she knew, as someone has said:

> “It is a crime to cultivate beauty and despise one’s reputation.”

She knows that “a good name is better than precious ointments” (Eccl. 7). She knows that “the memory of the righteous is with praises, but the name of the wicked shall rot” (Prov. 10). She knows, according to the Apostle, that the good fragrance of Christ is in every place (2 Cor. 2). Truly, then, she was like a fragrant violet: whose fragrance not only suffused human beings, but also turned angels to admiration of itself. Truly she was fragrant, whose scent filled not only [Col. 1026A] earth but heaven as well. Finally, every violet naturally bends its head—that is, its little flower—downward, and thus fittingly expresses humility. Who could doubt that this virtue was outstandingly present in blessed Mary? For when the angel announced that she was to be the Mother of God, and therefore truly lady of the world and queen of heaven, she humbly replied: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord” (Luke 1). Thus this violet truly possessed the quality of bending its head downwards: in becoming greater, she humbled herself the more, choosing “not to think highly of herself, but rather to associate with the humble” (Rom. 12). For she already had written upon her heart: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, and whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14); and likewise: “Before ruin the spirit is exalted, and before glory it shall be humbled” [Col. 1026B] (Prov. 16). Rightly, therefore, blessed Mary was a violet in all the ways stated above, since she truly practised all that was said mystically of it.

And we, dearest brethren—we, I say—should be violets. Let us imitate the blessed Virgin as far as we can. Let us be, as it were, naturally cold through the extinction of carnal fire; green through the beginning of righteousness and through its continuance, or through the unfading hope and expectation of heavenly goods. Let us be purple by rightly governing ourselves. Let us be fragrant among all people by acquiring a good name; let us lower our heads by always thinking most humbly of ourselves. Let us conform ourselves, according to our strength, to the blessed Virgin in holiness, that we may deserve to become her companions in blessedness. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XLVII. On the Assumption of Blessed Mary, Ever-Virgin

[Col. 1026C]

“I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on Mount Zion. I was exalted like a palm tree in Kadesh, and like a plantation of roses in Jericho” (Ecclus. 24).

These words, beloved, which we have set before you, are described in Ecclesiasticus in praise of Wisdom, as though Wisdom itself were speaking; and today they are most fittingly recited in churches in praise and glory of the most blessed Virgin Mary, whose feast of Assumption we celebrate, in her person, as though she were suitably commending herself. For she was rightly a cedar, cypress, palm, and so forth—together with the further things which follow there—since she shone resplendent, filled with all the virtues signified by them.

The cedar is a tree of Lebanon, tall and very resistant to decay. Lebanon, moreover, whose name is interpreted “whitening,” often signifies the present age, which shines temporarily with some kind of brightness. Therefore the blessed Mother of God was rightly a tree of Lebanon, because she took her bodily origin from the present age. But, raising herself to things on high, she surpassed Lebanon’s height, because by the loftiness of her virtues she immeasurably transcended all the world’s glory. She was also incorruptible, since, remaining an uncorrupted virgin, she became a mother. Finally, she rightly said that she was exalted like a cedar, since, ever remaining inviolate, she saw herself raised above all creatures—first by grace and afterwards by glory. “And like a cypress on Mount Zion.” Cypress wood has a strength nearly akin to cedar [Col. 1027A]: suited for the beams of temples, it never yields beneath a burden because of its impenetrable solidity, but persists in the firmness it first possessed; and it fittingly signifies strength. Zion also, whose name is interpreted “watchtower,” is rightly understood as the holy Church, which loftily contemplates the beauty of heavenly good. Blessed Mary, therefore, is aptly said to have been exalted like a cypress on Mount Zion: while she lived in the world, powerfully subduing all worldly things and courageously ascending by the steps of virtues to heaven, she contemplated the glory of divinity above all the Church’s faithful; and now she beholds it above all heavenly spirits.

“I was exalted like a palm tree in Kadesh.” We read in the Old Testament that the people of Israel twice drank in the desert from water brought forth from a rock: first at Rephidim, and second at Kadesh [Col. 1027B]. These two places fittingly signify a twofold compunction within us: one born from recollection or sorrow for sins; the other arising from desire for future rewards. This is also rightly inferred from the interpretation of the places themselves. For Rephidim, which signifies the first, is interpreted “health of judgment” or “vision of the mouth sufficient for them.” But Kadesh means “holy.” Therefore we drink water at Rephidim when, inwardly judging ourselves rightly concerning our sins, we are pierced with compunction, and through prudent oral confession are sufficiently washed from them. But we drink at Kadesh when, devoutly and holily kindled and melted by desire for heavenly goods, we are intoxicated, mingling our drink joyfully with tears. The palm [Col. 1027C] signifies victory. Blessed Mother of God, then, rightly glories that she was exalted like a palm at Kadesh, because, having powerfully and victoriously subdued spiritual enemies, she was most sweetly given drink—not by sorrow for sins, but by love for heavenly rewards.

The water given to the people at Rephidim may also be understood as the gift of the Holy Spirit, granted to the faithful for righteousness in the world; while the water given at Kadesh is the water of the heavenly spring, granted to the glorified for glory in heaven—so that the former is given in merit and the latter in reward. Of the first it is written: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). To the second belongs what John says in the person of Christ: “To the thirsty I shall give freely from the spring of the water of life” [Col. 1027D] (Rev. 21). For whoever thirsts for righteousness shall be refreshed by glory.

Blessed Mary, therefore, rightly declares that she was exalted like a palm in Kadesh, because she possesses the sweetness of the heavenly spring more excellently than all spirits. “And like a plantation of roses in Jericho.” The rose, which is red, fittingly signifies passion. And if the rose signifies passion in its redness, then in being planted it fittingly signifies compassion. Compassion is in the heart; passion in the body. Compassion lies hidden; passion is manifest. Thus a rose is planted when compassion is implanted in the heart; it produces its red flower when it proceeds into the effect of suffering. Jericho means “moon,” and is taken for the failing of the flesh or the decline of the present age [Col. 1028A]. It is clear, therefore, that the Mother of God was like a plantation of roses in Jericho, because amid the decline of the present age she shone outstandingly and uniquely through the virtue of compassion. For “a sword passed through her own soul” (Luke 2). And who could worthily weigh what sword of sorrow she endured when she saw her only-begotten Son hanging and dying upon the cross?

“Like a beautiful olive tree in the fields, and like a plane tree beside the waters.” The olive signifies mercy. Blessed Mary, therefore, was an olive through mercy, and the more precious in mercy as she was more excellent in grace. She was rightly in the fields: in the open plain of the present age and in the breadth of the holy Church spread throughout all lands, so that all sinners might look to her freely and without hindrance, flee to her, seek counsel from her, and receive help through her; being reconciled to God through her, gladdened by pardon, enriched by grace, illumined by faith, strengthened by hope, justified by charity, trained in other virtues, adorned with good works, and at last made blessed by glory.

“And like a plane tree beside waters in the public squares” [Col. 1028B]. But the earlier ending we have adopted seems better, so that it reads: “like a plane tree beside waters.” The plane tree is named from the breadth of its leaves, or because the tree itself is spreading and wide. For the Greeks call broad **πλατύς** (*platys*). Leaves signify good works. For just as it is clothed and adorned with its leaves, so the righteous person is clothed and adorned with good works. Therefore the blessed Mother of God rightly says that she was like a plane tree beside waters, because, watered with divine gifts, she was always enlarged in good works. Hence, after receiving the angelic announcement that she was to be the Mother of God (Luke 1), she immediately went into the hill country of Judaea to Elizabeth, of whose conception she had heard—not to test the angel’s word by a woman’s testimony, but to render diligent service, as a young virgin, to a woman advanced in age.

“In the public squares I gave forth fragrance like cinnamon and balsam.” Sellers of spices, sitting in the public squares at fairs, display different kinds of spices, and those spices fill the squares with the sweetness of their scent. So the possessors of spiritual spices delight those who pass through the broad ways of vices with the fragrances of virtues and good works, and by the scent of their reputation turn them back from the way of wickedness [Col. 1028D]. Cinnamon, although it has a pleasant scent and may therefore signify the holy Virgin’s renown, nevertheless fittingly signifies praise and thanksgiving because it forms its bark in the manner of a reed. This appropriately suits the blessed Virgin, who, when she heard from Elizabeth that the angel’s words would be fulfilled in her, immediately burst forth in praise and thanksgiving, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1). Balsam, however, expresses Blessed Mary’s good reputation by its scent. Thus we also sing of her that her scent was beyond estimation in her garments, and that flowers of roses and lilies of the valleys surrounded her like spring days (Ecclus. 50). This especially suits the blessed Virgin Mary, who immeasurably filled the whole world [Col. 1029A] with the fragrance of the finest reputation.

“And like chosen myrrh I gave the sweetness of fragrance.” Myrrh, because of its bitterness, signifies mortification of the flesh. This virtue shone uniquely in blessed Mary, because she was uniquely chaste. Therefore she fittingly declares that she gave not fragrance, but the sweetness of fragrance. By these virtues, beloved, the blessed Mother of God was exalted in the world through merit and is now exalted in heaven through reward. Let us therefore celebrate the feast of the most sacred Virgin with deepest devotion, that we may imitate her according to our strength; so that we too may be, in whatever measure, like a cedar through incorruption; like a cypress through strength; like a palm through victory; like a plantation of roses through brotherly compassion [Col. 1029B]; like an olive through mercy; like a plane tree through good action; like cinnamon through praise and thanksgiving; like balsam through good reputation; and like myrrh through mortification of our flesh. Let us imitate her in good conduct, so that by her merits and prayers we may deserve to be joined to her in blessedness. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XLVIII. On the Nativity of the Lord

“He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (Ps. 18).

There are different kinds of tabernacles, and of those dwelling in tabernacles, as we have learned by hearing, seeing, and reading [Col. 1029C]. Shepherds, guards, merchants, soldiers, exiles, pilgrims, travellers, and poor people commonly dwell in tabernacles. There are also tabernacles of the wicked and tabernacles of the righteous. Christ was all these things, except only that he was not wicked. For although, according to the prophet, he “was reckoned with the wicked” (Isa. 53), and, according to the Apostle Paul, “was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3), nevertheless “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 1). Thus Christ was shepherd, guard, merchant, soldier, exile, pilgrim, traveller, poor person, and righteous person—indeed, he was righteousness, always is, and always shall be.

The song of King Hezekiah informs us that shepherds dwell in tabernacles, when it says: “My generation has been taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherds’ tent” (Isa. 38). Christ was a shepherd, as he first said of himself through the prophet and then in his own words. Through the prophet he says: “I shall feed my flock as a shepherd feeds his flock on the day when he is among his scattered sheep” (Ezek. 34); and shortly afterwards: “I shall feed them in most fertile pastures, and their pastures shall be on the lofty mountains of Israel” (ibid.). Isaiah says of him: “Like a shepherd he shall feed his flock; in his arm he shall gather the lambs, and in his bosom he shall lift them; he himself shall carry those with young” (Isa. 4). And he says of himself: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep” (John 10).

Isaiah also indicates that guards have tabernacles, when he says: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber field” [Col. 1030A] (Isa. 1). And Christ was a guard, as the Psalmist says: “He who guards Israel neither sleeps nor slumbers” (Ps. 120)—that is, the person who sees God, provided that he sees him with both eyes: namely, the eye of knowledge and the eye of love. For some are spiritually one-eyed: they see God only with the eye of knowledge, not also with the eye of love. Such people are not of Israel’s race, unless perhaps they are called stepchildren and have no share in Israel’s inheritance. For the true Israelite, although he limps beneficially on one foot after the manner of his father, nevertheless sees clearly with both eyes.

Therefore, if you wish to be guarded by Christ, be Israel, so that you may see God with both eyes: the eye of knowledge [Col. 1030B] and the eye of love; the eye of faith and the eye of action; the eye of reason and the eye of good will; the eye of learning and the eye of wisdom; the eye of judgment and the eye of righteousness; the eye of understanding and the eye of affection. Let Christ see in you these two eyes—the eye of knowledge, faith, reason, learning, judgment, and understanding; and the eye of love, action, good will, wisdom, righteousness, and affection—if you wish him to guard you.

The Psalmist expresses these two eyes when he says: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God” (Ps. 13). For when he says “one who understands,” he expresses the first eye: knowledge, faith, reason, learning, judgment, and understanding, all of which must be taken under one meaning. But when he says “one who seeks,” he denotes the other: love, action, good will, wisdom, righteousness, and affection, all of which likewise must be comprehended under one meaning. The things first described—knowledge and the rest—belong to the truth that is in us. Those placed second—love, and so forth [Col. 1030C]—belong to goodness. By the former we shine; by the latter we burn warmly. By the former, according to the teaching of our masters, the divine image is re-formed in us; by the latter, the divine likeness. Thus Christ is truly the guardian of one who, as has been said, is truly Israel.

Some had both eyes—that is, knowledge and love; some had only one, namely knowledge; some had neither, because they had neither knowledge nor love. The first are good Christians; the second, bad Christians; the third, utterly unbelieving people.

We often see merchants dwelling in tabernacles at fairs. Christ, however, was a merchant. Do you wish to hear what sort of merchant? He gave his life in order to receive yours. He gave himself as Lord in order to free you as a slave. He gave himself as the natural Son in order to make you an adopted child. He gave himself to dishonour in order to restore you to glory. He gave himself to temporal punishment in order to restore you to eternal happiness. To this merchant’s transaction belongs what Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “You were bought at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” [Col. 1030D] (1 Cor. 6). And blessed Peter says: “Knowing that you were redeemed from your vain manner of life handed down by your fathers, not with corruptible gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Jesus Christ, like that of an unblemished and spotless lamb” (1 Pet. 1).

Military duty compels soldiers, or those on campaign, to remain in tabernacles. Christ was a soldier: a vigorous soldier, a strong soldier. For he is the strong one—indeed, the stronger one—who conquered the strong, armed man guarding his courtyard and peacefully possessing all his goods; he took away all his weapons in which he trusted and distributed his spoils (Luke 2). Hence he himself said: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12). The strength of this soldier, fighter, and conqueror is declared in Scripture, where it says: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden; before his face death shall go” (Hab. 3). He was truly strong, who through the cross defeated the devil [Col. 1031B] and all aerial powers, overcame the world, sin, and death, and, having broken the gates of hell, led our captivity captive (Eph. 4); and as the King of glory, the Lord strong and mighty in battle (Ps. 23), entered as a manifest victor through the gates of the heavenly homeland.

Necessity often compels exiles, pilgrims, travellers, and poor people to dwell in tabernacles. Christ was an exile because he underwent our exile—not because he was deserving of it, but because he so chose; not constrained, but voluntarily; not by losing what was his own, but by gathering what was alien. Thus he was an exile in entering our exile, though willingly. “The Word walked and went out into the field. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1). He came forth from the Father and came into the world, not [Col. 1031C] to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him (John 16).

He was also a pilgrim. For concerning his pilgrimage and its action it is written: “That he may do his work, his work is alien; that he may perform his work, his work is strange to him” (Isa. 28). God’s work is to gather the souls he created and call them back to the joys of eternal light. But to be scourged, covered with spittle, crucified, die, and be buried is not, in his own substance, God’s work; rather, it is the work of sinful humanity, which deserved all these things through sin. Yet he himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood; and he who remains always incomprehensible in his own nature deigned to be apprehended and scourged in our nature, because [Col. 1031D] unless he had taken upon himself the things belonging to our weakness, he would never have raised us to the power of his strength.

Therefore, “that he may do his work, his work is alien; that he may perform his work, his work is strange to him,” because God incarnate deigned, in order to gather us to his righteousness, to be beaten for us as a sinful man. He did an alien work in order to do his own work, because by enduring our evils in weakness, he brought us, his creatures, to the glory of his strength.

Sacred Scripture declares that those on the road, or travellers, dwell in tabernacles: it testifies that the patriarch Jacob, when he departed from Laban, pitched his tents on Mount Gilead; and the children of Israel, journeying through the desert and making their way to the promised land, are read to have dwelt in tabernacles. Christ was a traveller, as David testifies: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (Ps. 109). And again: “He shall rejoice like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit unto its summit.” Hence Solomon, describing his course—or rather, his leap—in the person of holy Church, says: “Behold, he comes, leaping on the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song 2). For he made certain leaps: he came from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross to the tomb, and returned from the tomb to heaven. He made these leaps by leaping on mountains and bounding over hills, because he alone and uniquely surpassed the heights [Col. 1032B] of all the saints, both greater and lesser.

Christ was also poor. Although he was rich, he deigned to become poor for us, so that through his poverty and humanity he might grant us a share in his riches and divinity. He himself says of his poverty: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 6; Luke 2). This is also relevant: his blessed mother, the Virgin Mary, when the days of her purification were completed, came to the temple to offer for him not a lamb, the offering of wealthy women, but a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—that is, the offering of the poor (Luke 2).

The divine word testifies thus that the wicked also have tabernacles: “The tents of robbers abound, and they boldly provoke God, though he has given all things into their hands” [Col. 1032C] (Job 12). Finally, the Psalmist sings that the righteous have tabernacles: “The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tabernacles of the righteous” (Ps. 11). Hence the ancient righteous—namely Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—dwelt in huts in the lands of promise. They did not do this because of poverty, but for typological significance. For they were righteous; and by dwelling in huts they showed that they desired and sought not a city remaining here, but the city to come.

Hence also Jonadab son of Rechab, for the increase and example of righteousness, commanded his sons, saying: “You and your sons shall not drink wine for ever; you shall not build a house, sow seed, plant vineyards, or possess them; but you shall dwell in tabernacles all your days” [Col. 1032D] (Jer. 35). Jonadab gave these commands to his sons so that they might learn not to cling steadfastly to earthly things, nor intoxicate themselves with Babylon’s cup, but advance toward the heavenly Jerusalem by the steps of virtues and good works, and thirst with their whole desire for righteousness and heavenly sweetness, where, for so great a merit and example of righteousness, they would receive a fitting reward of glory. Thus, as a figure of eternal recompense, they deserved to hear: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his commandments, there shall not fail a man of the line of Jonadab son of Rechab standing in my presence all days” (ibid.).

The ancient fathers, dearest brethren, handed down to us such an example of holy conduct [Col. 1033A]. But we, having utterly forgotten so great an example, build no longer tabernacles—not even houses—but palaces and royal halls. Yet this seems tolerable to many on account of the necessity, usefulness, and repose of posterity, provided that the inward and enduring edifice of souls is not neglected on account of this outward and perishing construction.

Christ, however, was truly righteous. Hence God the Father says of him through Isaiah: “By his knowledge he himself shall justify many of my righteous servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities” (Isa. 53). Therefore Christ, as shepherd, guardian, merchant, soldier, exile, pilgrim, traveller, poor person, and righteous person, remained in a tabernacle and placed his tabernacle in the sun. His tabernacle was his human manner of life. Of this tabernacle—that is [Col. 1033B], his manner of life—Baruch says: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned against him. He discovered every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant and Israel his beloved. After this he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3).

He placed his tabernacle in the sun (Ps. 18), because he placed it in the manifest knowledge of human beings, amid the heat of persecution and affliction, hunger and thirst, blasphemy and beating, passion and death. “And he himself is like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber” (ibid.). Christ is the bridegroom; the Church is the bride; the six water jars are the six ages; water is the letter; wine is spiritual understanding. The prophets are harpists; John the Baptist or the apostolic order is the bridegroom’s friend; the children of the wedding are each of the faithful; and the bridal chamber [Col. 1033C] of the marriage was the womb of the incorrupt Mother, in which God was joined to human nature, and from which he came forth as bridegroom in order to unite the Church to himself.

The first place of the wedding was Judaea, in which the Son of God deigned to become human, consecrate the Church through participation in his body, and confirm her through the pledge of his Spirit. But once the Gentiles had been called to faith, the desired joys of that wedding reached the ends of the earth. “Like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber.” It is customary for bridegrooms, when they first leave the bridal chamber, to proceed in white garments coloured red or with another colour. Christ, however, was white and red: white with virginity, red with passion. Hence his bride, the holy Church, says of him in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy” [Col. 1033D] (Song 5): white, that is, through the purity of virginity; ruddy through the shedding of blood.
