Brethren, let us imitate the master as disciples, the lord as servants, the king as soldiers. Let us be shepherds, diligently feeding ourselves and others with the pastures of sacred doctrine. Let us be guards, watchfully guarding ourselves and others insofar as we can. Let us be merchants, shrewdly exchanging earthly things for heavenly. Let us be soldiers, manfully defending our spiritual goods. Let us be exiles and pilgrims, truly recognizing ourselves to be exiles and pilgrims. Let us be travellers, moving day by day toward the heavenly homeland by the steps of virtues and good works [Col. 1034A]. Let us be poor, possessing only food and clothing. Finally, let us be righteous, living rightly before God and human beings.

Let us dwell in tabernacles, but ones becomingly constructed out of the branches of virtues and good works. Let each of us place his tabernacle in the sun with Christ, so that we may go forth with Christ outside the gate, bearing his reproach with him (Heb. 13). Or rather, let it be in the sun so that, for his love, we may be, as the Apostle says of himself, “in labour and hardship, in many vigils, in hunger and thirst, in many fastings, in cold and nakedness” (2 Cor. 11), and in all the other things he enumerates above and below. Let us also go forth, according to our measure, like a bridegroom from the bridal chamber, so that, if not white through virginity, we may at least be white through chastity; and red through suffering or at least compassion [Col. 1034B]. In all these things, let us imitate Christ according to our strength if we desire to reign with him. For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked. Therefore let us follow Christ by holy living in time, so that we may follow him in eternity. May the same Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XLIX. On the Circumcision of the Lord

“Let us go as far as Bethlehem and see this thing which has happened, which the Lord has made known to us” (Luke 2).

Brethren, we ought to be both shepherds and sons of shepherds: sons, namely, of the ancient Fathers, who were shepherds and became our fathers in the faith [Col. 1034C]. They themselves also passed over to see the Lord, because by dwelling in huts they showed that they sought not a city remaining here but the city to come; and they left us a pattern and example for seeking it. We therefore ought ourselves to be shepherds, feeding and guarding our flocks. Our flocks are our thoughts and affections, our senses and desires, our speech and actions. In these flocks we have lambs through purity, sheep through innocence, and wethers—that is, castrated rams—through continence. We have the ram, leader of all the flocks: rational understanding, having two horns implanted in it by God and standing high—namely, the two Testaments. We ought to feed these flocks upon the pastures of the divine page and guard them [Col. 1034D] through the whole night of the present age from the snares of the deceitful thief and the assault of the ravening wolf. Far from our flocks, brethren, be the pig of filthy uncleanness and the goat of stinking disgrace!

Therefore, if we are sons of shepherds and shepherds, and if we are Hebrews, let us pass over and see Christ not only born but also circumcised. Perhaps on the day of his birth we passed over and saw him born; but let us pass over still further and see him circumcised. Let us see, I say, and love. Let us see truth and love goodness. Truth and goodness are two things which, if we have both, we ought to seek nothing further. “Seek first,” he says, “the kingdom of God and his righteousness” (Matt. 6). The kingdom of God is truth; his righteousness is goodness. If you seek these two as you ought, the rest shall be added to you [Col. 1035A]. Why labour to seek these things, rather than things which you can possess freely? Thus there are two things chiefly to be sought: truth and goodness. But would that human beings were as eager in seeking goodness as they are found curious in seeking truth! I do not know how it is, but it is natural to human beings to seek truth even when they do not love goodness. For everyone wishes so much to know the truth that no one wishes to be deceived. But truth does not willingly come without goodness; or, if it comes, it does not come from those parts or that region in which salvation is found.

Let us, dearest brethren, seek both, so that through both we may be able to find Christ and be renewed in him, as the Apostle urges us, saying: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind” [Col. 1035B] (Eph. 4)—that is, in your mind, which is spirit, or which is a spiritual reality. For it is fitting that we be renewed, because “the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5; Rev. 21). A new mother, a new son, a new joy, a new song, a new child, new cradles, a new circumcision, a new name, a new sign, new worshippers, new gifts, a new bridal chamber, a new bridegroom, a new bride, new weddings, a new miracle, new bridegroom’s friends, new guests, new harpists, a new offspring, a new prince, a new commonwealth, a new battle, a new victory, a new peace, new righteousness, a new sacrifice, a new testament, a new inheritance, a new people, a new rite, a new year. All these things signify and correspond to newness, so that we may walk in newness of life.

A new mother: a virgin mother. A new son: God and man. A new joy: the joy of angels at the salvation of human beings. A new song: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2). A new child: true because pure, because “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” [Col. 1035C] (1 Pet. 2). New cradles: animals’ mangers. A new circumcision: because it was in flesh without sin. The new name Jesus: because he himself saves his people from their sins (Matt. 1). A new name: because “there is no other name given under heaven to human beings in which we must be saved” (Acts 4). A new name: because at the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2). Likewise the new name Christ, from which Christians are called: a new name, I say, Christ, because he was anointed not with material oil like the rest, but with the spiritual oil of gladness beyond his companions (Ps. 44); in that name, “whoever is blessed upon earth shall be blessed in God.” Amen.

A new sign: a new star. New worshippers: Gentile Magi. New gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. A new womb: the Virgin’s womb. A new bridegroom: Christ. A new bride: the Church. New weddings: the union of Christ and the Church. A new miracle: water made wine. New bridegroom’s friends: angels. New guests: apostles. New harpists: prophets. A new offspring: spiritual souls. A new prince: the Prince of Peace, who shall reign in the house of Jacob for ever, and [Col. 1036A] of whose kingdom there shall be no end (Luke 1). A new commonwealth: heaven and earth. For he indeed “made both one” (Eph. 2), because he made the homeland of the heavenly and earthly realms one commonwealth. A new battle: because, as it is written, “The Lord chose new wars,” so that wisdom might assail malice and Christ’s humility the devil’s pride. A new victory: because the strong armed guardian of his courtyard, the prince of the world and ruler of darkness, was cast out, and every aerial power was overthrown with him. New righteousness also, and new peace, because “in his days righteousness and abundance of peace arose, until the moon be taken away” (Ps. 71). A new sacrifice: Christ’s passion. A new testament: the word of the Gospel. A new inheritance: the kingdom of heaven. A new people: the Christian people. A new rite: Christianity. A new year: the year of divine favour, that is, the time of grace. Therefore, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind.”

What the Apostle says, “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” was said of old through Jeremiah, when he declares: “Be circumcised for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem” (Jer. 4). For that spiritual circumcision is itself true renewal. But just as, according to the letter, some were men of Israel and others men of Judah or inhabitants of Jerusalem, so, according to the spiritual sense, these must be understood as one group and those as another. Thus the men of Israel are all carnal and conduct themselves carnally; but the men of Judah, or inhabitants of Jerusalem, are holy and spiritual, living spiritually. This, brothers, is what we especially ought to be—we who live in a community and have professed fellowship, chastity, obedience, and the amendment of our conduct. Therefore the foreskins of the men of Israel are exceedingly shameful and monstrous: they are the works of the flesh itself. “These are fornication, uncleanness, shamelessness, sensuality, idolatry, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, angers, strifes, dissensions, sects, envies, murders, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these; concerning which I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (Gal. 5).

But on this day, which they call New Year’s Day, the men of Israel shamefully grow old amid the monstrosities of their foreskins. For today, more than on other days of the year, they devote themselves to divinations and auguries, [Col. 1036D] vanities and false madnesses. Today they anticipate one another with gifts in the observance of vain and superstitious intentions; today, carried away by the furies of their debauchery and inflamed by the fires of diabolical instigation, they rush to church, and profane the house of God with empty and foolish talk—where sin will not be absent but rather present—with wicked rhythmic utterances too, laughter, and guffaws. And whoever speaks evil more cleverly “is the more praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 10). Today also certain clerics—of whom it seems to have been written that “their clerics shall not profit them”—“prophesy in Baal” (Jer. 2), “and divine falsehood” (Ezek. 13); and some priests “clap their hands” (Lam. 2), and the people love such things. “They sacrifice to demons [Col. 1037A] and not to God, to gods whom they did not know; new and recent gods came, whom their fathers had not worshipped” (Deut. 32).

Such are the foreskins of the men of Israel: long, monstrous, and deformed, apart from those things hidden within. “For it is shameful even to speak of the things done by them in secret” (Eph. 5). But why are they such? Perhaps because Eli’s eye has grown dim and cannot see the lamp of God; his sons sin, and he does not correct them, and they deserve death (1 Sam. 3–4). Likewise Zipporah the mother delays to circumcise her firstborn; and it is to be feared that the Lord may come and kill him (Exod. 4). Zipporah is the Church; her firstborn is the clergy; her second-born, the people; the sharp stone, Christian faith; the bridegroom of blood, Christ, who did not come to bring peace upon earth but a sword [Col. 1037B] (Matt. 10).

But since these matters concern bishops and priests who have the care of souls, let us turn the words upon ourselves, who, in comparison with secular people, ought to be men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, most devoted praisers of God and most perfect contemplators of the highest peace.

Leaving aside secular people and those who live carnally, then, let us examine, cut off, and cast away the monstrous foreskins of our own people. For in some who make a show of religious life by their habit, shameful, foul, and at times long foreskins grow again. Hence the Lord said to Jerusalem—by which those who live under a religious profession are especially signified—“When you were born, on the day of your birth your navel-string was not cut” (Ezek. 16). And [Col. 1037C] again: “You committed fornication beyond all precedent and all future possibility” (ibid.). Again: “You surpassed your sisters Sodom and Samaria in your sins, acting more wickedly than they. For they were made holy by you” (ibid.). And again, concerning the same city: “She despised my judgments, so as to be more ungodly than the nations” (Ezek. 5). And again: “Faithless Judah justified her own soul” (Jer. 3). Similar to this is what Isaiah says: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23). Moreover, the tax collector “went down to his house justified rather than the Pharisee” (Luke 18).

For, what cannot be said without grave sorrow, those who have vowed religious life to God sometimes, even while remaining in the very habit of religion, relapse into their vomit with such madness that secular people seem righteous by comparison with them [Col. 1037D]. Indeed, what wickedness is worse than the wickedness of the Pharisees? What angers, what quarrels, what dissensions are more bitter and dangerous than those which today rage fiercely in congregations of brothers, stirred up by the devil? It now seems altogether to be a fault in some that “they have lawsuits among themselves” (1 Cor. 6). It is to be feared that the queen of the South, who came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and the men of Nineveh, who did penance at Jonah’s preaching, may rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it (Luke 11), because God has given them opportunity for repentance and they misuse it for pride. It is to be feared that Tyre and Sidon and the land of the Sodomites will fare more gently on the day of judgment than these, because if they had possessed as great a knowledge of divinity and of the divine commandments as [Col. 1038A] these possess, they would long ago have done penance in ashes and sackcloth (ibid.).

But now there is wickedness in their dwellings, in their midst. Why do they not rather suffer injury? Why do they not rather endure fraud? Instead, they pursue lawsuits, not only among themselves or before religious persons, but, as the Corinthians did before wicked believers, so these do before secular authorities. Yet, brothers, we do not say this in order to rebuke those who freely exercise vengeance in congregations for God and with God, in zeal for justice, and render recompense to the proud; who rise up against evildoers and stand against workers of iniquity (Ps. 93); who, at Moses’ command, do not spare even friends from the sword, cutting off idolatry; who, with Phinehas, slay the fornicators (Num. 25), punishing the flesh’s lust; who, with [Col. 1038B] Samuel, cut the king of Amalek into pieces (1 Sam. 15), killing every earthly desire. But there are certain carnal persons in the Church to whom these things apply: while they stubbornly wish to accomplish their own desires, such foreskins easily grow again.

May such foreskins as we have mentioned be far from us, beloved! Far be it from us to be “in revelries and drunkennesses, in beds and shamelessnesses, in strife and jealousy” (Rom. 13).

Besides these, there are foreskins among those who live under rule, smaller than those already mentioned: for example, the unnecessary walking about or riding abroad of officials; the sorties from the cloister and dissolute roaming of cloistered persons; proud bearing and gesture in both; disorderly action or speech; earthly thought or desire. [Col. 1038C] For we often see not only elders going out on household business, but younger men too wandering through streets and squares. We see cloistered persons frivolously darting out of their cloisters and, before returning, inspecting every workshop; they seem to behave like a bear tied to a post, which, unable to extend its step farther, strives to circle about the very post. We see many of both sorts affect small tonsures, long hair, and long garments, with sleeves hanging from their clothes down to the ground: walking on their feet like human beings, but flying with their arms like birds; jostling with their shoulders, speaking with a finger, signaling with their eyes, turning their faces in different directions, and twisting their mouths into guffaws. We also see many of this [Col. 1038D] kind doing many disorderly things, speaking trifles—and not only trifles, but shameful and harmful things. Of the thoughts and desires of such people, hidden within, we can know nothing except insofar as we detect them from such signs. For it is written: “A man’s clothing, his manner of walking, and the laughter of his teeth declare these things about him” (Ecclus. 19). Let all such persons, since they seem neither cold nor hot, fear lest they be vomited from God’s mouth (Rev. 3).

Everything that is a foreskin—everything said above—must be cut off and cast away, whether it belongs to the outward or the inward person. But let our circumcision be perfect, as befits men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: not that Judah whose sin “is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point” (Jer. 17), but that Judah of whom the Lord says, “Judah is my king” (Ps. 59); nor that Jerusalem whose navel-string was not cut (Ezek. 16), but that Jerusalem whose name the Lord’s mouth has called new (Isa. 62). Let our circumcision be such that “all bitterness, anger, indignation, blasphemy, and all malice” may be taken away from us (Eph. 4–5), and that “fornication and every uncleanness or covetousness may not even be named among you, as befits saints” (Eph. 5).

But behold: we who have the office of circumcision and hold the knife for circumcising, while we aim to perform circumcision, fear causing a killing. For weak brothers, when rebuked, are sometimes wounded with such pain that from the rebuke from which they ought to receive an increase of righteousness, they suffer loss instead. [Col. 1039B] For a bruised reed is easily broken, a smoking piece of wood is lightly extinguished, a weak vessel, when rubbed too harshly, quickly breaks, and a light vessel with a shallow bottom, when pushed, is quickly overturned and what is inside is easily spilled. For:

> A light vessel is an empty vessel, a futile vessel, a vessel unsound;
>
> It rashly spills what has been entrusted to it.

Nevertheless, where necessary, we must always rebuke, because “all things work together for good to those who are called saints according to the purpose” (Rom. 8). Let us cleanse ourselves, then, and with the new year be renewed in the spirit of our mind, and put on the new man, “who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. 4). Let us be renewed in the new man through a new circumcision, in this new year in [Col. 1039C] this world, so that we may deserve to be renewed in him in heaven. May our Lord Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON L. On Certain Apostles

“I will place a sign among them, and I will send from them those who have been saved to the nations—to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, holding the arrow; to Italy and Greece, to the distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they shall proclaim my glory to the nations, and they shall bring all your brothers from all nations as an offering to the Lord, on horses and in chariots and in litters and on mules and in carts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord, just as if the children of Israel were bringing an offering in a clean vessel into the house [Col. 1039D] of the Lord; and I will take some of them as priests and Levites, says the Lord” (Isa. 66).

In these words the Lord speaks through the prophet to the Jews, plainly declaring that from among those of their race whom he would call to faith through the grace of redemption, he would choose—or rather pre-choose—apostles, distinguish them by a certain prerogative of heavenly grace, send them to the nations, and through their ministry join those chosen from among the nations to the Jews in a common faith. For divine providence so ordained that Gentiles should be joined with Jews in faith, so that there might be one God and one worship, one high priest and one Church, one faith and one baptism, one cornerstone and one house, one householder and one household, one teacher and one school, one emperor and one commonwealth, one [Col. 1040A] leader and one army, one testator and one inheritance, one husbandman and one vine, one king and instructor and one people following him, one shepherd and one flock.

The holy apostles themselves, who were to be sent to preach throughout all the earth, besides those spiritual goods which they deserved to receive by hearing Christ’s teaching, seeing his miracles, and beholding his passion, resurrection, appearances, and ascension, were distinguished above other mortals, either uniquely or exceptionally, by certain further gifts of heavenly grace. Such gifts were the firstfruits of the Spirit, knowledge of languages, understanding of heavenly mysteries—as when blessed John understood that “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1)—the grace of miracles and wonders, power to tread upon the strength of evil [Col. 1040B] spirits, and wisdom for overthrowing the doctrines of philosophers. Hence blessed Paul speaks thus of the glory of apostolic dignity: “According to revelation the mystery was made known to me, which in other generations was not made known to the children of men, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets, namely, the new prophets in the Spirit: that the Gentiles are co-heirs, fellow-members of the body, and sharers in his promise in Christ Jesus” (Eph. 3). In all these things God placed a sign in the apostles, that they might be ministers to the nations and stewards of evangelical preaching.

“And I will send from them,” he says, “to the nations—to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia holding the arrow, to Italy and Greece, to the distant islands.” He sets forth and distinguishes by name six things: the sea, Africa, Lydia, [Col. 1040C] Italy, Greece, and islands, in order to signify, through the perfection of the number six, that the fullness of the Gentiles would enter perfectly into Christian faith through apostolic and evangelical preaching proclaimed throughout the whole world. The sea, named first, and the islands, placed last, ought to be explained together rather than separately, because they are neighbors in their physical position. Thus the sea, which never remains in the same condition but is always in motion, rightly signifies those who fluctuated through the worship of different idols or through various vices. The islands, however, which stand unmoved amid the waves, fittingly represent those who lived in faith in the true God and in good conduct. Job, for example, was like an island: though a Gentile, a man without the Law amid unbelievers and sinners, he believed rightly and lived holily. And concerning such persons [Col. 1040D] the Apostle says: “When Gentiles who do not have the Law naturally do the things of the Law, these, having no Law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts accusing or else defending one another, on the day when the Lord will judge the secrets of human beings according to my Gospel through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 2).

Or certainly, under the name of islands we may suitably understand those Gentiles who persisted in the worship of some single image, or in the pleasure of any single vice, and did not fluctuate among different things. Then come Africa, Lydia, Italy, and Greece. Of these four regions Lydia lies to the east, Italy to the west, [Col. 1041A] Greece to the north, and Africa to the south. These four therefore rightly designate the four quarters of the world, and figure the apostolic preaching that would be spread throughout the whole world.

Another interpretation: Lydia, which is in the east, where the sun’s radiance first shines out, signifies cunning. Italy, which is in the west, where the sun’s brightness fails, signifies ignorance—cunning, I mean, in evil; ignorance, of good. And observe that, when he has said “to Lydia,” he adds, “holding the arrow.” For Lydians are wise archers. “The children of this age are wiser in their generation in evil cunning than the children of light” (Luke 16). Their heart, devising evil, is a quiver; their mouth and tongue, a bow; their speech, an arrow; the hearer’s wicked assent and his heart’s delight, the wound. “For evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). Greece, which stretches toward the north, where the sun’s warmth grows cool, expresses the cold malice of the human heart. Hence the prophet Jeremiah says concerning Jerusalem: “As a cistern makes its water cold, so she makes her wickedness cold” [the printed reading is *militiam*, “military service,” apparently corrupt] (Jer. 6). Africa, which lies in the south, where the sun burns, signifies lust and sensuality.

Thus the Lord sends, as it were, to all these places to call his elect, because through holy preaching he leads them away from the vices which, as we have said, they signify, onto the way of truth and righteousness. Some, therefore, are called from the sea, others from islands, others from Lydia, others from Italy, others from Greece, others from Africa: because some are justified through God’s grace from the harmful fluctuation of vice, others from obstinate fixedness, [Col. 1041C] others from the cunning of this present age, others from blindness of mind, others from malice, and others from sensuality.

“I will send,” he says, “to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory, and they shall announce my glory to the nations.” Hence the saying: “Those to whom it was not announced concerning him shall see” (Isa. 66). For Jesus died for the nation—and not only, that is, for the Jewish nation, but in order that he might gather into one the children of God who were dispersed, that is, those predestined from among the Gentiles to eternal life (John 11): into the unity of faith with the chosen Jews. “And they shall bring your brothers from all nations as an offering to the Lord.” Your brothers always by predestination, then also by faith, but meanwhile enemies through the worship of idols. An offering to the Lord: the apostles offered to the Lord the souls of the Gentiles whom they had gained by their preaching, as the fruit of their labors. [Col. 1041D]

“On horses, and in chariots, and in litters, and on mules, and in carts.” A horse is an animal trained by the bridle, suited for war, swift of foot, and useful and necessary for carrying or drawing burdens. Therefore, in being bridled, it signifies restraint of vices; in being suited for war, subjection of demons; in being swift of foot, promptness in good work; in drawing or carrying burdens, obedience and endurance in any fruitful labor. Chariots signify the fulfillment of the four Gospels, or the exercise of the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. A litter is said to be a kind of vehicle in which the person carried rests as if in a bed; thus it suitably signifies the repose of inward contemplation. A mule is a barren animal, and therefore expresses the continence of those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. A cart has two wheels and thereby signifies wisdom and teaching.

Those, then, who vigorously restrain their vices, powerfully overcome demons, perform good works without sloth, and obediently endure labors laid upon them, are brought on horses. Those who fulfill in deed the precepts of the four Gospels and manfully practice the four chief virtues are brought in chariots. Those who leave behind the affairs of the active life and rest in the peace of divine contemplation [Col. 1042B] are brought in litters. Those who, despising carnal allurements and setting marriage aside, love the purity of chastity, are brought on mules. Those who devote themselves to the pursuit of wisdom and diligently attend to the word of teaching are brought in carts.

“To my holy mountain Jerusalem.” The holy mountain is Christ; Jerusalem is the Church. Jerusalem is built upon the mountain: the Church is founded upon Christ. “Just as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.” The offering is understood especially as love, without which other things do not deserve life before God. A clean vessel is a clean heart, a clean body, a clean work. “And I will take some of them as priests and Levites.” This, beloved, especially concerns us, who perform priestly and Levitical office in God’s house [Col. 1042C] and minister at the altar in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. For this is our saving and splendid dignity, provided that by serving worthily, according to the capacity of human frailty, we preserve it.

Concerning the sublimity of this dignity and ministry, blessed Gregory writes thus in the book of *Dialogues*: “Who among the faithful can doubt that, at the very hour of immolation, at the priest’s voice, the heavens are opened in that mystery of Jesus Christ; that choirs of angels are present; that things below are joined with things above; that earthly things are united to heavenly; and that visible and invisible things become one? But when we do this, it is necessary that we sacrifice ourselves to God in contrition of heart. For we who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s passion ought to imitate what we do. Then [Col. 1042D] the offering will be truly for us, when we have made ourselves an offering.” From these words, brothers, we may judge what sort of persons we ought to be in our ministry.

But in order that you may exercise this same ministry with still greater reverence, we write to you a recent event, which we know with complete certainty because our abbot related and recorded it for us. A certain priest in the province of Sens, entrusted with the care of a baptismal church, performed parochial ministry. Inclined to fleshly desires, he defiled by feminine touch the members which ought to have served the sacraments. He preferred shameful and unlawful embraces to sacred pursuits, and did not preserve in practice the continence which he had promised by vow. Among others, he was accustomed to visit one particular little woman frequently; through her unclean cohabitation he corrupted his conscience inwardly [Col. 1043A] and his reputation outwardly. He had already become accustomed to his filth, and yet it was wickedness that did not permit him to grow old in it.

Very often, after the foul and illicit intercourse of his shamefulness, when he approached the Lord’s sacraments imprudently and shamelessly, a marvelous and pitiable vision met him, by which he might either be corrected though undeserving, or kept away though unworthy. In the very chalice he seemed to see the image of a venomous toad, crawling and swimming through the currents of the sacred liquid; and the horror of the sight scourged the wretched conscience of the fornicating priest. As though by true proofs and eyewitness certainty, the Apostle cried out to him: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 10). Yet he received it in fear and, amid these punishments, completed the sacrifices. He confessed to his archbishop that this had happened to him more than a hundred times, and only after a night in which he had made Christ’s members the members of a prostitute. [Col. 1043B]

At last pierced with compunction and mindful of God’s patience, which was leading him to repentance, he prostrated himself before his archbishop with a great outpouring of tears. He recounted the affair in order, confessed and renounced his former uncleanness, explained the manner of his correction through the matters we have mentioned above, resigned his parochial cure, and, entering the Cistercian order in a monastery, bore worthy fruits of repentance, as I believe. I was present when he alone disclosed to the archbishop alone what has been said, and in fear I gave praise to God, “who calls the things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4).

Let us examine our own life by such sayings, and consider whether we are in the regions [Col. 1043C] of the aforementioned vices, or in the vehicles of virtues, or in the order of priests and Levites. If we are in evil, let us turn away from evil; if in good, let us strive to advance from good to better, so that, aided by the merits and prayers of the apostles whose feast we celebrate today, we may deserve to attain their joys. May he grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LI. On Septuagesima

“By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, while we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136). We were citizens of Jerusalem and became citizens of Babylon. Jerusalem is Paradise; Babylon is the world. In the first parent, in whom we sinned, we were transferred [Col. 1043D] from Jerusalem to Babylon, from Paradise into the world, from homeland into exile, from jubilation into mourning, from rest into labor, from joy into sorrow, from freedom into slavery, from glory into disgrace, from pleasure into hardship, from happiness into misery, from delights into hunger, from wholeness into corruption, from life into death. Rightly, then, we sit; rightly we weep by the rivers of Babylon: the rivers of Babylon are the courses of our corruption, the courses of our mortality. Rightly we sit; rightly we weep, while we remember Zion, while we recall divine contemplation, which we lost when Adam sinned. Rightly we sit; rightly we weep, because we are not able worthily to sing in a foreign land the delightful and perfect song of the Lord—that pure and true *alleluia* which Adam, still innocent, sang with a most pure mouth, and which we lost when he sinned. “For praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15).

For which of us all—indeed, which mortal, however righteous—would dare to compare himself with the innocence which Adam had before sin? For Scripture testifies: “We all offend in many things” (Jas. 3); “all our righteousness is as a menstrual cloth” (Isa. 64); “a child of one day is not without sin upon the earth” (Job 15, according to the Septuagint); and “no living person shall be justified in God’s sight” (Ps. 142). Therefore, insofar as we are sinners, we sing the Lord’s song less worthily than he who was so righteous that he was not a sinner even in the least degree. Let us therefore sit [Col. 1044B] and weep. Let us sit by humbling ourselves; let us weep in grief for our exile. Let us sit, because it is vain for us, who eat the bread of sorrow, to rise before the light (ibid.). When, then, shall we rise? When God has given sleep to his beloved and the Lord’s inheritance has been revealed: children, the reward, the fruit of the womb (ibid.)—namely, the womb of the Church, which now bears her children through many tribulations.

Concerning this sitting and rising, blessed Peter says: “Humble yourselves beneath the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5). Let us also weep so that afterward we may laugh, because, according to Solomon, “there is a time for weeping and a time for laughing” (Eccl. 3): a time for weeping in the world, a time for laughing in heaven. For when the Lord has turned our captivity, our mouth shall be filled with joy [Col. 1044C] and we shall become glad (Ps. 125), because when “this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 13), we shall enter the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all, singing *alleluia* and rejoicing.

Certainly, the time of Septuagesima, upon which we now enter, signifies the entire duration of this present age, which turns through seven days, in which we are held under the hardship of our corruptibility and mortality. Hence, in order to signify our misery and groans, under which we are oppressed in this life, we fittingly now omit *alleluia* and *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, which are heavenly and angelic songs, and sing the long Tracts, which signify the long labors and pains [Col. 1044D] of the present life. For John testifies in the Apocalypse that *alleluia* is a heavenly song, where he says: “I heard the voice of many multitudes in heaven saying, Alleluia” (Rev. 19). That “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2) is the song of angels, no one among the faithful is unaware.

According to the rubric of the sacramentary and antiphonary, Septuagesima is reckoned from nine weeks before the Lord’s Passover, and ends after the Lord’s Passover on the seventh day, that is, Saturday. It begins on the Lord’s Day on which “The sorrows of death surrounded me” is sung, and ends on the seventh day of Easter week, that is, Saturday. We have a pattern and example for the institution and observance of this holy season in the seventy years during which the ancient people of God, their sins requiring it, were carried into Babylon and held in slavery; they sat and wept by Babylon’s rivers while remembering Zion. Thus the institutor of Septuagesima made these seventy days correspond to the seventy years, so that we too might sit and mourn in these days, because in certain sins we share fellowship with the former people. Yet they, because they served as slaves, suffered affliction unwillingly; whereas we, because we are free, undergo voluntary affliction. The number seventy, however, signifies not only that we must abstain and mourn during these days, but also that throughout the whole time of our life—which turns through seven days and in which we are exiles from the heavenly Jerusalem—we ought to be in repentance and mourning, especially if we have fallen into grave sins after baptism.

[Col. 1045B] Moreover, we read in the prophet Zechariah that, when the time was imminent for the captivity of God’s people to be ended, the angel who spoke in the prophet himself prayed to the Lord, saying: “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you are angry? This is the seventieth year.” And the Lord answered the angel with good and consoling words (Zech. 1). And we, beloved, have good words, consoling words: namely, the first resurrection, through which we await the second. We have justification, through which we hope for immortality. The Apostle sets forth these two things, one of which we possess in actuality and the other in hope, when he says: “If Christ is in you, indeed the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives because of justification. But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he shall also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8). [Col. 1045C]

We rise now: catechumens indeed through the grace of baptism, and not through penance. We rise now, I say, unto righteousness; but on the day of judgment we shall rise unto glory. *Alleluia*, which we sing daily at Mass on the six weekdays of Easter, signifies this first resurrection for us. The two *alleluias* which we sing on the Saturday of Easter week express both resurrections together, since that Saturday signifies the completion of our Septuagesima, that is, of our whole temporality. For now we sing, as it were, one simple *alleluia*, because we enjoy justification alone; but then we shall sing a double *alleluia*, when we enjoy immortality as well. The six Easter days signify, in the ancient people, the return from Babylon to Jerusalem; Saturday signifies their arrival. In us, they signify the number six of good works by which we ought to strive toward heavenly blessedness; Saturday, moreover, signifies entry into it. Or certainly, by the one *alleluia* which we sing daily during the six Easter weekdays, we may understand the first robe of the saints; by the double *alleluia* which we sing on Saturday, we may understand both the first and the second robe together.

Therefore we have good words, consoling words. What we possess is good; what we await is better. “For we know in part and prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away. Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13). [Col. 1046A]

Therefore, while we must always rejoice in the Lord because of these good and consoling words, so long as we live we must always sit and always weep; we must remember Zion, sigh for the heavenly Jerusalem, and say with the Psalmist: “If I forget you, Jerusalem,” etc. (Ps. 136). For so long as we live, we are exiles, captives, and pilgrims. Let us therefore be miserable, mourn, and weep. Let our laughter be turned into mourning and our joy into sorrow. Let us always remember Solomon’s saying: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7). And again: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. 14).

But, alas for sorrow! The rigor of the order has fallen into such decay, and the discipline of correction, the honorableness of religion, the seriousness, maturity, and modesty of holiness have been so degraded that, in the opinion of many, those who shrink from uttering witty words or words that provoke laughter, or who do not wish to contort themselves in guffaws, are judged hypocrites and ridiculed because they do not laugh. Yet among them, whoever dissolves himself inwardly and pours himself out in laughter and jest is called a witty, courtly brother of good cheer. But do we anywhere read that Christ brought laughter into the world or laughed? Far from it! Rather, we find that he was sorrowful and wept. Hence he says: “Woe to you who laugh now, for [Col. 1046C] you shall weep!” (Luke 6).

Let us therefore choose, beloved, to weep now so that afterward we may laugh, and to be sorrowful so that we may rejoice. A certain holy Father teaches us perfectly, in few words, that we must utterly abhor the laughter of foolish merriment. When he saw a certain brother laughing, he said to him: “Before heaven and earth, we shall render God an account of our entire life—and are you laughing?” Therefore, brothers, we who profess holiness not only by word but also by tonsure and dress—let us, I say, set aside the voice of useless joy and vain gladness; renouncing trifling speech, laughter, jokes, and the softness of vices, let us prefer the severity of virtues. For through the bitterness and severity of virtues and good works we shall attain the kingdoms of heaven. “For if we sow in tears, we shall reap in joy.” May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON LII. Likewise, on Septuagesima
Over the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered you, O Zion (Ps. 136). The ancient enemy, dearly beloved, who by his cunning drove our first parents from Paradise and made them subject to the misery of this present life, continually lies in wait for us while we are established in the spiritual Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of heavenly peace—in order to draw us away from the joys of its pleasantness and, carrying us off into Babylon—that is, the confusion of vices—to subject us to his servitude. For Jerusalem fittingly signifies the spiritual life [Col. 1047A], Babylon the carnal life; Nebuchadnezzar, the devil; captivity, sin.

Spiritual men, living in the spiritual Jerusalem, have various spiritual houses and, in them, various spiritual riches. They have houses through good conduct. For houses aptly signify conduct, because it is in them that we live. Smaller houses signify the beginning of good conduct; larger ones, the perfection of that conduct; the greatest, its consummation. The house of spiritual conduct is well founded upon the firm rock through faith; it is high through hope, broad through charity, and long through the long-suffering expectation of future goods. This spiritual house of the righteous man, and especially of the perfect man, is full of goods and gifts, as it is written: “Glory [Col. 1047B] and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures,” etc. (Ps. 111). And Wisdom, with whom the righteous person dwells, says in one place: “With me are riches and glory, lofty [or: proud; *superbae*] possessions and righteousness” (Prov. 8).

Thus the righteous and perfect inhabitant of Jerusalem—that is, the spiritual man—has, I say, in the house of his conduct: the gold of wisdom; the silver of eloquence; the grain of doctrine; the wine of holy joy; the oil of mercy; precious stones through the splendour of virtues; ornaments of varied garments through the performance of good works. He also has various kinds of vessels: “every small vessel, from the vessels of bowls even to every vessel of musicians” (Isa. 22). By bowls, from which is offered wine that gladdens the human heart, is rightly signified the grace of imparting consolation; [Col. 1047C] by musical vessels, the grace of divine praise. Finally, he has many spices, by which is figured the grace of good repute. But we do not delay over explaining all these riches, because we speak to those who know the law, and in other sermons we have often explained what matters of this kind signify mystically.

Therefore, when things are so ordered—that is, when the righteous are established in the beauty of peace and in abundant repose—the evil one comes with an army of tempting demons and flattering vices. He fiercely attacks the holy city, often captures it in certain persons, overturns the houses of their good conduct, deprives them of their spiritual goods, and takes them captive. If they prudently and manfully trampled upon the head of the ancient enemy—that is, the beginning of temptation [Col. 1047D]—they would not be conquered but would conquer; nor would the battle of temptation be for their guilt, but for their crown. Hence James says: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been proved, he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him” (Jas. 1). And earlier: “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience. But let patience have its perfect work, that you may be perfect and whole, deficient in nothing” (ibid.).

For the righteous person, who knows that, with the Apostle, he has obtained God’s mercy (1 Tim. 1), rejoices amid temptations and adversities and blesses God at every time. He knows that “he who endures to the end [Col. 1048A] shall be saved” (Matt. 10). He glories in labour and pain, and says with the Psalmist: “I found tribulation and misery, and I will call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114). Thus, whereas another calls upon God when tribulation comes, the holy man and unconquered warrior desires tribulation and misery to come, in order to exercise and prove himself. Understanding this, the Psalmist said to the Lord: “Prove me, O Lord, and test me; burn my reins and my heart” (Ps. 25).

Temptation, then, appears not to harm but to benefit, unless delight is admitted. But if delight is admitted and is not swiftly driven away, the strength of Christ’s soldier is weakened, as though he had already received a wound; and he stands, as it were, at the exit of his city, ready to surrender himself, defeated, to the enemy attacking and hurling missiles from without. If he consents, he has already surrendered himself and committed sin by consent alone, as it is written: “In your heart you work iniquities upon the earth” [Col. 1048B] (Ps. 57). For the will is reckoned as the deed; and there is no peace from God for human beings except for those of good will (Luke 2).

The first stage in this exile, therefore, seems to be delight; the second, deliberation; the third, action; the fourth, habit. Through these four, the whole path of this wretched exile is completed, all the way to the city of detestable confusion. Through these four the human mind is sometimes estranged from the vision of heavenly peace, so that, defiled and entangled by the totality of the seven principal vices, it is held captive in confusion, as if through a seventy-year number of years. And the seventy is indeed wretched in us—that is, the totality of present labours—but this seventy, the totality of vices, is much more wretched [Col. 1048C] and altogether more detestable. By the former we are miserable; by the latter we are also wicked.

Yet, by God’s disposing grace, such a soul, after it has been defiled by every vice and made the sport of every demon, strengthened by the word of life recovers its strength. It rises above the rivers of Babylon—that is, it sits over the flow of its own viciousness—and weeps because it has lost grace and committed guilt. By the command of Christ, the most mighty King, “the yoke shall decay because of the oil”; captivity is loosed, freedom is bestowed through compunction, confession, and satisfaction. Jerusalem is restored; the house of honourable conduct is rebuilt out of the stones and timbers of virtues and good works; and the soul redeemed by the Lord is wonderfully enriched with spiritual goods. “Its latter things become worse than its former”: “And the Lord blessed his latter end more than his beginning” (Job 42). For in place of its having been forsaken and hated, it is made “an eternal exaltation, a joy from generation to generation” (Isa. 60). It possesses joy and gladness; sorrow and groaning flee away. In place of its double confusion and shame, they shall praise its Father. And there is joy among God’s angels in heaven over one sinner doing penance, more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who need no repentance (Luke 15).

When the son who had perished is found, the Father rejoices; the best robe is brought forth, a ring is given on his hand and shoes on his feet; and, with the fattened calf killed, a feast is celebrated. Symphony and dancing are heard outside (ibid.) [Col. 1049A], and thenceforth there is “the sound of one feasting, in the voice of exultation and confession” (Ps. 41). Therefore now, dearly beloved, let us consider where we are. If we are outside Jerusalem, let us return to it as soon as possible. But if we see that we stand within it, let us hold fast what we possess, so that from that Jerusalem in which we now live we may deserve to pass to the heavenly one. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIII. On Making Confession and Paying Vows

“Behold upon the mountains the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace. Keep your feasts, Judah, and pay your vows; for Belial shall no longer pass through you: he has wholly perished” (Nah. 1).

It is read [Col. 1049B] in the book of Chronicles that, when Sennacherib was besieging Jerusalem, Passover could not be kept in the first month; but, after the army had been slain and Sennacherib’s death announced, Passover was celebrated in the second month (2 Chron. 32). Hence the prophet Nahum, addressing the people of God, says consolingly: “Behold upon the mountains the feet of one bringing good news, announcing peace,” etc. It is as though he said: “O Judah, do not be anxious. For, after your enemy has been slain in the temple of his god, a messenger comes to you, crossing the mountains and, as it were, announcing from a watchtower that Sennacherib is dead and the city delivered. Therefore, Judah, keep your feasts and pay to God the vows you promised on account of the enemy’s slaughter, because Belial—that is, the transgressor—shall not pass through you, since he has wholly perished.” The army, king, and empire of the Assyrians have utterly fallen [Col. 1049C].

These prophetic words, dearest brothers, insofar as they concern history according to what has been said, are to be believed with firm faith and embraced with every devotion. But we, who serve not according to the letter but according to the spirit, should leave aside those things that belong to the letter and seek, for our edification, what spiritual meaning lies hidden in them. Thus we may fittingly understand Sennacherib as the devil; his army as the whole multitude of demons and wicked people; Jerusalem, the holy city, as the universal Church; the siege as temptation or persecution; the killing of the king and his army as the overthrow of spiritual enemies; the mountains as virtues; the messenger [Col. 1049D] as teachers; the Jewish people as the people of believers; peace divinely bestowed as inward repose; and the celebration of Passover or any feast as the honourableness of holy conduct through the performance of a good work.

But now let us return to each point and describe them more fully. King Sennacherib signifies the devil. For he is king over all the children of pride and ruler of these darknesses—that is, of spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places. Jerusalem, which is the holy city and is interpreted “vision of peace,” rightly figures the holy Church, which is built as a city and sublimely contemplates the joys of inward, heavenly, and eternal peace. Therefore Sennacherib, with his army, surrounds and attacks the city Jerusalem when the ancient enemy, with his accomplices—demons or reprobate men—harasses and wears out the holy Church by temptations and persecutions. But through heavenly grace he flees, as though his army had been lost, and is slain when his entire endeavour is brought to nothing [Col. 1050A].

Mountains in Sacred Scripture can signify the virtues that, raising us from earthly things, lift us to heavenly things. One mountain is prudence; one mountain is fortitude; one mountain is justice; one mountain is temperance. Or rather, according to the evangelical description, one mountain is humility; one mountain is gentleness; one mountain is compunction of mind; one mountain is the desire for righteousness; one mountain is mercy; one mountain is purity of heart; one mountain is the inward peace of the mind.

The messenger or evangelist of peace is the universal order of preachers. This messenger is the company of prophets, the choir of apostles, the army of martyrs, the assembly of confessors. The feet of this messenger are principally understanding and affection. Through understanding, when it is rightly directed, error is avoided; through affection, corruption is guarded against. Understanding proceeds and advances through knowledge of the truth; affection through love of virtue. Concerning these mountains and the feet of this messenger, most purely walking upon those mountains, Isaiah speaks thus: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and preaching peace, announcing good, preaching salvation, saying: ‘Zion, your God shall reign’” (Isa. 52). Your God shall reign, not Sennacherib, not the devil.

By the Jewish people we understand the people of believers who confess God. For Judah [Col. 1050C] is interpreted “confessing.” Thus that people is rightly understood through Judah which confesses God not only with the lips but also in deed and truth. But those who honour God with their lips while their heart is far from him (Mark 7), and who, while confessing that they know God, deny him by their deeds (Titus 1), are the seed of Canaan, not of Judah.

There is one confession of sin and another of praise. Indeed, how pernicious and dangerous it is for a sinful person to conceal his sins, and how fruitful—indeed, necessary—it is to confess them, is declared by many authorities in Holy Scripture. Hence that passage in the Psalm: “Because I kept silent, my bones grew old, while I cried out all day long. By day and by night your hand was heavy upon me; I was turned in my misery while the thorn is fixed” [reading uncertain] (Ps. 31). This concerns the ruin brought by silence. “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my injustice. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (ibid.). This concerns the benefit of confession.

And Solomon says in Proverbs: “He who conceals his crimes shall not be set right; but he who has confessed and forsaken them shall obtain mercy” (Prov. 28). The words “he who conceals his crimes shall not be set right” demonstrate the ruin of silence; the addition, “but he who has confessed,” etc., demonstrates the benefit of confession. Blessed James also shows this benefit in the New Testament, saying: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (Jas. 3). The ancient law likewise commands confession and sends people to priests so that they may confess their sins and receive pardon. If, therefore, transgression was then wiped away by offering and confession, when there was still only a shadow and confession of sin ought rather to fear punishment than expect mercy, how much more should confession now be made under grace, when punishment is not so much to be feared as pardon hoped for?

Finally, blessed Augustine testifies that confession is altogether necessary for a sinner, saying: “No one can be justified from sin unless he has confessed before the sin.” Likewise Bede, on the Epistle of James: “Without confession,” he says, “sins cannot be forgiven.”

By such great and numerous authorities we are taught, dearly beloved [Col. 1051B], that confession is not merely useful but necessary for the sinner. But if perhaps the sinner truly repents and yet, through an intervening emergency, cannot come to confession, it must firmly be believed that in him the highest Priest accomplishes what a mortal could not; and before God that is held to be already done which the person truly wished but was unable to fulfil, because not contempt but necessity excluded confession. “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33). And the Psalm says: “I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31). And the lepers, while going to show themselves to the priests, were cleansed (Luke 17).

For the salvation of the sinner begins when he truly groans over his sins. Yet that salvation is made complete when he confesses with his mouth that for which he groaned. And although, as has been said, this completion of salvation is prevented by an emergency, it is nevertheless fulfilled by the highest Priest, to whom all things are possible. In making confession, however, this distinction should be observed: daily and slight sins should be confessed mutually to equals, so that we may be saved by prayers offered for one another. But the uncleanness of a graver leprosy we should disclose to the priest—that is, to our highest superior, namely the abbot—so that we may endeavour to be justified according to his judgment.

For there is a common confession and penance in the Church which we make daily to one another; in it, through prayer poured out for one another, we obtain pardon and remission for daily [Col. 1051D] and slight sins. But the guilt of a graver fault we disclose by individual confession to the priest, and according to his counsel, by presenting the offering of satisfaction, we obtain forgiveness of sin. There are certain sins that would be regarded as very slight unless Scripture showed them to be more serious than people suppose. Who, for example, would consider someone who says to his brother, “Fool!” guilty of Gehenna, unless Truth himself had said it? (Matt. 5). Yet he immediately provided a remedy for this wound in the command of brotherly reconciliation, saying: “If you offer your gift before the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then, when you return, you shall offer your gift” (ibid.).

Or who would think how great a sin it is to observe days, months, and years, as do those who wish or do not wish to begin something on certain days, months, or years because, according to the empty teachings of human beings, they regard particular times as fortunate or unfortunate—unless we weighed the greatness of this evil from the Apostle’s fear, when he says to such persons: “I fear for you, lest perhaps I have laboured among you in vain” [Col. 1052A] (Gal. 4).

There are also certain other sins that would seem to some persons to be no sins at all unless they were made known by the testimonies of Sacred Scripture. A man’s intercourse with his wife not for the begetting of children but only for carnal pleasure and lust might be thought not to be sin, unless the Apostle, speaking of this duty, had said: “Do not defraud one another, except perhaps for a time by mutual consent, that you may be free for prayer; and return together again, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control,” and had added: “But I say this by way of concession, not commandment.” Who can deny that it is sin when apostolic authority admits that forgiveness is granted to those who do it?

It might likewise be thought not to be a sin if a brother disputed with his brother over his own affair, not outside the Church but within it, and not before wicked people, whom the Apostle rebukes terribly, but before believers; he might say that he suffers an injustice which he desires a judge’s verdict to remove from him. I say, this might be thought not to be a sin unless the Apostle added: “Already indeed it is altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another” (1 Cor. 6). And lest anyone, flattering himself and claiming to have a just case, should wish to excuse himself on this account, the Apostle immediately meets such thoughts by saying: “Why do you not rather accept injury? Why do you not rather suffer fraud?” (ibid.). But the Lord says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and contend with you in court, let him have your cloak also” (Matt. 5). And elsewhere: “From one who has taken what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke 6). Thus he forbade his own people to have litigation over secular affairs with others; and from this teaching the Apostle calls it a fault among those who contend.

Nevertheless, since he permits it to take place in the Church, with brothers judging brothers, while terribly forbidding it outside the Church, it is evident that this is allowed by way of pardon to the weak. He also indicates that it can be allowed to the weak where, above, he said reproachfully: “Is there then no wise person among you who can judge between his brother? But brother contends in court with brother—and this before unbelievers?” (1 Cor. 6).

Because of these and similar sins, and also other sins perhaps less than these, which occur through offences of word and thought, and because the Apostle James confesses and says, “For in many things we all offend” (Jas. 3), we must pray to the Lord daily and frequently, saying: “Forgive us our debts,” etc. (Matt. 6), and not lie in what follows: “As we also forgive our debtors” (ibid.). What sins are light and what are grave must therefore be weighed not by human but by divine judgment.

[Col. 1053A] Concerning diligence in confession, blessed Augustine writes as follows: “Let the sinner consider the character of the crime in its place, time, persistence, variety of persons, the temptation by which he committed it, and the manifold performance of the vice itself.” For the fornicator must repent according to the eminence of his rank or office; or according to the character of the prostitute and the character of his act; and according to how he performed the shameful act—whether in a sacred place, whether at a time appointed for prayer, such as festivals and seasons of fasting. Let him consider how long he persisted, and weep because he sinned so persistently; and let him consider by what assault he was overcome in such persistence. For there are some who are not merely conquered but offer themselves voluntarily to sin: they do not wait for temptation but anticipate pleasure.

[Col. 1053B] And let him consider within himself by what manifold action of vice he sinned pleasurably. All this variety must be confessed and wept over, so that, when he has recognized what sin is, he may swiftly find God merciful. In recognizing the increase of the sin, let him discover at what age he was, of what wisdom, and of what order. Let him dwell on each of these points and perceive the measure of his crime, cleansing every quality of vice with tears. Let him weep for the virtue that he lacked in the meantime. For it must be lamented not only that he sinned, but also that he deprived himself of virtue. Let him also weep because, by offending in one point, he became guilty of all (Jas. 2). For he proved ungrateful, who, though full of virtues, did not fear God at all. Every sinner becomes more blameworthy in proportion as he is more acceptable to God. Thus Adam sinned more grievously because he abounded in every good.

In another way, by offending in one point he became guilty of all, because every virtue suffers loss from a single vice. Let him place himself wholly under the judgment and authority of the priest, reserving nothing of himself for himself, so that at the priest’s command he may be prepared to do everything to recover the life of his soul which he would do to avoid bodily death—and this with desire, because he recovers an infinite life. For one who is to become immortal ought gladly to do what, as one destined to die, he would do to postpone death. Let him always entreat God; let him offer God his mind and contrition of heart, and then, with assurance, offer what he can from his possessions. For “God looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4). He said first “upon Abel,” and then “upon his gifts.” Therefore the alms of the giver’s heart must be offered. One must consider not how much he gives, but with what mind and what affection he gives what he can.

Therefore, one who wishes to redeem his sins through a temporal offering should first offer his mind. Let him beware, led by shame, of dividing his confession within himself, so that he wishes to disclose different matters to different priests. For some conceal from one what they reserve to disclose to another; this is to praise oneself and tend toward hypocrisy, and always to lack the forgiveness which one vainly thinks to attain. Let him also beware lest he approach the Lord’s body before he is strengthened by a good conscience; and let him grieve that he does not yet dare to receive the saving food which he greatly desires. Let one who wishes to obtain the perfect grace of remission also restrain himself from games and worldly spectacles. [Col. 1054A] These are the worthy fruits of penance, disentangling the captive soul and restoring it to freedom.

Let us confess, dearly beloved, according to what has been said, everything in us that is sin and crime, so that in confession we may worthily sing those things that belong to divine praise; for “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Sir. 15). Whoever does not disclose the old things by confession does not bring forth the works of a new life. Whoever does not know how to mourn what weighs him down cannot bring forth what lifts him up.

Therefore let us confess and lament our sins, in which we have grown old, so that in the confession of divine praise we may be able to utter new songs. Of this confession it is written: “His confession is above heaven and earth” (Ps. 148): above heaven, namely through angels; above earth, through holy people. Likewise the Lord says through the Psalmist: “The sacrifice of praise shall honour me; and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49). Let whoever can consider how great a gift, how great a good it is worthily to praise God. In a manner suited to human capacity, that person worthily praises God who sings his praise with a pure heart and mouth. That person praises well who turns over in his heart what he utters with his mouth. That person praises well who has uprightness in his heart and praise upon his lips. For “praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32). Thus that person alone truly praises who demonstrates by life what he cries with his mouth.

There are people who praise God abundantly—indeed, excessively—with their mouths: tossing themselves about with unrestrained gesture, they indecorously shout his praise in disorderly voices. Yet by living badly, they blaspheme his commandments through contempt. While they praise God with their voice alone, though denying him by their deeds, they nevertheless think that they possess the vessels of song. They do not notice what is written in Malachi: “Behold, I shall cast an arm upon you and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities” [Col. 1054C] (Mal. 2).

But let us, dearly beloved, cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit. Being without spot or wrinkle, let us fittingly sound forth the praise of our Creator, because there is the way by which the salvation of God is shown and seen. “God is indeed known in Judah, but his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). By Judah, confession is understood; by Israel, contemplation. Therefore God is known in confession of sin, but better known in confession of praise. Yet he is most fully known, and his name is great, in contemplation of his majesty. Confession of sin belongs to beginners; confession of praise to those advancing; contemplation of divinity to the perfect.

Thus that people is rightly called Jewish which confesses God not only by voice but by conduct. Peace is granted also to such a people after its enemies have been extinguished, when, with the temptations of demons and persecutions of wicked people checked, inward repose for attending to God is divinely bestowed upon it. Finally, that person celebrates the Lord’s feasts who, by living well, honours God according to his strength for the received benefit of peace.

“And pay,” he says, “your vows.” A vow is a certain attestation of a voluntary promise, referring most properly to God alone and to the things that are God’s. For to make a vow is to establish oneself as bound and indebted to God by the attestation of a voluntary promise [Col. 1055A]. One who simply promises pledges that he will do something; but one who makes a vow calls witnesses to his promise and confirms his promise.

But we have learned from Scripture’s teaching that some vows are not to be kept. For it is written: “The vows of fools are to be broken.” By vows of fools we understand those made either concerning evil, or concerning a good thing in an evil manner. For example, if someone vowed to kill another person, or vowed that he would do anything else in which guilt was evident, this would be a vow concerning evil and would itself be evil; therefore it should not be paid. The first fault was to make the vow; the second would be in the act, if it were fulfilled.

Likewise, a vow made concerning a good thing, if it is not well made, is reckoned among the vows of fools that must be broken. A vow, even though it concerns a good thing, is not well made if it vows what is unlawful or what is not expedient. It is unlawful if a woman vows continence without her husband’s consent—or rather, against his objection. It is not expedient if someone promises by vow that, in fasting or any other work, he will do something beyond his strength and capacity. All these are reckoned among the vows of fools: vows that are either perverse and unlawful or indiscreet.

Again, certain vows admit substitution, while others do not. You have vowed gold; you may pay silver, because what is of lesser value may be greater in weight. You have vowed a pilgrimage to the Lord: it admits substitution if perhaps it is more expedient—as may happen—for you to remain in your own country and home. For if you can render there something else of equal value, whether in the labour of work, the devotion of virtue, or the usefulness of administration, it admits substitution [Col. 1055C]. You have vowed a fast, and here too substitution can occur, if perhaps this is not expedient—as may happen.

I say something further. You have vowed to serve God in a certain place, or in a particular habit, or in some community: I say that all this can be changed, because a place may be destroyed, people may die, and a habit may be altered. Do you suppose that you lose your soul because some place is laid waste or because people die? Only do not let what happens to them happen through you, nor let there remain undone in you what ought to have been done by you. There is no danger to you where there is no fault of yours. Do what you can, and as much as you can, and that is sufficient for you. No more is required from a good will than it is able to give.

But if you have vowed any of these things, or something similar, which can either be taken away against one’s will or changed by those willing it, and are in fact able to fulfil what you vowed, the substitution of your vow is not in your own discretion—even if you see some greater or better thing to be done. A dispensation may indeed be made for you, but it ought not be made by you. For, so far as lies in you, you owe what you vowed—this very thing and no other. You may not exchange one thing for another; but your superior, the administrator, may, if he knows it to be expedient and wishes, accept something else. If the same thing is given by you, it is a debt. If something else is accepted from another source, it is an indulgence.

Again, you have vowed your virginity to God and, after the vow [Col. 1056A], have lost it. Virginity, once lost, cannot be restored or recovered. What, then, will you give back to God for what you vowed and irrecoverably lost? Hear: restore your penance; restore contrition; restore humility. For bodily virginity, restore humility of heart. For flesh that has been broken, break your heart. You owed humility in itself even if you had retained virginity; and yet, if you cannot restore virginity, restore humility in its place, and it will make satisfaction both for itself and for virginity. See how great is the power of humility. Virginity is the companion of humility, and humility the companion of virginity; nevertheless, if humility is absent, virginity cannot make satisfaction, but if true humility is present, it can make satisfaction even if virginity is absent.

There is, however, a certain vow that admits no substitution. Hear Truth saying: “What exchange shall a man give for his soul?” (Matt. 16). It is as if he said, “None.” You see, then, that there is one thing that receives no substitution and admits no dispensation. If you vow this—or rather, because you vow it, for you cannot be good if you do not vow it—pay what you vowed, and pay the very thing you vowed. If you wish to give something else in exchange for it, he does not accept whatever that other thing may be. “Make vows,” he says, “and pay them to the Lord your God, all you who are around him and bring gifts to the Terrible One—to him who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible to all the kings of the earth” (Ps. 75).

Therefore vow and pay your spirit to God. If you vow and pay it, he will receive it. If you do not vow, or after your vow refuse to pay, he will take it away. If he takes away the spirit of princes, will he not be able to take away [Col. 1056C] your spirit? Therefore, if you pay it, he will reward you for what you have given; if you do not pay it, he will condemn you for what you have withheld. If you vow your soul, pay your soul. Do not think that you can pay your money in place of your soul. That would be to vow more and pay less, and it would not be an equal recompense. If you give what is yours to God and yourself to the devil, it is not an equal division. Along with your soul you may give God your money; you cannot give it instead of your soul, unless perhaps you wish to give your money for your soul in such a way that, when money has been given, your soul may become more acceptable through it. The soul, then, is the one thing that admits no substitution.

Finally, one kind of vow is hidden and made before God alone; another is manifest, also before human beings. A hidden vow broken is sin; a manifest vow broken is both sin and scandal. In the former God is offended; in the latter one sins against one’s neighbour. Better, however, not to vow than to vow and not to pay. This is like the judgment of blessed Peter: “It is better not to know the truth than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down” (2 Pet. 2).

“Keep,” he says, “your feasts and pay your vows, because Belial shall no longer pass through you: he has wholly perished.” If by Belial, which is interpreted “without a yoke,” we fittingly understand the devil, then by Belial in his entirety we may not unfittingly understand the devil together with the whole multitude of demons and reprobate people. Belial in his entirety perishes for us [Col. 1057A] when the devil, together with all evil spirits and reprobate people, being divinely restrained, loses the power to persecute and tempt us. And our God reigns, because when the kingdom of the devil falls in us, the kingdom of Christ arises and remains.

Therefore now, dearly beloved, if we are not the seed of Canaan but Judah—namely that Judah of whom it is written, “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. 49)—let us first confess our sins, then offer the sacrifice of praise to the Lord, and pay our vows to the Most High in due time, so that we may reign with him in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIV. In Lent

[Col. 1057B]

You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample down the lion and the dragon (Ps. 90 [91]).

At this most sacred season, dearly beloved, as the holy custom annually sets before us, the heavenly trumpet is heard in the camp of the Church; the Christian army is summoned; the pay of spiritual instruction is distributed; Christ’s soldier is girded; he enters the field of holy abstinence to do battle with the devil; fortified with the weapons of virtues and good works, he advances; battle is joined, victory is hoped for, the enemy is conquered, triumph is borne home, the crown is bestowed, and the peace sought through war is possessed more securely. Christ’s soldier ought not, when the trumpet of heavenly exhortation sounds, to tremble at the encounter with a mighty enemy [Col. 1057C], since the teaching of the Gospel history tells him that his leader, strong and armed, overcame him long ago. The strong armed man is the devil; his court is the world; his weapons of deceit are spiritual frauds and wiles; the vessels are human beings; the stronger one who comes upon him is Christ; the plundering of the vessels is the redemption of human beings (Luke 11).

Christ therefore came into the world in order to free the human race, and to send upon the earth not peace but a sword (Matt. 10). “Cursed, therefore, is he who does the work of God negligently, and who keeps his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). And, as Solomon says, first there is a time of war, and afterwards a time of peace (Eccles. 3). The time of war is in the world; the time of peace is in heaven. Let us therefore fight according to our strength, so that, victory attained, we may rejoice in peace. But if we neglect to fight and conquer, we shall be attacked and conquered. For our enemy [Col. 1057D] neither sleeps nor slumbers (Ps. 120 [121]), but goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour (1 Pet. 5).
