In explaining this statement, let us take not our own words, but those of blessed Cyprian: “He,” he says, “goes about each one of us; and like an enemy besieging a closed city, he explores the walls and tests whether there is any part of the members less firm and less faithful, by whose entrance penetration may be made into the interior.” He presents enticing forms to the eyes, and torches of pleasure [the text reads *faces voluntatis*, “torches of will”], in order to destroy chastity by sight. He tempts the ears through melodious music, so that by hearing a sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue to fault; by injuries that incite, he urges the hand toward the wantonness of the heart. To make a person fraudulent, he sets unjust gains before him. To capture the soul through money, he suggests ruinous [Col. 1058A] profits; he promises earthly honors in order to take away heavenly ones. He displays false things in order to steal away true ones. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens plainly and openly. He holds out the terror of a troubled persecution in order to overthrow the servants of God—ever restless and ever hostile, deceitful in peace and violent in persecution. Therefore the mind must stand equipped and armed against all the devil’s deceptive snares or open threats, as ready to resist as the enemy is always ready to attack.

Now there are four things—the asp, basilisk, lion, and dragon—which we set at the beginning of the sermon, and through which we can and ought to understand the devil’s universal malice. They relate concerning the asp that, when it begins to suffer an enchanter who summons it from its cave by certain special spells, if it does not wish to come out, it presses one ear to the ground and blocks and covers the other with its tail; thus, not hearing those magical utterances, it does not emerge. Therefore the asp, which stubbornly preserves itself against the enchanter’s voice by blocking its ears so that it may not emerge, fittingly represents the devil’s deaf and insensible obstinacy against us. Hence it is said in the psalm concerning those whom he makes hardened in evil and obstinate through the fault of their own malice: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which will not hear the voice of charmers, nor of the enchanter charming skilfully” (Ps. 57 [58]).

The enchanter charms skilfully when the learned teacher preaches wisely and strives with all [Col. 1058C] his strength to lead the sinner from the hidden places of his perversity to the light of truth. But the asp blocks its ears with earth and tail, so that it may not hear the enchanter’s voice and come out, when the sinner, on the one hand overcome by love of earthly things, and on the other flattering himself with hope of a future amendment—which some are thought to attain near the end of life or at its very end—labors by every means not to obey the righteous person’s warnings in the present. Thus the asp fittingly represents the devil, who stubbornly persists in his malice against us as though deaf and insensible. It also rightly signifies the sinner who, driven into his evil habit, stubbornly resists lest he yield to righteous warnings.

But we, dearly beloved, should continually and long charm the devil—whom we said is principally denoted here [Col. 1058D] by the asp—by prayers poured out to God and holy admonitions directed to one another, until we mightily cast out from our own hearts and those of our brethren both his obstinacy by which he rages against us and his deadly venom.

*Basilisk* in Greek is rendered in Latin *regulus*, “little king,” because it is king of serpents: indeed, those seeing it flee, since it kills serpents with its breath; nevertheless, it is overcome by weasels. A weasel is said to be, as it were, a “long mouse,” for *telon* [τέλον] means “long.” A weasel, therefore, is a long, small, and clever animal. Through the basilisk, then, because it is king among creatures of its own kind, we rightly understand the devil’s pride. For he is “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41). He also kills serpents with his breath, when, by breathing evil suggestions upon some who ought to be prudent as serpents, he often puts them to death through sin [Col. 1059A]. Yet he is overcome by weasels when he is defeated by those who are small through humility of heart, long—or rather long-suffering—through perseverance in good work, and prudent through the keenness of discernment.

The lion, which fiercely rages against other beasts, rightly denotes by its ferocity and savagery the devil’s savage cruelty. Finally, the dragon has its strength not in its teeth but in its tail, and harms more by lying in ambush and hiding than by raging openly; not even the elephant is safe from it by reason of its body’s size. For, hiding around the paths by which they customarily walk, it binds their legs in knots and kills them once suffocated. Therefore, as the lion expresses the devil’s manifest cruelty, so the dragon [Col. 1059B] fittingly denotes his hidden cunning. Thus, as was shown above, the devil is an asp by insensible obstinacy, a basilisk by exalted pride, a lion by manifest savagery, and a dragon by hidden malice. But Christ’s soldier conquers and tramples down the asp, basilisk, lion, and dragon when he wisely and mightily defeats all his wickedness, which is figured by these four.

To win the palm of this victory we are also encouraged by the Savior’s own words, when he says, speaking to the apostles: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke 10). For he gave power to overcome hostile powers not only to the apostles but also to all his faithful people; he deigned to give an example of fighting against them not only to those apostles but to all who believe in him. Hence too he said to the eleven apostles as they reclined: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons” (Mark 16). And again, shortly afterward: “They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not harm them” (ibid.).

But, brothers, because we do not do these things bodily and visibly, do we therefore not believe? Far from it! Holy Church, as blessed Gregory says, now does spiritually every day what it then did bodily through the apostles. For when her priests, by the grace of exorcism, lay hands upon believers and forbid evil spirits to dwell in their minds, [Col. 1059D] what else do they do but cast out demons? And when through their good exhortations they remove malice from other people’s hearts, they take up serpents. And when they hear deadly suggestions but are nevertheless not drawn into evil action, they indeed drink what is deadly, but it does not harm them.

By all these things we are taught, brothers, to love not so much bodily signs, which may be held in common with the reprobate, as the spiritual signs of which we have spoken. These are all the safer because they are more hidden; and the less glory they bring among human beings, the greater is their reward before God. Hence too, when the disciples rejoiced because unclean spirits were subject to them, the Lord said: “Do not rejoice because spirits are subject to you. But rejoice because your names are [Col. 1060A] written in heaven” (Luke 10).

Therefore, dearly beloved, as we are about to fight the spiritual enemy, let us put on spiritual weapons: let us have the shield through faith, the helmet through hope, the breastplate through charity, the sword of the Spirit—which is the word of God—through preaching, and the long lance, raised toward God and directed against the enemy, through devout and unceasing prayer. Let us sit upon our beast of burden, so that we may subdue the wantonness of our flesh; let us put upon it the bridle of temperance and discernment, so that we may restrain it from what is unlawful and direct it along the path of righteousness. Let us urge it with the spurs of fasting and vigils, lest it grow sluggish in the exercise of virtues and the performance of good works. Let us be strong in war and fight with the ancient serpent, so that we may receive the eternal kingdom [Col. 1060B]. Let none of us grow sluggish while fighting enemies in the camp of this present life, lest, overcome, he lose the eternal kingdom. For the crown of the heavenly kingdom is reserved not for one who fights sluggishly, but for one who fights manfully and lawfully. Hence a certain poet aptly says:

> Shake off lethargy, you who seek heaven’s honor:  
> The glory of the heavenly kingdom will not be given to the slothful.

May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LV. On the Feast of Blessed Mary

“Like storax and galbanum, onycha and stacte, and like uncut Lebanon I gave forth fragrance in my dwelling; and my scent is like unmixed balsam. And like a terebinth I spread out my branches, and my branches are of honor and grace. I, like a vine, bore the fruit of sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are fruits of honor and dignity” (Ecclus. 24).

These most holy words, dearly beloved, which are most elegantly set forth in Ecclesiasticus through Jesus son of Sirach in praise of wisdom, are fittingly applied to the praises and magnificent virtues of the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary. For she, having been granted heavenly wisdom more fully than other mortals, overcame malice through the virtues represented by the things described here; she obtained the palm and possesses the crown. Truly, the Lord is her strength and praise, and has become her salvation: strength in battle, praise in victory, salvation in glory. Thus the blessed Virgin Mary can most rightly extol her virtues in praises of wisdom through the mouths of all the faithful, and commend the glory of her dignity throughout the whole Church. Let her therefore say—let her say, I repeat—uniquely before all mortals, let her say preeminently: “Like storax, galbanum, onycha, and stacte; and like uncut Lebanon I gave forth fragrance in my dwelling. And my scent is like unmixed balsam,” and so forth.

Storax, as books of natural science report, when taken in a drink removes hoarseness and clarifies the voice. It therefore fittingly represents the grace of divine praise. Blessed Mary clearly possessed this grace, because, having been pronounced blessed by Elizabeth for her faith, she sang praises to God, saying: “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1). She was therefore like storax, because, with her voice purified by heavenly grace from the hoarseness of sin, she most worthily sang the praise of God [Col. 1061A].

The fumigation of galbanum, as the same books attest, puts creeping things to flight. Creeping things fittingly signify the intrusion of shameful thoughts into human hearts. Thus the blessed Mother of God was truly like galbanum, because she drove every intrusion of unclean thought from the entrance to her heart. *Ungula*, as natural philosophers teach, is an herb shaped like a horse’s hoof and called by them *ungula caballina*, “horse-hoof.” Since it is of a cold nature, it can signify the extinction of badly enticing carnal desire. Therefore blessed Mary is rightly believed to have been like *ungula*, since there can be no doubt that she powerfully extinguished in herself the fire of carnal desire with the dew of heavenly grace [Col. 1061B].

*Gutta* drives away every swelling and puffiness, and for this reason fittingly expresses the virtue of perfect humility. The holy Mother of God possessed this virtue preeminently: when she was called the Mother of God by the angel, she humbly answered, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word” (Luke 1). “And like uncut Lebanon.” *Lebanon* means “whitening.” Blessed Mary, therefore, was like Lebanon through the whiteness of chastity, “uncut” through the integrity of virginity. Some say “unburned”: for she was like unburned Lebanon, because the pure-white flower of her chastity was not scorched by the fire of lust.

“Like storax,” he says, “and galbanum, onycha, and stacte; like uncut Lebanon I gave forth fragrance in my dwelling” [Col. 1061C]. For the glorious Virgin Mary—often named, always to be named, and never to be passed over in oblivion—made her dwelling fragrant with such spices, because through such virtues she set her holy way of life ablaze in order to drive away the cold of malice.

“And my scent is like unmixed balsam.” The balsam tree resembles a vine in trunk and rue in its leaves, which are paler and always remain. The tree is called *balsamum*, its wood *xylobalsamum*, and its fruit or seed *carpobalsamum*. When the bark of balsam is pierced by iron hooks, it emits a drop of extraordinary fragrance. It is adulterated by mixing in cypress oil or honey. If it is pure, it has such power that, when the sun has become hot, it cannot be held in the hand. The scent [Col. 1061D] of the blessed Virgin Mary is like unmixed balsam, because no stench of infamy corrupts her holy and sincere reputation, which filled earth and heaven.

“I spread out my branches like a terebinth; and my branches are of honor and grace.” The terebinth is a tree whose resin excels all other resins. It therefore fittingly signifies charity, of which it is said: “I show you a still more excellent way. Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels,” and so forth (1 Cor. 12–13). And shortly afterward: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, charity; but the greatest of these is charity.” This terebinth rises to heaven through love of God, and spreads its branches throughout the whole world through love of neighbor. Its branches are the exercise of the other virtues and the performance of good works. They are of honor [Col. 1062A] because of reverence, and of grace because of beauty: of honor for others, of grace in themselves. Its fruit is the delight of a good conscience inwardly before God; its leaves are the beauty of a good example outwardly before one’s neighbor. Blessed Mary therefore spread out her branches like a terebinth, because she was full of charity: she loved God above all things and her neighbor as herself.

“I, like a vine, bore the fruit of sweetness of fragrance.” The vine bears fruit when it flowers, and its fruit intoxicates. Thus blessed Mary, through the flower of her virginity, bore Christ, the cluster of our redemption, who intoxicates his elect in the world with the wine of grace and in heaven with the wine of glory. That cluster or fruit of this vine—that is, Christ—is well signified by the cluster which the two Israelite men, the scouts, carried into the wilderness upon a pole [Col. 1062B]. For he is the fruit of life to us, by which we are fed; and, as has already been said, he first pours out to us the wine of grace and then that of glory, by which we are intoxicated.

The two men, the scouts, represent the prophets and apostles, who, with the Holy Spirit as guide, explored the secrets of the heavenly homeland and brought Christ to us into this world through their Scriptures. The wood of the pole signifies the wood of the cross. And just as the man preceding among the two men carrying the cluster did not see the cluster hanging behind his back on the pole, so the preceding company of prophets did not see Christ on the cross. But the one following saw the cluster, because the choir of apostles, which remained in the world after him and departed the world after him, beheld him present in the flesh, suffering on the cross [Col. 1062C].

The ten scouts who turned the hearts of the children of Israel away from entering the promised land by evil words signify the unbelieving Jews placed under the Decalogue of the Law, who refuse to seek the heavenly promises through faith in Christ. But the two scouts who faithfully exhorted the people to enter that land represent the chosen Christians placed under the two commandments of charity, who desire with all their heart to enter the delight of the heavenly homeland.

The fruit of this vine is appropriately called “sweetness of fragrance,” because, through its breathing forth and proclamation, it is fragrant to us from the earth because it is sweet in heaven. But he who is now for us sweetness of fragrance in the world will afterwards be sweetness of taste for us in [Col. 1062D] heaven: he who is now sweetness of fragrance in faith will then be sweetness of taste in contemplation; he who is now sweetness of fragrance in hope will then be sweetness of taste in reality. “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then we shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13).

“And my flowers,” he says, “are fruits of honor and dignity.” The flowers of the blessed Virgin—that is, her virtues, chastity, charity, and humility, blooming without withering—are flowers of honor and dignity, because Christ, her fruit, who came forth from the Virgin adorned with these flowers, grants honor and dignity to his elect upon earth and promises to give them to those same persons in heaven. The blessed Mother of God therefore bore fruit like a vine, because she brought forth Christ, the true cluster, who never ceases to intoxicate us with the wine of grace and glory. But [Col. 1063A]—what is wonderful to say—this fruit alone did not take the flower from his mother, but preserved and beautified it.

Therefore the blessed and undefiled Virgin Mary, beyond other mortals, was filled with the spices of heavenly wisdom: like storax, through the clearest—that is, most worthy—singing of divine praise; like galbanum, through the expulsion of every unclean thought; like *ungula*, through the extinction of carnal desire; like *gutta*, through the suppression of all self-exaltation; like uncut Lebanon, through the integrity of pure-white chastity; like unmixed balsam, through sincere reputation; like a terebinth, through true charity; like a vine, through singular fruitfulness.

There are very many things, brothers, which could, indeed ought, to be said about all these matters in praise of the holy Virgin Mary; but the shortness of time and the extended celebration of divine praise forbid us to dwell upon them longer. Nor should we hold the day up with speech; for, as a word spoken at the proper time is best, so one who moderates his lips is most prudent. Let us now therefore return to ourselves and strive according to our strength to imitate blessed Mary in the things that have been said, so that through her merits and prayers we may be glorified with her. Let us too be like storax, celebrating God’s praise with the voice of our hearts made clear; like galbanum, fumigating away the creeping things of useless thoughts by devout prayers; like *ungula*, extinguishing the lust of the flesh; like *gutta*, subduing the pride of the heart; like Lebanon, guarding bodily chastity; like balsam, spreading a good reputation everywhere; [Col. 1063C] like a terebinth, loving God above all things and our neighbor as ourselves. In all these things let us imitate blessed Mary during the brevity of time, so that with her we may deserve to glory in the duration of eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LVI. On the Obedient Soul

We read in the page of the Old Testament concerning Ruth the Moabitess that, clinging to Naomi her mother-in-law and obeying her commands, she deserved to be joined in marriage to Boaz, a powerful and wealthy man (Ruth 1). Naomi, whose name means “beautiful,” signifies an ecclesiastical teacher and pastor, adorned with various gifts of heavenly grace not only outwardly but also inwardly; one who, according to the Apostle, rejects the hidden things of dishonor, does not walk in craftiness, and does not adulterate the word of God. She is represented by a woman because she does not cease to bear and nourish spiritual offspring for God through her preaching. Hence the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4).

Ruth, whose name means “hastening,” signifies the soul that promptly obeys the holy admonitions of its superior, weaving no delays into the execution of commands. It knows that the Lord desires not so much holocausts or victims as obedience to his voice; and that obedience is better than sacrifice, and listening more than offering the fat of rams, since resistance is like the sin of divination and refusal to comply like the crime of idolatry (1 Sam. 15). Ruth therefore truly and rightly hastens when the obedient soul promptly bends its ear to all that is commanded it, whether such things seem honorable or shameful [Col. 1064A].

It must be known, however, that obedience is sometimes no obedience at all if it contains something of one’s own; and sometimes it is slight, even if it contains nothing of one’s own. For when a high position is commanded, the person who longs for it by his own desire empties obedience of its virtue. But when acts of humiliation proper to oneself are commanded, unless the mind desires them of itself, obedience diminishes its own merit, because it descends to them unwillingly. Hence Moses humbly refuses leadership of the people (Exod. 3). Paul boldly says: “I am ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem but also to die” (Acts 21).

Ruth therefore left her land and gods for Naomi’s sake when the truly obedient soul, stirred by the word or example of an ecclesiastical teacher, entirely sets aside all earthly things and delights offered by demons. It clings to that teacher inseparably when it gives a friendly assent to the precepts of his teaching. It follows him along every way in which he walks when it imitates him in avoiding vices and practising virtues. Finally, it dwells with him in Bethlehem when, within holy Church, it lives holily and honorably under his counsel or governance.

Boaz, whose name means “strength of God,” was a powerful man and one of great wealth, who had harvesters [the Latin appears as *mes ores*], and whose field was the one in which Ruth gathered ears of grain (Ruth 2); he signifies Christ. For with the Apostle we believe and confess Christ as “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1), who is a powerful man because “all power in heaven and on earth has been given to him” (Matt. 28) [Col. 1064C]. He is also of great wealth because in him are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2).

His field is holy Scripture. This field has barley here through the Old Testament, and wheat there through the New Testament. The harvesters are preachers who daily reap in this field teachings from which faithful souls may feast and be splendidly nourished. But the imperfect and weak do not reap sheaves; rather, they gather ears, because they grasp not the greatest things but the least. They do well to stand in the field from morning until evening, as Ruth did, because they labor manfully in order to proceed from the very beginning to perfection. Hence Boaz commanded his harvesters that, if they wished to reap with them—that is, to investigate and grasp greater things—they should not prevent them; rather, they should deliberately give them even from their own sheaves, so that they might not negligently instruct them even from their own teachings.

He also commanded his harvesters that no one should cause trouble to Ruth as she gathered ears, because every precaution must be taken lest anyone place a stumbling block before a soul beginning in goodness—that is, one recently come to faith or a good manner of life. Hence the Savior says: “Whoever receives one little child in my name receives me” [Col. 1065A] (Matt. 18). “But whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were drowned in the depth of the sea” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones. For I tell you that their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Rom. 14 [citation as printed]). A little one is one who begins what is good and has not yet ascended to the strength of virtue or the height of perfection.

Blessed Paul likewise says concerning not bringing the trouble of scandal upon weak brethren: “Rather judge this: not to place a stumbling block or offence before a brother.” And again: “Do not by your food destroy the one for whom Christ died” (ibid.). Hence he says again: “If food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat” (1 Cor. 8) [Col. 1065B]. And thereafter: “Give no offence to Jews, Gentiles, or the Church of God, just as I please everyone in all things, seeking not what is useful to myself but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10).

Boaz allowed Ruth to eat bread with his servants, dip her morsel in vinegar, and, when thirsty, drink from the water that was by the little burdens; because Christ, the most merciful master of the household, graciously gives the recently converted soul, together with his elect, the bread of sound teaching, lest it fail on the way of virtue and good work; the sharply pricking vinegar of fear, of which it is written, “Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I feared your judgments” (Ps. 118 [119]), lest it dissolve in prosperity; and the water of refreshing consolation, lest it be broken in adversity. For bread sustains, vinegar pricks, and water refreshes.

“If you are thirsty,” he says, “go to the little burdens and drink the waters of which the servants drink.” It should be noted concerning the water that one is commanded to seek it at the little burdens, because whoever willingly puts his shoulder beneath the burden of practising virtue and performing good work thereby deserves the refreshment of divine consolation. Hence the Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [94]). And again: “In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands in the night before him, and I was not deceived. My soul refused to be consoled”—that is, by earthly consolation—“I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76 [77]), having received, namely, divine consolation [Col. 1065D].

But whoever withdraws himself from the loving burden of virtue and good work deprives himself of the refreshment of heavenly consolation. Thus it is well said of Wisdom that it “is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28). Let whoever desires to drink the water of saving wisdom therefore go to the little burdens—that is, to the exercise and labor of virtue and good work. Moreover, Boaz’s saying not “burdens” but “little burdens” seems to accord with the Lord’s saying: “My yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11). And blessed John says: “His commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5).

For the divine commandments, called unbearable by the reprobate, are somewhat burdensome indeed to beginners and the weak, but are proved light to the perfect. The Psalmist shows that they are light to those who love God perfectly, saying: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118 [119]) [Col. 1066A]. Therefore Ruth has bread, vinegar, and water with Boaz’s servants, because the truly penitent soul has, together with pure and chosen souls believing in Christ, bread in instruction, vinegar in rebuke, and water in visitation. This bread gives the strength of sustenance, the vinegar the wholesomeness of fear, and the water the refreshment of consolation. The remnants of food that Ruth gathered can be understood as certain lesser words of sacred teaching, which the perfect leave behind when they both practise greater things in themselves and distribute them to others. Ruth gladly gathers these lesser things because to the hungry soul every least thing, even bitter things, seems great and sweet.

“Do not go,” he says, “to gather in another field; do not depart from this place, but join my maidens, and follow where they reap.” The other and foreign field is every book of heretics, in which Boaz dissuades Ruth from gathering ears, because Christ warns the soul converted to him not to receive the evil assertions of heretics. It is truly joined to his maidens then, and follows them in reaping, when it faithfully clings to holy souls and imitates them in sacred reading [Col. 1066B].

Thus Ruth, a foreign woman, gathers ears in Boaz’s field when the sinful but converted soul diligently reads the words of God; and it beats and threshes the gathered crop with a rod when, through careful meditation, it rightly distinguishes truth from falsehood, or spiritual meaning from the letter, in what it reads. Finally, it carries the gathered and threshed grain home when it commits what it reads and meditates upon, within its holy way of life, to the effect of good work. For the house in which one lives rightly signifies one’s way of life. Hence a certain Wise Man says: “Unless you hold yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown” (Ecclus. 27)—that is, your good way of life. Or certainly, to carry the gathered and threshed harvest home is to place within the conscience, through the desire and effect of virtue and good work, the good things known and tested through reading and meditation.

When these things had been done, Naomi saw that her daughter-in-law had found great favor with Boaz and gave her advice by which she could find still greater favor. So every good pastor, when he perceives that Christ’s grace has grown strong in the soul entrusted to him [Col. 1066D], devotes effort so that it may have still greater favor with Christ. She therefore says:

“My daughter, I shall seek rest for you, and shall provide for you, that it may be well with you. This Boaz, to whose maidens you have been joined in the field, is our kinsman; and even tonight he is winnowing the barley threshing-floor. Therefore wash, anoint yourself, put on finer garments, and go down to the threshing-floor. Do not let the man see you until he has finished food and drink. But when he goes to sleep, mark the place where he sleeps; then come, uncover the cloak with which he is covered at his feet, throw yourself down, and lie there. He himself will tell you what you ought to do” (Ruth 3).

Naomi is the ecclesiastical pastor; Ruth, the subject; Boaz, Christ; kinship, goodness. This kinship is not made by relationship of blood, but by affinity of holiness [Col. 1067A]. Hence the Savior says: “Whoever does the will of my Father, that one is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 12). And blessed John says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God—to those who believe in his name—who were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1).

Night is the present life, while under the veil of sacraments we receive the grace of heavenly gifts. It is night while we do not see one another’s consciences, but do not know what one thinks of another. It is night because we see through a mirror and in an enigma, not yet face to face, and we walk by faith, not yet by sight (1 Cor. 13). In this night Boaz winnows his threshing-floor, because Christ diligently purges not only holy Church from its persecutors or ill-living people, but also each faithful soul from evil thoughts and from false and carnal understanding in sacred Scripture [Col. 1067B].

Certainly, the faithful and obedient soul is washed when it is cleansed from the filth of former sin by frequent tears. Hence Jeremiah exhorts: “Bring down tears like a torrent day and night; give yourself no rest, and let not the pupil of your eye be silent” (Lam. 2). Ointments are spiritual gifts, because, just as bodily wounds or pains are healed and soothed by ointments, so the wounds or pains of souls are healed and soothed by sacred gifts. Concerning these gifts the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness” (1 Cor. 12). “To one indeed is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the grace of healings, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another interpretation of utterances” (Isa. 2 [citation as printed]).

And Isaiah says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him.” These gifts, brothers, are true ointments, and receiving them is true anointing. But the virtues arising from these gifts are also not inappropriately called ointments, because their exercise is perfect anointing: it consumes in us the worms of vices and restores to health the affections wounded by sins. Garments are works. Finer garments are outstanding works, such as the six [Col. 1067D] works of mercy: giving bread to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and so forth. If anyone is surrounded by these, he is adorned as it were with clean and precious garments.

Accordingly, after the gathering and threshing of the ears, Ruth is washed, anointed, and clothed, because the faithful soul, after receiving through reading and meditation the knowledge of truth contained in the Scriptures, is washed by contrition, anointed by the pursuit of spiritual gifts and the practice of virtues, and clothed by good conduct. Once these things are arranged, to go down to the threshing-floor is for anyone, after benefits have been received, to humble himself within the level ground of his heart. For a person is, as it were, above himself through pride; but by humility he returns to himself and descends into himself. There is also another humility, which precedes this one [Col. 1068A], but the former is for receiving a benefit; this one, however, is for increasing the benefit.

To uncover the garment at the feet and there cast oneself down or lie down is humbly to investigate and consider the mystery of our redemption, and humbly and unceasingly to request Christ’s perpetual union through faith in his incarnation. Yet let the soul by no means presume upon so great an approach and familiarity unless it sees him gladdened by food and drink and laid in the bed of peace and rest. Christ’s food and drink are that his Father’s will should be done. Hence he says to his disciples: “I have food to eat which you do not know. My food is to do the will of him who sent me, that I may complete his work” (John 4).

Therefore let no soul dare in any way to examine, handle, receive, or ask great things of Christ’s mystery [Col. 1068B], unless, after first presenting holy works, it recognizes that he is made glad and peaceful toward it. “What fellowship has a pot with a kettle?” (Ecclus. 13). “For when they strike together, it will be broken.” And the Apostle says: “He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11).

Thus, when Moses, after the death of Nadab and Abihu, rebuked Eleazar and Ithamar concerning the goat which he found burned, because they had not eaten it, Aaron answered him: “A sacrifice for sin and a burnt offering have today been offered before the Lord. But what you see has happened to me. How could I have eaten it, or how could I have propitiated the Lord?” Or, as some read: “How could I have pleased the Lord in the ceremonies while my mind was grieving?” (Lev. 20 [the reference appears to be erroneous]). Concerning prayer also [Col. 1068C] it is written: “He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28).

Whoever, then, wishes in any manner to approach God or ask anything from him must first strive to make his conscience serene before him by doing good works and humbling himself; and thereby, as it were, to refresh Christ with food, cheer him with drink, and render him peaceable toward himself. Yet the food and drink which Boaz took were not from Ruth’s giving but from Boaz’s own resources, because our action is Christ’s gift and does not arise from our own ability but from heavenly grace. For it depends “not upon him who wills nor upon him who runs, but upon God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

“He,” he says, “will tell you what you ought to do.” For if we obediently [Col. 1068D] do what our superior commands us, thereafter Christ’s anointing teaches us concerning all things (1 John 2). Finally, Boaz praises Ruth because she did not follow the young men; and Christ praises the soul faithfully approaching him because it does not follow demons or reprobate people, swift and fickle in wrongdoing.

Now therefore, most dear to us, returning to ourselves, let us strive through all these things to be instructed in the knowledge of truth, inflamed with love of goodness, stirred to the practice of virtue, formed for the accomplishment of good works, and prompted to earn the reward of salvation. Let us leave our land and our gods, renouncing our former wickednesses and the suggestions of demons; let us follow our shepherd, imitating him in what he rightly does; let us cleave [Col. 1069A] to him by loving him truly. Let us obey him, diligently performing all that he commanded. Let us dwell with him in Bethlehem, conducting ourselves honorably with him in the holy Church.

Let us gather and thresh ears in Boaz’s field, carrying them into our house by reading and meditating upon our Saviour’s words and storing them, as has been said above, in our memory or conscience. Let us not gather in another’s field, rejecting the corrupt assertions of heretics. Let us wash ourselves by mourning our crimes; let us anoint ourselves by pursuing spiritual gifts, and especially by following virtues—above all charity—according to the Apostle; let us clothe ourselves by putting into effect the six works of mercy. Finally, let us go down to the threshing-floor by humbling ourselves within our heart; let us uncover the garment [Col. 1069B] which covers him at the feet, investigating the mystery of our redemption with humble consideration; and there let us cast ourselves down and lie, humbly and without ceasing asking to be joined to him through the end of his Passion.

For by persisting in such things we shall deserve, like Ruth from Boaz, first to receive three measures of grain through faith in the holy and undivided Trinity; then six measures through the perfection of all holiness; and finally to be joined to him in the bridal chamber—on earth through a taste of inward sweetness, and in heaven through the glory of blessedness. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, he who is God blessed for ages. Amen.

## SERMON LVII. On any prelate or teacher

[Col. 1069C] Boaz said to Ruth: “I do not deny that I am a kinsman, but there is another kinsman nearer than I. If he should wish to retain you by right of kinship, the matter is well accomplished. But if he should not wish it, I shall receive you without doubt” (Ruth 3).

Ruth, whose name is interpreted “hastening,” rightly prefigures the holy Church, which hastens with all devotion to fulfil the commandments given her from heaven. Her husband is fittingly understood to be Christ, of whom it is written: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3). And the blessed Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, that he himself might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle, but that she might be holy and [Col. 1069D] immaculate” (Eph. 5).

To this bride the same bridegroom became in a certain sense, as it were, dead from the time when he ceased, as a human being, to live and converse among human beings; from the time when, as the Apostle says, “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2). For although Christ, risen from the dead, now dies no more and death no longer has dominion over him—“for in that he lives, he lives to God” (Rom. 6)—yet, insofar as he has departed into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself, and is bodily absent, he is in a certain sense dead to her.

His kinsman—indeed, his nearer kinsman—is the body of ecclesiastical prelates. For although all true Christians are rightly called Christ’s kinsfolk, as he himself testifies, saying: “Whoever does the will [Col. 1070A] of my Father, he is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matt. 22 [the citation appears erroneous]), nevertheless ecclesiastical shepherds, whose ministry it is, by teaching, baptizing, instructing believers in the other sacraments, and confirming them, to beget spiritual seed for Christ, are especially his nearer kinsmen. Of this seed of Christ Isaiah says: “If he gives his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed, and the will of the Lord shall prosper in his hand” (Isa. 53).

So that this seed may not fail at any time, Christ’s kinsman—that is, the choir of holy prelates—must take every means to guard against this through preaching. But when holy teachers preach, they beget not for themselves but for the Lord, because in begetting spiritual offspring by teaching they seek not their own praise but Christ’s. And because they do everything for God’s glory, they can truly say: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113).

These prelates, or holy teachers, as it were, have two stockings within: knowledge of truth and love of virtue; and two shoes visible outside: the word of preaching and the example of good work. Whoever lacks either one or both of these shoes is unfit to raise up seed for Christ. For, to use not our words but those of the holy Fathers: an ecclesiastical teacher ought to shine both in life and in doctrine. Doctrine without life makes one arrogant; life without doctrine makes one useless. A priest’s preaching must be confirmed by works, so that what he teaches in word he may demonstrate by example. [Col. 1070C] For that doctrine is true which a manner of life follows. Nothing is more shameful than for anyone to neglect in deed the good which he preaches. Preaching is usefully delivered insofar as it is effectively fulfilled.

Therefore every teacher ought to be zealous both for good conduct and for good preaching, for one without the other produces no advancement. As doctrine does not suffice without life, so life does not suffice without doctrine. Every prelate must certainly live holily for the sake of example and teach devoutly because of the office of his administration, being certain that his own righteousness will not aid him, from whose hand the soul of a subject is wholly required. What advantage is it not to be punished for one’s own sin, if one must be punished for another’s?

I lie if the Lord does not say this through the prophet with a declaration of terror: “Son of man, if, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you have not spoken so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if a righteous man, having turned aside, commits iniquity, he shall die because you did not announce it to him; and I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you announce to the righteous man that he should not sin, and he does not sin, he shall surely live, because you announced it; and you have delivered your own soul” (Ezek. 3).

It is clear, therefore, that neither doctrine without life nor life without doctrine suffices for a prelate, if he is to be able to beget spiritual offspring for Christ. If one of these happens to be lacking [Col. 1071A], it is better, of the two imperfections, to possess holy rusticity than sinful eloquence. But if both are absent, he will be not only useless for raising up seed to Christ but also harmful both to himself and to those entrusted to him, like an unfruitful tree occupying the ground.

Therefore the holy Church rightly does not recognize as Christ’s kinsman such a shepherd who presides in name only and not in reality, with power but not with usefulness. Before Boaz—that is, before any ecclesiastical teacher rich in the word of wisdom and knowledge and powerful in the strength of virtues—she humbly seeks the raising up of spiritual seed for preserving the perpetuity of the Christian name. For an ecclesiastical teacher is Christ’s kinsman through the grace of teaching; but a shepherd entrusted with the care of souls is nearer through the duty and obligation [Col. 1071B] of pastoral care.

When he has been reverently admonished before the elders of Bethlehem—that is, the more perfect men of the holy Church—to endeavour in the care enjoined upon him, if he refuses to fulfil it, then often, by God’s disposing grace, he loses, as it were, both shoes: he abandons the care of governance by which he ought to have made the holy Church fruitful with spiritual offspring; and the ecclesiastical teacher receives both shoes when, being appointed in his place, he unceasingly instructs the holy Church by word and example, so that it may be made fruitful with spiritual seed to Christ’s honour.

Thus the council of the apostles appointed Matthias in Judas’s place; and in the place of the Jews the fullness of the Gentiles entered, as the Lord himself said to the Jews: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” [Col. 1071C] (Matt. 21). Hence it is said to the bishop of Philadelphia: “Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown” (Rev. 3). Hence also it is said to the bishop of Ephesus: “I have a few things against you: you have left your first charity. Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen; repent and do the first works. But if not, I shall come to you soon and remove your candlestick from its place” (Rev. 2).

For the candlestick of any reprobate shepherd is removed from its place when the ecclesiastical dignity conferred upon him is taken away—because his sins demand it—from one useless and unworthy, and transferred to another, and bestowed upon him as one worthy and fruitful. We often see this happen: reprobates are driven from their position, and others are appointed in their place, through whom ecclesiastical duties are exercised as they should be.

Finally, such a shepherd is deservedly called unshod, because he is stripped of the protection of word and example, insofar as ecclesiastical ministry is concerned, and is deprived of the merit and reward of both. While he loves to generate and perpetuate the household of his own vices, he leaves to another the shoes of preaching and action by which he ought to have armed his own people for the preparation of the Gospel of peace. But would that, according to the Psalmist’s imprecation, “his offspring might be given to destruction; in one generation may his name be blotted out” (Ps. 108).

All things, however, which belonged to the dead pass into the possession of the one using his privilege, because especially holy and perfect rulers of souls both do the works which [Col. 1072A] Christ did and do greater works than these. Yet they buy all these things, according to the interpretation given concerning Elimelech’s portion of the field to be sold, when they renounce their own possessions and wills in order to obey the divine will. Hence blessed Peter said to the Lord: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you.” So too the prudent merchant, having found one precious pearl, gave all that he had and bought it (Matt. 13).

The elders of Bethlehem said to Boaz: “May God make this woman who enters your house like Rachel and Leah, who built the house of Israel” (Ruth 14 [source citation; presumably 4]). The elders of Bethlehem pray to Boaz for Ruth, because all who are perfect in the holy Church assist the ecclesiastical prelate and the whole congregation entrusted to him by continual [Col. 1072B] prayers. And just as Rachel and Leah built the house of Israel, so Ruth builds the house of Boaz when the holy congregation entrusted to a faithful prelate, and made fruitful with spiritual seed through his ministry, multiplies for him spiritual offspring: namely, spiritual men, some quiet in contemplation, others laborious in action.

And she is an example of virtue in Ephrathah when her obedience shines in the universal Church; and she has a celebrated name in Bethlehem when she spreads a distinguished reputation throughout the whole Church. Finally, Boaz’s house, from the seed which the Lord gives him from her, becomes like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, when many begotten from it by his preaching, cleansed from former sins by the most health-giving bitterness of confession and then distinguished from many others especially by the gift of knowledge and virtue, sometimes deserve to be raised to the height of ecclesiastical governance.

For Tamar is interpreted “bitterness,” Judah “confessing,” and Perez “division.” And the offspring of Perez, whom Tamar bore, was in this respect divided far from the other tribes of Israel’s sons: royal dignity proceeded from it, as is also declared in the Book of Ruth, where it is written: “Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon; Salmon begot Boaz; Boaz begot Obed,” namely by Ruth; “Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot King David.”

Now therefore, most dear ones, returning to ourselves [Col. 1072D], let us always desire that this spiritual Boaz should preside over us, and let us fear to have that useless kinsman reign over us. When a good shepherd is given to the Church, it is God’s gift. But when a reprobate rules, it is because human sins require it, since God causes “a hypocritical man to reign over a nation and over all people because of the sins of the people” (Job 34). Therefore an unruly ruler is not to be judged by the people, since they should rather know that they have deserved to receive the rule of a perverse bishop. For God orders the lives of rulers according to the merits of peoples, as in the example of David’s sin, in comparison with rulers who transgress because of the merit of the people.

But if a ruler should depart from the faith, then he must be rebuked by his subjects. For reprobate morals, however, he is to be endured [Col. 1073A] rather than sternly censured by the people. Therefore, most dear ones, let us not presume rashly to tear apart such prelates for things which they administer disorderly. And according to the judgment of blessed Gregory, let none of us rashly reproach his shepherd’s sentence, even if he has been bound unjustly, lest, though he has been bound unjustly, the sin which was not present become present through the pride of swollen reproach.

But if we see the true Boaz diligently raising up spiritual seed in order to spread Christ’s name through the word of preaching and the example of good work, let us rejoice. Let us strive to be his companions in merit by living well ourselves and by admonishing one another, so that we may deserve to become his companions in reward. May our Lord Jesus Christ grant this to us, he who is in all things [Col. 1073B] God blessed for ages. Amen.

## SERMON LVIII. What the necessities of human life signify

In Ecclesiasticus we read that the author of that book, mentioning the things necessary for human life, says: “The beginning of the necessities of human life is water, fire, and iron, milk and fine wheaten bread, and honey, and a cluster of grapes, and oil, and clothing” (Ecclus. 39); and elsewhere, after listing some of these, he adds “a house sheltering shame.” For in an earlier passage he had said: “The beginning of human life is water, bread, clothing, and a house sheltering shame” (Ecclus. 29).

Here he now adds several other things, some sweeter, more pleasant, and more agreeable than the former, such as milk, honey, a cluster of grapes, and oil, because as the misery of human frailty increased with the passage of time [Col. 1073C], it was necessary that its necessities should also increase. And as frailty increased, necessity consequently increased. Necessity is that without which something cannot exist. But since he has set forth these things according to what is necessary to the flesh, let us now turn them toward the spirit and investigate how they may be understood spiritually, for the instruction of our mortality.

In sacred Scripture, water sometimes signifies the grace of contrition and tears. There are two kinds of contrition, prefigured by the water twice brought forth from the rock in the wilderness: one which arises from sorrow for guilt and fear of punishment; the other which is generated by consideration of heavenly gifts received and divine love. These two kinds of contrition are clearly distinguished by the prophet Isaiah, where he says: “Everyone left in Zion and remaining in Jerusalem shall be called holy, everyone enrolled for life in Jerusalem, when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the blood of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning” (Isa. 4).

By the spirit of judgment is indicated contrition arising from fear; by the spirit of burning, contrition arising from love. For divine judgment brings fear, whereas divine burning bestows love. As there seem to be two kinds of contrition, so likewise there are two kinds of sin: one in the flesh, the other in the spirit—that is, one carnal, the other spiritual. In the flesh is lust; in the spirit, malice. Lust is a stain; malice, a wrinkle. The stain of lust is expressed by “filth”; the wrinkle of malice by “blood.” That malice of heart is expressed by blood is openly shown where its remedy is mentioned. Hence Jeremiah says: “Wash your heart from malice, Jerusalem, that you may be saved. How long shall harmful thoughts remain in you?” (Jer. 4).

Indeed, the spirit of judgment washes filth when a person, struck by fear of divine judgment, makes bitter to himself those things which had been sweet to him according to lust. And the spirit of burning washes blood when a person who had been bitter toward his neighbour is touched by the burning of heavenly love and becomes inwardly sweet toward that same neighbour. Thus the grace of contrition washes all sins, whether carnal or spiritual, because the spirit of judgment cleanses filth and the spirit of burning [Col. 1074B] cleanses blood.

Although we distinguish matters thus, saying that filth is washed by the spirit of judgment and blood by the spirit of burning, we should nevertheless understand that each works in both places, cleansing both filth and blood. For fear and love, poured out through the Holy Spirit for the justification of sinners, cooperate with one another in such a way that, whether sins be carnal or spiritual, they are effectively washed away, fear going before and love following.

And because true confession plainly accompanies true contrition, it is fitting that, after declaring water necessary, he immediately added that fire also is necessary. Fire signifies confession, for fire is red and confession bears the blush of shame. Hence Paul says: “What fruit did you then have in those things of which you are now ashamed?” (Rom. 6). We may also understand fire to signify the labour of satisfaction, such as fasts and other things of that kind. Those whom the fire of this labour cleanses perfectly by burning them in the present age are by no means tormented in the age to come by hellfire or purgatorial fire.

The Psalmist clearly expresses the fruit of this fire and water when he says: “We passed through fire, and you brought us out into refreshment” (Ps. 65). For we pass through water and fire and are led into refreshment when, cleansed by contrition and confession, or also by satisfaction, we rest from the distress of sorrow and fear which we suffered because of our sins. Only one who has deserved, by divine grace bestowed, to experience this refreshment truly knows its delight [Col. 1074D].

And iron. When iron is used in a good sense, it is rightly understood as the virtue of severity. Therefore after water and fire he declares iron necessary, because after renouncing evils committed by weeping, confessing, and even making satisfaction, unless we resist with the sword of great severity the enticements of temptations, as the ancient enemy rages against us more fiercely than usual, we are quickly dragged back by the snare of allurements to the evils which we had left, or indeed to more serious sins. Then “the last state becomes worse than the first” (Luke 11), when seven spirits more wicked than the spirit which had formerly possessed us enter and dwell in us with him.

[Col. 1075A] Therefore it is necessary that, in these assaults, we crush the head of the ancient enemy with the severity of great discipline and dash his little ones against the rock.

And milk and bread. As we understand from various passages of Scripture, milk fittingly denotes teaching to be offered to beginners, and bread teaching to be offered to the perfect. Thus concerning this milk blessed Peter says to those who had recently believed: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, that by it you may grow unto salvation” (1 Pet. 2). And blessed Paul says to the Corinthians: “I could not speak to you as spiritual persons, but as carnal; as little children in Christ I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3). Rebuking the Hebrews, he says: “Though by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need to be taught what are the elementary beginnings of the sayings of God, and you have become such as need milk, not solid food. For everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a child” (Heb. 5). Concerning bread he immediately adds: “But solid food is for the perfect, who through habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil” (ibid.). And he says to the Corinthians: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2).

Thus simple teaching is necessary for beginners, like milk for little children; deep and manifold teaching is necessary for the perfect, like bread for adults. Notice that after saying “bread” he added “fine wheaten,” because, when the bran of the letter has been removed, the flour of spiritual understanding is dispensed to the perfect. Therefore after water, fire, and iron, he says that milk with bread is necessary so that the athlete of Christ—whom water and fire render clean and purified from past guilt, and whom iron arms against the deadly enticement of the ancient enemy—may be made strong by milk and bread for the practice of virtues and the accomplishment of good works.

And honey and a cluster of grapes. Divine mercy is accustomed, before those converted from unbelief to faith or from guilt to repentance enter upon the laborious practice of virtues and good works after receiving knowledge of the truth, to bestow upon them some inward sweetness and consolation, and thereby effectively to urge them toward spiritual merit and the reward of merit. Hence blessed Peter, exhorting those recently converted to faith to grow unto salvation, says: [Col. 1075D] “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Pet. 2). Hence Job says to the Lord concerning a human being magnified through divine grace: “You visit him at dawn, and suddenly you test him” (Job 7).

The Lord visits a person at dawn and suddenly tests him when, at the beginning of his conversion or manner of life, he mercifully shows him what the flavour of inward sweetness and the taste of heavenly consolation are; and immediately tests him in the furnace of perfection of life, like a potter’s vessel, so that thereby the person may learn how much progress he makes. Of this temptation or testing it is written: “The furnace tests the vessels of a potter, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclus. 27). But the tribulation of the righteous consists in practising virtues and performing good works.

Concerning this temptation [Col. 1076A] or testing of the righteous it is written: “God tested them and found them worthy of himself; he tested them like gold in a furnace and received them as sacrificial burnt offerings” (Wis. 3). Therefore the Lord, as we have said, visits his chosen one at dawn through consolation, but suddenly tests him through exercise. Hence again it is written: “You shall delight the goings forth of morning and evening” (Ps. 64). The Lord delights the goings forth of morning and evening because he gladdens the beginning of a good way of life by consolation and its end by recompense. But he assigns the middle of the day not so much to delight as to burning heat, because he assigns the middle period of merit not so much to consolation as to rigorous testing.

Because, then, before the rigor of testing, the Lord sometimes pours into the soul the sweetness of his consolation, he rightly declared honey and a cluster of grapes necessary after the things stated above. Honey, having a sweet taste, and a cluster containing wine, which intoxicates, can signify inward sweetness and spiritual consolation. But it must carefully be noted that he said not “honeycomb” but “honey,” and that he said not “wine” but “a cluster,” and specifically a cluster of grapes. For there appear to be two kinds of consolations: one is poured into us without coverings; the other is bestowed, as it were, through certain wrappings and husks, mediated in some way by sacred things or others of this kind.

The first may therefore be represented by honey, the second by a cluster. Alternatively, by honey we may understand any—even the smallest—inward spiritual sweetness pleasantly savoured; by a cluster, a greater consolation powerfully intoxicating the mind. This is aptly called a cluster of grapes (*uva*), belonging to the good, not of wild grapes (*labrusca*), belonging to the wicked, concerning whose grape, cluster, and wine it is written: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 32).

Therefore, just as every person converted from guilt is cleansed and purified through the water of contrition and the fire of confession, or also of satisfaction; just as he is armed by the iron of severity against the assault of demons who wickedly entice through the desires of the flesh; and just as he is nourished and strengthened by the milk and bread of doctrine for the practice of virtues [Col. 1076D] and good works: so through the honey and cluster of inward sweetness and consolation he is wonderfully encouraged to earn heavenly joy even through sadness and bitterness. Nor does he hesitate to pass through the bitter cup of present evil to the delight of the heavenly good when he has been permitted beforehand to taste even slight drops of that cluster.

And oil and clothing. What does oil signify except the virtue of charity? And what better than the necessity of good work is understood through clothing? For oil by its nature is accustomed to float above all liquids with which it is mixed. And the Apostle, about to speak of charity, says: “Yet I show you a more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, etc.” (1 Cor. 12–13). Therefore charity is rightly signified by oil [Col. 1077A], and not only charity but the totality of the other virtues is included and signified as well. Read the Apostle’s words that follow what we have cited above, and you will find that charity contains the other virtues and that whatever is without charity has no value at all for obtaining eternal life.

This author, therefore, intending here to speak of virtues, fittingly set forth that which charity signifies by oil, because the totality of the other virtues is represented through it. Charity is truly oil: in other virtues—humility, patience, abstinence, continence—something sometimes terrifies us by its harshness; but charity charms us by its sweetness. For it softens, seasons, and makes gentle everything by its sweetness.

Good work is designated by clothing, because clothing is as necessary to the body as good work is necessary to the soul; and as clothing surrounds us outwardly, so good work gives us honour before our neighbour. “And a house,” he says, “sheltering shame.” By house, as we have said elsewhere, is meant one’s manner of life, because each person lives in it. A house shelters shame when a good way of life conceals guilt from the divine eyes. Every practice of virtues, performance of good works, and discipline of character belongs to building this house. Therefore he placed the house last, after he had perfectly encompassed the entire fruit of our labour.

Thus it is necessary for us, most dear ones, to possess [Col. 1077C] water through contrition; fire through confession and satisfaction; iron through severity; milk and bread through sound teaching; honey and a cluster through divine consolation; oil and clothing through virtue and action; and a house through good conduct. Yet two things besides all these are necessary: righteousness and glory. Righteousness in the world; glory in heaven. Righteousness in merit; glory in reward. Righteousness begins the spiritual life; glory completes it. How will one possess the end who neglects to possess the beginning? One goes by righteousness and arrives by glory. Let us labour, therefore, brothers, to possess righteousness, so that through it we may deserve to possess glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God blessed [Col. 1077D] for ages. Amen.

## SERMON LIX. On Absalom as signifying the Jews, and David as signifying Christ; that is, on the things which Christ suffered.

In the Second Book of Kings we read that Absalom cruelly persecuted David, his father, and that David himself, driven across the Jordan, was sustained with food and drink and honored with gifts by three men of that region (2 Kings 15 ff.). Now Absalom—“beautiful and noble”—signifies the Jewish people, adorned with legal commandments and ceremonies, ennobled by kingdom, priesthood, and Temple, and for that reason exalted above itself through excessive pride. David, however, who was ruddy, handsome, and strong, signifies Christ: ruddy through the Passion of his flesh, handsome [Col. 1078A] through the glory of his divinity, strong through the power of his majesty. The prophet had once anointed him king at the divine command, because God had long before foretold by the prophetic voice that this one would be anointed. David was transferred from the flock of sheep to the rule of men, and Christ from the sheepfold of the Jews to the kingdom of the Gentiles. David killed Goliath the Philistine; Christ killed the devil. David had Saul, a rejected king, as persecutor; Christ had the devil. Therefore Absalom signifies the Jewish people, David Christ. Absalom persecuted David his father; the Jewish people persecuted Christ. Hence Isaiah says: “I have nourished and raised up sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1). Shimei cursed David, but David did not answer him; and Christ, when he was cursed, did not threaten in return.

[Col. 1078B] Ziba, abandoning his lame master Mephibosheth, followed David with food and drink in order to refresh his men; and Paul, abandoning the whole body of the Pharisees, which limped from the paths of righteousness, though he had served it in the persecution of the saints, followed Christ in order to satisfy Christ’s faithful people with teaching and consolation. “Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is yours,” David says to Ziba; and Christ granted Paul the fullness of wisdom which he had taken away from the faithless Pharisees. Absalom violated David’s concubines, whom David had left behind; and the assembly of Jewish teachers, which had specially usurped the governance of the people, does not cease to corrupt souls left by Christ by teaching the Law carnally. Jonathan and Ahimaaz, who informed David so that he might cross the Jordan, signify the patriarchs and prophets [Col. 1078C] who foretold through figures and oracles that Christ would leave Judaea and pass over to the Gentiles. David, while Absalom pursued him, left Judaea and fled across the Jordan to the Gentiles; and Christ, when the Jews persecuted his apostles, left Judaea and passed in the apostles to the Gentiles. This is what Paul said to the Jews themselves: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13). Many of the children of Israel followed David across the Jordan; and after the Gospel began to be preached to the Gentiles, many Jews believed in Christ. Ahithophel, whose name is interpreted “the ruin of a brother,” represents Judas, who plotted Christ’s ruin [Col. 1078D] and gave the Jews counsel against Christ; and both perished by hanging. Absalom pursues David across the Jordan; and Jewish unbelief endeavors to destroy Christ’s faith not only among its own people but also among the Gentiles. David is honored across the Jordan by three men with various gifts; and Christ is glorified among the Gentiles who receive faith in the Holy Trinity through various virtues and good works. For the history in the Book of Kings relates that David was honored with gifts across the Jordan, saying:

“When David came to the camp, Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbath of the children of Ammon, and Machir son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim, offered him beds, rugs, earthenware vessels, wheat, barley, flour, parched grain, beans, [Col. 1079A] lentils, chickpeas fried in oil, honey, butter, sheep, and fat calves; and they gave them to David and the people with him to eat.”

In all these things is shown the active devotion of converted Gentile peoples. Yet in those things which pertain to food, the nourishment and consolation of sacred teaching are especially expressed. In the earthenware vessels, however, are figured good works and certain virtues which, at the end, when that which is perfect has come and that which is partial has been done away with, will be broken and destroyed. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “Whether there be prophecies, they shall be done away; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13). Considering this, the Psalmist seems to cry out in wonder: “Come and see the works of the Lord, what wonders he has set upon the earth” [Col. 1079B] (Ps. 45), that is, upon human nature, which is certainly earthly. “He makes wars cease to the end of the earth; he will break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire” (ibid.). For the Lord will remove wars to the end of the earth when, at the end of life, he causes every temptation altogether to cease. He will also break the bow, shatter the weapons, and burn the shields with fire when, by the immediate brightness of the vision of himself and the fullest perfection of charity, he will make void preaching, sacraments, works, and certain virtues—namely faith, hope, prophecy, tongues, and knowledge. In the beds and rugs, which pertain to adornment, the fitting beauty of ecclesiastical ornament is signified. Therefore those who honored David across the Jordan [Col. 1079C] with their gifts represent those who, being Gentiles and possessing faith in Christ, render him faithful service daily. But those who disdained to follow David out of Judaea plainly represent the Jews who, despising faith in Christ, departed through unbelief from his paths. At that time the lame Mephibosheth alone bore their type; David reproached him for having remained alone behind from his company. Hence Christ himself sang through the Psalmist:

“You will deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will set me as head of the Gentiles. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me. Foreign sons lied to me; foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths” (Ps. 17).

Indeed, those who went out with David and crossed the Jordan with him [Col. 1079D] represent the apostles and the faithful of the primitive Church converted from the Jews, who, driven out of Judaea by Jewish persecution, were compelled to pass over to the Gentiles.

Accordingly David reviewed his people and set over them commanders of thousands and commanders of hundreds. He placed a third part of the people under Joab’s hand, a third under the hand of Abishai, and a third under the hand of Ittai, who was from Gath. David reviewed his people across the Jordan because Christ saw his faithful people multiplied in their minds. He set commanders of thousands and hundreds over them because he first set in the Church apostles, secondly prophets, thirdly teachers, then powers, then gifts of healing, helps, governments, and kinds of tongues (1 Cor. [Col. 1080A] 12). It should be carefully noted that neither more nor fewer than three rulers are set over the people of God. Each portion of the people is called a third, so that it may plainly be signified that both prelates and subjects ought to be worshippers of the Holy Trinity. In this war David is a protection to his people while remaining in the city; he does not go out with them to fight bodily. So Christ now does not personally dispute with his faithful people against the faithless, but, seated in the heavenly city, intercedes with the Father for his own. In this war Absalom and many who are with him die, because both the faithless Jewish people and all who endeavor with them to assault Christ’s kingdom, unless they repent, are punished with eternal death. This is most plainly indicated where Absalom, after being killed, is said to have been thrown into a great pit: [Col. 1080B] for the great pit is hell. Absalom hangs in an oak between heaven and earth because the Jewish people, lifted up against Christ, possess neither the land once granted to them nor heaven. For the oak, a lofty and unbending tree, rightly signifies pride. This oak is said in the same place to have been great and dense because Jewish pride is proved both great through self-estimation and dense through blindness. The mule upon which Absalom rode figures the carnal and fruitless observance of the Law. It passed on while Absalom hung suspended, because, while the Jewish people persisted in their pride, the Law came to its end through grace. His excessive hair upon his head rightly signifies the superstition of Jewish self-estimation. [Col. 1080C] Finally, Absalom is slain by three spears because he is condemned by the faith of the Holy Trinity, which that people hates and rejects. By Joab any perfect teacher is signified. By his ten young armor-bearers, who struck Absalom after him, is represented a band of his disciples made strong in the knowledge of the Decalogue. Thus all wound Absalom unto death who declare that the aforesaid people must be struck with perpetual death because of its unbelief. Moreover, all who escaped from the people of Israel and were later reconciled with David their king plainly represent the remnant who will be saved after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. David mourned Absalom’s death; and Christ wept over that nation, which he knew would perish because of its unbelief, saying: “If you too had known, etc.” (Luke 19). [Col. 1080D] David wished his son to be spared for him; and Christ especially desired that the Jews, to whom he was first specially sent, should come to the knowledge of truth.

Having considered these matters according to allegory, let us return to tropology, so that, just as we have spoken of those things which instruct us in knowledge, we may henceforth seek those which form us in righteousness. For knowledge is of no benefit when righteousness is not its companion. Let us therefore take every precaution not to perish with the faithless, either by believing wrongly or acting wickedly; but, with Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai—that is, with those who are truly faithful—let us render faithful service to Christ. Let us offer him beds, rugs, and so forth. By the beds, which the Holy Spirit [Col. 1081A] placed first in this passage, he signifies for us the repose of inward contemplation. He therefore placed first what he loves above all else. Thus the Psalmist says: “The Lord loves the gates of Zion above all the tabernacles of Jacob” (Ps. 86). For the Lord loves even the beginning of heavenly contemplation above all the works of good conduct, preferring it in love; for by Zion is understood heavenly contemplation, and by the gates of Zion the beginning of that contemplation. By Jacob is meant the doer of good work; by tabernacles, every structure of good conduct. So also rugs, because they make beautiful the house in which they are spread out, can signify the dignity of holy conduct. Earthenware vessels signify our fragile bodies, which we then offer [Col. 1081B] to Christ when we devote them to his service.

“Wheat, barley, and flour of parched grain,” that is, pure flour. By wheat the New Testament, and by barley the Old Testament, is understood. By the flour of parched grain is plainly expressed the spiritual understanding of both. Therefore we offer wheat, barley, and flour of parched grain to Christ when, out of love for him, we faithfully dispense both Testaments, according to both the letter and the spiritual understanding, by reading, meditating, speaking, and acting.

“And beans, lentils, and fried chickpeas.” What fish are after loaves in the Gospel, those previously mentioned legumes can be understood to be after wheat, barley, and flour in this passage. For by wheat, barley, and flour, just as there by loaves, may be signified the precepts of sacred Scripture; and by beans, lentils, and chickpeas here, just as there by fish, the examples of the holy Fathers. Appropriately, whether fish after loaves in the Gospel or legumes after wheat, barley, and flour here, these are placed in sequence because, just as we consume each pair of bodily foods to sustain our bodies, so we use both the words of sacred Scripture and the examples of the righteous for the justification of our souls. We are nourished by precepts when we obeyingly put them into practice; we are nourished by examples when we humbly imitate them. “Beans,” he says, “and lentils, and fried chickpeas.” We know that beans are larger than lentils, and lentils smaller than beans. By beans, therefore, [Col. 1081D] greater examples are fittingly understood; by lentils, lesser examples of the saints. By fried chickpeas, however, the passion of holy martyrs alone seems to be figured: for human flesh is fried when it is tortured by the straits of suffering. Thus we give wheat, barley, and flour to Christ when we perform his commandments contained in the Scriptures. We give him beans, lentils, and fried chickpeas when we imitate the examples of his saints.

“And honey, butter, sheep, and fat calves.” Honey is sweet; butter is rich; a sheep is an innocent animal; a calf is obedient. For so long as it is a calf, it is readily driven even at the motion of one who threatens. By honey, then, we understand inward sweetness of heart; by butter, brotherly charity; by sheep, innocence; by fat calves, heartfelt obedience. We therefore give honey, butter, sheep, and calves [Col. 1082A] to Christ when we truly serve him through the virtues signified by these things. Let us give, beloved, the mystical gifts which have been mentioned; let us give them, I say, to Christ by faithfully serving him in the world, so that we may deserve to be rewarded by him in heaven.
