May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LX. On All the Saints

Christ Jesus our Savior, most beloved, the bridegroom of the holy universal Church, elegantly praises in the Song of Songs the varied and manifold fruit of this his bride, in order by praise to stir and inflame her toward greater things. He says in one passage:

“You are a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain. Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates with the fruits of orchards. Cyprus with nard; nard with saffron; calamus and cinnamon with every tree of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes with all the finest spices” (Song 4).

For in all these things the bride’s good is elegantly commended by the bridegroom; and the bridegroom rejoices with and congratulates his bride. In the same Song of Songs, the holy Church herself is called by various names. At one time she is called bride, at another friend, at another sister, at another dove, and at another beautiful or fair. She is indeed a bride through faith, a friend through love, a sister through participation in the heavenly inheritance, [Col. 1082C] a dove through simplicity, and fair through the beauty of righteousness.

“You are a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed.” By the garden we understand the holy conduct of the holy Church, from which we see the shoots of virtues and good works continually springing. This garden is aptly called enclosed because it is fortified on every side by the strong defense of discipline, lest the deceitful enemy break in anywhere, uproot the planting of righteousness, and carry it away. It is openly named twice so that its twofold fruit—faith and action; or marriage and continence; or even the distinction between God and the people; or, certainly, the active and contemplative life—may plainly be expressed. Thus it is said:

“You are a garden enclosed, my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a sealed fountain.” By the fountain of this garden [Col. 1082D] heavenly wisdom is understood. This fountain is divided, as if to water paradise, into four rivers when divine wisdom is distributed throughout the whole Church by the preaching of the four Gospels. It is also fittingly said to be sealed, because the wisdom of God is veiled in sacred Scripture by many and various enigmas. Hence Paul says: “We speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined for our glory” (1 Cor. 2). This is the sealed book of which Isaiah says: “When they give it to one who knows letters, saying, ‘Read,’ he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed’” (Isa. 29). This is the same book of life which blessed John saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne, sealed with seven seals, [Col. 1083A] which no one in heaven, on earth, or under the earth was able to open, except the lion alone from the tribe of Judah, who conquered, who is like a slain lamb having seven horns and seven eyes, which are the seven spirits of God sent into all the earth (Rev. 5). Therefore, since he alone can open this fountain or book, he could rightly say to his disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Matt. 13). Elsewhere it is written of him and these same disciples: “Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24). No one, therefore, can draw the saving taste of this fountain unless the Savior, who alone opens and shuts, deigns to open its seal for him. Nor can anyone have the shoot of this garden unless this fountain provides him with saving irrigation. That the Savior [Col. 1083B] opens the stream of this fountain to some and shuts it to others he himself shows when he says to his disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables, that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Matt. 13). And elsewhere he says to the Father: “I give thanks to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11). Thus the garden is enclosed and the fountain sealed: the garden enclosed by discipline, the fountain sealed by figure. The garden is enclosed lest the deceitful enemy break in; the fountain sealed lest a stranger drink from it. The garden is righteousness; the fountain, wisdom. First the bridegroom sets forth the garden sprouting and the fountain watering. Then he expresses more fully the fruit of sprouting and irrigation, saying:

[Col. 1083C] “Your shoots are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of orchards,” and so forth. The shoots of the holy mother Church are her spiritual offspring, especially in this passage the martyrs, who are designated by the name of pomegranates. The holy Church sends them forth from the world and brings them into heaven, yet does not lose them: she sends and entrusts them to Christ. Pomegranates are sharp with juice within and red in their seeds, and thereby figure martyrs, who may rightly be said to be red not only outwardly but inwardly also. For there are two kinds of martyrdom, one inward and the other outward, one in the heart and the other in the flesh. That which is outward is of no value if that which ought to be inward is lacking, because the suffering of the flesh profits nothing to one who lacks compassion of heart. [Col. 1083D] For all the glory of the king’s daughter, as it is written, is from within (Ps. 44). These shoots of pomegranates are compared to paradise because, just as paradise is filled, thickened, and adorned with diverse trees, so the holy Church is filled, thickened, and adorned with innumerable martyrs. What most expert reckoner could comprehend even their hundreds or thousands in number? Some, as a certain Scripture cries out (Heb. 11), were killed by the sword; some burned in flames; some beaten with scourges; some overwhelmed by the danger of the sea; some flayed alive; some had their nostrils pierced; some were tortured on the gallows; some consigned to chains; some deprived of their tongues; some buried beneath stones; some afflicted by cold; some worn down by hunger; others, with their hands cut off [Col. 1084A] or their other limbs mutilated, nakedly endured in the presence of the people a spectacle of disgrace for the Lord’s name.

Yet it may seem strange how martyrdom is compared to paradise, since martyrdom has bitterness while paradise has delight. But if we consider the matter more carefully, it will not seem strange, because every kind of torment was delightful to holy martyrs; and everything that hostile power could inflict upon them for the name of Christianity was sweet to them—or rather, too little. Thus it is written of the apostles: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were judged worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 3). And the apostle Paul, considering it a great gift to suffer for Christ, wrote to the Philippians: “It has been granted to you for Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1).

[Col. 1084B] “With the fruits of orchards.” Holy martyrs have fruits in the world and fruits in heaven: in the world, fruits of righteousness; in heaven, fruits of glory; in the world, fruits of merit; in heaven, fruits of reward. “Cyprus with nard, nard with saffron.” Cyprus is said to be an aromatic plant in Egypt with a white and fragrant seed, which is cooked in oil and pressed. From it an ointment is prepared which is called royal. Therefore cyprus fittingly signifies the gift of governance, that is, discernment, or certainly the rulers of souls themselves. Nard is a lowly plant. It therefore signifies humble subjects. Saffron is golden in color and therefore rightly designates teachers radiant with heavenly wisdom. Cyprus plants, [Col. 1084C] I think, are mentioned in the plural, while the things which follow are written individually, so that we may recognize by this that every prelate ought to abound more than all others in every virtue and good work. Hence blessed Augustine gives this command concerning a prelate:

“Toward all, let him offer himself as an example of good works; let him correct the unruly, console the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient with all. Let him gladly maintain discipline and impose it in a manner that commands fear. And although both are necessary, let him desire more to be loved than feared.”

Taught by such words of blessed Augustine, every prelate must strive to surpass those entrusted to him in every goodness, so that, severe toward some and gentle toward others, made all things to all through the fullness of his virtues, he may gain all. Cyprus is with nard when prelates humbly subject themselves with those under them to the divine commandments. Hence it is written: “Have they appointed you ruler? Do not exalt yourself; be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclus. 32). When holy rulers rightly say what they ought, and humbly do with those subject to them what they say, then truly cyprus is with nard. Nard is with saffron when crowds of humble subjects, drawing near to the feet of holy teachers shining with the brightness of heavenly wisdom, willingly hear saving teaching from them and faithfully yield to their words by belief and action, fulfilling the command of James: “Let every person [Col. 1085A] be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (Jas. 1). In such persons the testimony of Moses is likewise fulfilled: “Those who draw near to his feet shall receive from his teaching” (Deut. 33). For the Lord’s feet are holy teachers, who carry him to the hearts of hearers by their preaching. Those who humbly approach these feet receive his teaching through them, because, as it is written: “He who walks with the wise shall be wise, but the friend of fools shall become like them” (Prov. 13).

“Calamus and cinnamon.” Calamus is a small aromatic tree with strong purple bark, useful for healing discomforts of the internal organs. Thus it can signify all who are pierced by the fear of God concerning their sins—for the fear of God is the beginning of wisdom—and who cleanse the spiritual inward parts of their hearts from the troublesome accumulation of shameful thoughts by true confession. For just as a discomfort of the inward parts is healed by calamus, so in all who truly repent the hidden places of conscience are cleansed of their wickedness through perfect confession. Thus calamus signifies all who, in themselves or in others, drive out by the grace of compunction, confession, or even more forceful admonition, the troubles caused by inwardly hidden sins. Cinnamon is a short, fragrant, sweet, ash-colored tree, twice as excellent as calamus for medicinal use. It is called cinnamon because its bark is formed like a reed. And because boys customarily form a sound with their mouths through a reed cut for this purpose, cinnamon can signify the confession of holy priests—namely Jerome, [Col. 1085C] Gregory, Augustine, Ambrose, and all such persons. For, since they not only believe in the heart unto righteousness, but also confess with the mouth unto salvation, holy confessors can be signified by cinnamon, whose bark is bent around in the shape of a sound-producing reed, on account of their utterance of a saving sound. Therefore, just as we understand by calamus penitents who through true confession drive the troubles of sins out of their hearts, so let us understand by cinnamon holy confessors.

“With every tree of Lebanon.” Lebanon is interpreted “whitening.” The trees of Lebanon grow higher than other trees. Thus in Ezekiel, in describing the loftiness—or rather, the pride—of Assyria, it is said: “Behold, Assyria was like a cedar in Lebanon, beautiful in branches, thick in foliage, lofty in height, and its top was raised among the dense boughs” (Ezek. 31). Therefore, by the trees of Lebanon we fittingly understand the choirs of holy virgins, who raise themselves on high through the loftiness of their purity and draw nearer than others to heavenly goods through the exalted gifts of their purity. For virginal perfection is not so much an earthly as a heavenly life, not so much a human as an angelic one, because virginity is ever akin to the angels. Thus the trees of Lebanon are holy virgins: Agnes, Cecilia, Agatha, Lucy, and all the others whose names cannot be listed here. Therefore the holy mother Church possesses, together with the things mentioned above, the trees of Lebanon, because together with the aforesaid saints [Col. 1086A] she possesses sacred virgins, white through lofty purity and exaltedly raised toward heavenly goods.

“Myrrh and aloes.” These two spices have bitterness and are therefore useful against the decay of bodies if they are applied to them. Myrrh has greater power than aloes; accordingly, let us understand continence by myrrh and abstinence by aloes. It is burdensome to abstain; more burdensome to be continent. Myrrh and aloes repel worms and the decay of bodies; continence and abstinence repel from heart and flesh the corruptions of vices. Or, certainly, by myrrh and aloes in this passage we better understand those who are continent and abstinent, exercising themselves through these virtues. “With all the finest spices.” The finest spices are the principal gifts, such as charity and prophecy. Thus Paul, having listed the spiritual gifts, says: “And I show you yet a more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and angels,” etc. (1 Cor. 12–13). And shortly afterward: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; but the greatest of these is charity” (ibid., 13). “Pursue charity; desire spiritual gifts,” that is, desire divine gifts; “but especially that you may prophesy,” that is, preach. Therefore he first commended charity, and then prophecy, that is, preaching, because preaching is more concerned with the fruit of charity.

Thus the holy mother Church has a garden through good conduct, enclosed through discipline; a fountain through wisdom, sealed through figure. She has a paradise of pomegranates in suffering martyrs, [Col. 1086C] cyprus in prelates who rule, nard in humble subjects, saffron in learned teachers, calamus in compuncted penitents. She has cinnamon in confessors, trees of Lebanon in virgins, myrrh in the continent, aloes in the abstinent, and all the finest spices in the principal spiritual gifts. These are the spiritual riches of the holy mother Church: the riches of the sprouting garden and the watering fountain. Beloved, let us imitate mother Church in all these things, so that we may deserve with her to see the bridegroom in his beauty and to rejoice with the bride in heaven. Let us too have a paradise of pomegranates, frequently suffering adversity for Christ and daily sharing the suffering of the oppressed; cyprus, [Col. 1086D] governing ourselves with discernment; nard, humbly submitting ourselves to our prelates; saffron, shining with the light of wisdom; calamus, driving our sins from our hearts by confession and mourning; cinnamon, singing thanks for benefits received; trees of Lebanon, displaying works of purity; myrrh, restraining ourselves from the enticements of the flesh; aloes, abstaining even from lawful foods; and all the finest spices, possessing the principal gifts. This is the way; let us walk by it, that we may come to the joy possessed by thousands of saints. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is God, blessed for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXI. On the Works of the Six Days

[Col. 1087A]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). On the first day he made the primal light; on the second day, the firmament; on the third day, he gathered the lower waters into one place; on the fourth day, he made the heavenly lights; on the fifth, birds and fish; on the sixth, beasts. Therefore, after the world had been created, arranged, and adorned, and after everything necessary, useful, and pleasing for the human body had first been prepared, God made man on that same sixth day, lord of all and possessor of the universe. Although created later in time, he was nevertheless found prior in purpose and superior in dignity to the rest. For God made this perceptible world for man, [Col. 1087B] so that the world might be subject to the human body, the body to the spirit, and the spirit to its Creator. Since man was made of a twofold nature, his Creator prepared two goods for him: one visible, the other invisible; one bodily, the other spiritual; one transient, the other eternal; both complete and both perfect in their own kind; one for the flesh, the other for the spirit, so that in the one the sense of the flesh might be nourished with delight, and in the other the sense of the mind might be filled with blessedness. Visible things for the flesh, invisible things for the spirit; for the flesh, consolation; for the spirit, joy. Of these goods he gave one and promised the other: one to be possessed freely, the other to be sought through merit. He freely gave the visible good, but set forth the invisible good as something to be sought by merit, so that through the gratuitous gift both the excellence of the promise and the faithfulness of the promiser might be proved.

[Col. 1087C] But after man, darkened by the gloom of sin, lost the eye of contemplation, this whole universe of visible things not only provides him support for bodily sustenance, but also aid for attaining divine knowledge. For it is written: “His invisible things are clearly perceived, being understood through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1). There are three invisible things of God: power, wisdom, and goodness. From these three all things proceed. Power creates, wisdom governs, goodness preserves. Yet, just as these three are ineffably one in God, so in operation they cannot be separated. Power creates wisely through goodness; wisdom governs kindly through power; goodness preserves powerfully through wisdom. The immensity of creatures manifests power, their beauty wisdom, and their usefulness goodness. Therefore the creation of visible things is a great gift of God and a good for humanity: through it the human body is sustained, and the mind, illuminated by contemplating these things, is wonderfully raised to knowledge, admiration, and love of its Creator.

[Col. 1087D] Indeed, God, though hidden, comes to human knowledge in four ways: inwardly in two ways and outwardly in two ways. Inwardly through reason and inspiration; outwardly through creation and teaching. Reason and creation belong to nature; inspiration and teaching belong to grace.

Having set these matters in order, and briefly treated the works of the six days, let us see what moral teaching lies hidden in them [Col. 1088A], and diligently inquire what may contribute to our edification.

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Heaven is the spirit; earth, the body. By heaven we fittingly understand the human spirit, formed in the image and likeness of God, created to know, love, seek, and possess heavenly goods. By earth we understand the human body, which is earthly and will shortly return to earth. As it is written: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. III). The spirit is heaven, because it conceals and hides from us, at its own will, the things that are within it, as it is written: “For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man which is in him?” (I Cor. II). The body is earth, because it is worn away daily until it returns to earth. Therefore the spirit is heaven [Col. 1088B], and the body earth, because, just as heaven is higher and more substantial than earth, so the spirit is more excellent than the body.

The world in its first confusion is the human being in his iniquity. For just as, in the primordial world still confused, there was neither light nor the order to come, so in the person subject to iniquity neither does light shine through knowledge of truth nor is there order through the ordering of righteousness. And God, as it were, creates the first light amid the confusion when he illuminates the sinner, confused by diverse crimes, with the rays of inward light, so that he may recognize what he is and what he ought to be, and may set himself in order according to the rule of right living. The first light, therefore, signifies knowledge of sin.

The firmament between the upper and lower waters is discernment between vices and virtues. For the lower waters [Col. 1088C] signify vices, and the upper waters virtues. A firmament, as it were, is placed between the two waters when, through the virtue of discernment, virtues are separated from vices and vices from virtues. Then comes the gathering of the waters which were beneath the firmament. The gathering of waters signifies the restraining of vices. Since vices cannot in this life be entirely emptied out or eliminated from the inner recesses of human nature because of the impulses naturally implanted in us, they must, as far as is possible through divine grace, be restrained, confined, and brought together into one place, lest they spread everywhere, occupy everything, and corrupt us; lest they hinder our senses from the search for truth, our affections from the practice of virtue, and our members from the performance of good [Col. 1088D] works.

For just as earth covered by waters cannot germinate, so we, entangled in vices, are unable either to seek truth with our senses, practise virtues with our affections, or offer good works with our bodily members. Therefore, when the waters are gathered into one place, the air becomes bright and warm, and the earth germinates: so, when vices are restrained, our soul shines through knowledge, grows warm through love, and the flesh bears fruit through good action.

The creation of the lights signifies a perfect apprehension of truth, once the cloudy blindness of ignorance has been put aside. The sun may signify knowledge of those things pertaining to the holy Church; the stars, knowledge of those things pertaining to each creature or to each faithful soul. The fishes, which toil in the depths, that is, in the waters, signify the concern of good action carried on amid the waves of this passing life [Col. 1089A]. The birds, which fly to the heights, signify contemplation of heavenly things, by which we are raised from the lowest things to the highest. Land animals figure the senses of our body, because they share, as it were, in human sensation; for animals are created in us when the senses of our body, previously corrupted by vanity, are renewed through divine grace.

When these things have thus been arranged, at last man is made in the image and likeness of God. For when virtues and good works have been so ordered within us, the sinner, who was formerly shapeless and unlike God through guilt, becomes conformed and similar to God through righteousness. Finally, the man formed is transferred into the paradise of delight [Col. 1089B], because the sinner reborn in the world through grace is raised into heaven through glory.

Therefore: heaven, the spirit; earth, the body; the creation of the first light, knowledge; the firmament between the lower and upper waters, discernment between vices and virtues; the gathering of the lower waters, restraint of vices; the bringing forth of shoots, the performance of good works; the creation of the lights, perfect knowledge of truth; fishes, good action; birds, contemplation; the creation of animals, restoration of the bodily senses; the formation of Adam, the perfection of the righteous; Adam in paradise, the righteous in heaven.

Behold, brothers, another world. This greater, sensible world was created before every day; arranged in the first three days; and adorned in the [Col. 1089C] following three. Let us see, beloved, whether, just as we possess existence through creation, we also possess order through righteousness and adornment through good conduct. Let us see whether in us there is the first light through knowledge of our sins; the firmament through discernment of vices and virtues; the gathering of waters through restraint of vices; shoots of trees and plants through the practice of virtues. Let us see whether there are lights through knowledge of truth, fishes through the performance of good works, birds through the flight of contemplation, land animals through incorruptibility of the senses. Let us see whether human dignity, deformed by guilt, has been reformed in us through righteousness; and whether we shall see all that we have done to be [Col. 1089D] very good, when we keep Sabbath with God and in God now through a good conscience, and then shall keep Sabbath in those things through glory, so that there may be fulfilled in us what is written: “There shall be Sabbath after Sabbath” (Isa. LXVI). May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXII. On Noah’s Ark

“All flesh had corrupted its way through unlawful union, and Noah found grace before the Lord. And the Lord said to Noah: Make yourself an ark of planed timbers; and you shall enter it—you, your three sons, your wife, and your sons’ wives. Of every kind of clean animal and bird, take seven and seven; but of unclean animals [Col. 1090A], two and two. For I shall bring the waters of the flood and shall destroy man, and all things which I made for man, in which is the breath of life,” etc. (Gen. VI).

Since I speak to those who know the law, brothers, it seemed good to me to run briefly through the meaning of the ark, leaving fuller gleanings for your own hand. Corruption of the way is the committing of sin; the ark, the Church; Noah, prelates; his household, those subject to them; the inundation of the flood, the temptations of the age. Individual timbers are individual souls; the smoothing of the timbers, the justification of souls; the inner coating, charity in the affections of the heart; the outer coating, charity in the performance of works; the little chambers and the three storeys, diverse orders and diverse merits; the twofold chambering, good action and contemplation; the threefold chambering, marriage, continence, and chastity. The length [Col. 1090B] of the ark is perfect knowledge through the three times of the holy Trinity; its breadth, the effect of good work toward one’s neighbour; its height, the excellence of the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity; the animals are the active; the birds, the contemplative; food, Scripture; forty days, the present life; the mountains of Armenia, the sublimity of eternal life; the receding of the waters, the removal of temptations and persecutions.

Now therefore, brothers, since through faith and baptism we are in the ark, let us see whether we are such as we ought to be: namely, whether we are not among the unclean but among the clean animals and birds. Although in the present Church both kinds seem mingled together according to the effect of certain persons’ works or their reception of the sacraments, nevertheless into the heavenly homeland [Col. 1090C] nothing unclean or defiled shall enter.

Therefore let none among us who are devoted to good action imitate the wolf in rapacity, the hare in useless timidity, the fox in cunning, the bear in grumbling, the dog in quarrelling, the lion in cruelty, the ass in stupidity, or the sow in uncleanness. The eagle flies higher than other birds and therefore fittingly signifies pride. The vulture is thought to be named from its slow flight, because, owing to the size of its body, it does not have swift winged flights; it therefore rightly figures sloth. Likewise the kite, because it is rapacious, expresses rapacity. By the raven, because it tears with its beak, we understand detraction. When the owl cries, it imitates weeping or groaning; it therefore signifies sadness. [Col. 1090D] The night-owl is so called because it flies about at night and cannot see by day. Hence ignorance is understood through it. The magpie articulates words in an approximation of the human voice; though it cannot form language in speech, it nevertheless imitates the sound of human utterance. Of it someone aptly said:

> Talkative magpie, with a sure voice I greet you as master.  
> If you did not see me, you would deny that I am a bird.  
> (MARTIAL, *Epigrams*, XIV.76.)

The magpie, therefore, signifies chatter. The hoopoe, a most filthy bird, dwelling in human excrement and feeding on unclean dung, figures the foulness of human flesh or the stench of a bad reputation. Let none among us who have undertaken to devote themselves to contemplation be an eagle through pride, a vulture through sloth [Col. 1091A], a kite through rapacity, a raven through detraction, an owl through harmful sadness, a night-owl through ignorance, a magpie through chatter, or a hoopoe through foulness and ill repute.

Concerning people of this sort, who follow not the things of sound reason but those of corrupted sensuality, Boethius says in the book *The Consolation of Philosophy*:

> It happens that, when you see someone transformed by vices, you cannot suppose him to be a human being. If he burns with greed and violently snatches what belongs to others, you will call him like a wolf. If, fierce and restless, he exercises his tongue in quarrels, you will compare him with a dog. If he is a hidden plotter and rejoices in stealing through frauds, he is the equal of foxes. If he roars, unrestrained in anger, he is thought to possess the spirit of a lion. If, fearful and flighty, he dreads things not to be feared, let him be considered like a stag. If sluggish and stupid, he lives as an ass [Col. 1091B]. If fickle and inconstant, he shifts his pursuits and differs in no way from birds. If he plunges himself into foul and unclean lusts, he is held fast in the filthy pleasures of a sow. Thus it comes about that one who, having abandoned uprightness, has ceased to be human, is turned into a beast, since he cannot pass into the divine condition.

But since above we said that active persons are signified by walking animals and contemplative persons by flying creatures, let us return to our point and see whether there are any among us who carry some unclean thing with them by which they are made strangers to entrance into the heavenly homeland. For although sinners and unclean persons are never lacking in Noah’s ark—that is, in the universal Church of Christ—nevertheless we must always desire, and as far as we can take care, that in our own three-storey house or upper chamber—that is, in our own household—there should be no one who, through his own fault in thought or deed, in effect or affection, is unworthy of the heavenly fellowship of the saints [Col. 1091C].

For in every condition and rank of this life the worst are mixed with the best; and while the present age runs its course, tares are with ears of wheat, chaff with grain, serpents with fishes, and kids with lambs. Yet although the company of sinners is very burdensome and troublesome to the righteous, it is by no means unprofitable; for though the righteous do not have from them an example of good living, they do have through them an exercise. There is no Abel whom Cain’s malice does not test.

Therefore, in the Gospel, to show that the malice of the wicked is useful to the good, the Lord, while setting forth the parable of the tares [Col. 1091D] and the good seed, related that the master of the field said: “Let both grow until the harvest” (Matt. XIII). Hence he says through the Psalmist: “Do not kill them, lest my people ever forget” (Ps. LVIII). Hence also it is said through Solomon: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song II).

Nevertheless, by every means, beloved, let us labour to rebuke, admonish, and correct those brothers who behave more laxly, lest, when the Judge comes to separate the clean from the unclean, it befall them to enter not glory with the clean but punishment with the unclean. Rather, let us strive together that all of us may deserve to enter the heavenly homeland among the blessed who are to be placed at his right hand, and to contemplate the King in his beauty. May Jesus [Col. 1092A] Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXIII. On Gideon, for the Nativity of the Lord

“You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor, as in the day of Midian” (Isa. IX). These prophetic words refer principally to Christ. Hence, after very few intervening words, the same prophet—namely Isaiah, whose words these are—plainly prophesies concerning him, saying: “A little child is born to us; a son is given to us; and his rule has been placed upon his shoulder. His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His dominion shall be multiplied [Col. 1092B], and there shall be no end of peace. He shall sit upon David’s throne and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness from now and for ever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this” (ibid.).

“You have overcome the yoke of his burden, the rod of his shoulder, and the sceptre of his oppressor.” The yoke is guilt; the rod, punishment; the sceptre, eternal condemnation. We were pressed by the yoke, beaten with the rod, condemned by the sceptre. The oppressor is the devil; the victor, Christ. For when Christ entered the world by assuming our flesh, he, as one stronger coming upon the strong man armed who guarded his court, drove him out and plundered his goods (Luke II). The strong man armed is the devil; the court, the world; the stronger one coming upon him, Christ; the goods, souls; the plundering of the goods, the redemption of souls; the driving out of the strong man armed, the binding [Col. 1092C] of the devil.

Therefore, now that our oppressor has been overcome and his yoke, rod, and sceptre broken, we must take up the prophetic taunt, as the aforesaid prophet mystically commands us, saying: “And it shall be on that day, when the Lord gives you rest from your labour, your distress, and the hard bondage in which you formerly served, that you shall take up this taunt against the king of Babylon and say: How has the oppressor ceased! The tribute has rested! The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, which struck peoples in wrath with an incurable blow, which subjected nations in fury and cruelly persecuted them. The whole earth has rested and been still; it has rejoiced and exulted. The fir trees also rejoice over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: since you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down” (Isa. XIV).

Since, therefore, the yoke has rotted away because of the oil, the rod of our striker has been crushed, and the sceptre of our oppressor broken, we ought rightly to exult over the conquered one and praise the victor. But now let us consider how the spiritual battle was fought and how victory was achieved.

“As in the day of Midian.” We read in the book of Judges that after Deborah’s death the children of Israel sinned against the Lord, and he handed them over into the hand of Midian for seven years; and they were severely oppressed by them. But Gideon, at the Lord’s command, fought against them, overcame them, and freed the people of Israel, etc. (Judg. VI). Since the history is known, and I speak to those who know the law, it seems long and superfluous to repeat the whole story. Let us omit the narration of the history, attend to those things that pertain to the spiritual meaning, and see in what way Christ, our warrior and our Saviour, overcame the yoke of our burden, the rod of our shoulder, and the sceptre of our oppressor, as in the day of Midian [Col. 1093A].

Midian is interpreted “iniquity.” Therefore the people of Midian aptly signify the whole multitude of demons, who never work righteousness but always iniquity. The four princes of Midian—Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, and Zalmunna—aptly figure all the princes of demons. They may be designated by the number four because they attack us and wage war against us through the four quarters of the world; or indeed because they draw us toward the four vices signified by the four quarters of the world. The east, where light rises, expresses cunning [Col. 1093B], because “the children of this age are more prudent than the children of light in their generation” (Luke XVI). The west, because there the sun sets and the upper part of the earth loses light, figures ignorance. Likewise the south, because it is hot, signifies lust; and the north, because it is cold, signifies malice. Thus the princes of demons are four in general, since by these four vices they scatter us, as it were, and divide and destroy us among the four principal winds.

I think these also are the four angels whom in the Apocalypse we read were forbidden to harm the earth, the sea, and the trees, where it is said: “And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the seal of the living God; and he cried with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it had been given to harm the earth and sea, saying: Do not [Col. 1093C] harm the earth, the sea, or the trees until we have sealed the servants of our God upon their foreheads” (Rev. VII). The earth are those who dwell steadily and firmly in the conduct of a holy life. The sea are those who fluctuate in outward actions, moved by the necessities of the present life. The trees are those who, growing upward in lofty divine contemplation, bear fruit. The princes of wicked spirits are forbidden to harm all these, when by a hidden divine ordering they are restrained from injuring them. They inflict upon them a wonderful and miserable injury whenever, their sins demanding it, they are by the same ordering released and able to prevail over them through their temptations.

Thus it is fittingly said in the book of Judges that the children of Israel were grievously oppressed [Col. 1093D] by the Midianites: “They and all their herds came with their tents, and like locusts they filled everything, an innumerable multitude of men and camels, devastating whatever they touched” (Judg. VI). They cover their land like locusts because they are light and flit about, and oppress their carnal senses and affections with their perversities. As the same history relates, they lie in the valley—namely through the depth of despair—to the north through the coldness of malice, beside the mountain through fellowship with pride. For pride is always joined to demons. Their camels, on which they ride, are reprobate human beings, bent down toward earthly things, enormous and burdened with the hump of sins. These camels, plainly, are as innumerable as the sand of the sea, because [Col. 1094A] the number of fools barren in good work is infinite (Eccl. I).

And the Midianites with their camels devastate every crop of the children of Israel while it is still in blade: that is, demons, by stirring up persecutions through reprobate people, destroy in those who seemed to live rightly the tender growth of virtues and good works. Finally, they leave them nothing pertaining to life, when they kill in them the principal virtues—neither oxen, nor sheep, nor asses—because they take away from them continence, innocence, and patience.

Thus spiritual Israelites serve the spiritual Midianites for seven years: that is, throughout all the time in which they abandon God, submit themselves to vices, become entangled in sins, lack virtues, and have no good works. And although, as is written in that history [Col. 1094B], they make for themselves caves and caverns in the mountains and very strong places for fighting, nevertheless they cannot resist their enemies or escape hostile hands. For once we have abandoned God and are abandoned by him, our enemies become, according to Jeremiah, “swifter than the eagles of heaven; they pursue us over the mountains and lie in wait for us in the wilderness” (Lam. IV).

There must come the vigorous purifier of wheat, the bravest of men—namely that Gideon who destroys in the world the altar of idolatry, cuts down the grove of ignorance, offers to God the Father the bull—that is, the fatted calf, namely himself—and seeks no sign either in the fleece or in the dew, but openly displays that which both signify; who overcomes the enemies, frees his people, and [Col. 1094C] saves them. How? By the sound of trumpets, the breaking of jars, and the lighting of lamps.

Christ caused the trumpet to sound when he preached the Gospel. He broke the jar when he underwent the Passion. He lit the lamp when he performed miracles. The trumpet also sounded when he praised the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. XI). For just as there is a trumpet of preaching, so too there is a trumpet of praise, as it is written: “Sound the trumpet at the new moon” (Ps. LXXX); and again: “Praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (Ps. CL).

He broke his little jar, as the Prophet had announced, saying: “Behold, the Lord, the ruler of hosts, [Col. 1094D] shall break the little jar in terror, and those lofty in stature shall be cut down” (Isa. X). The little jar is human flesh. The Lord broke the little jar in terror, because at Christ’s death human beings were terrified, and demons too were terrified. Human beings were terrified because those who had gathered at that spectacle, seeing the earthquake and the other things which happened, returned beating their breasts (Luke XXIII). Demons too were terrified, because they saw him immediately bind the devil, break the bars of the abyss, penetrate the depths of death, and powerfully lead forth his elect as a captive captivity. Those lofty in stature were cut down because proud people were deprived of their ancient dominion.

Christ also lit the lamp when he displayed good works in the world in many ways. Hence he said to the Jews: “I have shown you many good works from my Father” (John X). Gideon summoned thirty thousand men to his battle, but conquered with three hundred (Judg. VII); and in Christ’s army “many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. XX). Those three hundred men signify all the elect who are truly armed either with faith in the holy and undivided Trinity or with the protection of the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity [Col. 1095A]. They drink neither with bent knee nor with their mouths immersed in the waters at the river’s edge, because in passing things they seek not superfluities but necessities only. But the reprobate drink the waters of the stream with bent knee and mouths immersed in the waters, because they plunge themselves wholly into the fleeting delights of passing things.

Gideon overcame his enemies not only on this side of the Jordan but beyond it also; Christ conquered demons not only in Judaea but among the Gentiles as well. Thus Gideon fought; thus Christ fought and conquered. Therefore, brothers, let us consider how we may fight so as to conquer. “What you see me do,” Gideon said to his men, “do likewise; and cry out to the Lord and to Gideon” (Judg. VII). Thus Christ wishes us to fight alongside him, cry out, and conquer. For he gave us an example, that as he did, so we might do. This seems to be the point of his saying: “Those who believe in me shall do the works which I do, and shall do greater things than these” (John XIV).

We have not only Christ as champion and Saviour, but also our prelate, who acts in his place, who ought to go before us in battle and show us by example how to fight [Col. 1095C]. Would that he were Gideon and not Abimelech. For Abimelech signifies a reprobate and wicked prelate, who seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Abimelech slaughtered his brothers upon one stone; the wicked prelate destroys his brothers by his harshness. Abimelech killed the people of his city and scattered salt in it; likewise the reprobate prelate kills by word and example the subjects entrusted to him in his Church, leaving within it, insofar as his perversity is permitted, neither wise person nor wisdom. Let the men of Shechem have Abimelech; may we have Gideon.

“The trees of the forest,” he says, “went to appoint a king over themselves. They came to the olive, the vine, and the fig, all of which refused to reign over them and to be promoted among them. Then the trees said to the bramble: Rule over us. It answered: If you truly appoint me king over you, come and rest beneath my shade. But if you do not wish it, let fire come forth from the bramble and devour the cedars of Lebanon” (Judg. IX).

In Jotham’s parable the forest trees are the men of Shechem and the bramble is Abimelech. But in the mystical sense, what could we understand more rightly by the trees of the forest than nations or any fruitless communities, and people old and inveterate in sins and fit for eternal fires? By the olive we may understand some faithful person excellent in the virtue of mercy. By the vine, because Christ, who is the wisdom of God, says, “I am the vine” (John XV) [Col. 1096A], and because it is written, “Wine moderately taken sharpens the mind,” we understand any righteous person distinguished in the virtue of wisdom. Finally, by the fig we understand another person outstanding in the grace of inward sweetness, for the fig has sweet fruit.

The forest trees come to the olive, vine, and fig in order to receive a king from them, when any fruitless thoughts seek a merciful, wise, gentle, or sweet person as prelate. But the olive, vine, and fig tree reject such rule, because the elect fear that, if they are established over the wicked, they will be deprived of their own fruit by the wickedness of those people and will help them in no way. Then the trees raise the bramble over themselves as king when wicked people demand as ruler another wicked person, covered with the thorns of sins. These too are devoured by reciprocal fire, when the perverse subjects and their perverse prelate are disturbed by one another’s fury. Of such people, and of such fire and devouring, the prophet says: “Your spirit, like fire, shall devour you” (Isa. XXXIII) [Col. 1096B]. For they envy one another, bite one another, and consume one another. But let us now return to our subject.

Therefore Christ overcame the yoke of our burden and the sceptre of our oppressor, as in the day of Midian, because by the trumpet of his preaching, the Passion of his death, and the performance of good action he defeated the demons and freed us from their dominion. We also have another Gideon: namely, our prelate, who acts in this battle in the place of Christ the champion and Saviour, daily defeating our enemies with Christ’s help [Col. 1096C].

With Gideon this man must offer unleavened bread, namely simple teaching; a kid, through penitence; the same kid cooked, through love; and pour incense over it through compunction. He must also offer the bull, namely himself, so that, even if he is not granted in deed to die for his people, he may nevertheless always be prepared in will to die for them. “I shall enter a part of the camp,” Gideon says, “and follow what I do” (Judg. VII). Thus every prelate ought to present to those subject to him a pattern of good living, lest he be proved to belong to the number of those who say and do not do, who bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon people’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their own finger (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore he should enter the enemy camp not only by arranging what is useful and necessary, or by providing against evils and providing for the practice of goods, but also by doing these things. Let him enter a part of the camp by fulfilling his ministry. Let him enter a part of the camp, for he cannot do everything alone, because Moses’ hands are heavy and need to be supported by the assistance of others [Col. 1096D]. Let him sound his trumpet by preaching and singing; break the jar by fasting and keeping vigil; light the torch by practising virtues and performing good works. And let us cry out to the Lord and Gideon, imitating him in all these things.

But there are certain carnal people, even cloaked in the habit of religious life, whose trumpet-blast is wholly carnal. For they never speak of religious observance, never of reforming the order, because, according to the apostolic saying, they savour not the things of the spirit but those of the flesh (Rom. VIII). “We sleep too little,” they say; “we eat too little; we live most poorly.” If these people are not filled, they often not only murmur but quarrel. May they at least have peace when filled. Yet we do not reproach people for speaking thus of the necessities of the body. But it is remarkable in our eyes that they always speak of carnal matters and never of spiritual things. For to speak, as is fitting, of the necessities of the human body is praiseworthy, since no one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it. Yet to speak of what pertains to the spirit is altogether necessary, since the human spirit is the better part of the human being—or indeed, as a certain philosopher says, the human being himself. “The mind,” he says, “is whatever each person is” [Col. 1097A].

Others open their mouths wide enough in the refectory for eating and drinking, but in choir often or always shut them for reading and singing. Others, with no smaller fault but greater madness, while confessing to the Lord, shake their heads too little in heart and too much with their mouths, falsify their voices, make their chant effeminate, and, captivated by the spirit of vainglory, screech and hiss rather than sing in the divine praise.

Therefore now, beloved, let us fraternally rebuke and correct one another in all these things, so that, with our trumpet sounding well, we may terrify the camps of the enemies. Moreover, the divine word, which we say is figured by the trumpet whether preached or sung, is understood in this same history through bread or a sword. “Someone recounting a dream,” he says, “said to his neighbour: ‘I saw a dream, and it seemed that a barley cake, baked under ashes, rolled down [Col. 1097C] into the camp of Midian; and when it reached the tent, it struck it, overthrew it, and levelled it completely to the ground.’ The man to whom he spoke replied: ‘This is nothing other than the sword of Gideon. For God has delivered Midian and all its camp into his hands’” (Judg. VII).

Therefore the word of God is a trumpet, bread, and a sword. It is a trumpet because it sounds in the ears. It is bread because it nourishes the mind of those hungering for righteousness. It is a sword because it penetrates the secrets of hearts. Hence the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart; and no creature is invisible in his sight” (Heb. IV).

But we must not only sound the trumpet, as has been said, through preaching, chanting, or singing; we must also break the jar, crucifying our flesh with its vices and desires. Yet there are many in religious orders who, though they have professed religion, shrink from its healthful harshness, always wishing to live in luxurious ease and asserting that God requires no hardship from abstaining from meat. But we, beloved, should break this little jar in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, labour and hardship, and other such things. Let us light our lamps, that we may practise virtues and display good works. With such weapons we shall overcome our enemies, obtain victory, and possess the palm—yes, the golden [Col. 1098A] palm. So Gideon, of whom this discourse speaks, obtained a golden palm when he requested and received from his army golden earrings from the enemies’ spoil. So too, brothers, if we contend lawfully, we shall possess the golden palm, that is, heavenly glory. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXIV. On the Apostles Peter and Paul
God made two great lights: the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night, and the stars (Gen. 1). Perhaps you wonder, brethren, why, when we are about to address you on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, we lay the foundation of our sermon in matters contained in the works of the six days. Yet we do this not without reason [Col. 1098B], since through the creation of the world we fittingly understand the regeneration of the human race, and through the adornment of heaven and earth the beauty and comeliness of the universal Church. Heaven signifies those things which are exalted in the holy Church; earth, those which are lowly. Heaven signifies prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives; earth, subjects, the imperfect, and the active. For prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives are superior to subjects, the imperfect, and the active, whether by the authority of their title, the distinction of their rank, or the merit of their virtue. Subjects, the imperfect, and the active are inferior to prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives. The adornment of the heavens expresses the virtues of the perfect; the adornment of the earth, the virtues of the imperfect. Divine contemplation adorns the former, as heavens raised on high; good action beautifies the latter [Col. 1098C], like earth still lying below. The former protect by continual prayers; the latter are protected. Heavenly grace is bestowed on the former, and through them conveyed to the latter. Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “I shall hear the heavens, and they shall hear the earth” (Hos. 2). And elsewhere it is written: “The Lord shall open his best treasure, heaven, that he may give rain to your land in its season” (Deut. 28).

Since, therefore, through the creation of the world we fittingly understand the restoration of the human race, and through the ordering and adornment of heaven and earth the order and beauty of the universal Church, what ought we more properly to understand by the two great lights—the sun, namely, and the moon—than the holy apostles whose feast we celebrate, that is, Peter and Paul [Col. 1098D], who are truly lights by grace and great by excellence? Peter surpasses the others in the excellence of authority; Paul, in the excellence of preaching. Peter is the sun; Paul the moon: Peter, the sun, through the power divinely bestowed on him; Paul, the moon, through the wisdom bestowed on him from heaven. God made the greater light when he said to Peter: “Flesh and blood did not reveal to you the sacrament of faith, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16); and he commanded him then to shine in heaven when he entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven. He made the lesser light when he struck Saul down and raised Paul up, and in him extinguished bodily light for a time but kindled spiritual light forever.

But now let us see how he commanded the greater light to rule [Col. 1099A] the day, and the lesser light to rule the night. Judaea is fittingly signified by the day, for it was illuminated by the teaching of the Law and the prophets as by a certain brightness of heavenly light. In this respect, indeed, it shone before the Gentiles to no small degree: it possessed not only the natural law but also the written law. Hence the Apostle, disputing concerning Jews and Gentiles, says: “What advantage then has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Rom. 3).

The Gentile world is rightly represented by the night, for it was formerly covered in the darkness of its own blindness. Was not the Gentile world a dark night, when even its wise men, though they had known God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts [Col. 1099B], and their foolish heart was darkened? “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things” (Rom. 1). Although they had known God by naturally apprehending him, they did not glorify him as God by worshipping him in righteousness, nor did they give thanks by praising him for the benefit received; rather, through pride they became vain in their thoughts. And their foolish heart was darkened through ignorance. For pride, while it fills the mind with smoke, darkens those deprived of the brightness of their own light. Professing through pride and boasting that they were wise through knowledge received, they became fools through the working of pride, by blind and blinding [Col. 1099C] ignorance.

The extent of the folly into which they fell is shown when he immediately adds concerning idolatry: “And they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, and of four-footed beasts, and of creeping things.” And shortly afterward: “God gave them over to dishonourable passions; for their women burned in desire toward one another; and, since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things unfitting: filled with all iniquity, malice, fornication, avarice, wickedness; full of envy, murders, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, detractors, hateful to God, abusive, proud, arrogant, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish [Col. 1099D], disorderly, without natural affection, without fidelity, without mercy” (ibid.). Rebuking this sharply under the person of a single human being, Paul, whose words these are, says: “By your hardness and impenitent heart you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and revelation of the just judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works” (Rom. 2).

Thus abyss calls to abyss, when fault begets fault. The fault of pride produced in them the blindness of ignorance; the blindness of ignorance produced the impiety of idolatry; the impiety of idolatry produced the stain of lust; and the stain of lust, with the aforementioned evils working together, produced the enormity of every injustice, which at last produced contempt and the hardness of impenitence. Behold how the Gentile world was a dark night. But the greater light ruled [Col. 1100A] the day and the lesser light the night when Peter preached to the Jews and Paul to the Gentiles. Paul clearly declares this in the Epistle to the Galatians: “When they saw,” he says, “that the Gospel of the uncircumcision had been entrusted to me, as that of the circumcision to Peter—for he who worked through Peter for the apostleship of the circumcision also worked through me among the Gentiles,” etc. (Gal. 2).

Thus Judaea is the day, not the Gentile world; Peter the greater light, Paul the lesser light. Although Paul was the preacher to the Gentiles, although he was a vessel of election, although he laboured more than all the others, although he was in no way inferior to the great apostles, although he was caught up into the third heaven and into the paradise of God and there heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter, I nevertheless do not think that I detract in anything from his eminence [Col. 1100B] when I compare him to the lesser light, that is, the moon, and Peter to the greater, that is, the sun. For it is established that to Peter alone was said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church. And I shall give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16). And to Peter alone, at the Lord’s command, it was granted to walk upon the waters of the sea; and upon Peter alone, among and before the others, pastoral care was principally and specially imposed by the Lord when he said: “Feed my lambs” (John 21).

Yet both are great, both wonderful, both praiseworthy and worthy of proclamation; both are brothers in suffering, and on one day, in one place, endured the sentence of one tyrant. Therefore, although for the convenience of our argument we have above distinguished them in accordance with the aforesaid lights, it is not certain which should be preferred to which, since those who are equal in suffering may be judged not unequal in merits. And although faith stands out in Peter and doctrine excels in Paul, nevertheless the fullness of faith is Paul’s teaching, and Peter’s belief is the foundation of doctrine. These are the two chief towers in the Church, two bulwarks, two leaders, two heralds, two pillars, two olive trees, two lampstands: towers by rising high, bulwarks by defending, leaders by fighting, heralds by preaching; pillars by sustaining, olive trees by showing mercy, lampstands by shining.

It must certainly be known that, although the power of loosing and binding appears to have been given by the Lord to Peter alone, it was nevertheless, without any doubt [Col. 1100D], given also to the other apostles, as he himself testifies: after the triumph of his passion and resurrection, appearing to them, he breathed upon them and said to them all: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20). And even now the same office is entrusted throughout the whole Church to bishops and priests: namely, that, after the cases of sinners have been examined, whoever they see to be humble and truly penitent, these they may mercifully absolve from the fear of everlasting death. Likewise, although Paul received in an eminent manner the special gift of teaching, it must nevertheless be recognized that the other apostles were perfectly endowed with the grace of his teaching, since the Lord himself imposed upon them the ministry of teaching when he said: [Col. 1101A] “Going forth, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (Matt. 28).

God therefore made two great lights, that the greater light might rule the day and the lesser light the night. “And let them,” he says, “be for signs and seasons and days and years; and let them shine in the firmament of heaven and give light to the earth” (Gen. 1). So far as the literal sense is concerned, we know that the bodily lights of heaven serve as signs of storm and fair weather, as signs for navigation, and for many other such purposes. They are also for seasons, because by their course, rising, and setting the four seasons of the year are determined and completed. They are for days [Col. 1101B] and years, because these are completed by their—and especially the sun’s—rising, course, and setting.

Thus these spiritual lights are signs for us when they furnish us examples of avoiding evil and doing good. They are also for seasons, in that they plainly teach us that no one ought to hope in the uncertainty of riches, which pass away with the seasons. Hence blessed Paul says: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep, as though they did not weep; those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it: for the form of this world passes away” (1 Cor. 7). And to Timothy: “Command the rich of this world not to be high-minded, nor to hope in the uncertainty of riches” (1 Tim. 6). They are for seasons [Col. 1101C] for us when they instruct us to seek eternal things amid temporal things. Thus the same Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

By days we understand the beginning of good works, but by years their completion. These holy heavenly lights therefore provide and determine days and years for us, because by their precepts they reasonably and discerningly enlighten us toward the beginning and perfection of good works, as the aforesaid apostle exhorts, saying: “I beseech you, brethren, by the mercy of God, that you present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—your reasonable service” (Rom. 12). Finally, these lights shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth, because they shine wonderfully among those established in heavenly conduct [Col. 1101D], and grant to the lower and imperfect the light of righteousness by instructing them with words and inflaming them with examples. For holy persons who are perfect are established in heavenly conduct: on the way, by grace; in the homeland, by glory. Here by righteousness; there by the first robe, until they receive also the second. Hence the aforesaid Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). The imperfect, however, still dwell as it were on earth, since they often labour in earthly toils. Therefore the former are fittingly designated by the name of the firmament, and the latter by the name of earth. Thus have we spoken of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and have set forth their great brightness according to the two greater lights of heaven, not as we wished, but as we were able.

[Col. 1102A] “And the stars.” As we understand Peter and Paul through the two greater lights of heaven according to the foregoing interpretation, so we must understand the other apostles through the stars. For although all the apostles are great and all alike and jointly endowed with heavenly grace, yet I do not know by what arrangement Peter and Paul seem to excel the rest by a certain special strength of faith in heaven: to Peter, as a good steward, he gave the keys of the kingdom of heaven; upon Paul, as a capable teacher, he imposed the office of instructing the Church. Therefore these two greatest lights, like sun and moon, do not appear fixed in one place: the care of the universal Church is entrusted to Peter, and the teaching of all nations committed to Paul. But all the others, like stars in the firmament, appear each fixed [Col. 1102B] in one place, since each preached in a single kingdom. John preached in Asia; Andrew in Achaia; Matthew in Ethiopia; James the Greater and James the Less in Judaea; Philip in Scythia; Thomas in Greater India; Bartholomew in Lesser India; Simon and Jude in Persia.

But it was not so with Peter and Paul. Peter, leaving the others in the boat and walking on the waters of the sea, received a sign that he would be chief of all ecclesiastical rank. Paul, for his part, “from Jerusalem, and round about as far as Illyricum, fulfilled the Gospel of Christ.” Therefore, though all shine upon us together from heaven, offering the light of truth amid the darkness of the present life and teaching us how we may ascend from Babylon to the heavenly Jerusalem, blessed Peter and Paul [Col. 1102C], whose feasts we celebrate, irradiate us with a certain special brilliance of heavenly righteousness.

Now therefore, beloved, illumined by the splendour of such great lights, “we are all children of light and children of the day, not of the night nor of darkness” (1 Thess. 5). Let us “cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light” (Rom. 13). Yet not this only: let us also be transformed from brightness to brightness, as by the Spirit of the Lord; that is, let us not merely abandon evils and acquire goods, but even among good things always pursue those which are greater, so that, ascending from virtue to virtue, through the merits and prayers of the blessed apostles, we may deserve to see the God of gods in Zion. May Jesus Christ, our Lord, who is God blessed for ever [Col. 1102C], deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXV. On the Nativity of Blessed Mary

As a thorn produced a rose, so Judaea produced Mary. The ancient people, brethren—the Israelite people—was like a certain tree: it had its root in Abraham; it put forth its trunk in Isaac and Jacob; it rose up and multiplied branches and twigs in the twelve patriarchs and their sons. On account of the richness of the faith and righteousness of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and of certain persons born from them, it deserved in some places of Scripture to be called an olive tree or a vine; but because of the depravity of some—indeed, of many—who descended from it, it may more especially be compared to a thorn.

Hence, to show its preceding goodness [Col. 1103A] and its subsequent depravity, the Lord says through Jeremiah: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true seed; how have you turned into a degenerate, foreign vine?” (Jer. 2). And shortly afterward Jeremiah himself says: “The Lord called your name ‘a luxuriant olive tree, beautiful, fruitful, and fair.’ At the sound of a great utterance, fire was kindled in it” (Jer. 11). Scripture testifies that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and most of those born from their stock pleased the Lord, and that the Lord spoke with them or through them; thus we recognize that this people is deservedly compared to a vine or vineyard, an olive tree, or even a fig tree.

But now let us see how and why, because of the impiety of many of its children [Col. 1103B], this same people ought rightly to be compared to a thorn, which produces sharp pricks and wounds cruelly; and we shall find that many thorns of its cruelty may be counted from the testimonies of sacred speech. First, then, concerning the thorns of that people’s cruelty we read that Joseph was unjustly hated by his brothers, stripped of his long robe, put into a pit, and finally cruelly sold to Ishmaelite merchants to be taken away among foreign and unknown peoples. In Egypt too, when afflicted by Pharaoh, though they should have shown patience in adversity, they angrily said against Moses and Aaron: “You have made our odour stink before Pharaoh and his servants, and have given him a sword to kill us” (Exod. 5).

After they had departed from Egypt, before crossing the Red Sea, when they saw the Egyptians following them, they raged against Moses and said: “Perhaps there were no graves in Egypt, and so you brought us out to die in the wilderness. What did you mean by doing this, by bringing us out of Egypt? Is this not what we told you in Egypt, saying: ‘Go away from us, that we may serve the Egyptians; for it is much better to serve them than to die in the wilderness’?” (Exod. 14). But after the crossing of the Red Sea, in the wilderness of Sin they angrily said against Moses and Aaron: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to satisfaction. Why have you brought us into this wilderness, to kill this whole multitude with hunger?” (Exod. 16).

But since the Psalmist, because of the manifold wickedness of their depravity, cries out not in inquiry but in astonishment [Col. 1103D] and amazement: “How often did they provoke him in the wilderness, and turn the Most High to anger in the waterless place?” (Ps. 105), what need is there laboriously to describe their disputes one by one and enumerate their various quarrels, by which they provoked the Lord and Moses in the camp, and Aaron the holy one of the Lord? Likewise, when established in the promised land, they sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know; they abandoned God who had begotten them and forgot the Lord their creator. They destroyed his altars and killed the prophets. Finally, to complete the measure of their condemnation, they crucified and killed the author of life.

By these and such perversities, like the most cruel thorns [Col. 1104A], that faithless people was ever bristling; nor did it cease to tear and make bloody the flowers proceeding from itself—that is, the prophets and other righteous people born from it. Some of these were sawn asunder, such as Isaiah; some stoned, such as Jeremiah in Egypt and Ezekiel in Babylon; some killed by the sword, such as Uriah and Josiah; others, fleeing their threats, wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, such as Elijah, destitute, distressed, afflicted—persons “of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11; the citation is printed as Heb. II). Its rulers also “slew the widow and the stranger, and killed the fatherless,” and said, “The Lord shall not see” (Ps. 94; printed XCXIII).

Concerning such most cruel prickings, the Lord reproving the scribes and Pharisees also says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who build the tombs of the prophets [Col. 1104B] and adorn the monuments of the righteous, and say: ‘If we had been in the days of our fathers, we would not have been their partners in the blood of the prophets.’ Thus you bear witness against yourselves that you are the sons of those who killed the prophets” (Matt. 23). And shortly afterward: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you” (ibid.).

This tree also had leaves that would not remain forever but would one day fall: namely, the carnal observances of the Law. Paul indicates their passing away when, speaking of them, he states the parable of the present time: “According to it gifts and sacrifices were offered which could not, as regards conscience, make perfect the worshipper, consisting only in foods and drinks and various washings and ordinances of the flesh imposed until the time of reformation” (Heb. 9). And elsewhere: “The preceding commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness. For the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). For the Law had “a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things.”

Therefore, we understand Abraham as the root of our tree; Isaac and Jacob as its trunk; the twelve patriarchs as its branches; their sons as its many twigs; carnal observances as its leaves; the righteous of old, especially the prophets, as its flowers; and the perversities of that same people as its thorny pricks. Among these flowers, blessed Virgin Mary shines more gloriously than the rest: she surpasses not only the righteous of old but all righteous persons by her beauty.

But since we have explained how the Jewish people [Col. 1104D] is compared to a thorn, let us say how blessed Mary is signified by a rose, that is, by the flower itself. Four things seem distinguishable in a rose: its nature, form, colour, and fragrance. A rose is cold by nature, broad in form, white or red in colour, pleasant in fragrance. By its nature, therefore, it signifies the extinction of vices; by its form, charity; by its colour, purity and suffering—or, rather, compassion; by its fragrance, good repute. All these things, except bodily suffering, most fittingly apply to blessed Mary, whose nativity we celebrate today. For, to pass over the other matters which are sufficiently well known, blessed Mary possessed the virtue of compassion because, as it is written, a sword of sorrow pierced her soul (Luke 2).

Therefore, as stated above, Judaea is the thorn and Mary the rose. And [Col. 1105A] as a thorn produced a rose, so Judaea produced Mary: that cruel people brought forth this mercy. For what is more cruel than the Jewish people, of whom it is written: “The sea-monsters have uncovered the breast; the daughter of my people is cruel, like the ostrich in the wilderness” (Lam. 4)? And again: “The iniquity of the daughter of my people has become greater than the sin of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment and no hands were laid upon it.” But what is more merciful than blessed Mary, who is called the mother of mercy by all the faithful and is proved to be the mother of mercy by all who invoke her with true faith?

But since we cannot sufficiently describe the wickedness of Judaea and the ever-praiseworthy goodness of blessed Mary, let us turn the pen upon ourselves and diligently consider how we should depart from the former and imitate the latter [Col. 1105B]. Let us not, therefore, imitate impious Judaea so as to be thorns—those thorns, I mean, of which David says: “Transgressors shall all be plucked up like thorns, which are not taken away with hands; and if anyone wishes to touch them, he shall arm himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, and they shall be burned up with fire unto nothing” (2 Sam. 23). These thorns are cruel, cruel and detestable. They are not taken away with hands because they cannot be plucked from their cruelty by human power, but only by divine power. And if anyone wishes to touch them, he shall arm himself with iron and the shaft of a spear, because the bestial cruelty of some is in no way restrained unless it is struck by the harshest and most severe rigour of justice. Finally, they are burned up with fire unto nothing because, condemned to the flames of Gehenna, they are reduced to nothing insofar as pertains to what they were in the world.

Let us not, brethren, be such thorns or like them. The bitter fruit of thorns is a bloody prick, and thorns are seldom suited to any purpose except fire and burning. And what is more bitter than sin, or what is more grievous than the eternal fires in which sinners are burned? Let us imitate blessed Virgin Mary, especially according to what we have said above about the rose: according to its cold nature, let us extinguish the flames of our vice; according to its form, let us spread our hearts more broadly in love of God and neighbour. Let us be ruddy—if not by shedding blood for Christ, at least by showing compassion to his infirm members—and fragrant by spreading good repute everywhere [Col. 1105D]. Let us avoid Jewish wickedness by turning away from evil; let us imitate the holiness of blessed Virgin Mary by doing good, so that through her merits and prayers we may deserve to escape condemnation and attain blessedness. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXVI. On Praising God, on the Feast of Any Saint

From many passages of sacred Scripture we have learned that God is wonderful and praiseworthy in his saints, and the more praiseworthy in proportion as he is more wonderful. The holy Psalmist sets before us various modes of divine praise in the last psalm of his book, where he says: [Col. 1106A] “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and harp; with timbrel and choir; with strings and organ. With well-sounding cymbals; with cymbals of jubilation” (Ps. 150). And, to teach beforehand that all these are to be understood not of bodily but of spiritual instruments, he immediately adds: “Let every spirit praise the Lord”—that is, every angelic and human spirit. Let us therefore see what all these things signify spiritually.

The trumpet has a terrible sound, and thereby represents that preaching which strongly terrifies us either concerning the shortness of the present life or the duration of future condemnation: concerning the shortness of the present life, as where it says, “Now the axe is laid to the root of the tree” (Matt. 3); concerning the duration of future condemnation, as where it says, “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be extinguished” [Col. 1106B] (Isa. 66). Since we have sufficiently spoken above in a certain sermon on the difference between trumpets, that is, the kinds of preaching, we do not now care to repeat the same matters.

“Praise him with psaltery and harp.” The psaltery is divine contemplation; the harp, good action, because the psaltery sounds from above and the harp from below.
