This psaltery is indeed called well “ten-stringed” in sacred Scripture, because in divine contemplation the whole sequence of the Law is truly and perfectly fulfilled. This spiritual harp has six strings: the six works of mercy, namely, giving food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and so forth. Christ himself urges us to play this harp and through it sing praise to God, when he says: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11). And he rebuked the ancients for contempt through the prophet, saying: “Refresh the weary; this is my refreshment, and you would not hear” (Isa. 28).

“Praise him with timbrel and choir.” A timbrel is made from dried hide stretched over a wooden hoop; young women who play the timbrel commonly use it, having no finer instruments. The timbrel fittingly signifies abstinence, through which the flesh is dried, made lean, and stretched. Paul seems to express this timbrel when he says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5).

But because abstinence is of no avail unless concord accompanies it, he rightly added “and choir” after saying, “Praise him with timbrel.” A choir is a harmoniously balanced gathering [Col. 1106D] of voices; therefore concord of conduct is designated by the choir. Those who seek to praise the Lord with the timbrel of abstinence but not also with the choir of concord are rightly reproved in their fasts, as it is said through the prophet: “Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and strike wickedly with the fist. Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the fast that I have chosen, for a person to afflict his soul for a day?” (Isa. 58). And shortly afterward: “Is not this rather the fast that I have chosen? Loose the bonds of impiety; undo the bundles that oppress” (ibid.). Therefore whoever wishes to please the Lord by praising him with the timbrel of abstinence should endeavour also to please him by praising him with the choir of concord.

“Praise him with strings [Col. 1107A] and organ.” The strings signify virtues. Strings are stretched in order to produce sound; virtues are exercised in order to yield fruit. The stretching of strings, therefore, is the exercise of virtues; the sound of strings, the usefulness of virtues. They praise God with strings who honour him by living rightly through holy virtues; and their strings sound harmoniously when their virtues agree uniformly in producing praiseworthy righteousness. Those virtues too give forth a clear sound which are dried of every moisture, because virtues not moistened by the watery flux of vices sound sweetly to God. Finally, strings make no sound unless touched, because virtues do not shine forth at all unless first exercised amid adversities. The sound of strings is strengthened and formed by the hollow of the wood near them; but the goodness of virtues is commended by the inward and hidden intention of the doer.

An organ is like a tower constructed of various pipes, which sounds by the blast of bellows. What, then, do we understand by the bellows except more perfect teachers filled with spiritual teaching, and what more fittingly by the organ than the assembled body of hearers who are disciples? The organ is filled by bellows in order that it may give forth sound through its pipes; and the company of disciples is filled by teachers full of the Holy Spirit with spiritual teaching, in order that through their faculties and members—or, indeed, virtues and works—it may offer praise to God. Therefore God is praised by us in the organ when he is glorified in our hearers through our spiritual teaching and their good conduct. Thus we fulfil what is written: “Glorify the Lord in teachings” [Col. 1107C] (Isa. 24). The organ has the shape of a tower because the multitude of disciples ought always to be strong and lofty in resisting enemies. Therefore we praise the Lord with strings when we exercise virtues in ourselves; with the organ when we advance others in one way or another toward the praise of God.

“Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.” Cymbals strike one another and thus give sound; they signify the reciprocal honour by which righteous persons outdo one another, together with the mutual exhortation by which they admonish one another always to act better and praise God more devoutly. Concerning these cymbals and their mutual striking, or harmony, blessed Paul says: “Loving one another with brotherly charity, outdoing one another in honour” [Col. 1107D] (Rom. 12). And again: “I myself also am certain concerning you, my brethren, that you yourselves are full of love, filled with all knowledge, so that you are able to admonish one another” (Rom. 15; the citation is printed as Rom. XI). These, indeed, are well-sounding cymbals: the reciprocal holy admonitions of saints toward greater progress.

The cymbals of jubilation are fittingly our lips, which, when they strike one another in praising God, sweetly express the delightful joy of his jubilation. Jubilation is an ineffable joy which can neither be kept silent nor adequately expressed. The Church represents it at its principal feasts by forming varied melodies around the same syllable, as at the Nativity of the Lord is sung *tanquam sponsus*, “as a bridegroom,” as though unable to express the gladness of the mind.

Now therefore [Col. 1108A], beloved, let us praise the Lord with the sound of the trumpet, as has been said, by preaching; with the psaltery, by contemplation; with the harp, by good action. Let us praise him with the timbrel, by abstinence; with the choir, by concord. Let us praise him with strings, by exercising virtues in ourselves; with the organ, by instructing and urging others through spiritual teaching toward divine praise. Let us praise him with well-sounding cymbals, by mutually admonishing one another toward better things; with cymbals of jubilation, by always singing his praise with our lips. Let us, I say, praise the Lord, because divine praise is for us a special song of singular joy.

Let us praise the Lord, because if we praise him as we ought, we shall be the people of whom he says: “This people I have formed for myself; it shall declare my praise” [Col. 1108B] (Isa. 43). Let us praise the Lord, because “the sacrifice of praise honours him; and there is the way by which he will show us his salvation” (Ps. 49). Let us praise the Lord, whom, Scripture testifying, all his works praise—not only sentient things, but also things without sense and without feeling. And since not all of us can do all things, and each has his own gift from God, let each of us sing divine praise by working excellently in that wherein he recognizes that he has, as it were, a particular grace.

Therefore let us all praise the Lord; let each of us praise him. Let us praise him by our conduct; let us praise him upon earth with righteous people in time; let us praise him with our voices, so that through the merits and prayers of the saints whose feasts we celebrate today, we may deserve to praise him above heaven [Col. 1108C] with the angels in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXVII. On the Allegory of Four Kings Fighting against Five Kings
It came to pass that Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Pontus, Chedorlaomer king of the Elamites, and Tidal king of the Nations made war against Bera king of the Sodomites, against Birsha king of Gomorrah, against Shemeber king of Zeboiim, against Shinab king of Admah, and against the king of Bela—that is, Zoar (Gen. 14).

The four kings mentioned above are all the demons. They may be said to be four because they assail us from the four winds, or because they strive to overthrow the four principal virtues within us. Of these, Chedorlaomer—who stood among the others as their head and prince, and for whose sake the war was principally undertaken—particularly represents the devil, who holds primacy among the other evil spirits in attacking or overcoming believers. Chedorlaomer is interpreted as “generation of a sheaf,” or “a handsome sheaf,” because the devil, as it were, begets a collection of evils when by his wicked suggestions he produces them in evil; and carries them in his hand like a handsome sheaf when he bears those adorned with the deceptive beauty of this world to torments.

He is king of the Elamites. Elam is interpreted as “age” or “world,” and signifies the whole company of people who love the world and walk about in the circuit of their perversity, as it is written: “The wicked walk about on every side” (Ps. 11). Elamites are also interpreted as “opponents” or “despised persons.” The devil is king of the Elamites, that is, of all those who oppose the faithful and are deservedly despised by them. Finally, all reprobate spirits are kings, because, according to the Apostle, they are “the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. 6).

The region of the Pentapolis, arranged in its five cities, is the sensuality of human flesh, distinguished by its five properties. The five bodily senses are the kings of this region, insofar as they rule over external affairs, naturally and properly assigned and allotted to them according to their fivefold distinction. But the four aforesaid kings overcome the five subordinate kings when evil spirits corrupt the bodily senses by wicked pleasures.

And for twelve years the Pentapolis serves Chedorlaomer in its five kings when the whole multitude of people living carnally renders to the devil, in the five corrupted senses of the body, the service which it ought to have rendered to God according to apostolic teaching. It withdraws from him in the thirteenth year when, according to the right faith of the Holy Trinity, it determines upon the Decalogue of the Law. But when a company of carnal persons, pierced by the fear of God, resolves to renounce its wickedness, then the devil rages more fiercely against it. Hence in this history it is written that, when the five kings of the Pentapolis withdrew from Chedorlaomer, he assembled his allied kings and made war against them.

Yet this battle was by no means fought in a place suitable to the advantage of the five kings. For it is written that they drew up battle against the four kings in the woodland valley. Now the woodland valley had many pits of bitumen. Therefore the king of Sodom and the king of Gomorrah turned their backs and fell there; and those who remained fled to the mountain. They took all the possessions of Sodom and Gomorrah, and everything belonging to food, and departed; also Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, who dwelt in Sodom, and his possessions. And one who had escaped reported it to Abram.

So it is, dearly beloved: we often see that certain people resolve to serve God, yet do not perfectly renounce their wickedness; and it happens not that they conquer their enemies, but that, struck down by their enemies, they fall and lose their possessions—that is, their virtues and the good works they have already begun. For what is signified by the woodland valley except earthly and fruitless activity? What by the pits of bitumen except the depth of bitter adhesiveness, or indeed the abyss of sticky and perverse habit? Therefore, if we intend to fight our spiritual enemies, let us not descend into the valley of vices, but climb the mountain of virtues, that we may conquer—or at least escape.

“They took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother.” Abram, whose name is interpreted “exalted father,” signifies understanding, which seems to surpass and preside over the other faculties of the soul. His brother Haran, whose name is interpreted “exalted,” denotes affection, given to a human being not so that it may cling to what is lowest, but so that through it the person may always adhere to what is highest. Therefore, if Abram in mystical signification is rational understanding and Haran his brother is the affection of the heart, we may fittingly understand Lot as the effect of a good work. For the effect of a good work is born from the heart’s affection.

Nor is it surprising that, when Haran is dead and Abram absent, Lot is captured and carried away. For when the heart’s affection dies through sin and diligent understanding is absent through negligence, the effect of a good work is immediately estranged from the rectitude of good intention and entirely deprived of its goods. These goods may be called the six works of mercy. The messenger who reports these things to Abram is the worm of an evil conscience, which, after all else has been carried away, is accustomed to remain alone.

When he learns this, the exalted father, joined by three hundred and eighteen servants born in his household—that is, the other powers of the soul—pursues and defeats the enemies, and by overcoming with the three hundred and eighteen servants brings back the spoil of virtues and good works. Three hundred, according to the assertion of the teachers, signifies the letter tau, which has the form of a cross. Thus, in the sacrament of the cross, in the tenfold number of the Law, and in the eightfold number—that is, the hope of future blessedness—our Abram fights, conquers enemies, frees citizens, and recovers the spoil.

Melchizedek, priest of God Most High and king of Salem—that is, Christ, who always rejoices and exults in our victory—meets him as he returns from the slaughter of the kings. He brings forth bread and wine, sharing with him the sacrament of his body and blood; he blesses him by multiplying him in spiritual gifts; and Abram gives him tithes of everything he has gained, not proudly ascribing the perfection of virtues and good works to his own strength, but humbly attributing it to him and saying: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to thy name” (Ps. 113).

And now, most beloved, let it be shameful for us to dwell with Lot in Sodom—that is, in carnal pleasure—and about the Jordan, that is, in the descent of worldly affairs. Let us fear, from his example, being plundered and captured. Let us always climb to safer places—that is, to the more secluded summits of virtues—so that, more secure against these dangers, we may more readily deserve heavenly goods. May Jesus grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXVIII. Morally, on eight lands full of different things.

[Col. 1110D]

“The earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 32). We have determined here to describe several different lands, for the clearer exposition of the proposed discourse, so that from their description we may disclose for ourselves several understandings of spiritual meanings.

There is, then, a land full of the wrath of the Lord, and a land full of the Lord’s rebuke. The land full of the Lord’s wrath is hell; the land full of the Lord’s rebuke is purgatorial fire. For hell may fittingly be called full of the Lord’s wrath, because there those feel his wrath in its fullness who have despised either wholly to refrain here from damnable sins or, after falling, to amend themselves.

The Lord makes mention of this land, which is lowest of all lands and lies in the final region, when he speaks to Ezekiel concerning the condemnation of certain gentile princes and their peoples, saying: “Son of man, sing a lament over the multitude of Egypt, and cast it down, both it and the daughters of strong nations, to the lowest land with those who go down into the pit” (Ezek. 32). And afterward: “There are Assyria and all her multitude; around it are its graves—all slain, and those who fell by the sword, whose graves were given in the lowest parts of the pit. And her multitude was made round about her grave. There is Elam and all her multitude round about her grave: all these slain by the sword, who went down uncircumcised into the lowest land; who set their strength in the land of the living and bore their shame with those who go down into the pit” (ibid.); and similarly the remaining things said concerning certain other kings and peoples.

This land, therefore, is truly full of the Lord’s wrath: in it is death without death, an end without end, decay without decay. There the worm is always eating; there the tormentor is always striking:

> This is the place for the unworthy, where the fire is not extinguished.  
> Neither the one tormented nor the one who torments shall die.

Nor should it be carelessly overlooked that condemned princes are said to be among those condemned with them and in their midst. For it is just that those who here were, as it were, a pillar and foundation in sin should there be in the midst of torment. Each individual grave of all these persons is the individual torment of each.

But the land full of the Lord’s rebuke or correction may aptly be called purgatorial fire. The difference between rebuke (*correptio*) and correction (*correctio*) seems to be this: rebuke is when someone is reproved, even if not amended; correction, however, is when he is also amended. Therefore purgatorial fire is rightly called a land full of the Lord’s rebuke and correction, because there those receive the Lord’s full rebuke and undergo correction who, having withdrawn in this world from sins already committed, neglected to cleanse themselves through full satisfaction, or indeed were forestalled by death and could not do so.

The torment of this fire must be believed to surpass all pains of present satisfaction. For “the present momentary and light affliction of ours works in us beyond measure an eternal weight of glory on high” (2 Cor. 4). But there, for negligence or prolonged contempt, the torments of a more grievous flame are owed and inflicted, as is shown by many revelations of the saints and passages of Scripture.

There is also a land full of the Lord’s delight, and a land full of the Lord’s sustenance. The land full of the Lord’s delight is paradise; the land full of the Lord’s sustenance is this world. Paradise is a land full of the Lord’s delight, not that delight which he himself is, or which is in him substantially and eternally, but that which has been created by him or through him, temporal and mutable.

Paradise is full of delight because from the beginning it is believed that in it were made all things fully necessary, useful, convenient, pleasing, and delightful for human use. There is there a perpetual temperateness of air, most pleasing to human nature; and the tree of life, most powerful by its virtue to preserve human life incorruptible and immortal. There, if humankind had remained in righteousness, the variety of diverse colors would always have charmed and delighted sight; birdsong, hearing; the fragrance of flowers, smell; the savor of fruits, taste; and the sweetness of all kinds of things, touch.

This world is also not unfittingly called a land full of the Lord’s sustenance. For in this world, by the working of planets as they approach or recede, and by the cooperating power of the early and latter rain, God fully provides and administers, through things that generate and sprout—unless sin sometimes obstructs it—all things necessary for the sustaining of human life. And even if pleasure is sometimes sought or thought to be possessed in the delights or riches of this world by those who walk according to the flesh, nevertheless no one of sound understanding should believe that true pleasure is in things which, according to the Lord’s saying, are compared to thorns.

There is likewise a land full of the Lord’s anger, and there is the land which, as we set forth at the beginning of this sermon, is full of the Lord’s mercy. Thus the land full of the Lord’s anger is the whole company of sinners; the land full of the Lord’s mercy is fittingly understood as the whole company of penitents.

The land full of the Lord’s anger is the whole company of sinners because the Lord is truly believed to be fully angry with those whom he permits, according to the desires of their hearts, to go on in their own devices. Was he not angry with those whom, as the Apostle says—and as we set forth above in a certain sermon—he “gave over to a reprobate mind, to do things which are not fitting, being filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication” (Rom. 1), together with the other dreadful and detestable vices and sins subsequently described there?

He signified that the ancient people would fall into the miseries of this land when he threatened through Moses: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, that their foot may slip” (Deut. 32). Isaiah uttered a tearful complaint to the Lord concerning dwelling in this land, saying: “Behold, thou wast angry, and we sinned” (Isa. 64). Finally, the Psalmist restrains us from this land when he says: “Lay hold of discipline, lest at any time the Lord be angry and you perish from the right way” (Ps. 2).

But the land full of the Lord’s mercy is manifestly the whole company of those truly repentant, since the Lord himself says through Ezekiel the prophet: “If the wicked man repents of all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my commandments and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die. I will not remember any of his iniquities which he has committed. In his righteousness which he has done he shall live” (Ezek. 18).

This is the land in which that joyful praise of the Psalmist is sung solemnly and distinctly every day—indeed, continually:

> “The Lord is compassionate and merciful, patient and abundant in mercy. He will not be angry for ever, nor threaten unto eternity. He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Ps. 102),

and the rest that follows.

Finally, there is a land full of the Lord’s grace, and a land full of the Lord’s glory. The land full of the Lord’s grace is the holy Church. Hence Paul, writing to the Church of the Corinthians, says: “In all things you have been enriched in Christ, in every word and in all knowledge, as the testimony of Christ has been confirmed in you, so that you lack no grace” (1 Cor. 1). Again, in the same Epistle, concerning the multiplicity of God’s manifold grace which is in the Church, he says: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith; to another the grace of healings; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances. But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12).

Therefore heavenly grace is poured into the holy Church; and while it is sufficiently distributed among its individual members, it is shown to be full and perfect in the whole body. Certainly the land full of the Lord’s glory is the heavenly country. For although heaven and earth are full of his glory, that country is not unfittingly called in a singular sense full of his glory, in which his glory is seen not through a mirror and in an enigma, nor in part, but manifestly and fully.

We are insufficient either to write its glory by hand, utter it with the tongue, or conceive it by thought, because God himself, who is that glory, is incomprehensible to thought. For it is not possible to conceive what God is, even if one can believe that he is; nor can one comprehend what he is like. Hence the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2). And the Psalmist says: “How great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord, which thou hast hidden for those who fear thee!” (Ps. 30).

Therefore, as has been shown above, hell is full of the Lord’s wrath; purgatorial fire, of rebuke; paradise, of delight; the world, of sustenance; the whole company of sinners, of anger; the whole company of penitents, of mercy; the holy Church, of grace; and the heavenly country, of glory.

The heavenly country is indeed the final end of all things at the highest point; hell is the final end of all things at the lowest. The way to the end which is highest is righteousness. The way to the end which is lowest is sin. To the end which is highest the elect tend and arrive. To the end which is lowest the reprobate tend and arrive. And divine Wisdom, which is the creator and ruler of all things, “reaches from end to end mightily and disposes all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). It reaches from the end which is highest to the end which is lowest: from the end of blessedness to the end of damnation, here repaying the good with the rewards of life, there repaying the evil with the wages of death. It reaches mightily from end to end because it does not fall short within the bounds of either recompense; and it disposes all things sweetly because it exceeds in nothing the measure of equity.

Brothers, we have touched on these matters briefly and leave greater things for your investigation. And now, dearly beloved, let us return to ourselves as soon as possible. Let each carefully examine his own conscience and diligently consider where we are and whither we are tending. May the Lord grant that, while we live, we may remain in the land full of the Lord’s mercy, so that, passing through the land full of the Lord’s grace, we may reach the land full of the Lord’s glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord grant this to us, he who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXIX. On the Ascension of the Lord: on praising God through every creature.

[Col. 1114B]

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy winds which fulfil his word,” etc. (Ps. 148).

Above, brothers, in the psalm from which these words are taken, the holy Psalmist invited certain heavenly beings—namely angels, sun, moon, and stars—to praise the Creator. Now he descends to invite to his praise the things which we have set forth and the rest that follows. “Praise the Lord from the earth,” he says, “dragons and all deeps.”

Not only the things written in this passage, but all bodily things which exist, praise God insofar as they possess and retain their own place for the adornment of the universe. All visible things also continually and sublimely praise God in this respect: being wonderfully created and fittingly arranged by God, they constantly move and invite us, by contemplation of themselves, to admire and praise God.

But because we must discuss not so much what the letter outwardly sounds as what sweetness spiritual understanding contains inwardly, let us enter upon the examination of moral meanings and see what moral edification lies hidden in the things here described according to the letter.

“Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all deeps.” As blessed Augustine says, there are no animals greater than dragons upon the earth. Although they are very destructive creatures, they nevertheless contain something by which they may be placed in a good signification. For since nothing that exists is wholly deprived of participation in goodness—because, as Scripture testifies, “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1)—even whatever is lowest and least, and whatever appears deformed in comparison with other things, may signify some good.

Therefore dragons, because they surpass other creatures in magnitude of body, signify those who transcend others by great merit of righteousness or by the reputation and authority of a good name. Thus we admire and imitate Abraham among the patriarchs, Isaiah among the prophets, John among the evangelists, Peter among the apostles, Stephen among the martyrs, Nicholas among the confessors, and blessed Mary among virgins.

Deeps are of great profundity and cannot be penetrated by human sight. They therefore rightly designate those who surpass others in the hidden and mystical depth of heavenly wisdom and knowledge. Paul, wondering at and exclaiming over this depth, says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counsellor?” (Rom. 11). And the Psalmist says: “Thy judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35). And Solomon says: “The righteous and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; and yet a person does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred” (Eccles. 9). Therefore deeps may fittingly represent those to whom, beyond others, it has been granted either to know hidden things in the mysteries or to investigate more profoundly the secrets of divine judgments.

Fire likewise especially denotes those whose mind, kindled by charity, burns more fervently. For charity is the perpetual fire which ought never to fail upon the altar of the Lord (Lev. 6), that is, in the secret place of the human heart. This is the fire of which the Lord himself says: “I came to send fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it be kindled?” (Luke 12).

Hail strikes as it falls and thereby plainly figures those whose speech is severe and sharply chastises the lax and restless. Yet there are some who suppose themselves to live innocently while they do not rebuke those who sin. Rebuking them, blessed Augustine says: “You are not the more innocent if, by keeping silent, you permit your brothers—whom you can correct by judging—to perish.” And blessed Gregory says in the *Pastoral Rule*: “Those who behold their neighbors’ evils and yet suppress their tongue in silence are like persons who, seeing wounds, withhold the use of medicine; and they become authors of death precisely because they were unwilling to cure the poison which they could have cured.”

Let those hear this who, through fear, affection, or acceptance of a gift, avoid exposing the deadly sins of others: unless they disclose them for the sake of correction and salvation, they become like the sinners; and when one sins while the rest remain silent and do not correct him, danger threatens all. For whoever sees evil and keeps silent falls not only into the Psalmist’s saying, “If thou didst see a thief, thou didst run with him, and didst set thy portion with adulterers” (Ps. 49), but must also cry out with Isaiah and say: “Woe is me, because I have kept silent, because I am a man of unclean lips” (Isa. 6). Whoever sees evils and is silent, therefore, is a man of unclean lips and turns the sinner’s crime back upon himself.

Snow is white and thus rightly bears the type of those who shine through purity. Water is constrained by the force of cold and reduced to ice. Ice, then, truly represents those who restrain the unstable things of their mind and flesh by the severity of discipline. “Stormy winds”—that is, wind which now raises storms and now calms them—signify the Holy Spirit, who now raises and now humbles the thoughts of the human mind. Thus those who adhere to God, who is spirit, through love may not unfittingly be called spirits. For “he who adheres to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6).

But anyone wishing to understand evildoers by these things may understand malicious persons by dragons, deceitful persons by deeps, the covetous by fire, persecutors by hail, hypocrites by snow, the hardened by ice, and those who disturb and are disturbed by stormy wind. The Psalmist calls all these to the praise of God when, in these words, he subtly invites them to turn from evil to good. Yet it seems better that dragons and the remaining things be said to signify the good, because of what is added: “which fulfil his word.” For the good without doubt fulfil God’s word, because they obey the Lord’s commandments.

It follows:

“Mountains and all hills, fruitful trees and all cedars, wild beasts and all cattle, creeping things and winged birds.”

Mountains represent the advanced and perfect; hills, beginners and imperfect persons. Thus not mountains alone praise God, but hills too are counted among those who sing the praise of God. Let not hills therefore despair—that is, those who have begun good though they have not yet completed it. For it is written: “Thine eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in thy book” (Ps. 138). If all, then both small and great. What does “thine eyes saw” mean? They approved. What does “they shall be written in the book” mean? They shall be saved. Therefore even the imperfect shall be saved.

For those who are imperfect are something and are persons; they are counted in the number and written down. But those who are nothing are nobody and can neither be written nor numbered, since they possess nothing. Therefore “to everyone who has shall be given, and he shall abound” (Matt. 25). To everyone possessing merit, reward shall be given. He did not say, “Reward shall be given to one with great merit, and shall not be given to one with small merit”; but, “To everyone who has shall be given, and he shall abound.” Therefore even one who has small merit, when he receives reward, shall have enough, although he shall not have as much as one who has great merit. Only the person who has nothing of merit is excluded from receiving reward.

Therefore all who die in the Lord are blessed (Rev. 14), because after the merit of virtue they attain the reward of blessedness. Those die in the Lord who, though dying in the flesh, are found living in the Lord. How living? Existing in faith, hope, and charity.

Fruitful trees are those who bestow upon others the fruit of life-giving teaching. Cedars are those who, despising earthly things, raise themselves on high to hope for heavenly things. By wild beasts we understand all wild and untamed animals which wander in solitary places and flee human sight. By cattle we understand domestic and gentle animals. Wild beasts, therefore, rightly signify those who lead a solitary life; cattle, those who live socially with others. Serpents crawl upon the earth and are prudent. Birds fly to the heights and draw near to heavenly things. Thus serpents may fittingly represent all who administer the matters belonging to the active life; birds, all who raise themselves on the wings of virtues to contemplate heavenly things.

It follows:

“Kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; young men and virgins, old men with the younger: let them praise the name of the Lord, because his name alone has been exalted.”

By kings we understand all who rightly preside over others. By peoples we understand all who humbly obey their prelates. Princes seem to be so called as those who first begin. Princes, therefore, rightly signify those who go before others by the example of a good work and form them toward righteousness. Hence it is written of the Lord himself: “What Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). And blessed Peter says to prelates: “Not as lording it over the clergy, but made an example to the flock” (1 Pet. 5).

Judges are those who truthfully discern true from false and good from evil. Strength flourishes in young men. Young men, therefore, aptly represent those who are strong in battle and conquer the evil one. Addressing such persons, blessed John says in his Epistle: “I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, and you have conquered the evil one” (1 John 2).

By virgins we understand all who possess the virginal integrity of the body, or indeed those who possess integrity of faith and mind, who adhere to Christ the bridegroom and do not consent to the devil, the corrupter. By old men, finally, we may understand all who are mature in seriousness; by younger persons, all who are vigorous in the swiftness of good work. All these mentioned above sing God’s praise by living rightly. Blessed is the person who truly knows himself to possess even one of the things mentioned; wretched and miserable is the person who sees himself empty of all the goods signified above.

And now, brothers, let us look back upon ourselves and consider whether we are among the number of all those whom we have described above by some grace. Let us see whether we are dragons, surpassing others at least by the greatness of some virtue or reputation; whether we are deeps, containing, insofar as our frailty can bear it, the hidden depth of divine wisdom and knowledge. But these things are exceedingly great and perhaps entirely surpass our smallness; they are not common to all, but singular to few.

If, therefore, we cannot excellently be dragons and deeps, let us at least be fire by fervor of spirit; hail by rebuking the restless; snow by shining through purity; ice by restraining what is wrongly unstable in us; spirits by adhering through love to God, who is spirit. Let us be mountains through perfection, or at least hills through the beginning of good; fruitful trees by giving others the fruit of teaching; cedars by raising ourselves on high to hope for heavenly things.

And if we cannot be wild beasts by leading a solitary life, let us be cattle by living gently with others; serpents by prudently managing the affairs of the active life; birds by flying out toward the contemplation of heavenly things. If we are not in the number of kings by presiding over others, let us at least be in the number of the people by humbly obeying our prelates. Let us be princes by giving others an example of righteousness. Let us be judges by discerning what is right. Let us be young men by conquering the evil one; virgins by possessing integrity, if not of body, at least of faith and mind. Finally, let us be old men by the gravity of maturity, and younger persons by the swiftness of good work.

Let each person praise the Lord according to the gift specially bestowed upon him. For not all of us can do everything. And because we sing these things on each of the nights of the year, while we utter them with our mouths, let us consider whether we hold them in our hearts. For it is especially our ministry to praise the Lord. His praise is then acceptably sung when what is uttered by the mouth is held in the heart.

“Because his name alone has been exalted.” Just as he alone is, because he truly is and is unchangeably, so his name alone is truly exalted. And although the creature has its own being and lofty being, nevertheless its existence bears no comparison to the essence of the Creator, nor its height to his excellence. For “all nations are before him as though they were not; they are reckoned to him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40); and “a thousand years in thy sight are as yesterday, which has passed” (Ps. 89).

Hence all the saints, when they advance in the vision of God, the more they behold the inner things of divinity, the more they know themselves to be nothing. For nowhere do we read that Abraham professed himself to be ashes except when he merited to have discourse with the Lord. He might perhaps have thought himself to be something had he not perceived the true essence which is above him. But when he was raised above himself to contemplate the Unchangeable One, filled with the power of so great a contemplation, seeing him, he saw himself to be nothing but dust.

For he alone truly is because he alone remains unchangeably. Whatever is now thus and now otherwise is close to non-being. For it cannot remain in its own state; and in a certain manner it goes toward non-being when it is led into something else through the alternation of times.

And blessed Dionysius testifies in the following words that no essence, light, or life can bear any comparison to the incomprehensible infinity of divinity:

> “At times the traditions of the Scriptures, which reveal the blessedness of divinity, praise the divine rationality as reason, intellect, and essence, declaring his wisdom and truly existing subsistence, and the true cause of the subsistence of things that are; and they call him, as it were, light, form, and life.”

And although these things—namely reason, intellect, light, and the other visible things through which the invisible things of God are sometimes understood—excel and appear loftier for signifying what belongs to divinity, nevertheless such likenesses fall short of divine truth. For he is above every essence and way, with no light characterizing him; and every reason and intellect are left incomparably distant from any likeness of him.

Therefore, because God alone truly is, because he also is unchangeably, his name alone has rightly been exalted and must be exalted. Especially in this sacred solemnity, on which the only-begotten Son of God, coeternal with the eternal Father, ascended into heaven in the substance of our flesh and took his seat at the right hand of Majesty on high. Today, I say, his name has been exalted singularly and solemnly [Col. 1119A] and must be exalted, because today “the Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109). Today he who came from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah, splendid in his robe, advancing in the greatness of his strength (Isa. 63), entered gloriously into the kingdoms of heaven, as the princes of heaven opened their gates—long closed against human nature—and the everlasting gates lifted themselves up (Ps. 23). Today the Son of Man came to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honor and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and languages shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed (Dan. 7). Today our forerunner entered, beyond the inner veil, into heaven itself, into the tabernacle [Col. 1119B] not made by hands, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood; once for all he entered the holy places, having found eternal redemption. He was made a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, that he may now appear before the face of God for us and intercede for us (Heb. 6, 7, 9). And now, beloved, we began our discourse from earthly things; but through it let us also ascend to the inner things of heaven. Would that, as we ascend in word, so we may ascend in mind; as we ascend in speaking, so we may ascend by worthy praise. Let us therefore praise the Lord with the heart; let us praise him with the mouth in time, that we may deserve to praise him in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is, etc., deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON LXX. On the Day of Pentecost

[Col. 1119C]

“The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83).

Beloved, humanity was made in the image and likeness of God so that it might share, by grace, in that good which God is by nature. It was made in God’s image according to reason, and in God’s likeness according to love; in the image according to the knowledge of truth, in the likeness according to the love of virtue; in the image according to understanding, in the likeness according to affection. Thus God the Maker formed human nature in his image and likeness, so that, through being made in God’s likeness, it might love God and, by knowing and loving God, [Col. 1119D] possess him; and by possessing him, be blessed.

For in one element, namely fire, there are two things distinct and separate from each other: brightness and heat. Brightness is not heat, nor heat brightness, because brightness shines and is seen, whereas heat burns and is felt. Brightness neither burns nor is felt, and heat neither shines nor is seen. Yet in the human creature God’s image and God’s likeness appear distinct from each other and, in a certain manner, separated. For according to that good by which human nature was made in God’s image, it shines forth toward knowledge; and according to that good by which it was made in God’s likeness, it grows warm toward love. That image and likeness of God may be understood according to the foregoing distinctions is declared by teachers in the words of the Psalmist: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked [Col. 1120A] upon us; you have given joy to my heart” (Ps. 4). By the light marked upon us or in us they distinguish the divine image in us, which they assign to the discernment of reason; but by joy they distinguish the divine likeness, which they locate in the delight of love.

Therefore, when humanity had been created in God’s image and likeness, and had been established, as it were lord of the world, by God’s providence in a place of delights, as in God’s more excellent portion; when, by that same providence, reason had been joined to humanity to warn it to preserve the goods it possessed, and when it had been equipped, through a command of obedience working together with grace, to seek and obtain the goods it was to possess: the devil saw and envied the fact that humanity [Col. 1120B] would ascend through obedience to the place from which he himself had fallen through pride. But because he could not harm humanity by force, he turned to deceit, so that he might trip humanity by guile, whom he could not overcome by strength.

Thus, in deceiving humanity, the devil inflicted upon it two principal evils opposed to the two principal goods already mentioned; he wounded it with two deadly blows. In that by which humanity had been made in God’s image according to reason, he wounded it through ignorance of the good. In that by which it had been made in God’s likeness according to love, he wounded it through desire for evil. These are the two principal evils from which all the remaining evils of humanity proceed. From ignorance comes *delictum*, failure; from concupiscence comes sin. A failure is when what ought to be done is not [Col. 1120C] done. Sin is when what ought not to be done is done.

Humanity, therefore, stripped and wounded—stripped of goods and wounded with evils—was left half alive. For although the divine likeness, which consists in love, can be wholly corrupted in human nature, the divine image, which consists in reason, cannot be wholly erased. Though humanity may be so affected by wickedness as to love no good at all, it cannot be so blinded by ignorance as to know no truth at all. This is evident in the devil himself, the prince of evil: although he is so corrupted that he loves no good, he cannot be so blinded as to know no truth. Humanity is therefore rightly said to have been left half alive, because, although it was corrupted in part through the primordial evils, [Col. 1120D] it was not wholly blinded. Indeed, even after its wounds it lived in that some spark of perception, however slight, remained within it. Thus the hostile sword did not utterly destroy humanity, since it could not wholly erase in it the dignity of natural good.

The Psalmist agrees with this understanding when he says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Ps. 50), signifying the divine likeness in himself by the clean heart and the divine image by the right spirit. In asking that a clean heart be created in him but that a right spirit be renewed, he fittingly indicated both that the divine likeness can be wholly corrupted and that the divine image can in no way be entirely erased. For where no good remains, good—if it is restored—[Col. 1121A] is created; but where some good still remains, it is renewed. Purity of heart consists in perfect love of God, while rectitude of spirit consists in sound reason. The same sense is also expressed by the other Psalm passage: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103).

Humanity, then, had been placed in honor through the two principal goods mentioned above, but it did not understand that it had been placed in honor. By consenting to the devil, it corrupted in itself, through the two evils already mentioned, those two goods. But because it could neither drive out evils nor restore goods by itself, divine providence bestowed two principal remedies, by which it might heal the evils inflicted upon it and recover the goods it had lost: namely, counsel and help. Yet, that humanity might recognize its disease, [Col. 1121B] it was first left entirely to itself, lest it perhaps judge grace superfluous if it had not first recognized the deficiency of its own weakness. Therefore the period of natural law was established, so that nature might act by itself—not because it could accomplish anything by itself, but so that it might recognize that it could not.

Nature, then, left to itself, began to wander from truth through ignorance; and it was convicted of blindness, later also to be convicted of weakness. The written Law was given to illumine ignorance, but not to strengthen weakness, so that humanity might be helped in that respect in which it recognized its own deficiency, while in the respect in which it thought it could stand by itself, it might be left to itself. Having therefore received knowledge of the truth through the Law, it began to strive to make progress; but, weighed down by concupiscence, because it did not have assisting grace, it failed in the work of virtue. [Col. 1121C]

The apostolic saying accords well with this: “By works of the Law no flesh shall be justified before him” (Rom. 3). Likewise: “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). Why? What came through the Law? Knowledge of sin only—this is to be understood. Through the Law came only knowledge of sin, not also its consummation. The Law prescribed by teaching, but humanity, having counsel through the Law and not help, failed in doing. For the Law gave knowledge of what ought to be done, not strength to accomplish it. A poor sick person remains in sickness unless the physician who gives counsel for escaping the disease also supplies the antidote of medicine. So one weakened by sin cannot be justified from sin through the Law alone, unless grace is given, which is the medicine of sin. [Col. 1121D]

Thus humanity was convicted in both respects: namely, that by itself it can neither know truth nor accomplish good. During the time of natural law it was convicted of blindness; during the time of the written Law, of weakness. Therefore the prophet David, seeing that neither nature nor Law could suffice to liberate humanity, understanding grace to be necessary, and observing divine goodwill toward the human race in the Law, consoled himself and all who would place their trust in God’s grace rather than in the works of the Law, saying: “The Lord will give grace and glory” (Ps. 83).

After humanity had thus recognized its blindness and weakness, the Law was suitably given which would both illumine the blind and heal the weak: it would illumine ignorance and cool concupiscence; [Col. 1122A] it would illumine toward knowledge of truth and kindle toward the love of virtue. Therefore the Spirit was given in fire, that it might have both light and flame: light for knowledge, flame for love.

This excellent and perfect gift, descending from above from the Father of lights (Jas. 1), has a sacred solemnity that is not new, unknown, or sudden, but ancient, celebrated, and authoritative: it was once typologically celebrated through Moses and the children of Israel on Mount Sinai. For “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1). The Law was given on a high mountain; grace was given above, in the upper room. The Law was given amid fiery flashes; grace was given in fiery tongues. The Law was given to twelve tribes; grace was first given to twelve apostles. [Col. 1122B] The Law was written on two tablets; grace is fulfilled in the two commandments of charity. The Law was written by God’s finger on tablets of stone; grace is written by the Holy Spirit in human hearts. The Law was given on the fiftieth day after Passover had been celebrated in the land of Egypt; grace was given on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection. “When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, the disciples were together in the same place, and suddenly there came from heaven a sound of a violent wind,” etc. (Acts 2).

The fullness of this Spirit is in the head; participation in it is in the members. The head is Christ; the member is the Christian. One head, many members; and one body consists of head and members, while in the one body there is one Spirit. Therefore, if there is one body and one Spirit, whoever is not in that [Col. 1122C] body cannot be made alive by the Spirit, as it is written: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8). For whoever does not have Christ’s Spirit is not a member of Christ. In one body there is one Spirit. Nothing in the body is dead; nothing outside the body is alive.

This is the anointing upon the head which descends upon Aaron’s beard and even to the hem of his garment (Ps. 132). The head, as has been said, signifies Christ, who is the head of all the faithful. The beard, which clings to the head and is a sign of manliness, signifies the apostles, who clung to Christ while he lived in the world; and, clinging to him, ate and drank with him, heard his saving teaching, and saw his miracles. After [Col. 1122D] his Ascension, strengthened manfully by receiving the Holy Spirit more fully, they acted courageously, because they preached his faith throughout the kingdoms of the world; for his name they were handed over to councils, scourged in synagogues, and led before kings and governors—and in all these things they conquered.

Therefore the anointing of the Holy Spirit, which is in the head according to fullness, descended into the beard—that is, upon the apostles—according to participation, when he said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit”; and when, after his Ascension, he sent them that same Spirit and distributed the grace of languages. It descends to the hem of the garment because the same Spirit is granted to those holy persons who are to exist even at the end of the world.

And now, beloved, let us look to ourselves and see whether we have been cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit [Col. 1123A], so that in this his sacred solemnity we may worthily deserve to possess or receive the Holy Spirit. “Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins. For the holy Spirit of discipline will flee from deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be reproved by the iniquity that comes upon it” (Wis. 1). Let us finally imitate our fathers, namely the holy apostles, from whose acts our order has been derived. For it is highly praiseworthy and worthy of imitation what is written of them: that they were together in the same place. Let us also, brothers, be together—not only by dwelling in one place, but also in one faith, hope, charity, devotion, prayer, invocation, and expectation of the Holy Spirit—so that we may deserve together to be in the reception [Col. 1123B] and participation of him, and thus, justified through him in time, may together be glorified in eternity. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXI. On the Apostles and Other Preachers

The Ark is carried round Jericho for a circuit of seven days amid the sounding of trumpets; Jericho is overthrown; Rahab is saved by placing a scarlet cord in the window; and Achan is stoned for stealing a bar and a cloak (Josh. 6–7).

Jericho, which is interpreted “moon,” signifies the present age, which, like the moon, is brought to fullness and decline: now it grows and is raised up through prosperity, now it diminishes [Col. 1123C] and is humbled through adversity. We see the cycles of the years through which the world revolves. When the sun in springtime opens the pores of the earth, like the first moon displaying its first light, we see it bring forth shoots. Then, just as through daily progressions we see the moon come to fullness, so we observe all things that spring from the earth attain their maturity and perfection in summer through the enlivening of heat and the fostering of moisture. Afterwards, like the waning moon, they diminish, as they die in autumn when natural heat and moisture fail. Finally, in winter, they return, as it were, to a kind of moonless interval: worn down by the harshness of cold, they retreat again into the hidden bosom of nature and withdraw [Col. 1123D] themselves from our sight.

So also in human beings, beasts, birds, and fishes, we see that, after they come into being, they first labor to attain perfection and then hasten through decay toward non-being. Thus, thus we see the glory of the present age now arise, now increase, now be exalted, now diminish, now return to nothing. The Ark signifies Christ. The Ark is carried around Jericho for seven days while Christ is preached in the world until the end of the age, which revolves in the cycle of seven days. The bearers of this Ark are the holy apostles and preachers, concerning whom it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). The bronze trumpets signify the strong and invincible authority of preaching. The holy preachers hold them in their hands while [Col. 1124A] sounding them, because they fulfill in deed what they proclaim with their voice.

The walls of Jericho signify philosophical arguments or the cult of idols, strengthened and exalted throughout the circuit of the world. They fell through the carrying around of the Ark and the sounding of the trumpets, because they perished through Christ’s preaching resounding throughout the earth. The men of Jericho are slain when those devoted to the world and worldly business are condemned forever. Rahab the harlot signifies the Church chosen from among the nations, which formerly served and was subject to many lovers, that is, to many demons. Rahab, in order to be saved, placed outside in the window the scarlet cord that she had within her house; and the holy Church, in order to be saved, confesses with her mouth Christ’s passion, which she believes in her heart.

Achan steals a golden bar and a cloak [Col. 1124B] and is stoned in the Valley of Achor; likewise, any false Christian or heretic who introduces into the Church philosophical wisdom, figured by the golden bar, and secular culture, signified by the cloak, is condemned in hell. All that belongs to him is also consumed by fire, when his body, soul, and whatever he possesses in either are burned in the conflagration of Gehenna. Gold, silver, and every kind of metal, whether from Jericho or other cities, are purified by fire and taken up for the Lord’s work; thus philosophical wisdom, eloquence, and any teaching of theirs, once purified of every stain of error by the examination of Holy Scripture, [Col. 1124C] are not rejected in the ministry of divine preaching. A curse falls upon whoever rebuilds Jericho; and cursed is whoever restores and rebuilds through evil speech or example the worldly wickedness destroyed in the baptized.

“Hiel of Bethel built Jericho. He laid its foundation in Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates in Segub his youngest” (3 Kgs. 16). Hiel means “living for God”; Bethel, “house of God.” Thus Hiel of Bethel rebuilds the walls of Jericho, destroyed by Joshua and devoted to destruction, whenever someone who has taken up a religious habit in the Church returns to deeds of wickedness which the Lord Jesus forgave him on the day of baptism, and, by living luxuriously, resumes the pomps of the devil which he himself had anathematized. And when he prefers doctrines of error or pagan fables to the ecclesiastical truth [Col. 1124D] in which he had been instructed, he revives the ruins of Jericho as though leaving Bethel. He also loses the foundations of faith from which good buildings ought to begin, and the enclosures of good action by which they ought to be completed.

Alternatively: he lays its foundation in his firstborn and its gates in the last of his children, because through this fault he loses both the gift of nature which he first received and the gift of grace which he received last, so that neither can now avail for salvation. Let us detest, beloved, Hiel of Bethel, and not imitate his wicked deeds, lest, if after baptism or after taking the habit of conversion we presume to rebuild in ourselves or others the works of the devil or his pomps, which we renounced, we subject ourselves, together with the offspring of our virtues and good works, to eternal [Col. 1125A] curse.

But if we observe among ourselves an Achan, defiled by spiritual transgression and spiritual anathema, let us immediately bring him to the valley of humiliation and overwhelm him with stones—that is, harsh words—so that, so far as lies with us, he may die to the devil and live to God. Otherwise, if we bear his fault, we shall be convicted before the just Judge of consent to sin and found sharers in his defilement. To consent is to remain silent when one is able to rebuke. Let us therefore always remember that through the man Achan all Israel was troubled.

This also appears to be the point of Paul’s words to the Corinthians about that one fornicator: “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump? Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new dough, as you are [Col. 1125B] unleavened” (1 Cor. 5). We must correct among ourselves not only the greatest sins but every least sin, lest, if they grow and become strong, they become difficult or altogether impossible to amend. For “blessed is he who takes and dashes his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136); and again, “Whoever despises small things shall gradually fall away” (Ecclus. 19). Nor should we wish to be considered merciful by hiding, overlooking, or tolerating others’ faults. For as “the wickedness of a man is better than a beneficent woman” (Ecclus. 42), so the daughter of Judah who does not tolerate wickedness seems more praiseworthy than the kings of Israel who are foolishly merciful.

The saying of Saint Augustine also seems to have regard to this: “If your brother has a wound in his body which, fearing incision, he wishes to conceal, would it not be cruel for you [Col. 1125C] to keep silent and merciful for you to reveal it? How much more, then, ought you to disclose a spiritual wound, lest it rot more grievously in the heart?” Let us therefore strive to carry the Ark of wisdom around among different hearers by preaching, and in them overthrow on every side, through the cry of our preaching, the fortifications of the devil. The holy prophets encourage us to this work: preaching God’s word and rebuking tyrants, they “went about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11). The holy apostles, whose solemnities we celebrate today, set us an example in the same work. They went throughout kingdoms, regions, cities, forts, houses, and villages, and powerfully destroyed idolatrous impiety [Col. 1125D] together with the perversity of worldly desire, as the sound of their preaching resounded everywhere.

Therefore, beloved, following their footsteps according to our measure, let us serve as soldiers in all these things under God, under Jesus our new prince, now that Moses, our first leader, has died. Moses, who gave the Law, signifies the Law. When Moses died—that is, when the Law, according to carnal and old observances, had died, been fulfilled, or ended—Jesus our Savior, who saves his people from their sins (Matt. 1), Jesus, I say, the Son of God, was manifested as prince over God’s people, in order, once the enemies of God had been conquered, to distribute gifts to the people (1 Cor. 12).

For Jesus son of Nun, as Jerome says, “prefiguring the Lord not only in his deeds but also in his name, [Col. 1126A] overthrows the kingdoms of enemies beyond the Jordan, divides the land among the victorious people, and describes throughout individual cities, villages, mountains, rivers, torrents, and borders the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and the heavenly Jerusalem.” Thus our Jesus, having cast out the prince of this world and his soldiers, works in the elect: now “to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for usefulness; to one indeed, through the Spirit, a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge; to another, faith; to another, gifts of healings; to another, working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of languages; to another, interpretation of utterances” (1 Cor. 12). Afterwards, to each according to the distinction of gifts will be granted a corresponding distinction of heavenly goods, and rewards will be given according to merits.

Let us not therefore, brothers, grow slack in [Col. 1126B] battle, like the children of Israel, to whom Joshua said: “How long will you languish in idleness and not enter to possess the land which the Lord God of your fathers has given you?” (Josh. 18). Let us therefore fight manfully in time, that we may be crowned gloriously in eternity. May Jesus Christ, etc., deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON LXXII. On the New Year, or on the Feast of Saint John the Baptist

“You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness, and your fields will be filled with abundance. The beautiful places of the wilderness will grow rich, and the hills will gird themselves with exultation,” etc. (Ps. 64).

As God is admirable and praiseworthy in creatures, so he is admirable and praiseworthy in the Scriptures. For just as he instructs and incites us through creatures to know and love him, so he teaches and admonishes us through the Scriptures toward [Col. 1126C] both. Hence even in these few words which we have set forth, he typologically describes for us in diverse ways the various virtues of different persons, so that we may be instructed and encouraged in various ways: to turn away from evil and do good; to walk without stain and work righteousness; to escape punishment and obtain glory.

“You will bless the crown of the year of your goodness.” The year of divine goodness is the universal time of grace, extending from the Lord’s Incarnation to the end of the world. The two preceding periods—namely, the time of natural law, which was from Adam to Moses, and the time of written Law, which was from Moses to Christ—were like two years of divine wrath. For human beings, however [Col. 1126D] righteous, whether prophet or more than prophet, had not yet, before the price of redemption had been offered, complete peace with God, because all who died were meanwhile excluded from entrance into the heavenly country.

But after Christ came in the flesh and reconciled the Father to us through his passion, there came to be a year of divine goodness, because, as the Apostle says, “the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared” (Titus 3). The Lord blesses the crowns of this year while throughout its whole course he continually pours out the gifts of his grace upon us, so that, watered by the dew of grace, we may bear fruit by which we may carry sheaves of righteousness into the heavenly storehouses.

By the full blessing of this year, our fields are filled with abundance; the beautiful places of the wilderness with richness; the hills gird themselves with exultation; [Col. 1127A] the rams are clothed with a garment; and the valleys abound with grain. Fields, because of their width and flatness, signify married persons, who, using themselves and their possessions according to the marital law, walk more freely, as it were, in broader and flatter places. They are unable to imitate those who walk by the narrow and arduous path of continence, renouncing their own wills and possessions and nakedly following the naked cross.

By the beautiful places of the wilderness we fittingly understand holy solitary persons, who live far from the world’s tumult in wooded wilds and deserted places, and adorn and embellish those same places by their holy manner of life. Elijah was among these beautiful places of the wilderness, when he sat alone for many days by the brook Cherith, when he rested under a juniper tree [Col. 1127B] in the wilderness of Beersheba, and when he remained in a cave on Mount Sinai. Among the beautiful places—indeed, the most beautiful—of the wilderness was blessed John the Baptist, who, clothed in camel hair, ate locusts and wild honey in the wilderness and drank water.

The beautiful places of the wilderness were also the innumerable multitudes of Egyptian monks, of whom hundreds and thousands lived in different places of the desert. The beautiful places of the wilderness are the many thousands of monks or canons now living in wooded wilds or solitary places, such as the Carthusians, Cistercians, Premonstratensians, those called of the Great Mount, and many other hermits or anchorites, whether many together or few, or alone, dwelling in deserted places and adorning the wilderness itself by the perfection of their holiness. [Col. 1127C] For all such persons adorn the wilderness by the beauty of their righteousness, living there religiously through example, speech, silence, abstinence, labor, continence, manual labor, rough clothing, hard beds, continual vigils, the spiritual melody of chants, persistence in prayers, generosity in almsgiving, kindness in hospitality, and finally the practice of every virtue and the performance of good works.

These, then, are truly the beautiful places of the wilderness; and in the things mentioned they grow wonderfully rich every day, not in the flesh but in the spirit. For while they mortify the flesh, they enrich the spirit; while they weaken the flesh, they strengthen the spirit; while outwardly taking little from the flesh, inwardly they bestow much upon the spirit. For [Col. 1127D] “the present, momentary, and light affliction” of theirs works in them “beyond measure in sublimity an eternal weight of glory,” since they look not at what is seen but at what is unseen. For the things seen are temporal, but those unseen are eternal (2 Cor. 4).

The hills, however, fittingly signify those who raise themselves in this life from earthly things to contemplate heavenly things. Those who are now hills in the world through contemplating heavenly things will afterwards become mountains in heaven through eternal contemplation. For what they now receive from contemplation is imperfect, but what they will then possess will be perfect. This seems to be the point of the Apostle’s saying: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know even as [Col. 1128A] I have been known” (1 Cor. 13); and above: “For we know in part and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (ibid.).

That the little knowledge of God now given to the saints is slight in comparison with what is reserved to be given them in the future is intimated by Solomon’s statement concerning grinders, that they see through openings, and by the Lord’s command, when he bade the prophet prophesy: “Son of man, drip” (Eccl. 12; Ezek. 20); by the fingers seen writing in Daniel (Dan. 5); and also by the fact that, in the measurement of the spiritual building, after six cubits—which signify good works—there is added a palm, which expresses present contemplation (Ezek. 40). For what the image seen in a mirror is to the reality of the body; what [Col. 1128B] sight through an opening is to full vision; what a drop is to the ocean; what a finger is to the whole body; what a palm is to a cubit; what the smallness of a hill is to the greatness of a mountain: such appears to be the contemplation granted to saints in time in comparison with that which is reserved to be granted in eternity.

The hills, therefore, are contemplatives, raised above earthly things and illumined before others by the sun of righteousness. Of them it is aptly said that “they will gird themselves with exultation” (Ps. 64), because true exultation belongs to those who possess contemplation. Those to whom it has already been granted, however faintly, to see the joys of the heavenly good ought rightly to rejoice. But what joy can there be for me, since I sit in darkness and do not see the light of heaven? (Job 5).

And it should be noted that he says, “they will gird themselves.” We gird ourselves in front for service, [Col. 1128C] beneath for walking, and around for fighting. Since we gird ourselves in front for service, it is rightly written of the Lord, when he wished to serve his disciples by washing their feet, that, having taken a towel, “he girded himself” (John 13). We gird ourselves beneath for walking, lest our feet be hindered by flowing garments. We gird ourselves around for fighting, as is said in the Psalm: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one” (Ps. 44). Therefore the hills gird themselves with exultation, because the more keenly holy contemplatives behold heavenly joys, the more stoutly they arm themselves against the ancient enemy. Thus, as they receive grace for grace, there is fulfilled in them [Col. 1128D] what is written: “Let the righteous still be justified, and let the holy still be sanctified” (Rev. 22).

“The rams of the sheep are clothed, and the valleys will abound with grain.” By the rams, which are leaders of the flock, we understand holy prelates, who daily lead the Lord’s flock to spiritual pastures and vigilantly guard it against the attacks of spiritual wolves. They have two horns: one through the example of good work, the other through the word of preaching; with these they must drive ravening enemies from their territories. They also possess a fleece of their own wool—that is, a garment—which is the uprightness of good morals. By valleys, finally, we understand humble subjects. Just as barley in Holy Scripture signifies the doctrine of the Old Testament, so grain signifies [Col. 1129A] the doctrine of the New. Therefore valleys abound with grain when all subjects and humble persons are filled with the knowledge contained in the sacred Gospel.

Thus, by fields we fittingly understand married persons because they more freely use temporal possessions; by the beautiful places of the wilderness, solitary persons because of their more secluded life; by hills, contemplatives because of their more eminent grace; by rams, prelates because of their higher authority; and by valleys, subjects because of their humbler subjection. We also understand by the abundance of the fields the effect of good works among married persons; by the richness of the beautiful places of the wilderness, the fullness of charity and the perfection of the other virtues among solitary persons; by the exultation of the hills, a taste of heavenly joys among contemplatives; by the clothing [Col. 1129B] of the rams, uprightness of morals among prelates; and by the grain of the valleys, sacred knowledge among subjects.

Now, dearest brethren, looking back upon ourselves, let us see whether we are any of those whom we have described above, whether we possess anything of their fullness. Certainly we are not fields, nor ought we to be. For our profession, our habit, and the witness borne by our tonsure transcend the flatness of those fields—that is, the more unrestricted way of life of married persons; and therefore we must ascend to a higher degree of life. Far be it from us to belong to the company of the married, to be anxious about the things of the world, to be divided, to consider how we may please a wife. For we ought to consider the things of God, so as to please God and to be holy in body and mind. Yet although [Col. 1129C] we ought not to be fields, through this lower manner of life and its broader liberty we should nevertheless possess their fruitfulness by the perfect performance of the six works of mercy. For to whom is it more fitting to exercise works of mercy than to those who profess the religious life by habit and tonsure? But we must fear, brothers, lest we do these works not from regard for mercy, but from respect of persons. Sometimes some rich abbot, our neighbor, comes, who has had us honorably served in his house with various dishes set before us; immediately we run about, stir up the household, order various dishes to be prepared, and declare that he must be honorably served. This, certainly, is right. For he deserved it, [Col. 1129D] and, if occasion again presents itself, will deserve it still. But at another time a poor monk arrives, a stranger, fasting, exhausted by heat or frost, afflicted all day by rain or winds; and when he asks the steward what he is to eat, the cold reply is given: “He will have enough,” they say; “he will have eggs.” Such things do not seem to accord with Christ’s words when he speaks of giving a feast, saying: “When you make a luncheon or dinner, do not invite your friends, nor your brothers, nor your kinsmen, nor rich neighbors, lest perhaps they also invite you in return and repayment be made to you. But when you make a banquet, invite the poor, the disabled, the lame, and the blind; and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14).

From these words anyone who wishes may perceive that, [Col. 1130A] while we return with such painstaking care the service done us by those who have honorably entertained us in this manner, the repayment appears to be one of human merit; but when we show every kindness, solely from the regard of charity, to those who have never served us, we fulfill Christ’s commandment. Therefore let us not serve poorer guests negligently, because those poorer in worldly goods are often richer in faith. Perhaps also some brother who is rich—that is, born of the rich, or influential in the house—lies ill with some infirmity. Immediately he is visited and comforted by all, and every care is devoted to his service. At another time another brother who is poor—that is, born of the poor and of no influence in the house—lies weighed down by a more severe illness; perhaps he is neglected and despised, and suffers annoyance from those who serve him in the morning, [Col. 1130B] so much so that he may justly complain in the Psalmist’s words: “They added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 68 [69]). And concerning such care or neglect, a certain versifier aptly said:

> If a rich man lies ill, though wasted by a slight fever,  
> A mounted monastic troop bursts into his chamber;  
> If a poor man lies burdened by sickness or by death,  
> Where no hope summons them, they pass by, valuing him not,  
> Like a cripple [or “a nail”: *clavus*; the reading is uncertain] hurled into the Lord’s mill.

We say all these things, brothers, so that we may perform works of mercy not according to respect of persons but according to charity and the need of each individual. Nor, in saying this, do we urge you not to show honor to persons worthy of [Col. 1130C] honor, for it is written: “To whom honor, honor”; but we exhort you not to withhold from others anything due in charity (Rom. 13). Therefore we are not fields, nor ought we to be; but would that we might not lack their fruitfulness. And just as we are not fields because we ought not to be fields, so we are not the beauties of the wilderness, because we cannot be these. For how can we belong among the beauties of the wilderness, we who eat rich food, drink mead, and, compared with them, are clothed in soft garments? How can we belong among the beauties of the wilderness, we who are far removed from the desert and almost joined to the world? For, I fear, we dwell with Reuben among the boundaries, so as to hear the bleating of the flocks. We dwell, so to speak, between [Col. 1130D] the boundary of the spiritual life and the boundary of the secular life. We hear the bleating of flocks—that is, the games, cries, songs, and uproars of people running in herds toward damnation through various sins.
