We cannot therefore be the beauties of the wilderness; but would that we might share their richness, that is, their charity and other virtues! But we ought to be hills—would that we were!

For this is why we live in quiet, silence, reading, meditation, prayer, and the chanting of divine praise: that we may more readily and more perfectly cleave to heavenly contemplation. Indeed, among all the spiritual goods that can be acquired or possessed in this present life, contemplation is the best. For Mary chose the better part, [Col. 1131A] which shall not be taken away from her (Luke 10). There are three things in which the human mind now exercises itself: thought, meditation, and contemplation. The greatest of these is contemplation. Thought is when the mind is touched fleetingly by awareness of things, when the thing itself suddenly becomes present to the mind by its image, either entering through the senses or rising from memory. Meditation is the persistent and keen reconsideration of a thought, striving either to unfold something involved or to penetrate what is hidden by searching. Contemplation is the clear-sighted and free gaze of the mind, diffused everywhere over the objects to be perceived. The difference between contemplation and meditation is this: meditation is occupied with investigating one matter, whereas contemplation extends to apprehending many or diverse matters. Contemplation, [Col. 1131B] therefore, is the clear-sighted and free gaze of the mind, spread everywhere over the things to be perceived: clear-sighted, that it may penetrate the depths; free, that it may not be weighed down and hindered by earthly desires; spread abroad, that it may comprehend many things or all things. Let us therefore see whether we possess this gaze of the mind, so that we may deservedly be and be called hills through contemplation—though I venture to say much about contemplation because, in respect of experience, I know utterly nothing of what it is. Nor are we rams, because we do not lead the Lord’s flock. Yet though we are not rams in leading the flock, would that we had the horns of these rams through the example of good work and the word of preaching, and their covering through the uprightness of good morals! Finally, although we cannot perfectly be the beauties of the wilderness, hills, [Col. 1131C] and rams, let us at least strive to be valleys through humble subjection, so that with them, according to our measure, we may be able to cry aloud and sing a hymn: to cry aloud in time, to sing a hymn in eternity. Why cry aloud in time and sing a hymn in eternity? Because one who is far off cries aloud; one who is near speaks. We are far off in time, because “while we are in the body, we are away on pilgrimage from the Lord” (2 Cor. 5). We shall be near in eternity, because “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3). Therefore, just as then we shall see eye to eye, so we shall speak mouth to mouth. To cry aloud, then, is to praise God in time; to sing a hymn is to praise God in eternity. But what and how great, and of what kind, will be the sweetness, delight, and blessedness of that hymn, [Col. 1131D] we cannot know until we come to the fountain of life, are made drunk from the abundance of God’s house, and he gives us drink from the torrent of his delight (Ps. 35 [36]); and until we see light in light, the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. For when the Son has delivered the kingdom to God the Father, when he has abolished every principality, authority, and power, and God is all in all (1 Cor. 15), then, singing this hymn with the angels and all the saints, we shall perfectly know the nature of its inestimable melody. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXIII. On the Feast of Saint John the Baptist

“The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” [Col. 1132A] (Ps. 91 [92]).

The life of blessed John the Baptist, dearest brethren, whose nativity we celebrate today, speaks wholly to us; it is wholly a sermon to us; it wholly calls us back from evil and exhorts us to good. Nor only the things contained in his most holy life, but also those that precede or follow his life, when carefully considered, call us back from sin and form us in righteousness. Before his conception, his annunciation speaks to us; after his death, the renown of his virtues; in his life, his entire holy manner of life. For as the varied diversity of precious stones shines in a garment, so in blessed John the multitude of diverse virtues and the beauty of that very multitude shine forth for us: contempt for the world, love of God, abstinence [Col. 1132B] in food, harshness of dress, the quiet of solitude, the word of preaching, bodily virginity, humility of heart, strict severity, confession of truth, the power of patience, and the fragrance of a good reputation. He is the dawn of the true sun, the forerunner of the Redeemer, the soldier of the heavenly king, the herald of the judge, the voice of one crying out. He is the prophet of the One to come, the Lord’s minister, the identifier of the Lamb, Christ’s Baptist, the bridegroom’s friend. He is the preacher of repentance, lover of chastity, persecutor of lust, witness to righteousness, defender of innocence. He is the son of holy parents, privy to heavenly secrets, the joy of his relatives, the rejoicing of his neighbors, the admiration of all. He is, with the apostles—indeed before the apostles—the messenger of Christ, the light of the world, the salt of the earth, a lamp upon the lampstand, [Col. 1132C] a city set upon a mountain. He was announced by an angel, sanctified in the womb, made glorious in the world, crowned by martyrdom, glorified in heaven. He is therefore deservedly extolled throughout the world by the voices of the faithful, proclaimed in words, honored in praises, and commemorated in solemn observances.

He is compared to the palm and the cedar. Truly he is a palm, truly a cedar: a palm through righteousness, a cedar through glory. For, as blessed Gregory says in the *Moralia*, the life of the righteous is fittingly compared with a palm, because a palm is rough to the touch below and, as it were, wrapped in dry bark, but above is beautiful both in appearance and in fruit. Below it is constricted by the enveloping layers of its bark, but above it spreads in the breadth of lovely greenness. The palm has another quality [Col. 1132D] by which it differs from every kind of tree. Every other tree stands broad in its strength close to the ground, but narrows as it grows upward; and the higher it rises, the more slender it becomes aloft. The palm, however, begins narrower at its base and rises in greater strength near its branches and fruits; and, though it grows from a slender base, it increases toward the summit in more expansive strength. To what other plants, then, are earthly minds found similar, broad below and narrow above? For all lovers of the world are strong in earthly matters and weak in heavenly ones. They desire to labor unto death for temporal glory, yet for the hope of eternity they do not endure even a little labor. For earthly gain they bear injuries of every kind, yet for heavenly reward they refuse to endure [Col. 1133A] even the slightest insults of speech. They are strong enough to wait upon an earthly judge all day, but in prayer before the Lord they grow weary in the space of a single hour.

There are also some who, when they seek heavenly things and abandon this world’s harmful deeds, fail every day from the beginning of their undertaking through the faint-heartedness of inconstancy. To what else shall I call them similar but to the remaining shrubs, which do not rise such as they first spring up below? For when they enter a religious manner of life, they do not persevere as they began. And, as with trees, they are expansive in their beginning but grow slender, because with the passing increase of time they suffer losses of virtue. Gradually their heavenly desires languish; and those who had proposed robust and strong things [Col. 1133B] bring weak and infirm things to completion. As they advance in age, they grow, as it were, pliant. But the palm, as has been said, is broader at the top than it was when it began from the root, because the conduct of the elect often accomplishes more in its ending than it proposes at its beginning; it often begins more tepidly but completes its final course more fervently. Indeed, because it always judges itself to be beginning, it endures untiringly in newness. Isaiah speaks as though of the other trees where he says: “Boys shall fail and grow weary, and young men shall fall in weakness” (Isa. 40). But concerning the palm he adds: “Those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall take up wings like eagles; they shall run and not grow weary; they shall walk and not fail” (ibid.).

There are, however, some [Col. 1133C] who, after beginning strong things, not only grow lukewarm in what they have begun, but also shamefully fall into vices; and, having begun in the Spirit, they end in the flesh (Gal. 3). The poetic saying aptly applies to them:

> If a painter should wish to join a horse’s neck  
> To a human head, and to add varied feathers  
> To limbs assembled from every side, so that a woman, fair above,  
> Ended foully in a black fish—  
> Once admitted to see it, could you, my friends, restrain your laughter?  
> (*Horace, Art of Poetry*, lines 1–5.)

For the spiritual work which they begin is human, rational, and very beautiful; but the vice in which they end is altogether bestial, foul, and black. [Col. 1133D] Those alone, therefore, seem comparable to palms who, though the things they begin are small, few, and constrained (*arcta*, evidently misread in the source as *acta*), nevertheless complete great, many, and ample things.

The cedar is said to excel other trees in height, and therefore heavenly glory, than which nothing is more exalted, is fittingly expressed by the cedar. The palm too has its height, by which the height of righteousness is signified; but it is in no way equal to the cedar, by which the height of glory is figured. And we should carefully observe what Scripture says: “He shall flourish like the palm; he shall multiply like the cedar.” For in the present life, through righteousness, we have the flower—that is, the hope of receiving the future fruit; but in the future we shall receive through glory the fruit of that flower. That fruit is rightly called manifold, because “in keeping the judgments of the Lord there is great reward.” Blessed [Col. 1134A] John, therefore, is beyond the other saints both palm and cedar: palm through righteousness, cedar through glory; palm in the world, cedar in heaven; palm in merit, cedar in reward; palm because righteous, cedar because blessed. The more righteous he is, the more blessed; more righteous on the way, more blessed in his homeland.

Therefore, dearest brethren, let us labor with all our strength to be palms with blessed John, so that afterward we may be able to be cedars with him. Let none of us, by living perversely, imitate the other trees, broad below and slender at the top; let none be like the remaining shrubs; let none be weak in spiritual matters and strong in carnal ones. Let us all alike cut short the fleeting pleasures of the flesh and enlarge the inner chambers of our minds, so that we may flourish like a palm through righteousness in time, and multiply like a cedar through glory in [Col. 1134B] eternity. May the Lord deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXIV. On the Feast of the Same Saint John the Baptist

“John is his name, and many shall rejoice at his birth” (Luke 1).

“John” is interpreted “God’s grace.” This most holy name, dearest brethren, given to a most holy man, reverently announced by Gabriel, spoken by Elizabeth when filled with the Holy Spirit, and indicated in writing by Zechariah, must without doubt be believed to have been divinely ordained. For not without reason did he bear such a name, he who shone in grace above those born of women; whom grace sanctified in the womb; who, at the voice of blessed Mary, leaped for joy through grace at Christ’s presence; who, still a child, strengthened by grace, renounced [Col. 1134C] the world and entered the wilderness; and who until the day of his manifestation to Israel devoted himself to God alone, clothing himself in camel’s hair, binding himself with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, and drinking water. He deserved to be called John, since he was the herald and preacher of heavenly grace, whose bearer and giver Christ himself was. Thus John himself says: “I indeed baptize you with water,” that is, unto repentance; “but he who is to come after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Luke 3). For “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1).

Therefore, brothers, since we celebrate throughout the whole world the venerable nativity of so great a man, let us rejoice with all our [Col. 1134D] hearts, that we too may be participants in the saying written: “Many shall rejoice at his birth.” At his nativity, as is seen more with the eyes than read in books, many rejoice, because Christians rejoice; and, as report bears witness, pagans also rejoice. At his nativity many rejoice: the poor rejoice, servants rejoice, the good rejoice, the evil rejoice. The poor rejoice because they see the ripening of the harvest drawing near. Servants rejoice because they see the end of their labor and the time for receiving their wages at hand. The good rejoice with joy that is in the Holy Spirit. The evil rejoice with joy that is in the world. Now worldly joy is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. In the lust of the flesh is the joy of foulness; [Col. 1135A] in the lust of the eyes, the joy of curiosity; in the pride of life, the joy of vanity. For everyone who is proud becomes empty. This kind of joy, which is in the world, belongs only to the reprobate: those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 2); who delight in vanities and false madness, in the superstition of games, the practice of vices, and the commission of sins; who fill themselves with precious wine and ointments, and let not the flower of time pass them by (Wis. 2); who crown themselves with roses before they wither and wish to leave signs of their mirth everywhere. In these things rejoice those who, condemned in hell, grieve and say: “We wandered from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness did not shine upon us, and the sun of understanding did not rise for us. We were wearied in the way of iniquity and [Col. 1135B] destruction, but we did not know the way of the Lord. What profit did pride bring us, or what did the boasting of riches confer upon us?” (Wis. 5).

Therefore, dearest brethren, since worldly merriment is the way to everlasting sorrow—for “laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14)—let us regard laughter as error, and say to joy: “Why are you vainly deceived?” (Eccl. 2). “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for there the end of all people is brought to mind, and the living person considers what shall be. Anger is better than laughter, because through sadness of face the mind of the sinner is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sorrow” (Eccl. 7), because they know that the sorrow which is according to God produces a steadfast repentance unto salvation.

But sorrow too has its miserable form, [Col. 1135C] just as joy has its foolish form; both are evil. For “the sorrow of the world produces death” (2 Cor. 7). Thus there are two persons: one sorrows miserably, the other rejoices foolishly.

> One loves tears; another loves to twist his face in laughter;  
> And madness alike possesses them all in diverse ways.  
> But you, my son, will proceed most safely by the middle path.  
> Fly between the two; let discretion alone please you.  
> Virtue is the mean, withdrawn from vices on either side.

For just as between the vice of sticky grasping and the vice of slippery prodigality lies the virtue of generosity, which is exercised with discretion, so between bitter worldly sorrow and its empty merriment lies spiritual exultation, which is exercised with fear. [Col. 1135D] For exultation without fear is sometimes the mother of sins, while fear or sorrow without exultation is a certain bitterness in life. Nor should anyone say that the sorrow according to God differs from the joy of this or any solemn feast, since it is plainly often the true path to the joy that is in the Holy Spirit. When, moreover, we rejoice in the Lord, we may already trust that we have received something of the reward, since that joy which is received from the Lord and in the Lord is the blessedness of a rational creature. Let us therefore, dearest brethren, rejoice with great joy on this holy nativity of blessed John the Baptist. But let the exultations in our mouths be those of God, not of the world, so that through this holy joy we may deserve [Col. 1136A] to attain heavenly glory. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXV. Homily, or Sermon, on Balaam and the Children of Israel for the Feast of Any Saints

We read in Numbers that, after the children of Israel had departed from Egypt and were making their way through the wilderness to the land of promise, Balak resolved to oppose them and hired Balaam to curse them. But God turned his curse into a blessing. We shall run through the words of this history for you according to their spiritual sense, so that from them, according to our ability, we may build up the holiness of your conduct.

That people, now designated by the name Jacob and now Israel, signifies the people of the truly faithful: they are truly Jacob [Col. 1136B] while they struggle courageously against vices; Israel while they delight sweetly in the goodness of virtues. They are Jacob while they labor in earthly affairs on account of bodily necessity; Israel while they contemplate heavenly goods on high. Thus Balaam rightly said by a prophetic spirit: “Who can count the dust of Jacob, and know the number of Israel’s stock?” (Num. 23), so that by Jacob’s dust we understand active persons occupied with earthly matters, and by Israel’s stock contemplatives beholding heavenly things.

Balak, whose name is interpreted “licking,” “crushing,” or “enveloping,” signifies the devil, who licks with the blandishment of wicked temptation those whom he can, crushes them by the consent or accomplishment of sin, and entangles them in the bond of evil habit. Balaam, whose name is interpreted “vain people,” represents the whole [Col. 1136C] body of false Christians, who despise truth and follow vanity—especially those among them who seem to surpass others with a certain authority, whether by fleshly prudence, worldly learning, or the vain glory of philosophy. These, indeed, are like diviners in the eyes of the devil, all demons, and all lovers of the world, while they worship the empty wisdom of the world—or rather, by it, demonic impiety—through evil living. And while every day they add vices to vices or exchange one vice for another, they renew, as it were, the worship of new demons. For the text aptly applies: “New and recent gods came, whom their fathers did not worship” (Deut. 32). Like Balaam, they have one eye stopped up, because though [Col. 1136D] through knowledge they see that God is, they do not know what he is in respect of love. And while God looks down upon them from heaven to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God (Ps. 13 [14]), though there may be among them one who understands through knowledge, there is none who seeks through love.

Although, therefore, one eye is open in them while they believe rightly, the other is closed while they live wrongly. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 52 [53]). They have turned aside from good and become useless in evil. Like Balaam, they are hearers of God’s words but refuse to be doers. They see the visions of the Almighty through knowledge, but refuse to see them through action. They fall, and thus their eyes are opened: they fall through condemnation, [Col. 1137A] and thus their eyes are opened through perfect recognition of their former wickedness. For they do not perfectly know their own impiety until they feel the punishment which they earned through it.

Alternatively: they fall when some of them, at times pierced with compunction, are humbled from their pride; and thus their eyes are opened when they are perfectly illumined by God. For in this way God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4). Or certainly, just as Balaam himself says of himself below, that he has open eyes when fallen, so the proud wise persons of the world fall with open eyes, because they know what is true but nevertheless do not cease to do what is wicked. Balak first sent noble princes to Balaam, then nobler ones, because the devil sends demons to tempt the strong; and if those do not prevail, [Col. 1137B] he then sends stronger ones, that they may bend to their suggestions the crafty and eloquent men of the world, so that these may curse the conduct of the righteous—that is, disparage it by their slanders—and thereby diminish their good reputation, and thus render any simple and less cautious persons slothful, negligent, and faint-hearted in doing good.

Slander itself is the curse; commendation itself is the blessing. For nowhere in this entire blessing of Balaam do we read that he prayed good things for the children of Israel; rather, he only pronounced good things concerning them, or foretold them. And because the wise of the world seem, in the eyes of the devil and lovers of the world—and even in the eyes of some simple righteous persons—to possess great authority to praise or blaspheme, and because it is thought that some are brought low by their [Col. 1137C] disparagements while others are raised high by their praises, Balak aptly sends this message to Balaam through messengers:

“I know that he whom you bless is blessed, and he upon whom you heap curses is cursed” (Num. 22).

The Lord’s people are said to have covered the face of the earth, because “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20); and the devil fears that even any false Christians may sometimes be converted and oppose him with the rest, as long as he does not yet see them to be with him through a denial of faith. But the righteous destroy Balak’s people like grass even to the root, because the righteous customarily investigate and refute not only evil deeds but also evil counsels at their root. “For the spiritual person judges [Col. 1137D] all things, but is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2).

The price of divination and cursing, which Balak’s messengers held in their hands, may be believed to have been gold or silver, or both. Thus Balaam seems to have answered them: “If Balak should give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot alter the word of my God” (Num. 22). He made these messengers remain with him for the night, to inquire whether he could go with them or not, because it belongs to evil persons to seek counsel in darkness, not in light, concerning how they may carry out works of darkness. Rebuking them, Isaiah says: “When they say to you, ‘Seek those who consult spirits and diviners, who busy themselves with their incantations’: should not a people seek a vision from its God? On behalf of the living and the dead? Rather, to the law [Col. 1138A] and to the testimony!” (Isa. 8).

The gold and silver which we believe to have been the price of cursing signify worldly wisdom and eloquence, a pernicious abundance of this wealth, loved with all their hearts by all who are most vain among the vain. Hence they incline to diabolical suggestions, so that they may be thought wiser and more eloquent than others in the eyes of lovers of vanity. They are also brought from the mountains of the east to curse, because their inclination to disparage the good proceeds from pride and cunning. For mountains signify pride; the east, where worldly light rises, signifies cunning.

The ass upon which Balaam sat fittingly signifies the company of foolish subjects, upon which those masters of error sit while they exercise the primacy of their [Col. 1138B] teaching among them by authority. But on the path of their wicked intention, the angel with drawn sword—that is, the angelic order with the terror of divine judgment—resists both. The ass first observes this angel or sword and abandons the path of wickedness; then Balaam, when he sees it, is terrified. For the simpler and less crafty are more easily and swiftly shaken by terror of divine judgment and restrained from the purpose of perversity they have begun than are those darkened by the shadows of greater pride and impious cunning. Meanwhile Balaam strikes his ass with spurs, because the ruler of those who love vanity, while still insufficiently frightened and not yet understanding divine judgment, afflicts the people subject to him with the harshest words and, as far as he can, compels them to continue with him on the path of iniquity [Col. 1138C].

The vineyards are the diverse congregations of the Church. The walls with which the vineyards are enclosed are the teachers by whom communities of the righteous are fortified. The narrowness of the path is the command of righteousness, or the careful discipline and subtle understanding of ecclesiastical doctrine. Balaam is led into this narrow place and his foot is crushed, because the perverse undertaking of his intention is proved to be contrary to God. There the ass speaks, because the company of subjects, aided by the authority of holy teachers, reasonably complains against him about the harshness of his oppressive justice. Finally, when he recognizes that he is proceeding against God in trying to curse God’s people, he is corrected by fear; and if he is not restrained from the malice [Col. 1138D] of his wicked will, he is at least restrained from the malice of slander. And his curse is turned into blessing, when, corrected by fear of divine judgment, he is compelled to be silent concerning evil and strives, though unwillingly, to proclaim good things concerning the righteous. Balaam too is slain by the sword of the children of Israel, when at the final judgment the leadership of those who follow vanity is condemned by the righteous.

Therefore Israel’s people are the company of the elect; Balak is the devil; Balaam is the leadership of those who pursue vanity; his ass is their discipleship; the journey on the road is the advancement of wicked intention; the angel who opposes him is the angelic order contradicting their wicked enterprises; the drawing of the sword is the threatening of judgment; the vineyard walls are the teachers of the churches; the narrowness of the road is the discipline of sacred doctrine; the injury to the foot is the rebuke of wicked action; the curse is disparagement; [Col. 1139A] the blessing is praise and commendation of the righteous.

These things, brothers, we have run through only on the surface, leaving the deeper things for you to investigate. But since the matters that remain to be explained concerning this history are lengthy, we have thought it good to end this sermon with what has been said and reserve what remains to be set forth later. Now, therefore, dearest brethren, since by faith we have gone out from spiritual Egypt and ought to travel through the wilderness and make our way toward the land of promise, let us see whether we are true Israelites. Egypt is the secular life; the wilderness, the spiritual life; the land of promise, the heavenly life. Egypt is the flesh; the wilderness, the soul; the land of promise, God. We are true Israelites if we see God not merely with the eye of knowledge but also with the eye of love. If we have these eyes [Col. 1139B] sound, we shall hold the straight path by which we shall enter the land of heavenly promise. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVI. From the Words of the Same Balaam, for the Feast of Any Saints

In the preceding sermon we said certain things concerning the children of Israel, Balak, Balaam, and the blessing by which he blessed the children of Israel. Now let us come to the words of that same blessing and see what moral instruction they contain within them. If anyone asks what significance belongs to the burnt offering of Balak, who signifies [Col. 1139C] the devil, we reply that not everything contained in the letter is to be bent to a spiritual meaning. Nor does a parable extend in every respect.

Balaam blessed the children of Israel three times, so that the blessing itself may be understood to have been given, though through a human being, yet not by a human being, but by the holy and undivided Trinity. The words of the first blessing are these:

> “Balak, king of the Moabites, brought me from Aram, from the mountains of the east. ‘Come,’ he said, ‘and curse Jacob; hasten and denounce Israel.’ How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed? On what ground shall I denounce one whom he does not denounce? From the tops of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall consider him. The people shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations. Who can count the dust of Jacob and know the number of Israel’s [Col. 1139D] stock? Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my last things be like theirs” (Num. 23).

Aram is interpreted “high” and signifies pride. Balaam, therefore, was rightly brought from Aram, or from the mountains, by the impious king to curse God’s people, because the disparagement of the good by evil persons, with the devil’s assistance, proceeds wholly from pride. Moab is interpreted “from the father” and signifies all the reprobate, among whom were those to whom it was especially said: “You are from your father, the devil” (John 8). Thus Balak, king of the Moabites, summons Balaam to curse Israel, because the devil, ruler of these darknesses—that is, of demons darkened through pride and impious people begotten from him through sin—sharply incites, from among those impious persons, the most impious, devoted to his worship through impiety, to [Col. 1140A] blaspheme the righteous through desire for vain praise and empty glory. Unless they are restrained by fear of divine power, they are so inflated among people with glory in their wisdom and power that they readily incline to commit the crime of slander and blasphemy. It has often been proved that this curse has harmed the righteous repeatedly and in diverse ways.

But when they see that the righteous are fortified by divine protection, struck by divine fear, they greatly dread that the curse of their own disparagement should be brought upon them. Yet they would gladly do so, were they not afraid that vengeance from above threatened them. Thus Balaam also, restrained by fear of God, kept silent concerning the curse which, if he had been allowed, he had resolved to bring upon God’s people, saying: “How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed? By what reason shall I detest one whom the Lord does not detest? From the tops of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall consider him” [Col. 1140B].

From the tops of the rocks or hills, the perfect lovers and teachers of this vanity consider God’s people when, terrified by divine fear, they raise their minds on high to contemplate it and carefully weigh how deservedly it differs from other nations. They see that in the Church “to one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge; to another faith; to another the grace of healings; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another interpretation of utterances” (1 Cor. 12). They see some labouring at good works, others flourishing in virtues, others shining by miracles [Col. 1140C], others humbly subject, others excellently presiding, all wishing to benefit all.

And when they behold the people of the righteous filled with the blessing of heavenly grace, terrified by the judgment from above, they in no way presume to bring upon it the curse of their blasphemy and disparagement. On the contrary, they bless it, when, though unwillingly, they speak concerning it the good that they see in it. For it is not by their own choice, but by divine judgment, that they proclaim in admiration the righteousness of the good—righteousness which they neither follow nor love. Hence Balaam rightly says later: “I cannot prevent the blessing.” The words of this blessing—that is, this proclamation—follow when it is said: “The people shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations.”

It is great praise, brethren, to say that “the people shall dwell alone” [Col. 1140D]. Would that this voice of praise might be in the hearts especially of monks and of those who proclaim a solitary life in one manner or another by their speech and display it by their dress. Let those blush and fear at these words who, having left their cloisters, often attend courts merely out of curiosity rather than necessity; who gladly go out to spectacles and frivolous entertainments; who love greetings in the marketplace, the first seats in synagogues, the places of honour at feasts, and to be called *rabbi* by men (Matt. 23).

In saying this, however, we ought not to be thought to condemn the authoritative, honourable, and religious persons of men who, according to place, time, and cause, assist the outward necessities of holy mother Church. For it is one thing to act at the prompting of curiosity, another to act at the direction of reason [Col. 1141A].

Ephraim, “a heifer trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10), is therefore excluded from this praise. But the people of the righteous dwell alone and are not reckoned among the nations, because all the other nations follow the desires of the flesh and the glory of the world, whereas the elect alone pursue righteousness and spiritual goods. Not only contemplatives but also actives dwell alone, while they do not share in the works of the reprobate.

Therefore, although it befit all the faithful to dwell alone, not so much through bodily residence as through unity of heart, it especially befits those surrounded by the habit of religion and professing the religious life to dwell alone—not only through the singularity of good works, but also, insofar as possible, through bodily residence. Their profession, their habit, and their order demand that they be far separated from others [Col. 1141B], not only from the wicked but also from those who do good, since they profess holiness above others by their habit. Those who are separated from others by a singular profession of religion ought not to be reckoned among the other nations by their bodily manner of life.

“Who can count the dust of Jacob, or know the number of the children of Israel?” In the preceding discourse we said that by the dust of Jacob the active ought to be understood, and by the number of Israel’s stock the contemplative. In the literal sense also, it is rightly believed that the people of Israel could not be numbered because of their multitude, as is gathered from many places in the Old Testament—for example, where Israel is said to have been innumerable as the stars of heaven and the sand on the seashore (Heb. 11). But with regard to spiritual understanding, the people of the righteous must be believed to be far more innumerable [Col. 1141C].

Thus David says: “But to me thy friends, O God, have been exceedingly honoured; their dominion has been greatly strengthened. I shall number them”—that is, if I should wish to number them—“they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. 138). Of the multiplication of carnal Israel it was said, “They shall be multiplied like the sand”; but of the multiplication of spiritual Israel—that is, the friends of God—it is said, “beyond the sand.”

Blessed John likewise, in the Apocalypse, after seeing twelve thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel, added: “After these things I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands” (Rev. 7) [Col. 1141D]. For just as, according to the testimony of Scripture, the days of Israel are innumerable (Ecclus. 37), so Israel itself is innumerable. Not only the active, who are far more numerous than the contemplative, but also the contemplative, who are fewer than the active, are innumerable. This is shown where, after first saying, “Who can count the dust of Jacob?” he added, “or know the number of Israel’s stock?” As though he said: no one. It follows.

“Let my soul die the death of the righteous, and let my latter end be like theirs.” The worldly-wise of this present age, who malign the righteous insofar as they can, when at times stirred by fear raise their minds to contemplate the life of the righteous, desire to die their death, though they refuse to imitate their life [Col. 1142A]. They love with their whole heart the lust of the flesh and the glory of the world, preferring these to virtues and good works; yet, with what face I know not, they wish to die with the righteous and receive their rewards. But he who bears their type, because he refused to live the life of the righteous, did not deserve to die their death. Without doubt, he would have been heard in the prayer in which he asked to die well, had he taken care after his prayer to live well.

From what has been said, brethren, let us gather the means by which we may advance on the way of God. Let us strive to dwell alone, and not to be reckoned among the nations through any unrest of dissipation. Let us strive, with Jeremiah, to sit alone and, in accordance with his words, to lift ourselves above ourselves (Lam. 3). Let us strive to live righteously with the righteous, that with them we may deserve to die well [Col. 1142B] and, aided by their merits and prayers, attain the glory above. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVII. On the Feast of Any Saints, on the Same Words of Balaam

Since in the preceding sermon we have, as far as we were able, set forth what is contained in the first blessing by which Balaam blessed the children of Israel, let us now proceed in order to explain what is contained in the second. Balak, grieving and bitterly complaining that Balaam was blessing the children of Israel, whom he had hoped he would curse, said to Balaam: “Come with me to another place, from which you may see part of Israel, though you cannot see the whole; from there curse him” (Num. 23) [Col. 1142C].

And he brought him to a high place, upon the summit of Mount Pisgah. When Balaam had withdrawn and returned after receiving God’s counsel, he said: “Stand, Balak, and listen. Hear, son of Zippor. God is not like a man, that he should lie; nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he spoken, then, and will he not do it? Has he uttered a word and will he not fulfil it? I have been brought to bless; I cannot prevent the blessing. There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel; the Lord his God is in him, and the shout of a king’s victory is in him. God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros. There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In their times it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done. Behold, the people shall rise like a lion and be lifted up like a lioness. He shall not lie down until he has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain.” [Col. 1142D]

Balak said to Balaam: “Do not curse him, nor bless him.” And he said: “Did I not tell you that whatever the Lord commanded me, that I would do?”

The devil has manifold cunning by which he attacks the righteous and daily attempts to overthrow them. Hence Balak summons Balaam from place to place to curse God’s people: for when the devil does not prevail against the righteous in one way, he tries another way so that he may conquer. He incites the vainest members of the vain people to corrupt, at least in part, the praise of the good by the curse of disparagement and blasphemy, so that, when he cannot destroy the reputation of the saints wholly, he may at least injure it in some part. For this is both to see in part and to curse in part.

[Col. 1143A] Balaam withdraws and seeks God’s will as to whether he can curse God’s people, because the vain people in temptations of this kind commonly gather themselves inwardly in order to inquire concerning God’s will in the matter. And when they recognize his goodwill toward his elect, they do not presume to cast upon them the darts of their curse. When they raise their minds higher in contemplation of them, they immediately turn aside to utter words of blessing. Hence, after receiving God’s counsel, Balaam says to Balak: “Stand, Balak, and listen; hear, son of Zippor. God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he spoken, then, and will he not do it? Has he uttered a word and will he not fulfil it? I have been brought to bless; I cannot prevent the blessing.”

“Stand, Balak,” as though it were said: “Cease, devil, to urge me to blaspheme the righteous [Col. 1143B]; for if I presume to do this, I gain damnation for myself and do not impede their salvation.” God, who does not change in heart, does not lie with his mouth; he does not change in purpose, nor lie in word. He himself proposed and promised that in Abraham’s seed he would bless all nations. Will he not then do what he has proposed? Will he not fulfil what he has said? Far be it! For “God is true, but every man a liar” (Rom. 3). Therefore, because God is true in his promises, his word is daily seen to be fulfilled. For the justification and salvation of the elect is his blessing.

Let the vain people therefore say: “Can I, then, nullify by my curses what God has decreed to fulfil? Indeed, [Col. 1143C] I have been brought to bless; I cannot prevent the blessing.” For when the reprobate are raised up to contemplate the life of the righteous, admiration itself compels them to proclaim the righteousness which they do not love. This praise in blessing proceeds not so much from their will as from the divine dispensation. Thus Balaam says: “I cannot prevent the blessing.”

The words of this blessing are: “There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord his God is with him, and the trumpet-call of a king’s victory is in him.” He removes evils from the spiritual people and proclaims their goods. He removes, namely, idol and image from the spiritual people—things which are known to have existed almost continually in the carnal people of old. He proclaims the goods which are truly and perfectly found in the spiritual people [Col. 1143D]. Hence the bridegroom, praising the bride, says: “My dove is one, my perfect one” (Song 6).

He removes all idolatry and unbelief from the spiritual people when he says: “There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel.” He proclaims its perfect liberation and freedom when he adds: “The Lord his God is with him, and the trumpet-call of a king’s victory is in him.” In that the Lord his God is with him, he no longer serves the spiritual Pharaoh in Egypt; in that the trumpet-call of a king’s victory is in him, he already sings with Moses in the desert the song of thanksgiving.

It should be carefully noted that he does not say “the trumpet-call of battle,” but “the trumpet-call of victory.” In the liberation of the earlier people there was no trumpet-call of battle, because the Lord fought for it, while it kept silence. Likewise, in the liberation of the later people there was no trumpet-call of battle, because Christ, who “did not open his mouth before the one shearing him,” liberated it by bearing its sins [Col. 1144A]. “He trod the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with him” (Isa. 63).

The first trumpet-call of victory, then, was the song sung by Moses and the children of Israel when they were liberated from the servitude of Pharaoh, king of Egypt: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified; horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exod. 15). The second trumpet-call of victory is the thanksgiving sung by spiritual Israel when liberated from the servitude of the devil. Of this trumpet-call of victory the Lord says through Isaiah, under the name of Zion: “Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51).

There is therefore no idol in spiritual Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel, because it has been liberated from the slavery of demons and brought out from the darkness of unbelief, since the Lord its God is with it and the trumpet-call of a king’s victory is in it. To strengthen this statement, he adds: “God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros” [Col. 1144B].

The rhinoceros is of an untameable nature; and God is altogether incomprehensible and invincible. *Rhinoceros* in Latin means “a horn in the nose.” Since by the nose we distinguish pleasant and foul smells, the nose rightly signifies the moderation of discernment; by the horn, however, we understand power. God’s strength, therefore, is like that of a rhinoceros, because God always exercises the power of his strength with the moderation of wondrous discernment. Hence it is written: “Thou, Lord Sabaoth, judgest all things with tranquillity” (Jer. 11). And of Wisdom we read: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8). To this sense also belongs the saying of the Psalmist: “He sent darkness and made it dark, and he did not provoke his words” (Ps. 104) [Col. 1144C].

Since, then, God brought spiritual Israel out of the Egypt of its former unbelief, no image of the old error is deservedly seen in it. But because there are many who bear the name of Christianity and do not bow their necks to images, yet devote themselves in sacrilegious fashion to various lots and divinations, he rightly proclaims concerning true Israel: “There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel.” For those who place their faith and hope in such vanities are false Israelites. Thus the Apostle, rebuking the Galatians, says: “You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear for you, lest I have laboured among you in vain” (Gal. 4) [Col. 1144D].

But in true Israel, just as there is no idol or image, so there is no augury, divination, incantation, or any superstitious observance, nor anything else proved contrary to the sacred faith. He still elegantly proclaims the spiritual goods of this people, in order to show it worthy not of cursing but of blessing: “In their times,” he says, “it shall be told to Jacob and Israel what God has done.” How? He himself will reveal it to them—he “who declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done thus to every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (Ps. 147).

The judgments or works of God are made known to the faithful at diverse times and in diverse ways [Col. 1145A]. They are made known through nature, through creation, through the law, through prophecy, and through grace. After death they are made known more fully in receiving the first robe; after the end of the age they will be made known most fully in receiving the second robe and possessing glory. Meanwhile, while we are on the way and not yet in our homeland, many things are hidden and few are manifest. Although many uncertain and hidden matters of divine wisdom are revealed to a human being (Ps. 50), nevertheless he does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love, since all such things are reserved uncertain for the future (Eccles. 9), and God’s hidden judgments over us are “a great deep” (Ps. 35). “Now we know in part; but then we shall know even as we are known” (1 Cor. 13). And thus, in their times, it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done.

“Behold, the people shall rise like a lion and be lifted up like a lioness.” He compares the life of the righteous to the noblest beasts, so that by this comparison he may clearly show the nobility of character in them. The lion signifies strong and perfect men; the lioness, the imperfect and weak. The lion signifies contemplatives; the lioness, actives. The lion is Israel; the lioness Jacob [Col. 1145B].

It is reported that, when the lion is hungry, it gives a roar whose terror stops and fixes the beasts that hear it; then, catching them, it drinks their blood and eats their flesh. In this also it surpasses the other beasts: it fears the fierceness of no beast. For “the lion, strongest among beasts, shall fear no encounter.” So, indeed, the people of the righteous—especially the company of preachers—when it hungers for the conversion of those living wickedly, emits the terror of preaching and restrains men living like beasts, lest they continue running through diverse vices. It drinks the blood of those whom it has, as it were, caught in its mouth, when it utterly consumes their cruelty. It kills them so that they may die to the world and live to God; and it eats them by incorporating them into itself, when through faith it joins and unites them to itself.

And as the lion surpasses beasts in fierceness, so it surpasses men in virtue, because, in order to refresh itself by the amendment of offenders, it fears no encounter with cruelty. It does not lie down until it has devoured the prey and drunk the blood of the slain, because it never ceases from capturing the souls of those to be saved, uniting them to itself, and consuming their cruelties, until it knows at the end of time that the full number of the elect has been completed [Col. 1145C].

[Col. 1145D] This proclamation of the righteous is often uttered by Balaam—that is, by the vain people—and thereby provokes Balak, that is, the devil who had suggested words of blasphemy and cursing, to anger. Hence Balak says to Balaam: “Do not curse him, nor bless him.” For the devil would prefer lovers of vanity to be wholly silent than to speak anything good about the good. But God orders it for the praise of his name that, even through the mouths of the wicked, the praise of the good may sometimes increase.

May the Lord grant us, beloved, always to share in the grace and praise of the righteous, so that, helped by their prayers and merits, we may deserve to enter with the righteous the homeland of the heavenly promise. May Jesus Christ our Lord, God blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXVIII. On the Feast of Any Saints, on Balaam’s Third Blessing

[Col. 1146A]

Since we have spoken of the matters written in the first two blessings by which Balaam blessed the children of Israel, let us now proceed to explain the matters contained in the third instance. Balak said to Balaam: “Come, and I will bring you to another place; perhaps it may please God that you may curse them from there.” And he brought him to the summit of Mount Peor.

When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord for him to bless Israel, he did not go away, as he had previously gone, to seek augury. Instead, turning his face toward the wilderness and raising his eyes, he saw Israel dwelling in its tents by its tribes. And as the Spirit of God rushed upon him, he said: “How beautiful are thy tabernacles, O Jacob, and thy tents, O Israel: like wooded valleys, like gardens watered beside rivers, like tabernacles fixed by the Lord, like cedars beside waters!” (Num. 23–24) [Col. 1146B].

Balak summons Balaam from place to place to curse God’s people, because the devil inflames vain men in diverse ways to blaspheme the righteous, so that, when he cannot diminish their praise in one way, he may do so in another. He also leads them to high places when he raises them, insofar as he can, into pride against the righteous. But the more frequently and sharply the vain people are tempted to curse the righteous, the more fully are they commonly taught concerning the goodwill God has toward them, and the more ready they become, not to curse, but to bless.

Thus, when Balaam saw on this third occasion that it pleased the Lord for him to bless Israel, he did not go away, as he had previously gone, to seek augury. Rather, turning his face toward the wilderness, raising his eyes, seeing Israel dwelling in its tents by its tribes, and with the Spirit of God rushing upon him, he said: “How beautiful are thy tabernacles, O Jacob, and thy tents, O Israel!”

The vain people turn their faces toward the wilderness when, in hidden reflection, they diligently consider what takes place in the conduct of those who live spiritually. They raise their eyes in order to see Israel when they exalt their minds in contemplation of them [Col. 1146C]. Restrained on the one hand by fear from uttering evil, and compelled on the other by admiration of the righteous not to keep silent concerning good, they burst forth in a voice of blessing, saying: “How beautiful are thy tabernacles, O Jacob, and thy tents, O Israel!”

“Tabernacles” may more properly be called those made of leaves and branches; “tents,” however, those stretched by sewing together material of skins and cloths. Therefore tabernacles, being made of less costly material, signify the performance of good works; tents, being made of better and more precious material, more properly signify the exercise of virtues. For the goodness of virtues surpasses works, because a person who has nothing to give may be saved without works; but without virtues—especially charity and certain others—he cannot be saved. There are also many who perform good works, but, because they are without charity, cannot thereby attain heavenly glory [Col. 1146D].

The material of tabernacles, then, seems chiefly to be the sixfold work of mercy; the material of tents, the threefold or sevenfold set of virtues. The six works are to give food to the hungry, drink to the thirsty, and so forth (Matt. 25). The three virtues are faith, hope, and charity. The sevenfold virtues are the seven virtues described in the Gospel (Matt. 5): the first is humility; the second, meekness; the third, contrition of mind; the fourth, desire for righteousness; the fifth, mercy; the sixth, purity of heart; the seventh, inward peace of mind.

There are also very many other virtues mentioned by Sacred Scripture which, when rightly exercised, are stretched out in the work of the spiritual tent. For the exercise itself is the stretching. Thus the performance of good works is itself the erection of spiritual tabernacles; the exercise of virtues is the stretching of tents or pavilions [Col. 1147A].

What the beauty of these tabernacles or pavilions is—or indeed how beautiful it is to dwell in them—is finely described in four ways when it is added: “Like wooded valleys, like gardens watered beside rivers, like tabernacles fixed by the Lord, like cedars beside waters.” The tabernacles and tents of the righteous, constituted by action and virtue, are like wooded valleys: valleys through humility, wooded through protection.

For from humility, which is the stable foundation of virtues and good works, virtues and good works arise; and just as thick and lofty woods arise from fertile valleys, and as springs issue forth in valleys and their confluence produces lofty trees, so gifts of grace are given to the humble, from which works and virtues are bestowed. And as anyone takes refreshment in valleys beneath the shade of thick and lofty trees, so as not to be burdened by the sun’s heat, so every righteous person is refreshed in his humility beneath the protection of virtues and good works, lest he be scorched by the heat of fleshly desire or by the visitation of heavenly wrath [Col. 1147B].

“Like gardens watered beside rivers.” Gardens are divided into diverse little plots, as diverse seeds are sown in their diverse beds and diverse shoots arise differently in them. In one place onions, in another leeks, in another cabbages find room; from the nourishment of the earth they put forth their shoots and grow to maturity. Likewise, in gardens of aromatic plants [Col. 1147D], different kinds occupy different places and receive nourishment for growth.

Just as above works were fittingly understood by tabernacles, so here virtues are understood by aromatic plants: so that the beauty and usefulness of vegetables may correspond to the beauty and usefulness of works, and the beauty and usefulness of aromatic plants to the beauty and usefulness of virtues. The rivers that water these two gardens are fittingly understood as the two kinds of compunction, which flow through human hearts in order that they may bear fruit in both directions. For when fear and love stir the heart on either side, the rivers of compunction immediately flow forth; and when they water the little plots of those hearts, they at once abundantly make them fruitful in producing the shoots of virtues and good works [Col. 1147C].

Therefore the tabernacles of Jacob—that is, the works of the active—and the tents of Israel—that is, the virtues of the contemplative—are like wooded valleys because they protect, and like gardens watered beside rivers because they feed. Although we distinguish these matters in this way, assigning works to the active and virtues to the contemplative, it should nevertheless be known that the active exercise virtues and the contemplative perform good works, although the performance of works seems to belong more to the active and the exercise of certain virtues especially to the contemplative.

“Like tabernacles fixed by the Lord.” The tabernacles of the righteous are always fixed and always moving: always fixed through the firm and continuous stability of righteousness; always moving through the continual growth of that same righteousness. They are fixed so that they may not fall away from righteousness; they move so that they may always grow in it. They are always fixed because “the man is gracious who has mercy and lends; he orders his words with judgment; he shall not be moved for ever” (Ps. 111). They are always moving, as Saul said to David: “By doing thou shalt do, and by being strong thou shalt prevail” (1 Sam. 16). And later it is written concerning David: “David advancing and ever stronger in himself” (2 Sam. 3) [Col. 1148A].

The tabernacles of the righteous, fixed by the Lord, remain always, because “the rain descended, the floods came, the winds blew and rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, because it was founded upon firm rock” (Matt. 7). They are always moving while their actions and virtues continually increase in the fruit of righteousness. Hence Paul writes to the Corinthians: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the growth of the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Cor. 9) [Col. 1148B].

“Like cedars beside waters.” Cedars are very lofty trees which, when they grow beside waters, as may be inferred from these words, raise themselves higher than usual. By waters are fittingly understood the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and godliness, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. 11).

That water may signify the Holy Spirit, the Lord shows in the Gospel where he says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly.” “But this,” he said, “concerning the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7) [Col. 1148C].

The tabernacles or tents of the righteous—that is, their actions and virtues—are like cedars beside waters because, receiving nourishment from the gifts of the Holy Spirit, they not only surpass human work and strength but even reach unto heaven. Hence Paul says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3).

Therefore the tabernacles or tents of the righteous—their actions and virtues, as stated—are like wooded valleys, because they protect; like watered gardens, because they feed; like tabernacles fixed by the Lord, because they are stable; like cedars beside waters, because they are lofty. Let us strive, brethren, to dwell in the tabernacles and tents of the righteous. Let us strive to imitate their works and virtues. Let us strive [Col. 1148D] to rest with the righteous in wooded valleys, in watered gardens, in tabernacles fixed by the Lord, beneath cedars beside waters.

Much indeed could be said about all these things, but we run through them only in summary, leaving deeper investigation to you. And because there remain many words concerning this third blessing, we have resolved to end this sermon with what has been said above and reserve what remains to be explained for later, lest, by stretching the discourse too long, we generate weariness in you.

Let us therefore take care, beloved, from what we have said, to conduct ourselves holily and honourably, so that we may silence the ignorance of foolish people; so that, if there are any who, imitating Balaam, wish to disparage us as evildoers, they may be put to shame [Col. 1149A] [Col. 1149B] and be compelled instead to proclaim what is right concerning us, considering our good conduct in Christ. Finally, let us strive with the righteous to advance from virtue to virtue, so that, aided by their merits and prayers, we may one day deserve to enter with them the homeland of the heavenly promise. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXIX. On the Feast of Any Saints. On the Same Third Blessing

“Water shall flow from his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters. His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed. God brought him out of Egypt, whose strength is like that of a rhinoceros. They shall devour the nations, his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows. Lying down, he slept like a lion and like a lioness; who will dare to rouse him? Whoever blesses thee shall himself be blessed, and whoever curses thee shall be reckoned under a curse.”

After the most beautiful conduct of the righteous has been beautifully described above, the same diviner Balaam, who bears the type of the vain people, still magnificently proclaims their praise, saying: “Water shall flow from his bucket, and his seed shall be in many waters.” In Sacred Scripture waters sometimes signify the Holy Spirit, sometimes sacred knowledge, sometimes corrupt knowledge, sometimes tribulation, sometimes passing peoples, and sometimes the minds of the good who follow the teachings of faith [Col. 1149C].

By water the infusion of the Holy Spirit is signified, as it is said in the Gospel: “He who believes in me, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7). By water holy knowledge is signified, as it is written: “He shall give him to drink of the water of saving wisdom” (Ecclus. 15). By water corrupt knowledge is figured, as the corrupt woman is described by Solomon.

Tribulations are often understood under the name of waters, as the Psalm says: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even unto my soul” (Ps. 68). By waters are expressed passing peoples, of whom it is written: “Cast thy bread upon passing waters” (Eccles. 11), that is, passing peoples, because after many days thou shalt find it. John also testifies that peoples are signified by waters, saying: “The waters are peoples” (Rev. 7). These waters pass away [Col. 1150A], because through mortality they flow toward death. We cast our bread also upon them when, whenever they need our service, we bestow upon them our benefit in charity. And we find it after many days, because after this life we receive it as a reward.

Finally, by water are signified the minds of the good who follow the teachings of faith. Hence Ezekiel says: “I heard the sound of the wings like the sound of many waters” (Ezek. 1). For the sound of the sacred faith, first made among a few saints, was afterwards multiplied from many waters—that is, from innumerable peoples.

Spiritual Israel’s bucket is Christ. For the ancient people he was the rock; for us he is the bucket: a rock, because he stands firm in himself; a bucket, because he made all things in measure. He poured out water for the ancients; he pours grace into us through the bucket [Col. 1150B].

From this bucket there flows to us the water of spiritual grace, the water of saving wisdom: the water of grace for righteousness, the water of wisdom for knowledge. This water, which that bucket itself contains, flows forth through fullness and flows into us through participation in that fullness. “For from his fullness we have all received” (John 1). “And his seed shall be in many waters.” Now, just as Christ is the bucket of the peoples, so his seed must likewise be understood as Christ. For Christ was born according to the flesh from that people. He is the bucket because by his grace he refreshes our spiritual thirst. He is the seed because by that same grace he regenerates us. He is the seed of whom it was said to Abraham [Col. 1150C]: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22); and to David: “From the fruit of your womb I shall set one upon your throne”; and through Isaiah: “Unless the Lord had left us seed, we should have been like Sodom and should have resembled Gomorrah” (Isa. 1). He is also the one of whom David says: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13), that is, Christ.

For although that evangelical householder had at different times, from the beginning of the dawning age, various righteous cultivators of his vineyard—and both the cultivator and the cultivation were good, that is, both just prelate and just subject—nevertheless no one possessed of himself what he was or what he did. Rather, all had it from this one, who was always faithfully awaited by all and mercifully bestowed upon all, and who by suffering brought it about that the good which they had done in faith in him should count to them as righteousness, through which they might return to the lost fatherland. Hence, because he alone proved to be the good of all, no righteous person entered that fatherland before his Passion, until he came, redeemed all, and, having redeemed them, opened to them the entrance of that same homeland. And because the righteousness of all was to be referred to him alone and ascribed to him alone, one of them spoke for all: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113). To you be glory, because our righteousness comes from your grace, not from our own strength. For, according to the prophetic utterance: “You, O Lord, have wrought all our works for us” (Isa. 26). With him, as Moses says, no one is innocent in himself [Col. 1151A] (Exod. 34).

This seed is that evangelical grain of wheat which, falling into the earth through the Incarnation and being put to death through the Passion, “bore much fruit” (John 12) through the justification of many ungodly persons, who are here signified by the multitude of waters. For “the waters are peoples” (Rev. 17), and many waters are many peoples. John signifies their innumerable multitude in the Apocalypse, where, after the forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel (Rev. 7), he testifies that he saw a great multitude which no one could number (ibid.). Isaiah calls this same multitude “long-lived seed,” when, after speaking much concerning Christ’s Passion and the redemption of humankind, he added in the person of God the Father: “If he shall set his soul as an offering for sin, he shall see long-lived seed” (Isa. 53). It remains in the world through grace, in heaven through glory.

“His king shall be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom shall be removed.” According to the letter, it is evident to everyone acquainted with the history written in the First Book of Kings that this too was true. For Saul went at the Lord’s command to destroy Amalek, its king, and everything alive that he found there; but in this he disobeyed the Lord, because he kept Agag, king of Amalek, alive. Therefore, when he returned from the slaughter, Samuel said to him: “The Lord has rejected you, that you should not be king over Israel” (1 Sam. 15). And shortly afterward: “Today the Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you and has given it to your neighbor, better than you.” When David had been anointed, the Spirit of the Lord came upon David from that day onward [Col. 1151C]; and it departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him (ibid.).

But in the spiritual sense the king of Israel is taken away because of Agag when an ecclesiastical superior, fighting against the devil in his rule not according to the divine command, is rejected. “And his kingdom shall be removed,” because “where there is no governor, the people shall fall” (Prov. 11 [printed: 2]). “God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros.” This statement occurs twice in this history, in order to show that God both created the world in wisdom and redeemed humankind in wisdom. In the creation of the world, God’s strength is rightly said to be like that of a rhinoceros, because it is written: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103). In the redemption of humankind also, God’s strength is fittingly called like that of a rhinoceros, because it is written: “Wisdom overcomes malice” (Wis. 7). Why God’s strength is said to resemble that of a rhinoceros has been explained above: “They shall devour the nations, his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them with arrows” (Num. 24). The enemies of spiritual Israel are especially fleshly Israelites. Hence it is aptly written: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Matt. 10); and again: “Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him have no confidence in any brother” (Jer. 9).

By “nations,” moreover, Gentiles are understood. Thus what is said here, “The nations shall devour his enemies,” is plainly and literally known to have occurred when the Romans, under the leadership of Titus, killed many thousands of Jews in the siege of Jerusalem, overthrew the walls, set fire to the Temple, led the remaining people who had escaped death into captivity, and scattered them through various regions [Col. 1152A]. Spiritually, however, the nations devour his enemies when those converted from the Gentiles to Christ’s faith overcome by their preaching either the perfidy of the Jews or the unbelief of any others who imitate Jewish perfidy; and, having conquered their unbelief, call them to faith, because they incorporate them into themselves. They break their bones when they soften, by the terror of divine threats, those among them who are harder and stronger. They pierce their bones with arrows when they penetrate their hard hearts with the most subtle words of Scripture, so as to bring Christ into them, kill them according to the flesh, and render them living according to the spirit [Col. 1152B]. Although we interpret these things in this way according to the spiritual sense, we do not deny that they happened literally to that ancient and fleshly people, when other nations overthrew other nations hated by that same people: Cyrus and Darius, for example, overthrew the Babylonians, and many others overthrew many others.

“He lay down and slept like a lion, and like a lioness: who shall dare awaken him?” But this too is known to have happened literally to ancient Israel, especially when David had subdued the surrounding nations and, in Solomon’s time, there was tranquil peace: there was no king or kingdom that presumed to trouble it or disturb its rest [Col. 1152C]. Mystically, however, these words particularly suit contemplatives and all the perfect, who live more quietly and securely the farther they are from earthly concerns and the noise of the world. They truly sleep peacefully in this respect: with the eyes of their heart shut to external things, they attend only to inward and eternal things. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song 5). No one dares awaken them, because their hosts are terrible “as an army arrayed in battle” (Song 6). Thus it is written of Solomon’s bed, which signifies contemplative souls: “Behold Solomon’s bed: sixty mighty men surround it, from the mightiest of Israel; all hold swords and are most skilled in war. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3).

Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed because perfect men, especially prelates, guard contemplative souls, in whom our Peaceful One especially rests. They are most skilled in war because they know most skillfully how to resist the assaults of the crafty enemy. And each one’s sword is upon his thigh because, lest they be destroyed by fleshly desire, they gird themselves most strongly with the virtue of abstinence and continence [Col. 1152D]. Therefore, with Christ’s grace assisting, enemies are kept far away from attacking them and prevented from disturbing them. It is therefore fittingly said of the righteous nation and the truly Israelite people that “he lay down and slept like a lion, and like a lioness whom no one dares awaken” [Col. 1153A], because, guarded by the strong watch of perfect men, it is not troubled even by the gates of hell.

“Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed; and whoever curses you shall be counted under a curse.” So that Balak may finally cease from his folly, Balaam firmly declares at the conclusion of this final blessing that everyone shall partake in that very thing which he has pronounced upon God’s righteous ones in blessing or cursing. “Whoever blesses you,” he says, “shall himself be blessed.” The Holy Spirit here most certainly speaks of that blessing which is not performed merely with the mouth, but proceeds from a blessed and benevolent heart. Balaam indeed blessed the children of Israel; but because he did so only with his mouth, unwillingly, and not from good will, he did not at all share in that blessing [Col. 1153B]. Rather, I would believe that he shared in the impious curse which he bore in an impious heart; and that consequently he fell into the guilt of giving wicked counsel against the children of Israel, and at last perished by their sword.

That one who curses God’s people shares in that curse is plainly proved by sacred authority, which says: “Revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6). For revilers will be punished with eternal curse among the other evildoers, when at the end it is said to them: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). And now, beloved, let us strive from what has been said to become participants in the blessing of the righteous, so that, aided by their merits and prayers, we may deserve to possess, both in the world and in heaven, the blessing by hereditary right [Col. 1153C]. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON LXXX. On the same history and Balaam’s blessing. A homily for the feast of any saints.

Balak, angry with Balaam, said, clapping his hands: “I called you to curse my enemies, but instead you have blessed them three times. Return to your place. I had indeed determined to honor you magnificently, but the Lord has deprived you of the honor prepared for you” (Num. 24). As is plainly recognized from these words, the devil becomes more fiercely angry in proportion as he repeatedly experiences openly that the efforts of his malice are not only ineffective but also work for good to the righteous, and that divine assistance gives them an outcome with the temptation [Col. 1153D]. For when he seeks to destroy the glorious life and progress of the righteous by the blasphemies of vain and profane people, and the sentence is, by divine providence, turned to the contrary, he grieves and complains bitterly.

The life of the righteous is blessed a third time by the vain people when their thought, word, and action are proclaimed by that people to be blessed. The vain people too are deprived of the honor arranged by the devil when they are entirely cheated of the favor of empty praise which they would have deserved by detracting through the oppression and diminution of the righteous persons’ glory. They return to their own place with the affair unfinished when, falling away from consideration and praise of the righteous, they relapse into their customary vices. Balak also returns by the way through which he came to his own place when the devil, frustrated in the result of his wicked intention [Col. 1154A], withdraws into the secrecy of his malice to devise other engines of deception.

Finally, although vain people do not dare openly to serve against the righteous by most wicked words, nevertheless, with envy still goading them, they sometimes rage against them by hidden schemes. Hence Balaam, as he went to his people, said: “Yet, as I go to my people, I shall give counsel what your people shall do to this people at the last time,” that is, at the end, before he is separated from it. This was the counsel that he gave him: namely, that virgins, by whose appearance chastity might be mocked, should be sent around their tents; that these women should labor meanwhile to entice to themselves the young men who turned aside toward them, so that they might make them transgress their ancestral laws and worship foreign gods; in order that, with their God angered against them, they might be humbled, even if only for a short time [Col. 1154B]. And this was done.

But Balaam, still raised by a fourth impulse of the spirit of prophecy, took up his parable and spoke certain things concerning Christ and again certain things concerning the spiritual people, which were to happen in the future and at a distance. He said: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel; it shall strike the leaders of Moab and lay waste all the children of Seth. And Idumea shall be his possession. The inheritance of Seir shall yield to his enemies; but Israel shall act valiantly. From Jacob shall come one who rules and destroys the remnants of the city.” After these predictions of the ruin of certain nations, he returned to his own place. Unless it were known from many testimonies of Holy Scripture that wicked persons, like some others, can possess the gift of prophecy [Col. 1154C] and certain other spiritual gifts, it would be very remarkable that this diviner, raised by a prophetic spirit, could have prophesied such lofty things concerning Christ and the people of the righteous.

“I shall see him,” he says, “but not now; I shall behold him, but not near.” As though he were saying: The wicked counsel which I gave you, when the children of Israel pass through your land, can be carried out; but the things I add will be fulfilled after a long time. “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a rod shall arise from Israel.” Christ is the star; Christ is the rod. A star because he enlightens; a rod because he chastises. He enlightens toward good; he chastises for evil. He enlightens the ignorant; he chastises offenders. “And it shall strike the leaders of Moab,” and so forth.
