The conversion of the Gentiles is plainly signified by all those whom this rod is said to strike [Col. 1154D]. For Christ struck the nations when, through his faith, he made them dead to the world in order that they might live to God.

What Balaam said of Christ—“It shall strike the leaders of Moab,” and so forth—also seems to have been later sung by David in the person of Christ: “Moab is the pot of my hope; into Idumea I shall stretch out my sandal,” that is, the faith of my Incarnation. “Foreigners are subject to me” (Ps. 59). For Moab is Christ’s pot when Gentile people, well cooked by love out of their own cruelty, refresh by holy living his desire by which he hungers for our salvation. He also stretches out his sandal into Idumea when he gives that same Gentile people the faith of his humanity. And foreigners are subject to him when those who are not from Israel also believe in him [Col. 1155A].

The primitive Church is signified where it says: “Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim is the strength of my head; Judah is my king” (ibid.). Then follows the conversion of the Gentiles, which is figured where it says: “Moab is the pot of my hope,” and so forth (ibid.). Christ strikes all these when, making them dead to the world, he renders them living to himself. The inheritance of Seir also yields to its enemies, and Israel acts valiantly, when the Gentile world submits its neck to the words of preachers, and the company of preachers vigorously disposes it toward good works. This strength of spiritual Israel first shone in the apostles and afterwards shone forth in the other righteous persons who followed. To the apostles, indeed, it was said: “Be strong in battle, and fight against the ancient serpent.” That this was not said to the apostles alone is evident from: “What I say to you, I say to all” [Col. 1155B] (Mark 13).

“From Jacob shall come one who rules,” namely Christ, “and destroys the remnants of the spiritual city Babylon.” For he destroys those whom he leaves for damnation. Their damnation is signified through the ruin of the subject nations, when it is added: “When he saw Amalek, he said: Amalek is the beginning of the nations; its end shall be destruction. He also saw the Kenite and said: Your dwelling is indeed strong; but even if you place your nest in the rock and are chosen from the stock of Cain, how long will you be able to remain? For Asshur shall take you captive. They shall come in triremes from Italy; they shall overcome the Assyrians and lay waste the Hebrews; and at last they too shall perish.” By the overthrow of these nations, therefore, we understand the damnation of all the wicked.

[Col. 1155C] At that time Israel was dwelling in Shittim, and the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who called them to their sacrifices. They ate and worshipped their gods, and Israel was initiated into Baal-peor. The Lord, angered, said to Moses: “Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gibbets before the sun” (Num. 25). The leaders seem to be punished because they ought to have punished the transgressors. Moses also said to all the judges of Israel: “Let every one kill his neighbors who were initiated into Baal-peor”; and on that day twenty-four thousand people died.

Shittim means “thorns.” Thus it is well said of the children of Israel that they dwelt in Shittim, that is, in thorns, when they sinned; for it is altogether credible that the thorns of preceding sins required them to fall into such grave crimes [Col. 1155D]. “Deep calls to deep” (Ps. 41), because fault generates fault. Elsewhere it is said of sinners: “Vengeance is mine, and I shall repay them in due time, so that their foot may slip” (Deut. 32). By their sacrifice to the idol we understand every kind of unbelief; by their fornication, every wicked action. Therefore, with both feet—those of faith and action—they limped from the straight path when they fell into the crimes mentioned above.

But in punishing fornication Phinehas proved remarkable and praiseworthy. Inflamed with zeal for justice, he pierced in their genitals Zimri, leader of the tribe of Judah, and Cozbi, a Midianite woman, while they were lying together; and he appeased God’s wrath raging among the people. Therefore the Lord established for him a covenant of peace and made him a prince, so that the dignity of the priesthood might be his forever [Col. 1156A] (Ecclus. 45 [printed: 65]). And now, beloved, considering these things in relation to ourselves: even if we do not suffer loss of our glory through the curses of vain people, let us nevertheless beware lest we fall into sin through their wicked counsels. And if we see any among us fallen into guilt through the deception of the devil and vain people, let us immediately remove evil from among us. Inflamed with zeal for justice after the example of Phinehas, let us punish it with the sword of our discernment, that, aided with the righteous by the merits and prayers of the righteous, we may deserve to enter the land flowing with milk and honey. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON LXXXI. On the feast of Saint Gregory: on the lampstand, concerning which Exodus 25 speaks.

[Col. 1156B]

“No one lights a lamp and puts it in a hidden place, nor under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that those who enter may see the light” (Luke 11). Brothers, the lampstand is the Church; blessed Gregory, whose festival we celebrate today, is the lamp. The lampstand is the Church, because the lampstand is beaten out with hammers and made an instrument of light; and holy Church, tested by temptations and thinned by the blows of persecutions, burns with the fire of heavenly wisdom and shines through the work of charity. The lampstand rests upon three feet, and holy Church is founded on faith in the Holy Trinity.

We read in Exodus that the Lord, commanding Moses to make the lampstand, said: “You shall make a lampstand beaten out of the purest gold: its shaft [Col. 1156C], its branches, its cups, its globes, and lilies proceeding from it. Six branches shall come out from its sides, three from one side and three from the other. There shall be three cups, as in the form of a nut, on each branch, and globes and lilies. This shall be the work of the six branches which are to proceed from the shaft. But on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups in the form of a nut, and globes upon each, and lilies. Thus the globes and branches shall be from it, all beaten out of the purest gold. You shall also make seven lamps and set them upon the lampstand, so that they may shine opposite it. The snuffers also, and the vessels in which the snuffed material is extinguished, shall be made of the purest gold. The whole weight of the lampstand, with all its vessels, shall be one talent of the purest gold” (Exod. 25).

Holy Church, then, is a beaten-work and golden lampstand. It is a lampstand because it is founded upon faith in the holy and undivided Trinity and established to contain the true and divine light. It is beaten work because, through the various blows of persecutions over the succession and length of time, it has been extended into growth in virtues and increase of its faithful people. It is golden because it is splendid with the radiance of inward charity [Col. 1156D]. The lampstand and the things proceeding from it were beaten work because “all who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). They were golden because every form of the saints’ righteousness is shown to shine brightly, whether through the flame of perfect charity or the light of wisdom.

By the shaft of the lampstand, which is evidently the strongest, greatest, and innermost part of it, and not merely straight but upright, we fittingly understand men in holy Church who are strongest in works, foremost in virtues, devoted to inward things, sublimely raised and elevated to contemplate heavenly things, and not bent to right or left to manage external affairs [Col. 1157A]. These are especially excellent before divine sight: those who “have chosen the better part, which shall not be taken from them” (Luke 10). Therefore four cups, globes, and lilies are commanded to be made in the shaft of the lampstand, whereas only three cups, globes, and lilies are described in the branches that proceed from it, in order to show by this that the merits of contemplatives surpass the life of active persons.

Alternatively, we may understand by the shaft—which is the strongest, principal, and central part of the lampstand, from which the other parts proceed and in which they have their foundation—Christ, who is the strength, beginning, and foundation of all saints, and who is in their midst, as he himself testifies: “Where two are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18) [Col. 1157B]. They truly proceed from him because whatever good they do, they receive from him. Hence he says: “I am the vine, and you are the branches” (John 15). As if to say: I am the shaft, and you are the branches. Just as a branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, and just as a branch of the lampstand cannot raise itself to support a lamp unless it remains in the lampstand’s stem, so neither can you bear the light of truth and faith unless you remain in me.

Thus Christ is the shaft, and all the other things proceeding from the shaft are all the faithful. In the shaft, the number four of the cups and the other things that follow is described, while in the branches only the number three is found, so that it may plainly appear from this that the good which is in Christ by fullness is in his faithful only through participation in that fullness. The branches proceeding from the shaft, and chief in the lampstand after the shaft, are the holy apostles and all preachers. They are rightly called branches because they are filled with the divine Spirit. As they preach the sacred faith to us, they sound sweetly like a new song. Of their sound the Psalmist sang: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18) [Col. 1157C]. They are described as six in number in order that their perfection may be signified by the number six. For six is a perfect number, both because God completed this world in six days and because six consists of its own parts.

As the branches signify preachers, so the cups signify hearers. Since wine is poured into cups, hearers of the word are rightly figured by cups. And as more liquid is poured into some cups and less into others, so more heavenly grace is bestowed through preaching upon some hearers and less upon others: to each according to the measure of faith and the measure of Christ’s gift.

Finally, when cups—that is, hearers—are filled and made drunk with spiritual wine, they are strongly encouraged toward the accomplishment of good works [Col. 1158A]. Hence globes are immediately added. Globes, because they are rolling bodies, represent the righteous who are swift in good works. A globe rolls in every direction, and the perfect activity of the righteous is neither slowed by adversity nor puffed up by prosperity; it is strong amid adversities and humble amid prosperities, having neither an angle of fear nor one of pride. Lilies signify heavenly recompense: through their greenness they figure the unfading nature of eternity; through their whiteness, the beauty of immortality. Thus branches, cups, and globes pertain to labor; lilies to recompense.

Three branches proceeded from the shaft on one side and three on the other because, before Christ’s Incarnation, there were holy persons in the time of the natural law, in the time of the written law, and in the time of the prophets, who mystically signified faith in the Holy Trinity; and after his Incarnation there are such persons in the time of the primitive Church, in the time of our election from the Gentiles, and in the final time when the remnant of Israel will be converted, who will preach that same faith [Col. 1158B]. Cups, globes, and lilies are described upon each branch because under both ancient and modern preachers, in each of the periods mentioned, faithful persons are found who thirst for the drink of grace, run in good works on God’s way, and await the unfading greenness of eternity and the incorruptible whiteness of immortality.

There were three cups, globes, and lilies on each branch in order to signify that in every age there have been rulers, continent persons, and married persons, who are figured in Ezekiel by Noah, Daniel, and Job. The cups were commanded to be made in the form of a nut, which has a hard shell and a sweet kernel, in order to show that sweetness is sometimes acquired with difficulty, but when it is possessed, tastes very sweet and is much loved.

If anyone asks how, mystically, the shaft, which signifies Christ, contained cups, globes, and lilies, let him prudently observe that Christ not only gives his elect knowledge of virtues, their practice, and their reward; he also displayed in himself the figure of a cup when he declared himself full of the Holy Spirit, of a globe when “he rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18), and of a lily when he was glorified with the Father [Col. 1158C]. Moreover, the final—that is, highest—cup, globe, and lily on the shaft rise higher than the branches, because the gifts which God bestowed upon Christ transcend every measure of human capacity. “For grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4); but “in him dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2) [Col. 1158D].

The seven lamps set upon the lampstand so as to shine opposite it are all prelates, who, placed over holy Church, shine toward those before them when by word and example they offer sinners the light of righteousness, heal the brokenhearted, and proclaim forgiveness to captives. We have often said that the number seven signifies universality. “The snuffers also, and the vessels in which the snuffed material is extinguished, shall be made of the purest gold.” There are certain precepts in the Scriptures to be observed perpetually both in this life and in the life to come, such as: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth (Matt. 22). There are others commanded to be observed during this life so that reward may be rendered in the future, such as: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16). There are still others which, though observed at the Lord’s command in the Old Testament, are now, with the Gospel shining forth, observed not according to the letter but according to their mystical sense, such as the rites of sacrifices and other matters of that kind.

When the apostles preached that these had come to an end and were to be observed only spiritually, the wicks of the lampstand were snuffed so that, renewed, they might shine more brightly, because, understood more sublimely, they might offer the light of doctrine more fully. To this renewal belongs what is written: “You shall cast away the old things when the new come” [Col. 1159B] (Lev. 26); and elsewhere: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21).

It is established that the apostles set aside the Sabbath before the Passion, and after the Lord’s Ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit put a complete end to legal sacrifices. Likewise, when mortal life has ended and immortal life succeeds, for the most part the works or gifts of light which we now use will cease, so that eternal rewards may follow in the presence of the divine vision. “Whether prophecies, they shall be abolished; whether tongues, they shall cease; whether knowledge, it shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13). The words of Holy Scripture that testify that these things are so to occur are golden snuffers because of their outstanding hope of future brightness. The vessels in which the snuffed material is extinguished are the hearts of the saints, in which these changes occur [Col. 1159C]; and they too are golden because they shine with the light of wisdom and the flame of charity.

Finally, the whole weight of the lampstand with all its vessels was one talent of the purest gold. For everything that God does, he does “in number, weight, and measure” (Wis. 11). In the spiritual sense these three can have the same meaning. The statement made above belongs to this weight or measure: “Grace has been given to each one of us according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4). Christ alone is excepted from this measure, for to him alone belongs what is written: “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3). For Christ, as was also shown above, possesses grace in its fullness, which is apportioned to the rest according to measure [Col. 1159D].

We therefore understand the lampstand as the Church; the shaft as Christ; the branches as preachers; the cups as hearers; the globes as workers; the lilies as recompenses; the lamps as prelates; the snuffers as the words of Holy Scripture testifying that certain works and virtues are at times abolished; the vessels in which the snuffed material was extinguished as the hearts of the saints in whom these things are abolished; and the weight of the lampstand as the measure of gift, merit, or reward. The talent, which is the greatest of weights, signifies perfection.

This lamp, then—blessed Gregory, whose festival we celebrate today—set upon the lampstand not in any ordinary place but at its summit, diffuses its rays farther and more widely in proportion as it was placed more highly [Col. 1160A]. Thus the lamp shines upon us with diverse rays, outstanding rays, splendid rays. It shines upon us through virtues; it shines through works; it shines through words; it shines through miracles; it shines through most rigorous religious discipline; it shines through most fragrant reputation; it shines through merit; it shines through reward. And now, beloved, let us walk by the rays of this lamp, so that, avoiding every byway and proceeding along the path of righteousness, we may come to the joys above. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXXII. On the Feast of All Saints.—A Tropological Exposition of Psalm 149.

The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting-places. In these and the following words, beloved, the dignity of the saints is declared, and beneath the brevity of a few words [Col. 1160B] their glory is set forth. “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting-places.” The glory of the saints is their good conscience, as Paul testifies when he says: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 2). Thus the saints are not inappropriately said to exult in glory when they exult in their good conscience. To this also pertains what the aforesaid Apostle says: “Let each one prove his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another” (Gal. 6).

The holy Psalm-writer—or rather, the Holy Spirit—places the glory of conscience before the other virtues of the righteous in the order of narration, not because it precedes them in order, but because it surpasses them in dignity. For virtue and good action come first, and by these [Col. 1160C] one proceeds and arrives at a good conscience. For who has a good conscience except one who knows himself, through virtue and action, to possess righteousness? Therefore only those exult in glory in whom there is a good conscience, which righteousness alone establishes.

“They shall rejoice in their resting-places.” The saints rejoice in their resting-places when, removed from the desires of the flesh, set at a distance from worldly cares, and established in inward peace, they contemplate heavenly goods in tranquillity. By resting-places, namely, in which one sleeps, inward repose is understood; and the mind truly attains this when it rests perfectly from outward things and attends only to inward things. The bride in the Song of Songs mentions these resting-places and this repose when she says: “I sleep, and [Col. 1160D] my heart is awake” (Song 5). Certainly, that person sleeps well and his heart is awake who, with the senses concerning outward things lulled to sleep, devoutly applies himself inwardly to contemplating interior things.

All carnal persons hate this repose of the resting-places, since outward things alone please them. Rebuking them subtly under the name of Ephraim, the prophet says: “Ephraim is a heifer taught to love threshing” (Hos. 10). For the heifer loves threshing because she eats of the ears of grain which she threshes. Thus all carnal people love outward occupations with all their hearts, not in order to serve the needs or usefulness of the Church, but so that they may refresh themselves as they please with more abundant and more luxurious food and drink, with empty words also and worldly vanities. Indeed, they complain that a serious loss is inflicted on them whenever outward matters to be guarded or administered [Col. 1161A] are not entrusted to them. But the saints, especially the perfect, are not so: they love inward things more, from which they derive more excellent joys.

Therefore it follows: “The exultations of God are in their throat.” The exultations of God are in the throats of the saints when they joyfully give thanks to God for benefits received. Hence the prophet says of Jerusalem—or rather, of the whole body of the righteous: “Joy and gladness shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51). But because it is not enough for anyone merely to do good unless he also destroys evil in others according to his ability, the text fittingly adds:

“And two-edged swords,” or swords sharp on both sides, “are in their hands, to execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples; to bind [Col. 1161B] their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles; that they may execute upon them the written judgment: this glory is for all his saints.” Thus the Apostle, when speaking of spiritual armour, says of the sword: “And the sword of the Spirit,” that is, the spiritual sword, “which is the word of God” (Eph. 6). And elsewhere: “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. 4).

Here swords are spoken of in the plural because the word of God consists of two Testaments. Perhaps this is what the Gospel saying refers to: “Lord, behold, here are two swords” (Luke 22). They are rightly sharp on both sides, because outwardly they cut away in us the lust of the flesh and [Col. 1161C] inwardly they prune the malice of the heart. They are sharp on both sides because they distinguish the good from the evil and the evil from the good. The saints hold swords in their hands because they put into practice by works the sacred words which they preach.

The purpose for which they hold them is also declared when it follows: “To execute vengeance among the nations, rebukes among the peoples.” In this place we may fittingly understand by “nations” the wicked, and by “peoples” the good—yet weak and imperfect. Thus the saints execute God’s vengeance among the nations with swords when, in accordance with the precepts of Holy Scripture, they excommunicate the wicked, or at least preach that vengeance will at some time come upon them. They make rebukes among the peoples when they reprove with sacred words whatever venial and light transgressions [Col. 1161D] occur among the good, whether perfect or weak. The wicked incur guilt deliberately, through an evil will and pride; the good offend through ignorance or weakness. And as the wickedness of the evil differs from the weakness of the imperfect, so vengeance appears to differ from rebuke. Wickedness and vengeance are graver; weakness and rebuke lighter.

“To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles.” Kings may here be understood as those whose office it is to govern others by the virtue of discernment. Nobles are those who seem to surpass others through the splendour of whatever dignity. The more exalted they are, the more easily and quickly they sometimes fall into fault. The saints bind them with fetters and iron manacles whenever they restrain their depravity by the authority of their holiness. Nor do holy prelates alone restrain these prelates and nobles who live ignobly from their perversities; their subjects also ought to restrain those same evildoers, so that their hands may not accomplish what they have begun, or, if they have begun it, may not become accustomed to it or persist in it longer. Unless subjects reject their evils with authority and oppose them, they should know themselves guilty of their seduction. For if Balaam’s ass had carried her rider onward even to the angel’s sword, would not both have incurred the sentence? But she opposed him, struck him with her hoofs, rebuked him with words contrary to her nature, and thus saved both herself and him. So also Paul withstood Peter to his face, because he was blameworthy (Gal. 2).

[Col. 1162B] That a prelate ought willingly to receive the correction of subjects, blessed Gregory shows in his *Pastoral Rule*, saying:

> “A prelate who strives to do wrong, yet sees others silent about it, is himself a witness against himself that he seeks to be loved more than truth, because he does not wish to be defended against himself. Thus Peter willingly accepted Paul’s rebuke. Thus David humbly listened to the correction of a subject; for good rulers, since they do not know how to be loved with private affection, regard from their subjects the word of free integrity as an act of humble obedience. Yet amid these things it is necessary that, when the mind of subjects can rightly perceive something, it should so come forth in a voice of freedom that freedom does not burst into pride; lest, when too unrestrained a liberty of speech is perhaps granted them, [Col. 1162C] humility of life be lost by them.”

“That they may execute upon them the written judgment.” The written judgment may be called the divine decree, established in the world by God as its author and committed to writing by the Fathers. The saints execute this judgment upon nations, peoples, their kings, and nobles when they punish some for obstinacy, reprove others for their transgressions, and restore them, so far as they can, to the integrity of virtues. And this is glory for all his saints: namely, that they themselves may be good through righteousness, and may exercise in punishing or rebuking others, according to the explanation given above, the grace bestowed upon them. “For all his saints,” that is, not only for the greater but also for the lesser. For although those of lower rank do not act with authority in punishing or [Col. 1162D] rebuking others, yet they cooperate with those who act authoritatively; and, if not by deed or word, at least by will. Hence: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Ps. 57). And if the righteous rejoices when he sees vengeance inflicted upon the wicked, he should be believed to rejoice much more when he sees forgiveness granted to sinners through correction and amendment, holiness restored—as there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance more than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance (Luke 15).

Therefore, as was said above, the saints shall exult in glory through the boasting of a good conscience; they rejoice in their resting-places through inward repose; God’s exultations are in their throat through thanksgiving; two-edged swords are in [Col. 1163A] their hands through the working of the sacred word; they execute vengeance among the nations by punishing the wicked; rebukes among the peoples by reproving offenders; they bind kings and nobles—even superiors—by reverently restraining them from perversity; in all these things they execute the written judgment by carrying out what God judges to be done through Scripture. Let us labour, beloved, to share in the good things said of the saints, so that we may deserve to be companions in their glory. May he deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXXIII. On the Feast of All Saints.—An Anagogical Exposition of Psalm 149

“The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice in their resting-places.” These words have been explained above according to their tropological sense [Col. 1163B]; but they may still be explained according to the anagogical sense, to which they seem to pertain even more. The saints, therefore, shall exult in glory because they not only now exult in glory, as was said above, through a good conscience in time, but after time shall also exult in glory through recompense in eternity. The more this glory is now unknown to our understanding and unexperienced by our affection, the more difficult it is to express.

For this glory is God himself, whom no one has ever seen (1 John 4), who is incomprehensible to thought; and when he illuminates his saints in heaven with the light of his brightness, he makes them perfectly share in the blessedness of his glory. Concerning this glory, in order that it may somehow be signified to us, it is written: “The righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom [Col. 1163C] of their Father” (Matt. 13). What brightness, then, do you suppose there will be when innumerable thousands of righteous persons are joined to innumerable thousands of angels? And if such inestimable brilliance will be in these creatures, who, I ask, can estimate the splendour of the supreme majesty—not only that which belongs to divinity, but also that of the humanity glorified in Christ, which most certainly surpasses incomparably the brightness of every creature?

For even concerning Christ himself, before his Passion and before the glory of his Resurrection and Ascension, it is written in his Transfiguration that “his face shone like the sun” (Matt. 17). We read in the Apocalypse concerning the angel who appeared to blessed John in the likeness of the Son of Man, that “his face [Col. 1163D] was like the sun shining in its strength” (Rev. 1). He chose the brightest visible creature to express the glory of that brightness when he said that his face shone like the sun in its strength—that is, at noon. Let him who can consider what is the eternal and immense brightness of incomprehensible and ineffable divinity, if the appearing likeness of the humanity glorified in Christ was so wonderful.

But the blessed glory, or glorious blessedness, of the righteous will be to be irradiated by the brightness of the supreme Divinity and of the humanity glorified in Christ, and to contemplate it without end. Thus it is again written in the Apocalypse that the heavenly city, namely Jerusalem, “has no need of sun or moon to shine in it; for the glory of God shall illumine it, and its lamp is the Lamb” (Rev. 21).

[Col. 1164A] Let one who can consider—but, I think, there is no one who can—how great the glory of the saints will be: when the good and faithful servant enters into the joy of his Lord (Matt. 25); when the good labourer, after the labour of his work, receives the gain of the denarius (Matt. 20); when the wise virgins, entering with the bride and bridegroom, rejoice forever in the heavenly bridal chamber (Matt. 25); when those receiving them into eternal dwellings give into their bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing (Luke 6); when God wipes every tear from the eyes of his saints, and there shall no longer be mourning, crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away (Rev. 21); when they shall possess joy and gladness, when [Col. 1164B] sorrow and groaning shall flee away, when we shall be filled from the abundance of God’s house and he shall give us to drink from the torrent of his delight, and when in his light we shall see light (Ps. 35); when our being shall know no death, our knowing shall know no error, and our loving shall know no offence; when we shall be at leisure and see, shall see and love, shall love and praise the magnificence of our Creator, who is God blessed above all things for ever.

Great, therefore, is the glory, as we said in the preceding sermon, of possessing a good conscience; but far greater is the glory of possessing eternal life. For it is a great thing if you are righteous, and incomparably greater if you are also blessed.

“They shall rejoice in their resting-places.” Here by the resting-places [Col. 1164C] of the saints we may understand their heavenly dwellings, of which the Saviour says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling-places” (John 14). Commending this same house, the prophet says: “O Israel, how great is the house of God, and how vast the place of his possession! Great is it and has no end; lofty and immeasurable” (Baruch 3). Of this place, too, the Saviour says: “I go to prepare a place for you” (John 14). In the dwellings of this house or place, while the saints live securely, peacefully, and tranquilly, they rest sweetly as in sleeping-chambers.

He says “in resting-places,” not “in a resting-place,” because there will be a difference in rewards according to the difference of merits. “For star differs from star in glory; so also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15). And elsewhere: “Each shall receive his own reward according to his labour” (1 Cor. 3).

[Col. 1164D] “The exultations of God are in their throat.” Then God’s exultations will be in their throats, because without end they will praise God, since they have escaped evils, received good things, and shall possess these forever without loss. Of this eternal praise of the saints the Psalmist says: “I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever” (Ps. 88). But what the exultation of the saints in heavenly glory is, what their rejoicing in these resting-places is, and what the exultations in their throats are, belongs to the knowledge and possession of those alone to whom it has been granted. Hence someone, speaking of the heavenly Jerusalem in rhythmic verse, aptly said:

> How greatly they rejoice in you,  
> How festively they feast;  
> [Col. 1165A] what affection binds them,  
> Or what jewel adorns the walls—  
> Whether chalcedony or hyacinth—  
> Those who are within know.

Since, then, there is no one who can know what will be the glory of the saints which they shall possess by seeing him, what their repose which they shall have by resting in their heavenly dwellings, or what exultations shall resound in their throats as they sing to God, let us meanwhile examine and heal our weakness, that we may someday deserve to attain those goods which we cannot yet see. Let us labour with all our strength to reach that light which shines in darkness and which darkness cannot comprehend.

“And two-edged swords are in their hands, to execute vengeance [Col. 1165B] among the nations, rebukes among the peoples,” etc. Having set forth the heavenly goods which the saints shall possess in the future, he returns to set forth the power which they shall exercise with the Judge on the day of judgment against those to be condemned. For the apostles and all who are most perfect are to be believed to judge the world with Christ. In their hands there will be two-edged swords for executing vengeance among the nations and rebukes among the peoples, because, according to the words of Scripture which they held and their opponents despised, they shall judge that these opponents ought to be punished eternally in soul and body.

For then the righteous shall stand with great constancy against those who afflicted them and took away their labours (Wis. 5). Then blessed Benedict shall stand for his monks; blessed Augustine for his clerics; blessed Peter, all the apostles, and ecclesiastical prelates for those entrusted to them, against the impious, unjust, and rapacious men who tormented them and unjustly plundered the possessions of the Church and the resources of the faithful; and, not permitting them to enter the gates of heaven, they shall cast them into outer darkness.

By “vengeance among the nations” we may understand the more severe punishment to be imposed upon those who have committed more grievous crimes. By “rebukes among the peoples,” we may understand the lesser torment in hell to be imposed upon those who have committed lesser offences. For adulterers shall be punished more severely than fornicators. Furthermore, because after the general punishment of the wicked a particular torment is specifically assigned to their kings and nobles, it is clearly shown [Col. 1165D] that, as it is written, “a very severe judgment shall be for those who rule” (Wis. 6), and “the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (ibid.). And again: “A stronger torment threatens the stronger” (ibid.). For it is just that those set over others, who through the power granted them act worse than others, should be confined more strictly under graver punishments than others in condemnation. And this is what is added: “To bind their kings with fetters and their nobles with iron manacles.”

The judgment which shall be exercised through the saints upon the reprobate on the day of judgment is called a written judgment because it has been written and established in the divine page by the holy Fathers. “This glory is for all his saints”: namely, that they may shine gloriously in themselves eternally and decree that the impious are to be punished by eternal torment according to their judgment.

[Col. 1166A] Let us consider, beloved, insofar as we can, what and how great is the glory of the saints, and let us labour that we may deserve to be their companions in the homeland. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us—he who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXIV. On the Feast of Saint Augustine. On the Perfection and Joys of the Church Militant and Triumphant

“My soul, bless the Lord, because he has delivered Jerusalem, his city. I shall be blessed if remnants of my seed remain to behold the brightness of Jerusalem. The gates of Jerusalem shall be built of sapphire and emerald, and all the circuit of her walls [Col. 1166B] of precious stone. All her streets shall be paved with white and pure stone, and through her lanes alleluia shall be sung. Blessed be the Lord who has exalted her, that his kingdom may be over her for ages of ages. Amen” (Tob. 13).

These words which we have set before you we have taken from the words of Tobit, by which, after recovering the sight of his eyes, he praised the Lord. Tobit means “good of the Lord.” Thus Tobit most rightly signifies the body of holy teachers and prelates, who is pre-eminently and truly the Lord’s good one, and is so called not only because by living holily he carries the Lord’s precepts into effect, but also because he instructs in faith the souls entrusted to him and forms them for right living. From the number of these prelates and teachers blessed Augustine, whose feast we celebrate today, was pre-eminent; [Col. 1166C] he taught his disciples and flock most perfectly and likewise trained them for the service of God. He also rightly urged his soul to bless the Lord, because he did not disregard the light of heavenly knowledge bestowed upon him.

By Jerusalem we understand the holy Church, which partly journeys on earth and partly is glorified in heaven. Here she exults; there she reigns. Here she is daughter; there mother. Yet she is one city, one Church, one dove, one beloved, one bride: a city through the cohabitation of citizens; Church through the gathering of the faithful; dove through simplicity; beloved through love; bride through faith. And the marriage is celebrated in both places, in the world and in heaven; but here in faith, there in sight; here in hope, there in reality. “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma; [Col. 1166D] but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Here at the wedding the wine of grace is offered; there the wine of glory is offered.

At the beginning of the passage set before us, it is also made known concerning this city that God delivered her; and at the end, that he exalted her. For he says:

“My soul, bless the Lord, because he has delivered Jerusalem, his city.” And at the end: “Blessed be the Lord who has exalted her.” First, indeed, he delivers her; then he exalts her. He delivers from evil; he exalts in good. He delivers on the way; he exalts in the homeland. He delivers through grace; he exalts through glory.

“I shall be blessed if remnants of my seed remain to behold the brightness of Jerusalem.” Let one who can consider how great is the love of spiritual fathers for their children: as may be understood from these [Col. 1167A] words, they regard the salvation of their children as their own, because they truly love it as their own and count it as belonging to them. Hence Paul says to the Thessalonians: “What is our hope, or joy, or crown of glory? Are you not so before the Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?” (1 Thess. 2). Paul expresses the same love when he says to the Galatians: “My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4). It should be noted that he does not say “my seed,” but “remnants of my seed.” For although many are called, few are chosen (Matt. 22); and even among the chosen, many are imperfect, while fewer are perfect for beholding the brightness of Jerusalem.

There are two brightnesses of the holy Church: one in time, the other in eternity; one in justification, the other in blessedness; one in merit, the other in reward. Yet however much she shines inwardly by the first, outwardly she is darkened, because “all who desire to live piously in Christ shall suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Of this brightness and this darkness the holy Church herself says in the Song of Songs: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1). Black outwardly through the distress of persecution, but beautiful inwardly through the brightness of love. “For though our outward human being is corrupted, our inward human being is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4).

But the words, “I shall be blessed if remnants of my seed remain to behold the brightness of Jerusalem,” seem to pertain rather to her future glory, which Isaiah promises her, saying: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illumine you; [Col. 1167C] but the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and your God shall be your glory”—that is, “your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not diminish; for the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be fulfilled” (Isa. 60).

Thus every holy prelate declares himself blessed if remnants of his seed remain to behold the brightness of Jerusalem, because he will truly be blessed when he sees in heaven, together with himself, some at least of those who now seem to imitate him in the world, contemplating the heavenly glory of the holy Church. He shall be blessed for his own good work, and blessed for the good conduct of those entrusted to him. For although in all saints there shall be a double glory, namely for the robe of the body and that of the soul, in holy prelates especially shall be fulfilled what is written: “In their land they shall possess double things” (Isa. 61)—for their own righteousness and that of those entrusted to them.

[Col. 1167D] “The gates of Jerusalem shall be built of sapphire and emerald, and all the circuit of her walls of precious stone.” The emerald signifies faith through its greenness. Sapphire, which bears the colour of the firmament, signifies good action. The greenness of the emerald signifies faith because, just as greenness first appears in things that germinate, so faith is first in the order of virtues, without which it is impossible to please God. The first gate of the holy Church is faith, which is represented in reversed order by the second stone, that is, the emerald; the second is action—namely, that action which comes through love of God and neighbour—which is expressed by the first stone.

[Col. 1168A] The first gate, faith, has, as it were, two leaves because of its two parts. For there are two things, and these two are one: Creator and Saviour; two divinities, but one reality. Yet “Creator” signifies one thing and “Saviour” another: Creator, because he made us; Saviour, because he saved us. The Creator and those matters which pertain to the Creator are one part of faith; the Saviour and those matters which pertain to the Saviour are the other. In the first part of faith it belongs to faith to confess the Creator and that all things which have being were made by him; in the second, it belongs to faith to worship the Saviour and confess that the lost have been restored by him, to whom blessedness has been given or shall be given.

The first part of faith concerns the obligation of nature; the second concerns the obligation of grace. We ought to believe the former because we were created by nature. We ought to believe the latter because we have been restored by grace. Therefore, if you believe the former, you possess one leaf of the first gate; if you believe the latter, you possess the other. But it is not enough to enter the first gate alone unless you also enter the second, because “faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2).

Action, however, is the second gate, represented by the first stone, namely sapphire. For every action performed through love of God and neighbour is more heavenly than earthly, because it is done not for earthly but for heavenly things; and for this reason it is represented by sapphire. It too appears to have two leaves. If you do what is good by loving God, you possess one leaf; but if you do good by loving your neighbour, you possess the other. Therefore, if you wish to be a citizen of Jerusalem, either in the present or in the future, you must enter both gates: faith and action—indeed, that action which is performed through love. For just as faith without action is dead, so action without love is empty.

“All the circuit of her walls is built of precious stone,” because the holy Church is surrounded on every side, in merit, by the firmness of her virtues, and, in reward, adorned all around by the brightness of heavenly rewards: so that in merit she may be firm, in reward bright; in merit she may lack no virtue, in reward no blessedness. Yet in both she is bright, in both firm, since now she is radiant in virtue and then in everlasting brightness.

But “all her streets are paved with white and pure stone”: white in good, pure [Col. 1168D] from evil. Thus all imperfect persons, who use earthly things more freely and broadly, are arranged in the most orderly manner in time by the purity of good works and in eternity by the beauty of rewards. Although they lack the strength of martyrdom, they are nevertheless white with the fine linen of their justification, which they possess through the purity of good action and the beauty of honourable conduct.

“And through her lanes alleluia shall be sung.” In the world and in heaven there are many orders of the holy Church. Since they differ among themselves either in merit or in reward, they make, as it were, many lanes. Through all these alleluia is sung, while divine praise is uttered both by those in heaven and by those on earth. Hence it is written: “His praise is above heaven and earth” [Col. 1169A] (Ps. 148). Although we explain these things which have been said according to both states of the holy Church, they refer more fittingly to the future. Therefore it follows:

“Blessed be the Lord who has exalted her, that his kingdom may be over her for ages of ages. Amen.” Although God’s kingdom is also over the Church in the present, it appears that it shall be far more fully so in the future: when every vexation of sin has ceased; when neither death nor mortality will rule over us any longer; when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing has put on immortality; when the Son has delivered up the kingdom to God the Father, and God shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15).

And now, beloved, let us see whether we are, as we ought to be, of the seed of blessed Father Augustine—that is, his imitators. Let us consider [Col. 1169B] whether, following his example, we love the word of God through reading, meditation, exposition, and preaching, according to the grace given us; whether by holy living we imitate with all our strength his most honourable religious discipline. For if we do these things, we are truly his seed; we shall truly contemplate with him the brightness of the heavenly Jerusalem. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXV. First Sermon on the Feast of Saint Michael.—From the History of the Book of Judith

The history of Judith is well known: how she killed Holofernes, commander of the army of the king of the Assyrians, who in the same history is called Nebuchadnezzar and is said to have reigned at Nineveh. When the victory had been achieved [Col. 1169C] and the spoils of the enemy gathered, the children of Israel gave Judith gold, silver, garments, gems, and every kind of household furnishing, all of which were shown to have been Holofernes’s personal property. And all the peoples rejoiced with women, virgins, and young men, with instruments and harps.

Then Judith sang this hymn to the Lord, saying: “Begin for the Lord with tambourines; sing to the Lord with cymbals; make melody to him with a new psalm; exult and call upon his name. The Lord who shatters wars—the Lord is his name. He has placed his camp in the midst of his people, that he might rescue us from the hand of our enemies” (Judith 16).

Judith signifies the Church; Nebuchadnezzar, the devil; Nineveh, the world; Holofernes, some most powerful [Col. 1169D] prince of demons, or the dominion of nations malignantly opposed to the Church. Judith cut off Holofernes’s head with his own sword because the holy Church confounds the pride of any hostile adversary by his own malice. For when the crafty enemy acts malignantly against the Church or any holy soul, and that Church or soul, with grace helping, escapes his malice, the same malice is turned back upon him, and by it he is slain. Hence it was said to the impious elder who maliciously opposed the righteous Susanna: “You have rightly lied against your own head” (Dan. 13). And again it is written: “Iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. 26). For it is just that whatever every impious person attempts against the righteous, he should himself be compelled to endure. “For all who take the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26).

[Col. 1170A] The spoils of the Assyrians signify wisdom, eloquence, certain works and virtues, and the discipline of good morals among the gentiles. In all these things, some elements are found useful for imitation. Gold signifies wisdom; silver, eloquence; garments, good works; gems, virtues; varied household furnishing, the ornaments of good moral character. The children of Israel take these things from their enemies and give them to Judith when all the faithful who practise them direct them to the praise and service of the Church. Thus, when the people of God departed from Egypt, they despoiled Egypt itself, from whose goods they constructed the tabernacle. Thus the righteous under the Old Testament consecrated to the service of the Temple what they had taken from their enemies.

“All the peoples rejoiced with women, virgins, and young men, with instruments and harps.” Women are those who act toward others with maternal affection, who beget and nourish them by the word of teaching. Paul was a woman, or mother, when he said: “My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4). And again: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 13). Virgins are those who rest from the business of teaching, who consider only the things that are God’s—not also the things that concern the neighbour through the office of teaching—and who labour only to please God in mind and body through holiness. Young men are those who do not grow old through any fulfilment of good work; rather, “their youth is renewed like an eagle’s” (Ps. 102), and although their outward person is corrupted, their inward person is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4).

With all these, the faithful peoples exult, and outwardly show in instruments—that is, spiritual songs—and in harps—that is, good works—the inward joy they possess from spiritual victory. For instruments are filled with wind in order to give a sound, and thus signify songs filled with the Holy Spirit. Harps, however, are touched by the hand in order to sound, and therefore good works are signified by harps.

Begin for the Lord with timbrels; sing to the Lord with cymbals; make melody to him with a new psalm. In this song the holy Church both gives thanks for the victory it has gained and instructs its faithful when they should sing in harmony with her. “Begin for the Lord with timbrels.” Attend, brethren. For, as may be understood from these words, “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15), who serves the will of his flesh. One who has given himself over to revelries and drunkenness, [Col. 1170D] beds and shameless acts, and neglects to chastise his flesh by abstinence and continence, cannot fittingly give thanks to God. The timbrel, made of dried and stretched skin, expresses affliction of the flesh. Therefore begin with timbrels, and afterwards sing with cymbals. Cymbals, which sound when struck together, signify our lips: when we strike them together in song, we give forth the sound of divine praise. Let timbrels therefore come first, so that cymbals may sound well; that is, let us first cleanse ourselves perfectly through affliction, so that afterwards we may fittingly and acceptably sing the praise of God. A psalm, whether so called from *psallere*, “to play,” or from Greek ψάλλειν (*psallein*), “to touch,” signifies the effect of a good work. [Col. 1171A] Begin, therefore, by chastising the flesh; sing to God with cymbals by praising him with your lips; make melody with a new psalm by doing good works. Rejoice, and invoke his name. Rejoice over benefits received; invoke him for those yet to be received. “The Lord crushing wars—the Lord is his name.” The Lord crushes wars because strength is from heaven, because he himself conquered the world; “the Lord” is his name—understand, he alone—for though there are many lords, yet he alone is Lord, because he is pre-eminent and unchangeable. He set his camp in the midst of his people, that he might deliver us from the hand of our enemies. This is the cause of victory; this is the cause of divine praise: that God set his camp in the midst of his people. But what is this camp except the army of angels, of whom Jacob, when he met them, said: “This is the camp of God” [Col. 1171B] (Gen. 32). God placed this camp in the midst of his people because, as Paul says, “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to minister for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1). Thus blessed Michael, whose feast we celebrate today, is reported in the Apocalypse to have fought and conquered the dragon with his angels, where it is said: “A great battle took place in heaven. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon; and the dragon fought, and his angels, and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any more in heaven” (Apoc. 12). For although all ministering spirits—that is, angels—are believed to be sent to minister for those who receive the inheritance of salvation, Michael is nevertheless designated by name in the battle and described as prince of the others [Col. 1171C], just as in the Old Testament he is mentioned as prince of the Israelite people—that is, of the people who see God.

“And a great battle took place in heaven.” It is as though it were said: Do not fear, faithful people, although demons rage against you by bringing temptations and stirring up persecutions; for the holy Church has great aids against all their devices—not only the teaching of holy doctors and preachers, but also the assistance of angels. And the battle was great because it was strong and prolonged in heaven—that is, in the holy Church while she is held in the world. Michael and his angels fought with the dragon, and the dragon and his angels fought: the former by helping the Church, the latter by attacking it; the former by suggesting wholesome things [Col. 1171D], the latter by counselling harmful things; the dragon and his angels by assailing the army of the good; Michael and his angels by restraining their assault. “And they did not prevail”: namely, the dragon and his angels did not prevail to remove the assistance of the holy spirits; “nor was their place found any more in heaven,” that is, in the holy Church, so as either to take righteousness from her or draw her into sin. For even if one of the faithful of the Church—we mean those “who are called saints according to purpose”—sometimes falls into sin, divine providence permitting and diabolical malice suggesting it, the devil by no means conquers in this; rather, he is conquered, because for those predestined to life even evil works together for good. Nor is this brought about so much by the powers of raging adversaries [Col. 1172A] as it is ordered by the provident disposition of the God who permits it, for the caution of the person who falls and rises again. Therefore the devil and his angels have no place any longer in heaven—that is, in the Church of such persons—because he cannot overcome those who know heavenly goods with a true heart and are predestined to attain them, so as to draw them into sin at his will or hold them there for as long as he wishes. Rather, since even this occurs by divine permission, their place is found on earth—that is, in those who love earthly things and despise to merit heavenly goods. Hence it fittingly follows: “And that great dragon, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who deceives the whole world, was cast down; he was cast down to the earth, and his angels were sent with him.” He is a dragon through the burning heat of envy; great through the eminence of pride; a serpent through the cunning of craftiness; ancient through the inveterate habit of sinning. Therefore now, dearest brethren, because holy Michael and his angels fight for us and with us, because those with us are more than those with them—for there is no number to God’s soldiers: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” [Col. 1172B] (Dan. 7)—let us act manfully against this dragon, who is figured by the king of the Assyrians, and by crushing his pride cut off his head, so that, when victory has been won, we may deserve to enter the heavenly Jerusalem joyfully with our Judith. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXVI. Second sermon on the feast of Saint Michael.—Likewise from the book of Judith.

[Col. 1172C]

“Assur came from the mountains, and from mountains from the north, in the multitude of his strength. His multitude stopped up the torrents, and their horses covered the valleys. He said that he would burn my borders, kill my young men with the sword, give my infants as plunder, and my virgins into captivity. But the Lord Almighty harmed him, delivered him into the hand of a woman, and confounded [pierced] him” (Judith 16). In these words the proud strength and stubborn threat of the devil are described, so that, when the holy Church overcomes him, her power may be shown more gloriously. Yet the beginning of the sermon declares that the devil’s rage against the Church proceeds from extraordinary [mere] pride. [Col. 1172D] For it is said: “Assur came from the mountains,” that is, from the swellings of his pride, by which in the beginning he wished to make himself equal to God and now wishes to be worshipped by man. Since mountains are sometimes used in a good sense, as in: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, whence help shall come to me” (Ps. 120); and where it is said of the inhabitant of Jerusalem that mountains surround him (Ps. 124), it is made clear by the repetition which follows that here they must be understood only in an evil sense: “and from mountains from the north,” since the Lord says, “From the north every evil shall be opened” (Jer. 1). And what do we understand more fittingly by the north, which is cold, than malice? Hence it is said of Jerusalem that “she made her malice cold, as a cistern makes its water cold” [Col. 1173A] (Jer. 6). Thus Assur comes from mountains in the north when the devil bursts forth from proud malice, or malicious pride, to persecute the righteous. He comes in the multitude of his strength because, to accomplish his wickedness, he gathers together the whole host of demons and malignant human beings. “His multitude,” he says, “stopped up the torrents, and their horses covered the valleys.” The multitude of the devil consists of demons; the horses on which they ride are persecutors. The torrents are teaching preachers; the valleys are humble hearers. The demons stop up these torrents, lest they pour out water upon the faithful, by delaying them from the office of preaching through whatever hindrances they can. Their horses likewise cover the valleys when persecutors oppress the humble. It is therefore a great scourge when the streams of preaching are taken away through diabolical temptations and humble hearers are oppressed by persecutions of the impious. Yet what the devil intends for harm returns, as the outcome proves, to the advancement of the elect, as it is written: “God will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear; but with the temptation he will give an outcome, so that you may be able to endure” [Col. 1173B] (1 Cor. 10).

“He said that he would burn my borders, kill my young men with the sword, give my infants as plunder, and my virgins into captivity.” By the borders of the Church we understand those who are weaker; by young men, the stronger; by infants, beginners; by virgins, those perfect persons living in continence or virginity, who reflect more deeply upon the things of God and how they may please God. The devil therefore threatens to burn the borders—that is, the outlying and weak—with the fire of carnal lust, as though they offered an easy encounter. He threatens to kill the young men—that is, the stronger, whom he knows cannot be overcome without a stronger assault—with the sword of malice in the heart. Further, he threatens to hand over infants—that is, beginners—as plunder, so that they may no longer grow in good; and virgins—that is, the perfect—into captivity, so that he may ensnare them in the bonds of sin and they may no longer rise to the height of perfection. The devil makes great threats, but through the bounty of God’s grace and the assistance of angelic spirits he is shamefully frustrated of his desire. For it follows: “The Lord Almighty harmed him, delivered him into the hand of a woman, and confounded him.” The Lord Almighty harms the devil because, by the power of his presence or in some other way, he restrains his perverse will; or certainly because God turns to his own just purpose the evil which the devil, with evil will and by God’s permission, prepares to do. That this is often accomplished through the ministry of angels is made most certain by many passages of sacred Scripture. In this work blessed Michael, whose feast we celebrate today, with his angels, as prince of God’s people, fights mightily for God’s people by God’s ordering and powerfully drives the ancient enemy from the borders of the Church. But since whatever God does in this spiritual war, whether by himself, through angels, or in any other way, in defeating the devil, he attributes wholly through his grace to the praises of the Church, it is fitting that, after “God harmed him” was said, there was immediately added: “and he delivered him into the hand of a woman” [Col. 1174A]. The holy Church calls herself a woman because she bears spiritual children for God, or certainly because in this battle, and in all that she does, she recognizes herself as weak and useless without God. “And he confounded him.” It is indeed a great humiliation for the devil that he is now overcome daily by weak souls, though he gloried in having conquered our first parents when they were placed in innocence. Thus he was conquered by blessed Job, stripped of all his possessions, bereft of sons and daughters, struck with a most grievous ulcer, wickedly counselled by his wife, harshly afflicted by his friends, and humbly placed upon a dungheap. This victory, therefore, is a great humiliation for the devil and a great glory for the Church. Hence it is added:

“For their mighty man did not fall by young men, nor did the sons of Titan strike him, nor did lofty giants set themselves against him; but Judith, daughter of Merari, undid him by the beauty of her face.” By young men we understand the strong and rash; by sons of Titan—that is, of the sun—the noble and distinguished; by giants, the powerful and proud. Such persons do not punish the ancient enemy, but rather fall by him. Nor did the Lord choose such persons for battle. Did he choose Alexander the Great or Caesar Augustus, that through them he might destroy the devil’s pride and cast down the glory of the world? Far be it! Whom, then, did he choose? The weak, the ignoble, the unlearned—rightly figured by a woman. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: “Consider your calling, brethren,” that is, the apostles through whom you and others were called to faith: “not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose what is foolish [Col. 1174C] in the world to confound the wise; and God chose what is weak in the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are” (1 Cor. 1). Behold Judith the woman. But how is she the daughter of Merari—that is, “bitterness”? Listen: “To this very hour we hunger and thirst, and are naked, and are beaten with fists, and are unsettled; and we labour, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and endure it; we are slandered, and we entreat. We have become as the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things until now” (1 Cor. 4). Although these words can also be understood of the rest of the faithful, they seem to be understood especially and pre-eminently [Col. 1174D] of the apostles. It is particularly the beauty—that is, the glory of the virtues, good works, and miracles—of these apostles and apostolic men which undoes and kills the devil in the elect. Therefore, dearest brethren, let us imitate Judith by loving chastity, subduing the flesh by fasts, praying devoutly to God, awaiting his mercy, and humbling our souls before him, that we may deserve to be her imitators by destroying the enemy and obtaining victory. And, having holy Michael and his angels as our help, let us make use of great confidence. For, as we sing on this feast, “the sea is shaken, the earth trembles, when the archangel Michael descends from heaven.” The sea is demons; the earth is reprobate people. The sea signifies demons because they are bitter, swollen, and restless. [Col. 1175A] The earth signifies reprobate people, not so much because they were taken from the earth and will return to it, as because, despising heavenly things, they attend only to earthly things. Yet when Michael descends from heaven, the sea is shaken and the earth trembles, because demons are restrained in terror from temptation and wicked people from persecution, while the faithful are delivered. Let us therefore act confidently in the battle, that, after victory is gained, we may be enriched with the crown. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXVII. Third sermon on the feast of Saint Michael.—From the same book of Judith.

“She put off the garments of her widowhood and clothed herself in garments of joy for the exultation of the children of Israel. She anointed her face with ointment. She bound up her tresses with a headband to [Col. 1175B] deceive him. Her sandals seized his eyes; her beauty made his soul captive; she cut off his neck with a dagger. The Persians were horrified at her steadfastness, and the Medes at her boldness. Then the camps of the Assyrians howled when my humble ones appeared, parched with thirst. The sons of maidens pierced them, and killed them like fleeing boys. They perished in battle before the face of my Lord. Let us sing a hymn to the Lord; let us sing a new hymn to our God” (Judith 16). At the end of the preceding sermon it was said that Judith undid and killed her enemy by the beauty of her face. Now these words describe in detail the adornments of her beauty by which she overthrew his heart. “She put off the garments of her widowhood and clothed herself in garments of joy.” The holy Church was a widow from the time when the first parent sinned until Christ came into the world. Throughout that period she was clothed in garments of widowhood—that is, in mourning and the spirit of sorrow. But when Christ came in the flesh, she was clothed in garments of joy—that is, in the oil of gladness and the mantle of praise. Hence Christ himself, foretelling through Isaiah, says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim pardon to captives and opening to those shut in; to proclaim a year acceptable to the Lord and a day of vengeance to our God; to comfort all who mourn and give strength to the mourners of Zion, and to give them a crown instead of ashes, oil of gladness instead of mourning, and a mantle of praise instead of the spirit of sorrow” [Col. 1175D] (Isa. 61). Therefore the holy Church clothed herself in her garments—here called “a garment of joy”—so that it may be understood of the wedding garment, that is, charity, when in the time of grace she is renewed by new acts. And this is in the exaltation of the children of Israel—that is, of all who see God not only with the eye of cruelty but also with the eye of love. She anoints her face with ointment in receiving the sacred chrism; she binds her tresses with a headband—that is, her thoughts with the strictness of divine fear—to deceive him. For in this the devil is strangely deceived: when he sees the faithful fear divine judgments, he then thinks all the more that he can delay them from good works through faintheartedness or cast them down into despair. “Her sandals seized his eyes.” Sandals are coverings for the feet [Col. 1176A], with which the holy Church is shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. Her sandals seize the eyes of the ancient enemy because the words of sacred preaching especially inflame his mind to rebuke the holy Church. For the more he sees the number of believers increasing, the more fiercely he burns and labours, if possible, to lessen them by corrupting them and corrupt them by lessening them. “Her beauty made his soul captive.” By beauty—that is, by the universal ordering of the holy Church—the soul of the devil is held captive, because, when he beholds her virtues and good works, his perverse will is so bound and restrained in its purpose that it cannot cease suggesting wickedness until, conquered by her, it falls. Hence it follows:

[Col. 1176B] “She cut off his neck with her dagger.” As was also said above, the devil is slain by his own sword, when he is condemned by the consciousness of that malice with which he rages to corrupt the Church. As is read in Esther, Haman prepared a gallows for Mordecai on which to hang him; but Mordecai was delivered, and Haman himself perished hanging on the same gallows. “The Persians were horrified at her steadfastness, and the Medes at her boldness.” “Persians” is interpreted as “those who tempt”; “Medes,” as “those who lie.” Those who tempt are evil spirits; those who lie are false Christians. Thus Persians and Medes are horrified at the steadfastness of the holy Church because demons and reprobate people are turned to amazed astonishment when they see the virtue and victory of the holy Church. “Then the camps of the Assyrians howled, because my humble ones appeared [Col. 1176C], parched with thirst.” “Assyrians” is interpreted as “those who direct,” and they signify heretics, who suppose that they and their followers direct themselves most rightly in their perverse doctrine. They also possess camps in which they dwell because they wage war against the Church by wicked disputations. These camps howl at the victory of the holy Church when heretics, grieving, cry out that their opinion has been shown false. The humble of the holy Church endure a grievous thirst when demons, wicked people, and especially heretics persecute her. For a time they are also, as it were, hidden, because, fearing to be corrupted by the perversity of heretics, they do not dare to show themselves outside the bosom of the Church. Nor do they safely draw from the streams of doctrine, because they fear to taste the wormwood of those heretics within them [Col. 1176D]. Once victory has been achieved, they openly show themselves, when they seek and find sacred Scripture without suspicion of perversity. When they appear, heretics grieve deeply because they see themselves conquered and those others victorious. “The sons of maidens”—that is, of Churches—pierce them, because with the arrows of preaching they pierce through their perverse assertions. “And they kill them like fleeing boys,” because they destroy them as weak, fearful, and inert persons fleeing away. For wickedness has no place to stand before the sight of goodness. “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4). “They perished in battle before the face of my Lord. Let us sing a hymn to our God.” This is now the third time that she attributes victory to the Lord, thereby showing herself a worshipper of the holy Trinity. First [Col. 1177A] she ascribes this victory to the Lord when she says that he set his camp in the midst of his people. Secondly, when she says: “The Lord Almighty taught him.” Thirdly here, when she says: “They perished in battle before the face of my Lord.” Therefore, dearest brethren, because in this spiritual battle the camp of God—that is, angelic aid—is in the midst of his people, and blessed Michael with his angels fights for us, let us act confidently and not fear. “For we have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear, but we have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). We have not come to tangible and accessible fire, whirlwind, darkness, storm, the sound of a trumpet, and the voice of words, which those who heard begged that no further word might be spoken to them; but we have come to Mount Zion [Col. 1177B], the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, the assembly of many thousands of angels, the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge of all, the spirits of the righteous made perfect, Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkled blood that speaks better than Abel’s (Heb. 12). Let us therefore stand firmly in battle, confident of victory. Once it has been won, let us sing a hymn with our Judith: let us sing a new hymn to the Lord, to our God. A new hymn, because when victory has been accomplished, old things have passed away and behold, all things have become new (Apoc. 21). Let us sing because we have been delivered from evil. Let us sing because we have been enriched by a benefit. Let us sing because we have received grace. Let us sing because we hope for glory. May Jesus Christ [Col. 1177C] our Lord, who is blessed for ever, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON LXXXVIII. On the commandment of love.

“You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart,” etc. (Deut. 6). After man abandoned his Creator through the primal fault and came into the misery of this world, he is subjected to many cares, occupied with activities, and wearied with labours. Yet among all things in which a person is stretched out beneath the sun, one thing is best and endures: namely, to serve God (Eccles. 1); for all other things are transitory, all other things are vain. Whoever therefore does not serve God is vain, and his life ought to be counted as nothing; it would be better for him not to be than to be evil, and not to live than to live badly. And even if such a person could possess in this present life Samson’s strength, Absalom’s beauty, Solomon’s wisdom, Asahel’s swiftness, Croesus’s riches, Alexander’s virtue, Octavian’s power—for he held the whole world in his power—and Enoch’s longevity, who, born at the beginning of the age, will not die until its end: even if, I say, he could possess such great and such things in the present life, none of them would profit him if he did not serve God. For when all these things had finally passed away, when he died, his flesh would become food for worms and his spirit would be given to demons and to the torments of hell, until on the day of resurrection all flesh should be restored to its original state; and then, having resumed the flesh through which and in which he sinned, he would again undergo eternal damnation [Col. 1178A]. It is therefore best to serve God, because even if throughout all his life a person is deprived of temporal and bodily supports, if he serves God, he passes from the misery of the present life to the blessedness of eternal life. Since, then, among all the goods of the present age which the human race pursues or attains, the sole best and enduring good is to serve God, we must seek by every means what it is to serve God; and, once it has been sought and found, we must persevere in it without failing. For only one who perseveres in it will be blessed. Brethren, in a brief, sweet, and delightful saying it is contained and declared what it is to serve God. To serve God is to love God. Whoever does not love does not serve; whoever loves serves; whoever loves little serves little; whoever loves much serves much; and whoever loves perfectly serves perfectly [Col. 1178B]. Whoever possesses temporal things—lands, vineyards, flocks, herds, costly garments, houses, silver, gold, or a wife whom he loves greatly—if he finds that he possesses one of these things, or all of them together, contrary to the love of God, ought to leave all things and put all things after divine love, placing it before all. Indeed, a person must give even his own life for the love of God, should it happen that he cannot preserve it together with that love. Thus Peter did; thus Paul did; thus the other apostles and Christ’s martyrs did, for they surrendered not only their possessions but themselves for the love of God. They too were human beings, and they left us an example of acting in this way [Col. 1178C].

We must therefore love God because he first loved us, giving us some of his manifold gifts and promising others; and in all these things, so to speak, he earned from us that he should be loved. The least gift God gave man, that he might be loved by man, is this whole world. For God made the world—the heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, stars, birds, fish, beasts of the earth, plants, trees, and whatever visibly subsists—for humankind.
