Since, then, this world is the least among God’s gifts, how great, do you suppose, is the greatest? The second gift of God is that he made man in his own image and likeness. It is altogether a great and wonderful gift for the thing made to become like and conformed to its Maker [Col. 1178D]. The third gift is the grace that he bestowed on us in redemption, because “he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8). The fourth gift he keeps and promises us: namely, the gift of future glory, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2). The first gift, therefore, we may call the good of creation; the second, the good of nature; the third, the good of grace; the fourth, the good of glory. For all these things we must love God. But how greatly must we love him? With our whole heart, whole soul, all our strength, and whole mind. With our whole heart, that is, wisely; with our whole soul, that is, sweetly; with all our strength, that is, strongly; with our whole mind, that is, mindfully—and in whatever other ways it may be said—for one cannot say too much of what cannot be loved too much. “And your neighbour as yourself” [Col. 1179A] (Matt. 22). We must love our neighbour as ourselves in deed, word, and desire. In a deed is a good work; in a word, sound counsel; in desire, longing. In all these ways let us love our neighbour on the way, with whom we shall have fellowship in the homeland. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON LXXXIX. On the first Sunday of Lent.

“Fearing Jezebel’s threats, Elijah, leaving his servant, went into the wilderness a journey of one day, and sat down beneath a juniper tree” [Col. 1179B] (3 Kings 19). Holy men are lifted up to the heights by the Spirit’s support. Yet so long as they are in this life, they are restrained by temptations lest they become proud. Thus Elijah, though he had advanced in so many virtues, later fled Jezebel—a woman, though a queen; and he who raised the dead, foresaw future things, and performed other notable deeds, struck with fear fled death from a woman’s hand, sought death from God’s hand, and did not receive it. In Elijah’s virtues the power of God was strong; in his weaknesses he recognized what he could be in himself. There he showed what he had received; here he safeguarded what he had received. In his miracles he was displayed; in his weaknesses he was preserved. Elijah, the prophet of the Lord, illustrious in life and miracles, signifies any faithful person. The impious king Ahab, the adversary of the Lord and of his commandments [Col. 1179C], signifies the devil, who is king over all the children of pride (Job 45) and rules them in deeds of sin. Jezebel, the shameless woman and Elijah’s continual enemy, expresses the impurity of the flesh, which always persecutes the righteous and opposes his deeds. Frightened at times by her threats—that is, temptations—Elijah, that is, the faithful person, although he may previously have shone with virtues and many good works, destroyed the prophets of Baal—that is, driven every infidelity and heretical perversity from his heart—and deserved that rain, that is, grace, should be given him from heaven, yet fears lest an occasion arise and Jezebel—that is, lust—kill him. He therefore obeys the apostolic counsel which says: “Flee fornication” (1 Cor. [Col. 1179D] 6). He flees fornication who leaves worldly dress and manner of life, and goes into the wilderness who takes up the habit and life of religion. The wilderness is spiritual life and religious observance because it is abandoned by many and inhabited by few. Elijah left his servant and entered the wilderness alone because it is right that any faithful person entering the spiritual life should leave behind all childish, vain, and frivolous things, and should do nothing childishly in eating, drinking, speaking, or any other action. By the juniper tree under which Elijah sat we may understand the severity of some religious order, such as monks, regular canons, or any other profession. For every religious profession appears like a juniper tree, possessing certain prickles of severity: namely, the observances of the cloister, the weariness of silence, fear of the superior, the discipline of the chapter, abstinence from food, and whatever similar things can prick by the harshness of their adversity. There are other prickles of this juniper tree as well: namely, extremely sharp and persistent temptations, which, like thorns, pierce the tenderness of souls [Col. 1180A].

There are four kinds of temptation. One is light and hidden; another light and manifest; another heavy and hidden; another heavy and manifest. A light and hidden temptation is when someone is lightly tempted, yet does not understand whether that concerning which he is tempted is evil for him. For example, when someone is lightly tempted concerning some office or position of authority: the temptation is light because he is tempted lightly, and hidden because he does not know whether what he desires is expedient for him. A light and manifest temptation is when someone is lightly tempted and is manifestly tempted concerning evil. For example, when someone is lightly tempted by fornication, the temptation is light because he is tempted lightly, and manifest because it is manifestly concerning evil. A heavy and hidden temptation is when someone is heavily tempted but does not know whether that concerning which he is tempted is harmful to him. For example, when someone is heavily tempted concerning authority or some ministry, the temptation is heavy because he is heavily tempted, and hidden because he does not know that the devil’s deceit is concealed there. For the devil tempts a person with exaltation so that through elevation he may fall more deeply into damnation. A heavy and manifest temptation is when someone is heavily tempted and manifestly tempted concerning evil. For example, when someone is heavily tempted by fornication, the temptation is heavy because he is heavily tempted, and manifest because it is manifestly concerning evil. The Psalmist fittingly designates these four kinds of temptation when he says: “You shall not fear the terror of the night, the arrow flying by day, the business walking in darkness, the assault of the noonday demon” [Col. 1180C] (Ps. 90). A light and hidden temptation is the terror of the night: terror because it is light, nocturnal because it is hidden. A light and manifest temptation is the arrow flying by day: an arrow flying because it is light; by day because it is manifest. A heavy and manifest temptation is the business walking in darkness [sic]: business because the temptation is heavy; walking in darkness because it is hidden. A heavy and manifest temptation is the assault and the noonday demon: assault and demon because it is heavy; noonday because it is manifest. These, therefore, are the kinds of temptation—the prickles, that is, of this juniper tree, of the religious order—because like prickles they pierce and sometimes tear the tenderness of souls [Col. 1180D]. This is not because the order is evil, but because the devil pricks the righteous more sharply by temptations the more he sees him passing, through the habit and life of a religious order, to higher and more hidden things.

Rightly, therefore, in accordance with what has been said above, a religious order is compared to a juniper tree, since it is proved to prick by its various harshnesses and temptations. Elijah, then, comes to this juniper when a righteous person, grieving over worldly things, submits himself to the austerities of some religious order [Col. 1181A]; and he asks that his soul may die when he longs to die wholly to the world and to live to God. Yet he finds not the death he asks for, but the sleep he does not ask for, because often a religious person, wearied by various temptations and adversities in the spiritual life, grows sluggish in progress in virtues and good works.

The guardian and awakener angel of Elijah is the superior, the guardian and faithful exhorter of the soul subject to him. When he sees Elijah—that is, the soul entrusted to him—sleeping under the juniper, that is, growing torpid under the order, he immediately awakens, feeds, and gives him drink: he urges him toward better things and teaches him from Holy Scripture both the more difficult matters, signified by food, and the easier matters, represented by drink. Elijah too, once awakened, eats and [Col. 1181B] drinks when the admonished subject patiently assents to the speaker’s words and does not contradict what is said. But he falls asleep again, because sometimes the subject, afflicted with much weariness, grows lukewarm again after the first admonition and instruction.

But Elijah is awakened and fed a second time by the angel when the subject is again admonished and instructed by a prudent and faithful superior: “Rise,” he says, “eat; a great journey remains for you.” It is as though he said: “If you trust in the order alone, know that it profits you nothing to have left the world merely in bodily fashion, existing only outwardly cloaked in the habit of religion before human eyes. Strive to advance further through virtues; help your neighbours by works of mercy; read, meditate, sing psalms, pray, work. A great journey remains for you, because you have advanced little so far [Col. 1181C] and have much further to advance.”

Finally Elijah eats and drinks, and goes in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, when the subject, well strengthened by the instruction given anew, advances through the practice of virtues and the performance of good works—in prosperities as in days, and in adversities as in nights—and, fulfilling the fourfold Gospel and the tenfold Law, comes to the summit of spiritual sublimity. There he is rightly said to stand in the repose of a cave, when he is ready, whenever the Lord calls him, to depart from the flesh. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XC. On the Purification of the Blessed Mary

[Col. 1181D]

The Shunammite said to her husband concerning Elisha: “I perceive that this man of God, who frequently passes by us, is holy. Let us therefore make for him a small upper chamber, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that, when he comes to us, he may stay there” (4 Kings 4).

Elisha, whose name means “salvation of God,” signifies Christ by the interpretation of his name, the working of miracles, the practice of virtues, the performance of good works, the holiness of an honourable manner of life, and by raising a dead man after Elisha’s death. The Shunammite, whose name means “captive” or “scarlet,” represents the soul which Christ redeemed by his blood from the captivity of the devil. Elisha often comes to the Shunammite woman because Christ [Col. 1182A] often comes to the soul in many ways. He comes through contemplation of created things; he comes through reading the Scriptures; he comes through the working of miracles; he comes through the preaching of his commandments; he comes through inward inspiration; he comes through adversity; he comes through prosperity; he comes by threatening evils; he comes by promising good things; he comes by removing evils; he comes by bestowing good things; he comes through knowledge of truth; he comes through love of virtue.

Christ comes to the soul by visiting it spiritually; he lodges with it by justifying it; at times he passes on by withdrawing grace from it. For sometimes he withdraws grace in part, so that the mind, which thinks too highly of itself, may be humbled. But he returns again when he pours it in again. The husband of this woman—that is, of the rational soul—is the intellect, which by powers and understanding implanted by nature or bestowed by grace ought to preside over the soul, counsel it, provide for it, govern and guide it, and beget from it offspring of virtues and good works. With this husband the soul takes counsel, saying: “I perceive that this man of God, who frequently passes by us, is holy.” Truly he is holy, because he is the Holy of holies, and no one is holy except through him.

“Let us make for him,” she says, “a small upper chamber, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that, when he comes to us, he may stay there.” The upper chamber, because it is raised aloft, signifies the spiritual manner of life. Paul had well made this upper chamber for Elisha when he said of himself and those like him: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3) [Col. 1182C]. Its being called small suggests humility. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4). Therefore, if the faithful soul ever does great things in the sight of its Creator, it considers them small.

On a bed we are accustomed to rest from labours and, in sleep, to disregard visible things. Therefore contemplation is rightly represented by the bed. Whoever abides in it rests from the labour brought by the assault of temptations and affliction, and, intent upon inward and eternal things, does not heed what is taking place outside. The table signifies Scripture. For as a table is filled with foods, so Holy Scripture is filled with sayings; and it gives us one refreshment through history, another through allegory, another through tropology, another through the Old Testament [Col. 1182D], another through the New. The chair signifies instruction. For teachers customarily sit when they instruct others. The chair rightly follows the table, because it is fitting that one who has learned Scripture by hearing or reading should give to others through teaching the good that he has recognized.

The lampstand is an instrument of light. A lampstand has below a base; above the base, an upright shaft; above the shaft, a rounded knob all around; and above the knob, a point upon which the lamp is set. The base of the lampstand has three branches, equal in length, equal in size, of one form, and equally distant from one another. It therefore signifies faith in the Trinity. For as is the Father, so is the Son, and so is the Holy Spirit, etc. The shaft of the lampstand, insofar as it is straight, expresses the uprightness of equity; insofar as it is raised, the elevation of good intention. The rounded knob signifies the mind’s circumspection. For the knob is, as it were, placed upon the lampstand when the mind, solicitously attentive to itself, bears itself about through circumspection. The point above signifies the subtlety of sound reason. The lamp set upon it expresses Christ. The wax is his humanity; the light, his divinity.

Thus the Shunammite woman, taking counsel with her husband—that is, the faithful soul instructed through understanding—makes for Elisha, that is, for Christ, an upper chamber through spiritual conduct, small through humility; she places a bed through contemplation, a table through reading the Scriptures, and a chair through instructing those beneath her. She also places in it a lampstand, the instrument of the true light: she makes its base through faith in the Holy Trinity [Col. 1183B], its shaft through upright equity and the elevation of good intention, its rounded knob through circumspection of mind, and its point through the subtlety of reason. This must be present in the lampstand, because the soul must always cling to Christ. The soul that knows how thus to prepare lodging for Christ deserves to have Christ as its guest and, through him, to possess the very Son of God. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XCI. The First Sermon on Christ’s Spiritual Banquet — From the Book of Esther

“In the third year of his reign King Ahasuerus gave a great banquet for all his princes and servants, for the mighty men of the Persians and the nobles of the Medes, and for the governors of the provinces before him, in order to display the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the greatness and magnificence of his power [Col. 1183C] for a long time—namely, one hundred and eighty days” (Esther 1).

The beginning of this kingdom was at Susa. Susa is a metropolis in Persia, a city said to have taken its name from the river Susi. There is the palace of Cyrus, of white and variegated stone, adorned with golden columns, ceilings, and jewels, containing an image of heaven and marked by gleaming stars. There Ahasuerus celebrated a banquet abounding in the greatest riches and delights. History recounts the pomp and royal splendour of this banquet; allegorically, however, it signifies Christ’s spiritual riches, which he distributes to every person.

He gave this banquet of delights in the third year of his reign, that is, in the time of the present age. Hence Christ himself preached in that third time, saying: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who was a king and made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. 22) [Col. 1183D]. In the third period of the age Christ revealed the mystery of his incarnation and most abundantly supplied the spiritual food of sacred preaching, as well as his body and blood. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace.

Ahasuerus means “door,” and by this signifies Christ, who says: “I am the door of the sheep” (John 10). “For all his princes and servants.” By the princes we understand prelates; by the servants, subjects. Princes are those who preside over others by example and word. Servants are those who faithfully obey their prelates. When they obey those set over them in all things, they are purified through obedience from every defilement [Col. 1184A] of flesh and spirit, and like children have nothing of the impurity of sin.

“For the mighty men of the Persians and the nobles of the Medes.” By the Persians, who are known to have surpassed the Medes in dignity and power, we understand the Jews; by the Medes, who were inferior to the Persians, the Gentiles. The Persians are put before the Medes in the description because the Jews are preferred to the Gentiles on account of the prerogative of the fathers and many other things. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15); and to the Apostles: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, nor enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matt. 10). And the Apostle says to the Romans: “What advantage then has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way: first indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them” (Rom. 3). And at the end of the same epistle: “I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises of the fathers; but that the Gentiles might glorify God for mercy” (Rom. 15).

They are mighty because neither words nor blows, neither life nor death, can separate them from the love of God. Hence the Apostle: “Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us. For I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither powers, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength [Col. 1184C], neither height nor depth, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8).

They are noble who scorn to be rendered base not only in deed but even by delight in sinful thought, “renouncing,” according to the Apostle, “the hidden things of disgrace and commending ourselves to every human conscience before God” (2 Cor. 4). “And the governors of the provinces,” that is, the prelates of the churches. To all these, therefore, Ahasuerus gave a banquet; and Christ granted participation in the delights of his grace to all whom these figures represent.

“Before him”: both with respect to his divinity, by which he is present everywhere, and with respect to his humanity, by which he was made manifest to the world. “Before him,” because they saw him eye to eye and their hands touched him. Or certainly, “before him” means according to his good pleasure. For he has, as it were, before himself those things which please him; but those which displease him he sees as if from afar. Hence it is written: “For he looks upon the lowly, and beholds the lofty from afar” (Ps. 137 [Vulgate]), that is, the proud. “To display the riches of the glory of his kingdom, and the greatness and magnificence of his power.”

Christ showed all these things in the world when he opened the minds of his disciples to understand the Scriptures and gave them the Holy Spirit, first by breathing upon them and afterwards by sending him from heaven. Of this manifestation Paul writes to the Ephesians: “In the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the children of men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets” (Eph. 3). And to Timothy: [Col. 1185A] “Manifestly great is the mystery of godliness: he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the Gentiles, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3).

Once Christ’s riches were known through the manifestation of the mystery, the riches of the present age immediately became worthless. The righteous, to whom heavenly glory was revealed and offered, left not only their own possessions but even themselves in order to attain it. Once enlightened by the knowledge of him, having tasted the heavenly gift, become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and likewise tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come (Heb. 6), they were inflamed with his love. Peter was crucified, Paul beheaded, Stephen stoned, Lawrence roasted, and others killed by other punishments [Col. 1185B], that they might participate in this banquet: in the world through grace, and in heaven through glory.

For the spiritual banquet begins on the way and is consummated in the homeland. What is now tasted beforehand from it is indeed little; but what is reserved to be tasted hereafter is great and beyond estimation. Hence the Psalmist: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30 [Vulgate]). “For a long time—namely, one hundred and eighty days.” Observe that even the specification of time serves the mystery of spiritual understanding. One hundred is a perfect number and signifies the perfection of human righteousness. Eighty, which is named from eight, expresses the future resurrection and blessedness. The whole good of humanity consists in these: in righteousness, whose perfection the number one hundred signifies, and in resurrection and blessedness, whose glory the number eighty represents. One hundred is placed first and eighty follows, because through the height of sanctification one comes to the eighth-numbered reality of resurrection and blessedness.

“And when the days of the banquet had been fulfilled, he invited all the people found in Susa, from the greatest to the least.” The days of the banquet seem to have been fulfilled when Christ said on the cross, “It is finished” (John 19); or certainly when the Holy Spirit was sent in fullness to the disciples gathered together. Then the days of the spiritual banquet were fulfilled—not because they then ceased to exist, but because then, and from then onward, they were to be celebrated in fullness. Susa is the city of the Gentiles, by which the calling of the Gentiles is signified [Col. 1185D]. “He invited all the people, from the greatest to the least.” This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). He invited the people from least to greatest because the Lord blessed the little together with the great.

Unhappy, brothers, is the soul that is absent from this banquet; and unhappy—or perhaps more unhappy still—is the soul that is present otherwise than it ought to be, that is, without a wedding garment. It seems more unhappy because, as Peter says: “It would have been better for that person not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment” (2 Pet. 2). But blessed is the soul that takes part now in Christ’s banquet not only in the name of Christianity but in its truth, because it may hope to be admitted to the heavenly and eternal banquet [Col. 1186A]. And now, beloved, just as we take part in this banquet now by profession, let us strive to take part in it also by virtue, so that we may deserve to take part in it in blessedness. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XCII. The Second Sermon on Christ’s Spiritual Banquet — From the Same Book of Esther

“And for seven days he commanded a banquet to be prepared in the vestibule of the garden and grove, which had been planted by royal cultivation and hand. Tents of sky-blue, fine linen, and hyacinth colour hung on every side, supported by cords of fine linen and purple, which were inserted into ivory rings and upheld by marble columns” [Col. 1186B] (Esther 1).

Great, beloved, is the fruit of spiritual understanding hidden in all these things, covered not only by the leaves of words but also veiled in varied figures of visible things, like a kernel firmly enclosed in its shell and husk. By the seven days, as we have often said, the whole of this time is expressed, because it revolves in the number of seven days. Throughout all this time Christ commanded a banquet of spiritual delights to be prepared for his faithful, so that spiritual food and drink might never fail them. But how much spiritual food each person inwardly receives is demonstrated outwardly by the display of a good life. As each person is inwardly nourished by grace, so is that person outwardly strengthened in virtue and action.

“Days,” he says. Evil people, indeed, hold their banquets at night, since their works are in darkness: “They rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. 2) [Col. 1186C]. “In the vestibule of the garden and grove, which had been planted by royal cultivation and hand.” That heavenly paradise, to be preferred to every good thing, is garden and grove: it is a garden because it satisfies by its sweetness; it is a grove because it delights by its beauty. It is a garden, caressing holy affections with the savour of its delight; it is a grove, holding the intellect in wonder at its beauty. It is a garden because it feeds; it is a grove because it shelters. It feeds with good things and shelters from evils.

The vestibule of this garden and grove is as though *nestibulum*, with *v* put for *n*, because one is not to stand there at all but to pass through and enter within. And no faithful person is to stand still in the present Church, but rather to pass from virtue to virtue until entering into the joy of his Lord and seeing the God of gods in Zion. In this vestibule the spiritual banquet is given and prepared: given through grace, prepared for glory; given on the way, prepared to be received in the homeland. But whether the statement that it “had been planted by royal cultivation and hand” is referred to the present state of this festivity or to the future makes no difference. Whatever is done in Holy Church, whatever is afterward received in the heavenly homeland, is wholly accomplished by royal cultivation and hand: by hand with respect to action, by cultivation with respect to adornment. Yet the things written here concerning the spiritual banquet and its varied ornament seem to pertain more to the vestibule than to the garden and grove—that is, to the present state of the Church rather than to the future [Col. 1187A].

“And tents hung on every side.” Things which hang are raised from the ground but do not yet touch heaven. These tents, therefore, are the virtues and good works of the righteous, which are lifted from the earth through devotion but have not yet reached heaven through recompense. They hang on every side because they have nothing imperfect about them. But because before God whatever good is done in the world is of little account unless it is coloured by the goodness of divine grace, it fittingly continues: “Of sky-blue, hyacinth, and fine-linen colour.” By these three colours—sky-blue, hyacinth, and fine-linen—we believe that the three greatest things which now remain are to be understood: faith, hope, and charity.

By the sky-blue [Col. 1187B] colour, because it is written, “God is spirit” (John 4), faith in the heavenly divinity is rightly understood. By hyacinth, because it resembles the colour of heaven, hope of heavenly reward is expressed. By fine linen, because it imitates the brightness of gold, the splendour of charity is signified. These three virtues colour all the tents of other virtues and good works, in that they adorn, commend, and bring to completion all that is done in one or another of them. They are, as it were, the colour of all, because they are their form and beauty.

“Supported by cords of fine linen and purple.” A cord has length, fine linen whiteness, purple redness. By these two kinds of cords, therefore, we understand two kinds of virtues: one greatest outwardly, namely bodily chastity; the other greatest inwardly, namely compassion of heart. The cord of fine linen is chastity of flesh; the purple cord is compassion of heart. When these two virtues continuously and patiently endure in us like stretched cords, they hold immovably both walls of our tents. Chastity outwardly supports manifest virtues; compassion inwardly supports hidden virtues. Whoever has these well stretched within himself need not fear the collapse of virtue or good work, since the whole structure of that person’s righteousness hangs upon them. For who need fear loss of the other virtues if one perfectly possesses perpetual chastity of body and true compassion of heart?

The perfection of these virtues—namely chastity and compassion—is signified when it is added concerning the cords, since they express these virtues, that “they were inserted into ivory rings” [Col. 1187D]. The cords of fine linen and purple were inserted into rings because chastity, expressed by fine linen, and compassion, expressed by purple, ought always to belong to the purest perfection. So long as the structure of our righteousness clings firmly to this perfection, it remains firm and unshaken.

It is further said of these cords, or virtues, that “they were upheld by marble columns.” By marble columns we understand the firm uprightness and upright firmness of holy teachers. Marble columns are teachers: columns because they are upright in righteousness, marble because they are firm in faith. Therefore cords of fine linen and purple are upheld by marble columns, because the wisdom of teachers works wondrously [Col. 1188A] to ensure that chastity in the flesh and compassion in the heart continually abide in the elect. Thus through the columns the fine-linen and purple cords are upheld, and through the cords the rest is supported: through teachers, chastity and compassion are strengthened in all, and through these virtues the others are strengthened.

Accordingly, first the tents are raised by the practice and performance of virtues and good works. Second, they are coloured and adorned by faith, hope, and charity. Third, they are supported by fine-linen and purple cords—that is, by chastity and compassion. Fourth, the cords themselves—that is, the virtues—are upheld by marble columns, that is, by the upright and firm instruction of teachers. And now, beloved, let us attend carefully, so that by grace we may now be in this vestibule adorned with such great tents, and may afterward deserve through glory to enter the garden and grove. May he grant this to us, etc.

## SERMON XCIII. The Third Sermon on Christ’s Spiritual Banquet — From the Same Book of Esther

“Golden and silver couches also were arranged upon a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone, which a painting of marvellous variety adorned. Those who had been invited drank from golden cups, and food was brought in vessels of one kind and another. Wine also, abundant and excellent, as befitted royal magnificence, was set forth. Nor was there anyone to compel the unwilling to drink; but as the king had ordained, appointing over his tables individual princes, each person was to take what he wished” (Esther 1).

Above, matters were stated concerning the spiritual ornament of the spiritual vestibule; now greater things are added to the earlier ones. For who does not know that contemplation is greater than all works and virtues? This is introduced when it says: “Golden and silver couches also were arranged upon the pavement.” By the couches is understood the repose of inward contemplation. In this repose the human mind watches more diligently for inward things precisely as it sleeps more deeply with regard to outward things. Hence the bride: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch” (Song 5) [Col. 1188C].

It says “couches,” not “a couch.” For what we now receive from contemplation is little compared with what we expect to receive. It was also fittingly said not that one couch was arranged, but that couches were arranged, because the mode of contemplation is varied and more is bestowed upon some, less upon others, in the gift of contemplation. For as grace is differently given in action according to the measure of Christ’s gift, so it is distributed in contemplation according to the capacity of those receiving it. Thus there are many couches, differently placed both because of the difference of gifts and because of the differing ranks of contemplatives.

“Upon a pavement laid with emerald and Parian stone.” A pavement, lower down and laid evenly, supports all furnishings—for example, couches, seats, and vessels. It therefore signifies the equanimity, humility, and labour of prelates. Although they are set over others in authority, they are subject in service, just as the Lord himself, who is prelate over all prelates, came not to be served but to serve and to give his life for many (Matt. 20) [Col. 1189A]. Thus he says to his disciples: “Let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as one who serves” (ibid.). Thus Paul called himself, through Jesus, the servant of those to whom he wrote. Thus Blessed Augustine says of a prelate: “In honour before you, let him be set over you; in fear before God, let him be laid beneath your feet.”

Prelates, therefore, are a pavement by humbling themselves before God, patiently bearing those committed to them, and laboriously serving them; for when they serve them with labour, they bear them as though set upon themselves. But great praise of prelates is expressed when the pavement is said to be laid with emerald and Parian stone and declared to be adorned with a painting of marvellous variety. Emerald is green; Parian stone is white. Emerald signifies faith; Parian stone, chastity and pure action. Thus the pavement is laid with emerald and Parian stone when the prelate is adorned with faith, chastity, and most pure action. It is also adorned with a painting of marvellous variety when the prelate imitates the diverse virtues of different righteous persons not merely for personal benefit but also as an example to others.

Abel is painted on this pavement through innocence, Noah through righteousness, Abraham through faith, Isaac through patience, Jacob through endurance, Joseph through continence, Moses through meekness, Joshua through fortitude, Samuel through charity, David through humility, Elijah through zeal for righteousness, Daniel through the virtue of abstinence; and the form of any saint is painted upon it when the prelate practises that saint’s virtues insofar as he can [Col. 1189C]. Although it was said of the universal Holy Church, “The queen stood at your right hand in golden raiment, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44 [Vulgate]), yet this beauty of variety ought to appear pre-eminently and, as it were, especially in the holy prelate, so that, shining with every virtue, he may become all things to all people in order to gain all (1 Cor. 9).

Augustine’s statement about a prelate agrees with this meaning: “Toward all,” he says, “let him offer himself as an example of good works; let him correct the unruly, console the faint-hearted, support the weak, be patient toward all, gladly maintain discipline, and impose it with awe.” And although both are necessary, let him seek to be loved by you more than feared. Thus the couches were upon the pavement because prelates support contemplatives by their care and labour. Or rather, the couches were upon the pavement when contemplatives, placed in repose, sometimes advance further than their prelates, who are wearied and troubled by care.

Let us see, brothers, how we stand upon this venerable pavement: whether, established in quiet, we contemplate heavenly things on high. For there are some who burden their prelates with many annoyances and make no progress in contemplation, though they have been placed in a place of rest. Rebuking them, Paul says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Obey your leaders and submit to them. For they keep watch as those who are to render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this is not advantageous for you” (Heb. 13) [Col. 1190A]. And a little earlier, holding prelates up as examples to others, he says: “Remember your leaders, who spoke to you the word of God; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (ibid.). And to the Thessalonians, concerning the charity and peace to be maintained with prelates: “We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labour among you and preside over you in the Lord and admonish you; and to hold them in greater love because of their work. Be at peace with them” (1 Thess. 5). Hence Augustine says to subjects concerning prelates: “By obeying, have mercy not only upon yourselves but also upon him, who, the higher his position, is involved in the greater danger.”

“Those who had been invited drank from golden cups, and food was brought in vessels of one kind and another.” Golden cups are the words of the Gospel, more precious than all else, gleaming as with gold through the wisdom of God, which is Christ. These words are rightly called cups because they are easily understood. Foods, however, are those words of Scripture which are grasped with difficulty and labour, such as the words of the prophets in many places. These foods are brought in vessels of one kind and another when the grace contained in them is bestowed on us now through the opening of figures, now through the administration of sacraments. The enigmas of Holy Scripture and the sacred veils of the sacraments are, as it were, vessels; when they are opened, the minds of the faithful are refreshed.

“Wine also, abundant and excellent, as befitted royal magnificence, was set forth.” What is more rightly understood by spiritual wine than the consolation of the Holy Spirit, by which the faithful mind is often inebriated? Of this inebriation it is written: “My intoxicating cup—how excellent it is!” (Ps. 22 [Vulgate]). And again: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93 [Vulgate]) [Col. 1190C]. “As befitted royal magnificence,” he says. For in bestowing his grace God considers his own goodness, not human merit. “Abundant and excellent” wine was set forth. It was abundant because “God gives abundantly and does not reproach” (Jas. 1); excellent because nothing in life is sweeter than the sweetness of the Holy Spirit. Hence a certain Wise Man said in wonder: “How sweet, O Lord, is your spirit in all things” (Wis. 12). It is excellent because this is the wine of which the master of the banquet said to the bridegroom: “But you have kept the good wine until now” (John 2).

The saying in the Song of Songs seems to accord with the meaning of this banquet: “Eat and drink, friends, and be inebriated, beloved ones” (Song 5). Eat food; drink the cup; be inebriated through wine. “Nor was there anyone to compel the unwilling to drink; but as the king had ordained, appointing individual princes over his tables, each person was to take what he wished.” From these words it may be perceived that God does not wish to have forced service. “There was no one,” it says, “to compel the unwilling to drink.” No one is compelled to receive a spiritual gift: God wants children, not slaves; service according to will, not according to necessity.

“As the king had ordained, appointing individual princes over his tables.” The tables are the Scriptures [Col. 1191A]; the princes are teachers and prelates. He appoints individuals because “to one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge” (1 Cor. 12), so that each may distribute to the rest what he has received in an outstanding degree, “that each person might take what he wished.” Preaching must be tempered according to the will, capacity, and benefit of each person, so that it may benefit all and harm no one, and may pass through every vice like a two-edged sword: cutting away pride without increasing timidity; imposing the concern of work upon the idle and sluggish without increasing excessive activity among the restless and inquisitive; and so with the rest.

Let us feast now, brothers, in the vestibule of the garden and grove through grace, so that afterward we may deserve to feast through glory in the garden and grove. May he deign to grant this, etc.

## SERMON XCIV. On the Holy Day of Easter

[Col. 1191B]

Today, dearest brethren, is the Paschal solemnity, which, because of its excellence, may be called the solemnity of solemnities, just as it is said, the Song of Songs, God of gods, King of kings, Lord of lords. For it is celebrated not only annually today, as other solemnities are, but is also continually and singularly commemorated on every Lord’s Day; and on the day of judgment, when “this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15), it will be consummated universally and perfectly. The more celebrated this solemnity is, the more abundant [Col. 1191C], sumptuous, and refined should today’s provision of food be. And since in this present solemnity, according to Christian custom, all Christians—little with great, laypeople with clergy—shall sit down at the great table, at the table of the rich, mighty, and wise Solomon, let us carefully attend to what is set before us (Prov. 23).

For our Solomon is rich toward all, namely those who call upon him (Eph. 2). He is mighty, because “all power is given unto him in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28). He is wise, because “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2). The royal wealth and delights of his table are declared figuratively and plainly in the Third Book of Kings, where it is said: “Solomon’s provision for each day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and [Col. 1191D] a hundred rams, besides venison of deer, gazelles, and buffaloes, and fattened birds” (3 Kings 4). All these things are found spiritually on the table of our Solomon.

On Christ’s table are found thirty cors of fine flour through faith in the Holy Trinity, and sixty cors of meal through good action. Fine flour, being without bran, rightly signifies faith because of faith’s purity. Meal, which is not without some bran, signifies good action because of the disturbance involved in action. Of this bran it is written: “Martha, Martha, thou art anxious and troubled about many things” (Luke 10). The ten fat oxen are the ten commandments of the Law: oxen, because they enjoin good continence; fat, because they contain twofold charity [Col. 1192A]. Is not charity’s richness present where it is said, “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart,” and so forth, “and thy neighbour as thyself” (Matt. 22)? Does it not express continence where it says, “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife, nor anything that is his” (Deut. 5)?

“And twenty pasture-fed oxen”: the pasture-fed oxen are all the remaining legal precepts, which are leaner than the fat oxen insofar as they do not describe so expressly and authoritatively as the Decalogue the aforesaid greatest virtues—namely charity and abstinence from evil. The commandments of the Decalogue were written by the finger of God, whereas the other commandments were written by the finger of man. Oxen signify continence because they lack genitals, just as bulls signify lust because they possess them [Col. 1192B]. The lesser commandments following the Decalogue are likewise, as has now been shown, called oxen because of the charity and continence which they too teach; and they are twenty because, in accordance with the Decalogue, they are administered in a twofold manner through the service of piety: on the one hand to friends, on the other to enemies.

Finally, rams, because they differ from other sheep in that they are horned and strike an adversary most fiercely with their very hard heads, fittingly express the most eminent meanings of Scripture. When these are brought forth, they strike and crush most grievously their enemy, the devil, and the wicked human neighbour. They are rightly described by the number one hundred, so that their perfection may be denoted. Therefore, on Christ’s table thirty cors of fine flour, sixty cors of meal, ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and a hundred rams are set forth, when the minds of the faithful are most fully refreshed through the diligence of teachers by the doctrine of faith, good work, the Decalogue, whatever other legal precepts there may be, and the most excellent senses of Holy Scripture—besides the hunting of deer, gazelles, buffaloes, and fattened birds [Col. 1192C].

We bring the hunting to the table of our Solomon when, by reading, meditation, and ranging through different books as through different forests, we hunt out certain meanings that are, as it were, new and less often heard, and dispense them to our hearers in some new and unusual mode of speech. Those who have been nourished more delicately upon the Scriptures refresh themselves most eagerly by this fresh and wholesome sweetness of meanings and words, just as those who eat daily at royal courts and on royal fare delightfully consume fresh and rich game [Col. 1192D]. In deer there is timidity; in gazelles, swiftness; in buffaloes, strength; in birds, the elevation of flight.

Therefore we bring deer to Christ’s table when we speak of fear; gazelles, when we speak of swiftness in good works; buffaloes, when we speak of the strength of that same work; birds, when we speak of contemplation. Notice that when he had said “birds,” he added “fattened.” For that contemplation is praiseworthy before God which is raised upward not only by knowledge of truth but also made rich by love of virtue. We may turn this whole statement to another sense: by fine flour and meal we may understand the doctrine contained in the precepts of the two Testaments [Col. 1193A]; by domestic animals, the examples of saints from among the nations slain for Christ—so that we have a twofold food, one in precepts, the other in examples. By oxen we may understand those who in the Old Testament persistently applied themselves to good works; by rams, those who, striking their enemies fiercely with the horns of their strength, drove them from their territories; by wild animals, those faithful people from the nations who are active; and by birds, those who are contemplative.

Nor are holy martyrs alone food of salvation to us by their examples: holy confessors also, and all saints, provide us with food by the examples of their lives. Though they did not fall by the sword, they nevertheless crucified their flesh with its vices and desires through fasts, vigils, and varied labours [Col. 1193B]. Moreover, we have food not only in precepts and examples, but also in sacraments, of which the greatest is the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. All of us ought to assemble today to receive it reverently and beneficially.

In praise of it blessed Gregory says in Book IV of the *Dialogues* (ch. 58):

> What member of the faithful could doubt that, at the very hour of the offering, at the priest’s voice the heavens are opened; that in this mystery of Jesus Christ the choir of angels is present; that the lowest things are joined to the highest, earthly things united with heavenly, and one thing made out of visible and invisible? But it is necessary that, when we do this, we ourselves be sacrificed in contrition of heart. [Col. 1193C]

For we who celebrate the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion ought to imitate what we perform. How salutary, necessary, and blessed it is to receive Christ’s body and blood holily, he himself deigned to make known, saying: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6).

But Paul shows how harmful it is for those who receive unworthily, when he says: “Whoever shall eat the bread or drink the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11) [Col. 1193D]. “Not discerning,” that is, not distinguishing it reverently from other foods. For he ought either to have examined himself and cleansed himself through penance, or at least to have abstained.

Hence Paschasius says in his book *On the Body of the Lord*:

> Whoever becomes either a member of a harlot or, by some grave offence, a member of the devil has certainly fallen away from Christ’s body, and therefore he is not permitted to touch Christ’s body. What, then, does the sinner eat and drink? Certainly not flesh and blood to his own benefit, but judgment. Why? Because he does not first examine himself.

Therefore, if anyone who has fallen from Christ’s body and become a member of a harlot or of the devil presumes to touch this most holy body, there is no doubt that he receives judgment for it and, liable to guilt, is joined with Judas: both because he fell and because, condemned in his conscience, he dared without penance and pardon of correction to profane the holy mysteries [Col. 1194A]. Another, about to approach communion, does not consider the sublimity of the sacrament and, by jesting, anger, or indignation, does not honour communion but dishonours it. Another indeed communicates reverently, having withdrawn from prolonged laughter, excessive speech, idle speech, obscene speech, and detraction, yet dishonours holy communion by other vices. Of such people it seems to have been said: “The graces of fools shall be poured out” (Ecclus. 20). For whatever good they draw in from morning to evening by reading, chanting psalms, praying, or any other means, they carelessly pour out again by giving themselves not merely to idleness but to unlawful pleasures.

Hence this most holy mystery, venerable even to angels, is seen in our times to have fallen into such great contempt, as though there were no Father to seek and judge the honour of Jesus Christ. Thus truth has been cast down, so that, as is read in Daniel, we see “the abomination” take place in the temple of God (Dan. 9) [Col. 1194B]. Therefore those who despise so great a sacrament ought greatly to fear divine vengeance. The aforesaid Paschasius accordingly says in the same book that those angels appointed for this purpose would even now destroy anyone who communicated unworthily even once, unless Christ’s goodness—on whose judgment all things depend—held back the sword and removed temporal death from certain persons so that they might repent [Col. 1194C].

Yet we have not only heard with our ears but have also read with our eyes, in various books, of most grave and terrible punishments divinely inflicted without delay upon such presumptuous persons. Saint Gregory of Tours says of a certain priest “to whom, on the Lord’s solemnity, it had been granted on account of his office to celebrate Mass: as soon as the moment of communicating arrived, he was immediately seized by epilepsy (*ἐπιληψία*), fell down foaming, and cast the sacred particle from his mouth; and, as many testified, he had been drunk that very night.” Likewise he says of a notorious deacon that “while he was carrying the box containing the Lord’s body, it slipped from his hands and returned through the air above the altar.”

Saint Jerome, in the *Lives of the Fathers*, says of blessed Eulogius that, “when he saw certain monks who were unclean approaching communion, he held them back, saying: ‘You had a desire for fornication this night. But you said in your heart: It makes no difference whether a righteous person or a sinner approaches the sacrament. And another had doubt in his heart, saying: What can communion do to sanctify me?’” He removed all these from communion in the sacrament until they were purified by penance and tears [Col. 1194D]. He likewise writes such things concerning Saint Macarius, Saint Piammon, and their monks.

Brethren, we have given these examples because in the holy Church there are “many weak and feeble, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11). We have written these things because perhaps someone among them will read them and, having heard them, correct himself concerning his negligence [Col. 1195A]. But may these dangers be far from you, and may the cause of such dangers also be far from you. For you are not in darkness, brethren, that these dangers should overtake you (John 12). For you are all children of light and children of God. You are not children of the night nor of darkness (1 Thess. 5). We also hope better things of you, and things nearer to salvation, though we speak in this way (Heb. 6).

Therefore, dearly beloved, frequent this mystery with humility and reverence; approach often for its glory, and always desire to become its participants. For this is the mystery which especially in the living relieves inward pains, heals wounds, conquers the enemy, frees from evils, assists in good things, bestows grace, increases righteousness; and in the dead washes away guilt, remits punishment, opens heaven, and grants life [Col. 1195B]. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCV. On the Table of the Presence from the Book of Exodus, in Praise of Holy Scripture

The Lord, speaking to Moses concerning the making of the table of the Presence, said: “You shall make a table of shittim wood, two cubits long, a cubit broad, and a cubit and a half high; and you shall overlay it with the purest gold. You shall make for it a rim all around; and for the rim itself a chased crown four fingers high, and above it another little golden crown. You shall also prepare four golden rings and set them at the four corners of the same table, at each foot [Col. 1195C]. The golden rings shall be beneath the crown, so that poles may be passed through them and the table may be carried. You shall also make the poles of shittim wood and overlay them with gold for carrying the table. You shall prepare dishes and bowls, censers and cups, in which libations are to be offered, of the purest gold. And you shall set upon the table the loaves of the Presence before me continually” (Exod. 25).

What is this table except Holy Scripture? Whenever it exhorts us to live well, it offers us the bread of life. We read that the table was made of shittim wood, and the truth of Holy Scripture is corrupted by no antiquity. In the likeness of the table, Holy Scripture has two cubits of length when it teaches us both parts of faith: namely, that by which we believe in the Creator and that by which we believe in the Redeemer [Col. 1195D]. It has a cubit and a half of height when it teaches us what is the height of hope and the beginning of contemplation. Finally, it has a cubit of breadth when it instructs us what is the breadth of charity. Thus Holy Scripture, very much like a table, has length, height, and breadth, teaching us perfectly faith, hope together with the beginning of contemplation, and charity.

This spiritual table is overlaid entirely with gold because it shines throughout not only with the splendour of miracles but also of heavenly wisdom. It has a rim: namely, the mouths of holy teachers. This rim is carried around its entire circumference because holy teachers leave nothing anywhere uncorrected. For holy teachers are, as it were, the rim around the table, since by Scriptural authority they rebuke the wicked everywhere for evil and instruct the good toward better things [Col. 1196A].

The two crowns that follow, one of which is called chased and the other a little golden crown, signify the two goods of the righteous: one in this world and the other in heaven. The first signifies righteousness, the second heavenly reward; the first, merit, the second, recompense; the first, a good conscience, the second, the glory that follows. Both goods are rightly compared to crowns, both because they are perfect and because they confer a crown.

The first is commanded to be chased because the effect of good work is now manifold and varied. It is also four fingers high because the righteousness of the saints, through the working grace of the Holy Spirit, is raised by exercise in the four principal virtues [Col. 1196B]. In the fingers the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and in the number four the four virtues—prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance—are figured. This crown was joined to the rim of the table because the righteousness of the saints is brought to perfection according to the exhortations of teachers. Above it was the little golden crown because heavenly glory follows righteousness and surpasses it. It is called a little golden crown so that gold may signify the radiance of contemplation.

Careful attention should be given to the fact that it is said to have been not golden but a little golden crown, so that the diminutive indicates that whatever is now perceived of that same good by contemplation is small in comparison with the fullness of the good to come. It is nevertheless great and beyond estimation because, Scripture testifying, “those things which were under him filled the temple” (Isa. 6). And if those things beneath him fill the temple, who can estimate of what kind and how great are the things that are in him, and which are himself? Therefore concerning that heavenly reward, called here the higher crown and little golden crown, it is written: “They shall give into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over” (Luke 6) [Col. 1196C].

The beginning of this table or little golden crown is already seen and perceived in the present by some through contemplation, and it will be perfected in the future, when God himself—who is the reward and crown of the righteous—will be seen not through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face. Therefore, in the first place is put the table; in the second, the rim; in the third, the chased crown; in the fourth, the little golden crown. The table is Scripture; the rim, the exhortations of teachers; the chased crown, the righteousness of the saints; the little golden crown, heavenly recompense [Col. 1196D].

The four rings are the four books of the Gospels, aptly called rings because they are perfect: for they hand down perfect doctrine concerning faith and action, merit and reward. They are placed at the four corners of the table, at each foot, when by their authority and perfection the four senses of Scripture are strengthened, and Scripture itself is made ready to be carried through the four regions of the world in its four senses by Gospel preaching.

The table has four feet because the words of the heavenly oracle are understood historically, allegorically, tropologically, or anagogically. History is when in plain speech it is related how a matter was done or said according to the letter, as when the people departing Egypt are said to have been saved by the blood of the lamb, or when the tabernacle made in the wilderness is described. Allegory is when, through mystical words or things, the present mysteries of Christ and the Church are signified: through words, as follows: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11) [Col. 1197A]. That is to say: the Virgin Mary shall be born from David’s stock, and Christ from her stock. Through things, as when the people saved from Egypt by the blood of the Lamb signify the Church set free from the devil’s condemnation by Christ’s Passion.

Tropology—that is, moral discourse—concerns correction and instruction in morals through open or figurative words. Openly, as follows: “Little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3). Figuratively, as follows: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let not oil fail from your head” (Eccl. 9) [Col. 1197B].

Anagogy—that is, discourse leading upward—is that which treats of future rewards and the life that is in heaven by mystical or open words. Openly: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5). Mystically: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the city,” namely, the heavenly city (Rev. 22).

Therefore the four rings are set on the four feet of the table so that, with poles passed through them, the table may be carried: that is, the books of the Gospels are joined to the four senses of Scripture so that, by their authority, Scripture itself may be preached everywhere through teachers. The rings themselves are golden because the Gospel books are splendid with the wisdom of God, which is Christ. These rings are also beneath either the first or the second crown because Gospel doctrine comes first in order; righteousness follows doctrine, and glory follows righteousness [Col. 1197C].

The poles by which the table was carried are preachers through whom Holy Scripture is preached. They are of shittim wood because it is right that those who preach holiness to others should themselves live free from the corruption of vices. They are overlaid with gold because they shine with divine wisdom.

“You shall prepare dishes and bowls, censers and cups.” The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of speech adapted to the capacity of hearers, because not everything is suitable for everyone. The wise must be taught differently from the foolish; the rich differently from the poor; the healthy differently from the sick; the old differently from the young; men differently from women; celibates differently from married people; prelates differently from subjects [Col. 1197D]. Dishes signify biting doctrine; bowls, abundant doctrine; censers, devout prayer; cups, limited knowledge. All these vessels belong to the table of the tabernacle and to offering libations. For whatever diverse things are said according to the diversity of hearers are found in the rule of Holy Scripture, and they stir the hearts of hearers to offer the Lord the vows of good works.

“And you shall set upon the table the loaves of the Presence before me continually.” The loaves of the Presence are the words of heavenly wisdom. They are aptly called loaves of the Presence because the word of salvation ought always to be open to all the faithful, and in the Church there ought never to be lacking a word of consolation, which the Lord, setting it before the world through preachers of truth, willed to appear in his sight and to abound without ceasing until the end for those who hunger and thirst after righteousness [Col. 1198A].

Therefore the table is Scripture; the rim, the mouths of teachers; the chased crown, the righteousness of the saints; the higher little golden crown, heavenly remuneration; the feet of the table, the senses of Scripture; the four rings, the books of the Gospels; the poles, preachers; the varieties of vessels, distinctions of speech; the loaves of the Presence, words of heavenly wisdom.

This table, brethren, is heaped with every kind of wealth and filled with all delights. If you desire loaves and fish, receive on it the five loaves and two fish (Matt. 14), or indeed the seven loaves and a few small fish (Matt. 15). Five thousand people were satisfied from the former, and twelve baskets were filled with their fragments; four thousand people were satisfied from the latter, and seven baskets were filled with their remains [Col. 1198B]. Receive, therefore, both these loaves and those, and the fish, though few, and know that food will abound and remain over.

If you desire meat, receive the fattened calf (Luke 15), the oxen and fattened birds which have been slain for you (Matt. 22). If you desire flavour, receive the grain of mustard, which indeed is very small, but cast into the earth it grows and becomes greater than all herbs (Matt. 13). If you desire butter and honey, eat both with Emmanuel, so that with him you may know to reject evil and choose good (Isa. 7). If you desire fruits of various kinds, receive all new and old fruits which the bride kept for the bridegroom, and eat nuts from the garden of nuts (Song 7) [Col. 1198C].

If you desire drink, receive choice wine, of which it is written: “But thou hast kept the good wine until now” (John 2). If you desire a fuller drink, bring forth wine and milk without any exchange, and drink with the bride your wine with your milk (Song 5). If you desire nectar-like spices, receive the consolations of God, which, according to the multitude of your sorrows in your heart, shall gladden your souls (Ps. 93). If you desire aromatics, receive cypress with nard, saffron, calamus, and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes with all the finest ointments (Song 4).

And because it is dangerous and shameful that, beside such a great table, we should waste away dying of hunger and die withered, let us eat and drink and be made drunk from those things that are now set before us on this table by grace, so that afterward we may possess them more perfectly through glory [Col. 1198D]. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us. Amen.

## SERMON XCVI. On Any Saint

“Myrrh, stacte, and cassia flow from your garments, from ivory palaces; from them daughters of kings have delighted you in your honour. The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded by variety” (Ps. 44).

In these words both the holiness of each of the faithful is expressed and the righteousness of the universal Church is figured. In the first verse the virtues of individual faithful persons are described; in the second the righteousness of the whole Church is declared [Col. 1199A].

“Myrrh, and stacte, and cassia.” Myrrh is very bitter, and therefore signifies the mortification of the flesh—not with respect to nature, but with respect to guilt. For nature must always be nourished; guilt must be destroyed. This myrrh belongs to all the elect: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5). But because earlier in this little book we have said much in a certain sermon about this myrrh and its kinds, let us now be content with fewer words and pass on to what follows.

Stacte (*gutta*) is a plant that suppresses swellings and therefore expresses the virtue of humility. How necessary it is, the Lord demonstrates in the Gospel when he says: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted, and he who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14). And again: “Whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child shall not enter it” (Matt. 18) [Col. 1199B]. Abraham truly possessed this when he said: “I shall speak to the Lord, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18). Jacob likewise possessed it truly when, speaking to the Lord, he said: “I am less than all thy mercies” (Gen. 32). When the apostate angel refused to possess it, he fell irrecoverably from heaven like lightning. When Adam’s descendants lacked it while building the tower of Babylon, they deserved confusion of speech. Thus in all other cases it always happens that “before ruin the spirit is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16).

Cassia, also called calamus (*fistula*), purges the belly and relieves nature of its superfluities; it therefore signifies the virtue of confession, which, when it expels the guilt of the mind through the mouth, unloads the mind itself of sin’s weight [Col. 1199C]. Thus by myrrh we understand mortification of the flesh; by stacte, humiliation of the mind; by cassia, confession of sin.

“From your garments.” The garments of Christ’s body, which is the Church, are the more perfect saints, by whom holy Church, like a person with garments, is surrounded and adorned. Of these garments, or saints, some are red, namely martyrs made red by their blood; others are hyacinth-blue and heavenly, namely confessors raised sublimely to contemplate heavenly things; others are snowy white, as virgins are; others black, as are the humble, who continually make themselves black through the remembrance of their sins; others of varied and mixed colour, namely those who share in diverse virtues and good works.

“From ivory palaces” [Col. 1199D]. By ivory palaces we understand chaste and continent communities. For elephants, whose bones are called ivory, are exceedingly chaste animals: they mate facing away from one another; bear offspring only once; do not lie down upon the ground; and live three hundred years. All these things suit righteous and chaste souls, if you wish to examine them closely. Therefore Christ’s garments come from ivory palaces, and myrrh, stacte, and cassia come from the garments, because individual faithful persons come from chaste and continent communities, and holy virtues and reputations for virtue come from those faithful persons.

“From them daughters of kings have delighted you in your honour.” Kings are holy prelates, who govern others by the virtue of discernment. Their daughters are the souls of holy subjects, nourished by their doctrine and adorned by their examples [Col. 1200A]. They are designated by the name not of sons but of daughters in order that their great devotion may be signified. For the female sex is exceedingly devoted, and wherever it turns itself toward love it burns wonderfully. Or rather, they are described under the name of daughters rather than sons so that, when it is shown that even weak and imperfect souls, signified by daughters, delight Christ by their holiness, it may be expressed more clearly how much the remarkable righteousness of the perfect pleases him. Therefore daughters of kings delight Christ in honour when devoted multitudes of subjects delightfully honour him by their goodness. This delightful honour, or honourable delight, proceeds from the aforesaid virtues and sweetly refreshes him when he sees those subjects living righteously by these virtues and providing others with examples of righteousness [Col. 1200B].

“The queen stood at your right hand in a golden garment, surrounded by variety.” As in the preceding verse the virtues and reputations for virtue of individual faithful persons are suggested, so in this verse the righteousness of the universal Church and the diverse multiplicity and manifold variety of that righteousness are designated. Holy Church is most rightly compared to a queen because she is united to the heavenly King and exaltedly crowned by him. She stands through faith and stands beside him through good intention. False believers, though they stand by rightly believing true things, nevertheless do not stand beside him by performing the good they do with right intention.

Elijah belonged to the number both of those who stand and of those who stand beside, when he said: “The Lord lives, in whose presence I stand” (3 Kings 17). For when he said “I stand,” he declared that he stood; but when he said “in whose presence,” he made clear that through intention he did not lack the divine presence [Col. 1200C]. Holy Church now stands beside God at the right through righteousness, so that in the future she may deserve to stand at the right in glory. Likewise the reprobate are now at the left through guilt, and at the end will be placed at the left for punishment.

“In a golden garment.” By the garment righteousness is to be understood; by the gilding, wisdom. Whatever holy Church performs, whether in exercising virtues or doing good works, is entirely adorned by the radiance of heavenly wisdom. For she imitates her Creator according to her ability: he made all things in wisdom; in ordering the universe he first created light and then arranged the rest; and, when all things had been arranged, “he saw all that he had made, and behold, it was very good” (Gen. 1) [Col. 1200D].

“Surrounded by variety.” Holy Church is not content with one virtue or one work, but desires to be surrounded by a multiplicity of virtues and adorned by a variety of good works, according to “the stewardship of the manifold grace of God” (1 Pet. 4). To this variety belongs the saying of blessed Peter: “Supply in your faith virtue; and in virtue, knowledge; and in knowledge, abstinence; and in abstinence, patience; and in patience, piety; and in piety, brotherly love; and in brotherly love, charity” (2 Pet. 1). And that of blessed Paul: “In all things let us show ourselves as ministers of God, in much patience,” and so forth (2 Cor. 6) [Col. 1201A].

Therefore by myrrh, stacte, and cassia we understand the virtues of the faithful; by the garments, the faithful themselves; by ivory palaces, their chaste communities; by the queen, holy Church; by her golden garment, her righteousness; by the variety, the manifold difference of that same righteousness. Therefore let us exercise virtues and good works with all our strength, so that with all the faithful and with holy Mother Church we may deserve to be crowned in the heavenly homeland. May Jesus Christ deign to grant this to us, and so forth.

## SERMON XCVII. On the Feast of Saint John the Baptist

“If you sleep between the midst of the choirs, the wings of the dove are silvered, and the hind parts of her back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67) [Col. 1201B].

In these sacred and few words, which the holy Psalmist sings to us through the Holy Spirit, he describes by spiritual signification the merit of the saints, the knowledge of the universal Church, and their reward. He denotes merit when he says, “If you sleep between the midst of the choirs”; the knowledge of holy Church when he adds, “the wings of the dove are silvered”; and reward when he concludes, “the hind parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.”

“If you sleep between the midst of the choirs.” The two choirs are the prophets and apostles. Between them sleep those who, taught on either side by their sacred sayings, happily rest in the peace of good conduct, free from the disturbance of demons. For all who live holily between the proclamations of the prophets and the preachings of the apostles are between the midst of the choirs. They also sleep when, occupied in good works, they are undisturbed by the assaults of temptations [Col. 1201C].

Of this blessed sleep of the saints it is said through Jacob under the name of Issachar: “Issachar is a strong ass, lying down between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent; and he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant under tribute” (Gen. 49). The people of the righteous are indeed a strong ass because they bear peacefully and courageously the weight of every tribulation. They lie down between the boundaries when, instructed by prophets and apostles, they rest in doing good works through the doctrine of both. They see that the rest of inward contemplation is good and that the land of heavenly blessedness is excellent; captured by love of both, they bow their shoulder to bear whatever burden is imposed. They also serve under tribute because they willingly give not only what is theirs but themselves for spiritual goods [Col. 1201D].

The company of the elect, therefore, sleeps between the two choirs, as has been said, and by this sleep acquires a heavenly reward. It sleeps, and, as Solomon says, “its sleep is sweet” (Prov. III).—“The wings of the dove are silvered.” The dove, as has often been said, is the holy Church. The holy Church, indeed, just as it lacks gall through charity, does not live on carrion through the corruption of dead works, chooses the better grains through the performance of God’s greater commandments, has groaning instead of song through repentance, often feeds the young of others through mercy, sits upon waters so that by reading sacred Scripture it may foresee the shadow of the hawk that is coming—that is, of the devil [Col. 1202A]—and nests among rocks by resting in the hidden places of Christ in lofty contemplation. It has two wings through love of God and neighbour: on the right, love of God; on the left, love of neighbour. The feathers of the right wing are those distinctions by which it is said: “You shall love your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind” (Matt. XXII). The feathers of the left wing are vow, counsel, and beneficence, by which we ought to love our neighbour as ourselves. These feathers, moreover, are silvered, because on love of God and neighbour “hang all the law and the prophets” (ibid.). Certainly, sacred speech is signified by silver, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. XI). Therefore, when the saints sleep between the two choirs, the dove’s feathers are silvered, because sacred knowledge is then fulfilled in the virtues of the holy Church, while the whole company of saints, resting in faith and works, carries out to the best of its ability the prophetic and apostolic commandments. “And the hind parts of her back are in the pallor of gold.” The hind parts of the back are the consequences of reward. They are most fittingly compared with gold, because, as gold surpasses other metals, so the heavenly reward leaves all other goods far behind by comparison with itself. Blessed John the Baptist, whose solemnity we celebrate today, slept between the two choirs not only in virtue but also in time, because he stood between prophets and apostles not only by holiness of life [Col. 1202C] but also by his place in time. “For the law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. XI). Let us imitate his holiness, insofar as heavenly grace may deign to grant it, so that by his merits and prayers we may deserve to attain heavenly joys. May Jesus Christ our Lord deign to grant this to us, he who is blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCVIII. On the Ascension of the Lord

“His praise is above heaven and earth; and he has exalted the horn of his people” (Ps. CXLVIII). Confession is of one kind for sin, of another for praise. But in this place it is understood only of praise.
