For the confession of God—that is, the praise of God—is above heaven through the blessed spirits, and above earth [Col. 1202D] through righteous human beings, and thus above heaven and earth. For everything that has been created is beneath him. But since above we have said much both about confession of sin and confession of praise, we leave these matters and pass to the rest.

“And he has exalted the horn of his people.” The horn of the Lord’s people is Christ. A horn proceeds from flesh, yet exceeds flesh. So Christ proceeded from virginal flesh, yet, having no sin, exceeded flesh. The saying of the Apostle accords with this: “What was impossible for the law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh through sin, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. VIII). For in this horn, just as it in some manner transcends flesh—because he came not in sinful flesh but only in the likeness of sinful flesh—the horn rises above every body, and Christ above the whole body of his members. Hence Zechariah, the father of blessed John the Baptist, says of him: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, because he has visited and wrought redemption for his people [of his people]; and has raised up for us a horn of salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke I). Christ is the horn because he proclaimed salvation to the world. Hence the Apostle says: “Coming, he preached peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near; because through him both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. II). Christ is the horn of God’s people because by him he terrifies and drives enemies from [Col. 1203B] its borders. He did not say “horns,” but “horn,” because our one teacher is Christ. Of him the Psalmist also says: “There is none that does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII), that is, Christ. Thus God, speaking to Abraham by promise, did not say, “In your seeds,” as though many nations would be blessed, but “in your seed,” as in one, which is Christ (Gal. III).

This our one and singular horn was especially exalted on this day, when the only-begotten Son of God, according to the humanity he assumed, penetrated all the heavens and, surpassing the highest ranks of the heavenly spirits, sat down at the right hand of the Father. Hence the Apostle says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is [Col. 1203C] above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of heavenly beings, earthly beings, and those under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II). Today, finally, Daniel’s vision was fulfilled, in which it is said: “I was looking in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man came, and he came even to the Ancient of Days; and they presented him before him. And he gave him power, honour, and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one which shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII).

“Therefore, having a great High Priest who has penetrated heaven, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession” [Col. 1203D] (Heb. IV). That confession, I say, which is above heaven and earth, which is made unto salvation, as it is written: “The sacrifice of praise shall glorify me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. XLIX). Let us confess upon earth, to whom angels confess above heaven, that God, who is rich in mercy because of the charity with which he loved us, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, raised us together, and made us sit in heavenly places in Christ Jesus (Eph. II). For we have been saved in hope (Rom. VIII). But until hope passes away and the reality follows, let us set ascents in our hearts in the valley of tears, in the place which we have set for ourselves (Ps. LXXXIII). The ascents are virtues; the valley of tears is the world; the place which we have set is the manner of life that [Col. 1204A] we choose. Some choose to be in the field, others at the mill, others in bed. Let us, therefore, in the place that we have chosen, set ascents in our hearts; or, according to blessed Peter, let us supply in our faith virtue, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge self-restraint, in self-restraint patience, in patience godliness, in godliness brotherly love, and in brotherly love charity (II Pet. I). For these are the ascents by which the tribes—the tribes of the Lord—go up to confess the name of the Lord (Ps. CXXI). Whoever holds the final step of this ascent, that is, charity, possesses God. “For God is charity; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV).

Blessed Peter placed faith itself as the first step of this ascent [Col. 1204B] because it is the first of all virtues, since without it it is impossible to please God (Heb. XI). He placed charity as the final step, because it is greater than all. Hence Paul, after describing spiritual gifts or virtues, added concerning charity: “And yet I show you a more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of men and angels” (I Cor. XII), etc. And shortly afterward: “But now these three remain: faith, hope, charity. But the greatest of these is charity” (ibid.).

Blessed Peter therefore fittingly placed faith first and charity last on the ladder of virtues, because faith begins the good in us and charity perfects it. But among the other virtues of the ladder, whichever you see higher up, if you consider rightly, you will see to be the more excellent. For who doubts that brotherly love is better than courage? Who does not know that godliness is more useful than knowledge? Who does not know that patience is more praiseworthy than self-restraint? Put otherwise: just as charity surpasses brotherly love and all other virtues in goodness, so brotherly love exceeds godliness and the remaining virtues placed below it. The same is to be understood of the rest. For just as a preceding virtue comes before the following one in order, so every following virtue surpasses the preceding one on this ladder in dignity. Hence the higher anyone climbs, the more firmly he places his foot, because he stands more securely as, by attaining more exalted virtues, he draws nearer to heaven.

“Supply in faith virtue,” etc. For faith without virtue is powerless [Col. 1204D] and idle; virtue without knowledge, undiscerning; knowledge without self-restraint, puffed up; self-restraint without patience, irascible; patience without godliness, inhuman; godliness without brotherly love, imperfect; brotherly love without charity, carnal. This ladder of ascent is, finally, distinguished by eight virtues because through it one reaches the eightfold number of beatitudes. Each is joined to another, so that their harmony may thereby be shown, and it may be shown that one perfect righteousness consists of them all and that one may reach a single glory through them. No one has ever seen that glory as it is in this mortal life. For, as blessed Gregory says:

> “However intensely the human mind may strive, even if it has already restrained the phantasms of bodily images from thought, [Col. 1205A] and even if it has already removed all circumscribed spirits from the eyes of the heart, nevertheless, while placed in mortal flesh, it cannot see the glory of God as it is. And whatever of that glory shines in the mind is a likeness, not the thing itself.”

Hence the prophet Ezekiel, describing what he had seen in the Spirit, did not say, “This is the vision of the glory of the Lord,” but “This is the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord” (Ezek. VIII). Yet this very vision of the likeness wonderfully gladdens the mind, because the things beneath it fill the temple. For the things beneath it fill the temple, because even those things that are seen in the likeness of his glory afford wonderful joys to the human mind. May Jesus Christ deign to grant us that glory. Amen.

## SERMON XCIX. On the Feast of Saint Augustine

[Col. 1205B]

“My heart has uttered a good word; I speak my works to the king. My tongue is the pen of a swiftly writing scribe” (Ps. XLIV). These words, beloved, which have been set forth, apply to prophets, apostles, and all teachers of the Church, and to all who, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, utter the word of God. Since this is unquestionably true of blessed Augustine, whose solemnity we observe today, we do not doubt that they apply to him. For his heart truly uttered a good word, since he preached the word of God in the holy Church until his final illness. He spoke his works to the king because he ascribed not to himself, but to Christ, the holy life he lived. His tongue became the pen of a swiftly writing scribe because, taught and guided by the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1205C] he dispensed the word of God most elegantly. Therefore we sing of him at this solemnity: full of the spirit of prophets and apostles, he made accessible to us the mysteries they foretold; after them, he shone forth first in the second grace of dispensing the word of God.

Ink is grace; the horn, or inkhorn, is Christ; the parchment is the hearts of the hearers. Just as a writer writes on parchment whatever he wishes with a pen from ink contained in a filled horn, so the grace of the Holy Spirit, filled in Christ and in the teacher’s tongue, instructs our hearts. This seems to be what Christ says to his disciples in the Gospel: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth; for he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you” [Col. 1205D] (John XVI). For as the Holy Spirit is not from himself, so he does not speak from himself, but from the Father and the Son, from whom he proceeds. And in speaking he distributes to us, as he wills, the grace that is in Christ. For from the fullness of Christ, in whom all treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden, we have all received (John I; Col. II).

Our hearts also, which we have said are figured by parchment and in which this spiritual writing is spiritually written, are prepared after the manner of material parchment: by bitter repentance they are made; by strict self-denial they are stretched; by the removal of all carnality they are scraped; and by firm stability they are formed into a square [Col. 1206A]. For just as everything round is liable to roll, so everything square is stable and firm. Dots signify number, lead weight, and the rule measure. For God made all things in number, weight, and measure. Although number, weight, and measure cannot be comprehended by us, they are not incomprehensible to God. The saying of the Gospel seems to accord with this spiritual number, weight, and measure, which we mark upon spiritual parchment: “A certain man going abroad called his servants and handed over his goods to them. To one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one, to each according to his own ability” (Matt. XXV). And again: “To whom more has been given, more will be required from him” [Col. 1206B] (Luke XII). And the Apostle says: “To each of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV).

The writing inscribed upon our hearts is truth. Concerning this inscription the Lord says through the prophet: “But this is the covenant which I will make with them after those days, says the Lord” (Jer. XXXI): “I will put my laws in their hearts, and I will write them upon their minds” (Heb. X). Finally, the writing-desk placed beneath this spiritual parchment, so that truth may be written upon the parchment itself, seems to be earthly support. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Cant. VIII), intending by the left hand bodily goods and by the right hand spiritual goods. For earthly things are supplied to the body so that the spirit may more easily sustain, undertake, and carry out divine things [Col. 1206C]. Therefore the Holy Spirit is the scribe; the teacher’s tongue, the pen; grace, the ink; Christ, the horn; hearts, the parchment; truth, the writing; earthly supports, the writing-desk.

Let us see, beloved, whether our hearts are suitable for truth, so that truth may be written upon them: whether they have been made by bitter compunction; stretched by the rigour of self-denial; scraped by the removal of all carnality; and formed into a square by firm stability. For the dots, lead, and rule—that is, number, weight, and measure—seem to belong to God alone. Let us therefore see whether the sacred words, administered to us by the Holy Spirit as scribe, by grace as ink, and by the tongue of Saint Augustine as pen, find room in our hearts. Saint Augustine says in our Rule [Col. 1206D]—indeed, it is the Holy Spirit speaking through his tongue filled with grace: “Before all things, let God be loved, and then one’s neighbour.” In what follows he gave many commands concerning continence, obedience, and common life, which are especially contained in our profession. Let us see whether these words of the blessed man have become strong in us. If this is found to be so, let us not doubt that the Holy Spirit has worked in us through his tongue. And let us hold in faith, love, and action not only what is contained in his Rule, but also the other things he wrote in expounding Scripture, teaching, and exhorting, so that we may obtain heavenly rewards. May Jesus Christ, who is, etc., deign to grant this to us.

## SERMON C. On the Feast of the Holy Cross

[Col. 1207A]

“When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished’; and, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John XIX). These words, beloved, which we have set forth are indeed brief, but most excellent, since they describe for us the completion of our redemption. Therefore, in the death of Christ all the enigmas of ancient figures signifying it, and all the utterances of the prophets foretelling it, were fulfilled. Hence the Lord himself said to the Apostles: “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and all things written through the prophets concerning the Son of Man will be fulfilled” (Matt. XX). “It is finished.” For in the death of Christ, according to typological meaning, there was fulfilled [Col. 1207B] what God did when he formed Eve from the side of sleeping Adam, because this signified that the holy Church would be redeemed by the blood flowing from the side of the dead Christ. There was fulfilled what Cain did when he killed his brother Abel through envy, because this was a sign that the Jewish people, through envy, delivered Christ to Pilate to be crucified. There was fulfilled, according to mystical meaning, what Abraham did when he placed his son Isaac upon an altar, with a pile of wood laid beneath him, in order to offer him to God, because this figured that the human race offered Christ, born from itself according to the flesh, upon the cross. There was fulfilled, according to the same meaning, what God did when, in the slaughter of the paschal lamb, he freed the children of Israel from the bondage of the Egyptians, because this indicated that spiritual Israelites would be rescued by Christ’s death from the yoke of demons. There was fulfilled [Col. 1207C] what Moses did when he sweetened bitter waters by wood and brought forth waters from the rock, because this represented that Christ, by the bitterness of his death, changed for us the severity of the Law into sweetness and caused spiritual streams to flow to us from himself, who is the true rock. There was fulfilled what the scapegoat did when it bore the people’s sins into the wilderness, because it was a type signifying that Christ would take away our sins. There was fulfilled what the woman of Zarephath did when she gathered two sticks, because this expressed that the Gentiles afterwards received faith in Christ’s passion. There was fulfilled what the angel Raphael did when, at Tobias’s marriage, he bound the demon driven out by the gall of a fish, because this indicated [Col. 1207D] that Christ, given gall to drink and embittered by death, overcame the devil.

The prophecies of the prophets were also fulfilled. There was fulfilled what Moses said: “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deut. XXI). Hence the Apostle also says that Christ “was made a curse for us” (Gal. III). There was fulfilled what David said: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII). And Isaiah’s prophecy was fulfilled, which says: “For the crime of my people I struck him” (Isa. LIII); and again: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (ibid.). Many enigmas of figures and proclamations of prophets signifying and announcing beforehand the death of Christ were fulfilled, brothers. But who could enumerate and explain them all? It is [Col. 1208A] finished, therefore. For whatever had to be done before Christ’s death was fulfilled in Christ’s death.

The death of Christ, therefore, is for us the perfect restoration of life; Christ’s death, our reconciliation with God; Christ’s death, the removal of guilt; Christ’s death, the bestowal of righteousness; Christ’s death, the locking of hell for us; Christ’s death, the opening of heaven; Christ’s death, the destruction of punishment; Christ’s death, the recovery of glory. Therefore it is finished. Finished is whatever pertains to the ending of evil. Finished is whatever pertains to the perfection of good. Fulfilled is what righteous Simeon foretold. Fulfilled is what Caiaphas, though reprobate, prophesied. Fulfilled is what detestable Judas promised the Pharisees [Col. 1208B]. Fulfilled is what Pilate, the unjust judge, unjustly decreed to be done. Fulfilled is what the unhappy Jew desired to his own destruction. Fulfilled is what God provided for our benefit. The Law is fulfilled. Prophecy is fulfilled. The angelic announcement is fulfilled. Fulfilled is what the righteous hoped for in the world. Fulfilled is what they afterwards awaited in hell. Fulfilled is that by holy living they deserved to possess heaven. Therefore it is finished.

But righteousness, completed in us by grace, is to be completed by glory through righteousness. Righteousness has been completed in effect; glory is to be completed in us by its cause. For all who truly believe in Christ are already righteous in effect, blessed in cause, and at last to be made blessed in effect. Concerning this cause of blessedness Paul speaks thus of Christ: “Having been made perfect, he became, for all who obey him, the cause of eternal salvation” [Col. 1208C] (Heb. V). For if, as he says elsewhere, “the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to our mortal bodies, because of his Spirit dwelling in us” (Rom. VIII).

It is therefore well said that Jesus, when he had received the vinegar, said, “It is finished,” and, bowing his head, gave up the spirit. The tasting of vinegar signifies the bitterness of death; the bowing of the head, the condescension of humility; but the giving up of the spirit is the completion of human redemption. Therefore in Christ’s death all things were fulfilled, since righteousness is fulfilled in the present and glory will be fulfilled in [Col. 1208D] the future. When? “When this corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” (I Cor. XV). “For when Christ, your life, shall appear, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III).

But, beloved, since we cannot sufficiently describe or worthily praise the passion of Christ, the redemption of the human race, let us turn the pen toward ourselves and see whether, according to our measure, we follow Christ’s footsteps by enduring evils. And since today we celebrate the solemnity of the holy cross and remember the Lord’s passion, it is fitting that we exhort one another concerning patience. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him”; and if we have been companions of his sufferings [Col. 1209A], we shall also be companions of his consolations (Rom. VIII). Attentive to this, the bride says: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Cant. I). Let us therefore strive to enter through the narrow gate and climb the strait and steep way, because there is no other entrance to righteousness or ascent to glory.

Now that this hundredth sermon, beloved, has been completed in this little book, we judge that the little book itself should be completed with this sermon. Let us therefore endeavour to fulfil in faith, hope, and love the things written in this sermon and little book, so that we may deserve to attain heavenly glory. May Jesus Christ our Lord, who is God blessed for ages of ages, deign to grant this to us. Amen.

[Col. 1209]

## SERMON ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

In which there is expounded, for the most part, what is drawn from the Song of Songs and is customarily sung in the Office of her Assumption.

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 1209] Receive, dearest brother, this small gift of my promise; and whatever you find in it other than is fitting, consider it your own, since you compelled me. You requested that I open for you by a brief exposition that eulogy, “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved” (Cant. IV), which the Church sings, taken from the Song of Songs, in praise of the mother and virgin. You were led to ask this especially, as you yourself confessed to me, because your monastery is consecrated in honour of that same virgin; and therefore it is altogether fitting that those who are marked by her special title should also be found most dear in singular devotion.

In yielding to these words, I think the exposition not unworthy for this reason: although the passages explained are not taken in the manner in which they occur in the sequence of the book as written, they nevertheless do not depart from the ancient authority; and the charity of her in whose praise they are spoken urges us to think that whatever may be acceptable to her ought to be of the greatest importance. I have already done this same thing in another chant, which likewise, compelled by a certain brother, I undertook to explain in a compilation arranged in the same manner. In it, although our exposition sometimes changed the words of the primary authority and their order, it nevertheless did not depart from the meaning of that primary authority. In expositions of this kind, while willingly complying with fraternal charity, I do not think that I should be blamed, even if they perhaps seem to have less gravity; for I judge that it makes little difference by what occasion, provided only truth is preserved, I provide for the edification of a brother.

## SERMON ON THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN

[Col. 1209]

[Col. 1209B] “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Cant. IV). These words, beloved, are known to us all and have been made known to all with great sweetness. They possess a sweetness of their own by which they delight, and from the sweetness of her to whom they are sung they receive a more abundant charm. For she herself is wholly sweet and wholly gracious, uniquely beautiful and singularly lovely. Therefore the praise of so beautiful a virgin must itself be beautiful, since in it the beauty of the beloved is praised and love for the beautiful one commended. The bridegroom of the virgin himself declares the praise of virginity; and to be praised by him is so much the greater because it is less possible than anything for him to be mistaken in praise of anyone. The author of beauty and judge of truth himself commends beauty and approves charity. He confesses that he loves the one whom he made lovable, and glories in being loved by her to whom he gave love.

O wondrous thing! He is both the son of a mother and the bridegroom of a virgin, the author of integrity and the fruit of fruitfulness. He himself praises his beloved, commends the beautiful one, and invites his friend. “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved.” O admirable lover! O singular teacher! What do you say? She is your mother; she is your beloved. And how is she your beloved? Are we to believe that your very mother is your beloved? [Col. 1211A] Or how can this be? Certainly she is your beloved and your mother: your beloved because untouched, your mother because fruitful. For you, the son of integrity and friend of fruitfulness, have as mother a virgin and as beloved one rejoicing in offspring. Your beloved, Mary, mother and virgin, first bore you. Afterwards your beloved, the Church, mother and virgin, was begotten from you. By coming in the flesh, you became the son of your bride, who is mother and virgin in body. By dying in the flesh, you became the begetter of your bride, who is virgin by faith. In being born from your bride, you received the substance of weakness; in dying, you gave your bride the sacraments of incorruption: in both respects a wondrous lover, in both respects a singular lover. You loved your bride so that you might be born in her, and you loved your bride so that you might die for her. And your bride is one; your beloved is one; your dove, your perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, one chosen by her who bore her (Cant. VI) [Col. 1211B].

Call, therefore, your bride; invite your beloved. You who are beautiful, call the beautiful one; you who are lovely, call the comely one; you who are beloved, call your unique one. Praise her beauty, lest she be afraid to approach the Beautiful One; speak of her loveliness, lest she fear to be joined to the most lovely One; say how you first came to her, loving and seeking love, so that she may hasten to come to you, loving and returning love. Speak, therefore, Lover: speak to your beloved of her own beauty; speak of your love, so that the beloved may love her lover, may desire more greatly to be loved, and may hasten more quickly to be joined to him. Speak, therefore, speak: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved.” Why then, beautiful one, do you hesitate? Why do you delay?

[Col. 1211C] “Show your face” (Cant. II). Come forth, that you may see the Beautiful One and be seen as beautiful. Why do you weave delays? You desire to see the Beautiful One, but perhaps you fear that you may be seen, even in some small respect, as not beautiful; and therefore perhaps you are afraid to go forth, tremble to be revealed, and blush to be presented. Remove fear; put away dread. “I,” says the beloved, “see you—I who call you. I have you present—I who invite you to come. For I do not call you in order that I may begin to see you, but in order that I may make myself openly visible to you. Therefore do not fear; rather, believe me who call you concerning yourself, because I would by no means call you if I did not see you prepared, if I saw you less worthy. I call you clean; I invite you sincere; I desire you wholly beautiful: ‘You are wholly beautiful, my beloved!’”

O what fellowship! The wholly beautiful One joins the wholly beautiful one to himself. “You are wholly beautiful [Col. 1211D], my beloved.” I am wholly beautiful, and you are wholly beautiful: I by nature, you by grace. I am wholly beautiful because everything beautiful is in me. You are wholly beautiful because nothing ugly is in you. “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” You are wholly a beautiful thing: beautiful in body, beautiful in mind. Bodily, the integrity of virginity makes you beautiful; in mind, the virtue of humility displays you as beautiful. Therefore you are wholly beautiful: snowy in body, sincere in mind. You are wholly beautiful; for beauty has left nothing in you which it does not possess; adornment holds the whole, loveliness possesses it, honourableness governs it. “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.”

O humble virginity and virginal humility! How did you come together into one? How are you in one fellowship, so as to produce such and so great a miracle? What have you done? You have so exalted the humble woman and so made the virgin fruitful [Col. 1212A] that a virgin bears the Son of God and a humble woman has God as bridegroom. No other woman was fitting for such a one, nor could any other such one be found for such a woman. O worthy one of the Worthy One; beautiful one of the Beautiful One; pure one of the Incorruptible One; lofty one of the Most High; Mother of God, bride of the eternal King! How beautiful you are, and how sweet: you whom the searcher of the reins approves, whom the inspector of hearts praises, whom the author of beauty loves, to whom the teacher of truth bears witness.

Listen therefore to his voice; incline your ear to his words. He is the one who speaks; he is the one who is heard; he invites you; he desires you to hear him; he says: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish [Col. 1212B] in you.” Exult and rejoice; rejoice beyond comparison; be glad singularly. Respond joyfully to the one who calls; hasten to come; hurry to meet him; receive the kingdom of the bridegroom; possess the inheritance of the Son. Do not delay any longer the desire of the lover; do not by postponement afflict the one who waits and desires you. Consider with what sweetness he invites you, and you will understand with what charity he awaits you.

Then, after he had said that no blemish was found in her—that she was pure and sincere, and untouched by anything that could displease—lest this praise perhaps still too little encourage the timid woman or inflame the modest one, he added further and continued, showing that she was not only immune and free from evil, but full of ineffable goods and endowed with every perfection of virtues, saying: “O my beautiful one! O my beloved! O my dove! My friend, I gladly embrace you; I gaze upon you with delight, because I see no blemish in you, because I behold you wholly beautiful; but far more, with ineffable delight, because I find you wholly full of sweetness. Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue; and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices” (Song of Songs 4).

Your lips, your tongue, your ointments: all are sweet, all pleasant, all worthy of praise. Your lips, your tongue, your ointments. Three things are commended: lips, tongue, and ointments. In the lips is the kiss; in the tongue, speech; in the ointments, scent and fragrance. Thus the whole Trinity came to the Virgin. For in her lips she had received from the mouth of the Father a kiss. In her [Col. 1212D] tongue she had received the Father’s Word. In the ointments she had received the Spirit of the Father and of the Word. Hence: your lips, your tongue, your ointments. “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue; and the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.”

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” Your lips possess both fullness and sweetness. Therefore, “your lips are a dripping honeycomb”: for, when pressed, they give forth sweetness. Thus, “your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” All is said by way of likeness: “your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” A honeycomb has honey and wax. Honey is divinity; wax, humanity. The honeycomb is the Word made flesh in the Virgin: therefore, “your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” In you divine and human nature, their old discord dissolved, were joined by the kiss of peace into perfect fullness and eternal union. In you divinity poured itself into humanity. Hence Christ, God and man, came forth from you in true humanity and perfect divinity. Therefore, “your lips are a dripping honeycomb.”

“I,” he says, “know what I proclaim; I have experienced what I praise. Your lips are a dripping honeycomb. Bound to you in love, I pressed your lips with the kiss of my mouth; at once I poured sweetness in and drew sweetness forth from sweetness. I impressed it greatly and drew it out greatly, because I poured it in fully and joined it perfectly. Therefore I deeply impressed sweetness and truly expressed pleasantness, when I joined what was mine with what was yours in you, and through what was yours came forth from you with what was both mine and yours. My divinity was honey, and your humanity was wax; from these I made myself a honeycomb, and became one. And behold, your lips are a dripping honeycomb. For what was impressed in you [Col. 1213B] was assumed from you, and the very thing made was full of sweetness in me. Thus now I am what I am, and I am what I became. What I became, I now am; but what I am, I always am. Yet I truly am both what I became and what I am: the one from you, the other before you. Your lips are a dripping honeycomb. O how sweet and pleasant you are, you who alone were worthy to receive in your conception the kiss of heavenly sweetness and, in giving birth, to distil the sweetness of the whole world!”

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” What is “honey and milk under your tongue”? It is the Father’s Word beneath your flesh. Why, then, beneath your tongue? Because it is the Word, and therefore beneath the tongue. “Honey and milk [Col. 1213C] are under your tongue”: not above the tongue, but beneath it, because the Word is hidden, and therefore honey and milk are beneath your tongue. “Honey and milk are beneath your tongue”: beneath your tongue, beneath your flesh. Beneath your tongue, because it is a word; beneath your tongue, because it is hidden. Honey and milk: God and man. Honey is divinity; milk, humanity. Honey comes from the dew of heaven, because the divine nature is above all things. Milk is pressed from flesh, because humanity was assumed from below. From flesh, flesh. Therefore it is milk, not flesh, beneath your tongue: for milk comes from flesh, not flesh itself; yet from flesh comes flesh, and flesh only—not the first flesh, but from the first flesh a second flesh; from old flesh, new flesh; from flesh requiring purification, sacrificial flesh. Therefore honey and milk are beneath your tongue, because in your flesh God is man, and beneath your flesh God and man are one Jesus Christ.

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are beneath your tongue; the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” For he himself says: “My spirit is sweeter than honey” (Ecclesiasticus 24). He rested in you in a singular manner—you who, above all others full of grace, were made Mother of the Son and temple of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices, because your exaltation exceeds every grace and your dignity surpasses every perfection. You were uniquely chosen; you were ineffably exalted. None could be like you in grace, through whom grace came upon all the children of men. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace; the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1). Therefore your grace is above every grace; your excellence above every merit—[Col. 1214A] loftier than all, holier than all. No one was full of grace as you were, you who alone, without precedent, gave birth as a virgin mother and preserved the lily of chastity together with the fruit of fecundity. Therefore the Holy Spirit rested uniquely in your humility, he who in your virginity performed a miracle comparable to none. Thus the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.

“Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are beneath your tongue; the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.” You received ointments for delight, ointments for beauty, ointments for fragrance. That ancient Mary, bearing the name only, did not leave you as heiress to leprosy; you had neither blemish nor wrinkle for ointments to wipe away. Rather, you received ointments so that they might commend your beauty and form more pleasingly. Therefore the fragrance [Col. 1214B] of your ointments surpasses all spices. Others are anointed for healing; others are anointed for strength; we all receive ointments out of necessity. But you, tender daughter and full of every grace, most dear in your delights, were anointed for the glory of your beauty and as a sign of love. Since you were to bear the Anointed One, you too were anointed, so that the ointment itself, which later he would receive uniquely in your womb, might first pour itself out excellently in you. He too received, above you, fullness beyond all his companions; you, after him, sweetness beyond all. Therefore the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.

“For now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. [Col. 1214C] Flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance; and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs 2). O wondrous fitness! Such things are prepared for one such as this. “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Your lips are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are beneath your tongue; the fragrance of your ointments surpasses all spices.”

If she is such, and has been praised so highly, this could not sufficiently commend her; it remained also to declare this, that she might know to what homeland she was being called and from what exile she was being led forth. Therefore both are mentioned, and everything is set in order: the beloved’s beauty, grievous exile, and sweet homeland. Praise is firm when it takes its beginning from the thing itself. For a person’s own qualities commend each one more truly. Therefore she herself is first praised; then those things which are hers are praised; and [Col. 1214D] all this serves to stir love. Adversities too are recalled, so that ardent desire may hasten to fulfillment and hurry away from the place where sadness sits, mourning dwells, and misery reigns. This is all exile. Then he praises her homeland and tells what joys, delights, great pleasures, and loveliness are there. And among all these: “Flowers have appeared; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.”

All things are full of love, and all resound with love: flowers, fragrance, song. There is nothing here that does not enter the mind, penetrate the heart, and pierce the affections. At the very hearing, the mind catches fire, desire burns, and the soul cannot contain its own longings. For one cannot hear without delight what is full of so great a sweetness. And whoever does not hear this for himself does not love it for himself. For it turns many toward itself whom it does not draw after itself; and though all love it in order to possess it, not all love it in order to follow it. But the beloved is called in order that she may come, since whoever does not come does not arrive. Thus it is recounted that she may hear, she is invited that she may come, and, coming, may arrive and take hold.

“The winter,” he says, “has passed; the rain has gone and departed.” This concerns exile. But concerning the homeland: “Flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” O wretched soul, who loves this and does not love that! Whoever you are, you are wretched if you love what ought so greatly to be fled—what, even if it were not fled, would nevertheless not remain. But if you do not love what ought so greatly to be loved, then, though living in yourself, you are dead, because he without whom you cannot live does not live in you.

Therefore the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. Flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in the land. The things recounted are familiar, but that for which they are recounted is not familiar. The forms of visible things, known to human sense, are themselves pleasant and sweet to human beings; they are set forth as likenesses, so that from them a person may think of what he does not know. And all these things run within the likeness: the winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed.

Behold, soul, do as you will: whether you love or do not love, the world passes away, and its desire. All that you love temporally passes away: what you love passes before you; finally you too pass away, and you pass beyond [Col. 1215C] the very things that you love. Why then should that which passes be loved—what was not to be loved even if it were not transitory? For when it stood, it harmed; when it passed away, it deceived. Cruel in the one respect, deceitful in the other. Hear rather what should make you rejoice: “The winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.”

What is winter? Is not mortal life winter, bound fast by the numbness of its corruption and darkened by the mist of ignorance? For it is sluggish in doing good and clouded in discerning. And what is the rain? For frost binds within, while rain rushing in from without dissolves. Thus rain consists in those troubles which, beyond innate occupation, press upon us daily, by which mortal life is worn away outwardly while held fast inwardly by the dire necessity of mortality. Therefore the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.

O happy soul that is able to hear: “The winter has passed!” For winter indeed always passes, but not all are worthy to hear this, except those for whom it passes before it has passed—that is, those by whom it is despised before it is overcome. For these, winter is grievous and summer is desired. These alone therefore deserve to hear, “The winter has passed,” so that, receiving consolation in its passing, they may rejoice because they had formerly sighed in affliction while it remained.

O blessed hour and time, desirable above all others, when that heavenly Bridegroom meets his beloved as she comes forth, after long desires, from the prison of the world, and gently invites his dear one to himself with consolation, saying: “Go forth with rejoicing, chosen among daughters. Let it not seem hard to you [Col. 1216A] to lay aside in death the garment of corruptible flesh, since even while living you knew that you did not love the flesh’s corruption. Do not tremble or be afraid: you escape exile; you are freed from misery. There will be no more pain or groaning, because these former things have passed away. For now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.”

Henceforth the body which is corrupted will not weigh down the soul, nor will the earthly dwelling press down the mind that thinks upon many things (Wisdom 9). For this is the winter that passes: its grievous numbness and frost are now melted when the south wind blows, and its dark mist is scattered when the sun of righteousness rises. Therefore now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. For because the winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed. After the prison-house of flesh you escape the world’s exile; nor do you any longer fear the evils of adversity, since, released from the law of mortality, you are no longer held in the corruption of flesh. Therefore the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. Unless mortality had been in you, adversity could have prevailed against you in nothing; and therefore, when through the death of the flesh you put off mortal corruption, you safely despise henceforth the whole world and the world’s opposing evils. Thus, because winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed. (“For now, now the winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed.”)

“Flowers have appeared; but the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” What does he mean by saying, “Flowers have appeared in our land”? Who are these flowers, what are the vineyards, what is the voice of the turtledove, and where is his land? Let it not happen to us as to the Jews, who said: “We do not know where this man is from” [Col. 1216C] (John 9). For if we know where he is from, we know his land; and we know who these flowers are, what the vineyards are, and what fragrance the flowering vineyards possess. Finally, we know the turtledove and the character of its voice. We know all things if we know where he is from.

And would that we did not know where he is from by hearing alone, lest perhaps we have merely heard a report and do not know the truth. For it is too little to have heard a report about him. Destruction and death could do this, and in this alone they glory; for nothing further is granted them. Therefore we must be taught concerning him not only by report but by experience, that we may taste and see that the Lord is sweet, and that his anointing may teach us concerning all things. If, therefore, his anointing is in us, we know where he is from, we know his land, and now we shall be able wisely to provide an explanation concerning the flowers, the fragrance of the vineyards, and the voice of the turtledove.

“For now the winter has passed, and the rain has gone and departed. Flowers have appeared, the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” Joyful things follow sorrowful ones. When what caused pain passes away, what delights succeeds: “Flowers have appeared in our land.” A great subject lies before us: to speak of flowers, vineyards, and the voice of the turtledove. For we know much concerning winter, rains, storms, and winds, and these matters have been stated clearly enough; there is no need for more to be said now, since enough has been said in the present discussion. Yet, as far as the sequence of the reading is concerned, these words seem to refer back to what preceded: “flowers have appeared” answers “the winter has passed”; while “the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance” answers “the rain has gone and departed.” Thus, because winter has passed, flowers have appeared; and because the rain has gone and departed, the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.

Winter has passed; flowers have appeared. For when the frost of winter, melted by spring warmth, is loosened, the earth, touched by warming rays, immediately opens itself to bring forth. Then buds and flowers emerge, and the earth is again clothed in its beauty. Thus winter has passed, and flowers have appeared in the land. Since the rain has gone and departed, the flowering vineyards immediately gave forth fragrance. For rains are hostile to flowers, and very heavy rains strike off the vineyard flowers; therefore, because the rain has gone and departed, the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.

[Col. 1217B] Therefore, when flowers were springing up and vineyards scattering their fragrance, the turtledove gave its voice, joy was made complete, and he said: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land; flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.” “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” “Our land,” he says—not “my land,” but “our land,” in order to share it with us.

If, then, that is our land where flowers have appeared, where flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance, and where the voice of the turtledove has been heard, this is exile—where, in a deserted, pathless, waterless land, in a foreign land, we cannot sing the Lord’s song, but say: “By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept, when we remembered you, Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” [Col. 1217C] (Psalm 136). Here there are nowhere flowers or flowering vineyards, but barren willows which have leaves and have no fruit. Nor is the voice of the turtledove heard here; rather, we hang up our instruments and cannot sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land. Therefore there is our land; here is our exile. We were created for that land and expelled to this one. Here we are pilgrims, destined to return there. Departing from there, we came here; departing from here, we return there.

Therefore, after winter has passed and the rain has gone and departed, flowers immediately appeared in our land, flowering vineyards gave forth fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove was heard in our land. Where these things were removed, those things immediately began to appear without delay. After the shaking brought by these things had passed from us, the fragrance of those things immediately reached us. When the groaning caused by these things fell silent, the harmony of those things immediately sounded in our ears, and the voice of the turtledove was heard.

He seems here to commend certain great joys in flowers, fragrance, and song. For these three alone are mentioned: flowers, fragrance, and song. We know that flowers belong to appearance, fragrance to scent, and song to delight. Appearance pertains to sight, fragrance to smell, melody to hearing. Why, then, are these alone selected and named before all the senses? Each sense has its own pleasures, and inner joys could also have been designated by taste, as it is written: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33); and again: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Col. 1218A] (Psalm 16); and: “You shall make them drink, O Lord, from the torrent of your delight” (Psalm 35). But whoever already tastes enjoys and has arrived at the end of his desires. Here, however, certain beginnings of everlasting life had to be signified, when all things are not yet consummated.

For the bride is still in the act of departing and is invited to come. She herself was already leaving the tent of her flesh and had turned in order to come. There her eyes were unveiled. And behold, as if from afar, she saw a land, a homeland, a lovely region—still invisible, yet more beautiful than all things she had hitherto seen—full of splendor and overflowing with delight, whose sight awakens eternal desires. There all things which in this age have seemed beautiful, whether already past, presently existing, or still to come, shine incorruptibly and are displayed, beyond all estimation, with a beauty far greater than had been believed. Therefore the bride, wholly fixed in contemplation upon this vision and gathering herself into herself, desired more fully to know whence so wondrous a beauty had suddenly shone forth.

As she burned with full attention toward it and could no longer contain herself for joy, behold, a most sweet fragrance stole in, and certain sweet songs were heard, and everything was wondrous beyond custom. Therefore flowers, fragrance, and song are mentioned; in all these that sweetness and delight of invisible goods is signified. It is said: “Flowers have appeared, the vineyards have given forth fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard.” All these are in one, and all are one: flowers, fragrance, and song. They are flowers because they display beauty; fragrance because it pours forth sweetness; song because it sounds sweetness. It is all this, and the whole is there, but still as if from afar. Whatever is seen there is beautiful, sweet, and delightful; but it is still as if from a distance. Therefore it is not yet perceived by taste or handled by touch, but, as though situated far off, is heard, smelled, and seen. Yet even so it wondrously refreshes the soul and draws it onward into everlasting desires.

Therefore she says: “Draw me; we will run after you in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song of Songs 1). And: “The voice of my beloved. My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song of Songs 5). “You are beautiful, my beloved, and fair, and wholly desirable: your head, your hair, your eyes, your lips. Flee, my beloved, flee; be like, my beloved, a gazelle or a young hart upon the mountains of spices” [Col. 1218D] (Song of Songs 8). Therefore flowers have appeared in our land; flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance; and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.

Thus eternal joys are signified by flowers, fragrance, and song. We have said that taste is passed over because he wished to show that these things were still far off, and that the bride had not yet arrived at them, but was invited to come; they were shown to her so that she might see, desire, and hasten. Therefore those joys were fittingly signified by flowers, fragrance, and song. For all these refresh from afar and delight when situated at a distance.

There are many more things that could still be said on these matters. But we are poor and limited in knowledge and speech, and cannot suffice for realities so immense and so exalted above our power. Yet we must not pass over what still suggests and offers itself for explanation. Since there are five bodily senses, two—touch and taste—come closer to impurities and are subject to defilement. Hence they cannot have refreshment wholly pure, but one requiring cleansing and purification. The other three, however, draw unmingled sweetness and turn their delights more toward the soul’s pleasure; for they refresh not out of necessity but for delight. There is, therefore, a great likeness in these things, nor could invisible realities be declared by clearer signs. As the eye is fed upon the form of things without defilement, and as the ear is delighted by the sweetness of sounds without corruption, [Col. 1219B] so those eternal joys pour in sweetness without bringing corruption. They refresh always and never fail. They feed, yet remain whole; they offer themselves for enjoyment, yet remain incorruptible.

Therefore flowers have appeared in our land, flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance, and the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. “Flowers have appeared.” What kind of flowers? Like lilies, roses, and violets; and there is no flower without its own form and particular beauty. Every beauty is there, where supreme beauty is. There is one good, and every good is in that good. If you name flowers, if you name fruits, everything is there. For there is also a tree, the tree of life, since it was said of Wisdom herself: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her, and those who possess her are blessed” [Col. 1219C] (Proverbs 3). The tree of life is planted beside streams of waters and shall give its fruit in its season; its leaf shall never fall (Psalm 1).

See that nothing is lacking there. Everything is there. It has flowers, leaves, and fruit; nor can leaves be lacking, for there is shade there also—not for darkness, however, but for refreshment. The bride herself testifies that there is shade there: “Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs 2). What, then, could you seek there and not find? Only what is not, is not there. For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. And what was made in him was life (John 1). For from him, through him, and in him are all things (Romans 11). When something begins to be seen in him, it does not begin to be in him when it begins to be seen; for what is there always is, and is always wholly there.

Hear further Wisdom enumerating her joys and delights: “I, like a vine, brought forth the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are fruits of honor and beauty [or: propriety]. I was exalted like a cedar in Lebanon, like a cypress on Mount Zion, like a palm in Kadesh, like an olive tree in the plains, and like a plane tree beside water in the streets” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

But lest perhaps this abundance induce forgetfulness in us, and, leaving flowers behind, we begin to count trees: for trees appear to contain a certain rigidity and hardness. But we are beginners and tender, and need soft and gentle things; therefore we turn again to flowers [Col. 1220A]. “Flowers,” he says, “have appeared in our land” (Song of Songs 2). Thus the contemplation of eternal Wisdom is being discussed, whose sight—desirable, full of every delight and beauty—draws forth everlasting desires. Therefore flowers have appeared in our land.

“Whoever enters through me,” Wisdom said, “shall go in and go out, and find pasture” (John 10). Therefore within is pasture, and it is itself the land in which flowers have appeared, whose perpetual greenness never withers; of it it was said: “Above every fair green thing” (Isaiah 2). How great, do you suppose, is the beauty in contemplating eternal Wisdom, where the forms of all things flourish without defect, remain without passing away, stand without corruption, and are eternal without change? If that which is not truly beautiful is so beautiful, what is that which is truly beautiful? Therefore flowers have appeared in our land.

The fruits have not yet appeared; they are reserved for the future. But meanwhile flowers have now appeared, to soothe the sight and kindle desire, because this is the present task while she has not yet arrived where she is invited to come. Therefore flowers have appeared in our land. In what land are they? Where is this land? Is this land neither in heaven nor on earth? For this land is both heaven and earth. It is earth because it nourishes and bears; it is heaven because it protects and illuminates. This land is within us and contains the whole world. Yet it is within, and is not seen except by those who are within. For this land is invisible, but only to those who see only visible things. This is the land where the light shines which the eyes of the wicked cannot see. This is the land in which flowers have appeared, because flowers have appeared in our land; the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. “Behold, the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” [Col. 1220C] (Matthew 3).

“The flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.” First it appeared; now, behold, it is perceived. Behold, the fragrance has reached even us. “The flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.” At first we saw flowers, and they were not the flowers of vineyards; yet flowers appeared in our land. But now vineyard flowers have given forth fragrance. There, delight; here, usefulness. There, pleasure; here, refreshment. There beauty appeared for delight; now the fragrance itself and the sweetness itself pour themselves in for pleasure and healing. It gradually approaches, grows ever more and more; sweetness grows in perception, knowledge in illumination. Yet one has not arrived at taste.

That intoxicating cup, from the abundance of his house, from the torrent of delight, is not yet offered to drink. For the bride still stands outside and must still be brought into the wine cellar; thus there is complete silence still about things of that kind. Only this is said: “The flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.” The flower is still present; the cluster is not yet. Winepresses are nowhere yet named, nor does new wine ferment in vats so that new wine may be put into new wineskins; for these are great things, reserved for the delights of the feast to come. For now, only the flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. We have heard only of vineyards and perceived their fragrance.

[Col. 1221A] “And the flowering vineyards,” he says, “have given forth fragrance” (Song of Songs 2). Therefore we have not been left altogether without hope: we have hope and run until we arrive. For flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. The hope of future intoxication has been given us, and hope itself meanwhile has its own refreshment, so that we may endure and not fail upon the way. For flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. In the flower is hope; in the fragrance, refreshment. Therefore flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.

And we run, follow, and hasten to be intoxicated; when we arrive, the vineyards will already be ripe and the wines pressed, we shall enter the wine cellar, and henceforth there will be no delay caused by the fragrance of flowering vineyards. For all these things are now only for a beginning and promise; and when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away (1 Corinthians 13). For now, therefore, flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.

It is a marvelous thing: there they are ripe, yet here, in keeping with our condition, they begin as flowers to have clusters not yet ripe. Nor should we therefore delay because the vineyards now flower, as though we must anticipate the vintage season if we run, but should wish to walk slowly because much still remains from flower to ripe cluster. Those vineyards are not like the other vineyards which we know. Their ripening is in you. For they begin to flower for you and ripen for you. They are always ripe in themselves; and they begin to be ripe for you when you begin to be ripe for them. If they delay, they delay because of you. For themselves, they hasten as much as you wish. Therefore do not fear, but hasten yourself. If you have already perceived the fragrance of those flowering vineyards, hasten to gather the ripe fruit.

For you have heard what was said to the bride. What was said to her was said to you, provided that you are one of the Bridegroom’s friends or one of the bride’s maidens. For all these are invited to one banquet: nor can either the bridegroom feast without his friends or the bride without her maidens. Hear, then, as addressed to yourself, what was said to her, because what was said to her was likewise said to you with her: “Rise,” he says, “hasten, my beloved, because the winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed, and now flowers have appeared in our land. The flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance.”

Finally he added, as though commending something unique and singular: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs 2). What can we now say about the voice of the turtledove? Yet lest it perhaps come into mind or arise in the heart that, since the turtledove has groaning for song, lamentation rather than song is signified here: we do not presently admit that interpretation among our joys. For the voice of the turtledove sings of love and affection; and the turtledove has a singular affection for the one to whom it sings—joy when present, longing when absent. Thus the voice of the turtledove is wholly about love; the turtledove knows nothing but love. And its love is singular, for it does not join a second to the one; and eternal, for it admits no second even after the first. Therefore the voice of the turtledove sings of love; the voice of the turtledove is the song of love.

Hearts burn at the voice of the turtledove, and the voice of the turtledove is heard. What, then, is this voice of the turtledove of which it is said: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard”? What does the voice of the turtledove sound? Does the voice of the turtledove have a meaning? What does it say? There is one thing that the voice of the turtledove sounds; it always sounds and resounds this same thing, and never grows weary. The turtledove never changes its voice, never alters its song; it always sings the same thing because it always loves the same thing. Therefore the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.

O voice of the turtledove, how sweet you are! Who shall be worthy to hear the voice of the turtledove? The turtledove sings in solitude and always loves solitude, because it seeks a singular love. Its voice shall not be heard in the streets, nor shall it utter its cry abroad. It resounds within; it sings inwardly. None can hear the turtledove except those who are within: those who withdraw into solitude, inhabit secrecy, and rest in silence. These are the ones who hear the voice of the turtledove.

In the terror of a night vision, when sleep is accustomed to seize human beings, then it opens the hearts of men and they hear its voice. There it reveals the hidden and secret word to its friends; they perceive the veins of its whisper, preserve its secret, and it itself weans and leads forth the bride into solitude. With sweet addresses it calls and admonishes her to go forth, so that there it may speak to her heart and give her understanding of love.

O beautiful one among daughters, you have heard the voice of the turtledove; you have heard and understood! It was speaking within, and you were within; therefore you heard and understood, and said: “The voice [Col. 1222C] of my beloved” (Song of Songs 2). For you understood that it was the voice of the beloved and spoke of love; because you heard and understood, you also loved and said: “The voice of my beloved.” You understood and spoke. For you would not have understood unless you had loved, because it was a word of love and could be understood only by one who loved. The beloved was speaking, and he was speaking to his beloved, and love was being commended.

Therefore, because you have heard the beloved’s voice and understood love, delay no longer; make no further pause. Rise swiftly, open the latch of your door, and go forth to him, so that you may see his face; and if he flees, follow him over the mountains of spices (Song of Songs 5). For you run securely because you come from Lebanon, because you come white and pure. You come chaste and spotless; therefore you run securely from Lebanon over the mountains of spices [Col. 1222D] (Song of Songs 8): from the merit of chastity to the reward of blessedness; therefore, from Lebanon over the mountains of spices.

There he awaits you who was born from you; there he has gone before you. There is your son and your beloved: he who calls you, invites you, goes before you as you come from Lebanon, and awaits you upon the mountains of spices. There flowers have appeared; flowering vineyards have given forth fragrance. There the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. Rise, hasten, my beloved, and come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned (Song of Songs 4).
